p.seg: Classics
Like rivers at their peak flow,
There is nothing that does not increase.
. "Shī·Tiān Bǎo".
The Master said: "I have seen him advance,
But never have I seen him stop."
"Analects".
Mencius said
Like a fire just ignited,
Or a spring just breaking through.
. "Mèngzǐ·Gōngsūn Chǒu".
The blade's edge is as if newly sharpened on the whetstone.
. "Zhuāngzǐ·Yǎngshēng Zhǔ".
Cross-referenced under "Talent and Beauty".
The sun rises from Yánggǔ,
And ascends upon Fúsāng.
. "Huáinánzǐ·Tiānwén Xùn".
Resplendent is the light of the rising sun.
. "Yángzǐ·Wǔ Bǎi".
Biographies
Those who learn while young,
Are like the light of the rising sun.
Liú Xiàng "Shuō Yuàn".
Collections
With a light carriage, skilled driving, and strong horses,
Alas! Knowing the path, you journey without rest.
Hán Wén.
Endlessly pointing to the long road,
Going forth, whipping the high-stepping carriage.
Same as above.
Like a robust person climbing a ladder,
The more steps taken,
The higher the ascent,
The more others look up to them.
Liǔ Wén.
The demeanor of a wild goose ascending gradually,
Ought to begin from this point.
"Bái Jūyì Collection".
Like the sun that never extinguishes,
Like the sea that never exhausts.
Táng Lǚ Wēn "Inscription on Fù Yán".
Observing its swift pace,
Galloping steadily forward.
Soaring on the whirlwind to reach the highest purity,
Hunting remnants of legacy and approaching Sōng and Dài mountains.
I see it advancing,
But never see it halt.
"Wéi Yìngwù Collection".
Our Dynasty
I admire your youth and being on the right path,
Like the rising sun at Fúsāng.
"Ōuyáng Collection".
Treading upon a clear path just begun,
The far-reaching achievements are hard to measure.
Dōngpō "Reply to Wáng Qīnchén's Letter".
Classics
When decline reaches its end, it topples,
How can it last long?
. "Yì·Pǐ Guà".
A withered poplar putting forth blossoms,
How can it endure?
. "Yì·Dàguò Guà".
The setting sun's glow,
How can it last long?
. "Yì·Lí Guà".
Snow falls thick and fast,
Melting upon seeing the sunlight.
. "Shī·Juélì".
Cross-referenced under "Unequal Strength".
A fowl's cry reaching the sky,
How can it last long?
. "Yì·Zhōngfú".
Mencius said
Between the seventh and eighth months,
When rain collects in the ditches,
They all fill up, but their drying out,
Can be awaited standing.
"Mèngzǐ".
A gale does not last all morning,
A sudden downpour does not last all day.
. "Lǎozǐ·Zìrán Chapter".
The morning mushroom knows not the end of the month.
On decaying soil, there are fungi,
Born in the morning,
Dead by the month's end.
"Lièzǐ".
The thickness of clouds and fog,
Ends in a moment;
The intensity of a rainstorm,
Does not last beyond a day.
"Wèizi".
History
In one's time, there is glory,
But it ends with death.
. "Shǐjì·Kǒngzǐ Shìjiā".
Those who serve others with their looks,
When beauty fades, favor wanes,
And when favor wanes, kindness ceases.
. "Western Hàn·Bān Gù Biography".
Flourishing in the morning,
Withered by evening.
Same as above.
Gathering to cling to life,
Like fish swimming in a cauldron,
Gasping for but a moment.
. "Later Hàn·Zhāng Gāng Biography".
Grass that blooms in the morning,
Falls withered by evening.
. "Wèi·Wáng Chǎng Biography".
Biographies
Those who learn in old age,
Are like walking at night holding a torch.
Liú Xiàng "Shuō Yuàn".
When rivers overflow,
It lasts no more than three days;
Gales and rainstorms,
Are over in a moment.
. "Shuō Yuàn·Tán Cóng".
Collections
Would you rather see the white snow on the steps,
How could it shine brightly in the spring sun?
Xiè Huìlián "Snow Rhapsody".
The glory of the hibiscus does not last a morning,
The mayfly hardly sees the evening.
Guō Jǐngchún "Roaming Immortals Poem".
Pressed by this fleeting light, urgent.
Dù's poetry.
How long can lavish blooms last?
Same as above.
Morning flies need not be driven away,
Evening mosquitoes cannot be swatted.
How long does their season last?
They feast with you wantonly.
When the cool breeze of the ninth month arrives,
They are swept away without a trace.
Hán Wén.
Small, carried by the wind past the curtain,
Faint, near the woods in the rain.
In the tenth month, heavy with clear frost,
Whither do they drift, to return?
Dù's "Firefly Poem".
Sick leaves often fall first,
Cold flowers only briefly fragrant.
Dù.
Serving others with one's looks,
How long can the favor last?
"Lǐ Bái Collection".
Puddle water has no source,
Full in the morning, gone by evening.
Hán Tuìzhī.
Floating clouds ascend to heaven, rain falls to earth,
A momentary union ends in parting.
"Zhāng Wénchāng Collection".
How long can a precarious stem endure?
"Yuán Zhěn Collection".
Cold ashes bury a dim fire,
Morning flames congeal into a dying candle.
"Bái Jūyì Collection".
Moreover, your spring-breeze face,
Soft and fleeting as fragrant grass.
The peach and plum hues in the mirror,
Cannot remain fair for ten years.
Like swallows in a tent or fish in a cauldron,
Clinging to life for a moment.
Morning's cloud-touching flower,
Evening's firewood on the ground.
Both same as above.
Much like foxes and rats,
Scurrying under cover of night.
Once the morning light rises,
They naturally crouch and shrink.
Lù Xuàngōng's writings.
Also like a small star about to fall, its brilliance flares suddenly.
Sīkōng Tǔshèng's writings.
Past spring, flowers fall on their own,
At dawn's end, the moon shines in vain.
Xǔ Yònghuì's writings.
Like the chirping of sparrows,
Once the sound stops, it's over.
Huángfǔ Shí.
Stealing a moment's extension.
"Wáng Wéi Collection".
Our Dynasty
The flourishing blossoms of plants and trees are like a passing gust of wind,
The pleasant sounds of birds and beasts merely brush past the ears.
． Ouyáng Xiū's "Preface to Seeing Xú Wúdǎng Off".
Floating clouds have no roots or stems,
Puddles can last but a moment.
Spring ice holds no true firmness.
Ouyáng Xiū's poem.
It is said that spring chill, autumn heat, and the vigor of old age
are three things
that ultimately do not last long.
Ouyáng Xiū's "Personal Letter to Shěn the Deputy Commissioner".
Ask how firm frost and ice may be,
Come spring, can they long endure?
"Collection of Lúanchéng".
Classic
Clouds move and rain falls,
bringing peace to all under heaven.
． "The Qián Hexagram of the Yìjīng".
Under the vast sky,
there is no land that is not the king's;
Along the shores of the realm,
there is none who is not the king's subject.
． "The Běishān Ode of the Shījīng".
Without these boundaries and borders.
． "The Sīwén Ode of the Shījīng".
When the Great Way prevails,
the world is shared by all.
Thus people do not only love their own parents,
nor only care for their own children.
Doors remain unbolted at night,
this is called the Great Unity.
． "The Lǐyùn Chapter of the Lǐjì".
Therefore, the sage regards all under heaven as one family,
and the central states as one person.
They dislike goods being discarded on the ground,
yet do not hoard them for themselves;
they dislike strength not being exerted from one's body,
yet do not exert it for their own sake.
Same as above.
All within the four seas are brothers.
． "The Yānyuān Chapter of the Lúnyǔ".
Masters
When the King of Chǔ lost his bow,
his attendants sought to retrieve it.
The king said: "The King of Chǔ lost his bow,
a person of Chǔ will find it—why search for it?"
Confucius said: "It is a pity his perspective was not broader.
He could have said: 'A person lost the bow,
a person will find it,'
why must it be Chǔ?"
"Family Sayings of Confucius".
From the perspective of their sameness,
all things are one.
． "The Dé Chōng Fú Chapter of the Zhuāngzǐ".
History
Within the borders,
what land is not the ruler's?
Those who eat the produce of the land,
who is not the ruler's subject?
． "Zuǒzhuàn, Tenth Year of Duke Zhāo".
All within the four seas are like one family.
． "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Qín Annals".
Harmony fills the six directions,
benevolence dwells in every household.
Unifying the masses of the world,
equalizing the myriad differences among beings.
Though varied, they are measured alike,
molded as one in the potter's kiln.
． "Hòuhànshū, Biography of Cuī Yīn".
Collections
All within the four seas are brothers,
who then is a stranger?
Sū Wǔ's poem.
How can the Héshì jade shine solely in Yǐng?
Holding the luminous pearl,
why should it be enjoyed only in Suí?
To hold the resources of the world,
is to share them with all under heaven.
Liú Yuèshí's letter.
Only by embracing a grand view,
can the myriad differences follow one track.
Lú Zǐliáng's letter.
No marsh fails to moisten,
not even the burrows of ants and crickets are missed.
"Stele of the Late Prince of Ānlù of Qí".
Peach and plum trees have wondrous qualities,
while ailanthus and oak lack graceful forms.
Yet all are bathed by auspicious clouds,
and blown by the same spring breeze.
Ouyáng Xíngzhōu.
When timely rain falls across the six directions,
all things escape withering and drought.
Lǐ Tàibái.
How to obtain thousands of spacious mansions,
to shelter all the poor scholars under heaven and bring them joy?
Dù Fǔ's poem.
The sage regards all with equal benevolence.
Hán Yù's "On the Origin of Humanity".
Viewing the outside as the inside,
treating a family as one person.
Hán Yù's writings.
If indeed regional inspectors show no favoritism to their own people,
and surveillance commissioners do not press harshly for taxes,
the inspector would say: "The people of my prefecture
are the people of all under heaven;
benefits should not be exclusively bestowed on them."
The surveillance commissioner would also say: "The people of a certain prefecture
are the people of all under heaven;
taxes should not be harshly collected from them alone."
If this is so, yet governance remains unequal and orders unenforced,
such a thing has never occurred.
Same as above.
The moistening of auspicious clouds
does not bypass the thorns and brambles.
"Collection of Wáng Wéi".
Recalling at fifteen, I aspired to build great houses,
intending to cover all the poor under heaven.
"Collection of Yuán Zhěn".
Worrying for others as for one's own flesh and blood.
Yáo the Assistant Director.
Benefiting the west while equalizing the east,
nourishing the interior while enriching the exterior.
"Tángwéncuì".
Heaven's intent
leaves nothing, however small, neglected;
like the sun's radiance,
it does not exclude the remote and obscure.
Same as above.
I have ever sought to greatly nourish all under heaven;
should one thing wither,
I would consider it my personal shame.
"Collection of Línchuān".
After all, the spring breeze does not pick and choose,
blossoms open and fall, each in its own time, evenly.
"Collection of Lúanchéng".
How to obtain a great robe stretching ten thousand zhang,
to cover the entire city of Luòyáng with you?
Grains and weeds alike,
are nourished by the same rain on the same day.
Vice Minister Bái.
Masters
From the perspective of their differences,
even the liver and gall are as distant as Chǔ and Yuè.
． "The Dé Chōng Fú Chapter of the Zhuāngzǐ".
"Huáinánzǐ" says: "The liver and gall are as far apart as Hú and Yuè."
History
Those in the same boat
can all become enemy states.
． "Shǐjì, Biography of Wú Qǐ".
Xiè Xuán's son was Huàn,
Huàn's son was Língyùn,
gifted with abundant and unrestrained literary talent.
Xuán said: "If I gave birth to Huàn,
how could Huàn not give birth to Língyùn?"
． "Jìnshū, His Biography".
Collections
When lost,
the liver and gall become Chǔ and Yuè.
Táng Xú Yànbó's "Essay".
Our dynasty
Even the liver and gall can be as distant as Chǔ and Yuè.
Dōngpō.
Classic
Confucius said: "Now, regarding people,
I listen to their words and observe their actions."
"The Analects".
Zhào Wénzǐ
spoke haltingly, as if words could not leave his mouth.
． "Lǐjì, Tángōng Part Two".
A gentleman does not judge others solely by their words.
． "Lǐjì, Biǎojì".
The Master said: "A gentleman does not select people based on their speech."
． "The Analects, Duke Wèi Líng".
Masters
Had Confucius selected people by their speech,
he would have erred with Zǎi Wǒ.
"Family Sayings of Confucius".
History
Xiàngrú stammered in speech,
yet excelled in writing books.
． "Shǐjì, Biography of Sīmǎ Xiàngrú".
Ní Kuān was deft with the brush,
but could not articulate clearly.
． "Shǐjì, Biographies of Confucian Scholars, Fúshēng's Biography".
Liú Rú was slow of speech,
but sharp in mind.
"Hòuhànshū".
Zhàng Shìzhī said: "Zhōu Bó and Zhāng Xiàngrú were called elders,
yet when discussing matters,
they hardly spoke a word."
． "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Hàn Wéndì's Annals".
Confucius said: "I once judged a person by his words,
and missed the mark with Zǎi Yǔ."
. "Records of the Historian: Biographies of Confucius' Disciples".
Emperor Wén ascended the Tiger Enclosure,
and questioned the Shanglin official about the animal register,
but he could not answer.
The granary keeper stepped in from the side to answer on his behalf,
responding endlessly like an echo.
The emperor decreed to appoint the granary keeper as the Shanglin magistrate.
. "Book of the Former Hàn: Biography of Zhàng Shìzhī".
Yáng Yīn in "Selection of Officials",
often judged people by their words.
"Book of the Later Wèi".
Zhū Pǔ claimed: "If I become chancellor,
peace could be achieved in just over a month."
The emperor believed him.
He appointed Pǔ as Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
Pǔ was mediocre, vulgar, pedantic, and eccentric,
with no other strengths.
When the appointment was issued,
the court and the public were greatly shocked.
. "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Zhāo Chapter".
Classic
Zhào Wénzǐ was so frail in stature that he seemed unable to bear his clothes.
This refers to his physical build.
. "Record of Rites: Tángōng Part Two".
Master
Confucius intended to judge people by their appearance,
but changed his view regarding Zǐ Zhāng.
"Family Sayings of Confucius".
Dāntái had the appearance of a gentleman,
but his conduct did not match his looks.
Same as above.
Judging by appearance is not as good as assessing the heart.
Xúnzǐ's "Against Physiognomy".
The appearance of King Xú Yǎn,
his eyes could look upward;
he could not look down at small objects,
only seeing them from afar.
The appearance of Confucius,
his face was like wearing a mask;
resembling a Fangxiàng exorcist.
The appearance of the Duke of Zhōu,
his body was like a broken stump;
the appearance of Gāo Yáo,
his complexion was like a peeled melon;
the appearance of Hóng Yāo,
his face had no visible skin;
the appearance of Fù Yuè,
his body was like a standing fish fin.
As if a fish were standing.
The appearance of Yī Yǐn,
his face had no beard or eyebrows.
Yǔ walked with a limp, Tāng was lopsided,
Yáo and Shùn had double pupils.
Two pupils.
Jié and Zhòu were tall, huge, and handsome,
the finest in the world,
their sinews and strength exceptionally powerful,
a match for a hundred men,
yet they died and their states perished,
becoming the great shame of the world.
Later generations speaking of evil,
must refer to them.
Now the disorderly rulers of common customs,
the frivolous youths of the villages,
are all beautiful, elegant, and charming,
wearing strange clothes and feminine adornments,
their vitality and demeanor imitating women,
women all wish to have them as husbands,
maidens all wish to have them as suitors.
Yet a moderate ruler would be ashamed to have them as ministers,
a moderate father would be ashamed to have them as sons,
a moderate elder brother would be ashamed to have them as younger brothers,
a moderate person would be ashamed to have them as friends.
Xúnzǐ's "Against Physiognomy".
Chǔ's Sūn Shū'áo,
had a bald head and a longer left side,
yet he made Chǔ hegemon.
Qì's Prince Gāo,
was tiny, short, and thin,
walking as if he could not bear his clothes,
yet during the rebellion of Lord Bái,
he executed Lord Bái,
stabilized the state of Chǔ,
as easily as turning his hand.
Same as above.
History
Jìn's Shū Xiàng went to Zhèng,
Zhèng's Zōng Miè stood under the hall,
and with one good remark,
Shū Xiàng said: "You are unimpressive in appearance,
if you had not spoken,
I would have nearly missed you."
. "Zuǒzhuàn: Zhāo 20th Year".
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān thought Liú Hóu was imposing and extraordinarily tall,
until he saw his portrait,
which looked like a gentle and beautiful woman.
. "Records of the Grand Historian: Hereditary Houses".
Yán Yánnián,
was short in stature but vigorous and capable,
quick in handling affairs,
even Zǐgòng and Rǎn Yǒu, skilled in governance,
could not surpass him.
"Book of the Western Hàn".
Shùn had double pupils,
and Xiàng Yǔ also had double pupils.
. "Book of the Western Hàn: Biography of Xiàng Jí".
Hé Xiū was simple, unadorned, and slow of speech,
yet elegant and thoughtful.
. "Book of the Eastern Hàn: His Biography".
Cross-reference to "Profound".
Zhōu Xiè was born with a recessed chin and a broken nose bridge,
his ugly appearance frightening people.
His mother wanted to abandon him,
but his father said: "Many sages and worthies had unusual looks.
The one who will prosper our clan,
is this child."
So they raised him.
. "Book of the Later Hàn: His Biography".
The Wèi emperor pointed at Cuī Hào and said: "You all look at this man,
frail, slender, and timid,
unable to bend a bow or hold a spear,
yet what he holds in his breast,
surpasses armor and weapons."
. "Comprehensive Mirror: Sòng Chapter".
Qí's Mèng Yè served as a legal officer.
Wáng Yuè saw his short and small stature,
and laughed without speaking.
But upon examining his judgments and decisions,
he said to Yè: "Your clarity in decision-making,
can be said to exceed the use of a large physique."
"Diǎn Lüè of the Three Kingdoms".
Hóu Jǐng had a shorter right foot,
archery and horsemanship were not his strengths,
yet he was full of strategies and calculations.
. "Comprehensive Mirror: Liáng Gāozǔ".
Yú Shìnán appeared as if he could not bear his clothes,
yet inwardly he was resolute and fervent.
. "Book of Táng: His Biography".
Wèi Zhēng's appearance did not surpass an average person,
yet he had courage and strategy.
. "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Tàizōng Chapter".
Tàixué academician Zhōu Shě recommended his cousin Xú Chī,
saying: "His physique is small and unimpressive,
as if unable to bear his clothes,
yet he is fit for this selection."
Thus he became the study attendant for the Prince of Jìn'ān.
Liú Pán's "Liáng Diǎn".
Cross-reference to "Outer Appearance".
Collection
Although my body is small,
my seasoned spirit spans the nine provinces.
Dù Fǔ's poem.
If the pulse is not ill,
even if thin, it is not harmful;
if the pulse is ill and one is fat,
then death is imminent.
Hán Yù's "Miscellaneous Sayings".
Although not full seven chǐ tall,
my heart rivals ten thousand men.
"Táng Wén Cuì".
Bó Lún's appearance,
did not hinder him as a worthy scholar.
"Bái's Encyclopedia".
Yànzǐ was short yet became chancellor of Qí,
Cài Yì was small yet assisted Hàn.
Gāo Chái was extremely ugly,
yet was esteemed for utmost filial piety among Confucius' disciples.
Same as above.
Our Dynasty
Yàn Yīng was not six chǐ tall,
yet his lofty integrity towered ten thousand rèn over Shǒuyáng.
Dōngpō's poem.
History
Judging by appearance,
one missed Zǐyǔ.
． "Records of the Historian: Biographies of Confucius' Disciples".
When Mèngcháng Jūn went to Zhào,
the people of Zhào came out to see him,
and laughed, saying: "At first we thought Lord Xuē would be imposing,
but now seeing him,
he's but a small man."
"Records of the Historian".
When Gǒng Suì was summoned for an audience,
his stature was short and small,
Emperor Xuān saw him,
and he did not match what he had heard,
so he inwardly belittled him.
． "Book of Han: His Biography".
Jiāng Chōng was imposing in person,
with a very robust appearance.
Emperor Wǔ saw him and found him remarkable, saying: "Yān and Zhào have many extraordinary men."
． "Book of Han: Biography of Xīfū Gōng".
Having seen personally that Yáng Zǐyún's rank and appearance could not impress people,
they therefore belittled his writings.
． "Book of Western Han: Biography of Yáng Xióng".
Yáng Yīn in "Electing Officials" often judged people by their looks,
leading to contemporary criticism: "The Minister in charge of elections,
is like a poor man buying melons,
only picking the big ones."
"Book of Later Wei".
Classic
Only after learning does one know one's inadequacies;
only after teaching does one know the difficulties.
． "Book of Rites: Record of Learning".
Knowing how to be a good son,
then one can be a father.
Knowing how to serve others,
then one can employ them.
． "Record: King Wén as Heir".
Son
If one does not approach the deep abyss,
how can one know the peril of drowning?
If one does not behold the vast sea,
how can one know the hazard of storms?
． "Family Sayings: Oath in Distress".
Without climbing high mountains,
one does not know the height of the sky;
without facing deep valleys,
one does not know the thickness of the earth;
without hearing the legacy of former kings,
one does not know the greatness of learning.
． "Xúnzǐ: Encouraging Learning".
Through fierce winds and torrential rains,
one then knows the value of a great house as shelter;
through tyrannical governance and harsh times,
one then knows the sage's role as a protective wall.
． "Yángzǐ: My Son".
Wénzhōng Zǐ said: "Only after long experience in handling affairs,
will one naturally understand."
"Wénzhōng".
History
Qí Gāo Qiáng said: "With three broken arms,
one knows how to be a good physician."
． "Zuǒzhuan: 13th Year of Duke Dìng".
Cross-reference to "Gaining wisdom through experience".
When Zhōu Bó was imprisoned by the court justice,
the jailers gradually harassed and humiliated him.
Bó gave a thousand pieces of gold to a jailer,
who then wrote
on a wooden tablet to show him.
After Bó was released,
he said: "I once commanded a million troops,
but how could I have known the power of jailers!"
． "Records of the Historian: Hereditary Houses".
Cross-reference to "Loss of power".
Hearing a hundred times is not as good as seeing once.
I wish to gallop to Jīnchéng,
to map out strategies for Your Majesty.
． "Book of Western Han: Biography of Zhào Chōngguó".
Drawing a circle on the ground as a prison,
one dare not enter;
carving a wooden figure as a jailer,
one dare not confront it.
． "Book of Western Han: Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān".
Tasting one morsel of meat,
one knows the flavor in the pot.
．． "History of Northern Dynasties: Biography of Wèi Cuī Hào".
Biographies
If one does not strike the great bell,
or beat the thunder drum,
one cannot know their sound.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World".
Taste one morsel to know the flavor of the whole pot, the seasoning of the entire cauldron.
"Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals".
Collection
After breaking an arm nine times, one becomes a physician—
now I understand why.
"Songs of Chu".
Who says sacrificing one's life is easy?

Jiǎ Jiān,
courtesy name Shìgù,
could draw a bow requiring three shí of strength.
The late Lièzǔ, knowing Jiān was skilled in archery,
personally tested him.
He placed an ox a hundred paces away,
summoned Jiān to shoot,
and asked, "Can you hit it?"
Jiān replied, "In my youth, I might have missed;
now that I am old,
I can surely hit it."
Kè laughed heartily.
He shot one arrow that grazed the ox's back,
another that skimmed its belly,
both just touching the skin and shedding some hair,
with identical precision top and bottom.
Kè asked, "Can you hit it again?"
Jiān said, "What is valued is making missing remarkable;
hitting it—what difficulty is there?"
With one shot, he hit it.
Jiān was then over sixty years old,
and all spectators admired his exquisite skill.
From "Yān Shū",
also recorded in "Comprehensive Mirror, Volume 98".

Wēng Wěi of Guànghàn could understand the sounds of birds and beasts.
Riding a lame horse in the wild,
he encountered a horse grazing in the field,
several li away,
their calls audible to each other.
Wēng Wěi said to his driver,
"That grazing horse is blind in one eye."
The driver asked, "How do you know?"
He replied, "It insulted this lame horse in our carriage,
and the lame horse retorted by calling it a one-eyed horse."
The driver did not believe him,
but upon going to check,
the horse was indeed blind in one eye.
From "Lùn Héng".

Bǎi Lǐ Xī did not let rank and salary enter his heart,
So when he fed the oxen, they grew fat.
- From "Shān Mù" in the Zhuāngzǐ.
Cross-reference "Concentration".
Gathering easily obtainable things into easily filled vessels,
With a heart longing for someone and set on the highway,
If divided, it cannot be filled.
From the Xúnzǐ.
A man from Qí who desired gold,
Dressed up and went to the market at dawn,
Came to where gold was sold,
Snatched the gold and ran.
Officials caught him,
Asked: "People were all around,
Why did you snatch someone's gold?"
He replied:
"When taking the gold,
I saw no people,
Only saw the gold."
From the Lièzǐ.
Cross-reference "Greed and Delusion".
When a bright blade is at one's chest,
The eyes do not see flying arrows.
- From "Qiáng Guó" in the Xúnzǐ.
Eyes cannot see clearly when looking at two things,
Ears cannot hear keenly when listening to two sounds.
From the Xúnzǐ.
Those chasing game do not see Tài Shān,
When desires are outward,
Then vision is obscured.
From the Huáinánzǐ.
Cross-reference "Greed and Delusion".
The eye examines the tip of an autumn hair,
But the ear does not hear the sound of thunder;
The ear tunes to the sound of metal and stone,
But the eye does not see the height of Tài Shān.
When focused on small things,
Then big things are forgotten.
From the Huáinánzǐ.
Have the left hand draw a square,
And the right hand draw a circle,
Commanding both to be completed at once,
Even with a mind holding compasses and square, and hands skilled in carving, it cannot be done,
Because the mind cannot focus on two things,
So the hands cannot work simultaneously.
Lí Lóu could discern the sharpness of an autumn hair,
But did not hear the sound of thunder;
Jì Zǐ listened to the melody of Qīng Jué,
But did not see the shape of Sōng and Dài mountains.
From Liú Xié.
History
There are things the eyes do not see,
Sounds the ears do not hear.
Even the worthy,
Cannot draw a square with the left hand,
And a circle with the right.
From the Records of the Grand Historian.
Dǒng Zhòngshū lectured behind curtains,
For three years without peeping into the garden.
- From the official biography in the Book of Hàn.
Cross-reference "Concentration".
Liú Jùn studied diligently,
Often reading while walking without rest,
Where there were pits and bumps on the ground,
He would often stumble and fall,
Only then realizing it.
From the Book of Liáng.
Biographies
Those whose eyes examine the tip of an autumn hair,
Their sight cannot see Tài Shān;
Those whose ears listen to the tones of clear and turbid,
Their hearing cannot perceive the sound of thunder.
Why?
Because their attention is biased.
- From the "Miscellaneous Sayings" chapter of the Garden of Persuasions.
Jiǎ Dǎo composed poetry,
When he was bitterly chanting,
Even if encountering nobles and dignitaries,
He would not notice them.
One day he saw the Capital Governor,
Rode his donkey without avoiding,
Was called and questioned,
Only after a long time did he come to.
- From the biography of Hán Yù in the Book of Táng.
Cross-reference "Poetry".
Chǔ Suìliáng wrote the funeral eulogy for Tàizōng,
Returning on horseback from court,
Mistakenly entered someone's house without realizing.
From the Anecdotes from Suí and Táng.
Collections
Looking up greedily at the birds,
Turned head and answered the wrong person.
From Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Our dynasty
When he was delighted with five things,
Tài Shān ahead went unseen,
Sudden thunder shattered pillars but he wasn't startled.
From "Biography of the Six-One Retired Scholar".
I would have people wield an axe with the left hand,
And hold a carving knife with the right,
Count flying geese with their eyes and keep rhythm with drums in their ears,
Nod to others with their head and recognize steps with their feet,
Even if they had the knowledge,
They would have no leisure for it.
From Sū Shì's "Record of the Great Compassion Pavilion".
Philosophers
Affairs and things tangle and slip,
Like untangling a messy hemp,
Like wading through startled waters,
On one hand, it makes one cautious,
On another, it makes one avoid,
On yet another, it serves as a warning.
Thus within a single day,
In a moment's time,
And in a tiny space,
It feels both fiery and icy.
From the Zǐhuázǐ.
A man who lost his axe,
Suspected his neighbor's son,
Watching his gait,
It seemed like stealing an axe;
His expression,
Like stealing an axe;
His speech,
Like stealing an axe;
Every movement and manner seemed like that of an axe thief.
Soon after, he dug
(Pronunciation: jué)
in the valley and found his axe,
Another day he saw his neighbor's son again,
His movements and manner bore no resemblance to an axe thief.
From the Lièzǐ.
Cross-reference "Judgment After Time".
When the heart is anxious and fearful, then the mouth holds fine food but doesn't know its taste,
The ears hear bells and drums but don't know their sound,
The eyes see embroidered robes but don't know their pattern,
Lying on light warm mats but the body doesn't feel their comfort.
From the Xúnzǐ.
Formerly, Mí Zǐxiá was favored by the lord.
The law of Wèi state: Stealing the lord's carriage to drive,
Was punished by foot amputation.
Mí Zǐ's mother fell ill,
Informed Mí Zǐ,
Who pretended to drive the lord's carriage,
The lord said: "How filial!
For his mother's sake,
He risked foot amputation."
When Mí Zǐ's looks faded and favor waned,
He offended the lord,
The lord said: "This is the one who once pretended to drive my carriage."
From the Hánfēizǐ.
Formerly, Mí Zǐxiá was favored by the lord of Wèi.
Strolling with the lord in the fruit garden,
Ate a peach and found it sweet,
Gave half to the lord to taste,
The lord said: "He loves me!
Forgot his own mouth and gave it to me."
When Mí Zǐxiá's looks faded and favor waned,
He offended the lord,
Who said: "This is the one who once fed me his leftover peach."
Same as above.
History
In the past, Minister Jiǎ was ugly,
but he married a beautiful wife.
For three years, she neither spoke nor smiled.
He took her to the marshlands,
shot a pheasant and captured it,
and only then did his wife begin to smile and speak.
Minister Jiǎ said: "Talent cannot be neglected—
had I been unable to shoot,
you would never have spoken or smiled."
． From Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāogōng 28th Year.
When Tián Dān was about to attack Dí,
he met Lǔ Zhònglián.
The latter said: "General, you will not be able to capture Dí."
Tián Dān said: "With the remnants of a defeated army from Jímò, I defeated the mighty state of Yān,
and restored the ruins of Qí.
Now, if I cannot take Dí,
why is that?"
Zhònglián replied: "When you were at Jímò,
you sat weaving baskets,
stood leaning on your spade,
and led by example for your soldiers.
At that time,
you had the resolve to die,
and your soldiers had no will to live—
that is why you defeated Yān.
Now, you enjoy tributes from Miǎnchí in the east,
and pleasures from Zīshàng in the west,
girded with a golden belt and galloping between the Zī and Miǎn rivers,
indulging in the joys of life,
with no resolve to die—
that is why you cannot win."
． From Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Zhōu Nǎnwáng 43rd Year.
Zǐxià,
a top disciple among the disciples,
still
said,
"When I go out and see the splendor and luxury, I delight in it;
when I come in and hear the Master's Way, I rejoice in it.
The two wage war in my heart,
and I cannot decide for myself,"
let alone those of mediocre or lesser ability,
steeped in lack of instruction,
and clad in established customs?
． From Shǐjì, Book of Rites.
Lǐ Guǎng was out hunting when he saw
a rock in the grass,
mistook it for a tiger and shot at it.
The arrow struck the rock and sank in,
but when he looked,
it was a rock.
Another day, he shot at it again,
but could not pierce it anymore.
． From the main biography in the Western Hàn history.
The rise and fall of things,
the ebb and flow of emotions,
follow inherent principles.
But when it comes to extreme shifts of honor and disgrace,
must it only be due to favor and infatuation?
When one shares the bed,
and receives affectionate favors,
even treacherous hearts and flawed conduct
are all deemed virtuous.
But when affection shifts,
and intimacy is severed,
even kind hearts and beautiful appearances
only seem more ugly.
When love rises,
the world cannot contain its height;
when favor falls,
even the nine regions offer no escape from fate.
． From the Eastern Hàn history, Treatise on Empresses.
Wéi Yào normally drank no more than two shēng of wine.
When Sūn Hào first treated him with special respect,
he often reduced the amount for him,
or secretly gave him tea instead of wine.
But when favor waned,
he was instead forced to drink,
and this was held as a crime.
From the History of Wú.
Yuè Guǎng once had a close guest
who had not visited for a long time.
Guǎng asked the reason,
and the guest replied: "Last time I was seated,
you offered me wine.
As I was about to drink,
I saw a snake in the cup,
felt very disturbed by it,
and fell ill after drinking."
At that time, on the wall of the Hénán office hall, there was a horn
painted with a snake in lacquer.
Guǎng realized the snake in the cup was its reflection.
He again set wine in the same spot,
and asked the guest,
"Do you see anything in the cup now?"
The guest replied: "What I see is the same as before."
Guǎng then explained the reason,
and the guest suddenly understood,
his chronic illness vanishing at once.
From the History of Jìn.
Fú Jiān was defeated at the Féishuǐ,
his remaining troops fleeing in disarray.
Hearing the wind and the cranes' cries,
they all thought the imperial army had arrived.
From the Biography of Xiè Xuán.
Cross-referenced under "Fear" and "Collapsing at the Rumor".
A record
tells that Xióng Qúzǐ was traveling at night
when he saw a reclining rock and mistook it for a crouching tiger.
He drew his bow and shot at it,
the arrow sinking into the metal, its feathers submerged.
Looking down,
he realized it was a rock.
When he shot at it again,
the arrow bounced off without a trace.
From Hánshī Wàizhuàn.
Yìng Chēn was the magistrate of Jí
and invited his registrar Dù Xuān for wine.
At the time, a red crossbow hung on the north wall,
its reflection shining in the cup,
appearing like a snake.
Xuān was disturbed by it
and fell ill,
saying, "A snake has entered my belly."
Later, Chēn had Xuān return to the same place,
set wine in the cup,
and again there was a snake.
He then told Xuān: "This is just the reflection of the crossbow on the wall,
nothing strange."
Xuān's worry then dissolved.
From Fēngsú Tōng.
On the plantain leaves, the rain holds no sorrow;
it is our own sentiment that hears the heartbreak.
From Yǎyán Xìshù.
Collected
examples: taking medicine to induce sweating may sometimes fail,
yet a flush of shame can bring a sudden drenching;
after a morning without food, one craves it ravenously,
yet Lǔzǐ, in mourning, felt no hunger for seven days;
sitting late at night, one grows drowsy for sleep,
yet with deep sorrow in heart, one stays awake till dawn;
a stiff brush combs the hair,
strong wine reddens the face,
but only a warrior's rage can make one's hair stand on end
and crown lift in a striking display.
． From Wénxuǎn, Jī Kāng's Essay on Nurturing Life.
In the past, Jiǎ's wife at the marsh
was moved to smile by a single arrow;
an ugly man thus changed his appearance,
a resentful wife thus shed her grievance.
From the Rhapsody on Pheasant Shooting.
In joy, one regrets the short night;
in sorrow, one complains of the long evening.
． From the Xuǎn love poem.
Cross-referenced under "Different Likes and Dislikes".
It is not that external things change,
but surely joy and sorrow alter with feeling.
Pān Ānrén.
It must be because people's hearts differ today,
not that the autumn fragrance fades overnight.
From Táng poet Zhèng Gǔ's poem "The Tenth Day Chrysanthemum".
The water in a ravine
is deep but a foot or so;
the mound on a hill
is high but a few yards—
people approach and play with them.
But when facing the sheer cliffs of Tàishān
or gazing at the raging waves of the great sea,
none do not tremble with fear,
dazed and losing themselves.
What is seen changes before them,
what is held within shifts easily.
From Hán Yù's writings.
Then I learned there is no fixed beauty;
likes and dislikes follow human feelings.
Bái Jūyì.
Offering food to someone
in their hunger and thirst—
a single meal is worth a fortune.
But when full, even delicacies from land and sea
are regarded as chaff.
Shěn Xiàxián.
This dynasty
Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng asked Guō Chóngtāo:
"In the past when I confronted Liáng in battle along the river,
even during severe cold and intense heat,
I wore armor and rode horses
without feeling weary.
Now I reside in deep palaces,
sheltered by vast buildings,
yet I cannot bear the heat.
Why is this?"
Chóngtāo replied:
"Your Majesty previously had the whole realm in mind,
but now you focus only on your personal comfort.
Hardship and ease,
involve different concerns -
this is natural by circumstance."
． From "Continuation of Shì Shuō, Tenth Chapter".
Those who discuss delicacies will salivate,
those who speak of filth will spit.
Neither has actually contacted me,
so how do the spitting and salivating arise?
From Sū Dōngpō's "On Nourishing Life".
If there are maggots in food,
those who see them will vomit;
those who eat without seeing them
never vomit.
Ibid.
Things that resonate with the same sound
need not be equal in pitch;
things that seek the same energy
need not be identical in substance.
． From "General Principles of the Yì Jīng, Part One".
History
Minister Qí recommended outsiders without rejecting enemies,
and recommended insiders without omitting relatives.
． From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, 21st Year of Xiānggōng".
Cross-reference: "Devoted to public duty, forgetting private interests".
When Wèi Xiànzǐ administered governance in Jìn,
he appointed Wèi Wù as magistrate of Gěngyáng.
Xiànzǐ
was a son of a concubine.
． From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, 28th Year of Zhāogōng".
When Yǔ Liàng was in Wǔchāng,
his assistants including Shāng Hào
went together one autumn night to climb the south tower.
Unexpectedly, Liàng arrived,
and as everyone rose to avoid him,
he said: "Gentlemen, stay awhile.
This old man finds quite some delight here too."
He then sat on a folding chair
and conversed and recited poetry with Hào and others.
From "History of the Jìn Dynasty".
When a scholar's family in Wúzhōng had fine bamboo,
Wáng Huīzhī wanted to see it.
He went straight to the bamboo grove
and chanted poems for a long time.
The host cleaned and offered him a seat,
but Huīzhī paid no attention.
As he was leaving,
the host closed the gate,
which Huīzhī appreciated,
and he left completely satisfied.
． From "Biography of Wáng Huīzhī in History of the Jìn Dynasty".
After Táo Qián cut off visits to provincial authorities,
his villagers like Zhāng Yě, Yáng Sōnglíng, and Páng Zūn would invite him when they had wine.
He would join them at the drinking spot,
and even if he didn't know the host,
he would cheerfully feel no offense,
returning home when happily drunk.
． From "His Biography in History of the Jìn Dynasty".
Cross-reference: "Forgetting formalities with each other".
Someone reported that Chancellor Wèi Zhēng favored his relatives.
The Emperor had Wēn Yànbó investigate,
who said: "Zhēng doesn't maintain formalities
or avoid suspicion from afar.
Though his heart is without selfishness,
he still deserves blame."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Tàizōng".
When Cuī Yòufǔ became chancellor for less than a year,
he appointed nearly eight hundred officials,
mostly considered appropriate.
The Emperor said: "Some criticize that many officials you appointed
are relatives or acquaintances.
What say you?"
Yòufǔ replied: "To recommend candidates, one must know their ability and conduct.
Only if I know them
can I have some understanding.
If I've never heard of them,
how can I know their words and deeds?
The reason for this criticism
lies precisely here."
． From "His Biography in Old History of the Táng Dynasty".
Cross-reference: "Devoted to public duty, forgetting private interests".
When Wéi Guànzhī was Imperial Censor,
he recommended his brother Wéi Xiè as his replacement.
． From "His Biography in New History of the Táng Dynasty".
When Gāo Yuányù was Vice Censor-in-chief,
Emperor Wénzōng found it hard to replace him,
so he recommended his brother Gāo Yìshǎo as capable for the post,
who was thus appointed.
Ibid.
Biographies
Wáng Huīzhī of Jìn had outstanding talent.
When young, he served as advisor to Huán Chōng.
Once following Chōng,
it rained,
so he dismounted and entered Chōng's carriage,
saying: "How can you独占 a carriage
and not accommodate a national scholar?"
From "Shì Shuō".
Cross-reference: "Subordinates".
Collections
In ancient times, those who understood others
didn't wait to be asked before bestowing virtue -
they simply recommended the capable.
Those who received virtue
didn't wait until success to give thanks -
they simply felt the understanding.
Thus, without knocking, there was resonance;
without introduction, there was harmony.
Then recommendations would surely come,
and gratitude would be profound.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's "Preface".
This Dynasty
Wáng Zǐyóu's love for bamboo
led him to visit without consulting the host;
Táo Yuānmíng's riding in a carriage
would stop for wine when meeting a Daoist priest.
From "Collection of Ōuyáng Xiū's Literary Works".
Cross-reference: "Leisure and Comfort".
Masters
They delight in their customs,
are content in their dwellings.
Neighboring states are visible to each other,
the sounds of chickens and dogs are audible,
yet people grow old and die without visiting each other.
In such times,
perfect governance is achieved.
． From "Zhuāngzǐ, Opening Trunks".
Fish forget each other in rivers and lakes;
people forget each other in the art of the Way.
． From "Zhuāngzǐ, The Great Ancestral Teacher".
Lièzǐ rode the wind and returned,
saying: "I truly don't know whether the wind rode me,
or I rode the wind?"
． From "Lièzǐ, The Yellow Emperor".
Neighboring states are visible to each other,
the sounds of chickens and dogs are audible,
people grow old
without visiting each other.
． From "Lǎozǐ, Chapter Ten".
A man by the sea who loved seagulls
would go to the sea every morning
to wander with them.
The seagulls that came to him
numbered in the hundreds.
． From "Lièzǐ, Heaven's Gifts".
Zhuāng Zhōu dreamed he was a butterfly,
then suddenly awoke,
saying: "I don't know whether Zhōu dreamed he was a butterfly,
or the butterfly dreams it's Zhōu?"
． From "Zhuāngzǐ, Discussion on Making All Things Equal".
Cross-reference: "Broad-mindedness".
Villages are separated by distance,
the sounds of chickens and dogs are audible,
people grow old and die
without visiting each other,
for they are self-sufficient.
． From "Wén Zhōngzǐ, Establishing Destiny".
History
Táo Qián cut off visits to provincial authorities.
His villagers like Zhāng Yě, Yáng Sōnglíng, and Páng Zūn would invite him when they had wine.
He would join them at the drinking spot,
and even if he didn't know the host,
he would cheerfully feel no offense,
returning home when happily drunk.
． From "His Biography in History of the Jìn Dynasty".
Cross-reference: "Not Sticking to Formalties".
Biographies
In the time of Yáo, there was an old man beating the ground by the roadside,
saying:
"I rise with the sun and work,
rest when it sets,
drink from a well I dug,
eat from fields I plow—
what power does the emperor hold over me?"
From Tōng Lì,
also seen in Dìwáng Shìjì.
Sīmǎ Décao once visited Páng Dégōng,
encountering him while he was crossing the Miǎn River
to pay respects at his ancestors' graves.
He entered directly into his home,
called out to Dégōng's wife and children,
who all lined up to bow in the hall
and hurried to prepare offerings.
Soon after,
Dégōng returned,
went straight in to join them,
not knowing who the guest was.
From the annotation in Shǔ Zhì, "Páng Tǒng Zhuàn," citing Xiāngyáng Jì.
Collection
The people of Yáo's time did not realize Yáo's presence,
only enjoying peace and idly beating the ground.
From Yuán Zhěn's collection.
Chickens rest, birds without doubt.
Mèng Hàorán.
Born between heaven and earth,
yet unaware of their height and depth;
drinking from rivers and seas,
ignorant of their vastness and profundity.
From Zhāng Yuè's writings.
Just ask the host to sweep the floor empty,
I'll bring my own wine, cup, and strings.
Bái Lètiān.
Our dynasty
For years, no letters exchanged,
who knows my laziness?
We meet beyond the cosmos,
why bother with complexity or simplicity?
Hòushān.
Hán Wèigōng delighted in employing renowned scholars,
sometimes without having met them;
once appointed,
they didn't even know who recommended them.
From his biography.
Classic
After nine years,
efforts yielded no success.
From Shū, "Yáo Diǎn."
To act deceitfully
tires the heart and blunders the day.
From Shū, "Zhōu Guān."
Like plowing without a plowshare.
From Jì.
Masters
It's like climbing a tree to catch fish.
To help it grow,
one who pulls up the seedlings,
not only does no good,
but also harms them.
From Mèngzǐ.
Also appears in "Self-made unrest" and "Love turns to harm."
Zhū Pēngmàn learned dragon-slaying from Zhīlí Yì,
spent all his family's wealth,
mastered the skill in three years but had no use for it.
Pushing a boat on land,
labor without gain.
From Zhuāngzǐ.
History
Tongues worn out, ears deafened,
yet no success seen.
From Zhànguó Cè.
Trying to catch the wind or grasp a shadow,
ultimately unattainable.
From Qián Hàn, "Jiāosì Zhì."
Following it is like chasing a shadow.
From Xī Hàn, "Zhǔfù Yǎn Zhuàn."
Lù Zhǎn dyed his white hair,
hoping to charm a concubine.
But the dark color didn't last long,
speckles of white soon reappeared.
From Sòng, "Xiè Língyùn Zhuàn."
Lips rot, teeth fall out, yet unaware of any benefit.
From Rúlín Zhuàn.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng devoted his mind to Buddhism,
Jiǎnwén focused intently on the Dharma,
emptied the treasury to support the monastic community,
exhausted human resources to build temples and pagodas.
Until the three Huái rivers boiled with waves,
the five ridges smoked with turmoil,
clinging to life like a bear's paw,
drawing last breaths from a sparrow's chirp,
their descendants perished without respite,
the state fell in an instant to ruins—
the sign of retribution,
how misguided it was!
From Tōng Jiàn, Táng Tàizōng.
Collection
Using a straight needle as a hook,
what fish could one ever catch?
From Chǔ Cí.
Even if every household had a mouth to boast,
the slander would only worsen.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
Pecking all over the Dèng forest for one insect,
the insect's hole not pierced, the long beak worn bald.
From Yuán Zhěn's collection.
Scooping earth to move a mountain, hoping it will vanish;
tossing stones to fill the sea, wishing it would brim.
How long to catch the wind with a rope?
When will slicing water with a knife ever cut it?
Wéi Yìngwù.
At home, storing ancient and modern calligraphy,
ink shades illuminating chests and baskets.
When hunger comes, leaning on an empty bed,
not a single character fit to cook.
Dōngpō.
Even if each house had a mouth to explain,
and markets displayed gold to hire people,
none would believe,
and criticism wouldn't cease.
From Dōngpō's "Letter to the Emperor."
A short rope, though skillfully used,
can never draw from the depths.
Hòushān's poem.
Cooking sand for porridge never satisfies hunger.
Shāngǔ's poem.
Counting sands in the sea only traps oneself in toil.
From Yǒngjiā Zhèngdào Gē.
Classic
Like taking, like carrying.
From Shī.
Masters
The sword of the Xīróng, Kūnyú,
cuts jade as if slicing through mud.
From Lièzǐ, "Tāng Wèn."
Páo Dīng dissecting an ox,
the blade swishes smoothly.
Sound: mài.
Every move in harmony with the rhythm.
From Zhuāngzǐ, "Yǎngshēng Zhǔ."
Thin ice under the midday sun,
a thick fur coat meeting a fierce fire.
From Wèizi.
History
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú wielded horsewhips,
and captured dozens of cities in Zhào.
Lì Shēng leaned on the carriage rail,
and secured over seventy cities in Qí.
． From "Shǐ Jì: Liè Zhuàn".
Like singeing a goose feather over a stove's charcoal.
． From "Shǐ Jì: Jīng Kē Zhuàn".
Like six swift horses passing a crack.
． From "Shǐ Jì: Lǐ Sī Zhuàn".
Lifting Qín was as light as a goose feather,
taking Chǔ was like picking up something left behind.
From "Qián Hàn Shū".
As easy as turning one's hand over.
． From "Xī Hàn Shū: Lù Jiǎ Zhuàn".
Rotten flesh against a sharp sword.
． From "Xī Hàn Shū: Méi Chéng Zhuàn".
Like shooting a festering abscess with a strong crossbow.
From earlier "Hán Ān Guó Zhuàn".
Obtaining high office was like picking up mustard from the ground.
． From "Xī Hàn Shū: Xiàhóu Shèng Zhuàn".
Like the sting of a mosquito or horsefly,
one just drives it away.
． From "Xī Hàn Shū: Yán Yóu Zhuàn".
Breaking dry and decayed things requires little effort.
． From "Xī Hàn Shū: Biǎo".
Crushing the withered and breaking the rotten.
． From "Dōng Hàn Shū: Gěng Dēng Zhuàn".

they speak of wealth and profit.
From Yángzǐ.
A city wall ten fathoms high,
which even Lóu Jì cannot scale,
is due to its steepness;
a mountain a thousand fathoms high,
that even a lame goat can easily graze upon,
is because of its gentleness.
． From "Wǔ Dù" in Hánfēizǐ.
Hills and mounds cannot produce clouds and rain,
and stagnant waters cannot host fish and turtles,
because they are too small.
From Huáinánzǐ.
Cross-reference to "the small cannot accommodate the large."
On a morning with heavy fog,
one can write fine script,
but cannot see beyond a short distance.
From Huáinánzǐ.
On a barren, eroded mountain,
there are no trees of ten zhàng in height.
Same as above.
The eye can perceive the distant sky,
but cannot see the back of its own neck.
From Bàopǔzǐ.
The two eyes do not see for each other.
From Jiǎngzǐ.
At the foot of Kūnlún Mountain, jade is used to throw at crows;
by the shores of Pénglí Lake, fish is fed to dogs;
yet people do not cherish these,
not because they inherently disdain wealth,
but because they are abundant there.
From Liúzǐ.
Shǐ
Shū Xiàng's mother said: "In deep mountains and vast marshes,
truly dragons and serpents are born."
． From Zuǒzhuàn, 21st year of Duke Xiāng.
Like the eye seeing a fine hair,
but failing to see its own eyelashes.
． From "Yuè Family" in Records of the Grand Historian.
Between Qí and Lǔ, in literature and learning,
since ancient times, it has been their innate nature.
． From "Biographies of Confucian Scholars" in Records of the Grand Historian.
In the homes of the illustrious,
ghosts peer into their chambers.
． From "Biography of Yáng Xióng" in History of the Western Hàn.
Zōu and Lǔ adhere to classical studies,
Qí and Chǔ abound in clever debate,
Hán and Wèi produce men of extraordinary integrity.
． From "Biography of Zōu Yáng" in History of the Western Hàn.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
east of the mountains have produced ministers,
west of the mountains have produced generals.
． From "Biography of Zhào Chōngguó" in History of the Western Hàn.
In a city of ten thousand households,
there must be stores of ten thousand zhōng;
in a city of a thousand households,
there must be stores of a thousand zhōng.
． From "Treatise on Food and Money" in History of the Western Hàn.
A fierce tiger in the deep mountains
causes all beasts to tremble with fear;
but when it is in a well or cage,
it wags its tail begging for food.
． From "Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān" in History of the Western Hàn.
Those wearing cool linen clothes
do not suffer the stifling heat of intense summer;
those clad in warm fox furs
do not worry about the bitter cold of severe winter.
． From "Biography of Wáng Bāo" in History of the Western Hàn.
Cross-reference to "being prepared."
In the heavenly music of the celestial court,
there must be wondrous and beautiful sights;
in the imperial palaces and royal residences,
there must be treasures of extraordinary value.
． From "Biography of Mí Héng" in History of the Eastern Hàn.
Wealth and honor breed inhumanity,
indulgence leads to foolish maladies.
From the Táng historian's eulogy for Emperor Mùzōng.
In Hénán, the imperial city, there are many close ministers;
in Nányáng, the emperor's hometown, there are many close relatives.
． From "Annals of Emperor Guāngwǔ" in History of the Eastern Hàn.
Men of culture and distinction
are all in the central plains.
． From "Annals of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng" in Comprehensive Mirror.
Those who climb heights without fear
are condemned men;
those who do not sit under eaves
are sons of wealthy families.
． From "Biography of Mǎ Róng" in History of the Eastern Hàn.
Cross-reference to "different capacities."
The capital is where the cultured elite gather,
and where fame and reputation are made;
through leisurely networking,
one can succeed without toil.
． From "Biography of Zhāng Jiǔlíng" in History of the Táng.
Clear waters harbor no big fish.
． From "Annals of Emperor Hé of Hàn" in Comprehensive Mirror.
Zhuànjì
In the state of Chǔ, food is more expensive than jade,
and firewood costlier than cassia.
Those contending for fame do so at court;
those contending for profit do so in the marketplace.
From Strategies of the Warring States.
On mountain peaks, there are no beautiful trees,
harmed by excessive sun;
under great trees, there are no beautiful grasses,
harmed by excessive shade.
． From "Tán Cóng" in Garden of Stories.
Calling out with the wind,
the voice is not louder, yet many hear it;
waving from a hilltop,
the arm is not longer, yet it is seen from afar.
． From "Jiàn Běn" in Garden of Stories.
Cross-reference to "being in the right place."
Associating with the noble,
it is fragrant as entering a room of orchids;
after long without noticing,
one becomes transformed by it;
associating with the base,
it is rank as entering a place of salted fish;
after long without noticing,
one becomes transformed by it.
Therefore, the noble are cautious about whom they associate with or avoid.
Associating with the noble,
is like the lengthening day—
one does not realize it oneself;
associating with the base,
is like treading on thin ice—
with each step sinking lower,
how can one avoid falling through?
． From "Master Zēng's Illness" in Elder Dài's Book of Rites.
High mountains with dense forests
must harbor strange tigers and leopards nurturing their young;
deep abysses and great rivers
must contain flood dragons.
． From "Four Generations" in Elder Dài's Book of Rites.
In the woods, strong winds are common;
among the wealthy and noble, flattery is rife.
From Discourses on Salt and Iron.
Master Guǐgǔ said: "Have you not seen the trees by the river?
Servants break their branches,
wind and waves erode their roots;
do these trees have enmity with heaven and earth?
It is their location that causes it;
have you not seen the pines and cypresses on Sōng and Tài mountains?
Their upper branches reach the blue clouds,
their lower roots extend to the nether springs;
for a thousand autumns and a hundred years, they escape the threat of the axe—
do these trees have kinship with heaven and earth?
It is their location that causes it."
From Yú Bānyòu's Biographies of Noble Scholars.
Collection
Ascending heights makes one's thoughts roam far,
facing depths makes one's mind clear.
Annotation from "Zhāng Jǐngyáng's Poetry."
Also included under "Travel and Appreciation."
Where markets converge,
is the abyss of ten thousand merchants.
From Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ."
Lice on the head turn black,
musk deer eating cypress become fragrant.
Necks in rugged lands develop goiters,
teeth in Jìn turn yellow.
From Jī Kāng's "Essay on Nourishing Life."
The auspicious aura of the five imperial tombs is ever-present.
From Dù Fǔ's poetry.
The capital is a field of fame and profit,
where even at cockcrow there is no peaceful dwelling.
From Bái Jūyì.
With warmth and fullness within,
purity and integrity manifest without.
The southern mountains are rich with white clouds,
while Luòyáng is filled only with red dust.
Darkness gives birth to demons, and rot breeds worms.
Also from the same source.
Poor scholars lack color in their faces,
noble households abound in lightness and plumpness.
From Mèng Jiāo.
Carrying pearls and jade to the markets of a famous city,
there is none that will not sell;
taking them to the wilds of three households,
there is none that will not be stolen, leading to hardship.
From Huángfǔ Shí.
A barren nest has no returning feathers.
In wealth, it is easy to maintain appearances,
in poverty, it is hard to keep oneself well.
From Mèng Jiāo.
Since ancient times, humble gates have seldom seen carriage dust.
From Hán Wò.
Knowing you are a guest from the five imperial tombs,
you do not enjoy travels to Shímén.
From "The Collected Works of Liú Yǔxī."
Could swallows peeping at beams be found in the blue clouds?
In turbid waters, there should be no fish avoiding the hook.
A lone tree stands tall in the swift wind,
the vast lake shimmers under the bright moon.
From Xǔ Hún's writings.
Under pines and cypresses, no common grass grows;
among yuèzhuó birds, no ordinary fowl are found.
From Ōuyáng Zhān's writings.
Lodging by water, one knows the cold comes early; sorrowful sleep makes the night feel long.
From Lǐ Shāngyǐn's writings.
Water accumulates and deepens,
allowing fish in the vast abyss to leap;
wind gathers and thickens,
enabling wings that touch the sky to soar.
From Lǚ Wēn's writings.
A volcanic land has no cold spots,
a turbid stream has no clear source.
From "The Collected Works of Wáng Jiàn."
In our dynasty,
it is easy to gain renown while in poverty and low status,
but hard to avoid faults while in wealth and high position.
From Sū Shì's "Zhòng Xiān, Regional Defense Commissioner."
Near the sun, one knows dawn first;
where the sky is low, spring comes easily.
From Shào Yōng.
A waterfront pavilion gets the moon first;
flowers and trees facing the sun meet spring easily.
From "Famous Tales from the Hanlin Academy."
How does the young master know the autumn sun?
Born under ornate roofs,
and raised in the imperial court,
going out with large canopies,
entering to attend by the curtains,
where heat only reaches warmth,
and cold only reaches coolness.
From Sū Shì's "Rhapsody on the Autumn Sun."
Classics
How to gather people?
With wealth.
From "The Appended Judgments of the Yì Jīng."
Families with hereditary emoluments
seldom adhere to ritual.
Position leads to arrogance without intent,
wealth leads to extravagance without design.
From "The Book of Documents: The Charge to the Duke of Bì."
Masters
Zǐlù said: "Carrying heavy loads over long distances,
one does not choose where to rest;
with a poor family and elderly parents,
one does not choose the emolument to serve."
From "The School Sayings of Confucius."
A three-foot bank, an empty cart cannot climb;
a hundred-ren mountain, a loaded cart can ascend,
because of the gradual slope.
From Xúnzǐ.
Those in mourning clothes with hempen staffs
have no mind for music,
not that their ears do not hear,
but their attire makes it so;
those in embroidered robes and ceremonial caps
do not behave disrespectfully,
not out of矜持,
but their attire makes it so;
those in armor holding spears
have no cowardly spirit,
not because they are inherently fierce,
but their attire makes it so.
From "The School Sayings of Confucius: Three Forbearances."
Before the grass and wood offerings are displayed,
they are kept in boxes,
wrapped in embroidered cloth,
with the priest fasting to present them.
After they are displayed,
passersby tread on their heads and backs,
and gatherers take them to fuel their fires.
From "Zhuāngzǐ."
A proverb says: "Long sleeves are good for dancing,
abundant resources are good for trading."
This means ample means make work easy.
From "Hánfēizǐ."
With ample food and clothing, one knows honor and shame.
From "Guǎnzǐ."
When Yáo and Shùn were in power,
even ten Jiés and Zhòus could not cause chaos,
because the situation was ordered;
when Jié and Zhòu were in power,
even ten Yáos and Shùns could not bring order,
because the situation was chaotic.
From "Hánfēizǐ."
In the spring of a lean year,
even a younger brother goes hungry.
In the autumn of a abundant year,
even distant guests are fed.
From "Hánfēizǐ: Five Vermin."
A posthumous child does not long for its father,
having no image in the heart.
From "Huáinánzǐ: Forest of Sayings."
When people have surplus, they yield;
when in want, they contend.
Yielding gives rise to ritual and righteousness,
contending leads to violence and chaos.
Knock on a door for water,
and none will refuse,
because there is plenty;
in the woods, no one sells firewood,
on the lake, no one sells fish,
because there is abundance.
Thus, with plentiful goods, desires diminish;
with fulfilled needs, contention ceases.
From "Huáinánzǐ: Balanced Customs."
When Yáo was a commoner,
he could not command his neighbors.
Once he became sovereign,
his orders were followed and prohibitions heeded.
From "Shènzǐ."
The light of the bright moon
allows one to see far,
but not to write small characters;
on a morning of thick fog,
one can write small characters,
but not see beyond a short distance.
From "Huáinánzǐ."
Wealth does not require learning extravagance to be extravagant.
From "Rénzǐ."
When Shùn was making pottery,
he could not benefit his own lane;
but when he faced south as ruler of the world,
even the barbarians received his blessings.
From "Shīzǐ."
Carrying a bottle to beg for water,
holding a torch to seek fire,
and people do not stint,
not because they are naturally generous,
but because they have surplus.
From "Liúzǐ."
Hang a thousand gold in the market, and none dare take it,
because ownership is clear;
drop a single coin on the ground, and children contend for it,
because ownership is uncertain.
From "Fùzǐ."
History
The nature of those accustomed to rich fare is hard to correct.
From Guóyǔ.
Those who eat fresh and rich foods are often arrogant and unrestrained.
Ibid.
Those who are content can be led to practice righteousness,
while those in distress can be led to do wrong.
From Shǐ Qínshǐhuáng Jì.
Judicial officials compete with each other,
taking severity as wisdom.
Those who are harsh gain public fame,
while those who are fair often face future troubles.
Thus, all judicial officials wish for people to die,
not out of hatred for them,
but because their own safety lies in the death of others.
Human nature seeks comfort and delights in life,
but under pain, thinks of death.
Under the blows of the rod,
what confession cannot be obtained?
Thus, when prisoners cannot endure the pain,
they fabricate statements to show;
officials take advantage of this,
guiding them to clarify the charges;
fearing rejection when reporting to superiors,
they refine and meticulously frame the case.
Even if Gāo Yáo were to hear it,
he would still think death insufficient for the crime.
Why?
Because the crafted evidence is abundant,
and the artificially constructed crime is clear.
From Xīhàn Lù Wēnshū Zhuàn.
Those whose courage and strategy alarm their sovereign face personal danger,
those whose achievements overshadow the world receive no rewards.
From Tōngjiàn.
When food and clothing are sufficient, people know honor and shame;
when integrity and deference arise, disputes and lawsuits cease.
From Qiánhàn Shíhuò Zhì.
If a hundred people labor
but cannot clothe one person,
to hope that none below suffer cold
is impossible;
if one person tills the land
while ten gather to eat,
to hope the world knows no hunger
is impossible;
when hunger and cold pierce the people's skin,
to expect them not to turn to treachery and evil
is impossible.
From Tōngjiàn Hàn Wén.
The orphan is easily wounded,
the poor are easily moved.
From Dōnghàn Bǐng Yuán Zhuàn.
When the root is weak
and the branches grow strong,
in the end, there will be events of conflict and upheaval,
such is the inevitable trend.
From Tōngjiàn Hàn Guāngwǔ.
Those born rich are arrogant,
those born noble are proud.
Those born to wealth and nobility who are not arrogant and proud
have never existed.
From Tōngjiàn Hàn Hé Jì.
While power remains, no authority is beyond reach;
once power is lost, not even one's own life is secure.
From Tōngjiàn Hàn Xiàn Jì.
Nobility does not expect arrogance, yet arrogance comes on its own;
wealth does not expect extravagance, yet extravagance comes on its own.
From Táng Wèi Zhèng Zhuàn.
The poor do not learn frugality,
the rich do not learn extravagance;
it is not human nature,
but circumstance that makes it so.
From Wèi Zhì.
Cross-reference "does not require artificial shaping."
When a grand house is newly built, the master builder stands under it first;
when fine grain ripens, the farmer tastes it first.
From Wèi Zhì Wáng Càn Zhuàn.
Jìn Liú Yì said: "The highest ranks have no one from humble families,
the lowest ranks have no one from powerful clans."
From Tōngjiàn.
Sòng Míngdì decreed: "The highly placed fear peril and danger,
the lowly worry about dying in ditches."
From Tōngjiàn Sòng Jì.
Xīn Xióng said: "The reasons why men forget themselves in battle,
and fear not facing sharp blades,
are first, to seek glory and fame,
second, to covet great rewards,
third, to fear punishment,
fourth, to avoid disaster and difficulty.
Without these reasons,
even a sage ruler cannot command his ministers,
nor a kind father urge his son."
From Tōngjiàn Liáng Gāozǔ.
Zhū Jìngzé said: "Hasty steps leave no good tracks,
tightly strung strings produce few harmonious sounds."
From Xù Shìshuō.
People long at peace become arrogant and indolent, hard to instruct;
those who have experienced turmoil, sorrowful and bitter, are easily transformed.
It is like the hungry are easily fed,
the thirsty easily given drink.
From Tōngjiàn Táng Tàizōng Jì.
Biographies state:
The market,
full in the morning,
empty by evening,
is not loved in the morning and hated by evening;
people go where survival is sought,
and leave when it is gone.
From Zhànguócè.
Nobility does not expect wealth, yet wealth comes; wealth does not expect fine food, yet fine food comes;
fine food does not expect arrogance and extravagance, yet they come.
Ibid.
If one races alongside a steed,
then man cannot outrun the steed;
but seated in a chariot driving the steed,
then the steed cannot outrun man.
From Lǚshì Chūnqiū.
Why should fishermen and craftsmen worry about the exhaustion of mountains and seas?
Liú Zhījī's Shǐtōng.
Collection:
No river flows backward in Guǎngchuān.
From Xuǎn Xiè Língyùn's poetry.
Where money is present,
danger can be turned to safety,
death to life;
where money departs,
nobility can become baseness,
life can lead to death.
Lǔ Bāo's Qián Shén Lùn.
When great waves shake the valleys,
no fish in the river remains calm;
when fierce storms sweep the fields,
no branch in the forest stays still.
Yīn Zhòngwén's Biǎo.
High winds destroy the finest trees.
Lǐ Tàibái.
In youth, one delights in new friends;
in decline, one longs for old companions.
Hán Wén.
Cross-reference "different inclinations."
Literary works
often arise from travels and humble origins;
as for nobles and dignitaries,
content and satisfied,
unless naturally inclined and fond of it,
they have no leisure to engage in it.
Peaceful tones are bland,
while sorrowful sighs are profound;
joyful words are hard to perfect,
but expressions of hardship easily resonate.
Both from the same source.
With head tethered and feet tied,
even a steed cannot take a step.
Where nothing hinders the way,
a lame turtle travels a thousand miles.
In hot weather, no well is cool.
When the sun is at its zenith,
objects cast no slanting shadows.
Liú Bīnkè.
A short thread cannot make a long seam.
Mèng Dōngyě.
Neighbors rich, the chicken often visits;
home poor, guests gradually dwindle.
Yáo Shàojiān.
The Long River refuses to flow west.
Bái Lètiān.
Scions of noble families tread high positions,
while the talented remain in lowly posts.
Such is the lay of the land,
not a recent phenomenon.
Zuǒ Tàichōng's Yǒngshǐshī.
In high status, one often forgets the lowly.
Cáo Zǐjiàn's Zèng Dīng Yí.
Our dynasty
At vermilion gates lie leftover grains,
Swallows and sparrows come from miles away.
But official gates stand cold as ice,
A hundred pleas yield not one promise.
From Sū Dōngpō's poetry.
When full, leftover meat remains;
When starved, no extra greens are found.
Sweet wells are drained the earliest,
Bitter plums survive untouched and sound.
Also from the same source.
With a whip, one confronts a fierce tiger,
Shouting and striking with all might.
Barehanded, meeting a lizard,
One turns pale and flees in fright.
From "Collection of Lǎoquán Xiānshēng".
Bare-chested, hand on sword,
Even Wū Huò dares not approach.
Helmeted, armored, sleeping with weapons,
A child may draw his bow and encroach.
Where profit lies,
All under heaven flock.
Thus, a family of wealth,
Wishing to act,
Causes a market of a hundred shops
To lose its peaceful habitat.
From "Collection of the Three Sūs".
Looking up from below,
Boundless wealth and honor seen;
Looking down from above,
Endless poverty and misery keen.
By Shào Yáofū.
Classic
How can one avoid such a fall?
From "Shū·Wēizǐ".
Alas, it's done!
Heaven has willed it so,
What is there to say?
From "Shī·Běimén".
What can be done about it?
From "Shī·Jūnzǐ Xiélǎo".
Alas, what use is regret now?
From "Shī·Zhōnggǔ Yǒu Tuī".
What's past is not to be blamed.
From "Analects".
I see no way to deal with this.
Same as above.
History
Once done, it's not reproached.
From "Hànshū·Chē Qiānqiū Biography".
Yáng Yànxún said: "It's like a household with a son
Whom even parents cannot control—
What can be done?"
From "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn·Five Dynasties, Jìn Gāozǔ".
Biographies
A night traveler may avoid wrongdoing,
But cannot stop dogs from barking at him.
From "Strategies of the Warring States".
Our dynasty
Attack it temporarily, and it grows stronger;
Suppress it unextinguished, and it flares fiercer,
Until it reaches a point of helplessness.
From "Collection of Ōuyáng".
The trouble of the world
Is none greater than not knowing why things are as they are;
Not knowing why things are as they are
Is like folding hands awaiting chaos.
From Sū Dōngpō's prose.
Classic
If it can be stopped,
Then I wish to stop it.
From "Lǐjì·Tángōng Xià".
Masters
One should stop when it's time to stop.
From "Mencius".
Can this not be ceased?
From "Mencius".
History
It brings no harm to Lǔ,
But only seeks fame,
Which turns into ill repute.
From "Zuǒzhuàn".
When Nìng Xǐ of Wèi monopolized power,
Gōngsūn Miǎnyú requested to kill him.
The duke said: "The outcome is uncertain;
It may only earn ill repute—
Let it be."
From "Zuǒzhuàn·Year 27 of Xiānggōng".
It won't suffice to harm Wú,
But would kill many scholars of the state;
Better to desist.
From "Zuǒzhuàn·Year 8 of Āigōng".
Masters
Misfortune is
Where fortune leans;
Fortune is
Where misfortune hides.
Who knows its ultimate end?
From "Lǎozǐ·Chapter 58".
A man of Sòng who practiced benevolence and righteousness,
Unwavering for three years,
Saw his black cow bear a white calf for no reason,
And asked Confucius about it.
He said: "This is auspicious,
Offer it to the Supreme Deity."
A year later,
His father went blind without cause,
And the cow bore another white calf.
His father again sent his son to ask Confucius.
The son said: "Last time we asked, you lost your sight,
Why ask again?"
The father said: "The sage's words seem roundabout but later fit.
The matter isn't fully understood,
So ask once more."
The son went to ask Confucius again.
Confucius said: "It is auspicious."
And again advised a sacrifice.
The son returned to relay the message.
The father said: "Follow Confucius's words."
Another year passed,
And the son went blind without cause.
Later, Chǔ attacked Sòng,
Besieging the city,
Where people exchanged children to eat,
And split bones for fuel.
All able-bodied men fought on the walls,
And more than half perished.
This man and his son, being blind, were exempt.
When the siege lifted, their sight was restored.
This is called misfortune and fortune leaning on each other.
From "Lièzǐ·Shuō Fú".
Celebrants in the hall,
Mourners at the gate.
Misfortune neighbors fortune,
None know its door.
From "Xúnzǐ·Dà Lüè".
A fire breaks out and rain falls;
The fire is misfortune,
The rain is fortune.
Thus, within misfortune lies fortune.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
Where misfortune leans,
Turns into fortune;
Where fortune hides,
Reverses to misfortune;
What appears as ominous,
May bring good luck;
What descends as auspicious,
May circle back to calamity.
Those who know misfortune can become fortune,
Fortune can become misfortune,
Ominous signs can bring good,
Auspicious signs can turn ill,
May discuss the nature of things.
From "Lièzǐ".
History
Sīmǎ Hóu of Jìn said: "Some states are solidified through many difficulties,
expanding their territories;
others perish without experiencing hardships,
losing their domains.
Qí gained Duke Huán through the Zhòngsūn calamity,
while Jìn obtained Duke Wén through the Lǐ and Pī disasters,
thus becoming hegemon.
Wèi and Xíng, though untroubled,
were nonetheless lost to enemies.
" (Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāo 4)
Cross-reference: "Events defy fixed judgments"
Those who share in the rewards
must also share in the punishments.
(Referring to Gōngsūn Qīng of Qí)
" (Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāo 20)
Misfortune lies where blessing leans;
blessing lurks where misfortune hides.
Grief and joy gather at the same gate,
auspicious and ominous share one domain.
" (Shǐjì, Biography of Master Jiǎ)
When Gōu Jiàn was trapped at Kuàijī,
he sighed deeply: "Shall I end here?"
Zhǒng replied: "Tāng was imprisoned at Xiàtái,
King Wén confined at Yǒulǐ,
Chóng'ěr of Jìn fled to Dí,
Xiǎo Bái of Qí escaped to Jǔ,
yet all eventually became kings or hegemons.
Judging from this,
how could this not turn out to be fortunate?"
" (Shǐjì, Yuè Hereditary House)
Cross-reference: "Consolation"
When Yīng Bù was young, he met a physiognomist
who said: "You will be tattooed and then become king."
Later, when punished with tattooing,
he indeed became a king.
(Shǐjì)
Dòu Guǎngguó,
coming from a poor family,
was abducted and sold.
While charcoal-burning in the mountains for his master,
he and over a hundred others slept beneath a cliff in the cold.
When the cliff collapsed,
