but declined the summons.
Zhāng Fèng sighed and said, "The virtuous are indeed unfathomable.
His joy back then
was for his parent's sake."
_Book of Later Hàn_.
Vessels of great capacity are not for immediate use.
. _Book of Eastern Hàn: Biography of Sòng Hóng_.
For a tranquil official,
daily accounts may seem insufficient,
but monthly accounts show a surplus.
. _Book of Eastern Hàn: Annals of Ān_.
Cross-reference "tranquility."
Wáng Dǎo,
through handling affairs, achieved merits;
though there was no daily gain, the annual account showed a surplus.
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Reign of Jìn Yuándì_.
How can floods and droughts be blamed on Yáo and Tāng?
. _Book of Eastern Hàn: Biography of Cài Yōng_.
Wèi Shū,
not valued by his fellow villagers,
later became the senior officer to General Zhōng Yù.
Yù often practiced archery with his aides,
and Shū usually just kept score.
Later, when they were short a participant,
they included Shū to make up the number.
Shū's demeanor was calm and elegant,
and he hit every shot without fail,
astonishing everyone present,
with no one able to match him.
Yù said, "My failure to fully appreciate your talent
is just like this archery."
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Reign of Wèi Yuán_.
Wáng Zhàn,
initially possessing hidden virtue,
was unknown to others,
and even his brothers and clan considered him foolish.
His nephew Wáng Jì looked down on him,
and once visited Zhàn,
seeing a copy of _The Book of Changes_ by the bed.
Jì asked him to explain it.
Thereupon, he analyzed its profound principles,
subtle and wonderfully intriguing,
all of which Jì had never heard before.
Emperor Wǔ also thought Zhàn was foolish,
and upon seeing Jì,
often teased him about it,
but Jì said, "My uncle is certainly not foolish."
_Book of Jìn_.
Initially,
when Lù Jī went to Luòyáng,
intending to write the "Rhapsody of the Three Capitals,"
he heard that Zuǒ Sī was composing it,
clapped his hands and laughed,
writing to his brother Lù Yún, "When it's finished,
we can use it to cover wine jars."
But when Sī's rhapsody came out,
Jī was utterly amazed,
admitting he could not improve upon it,
and so he stopped writing.
. _Book of Jìn: Biography of Zuǒ Sī_.
Cross-reference "heartfelt admiration."
Initially,
when Tuòbá Kūduō attacked Guī,
Mò Tí, thinking Guī too young,
sent an arrow to Kūduō, saying, "How can a three-year-old calf bear a heavy load!"
Guī harbored a grudge.
By this time,
he had someone show the arrow to Tí and said to him,
"How did the three-year-old calf turn out?"
Tí and his son wept together.
The next morning,
they were captured and executed.
Cross-reference "disaster from words."
Wáng Jìngzé's mother often told people,
"Jìngzé deserves to have drums and horns blown for him."
People laughed and said, "It's enough if your son gets to blow horns for others."
Later, he indeed was enfeoffed as a marquis,
and granted drums and horns.
_Book of Southern Qí_.
Cáo Jǐngzōng greatly defeated the Wèi army,
and returned triumphantly.
The Emperor held a banquet at Huáguāng Hall,
ordering Left Vice Director Shěn Yuē to assign rhyme words for poetry.
Jǐngzōng did not get a rhyme,
and looked displeased,
requesting to compose a poem.
The Emperor said, "You have many talents,
and are outstandingly capable;
why limit yourself to a poem?"
Jǐngzōng, already drunk,
insisted on composing.
The decree allowed Yuē to assign the remaining rhymes,
leaving only "contest" and "ailment."
Jǐngzōng then took up the brush,
and finished in no time,
his verse reading: "Departing, my children grieved my return;
reed pipes and drums contend.
I ask the passersby,
how do I compare to Huò Qùbìng?"
The Emperor was exceedingly pleased.
Yuē and the court officials marveled all day, and the decree ordered it recorded in history.
_Book of Liáng_.
Chén Qìngzhī said, "I initially thought north of the Yangtze was all land of barbarians,
but upon reaching Luòyáng,
I realized the cultured and talented are all in the Central Plains,
beyond what Jiāngdōng can match."
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Liáng Gāozǔ_.
Yóu Yǎ of Wèi said, "Formerly, Minister Cuī stated,
'Gāo Shēng is richly talented and learned,
but lacks resolute integrity.'
I too thought so.
But when the Minister faced charges,
and the decree confronted him,
his voice faltered and legs trembled,
barely able to speak.
Gāo Zǐ alone elaborated on the facts,
with clear and discerning arguments,
and a lofty, resonant tone.
The sovereign was moved,
and the listeners were all stirred in spirit;
is this not resolute integrity?"
_Comprehensive Mirror_.
Gāo Shēng refers to Gāo Yǔn.
Emperor Tàizōng ordered Féng Déyí to recommend talents,
but after a long time, he had recommended none.
The Emperor questioned him,
and he replied, "It's not that I haven't tried,
but there are no extraordinary talents nowadays."
The Emperor said, "A gentleman employs people like tools,
each according to their strengths.
The real worry is not recognizing them;
how can you slander an entire generation!"
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Táng Tàizōng_.
Cross-reference "shallow judgment."
Fēng Chángqīng,
orphaned and poor in youth,
was thin with droopy eyes,
and one leg slightly shorter,
sought to be Gāo Xiānzhī's aide,
but was not accepted.
Chángqīng waited daily for Xiānzhī's comings and goings,
never leaving his gate,
for dozens of days,
until Xiānzhī reluctantly kept him.
When the Dáxī tribe rebelled,
Chángqīng privately drafted a victory report to show Xiānzhī,
which said everything Xiānzhī had in mind,
and from then on, the whole office marveled at him.
When Xiānzhī became military governor,
he appointed Chángqīng as his assistant.
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Táng Xuánzōng_.
Sāng Wéihàn made decisions as matters arose,
seemingly without prior thought,
leading others to doubt his negligence;
but upon careful deliberation,
none could change his rulings.
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Five Dynasties, Jìn Gāozǔ_.
Biographies
Zhāng Huà saw Chǔ Táo,
and said to Lù Píngyuán: "You brothers are like dragons leaping at the river's crossing,
while Gù Yànxiān is like a phoenix singing at morning sun.
I thought the treasures of the southeast were exhausted,
never expecting to see Chǔ Táo again."
Lù replied: "You simply haven't noticed those who neither sing nor leap."
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World".
When the phoenix first rises,
within twenty paces around it,
sparrows chuckle with mocking chirps;
but when it ascends to the sun,
bending and stretching,
soaring among the clouds,
the sparrows beyond the fences realize they cannot match its distance.
A scholar in coarse cloth,
never fully dressed,
eating coarse food,
never fully satisfied,
may be shamed by worldly men;
yet when he emerges, he secures myriad deliberations,
and when employed, he prolongs the people's lives,
then worldly men realize they cannot match his distance.
From "Han's Outer Commentary on the Poetry".
Collection
The kun as a fish
dives in the azure sea,
swims in the dark currents,
sinks its gills in the Bo Sea,
lashes its tail beneath wind and waves,
yet minnows in a pond or well
think they can compare with it.
The peng as a bird
preens its feathers,
indulges in drinking and pecking,
folds its wings between heaven and earth,
bends its neck by the rivers and seas,
yet pairs of wild ducks or geese
think they can belittle it.
But when its wings spread across the sky,
riding the wind for ninety thousand li,
shaking scales across the sea,
striking waves for three thousand miles,
how could it borrow wings from mulberry trees,
seek strength from water plants,
rely on trickles from riverbanks,
or wait for dust-raising winds from ant hills?
By Luò Bīnwáng.
People are hard to know,
a trouble even for Yáo and Shùn;
how can one judge their abilities
by a single question or answer?
From Duke Lù Xuān's writings.
Do not say it's but an inch of iron—
in use, it becomes a long weapon.
By Bái Lètiān.
Our Dynasty
All say the city lacks a stunning beauty,
unaware that behind vermilion doors lies a fair one locked away.
From the "Línchuān Collection".
Liú Zhōngshān said to Wáng Zēng: "As a top graduate in three exams,
you'll never lack for food and clothing."
Zēng replied: "My lifelong ambition
lies not in mere warmth and fullness."
From "Dōngxuān Notes".
Classics
How does it harm the sun and moon?
From the "Analects".
Masters
What belongs to the gentleman's nature,
does not increase with great success,
nor decrease with poverty and seclusion.
From "Mencius".
The wheat of Shànfǔ for one year,
does not strengthen Lǔ if gained,
nor weaken it if lost.
From "Family Sayings of Confucius".
The whole world praising him does not encourage him more,
the whole world blaming him does not discourage him more.
From "Zhuangzi: Free and Easy Wandering".
Under heaven, no water is greater than the sea;
countless rivers flow into it,
yet it never fills though it never stops;
the尾闾 drains it,
yet it never empties though it never ceases.
From the chapter "Autumn Floods".
Pour into it, and it does not overflow;
dip from it, and it does not run dry.
From the chapter "Heaven and Earth".
In Yǔ's time, nine floods in ten years,
yet the waters did not rise more;
in Tāng's time, seven droughts in eight years,
yet the shores did not recede more.
Both from "Zhuangzi".
Cannot destroy a single hair of the mountain.
From "Lièzǐ: Questions of Tāng".
Wealth and honor cannot add to it,
poverty and lowliness cannot subtract from it.
From the chapter "Āi Gōng" in "Xúnzǐ".
It does not exist because of Yáo,
nor perish because of Jié.
From "Xúnzǐ".
Praise and blame to oneself
are like a mosquito's passing bite.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
Thirsty, drink from the river—
your belly fills, but the river does not dry up.
Same as above.
With Yáo and Shùn ruling above,
even ten Jiés could not cause chaos,
such is the power of order.
From "Hánfēizǐ".
History
On the banks of rivers and lakes,
or islands in the Bo Sea,
geese gathering do not make it more,
pairs of ducks flying do not make it less.
From "History of the Western Hàn: Biography of Yáng Xióng".
Like losing one hair from nine oxen.
From "Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān".
Just as jade from Zhōng Mountain,
stones from the Sì River bank,
piling up jade tablets does not make them more abundant,
mining floating musical stones does not deplete them.
From "Biography of Cài Yōng".
Like the forests of Héngyáng,
the foothills of Dài's shadow,
cutting giant trees does not make them sparse,
planting saplings does not make them dense.
From "History of the Later Hàn: Biography of Cuī Yīn".
Dust added to Tài or Sōng Mountains,
frost gathered on Huái River or the sea,
though it brings no benefit, it does no harm.
Later, from "Biography of Yáng Lún".
Like that white jade,
pure without a speck of dust,
clear, yet not more so in purity,
muddy, yet not stained.
From Yuán Hóng's "Eulogy on Three Kingdoms' Famous Ministers".
Yú Zhòngxiáng,
with fine treasure as his essence,
carving and polishing make him brighter,
unable to diminish him.
From "History of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Yú Fān".
Táng's Duàn Zhìchōng said: "A foot of fog obscuring the sky
does not diminish its vastness;
an inch of cloud dotting the sun
does not harm its brightness."
From "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Records".
Biographies
The swan goose flies high, reaching the sky,
yet what it relies on
is its six wing feathers.
The down on its belly,
the feathers on its back,
add or remove a handful,
and its flight is neither higher nor lower.
From Liú Xiàng's "New Prefaces".
Zǐgòng said: "If I praise Confucius,
it's like adding a handful of soil to Tài Mountain—
clearly, it brings no increase;
if I do not praise Confucius,
it's like taking a handful from Tài Mountain—
clearly, it causes no loss."
From "Han's Outer Commentary on the Poetry".
In a single room,
adding one person
does not make the candle brighter;
removing one person
does not make it darker.
From "Biographies of Exemplary Women".
Collection
Blue flies cannot defile the pendant jade,
Heretical arguments cannot confuse Confucius or Mozi.
． From "Wénxuǎn: Discourse on the Virtue of the Four Masters".
Torrential rains may gather suddenly,
Yet rivers and seas do not consider themselves abundant;
Loaches and eels may flee together,
Yet the fine net does not consider itself empty.
Thus, Xǔ Yóu hid from Yáo and lived in seclusion,
But the Táng dynasty did not decline because of it;
Bó Yí and Shū Qí felt ashamed of the Zhōu and starved afar,
Yet King Wén and King Wǔ were not demeaned.
Same as above.
All rivers flow into the Eastern Sea,
Yet it neither empties nor overflows.
Mud and dregs cannot make it turbid,
Nor do clear waves make it purer.
Wéi Yìngwù.
The purity of the Huái and Jì rivers,
If blemished by a hair's breadth,
Truly does not harm their essence.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
The eclipse of the sun and moon,
The flaw in a great jade tablet,
How can these diminish their brightness or devalue their treasure?
Same as above.
The filthy remain filthy,
But cannot harm my purity;
The narrow remain narrow,
But cannot harm my breadth;
The obscure remain obscure,
But cannot harm my clarity.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
Losing one star,
Felling one tree,
Cannot diminish the radiance of heaven and earth.
From "Táng Wén Cuì".
Like a grain of rice in a great granary,
Adding one more to ten thousand bushels.
Same as above.
What praise cannot enhance,
Slander cannot damage;
What honor cannot move,
Disgrace cannot affect;
What profit cannot entice,
Harm cannot trouble.
Same as above.
Should I be the tip of an autumn hair,
I would still find myself sufficient and not see my smallness;
Should I be the slope of Mount Tài,
I would still have no excess and not see my greatness.
From "Táng Wén Cuì".
Cross-reference "Having Steadfastness".
Drawing water all year without end,
Neither depleting nor overflowing.
From "Yuán Zhěn's Collection".
Classics
When the noble person speaks of the great,
Nothing in the world can contain it;
When speaking of the small,
Nothing in the world can split it.
． From "The Doctrine of the Mean".
The Way of the noble person
Begins with ordinary men and women,
But in its utmost reaches,
It illuminates heaven and earth.
Same as above.
Observing all things under heaven,
None can match its virtue.
． From "The Book of Rites: Ritual Vessels".
The Great Way is not a vessel.
． From "The Book of Rites: Record of Learning".
The noble person is not a vessel.
． From "The Analects: Governance".
Masters
Its grace extends for ten thousand generations, yet it is not called benevolent;
It is older than antiquity, yet it is not called aged;
It covers and carries heaven and earth, carves all forms, yet it is not called skillful.
． From "Zhuāngzǐ: The Way of Heaven".
A thousand miles distant
Cannot encompass its greatness;
A thousand ren high
Cannot fathom its depth.
From the chapter "Autumn Floods".
It is above the Supreme Ultimate, yet not considered high;
It is below the Six Extremes, yet not considered deep;
It existed before heaven and earth, yet not considered ancient;
It is older than high antiquity, yet not considered old.
． From "Zhuāngzǐ: The Great and Venerable Teacher".
Histories
Zhuāng Zhōu's words are vast and unrestrained,
So that kings and nobles could not confine him.
Same as above.
Deep, it penetrates the Yellow Springs;
High, it emerges from the azure heavens;
Great, it embraces the primal energy;
Fine, it enters into the formless.
From the former "Biography of Yáng Xióng".
Wáng Róng once regarded Shān Tāo as unpolished jade and unrefined gold,
Whose treasure people could admire,
But none could name its vessel.
． From "Jìn Shū: Biography of Wáng Róng".
Collections
Brighter than the sun and moon, yet not enough to be called luminous;
Loftier than Mount Tài, yet not enough to be called high;
Vaster than heaven and earth, yet not enough to be called all-encompassing.
From Hán Yù's "Eulogy for Bó Yí".
Purer than fine jade, yet not enough to be its preciousness;
More fragrant than orchids, yet not enough to be its elegance.
Pí Rìxiū.
Firmer than metal or stone, yet not enough to be its steadfastness;
More serene than ice or jade, yet not enough to be its purity.
From "Táng Wén Cuì".
Intertwining clouds and mist
Are not enough to capture its demeanor;
The endless flow of water
Is not enough to capture its sentiment;
The lushness of spring
Is not enough to capture its harmony;
The clarity of autumn
Is not enough to capture its character;
Sailing ships and charging steeds
Are not enough to capture its courage;
Earthen coffins and ancient tripods
Are not enough to capture its antiquity;
Blooming flowers and beautiful women
Are not enough to capture its colors;
Desolate kingdoms and crumbling palaces,
Thorny bushes and barren mounds,
Are not enough to capture its sorrow and regret;
Whales gaping and turtles leaping,
Ox-headed ghosts and snake-bodied spirits,
Are not enough to capture its fantastical absurdity.
From "Táng Wén Cuì".
Flowing and halting like water's transformations,
Moving like a dragon's dance.
It is said the Way cannot be praised by one virtue,
Nor judged by one action.
Huángfǔ Shí.
Our Dynasty
When the Son of Heaven possesses the Way,
His virtue cannot be named;
When the ministers possess virtue,
Their talents cannot be seen.
Thus, in the Hàn dynasty,
The annals of Emperors Wén and Jǐng record no remarkable events,
And the biographies of Táng's Fáng Xuánlíng and Dù Rǔhuì list no great achievements.
From "Edict Appointing Lǚ Dàfáng as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs".
Just as the wonder of heaven and earth
Creates and transforms all things,
Moving and stationary,
Without distinction of small or great,
Leaving no trace,
Yet achieving perfection in their work.
From Ōuyáng Xiū's "Epitaph".
Classics
Such are the sages,
Who see clearly a hundred miles ahead.
Such are the foolish,
Who rejoice in madness and folly.
． From the "Shī·Sāng Róu".
One who is rich in benevolence but poor in righteousness is affectionate but not revered;
One who is rich in righteousness but poor in benevolence is revered but not affectionate.
． From the "Jì·Biǎo Jì".
Those who are born with knowledge are the highest;
Those who learn and acquire knowledge come next;
Those who learn through difficulties are next again;
Those who face difficulties but do not learn—such people are the lowest.
． From the "Yǔ·Jì Shì".
The Master said, "Huí's heart did not stray from benevolence for three months,"
"While others only attained it by the day or the month."
From "Yōng Yě".
To those above the average, one may speak of higher things;
To those below the average, one may not speak of higher things.
From "Gōng Yě Cháng".
The Master said, "The noble person remains steadfast in poverty,"
"While the petty person, when poor, becomes reckless."
From "Wèi Líng Gōng".
Like the walls of a palace,
Cì's wall is only shoulder-high,
Allowing a glimpse of the beauty within.
The Master's wall is several ren high,
And without finding the gate, one cannot enter.
From "Zǐ Zhāng".
The Master said, "The noble person aspires upward,"
"The petty person descends downward."
From "Xiàn Wèn".
The Master said, "The noble person is composed but not arrogant,"
"The petty person is arrogant but not composed."
From "Zǐ Lù".
The Master said, "The noble person is easy to serve but hard to please."
"If pleased improperly, he is not pleased;"
"And in employing people, he matches them to their abilities."
"The petty person is hard to serve but easy to please."
"Even if pleased improperly, he is pleased;"
"And in employing people, he demands perfection."
Same as above.
Zǐ
The qílín compared to common beasts,
the fènghuáng compared to flying birds,
Tài Shān compared to small mounds,
rivers and seas compared to puddles.
Mencius.
Cì progressed daily,
while Shāng regressed daily.
Cì liked befriending those superior to himself,
while Shāng liked befriending those not superior to himself.
Family Sayings of Confucius.
If Lǔ Mù Gōng had no one by Zǐsī's side,
he could not have kept Zǐsī content;
if Xiè Liǔ and Shēn Xiáng had no one by Mù Gōng's side,
they could not have secured their own positions.
Mencius, Gōngsūn Chǒu II.
A man fond of fame could yield a state of a thousand chariots,
but if it were not such a man,
even a bowl of rice or soup would show in his face.
Mencius, Jìnxīn II.
Yáng Zǐ advocated for self-interest,
refusing to pluck a single hair to benefit the world.
Mò Zǐ advocated universal love,
willing to be rubbed bare from head to heel to benefit the world.
Mencius, Jìnxīn I.
Cross-referenced with "Failing to Attain the Middle Way" and "Different Inclinations."
The way of heaven
diminishes the excessive
and supplements the deficient;
the way of man
diminishes the deficient
and offers to the excessive.
Lǎo Zǐ, Chapter 77.
Gōngyí Bó was renowned for his strength,
and King Xuān of Zhōu summoned him, asking,
"How strong are you?"
He replied, "My strength can break the leg of a spring locust
and withstand
the wing of an autumn cicada."
The king said, "My strength can tear the hide of a rhinoceros,
drag nine oxen by the tail,
yet I still regret its weakness."
Liè Zǐ.
In ancient times, there was a great chūn tree
that considered eight thousand years as a single spring and autumn.
On decaying soil grew fungi,
born at dawn and dead by dusk.
In spring and summer, gnats and midges
are born with the rain
and die upon seeing the sun.
In the vast sea, there is a fish
thousands of miles wide,
its length matching its width,
named the kūn.
There is a bird
named the péng,
its wings like clouds hanging from the sky.
In riverbanks, tiny insects thrive,
called jiāo míng,
swarming to rest on a mosquito's eyelash
without touching each other.
They come and go,
unnoticed by the mosquito.
Liè Zǐ, Tāng Wèn.
When Lord Yuán of Sòng planned to commission a painting,
many artists arrived,
licking brushes and mixing ink,
with half waiting outside.
One artist came late,
calm and unhurried,
accepting the salute without standing,
then went to his lodging.
The lord sent someone to observe him,
and he was found stripped, sitting cross-legged.
Zhuāng Zǐ.
Confucius said to Zǐlù,
"Those who travel waters without avoiding jiāo and dragons
display the courage of fishermen;
those who travel land without avoiding rhinoceroses and tigers
display the courage of hunters;
those who face crossed blades and regard death as life
display the courage of martyrs;
those who know poverty is fated,
success timely,
and face great perils without fear
display the courage of sages."
Ibid.
Great wisdom is broad and calm,
petty wisdom is narrow and fretful.
The master steps, and I step;
the master quickens, and I quicken;
the master runs, and I run;
but when the master dashes off leaving dust behind,
I can only stare after him.
Zhuāng Zǐ, Tián Zǐ Fāng.
Cross-referenced with "Matters Have Difficulty and Ease."
A frog in a sunken well said to a turtle from the Eastern Sea,
"The joy of the well's rim is supreme!"
The turtle's left foot had not yet entered
when its right knee got stuck.
Zhuāng Zǐ, Qiū Shuǐ.
The péng migrates to the southern sea,
splashing water for three thousand miles,
soaring on a whirlwind ninety thousand miles high.
Cicadas and doves dart up in flight,
reaching elms and sandalwoods,
while quails leap up
only a few yards before descending,
fluttering among weeds.
Zhuāng Zǐ, Xiāo Yáo Yóu,
also from Zhuāng Zǐ.
To court death recklessly
is the courage of petty men.
Xún Zǐ.
The noble man, if capable, is generous and straightforward in guiding others;
if incapable, he is respectful and humble in serving others.
The petty man, if capable, is arrogant and perverse in belittling others;
if incapable, he is envious and slanderous in undermining others.
Xún Zǐ, Bù Gǒu.
The King of Chǔ had a white ape
and shot at it himself,
but it caught the arrows and played;
when he had Yǎng Yóu Jī shoot it,
as soon as he adjusted the bow and fitted the arrow,
the ape clung to a post and wailed before it was released.
Huái Nán Zǐ.
Tài Shān compared to small mounds,
great rivers compared to puddles.
Mencius.
The way of Zhòngní
is like the four great rivers,
traversing the central states
and finally entering the great sea.
The ways of others
are like northwest streams,
regulating the lands of barbarians,
some flowing into the Tuó,
some lost in the Hàn.
Yáng Zǐ, Jūn Zǐ.
A fine horse needs no whip to run,
a nag cannot advance even with double whipping.
Huái Nán Zǐ.
Xǔ Yóu perfected himself alone,
while Tài Gōng benefited the world broadly.
Kǒng Cóng Zǐ, Jì Wèn.
Ordinary trees cannot emulate pines and cypresses,
common insects cannot learn from tortoises and cranes.
Bào Pú Zǐ, Duì Sú.
Where clarity reaches,
even in dark, shadowy places or on hair-thin objects,
it finds no difficulty;
where it does not reach,
even with the sun and moon shining in the sky or Sōng and Dài peaks towering through clouds,
it cannot perceive them.
Bào Pú Zǐ, Wēi Zhǐ Lùn.
What tigers and leopards leave
is what foxes and mice fight over;
what Táo Zhū discards
is what Yuān and Yán lack.
Bào Pú Zǐ, Qū Huò Lùn.
Earthen bowls and wooden cups abound by every door,
golden goblets and jade vessels are rare in ten thousand homes.
Also from Bào Pú Zǐ.
In the flow of great rivers,
rotten corpses float and pile up,
yet people drink from them—
because their volume is vast.
Water in a basin or bowl,
if a mouse dips its tail,
must be vomited and discarded—
because its volume is small.
Liǔ Zǐ.
When Zǐyóu governed Wǔchéng,
Zhòngní sighed about "killing a chicken with a ox-cutter;"
when Yīn Hé was to be a town magistrate,
Zǐchǎn advised against "assigning silk-cutting to a novice."
Ibid.
Shī Kuàng said to Duke Píng of Jìn,
"Those who learn in youth
are like the light of the rising sun;
those who learn in prime
are like the light of the midday sun;
those who learn in old age
are like walking at night with a torch."
Fàn Zǐ, Jì Rán.
History
Zǐpí said: "The nobleman strives to understand the great and the distant,
while the petty man strives to understand the small and the near."
． From *Zuozhuan*, 31st Year of Duke Xiāng.
Zǐpí drilled troops at Kuí,
completing the task by morning's end,
without executing a single person.
Zǐyù again drilled troops at Wěi,
finishing only by day's end,
flogging seven men,
and piercing the ears of three.
． From *Zuozhuan*, 27th Year of Duke Xī.
The foolish are blind to accomplished matters,
while the wise perceive what has not yet taken form.
． From *Records of the Grand Historian*, House of Zhào.
Thus, when deceit meets deceit,
there is still room for skill or clumsiness.
When deceit confronts integrity,
it is like using an awl to topple Mount Tàiháng.
． From *Comprehensive Mirror*, Chapter 6.
When Zǐchǎn governed Zhèng,
the people could not deceive him;
when Zǐjiàn governed Shànfù,
the people could not bear to deceive him;
when Xīmén Bào governed Yè,
the people dared not deceive him.
． From *Records of the Grand Historian*, Biographies of Jesters.
Cross-reference "Different Paths, Same Destination."
Thus, when Jié deceives Jié,
there is still luck in being skillful or clumsy.
When Jié deceives Yáo,
it is like throwing an egg at a stone,
or stirring boiling water with a finger.
As if plunging into water or fire,
one is scorched and submerged.
From *Comprehensive Mirror*.
When laborers use blunt tools,
they strain their sinews and weary their bones,
toiling all day long.
But when a skilled smith casts the raw material of Gānjiàng,
quenches its edge in clear water,
and sharpens it on Yuè's whetstone,
it cuts through dragons in water,
and slices rhinoceros hide on land.
． From *Book of Hàn*, Biography of Wáng Bāo.
Those clad in felt and fur
are hard to converse with about the fine texture of pure silk;
those who eat wild herbs and dry provisions
are unfit to discuss the flavors of the grand sacrifice.
Same as above.
Petty wisdom is self-serving,
despising others and esteeming oneself;
the enlightened, with broad vision,
find nothing unacceptable.
From *Book of Hàn*, Biography of Jiǎ Yì.
Measuring lengths and comparing sizes,
weighing authority and strength,
they cannot be spoken of in the same breath.
From *Book of Hàn*, Biography of Xiàng Jí.
The blind cannot see what is right before them,
while Lí Lóu illuminates corners a thousand miles away.
From *Book of Hàn*, Biography of Yáng Xióng.
Though men may be lowly, each acts as the yang of his household;
though women may be noble, each acts as the yin of her state.
From *Book of Hàn*, Biography of Dù Yè,
also in *Book of Hàn*.
The supremely wise do not dwell in danger to seek luck,
the moderately wise can turn danger into achievement,
and the utterly foolish remain complacent in danger until they perish.
． From *Book of Later Hàn*, Biography of Wú Hàn.
The wise plan according to the times,
while the foolish act against reason.
From *Book of Later Hàn*, Biography of Zhū Fú.
The wise follow circumstances to cultivate virtue,
while the foolish oppose them and bring harm upon themselves.
From *Book of Later Hàn*, Biography of Zhì Yùn.
Those who climb heights without fear
are condemned men;
those who do not sit under eaves
are sons of wealthy families.
From *Book of Later Hàn*, Biography of Mǎ Róng.
Cross-reference "Their Environment Makes Them So" section.

Guǎn Níng and Huà Xīn were hoeing vegetables together when they saw gold on the ground. Níng hoed on without a glance, treating it no differently from tiles and stones, while Xīn picked it up and threw it away. People thus knew their superiority and inferiority.
． From *Comprehensive Mirror*, Eastern Hàn.
Fèi Yī, as Imperial Secretary, often attended to affairs from morning till evening,
during which he received guests,
ate, drank, and amused himself,
even adding board games,
yet always fulfilled everyone's joy.
When Dǒng Yǔn replaced Yī,
within ten days,
many matters came to a standstill.
From *Records of the Three Kingdoms*, Shǔ.
Huán Wēn came to court.
Some said he intended to kill Wáng and Xiè.
Xiè Ān's expression remained unchanged,
while Tǎnzhī sweated so profusely it soaked his clothes,
and he held his tablet upside down.
． From *Comprehensive Mirror*, Jìn Annals.
Someone said to Huà Tán: "The proverb says the difference between people
is like that between nine oxen and a hair—
can this be true?"
Tán replied: "In the past, Xǔ Yóu and Cháofù declined the honor of being Son of Heaven,
while market scoundrels fight over half a coin's profit.
The difference between them
is far greater than that between nine oxen and a hair!"
． From *Book of Jìn*, Biography of Huà Tán.
The Wèi emperor held Rènchéng King Xié's hand and said: "The two Cáos envied each other for talent and fame,
but you and I are close through virtue and morality."
． From *Comprehensive Mirror*, Qí Míng Annals, Part 2.
Gù Yuèzhī was the same age as Emperor Jiǎnwén,
yet his hair turned white early.
The emperor asked the reason,
and he replied: "The nature of pine and cypress
remains lush even after frost;
the common substance of willow
withers at the approach of autumn."
． From *Book of Jìn*, His Biography.
Cross-reference "Quick in Response" section.
Yán Jùn and Xiè Zhuāng served as Ministers of Personnel.
People of the time said: "Yán Jùn scowls and gives office;
Xiè Zhuāng smiles and does not."
From *Book of Sòng*.
Qí Shénwǔ ordered his sons to each untangle a mess of silk threads,
but the emperor alone drew a knife and cut it,
saying: "The tangled must be severed."
． From *History of the Northern Dynasties*, Annals of Wén Xuān.
Pine and cypress grow alone, robust and upright,
with nothing to rely on; dodder, weak and unable to stand, must cling to other trees.
． From *Book of Táng*, Biography of Lǐ Déyù.
The upright are like pine and cypress,
standing independently without support;
the wicked are like vines,
unable to rise
without attaching to other things.
． From *Comprehensive Mirror*, Táng Wénzōng.
Lǐ Shèng sought a marriage alliance for his son with Yán Shǎng,
but was refused.
Shèng said to others: "We military men are straightforward;
over a cup of wine, grudges are forgotten
and no longer stored in the heart.
Not like scholars, who are hard to offend;
outwardly they may reconcile,
but inwardly they harbor resentment as before.
How can I not fear?"
． From *Comprehensive Mirror*, Táng Dézōng.
Mud walls and bamboo horses
are the joy of children;
adorned with gold, jade, and silk
is the joy of women;
trading to have what one lacks
is the joy of merchants;
high office and generous salary
are the joy of officials;
facing no match in battle
is the joy of generals;
peace and unity across the land
is the joy of emperors.
． From *Book of Táng*, Chronicles of the Western Regions, Yānqí.
From historical records.
The noble man attains his time like water,
the petty man attains his time like fire.
． From "Shuō Yuàn Tán Cóng" chapter.
Guō Línzōng said: "Fèng Gāo's capacity,
may be compared to a side-flowing spring,
clear yet easily scooped.
Shū Dù is vast like a thousand-qǐng lake,
unclear when settled,
unmuddied when stirred,
impossible to measure."
From "Shì Shuō".
． ○From "Hòu Hàn Huáng Xiàn Zhuàn".
Guǐ,
pronounced as jiǔ,
refers to a spring flowing from the side.
Làn,
pronounced hù zhǎn fǎn,
refers to a spring flowing directly upward.
"Máo Shī" mentions lined guǐ springs,
and also bì fèi làn springs,
with the same meaning.
Nowadays people often mistakenly write it as fàn làn,
which is incorrect.
This passage should only be recorded in "Hàn Shū".
Xiàhóu Tàichū once leaned against a pillar writing,
when heavy rain came,
a thunderbolt shattered the pillar he leaned against,
his clothes were scorched,
yet his expression remained unchanged,
and his writing continued as before.
The guests and attendants all stumbled and could not stand firm.
From "Shì Shuō".
Yáng Xiū served as Chief Clerk to Chancellor Cáo Cāo.
When they reached Jiāngnán,
reading eight characters on Cáo É's stele,
Cāo asked Xiū,
Xiū said: "I know them."
Cāo said: "Let me think about it."
After traveling thirty lǐ,
he finally figured it out.
He ordered Xiū to explain,
Xiū said: "Yellow silk means 'absolute' (jué);
colorful thread forms the character jué.
Young woman means 'wonderful' (miào);
a young woman forms the character miào.
Granddaughter means 'good' (hǎo);
a daughter's child forms the character hǎo.
Mortar for pungents means 'words of resignation' (cí);
receiving pungent flavors forms the character cí."
Cāo said: "Exactly as I thought."
Common saying: Whether one has wisdom or not,
is tested over thirty lǐ.
From Péi Qǐ's "Yǔ Lín".
Confucius said: "Benevolence and righteousness move the ruler,
wealth and beauty move petty men."
From "Yuè Dòng Shēng Yí".
In Lǔ, there was a man living alone in his house,
and a widow neighbor also living alone in her house.
One night, a violent storm came and destroyed her house,
the woman rushed to seek shelter with him,
but the man closed his door and did not let her in,
saying:
"I have heard that men under sixty do not live in seclusion.
Now you are young,
and I am also young,
I cannot take you in."
The woman said: "Why can't you be like Liǔxià Huì,
who sheltered a woman not reaching the gate,
and none in the state spoke of impropriety."
The man said: "Liǔxià Huì could do it,
but I certainly cannot."
From "Máo Gōng Shī Zhuàn".
Collection
How can a salamander in a foot-wide pond
measure the vastness of rivers and seas with the giant kūn fish?
How can a quail within a hedge
fathom the height of heaven and earth with the phoenix?
From "Chǔcí".
Also see "The small cannot comprehend the great".
The marshland compared to the handsome Zǐdū,
the anthill mound compared to the Fānglú mountain.
From Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Wèi Fù".
The fading light of the mulberry and elm trees at dusk,
surpasses the first glow of the evening star Chánggēng.
Same as above.
The tiny jiāomíng builds its nest on a mosquito's eyelash,
while the great péng bird fills the corners of the sky.
From Zhāng Huà's "Jiāoliáo Fù".
Once soaring to the blue heavens,
it never sings again for generations.
How could it content itself with quails and sparrows,
fluttering playfully in the courtyard?
From a poem by Ruǎn Bùbīng of Jìn.
A team of worn-out nags
cannot gallop a thousand-mile journey;
flocks of swallows and sparrows
cannot employ their six-winged might.
From Bān Shūpí's "Essay".
The lone pine thrives in late years,
while common trees love the fragrant spring.
By Chén Zǐ'áng.
Also see "Each thing has its proper place".
Nest-masters Xǔ Yóu and Cháo Fǔ disdained the entire realm,
yet merchants haggle over a single coin.
From Cáo Zhí's "Yuèfǔ Song".
Countless stars adorn the blue sky,
but only the moon shines brightly.
By Lǐ Tàibái.
Also see "Things appear by contrast".
Sparrows chirp at dawn seeking food,
turtledoves coo at dusk flocking together.
Only the season-knowing crane,
though it cries, does not do so for itself.
From Hán Wén.
Those lacking inwardly are anxious to be known by others.
Abundant and overflowing,
their fame spreads in all directions.
Nowadays, people traveling a few hundred miles,
leave home bewildered,
wearing expressions of pitiable parting sorrow,
carrying bedding to duty at the Three Departments,
endlessly instructing and looking back at their maids,
chattering without cease.
Yet you, sent ten thousand miles to foreign lands,
show not the slightest hint in word or expression—
is this not the true mark of a man who knows what truly matters?
An unskilled cutter,
bleeds his fingers and sweats with shame;
while the master craftsman watches aside,
hands tucked in sleeves.
One who does not understand words,
should not be spoken with;
one who understands words remains silent,
yet their meaning is conveyed.
The strong are sure to show anger in words,
the timid are sure to show it in their faces.
All from Hán Wén.
Not anxiously striving for advancement,
nor exulting in gain or lamenting loss.
With zither on the left and wine壶 on the right,
joyful all day long—compared to those who,
fearful and trembling, constrained by deceit and betrayal,
their honor not covering their shame throughout life,
and unable to stop—are they not alone at ease?
From Liǔ Wén.
The noble man is suited for high position,
not for lowly station;
the petty man is suited for lowly station,
not for high position.
From Liǔ Wén's "On Slander and Praise".
The enlightened man is straight as a bowstring,
the petty man crooked like a hook.
By Dù Gōngbù.
The wise man ponders a thousand times daily,
the fool has but four worries.
By Mèng Dōngyě.
The noble man is steadfast as mountains,
the petty man quarrels over trifles.
Clumsy hooves look back bruised and worn,
soaring wings leave behind grain and provisions.
The noble man has the nature of fragrant osmanthus,
flourishing in spring, even more abundant in winter.
The petty man has the heart of a hibiscus flower,
present at dawn, gone by evening.
All by Mèng Dōngyě.
Grasses of all lengths sprout,
birds of all pitches sing.
By Yuán Wēizhī.
The sage purifies his mind and silences slander,
thus able to illuminate the principles of the world;
therefore his mind is clear and settles the foolish.
The fool burdens his mind and neglects the external,
thus obscuring the principles of the world;
therefore his mind is dusty and entangled.
By Huángfǔ Shí.
Xiàng Jí accepted the surrender of two hundred thousand Qín soldiers,
but fearing their treachery,
had them all buried alive in one move—
his precautions were excessive indeed.
Hàn Gāo, open-minded and magnanimous,
welcomed all scholars under heaven who came to him,
employing them without suspicion—
his preparedness could be called lax.
Yet Xiàng fell,
while Liú prospered.
Hoarding suspicion versus extending trust—
their outcomes certainly differ.
By Lù Zhì.
Appearances vary by group,
distinctions abound in countless ways.
By Huángfǔ Shí.
Striving to amass and thicken the stores in one's coffers—
that is the wealth of a common man;
striving to distribute and win the hearts of the masses—
that is the wealth of a sovereign.
From Lord Lù Xuān's writings.
Butchering sheep in the market—
to suit the taste of the multitude;
carving jade in the mountains—
awaits the recognition of a discerning eye.
Greedy for daily gain, one wields the knife;
profiting from yearly plans, one stores treasures in boxes.
By Liú Bīnkè.
Língzhī mushrooms, shàpú plants, and all fruits sprout together,
yet the radiant and outstanding stand out from their kind.
Same as above.
That resembles the heart of a noble man,
upright and steadfast through ice and frost.
This resembles the face of a petty man,
changing with warmth and cold.
By Bái Lètiān.
The chūn tree lives eight thousand springs,
the hibiscus flower does not last a night.
Sunflowers wither yet still face the sun,
weeds break and bid spring farewell.
Pointing to the dust below,
the mayfly's life is truly pitiable.
Have you not heard of the Gūshè mountain,
where millennial ice and snow grace the skin?
Some end as mincemeat on the chopping board,
others fly like luán phoenixes beyond the heavens.
All from "The Collected Works of Bái Lètiān".
The eagle, hungry, often pecks at foul meat,
the phoenix, hungry, still awaits jade nectar.
From Zhāng Yuè's writings.
Yán Huí, with his single bamboo bowl and gourd, barely sustained himself;
rich flavors never reached his lips,
and he did not reach thirty years of age.
Zhāng Cāng, indulgent in love,
boundless in his excesses;
concubines filled his inner chambers,
yet he lived over a hundred years.
Same as above.
Also see the section "Matters Hard to Question".
The péng bird carries the sky on its back, the turtle drags its tail—
clouds and mud cannot roam together.
All from Zhāng Yuè's writings.
How can the cicada expect to see frost and snow?
The wise and profound are hard for vulgar minds to understand.
From Dù Mù's writings.
The noble man prefers small hardships for great attainment,
the petty man prefers small gains for great ruin.
By Chéng Yàn.
The tranquil often find ease at night,
the wealthy seldom show worry.
By Yáo Shàojiān.
The swift-footed aim for a thousand miles,
the stranded fish thirst for a single pool.
By Zhāng Chéngjí.
The wise man is troubled by ten concerns,
the enlightened man lightens a hundred worries.
From Xǔ Yònghuì's writings.
For the most foolish to face the most sage,
the extremely lowly to face the supremely尊—
merely hoping to strengthen oneself
is unattainable.
From "Táng Wén Cuì".
Small things lack great ambitions.
Same as above.
Orchids and huì grass, though cherished,
their fragrance fades with the season.
How unlike leaves that brave the frost,
still lush in color at year's end.
By Wéi Yìngwù.
The way of the sage is like a broad road,
the ways of the various schools are like crooked paths.
By Pí Rìxiū.
Our dynasty
Yán Lìběn initially advanced through literary talent,
yet ultimately suffered the disgrace of being treated as a mere painter.
I disagree with this assessment.
When Xiè Ānshí wanted Wáng Zǐjìng to inscribe the plaque for the Tàijí Hall,
he alluded to the story of Wéi Zhòngjiāng to persuade him.
Zǐjìng replied: "Zhòngjiāng
was a high minister of Wèi,
and in principle should not have done such things.
If this were the case,
it shows why the virtue of Wèi did not last long."
Had Lìběn possessed Zǐjìng's nobility of character,
who would have dared treat him as a painter?
Ruǎn Qiānlǐ was skilled at playing the qín,
and would play for anyone regardless of status or age.
His spirit was serene and harmonious,
unaware of who was listening.
When his brother-in-law Pān Yuè asked him to play,
he played from day to night without showing displeasure.
Those who understood knew he could not be affected by honor or disgrace.
Had Lìběn possessed Qiānlǐ's enlightenment,
who could have disgraced him as a painter?
From Sū Shì's "Postface to Zhū Xiàngxiān's Painting".
The guests of Zhái Gōng
abandoned him between life and death, honor and disgrace,
while his retainers
betrayed him in the blink of an eye.
Zhai blamed his guests,
while this lord blamed himself,
treating his retainers more generously -
far more virtuous than the ancients.
From Sū Shì's "Preface to Monk Qín's Poetry Collection".
The "lord"
refers to Ōuyáng Xiū.
In ancient times, the Master was incorruptible yet did not act differently from the crowd,
courageous yet without excessive discipline,
filial without being subservient to his parents,
loyal without offending his ruler.
All these
represent the Master's completeness.
Yuán Xiàn's incorruptibility led to poverty,
Gōngliáng Rú's courage to fighting,
Zēngzǐ's filial piety to subservience to his parents,
Zǐlù's loyalty to offending his ruler.
All these
represent these disciples' one-sidedness.
From "Letter to Grand Marshal Hán".
In the past, Táng Tàizōng, amid military affairs,
could still summon Lǐ Jìng from retirement in old age,
while Mùzōng and Wénzōng, in times of peace and comfort,
could not employ Péi Dù before he fell ill.
The effects on order and chaos
are thus evident.
From "Imperial Response to Wén Yànbó's Request to Retire, Denied".
Petty men see position as favor,
seeking it yet unable to obtain it;
noble men see favor as worry,
declining it yet unable to refuse.
From "Edict Denying Shàngshū Right Chancellor Hú Zōngyǔn's Resignation".
Noble men are as hard to know as the qílín and phoenix -
they rise at the first sign,
circling before alighting;
how could one wave them away?
Petty men advance as easily as maggots and flies -
wherever foulness gathers,
thousands appear instantly;
how could one need to summon them?
From "Memorial on Zhōu Chóng's Unauthorized Discussion of Sacrificial Companions",
also by Sū Shì.
The wealthy delight in splendid colors,
embroidery shimmering around seats.
The poor ashamed of their plainness,
bring out mortars and mills.
Sū Shì.
You are like the great river flowing a thousand miles daily,
I like this water beneath countless mountains.
The enlightened man's thousand-jūn crossbow,
once relaxed, is hard to draw again.
The inferior man's monkey cap,
though tied, still jumps and prances.
Thus we know the difference between wise and foolish,
is not merely like nine oxen's hairs.
The enlightened man befriends all within the four seas,
the narrow-minded man guards one village.
The phoenix sees virtue's glow,
soars far without waiting for the swallow's dispatch.
The swallow
clings to house and courtyard,
darting through thousands of turns.
Like street performers painting faces red and blue,
seductive songs and wild dances dazzle children.
But Lady Xiè's plain countenance,
serene, possesses the woodland breeze.
Also Sū Shì's poems.
When ancient noble men found no employment in the world,
they would寄托于things to divert themselves.
Ruǎn Jí used wine,
Jī Kāng used the qín.
Had Ruǎn no wine,
or Jī no qín,
then even eating plants and befriending deer,
they would have felt unsettled.
Only Yán Huí, drinking water and eating beans in his narrow lane,
needed no external假借yet remained joyful -
this is why Confucius sighed that he was unsurpassable.
From "Collection of Lúanchéng".
All others served their lord with strength,
only this lord upheld the Way in office.
Those relying on strength leave when it declines;
those upholding the Way are hard to retain when it soars.
Ibid.
How joyful the autumn swan,
riding wind through empty skies!
How sorrowful the autumn insect,
grieving all night by the wall!
Autumn wind watches willow and reed stumble,
year's end finds only pine and cypress firm.
Torrential Hé and Wèi run muddy,
sparkling Jiāng and Hàn flow clear.
Also ibid.
Great and small exhaust roc and quail,
long and short show in tree and hibiscus.
Huáng Tíngjiān's poem.
My poetry is like Cáo and Kuài,
shallow, failing to form a state.
Yours is like great Chǔ,
swallowing five lakes and three rivers.
Ibid.
Cross-reference "Clear Self-awareness".
The Tài'ē sword, though lacking a tip, remains unbroken;
the leaden blade cannot serve all purposes.
Chén Shīdào's poem.
My wall reaches only shoulders, easily seen over;
your talent looms like a great metropolis.
Ibid.
In chess, skill differs little -
but strong players recognize the first move,
the subsequent plays;
whereas weak players
take later moves for first moves.
When Qíng Bù, in desperation, came to surrender,
Gāozǔ washed his feet, not rising, to break his spirit.
Bù nearly killed himself,
but seeing the attendants serving Hàn's king like his own,
then rejoiced beyond expectation -
this is recognizing the first move.
When Hóu Jǐng, in desperation, came to Liáng Wǔdì,
he hastily granted him land and title.
Later, whenever Jǐng demanded anything, he harshly refused.
Thus Jǐng rebelled and Liáng fell -
this is taking later moves for first moves.
From "Collection of Mingdào".
Cross-reference "Improper Handling".
People have measures like pecks and pints,
some like bells and tripods,
some like rivers,
some like heaven and earth.
The peck-and-pint measure is negligible;
bell-tripod and river measures are vast indeed,
yet they overflow when full.
Only heaven-earth's measure cannot be diminished or increased -
who but sages can embody it?
Generally, those who seek fame
lack inner fulfillment;
the fulfilled
naturally care not for fame.
Ice and crystal are not without light,
but compared to jade,
they lack its warm, moist,含蓄quality -
not so glaring.
Like water stored at a ten-thousand-rèn source:
once released,
it rushes and gushes
straight to the sea -
its source is deep.
But puddle water
flows then dries abruptly,
never reaching far -
its source is shallow.
Also from "Collection of Mingdào".
Hán Qí only sought to tolerate petty men,
not sharply dividing good and evil, black and white, so they resented him less;
while Fàn Zhòngyān, Fù Bì, Ōuyáng Xiū, Yīn Sū always distinguished noble from petty,
so petty men's envy grew daily.
From "Surviving Sayings".
Hán Qí said: "Lǚ Yĭjiān took recommending worthies as his duty, claiming gratitude for himself,
so scholars of the time were under his control;
only Ōuyáng, Fàn, and Yīn repeatedly gathered and lost them,
never falling under his control."
The Way of sages
is like heaven and earth:
between them,
nothing is lacking.
The way of common people
is like mountains and rivers,
hills and valleys,
birds and beasts,
plants and trees,
insects and sand -
each fulfills its role,
unaware of what lies beyond.
Heaven and earth encompass all things without exception,
and extend universally to everything.
Also from "Yí Shū".
Sīmǎ Wēngōng said:
"At the juncture of merit and fame,
it is difficult for ministers to position themselves appropriately.
As Emperor Gāo once acknowledged,
there were only three outstanding heroes.
Huáiyīn was executed,
Xiāo Hé was shackled and imprisoned—
was it not because they trod the path of prosperity to its peak without knowing when to stop?
Hence, Zǐfáng sought refuge in the realm of immortals,
abandoning the human world,
treating merit and fame as external matters,
and disregarding glory and profit.
He can truly be called a man of wisdom who preserves himself,
and Zǐfáng exemplified this.
Some presented over ten portraits and official appointments of Dí Liánggōng,
to Dí Qīng,
claiming they were his distant ancestors.
Dí Qīng declined,
and sent them back.
Compared to Guō Chóngtāo weeping at Guō Zǐyí's tomb,
Dí Qīng's conduct was far superior.
From "Bǐ Tán".
Figures like Hàn's Jí Àn, Xiāo Wàngzhī, Lǐ Gù,
Wú's Zhāng Zhāo,
Táng's Wèi Zhènggōng, Dí Rénjié,
all sacrificed themselves for righteousness,
unswayed by summons,
undaunted by dismissal.
Standing solemnly in court,
they made wolves, jackals, and foxes
turn against each other,
thus able to avert disasters before they formed,
and rescue crises before collapse.
If all were like Chancellor Gōngsūn, Zhāng Yǔ, Hú Guǎng,
even by the hundreds or thousands,
how could they be relied upon in emergencies?
From "Wáng Yuánzhī Huàxiàng Zàn".
"Xīn Xù".
The green pine, steadfast in integrity, faces peril unyieldingly,
its stern dignity impervious to violation.
Plantains and lotus are unworthy of note,
cluttering and sullying only the pond and rails.
From "Ōuyáng Wénjí".
Newly risen scholars delight in boldness and sharpness,
while the experienced often act with caution.
Same as above.
To exhaust all things under heaven
and attain every desire
is the joy of the wealthy and noble.
From "Fú Chá Shān Shuǐ Jì".
Others, when polished,
vie to reveal their edges,
but you alone remain unadorned, your simplicity unseen.
From "Jì Hú Tàibó Wén".
All things have their roles,
only the aimless drift like dust.
Noble and base alike become one mound of earth,
yet sages and worthies shine like stars and sun.
From "Ōuyáng Wénjí".
Few men live to a hundred, rare since ancient times,
but a pine reaching a thousand years is not yet old.
From "Línchuān Jí".
Pine sprouts on the ground vary in height,
ducks and cranes by nature differ in length.
With short wings, flying low,
content with mere grains;
while the hidden dragon leaps on its own,
yearning to gleam afar amid wind and clouds.
Also from the same.
Zǐ
Zhōu Wén favored unpalatable pickles,
not exchanging them for the flavors of grand sacrifices;
Wèi Míng enjoyed the sound of chiseling,
not trading it for the harmony of strings and pipes.
From "Bàopǔzǐ Biàn Wèn" chapter.
Collection
Each person has their own preferences.
The fragrance of orchids and angelicas
is loved by many,
yet by the sea, there are those who chase after stench;
the music of "Xián Chí" and "Liù Jīng",
joyful to most,
yet Mò Dí criticized it.
From Cáo Zǐjiàn's letter.
In joy, one laments the short night,
in sorrow, complains of the long evening.
From "Xuǎn Qíng Shī".
Cross-reference "The mind changes with circumstances".
Most hearts love gold and jade,
most mouths crave wine and meat.
Why then does the old man by this stream,
find contentment with just a gourd to drink?
Bái Lètiān.
Once, the King of Qí loved the yu,
and a man seeking office in Qí
went there playing the sè.
For three years, he couldn't gain entry,
and exclaimed, "My sè playing can move ghosts and gods!"
A bystander scolded him: "The king loves the yu, yet you play the sè;
however skilled you are,
what can you do if the king doesn't favor it?"
From Hán Wén's "Dá Chén Shāng Shū".
Classic
Those close yet not in harmony
have aspirations that differ.
From "Yì Lüè Lì".
Cultivating virtue,
the heart is at ease and days are blessed;
engaging in deceit,
the heart labors and days worsen.
From "Shū Zhōu Guān".
The good person does good,
as if each day is insufficient;
the wicked person does evil,
also as if each day is insufficient.
From "Tài Shì Zhōng".
The noble person dwells in ease awaiting destiny,
the petty person takes risks seeking luck.
From "Jì Zhōng Yōng".
The noble person follows the mean,
the petty person opposes the mean.
Same as above.
Teaching with gentleness and patience,
not retaliating against wrongdoing,
is the strength of the south.
Sleeping with arms and armor,
dying without regret,
is the strength of the north.
Also from "Zhōng Yōng".
The benevolent use wealth to cultivate themselves,
the unbenevolent use themselves to amass wealth.
From "Dà Xué".
Virtue perfected is superior,
skill perfected is inferior.
From "Yuè Jì",
The Master said: "The noble person understands righteousness,
the petty person understands profit."
From "Yǔ Lǐ Rén".
The Master said: "The noble person cherishes virtue,
the petty person cherishes land;
the noble person cherishes laws,
the petty person cherishes favors."
Same as above.
Ancient learners studied for self-improvement,
modern learners study for others' approval.
From "Xiàn Wèn".
Those whose paths differ
do not consult each other.
From "Wèi Línggōng", also in the Analects.
Zǐ
Bóyí died for fame at the foot of Shǒuyáng Mountain,
while Dào Zhí died for profit atop Dōnglíng.
Zhuāngzǐ.
The arrow-maker fears only that his arrows might not harm people,
while the armor-maker fears that they might.
So it is with the shaman and the coffin-maker.
Mèngzǐ.
To be rich is to be without benevolence,
to be benevolent is to be without wealth.
Mèngzǐ: Téng Wéngōng I.
He who rises at cockcrow
and diligently does good
is a follower of Shùn;
he who rises at cockcrow
and diligently seeks profit
is a follower of Zhí.
Jìn Xīn Shàng,
also from Mèngzǐ.
The multitude values profit,
the incorruptible value fame,
the worthy esteem purpose.
Zhuāngzǐ: Kèyì Chapter.
To be like Yáo or Shùn is to be ever secure and honored,
to be like Jié or Zhí is to be ever endangered and disgraced.
Xúnzǐ: Róngrǔ Chapter.
He who puts righteousness before profit is honored,
he who puts profit before righteousness is disgraced;
the honored are ever successful,
the disgraced ever thwarted;
the successful often control others,
the thwarted are often controlled by others.
The talented and sincere are ever safe and benefited,
the reckless and fierce are ever endangered and harmed;
the safe and benefited are often happy and at ease,
the endangered and harmed are often anxious and perilous;
the happy and at ease often live long,
the anxious and perilous often die young.
The noble man speaks of what is constant,
the petty man speaks of what is strange.
Also from the same.
The earthworm has no sharp claws or teeth,
no strong muscles or bones,
yet it eats the dust above
and drinks from the yellow springs below,
because it concentrates its mind;
the crab has six legs and two pincers,
yet without the burrows of snakes or eels it has no refuge,
because it is restless in mind.
Quàn Xué Chapter.
Cross-reference "Wisdom not equal to folly."
Sincerity and spirit produce trust,
boasting and extravagance produce confusion.
Bù Gǒu Chapter.
The noble man admires what lies within himself,
and does not admire what lies with Heaven;
the petty man neglects what lies within himself,
and admires what lies with Heaven.
Tiāndào Chapter,
also from Xúnzǐ.
Maidens long in spring,
scholars grieve in autumn.
Huáinánzǐ.
Fishermen head for the deeps,
woodcutters head for the hills.
Now, from Jīzǐ's perspective, Bǐgān seems foolish;
from Bǐgān's perspective, Jīzǐ seems base;
from Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Yīng's perspective, Bóyí seems stupid;
from Bóyí's perspective, Guǎn and Yàn seem greedy.
Choices and rejections differ,
desires and aversions oppose,
yet each delights in his own pursuits—
whom shall we have to judge them?
Qí Sù Xùn,
also from Huáinánzǐ.
The incorruptible are always happy with no desires,
the greedy are always anxious with never enough.
Wénzhōngzǐ.
What delights children
is what the elderly disapprove of;
what entertains the ears and eyes
is what troubles the mind and thoughts.
Wàncāngzǐ.
When common folk converse,
they speak of wealth and profit;
when gentlemen converse,
they speak of benevolence and righteousness.
Yángzǐ.
In the history,
Zǐ Hǎn said: "I regard non-greed as my treasure,
you regard jade as your treasure."
Zuǒ Zhuàn: Xiānggōng 15th Year.
Those who contend for fame do so at court,
those who contend for profit do so in the marketplace.
Zhànguó Cè.
Shūsūn Tōng summoned over thirty scholars from Lǔ.
Two scholars from Lǔ refused to go.
Qián Hànshū: Shūsūn Tōng Biography.
Chén Zūn often said to Zhǎng Sǒng: "You recite the classics,
torment yourself with restraints,
daring not to slip,
while I indulge my whims,
drift amid the vulgar world,
yet my official rank and achievements
are no less than yours,
and I am somewhat happier alone—
isn't that better!"
Sǒng replied: "Each person has his own nature,
and decides his own strengths and weaknesses.
You couldn't be like me if you tried,
and if I imitated you, I'd fail.
Even so,
imitating me is easy to maintain,
imitating you is hard to manage—
such is my constant way."
Qián Hànshū: His Biography.
Scholars of the mountains and forests
go and cannot return;
scholars of the court
enter and cannot leave.
Qián Hànshū: Wáng Jí Eulogy.
Eagerly seeking wealth and profit,
always fearing scarcity and want—
this is the mind of the common people;
eagerly seeking benevolence and righteousness,
always fearing inability to transform the people—
this is the mind of the great officers.
Zīzhì Tōngjiàn: Hàn Wǔdì Annals.
Kǒng Fèn was the commandery aide of Wǔdū,
and followed Dòu Róng to the court.
The various governors and magistrates had goods and wealth filling carts and covering the rivers and marshes, only Fèn had no assets and went on his way in a single carriage.
Zīzhì Tōngjiàn: Hàn Guāngwǔdì Annals.
Those who seek to expand territory end in desolation,
those who seek to expand virtue end in strength;
those who are content with what they have find peace,
those who covet what others have bring ruin.
Same as above.
Wéi Biāo said: "Loyal and filial people

集
The world's affairs first yield to humility,
Merchants compete for the tiniest profits.
"Collection of Chén Zǐ'áng".
The honest detest the greedy,
The trustworthy abhor the false,
The wise do not scheme for fools,
The brave do not die for the cowardly,
Such are the contrasts in inclinations.
Same as above.
Eagles seize the moment to soar away,
Steeds turn their heads and whinny for their masters.
Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Emptiness and purity bring tranquility to noble minds,
Noise and vulgarity bind the worldly.
Same as above.
In youth, one delights in new acquaintances,
In old age, one longs for old friends.
Hán Yù's prose.
Cross-reference to "the situation makes it so".
If one follows the river downstream without stopping,
Though speed may vary, one will surely reach the sea;
But if one loses the right path,
Even if swift, without halting,
One will never fortunately arrive.
Same as above.
Living in seclusion in the wilderness,
Ascending heights to gaze afar.
Sitting all day beneath lush trees,
Cleansing oneself in clear springs.
Gathering from the mountains, delicacies to eat,
Fishing in the waters, fresh catches to savor.
Rising and resting without fixed times,
Only seeking comfort and ease.
Waiting at the doors of nobles and officials,
Rushing along the paths of power and influence.
Feet hesitating to step forward,
Mouth stammering when about to speak.
Remaining in filth without shame,
Violating laws and facing execution.
Hoping for a one-in-ten-thousand chance,
Continuing until old age and death,
In terms of character,
How do such people compare in worthiness or unworthiness?
．"Sòng Lǐ Yuàn《Xīn Xù》",
You emerge as clouds from the mountains,
I become a crane entering a cage.
Bái Lètiān.
Cháo Fǔ and Xǔ Yóu remained recluses all their lives,
Xiāo Hé and Cáo Shēn were busy until old age.
Whales devour and sharks battle, churning waves to blood,
While fish in deep streams joyfully remain unaware.
Beasts find joy in mountains and valleys,
Fish find joy in ponds and pools.
Insects find joy in deep grass,
Birds find joy in high branches.
All same as above.
Cross-reference to "finding proper reliance".
When flowers bloom, butterflies fill the branches,
When flowers fade, butterflies fly away.
Only the old nest's swallows,
Return even when the master is poor.
Táng Dynasty Yú Wǔ's poem.
Gōngsūn Hóng served as chancellor,
Opening the eastern pavilion to welcome the worthy.
By the time of Gōngsūn Hè and Liú Qūmáo,
It had deteriorated into a stable.
"Bái Tiē".
Under a foul tree, all others rest,
By the greedy spring, only I stay sober.
Wēn Fēiqīng.
Boasters die for power,
Martyrs sacrifice for fame, the greedy,
Drown in wealth.
Same as above.
Just like boats and carriages,
Each rushes on different paths.
Yáo Shǎojiān.
They hesitate at the gates of ministers and scholars,
While I wander freely in the realm of sages and worthies;
They ride in carriages through markets of fame and profit,
While I tread with sandals in gardens of literature and history.
Huángfǔ Shí.
You ascend on azure clouds away,
I gaze toward green mountains, returning.
Mèng Hàorán.
Cross-reference to "self-lament".
Steeds yearn to head north,
Partridges wish to fly south.
Mèng Dōngyě.
The wise value strategy,
Which fools do not heed;
The brave sacrifice their lives,
Which the timid do not follow.
Lù Zhì "Memorials".
Cloud-dragons and well-frogs,
Are fated not to meet.
Liú Bīnkè.
The greedy man spins like an ant on a millstone,
The cold official climbs like a fish up a pole.
"Lěng Zhāi Yè Huà".
The petty man's love for his ruler,
Seeks momentary pleasure,
Unlike the loyal minister's love for his ruler,
Who finds joy in securing the state.
"Luánchéng Jí".
Hearing hairpin sounds from next door,
And feeling desire stir,
How can it not be called breaking precepts?
Amidst heaps of gold and silver,
And crowds of nobles in crimson and purple,
If the heart remains unmoved,
How can it be called breaking precepts?
Lord Xú, like the lush pine at the ravine's depth,
Lord Chén, like the lofty pillar in the hall.
The deep ravine protects the pine from being felled,
The hall collapses, the pillar breaks, crushing its form.
Their paths and stations differ irreconcilably,
Like the sun and moon coursing east and west.
All same as above.
史
Jì Wénzǐ's concubines did not wear silk,
The people of Lǔ praised this as virtuous.
Gōngsūn Hóng wore cloth garments,
Yet Jí Àn mocked him for deceit.
The facts are similar,
But praise and blame differ.
．"Dōng Hàn Wáng Liáng Zhuàn".
Péi Mín guarded Běipíng,
Where tigers were abundant,
Mín was a skilled archer,
Once killing thirty-one tigers in a day,
He rested at the mountain's foot.
An old man said: "These are biao (lesser tigers).
Further north,
Lies a true tiger; if you encounter it,
You will be defeated."
Mín did not believe,
Spurred his horse angrily forward.
He saw a tiger emerge from the woods,
Small but fierce,
Crouched and roaring mightily,
Mín's horse recoiled in fear,
His bow and arrows fell,
From then on, he never hunted again.
"Xīn Táng Shū".
本朝
Authority without virtue,
Though fierce, inspires no fear;
Insight without virtue,
Though sharp, earns no respect.
My lord cultivates virtue from his seat,
Yet his authority repels enemies a thousand miles away.
Retiring at home, yet people regard him as if at court,
Can this not be called virtuous authority?
Sū Dōngpō "Inscription for the Hall of Virtuous Authority".
My lord,
Refers to Wén Lùgōng》.
经
The benevolent see it and call it benevolence,
The wise see it and call it wisdom.
．"Yì Xì Cí".
Those who know me,
Say my heart is troubled;
Those who do not know me,
Ask what I seek?
．"Shī Shǔ Lí".
Only the wise,
Say I am toiling;
But the foolish,
Say I am boastful.
"Hóng Yàn".
In the past,
Yán Shūzǐ once lived alone in his house,
A widowed neighbor also lived alone in hers,
One night, a storm destroyed her house.
The woman rushed to his door,
Yán Shūzǐ let her in,
Had her hold a candle,
Burned it until dawn and it extinguished,
Then tore down part of his roof to continue the light.
He considered this insufficient to avoid suspicion.
If one were truly careful,
It should be like the man from Lǔ.
A man lived alone in his house,
A widowed neighbor also lived alone in hers,
One night, a storm destroyed her house.
The woman rushed to seek shelter,
He closed the door and did not let her in.
Annotation to "Máo Shī".
子
He who understands me,
is it not the "Chūnqiū"?
He who blames me,
is it not the "Chūnqiū"?
"Mèngzǐ Téng Wén Shàng".
View it from its differences,
like liver and gall, Chǔ and Yuè;
view it from its sameness,
all things are one.
"Zhuāng Dà Zōngshī".
What the ancient called determination,
was not about official rank;
what is now called determination,
is about official rank.
"Shàn Xìng Piān".
Zǐlù saved a drowning person and accepted a cow as thanks.
Confucius said: "Lǔ must be fond of rescuing people from difficulties."
Zǐgàn redeemed a person
but did not accept gold from the treasury,
Confucius said: "Lǔ will no longer redeem people."
Zǐlù took and encouraged virtue,
Zǐgàn gave up and ceased goodness.
"Huáinánzǐ Qí Sù Xùn".
Lǎozǐ said: "Governing a large country is like cooking a small fish."
For those who are lenient, it is said not to disrupt;
for those who are harsh, it is said to just make it salty and sour.
Same above.
The envoy from Shǐ
Wáng Sūn was engaged in diplomacy in Jìn,
Zháo Jiǎnzǐ asked: "How many treasures are the white jades of Chǔ worth?"
He replied: "What Chǔ treasures are those
called Guān Shèfù,
who could compose instructive words.
Also the left historian Yǐxiāng,
who could expound instructive classics.
These are the treasures of the state of Chǔ.
As for the white jades,
they are merely toys for scholars,
how could they be deemed treasures?"
"Guóyǔ Chǔ Yǔ".
Mutual understanding: "Skillful in responding."
Liáng Wáng said: "I have ten pearls, each an inch in diameter, illuminating twelve chariots before and after.
Does the king also have treasures?"
Qí Wēi said: "What I call a treasure differs from the king's.
I have four ministers
Shànzǐ, Zhōngshǒu, Xìnzǐ, Qiánfū.
They illuminate a thousand miles;
how can only twelve chariots compare?"
Liáng Wáng was ashamed.
"Shǐ Qí Shìjiā".
The virtuous truly value their death.
Servants and concubines,
are moved and commit suicide out of despair.
"Qián Luán Bù Zhuàn".
Chén Dēng met Lǚ Bù and said: "Dēng told Cáo Gōng:
'Raising the general is like raising a tiger;
one must feed it meat,
if not fed, it will bite people.'
Duke said: 'It's not as you say.
It's like raising an eagle;
when hungry, it serves,
when full, it flies away.'"
"Tōng Jiān Dōng Hàn".
Sūn Bǎo said: "Zhōu Gōng is supremely sage,
Shào Gōng is greatly wise,
yet they did not agree with each other."
"Qián Hàn Sūn Bǎo Zhuàn".
The Crown Prince saw the Emperor's unrelenting diligence,
and taking an opportunity advised: "I wish for Your Majesty to conserve your energy,
relax and rest."
The Emperor said: "I enjoy this myself,
I am not weary."
"Tōng Jiān Hàn Guāng Wǔ".
The strategy of supervising the army lies in holding firmly,
not in seeing the timeliness of opportunities.
"Tōng Jiān Hàn Xiàn Dì".
Xiè Tàifù sat in the yard at night,
the moonlight was flawless,
he sighed at its beauty.
Xiè Jǐngzhòng abruptly said: "I think it lacks the adornment of light clouds."
Tàifù replied: "Your heart is not pure,
thus you wish to taint the pure moon."
"Jìn Shū".
Xiè Wàn said: "The three Xiè flatter the Way,
the two how deceitful to Buddha."
Same above.
Imposing name and reality is like chaff under the pillar,
playing with the pure void is like bran and chaff on the mat.
"Chén Shū Mǎ Kòu Zhuàn".
Cuī Qún said: "All take Ān Lùshān's rebellion in the 14th year of Tiānbǎo as the beginning of chaos,
I alone think it began in the 24th year of Kāiyuán when Zhāng Jiǔlìng was dismissed,
and Lǐ Línfǔ was fully entrusted.
This marked the division between order and chaos."
"Táng Shū".
Zhōu Gōng embraced the child, causing Shào Gōng to doubt him,
the intentions of Zhōu Gōng,
Shào Gōng did not know.
"Xīn Táng Shū Xīnluó Zàn".
Shǐ Hóngzhāo said: "Stability of the nation lies in long spears and great swords,

Wáng Zhāng said: "Without the brush,
from where will financial resources come?"
"Tōng Jiān Zhōu Tàizǔ Jì".
When
Wǔ Wáng and Zhōu Gōng,
sage men,
led the virtuous scholars of the world,
and the feudal lords of the world,
and went on their campaign, no one was heard to oppose.
Only Bó Yí and Shū Qí,
thought it impermissible.
Yīn had already fallen,
the world revered Zhōu,
these two people alone were ashamed to eat its grain,
starving to death without looking back.
From this we can say,
was this done for gain?
Their faith in the Way was steadfast and self-knowledge clear.
Hán Wén "Bó Yí Song".
The father of the Tai Shi Gong was named Tán,
thus "Shǐ Jì" does not contain the character Tán,
in "Jì Bù Zhuàn", Zhào Tán is changed to Zhào Tóng.
Fàn Yè's father was named Tài,
thus "Hòu Hàn" lacks the character Tài,
both Guō Tài and Zhèng Tài are written as Tài.
Lǐ Áo's father was named Chǔjīn,
therefore writing always uses the current rather than chí for zī.
Hán Yù wrote "Huì Biàn" for Lǐ Hè to uphold a non-referencing stance,
thus his father Zhòngqīng never concealed the name.
The son of Cáo Zhì Zhī, Tài, argued that simplicity was not enforced,
never avoiding the character Zhì.
In "Sān Guó Zhì", even the names of lords are not avoided,
saying achievement depends on authority,
this criticizes Sūn Quán's name.
"Kǒng Shì Zá Shuō".
In our dynasty,
the elderly feel time flies,
the idle know days are long.
The sun and moon are emotionless,
the human heart has leisure and toil.
"Ōu Gōng Jí".
Chén Tuán said Qián Ruòshuǐ has immortal bones,
the Māyī Daoist said: "This person is courageous enough to retreat from rushing currents."
"Dōngpō Jí".
People all plant elms and willows,
waiting to sit under ten acres of shade.
I alone plant pines and cypresses,

"Dōngpō Shī".
As years change, children rejoice,
yet it grieves the heart of the old.
"Línchuān Jí".
Harvesting years bring joy to the farming family,
autumn winds bring sorrow to the traveler.
Same above.
Bái Lètiān's poem says, "In the absence of events, days and months are long,

Mèng Dōngyě's poem says, "Upon leaving the door there is obstruction,
who says heaven and earth are wide";
these are the words of narrowness.
"Qīng Xiāng Zá Jì".
At the outset of new laws by the court,

"Yán Xíng Lù".

"Míngdào Jí".
The classic

they instead call me presumptuous.

Zǐ
A tree that has stood for a hundred years,

adorned with blue and yellow patterns,
has its leftover pieces discarded in a ditch.
Comparing the sacrificial vessel to the discarded pieces in the ditch,
there is a distinction between beauty and ugliness.

A tree survives its natural lifespan by being useless,

His family highly praised their son's wisdom,
but suspected the neighbor's father.

With a light carriage and strong horses,

Both from the same source above.
Shǐ
Yù Ràng,

but remained unknown.

who greatly honored and favored him.

The bright moon's pearl,

Gnarled tree roots,

"Zōu Yáng Zhuàn".

"Běnzhuàn",

Those in power ascend to the clouds,

Both from the same source above.
Bǎilǐ Xī in Yú led to its fall,

Thus, without cause before one,

If someone speaks for you first,

"Zōu Yáng Zhuàn".
Lifted, they soar above the clouds;

Used, they become tigers;
unused, they become rats.
"Dōngfāng Shuò Zhuàn".
Like plants growing in mountains and forests,
birds and fish breeding in rivers and marshes.
Those catching the season flourish,
those missing it wither.
"Bān Gù's Xùzhuàn",

The emperor promoted Gōng's response as the best,

"Zīzhì Tōngjiàn".
Pān Yuè, handsome in appearance,

See "Shìwù Xiāngxíng".
It's not that orchids resent and osmanthus befriend,

Yet life and death differ,

Same source,
Lù Jī et al.'s "Zàn".
Fine jade concealed in rough stone,

a skilled artisan polishes it,

Cross-reference "Shízhě Nán Qī".
Fàn Zhěn of Qí said, "Human life is like tree blossoms blooming together,

"Táng Shū".
Wénběn's talents and strategies,

Same source,

Same as above.

Same as above.

Both same as above.

Our dynasty

Classic

Master

History

Classic

Biographies
A noble steed, harnessed to a salt cart, ascended Tàiháng Mountain,
but lingered and strained under the yoke, unable to proceed.
Bólè encountered it,
alighted from his carriage, clasped it, and wept.
Thereupon, the steed lowered its head and snorted,
raised it and neighed,
its voice reaching the heavens,
as if emanating from metal or stone.
Why was this?
It had found in Bólè one who understood its worth.
"Strategies of the Warring States".
Cross-reference "Being Understood".
Qí Guǎngníng Wáng Xiàohéng once kept a watchdog,
preventing outsiders from approaching.
Whenever Xiàohéng went hunting,
he would command it to fetch arrows.
It also understood calls.
Summoning attendants,
it would tug at their clothes to approach.
"Outline of Three Kingdoms History".
Bees form two processions in response to tides.
"Běiyǎ".
If a hunting dog is lost in the mountains and forests,

the dog will bark and howl,
responding to its owner.
Though dogs are of a different species,
they respond when called

"Lùnhéng".
During the crisis of Zhèng Zǐyáng,

lost cattle led to defeat.
In those times,
even dogs and cattle could lead men.
"Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals".
Lù Jī had a dog named "Huáng'ěr".
When Jī took office in Luòyáng,
he often kept it by his side.
This dog was clever and perceptive,
able to understand.
Once lent to someone three hundred lǐ away,
it found its way back on its own,
reaching home in one day.
Jī, detained by official duties in the capital,
had long been without news from home.
Jī jokingly said to the dog:
"We've had no letters from home;
can you carry a message galloping back to fetch news?"
The dog joyfully wagged its tail,
vocalizing in response.
Jī tried writing a letter,
placed it in a bamboo tube,
and tied it to the dog's neck.
The dog took the post road,
swiftly heading towards Wú.
When hungry, it foraged in grass,
eating meat to satiate itself.
Whenever encountering large waters,
it would approach ferrymen,
drooping ears and wagging tail,
earning their pity and affection.
Thus called aboard,
once near the shore,
it leaped up and sped away like flight,
directly reaching Jī's household,
holding the bamboo tube and vocalizing to alert people.
Jī's family opened the tube to retrieve the letter,
after reading it,
the dog again vocalized to them,
as if requesting something.
The family prepared a reply,
placed it inside the bamboo tube,
and again tied it to the dog's neck.
Having received the reply,
the dog raced back to Luò.
Calculating a human journey of fifty days,
the dog's round trip took only half.
"Records of the Strange".

So they released an old horse and followed it,

Traveling in the mountains without water,
Xí Péng said: "Ants dwell on the sunny side in winter,
on the shady side in summer;
an inch of ant soil indicates water at a ren's depth."
They dug the ground,
and indeed found water.
With the wisdom of Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng,
when facing the unknown,
they did not hesitate to learn from an old horse and ants.
Nowadays, people fail to use their foolish minds to learn from the sages' wisdom,
is that not a mistake?
"Hánfēizǐ".
Qí raised an army to attack Chǔ,
Zǐfā led troops to resist them,
but the army retreated thrice.
Chǔ's worthy officials exhausted their strategies and sincerity,
yet the Qí army grew stronger.
Then a market thief came forward and requested: "I have a minor skill,
I wish to perform it for you."
Zǐfā said: "Agreed."
Without questioning, he sent him off.
The thief then stealthily untied the Qí general's tent curtain at night and presented it.
Zǐfā had someone return it,
saying: "A soldier gathering firewood
found the general's curtain,
and sends it back to your office."
The next night, he went again,
taking the general's pillow.
Zǐfā again had it returned.
The following night, he returned once more,
taking the general's hairpin.
Zǐfā again had it returned.
The Qí commander heard of this,
and was greatly alarmed.
The general and officers deliberated: "If we do not leave today,
the Chǔ army might take our heads."
So they withdrew their troops and departed.
Hence it is said: Nothing is too insignificant or weak in skill,
it depends on how the ruler employs it.
. "Huáinánzǐ: Responses of the Way".
History
Like adding dust to Mount Tài,

it causes no harm either.

Táo Kǎn served as the Grand General Who Conquers the West and Governor of Jīng Province.
At that time, when building ships,
he ordered that all wood chips and bamboo scraps be collected and stored,
which no one understood.
During a formal assembly,
after snow had just stopped and the sky cleared,
the snow in front of the hall was still wet,
so he spread the wood chips on the ground.
When Huán Wēn launched a campaign against Shǔ,
he used the bamboo scraps stored by Táo Kǎn to make nails for shipbuilding.
His meticulous and comprehensive management
was always of this kind.

Bù was greatly angered,

Upon exiting to his quarters,
he found the furnishings, food, drink, and attendants identical to those of the King of Hàn's residence,

From the "Biography of Qíng Bù, Former Hàn".

Collection

Master

yet inquires about not using teeth to tear meat,
this is called not knowing what is essential.
From "Mèngzǐ, Jìn Xīn Shàng".
To kill a warhorse in pursuit of a fox,

From the "Huáinánzǐ".

Yáng Hù oversaw Jīngzhōu,

Whenever engaging in battle with men of Wú,
