never resorting to schemes of surprise attack.
If any generals or commanders wished to propose cunning or deceptive strategies,
he would make them drink strong wine,
preventing them from speaking.
If he captured two children from Wú as prisoners,
he would send them back to their families.
When his army marched through Wú territory,
cutting grain for provisions,
he would always calculate the amount taken,

he always remained within Jìn territory.

he would have them all sealed and returned.
From the "Basic Biography, Jìn History".
Wèi Yuánzhōng submitted a sealed memorial,

while those who speak of military affairs prioritize horsemanship and archery without knowing strategy.
From the "Tōngjiàn, Táng Gāozōng".

Master
Now, as for Zhāngzǐ,

Because he had offended his father,
he could not be near him,
so he sent away his wife and distanced his son,

His intention was that if he did not act thus,
this would be a great crime,
and this is what Zhāngzǐ was about.
From the "Mèngzǐ".
When a master carpenter uses wood,

He knows that what it hinders is minor,
and in the end, it becomes an invaluable vessel.
From the "Kǒngcóngzǐ".
Now, Yán Zhuōjù
was a great bandit of Liángfù,
yet he became a loyal minister of Qí;
Duàn Gānmù

bringing peace to its perils,

Jǐngyáng

Lose a sheep but gain an ox,

Same as above.

Do not let one fault overshadow great virtue.
． From "Zuozhuan, the 32nd Year of Duke Xi".
Cáo Zǐ was a general of Lǔ,
defeated three times in three battles,
and lost five hundred lǐ of territory.
Had Cáo Zǐ made plans without looking back,
deliberated without retreating a step,
cut his throat and died,
then his name would inevitably be known as a defeated general captured by the enemy.
Cáo Zǐ abandoned the shame of three defeats,
and withdrew to strategize with the ruler of Lǔ.
He confronted Duke Huán on the altar platform,
and in one morning recovered all that was lost in three battles.
In such a case,
it was not that he was incapable of achieving minor integrity and practicing small principles,
but he believed that sacrificing one's life and body,
cutting off one's lineage and posterity,
without establishing merit and fame,
was not wise.
Therefore, he set aside the resentment of momentary anger,
to establish a lifelong reputation;
he abandoned the principle of indignant stubbornness,
to secure achievements spanning generations.
． From "Records of the Grand Historian: Lǔ Zhònglián".
"Endure the Small to Achieve the Great".
Guǎn Zhòng was not ashamed of being in prison but ashamed that the world was not well-governed;
he was not ashamed of not dying for Prince Jiǔ but ashamed that his authority was not trusted by the feudal lords.
Same as above.
Had Wǔ Zǐxū followed his father Wǔ Shē to death in that era,

The great Hàn dynasty ruled over ten thousand lǐ;

"Endure the Small to Achieve the Great".
The principle of the Spring and Autumn period

If an archer hits the target a hundred times but misses once,

Huà Yuán of Sòng slaughtered sheep to feed his soldiers,
but his charioteer Yáng Zhēn was not given any.
When battle came, he said:
"Yesterday with the sheep, you were in charge;
today's affairs,
I am in charge."
He drove into the Zhèng army,
thus causing defeat.
The gentleman said Yáng Zhēn was not human,
for due to his personal resentment,
he ruined the state and brought calamity upon the people."
． From Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xuān year 2.
Unable to endure one moment of shame,
one ends up shamed for a lifetime.
From Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Zhāo year 31.
Fighting over trivial matters until they exhaust their people.
From Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Chéng year 12.
Earlier,
men of Wǔchéng detained those of Zēng who were steeping rushes,
saying:
"Why do you make our water turbid?"
When the Wú army arrived,
the detainees guided them
to attack Wǔchéng,
and it was captured.
From Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Āi year 8,
also from Zuǒzhuàn.
Shí Qízi said:
"Gaining one man but losing a state,
allying with the wicked and abandoning the good,

Jìn sent Xì Kè to Qí.
Xì Kè was hunchbacked,
and the mother of Duke Qíng of Qí watched from a tower and laughed at him.
Xì Kè angrily said:
"If I do not take revenge on Qí,
may Hé Bó bear witness!"
Later he joined Lǔ and Wèi to attack Qí.
From Shǐjì.
Bāo Sì did not like to laugh,
and King Yōu tried every means to make her laugh,
but she still would not laugh.
King Yōu set up beacon fires and great drums;
when invaders came, he would light the beacon fires.
All the feudal lords came,
but when they arrived there were no invaders,
and Bāo Sì then laughed heartily.
King Yōu was pleased
and repeatedly lit the beacon fires.
Afterwards, they were not believed,
and the feudal lords increasingly did not come.
． From Shǐjì, Basic Annals of Zhōu.
Separately seen in the "Indulging Desires" section.
There was a lame man who walked unsteadily,
and a beautiful woman of Lord Píngyuán laughed at him.
The lame man went to Lord Píngyuán's gate
and said:
"The reason scholars come from a thousand lǐ away
is because you, my lord, value scholars and disdain concubines.
I wish to have the head of the one who laughed at me."
Lord Píngyuán did not kill her.
After over a year,
more than half of his guests and retainers gradually left.
． From Shǐjì, his basic biography.
Táo Zhūgōng's middle son killed a man
and was imprisoned in Chǔ.
Zhūgōng sent his eldest son
with a letter to his old friend Zhuāng Shēng,
offering a thousand pieces of gold.
When the eldest son arrived at Zhuāng Shēng's home,
Zhuāng Shēng did not intend to keep it
but planned to return it after the matter was accomplished.
Zhuāng Shēng went to see the King of Chǔ
and said:
"A certain star is harming the King of Chǔ."
The king then sealed the treasury of three coins.
A noble of Chǔ told Zhūgōng:
"The king is about to issue a pardon."
The eldest son thought that since there was a pardon,
his younger brother would surely be released,
and it would be pointless to waste a thousand pieces of gold on Zhuāng Shēng,
so he went to see Zhuāng Shēng again,
saying:
"Initially, I sought my brother's exemption,
but now he is to be pardoned,
so I bid you farewell."
Zhuāng Shēng knew he wanted the gold back
and said:
"You may go into the room and take the gold yourself."
The eldest son immediately went in and took the gold,
then left.
Zhuāng Shēng was ashamed to have been tricked by a youth,
so he went to see the King of Chǔ and said:
"When I previously spoke of the star,
Your Majesty said you would cultivate virtue in response.
Now that I have come out,
everyone on the road is saying that the rich man Táo Zhūgōng's son killed someone and is imprisoned in Chǔ,
and his family has bribed your attendants with much gold.

he scolded the Marquis of Qí like a domestic dog,
without inner trembling.
Liǔ Wén.
Not reaching one state but spreading throughout the world,
not fitting one era but flowing through all ages.

Famed throughout the world yet not reaching the court,
wisdom encompassing all things yet not suiting one person.
"Wéncuì".
Our dynasty
Yǐn Shīlǔ,
in all matters, if there was something minor yet pitiable,
he would be sorrowful and unable to bear exposing it;
in appearance and demeanor,
but when facing major principles and deciding great affairs,
his heart was like metal or stone,
unchangeable even with cauldrons and boilers before him.

Classics
Rather than kill the innocent,

Masters
Rather be pricked a hundred times with a needle,

rather pull a heavy weight once,

rather be hungry for one month,

History
Even casting many nets to catch one bird may fail,
how much more spreading a thousand-eyed net to ensnare all things and hoping to catch everything within it?

Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established the Harmony Office,
sang of heavenly auspices,
which was not unadmirable,
yet could not prevent the edict of sorrow.
Wáng Mǎng founded the Yìhé Office,
investigated pitch pipes,
which was not unrefined,
yet could not save him from the disaster at Jiàntái.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn set the flute's standard,
tuned metal and stone instruments,
which was not inexact,
yet could not avert the disaster at Píngyáng.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng established four instruments,
harmonized the eight tones,
which was not unperceptive,
yet could not escape the humiliation at Táichéng.
Thus, even if the music of Sháo, Xià, Huò, and Wǔ
still existed in the world,
if the rest is unworthy of it,
it could not transform even one man,
let alone the whole world!
. "Tōngjiàn Táng Tàizōng".
Biographies
Would one refrain from saving a drowning person merely for fear of getting one's feet wet?
From Liú Xiàng's "New Prefaces".
In ancient times, Confucius had the strength to lift a city gate bar,
yet he was not renowned for his physical power.
Why so?
Because the virtue of a great sage
encompasses numerous excellences;
one cannot take a minor skill
and regard it as the foremost among all conducts.
From "Generalities on History".
Collected Sayings
If one receives a gift of a thousand gold pieces daily,
and is promoted nine times in a year,

but to claim to the world that this makes one a true confidant is not so.
From Hán Yù's "Letter to Zhāng Fēngjiàn".
Even if one emerges untested among ten thousand,

how could there be limits?
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
Cross-reference "Heartfelt Admiration".
Classics
Bì (Adornment) means ornamentation.
When ornamentation is carried to the extreme, then prosperity reaches its end,
hence it is followed by Bō (Peeling Away).
Bō means stripping away.
Things cannot be exhausted forever;
after peeling away reaches the top, it reverts to the bottom,
hence it is followed by Fù (Return).
． From "Sequence of the Hexagrams" in the "Book of Changes".
Tài (Peace) means smoothness.
Things cannot remain smooth forever,
hence it is followed by Pǐ (Obstruction).
Ibid.
There is no level ground without a slope,
no departure without a return.
From the "Tài Hexagram".
Cross-reference "Vigilance and Warning".
When joy reaches its peak, sorrow follows.
． From "Record of Music" in the "Book of Rites".
Zǐyóu said: "In serving a prince, repeated remonstrance leads to disgrace;
among friends, frequent admonition results in estrangement."
． From the "Lǐ Rén" chapter of the "Analects".
What is exceedingly beautiful must have something exceedingly evil.
． From "Zuǒ Zhuàn", the 27th year of Duke Zhāo.
Masters
Those who advance too hastily
will retreat quickly.
． From "Mencius", "Jìn Xīn Shang".
Things of great beauty
are instruments of ill omen.
From "Lǎo Zǐ".
If criticism and scrutiny are too extreme,
there will inevitably be base minds that respond in kind.
． From "Zhuāng Zǐ", "The Human World".
Cross-reference "Do Not Push Things to the Extreme".
When people are numerous, they can overcome Heaven,
but when Heaven is settled, it can also respond to people.
From "Xún Zǐ".
A thousand years must bring a return to ancient constants.
． From the "Rhapsody" chapter of "Xún Zǐ".
When things reach their peak, they decline;
when joy reaches its extreme, it turns to sorrow.
From "Huái Nán Zǐ".
Smoke arises from fire but can stifle the fire;

when ice melts, water flows freely.
． From Liú Zǐ's "On Guarding Against Desires".
Histories
Stopping the mouths of the people
is worse than damming water.
If water is blocked and bursts through,
it will inevitably injure many.
From "Discourses of the States".
If full without reduction, it will topple;
if full without maintenance, it will tip over.
． From "Records of the Grand Historian", "Book of Music".
When things flourish, they then decline;
when time reaches its extreme, it turns.
． From "Records of the Grand Historian", "Treatise on the Balanced Standard".
With wine to excess comes disorder;

it is said one should not go to extremes,
for at the extreme, decline sets in.
． From "Records of the Grand Historian", "Biographies of Jesters".
What blazes fiercely will be extinguished;
what thunders loudly will be cut off.
． From "History of the Western Hàn", "Biography of Yáng Xióng".
The Qín built palaces so magnificent to this extent,
yet their descendants could not even find a hut to dwell in.
They constructed imperial roads so splendid to this extent,
yet their descendants could not even find a bypath to set foot on.
They made burials so extravagant to this extent,
yet their descendants could not even find a weed-covered mound for interment.
． From "History of the Western Hàn", "Biography of Jiǎ Shān".
Cross-reference "Bequeathing Calamity".
High position truly hastens a fall;

． From "History of the Former Hàn", "Treatise on the Five Elements".
Powerful clans are prone to collapse.
． From "History of the Eastern Hàn", "Eulogy for Yīn Jù".
Cross-reference "Power Cannot Be Relied Upon".
In the former Warring States period,

． From "History of the Eastern Hàn", "Biography of Shēntú Pán".
Poverty is born from wealth,

danger from security.
From "Biography of Wáng Fú".
The steepest heights crumble,
the leafiest branches break,

From Zhào Yè's "Chronicles of Wú and Yuè" of the Later Hàn.

At the height of joy, sorrow is abundant.
From Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's "Song of the Autumn Wind".

It is not the millet that is fragrant,

thought it delicious,

From "Liè Zǐ".

The steeds from Qūchǎn,

Yàn Fǔ.

Face to face.

"Qiūshuǐ" chapter.

the manuscript was not yet finalized.
Grand Master Shàngguān wanted to seize it,
but Qū Yuán refused to give it,
leading to slander against him.
The king, angered, distanced himself from Qū Yuán.
He composed "Lísāo",
and after being alienated,
he no longer held his position.
When King Qǐngxiāng ascended the throne,
Qū Yuán was exiled to the south of the Yangtze River.
_Shǐjì_,
same as above.
Wú Qǐ served as chancellor of Chǔ,
clarifying laws and carefully issuing decrees,
reducing non-essential officials,
and dismissing distant relatives of the royal clan,
to support and nurture warriors for battle.
His focus was on strengthening the military,
refuting the rhetoric of itinerant persuaders advocating horizontal alliances.
He pacified the Bǎiyuè in the south;
annexed Chén and Cài in the north,
repelled the Three Jìn;
and attacked Qín in the west.
The noble relatives of Chǔ all sought to harm Wú Qǐ.
_Shǐjì_,
same as above.
Those whose courage and strategies alarm their sovereign endanger themselves;
those whose achievements overshadow all under heaven receive no rewards.
． _Shǐjì, Biography of the Marquis of Huáiyīn_.
Yáng Xiū possessed outstanding talent,
and served as Registrar to Chancellor Cáo Cāo.
Once, when Cáo Cāo was about to travel,
Yáng Xiū anticipated that he would inquire about external affairs,
so he prepared responses in advance,
instructing the guards: "If orders are issued,
convey them accordingly."
It turned out as he predicted.
Cáo Cāo was surprised by the speed,
investigated the matter,
learned the truth,
and grew resentful of Yáng Xiū.
Later, he had Yáng Xiū executed on some pretext.
_Hòu Hànshū_.
The fragrant herb burns itself with its own scent;
the oil consumes itself with its own light.
． _Xī Hànshū, Biographies of the Two Gǒngs_.
Biographies
record that Cháo Cuò died due to his wisdom.
． _Dōng Hànshū, Biography of Gěng Tán_.
Cunning individuals with many talents may inevitably bring disaster;
thus, Fēng Shū died for his brilliance,
and Dèng Xī perished for his eloquence.
． _Tángshū, Eulogy for Yuán Zǎi and Others_.
Luxuriant blossoms break the branches;
rich fat ruins the bones.
_Wénxīn Diāolóng_.
Purity attracts dust;
whiteness attracts grime.
The stains from blue flies
often land on white silk.
_Lùnhéng_.
Those who achieve merits surpassing the age
are bound to bear the burden of defying conventions;
those with unique insights
are sure to incur the resentment of the masses.
_Zhànguócè_.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Liú Xīyí, Wáng Chānglíng, Zǔ Yǒng, Zhāng Ruòxū, Mèng Hàorán, Cháng Jiàn, Lǐ Bái, Dù Fǔ,
though renowned for their literary talents,
all wandered in obscurity and misfortune,
a result of relying on their talents and being frivolous.
_Mínghuáng Zálù_.
The tree is broken for its outstanding beauty;
the orchid is burned for its fragrance.
． _Jìnshū, Eulogy for Ānpíng King Sīmǎ Fú_.
Collections
When one's conduct rises above the crowd,
people are sure to criticize it.
． _Wénxuǎn, Lǐ Xiāoyuǎn's "Discourse on Fate"_.
When a tree stands out in the forest,
the wind will surely break it;
when a mound protrudes from the bank,
the current will surely erode it.
Same as above.
All admire the beautiful feathers and plump flesh,
like those of peacocks.
Thus, they perish without crime.
Though they hide in reeds to avoid arrows,
they end up slain in this world.
The fierce hawk is tethered for its prowess;
the clever parrot is caged for its wit.
Zhāng Huá's "Rhapsody on the Wren".
The orchid is destroyed for its fragrance;
the jade is broken for its fine grain.
Things fear strength and fragrance;
people shun brightness and purity.
． _Wénxuǎn, "Eulogy for Qū Yuán"_.
Fragrant herbs and oils consume themselves.
_Táng Wéncuì_.
The musk deer incurs harm for its scent;
the monkey invites arrows for its cunning.
The elephant is burned for its tusks;
the fish exposes its scales for greed of bait.
Both same as above.
Wú Zǐxū was cast into the Wú River;
Qū Yuán ultimately threw himself into the Xiāng River's shores.
Lù Jī, with his heroic talent, could not protect himself;
Lǐ Sī regretted not retiring early.
How can one hear the cranes of Huátíng again?
What use to speak of the greyhounds of Shàngcài?
Lǐ Tàibái.
Lacquer is cut for its usefulness;
oil burns itself for its light.
Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Objects with flavor are bound to attract worms;
people with talent are sure to face slander.
Liú Bīnkè.
The old turtle, gutted,
would be better off without divine spirit.
Bái Jūyì.
Multiple talents do not bring fortune;
a short fate accompanies intelligence.
Same as above.
Thus, I know that early success and many talents
seldom last long in this world.
Why do fragrant oils burn themselves?
Both same as above.
When deeds are accomplished, slander arises;
when virtue is high, calumny comes.
Hán Yù's writings.
In the birth of all things,
none wish to be material.
The sacrificial vessel, painted green and yellow,
is a disaster for the wood.
Hán Yù's "Eulogy for Liǔ Zǐhòu".
Jade fears to leave the rough stone;
once out, it first becomes dust.
Pine and cypress fear to leave the mountains;
once out, they first become firewood.
Mèng Jiāo.
The straight tree is the first to be felled;
the hard stone is also attacked by others.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng.
Hard jade breaks;
bright oil burns itself.
Teeth break from hardness;
oil is consumed for its light.
Same as above.
Our dynasty
The pheasant mirrors itself in green water,
how foolish its self-love.
Literary brilliance, used by the world,
only burdens the physical form.
_Línchuān Collection_.
Trees have galls,
stones have halos,
rhinoceros horns have channels,
all used to please people,
yet these are ailments of the things.
Sū Shì.
Fragrant herbs and oils both burn themselves;
ivory and kingfisher feathers destroy their bodies.
Same as above.
Classics
Disaster comes from the mouth.
． From "Yì Shùn Guà Zhèngyì".
Only the mouth brings shame.
． From "Shū Shuō Mìng Zhōng".
Not the tongue's utterance,
but the body's exhaustion.
From "Shī".
Words wasted and vexatious,
easily spoken but hard to regret,
easily drown a person.
． From "Jì Zī Yī".
A gentleman drowns by his mouth.
Same as above.
Drowning,
is caused by the cover of words.
To fend off others with a glib tongue,
often incurs their hatred.
From "Yǔ".
Many words lead to many failures.
The mouth is the gate of disaster.
From "Jiā Yǔ".
Speaking of concealed matters,
such actions endanger one's life.
From "Hán Zǐ".
Words can summon disaster.
From "Xún Zǐ".
Words that harm others,
cut deeper than spears and halberds.
Same as above.
No disaster is greater than excessive speech.
From "Wén Zhōng Zǐ".
Careless words invite sorrow.
From "Yáng Zǐ".
The mouth and tongue,
are the palace of calamity and the mansion of ruin.
From "Jiā Yǔ".
The harm of misspoken words,
is not less than piled blades.
． From the chapter "Liú Zǐ Jǐn Yán".
History
Shū Xiàng said: "The words of petty men
are presumptuous and unsubstantiated,
thus blame and misfortune befall them."
． From "Zuozhuan, Eighth Year of Duke Zhao".
Jìn's Bó Zōng, every time he attended court,
his wife would warn him: "You are fond of speaking bluntly,
and will surely meet with disaster."
Later, the three Xì families of Jìn harmed Bó Zōng.
． From "Zuozhuan, Fifteenth Year of Duke Cheng".
The three families besieged the city with the state's army and flooded it,
yet the wall remained unsubmerged for three ramparts' height.
The people showed no intention to rebel.
Zhì Bó, while inspecting the water,
said: "Now I know that water can destroy a state."
Huán Zǐ nudged Kāng Zǐ with his elbow,
and Kāng Zǐ stepped on Bó Zǐ's instep,
hinting that the Fén River could flood Ānyì,
and the Jiàng River could flood Píngyáng.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ sent men at night to breach the dikes and flood Zhì Bó's army.
Zhì Bó's troops were thrown into chaos while trying to save themselves from the water,
and they subsequently killed Zhì Bó.
From "Comprehensive Mirror".
Cross-reference "Bringing Defeat Upon Oneself".
Long ago, Zhèng Wǔgōng wanted to attack Hú,
so he married his daughter to its ruler.
Then he asked his ministers:
"I wish to use military force;
who should we attack?"
Guān Qísī said: "Hú can be attacked."
Wǔgōng then executed Guān Qísī, saying: "Hú
is a brotherly state;
why do you speak of attacking it,
and for what reason?"
． From "Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Hán Fēi".
Mistakenly misspeaking,
led to humiliation by officials.
． From "Book of Han, Biography of the Three Kings of Wén".
Crime incurred by speech.
From "Book of Han".
When Lǐ Líng surrendered to the Xiōngnú,
the Emperor asked the Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān,
who spoke highly: "Lǐ Líng served his parents with filial piety,
was trustworthy with scholars,
and bravely risked his life for the state's emergencies.
Now that an unfortunate event has occurred,
ministers who only care for their own safety and families immediately magnify his faults;
this is truly grievous!"
The Emperor considered Qiān's words deceitful,
as advocating for Lǐ Líng,
and sentenced Qiān to castration.
． From "Book of Han, Biography of Lǐ Líng".
I have suffered this calamity due to my speech,
greatly shaming my ancestors before my fellow villagers.
Same as above,
from "Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān".
Zhāng Chǎng's subordinate Xù Shùn privately went home, saying: "He's just a Metropolitan Governor for five days;
how can he still handle cases!"
Upon hearing this, Chǎng
arrested and imprisoned Shùn until he died.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Hàn Xuāndì".
Regional Governor Hán Bó reported: "There is an extraordinary man,
ten feet tall,
with a girth of ten arm-spans,
who came to my office,
saying he wishes to fight the Hú barbarians.
He calls himself Jù Wúbà,
hailing from Pénglái,
too large for a light carriage to carry,
and three horses cannot bear him.
He sleeps using a drum as a pillow,
eats with iron chopsticks;
this is how Heaven assists the Xīn dynasty.
I hope to welcome him.
If the capital's gates cannot accommodate him,
we should widen and heighten them,
to show the various barbarians,
and pacify the world."
Bó intended to satirize Wáng Mǎng.
Mǎng heard of it and disliked it,
detained Wúbà at his location,
changed his surname to Jùmǔ,
claiming it was due to the Empress Dowager Wénmǔ's auspicious sign for hegemony.
He summoned Bó and imprisoned him,
for saying what was inappropriate,
and executed him publicly.
． From "Book of Han, Biography of Wáng Mǎng".
Those who speak do not receive the blessing of being heeded,
but immediately suffer the disaster of being framed.
Now all are silent and tongue-tied,
taking me as a warning.
． From "Book of the Later Han, Biography of Cài Yōng".
After Dǒng Zhuó was executed,
Cài Yōng, while sitting with Minister over the Masses Wáng Yǔn,
unexpectedly sighed over it,
showing emotion.
Yǔn angrily rebuked him,
had him arrested and tried.
Yōng then died in prison.
Same as above.
Cài Yōng said: "If ruler and minister are not discreet,
the former faces the warning of leaked words,
the latter risks the calamity of losing one's life.
I hope my memorial is suppressed,
so that loyal officials are not resented by treacherous enemies."
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor read it and sighed.
He then got up to use the restroom;
Cáo Jié peeked at it from behind,
and told everything to those around him,
so the matter leaked.
Those whom Yōng had dismissed
glared with resentment, planning revenge.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Hàn Língdì".
Crime incurred by speech.
Same as above.
Dòu Róng wrote to Wěi Xiāo, saying.
Yuán Shào again advised Hé Jìn: "Previously, Dòu Wǔ intended to eliminate the inner favorites but was instead harmed,
solely because his words were leaked."
Chén Lín said: "A proverb says 'cover the eyes to catch sparrows';
even with tiny creatures, one cannot succeed by deception,
let alone in major affairs!"
Same as above,
from "Annals of Hàn Xiàndì".
Xǔ Yōu, arrogant due to his achievements,
once called Cáo Cāo by his childhood name in public: "So-and-so,
without me,
you wouldn't have obtained Jìzhōu!"
Cāo laughed and said: "You are right."
But inwardly displeased,
he later killed him.
Same as above.
Kǒng Róng, in responding to Sūn Quán's envoy,
made slanderous remarks,
and was executed publicly.
From "Book of the Later Han".
The Emperor toured the rear garden,
feasting with great pleasure.
Lady Guō requested to invite the Empress,
but the Emperor refused,
and forbade his attendants from disclosing it.
The Empress found out;
the next day,
she asked the Emperor: "Yesterday's feast in the north garden,
was it enjoyable?"
The Emperor, thinking his attendants had leaked it,
had over ten of them killed.
He forced the Empress to commit suicide.
．． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of the Three Kingdoms, Wèi Míngdì".
Jī Kāng wrote to Shān Tāo,
stating his inability to conform to vulgar customs,
and disparaging Tāng and Wǔ.
Sīmǎ Zhāo heard of it and was angered.
He then had Jī Kāng killed.
Same as above,
from "Annals of Jìn Yuándì".
Zhōu Yǐ said: "This year, I'll kill the traitorous slaves,
and get a gold seal as big as a dou-measure to hang from my elbow."
Wáng Dǎo deeply resented this.
Yǐ was killed by Wáng Dūn.
． From "Book of Jin, Biography of Zhōu Yǐ".
Initially,
when Tuòbá Kūduō attacked Guī,
Mò Tí, thinking Guī young,
secretly sent an arrow to Kūduō, saying: "How can a three-year-old calf bear a heavy load!"
Guī held a grudge.
By this time,
he sent someone to show the arrow to Tí, saying: "How did the three-year-old calf turn out?"
Tí and his son wept facing each other.
The next morning,
they were arrested and executed.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Jìn Āndì".
Cross-reference "Cannot Be Underestimated".
King of Qín, Duò, had a stern and rigid nature.
Someone told Duò: "Lord Dǒng is immensely favored;
you should lower yourself a bit to associate with him."
Duò said: "What kind of chicken or dog is Dǒng Lóng,
that a man of state should speak with him?"
When celestial anomalies occurred,
Róng told the Qín ruler Shēng: "Heaven's reprimand is severe;
it should be answered with an important minister."
So they killed Wáng Duò.
Saying to him: "Do you still dare compare Dǒng Lóng to a chicken or dog today?"
Same as above,
from "Annals of Jìn Āidì".
The Crown Prince always disliked Xīchāng Hóu Luán,
once telling Zǐ Liáng: "I really dislike this person in my heart,
though I don't know why;
it must be because he has little fortune."
When Luán came to power,
none of the Crown Prince's descendants survived.
From "Annals of Qí Gāozōng".
Much speech brings much trouble.
From "Annals of Liáng Wǔdì".
Hèruò Bì harbored resentment;
the Emperor imprisoned Bì,
saying to him: "I appointed Gāo Jiǒng and Yáng Sù as chancellors,
yet you often declared: 'These two are only fit for eating rice!'
What do you mean by this?"
From "Annals of Suí Gāozǔ",
and "Comprehensive Mirror".
When Hè Ruòbì's father Dūn was facing execution,
he called Bì and said:
"My ambition was to pacify Jiāngnán,
but this wish remains unfulfilled.
You must accomplish my ambition.
Moreover, I die because of my tongue,
you must not fail to reflect on this."
Thereupon he took an awl to pierce Bì's tongue until it bled,
admonishing him to guard his speech.
《Suí Shū》.
Sū Ānhéng,
being arrogant and fond of the extraordinary,
when Crown Prince Chóngjùn executed Wǔ Sānsī,
Ānhéng claimed "this was my stratagem".
After the Crown Prince's defeat,
someone reported him,
and he was executed.
． 《Tōng Jiàn Táng Zhōngzōng》.
In matters of state importance,
to speak while fearing it inappropriate to one's position,
is indeed culpable,
hence I wrote "Statement of Guilt".
． 《Xīn Táng Shū Dù Mù》.
Dù Fǔ once drunkenly ascended Yán Wǔ's bed,
stared and said:
"Yán Tǐngzhī actually has such a son!"
Wǔ resented this.
One day,
he intended to kill Fǔ,
gathering officers at his gate.
As Wǔ was about to depart,
his hat caught three times on the curtain.
His attendants informed his mother,
who rushed to intervene and stopped him.
． 《Xīn Táng Shū Dù Fǔ Zhuàn》.
Biographies
say those who err in speech forfeit their lives.
Improper speech
instead injures oneself.
Also from 《Shuō Yuàn》.
Magpies' cries chatter-chatter,
crows' clamor grab-grab.
Struggling in the courtyard,
they expose themselves to pellet shots.
Hán's writing.
Debates within the tent make others deem you rebellious,
critiques in the court make others think you subversive.
Will you not take warning,
and instead babble to endanger your life!
Same as above,
《Admonition on Speech》.
Since speech brings me calamity,
there is no way to conceal my words,
those who can avoid such faults
are indeed few.
Explanation of Speech.
To fully express opinions and expose others' faults
is why Guó Wǔzǐ was killed in Qí.
《Discussion on Remonstrance Ministers》.
Cross-reference to "Incurring Misfortune".
Also Hán's writing.
Not choosing words while in peril, indeed at the brink of multiple disasters.
Liǔ's 《Fu on Chastising Faults》.
One word creates sickness,
wisdom cannot clarify it.
Liú Bīnkè.
When verbal warfare arises,
its punishment is severe.
Same as above.
Zhì Bó erred in his words about the Guàn River.
《Bái Tiē》.
Classic
The gentleman, hearing bell sounds, thinks of military officers;
hearing chime stones, thinks of ministers who died defending borders;
hearing zithers and lutes, thinks of righteous and principled ministers;
hearing reed pipes and flutes, thinks of ministers who store and gather;
hearing war drums, thinks of commander ministers.
History
The King of Yuè sent Hòu Yōng to pay a courtesy visit,
and discuss the fields of Zhū,
demarcating the border at Táishàng.
They swore an alliance at Píngyáng,
with three ministers accompanying.
Kǎngzǐ was troubled by this,
and when mentioning Zǐgòng,
said: "If he were here,
I would not have come to this!"
Wǔbó said:
"We would certainly have summoned him."
Wénzǐ said: "Another day we shall remember him."
. "Zuǒzhuàn, 27th Year of Duke Āi".
Yuè defeated Wú,
relocating King Fūchāi of Wú to Yǒngdōng,
granting him a hundred households to reside.
The King of Wú said: "I am old now,
and cannot serve Your Majesty.
I regret not following Zǐxū's advice,
bringing this upon myself."
. "Records of the Grand Historian, House of Wú".
When a family is poor, they think of a good wife;
when a state is in chaos, they think of a good chancellor.
. "Records of the Grand Historian, House of Wèi".
The Emperor arrived at Guǎngwǔ,
pardoned Liú Jìng,
saying: "I did not heed your advice,
thus suffering at Píngchéng."
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Han Emperor Gao's Annals".
Zhāng Chǎng was dismissed and became a commoner,
living as a fugitive.
After several months,
law and order in the capital slackened,
alarm drums frequently sounded,
and bandits arose in Jìzhōu,
the Emperor recalled Chǎng's effectiveness,
sending an envoy to summon him from his home.
Chǎng faced serious charges,
and when the envoy arrived,
his wife and family wept,
fearful and anxious,
but Chǎng alone laughed and said: "I am a fugitive commoner,
local officials should arrest me.
Now an envoy comes,
this means the Emperor wishes to employ me."
He packed and followed the envoy,
to the official carriage.
The Emperor received Chǎng in audience,
appointing him as Governor of Jìzhōu.
Upon Chǎng's arrival in the region,
bandits vanished without a trace.
Ibid., "Annals of Han Emperor Xuān".
Bandits rose in groups in Yǐngchuān,
the commander in Hédōng also rebelled,
the capital was in turmoil.
The Emperor heard and said: "I regret not heeding Guō Zǐhéng's words."
Ibid.,
"Annals of Han Emperor Guāngwǔ".
Mǎ Yuán campaigned south against Jiāozhǐ,
leisurely telling his subordinates: "My cousin Shǎoyóu often pitied my lofty ambitions,
saying: 'A scholar lives but one lifetime,
seeking only adequate food and clothing.
Striving for surplus,
only brings hardship.'
When I was between Làngbó and Xīlǐ,
with mire below and fog above,
poisonous vapors steaming.
Looking up at kites falling into the water,
lying down I recalled Shǎoyóu's lifelong words,
how precious they were!"
. "Book of Later Han, His Biography".
The King of Hàn attacked Wú and was defeated,
by then Fǎ Zhèng had died,
Liàng sighed: "If Xiàozhí were alive,
he would certainly have restrained His Majesty from marching east.
Even if they had gone east,
it would not have led to such peril."
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Three Kingdoms".
Wáng Xiànzhī and his brothers,
before Qiè Chāo passed away,
when visiting Yīn,
would tread carefully to inquire after him,
observing the rites between uncle and nephew.
After Chāo died,
their visits to Yīn became negligent,
wearing clogs to see him.
Yīn often sighed: "Had Jiābīn not died,
would these rodents dare act so!"
. "Book of Jin, Biography of Qiè Chāo".
Yīn,
was Chāo's father.
Cross-referenced under "Fickleness".
Emperor Wén of Sòng said: "If Tán Dàojì were alive,
how could the northern cavalry come this far?"
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Sòng".
With Wú pacified,
ministers offered congratulations.
The Emperor raised his cup with tears: "This is the achievement of Grand Mentor Yáng."
Ibid.,
"Jìn Emperor Wǔ, 1st Year of Tàikāng".
The Turks besieged Yànmén,
Emperor Yáng sighed:
"Had Chángsūn Shèng been alive,
he would not have let the Xiongnu come this far."
"Book of Suì".
Liú Xíngběn,
was Tutor to the Crown Prince.
Prince Yǒng respected and feared him.
Later he died.
When the Crown Prince was deposed,
the Emperor said: "Had Liú Xíngběn been alive,
Yǒng would not have come to this."
◇Yuán Yán was Chief Minister to the Prince of Shǔ.
Later the prince gradually broke laws and was punished,
the Emperor said:
"Had Yuán Yán been alive,
would my son have done this!"
Both ibid.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng reported that Ān Lùshān showed signs of rebellion,
requesting his execution for crimes,
but the Emperor released him.
After Jiǔlíng's death,
the Retired Emperor in Shǔ,
recalling Jiǔlíng's foresight,
issued an edict mourning and posthumously honoring him.
"Book of Táng".
The campaign against Gāolì,
withdrew the army.
The Emperor, unable to achieve success,
deeply regretted it,
sighing: "If Wèi Zhēng were alive,
he would not have let me undertake this campaign!"
He ordered sacrifices to Zhēng with a young animal,
re-erected his stele,
summoned his wife and children to the imperial camp,
and rewarded them.
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Emperor Tàizōng".
When the position of Vice Minister of Justice was vacant,
the Emperor said: "I have found the right person.
Formerly Lǐ Dàorù opined in Zhāng Liàng's case 'evidence of rebellion is insufficient',
his words were correct,
though I did not heed them,
I regret it to this day."
Thus he appointed Dàorù as Vice Minister of Justice.
Ibid.
Emperor Tàizōng returned from Liáodōng,
saying: "If Wèi Zhēng were alive,
would I have undertaken this campaign?"
"Book of Táng".
Biographies
After Jì Zūn died,
at every court assembly,
the Emperor often sighed: "Where can I find one as public-spirited and devoted to the state as General Jì!"
"Dōngguān Hànjì".
Collection
In continuous rain, I long for a worthy aide;
facing portraits, I recall my veteran minister.
Dù Fǔ's poem.
Chanting verses of frost and snow,
I forever cherish the grace of the phoenix.
Bái Jūyì.
Deeds remain only in records,
banners should spread their fame.
Their voices unseen, unheard,
war drums deepen my longing.
Ibid.
Hearing war drums, I recall famed generals;
viewing portraits, I long for veteran ministers.
Lǐ Déyù.
Xiang bamboo's old spots make me think of the emperor's son;
river thoroughwort's first green grieves for the poet of sorrows.
Liú Chángqīng.
Our Dynasty
When Duke Wèi of Hán died,
scholar-officials sighed: "Why did Heaven not leave Ōuyáng Xiu alive to write Duke Wèi's epitaph before his death!"
"Separate Records of Duke Wèi of Hán".
Lú Tóng and Hán Yù are not here,
no mighty prose to subdue a hundred monsters.
"Collection of Ōuyáng Xiu".
Classic
The leader of ten thousand men
can be observed for his governance.
． From "Shū Xiàn Yǒu Yī Dé".
"Fēng Yǔ",
longs for the gentleman.
In times of chaos, one longs for the gentleman,
who does not alter his principles.
Wind and rain dark as night,
the cock crows unceasingly.
． From "Shī Fēng Yǔ".
Observe the vessel and know the artisan's skill,
observe the words and know the person's wisdom.
． From "Jì Lǐ Qì".
When the year grows cold,
then we know how the pine and cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
． From "Yǔ Zǐ Hǎn".
A gentleman
is not tolerated,
then his true nature is revealed.
From "Jiā Yǔ".
Cross-reference "Not Carelessly Conforming" and "The Great Way Is Not Tolerated".
When the six relations are discordant, filial piety and parental affection appear;
when the state is in chaos, loyal ministers emerge.
From "Lǎo Zǐ".
Send him far to know his loyalty,
keep him near to observe his respect,
burden him to see his ability,
entrust him with wealth to examine his benevolence,
question him suddenly to test his wisdom,
impose urgent deadlines to gauge his trustworthiness,
make him drunk to observe his discipline,
place him in mixed company to watch his demeanor,
confront him with danger to judge his integrity.
From "Zhuāng Zǐ".
Nourishing the living is not enough to be considered a great affair,
only sending off the dead can be considered a great affair.
． From "Mèng Zǐ Lí Lóu Xià".
Observe what he does when in poverty,
observe whom he associates with when successful.
From "Liè Zǐ".
In poverty, see his integrity;
in wealth, see his righteousness;
in life, see his love;
in death, see the grief he evokes.
． From "Yǐn Dèng Zǐ Xiū Shēn".
Without the cold of the year, one cannot know the pine and cypress;
without difficult affairs, one cannot know the gentleman.
． From "Xún Zǐ Dà Lüè".
When the boat capsizes, the good swimmer is revealed;
when the horse gallops, the skilled driver is seen.
． From "Huái Nán Zǐ Shuō Lín Xùn".
Like the jade of Zhōngshān,
the pine of the cold ridge,
they are no different from common stone and willow when compared.
But when burned in furnace coals for three days without losing their luster,
or placed in accumulated ice all year without their leaves withering,
then one knows they differ from other jades and trees.
From "Liú Zǐ".
History
Lǐ Kè said: "Observe whom he befriends when at home,
whom he associates with when wealthy,
whom he recommends when successful,
what he refrains from when in poverty,
what he does not take when poor."
． From "Shǐ Wèi Shì Jiā".
Cross-reference "Close Examination".
When the whole world is turbid,
the pure scholar emerges.
． From "Shǐ Jì Bó Yí Zhuàn".
Féi Yì said: "The upright minister's integrity is seen when hardship comes;
the loyal minister's conduct is clear when troubles accumulate."
Same as above.
"Zhào Shì Jiā".
When Huáiyīn, Qíng Bù, and others were all executed,
Xiāo Hé's achievements shone brightly.
"Xiāo Hé Shì Jiā".
When the world is dark and turbid, loyal ministers emerge.
"Wèi Wáng Bào Zhuàn".
The dog thief and the cock crower—
Mèng Cháng Jūn listed these two among his guests,
bringing much shame.
But when the crisis in Qín arose, it was these two's skills that saved him.
"Mèng Cháng Jūn Zhuàn".
Cross-reference "Inclusive Acceptance".
All above from "Shǐ Jì".
Jù Mèng,
a gambler.
When his mother died,
over a thousand carriages of guests attended the funeral,
showing he had exceptional qualities.
． From "Xī Hàn Yuán Àng Zhuàn".
Without encountering gnarled roots and tangled knots,
how can one distinguish a sharp tool?
． From "Hòu Hàn Yú Xǔ Zhuàn".
When Wáng Xiáng passed away,
those who rushed to mourn were either virtuous court officials
or close relatives and former subordinates,
with no miscellaneous visitors at the door.
． From "Jìn Shū Běn Zhuàn".
Cross-reference "Mourners at the Door".
Wáng Zhàn said: "How can one distinguish a horse on a straight, level road?
Only when it runs on ant hills."
． From "Jìn Jì Dèng Càn Zhuàn".
Táng's Lǐ Yíjiǎn impeached Yáng Píng,
who was demoted to Línhè尉;
only Xú Huì went to Lántián to bid him farewell.
Later, Yíjiǎn recommended Huì as a censor.
Huì said, "I've never even seen your face in my life,
how did you come to select me, Yí?"
Jiǎn replied, "You did not fail Yáng Línhè,
would you dare fail the state?"
"Tōng Jiàn".
Cross-reference "Forgetting Self for Public Duty".
It is between life and death
that one's integrity is revealed.
． From "Táng Yuán Déxiù Zhuàn".
In fierce winds, the tough grass is known;
in turbulent times, the loyal minister is recognized.
Táng Tàizōng's poem to Xiāo Yǔ,
see "Běn Zhuàn".
Lǐ Shìjì often attended banquets;
the emperor once said to him calmly, "Among my ministers, I seek one to entrust with my orphaned children,
none surpass you.
You did not fail Lǐ Mì in the past,
how could you fail me now!"
． From "Tōng Jiàn Táng Tàizōng".
Mǎ Wénjǔ said, "Without encountering a formidable enemy,
how can a warrior show his mettle?"
Same as above.
Collection
Better after frost and snow,
to see the heart of bamboo and cypress alone.
Jiāng Yān's poem.
In perilous times, a minister's integrity is seen;
in chaotic ages, loyalty is recognized.
． From "Xuǎn Bào Míngyuǎn Shī".
Supporting the falling, one then knows the value of long-term strategy.
Dù's poem.
In times of turmoil,
uprightness shines even brighter.
Liú Bīnkè.
After fire, jade is revealed;
after frost, pine and cypress are known.
Same as above.
A scholar's integrity is seen in adversity.
Hán's prose.
In rainy darkness, the faithfulness of the cock's crow is recognized;
in high winds, the falcon's strike shows its power.
Bái Lètiān.
Only through grinding and dyeing is its hardness and purity revealed.
Dù Mùzhī.
In a light breeze, one feels the fragrance of fir filling the air;
under scorching sun, the coolness of bamboo is known.
Lǚ Héshū's prose.
Without the fire of a hundred smeltings,
who would know the essence of an inch of gold?
Mèng Dōngyě.
Cross-reference "Truth Is Hard to Erase".
Split the pine to see its steadfast heart;
crack the bamboo to view its straight grain.
"Táng Wén Cuì".
If heaven had no snow and frost,
green pines would be no better than grass.
If earth had no mountains and rivers,
who would value level roads?
Táng Yú Xù's poem.
When all trees are bare and shaking,
then the true color of bamboo is seen.
Mèng Dōngyě's poem.
Cross-reference "Things Revealed by Contrast".
Our dynasty
Wielding the brush, one longs even more for a decisive battle,
Repeated hardships reveal the poet's true talent.
From the "Línchuān Collection".
When horses are in the stable,
Nags and steeds mingle together,
Drinking water and eating hay,
Neighing, kicking, and biting,
It is hard to tell their differences.
But when pulling heavy carts,
On level roads,
Without frequent whipping,
Or troublesome driving,
A single tug of the reins and a thousand miles are covered.
At that time,
If nags try to keep pace,
Even with broken wheels and torn reins,
Injured tendons and bones,
Chasing day and night without rest,
They fall far behind, unable to catch up.
From "Línchuān's Writings".
Only upon finding the path does one understand the heart of yesteryear.
From Dōngpō's poem.
In the cold of winter among countless trees,
Match the tall pine with the giant cypress;
As stars fade in the night,
The bright moon stands in awe of the evening star.
From Dōngpō's "Congratulatory Address for Attendant Lin".
See also "Things Revealed by Comparison".
Fire's reign of four hundred years wanes, its spirit fades,
Who will replace it? It is the one from Dangtú High.
Extreme villainy and cruelty are hard to seize,
Only then is known the firm foundation laid by Wén and Jǐng.
From the same source, "Ode to an Ancient Inkstone".
Only because Luán Bù did not abandon Péng Yuè's command,
Did Emperor Gāozǔ recognize his worth;
Only because Lǐ Jì did not betray Lǐ Mì's trust,
Did Emperor Tàizōng commend his righteousness.
From the "Luánchéng Collection".
Those who receive kindness and cannot bear to betray it,
Will surely be filial as sons and loyal as ministers.
From the "Míngdào Collection".
Without being tempered by great fire,
How can true gold be obtained?
From the "Luánchéng Collection".
Observe on a windy, cold night,
Who stands firm at the door.
From Shào Yáofū's poem.
Classics
Knowing one's insufficiency,
Then one can reflect upon oneself;
Knowing one's difficulties,
Then one can strengthen oneself.
From "Records of Learning" in the Book of Rites.
Philosophers
When Confucius considered judging a person by appearance,
He changed his view after meeting Miè Míng;
When he considered judging by speech,
He changed after encountering Zǎi Wǒ;
When he considered judging by demeanor,
He changed after knowing Zǐ Zhāng.
From the "Family Sayings of Confucius".
Thus stirring the heart, enduring the nature,
To enhance what one lacks.
One often errs,
Then can correct.
Troubled in heart,
Weighed in thought,
Then one arises.
Evident in complexion,
Expressed in voice,
Then understood.
From "Mencius - Gào Zǐ II".
Those who possess virtue, wisdom, and skill,
Often thrive through hardship.
Only the solitary minister or the disfavored son,
Their hearts anxious with care,
Their thoughts deep with concern,
Thus they attain understanding.
Same as above,
From "Mencius - Jìn Xīn II".
Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn conceived his ambition for hegemony in Cáo,
King Gōujiàn of Yuè conceived his in Kuàijī,
Duke Huán of Qí, Xiǎo Bái, conceived his in Jǔ.
From "Xúnzǐ".
Lǎozi studied under Shāng Róng,
Seeing the tongue, he learned to uphold softness.
Lièzǐ studied under Húzǐ,
Observing the shadow and post, he learned to hold back.
From "Huáinánzǐ - Miù Chēng Xùn" with note: "Form comes first, then shadow."
Yáo encountered floods and thus valued high land,
Tāng faced great drought and thus prized water.
From "Fùzǐ".
History
Gāo Qiáng of Qí said: "With three broken arms, one becomes a good physician."
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn - Dìng 13".
See also "Knowledge Through Repetition".
Emperor Gāozōng heeded the warning of the calling pheasant,
Rectified himself and followed the right path,
Thus enjoying a lifespan of a hundred years.
From "Western Hàn - Biography of Dù Qīn".
If the tree had not grown in the court,
Tàiwù would not have prospered;
If the pheasant had not cried at the cauldron,
Wǔ Dīng would not have been honored as an ancestor.
From "Jìn Shū - Biography of Guō Pú".
Collections
A physician is made after nine broken arms.
From "Chǔ Cí".
Three breaks make a skilled doctor.
By Liú Bīnkè.
Classics
Lush and sweet is the pear tree,
Do not cut it, do not harm it,
For Shào Bó rested beneath it.
From the "Book of Songs - Gǎn Táng".
Philosophers
Without Confucius,
How would the starving man of the Western Mountains and the dismissed official of the Eastern State be known?
From "Yángzǐ".
The jade of priceless worth,
Its light buried in Jīng Shān;
The pearl that glows at night,
Its radiance hidden in Yù Pǔ.
Jade flies without wings,
Pearls walk without feet.
Their fame spread on the Zhāng Huá Terrace,
Their brilliance displayed in silken halls,
Is all due to human effort.
From "Liúzǐ".
Had Liǔxià Huì not met Confucius,
His chaste conduct would not have been revealed,
Remaining merely a repeatedly dismissed official;
Had Jì Bù not met Cáo Qiū,
His promise of a hundred gold would not have been praised,
Staying an ordinary captive.
Same as above.
History
Although Bó Yí and Shū Qí were virtuous,
their names became more illustrious because of the Master.
For common people in the alleys
who wish to cultivate their conduct and establish their reputation,
unless they attach themselves to eminent figures,
how can their fame be transmitted to later generations?
. "Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of Bó Yí".
Master Máo then went to Chǔ once,
making Zhào's importance surpass the Nine Tripods and the Great Bell.
Same as above,
"Biography of Plain Yuan".
Yǔ Chéng studied at the imperial academy,
working as a servant for the students.
Later, he was able to lecture and recite,
but considering himself of lowly status,
he always took the lowest seat.
Students and erudites all came to consult him,
and from then on, the lowest seat became esteemed in the academy.
. "Later Han History: His Biography".
Governor of Hénán Yáng Zhì visited Zhào Yī,
their conversation lasted until dusk,
and they were extremely joyful.
Zhì then together with Minister over the Masses Yuán Féng jointly praised and recommended him.
His fame stirred the capital,
scholars and officials longed to witness his demeanor.
Same as above,
"Biography of Zhào Yī".
Ruǎn Jí saw Zhāng Huà's "Rhapsody on the Wren" and said: "This is the talent of a king's assistant!"
From then on, his reputation began to flourish.
"Book of Jìn".
Zuǒ Sī composed the "Rhapsody on the Three Capitals",
but adults did not value it.
Sī showed it to Zhāng Huà,
who praised it profoundly,
and additionally wrote a preface.
The wealthy and noble vied to copy it,
causing paper to become expensive in the capital.
"Book of Jìn".
Xǔ Xún moved to reside at the cliff of Gāotún,
often roaming and interacting with the Buddhist monk Zhī Dùn, as well as Xiè Ānshí, Wáng Xīzhī, and others.
Now Gāotún is called "Xǔ Dù Cliff".
Xiè Ān had a great reputation,
and was admired by people of his time.
There was a man who left his county post,
and returned.
Ān asked about his resources for returning,
he replied: "I have fifty thousand palm-leaf fans."
Ān then took one of medium quality and held it,
scholars and commoners vied to buy them,
and the price increased severalfold.
"Book of Jìn".
Yáng Xióng wrote the "Great Mystery",
and later encountered Lù Xù,
whereupon the Way of the Mystery became clear.
"Biography of Wáng Chángwén".
Wáng Dǎo served as Minister over the Masses,
at that time the treasury was empty and exhausted,
with only several thousand bolts of ramie cloth in the storehouse,
which could not be sold.
He then, together with court worthies, made unlined garments from the ramie cloth,
whereupon scholars uniformly wore them,
and ramie cloth suddenly became expensive.
When the officials sold it,
one bolt was worth a piece of gold.
Such was the admiration for him at the time.
Wáng Xīzhī saw an old woman
holding hexagonal fans for sale.
Xīzhī wrote on her fans,
five characters on each.
The old woman initially sighed in dismay.
He then said to the old woman: "Don't worry,
just say it is written by Wáng Yòujūn,
to ask for a price of a hundred pieces of gold."
The old woman did as told,
and people vied to buy them.
The above all from "Book of Jìn".
Biographies
There was a man who had a fine horse for sale,
he stood in the market for three mornings,
but no one recognized its value;
once Bó Lè glanced at it,
in one morning the horse's price increased tenfold.
"Strategies of the Warring States".
Guō Línzōng traveled to Luòyáng,
and first met Governor of Hénán Lǐ Yīng,
Yīng found him extraordinary,
and they became friends,
whereupon his fame shook the capital.
"Separate Biography of Guō Línzōng".
Regarding the Cílián River,
in the past, Lǐ Zǔrén lived here,
ten brothers all were kind, filial, honest, and deferential,
hence the river was named so.
"Record of Jiāozhōu".
Liáng's Gù Zǒng initially served as a county clerk.
One evening he met two men,
who claimed to be Wáng Càn and Xú Gàn,
saying: "In the past, we were in the same office with you,
you were Liú Zhēn."
They then recited his surviving writings,
Zǒng awakened,
and presented several pieces of the surviving writings to the magistrate,
who treated him very generously.
It was said at the time: "The dead Liú Zhēn still protects the living Gù Zǒng."
"Extensive Records of the Taiping Era".
A scholar is not a jade disc,
it is the discussers who set the price.
"Discourses on Principles".
Cross-reference "Seeking Assistance".
Bái Lètiān presented his poems to Gù Kuàng,
who then praised him,
and his reputation greatly soared.
"Tales of Seclusion and Leisure".
Collections
In the past, when Ōu Yě changed his gaze,
the lead knife gained value;
where Bó Lè looked,
the nag became worth a hundredfold.
. "Wénxuǎn: Cáo Zhí's Memorial".
The night-shining jade disc
manifests its value in Hé Shì's shop;
the thousand-lǐ steed
establishes its merit in Bó Lè's courtyard.
"Imperial Reader of Arts and Letters" records: "Yìng Qú's letter recommending Hé Lǜzé."
Once being appraised,
one becomes an excellent scholar.
Lǐ Bái.
With one glance of honor,
the inferior horse surpasses the mountain deer;
with the weight of a single word,
the fish's eye exceeds the divine snake.
Luò Bīnwáng.
With the praise of one word,
the eastern mound equals the western mountain;
with the honor of one meeting,
the Zhèng uncut jade surpasses the Zhōu treasure.
. "Preface to Wáng Yànshēng's Collected Works".
Cross-reference "Gratitude".
In the past, on Yú Bǎn's slope,
the exceptional steed and the inferior horse were both weary;
in Wú's kitchen,
the solitary tóng tree was burned together with firewood.
Meeting Wáng Liáng and Bó Yē,
they then soared in fame for a thousand ages.
If this poem had not met Wáng Jūn,
it would have been just several tens of sheets of old paper.
. Táng Wéi Tāo's "Preface to Mèng Hàorán's Collection".
The Chùzhōu edition,
Wáng Jūn named Shìyuán,
during the Tiānbǎo era obtained the "Collected Works of Mèng Hàorán",
Shìyuán wrote a preface for it.
Sòng Guǎngpíng sunk in low positions,
Sū Gōng Wèidào as an envoy,
Guǎngpíng presented to him the "Rhapsody on the Plum Blossom",
Sū praised it highly,
and from then on he was listed among the famous.
From this it is known that even outstanding talents,
cannot stand outside of literature,
still using a few words to borrow praise from the mouths of predecessors,
riding on their influence to then raise their heads in their time.
How much more so the mediocre,
who can distinguish themselves?
Liú Bīnkè.
Cross-reference "Seeking Assistance".
Beauty is not beautiful by itself,
but becomes manifest because of people.
The Orchid Pavilion,
had it not encountered Yòujūn,
then its clear rapids and tall bamboos,
would have been overgrown in the empty mountains.
Liǔ Wén.
Our Dynasty
Goose feathers gifted from a thousand lǐ away,
are valued because of the person.
Ōu Gōng.
Mount Xiàn overlooks the Hàn River,
viewed from afar it appears lofty,
yet it is among the smaller mountains,
but its name is especially prominent in Jīng,
is it not because of the person?
Who is that person?
It is Yáng Hù, Shūzǐ, Dù Yù, Yuánkǎi.
"Record of the Xiàn Mountain Pavilion".
Wēn Gōng built the Garden of Solitary Joy,
among the gardens in Luòzhōng it was the most simple and plain,
but because of the lord's reputation,
people would surely visit in spring.
"Collection of the Path of Enlightenment".
. Cross-reference "Category of Gardens and Ponds in the Gate of Livelihood".
Huáng Shūdù was serene and unpretentious,
but with one word from Guō Línzōng,
he has been regarded as Yánzǐ to this day.
Shūdù's virtue,
was not outwardly visible at all,
yet later generations still believe,
solely because of Línzōng's esteem.
Dōngpō's "Letter of Thanks for the Grand Guardian Writing the Epitaph for My Father".
Classics
Nowadays when people appoint Confucian scholars,
they often wrongly use "Confucian" as a term of reproach.
． From "Records of Confucian Conduct".
Even with the talents and virtues of Zhōu Gōng,
if one is arrogant and stingy,
the rest is not worth observing.
． From "Analects · Tàibó".
Masters
If the beauty Xīzǐ is covered with filth,
people will all cover their noses and pass by her.
From "Mèngzǐ".
The five grains
are the finest among seeds.
But if they do not ripen,
they are inferior to weeds.
Same source,
"Gàozi Shàng".
If a basin of water is set level and undisturbed,
the sediment will settle at the bottom,
while clarity remains on top,
allowing one to see one's beard and eyebrows and discern patterns.
But if a breeze passes over it,
the sediment stirs below,
and the clarity becomes disturbed above,
one cannot obtain a correct reflection of the larger form.
From "Xúnzǐ".
The root of the lán huái is called zhǐ,
but if soaked in wastewater,
the gentleman will not go near it.
Same source,
"Quànxué" chapter.
Note: "Xiǔ,
means urine."
Water's nature is clear; what makes it turbid
is soil stirring it up;
a forest's nature is still; what makes it move
is wind shaking it;
human nature is upright; what makes it evil
is desires confusing it.
From "Liúzǐ".
River water desires to be clear,
but sand and soil defile it.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
History
One fragrant herb and one stinking weed together,
after ten years the odor still remains.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn".
If weeds flourish and crops are defiled,
why not hoe them?
． From "Yán Yánnián's Biography" in History of the Western Hàn.
Loyal as Yùquán,
trustworthy as Biàn Hé,
wise as Sūn Bìn,
wronged as Xiàng Bó,
talented as Sīmǎ Qiān,
eminent as Zǐ Zhèng,
once subjected to punishment,
they were disgraced for life.
． From "Guō Tài's Biography" in History of the Eastern Hàn.
The Jīng River becomes turbid by the Wèi.
Same source,
"Jiǎ Biāo's Biography".
If a mountain has rotten soil,
though large, it will crumble;
if a tree has borers,
its glory easily falls.
． From "Historian's Eulogy on Emperor Xuánzong" in History of the Táng.
Collections
I strung huì and zhǐ to wear as adornments,
but passing a fish market, they lost their fragrance.
From "Chǔ Cí".
Endowed with a lofty and bright nature,
yet not free from the burden of baseness and turbidity.
． From "Elegy" in the Selections of Refined Literature.
Once a blue fly stains it,
white jade becomes wronged.
From "Collection of Chén Zǐ'áng".
This Dynasty
Gentlemen and petty men are like ice and charcoal,
absolutely cannot share the same vessel.
If both are collected and employed,
the petty men will surely prevail;
when fragrant and foul are mixed,
in the end, the stench will dominate.
From Dōngpō's "Epitaph for Duke Fù Zhèng".
Does nature have joy and anger,
just as water has waves or not?
Reply: "Tranquilly calm as a mirror
is water's nature;
but when passing over sand and stones,
or where the terrain is uneven,
it becomes turbulent and rapid,
or when wind blows over it,
it forms raging waves and surges—
is this water's nature indeed!"
From "Collection of Illuminating the Way".
Masters
Thus, though carved mìn stone may be ornate,
it cannot match the brilliance of jade.
． From "Xúnzǐ · Fǎxíng".
The brightness of a hundred stars
is not equal to the light of one moon;
ten windows all open
do not match the illumination of one door.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
A leopard fur mixed with others
is not as good as a pure fox fur.
Same source.
History
Zhào Liáng said: "The skins of a thousand sheep
are not equal to one fox's underarm fur."
． From "Biography of Lord Shāng" in Records of the Grand Historian.
A hundred birds of prey
are not equal to one osprey.
Quoted in "Memorial Recommending Mí Héng".
． Also seen in "Zōu Yáng's Biography" in History of the Western Hàn.
Jade is tested by grit.
． From "Jiǎ Biāo's Biography" in History of the Eastern Hàn.
Biographies
For one who fishes for giant fish,
lowering a thousand hooks to catch it
depends on one fish trap;
for one who catches high-flying birds,
setting ten thousand nets to capture it
relies on a single mesh.
From "Generalities on History".
Collections
Sparrows' noise makes the crane's stillness known.
By Gāo Dáfū.
Classics
Like weeds among seedlings,
or chaff in millet.
． From "Zhòngshì's Declaration" in the Book of Documents.
Masters
Tasting jade nectar makes one know the insipidity of coarse broth.
． From "Bàopǔzǐ · Gold" chapter.
Collections
The patterns of tiger and leopard
shine brighter than those of dogs and sheep;
the sounds of luán and phoenix
ring clearer than those of crows and magpies;
the glow of gold and jade
outshines that of tiles and stones.
By Huángfǔ Shí.
Cross-reference "Things Compared".
Masters
The arrow-maker only fears he cannot harm people.
From "Mèngzǐ".
History
The officials in charge of trials all desire people to die,
not because they hate them,
but because their own security lies in the death of others.
. _Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Emperor Xuan of Han_.
Cross-reference "It's the circumstances that make it so."
During the Wei period, the plaque of the Lingyún Hall had not been inscribed,
when the craftsman mistakenly nailed it up,
making it impossible to take down.
So they had Wéi Zhòngjiāng write on it while suspended.
By the time he finished,
his hair and beard had turned completely white,
and he was barely breathing.
Returning home, he told his disciples,
"You should never use this method."
. _Book of Jin, Biography of Wáng Xiànzhī_.
King Fú Shēng of Qin ate too many dates at night,
and by morning had fallen ill.
He summoned the imperial physician Chéng Yán,
ordering him to diagnose it.
Yán said, "Your Majesty has no other ailment,

The duke said, "The minister

He said, "It can be transferred to the common people."
The duke said, "If the people die,

He said, "It can be transferred to the year."

Zǐ Wéi said, "You have spoken three words of utmost virtue,
