Things of like kind gather together.
From "Yuè Jì".
Masters:
When the yang mirror faces the sun,
it ignites into fire.
From "Zhuāngzǐ".
Shī Wén learned to play the qín from Shī Xiāng.
In spring, he plucked the shāng string to summon the Nángōng note,
and cool winds gathered,
with plants bearing fruit.
In autumn, he plucked the jué string to excite the Jiázhōng note,
and warm winds gently circled,
with plants blooming.
In summer, he plucked the yǔ string to summon the Huángzhōng note,
and frost and snow fell together,
with rivers and ponds freezing suddenly.
In winter, he plucked the zhǐ string to excite the Ruíbīn note,
and sunlight blazed fiercely,
with solid ice instantly melting.
At the end,
he struck the gōng note and combined all four strings,
whereupon auspicious winds soared,
propitious clouds floated,
sweet dew descended,
and sweet springs gushed forth.
． From "Lièzǐ: Tāng Wèn".
If firewood is laid out evenly,
the fire seeks the dry parts;
if the ground is level,
water seeks the damp parts.
Plants and trees grow in clusters,
birds and beasts gather in groups,
each thing following its own kind.
． From "Xúnzǐ: Quàn Xué".
When heaven is about to rain,
though the overcast has not yet gathered, fish are already gasping, and mountain clouds steam around pillar bases.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
Add firewood to the fire,
and the dry parts will burn first;
pour water on level ground,
and the damp parts will be soaked first.
From "Dèngzǐ".
History:
Crickets await autumn to chirp,
mayflies emerge in the shade,
tigers roar and winds become sharp,
dragons rise and bring clouds.
From "Wáng Bāo Sòng".
When the south wind arrives, the Huángzhōng note responds;
when the harmonious wind stirs, fish rise to the ice.
． From "Hòu Hàn Shū: Cài Yōng Zhuàn".
When virtue permeates the wilds,
benevolent beasts gather there.
From "Hòu Hàn Shū".
When the winged dragon soars,
clouds and mists densely follow;
when the raging wind bursts forth in anger,
countless apertures howl without prior agreement,
for things naturally move each other.
． From "Táng Shū: Péi Jì Zàn".
The shadow resembles the form,
the echo rushes to the sound,
moving in tandem, each responding according to its kind.
From "Táng Shū".
Biographies:
The ox of Wù pants at the sight of the moon.
From "Shì Shuō Xīn Yǔ".
Clams, crabs, pearls, and turtles
wax and wane with the moon.
From "Kuàijī Xiānxián Zhuàn".
Mussels, clams, turtles, and pearls
wax and wane with the moon.
The moon
is the essence of the great yīn.
Hence, creatures like turtles and clams
flourish or decline accordingly.
"Lǚshì Chūnqiū" says: "At the full moon, clams are full;
at the new moon, clams are empty."
From "Dà Dài Lǐ".
They chirp when frost descends.
From "Shānhǎi Jīng".
The sun emerges and roosters crow,
responding by kind.
From "Chūnqiū Shuō".
When ants seal their nest entrances,
heavy rain is approaching.
From Jiāo Gòng's "Yì Lín".
When the Táng dynasty musical bells were scattered,
they were missing only the zhǐ note.
Lǐ Sìzhēn found a bell on a funeral carriage,
entered and shook it in the southeast corner,
and indeed there was a response.
Thereupon, they dug
and found a piece of stone,
which they divided into four parts,
filling the missing gaps in the musical bells.
From "Dà Zhōu Zhèng".
Collections:
Those with the same tone harmonize,
those of the same kind resemble each other.
Flying birds call to their flock,
deer cry to seek their companions.
From "Chǔ Cì".
Strike the gōng note and gōng responds,
pluck the jué note and jué vibrates.
When a tiger roars, valley winds arise;
when a dragon rises, auspicious clouds follow.
The resonance of sounds
speaks to how things of like nature influence one another.
Same as above.
Call and response echo,
mates and pairs follow each other.
From "Xuǎn Shī".
The pearl in the clam's womb
waxes and wanes with the moon.
From "Xuǎn Dōngdū Fù".
When hidden thunder comes from heaven,
insects have already heard it;
when floating clouds appear in the Milky Way,
the pillar bases are the first to be moistened.
From Rén Xiàogōng's memorial.
Classics
If you make sweet wine,
you are the yeast;
if you prepare a harmonious soup,
you are the salt and plum.
From "Shū·Shuō Mìng Xià".
Only the Duke of Zhōu could carefully begin it,
only Jūn Chén could harmonize its middle,
only the Duke could complete its end.
From "Bì Mìng".
In drafting decrees,
Bì Chén would draft them,
Shì Shū would discuss them,
the messenger Zǐyǔ would polish them,
and Dōnglǐ Zǐchǎn would refine them.
From "Yǔ".
See also "The strength of many is hard to achieve".
History
Yànzǐ said: "Harmony is like a soup,
where water, fire, vinegar, sauce, salt, and plums are used to cook fish and meat,
heated with firewood.
The chef blends them,
balances the flavors,
adding what is lacking
and reducing what is excessive.
The gentleman eats it
to calm his heart."
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn·Zhāo 20".
The wise plan,
the brave act,
the benevolent guard.
From "Gǔliáng Zhuàn".
Metal, wood, water, and fire,
firm and soft complement each other,
then achieving harmony,
can be put to use.
From "Dōng Hàn Yuán Tán Zhuàn".
Gathering essence and uniting spirit,
they enhance each other's brilliance.
Even if Bóyá played the Dì Zhōng
or Féng Ménzǐ drew the Wū Háo bow,
it would not suffice to illustrate their meaning.
Thus, a sage ruler must await worthy ministers to expand his achievements,
and talented scholars also await enlightened rulers to display their virtue.
From "Tōng Jiàn·Hàn Xuān Jì".
Yuè Guǎng excelled in clear conversation but not in writing;
when about to resign his post,
he asked Pān Yuè to draft his memorial.
People of the time all said: "If Yuè did not borrow Pān's pen,
and Pān did not adopt Yuè's ideas,
they could not have achieved such excellence."
From "Jìn Shū".
Táng historians praised Yuán Chóng for adeptly adapting to accomplish the world's affairs,
and Sòng Jǐng for skillfully upholding principles to maintain the world's integrity.
Though their ways differed,
they both achieved order.
From "Táng Shū·Sòng Jǐng Zhuàn".
See also "Different paths lead to the same end".
Lǐ Huá composed the "Yuán Déxiù Stele",
Yán Zhēnqīng inscribed it,
Lǐ Yángbīng carved the seal script heading.
Later people vied to copy it,
calling it the "Stele of Three Perfections".
From "Táng Shū".
See also "Admiration and yearning".
Wáng Yìfāng said: "The Son of Heaven appoints dukes, ministers, senior officials, and scholars,
desiring them to complement each other like water and fire,
or salt and plum enhancing one another.
They should not insist solely on their own right or wrong."
From "Táng Shū·Běn Zhuàn".
Biographies
A precious fur coat is warm due to many pelts,
a grand hall is built with numerous materials.
From "Shǐ Tōng".
Also included in "The strength of many is hard to achieve".
Under heaven, there is no pure white fox,
yet there are pure white fur coats,
made from many white pieces.
From "Lǚshì Chūnqiū".
Collections
Scholars who achieve great fame and prominence in their time
all have predecessors of renown
paving the way for them.
Those whose glorious legacy shines on later generations
also all have successors of renown
carrying it forward.
Without predecessors,
even excellence remains obscure;
without successors,
even grandeur does not endure.
These two types of people
are invariably interdependent.
From Hán Yù's "Letter to Yú Dí".
Common scholars,
living in poverty and obscurity,
must rely on the influence of nobles and officials
to achieve their aspirations;
nobles and officials with illustrious achievements
must borrow the praise of common scholars
to spread their fame.
Thus, common scholars,
though humble, need not flatter;
nobles and officials,
though exalted, need not be arrogant.
Their circumstances require mutual support,
and their roles provide for each other in sequence.
Same as above,
from "Letter to Secretary Xíng of Fèngxiáng".
Predecessors,
with the right person to rely on,
see their virtue manifest and fame spread;
successors,
with the right person to guide them,
achieve illustrious careers and attain rank.
Same as above, from "Seeing Off Magistrate Xǔ of Yǐngzhōu".
Wǔ Dīng,
a worthy ruler,
and Fù Yuè,
a worthy minister—
Wǔ Dīng cited metal sharpened on a whetstone to command his minister,
while Yuè used wood straightened by the ink-line to admonish his ruler.
From Lù Xuàn's writings.
Those skilled in governing
spread benevolence to nurture authority,
and nurture authority to honor benevolence.
Authority, when nurtured, remains unbroken;
benevolence, when honored, bestows grace.
Same as above.
Silk and tong wood differ in nature, yet their sounds blend naturally.
From "Wéi Yìngwù Collection".
Ice and jade shine together,
pepper and orchid share their fragrance.
From Zhāng Jiǔlíng's writings.
Ice placed in a white jade pot
first reveals its clarity and purity.
Pearls strung on deep red threads
first show their bright transparency.
From "Yuán Zhěn Collection".
Like many streams converging,
forming a great river;
clouds rising from numerous peaks,
blending into one atmosphere.
From "Lǚ Héshū Collection".
See also "The strength of many is hard to achieve".
Our Dynasty
Duānxī inkstone from Xuānchéng's control,
Wángwū pine soot and purple hare brush;
adding the old minister's calligraphy,
nothing in the world matches these five excellences.
From "Luánchéng Collection".
History
Now two tigers fight,
and inevitably, one must perish.
From "Tōng Jiàn".
See also "Inevitably opposed".
Zhū, Péng, Guàn, and Jiǎ,
heroes of their time,
attacking each other out of love and hate,
could worry the state.
Like insects biting each other,
they only end up harming themselves.
From "Hòu Hàn Shū·Kǒng Róng Zhuàn".
Those who contend with wisdom are exhausted,
those who contend with strength are defeated.
From "Tōng Jiàn·Hàn Xiàn Jì".
Biographies
Hán Lú,
the fastest hound in the world;
Dōngdū Qūn,
the craftiest hare in the world.
Lú pursued Qūn,
circling the mountain three times,
the hare exhausted itself ahead,
the hound collapsed behind,
and both hound and hare died.
*Strategies of the Warring States*.
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ was about to stab a tiger,
when Biàn Shùzǐ said: "Two tigers are feeding on an ox.
The ox is tasty, so they will surely fight over it;
fighting will lead to combat,
in which the larger will be injured
and the smaller will die.
Then stab the injured one,
and with one move, you will gain the fame of capturing two tigers."
Shortly after,
the two tigers indeed fought,
the larger was injured,
and the smaller died.
*Later Narratives of the Spring and Autumn*.
Sū Dài said: "I passed by a small stream
and saw a small clam just emerging to sun itself,
when a snipe pecked at its flesh,
and the clam closed, trapping its beak.
The snipe said: 'If it doesn't rain today,
nor tomorrow,
there will be dried clam meat.'
The clam also said: 'If you don't come out today,
nor tomorrow,
there will be a dead snipe.'"
Neither would yield to the other,
and a fisherman caught them both.
*Later Narratives of the Spring and Autumn*.
Cross-reference: "Yielding advantage to others."
Classics
The way of the noble person
is to either emerge or withdraw,
to either remain silent or speak.
*Yi Xici*.
Ways run parallel without conflicting.
*Record of the Doctrine of the Mean*.
Cross-reference: "Different paths lead to the same goal."
The Master said: "Those whose paths differ
do not consult with each other."
*Analects*.
Wēizǐ left them,
Jīzǐ became a slave,
and Bǐgān remonstrated and died.
*Analects*.
History
Wǔ Yún and Shēn Bāoxū were friends.
When he fled,
he told Bāoxū: "I will surely restore the state of Chǔ."
Bāoxū said: "Strive hard!
If you can restore it,
I will surely be able to revive it."
*Zuo Tradition, 14th Year of Duke Dìng*.
Zǐ Hǎn said:
"I regard not being greedy as my treasure,
while you regard jade as your treasure.
If you give it to me,
we both lose our treasures.
It is better for each to keep their own treasure."
*Zuo Tradition, 15th Year of Duke Xiāng*.
"Different capacities."
Chǔ's Wǔ Shàng said to his brother Yún: "You go to Wú,
I will return to die.
I can die,
and you can seek revenge."
*Zuo Tradition, 20th Year of Duke Zhāo*.
Zhāng Sǒng said: "Each person has their own nature,
and decides their own strengths and weaknesses.
If you want me to be like you, I cannot,
and if I imitate you, I will also fail."
*Western Hàn, Biography of Chén Zūn*.
Cross-reference: "Each has their own strengths."
Xiāo Wàngzhī became a court gentleman by taking the examination,
and was assigned as guard of the Small Garden East Gate.
Wáng Zhòngwēng had a grand entourage and was highly favored,
and turning to Wàngzhī, he said: "Unwilling to be ordinary,
you instead hold a gatekeeper's post?"
Wàngzhī said: "Each follows their own will."
Same as above,
*Biography of Xiāo Wàngzhī*.
Wáng Yáng was the governor of Yìzhōu,
and on his inspection tour, he reached the Jiǔzhébǎn slope at Ánglái,
and sighed: "Having received my parents' legacy,
how can I repeatedly risk such danger!"
Later, he resigned due to illness.
When Wáng Zūn became governor,
and reached that slope,
he asked his official: "Isn't this the path Wáng Yáng feared?"
The official replied: "Yes."
Zūn urged his driver: "Drive on!
Wáng Yáng was a filial son,
Wáng Zūn is a loyal minister."
*Biography of Wáng Zūn*,
also same as above.
Wǔ was perfectly virtuous,
yet ultimately preserved the purity of Gūzhú.
*Later Hàn, Biographies of Hermits*.
Yuán Yì advised Cài Xīngzōng: "Uncle, you should now take up residence west of Shǎn,
while I am in Xiāng and Miǎn;
if anything happens,
we can jointly achieve the merits of Huán and Wén."
Xīngzōng said: "You wish to secure safety outside,
I wish to avoid disaster at the center;
each follows their own will,
is that not good!"
*Comprehensive Mirror, Sòng Míng Records*.
When Shěn Qìngzhī died,
his son, court attendant Wénshū, wanted to flee,
and said to his brother, mid-level court official Wénjì: "I can die,
and you can seek revenge."
Thereupon, he drank Qìngzhī's poison and died.
Wénjì took up a blade, mounted a horse, and departed.
Same as above,
*Sòng Tàizǔ*.
Mǎ Shū said: "Those who value rank and emolument regard Cháo and Yóu as fetters;
those who love mountains and forests regard Yī and Lǚ as petty officials;
those bound by name and reality see the words of the pillar officials as worthless,
while those who delight in purity and emptiness consider the discourses at banquets as chaff."
*Chén History, His Biography*.
Also "Different orientations."
Some mingle with the dust of the world,
drifting with the waves as they pass;
others defy the times and correct customs,
gazing toward the rivers and lakes as they go alone.
*Northern History, Preface to Biographies of Hermits*.
Also "Different orientations."
Collections
Valued for utility, then the camphor tree is prized;
cherished for longevity, then the altar oak is esteemed.
Liú Bīnkè.
All beasts dance with the phoenix to the music of Sháoxiāo,
each expressing their utmost joy;
why would they have time to reflect that their forms are unlike?
*Collection of Yuán Wēizhī*.
Tàigōng fought at Mùyě,
Bóyí starved at Shǒuyáng.
Contemporaries called sage and worthy,
their advance and withdrawal did not hinder each other.
*Collection of Bái Lètiān*.
You know the breadth and narrowness within heaven and earth,
eagle, osprey, phoenix, and luan each fly their own way.
Twin phoenixes perch on the parasol tree, fish swim among the algae,
soaring and sinking according to their lot, each carefree.
Also same as above.
This dynasty
Roc and quail, carefree, each aware of their own.
*Línchuān Collection*.
Classics
Kuí,
was proficient in music but not in rites.
*Record, Confucius at Leisure*.
Virtuous conduct: Yán Yuān, Mǐnzǐ Qiān, Rǎn Bóniú, Zhònggōng.
Speech: Zǎi Wǒ, Zǐgòng.
Governance: Rǎn Yǒu, Jìlù.
Culture and learning: Zǐyóu, Zǐxià.
*Analects, Xiānjìn*.
Mèng Gōngchuò would excel as a senior in Zhào or Wèi,
but could not serve as a minister of Téng or Xuē.
*Analects, Xiànwèn*.
Also entered under "Different capacities."
The wisdom of Zāng Wǔzhòng,
the lack of desire of Gōngchuò,
the courage of Biàn Zhuāngzǐ,
the arts of Rǎn Qiú.
All from *Analects*.
Zǐ
Huáliú, Qíjì,
can gallop a thousand miles in a single day,
yet at catching mice, they are no match for the wildcat.
*Zhuāngzǐ*.
To assess the high and low,
inspect the barren and fertile,
and arrange the five grains,
a gentleman is no match for a farmer;
to judge beauty and ugliness,
distinguish the noble and base,
a gentleman is no match for a merchant;
to set the compass and square,
lay out the ink-line,
and prepare tools for use,
a gentleman is no match for a craftsman.
*Xúnzǐ: Rúxiào*.
The day knows not the night,
the moon knows not the day;
the sun and moon are bright, yet they cannot combine their light.
*Huáinánzǐ*.
Xī Zhòng could not become Féng Méng,
Zàofǔ could not become Bólè.
Same as above,
*Chùzhēn Xùn*.
The historian
Píchén was skilled in planning,
but in the wilds he succeeded, while in the city he did not.
*Zuǒzhuàn, Xiānggōng 31*.
Confucius said:
"A good farmer can sow but cannot necessarily reap;
a good craftsman can be skillful but cannot necessarily be compliant."
*Shǐjì: Kǒngzǐ Shìjiā*.
Sòng Yì said to Xiàng Yǔ:
"In donning armor and wielding weapons,
I am no match for you;
in sitting and devising strategies,
you are no match for me."
*Tōngjiàn: Qín Èrshì Jì*.
Fàn Lǐ said:
"Within the borders,
in matters concerning the people,
I am no match for Wén Zhǒng;
beyond the borders,
in controlling enemy states,
and making decisive judgments,
Wén Zhǒng is also no match for me."
*Guóyǔ*.
Huáng Bà's talent lay in governing the people,
but when he became chancellor,
his demeanor fell short of Bǐng and Wèi,
and his achievements were inferior to when he governed commanderies.
*Xīhàn: Huáng Bà Zhuàn*.
Zhāng Sǒng said to Chén Zūn:
"Each person has their own nature,
and their strengths and weaknesses are self-determined.
For you to try to be like me is impossible,
and for me to imitate you would also lead to failure."
Same as above,
*Chén Zūn Zhuàn*.
See also "Each follows their own will."
Xuē Xuān rose from a petty official
to become chancellor.
He was a model for officials of his time,
but when he occupied a high position,
he lost his reputation due to harsh scrutiny,
showing that one's capacity indeed has limits.
*Xīhàn Běnzhuàn*.
Chén Píng said: "In openly rebuking and arguing at court,
I am no match for you;
in preserving the altars of state,
and securing the future of the Liú clan,
you are also no match for me."
Same as above,
*Wáng Líng Zhuàn*.
Zēngzǐ excelled in filial piety,
but he was indeed dull and slow;
in literary arts, he was no match for Zǐyóu and Zǐxià,
and in governance, he was no match for Rǎn and Jì.
Now, if one wishes to combine all these in a single person,
even if there is something admirable,
there will inevitably be deficiencies within.
*Tōngjiàn: Hàn Shùn Jì*.
Zhūgě Liàng excelled in military administration,
but was weak in unconventional strategies;
his ability in governing the people
surpassed his skill in generalship.
*Shǔzhì Běnzhuàn*.
Lǚ Yì governed with simplicity and without complexity,
and was known for his clarity and competence;
but when he held high office,
his reputation suffered compared to when he served in commanderies and counties.
Same as above.
In commanderies, he was praised,
but at court, he was diminished.
Same as above,
*Chén Shòu's Commentary*.
Sūn Cè said to his younger brother Sūn Quán:
"In leading the masses of Jiāngdōng,
making decisive moves between two battle formations,
and contending with the world,
you are no match for me;
in promoting the worthy and appointing the capable,
ensuring each gives their utmost,
and preserving Jiāngdōng,
I am no match for you."
*Wúzhì Běnzhuàn*.
Zhì Yú and Tàishū Guǎng both served as high ministers.
Whenever they attended official gatherings,
Guǎng would speak,
and Yú could not respond;
Yú would write,
and Guǎng could not reply.
Yuè Guǎng was skilled in clear discourse but not in writing;
when he was about to yield his post to Yǐn,
he asked Pān Yuè to draft a memorial for him.
Some people of the time said:
"If Guǎng had not borrowed Yuè's brush,
and Yuè had not adopted Guǎng's ideas,
they could not have achieved such excellence."
*Jìnshū*.
See also "Mutual support achieves excellence."
Xiè Kūn said:
"In presiding solemnly at court,
setting a standard for all officials,
I am no match for Liàng.
(Yǔ Liàng.)
But in roaming hills and valleys,
I consider myself superior."
*Jìnshū*.
Chǔ Tǐng was praised for his practical ability.
When he served as a county clerk,
and a matter did not go well,
the magistrate wanted to whip him.
Tǐng said:
"Each thing has its proper use;
timber fit for rafters is not suitable for fences."
*Jìnshū*.
See also "Great talent used for small tasks."
The ancients said:
"For farming, ask the slave;
for weaving, ask the maid."
This means each has their own abilities.
*Suíshū*.
Shǐ Simíng said:
"Lǐ Guāngbì excels in defending cities;
now he has come out into the open field,
so he will be captured."
*Tōngjiàn*.
Zhūgě Liàng was clear-sighted in governing the state and served as chancellor;
Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi were the bravest in the army and served as generals.
Same as above,
*Hàn Xiàn Jì*.
Biographies
Cáo Mèi, wielding his three-foot sword,
could withstand an entire army;
but if Cáo Mèi were to lay down his three-foot sword
and take up a hoe to work the fields with farmers,
he would be no match for them.
*Zhànguócè*.
When apes and monkeys leave the trees and take to the water,
they are no match for fish and turtles;
when traversing dangers and scaling heights,
even a Qíjì is no match for a fox.
Same as above.
Gù Shào said to Páng Shìyuán:
"Who is better, you or I?"
He replied:
"In molding and refining worldly customs,
floating and sinking with the times,
I am no match for you;
but in discussing the remaining strategies of kings and hegemons,
and observing the crucial points of fortune and misfortune,
I seem to have a slight advantage."
Shào also accepted his words.
*Shìshuō*.
Collection
The qín awaited Jī Zhōngsàn,
the cup thought of Ruǎn Bùbīng.
"Yuán Wēizhī Collection".
Zǐcháng excelled in writing,
and I excel in argument.
Liú Bīnkè.
Lián Pō was skilled in military matters but lacked in literature,
Xiè Tiào was able in literature but not in martial arts.
"Dù Xún Hè Collection".
Heaven creates all things,
but rare is their combined utility,
with inherent strengths,
must come inherent weaknesses,
talents complement each other,
but they also diverge.
When something is fully formed, tools and objects are not left without use; if one seeks perfection, then everything else is discarded.
Therefore, a skillful carpenter follows the wheelwright's function,
thus straight and bent wood is never wasted.
An excellent driver adapts to both rough and smooth terrains,
thus the mediocre and the excellent horse do not lose their nature.
Writings of Lù Xuāngōng.
See "According to the capability of the material, it is utilized".
In our current dynasty,
Chuí was skilled at making bows but could not shoot,
Xī Zhòng was skilled at making carts but could not drive.
Ōu Gōng wrote "Preface to Méi Shèngyú Collection".
All things have what they cannot do,
thus they also have what they are best suited for.
At night, thieves are not deterred by horses,
and during the day, the water clocks are not maintained by roosters.
Writings of Shāngǔ.
Historian Kuǎi Tōng said:
"The dog of Zhī barks at Yáo,
not because of its master's lack of virtue. "
"Records of the Grand Historian".
Jìn abolished the Luán family,
ordered the ministers of Zhèng to not act.
The minister of the Luán family, Xīn Yú, acted,
officials arrested him and presented him to Duke Xiàn,
saying:
"The state has a great command,
why do you defy it?"
He replied:
"From my ancestor's time,
we serve loyally without usurping in the State of Jìn,
and have served the Luán family for three generations now.
Hence, I dare not fail to act."
"Discourses of the States".
Téng Gōng said: "What crime did Jì Bù commit?
Ministers serve their lords as required by duty.

_Huáinánzǐ_.
Some who wish to benefit them,
end up harming them instead;
some who wish to harm them,
instead end up benefiting them.
This reversal of benefit and harm,
this gateway to misfortune and fortune,
must not be left unexamined.
． _Huáinánzǐ_ "Rénjiān Xùn".
Cross-reference "zhì chá".
Histories
Under heaven, sovereigns and worthy men have been numerous,
honored in their time,
but gone when they passed away.
Kǒngzǐ was a commoner,
yet his teachings have been passed down for over ten generations,
and scholars revere him.
． _Shǐjì_ "Kǒngzǐ Shìjiā".
Yōng created resentment yet was first rewarded, oh,
Dīng followed kindness yet was executed.
． _Xī Hàn Bān Gù zhuàn".
White-haired as if newly met,
carriage covers tilted as if old friends.
Ibid.,
"Zōu Yáng zhuàn".
Just like water and fire,
they extinguish yet also give rise to each other.
Benevolence and righteousness,
reverence and harmony,
are opposites yet all complement each other.
． _Xī Hàn Yìwénzhì".
A thousand jūn float, while zīzhū sink.
_Hànshū_.
The soft can overcome the hard,
the weak can overcome the strong.
． _Dōng Hàn Zāng Gōng zhuàn".
Jíe and Zhòu were noble as Sons of Heaven,
yet common servants were ashamed to be compared with them,
because they were without righteousness;
Yí and Qí were lowly as ordinary men,
yet kings and nobles vied to be their companions,
because they had virtue.
． _Tōngjiàn_ "Hàn Shāng Jì".
Those who once were my nursing descendants,
now are all my blood-drinking enemies.
Ibid.,
"Hàn Xiàn Jì".
Empress Wǔ selected men through the Yì,
while Dézōng lost scholars through meticulousness.
． _Tángshū_ "Lù Zhì zhuàn".
Biographies
In the past, when Qín attacked Qí,
it decreed: "Whoever dares to gather firewood within fifty paces of Liǔxià Jì's grave mound,
will be sentenced to death without pardon;
whoever can obtain the head of the King of Qí,
will be enfeoffed with ten thousand households."
From this we see,
the head of a living king is not as good as the grave mound of a dead scholar.
_Zhànguócè_.
Mǎ Yuán was slandered because of job's tears,
Wáng Yáng sought fame because of a leather bag.
_Xù Hànshū_.
Sounds that have sound do not exceed a hundred lǐ,
sounds without sound extend to the four seas.
． _Shuōyuàn_ "Zhènglǐ" chapter.
During Shùndì's reign,
a ballad in the capital said: "Straight as a bowstring,
die by the roadside;
crooked as a hook,
yet become a marquis."
_Fēngsútōng_.
Collections
The omen of mulberry and grain instead brought blessing to Dà Wù,
the auspice of the great bird ultimately became a disaster for Dì Xīn.
_Lǐ Tàibái jí_.
Cross-reference "huò fú yǐ fú".
Yáo's Dānzhū,
Shùn's Shàngjūn,
King Wén's Guǎnshū and Càishū,
their influences were not unwholesome,
yet they ended up wicked;
Gǔsǒu's Shùn,
Gǔn's Yǔ,
their influences were not unvirtuous,
yet they ended up sage.
Hán Wén "Yuán Xìng".
Since ancient times, many have gained position through merit and virtue,
yet do not receive constant sacrifice;
Gōulóng, Qì, and Kǒngzǐ,
all did not gain position,
yet receive constant sacrifice.
But none compare to Kǒngzǐ's greatness.
Hán Wén.
Who would say the younger perish while the elder survive,
the strong die young while the sick remain whole!
Hán "Jì Wén".
The softest instead becomes hard.
Wéi Yìngwù piān.
The king of Shāng prospered because of mulberry and grain,
and grew great because of pheasants crowing;
the ruler of Sòng lived long because of the law star,
Zhèng declined because of dragons,
Lǔ weakened because of the qilin,
the white pheasant doomed Hàn,
the yellow rhinoceros killed Wǎng Mǎng.
Liǔ Wén.
Wealth and honor also have bitterness,
bitterness lies in a heart full of worry.
Poverty and lowliness also have joy,
joy lies in bodily freedom.
_Bái Lètiān jí_.
Sū Wǔ nonetheless returned alive,
while Dèng Tōng ultimately died of hunger.
Dù Mùzhī.
A hundred victories hardly make one adept at assessing the enemy,
three fractures make a good physician.
Liú Bīnkè.
Our dynasty
Glamour and splendor are momentarily delightful,
But in a blink, they scatter like floating clouds.
Simplicity and detachment yield a flavor that grows richer,
Remaining unchanged from start to finish.
From "The Collection of Ōu Gōng."
It is inherent that things may change from a state of peace,
And likewise, one may seek safety through peril.
From Dōngpō's rhapsody.
Throughout my life, I have faced many hardships,
Often testing them with my own person.
All who have saved me from distress
Were people I once held in awe;
Those who pushed me into danger
Were once those I found pleasing.
From Dōngpō's "On Resilience."
Cross-reference: "One knows only after experiencing."
All things must eventually come to an end,
And those relying on form for permanence
Are especially short-lived.
Even the solidity of metal and stone
Can decay in an instant,
While achievements and literary works
That are passed down through generations
Last somewhat longer.
From Dōngpō's "Record of the Ink Marvel Pavilion."
The wealth and status of Zhōu Gōng
Were not as fulfilling as the poverty of Confucius.
With Shào Gōng's virtue
And the kinship of Guǎn and Cài, yet they did not understand his heart—
With whom could Zhōu Gōng share the joy of his wealth?
But those with whom Confucius shared his poverty
Were all talented and virtuous under heaven,
Which was enough to find joy in it.
From Dōngpō's "Letter to Méi Zhíjiǎng."
A flood that reaches the heavens
Cannot last a full morning,
Yet a trickle of water
Can wear through stone.
From Dōngpō.
A forged arrow may not be perfectly crafted,
Yet a stray shot might still hit the target.
From Huáng Shān.
The emperor planted fine orange trees,
But by midlife, many turned to bitter trifoliate oranges.
Ibid.
Gray hair holds no special intent,
Yet across eras, there are kindred voices.
From Hòu Shān.
Cross-reference: "Separation and reunion know no closeness or distance."
Cài Tiānshēn obtained Sīmǎ Guāng's "Epitaph for Lǚ Xiànkě"
And presented it to Wáng Ānshí.
Initially, Tiānshēn intended to incriminate Sīmǎ Guāng.
But Ānshí, upon receiving it,
Hung it on his wall
And said to his disciples: "Jūnshí's writing
Is truly the prose of the Western Hàn!"
From "Records of Things Seen and Heard."
Trusted yet suspected,
Loyal yet slandered.
Classics
Meeting the lord in a narrow lane.
From "The Yìjīng, Guà of Kuí."
Yī Chuān remarked: "A lane is a winding path."
Not before me,
Nor after me.
From "The Book of Songs, 'First Month'."
Why not from the north,
Why not from the south.
From "Who Is This Man?"
History
Encountering the calamity of Yáng Jiǔ,
The convergence of Bǎi Liù.
From "History of the Western Hàn, Biography of Wáng Mǎng."
Collections
It happened precisely at that time.
From "Selected New Discourses."
Just when the people were facing such times.
From Hán Yù's writings.
Masters
The tree desires stillness, but the wind does not cease;
The son wishes to care for his parents, but they do not wait.
From "Family Sayings, 'Reflections on Devotion'."
All people desire wealth, honor, and longevity,
Yet none can avoid the misfortunes of poverty, low status, and early death.
The heart yearns for wealth and long life,
But poverty and premature death occur—
This is failing to reach what one wishes to attain.
From "Hán Fēizǐ, 'Explaining the Lǎo Zǐ'."
The sun and moon wish to shine,
But floating clouds obscure them;
The orchid grove wishes to bloom,
But autumn winds blight it.
From "Wén Zǐ."
History
Yáng Hù of Jìn said: "In life, things not going as wished
Often account for seven or eight out of ten."
From "History of Jìn, His Biography."
Although Xiè Ān accepted the court's commission,
His longing for Dōngshān never faded.
When stationed at Xīnchéng,
He prepared for a sea voyage,
Intending to return east by river
Once his duties were roughly settled.
But then he fell gravely ill.
Feeling his original ambition unfulfilled,
He deeply lamented the loss.
From "History of Jìn, His Biography."
Collections
Catching the opportunity of wind and clouds,
Yet time passes and age advances.
From "Selections of Refined Literature, Wú Jìzhòng's Letter."
Alas, in this place of joy and mirth,
We are no longer in our youth.
From Dù Fǔ's poetry.
When ears go deaf and eyes grow dim,
Music is played in the hall;
When teeth have fallen out,
Meat and wine pile high on the plate.
What comes goes as soon as it arrives,
Leaving excess without inner fulfillment.
From Bái Lètiān.
Glory and youth
Avoid each other like dawn and dusk.
Just as fate begins to favor,
Youth and looks have already departed.
Ibid.
Bound to office at court,
My wishes remain unfulfilled.
From Hán Yù's writings.
Vainly encountering bright sunshine,
Yet how can it dispel the gloom within?
From "The Collection of Yuán Wēizhī."
Our Dynasty
After a year in governance,
Half that time was spent ill.
From Dōngpō's "Stele Inscription for Sīmǎ Guāng."
Greasing the cart and feeding the horse for a long journey,
Aiming to cover a hundred miles in a day from the start.
Unaware of traps along the way,
High mountains, setting sun, and thorny paths.
From "The Collection of Luán Chéng."
Books that delight are quickly finished,
Guests one longs for never come.
So it often is with worldly affairs—
How many times in a lifetime does the heart truly open with joy?
From Hòu Shān.
Fine scenes are rare, and good meetings few.
From "Records of a Weary Traveler."
Classics
There are sprouts that never flower!
And flowers that never bear fruit!
From "The Analects, Zǐ Hǎn."
Masters
Heaven and earth are not all-powerful,
Sages are not all-capable,
And no thing is of all uses.
From "Liè Zǐ, 'The Heavenly Gifts'."
Thus, beautiful wings harm the bones,
Lush branches harm the roots—
To have both perfections
Is impossible under heaven.
From "Huái Nán Zǐ, 'Discourse on Interpretation'."
Yáo had no son,
Shùn had no father—
Better to have Yáo as father and Shùn as son.
From "Yáng Zǐ."
History
Féi Yì said: "If I wish to preserve my words intact,
how can I preserve my person intact?"
. From "Records of the Grand Historian: Hereditary House of Zhào."
Those endowed with teeth are deprived of horns;
those granted wings are given only two legs.
. From "Book of Hàn: Biography of Dǒng Zhòngshū."
Though Qiān was erudite and widely informed,
he could not use his wisdom to preserve himself whole.
Same as above,
"Eulogy for Sīmǎ Qiān."
Fàn Pāng's mother said: "Having already gained a fine reputation,
to further seek long life—
can both be obtained?"
. From "Book of Later Hàn: Biography of Fàn Pāng."
The integrity of loyalty and filial piety
are principles that cannot both stand.
. From "Book of Later Hàn: Biography of Yuán Shào."
Long days mean short nights;
when the sun is in the south, shadows point north.
If Heaven cannot bear to combine them,
how much less can humans encompass both?
Same as above,
"Biography of Zhāng Héng."
Rarely can talent and conduct be combined in one person.
. From "Comprehensive Mirror: Reign of Hàn Hé."
A loyal minister cannot be a filial son.
"Records of Wú."
Those who care for distant matters neglect the near;
those who serve external affairs simplify the internal.
. From "Comprehensive Mirror: Reign of Wèi Míng."
Jìn's Yáng Hù said: "In all under heaven, affairs that go against one's wishes
often account for seven or eight out of ten."
. From "Comprehensive Mirror: Reign of Jìn Wǔ."
Cross-referenced under "Things go contrary to one's wishes."
Zhōu Chǔ said: "The ways of loyalty and filial piety—
how can both be fully achieved!
Once I leave my parents to serve my lord,
how can my parents still have me as a son?"
. From "Book of Jìn: His Biography."
Cross-referenced under "Devote to public duty, forget private interests."
Since ancient times, loyal and worthy men
skilled in planning for the state are often unskillful in managing their own lives—
such cases are many.
. From "Book of Táng: Biography of Wáng Zhōngsì."
Yàng Yóujī's archery could pierce armor,
yet it did not prevent the flight at Yānlíng;
Lù Jī's discernment could analyze causes of downfall,
yet it could not save him from defeat at Héqiáo.
. From "Book of Táng: Biography of Wèi Yuánzhōng."
Biographies record:
Intent cannot be sharp in two directions;
affairs cannot flourish in two aspects.
What flourishes there must decline here;
what is long on the left must be short on the right.
"Garden of Persuasions."
No father is wiser than Yáo, yet his son Dānzhū was arrogant;
no son is wiser than Shùn,
yet his father Gǔsǒu was stubborn;
no elder brother is wiser than Shùn,
yet his brother Xiàng was arrogant;
no younger brother is wiser than the Duke of Zhōu,
yet his brother Guǎnshū was executed;
no minister is wiser than Tāng or Yǔ,
yet their lords Jié and Zhòu were overthrown.
"Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn."
Four-legged creatures lack wings and feathers;
horned creatures lack claws and sharp teeth.
. From "Dàidàilǐ: Chapter on Yì Běnmìng."
The pearl of bright moonlight
cannot be without flaws;
it is not perfectly even.
The jade that glows at night
cannot be without blemishes.
"Shǐ Tōng."
Pleasing petty men,
one incurs the ridicule of gentlemen.
Same as above.
The pheasant displays five colors,
yet flutters only a hundred paces,
for its flesh is abundant and strength heavy;
the eagle and hawk lack brilliance,
yet soar to the heavens,
for their bones are strong and spirit fierce.
"The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons."
Collection:
Sometimes a foot is too short,
sometimes an inch is long enough;
wisdom sometimes fails to discern,
calculation sometimes falls short,
spirit sometimes cannot penetrate.
"Chǔ Cí."
Sweet melons cling to bitter stems;
fine dates grow on thorny branches.
Ancient poem.
Gǔsǒu had keen ears but lacked Líng Lún's discernment.
. From "Xuǎn: Linked Pearls."
Beautiful objects often suffer from falsity;
ugly vessels are mostly sturdy.
Wèi's Ruǎn Yǔ "On Ornament and Substance."
Fine seasons, beautiful scenes,
joyful hearts, pleasurable events—
these four are hard to combine.
. Xiè Língyùn "Preface to Imitating the Crown Prince of Wèi's Collection of Poems from Yèzhōng."
Pearls that outshine chariots cannot be without blemishes;
jades worth multiple cities cannot be without flaws.
Lù Zhì "Memorials."
Life is half sorrow and half joy;
heaven and earth have both smooth and adverse courses.
Dù's poetry.
Lychee is no famous flower;
peony bears no sweet fruit.
Bái's poetry.
On moonlit, clear-breezed mid-month nights,
while ten thousand people enjoy themselves, one man grieves.
Same as above.
Having already stolen fame in one's time,
yet also wanting to grasp the wealth and honor of the age—
if you were the Creator,
would you grant both to one person?
"Collected Works of Bái."
Poets, fate thin, mostly lack rank;
generals, merit high, seldom possess literary grace.
Same as above.
With the talent of Yáng and Sīmǎ,
they knew not of moral transformation;
with the way of Xún and Chén,
they knew not of literary composition.
Liǔ Miǎn "On Literature."
Cross-referenced under "Gain here, lose there."
Crossing the river together,
the timing depends on the wind:
those going downstream meet good fortune,
those going upstream meet misfortune;
farming the fields together,
the timing depends on moisture:
some reap the benefit of early sowing,
others suffer the plight of late planting.
Liú Bīnkè.
Cross-referenced under "Circumstances differ."
Guāngwǔ emerged from a collateral line,
Shǎokāng did not reach his father as ruler.
"Collected Works of Wáng Wéi."
Sun and moon, lofty and bright,
sometimes decline and set;
pearls and jade, pure and flawless,
are not free from imperfections.
Oūyáng Zhān's writings.
Complete success is hard to maintain;
great fame is hard to uphold.
The sun blazes by day but lacks serene charm;
the moon gleams by night but gives no warming light.
Lǐ Wénráo.
Eagles and hawks are not trained for galloping;
thoroughbreds are not assigned for soaring.
Same as above.
Zhōu Bó and Huò Guāng, though they had meritorious deeds,
knew not the ways of Confucian scholarship;
Méi Gāo and Yán Jì excelled in literary composition,
yet never reached the court's high halls.
High rank brings near disaster;
great wealth often lacks benevolence.
Both same as above.
To be both close to parents and noble in rank—
since ancient times, rarely combined.
Lǎo Lái could only vainly display colorful garments,
much ashamed of official insignia;
Pān Yuè could only offer longevity wine,
truly lacking in ceremonial vessels.
Sīkōng Tǔshèng's writings.
The worthy need not be noble;
the long-lived need not be worthy.
"Collected Works of Huángfǔ Shí."
Jīng jade cannot be without flaws;
Suí pearls cannot be without blemishes.
"Táng Wén Cuì."
Praised highly for a thousand years,
yet his way was thwarted in his time.
Heaven gave him talent,
but man denied him destiny.
Same as above.
Our dynasty
The learning of a noble person,
whether applied in their career
or manifested in their writings,
often suffers from the difficulty of excelling in both.
For those who encounter favorable times,
their achievements shine in the court,
and their fame is glorified in historical records,
so they often regard writing as a trivial matter,
and moreover, some lack the time or ability for it.
As for those who are frustrated in their ambitions,
living in obscurity and poverty,
they ponder with a troubled mind and extreme concentration,
and all their feelings of indignation and having no outlet in the world
are poured into their literary compositions.
Hence it is said that the words of the distressed are easily refined,
such as Liǔ Zōngyuán and Liǔ Yǔxī of the Táng, uncelebrated for their careers,
while Yáo Chóng and Sòng Jǐng left no mark in literature.
Even these four individuals could not achieve both,
let alone those beneath them!
From Ōu Yángxiū's "Collected Works of Hán Jiǎnsù."
One person in a hundred generations,
a moment in a thousand years.
Only time and such individuals,
rarely matched, often extraordinary.
From Sū Shì's "Eulogy for Sīmǎ Guāng."
Only literature is immortal,
and having a son is like not dying.
Even those wealthy, noble, and long-lived,
may not necessarily have both.
From Sū Shì's "Eulogy for Liǔ Zōngyuán."
Farming desires rain, reaping desires sun;
those leaving with the wind are envied by those coming against it.
If every prayer were answered,
the Creator would need a thousand changes a day.
From Sū Shì's poem.
Thus destined to be poor to the bone,
yet wishing for endless life.
Same as above.
Jiǎ Yì of the Hàn,
eloquent and brilliant,
only reached the rank of a feudal lord's minister,
while Chén Píng and his kind
truly became high officials;
Hán Yù of the Táng,
upright and outstanding,
ended as the governor of the capital,
while Péi Dù and his peers
truly served as chancellors.
Chén Píng and Péi Dù can hardly be called literary,
while Hán Yù and Jiǎ Yì often lamented their lack of opportunity.
For in this world, individuals
must have strengths and weaknesses;
and Heaven, in endowing people,
cannot grant everything.
From the "Luánchéng Collection."
See also "Things Contrary to Expectation."
Since ancient times, beauties have often been fated to suffer.
By Chén Shīdào.
Classics
Like planning a journey without moving,
thus one cannot advance on the road.
From "Máo's Commentary on the Shījīng, Xiǎo Mín": "Sitting to plan distances without walking,
this means not moving a step forward on the road."
History
Hearing is not as good as seeing.
From the "Book of Later Hàn, Biography of Mǎ Yuán."
Hearsay differs from actual facts,
calculations afar differ from facing the situation.
From the "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn."
Zhào Chōngguó said: "A hundred hearings are not as good as one sight.
Military matters are hard to assess from afar;
I wish to rush to Jīnchéng,
to draw maps and present strategies."
From the "Book of Hàn, Biography of Zhào Chōngguó."
Classics
The state and the world
can be well-governed;
ranks and emoluments
can be declined;
sharp blades
can be trodden upon;
but the Mean
cannot be achieved.
From the "Record of the Mean."
The Master said: "To be poor and without resentment is difficult;
to be rich and without arrogance is easy."
From the "Analects, Xiàn Wèn."
Masters
To carry Mount Tài under one's arm and leap over the North Sea,
and tell someone, 'I cannot,'
is truly being unable.
To break a twig for an elder,
and say, 'I cannot,'
is not being unable,
but unwilling.
From the "Mèngzǐ."
The day before Jiǎ is easy,
the day after Jiǎ is hard.
From "Yáng Xiānzhī."
A guest painting for the King of Qí
was asked, "What is hardest to paint?"
He said, "Dogs and horses are hardest."
"What is easiest?"
He said, "Ghosts and spirits are easiest."
Dogs and horses
are known to everyone,
seen day and night,
and hard to depict accurately,
so difficult.
Ghosts and spirits,
having no form,
and being formless,
cannot be seen,
so easy.
From the "Hánfēizǐ."
Yǔ could channel rivers and dredge waterways
to benefit the world,
but could not make water flow west;
Jì could open fields and clear wilderness for the people to farm,
but could not make grain grow in winter.
From the "Huáinánzǐ."
History
Carving metal and stone is hard to achieve,
breaking dry rot is easy to accomplish.
The way of officials is to learn from laws and decrees,
which can be asked and known;
but ability or inability
depends on innate talent,
how can it be learned?
From the "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn."
Those who accomplish deeds
are easily recognized for their merits;
those who plan at the outset
are hard to discern due to hidden principles.
From the "Book of Later Hàn, Biography of Pī Tóng."
Wèi's Hán Xiǎnzōng said: "For craftsmen's families to adopt scholars' customs and rites,
a hundred years may not suffice;
for scholars' sons to mimic craftsmen's manners,
one day is enough."
From the "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Sòng Records."
Biographies
Loyalty in times of order is easy,
loyalty in times of chaos is hard.
From the "Lǚshì Chūnqiū."
Collections
More precarious than piled eggs,
harder than ascending to heaven;
easier than turning the palm,
more secure than Mount Tài.
From the "Wénxuǎn."
Measuring the sky with a gnomon,
lengths can be gauged;
fathoming water by the abyss,
depths are hard to discern.
From the "Wénxuǎn, Series of Pearls."
Strength can be forced to achieve results,
but the mind cannot be forced to gain wisdom.
From Hán Yù's prose.
Changing the new to the old is easy,
maintaining the old as new is hard.
From Mèng Jiāo.
This Dynasty
The Way can be learned through study,
virtue can be achieved through effort,
but the insight to know people cannot be learned,
it must come from natural talent.
Like Xiāo Hé recognizing Hán Xìn,
how could there be a method to pass on?
From Sū Shì's "Response to the Imperial Examination."
Just as rivers shift their courses,
to manage them by following their flow
is easy to accomplish;
to force them back against their will
is hard to achieve.
From Sū Shì's "Memorial on the Examination System."
Masters
Even with Lí Lóu's keen eyesight,
and Gōngshūzǐ's ingenuity,
without compass and square,
one cannot form circles and squares;
even with Shī Kuàng's acute hearing,
without the six pitch pipes,
one cannot correct the five notes.
． _Mèngzǐ: Lí Lóu I_.
Even robbers have their principles.
_Zhuāngzǐ_.
Gōngshū cannot surpass the marking line.
． _Xúnzǐ: Fǎ Xíng_.
To abandon laws and govern,
even Yáo could not rectify a single state.
If impartial officials uphold the law,
and clumsy craftsmen hold to compass, square, and measurements,
then not one in ten thousand will be lost.
_Hánfēizǐ_.
Without a plumb line,
even Lǔ Bān cannot determine straight and crooked.
_Huáinánzǐ_.
Cutting wood to make chess pieces,
scraping leather to make a ball,
all have their methods.
_Yángzǐ_.
History
It is like hunting:
if one is skilled in archery and charioteering, one can capture game;
but if one has never mounted a chariot or shot an arrow,
one will fear only defeat and overturning,
how could there be leisure to think of capturing game?
． _Zuǒzhuàn: Xiānggōng 30_.
If not trained to be an official,
look to accomplished affairs.
． _Western Hàn: Biography of Jiǎ Yì_.
In planning affairs, one must consult ancestors;
in issuing decrees, one must consult ancient sayings.
． _Western Hàn: Biography of Hán Ān Guó_.
Classics
If ascending to a height,
one must start from below.
If traveling afar,
one must start from near.
． _Shūjīng: Tàijiǎ III_.
When a gentleman builds a residence,
the ancestral temple comes first,
stables and storerooms next,
living quarters last.
． _Lǐjì: Qū Lǐ II_.
In all painting, applying colors comes after the plain groundwork.
． _Zhōulǐ: Kǎogōng Jì_.
In all household creation,
sacrificial vessels come first,
utensils for daily use come last.
Ibid.
None enter a room without going through the door.
． _Lǐjì: Jūn Lǐ_.
The way of the gentleman,
is like traveling afar must start from nearby,
like ascending high must start from low.
_Zhōngyōng_.
Things have roots and branches,
affairs have beginnings and ends.
Knowing what comes first and what follows,
then one is close to the Way.
_Dàxué_.
The Master said: "In painting, applying colors comes after the plain groundwork."
． _Lúnyǔ: Bā Yì_.
Masters
If the hall is not swept,
then one cannot attend to weeding the wild grasses in the outskirts.
． _Xúnzǐ: Qiáng Guó_ note: "If the hall is not yet cleaned,
one cannot look after the grasses in the outskirts."
If the dyer applies blue first and then black, it is acceptable;
if black first and then blue, it is not;
if the artisan applies lacquer first and then cinnabar, it is acceptable;
if cinnabar first and then lacquer, it is not.
All things are like this,
so precedence and sequence,
cannot be disregarded.
． _Huáinánzǐ: Shuō Shān Xùn_.
History
Qiáo has heard that one learns before entering government,
but has not heard of learning through governing.
． _Zuǒzhuàn: Xiānggōng 31_.
It is like sailing a boat:
though one does not cross the swift current directly,
one should gradually proceed along it,
slowly steering toward the destination,
and then one can cross.
_Zīzhì Tōngjiàn_.
Collections
Spring rain moistens the tree,
from leaves to roots.
_Wénxuǎn_.
To make branches and leaves flourish,
one must first save the roots and trunk.
Bái Jūyì.
Our Dynasty
Nowadays, those praised as good at cursive script may not master regular or running script—
this is utterly mistaken.
Regular script gives rise to running script,
running script gives rise to cursive;
regular is like standing,
running is like walking,
cursive is like running;
none can run without being able to stand or walk.
Dōngpō's _Comments on the Calligraphy of the Six Tang Masters_.
Masters
A man who lost his axe
suspected his neighbor's son:
watching his gait,
it seemed like stealing an axe;
his expression,
like stealing an axe;
his speech,
like stealing an axe;
every movement and manner seemed that of a thief.
Soon after, he dug in his valley and found his axe.
Another day,
he saw his neighbor's son again,
and his movements and manner bore no resemblance to a thief.
． _Lièzǐ: Shuō Fú_ chapter.
Cross-reference "Mind follows after events."
History
Zāng Wénzhòng,
after his death,
his words stood.
． From "Zuǒ Xiāng 25".
When Zǐchǎn had been in government for one year,
the people chanted about him: "They take our clothes and hats and store them away,
they take our fields and plots and organize them.
Whoever kills Zǐchǎn,
we will join him!"
After three years,
they chanted again: "We have sons and younger brothers,
Zǐchǎn teaches them.
We have fields and plots,
Zǐchǎn makes them prosper.
If Zǐchǎn were to die,
who would succeed him?"
． From "Zuǒ Xiāng 30".
Zǐshùn said: "It has long been impossible to discuss beginnings with the people!
Those in ancient times who were good at governance,
could not avoid slander at first.
When Zǐchǎn was minister of Zhèng,
it took three years for the slander to stop;
when our former lord was minister of Lǔ,
it took three months for the slander to stop.
Now that I am newly in government,
though I cannot match the worthies,
how could I know about slander!"
． From "Shì Jiān Zhōu Jì".
Zǐshùn said: "When our former lord was minister of Lǔ,
people chanted: 'In fawn fur and apron,
cast him away without fault;
in apron and fawn fur,
cast him away without blame.'
After three months,
when governance had transformed,
the people chanted again: 'In fur robes and ceremonial cap,
truly we get what we desire;
in ceremonial cap and fur robes,
he benefits us without selfishness.'"
Same as above.
After Zhāng Tāng died,
his family assets were worth no more than five hundred gold.
His brothers and sons wanted to bury him lavishly,
but his mother said: "Tāng was a great minister to the Son of Heaven,
who died with a tarnished reputation from evil words,
why bury him lavishly!"
They carried him in an ox cart,
with a coffin but no outer coffin.
When the Son of Heaven heard this,
he then fully investigated and executed the three Chief Clerks.
． From "Tōng Jiàn Hàn Wǔ Jì".
Liú Jìng was sent to the Xiōngnú,
and upon return said: "They cannot be attacked."
At that time, Hàn troops had already marched.
The Emperor was angry,
and had Jìng imprisoned in shackles.
When they reached Píngchéng,
the Xiōngnú surrounded the Emperor,
and it took seven days to break free.
The Emperor pardoned Jìng,
saying: "I did not heed your advice,
and thus was trapped at Píngchéng.
I have already executed the previous ten envoys who said they could be attacked."
He then enfeoffed Jìng as a marquis.
． From "Shǐ Běn Zhuàn".
Whenever Chōngguó submitted a memorial,
it was immediately given to the ministers and councilors for discussion.
Initially, those who agreed with Chōngguó's plan were three in ten,
midway five in ten,
and finally eight in ten.
． From "Xī Hàn Běn Zhuàn".
Where he served, he had no illustrious reputation,
but after leaving, he was often remembered.
． From "Xī Hàn Hé Wǔ Zhuàn".
Only after death,
is right and wrong finally determined.
From "Sīmǎ Qiān Zhuàn".
Wáng Yì and Yán Yóu said to Huán Tán: "You often praise Yáng Xióng's writings,
could they possibly be passed down to later generations?"
Tán said: "They will definitely be passed down.
It's just that you and I will not live to see it."
More than forty years have passed since Xióng's death until now,
and his "Fǎ Yán" has become widely circulated.
From "Yáng Xióng Zhuàn",
also in "Xī Hàn".
In the past, Biàn Hé presented a treasure,
and suffered severed feet as a result;
Língjūn offered loyalty,
and ultimately drowned himself.
Yet the jade of Héshì,
shone for a thousand years;
the writings of Qūzǐ,
are admired by all generations.
． From "Dōng Hàn Bān Gù Zhuàn".
Chén Shí served as an Officer of Merit,
when the Palace Regular Attendant Hóu Lǎn requested the Grand Administrator Gāo Lún to appoint an official,
Lún instructed to assign him as a Literary Scholar.
Shí knew the man was unsuitable,
and carrying the document requested an audience.
He said: "This man should not be appointed,
but the Regular Attendant Hóu's request cannot be refused.
I beg to appoint him externally."
Lún agreed.
Local opinion found the appointment strange.
Lún later explained to others: "I previously appointed an official for Regular Attendant Hóu,
Chén Jūn secretly returned the instruction to me,
and made the appointment externally.
I heard critics faulted him for this,
this blame was due to my fear of powerful forces,
Chén Jūn can be said to be one who claims faults as his own."
Shí thus took the blame upon himself,
and those who heard sighed in admiration.
Same as above,
from "Běn Zhuàn".
Cross-reference to "Sharing Blame".
Some critics mocked Chén Qún for holding office silently.
During the Zhèngshǐ era,
an edict was issued to compile memorials from ministers into "Famous Ministers' Memorials",
and court officials then saw Qún's admonitions,
all sighing in admiration.
．． From "Tōng Jiàn Sān Guó Wèi Míng Jì".
Yuè Guǎng served as Imperial Secretary,
and wherever he served, he had no remarkable achievements at the time,
yet after leaving,
he was remembered by later people.
From "Jìn Shū".
Initially,
when Wáng Dūn raised troops.
Zhōu Yǐ submitted a memorial to save Wáng Dǎo,
with very earnest words.
Dǎo did not know about the rescue,
and held a grudge against him.
After Dūn killed Yǐ,
Dǎo later sorted through old documents in the Secretariat,
and saw Yǐ's memorial pleading for him,
with sincere and earnest words.
He held the memorial and wept.
． From "Jìn Shū Zhōu Yǐ Zhuàn".
Wáng Dǎo said: "People say I am confused,
but later generations will remember this confusion."
From "Shì Shuō".
In office, he had no contemporary praise,
but after leaving, he was remembered by people.
． From "Jìn Shū Xiè Ān Zhuàn".
Jìn's Wáng Xún said: "Wáng Líng argued at court,
Chén Píng was cautious and silent,
but what matters is how things turn out in the end?"
． From "Tōng Jiàn Jìn Shū".
Yáng Chéng held the position of Remonstrance Official,
scholars thought he would die at his post,
and the world feared him more.
After accepting the appointment,
other remonstrance officials debated trivial matters incessantly,
and the Emperor grew weary and annoyed,
while Chéng gradually became familiar with gains and losses,
yet still refused to speak.
Hán Yù wrote "Essay on the Remonstrance Official" to criticize him.
After eight years in office,
people still could not discern his limits.
When Péi Yánlíng falsely accused and exiled Lù Zhì and others,
the Emperor was furious,
and no one dared to speak.
Chéng submitted a memorial strongly condemning Yánlíng's crimes,
passionately invoking righteousness,
and defending Zhì and others,
for several days without cease.
Listeners were chilled with fear,
but Chéng grew more determined.
． From "Táng Shū Běn Zhuàn".
Cross-reference to "Cannot Be Measured Shallowly" and "Cannot Be Fathomed".
If the worthy cannot achieve their ambitions in the present,
they will surely gain honor in the future,
all ancient writers were like this.
． From "Táng Liǔ Zōngyuán Zhuàn".
Biography
In the second year of Tiānhàn,
the Western Kingdom of Huánshān presented Lute-Mending Glue and Jíguāng Fur Robe.
The Emperor received them and stored them in the treasury,
unaware of the wonders of these two items.
Considering the tribute unremarkable,
he detained the envoy without sending him back.
When the Emperor visited Huálín Garden,
he shot a tiger but his crossbow broke,
the envoy accompanying the cortege offered a portion of the glue,
and moistened it with his mouth to mend the string.
The Emperor was astonished,
then had several warriors pull it opposite ways,
but it did not break all day.
The fur robe did not sink after a month in water,
nor burn when put in fire.
The Emperor valued it greatly, richly rewarded the envoy, and sent him back.
From "Shí Zhōu Jì".
The wood of Yùzhāng,
takes seven years to distinguish from the outside.
From "Guǎng Zhì".
Collection
Though spring blossoms are fair,
They await autumn's fruit;
Though water-polished jade gleams,
It awaits the sun's revelation.
From Péi Zhǐ's "Admonitions for Women Historians" of Jìn.
Wén Zhòng passed, yet his words endure;
Zǐ Chǎn perished, but his benevolent legacy remains.
From "The Collected Works of Zhāng Jiǔlíng".
Peach and plum blossoms may seem lonely in their prime,
But after frost and snow, they flourish verdant.
From Lǐ Yìshān's writings.
An arrow may miss the target at first shot,
Yet refined copper is known only after repeated smelting.
From "The White Compilation".
Testing jade requires three full days of firing,
Judging timber demands a seven-year wait.
When Duke of Zhōu feared slanderous rumors,
And Wáng Mǎng feigned humility before usurpation –
Had they died in those moments,
Who would discern their true nature through ages?
By Bái Jūyì.
Through countless washings and siftings, though arduous,
Only when wild sand is blown away does gold appear.
By Liú Yǔxī.
Blessings may not rest upon oneself,
But fortune surely flows to descendants.
From "Táng Wén Cuì".
Most who gain no renown in life
Earn lasting fame after death.
Yáng Xióng's "Model Sayings" flourished posthumously,
While Sīmǎ Qiān's "Records" went unrecognized in his lifetime.
From "The Collected Works of Liǔ Zōngyuán".
One may praise antiquity freely,
But dare not judge the present.
Huán Tán also said: "Having seen Yáng Zǐyún's unimpressive appearance,
Who would transmit his works?
Even with Zhuāng Zhōu's breadth,
Qū Yuán's pathos,
Mèng Kē's depth,
Lǐ Sī's vigor,
Sīmǎ Qiān's rigor,
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's richness,
Jiǎ Yì's clarity,
or Yáng Xióng's focus –
were they contemporaries,
The world's sages would be rare indeed."
Thus we see
Ancients were often scorned in their time
But honored by posterity.
From Hán Yù's writings.
Our dynasty
Is like polishing a mirror –
Unworn, it shines brighter.
One era's brevity
Versus eternity's span.
From Ōuyáng Xiū's "Eulogy for Sū Zǐměi".
Good medicine tastes bitter,
Its efficacy seen in curing grave ills.
Loyal advice first repels,
Yet when crisis comes, regret avails not.
From "The Collected Works of Ōuyáng Xiū".
Like eating olives –
The true flavor grows with time.
Ibid.
If posterity lacks impartiality,
No sage would be remembered today.
Ibid.
Pines and cedars grow in mountain forests,
Initially choked by weeds,
Trampled by cattle;
But ultimately,
They endure seasons and millennia unchanged –
Such is heaven's decree.
From Sū Shì's "Record of the Three Locusts Hall".
Momentary humiliation,
Eternal trustworthiness.
From Sū Shì's "Preface to Wáng Yuánzhī's Portrait Eulogy".
Even Emperor Yáo's wisdom
First tested Gǔn;
Even Confucius' sagacity
Doubted Zǎi Yú.
From Sū Shì's "Dismissal Edict for Lǚ Huìqīng".
A man's virtue is recognized only after his passing.
From "The Collected Works of Sū Zhé".
Truly like tasting olives –
Bitter at first, then lasting flavor emerges.
From Huáng Tíngjiān's poem.
Hard to argue with words alone –
Clear water reveals stones naturally.
Ibid.
Biàn Hé possessed a rare jade,
Unknown in Chǔ state.
Though knowing jade from stone,
He awaited recognition's hour.
Ibid.
Cross-reference "Resolving Disputes" and "Truth Is Hard to Erase".
Classics
The city wall returns to the moat.
From "Yì Jīng · Hexagram Tài".
Vast heaven above,
When will constancy return?
From "Shī Jīng · Odes of Táng · Pheasant Feathers".
High banks become valleys,
Deep valleys turn to hills.
From "Shī Jīng · October之交".
Cross-reference "Physics of Fullness and Emptiness".
Philosophers
Rottenness transforms into marvel,
Marvel reverts to rottenness.
From "Zhuāngzǐ".
Historical Accounts
Mágū told Wáng Fāngpíng: "Since my attendance,
I've seen the Eastern Sea turn to mulberry fields thrice.
Recently at Pénglái,
The waters have shallowed by half since last meeting."
From Yán Zhēnqīng's "Record of the Mágū Altar".
Anthologies
Lamenting Tài Shān becoming a moat.
Land beneath city walls.
From "Chǔ Cí".
Splendor fades into decay,
Halls overgrown with thorns.
From Ruǎn Jí's "Poems of Hidden Feelings".
Kōngsāng's village became vast rivers,
Lìyáng's capital turned to fish and turtles.
From Liú Xiàobiāo's "Discourse".
Cycles of reversal,
Swift as swirling waves.
From "Selection: On Ending Friendships" in Wén Xuǎn.
In a human century,
The physical world changes thousands of times;
Passions for fame, gain, favor, and disgrace arise,
Traces of love, hate, slander, and praise emerge.
By Luò Bīnwáng.
Eastern Sea waves touch heaven,
Thrice becoming mulberry fields.
High banks tower over roofs,
Suddenly changing to streams and valleys.
If heaven and earth transform thus,
How can human relations remain constant?
By night, vengeance with naked blades;
By morn, steadfast as metal and stone.
From Lú Tóng's writings.
Our Dynasty
The radiant lotus and caltrop,
The fragrant orchid and angelica,
With fine flowers and trees planted in shaded rows –
These were yesterday's misty thorns.
Tall eaves and giant rafters,
Where water reflections and sunlight shimmer –
Spacious, serene depths echoing far and breeding cool breezes –
These were yesterday's crumbling walls and deserted ruins.
On festive days and seasons,
Men and women singing with pipes and strings –
These were yesterday's gloomy storms and cries of beasts.
From Ōuyáng Xiū's writings.
Where once wild grasslands lay,
Veiled in frost and dew,
Hiding foxes and snakes –
Who then could foresee
The Língxū Tower rising?
Rise and fall, creation and ruin cycle endlessly;
The tower may yet return to wilderness –
None can know.
From Sū Shì's "Record of the Língxū Tower".
The world's ways are like chess –
Changes allow no undoing.
From Sū Shì's poem.
[End of Scroll]
Philosophers
The winged serpent flies without feet.
． From "Xúnzǐ: Quànxué".
There was a man of the Yú family,
who ascended a high tower,
overlooking the main road,
set out music and laid out wine,
and played at dice in the tower.
Knights-errant passed by in company.
A kite happened to drop a rotten rat, which hit them.
The knights-errant said to each other:
"We did not offend him,
yet he insults us.
We must destroy his household."
On the appointed night they gathered,
and assembling their forces, attacked and annihilated the Yú family.
． From "Lièzǐ: Shuō Shī".
Cross-reference "Incurring Misfortune".
To guard against thieves who rifle trunks, search bags, and break open boxes,
one must bind them with cords and ropes,
and secure them with locks and bolts.
Yet when a great thief comes,
he shoulders the box, lifts the trunk, and carries off the bag,
only fearing that the cords, ropes, locks, and bolts are not secure enough.
． From "Zhuāngzǐ: Qūqiè Piān".
Cross-reference "Creating Opportunities for Others".
The thin wine of Lǔ caused the siege of Hándān.
Also from the same source.
To hide a boat in a ravine,
or a mountain in a marsh,
may be called secure.
Yet at midnight a strong man
may carry them away on his back.
． From "Zhuāngzǐ: Dàzōngshī".
Praise and blame sprout and grow,
yet it cannot illuminate them.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
The moon illuminates the world,
yet is eclipsed by the toad.
The flying serpent rides the mist,
yet is endangered by the centipede.
The crow's strength can overcome the sun,
yet is bested by the quail's etiquette.
From the same work,
"Shuōlín Xùn".
When Chǔ assembled the feudal lords,
both Lǔ and Zhào presented wine to the King of Chǔ.
The royal wine steward requested wine from Zhào,
but was refused.
Angered, the steward
exchanged Zhào's rich wine for Lǔ's thin wine
and presented it.
The King of Chǔ, thinking Zhào's wine was thin,
thereupon besieged Hándān.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
History
Chén Shè,
a man born of humble means with a broken jar for a window and a rope as a door hinge,
a common laborer,
and one conscripted for forced labor,
whose abilities fell short of the average,
possessing neither the virtue of a Zhòngní or Mò Dí,
nor the wealth of a Táo Zhū or Yī Dùn,
stepped forward from the ranks of soldiers,
and rose abruptly from the fields,
leading weary and scattered troops,
commanding a few hundred men,
turned to attack Qín.
They cut trees to make weapons,
raised poles as flags,
and the people under heaven gathered like clouds and responded like echoes,
carrying provisions and following like shadows.
The heroes east of the mountains then rose together and brought about the downfall of the Qín clan.
．． "Records of the Grand Historian: Qín Annals, Jiǎ Shēng's Discourse."
All the generals thought they had obtained the rank of great general.
When the appointment was made,
the great general turned out to be Hán Xìn,
and the entire army was astonished.
． "Western Hàn: Biography of Hán Xìn."
A Chǔ envoy was in Jiǔjiāng,
urgently pressuring Yīng Bù to dispatch troops.
Suí Hé entered directly,
sat above the Chǔ envoy,
and said, "The King of Jiǔjiāng has already pledged allegiance to Hàn;
how can Chǔ demand troops from him?"
Bù was taken aback.
The Chǔ envoy rose.
Suí Hé then persuaded Bù, saying, "The matter is already settled;
you should kill the Chǔ envoy now,
do not let him return,
and quickly join forces with Hàn."
Bù said, "As the envoy instructs."
Thereupon, he killed the Chǔ envoy,
and raised troops to attack Chǔ.
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Hàn Gāozǔ."
Chancellor Hé Yǐ believed that the land in Cháng'ān was cramped,
and there was much empty land in the Shanglin Park,
left unused.
He wished to allow the people to enter and farm it,
not collecting the straw,
leaving it as food for birds and beasts.
The Emperor was greatly angered and said, "The Chancellor has taken much wealth from merchants,
and now he requests my park for them!"
He handed the Chancellor over to the Commandant of Justice,
who imprisoned him in shackles.
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Hàn Gāozǔ."
Cháo Cuò, planning for the state's long-term interests,
found disaster befalling himself instead.
． "Western Hàn: Biography of Jīng and Yān."
When the young men of various families saw Guāngwǔ in a crimson robe and large hat,
they exclaimed in surprise, "Even the cautious and honest one is doing this!"
． "Eastern Hàn: Annals of Guāngwǔ."
Zhūgě Liàng died in the army.
Chief Clerk Yáng Yí organized the troops and withdrew.
The common people rushed to inform Sīmǎ Yì,
who pursued them.
Jiāng Wéi ordered Yí to reverse the flags and beat the drums,
as if about to advance toward Yì,
who then gathered his troops and retreated,
not daring to press close.
A proverb says, "A dead Zhūgě puts a living Zhòngdá to flight."
Yì heard this,
laughed, and said, "I can predict the living,
but not the dead, that is why."
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Wèi Míngdì."
The high cicada rests in the light shade,
unaware that the mantis stalks it from behind.
． "Book of Jìn: Biography of Shí Bāo."
If a wasp or scorpion stirs in one's sleeve,
even a brave man will be startled.
"Book of Jìn."
Consider that disaster arises unexpectedly,
and even with wisdom and courage, there is no way to apply them.
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Jìn Yuándì."
Wáng spoke to King Shī Hǔ of Zhào, saying, "In the harsh winter, with snow and cold,
the Crown Prince is sending tens of thousands to cut timber for the palace, forcing them into labor.
Laments fill the roads,
and Crown Prince Xuān is angry.
When Mars remained in the Fang constellation, Xuān had the Grand Astrologer,"
order Zhào Lǎn to say to Hǔ, "It is fitting that a noble minister with the surname Wáng should bear the blame."
Hǔ said, "Who would that be?"
Lǎn said, "None more noble than Commandant Wáng."
Hǔ, reluctant and regretful, immediately had Lǎn name another,
and only the Director of the Central Secretariat, Wáng Bō, was mentioned.
Hǔ then issued an edict condemning Bō for his earlier
discussion of the matter of the hawk arrow,
and had him and his four sons executed by waist cutting.
Same as above.
"Annals of Jìn Mùdì."
Ruǎn Zhān always held the theory that ghosts do not exist.
Suddenly, a guest arrived, announcing his name to visit Zhān.
After exchanging pleasantries,
they casually discussed philosophy and logic.
The guest was very talented and eloquent,
and Zhān conversed with him.
After a long while, the topic turned to ghosts and spirits,
and they debated intensely.
The guest was eventually defeated,
then changed his expression and said, "Ghosts and spirits
have been passed down by sages and worthies throughout history;
how can you alone claim they do not exist?
I myself am a ghost."
Thereupon, he transformed into a strange shape,
and in a moment, vanished.
． "Book of Jìn: Biography of Ruǎn Zhān."
Dù Bì of Wèi said, "After the state of Chǔ perished,
the disaster extended to the trees in the forest;
when the city gate caught fire,
the calamity reached the fish in the moat."
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Liáng Annals," also see "Implication."
Dù Bì of Wèi said, "Disaster arises among one's own flesh and blood,
and strife starts from the heart."
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Liáng Annals."
Emperor Suí said, "It is like a fierce tiger,
whom no creature can harm,
yet it is instead gnawed and eaten by the insects in its fur."
Same as above,
"Chén Annals."
Also see "Disaster Arises from Neglect."
A sudden thunderclap leaves no time to cover one's ears.
． "Book of Táng: Biography of Lǐ Jìng."
Wáng Jūnkuò, the military governor of Yōuzhōu,
was arrogant, unrestrained, and often acted unlawfully,
and was summoned to court.
Chief Clerk Lǐ Xuándào,
a nephew of Fáng Xuánlíng,
entrusted Jūnkuò to deliver a letter.
Jūnkuò opened it privately,
but could not read the cursive script,
and suspected it accused him of crimes.
When he reached Wèinán,
he killed the courier station official and fled.
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Tàizōng."
Yáo Chóng and Zhāng Yuè served together as chancellors.
Zhāng held a grudge against Chóng.
When Chóng fell ill,
he warned his sons, saying, "Zhāng is a man who enjoys fine clothing and curios;
after my death,
display all my lifetime's fine clothing, curios, precious belts, and valuable vessels,
arranging them before the curtain.
If Zhāng pays no attention,
your family and clan will be doomed;
if he looks at them,
we will have nothing to fear.
Then ask him to write my epitaph.
Once you obtain his text,
copy it immediately and present it to the emperor,
and have a stone prepared and polished in advance,
ready for engraving as soon as it arrives.
Chancellor Zhāng is often slower than I in reacting to matters;
a few days later, he is sure to regret it.
If he demands the epitaph back,
using the excuse of revising it,
lead him to see the engraved stone,
and inform him it has already been reported to the emperor."
After Chóng's death,
Zhāng indeed came,
and his eyes lingered on the fine garments and curios three or four times.
Within a few days, the text was completed,
narrated fully and in detail.
A few days later,
Zhāng indeed sent a messenger to retrieve the manuscript,
claiming the wording was not thorough enough,
and he wished to make deletions and revisions.
Yáo's sons led the messenger to see the stone,
and informed him it had been presented to the emperor.
The messenger returned and reported,
and Zhāng, clapping his chest in regret and anger, said, "A dead Yáo Chóng could outwit a living Zhāng Yuè;
only today do I realize how far my talent falls short."
． "Old Book of Táng: His Biography."
Also see categories "Heartfelt Admiration" and "Judgment."
Zhāng Xún defended Yōngqiū,
and Líng Hú Cháo led troops to besiege it.
When the city ran out of arrows,
Xún tied straw into over a thousand figures,
dressed them in black clothes,
and lowered them down the city walls at night.
Cháo's soldiers vied to shoot at them,
and after a long while,
realized they were straw men.
Upon retrieving them,
they gained several hundred thousand arrows.
Later, they again lowered men down at night,
and the enemy laughed,
taking no precautions.
Then, with five hundred daring warriors, they attacked Cháo's camp,
throwing the army into great chaos.
"Book of Táng."
Also see category "Surprise Tactics."
Lǐ Pó,
the son of Lǐ Bì,
Yáng Chéng fully listed Pèi Yánlíng's faults and evils,
intending to submit a secret memorial.
Considering Pó the son of an old friend,
he had him transcribe it.
Pó went straight to report it to Yánlíng.
Yánlíng first went to the emperor,
explaining everything on his own behalf.
When the memorial was submitted,
the emperor considered it baseless,
and did not examine it.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Táng Dézōng".
Biographies
Termites and caterpillars topple pillars,
while gadflies and mosquitoes drive away cattle and sheep.
． From the "Garden of Persuasions: Talks on Collected Sayings" chapter.
Collections
Thus, conflicts arise from beneath the imperial carriage,
and barbarians approach close by.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Admonition Against Hunting",
also see "Disasters arise from negligence".
When the Liáng rebellion occurred,
Lù suffered its poison;
during the Xú calamity,
Zhèng fell victim to its harm.
From "Táng Wéncuì".
Also see "Implicated".
Lǔ's wine led to the siege of Hándān,
the flying kite brought disaster to the gambler.
Liú Bīnkè.
Originally relying on local reputation,
who would expect humiliation in the mud?
Liú Chángqīng.
A hundred birds fear humans and roost in the woods,
yet still end up caught in nets and butchered for meat.
Wéi Yìngwù.
Loosening a belt only to form a knot.
Same as above.
A sudden clap of thunder leaves no time to cover ears,
a flash of lightning gives no chance to close eyes.
From Jiāng Zǐyá's "Six Secret Teachings".
Our dynasty
Using an axe to split firewood,
one might say it's sure to succeed,
but if not following its grain,
the axe may break,
while the wood remains unsplit.
From Dōngpō's "Draft Policy Response for the Imperial Examination".
The white gull's nature belongs to the blue waves,
never expecting nets and snares in the dusty world.
From the "Línchuān Collection".
Vainly speaking of abolishing nobles to establish commanderies,
Zhào Gāo originally wasn't enfeoffed as a marquis.
Shào Yáofū's "Poem about Qín".
Classics
A withered poplar puts forth shoots.
． From the "Yìjīng: Great Excess".
The fish net is set,
but a swan gets caught in it.
． From the "Book of Songs: New Tower".
Shoot that small wild boar,
kill this great rhinoceros.
From the "Auspicious Day Poem".
Masters
There is unexpected praise.
． From "Mèngzǐ: Lí Lóu Part Two".
Lì Zhī of the Jì clan was the daughter of the border official of Ài.
When the state of Jìn first obtained her,
she wept till tears soaked her lapel;
but when she reached the king's place,
shared the king's bed,
and ate fine grains and meats,
she later regretted her earlier tears.
． From the "Zhuāngzǐ: Discussion on Making All Things Equal" chapter.
Histories
Qín burned books, yet the "Yìjīng" survived as a work on divination,
and its transmission never ceased.
． From the "Hàn History: Treatise on Literature".
When they were wielding knives as butchers or selling silk,
how could they have known they would follow the tail of a steed,
leave their names in the Hàn court,
and pass virtue to their descendants?
． From "Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of Guàn Yīng".
Also see "The unpredictability of life".
Cast off coarse garments and don embroidered robes,
abandon spade and construction for ornate carriages.
From the "Book of Later Hàn".
Yuán Zài served in the secretariat,
when an elder came seeking help.
Zài gave him a letter for Héběi.
The elder reached Yōuzhōu,
opened and looked at it,
finding not a single word,
only a signature.
Greatly regretting it,
angry and wanting to return,
he tried visiting a court official.
Shortly after,
he was requested to present the letter,
hosted as an honored guest,
lingered for several days,
and presented with a thousand bolts of silk.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Táng Records".
Bì Xián entered the Hànlín Academy as an academician.
The Dǎngxiàng tribe harassed Héxī,
so Emperor Xuānzōng summoned him to consult on border affairs.
Xián drew on ancient and modern examples,
detailing the Qīng's vulnerabilities thoroughly.
The emperor, pleased, said: "I need to select a capable commander.
Who would have thought that Lián Pō and Li Mù were in my own office?
Will you go on my behalf?"
． From the "New Táng History: His Biography".
Biographies
With one pot of food, he gained two scholars.
． From "Strategies of the Warring States: Zhōngshān".
Crown Prince Dān of Yān was a hostage in Qín,
treated disrespectfully by the Qín king,
and sought to return home.
The Qín king said: "When crows' heads turn white
and horses grow horns,
then I'll allow you to return."
Dān looked up to heaven and sighed: "Crows' heads turn white,
horses immediately grow horns,
and the Qín king releases me to return!"
From "The Spring and Autumn Annals of Lǚ Bùwéi".
Gù Zǒng was a county clerk,
frequently whipped,
so he fled to the ruins and tombs.
There, two yellow-clad men said: "Does Lord Liú recall our past association?
We are Wáng Càn and Xú Gàn,
and you, in your previous life, were Liú Zhēn."
Then they took a book from their sleeve, saying: "This is your collection."
Zǒng perused it
and became thoroughly enlightened.
He then took the collection to see the county magistrate,
who exclaimed in shock: "We cannot have Lord Liú Gàn as a minor clerk."
