Immediately treated him with guest rites.
Hence it's said: "The dead Liú Zhēn still protects the living Gù Zǒng."
From Niú Sēngrú's "Records of the Mysterious and Strange".
Collections
Leave coarse vegetables and straw sandals behind
to enjoy fine grains and meats.
From "Selections of Refined Literature".
People were astonished at the sight,
as if seeing the ribbon of office on Zhū Mǎichén.
From Liáng Liú Xiàoyí's "Letter of Thanks".
Seeking sound to find the instrument,
coming empty but returning full.
From "Táng Wéncuì".
Classics
The Yīn mirror is not far,
it lies in the time of the Xià dynasty.
． From the "Book of Songs: Greater Odes".
Also see "Warnings and Admonitions".
To cut an axe handle, to cut an axe handle,
the pattern is not far.
From "Cutting an Axe Handle".
The Way is not far from man.
． From the "Book of Rites: The Doctrine of the Mean".
Masters
With a glance, the Way is perceived.
From "Zhuāngzǐ".
Histories
Mǎ Yuán, before the emperor, piled rice to form mountains and valleys,
pointing out the terrain,
showing the paths for the troops to take,
analyzing the twists and turns,
making everything clear and understandable.
The emperor said: "The enemy is now in my sight."
From the "Book of Later Hàn".
Also see "Silent understanding".
Classics
Punishment does not extend to descendants.
． From Shū·Dà Yǔ Mó.
Exterminate their chief leaders,
but do not punish those coerced into following.
． From Shū·Sì Zhēng.
Do not harbor anger toward the stubborn,
nor demand perfection from any single person.
From Shū.
Owl, oh owl,
you have taken my young,
do not destroy my nest.
． From Shī·Chī Xiāo.
The noble person does not exhaust others' joy,
nor drain others' loyalty,
thus preserving relationships.
． From Lǐjì·Qū Lǐ Shàng.
The ruler does not surround marshes during spring hunts,
ministers do not wipe out whole herds,
scholars do not take fawns or eggs.
Same as above.
Leave surplus and dare not exhaust.
． From Lǐjì·Zhōng Yōng.
The noble person governs people according to their nature,
stopping when they reform.
Same as above.
If the noble person measures others by righteousness,
it becomes hard to be human;
if measuring others by human standards,
then the worthy can be recognized.
． From Lǐjì·Biǎo Jì.
The Master fished but did not use nets,
hunted but did not shoot roosting birds.
． From Lúnyǔ·Shù Ér.
The Master
Zhòngní never went to extremes.
． From Mèngzǐ·Lí Lóu Xià.
When pressure becomes too extreme,
inevitably base hearts will respond.
． From Zhuāngzǐ·Rén Jiān Shì.
Cross-reference "Things reverse at their extreme."
Water too clear breeds no fish;
people too discerning have no followers.
From Kǒngzǐ Jiāyǔ.
Cross-reference "Harsh Scrutiny."
Duke Dìng of Lǔ asked Yán Huí: "Have you heard of Dōngyě Bì's skill in driving?"
Reply: "Skilled he is indeed.
However,
his horses will surely bolt.
Shùn was adept at directing people,
while Zàofǔ was skilled with horses;
Shùn never pushed his people to exhaustion,
nor Zàofǔ his horses.
Thus Shùn had no bolting people and Zàofǔ no bolting horses.
Now Dōngyě Bì's driving—
mounting, holding reins and bit,
posture is correct;
walking, trotting, galloping,
all maneuvers complete;
traversing dangers, going long distances,
horses' strength exhausted;
yet his mind still endlessly demands more from them."
From Kǒngzǐ Jiāyǔ.
One who sees fish in deep pools meets misfortune;
one who discerns hidden secrets invites disaster.
From Lièzǐ.
Cross-reference "Harsh Scrutiny."
Burning forests to hunt,
will leave no game later;
deceiving the people,
will leave no followers later.
From Hánfēizǐ.
Burning forests to hunt,
may gain more game now,
but will leave none later.
From Huáinánzǐ.
History
A driver who doesn't understand his horses' condition.
From Shǐjì.
Fūchāi and Zhì Bó perished through excessive warmongering.
． From Xī Hàn·Lù Jiǎ Zhuàn.
Huáng Bà said: "In governance,
simply remove the most excessive aspects."
From his biography.
Things forbid extremity.
From Féng Fèngshì Zhuàn.
The intelligent and penetrating guard against excessive scrutiny.
From Kuāng Héng Zhuàn,
both in Xī Hàn.
Dǒng Zhuō said:
"Do not press a desperate enemy,
nor pursue retreating troops."
． From Hòu Hàn·Huángfǔ Sōng Zhuàn.
Too rigid, and it breaks;
too scrutinizing, and no followers remain.
． From Jìn·Liú Kuí et al.
Drumming too long wastes breath;
shouting too often exhausts strength.
． From Tōngjiàn·Sòng Tàizǔ.
Cross-reference "Affairs Should Be Sustainable."
Wéi Ruì said: "A general should know timidity sometimes,
not just rely on courage."
． From Tōngjiàn·Liáng Wǔ Jì.
Distinguishing good and evil too clearly
can also lead to mistakes sometimes.
． From Tōngjiàn·Táng Tàizōng.
Thunder crashes, lightning strikes—
heaven's wrath—
yet cannot last a full morning.
How could a sage ruler
hold wrath against ministers for a lifetime?"
． From Táng Shū·Wú Wùlíng Zhuàn.
Burning clothes for being stained,
felling trees for being worm-eaten—
doesn't this cause more harm?
． From Tōngjiàn·Táng Zhāozōng.
Biographies
Yuè Yì said: "Noble friends part without bitter words;
loyal ministers leave state without cleansing their name."
From Zhànguó Cè.
Divorcing a wife should leave her remarriageable.
Same as above.
Jìn's Yōng Jì said: "Draining ponds to fish
may catch fish now,
but next year there will be none;
burning marshes to hunt
may catch game now,
but next year there will be none.
Deceptive methods
may bring temporary gains,
but future harvests will fail—
not a lasting strategy."
From Lǚshì Chūnqiū.
Collections
Allow chance for later redemption
to amend past wrongs.
Bái Jūyì.
Should not bind and drive them
like oxen or horses—
haste leads to failure.
Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
Pushing something to its desperate end
is what the noble person avoids.
Dù Mù.
Cross-reference "Generosity."
The essence of things
is heaven and earth's secret treasure,
hence gold hidden in sand,
jade confined in rough stone.
Coral groves
flourish in deepest oceans;
luminous pearls
rest in the black dragon's jaw.
Digging relentlessly
brings exhaustion or disaster.
So too with writing:
moderate gains
yield abundant rewards;
deep extraction
leads to personal ruin.
From Sūn Qiáo's collection.
This dynasty
When sages enforce laws,
like thunder shaking grass,
though fierce in wrath,
they ultimately desire life;
when rulers punish subjects,
like parents disciplining children,
though strict in beating,
they cannot bear to cause death.
Sū Shì's "Petition for Chángzhōu."
Fine wine is best when slightly drunk;
lovely flowers viewed while half-open.
Sháo Yōng.
Classics
A man of Biàn wept like a child at his mother's death.
Confucius said: "Grief is grief indeed,
but hard to sustain.
Ritual exists
to be transmitted,
to be sustained—
hence wailing has its measures."
． From Lǐjì·Tán Gōng Shàng.
Masters
Lǔ law compensated rescuers from the treasury,
but Zǐgòng declined payment.
Confucius said: "From now on,
no one from Lǔ will ransom people from other states."
From Kǒngzǐ Jiāyǔ.
History: Drumming too long wastes breath;
shouting too often exhausts strength.
． From Tōngjiàn·Sòng Tàizǔ Jì.
Classic
An old horse is treated as a colt again,
without regard for its future.
The Book of Songs.
The commentary on "Jiao Gong" says: not reflecting on the consequences,
until old age comes,
how others treat one will likewise be so.
Words spoken with defiance
will be met with defiance in return;
wealth acquired unjustly
will be lost unjustly.
． The Record of the Great Learning.
Zi
What comes out of you
will return to you.
． Mencius, King Hui of Liang, Part II.
If the ruler regards his ministers as dogs and horses,
then the ministers will regard the ruler as a mere stranger;
if the ruler regards his ministers as dirt and weeds,
then the ministers will regard the ruler as an enemy and foe.
Same as above,
Li Lou, Part II.
A man was escorting his wife to her parents' home,
and on the way, he saw a mulberry-picking woman;
delighted, he spoke with her.
But when he turned to look at his own wife,
she too had someone beckoning to her.
． Liezi, Chapter "Explaining Conjunctions".
Those who harm others
will inevitably be harmed in return.
． Zhuangzi, The Human World.
Thus, Shāng Yāng established laws and was torn apart by dismemberment;
Wú Qǐ enforced harsh measures and was torn apart by chariots.
． Huainanzi, "Miu Cheng Xun".
History
King Líng of Chǔ heard of the deaths of the many princes,
and said: "I have killed many men's sons,
can I escape this fate?"
． From "Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāo 12".
Cross-reference category "Knowing Remorse".
Shāng Jūn fled to the pass,
wanting to lodge at an inn.
The innkeeper did not know he was Shāng Jūn,
and said: "By Shāng Jūn's law,
lodgers without identification are punished."
Shāng Jūn said: "The harm of making laws has reached this extent!"
He left for Wèi.
． From "Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Annals".
Wèi Yāng internally employed knives and saws,
externally deepened axes and execution blades,
judged prisoners by the Wèi River,
turning it entirely red, yet those who escaped
had nowhere to hide,
and nowhere to shelter; he died torn apart by chariots.
． Annotation from "Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Shāng Jūn".
No misfortune is greater than killing those who have surrendered,
this is why the general could not become a marquis.
． From "Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Lǐ Guǎng".
Generals of the Three Dynasties
were what the Daoists warned against;
from Guǎng to Líng,
their lineage was extinguished.
Same as above.
Yì Zòng executed many people.
The emperor visited Dǐnghú and Gānquán,
finding the roads poorly maintained.
Angered, the emperor said: "Does Zòng think I will not travel this road again?"
He bore a grudge.
Yì Zòng was executed in the market.
． From "Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Annals".
The prohibitions of old Qín
only aided the ambitious and hastened its own downfall.
． From "Book of Hàn, Biography of Yuán Àng".
Cross-reference "Providing Opportunities for Others".
Those who suppress others
will be suppressed in turn;
those who bully others
will be bullied in turn.
． From "Records of the Three Kingdoms, Wèi, Biography of Wáng Chǎng".
Chéng Pǔ killed several hundred captives,
ordering them all thrown into fire,
and soon fell ill, lost his voice, and died.
"Records of Wú".
Yǔ Yì sent wine to the Governor of Jiāngzhōu, Wáng Yǔnzhī.
Yǔnzhī detected poison,
fed it to a dog,
which died,
and secretly reported it.
The emperor said: "The elder uncle has already thrown the realm into chaos;
must the younger uncle do the same?"
In February,
Yǔ Yì drank poison and died.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Jìn, Mùdì".
Liú Yì fled at night to the Niúmù Buddhist Temple.
Earlier,
when Huán Wèi was defeated,
he fled to the temple's monk Chāng,
who hid him;
Yì killed Chāng.
Now,
the temple monks refused him, saying: "Our late teacher sheltered Huán Wèi,
and was killed by General Liú;
we dare not shelter a stranger now."
Yì sighed: "To be hoist with one's own petard
has come to this!"
He then hanged himself.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Jìn, Āndì".
Wèi's Chéngyáng King, Yuān, fled to the south of the mountains,
reaching the home of former Luòyáng Magistrate Kòu Zǔrén.
Zǔrén's family had three governors,
all promoted by Yuān,
so, relying on past kindness,
he sought refuge there.
Yuān had a hundred catties of gold
and fifty horses;
Zǔrén coveted his wealth,
and though he outwardly welcomed him,
privately told his family: "I hear Ěrzhū Zhào is offering a reward for Chéngyáng King;
the captor will be enfeoffed as a marquis of a thousand households—
today, wealth and honor have arrived!"
He then frightened Yuān, claiming officials were coming to arrest him,
urging him to flee elsewhere,
and had him ambushed and killed on the road,
sending his head to Zhào.
Zhào dreamed that Yuān told him: "I have two hundred catties of gold and a hundred horses at Kòu Zǔrén's house;
you may take them."
Awakening,
Zhào believed the dream true,
immediately arrested Zǔrén,
demanding the gold and horses.
Zǔrén, thinking someone had informed,
confessed readily,
saying: "I truly obtained a hundred catties of gold and fifty horses."
Suspecting concealment,
Zhào pressed based on the dream;
Zǔrén's family originally had thirty catties of gold and thirty horses,
all given to Zhào,
who still doubted,
grew angry,
seized Zǔrén,
hung his head from a high tree,
weighted his feet with heavy stones,
and beat him to death.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Liáng, Gāozǔ".
Empress Wáng had no son,
while Consort Xiāo was favored,
so the Empress resented her.
She secretly had Wǔ shì grow out her hair,
urging the emperor to take her into the palace,
hoping to undermine Consort Xiāo's favor.
Wǔ shì was clever and cunning,
versed in stratagems;
upon entering the palace,
she served the Empress with humble words and deference.
The Empress adored her,
often praising her to the emperor.
Soon, she was greatly favored.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng, Gāozǔ".
Suǒ Yuánlǐ, under Empress Wǔ, served as an investigator,
creating an iron cage to confine prisoners' heads,
adding wedges
until their skulls split and they died.
Later, for his harshness
and accepting bribes,
he was arrested and tried;
he denied the charges,
but the officer said: "Fetch your iron cage!"
Yuánlǐ then confessed
and died in prison.
"Book of Táng".
Zhōu Xīng, skilled in law, served as an autumn official;
later, someone accused him of treason,
and an edict ordered Lái Jùnchén to interrogate.
Initially unaware of the accusation,
Xīng was dining with Jùnchén,
who said: "Prisoners often deny charges;
what to do?"
Xīng replied: "Easy—
place them in a large vat,
surround it with burning charcoal,
and they will confess to anything."
Jùnchén then had a vat and fire brought,
and slowly said: "An edict investigates you;
please try it."
Xīng kowtowed and confessed.
"Book of Táng".
Yuán Zǎi was domineering,
and the emperor wished to execute him.
He was arrested at the administration hall
and ordered to commit suicide in Wànnián County.
Zǎi requested the executioner: "Make it a quick death!"
The executioner said: "Sir, you must endure some disgrace;
do not blame me!"
He then stuffed a dirty sock into his mouth and killed him.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng, Dàizōng".
Robbers desecrated Guō Zǐyí's father's tomb.
Zǐyí appeared before the emperor,
weeping: "I long commanded troops,
unable to prevent violence;
soldiers often robbed tombs,
and today this befalls me—
it is heaven's punishment,
not human affairs."
Same as above.
Those who falsely accuse the innocent
will suffer the same fate.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng, Dézōng".
Lù Yán served as chancellor,
secretly proposing: "When officials of the third rank or higher are ordered to die,
have the envoys cut out a three-inch piece of their throat to present,
proving their death."
Now,
he faced this fate himself,
dying on the very couch where Yáng Shōu had been ordered to die.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng, Yìzōng".
Yáng Xíngmì said: "I prefer leniency,
but Yuán Xí often urged me to kill—
this is why he did not live long!"
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng, Xīzōng".
Biographies and records.
Those who enjoy speaking of others' faults
will have their own faults spoken of by others;
those who delight in hating others
will likewise be hated by others.
. From "Garden of Persuasions: Collected Talks."
The Zhāng Yìzhī brothers vied in extravagance,
and after they were executed,
the common people sliced their flesh to pieces,
which was then called "galloping horse retribution."
From "Records from Court and Country."
Harming the virtuous
brings calamity for three generations;
obstructing the virtuous
brings harm upon oneself.
From "Huang Shí's Three Strategies."
Collected
Hán Fei set up arguments to curry favor with the ruler,
while Lǚ Bu carried out deceit to betray the state.
After "On the Difficulties of Persuasion" was expounded,
he himself was imprisoned;
when Qín's goods became expensive,
his lineage also fell.
From Zhāng Mèngjiān's "Guest's Banter."
Consort Bān wiped tears and embraced her maid,
while I have ostracized countless people.
From "Yuán Zhěn's Collection."
Cross-reference "Knowing Remorse."
Our Dynasty
When Lú Duōsùn was banished to Zhūyá,
Lǐ Fú met with Zhào Pǔ
and said that although Zhūyá was overseas,
its water and soil were not particularly bad,
whereas Chūn Prefecture, though inland,
was certain death for anyone sent there.
Pǔ nodded in agreement.
Later, when Fú himself was banished to Xuān Prefecture,
the emperor was angry,
and before it subsided, Pǔ related the whole matter,
whereupon Fú was appointed to Chūn Prefecture and died upon arriving.
From "Garden of Talks."
When Kòu Zhōngmǐn was banished,
Dīng Jìngōng and Féng Zhěng were in the secretariat.
Dīng, holding the brush,
first intended to banish him to Yá Prefecture,
but then suddenly had doubts
and proposed Léi Prefecture instead.
When Dīng himself was later banished,
Féng then proposed Yá Prefecture for him.
People of the time delightedly said:
"If you meet Kòu, the Registrar of Léi Prefecture,
remember, where in life do people not meet again?"
From Ōu Yángxiū's "Records of Returning to the Fields."
When Dīng Wèi was chancellor,
he expelled Lǐ Dí.
At that time, Sòng Shòu, as drafter, requested the charge, saying to Wèi:
"In the Spring and Autumn, 'having no leader,'
under Hàn law, 'unprincipled.'"
And when Wèi was banished to Zhūyá,
Sòng, still drafter, wrote the edict:
"The warning against 'having no leader' is deeply inscribed in the classics;
the punishment for 'unprincipled' cannot escape Hàn law."
All under heaven were pleased.
From "Records of Lóng Prefecture."
After Shí Jiè died,
Xià Sǒng said to Emperor Yīngzōng:
"Jiè is not really dead;
he has fled to the Hú."
So an imperial envoy was sent
to open Jiè's coffin and verify the truth.
Later, when Xià Sǒng himself died,
Wú Kuí said:
"Xià Sǒng was full of deceit,
and now he is dead."
Emperor Rénzōng went to his home
and ordered a chief eunuch to remove the veil from Sǒng's face and look.
The world says that opening the coffin and removing the face veil
both stem from the sovereign's suspicion alike,
could this also be called retribution?
From "Dōngxuān's Notes."
Cáo Pī, at the time, felt no shame,
daring to say that Shùn and Yǔ received it from Yáo.
As he gained it thus, so he lost it,
who knew three horses would share one trough?
From "Ōu Yángxiū's Collection."
Those who poison the world with laws
never fail to have it rebound upon themselves and their descendants.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn and the First Emperor of Qín
were both resolute in killing.
Thus, their sons—like the benevolent Fúsū
would rather die than plead;
like the defiant Crown Prince Lì
would rather rebel than protest.
From Dōngpō's writings.
Lǚ Bù served Dīng Yuán,
then killed Dīng Yuán;
served Dǒng Zhuó,
then killed Dǒng Zhuó.
Liú Láozhī served Wáng Gōng,
then turned against Wáng Gōng;
served Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn,
then turned against Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn.
Lǚ Bù was executed by Lord Cáo,
and Láozhī was killed by the Huán family.
From "Luánchéng's" writings.
Classics
If crossing the river in the same boat,
why worry about the Hú and Yuè having different hearts?
From "Brief Examples of the Yì."
If the common people have enough,
how can the ruler not have enough?
If the common people do not have enough,
how can the ruler have enough?
. From "Analects, Yānyuān."
Masters
If those below are poor, those above are poor;
if those below are rich, those above are rich.
. From "Xúnzǐ: Enriching the State."
People of Wú and Yuè,
crossing the river in the same boat,
encounter wind and waves midstream,
and rescue each other like left and right hands
because their peril is the same.
. From "Kǒng Cóngzǐ: On Circumstances."
Crossing the sea in the same boat,
meeting wind midstream,
they rescue from peril as one,
for their worry is the same;
setting nets for hunting,
their calls and responses do not differ,
for their benefit is equal.
Thus, those in physical pain
cannot but cry out;
The Earl of Zhèng said to Zhú Zhīwǔ: "If Zhèng perishes,
it would also be disadvantageous for you."
. From Zuǒzhuàn, the 30th year of Duke Xī.
"The cheekbone and the jawbone depend on each other;
when the lips are gone, the teeth are cold."
This saying refers to Yú and Guó, doesn't it?
. From Zuǒzhuàn, the 5th year of Duke Xī.
Xiāo Tóngshūzǐ is no other
than the mother of our ruler.
If we speak in terms of equals,
then she is also the mother of the ruler of Jìn.
From Zuǒzhuàn.
The Minister of the Left said: "When great ministers are not obedient,
it is a disgrace to the state."
From Zuǒzhuàn.
Zǐchǎn said to Zǐpí: "You, in the state of Zhèng,
are the ridgepole.
If the ridgepole breaks and the rafters collapse,
I, Qiáo, will be crushed beneath them."
. From Zuǒzhuàn, the 30th year of Duke Xiāng.
The ruler's ministers and assistants
are called his limbs.
If a limb is impaired,
what sorrow could be greater?
. From Zuǒzhuàn, the 9th year of Duke Zhāo.
Zōng Lì, the Minister of War of the Shūsūn clan, said to the multitude: "I
am a household servant,
and dare not concern myself with state affairs.
But in general, having the Jì clan or not having it—
which is more advantageous for me?"
They all said: "Without the Jì clan,
there would be no Shūsūn clan."
. From Zuǒzhuàn, the 25th year of Duke Zhāo.
Chéng
is the protective barrier of the Mèng clan;
without Chéng, there would be no Mèng clan.
. From Zuǒzhuàn, the 12th year of Duke Dìng.
Now Lǔ
is the lips and teeth of Qí and Jìn;
if the lips are gone, the teeth are cold.
. From Zuǒzhuàn, the 8th year of Duke Āi.
Yuè Yǔ of Sòng said: "The ducal clan
is the branches and leaves of the ducal house.
If they are removed,
then the trunk and roots will have nothing to shelter them."
From Zuǒzhuàn.
When the people are truly emaciated,
how can the ruler be fat?
From Guóyǔ.
King Hàn said: "My father is your father."
From Hànshū.
When the King of Huáinán rebelled,
the Prime Minister said: "Last year, Péng Yuè was killed;
the year before, Hán Xìn was killed.
These three men
were men of the same body.
Fearing that disaster would turn upon themselves,
they therefore rebelled."
. From Tōngjiàn, Annals of Hàn Gāozǔ.
When the branches and leaves fall,
the trunk and roots have nothing to shelter them.
. From Xī Hàn, Biography of Liú Xiàng.
Generals, ministers, and high officials
share the same body as the head;
they ride together in the same carriage,
and cross the river in the same boat.
If the carriage overturns or the boat capsizes,
they truly share the calamity.
. From Hòu Hàn, regarding Zhū Mù.
Tián Fén said: "Chéng Bùshí and Lǐ Guǎng are both Commandants of the Guards of the Eastern and Western Palaces.
Now you have publicly insulted General Chéng;
do you not, Zhòngrú, leave any ground for General Lǐ?"
. From Xī Hàn, Biography of Guàn Fū.
Lǐ Gù said: "It is like within one gate,
the affairs of one family:
in safety, they share the blessings and celebrations;
in danger, they share the disasters and defeats."
. From Tōngjiàn, Annals of Eastern Hàn.
It is like striking the trunk of a tree:
all the branches shake.
. From Eastern Hàn, Biography of Lǐ Gù.
See also "Influence and Response."
It is like the head and the feet depending on each other.
. From Tōngjiàn, Annals of Hàn Huándì.
Lǚ Fàn said: "It is like crossing the sea in the same boat:
if one thing is not secure,
all will suffer the disaster."
Ibid.,
Annals of Eastern Hàn.
Mùróng Chuí said: "Qín and Jìn are like tiles thrown together;
they rely on each other for strength.
If one wins, both become powerful;
if one is defeated, both collapse."
From Annals of Jìn Wǔdì.
The ruler and ministers are like father and son;
they share weal and woe.
From Annals of Táng Gāozǔ.
The Emperor once said to the dukes and ministers: "If a ruler is self-willed, rejects remonstrance, and considers himself wise,
and his ministers flatter and follow his wishes,
then once the ruler loses the state,
how can the ministers alone preserve themselves?
For example, Yú Shìjī and others fawned upon Emperor Yáng to preserve their wealth and rank;
after Emperor Yáng was assassinated,
Shìjī and others were also executed."
From Annals of Táng Tàizōng,
also ibid.
Biographies and Records
It is like crossing a river in the same boat:
if they cross, all share the benefit;
if they fail, all share the harm.
From Tàigōng Liùtāo.
Never has it been seen that the son is rich and the father poor.
From Tōngdiǎn.
Classics
When planners are too many,
the plans are not accomplished.
When words fill the court,
who will take responsibility for the fault?
. From Shījīng, Xiǎoyǎ.
Masters
The great road loses the sheep because of its many forks.
. From Lièzǐ, chapter "Shuō Fú."
A hundred doctors attending one illness
only serve to create doubts,
and cannot effect a single cure.
. From Zhuāngzǐ, "Rénjiānshì."
When great ministers share power equally, the fate of Wèi becomes chaotic.
Sīmǎ Xuānwáng and Cáo Shuǎng vied for power.
From Wénzhōngzǐ.
Histories
The fox-fur robe is luxuriantly fluffy,
One state with three lords,
To whom should I give my allegiance?
. From Zuo Tradition, 5th Year of Duke Xi.
When Duke Jiǎn of Qí was in Lǔ,
Kǎn Zhǐ enjoyed his favor.
Upon ascending the throne,
he put him in charge of governance.
Chén Chéngzǐ always feared him.
A charioteer named Yāng addressed the duke: "Chén and Kǎn
cannot coexist; you must choose between them."
The duke did not listen.
. From Zuo Tradition, 14th Year of Duke Āi.
When the ruler of Chǔ was chief minister,
he used a royal banner.
The taro officer Wú Yǔ said: "One state with two rulers—
who can endure this?"
From Zuo Tradition.
King Xuān of Hán wanted to employ both Gōng Zhòng and Gōng Shū in governance,
and consulted Miù Liú.
The reply was: "It cannot be done.
Jìn used six ministers and the state was divided;
Duke Jiǎn of Qí used both Chén Chéngzǐ and Kǎn Zhǐ and was killed;
Wèi used Xī Shǒu and Zhāng Yí and lost the land west of the Yellow River.
Now if you employ both,
the stronger will form cliques within,
the weaker will rely on external powers.
If ministers form internal cliques to defy the ruler,
or forge external alliances to cede territory,
your state will be in peril!"
. From Comprehensive Mirror, Reign of King Xiàn of Zhōu.
The nine ministers took turns wielding power,
and matters were not decided by the chancellor.
Ibid,
from Annals of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
Governance issued from multiple gates,
influential families
recommended and supported each other in turn,
as if in a market exchange.
From Annals of Emperor Huì of Jìn.
Penal laws were inconsistent,
litigation proliferated,
and Liú Sòng memorialized: "In recent times,
laws have gradually multiplied in sources,
edicts become highly inconsistent,
officials do not know what to uphold,
the people do not know what to avoid,
the crafty thereby peddle their schemes,
and those above find it hard to restrain those below."
Ibid.
Dual governance divides power,
rarely failing to lead to disaster.
From Annals of Emperor Chéng of Jìn.
At that time, there was no fixed office of chancellor;
anyone with whom the ruler discussed governance
and entrusted with机密 matters was a chancellor.
. From History of the Southern Dynasties, Annals of Emperor Gāozǔ of Sòng.
Zhāng Hóngcè said:
"One state with three lords is already unbearable,
let alone six nobles at court together,
who are bound to plot against each other."
. From Annals of Marquis Dōng Hūn of Qí.
All major authority in the empire reverted to the central palace for promotions, demotions, life, and death,
decided by her word,
while the emperor merely folded his hands;
inside and out, they were called the Two Sages.
From Annals of Emperor Gāozōng of Táng.
Obliquely appointed officials were all commissioned without going through the two departments,
and the two departments dared not submit objections.
From Emperor Ruìzōng of Táng,
all the above from Comprehensive Mirror.
Collection:
One state with three lords,
ten sheep with nine shepherds.
From a text by Lù Xuān Gōng.
History:
Qí attacked Chǔ.
The ruler of Chǔ sent a message to the army: "You dwell by the northern sea,
I by the southern sea,
and even galloping horses or cattle would not reach each other.
I did not expect you to tread on my land."
. From Zuo Tradition, 4th Year of Duke Xi.
In Zhèng, dragons fought,
and the people requested a sacrifice.
Zǐchǎn said: "When we fight,
the dragons do not appear to us.
When dragons fight,
why should I alone appear to them?
I have no need of dragons,
nor do dragons have any need of me."
. From Zuo Tradition, 19th Year of Duke Zhāo.
Cross-reference to "Upholding Integrity."
Collection:
Whales devour,蛟 dragons battle, waves turn to blood,
while fish in the deep stream joyfully know nothing.
Bái Lètiān.
The Yuè people regard the Qín people's fat or thin
with sudden indifference, neither joy nor sorrow in their hearts.
Hán Wén.
Masters:
Birds, when cornered, will peck;
beasts, when cornered, will pounce.
From Family Sayings.
Humans, when cornered, become deceitful;
horses, when cornered, become unruly.
Ibid.
Fish
moisten each other with their breath,
and dampen each other with their foam.
. From Zhuāngzǐ, "The Movement of Heaven."
This is only about saving lives, fearing insufficiency,
so how could there be leisure for propriety and righteousness?
. From Mencius, King Huì of Liáng, Part One.
History
Zhèng Zǐjiā said: "A dying deer does not choose the shade."
． _Zuozhuan, 17th Year of Duke Wen_.
Driven to take desperate risks,
how can one be selective in extremity?
Same as above.
The Sòng envoy Huà Yuán entered the Chǔ army camp at night,
ascended to Zǐfǎn's bed,
and said: "My lord sends me to report our distress,
saying:
'In our humble city, we exchange children to eat,
and split bones for fuel.
Even so,
a treaty under the city walls,
even if it means the state's destruction, we cannot accept.'"
． _Zuozhuan, 15th Year of Duke Xuān_.
When people are in dire straits, they revert to fundamentals,
thus in toil, suffering, and exhaustion,
they never fail to cry out to heaven;
in pain and anguish,
they never fail to call for their parents.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Qū Yuán_.
Nowhere to place one's footsteps.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Xī Shǒu_.
The cold prize short coarse garments,
the hungry savor chaff and husks.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Annals of Qín Shǐ Huáng_.
In the late era of Qín,
they burned the Books of Songs and Documents,
buried Confucian scholars alive,
and the Six Arts were thus lost.
When Chén Shè became king,
the various scholars of Lǔ took the ritual vessels of the Kǒng family and went over to King Chén.
Kǒng Jiǎ became Erudite for King Chén.
．． _Records of the Grand Historian, Preface to the Biographies of Confucian Scholars_.
Dīng Gōng,
a general under Xiàng Yǔ,
pursued and cornered Gāozǔ west of Péngchéng.
In close combat,
the King of Hàn was in peril,
and turning to Dīng Gōng said: "Should two worthies oppress each other?"
． _Book of Hàn, Biography of Jì Bù_.
Fán Kuài said: "Now others are the knife and board,
we are the fish and meat,
what is there to decline?"
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Hàn Gāozǔ_.
The Emperor was at Jìnyáng,
hearing that Mòdú was at Dàigǔ,
wished to attack him.
He sent men to spy on the Xiōngnú,
Mòdú hid his strong warriors and fat oxen and horses,
showing only the old and weak and emaciated animals.
Ten groups of envoys came,
all saying the Xiōngnú could be attacked.
Mòdú unleashed four hundred thousand elite cavalry,
surrounding the Emperor at Báidēng for seven days.
The Emperor employed Chén Píng's secret plan,
sending an envoy to secretly bribe the Yānzhī.
He escaped through a gap in the encirclement.
Same as above.
Wèi Bó said: "When a household is on fire,
does one have time to first inform the elders
before putting out the fire?"
． _Book of Hàn, Biographies of the Five Kings of Gāozǔ_.
Cross-referenced under "Expediency and Adaptation".
Human nature is such that,
if one does not eat for a day, one hungers;
if one does not make clothes for a year, one feels cold.
When the belly is hungry and gets no food,
the skin is cold and gets no clothing,
even a compassionate father cannot keep his children.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Hàn Wéndì_.
The cold do not wait for light and warm clothing,
the hungry do not wait for sweet and delicious food.
When hunger and cold befall the body,
one disregards shame.
． _Book of Hàn, Treatise on Food and Money_.
Under the rod and cane,
what confession cannot be obtained?
． _Book of Hàn, Biography of Lù Wēnshū_.
When a good man is in distress,
help is as urgent as a missed meal.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Hàn Shùndì_.
Those in a situation of myriad deaths
must have a heart set on fighting to the death.
Same as above,
_Annals of Hàn Xiàndì_.
Like mulberry leaves falling and tiles crumbling,
the situation is clear.
． _Book of Later Hàn, Biography of Mǎ Róng_.
Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
Liú Yù, Liú Yì, Hé Wújì, and others plotted restoration.
Xuán was terrified,
fled to Shǔ,
Fèi Tián, Máo Yòuzhī attacked Xuán.
He was struck by an arrow,
which his son Shēng promptly pulled out.
The Protector of Yìzhōu, Féng Qiān, drew his sword and advanced,
Xuán said: "Who are you?
How dare you kill the Son of Heaven!"
Qiān said: "I kill the traitor who called himself Son of Heaven."
Then he beheaded him.
Shēng said: "I am the Prince of Yùzhāng,
gentlemen, do not kill me."
They executed him at Jiānglíng.
． _Book of Jìn, Biography of Bó Xuán_.
Dòu Jiàndé's battles went unfavorably,
he was struck by a lance.
Yáng Wǔwēi pursued him,
Jiàndé fell from his horse and said: "Do not kill me,
I am the King of Xià."
Wǔwēi captured him.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Táng Gāozǔ_.
Biographies and Records
Holding a leaking jar,
pouring water into a scorched pot.
_Strategies of the Warring States_.
A desperate monkey flees to the woods,
how can it choose the tree?
_A New Account of the Tales of the World_, Part 1.
Those who flee for their lives
do not avoid axes and halberds.
Wáng Yì's _Zhèng Bù_.
Prince Sī of Chén said: "The cold do not covet a foot of jade but long for short coarse garments;
the hungry do not desire a thousand gold but relish a single meal,
for things are urgently needed in their time."
Jiǎ Sīxié of Later Wèi, _Essential Techniques for the Welfare of the People_.
Cross-referenced under "Using the Heavy to Illustrate the Light".
Wǔ Yuán's reliance on a fishing boat,
Jì Bù's hiding in a large willow cart.
_Family Instructions of the Yán Clan_.
Collected Works
Fish, when the spring dries up, moisten each other with foam;
birds, when near death, cry mournfully.
Liú Xiàobiāo's _Discourse_.
To relieve hunger, one does not await a tripod-cooked feast;
to rescue the drowning, one does not wait for proper conduct.
． _Selection of Policy Essays_.
A fish in a cooking pot
awaits its dissolution and decay.
． _Selection of Proclamations_.
Losing one's spirit and soul,
forfeiting direction and purpose.
_Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital_.
Cross-referenced under "Fear".
The peril of the Hú, their fate hangs by a thread in splitting bamboo.
Poem by Dù Gōngbù.
In a household lacking clothing and food,
even a stern father and compassionate mother
cannot control their children.
_Collected Works of Bái Jūyì_.
A cornered beast will grapple with humans,
a desperate deer will rush through narrow passes.
Dù Mùzhī.
A fish at its limit in a cooking tripod,
ants fearing their nest being searched.
Text by Sīkōng Tǔshèng.
Our Dynasty
Without the fierce tiger,
would the timid
dare to cross the deep valley?
_Collected Works of Lǎo Sū_.
Human nature, regardless of wisdom or folly,
none do not fear Heaven and revere their father.
Yet in pain they call for their father,
in dire straits they cry out to Heaven,
for feelings arise from within,
and words are spoken without choice.
How can one, because of their cries,
say they lack a heart of reverence and fear?
Sū Dōngpō.
Classics
After four generations, the mourning attire ends with the lightest hemp;
after five generations, baring the arm and removing the cap signifies the cessation of kinship;
after six generations, kinship is exhausted.
． _Book of Rites, Great Tradition_.
Masters
The influence of a nobleman lasts five generations before it is cut off;
the influence of a commoner also lasts five generations before it is cut off.
_Mencius_.
Histories
A set of fine gold ornaments does not exceed a hundred liang,
a year's beautiful clothes are no more than a few sets.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Sòng Tàizǔ_.
Biographies and Records
Wū Huò could lift a weight of a thousand jūn,
but at eighty years of age, he needed support to walk.
_Strategies of the Warring States_.
When the Qíjì steed is in its prime,
it can gallop a thousand li in a day;
but when it declines,
a nag can outrun it.
Same as above.
Collected Works
Extending years without death,
where does longevity ultimately cease?
"Chǔcí".
Even metal and stone eventually corrode and perish.
Xiè Huìlián's "Autumn Reflections Poem".
All flourishing things indeed face decay,
and mighty forces easily reach their extremes.
"Collection of Chén Zǐ'áng".
Radiant beauty does not last a thousand years.
"Lǐ Bái".
The wren nesting in the woods needs but one branch,
the field mouse drinking from the river only fills its belly.
"Zhuāngzǐ".
When the
pond dries up,
it's not said to start from the edges.
When the spring runs dry,
it's not said to begin from within.
． "Shījīng • Zhāo Mín".
Wise men build cities,
while clever women topple them.
． "Shījīng • Zhān Yǎng".
The ritual for a minister
is not to remonstrate overtly.
If after three remonstrations he is not heeded,
he should leave.
For a son serving his parents,
if after three remonstrations they do not listen,
he should follow them weeping and wailing.
． "Lǐjì • Qū Lǐ Xià".
In serving parents, conceal their faults but do not offend them;
in serving a ruler, offend him but conceal nothing;
in serving a teacher, neither offend nor conceal.
Same as above.
The noble man loves others with virtue,
the petty man loves others with indulgence.
"Tángōng Shàng".
Ritual for people
is like yeast for wine.
The noble man uses it to become generous,
the petty man uses it to become shallow.
"Lǐyùn",
also from "Lǐjì".
Cross-reference "Same Origin, Different Paths".
The Master said: "Only the highest wisdom and the lowest stupidity do not change."
． "Lúnyǔ • Yáng Huò".
If
people in the same room are fighting,
one may intervene to stop them,
even with hair disheveled and cap strings tied hastily.
That is permissible.
If neighbors are fighting,
and one goes to intervene with disheveled hair and hasty cap,
that is delusion,
and one might as well shut the door.
． "Mèngzǐ • Wàn Zhāng Xià".
Dying after exhausting one's path
is a proper fate;
dying in shackles
is not a proper fate.
Same as above,
"Jìn Xīn Xià".
The robber Zhí's reputation shines like the sun and moon,
passed down alongside Shùn and Yǔ.
Yet noble men do not value him,
for he does not conform to ritual and righteousness.
． "Xúnzǐ • Bù Gǒu".
Loving honor and hating disgrace,
loving profit and hating harm—
these are common to both noble and petty men.
But their ways of seeking them differ.
． "Xúnzǐ • Róng Rǔ".
When crossing a river in a double boat,
if an empty vessel bumps into it,
even a narrow-minded person does not get angry.
But if there is someone aboard that vessel,
one will shout curses at them.
Not angry then but angry now—
because before it was empty, now it is occupied.
"Zhuāngzǐ".
When a rabbit runs through the street,
a hundred people chase it,
greedy as they all are,
no one faults them,
because catching the rabbit is an undetermined share.
When piled rabbits fill the market,
passersby do not even glance—
not that they don't want rabbits,
but after shares are fixed,
even the lowly do not contend.
"Shènzǐ".
Cross-reference "Matters Have Fixed Shares".
The more a noble man hears and sees, the more sincere his heart becomes;
the more a petty man hears and sees, the more false his heart becomes.
Annotation to "Yángzǐ".
Fish fear not the net but the pelican;
the avenger blames not the sword but the wielder.
The net is mindless, but the bird has feelings;
the sword is heartless, but the man has intent.
"Liúzǐ".
Cross-reference "Intentional", "Unintentional".
History
When good men grow rich,
it is called reward;
when wicked men grow rich,
it is called calamity.
． "Zuǒzhuàn • Xiāng 28".
Gōngfǔ Wénbó held office in Lǔ,
and died of illness.
Sixteen women killed themselves in their rooms for him.
When his mother heard,
she refused to weep.
The steward said: "How can a mother not weep for her dead son?"
His mother replied: "Confucius,
a worthy man,
was driven from Lǔ,
and this son did not follow him.
Now he dies,
and sixteen women die for him.
This shows
he was thin to the worthy and thick to women.
Thus, from a mother's view, I am a worthy mother; from a wife's view, I would be a jealous wife.
So when the speaker differs,
people's hearts shift."
"Zhànguócè".
Cross-reference "Women's Insight".
The higher the virtue, the safer;
the higher the power, the more perilous.
． "Shǐjì • Rìzhě Zhuàn".
The "Shījīng" says "buy me wine if there's none",
yet the "Lúnyǔ" says "I do not drink bought wine"—
these two are not contradictory.
The "Shījīng" refers to a peaceful age,
when wine was brewed by officials,
harmonious and pleasant for people,
fit for consumption.
In the "Lúnyǔ", Confucius lived in Zhou's decline,
when wine was brewed by commoners,
weak, poor, and insincere,
hence he doubted and did not drink it.
． "Qián Hànshū • Shíhuò Zhì".
When Zhāng Shìzhī was commandant,
no one under heaven was wronged;
when Yú Dìngguó was commandant,
the people felt they were not wronged.
"Qián Hànshū".
Whenever Yáo and Sòng two men came to audience,
the emperor would rise for them,
and see them off from the balcony when they left.
When Lǐ Línfǔ became chancellor,
though favored more than Yáo and Sòng,
his ceremonial treatment was far inferior.
"Zīzhì Tōngjiàn".
Biographies
Loyalty in orderly times is easy,
loyalty in chaotic times is hard.
"Lǚshì Chūnqiū".
Cross-reference "Matters Have Difficulty and Ease".
Collections
All men must die,
some as weighty as Mount Tài,
some as light as a goose feather.
Sīmǎ Qiān's "Letter to Rèn Ān".
The historian blames Cuò's father for not matching Zhào Kuò's mother—
how shallow!

Assembling all talents,
gathering numerous artisans.
Some hold axes,
some hold saws,
all standing in a circle facing him.
The master carpenter holds a measuring line in his left hand and a staff in his right, positioned centrally.
Assessing the load-bearing of the beams,
judging the capability of the wood,
he raises his staff and commands: "Axe!"
Those holding axes rush to the right.
With a glance and point, he says: "Saw!"
Those holding saws hasten to the left.
Soon, the axe-wielders chop,
the knife-wielders carve,
all watching his expression,
awaiting his word,
none daring to decide on their own.
Those incompetent,
he dismisses with anger, yet none dare resent it.
He sketches the building on the wall,
within a foot capturing every detail of its design,
calculating to the finest measure to construct the great hall,
with no deviation.
Once completed,
he inscribes on the main beam,
"Built by so-and-so on such-and-such date,"
which is his name.
All the laborers who executed the work are not listed.
I looked around in astonishment,
then realized the greatness of his craft.
Subsequently, I sighed: "Has he set aside his manual skills,
focused his mind and intellect,
to grasp the essence of structure?
I've heard that those who labor with their minds govern others,
while those who labor with their strength are governed by others.
Is he not one who labors with his mind?
The capable are employed, the wise devise plans;
is he not one of the wise?
This is sufficient as a model for assisting the Son of Heaven and governing the realm!
Those who assist the Son of Heaven and govern the realm,
appoint and assign tasks,
direct and command,
organize the principles and adjust as needed,
standardize laws and regulations to bring order,
much like the carpenter uses compasses, squares, and ink lines to set standards.
Selecting scholars of the realm,
ensuring they fit their posts;
settling the people of the realm,
making them content in their livelihoods.
Observing the capital, one understands the countryside;
observing the countryside, one understands the state;
observing the state, one understands the world.
Whether far or near, small or large,
one can hold the map and investigate it all,
just as the carpenter sketches the building on the wall and completes the work.
Promote the capable and follow their lead,
so they feel no need for gratitude;
dismiss the incompetent and let them rest,
with none daring resentment.
Not flaunting ability,
not boasting of fame,
not attending to minor tasks,
not encroaching on other officials' duties,
daily discussing grand principles with the world's elite,
much like the carpenter adeptly directing the artisans without claiming their skills.
Only then is the way of governance achieved and all states well-ordered.
Once the way of governance is attained,
and all states are in order,
the people of the realm look up and say:
"It is the achievement of our prime minister." Later generations follow the traces and admire:
"Such was the talent of that prime minister." Scholars discussing the governance of Yīn and Zhōu,
mention Yī, Fù, Zhōu, and Shào,
while the diligent efforts of all the functionaries go unrecorded,
just as the carpenter inscribes his own name while the laborers are not listed.
How great is the role of prime minister!
One who comprehends this way,
is called a true prime minister.

Nothing is better than cultivating the foundation to overcome them.
In the past during the Warring States period,

may not have been inherently unkind.

yet borrows to eat—
people would still call him rich.
From Xúnzǐ.
Cross-reference "Not Rejecting the Coarse."
Jade from Zhōng Mountain,
heated in a furnace's charcoal,
for three days and three nights,
does not change its color.
From Huáinánzǐ.
Fine jade in muddy filth—
even the honest will not leave it.
Where beauty resides,
though defiled and shamed,
the world cannot deem it cheap.
Ibid.
Jade from Jīng Mountain,
hidden within its stones,
though buried under a thousand ren of earth,
cannot conceal its glow.
From Bàopǔzǐ.
Cinnabar can be ground but not stripped of its color;
orchids can be burned but not extinguished of their fragrance;
jade can be shattered but not altered in its whiteness;
gold can be melted but not changed in its hardness.
From Liúzǐ.
History
Like the eclipse of the sun and moon,
how does it impair their brightness?
． _Zuozhuan, 12th Year of Duke Xuan_.
From the casting of the five-zhu coin in the Han dynasty to Emperor Wen of Song,
over five hundred years passed.
Systems have risen and fallen through the ages,
yet the five-zhu coin remained unchanged,
demonstrating that its weight was exemplary,
and it suited the nature of currency.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Emperor Gao of Qi_.
White jade cast into mud
can never be defiled.
． _History of the Northern Dynasties, Biography of Mù Bì_.
Cuī Miǎn passed the imperial examination with top honors,
but those who failed bitterly slandered him.
Empress Wǔ ordered a re-examination by officials,
where Cuī Miǎn's responses proved even more refined,
and he was ranked first.
_Book of Tang_.
Though Gànjiàng sword may break,
its gleam remains undimmed.
． _Old Book of Tang, Yáng Yúlíng_.
Records state:
Zhōu had the Dǐ'è jade,
Sòng had the Jiélǜ jade,
Liáng had the Xuánlí jade,
Chǔ had the Hépú jade.
These four treasures,
though overlooked by craftsmen,
became renowned vessels of the world.
_Strategies of the Warring States_.
A stone may be shattered,
but its hardness cannot be taken away.
_Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals_.
A fine pearl measuring an inch,
though submerged in water a hundred fathoms deep,
cannot conceal its radiance.
_Han's Outer Commentary on the Classic of Poetry_.
A fine jade of one-foot diameter,
though buried under a thousand fathoms of earth, cannot hide its light;
a bright pearl measuring an inch,
though encased in a rock ten feet thick, cannot suppress its glow.
Yú Bānyòu, _Biographies of Noble Scholars_.
Collection:
Máoqiáng and Xīshī,
even skilled detractors cannot obscure their beauty.
． _Selected Essays: Four Masters' Discourse on Virtue_.
Even faded, the orchid's fragrance lingers.
． _Selected Linked Pearls_.
When a pearl shatters, it loses not its earthy hue;
when jade falls, it makes no sound of tile.
A broken sword still has inches of sharpness;
a shattered mirror still reflects in fragments.
_Collection of Yuǎn Zhěn_.
Present this to the mouths of the crowd:
even melted down, it remains gold.
Ibid.
A divine sword does not corrode in soil;
a rare cloth does not burn in fire.
_Collection of Yuán Wēizhī_.
Gold may be melted,
but cannot be made foul and rotten;
water may be muddied,
but cannot be turned to dust and filth.
Yuán Cìshān.
Cross-reference "Having Steadfastness".
Though white jade gathers dust and grime,
wiping it restores its brilliance.
_Collection of Wéi Yìngwù_.
Sinking jades and burying pendants—how can they not shine even in darkness?
Hiding calamus and orchids—why would their fragrance not endure?
Liǔ's _Lament for Qū Yuán_.
The aura of a hero under heaven,
remains awe-inspiring for a thousand autumns.
Liú Bīnkè.
Pearls cannot be dimmed by dust.
Ibid.
Catalpa and zi trees grow in deep forests;
though unknown to people,
it does not hinder their being timber for the world.
Essay by Ōuyáng Zhān.
Though a sword is buried, its spirit remains.
Bái Lètiān.
Without the tempering fire,
who would know the essence of an inch of gold?
Mèng Dōngyě.
A mirror broken does not change its reflection;
an orchid dying does not lose its fragrance.
Ibid.
Pound musk into dust—its scent persists;
twist lotus into strands—its threads endure.
Dù Mùzhī.
A pearl that illuminates a carriage—
its brilliance is hard to obscure.
_Tang Literary Essence_.
Like the sun and moon,
though seen eternally through the ages,
their light remains ever new,
this is why they are considered numinous.
Ibid.
The sun and moon eclipse and shine brighter after;
the Héshì璧 and Hé Pú jade remain luminous even in obscurity.
For fine timber, pearls, Mòyé swords, and Máoqiáng,
one never worries about concealment, boxing, bending, or striking as threats.
While gnarled wood, gravel, leaden dullness, and the hunchbacked may obstruct,
their revelation is merely a matter of time.
All ibid.
Have you not seen the Kūnwú iron smelting, flames flying,
red light and purple aura both blazing?
Skilled craftsmen forged it for years,
casting a treasured sword named Lóngquán.
Why speak of its abandonment mid-journey,
fallen and drifting by an ancient prison?
Though buried and sunk, seemingly useless,
still each night its spirit surges to the sky.
Guō Yuánzhèn's "Song of the Precious Sword".
Our dynasty:
It is like burying gold and jade—
their essence and brilliance remain undiminished.
_Collection of Ōu Gōng_.
The three lights—sun, moon, stars—remain untarnished through eternity.
Ibid.
Confucius and Mencius struggled all their lives,
slandered and exiled in countless ways.
If posterity were unjust,
there would be no sages today.
Thus, loyal and righteous scholars,
relying on this, face death unflinchingly.
Ibid.
This culture is like gold and jade;
discarded and buried in filth,
it cannot corrode.
Though neglected in its time,
it will surely be treasured by later generations.
Even while buried and unseen,
its essence and radiant energy can manifest spontaneously,
and nothing can conceal it.
Thus, when rejected, crushed, wandering in destitution,
its writings already spread across the world;
even its enemies and those who conspired to destroy it,
when faced with its writings,
cannot slight or obscure them.
． Ōu Gōng's "Preface to Sū Shì's Collected Works".
Gold,
tempered a hundred times into a mirror,
reflects all things without evasion.
But when tarnished and dulled by corrosion,
it becomes no different from a tile.
Yet, once treated by a skilled artisan's elixir,
polished to clarity,
it can reveal innards and count hairs.
For what can be dimmed is its light,
not its inherent nature.
Ōu Gōng's "Eulogy for Liú Jǐshì".
Noble and upright, towering and majestic,
buried underground,
one imagines it not decaying into soil,
but transforming into the essence of gold and jade;
if not,
growing into a thousand-foot pine,
or producing a nine-stemmed spirit fungus.
Ōu Gōng's "Eulogy for Shí Mànqīng".
Thus it is said: What endures without flaw is the Way;
what remains hidden yet ultimately revealed is sincerity.
Ōu Gōng's "Stele for Wáng Jūn, Hàn Court Gentleman".
Also know: Objects gain value with age;
treasures reveal themselves through repeated tempering.
_Collection of Ōu Gōng_.
A black moon in turbid water
can still be clear and bright.
Dōngpō's poem.
Bones may decay, but the heart's resolve is endless.
Ibid.
Tempered a hundred times, the will remains unchanged.
_Collection of Luánchéng_.
A divine pearl in muddy sand—
its radiance cannot be dimmed.
_Collection of Línchuān_.
When kalpa fires blaze,
only jade remains unburned.
Yáng Zhōnglì's "Eulogy for Liú Ānshì".
Gold, though tested a hundred deaths, does not transform.
Essay by Chén Wěi.
Tempered a hundred times, the fire extinguishes itself;
if the gold remains,
it is true gold.
． _Míngdào Ānzhèng Wàngquán Collection, Master's Chapter_.
End
Forced weeping,
though intense, lacks sorrow;
forced joy,
though smiling, lacks delight.
Huáinánzǐ.
A sheep in tiger's skin,
delights at seeing grass,
trembles at seeing jackals,
forgetting it wears a tiger's hide.
Yángzǐ.
History
Lù Zhǎn dyed his white hair,
hoping to please his concubine.
But the dark hue did not last long,
and the starlike white strands soon reappeared.
From "The Biography of Xiè Língyùn in the History of the Southern Dynasties".
Biographies
Yáng Jiǒng often called court officials "qílín xuàn".
When asked why,
he said:
"Those who stage unicorns nowadays
adorn its form,
drape it over a donkey,
making it seem a marvel.
But once the hide is removed,
it's still a donkey." From "Records of Court and Country".
Collections
Glowworms shine but are never fire,
dewdrops on lotus, round as they are, are not pearls.
Bái Lètiān.
In Qián, there were no donkeys until a meddlesome person brought one in by boat.
Finding it useless upon arrival,
he set it free at the mountain's foot.
A tiger, seeing this huge creature,
thought it divine and hid in the woods to observe.
Venturing closer cautiously,
it remained wary, unsure of its nature.
One day, the donkey brayed,
frightening the tiger so much it fled far,
fearing it would be devoured.
But over time, watching it closely,
the tiger sensed no special abilities
and grew accustomed to its bray.
Approaching from all sides,
it still dared not attack.
Edging nearer, it became bolder,
brushing, leaning, bumping, and provoking.
The donkey, enraged,
kicked out.
The tiger, pleased, reckoned,
"Its skill ends here!"
Then it pounced with a roar,
bit through its throat,
devoured all its flesh,
and left.
Liǔ Wén.
This Dynasty
Like cutting silk to make flowers:
they may look identical,
but lack the natural essence of creation.
Míngdào in "Records of the Two Chéngs".
Philosophy
Grand music is not for common ears;
"Plucking Willows" and "Yellow Blossoms"
make them chuckle with delight.
Zhuāngzǐ.
History
Walking the straight path,
one makes many enemies and few friends.
From "The Biography of Gài Kuānráo in the History of the Western Hàn".
Biographies
A singer in Yǐng began with "Lowlands" and "Bā Folk",
and thousands in the state joined in chorus.
With "High Hills" and "Gathering Ferns",
hundreds sang along.
But for "Spring Sun" and "White Snow",
only dozens could follow.
When he mixed sharp shāng and delicate zhǐ notes,
fewer than a handful could harmonize.
Thus, the loftier the tune,
the fewer the voices joining in.
Liú Xiàng's "New Prefaces".
Collections
Who appreciates the nature of pines and osmanthus,
when all compete for the shade of peaches and plums?
Hán Wén.
Those who bring goods to market to sell high
often find them hard to sell.
Same as above.
Only with Bó Lè do we recognize thousand-mile steeds.
Such horses are common,
but Bó Lè is rare.
Thus, even famed steeds
may be mistreated by stable hands,
dying side by side in stalls,
never known for their千里 prowess.
Also from the same.
This Dynasty
In times without Zhōng Zǐqī,
who understands the meaning of high mountains?
Without Jì Zhá,
who recognizes the music of a well-governed era?
Ōu Gōng's "Reply to Magistrate Xiàng's Poem".
"Plucking Willows" and "Yellow Blossoms" amuse many,
while "Spring Sun" and "White Snow" find few to join.
True connoisseurs are scarce under heaven,
let alone in the small state of Yǐng.
From the "Línchuān Collection".
Great talent has long been hard to employ,
lofty theories often seem impractical.
Pō Shī.
Classics
Diligently study day and night to be ready for questions,
hold loyalty and trust to await recommendation,
strive in action to merit selection.
From "The Conduct of the Scholar" in the Records.
To govern the state, first regulate the family;
to regulate the family, first cultivate the self;
to cultivate the self, first rectify the heart;
to rectify the heart, first sincere the will.
The Great Learning.
Only by harmonizing one's family
can one teach the people of the state.
Same as above.
Respectfulness, when close to ritual,
keeps disgrace at bay.
From the Analects, "Learning".
A gentleman values three things in the Way:
composing his countenance to avoid violence and arrogance,
setting his expression aright to approach trustworthiness,
and minding his words to stay clear of coarseness and error.
From "Tàibó".
To excel in his work,
a craftsman must first sharpen his tools.
From "Duke Wèi líng".
Philosophy
First establish the greater part,
and the lesser cannot be taken away.
From Mencius, "Gāozǐ II".
The great man rectifies himself,
and thus all things are rectified.
Mencius.
Those well-prepared in resources
survive famine years;
those firm in virtue
remain unswayed in corrupt times.
Same as above.
Better to dig a well than rely on others for water.
Huáinánzǐ.
By the river desiring fish,
it's better to go back and weave a net.
Wénzǐ.
One must love oneself first,
then others will love them;
one must respect oneself first,
then others will respect them.
From "According to Myself".
Is not a great vessel like the compass, square, and level?
First govern oneself,
then govern others.
From "Yáng Xiānzhī".
History
Zāng Wǔzhòng said: "Those in high positions
must cleanse their hearts,
unify themselves to treat others,
regulate their trustworthiness,
and only then can they govern people."
． From Zuǒzhuàn, Year 21 of Xiānggōng.
Just like a farmer,
who weeds and mounds the soil.
Although there may be famine,
there will surely be abundant years.
． From Zuǒzhuàn, Year 1 of Zhāogōng.
Only the flawless can punish others.
． From Zuǒzhuàn, Year 4 of Zhāogōng.
Gazing at fish in the deep waters,
it's better to go back and weave a net.
． By Dǒng Zhòngshū of the Western Hàn.
If you don't want others to hear,
better not to speak;
if you don't want others to know,
better not to do.
From Méichéng's Biography.
Collection:
High-flying birds not caught by light arrows,
deep-water fish not hooked by bait—
it's feared that the techniques of hooking and shooting are not yet perfected.
． Selected from "Memorial of Admonition".
Striving for outstanding fame,
how can one not sharpen outstanding tools?
Fighting in横行 formations,
how can one not develop横行 strategies?
Huángfǔ Shí.
Master:
What is naturally long cannot be cut short,
what is naturally short cannot be lengthened.
． From Zhuāngzǐ, "Webbed Toes" chapter.
Jiǎ Qióng asked: "How to stop slander?"
The Master said: "Do not argue."
He asked: "How to stop resentment?"
The Master said: "Do not contend."
． From Wénzhōngzǐ's "Inquiry into the Yì".
History:
Beyond the remote territories,
their rebellion does not warrant mobilizing troops,
their surrender does not warrant relaxing defenses.
Make it impossible for them to raid,
and impossible to submit as subjects.
．． From the Tángshū, Preface to the "Account of the Turks".
Also see "There is a way to control".
Collection:
If they do not know me,
and call me a robber like Zhí,
why should I fear?
If they do not know me,
and praise me as Confucius,
why should I feel honored?
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's "On Slander and Praise".
This dynasty:
The beautiful are beautiful themselves,
why should I rejoice?
The ugly are ugly themselves,
why should I be angry?
They leave on their own,
why should I feel lacking and pursue?
They come on their own,
why should I hinder and reject?
From the Línchuān Collection.
Teeth and hair are entrusted to Heaven,
their decay cannot be repaired.
Sū Dōngpō.
Classic:
Better if they do not come,
than that I neglect them.
Better if they do not come,
than that I am at fault.
． From the Shījīng, "Cutting Trees".
The noble person introspects without guilt,
and has nothing to shame his will.
． From the Record of the Zhōngyōng.
The Master said: "Do not worry about having no position,
worry about how to establish yourself;
do not worry that no one knows you,
seek to be worth knowing."
． From the Analects, "Lǐ Rén".
Loyal in advice and skillful in guidance,
stop if it is not accepted.
． From the Analects, "Yán Yuān".
The Master said: "Do not worry that others do not know you,
worry about your lack of ability."
． From the Analects, "Xiàn Wèn".
Master:
Regardless of premature death or longevity, cultivate oneself unwaveringly and await fate.
． From Mèngzǐ, "Jìn Xīn Shang".
The noble person can make himself worthy of honor,
but cannot make others necessarily honor him;
can make himself trustworthy,
but cannot make others necessarily trust him;
can make himself useful,
but cannot make others necessarily employ him.
Thus, he feels shame at not cultivating himself,
not at being slandered;
shame at being untrustworthy,
not at not being trusted;
shame at lacking ability,
not at not being employed.
． From Xúnzǐ, "Against the Twelve Masters".
Cross-reference to "Knowing Shame".
The noble person admires what lies within himself,
not what lies with Heaven.
． From Xúnzǐ, "The Way of Heaven".
The orchid grows in a secluded palace,
not ceasing its fragrance because none wear it;
the boat is on the river or sea,
not ceasing to float because none ride it.
The noble person acts righteously,
not stopping because none know of it.
． From Huáinánzǐ, "Explaining the Mountains".
History:
If the heart is without flaw,
why worry about having no home?
． From Zuǒzhuàn, Mǐngōng.
The people of Zhèng gathered at the village school,
to discuss the government.
Rán Míng said to Zǐchǎn: "Abolish the village school."
Zǐchǎn said: "When people gather there after work,
to discuss the government's merits and faults—
what they approve,
I will implement;
what they criticize,
I will correct.
They are my teachers,
why abolish it?"
． From Zuǒzhuàn, Year 32 of Xiānggōng.
If one can cultivate oneself,
why worry about lack of honor?
From the "Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò".
Scholars suffer from not understanding the classics.
If one understands the classics,
attaining high office
is as easy as picking up a mustard seed from the ground.
． From the "Biography of Xiàhóu Shèng" of the Western Hàn.
Introspecting without guilt,
why fear others' words?
． From the "Biography of Bān Chāo" of the Eastern Hàn.
Cross-reference to "Without Shame".
Yú Shìnán said: "If virtue is not cultivated,
even obtaining a qílín or phoenix
is ultimately of no help.
But if governance is without fault,
even with disasters,
what harm is there to the times?"
From the Tángshū.
Collection:
Students should worry about their studies not being refined,
not about the officials' lack of discernment;
worry about their conduct not being accomplished,
not about the officials' lack of fairness.
From Hán Wéngōng's "Advice on Learning".
Those who possess weapons like Zhànlú or Háocáo
worry about not getting rhinoceros hide to test them on,
not about their sharpness.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán.
The noble person embraces benevolence and righteousness,
fearing not even if heaven and earth collapse.
From the Collection of Wáng Jiàn.
This dynasty:
The clear fragrance does not diminish for lack of people.
From Ōuyáng Xiū's "Accompanying a Drink at the Rear Pavilion of Shànglín Court".
What cannot be taken lies with oneself,
to take or not lies with others.
From Sū Dōngpō's "Record of Four Bodhisattvas".
Those who know fate must exhaust human efforts,
then principles are fulfilled without regret.
Things that form must decay,
just as people who are born must die,
and states that rise must fall.
Although knowing this,
the noble person in nurturing the body
uses all means to prolong life and delay death;
in governing the state,
does all that can preserve existence and avert downfall;
persisting until无可奈何,
then stops—
this is called knowing fate.
From Sū Dōngpō's "Record of the Ink Marvel Pavilion".
Classic:
The sage, if heedless, becomes a madman;
the madman, if attentive, becomes a sage.
． From the "Book of Documents: Many Regions".
Ritual for a person
is like yeast for wine:
the nobleman uses it to enrich,
the petty person uses it to dilute.
． From the "Record of Rites: Evolution of Rites".
Cross-reference: "Same matter, different substance".
Mèngzǐ:
Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom
are not infused in me from without;
they are inherently mine.
Only, I have not reflected on them.
Hence it is said:
"Seek and you will obtain them;
neglect and you will lose them."
From the "Mèngzǐ".
If you wear the clothes of Yáo,
recite the words of Yáo,
and practice the deeds of Yáo,
then you are simply Yáo.
If you wear the clothes of Jié,
recite the words of Jié,
and practice the deeds of Jié,
then you are simply Jié.
From the "Mèngzǐ".
If Xīzǐ were covered in filth,
people would all hold their noses and pass by her.
Even an ugly person,
if purified and bathed,
may then sacrifice to the Supreme Deity.
． From "Mèngzǐ: Lílóu II".
Suppose there is a person
whose strength cannot lift a single chick—
then he is considered a weak person.
Now if it is said
that lifting a hundred jūn makes one a strong person,
then to bear the burden of Wū Huò
is simply to be Wū Huò.
Should one worry about not being able?
It is merely not doing it.
． From "Mèngzǐ: Jìnxīn II".
Human nature's goodness
is like water's tendency to flow downward.
Now take water:
strike it and make it splash,
and it can go over your forehead;
force it to flow,
and it can be made to go uphill.
Is this water's nature?
That humans can be made to do evil
is likewise with their nature.
． From "Mèngzǐ: Gàozǐ II".
Carve and then give up,
and even rotten wood won't break;
carve without ceasing,
and metal or stone can be engraved.
． From the "Xúnzǐ: Encouraging Learning".
Block its source,
open its channels,
and even rivers can be exhausted;
one step forward, one step back,
one left, one right,
and six fine steeds won't reach the destination.
． From the "Xúnzǐ: Cultivating Oneself".
Thus, if used well,
a state of a hundred lǐ can stand independently;
if used poorly,
then even Chǔ with six thousand lǐ becomes servant to its enemies.
． From the "Xúnzǐ: Zhòngní".
The sun, moon, stars, and constellations
were the same for Yǔ and for Jié.
Yǔ used them to bring order,
Jié used them to create chaos.
There are people who bring order,
but no fixed methods for order.
Yì's archery method was not lost,
but Yìs are not born in every age;
Yǔ's methods still exist,
but the Xià dynasty did not reign in every age.
With the right person, they survive;
without the right person, they perish.
． Both from the "Xúnzǐ: Way of Heaven".
He who accumulates deeply
spreads his influence widely;
he who accumulates thinly
spreads his influence narrowly.
Be a nobleman,
and you will often be safe and honored;
be a petty person,
and you will often be in danger and disgrace.
Both from the "Xúnzǐ".
A lame turtle can reach the goal,
while six fine steeds may not—
this is for no other reason
than that one does it,
and the other does not.
． From the "Xúnzǐ: Cultivating Oneself".
All streams learn from the sea and reach the sea;
hills learn from the mountain but do not reach the mountain.
． From "Yángzǐ: Learning and Conduct".
A horse that aspires to be a steed
is also a steed's kind.
A person who aspires to be like Yán Yuān
is also a disciple of Yán.
Same as above.
Cultivate goodness and you become a good person;
cultivate evil and you become an evil person.
． From "Yángzǐ: Cultivating Oneself".
To be feared or to be insulted
depends entirely on oneself.
． From "Yángzǐ: Five Hundred".
Govern with the right way,
and all the cunning in the world will serve you;
govern without the right way,
and all the cunning in the world will become your enemies.
From the "Yángzǐ".
Cross-reference: "Not a hair's breadth between".
Borrow a Confucian robe and books to read,
and if after three months you do not return them,
who can say you are not a Confucian?
From the "Yángzǐ".
Cross-reference: "Artificially shaped".
Plow the Way and you gain the Way;
hunt virtue and you gain virtue.
From the "Yángzǐ".
They are like water and fire:
used well, they bring blessing;
used poorly, they bring disaster.
． From the "Kàngcāngzǐ: The Way of War" chapter.
Now take Máo Qiáng and Xī Shī,
the beauties of the world:
if you make them handle rotten rats,
cover them with hedgehog skins,
dress them in leopard furs,
and gird them with dead snakes,
then even passersby in cloth clothes and leather belts
will all look askance and cover their noses.
But try having them apply fragrant oils,
straighten their moth eyebrows,
set hairpins and earrings,
dress in fine silks,
drag Qí gossamer,
powder white and paint black,
wear jade pendants,
then even kings, dukes, and great men
with stern wills and haughty conduct
will all feel stirred and pleased by their beauty.
． From the "Huáinánzǐ: Cultivation of Effort".
Cross-reference: "Not a hair's breadth between".
Thus, Wèi employed both Lóu Zhái and Wú Qǐ
and lost the Western Hé;
King Mǐn employed only Nào Chǐ
and died in the eastern temple,
for they had no method to govern them.
King Wén employed both Lǚ Wàng and Shào Gōng Shì and became king;
King Zhuāng of Chǔ employed only Sūn Shū Áo and became hegemon,
for they had a method to govern them.
． From the "Huáinánzǐ: Discussions on the Way".
History
In the first year of Duke Wén of Wèi's reign,
he had thirty war chariots;
by the final year of his reign,
this had increased to three hundred chariots.
. "Zuǒzhuàn, Mǐn 3".

Zhào Tuó declared himself emperor and rivaled the Central Plains.
The emperor then established a guard settlement for Tuó's ancestral tombs in Zhēndìng,
offering sacrifices seasonally;

granting them high positions and generous gifts to honor them.
He again sent Lù Jiǎ as an envoy to Nányuè,
bestowing a letter to Tuó that said: "Recently, I heard you mobilized troops at the border,
causing continuous disasters of conflict.
At that time,
Chángshā suffered greatly,
and Nánjùn even more so.
Even for your own state,
is this truly beneficial?
It must have killed many soldiers,
wounded good generals and officials,
widowed men's wives,
orphaned their children,
left parents alone,
gaining one but losing ten—
I cannot bear to do such a thing.
If I were to acquire your land now,
it would not make me greater;
if I were to acquire your wealth,
it would not make me richer.
South of the Fúlíng mountains,
you may govern it yourself.
However,
you have taken the title of emperor.
With two emperors standing side by side,
without a single envoy to communicate between them,
this is contention without humility,
which the benevolent would not do.
I wish to discard past grievances with you,
and from now on,
resume diplomatic exchanges as before."
Jiǎ arrived in Nányuè,
and the king of Nányuè, fearful,
kowtowed in apology,
admitting his fault and vowing to follow the clear decree,
to remain a vassal forever,
and offer tribute.
He issued an order to abandon the imperial system,
and declared himself a subject.

King Zhuāng of Chǔ had a beloved horse that died,
and he ordered his ministers to mourn it,
intending to bury it with a coffin and outer coffin in the rites of a senior official.
Those around him argued against it,
but he would not listen.
Mèng entered the palace gate,
looked up to the sky, and laughed loudly, saying:

what could it not obtain?

is too modest.

The King said:

He said:
"I request a coffin carved from jade,
an outer coffin of patterned catalpa,
with cedar, nanmu, and camphorwood for the joints,
mobilize armored soldiers to dig the tomb,
the elderly and weak to carry the earth,

sacrifice to it in the temple with the Great Tribute,

and Tián Dān gathers and feeds them;

and Tián Dān removes his robe to clothe them;

but actually harm them.
From Mèngzǐ.

Duke Mù's treatment of Zǐsī

which displeased Zǐsī;

The emperor of the Southern Sea was Shū,
the emperor of the Northern Sea was Hū,
the emperor of the Center was Hùndùn.
Shū and Hū sometimes met in Hùndùn's territory,
and Hùndùn treated them very well.
Shū and Hū planned to repay Hùndùn's virtue,
saying: "All men have seven apertures for seeing, hearing, eating, and breathing,
but this one alone has none.
Let's try boring some for him."
They bored one aperture each day,
and on the seventh day Hùndùn died.
From Zhuāngzǐ, Yìng Dì Wáng chapter.
Can the peng bird soar to heaven
without its six primary feathers?
If plucked and given to a turtledove,
wouldn't it be burdensome?
From Yángzǐ, Guǎ Jiàn.
Duke Wǔ of Zhèng and Jiāng of Zhuāng gave birth to Duke Zhuāng and Duàn of Gòng.
She wished to establish him,
and repeatedly requested this of Duke Wǔ,
but the duke refused.
When Duke Zhuāng succeeded to the throne,
she requested Jīng for him,
and had him reside there.
The younger brother completed his preparations,
intending to attack Zhèng,
and the lady was going to open the gates for him.
The duke ordered an attack on Jīng,
and the younger brother fled to Gòng.
From Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Yǐn 1st year.
Zǐpí of Zhèng wanted to make Yǐnhé a city governor,

From Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xiāng 31st year.
Emperor Hàn favored Yìn King Rúyì,

Empress Lǚ summoned the King of Zhào
and executed him.
From History of Western Hàn, Empress Lǚ's biography.
Emperor Xuān of Hàn emphasized penal laws,
trusting his secretaries.
Gài Kuānráo submitted a memorial saying: "Now we make legal experts into Zhōu and Shào,
and treat law codes as the Book of Songs and Book of Documents."
He also said: "The Five Emperors treated the world as public office,
the Three Kings treated it as family property.
Family means passing to sons,
office means passing to the worthy."
The Commandant of the Capital submitted that Kuānráo "intended to seize power,
and was greatly impious."
Reminder Gentleman Zhèng Chāng petitioned defending Kuānráo: "Above, he lacked connections like Xǔ and Shǐ,
below, he lacked support like Jīn and Zhāng."

was Emperor Xuān's father-in-law;
Shǐ Xuān

Zhāng Jīn

The emperor didn't listen,
and handed Kuānráo to the officials.
Kuānráo drew his sword and cut his throat below the northern gate tower.
From History of Western Hàn, his biography.
When position exceeds capability,

From History of Western Hàn, Flatterers' biography appraisal.
Such excessive favor
is actually harmful.
From History of Western Hàn, Bào Xuān's biography.
Dīng Gōng, serving under Xiàng Yǔ, pursued and cornered Gāozǔ,

From New Account of Tales of the World, Qīng Chǐ chapter.

Jífǔ became suspicious,

Duàn of Gòng's death

A certain Mr. Yǒng loved rats,

were left entirely to the rats.
Thus most food and drink were rat-leftovers.

New occupants
found the rats behaving as arrogantly as before, so they kept six cats,

hired servants to catch them.
They killed rats piled like hills.

How much lifelong joy,

The stable horse isn't unfed,

after placing them,
like discards.

worrying excessively,
inspecting morning and evening,
returning after leaving.
Some even scratch the bark to check vitality,
or shake roots to examine spacing,
making the trees' nature deteriorate daily.
Though called love,
it actually harms;
though called concern,
it actually opposes.
From Táng Liǔ Zōngyuán's Biography of Guō Tuótuó.
In our dynasty,

Zhāng Āndào, having retired in Nánjīng,
