It is a useless tree,
of no practical use,
hence it can live so long.
As for hawthorns, pears, oranges, and pomelos,
belonging to the fruit-bearing category,
when the fruits ripen, they are plucked and abused,
large branches break,
small branches are torn,
this is because their abilities bring suffering upon their lives,
thus they do not live out their natural years but die prematurely.
Zhuangzi.
The skillful toil and the wise worry,
while the incapable have no aims,
seeking only to eat their fill and wander freely,
like an unmoored boat.
Ibid.
The earthworm lacks sharp claws and teeth,
or strong sinews and bones,
yet it eats the soil above
and drinks from the springs below,
because it focuses its mind singularly;
the crab has six legs and two pincers,
but without the burrows of snakes or eels, it has nowhere to dwell,
because its mind is restless.
Xunzi, "Exhortation to Learning."
Cunning deceit is not as good as clumsy honesty.
Fùzǐ.
History
Speaking ten sentences with nine correct
is not as good as one silence.
Records of the Grand Historian.
Cross-referenced under "Prudent Speech."
Those who provoke perish,
those who remain silent survive.
Biography of Yáng Xióng, History of the Western Hàn.
The wise are doubted for their surplus,
while the simple are trusted for their lack.
Wú Hàn, History of the Eastern Hàn.
Zuǒ Xióng said: "A white jade cannot be carved; being carved often brings later blessings."
Comprehensive Mirror, Eastern Hàn.
Zhōu Yǐ and Zhōu Sōng both held high positions,
once during the winter solstice feast,
their mother raised a cup to toast her three sons,
Sōng said: "Bórén has great ambitions but limited talent,
heavy reputation but dim insight,
he delights in others' misfortunes,
which is not the way to preserve oneself;
I, Sōng, am stubborn and straightforward,
and also not tolerated by the world;
only Ānú, mediocre as he is,
will remain by mother's side."
Ānú
was the childhood name of Sōng's younger brother, Mó.
Book of Jìn, Biography of Zhōu Yǐ.
Biographies
Silence avoids excessive words,
caution avoids excessive actions.
A wooden horse cannot walk,
nor does it consume fodder;
a fine steed gallops a thousand miles a day,
yet the whip never leaves its back.
Garden of Sayings.
Anthology
Why is cleverness ever insufficient,
while clumsiness and hardship abound?
Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on a Leisurely Life."
The ox, as a creature,
plows a hundred acres daily,
yet people feel no shame,
benefiting the whole world,
its hide and horns are used,
but its flesh cannot be preserved.
It is inferior to a weak donkey,
following worn-out horses,
neither plowing nor pulling,
fed with beans and greens,
prancing on broad roads,
coming and going lightly,
braying loudly in the way,
startling listeners to avoid.
Though the ox has merit,
what benefit is it to itself?
Fate has its beauty and ugliness,
not by one's ability.
Liǔ Zōngyuán's "Rhapsody on the Ox."
Now, for no reason, I read books and histories,
wisdom only wearies the spirit.
All living things
wish not to be talented.
The sacrificial vessel, adorned in blue and yellow,
is a disaster for the wood.
Both from Hán Yù's writings.
The old turtle, its gut carved out,
would be better off without divine powers.
Bái Jūyì.
Cross-referenced under "Inviting Misfortune."
Clever women and talented men often have thin fates,
do not let your children suffer for being too capable.
Insects preserve their lives by being non-venomous,
trees fulfill their destiny by being useless.
The iron horse retires due to fatigue,
the lead knife is preserved for its dullness.
Both from Bái Jūyì.
Our Dynasty
Fools naturally fulfill their heaven-mandated lives,
wise men die by their wisdom, their grievances unredressed.
A clear stream a thousand fathoms deep
is not as good as a foot of murky water.
The sweet well dries up first,
the bitter plum is preserved whole.
Everyone wishes for clever children,
but I, harmed by cleverness all my life,
pray my son be foolish and dull,
to reach high office without disaster or difficulty.
Both from Sū Shì's poems.
Indeed, a thousand fathoms of clarity
are not as good as a foot of murk.
Chén Shīdào.
The clever speak,
the clumsy are silent;
the clever toil,
the clumsy rest;
the clever are crafty,
the clumsy are virtuous;
the clever meet misfortune,
the clumsy receive blessings.
Zhōu Dūnyí's "Rhapsody on Clumsiness."
Classic
The Master said: "Everyone says, 'I am wise.'
But driven into the nets, traps, and pitfalls,
they know not how to avoid them."
The Doctrine of the Mean.
The Master
Fish, turtles, and crocodiles still consider the abyss too shallow,
and dig burrows within it;
eagles and kites still regard mountains as low,
and build nests upon them.
When they are caught,
it is always with bait.
． From "Xúnzǐ Fǎxíng" chapter.
Cross-reference "Greed and Delusion".
The divine snake can break and reconnect itself,
but cannot prevent people from cutting it.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
Wisdom can understand others,
but cannot know itself;
divine power can protect things,
but cannot defend itself.
Thus the divine turtle is burned for its wisdom,
the spiritual snake is roasted for its divinity.
From "Lièzǐ".
Collection
When the orangutans saw wine and straw sandals,
they knew the villagers had set traps,
and even knew the family names of the trap-setters' ancestors,
shouting and cursing by name:
"You slaves want to trap us - we'll leave you behind!"
After repeating this several times,
they said to each other:
"Let's just try tasting the wine."
After tasting its flavor,
once they became drunk,
they took the sandals and put them on,
whereupon they were captured by people,
all caught,
with none escaping.
From "Táng Wéncuì",
Péi Yán's "Orangutan Inscription".
Cross-reference "Greed and Delusion".
Contemporary
The old fox, full of cunning schemes,
dwells securely in its wall burrow.
Listening to ice in deep winter to cross,
its considerations are indeed long.
Drawing itself into the trap
(drawing means pulling in),
even when dying it still leaps about.
From "Ōuyáng's Collection".
The tiger ultimately caught by mechanism,
the bird followed by pellets.
From "Línchuān Collection".
Classic
The nimble crafty hare,
meeting the hound is caught.
From "Máo's Poetry".
Philosophers
Fire burns hot but water extinguishes it,
metal is hard but fire melts it,
wood is strong but the axe fells it,
water flows but earth blocks it.
． From "Huáinánzǐ: Discourse on the Essential Art".
Now tigers and leopards are agile,
bears are powerful,
yet people eat their flesh and use their hides as mats.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
History
Duke Sòng hosted a joint feast for Jìn and Chǔ ministers,
with Zhào Mèng as guest of honor.
When Zǐ Mù spoke with him,
he couldn't respond.
Having Shū Xiàng speak for him,
Zǐ Mù still couldn't respond either.
． From "Zuǒzhuàn, 27th year of Xiānggōng".
Nìng Chéng lived in Nányáng,
when Yòng Zǒng arrived at the pass,
Nìng Chéng walked sideways in greeting,
yet Yòng Zǒng, full of arrogance,
showed no courtesy.
Arriving at the commandery,
he then prosecuted the Nìng family,
completely destroying their household.
． From "Records of Yì Zǒng".
Sū Qín feared Qín troops reaching Zhào would break the vertical alliance,
thinking no one could be used in Qín,
so he provoked Zhāng Yí,
sending him into Qín.
Zhāng Yí had traveled among various states without meeting opportunity,
becoming destitute in Chǔ,
so Sū Qín deliberately summoned and humiliated him.
A retainer said:
"Lord Sū worries Qín attacking Zhào will break the vertical alliance,
believing only you can gain power in Qín,
so he provoked you,
having me secretly provide your funds -
all part of Lord Sū's strategy."
Zhāng Yí said:
"Alas! I was in his scheme yet unaware,
I am not as wise as Lord Sū!
Thank Lord Sū for me."
While Lord Sū lives,
how dare I speak.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Zhōu Records".
Hàn had an expert archer named Lóu Fán,
when Chǔ challenged him,
he would shoot and kill them.
Ordered to shoot Xiàng Yǔ,
Xiàng Yǔ glared fiercely and shouted at him,
Lóu Fán's eyes couldn't see,
his hands couldn't shoot,
he fled back into the fortress,
not daring to emerge again.
． From "Western Hàn: Biography of Xiàng Yǔ".
Jí Àn was resolute.
Commentator Gǔ said:
"Resolute means firm-minded,
pronounced zhāng lì fǎn."
Sīmǎ Ān used legal technicalities maliciously,
Mèng Kāng said:
"Using legal technicalities to harm people."
Both served as two-thousand-bushel officials,
riding in the same carriage,
yet never dared share the same mat.
． From "Former Hàn: Biography of Nìng Chéng".
Eastern Wèi chancellor Gāo Huān attacked Yùbì,
Wéi Xiàokuān adapted flexibly to resist him.
The city had no water,
drawing from the Fén River,
Gāo Huān had the river diverted,
completed overnight.
Gāo Huān built earthen mounds south of the city,
wanting to use them for entry.
The city walls originally had two towers,
Wéi Xiàokuān bound wood to extend them,
keeping them always higher than the earthen mounds for defense.
Gāo Huān sent message:
"Even if you bind towers to heaven,
I'll tunnel underground to capture you."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Liáng Gāozǔ".
Fù Yì told his son:
"I've heard of diamond being extremely hard,
nothing can damage it,
only antelope horn can break it."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Tàizōng".
Ān Lùshān insulted all ministers,
only fearing Lǐ Línfǔ.
Whenever meeting him,
even in midwinter,
he'd sweat through his clothes.
Lǐ Línfǔ would seat him in the central secretariat,
soothing him with gentle words,
taking off his own robe to cover him,
making Ān Lùshān grateful,
confessing everything.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Xuánzōng".
Qín Xì was friends with Liú Chángqīng,
exchanging poetic gifts.
Quán Déyù said:
"Chángqīng considered himself 'Fortress of Five-Character Verse',
Xì attacked him with flanking maneuvers."
． From "Táng History: Basic Biography".
Biographies
The world has endless talent and wisdom -
Chén Píng once produced six wondrous strategies,
yet sitting quietly feared disaster reaching him.
Lù Jiǎ taught him to befriend the Grand Commandant,
also planning several matters regarding the Lǚ clan,
Chén Píng followed him,
ultimately executing the various Lǚ.
Thus Jiǎ's wisdom and strategy surpassed even Píng's.
From "Kǒng's Miscellaneous Sayings".
Cross-reference "The Player Is Bewildered",
also "Wisdom and Consideration".
Collection
Deer fear chū beasts,
chū beasts fear tigers,
tigers fear brown bears.
From Liǔ's writings.
Contemporary
Lambs distress tigers and leopards,
doves distress eagles and sparrowhawks.
The clever prepare traps and arrows,
the powerfully fierce still become constrained.
From "Línchuān Collection".
When Wáng Jīnggōng first joined administration,
he looked down on the court as if no one was there.
One day debating new laws,
he glared at the ministers:
"You all sit here without reading books!"
Zhào Qīngxiàn alone refuted him:
"You are mistaken, sir -
in the times of Gāo, Kuí, Jì, and Qì,
what books were there to read?"
Jīnggōng fell silent.
From "Shào's Later Records".
Cross-reference "Quick at Response".
A cartload of burning firewood,
He does not correct his own heart,
but resents those who rectify him.
The "Annotation" states: "Not restraining your own lustful heart, but instead hating those who are upright."
． From the "Odes: Jie Nan Shan".
Those drunkards do no good,
and feel ashamed if they are not drunk.
． From the "Odes: Bin Zhi Chu Yan".
Mencius
said of the village worthy,
"In speech, they do not consider their actions;
in action, they do not consider their speech.
They say: 'The people of old,
what did they do?
They walked alone and desolate.'"
． From "Mencius: Jin Xin".
A multitude of crooked things cannot tolerate the straight;
a host of perverse things cannot tolerate the correct.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
The straight ink-line is hated by warped wood.
From "Bàopǔzǐ".
The history
records the hatred of the upright and the vilification of the correct.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn".
He himself was without propriety, yet he condemned those who had propriety,
saying, "Why do you practice rites?"
Also from "Zuǒ Zhuàn".
Thieves hate the master of the house.
In the 15th year of Duke Chéng, the wife of Jìn's Bó Zōng said, "Thieves hate the master of the house."
Also seen separately in "Family Sayings of Confucius".
The base and flattering,
embracing emptiness while seeking advancement,
cruel and tyrannical,
such types as these
envy the good and hate the loyal.
． From "History of the Western Hàn: Biography of Lǐ Xún".
On the northern mountain there is an owl,
who does not clean its wings,
gluttonous and greedy,
feeding on putrid and rotten things,
yet it calls out long to the phoenix,
saying the phoenix is without virtue.
． From the commentary to "History of the Eastern Hàn: Biography of Zhū Huī".
Cross-referenced under the categories "Unaware of One's Own Ugliness" and "Frivolous Criticism".
In the Eastern Hàn, Kǒng Fèn was the commandery assistant of Wǔdū,
and strenuously practiced purity and integrity,
for which he was laughed at by the masses,
who thought that although he was in a position greased with fat,
he could not enrich himself.
From "Comprehensive Mirror".
Yáng Hù did not attach himself to or curry favor with the powerful at the central court,
and men like Xún Xù and Féng Dǎn all hated him for it.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Jìn Shìzǔ".
The wicked and deceitful vilify the upright.
． From "History of the Western Jìn: Biography of Zhāng Huà".
Yān's Fèng Yù said: "Having no integrity themselves,
they envy those who do."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Jìn Annals".
Cross-referenced under "Envy and Jealousy".
Those who are glib and cunning
call strong integrity the usurpation of power.
From "History of the Táng".
Biographies
record that Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said: "The beautiful woman
is the enemy of the ugly;
the man of great virtue
is shunned in times of chaos;
the conduct of integrity and uprightness
is hated by the wicked and perverse."
From "Shuō Yuàn".
Collections
record that scholars took Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozǐ as their masters,
and demoted the "Six Classics";
debaters considered emptiness and superficiality as clever argument,
and despised reputation and restraint;
those cultivating their conduct considered libertinism and turbidity as sophistication,
and belittled moral integrity;
those seeking office considered obtaining it by any means as noble,
and scorned holding to the right;
those in office considered being aloof and detached as lofty,
and laughed at diligence and conscientiousness;
those who relied on emptiness and vagueness, and were compliant and mindless, were all renowned throughout the land,
while those like King Wén, who had no leisure to eat until sunset,
or Zhòng Shānfǔ, who was untiring day and night,
were generally mocked and derided,
being reviled as dust and dirt.
． From "Jìn Annals: Gān Bǎo's General Discussion".
The solitary and upright
are hated by all the wicked;
the fair and just
are envied by a host of evil-doers.
From "Collected Works of Chén Zǐ'áng".
With a slave's countenance and kneeling posture, truly a beggar,
yet they in turn consider the upright and honest as mad and foolish.
Lù Lǔwàng.
Our dynasty
records those in office who refuse to worry themselves,
and also forbid others,
preventing them from worrying—
truly lamentable.
From "Collected Works of Ōuyáng Xiū".
Mencius
said this is like hating dampness yet living in a low place.
From "Mèngzǐ".
To be in a dust storm and wish not to have one's eyes blinded,
or to wade through water and wish not to get wet—
is impossible.
． From "Huáinánzǐ: Miù Chēng Xùn".
To blow on dust and wish not to have one's eyes blinded,
or to wade through water and wish not to get wet—
is impossible.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
History
records: To wish for profit in trade,
yet hate the noise of the market?
． From "Zuǒ Zhuàn: Zhāo Gōng Year 1".
Collections
say this is like wading across a stream yet being ashamed of getting one's feet wet.
From "Táng Wén Cuì".
The Master
said: The tree desires stillness, but the wind will not cease.
． From "Family Sayings of Confucius: Zhì Sī".
The sacrificial ox, adorned with embroidered trappings,
fed with hay and beans,
and led into the grand temple—
though it may wish to be a lonely calf,
can it attain this?
From "Lièzǐ".
The elephant loses its life because of its tusks,
yet cannot rid itself of their whiteness;
the fragrant plant is burned because of its scent,
yet cannot rid itself of its fragrance.
From "Sūzǐ".
History
records that Lǐ Sī, facing execution,
said to his son: "I wish to go with you again, leading the yellow dog,
and together chase crafty hares out the eastern gate of Shàngcài—
but can this be done?"
． From "Historical Records: His Biography".
A scholar cultivates himself at home,
only to be corrupted in the court of the Son of Heaven.
From "Comprehensive Mirror".
It is like ants walking on a millstone—
they walk slowly, but the millstone turns swiftly.
． From the Eastern Hàn Wáng Chōng's "Lùn Héng".
Liú Mùzhī of the Sòng said: "In poverty and lowliness, one often thinks of wealth and honor;
but having attained wealth and honor, one inevitably treads upon crisis.
Today, to wish to be a commoner of Dānyáng—
can it be done?"
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: History of the Jìn".
Liáng's Lǚ Chāo said: "It is like riding a dragon to heaven—
how can one stop halfway and descend?"
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Jìn Annals".
Empress Dúgū said: "Once riding a beast,
one inevitably cannot dismount."
From "History of the Suì".
When the eye sees what is desirable,
how can one stifle it in one's heart?
Once having formed private connections,
how can one break them off midway?
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Dézōng".
Lǐ Mì returned
and said to his sons and younger brothers: "I never desired wealth and honor,
but fate has gone against my wishes,
and now I have implicated you."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Dézōng".
Biographies
record: Oxen and horses, when driven by men,
do not enjoy bearing a weight of a thousand jun,
or traversing a thousand lǐ of danger—
the whip is painful.
From Yuán Huái's "Zhèng Shū".
集
A woman leaves her family to marry a man,
A minister offers his service to attend his lord.
Mí Zhènɡpínɡ's rhapsody.
Roaming mountain marshes,
Watching fish and birds,
My heart finds great joy in this.
Once taking office as an official,
Such pursuits are abandoned.
From Jī Kānɡ's "Letter Severing Ties with Shān Tāo" of the Jìn dynasty.
Departure and stay go against my wishes,
Looking up, I feel ashamed before the wings in the forest.
Dù Gōnɡbù.
Like a crane in a cage,
Its six wings cannot flutter on their own.
Riding a tiger, one dares not dismount.
Both from Hán Wén.
Though my heart soars with the cloud-reaching crane,
My body still touches the caged hawk.
Though the source of my mind is clear,
The dusty world is bitterly bustling.
Both from Yuán Wēizhī.
Opening a book, I cannot linger over it,
Submerged among official documents.
Worldly affairs are like a boat on waves,
How can it stay anchored, whether sailing up or down?
My heart yearns for the clear night,
But my body is bound by official duties.
Both from Wéi Yìnɡwù.
Once falling into the path of fame and office,
Vast as riding a wind-tossed boat.
Rushing through emotional waves, I am not free.
Both from Liú Bīnkè.
A post-house horse gallops on four hooves,
In pain and soreness without respite.
A mill ox blindfolded on both eyes,
In darkness and confinement, who knows?
The tree desires stillness, but the wind does not cease.
Both from Bái Jūyì.
I dislike being like a bolt of plain silk,
Measured and cut not by my own will.
Dù Mùzhī.
Following official documents, tethered by the yellow ribbon.
Mènɡ Hàorán.
Though a hundred hits depend on myself,
Ultimately, one call rests with the ruler.
Gāo Dáfū.
Cross-referenced in "There is a Way to Control."
Our dynasty
Only now do I realize, listening to the song from a golden cage,
Cannot match the free chirping in the woods.
From "Ōu Gōnɡ's Collection."
Drifting and adrift, not free, even prosperity is not within your power.
I live between heaven and earth,
Like an ant on a large millstone.
Trying hard to move right,
But unable to stop the wind-wheel from turning left.
Both from Dōnɡpō's poetry.
Once wrapped in official robes and headgear,
Long entangled by nets and snares.
From "Luánchénɡ Collection."
经
Even a skilled calculator cannot determine its numbers,
Even a sage cannot establish its constant principles,
Laws and regulations cannot standardize it,
Measures and weights cannot balance it.
From "Zhōu Yì Lüè Lì."
Like a fire spreading across the plains,
One cannot approach it.
From "Shū·Pán Gēnɡ Shànɡ."
Cross-referenced in "Nowhere to Apply Effort."
I myself cannot be spared,
How can I have leisure to worry about my descendants?
Meaning, I now fear I cannot even protect myself,
How can I spare time to worry about those after me?
From "Máo Shī."
Accomplished deeds need not be discussed,
Completed affairs need not be remonstrated,
The past need not be blamed.
From "Lún Yǔ."
子
The clarity of the eyes,
Can see objects a hundred steps away,
But cannot see one's own back,
Outside the curtains and walls,
Nothing is seen.
From "Zǐ Huá Zǐ."
In a state of ten thousand households,
If only one person makes pottery,
Is that sufficient?
From "Mènɡzǐ·Gào Zǐ Xià."
Like a seven-year illness,
Seeking a three-year moxa.
From "Mènɡzǐ."
The world certainly cannot be saved by a single hair.
From "Liè Zǐ·Yánɡ Zhū" chapter.
The ancients' eyes were short-sighted for seeing themselves,
Hence they used mirrors to view their faces.
From "Hán Fēi Zǐ."
A blind person cannot partake in the sight of patterns and colors,
A deaf person cannot partake in the sounds of bells and chimes.
From "Zhuānɡ Zǐ·Xiāo Yáo Yóu."
A blind person cannot appreciate the beauty of eyebrows and eyes or colors,
A sightless person cannot behold the sight of blue, yellow, and ceremonial robes.
From "Zhuānɡ Zǐ·Dà Zōnɡ Shī."
Lí Zhū's keen eyesight discerns the tip of a hair a hundred steps away,
But underwater, even a foot deep, he cannot see the shallows or depths,
Not because his eyes are unclear,
But because the conditions make it hard to see.
From "Shèn Zǐ."
A cocoon thin as morning dew,
Even a skilled woman cannot unwind it;
The sands of Zī and Shénɡ rivers,
Even a calculating boy cannot count them.
From "Lǔ Lián Zǐ."
A lame person seeing a tiger and not running away,
Is not bravery.
From "Huái Nán Zǐ."
Lí Zhū's keen eyesight,
Discerns the tip of a hair a hundred steps away,
But cannot see fish in the deep pool;
Shī Kuànɡ's sharp hearing harmonizes the eight winds' tunes,
But cannot hear beyond ten miles.
From "Huái Nán Zǐ·Xùn Dào Lùn."
Thus, a noble person can do good,
But cannot be certain to gain blessings;
He cannot bear to do wrong,
But cannot be sure to avoid calamity.
From "Huái Nán Zǐ·Miù Chēnɡ Xùn."
Blind Kuànɡ can tune sounds,
But Blind Kuànɡ cannot equalize uneven ears;
Dí Yá can taste flavors,
Pronounced hū lǎn qiē.
But Dí Yá cannot equalize uneven mouths.
From "Yánɡ Zǐ·Wèn Shén."
Ōu Yě cannot cast lead or tin into a Gàn Jiàn sword.
From "Bào Pǔ Zǐ."
Three inches of Ē Jiāo glue,
Cannot clear the Yellow River's muddiness;
A three-foot damaged basket,
Cannot save the salt pond's saltiness.
From "Fù Zǐ."
史
Jìn Bó Zōng said: "Though the whip is long,
it cannot reach the horse's belly."
. From "Zuǒzhuàn, Xuān Gōng 15th Year".
The Marquis of Jìn fell ill,
and the Earl of Qín sent a physician named Zhì,
who said: "The illness cannot be cured.
It is above the huāng and below the gāo,
where acupuncture cannot reach,
and moxibustion cannot penetrate.
Medicine does not arrive there,
so it cannot be treated."
. From "Zuǒzhuàn, Chéng Gōng 10th Year".
Cross-referenced under "Illnesses".
At the end of a whirlwind,
it cannot lift a goose feather.
From "Guóyǔ".
At the extreme of a strong crossbow,
the arrow cannot pierce Lǔ silk;
at the end of a gusting wind,
it cannot float a goose feather.
It is not that the beginning lacked force,
but that the end's strength has waned.
. From "Shǐjì, Hán Ān Guó's Biography".
For a fatal illness, there is no good physician.
. From "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Zhōu Dynasty Annals".
In the past, Yī Zhì was in Xià,
and Lǚ Wàng was in Shāng,
yet both states were not well-governed.
Was it that Yī and Lǚ did not wish to?
The situation made it impossible.
Same as above.
Spilled water cannot be gathered back.
. From "Dōng Hàn, Guāng Wǔ's Annals".
Even if ten thousand people cast it,
and one person seizes it,
it still cannot suffice;
how much more now if one person casts it,
then ten thousand people seize it!
Even using yīn and yáng as charcoal,
and all things as copper,
employing people who do not eat,
and using men who do not hunger,
it still cannot satisfy insatiable demands.

Méng Tián said: "From my ancestors to my descendants,
we have accumulated merit and trust with the rulers of Qín for generations.
Now I command over three hundred thousand troops,
and though I am imprisoned,
my power is sufficient to rebel.
Yet I know I must die and uphold righteousness,

so as not to forget the late emperor."

． 《Tōngjiàn, Qín Records》.
All of Chǔ's territories surrendered to Hàn,

． 《Shǐjì, Xiàng Yǔ's Annals》.
Sū Wǔ was exiled to the northern sea,
Chányú sent Lǐ Líng to the sea,
prepared wine and music for Wǔ,
and said to him: "You and your brother,
both previously committed suicide due to incidents.
When I came,
your esteemed mother had already passed away,
your wife, Zǐqīng, is young,
I heard she has remarried.
Only two sisters remain,
two daughters and one son,
now over ten years later,
their survival is unknown.
Life is like the morning dew,
why torment yourself so long?"
Wǔ said: "I have long considered myself
already dead.
If the king insists on making me surrender,
I ask to end today's joy,
and die before you."
Líng, seeing his utmost sincerity,
sighed and said: "Alas,
a man of righteousness!
The crimes of Líng and Wèi Lǜ
reach up to heaven."
Tears soaked his lapel,
and he parted from Wǔ.
Wǔ stayed among the Xiōngnú for nineteen years in total,
leaving in his prime,
and upon return,
his hair and beard were completely white.
． 《Tōngjiàn, Hàn Zhāo's Annals》.

Yǔ's men vied to kill him,

"This is a righteous man,
for dying with integrity, he may be given a sword."
Xù took the sword,
put his beard in his mouth,
looked at his attendants and said:
"Since I am killed by rebels,
do not let my beard be soiled."
He then fell on the sword and died.

History
Crown Prince Dān of Yān met Tián Guāng and said: "Yān and Qín cannot coexist,
I hope you will give this your attention."
Guāng said: "Among those I am close with,
Jīng Kē can be employed."
The Crown Prince said: "I hope you will not divulge this."
Guāng went to see Jīng Kē and said: "I spoke of you to the Crown Prince,
and the Crown Prince told me 'Do not divulge this,'
which shows he suspects me.
For one's conduct to make others suspicious,
is not the way of a principled knight-errant."
He intended to kill himself to inspire Jīng Kē,
saying: "I hope you will inform them that Guāng is already dead,
to prove I have not spoken."
Thereupon he cut his throat and died.
— "Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Annals."
Wǔ Zǐxū was in dire straits by the river,
begging for food along the way,
but did his resolve ever for a moment forget Yǐng?
Thus he endured humiliation to achieve merit and fame;
if not a man of fierce determination, who could have accomplished this?
— "Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Zǐxū."
Cross-referenced under "Unyielding Perseverance."
Wǔ Zǐxū remonstrated with the King of Wú,
but the Grand Steward Pǐ of Wú slandered him,
and the King of Wú granted him a sword to die by.
Zǐxū then told his retainer: "You must plant a catalpa tree on my grave,
so it can be made into vessels.
And gouge out my eyes to hang over the eastern gate of Wú,
that I may watch the Yuè army enter and destroy Wú."
Then he cut his throat and died.
"Records of the Grand Historian."
Péng Yuè once traveled with Luán Bù,
Péng Yuè rebelled,

Bù reported matters below Péng Yuè's head,
made offerings and wept for him,
and the officials arrested him and reported it.
Bù said: "Péng Yuè is already dead,
I would rather die than live.
I request to be boiled."
— "Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Annals."
Yù Ràng served Zhì Bó,
Zhì Bó was destroyed,
Ràng took a dagger to assassinate Xiāngzǐ,
but Xiāngzǐ released him.
Soon after,
he lacquered his body to cause sores,
swallowed charcoal to become mute,
and begged in the market,
saying: "The reason I do this,
is to shame all ministers in the world and future generations who serve their lord with divided loyalties."
After a while,
when Xiāngzǐ was traveling,
Ràng hid under a bridge,
the horses were startled,
and Xiāngzǐ then reproached Ràng.
Ràng said: "I am ready to accept execution,
but I wish to strike your garment to express my intent of revenge,
then I will die without regret."
Xiāngzǐ gave his garment to Ràng,
Ràng drew his sword, leaped three times and struck it,
saying: "Now I can report to Zhì Bó below."
— "Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Annals."
Cross-referenced under "Unyielding Perseverance."

Zhú said: "A loyal minister does not serve two lords,

The attendants wanted to stab Xiàngrú,

Xiàngrú turned to the Zhào historian to record: "On such date,

he became Minister over the Masses.
Earlier,
when Emperor Wǔ of Liáng was at the Western Residence,
he had associated with Yuē as an old friend.
Once his achievements were established,
and both divine and human will favored Yuē,
he often broached the subject,
but the emperor remained silent and did not respond.
Another day,
he again proposed: "Now is different from antiquity;
one cannot expect pure customs to govern all things.
The officials who cling to the dragon and phoenix
all hope to achieve some merit to secure their fortunes.
Even children and cowherds now know that Qí's reign is ending."
The emperor said: "I am still considering it."
Yuē said:
"When you first raised troops in Fán and Miǎn,
that was the time to consider.
Now the royal enterprise is already achieved;
what more is there to consider?
If the Son of Heaven returns to the capital,
and the ministers are in their positions,
then the roles of ruler and subject will be fixed,
with no further alternative schemes.
With a wise ruler above
and loyal ministers below,
who would still join you in rebellion?"
The emperor agreed.
Yuē went out,
summoned Fàn Yún,
and informed him.
When the emperor accepted the abdication,

over twenty officials including the Minister of Personnel Fàn Yún came to pay respects.

The Guǒ family of Qí was very wealthy,

The latter went from Sòng to Qí
to ask for the method.
Guǒ told him: "I excel at stealing.
In one year, I became self-sufficient,
in two years, well-off,
in three years, wealthy.
From then on,
I could benefit the whole neighborhood."
Xiàng was overjoyed,
understanding the word "stealing"
but not its true meaning.
So he climbed walls and broke into houses,
taking everything within reach,
leaving nothing untouched.
Before long,
he was convicted for the stolen goods,
and his family property was confiscated.
Believing Guǒ had misled him,
Xiàng went to complain.
Guǒ asked: "How did you steal?"
Xiàng described his actions.
Guǒ said: "Alas! Have you misunderstood stealing to this extent?
Now I'll tell you the truth.
I've heard heaven has its seasons,
earth its benefits.
I 'steal' heaven and earth's timely benefits—
the abundant rain from clouds,
the produce from mountains and marshes—
to grow my grain,
cultivate my crops,
build my walls,
and erect my house.
On land, I 'steal' birds and beasts;
in water, I 'steal' fish and turtles—
all born of heaven,
not owned by anyone.
Thus I 'steal' from heaven without penalty.
But gold, jade, treasures,
grain, silk, and wealth
are accumulated by people;
how could heaven grant them?"
Xiàng was greatly confused,
thinking Guǒ had deceived him again.
From Lièzǐ, "Heaven's Gifts."
A deceitful person
can deceive even within their own courtyard,
let alone from a thousand miles away.
From Xúnzǐ, "Against Physiognomy."
Foolishness compounded by more foolishness,
darkness deepened by further darkness.
Same as above.
Using a pole to measure a river,
and thinking the water shallow when the pole ends—
how deluded!
From Huáinánzǐ, "Forest of Persuasion."
Abandoning lush trees to perch on dry ones,
not shooting swans but crows instead—
hard to plan with such people.
From Huáinánzǐ.
One who wore armor and avoided arrows,
then wore it into water;
one who held a gourd to cross water,
then held it through fire—
can be called ignorant of categories.
A man of Chǔ encountered a storm while sailing,
and jumped into the water—
not that he didn't cherish life or fear death,
but confused about death, he forgot about living.
Both from the same text.
Not hearing is truly having no ears;
not seeing is truly having no eyes.
From Yángzǐ, "Asking about Enlightenment."
Sparrows nesting in a house,
with smoke pouring from the chimney
and beams about to burn—
unaware disaster is about to strike them.
From The Kǒng Family Masters' Anthology.
Treading on thin ice while waiting for summer.
From Bàopǔzǐ.
Content with bitter weeds,
unaware of sweet honey;
satisfied with thin wine,
unappreciative of fine liquor.
From Bàopǔzǐ.
Like sitting in a leaking boat,
or crouching under a burning house.
From The Wúzǐ.
A fool from Sòng found a Yān stone,
treasuring it as a great jewel.
A visitor from Zhōu came to see it;
the host, in ceremonial dress, unveiled the treasure
from ten layers of ornate cases,
wrapped in ten crimson cloths.
The visitor saw it
and chuckled: "This is just a Yān stone,
no different from a tile."
The host became furious,
and hid it even more securely.
From The Quēzǐ.
Cross-reference: "Self-Righteousness."
History
The Marquis of Jìn again borrowed a passage through Yú,
to attack Guó.
Gōng Zhīqí said: "Guó
is the outer shield of Yú.
If Guó perishes,
Yú will surely follow."
The Duke of Yú said: "Jìn
is of our same clan,
how could they harm me!"
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Xī 5th Year_.
Zhōuzǐ had an elder brother without wisdom,
unable to distinguish beans from wheat.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Chéng 18th Year_.
Ears that do not hear the harmony of the five tones,
are deaf;
eyes that do not distinguish the patterns of the five colors,
are dim.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Xī 24th Year_.
Does not understand speech.
_Zuǒzhuàn_.
To place fire under a pile of firewood,
and sleep on top of it,
while the fire has not yet ignited,
and call it safe.
The current situation,
how is it different from this?
． _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Wén Jì_.
Wearing a fox-fur robe inside out.
． _Xīhàn, Qiū Héng Zhuàn_.
Like wearing brocade to walk at night.
． _Xīhàn, Zhū Mǎichén Zhuàn_.
Confused and dim-witted, not knowing what to do.
． _Xīhàn, Xīfū Gōng Zhuàn_.
Galloping into the deep abyss, entering the tiger's mouth.
． _Dōnghàn, Mǎ Yuán Zhuàn_.
Yán Yán said: "Sitting alone in barren mountains,
releasing a tiger to defend oneself."
． _Tōngjiàn, Dōnghàn_.
Living in the peril of piled eggs,
yet planning for the security of Mount Tài;
engaging in deeds as fleeting as morning dew,
yet thinking of achievements to pass down through generations.
． _Dōnghàn, Wáng Fú Zhuàn_.
Cross-reference "not measuring oneself."
Climbing a mountain to gather pearls.
． _Dōnghàn, Liú Xuán Zhuàn_.
How could one know it will not succeed and yet shrink back, bite their tongue, fold hands, and follow the crowd?
． _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Guāngwǔ Jì_.
Zhāng Jiǎo started a rebellion,
Xiàng Xǔ submitted a proposal,
not wanting the state to raise troops,
but only to send generals to the riverbank to face north and recite the _Classic of Filial Piety_,
and the rebels would naturally be eliminated.
． _Dōnghàn, Xiàng Xǔ Zhuàn_.
Climbing a tree to seek fish,
walking backward to move forward.
． _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Shāng Jì_.
Sūn Ēn attacked Kuàijī.
The Neishǐ of Kuàijī, Wáng Níngzhī, whose family had long followed the Tiānshī Dào,
did not send out troops,
nor did he set up defenses.
Daily, in the Dàoist chamber, he kowtowed and knelt chanting.
His officials requested to send troops to suppress,
but Níngzhī said: "I have already requested the Great Dào,
to lend ghost soldiers to guard all key points,
each numbering tens of thousands,
the rebels are not worth worrying about."
When Ēn drew near,
only then did he allow troops to be sent out,
but Ēn had already reached the city.
On the day Jiǎyín,
Ēn captured Kuàijī,
Níngzhī fled,
Ēn captured and killed him,
along with his sons.
． _Tōngjiàn, Jìn Jì_.
The King of Jìn feasted with the later Shǔ ruler Liú Shàn,
and had former Shǔ courtesans perform,
all bystanders were moved to tears,
but Shàn laughed joyfully as if nothing was amiss.
The King of Jìn said: "How can a person be so heartless?"
Another day,
the King asked Shàn: "Do you miss Shǔ at all?"
Shàn said: "I am happy here,
I do not miss Shǔ."
Què Zhèng heard this and told Shàn: "If the King asks again,
you should weep and reply: 'My ancestors' graves
are far in Mín and Shǔ,
my heart grieves for the west,
there is not a day I do not think of it.'
Then close your eyes."
When the King asked again,
Shàn replied as before,
the King said: "How does this sound like Què Zhèng's words!"
Shàn looked up in surprise and said: "It is exactly as you say."
All attendants laughed.
． _Tōngjiàn, Jìn Jì_.
Emperor Ān was young and unwise,
unable to speak,
to the extent that he could not distinguish cold from heat or hunger from fullness,
eating, drinking, sleeping, and rising were all decided by others.
． _Tōngjiàn, Jìn Wǔ Jì_.
It is like a dog or pig growing fat,
unaware that disaster is about to strike.
．． _Jìnshū, Hán Bó Zhuàn Lùn_.
Opening the door to invite robbers.
． _Wú Zhì, Zhāng Zhāo Zhuàn_.
Húlǜ Guāng said: "The swan has already soared in the vast sky,
yet the netter still watches the swamp."
_Tōngjiàn_.
Letting others lead by the nose.
_Liáng Wǔ Jì_.
Wèi's Dù Bì said: "Raising the mantis' axe,
wearing the dung beetle's armor,
waiting in a dead-end rut,
sitting on a pile of firewood awaiting the blaze."
． _Tōngjiàn, Sòng Jì_.
Xiè Língyùn's son Fèng,
Fèng's son Chāozōng,
was gifted in writing,
the Emperor greatly admired and praised him,
saying to Xiè Zhuāng: "Chāozōng truly has the phoenix's feather,
it is as if Língyùn has returned."
At that time, the Right Guard General Liú Dàolóng was in the imperial presence,
and went to wait for Chāozōng,
asking to see the phoenix feather.
Chāozōng, thinking him ignorant and that he had invoked his father's name,
went barefoot back inside.
Dàolóng thought he was searching for the feather,
waited until dark without getting it,
and then left.
_Nánshǐ_.
About to journey a thousand miles,
yet abandoning the steed to ride a lame donkey.
． _Tōngjiàn, Liáng Wǔ Jì_.
Holding ice to seek warmth,
embracing charcoal hoping for coolness.
． _Wèi Zhì, Gāo Róu Zhuàn_.
The Emperor said: "It is like a hungry man,
eating his own flesh,
when the flesh is gone, he dies.
How foolish!"
． _Tōngjiàn, Táng Tàizōng Jì_.
Cross-reference "self-contradiction."
Sheltering under a rotten tree,
riding a boat made of glue.
． _Táng, Wéi Chéngqìng Zhuàn_.
Cross-reference "inviting disaster."
Wèi Zhēng said: "Formerly, Duke Āi of Lǔ said to Confucius: 'There is a man so forgetful
he moved house and forgot his wife.'
Confucius said: 'There are worse cases;
Jié and Zhòu forgot themselves.'
This is similar."
． _Tōngjiàn, Táng Tàizōng_.
Yáo Jì did not know money,
nor the count of its weight in mò and zhū.
． _Wǔdài, Jìn Jì_.
Historical records
Plugging a leaking boat yet disregarding the waves of Yáng Hóu,
then the boat capsizes.
_Zhànguócè_.
Like seeking fire in a well.
Same as above.
Abandoning the sunlight in the courtyard,
for the firelight in the room.
_Jiǎ Yì Shū_.
A man of Chǔ was crossing a river,
his sword fell from the boat into the water.
He hastily notched the boat, saying: "This is where my sword fell."
The boat moved on,
and he entered the water from the notched spot,
to search for it.
But the boat had moved,
the sword had not,
is this not perplexing?
_Lǚshì Chūnqiū_.
Cross-reference "stuck in mud."
Collection
Without distinguishing horizontal from vertical.
"Chǔcí".
The smartweed insect avoids mallows and violets,
Accustomed to bitterness, it does not complain of hardship.
． "Xuǎn Fàng Gē Xíng".
Filling a giant ravine with food,
Pouring drink into a leaky vessel.
Cáo Zǐjiàn's letter.
Taking the day one feels pain
As the beginning of the illness.
Jī Shūyè's "Yǎngshēng Lùn".
Following the tracks of an overturned cart.
"Wǔ Děng Lùn".
Thus knowing two and five,
But not recognizing ten.
"Biàn Mìng Lùn".
Drawing a form from its shadow,
Cannot capture its delicate beauty;
Observing fire through its ashes,
Does not see its blazing flames.
Lù Shìhéng's "Liánzhū".
Sitting on piled firewood waiting to ignite,
Pointing at the sun to compare its brilliance.
Pān Ānrén's "Xī Zhēng Fù".
Climbing Yángchéng to avoid danger,
Lying on Dǐzhù seeking safety.
Yǔ Xìn's "Āi Jiāngnán Fù".
Fools act against reason.
． "Wénxuǎn Shū".
What is the lamb's mouth for,
Silently dying at the slaughterhouse without a sound?
"Bái Chuán Jí".
Speaking of peace while sitting on firewood,
Talking of safety while nesting on a curtain.
Lǐ Yìshān.
Like leaving an orchid chamber for a fish market,
Abandoning fine wine for dregs and husks,
Shedding brocade for hemp cloth.
"Táng Wén Cuì".
As if blind in the midst of sun and moon,
Walking through perilous places,
Stumbling and falling down,
How can it be endured?
Same as above.
A fierce wind uproots a tree,
The tree falls, its roots exposed.
Above, several vines remain,
Still green, unaware.
Táng Yú Dú's poem.
Covering ears to steal a bell,
Claiming no one hears.
Liú Zhījǐ's "Shǐ Tōng".
Dull and unobservant,
As if deaf and blind.
"Shǐ Tōng".
This dynasty
Entrusting a fawn to a fierce tiger,
A fledgling to a soaring eagle.
． "Lèi Yào Xià".
How different from fleeing noise only to head to the market,
Or shunning shadows yet approaching the sun.
"Ōu Gōng Jí".
As if in a leaky boat,
Hastening toward the deep abyss,
Not abandoning it while still shallow,
And seeking a way to survive,
Yet excusing wet feet,
Is indeed the path to drowning.
Lǎo Quán's writing.
History
Méi Gāo composed texts swiftly,
completing them immediately upon receiving the imperial command.
． From "Biography in the Western Hàn History".
He dictated proclamations orally.
． From "Biography of Zhū Bó in the Western Hàn History".
Mí Héng composed rhapsodies,
without revising a single character,
his brush never pausing.
． From "Biography in the Eastern Hàn History".
Fèi Yī served as Imperial Secretary.
At that time, affairs were numerous,
and Fèi Yī's understanding surpassed others.
Whenever he reviewed documents,
with a brief glance,
he grasped their essential meaning,
several times faster than others,
yet never forgot them.
From "Records of Shǔ".
Liú Mùzhī served as Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
residing in the Eastern Bureau,
overseeing both internal and external affairs.
Liú Mùzhī managed court politics internally,
supplied military needs externally,
making decisions as fluidly as a flowing stream,
with no delays in handling matters.
Guests gathered like spokes around a hub,
presenting countless pleas and requests,
with consultations and reports from inside and outside,
filling the steps and rooms;
he read legal disputes with his eyes,
wrote replies with his hand,
listened to reports with his ears,
and responded verbally simultaneously,
without any confusion between tasks,
handling everything comprehensively and competently.
Moreover, he enjoyed hosting guests,
engaging in conversation, appreciation, and laughter,
remaining untired throughout the day.
Whenever there was a moment of leisure,
he would personally copy books,
perusing and collating them.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Jìn Ān Era".
Cross-reference to "Energy and Focus".
Wáng Tài composed poems by timing with a burning candle,
without revising the text.
．． From "Biography in the History of the Southern Dynasties: Sòng".
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng gathered over twenty scholars for a banquet to compose poems,
Xiāo Jiè dipped his brush and finished immediately,
without revising a word,
and the Emperor said: "Xiāo Jiè's literary piece
is a beauty composed on the spot."
From "Book of Liáng".
Fàn Yún excelled in writing essays and letters,
completing them as soon as he put brush to paper,
never drafting a manuscript,
leading contemporaries to suspect he had prepared them in advance.
From "Book of Liáng".
Péi Zǐyě's writings were elegant and swift;
when asked about his speed in writing,
Zǐyě replied: "Others complete with their hands,
I alone complete with my mind."
． From "Biography in the Book of Liáng".
Emperor Wǔ took authentic works of Zhōng Yáo and Wáng Xīzhī and gave them to Zhōu Xìngsì,
ordering him to select a thousand non-repeating characters,
and compose a rhymed text from them.
Xìngsì presented it after one night,
his hair and beard having turned white.
From "Book of Liáng".
Xiāo Wényǎn, Qiū Lìngkǎi, Jiāng Hóng, and others composed poems by striking a bronze bowl to set the rhythm,
finishing before the sound faded.
． From "Biography of Liáng Wáng Rú".
At that time, military documents numbered in the hundreds daily,
Lǐ Délín dictated to several people simultaneously,
with varied literary meanings,
yet without any corrections.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Chén Hòuzhǔ Era".
Liú Xuàn had a powerful memory and silent comprehension,
with no one to match him.
He could draw squares with his left hand,
circles with his right hand,
recite orally,
count with his eyes,
and listen with his ears,
performing these five tasks simultaneously,
without any omissions.
From "Book of Suí".
Qí Yuánkāng drafted military documents,
with his brush swishing swiftly,
producing several pages in a moment.
． From "History of the Northern Dynasties: Book of Qí".
The army had many affairs, and Rúhuì
analyzed and decided them as fluidly as a stream.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Táng Gāozǔ Era".
Péi Yányù at the inner court,
handled documents with agility,
earning the nickname "Downstream Boat."
From "Book of Táng".
Xiè Zhǐ,
excelled in writing.
When Wèi's Zhōngshān King Yuán Lüè returned north,
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng held a farewell banquet at the Wǔdé Hall,
composing a thirty-verse poem,
with a time limit of three ke (about 45 minutes).
Xiè Zhǐ completed it promptly.
From "History of the Southern Dynasties".
During Emperor Xuánzong's pacification of internal strife,
edicts and documents piled up,
yet Sū Tǐngshuò dictated and composed them,
detailing numerous merits and situations,
without any errors.
A clerk pleaded: "I beg you, sir, to slow down;
otherwise,
my wrist will fall off."
． From "Biography in the Book of Táng".
Líng Hú Chǔ served as secretary in Tàiyuán.
When Zhèng Dān died suddenly in his post without
leaving instructions for aftermath,
the army grew restless, on the verge of mutiny.
Suddenly, dozens of cavalrymen with swords approached Chǔ at night,
bringing him to the army gate,
where the generals pressured him
to draft a posthumous memorial.
Amidst the blades,
Chǔ grasped the brush and finished instantly,
then read it to the three armies,
moving all to tears,
thus gaining great renown.
From "Book of Táng".
Cross-reference to "Having Composure".
Fáng Xuánlíng handled military orders and official documents, sometimes while halting his horse,
composing texts and reasoning precisely,
all without drafting a manuscript.
． From "Biography in the Book of Táng".
When Zhū Cǐ plotted rebellion, the emperor fled to Fèngtiān.
At that time, the empire was in rebellion,
with urgent affairs piling up,
conscriptions and directives
in countless threads and aspects.
Within a single day,
hundreds of edicts were issued.
Lù Zhì wielded his brush to draft,
thoughts gushing like a spring.
At first, it seemed unplanned,
but once completed,
each was perfectly crafted.
Matters were suited to the occasion, and clerks had no time for documents,
while his colleagues all admired his ability.
． From "Biography of Lù Zhì in the Book of Táng".
Wáng Bó composed texts,
initially without deep contemplation;
he would first grind several pints of ink, then drink heartily,
pull the quilt over his face,
sleep until he awoke,
then take up the brush to complete the piece,
without changing a single character.
Contemporaries called Bó the "belly-draftsman."
． From "Biography in the Book of Táng".
Liǔ Gōngquán, skilled in poetry and rhapsodies, composed texts as soon as inspired.
Emperor Wénzōng of Táng said: "Cáo Zhi composed in seven paces,
but you do it in three."
From "Book of Táng".
Cross-reference to "Literature".
Xuē Shōu wrote letters, proclamations, and bulletins,
sometimes dictating on horseback,
with such comprehensiveness and speed as if precomposed,
never needing revision.
From "Book of Táng".
Wéi Chéngqìng composed texts swiftly without lingering thoughts,
even for major imperial decrees,
never drafting a manuscript.
． From "Biography in the Book of Táng".
Zhèng Mǐn served as Secretary of the Central Secretariat.
With edicts and documents arriving incessantly,
he never had stagnant thoughts,
and his words always hit the mark.
Lǐ Qīyún wrote with vigor and speed.
Lù Yǐ was skilled in literary composition with agility,
as rapid as an injection.
Both from the same source as above.
Anecdotes
Lǐ Tàibái, in the Hànlín Academy, responded to an imperial command,
． drafting the "Preface to the White Lotus Blossoms" and ten "Palace Poems,"
while heavily intoxicated.
A nobleman doused him with ice water,
and he sobered slightly.
Bái requested a brush before the emperor and wrote in one sweep,
without revising a word.
From "Collected Sayings".
Wēn Tíngyún excelled at composing short rhapsodies,
completing eight rhymes each time he crossed his hands eight times.
From "Trifling Tales of Northern Dreams".
Collection
Emperor Wén of Wèi halted his horse and inscribed his whip,
composing the "Rhapsody on Facing the Whirlpool."
Emperor Wén of Wèi's "Facing the Whirlpool Rhapsody."
Testing ten thousand words a day,
leaning on a horse, it can be awaited.
Lǐ Tàibái's "Letter to Hán Jīngzhōu."
Wielding the brush, words fall on paper like clouds and mist.
From Dù's poetry.
Enticed by a single moment or object,
expressed in a laugh or a chant,
spontaneously forming a piece.
Bái Lètiān.
Eloquent as a hanging river,
the brush never ceasing.
Fàn Chuánzhèng's "Stele Inscription for Lǐ Bái."
In our dynasty,
Yáng Dànián, whenever he wished to write,
would drink, gamble, play pitch-pot, and chess with his disciples and guests,
amidst loud conversations and laughter,
yet it did not hinder his contemplation.
On small square papers, he wrote finely,
wielding his brush like flying,
his prose flawless without corrections,
each time filling a sheet,
he would order his disciples to transcribe it.
The disciples grew weary from complying,
in a mere moment,
sometimes thousands of words.
From Oūyáng Gōng's "Records of Returning to the Fields."
A thousand words with one wave of the hand,
five cartloads no longer to be read.
From the "Collection of Dōngpō."
Sleeves folded, silently alone,
the draft already formed in the mind.
Writing like flipping water to compose a rhapsody, hands swiftly clasped; when putting pen to paper, wind and rain speed by,
the brush reaching where the spirit has already consumed.
Also from the same source.
Unrolling the scroll, five lines at a glance,
wielding the brush, ten thousand words pour out.
From the "Collection of Sū Zǐyóu."
Student Huáng studies poetry with great effort,
swift hands and quick tongue like an overturned basin.
Chén Hòushān.
Lazy and slow
In history,
Zhái Fāngjìn at age twelve or thirteen,
served in the prefect's office as a minor clerk,
known as slow-witted.
Yán Shīgǔ reads it as "dull."
Incompetent at tasks.
From the "Original Biography in the History of the Western Hàn."
Zhāng Héng, imitating Bān Gù's "Two Capitals," composed the "Two Metropolises Rhapsody,"
using it to offer subtle admonition,
and thought for ten years before completing it.
From the "History of the Later Hàn."
Zuǒ Sī, creating the "Rhapsody on the Capital of Qí,"
took a year to finish.
Wishing to write the "Rhapsody on the Three Capitals,"
he contemplated for ten years,
then completed the rhapsody.
From the "History of the Jìn."
Confucian slowness makes one unfit for critical matters.
From the "Records of Hǎixī Gōng in the Comprehensive Mirror of the Jìn."
Lǐ Chéng served as a Hanlin Academician,
by nature lazy,
he would arrive only after the sun passed eight bricks,
thus nicknamed "The Eight-Brick Academician."
From the "New Táng History Biography."
Biographies record
Zhāng Héng polished his "Metropolises" for ten years,
Zuǒ Sī refined his "Capitals" for a cycle of twelve years.
From "The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons."
Yáng Zǐ drafted the "Profound,"
taking years without completion.
From "Generalities on History."
Classics
Who knows in the morning and achieves by evening?
From the "Odes·Restraint" note: "Knowing early on."
Truly profound and vast,
his voice fills the road.
When he crawled as an infant,
he could discern and recognize,
and sought his own food.
From the "Odes·Birth of the People" note: "Able to crawl, then knowingly,
his mind already aware.
His appearance dignified,
capable of discrimination."
Early praised throughout the land.
From the "Record of the Doctrine of the Mean."
Masters
Confucius traveled east,
saw two children arguing,
asked them the reason,
one child said: "I believe the sun is closer at sunrise,
and farther at noon."
The other said: "I believe it's farther at sunrise,
and closer at noon."
The first child said: "At sunrise,
it's as large as a carriage canopy,
by noon,
it's like a plate or bowl,
isn't this the distant being small and the near large?"
The other said: "At sunrise, it's cool and refreshing,
by noon, it's like reaching into hot water,
isn't this the near being hot and the distant cool?"
Confucius could not decide.
The two children laughed, saying: "Who says you are knowledgeable?"
From the "Lièzǐ·Questions of Tāng."
Tóng Wū at nine years old,
engaged with me in profound writings.
"Yángzǐ" note: "Tóng Wū,
was Zǐyún's son."
Some ask: Gān Luó's insight,
Lǚ Bùwéi and Zhāng Pìqiáng's awakening of Chén Píng and Zhōu Bó,
all at twelve years old.
Yáng Chónglí.
Tiger and leopard cubs, though not yet patterned, have the spirit to devour an ox;
young swans, though not fully feathered, have the heart to span the four seas;
so it is with the birth of a worthy.
From the "Yīnzǐ."
History
The State of Chǔ sent Zǐ Yù to train troops,
and the senior statesmen all congratulated him.
Wén Wěi Jiǎ, still young,
arrived late,
and did not offer congratulations.
Zǐ Wén asked him why, and he replied:
"Zǐ Yù's failure
is your recommendation.
To recommend someone who will bring defeat to the state—
what is there to congratulate?
If his forces exceed three hundred chariots,
they will not be able to return.
If they do return and then I congratulate,
would that be too late?"
—From Zuǒzhuàn, 27th Year of Duke Xī.
When the Qín army passed by the northern gate of the Zhōu capital,
Wángsūn Mǎn, still a child,
observed them and said,
"The Qín army is frivolous and lacks propriety;
they are sure to be defeated."
—From Zuǒzhuàn, 32nd Year of Duke Xī.
Xiàng Yǔ attacked and captured Wàihuáng,
intending to massacre its people.
A thirteen-year-old son of a retainer of the Wàihuáng magistrate went to persuade Xiàng Yǔ, saying,
"Péng Yuè forcibly seized Wàihuáng,
so we temporarily surrendered.
If you, Great King, arrive and massacre everyone again,
how could the common people have any inclination to submit?"
After this,
more than ten cities in the Liáng region were terrified,
and none were willing to surrender.
—From Records of the Grand Historian, Annals of Xiàng Yǔ.
Qín Shǐhuáng sent Zhāng Táng to serve as chancellor in Yān,
but he refused to go.
Gān Luó said,
"Xiàng Tuó at seven years old became a teacher to Confucius.
Now I am already twelve years old;
please try me, Your Majesty."
The First Emperor then sent Gān Luó to Zhào.
—From Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Gān Mào.
Jiǎ Yì was over twenty years old,
the youngest among the officials.
Whenever an imperial decree was issued for discussion,
and the elderly scholars were unable to respond,
Jiǎ Yì would answer all the questions himself.
—From his biography in the Book of Hàn.
Sīmǎ Qiān at age ten could recite ancient texts.
At twenty, he traveled south to the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
ascended Kuàijī,
explored Yǔ's cave,
peered at Jiǔyí,
and floated on Yuán and Xiāng rivers.
—From his biography in the Book of Hàn.
Yìng Fèng was intelligent from a young age.
Since childhood,
everything he experienced
he could memorize without fail,
and he could read five lines of text at once.
—From his biography in the Book of Later Hàn.
Jiǎ Yì sought to test his skills by subjugating the Xiōngnú Chányú,
while Zhōng Jūn wished to use a long rope
to capture the powerful Yuè leader.
Their fervor in their early twenties
was praised by earlier generations.
—From Biography of Mí Héng.
During a solar eclipse,
which was not visible in the capital,
Huáng Qióng reported the event.
The Empress Dowager inquired about the extent of the eclipse,
and Huáng Qióng was unsure how to describe it.
Huáng Wǎn, then seven years old,
who was by his side, said,
"Why not say the remainder of the eclipsed sun is like the beginning of the moon?"
Huáng Qióng was greatly astonished
and immediately used his words to reply to the imperial inquiry.
—From Biography of Huáng Qióng in the Book of Later Hàn.
The capital hailed him as,
"Unparalleled under heaven,
the child Huáng of Jiāngxià."
—From Biography of Huáng Xiāng in the Book of Later Hàn.
Kǒng Róng showed exceptional talent from a young age.
At ten, he accompanied his father to the capital.
At that time, Lǐ Yīng, the Governor of Hénán, did not casually receive scholars.
Kǒng Róng went to his door and said,
"I am a family friend of Lord Lǐ."
The doorman reported this,
and Lǐ Yīng invited Kǒng Róng in,
asking,
"Did your esteemed grandfather
have a past friendship with me?"
Kǒng Róng replied,
"Yes.
My ancestor Confucius and Lǎo Jūn shared virtues
and were peers and friends;
thus, I and you have been family friends for generations."
All present sighed in admiration.
Chén Wěi arrived later,
and those seated told him what happened.
Wěi said,
"Clever when young,
not necessarily remarkable when grown."
Kǒng Róng retorted,
"From what you say,
you must not have been precocious, right?"
—From his biography in the Book of Later Hàn.
Kǒng Róng, the sixth child,
at four years old,
often ate dates with his elder brothers
and always took the smaller ones.
When asked why,
he answered,
"I am the youngest,
so it is proper to take the smaller ones."
From then on, his clan considered him extraordinary.
—From the Book of Later Hàn.
Zhāng Bà at seven years old

His parents said,
"You are too young
to manage that."
Zhāng Bà replied,
"I am capable of doing it."
—From his biography in the Book of Later Hàn.
Jiǎ Kuí, as a child at play,
often organized troops in formation.
—From the Records of Wèi.
Yú Fān had a proud spirit from youth.

a guest came to visit his brother but ignored Yú Fān.
Yú Fān chased after him and wrote,

and a magnet does not attract bent needles.
To pass by without acknowledging me,
is that not appropriate?"
—From a note in his biography in the Records of Wú.
Cháng Lín at seven years old
had a friend of his father visit.
The visitor asked Cháng Lín,

Cháng Lín replied,
"To address my father by his courtesy name in front of his son,
what bow is necessary?"
—From the Records of Wèi.
Zhūgě Zhān at eight was intelligent and adorable.
—From his biography in the Records of Shǔ.
Xún Yōu, styled Gōngdá,
had a grandfather named Xún Tán.
Xún Yōu was orphaned young.
When Xún Tán died,
a former subordinate named Zhāng Tuī requested to guard his tomb.
Xún Yōu, then thirteen,
suspected him
and said to his uncle Xún Qú,
"This official has a suspicious demeanor;
he might intend treachery."
Xún Qú realized the point,
interrogated him,
and indeed, he was a fugitive murderer.
Thus, they regarded Xún Yōu as extraordinary.
—From the Records of Wèi.

Zhāng Píng's grandfather, Zhāng Zhèn,

Píng said,
"Grandfather, how can you jest with my father using me?"

Cross-referenced under "Grandfather" and "Grandson."
Dèng Ài at eleven,
whenever he saw high mountains and vast marshes,
would point out locations for military camps.
Later, he became a great general.

Wáng Yǔnzhī in his childhood
was often kept by his uncle Wáng Dūn,
who took him along when going out in the same carriage
and shared a room when staying in.
Once, Wáng Dūn was drinking at night,
and Yǔnzhī pleaded drunkenness
and went to bed first.
Wáng Dūn and Qián Fèng plotted rebellion,
and Yǔnzhī, already awake,
heard all their words.
Fearing that Dūn might suspect him,
he deliberately vomited profusely where he lay,
soiling his clothes and face.
After Fèng left,
Dūn indeed came to check
and saw Yǔnzhī lying in vomit,
thinking him heavily drunk,
and suspected him no more.
—From his biography in the Book of Jìn.
Liú Zhàn, from his youth,
had the ambition to govern and often compared himself to Guǎn Zhòng and Zhūgě Liàng.

He picked up the brush and completed it immediately.

Lù Yún was equally famous as his elder brother Lù Jī from a young age,
and when Mǐn Hóng saw him as a child, he found him extraordinary,
saying: "If this child is not a dragon colt,
he must be a phoenix chick."
When Xiè Shàng was eight years old,

When asked why,
he said: "A tree by the roadside with so much fruit

They picked some and tried them,

Zǔ Yíng of the Northern Wèi Dynasty, at eight years old,

deeply engrossed in books.
His parents feared he would fall ill from overstudying,
but their restrictions could not stop him.
He often secretly hid embers in the ashes,
dismissed the servant boys,
and after his parents had gone to sleep,
he would light a lamp to read,
using clothes and quilts to cover the windows,
fearing the light would leak out

and relatives both inside and outside the family called him the "little sage."
He particularly excelled in composing writings.

Emperor Míng was intelligent and wise from a young age,
and was doted on and regarded as exceptional by Emperor Yuán.

he was once seated on Emperor Yuán's knee,
and it happened that an envoy from Cháng'ān arrived.
Emperor Yuán then asked him: "Which do you think is closer, the sun or Cháng'ān?"
He replied: "Cháng'ān is closer.
I've never heard of anyone coming from the side of the sun."
Emperor Yuán was amazed.
The next day,
during a banquet with officials,
he asked him again.
The reply was: "The sun is closer."
Emperor Yuán, taken aback,
said: "Why does this differ from what you said before?"
He answered: "I can see the sun when I look up,
but I cannot see Cháng'ān."

When Xiè Ān was four years old,

Thus, he gained a significant reputation from a young age.
From "The Book of Jìn".
Though the cypress and camphor trees are small,
they already possess the makings of pillars and beams.

Wáng Tài was clever and perceptive from a young age.

his grandmother scattered chestnuts on the bed for her grandchildren and nephews,

When asked why,

From "The Book of Sòng".
Liú Xiàochuò could compose writings at seven years old,

When Xiè Zhēn was eight years old,

From "The History of the Southern Dynasties".
Hé Xùn could compose poems at eight years old,
and Shěn Yuē said to him: "Every time I read your poems,

From "The Book of Liáng".
Xiāo Móhē, at thirteen years old,
charged into battle alone on horseback,

Xú Líng composed writings at eight years old,

When Wáng Sēngrú was young,

saying: "My father has not seen them yet,

From "The Book of Qí".
Yáng Yīn had a plum tree in his courtyard,

From "The Book of Gān Qí".
Hé Tuǒ was quick-witted from a young age.

Tuǒ immediately retorted: "And your surname, Gù—
is it the Gù as in caring for,
or the Gù as in old and new?"
From "The Book of Suí".
When Xuē Shìyōng was a child,
he would play with other children,
often drawing a city wall on the ground
and directing the children to simulate attacks and defenses.
Those who disobeyed his orders
were whipped.
The children, fearing him,
all complied orderly.
From the same source above.
When Yǔwén Xīn was a child,
he would play with others,
organizing them into squads
with precise movements and formations,
all obeying commands without fail.
Those who observed this found him extraordinary.
Lǐ Mì knew how to write at seven years old,
and Emperor Xuánzōng summoned him.
Upon arrival,
the Emperor was watching a chess game with Zhāng Yuè,
so he asked Yuè to test Mì's ability.
Yuè requested a poem on "square, round, movement, stillness,"
and Mì said: "Please outline the theme."
Yuè said: "Square like the chessboard,
round like the chess pieces,
moving as if the chess is alive,
still as if the chess is dead."
Mì responded: "Square like upholding righteousness,
round like employing wisdom,
moving as if deploying talent,
still as if achieving satisfaction."
Yuè then congratulated the Emperor on finding an extraordinary child.
． From "The New Book of Táng, Biography of Lǐ Mì".
Sū Tǐng was sharp and perceptive even in his youth,
able to read a thousand words at a glance
and recite them from memory.
． From "The Book of Táng, Biography of Sū Tǐng".
Lú Huáishèn showed exceptional talent even as a child,
and Hán Sīyàn exclaimed: "This child's potential is immeasurable."
From the same source above.
Yuán Chù, at nine years old, ascended the seat,
and his eloquent arguments flowed intensely,

． From "The New Book of Táng, Biography of Lǐ Mì".
Bái Jūyì, shortly after birth,
could point to the characters "zhī" and "wú" in books at seven months,

． From "The Official Biography in the Book of Táng".
Lǐ Hè could compose poetry at seven years old,
and Hán Yù and Huángfǔ Shí initially heard of it but did not believe it.

asked him to compose a poem,

titled "The Grand Carriage Passes By."
． From "The Book of Táng, Biography of Lǐ Hè".
Chǔ Wúliàng was diligent and studious from a young age.

Wúliàng, then twelve years old,
remained calm and continued reading undisturbed.
From "The Old Book of Táng".
Yán Wǔ was bold and straightforward as a child.
His mother, Péi, was not treated well by Yán Tǐngzhī,
who favored his concubine Yīng instead.
When Wǔ was just eight,
he wondered why and asked his mother,
who explained the situation.
Enraged, Wǔ took a iron hammer to Yīng's room
and smashed her head.
The servants were shocked
and reported to Tǐngzhī,
saying: "The young master killed Yīng in a fit of play."
Wǔ retorted: "How can a high official favor a concubine over his wife?
I killed her intentionally,
not in play."
． From "The Book of Táng, Biography of Yán Tǐngzhī".
Yán Wǔ had a noble and lively spirit,
was quick in perception and understanding,
and displayed the demeanor of an adult even in childhood.
The Old Book of Táng.
Peí Yán was executed.
Peí Yán's nephew, the Court Gentleman of the Court of the Imperial Stud, Péi Zhòuxiān, was seventeen years old.
He submitted a memorial requesting an audience to speak on matters.
Empress Wǔ summoned him for an audience,
and questioned him, saying:
"Your uncle plotted rebellion,
what more is there to say?"
Zhòuxiān replied:
"Your Majesty, as a wife of the Lǐ family,
upon the late emperor's passing, hastily seized the reins of government,
altered the designated heir,
alienated and dismissed members of the Lǐ clan,
while enfeoffing and elevating the various Wǔ relatives.
My uncle was loyal to the state,
yet you falsely accused him of crimes,
and executed even his descendants.
I truly lament Your Majesty's actions.
Your Majesty should promptly restore the throne to your son and return to rightful rule,
then you can rest peacefully and live in seclusion,
and the imperial clan can be preserved.
Otherwise, once the empire changes,
it will be beyond saving."
Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Táng Empress Wǔ.
Yuè Sīhuì's son, not yet ten years old,
was confiscated into the service of the Minister of Agriculture.
He was granted an audience,
Empress Wǔ inquired about his situation,
he replied:
"My father is already dead,
my family is already ruined.
I only regret that Your Majesty's laws are being manipulated by the likes of Lái Jùnchén.
If Your Majesty does not believe my words,
I beg you to choose among the court officials one who is loyal and upright, whom you have always trusted, and accuse him of rebellion, then hand him over to Jùnchén for interrogation—
there is none who would not confess to rebellion."
The Empress's mind became slightly awakened.
Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Táng Empress Wǔ.

Liú Yàn, at eight years old, presented a eulogy.
The emperor marveled at his youth,

Yuè said:

and he was called a "child prodigy,"
his fame shaking the age.
New Book of Táng, his biography.

"My elder sister used to hold me by the fence,

Wáng Zǐnián's Records of Omissions.
Hé Yàn was the grandson of the Grand General Hé Jìn.

By the age of seven or eight,
he possessed a naturally perceptive and understanding mind.

he had him join his sons in order of age.
Yàn subtly became aware of this;
when sitting, he would keep to his own mat;
when standing, he would stand apart.
Someone asked him the reason,
he replied:
"According to the rites: 'Those of different surnames should not be intermingled.'"

Emperor Xuánzōng greatly marveled at him.
Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng.
Xīn Pān was seven years old.

Zhōng said:
"Péi Kǎi is pure and comprehending,
Zhǒng Tóng,

Child Qū Jì at eleven,

two bold thieves seized him to sell in a market.
Jì feigned childish crying,
acting scared and trembling like a child.
The thieves underestimated him,
one left to trade,

King Zhuāng of Chǔ hosted a banquet for his ministers,
and as dusk fell and wine flowed freely,
the lamps and candles suddenly extinguished.
Someone tugged at the robe of a court beauty,
who swiftly tore off the tassel from the man's cap,
then reported to the king: "Bring torches quickly,
so we may identify the one with the broken tassel."
The king responded: "Having granted them wine until drunk,
how can I punish their breach of etiquette?
Should I disgrace my knights to highlight a woman's virtue?"
He then commanded all hundred-odd ministers to remove their cap tassels before relighting the torches,
and the feast concluded in utmost merriment.

In the past, Sòng Jiù, a senior official of Liáng, governed a border county,
where both sides grew melons near Chǔ.
Liáng's side watered frequently,
their melons were fine;
Chǔ's side watered little,
their melons poor.
Chǔ ordered people to sneak and damage Liáng's melons at night,
causing some to wither.
Liáng's captain wanted to retaliate,
but Sòng Jiù said,
"That would only foster enmity and share misfortune.
Have our people secretly water Chǔ's melons at night,
without them knowing."
Chǔ's melons improved daily.

I enjoy lying late,
but the gatekeeper insists on calling me,
first intolerance;
carrying a qín, singing outdoors,
hunting and fishing in the wilds, but officials guard me,
preventing free movement,
second intolerance;
sitting properly for hours,
legs numb, unable to move,
body full of lice,
scratching incessantly,
yet wrapped in official robes,
bowing to superiors,
third intolerance;
unaccustomed to letters,
disliking writing,
but worldly affairs abound,
papers pile on the desk,
not responding offends etiquette,
forcing myself to comply,
but unable to keep up,
fourth intolerance;
disliking mourning visits,
yet society values this,
already resented by the unforgiving,
to the point of being slandered,
though I startle and blame myself,
I cannot change,
never achieving faultless or praised state,
fifth intolerance;
disliking vulgar people,
but having to work with them,
or guests filling the room,
noise grating the ears,
dusty, smelly places,
endless variations of behavior,
right before my eyes,
sixth intolerance;
impatient at heart,
but official duties overwhelm,
affairs preoccupy the mind,
worldly concerns complicate thoughts,

He ordered Yí Shègū seized,
but they could not find him,
which increased his fury.
He threw himself onto his bed,

Duke Zhuāng was irritable and fastidious about cleanliness,

The emperor, enraged,
