Attendant, come out!"
Sōng replied, "I have never heard of a ruler personally rising to strike his attendant."
. — "Dōng Hàn: Zhōnglí Yì Zhuàn".
Yuán Tán had a harsh and impatient disposition by nature.
— "Wèi Zhì".
When Wáng Jùn attacked Wú,
he felt his merit was great
but was suppressed by Wáng Hún and his son;
each time he had an audience,
he would recount his efforts in the campaign
and the injustice he suffered,
unable to contain his resentment,
he would leave directly without taking leave.
. — "Jìn Shū: Běn Zhuàn".
Wáng Shù had an impatient temper;
once while eating an egg,
he tried to stab it with chopsticks,
but failed,
and flew into a rage.
He threw it to the ground,
the egg rolled round without stopping,
so he got off the bed and stepped on it with his clog's teeth,
again without success,
and became even more furious.
He put it in his mouth,
bit it open, and spat it out.
. — "Jìn Shū: Běn Zhuàn".
Xiè Mì was playing chess with a friend,
whose pieces in the southwest faced a doomed position;
another guest remarked, "The southwest wind is fierce—
it may capsize the boat."
and saved his position.
Xiè Mì was greatly angered
and threw the board to the ground.
. — "Nán Shǐ: Běn Zhuàn".
Huángfǔ Shí was impatient by nature;
once stung on the finger by a bee,
he hired children to collect bees,
then pounded them to extract their venom.
One day,
he ordered his son to copy a poem;
when a single character was wrong, he scolded him,
leapt up calling for a cane,
and before it arrived,
bit his son's arm until it bled.
— "Táng Shū".
Biographies:
The crab has two claws and eight legs,
yet without the burrow of an eel, it has no place to lodge,
because its heart is restless.
— "Dà Dài Lǐjì".
Wáng Sī was impatient;
once while holding a brush, a fly landed on its tip,
he flicked it away,
but it returned,
enraging Sī,
who rose to chase the fly,
failed to catch it,
then went back, took the brush, broke it, and discarded it.
— "Wèi Lüè".
Classics:
One must have forbearance,
then there can be success.
— "Shū: Jūn Chén".
Philosophers:
Gōu Jiàn entered Wú's service,
bearing arms as a groom for the King of Wú,
thus he was able to kill Fū Chāi at Gūsū.
— "Hánfēizǐ".
History
Someone slandered: "Zhí Bùyí has stolen a woman!"
Bùyí heard this,
and said: "I don't even have an elder brother."
Yet he never tried to clear his name.
. From "Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Biography."
Lián Pō served as a general of Zhào,
while Lìn Xiàngrú was appointed senior minister,
ranking above Pō.
Pō said: "If I see him,
I will surely humiliate him."
Xiàngrú heard this,
and refused to meet with him.
At each court session,
he would claim illness,
not wishing to contend for position with Pō.
Later, when going out,
he saw Pō from afar,
and turned his carriage to avoid him.
Xiàngrú said: "Even with the Qín king's authority,
I scolded him in court,
and humiliated his ministers.
Though I am inept,
would I fear General Lián alone?
I consider that the powerful Qín dare not attack Zhào
only because the two of us are here.
Now if two tigers fight,
neither can survive.
The reason I act this way
is to put the nation's crisis before personal grudges."
From "Records of the Grand Historian."
Also entered under the category "Devoted to Public Duty, Forgetting Private Interests."
Wèi Wǎn did not contend with other generals.
. From "Western Hàn, Basic Biography."
When Zhí Bùyí shared quarters with other court attendants,
one requested leave to return home,
mistakenly taking a fellow attendant's gold with him.
The gold's owner suspected Bùyí.
Bùyí apologized and admitted it,
buying gold to repay.
Later, the one who had taken leave returned and brought back the gold,
and the former attendant who had lost the gold was greatly ashamed.
Same as above.
Kòu Xún was in Yǐngchuān,
when a subordinate of Jiǎ Fù broke the law,
and Xún executed him.
Fù wanted to kill Xún with his own hand,
so Xún always avoided him.
From "Book of the Later Hàn."
Liú Kuān was once traveling,
when someone who had lost an ox came to identify it from Kuān's carriage,
and Kuān said nothing,
but dismounted and walked home.
After a while,
the identifier found his ox,
returned it,
and kowtowed to apologize.
Kuān said: "Things can look alike,
and mistakes can happen.
I'm grateful you troubled to return it,
why apologize?"
The community admired his lack of contention.
From "Book of the Later Hàn."
Zhuó Mào served under Kǒng Guāng,
and once while traveling,
someone claimed his horse.
Mào asked: "How long have you lost your horse?"
The reply: "Over a month."
Mào had owned the horse for years,
and knew the claim was wrong,
but silently untied it and gave it,
pulling the carriage away.
He turned and said: "If it's not your horse,
please return it to me at the chancellor's office."
Another day,
the horse's owner found his lost one,
and went to the office to return the horse,
kowtowing to apologize.
Chén Zhòng was in the attendants' quarters,
when a fellow attendant took leave to visit home,
mistakenly taking another's trousers.
The owner suspected Zhòng had taken them,
but Zhòng did not explain,
buying trousers to compensate.
Later, the one on leave returned,
and gave the trousers back to the owner,
revealing the truth.
Both same as above.
His nature was slow and easy,
harming no one.
Even if he suffered the humiliation of crawling between legs or the disgrace of Yúcì,
he did not feel belittled,
treating it like a passing mosquito bite.
. From "Book of the Later Hàn, Kǒng Róng's Biography."
Cáo Méng, styled Yuánwěi,
was known for benevolence and kindness.
A neighbor lost a pig,
similar to Méng's,
and came to his door to claim it,
but Méng did not argue.
Later, the lost pig returned on its own,
and its owner was greatly ashamed,
returning the claimed pig,
apologizing to Méng,
who smiled and accepted it.
From "Book of the Later Hàn."
Disciple Jiǎ Qióng asked about "ending slander,"
and Wáng Tōng said: "Do not argue."
Asked about "stopping resentment,"
he said: "Do not contend."
. From "Comprehensive Mirror, Suí Emperor Gāozǔ."
Zhí Bùyí bought gold to repay his fellow attendant,
Liú Kuān dismounted and returned the ox to the villager,
truly knowing that suspicions are hard to clarify,
and cannot be overcome by words alone.
. From "Táng History, Liǔ Zōngyuán."
Why must one probe their burrows and contend with ants over length?
. From "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Empress Wǔ."
Biographies
Sīmǎ Huī,
styled Décāo,
was called the "Water Mirror" by contemporaries.
Once, someone falsely claimed Huī's pig,
and Huī simply gave it to him.
Days later,
the one who lost the pig returned it.
Huī then kowtowed to thank him,
blaming himself,
and Huī also generously thanked him.
From "Dǒng Zhèng's Separate Biography."
Hé Suí,
styled Jìyè,
was pure, honest, and yielding.
Once, a butcher led a pig past,
and the rope broke at Suí's gate,
losing the pig by force.
He claimed the pig in Suí's pen,
and Suí led it to him.
The butcher later found his lost one and returned,
but Suí ultimately let him keep it.
From "Records of Huáyáng."
Collection
Have a mind like an empty boat.
Bái Jūyì.
Our dynasty
Hard to argue with words alone,
when water clears, stones are seen.
Huáng Tíngjiān's poem.
Classics
If you do not boast, none under heaven
will contend with you over ability;
if you do not brag, none under heaven
will contend with you over merit.
. From "Book of Documents, Great Yǔ's Counsels."
Masters
The way of heaven does not contend, yet excels at winning.
"Lǎozi."
Because he does not contend,
none under heaven can contend with him.
Same as above.
Histories
Lìn Xiàngrú yielded to avoid Lián Pō,
and his fame weighed as heavily as Tài Shān.
. From "Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Biography."
Classics
When your evil is full,
they point their spears at you.
When pacified and pleased,
they toast each other.
. From "Classic of Poetry, Joint Peak South Mountain."
Advancing someone as if placing them on your knee,
rejecting someone as if pushing them into an abyss.
. From "Book of Rites, Tángōng Part Two."
Masters
Horses, when pleased, rub necks;
when angered, turn backs and kick.
Dà jì fǎn.
"Zhuāngzǐ."
Frivolous in giving,
rash in slandering,
prone to likes and dislikes,
and frequent anger—
such is a petty person.
"Wénzhōngzǐ."
See also "Impatience and Irritability."
Histories
Few are those whose joy and anger follow proper measure,
Many indeed are those who are changeable.
． *Zuǒ Zhuàn*, 17th Year of Xuāngōng.
Wèi Shōu said: "Lift him and he would ascend to heaven,
Press him and he should sink into the earth."
． *Běi Shǐ*, his biography.
When fond of someone, they would drill through skin to make feathers emerge;
When disliking someone, they would scrub off grime to seek scars.
． *Xīn Táng Shū*, Wèi Zhèng's biography.
Collected sayings
The sovereign's heart, with its likes and dislikes, suffers from inconsistency,
Favor breeds feathers, disfavor breeds sores.
Bái Jūyì.
Classics
Only because it is profound,
Can it penetrate the will of all under heaven.
． *Yì Jīng*, Xì Cí.
Histories
Serene and deep, thus possessing strategy.
． *Shǐ Jì*, Zhuānxū's records.
The feelings of desire,
Do not intrude upon one's countenance and demeanor.
． *Xī Hàn*, Kuāng Héng's biography.
Silent and fond of deep, profound thoughts.
． *Xī Hàn*, Yáng Xióng's biography.
How profound is this man!
． *Xī Hàn*, Bān Gù's preface.
Hé Xiū was simple and plain, slow of speech,
Yet elegant and thoughtful.
． *Dōng Hàn*, his biography.
Cross-reference "Not Judging by Appearance."
Liú Rú,
Slow of speech but sharp in mind.
Same as above.
Although Yīn Hào was dismissed and exiled,
He uttered no words of complaint.
Composed in spirit and resigned to fate,
He continued conversing and chanting without cease,
So that even his family saw no grief of exile in him.
． *Jìn Shū*, his biography.
Bó Yí once said to Chǔ Póu: "Jìyě has the Spring and Autumn Annals within his skin."
Meaning he showed no praise or blame outwardly,
But held judgments within.
Xiè Ān said: "Though Póu does not speak,
The aura of the four seasons is already complete in him."
． *Tōng Jiàn*, Jìn records.
Yóu Yǎ said: "I have associated with Gāo Zǐ for forty years,
And never seen a trace of joy or anger on his face."
． *Tōng Jiàn*, Sòng Shìzǔ.
Yáng Wǎn had a calm and quiet nature,
Dwelling alone in one room,
With books and histories around him gathering dust,
Yet the mat was serene as ever.
． *Táng Shū*, his biography.
Lǐ Fān was calm and self-restrained.
Same as above.
Sòng Jǐng served as Minister of Justice,
Rushed by post to the court,
Sent the eunuch general Yáng Sīxù to greet him.
Jǐng's demeanor was composed and far-reaching,
None could fathom his depths,
And throughout the journey, he did not exchange a word with Sīxù.
． *Tōng Jiàn*, Táng Xuánzōng.
Biographies and records
Wisdom deep and courage steady.
*Zhàn Guó Cè*.
Collected sayings
His aura vast and profound.
*Chǔ Yuān Bēi*.
Wisdom and strategy deep and tranquil.
*Táng Wén Cuì*.
Philosophers
At the first appointment, he became as haughty as Lǚ;
At the second, he danced on the carriage;
At the third, he called his uncles by name.
*Zhuāng Zǐ*.
The learning of a petty person,
Enters the ear and comes out the mouth.
Between ear and mouth,
Is but four inches—
How can that beautify a seven-foot body?
*Xún Zǐ*.
Histories
To attain wealth and honor and not return to one's hometown,
Is like wearing embroidered robes and walking at night—
Who would know of it?
． *Shǐ Jì*, Xiàng Yǔ's records.
Hán Xìn pacified Qí,
Sent a message to the King of Hàn saying: "Qí is deceitful and fickle,
A state of repeated treachery;
Unless a provisional king is appointed to pacify it,
The situation will remain unstable.
I wish to be made provisional king."
． *Shǐ Jì*, his biography.
Fàn Jū would repay even the kindness of a single meal,
And avenge the slightest grievance.
Same as above.
His spirit soaring,
Very self-satisfied.
． *Shǐ Jì*, Yàn Zǐ's biography.
Those who feel insufficient,
See others as having more.
． *Xī Hàn*, Bān Gù's biography.
Huán Róng served as Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince.
The emperor bestowed upon him a carriage and horses.
Róng gathered his disciples for a grand assembly,
Displayed his carriage, horses, seals, and ribbons,
Saying: "What I receive today is due to the power of studying the past."
． *Dōng Hàn*, his biography.
Cross-reference "Arrogance and Conceit."
The kindness of a single meal,
The grievance of a sidelong glance,
None went unavenged.
． *Tōng Jiàn*, Hàn Xiàn's records.
Sāng Wéihàn acted on personal likes and dislikes, repaying the favor of a meal,
And avenging the slightest grievance,
For which people thought less of him.
．． *Tōng Jiàn*, Wǔ Dài Jìn Gāozǔ.
Yáng Yán alone held great power,
And devoted himself to repaying favors and grudges.
． *Tōng Jiàn*, Táng Dézōng.
Lǐ Xùn and Zhèng Zhù,
In their lives, repaid every thread of kindness and hair of grievance.
． *Tōng Jiàn*, Táng Wénzōng's records.
Biographies and records
After Zhāng Xiàobiāo passed the imperial exams,
He sent a poem to Bái Jūyì: "Passing the exams surpasses ten terms as an official,
Gilded like gold, I leave Cháng'ān.
As my horse approaches Yángzhōu's road,
I bid the people of the time to wash their eyes and see."
*Zhí Yán*.
Cross-reference "Arrogance and Conceit."
Collected sayings
Before composing a single line of Liú Chángqīng's poetry,
They already call Ruǎn Jí an old soldier;
Before writing a word of Luò Bīnwáng's prose,
They already curse Sòng Yù as a criminal;
Before recognizing the radicals of characters,
They loftily discuss Jì and Qì;
Before understanding punctuation in reading,
They look down upon Fú Qián.
Huángfǔ Shí.
Cross-reference "Not Knowing One's Limits."
Those lacking inner substance,
Are anxious for others to know them.
Hán Yù's writings.
One person's praise makes them feel more than sufficient,
One person's discouragement makes them feel inadequate.
Classics
The noble person, speaking of the great,
Nothing under heaven can contain it;
Speaking of the small,
Nothing under heaven can split it.
． *Lǐ Jì*, Zhōng Yōng.
Cross-reference "Ineffable."
Now take the earth—
A handful of soil in quantity.
Yet in its breadth and thickness,
It bears Mount Huà and Yuè without heaviness,
Shakes rivers and seas without leakage,
And carries all things.
Now take the mountains—
A fist-sized stone in quantity.
Yet in their vastness,
Grasses and trees grow on them,
Birds and beasts dwell on them,
And treasures abound.
Now take water—
A spoonful in quantity.
Yet in its unfathomableness,
Turtles, alligators, dragons, fish, and turtles thrive in it,
And goods and wealth multiply.
． *Lǐ Jì*, Zhōng Yōng.
Look up to it, and it grows higher;
Bore into it, and it grows harder;
Gaze at it ahead,
And suddenly it is behind.
*Lún Yǔ*.
The noble person is easy to serve but hard to please.
The master's wall is several ren high,
And one cannot enter without finding the gate.
Both from *Lún Yǔ*.
Philosophers
If Heaven could suddenly be measured,
Then its covering of things would be shallow;
If Earth could suddenly be fathomed,
Then its bearing of things would be slight.
Yángzǐ.
Water,
The more you measure it, the deeper it becomes;
The more you exhaust it, the farther it extends.
Ibid.
The great abyss as an entity,
Pours into it yet it does not fill,
Draws from it yet it is not exhausted.
Zhuāngzǐ.
Like the Milky Way, it has no limit.
Zhuāngzǐ: Xiāoyáo Yóu.
Boundless as Heaven and Earth,
Inexhaustible as rivers and seas.
Sūnzǐ.
Not serving as a storehouse of schemes,
Vast and without boundaries.
Liúzǐ.
History
Confucius went to Zhōu,
And inquired about rites from Lǎozǐ.
After Confucius departed,
He said to his disciples: "Birds, I know they can fly;
Fish, I know they can swim;
Beasts, I know they can run.
Runners can be caught with nets,
Swimmers can be caught with lines,
Flyers can be caught with arrows.
As for the dragon,
I do not know how it rides wind and clouds to ascend to Heaven.
Today I have seen Lǎozǐ,
Is he not like a dragon!"
Shǐjì.
Dài Liáng said: "Before I met Shūdù,
I thought myself inferior.
But having seen the man,
I look for him ahead,
And suddenly he is behind.
Truly he is difficult to fathom."
Dōng Hàn Huáng Xiàn Zhuàn.
Shūdù is vast like a thousand-qǐng lake,
Clarify it, yet it does not become clear;
Stir it, yet it does not become turbid;
It cannot be measured.
Ibid.
His family never saw any difference in his expressions of joy or anger.
Dōng Hàn Qiú Lǎn Zhuàn.
Xuē Shōu and Fáng Dù were entrusted as confidants,
And became even more attached to each other.
Xuē Yuánjìng was cautious and reserved,
Never expressing intimacy.
Qū Rǔhuì said: "The young recorder cannot be approached intimately nor kept at a distance."
Xīn Tángshū Běn Zhuàn.
Sūn Dēng's nature was without anger;
Someone threw him into the water,
Wanting to test his composure,
And upon emerging, he simply laughed heartily.
Jìnshū Yǐnyì Zhuàn.
Jiǎ Dān returned home from court,
Received and conversed with guests,
Yet was never weary all day.
His family and close attendants,
Never saw any sign of joy or anger on his face.
How could the virtuous gentlemen of old surpass this?
Jiù Tángshū Běn Zhuàn.
His demeanor was profound and far-reaching,
No one could fathom his depth.
Tángshū Sòng Jǐng Zhuàn.
Dù Rǔhuì followed Tàizōng on campaigns.
Participated in strategy sessions,
Handled confidential plans,
And resolved many matters without delay.
His subordinates all admired his talent,
But none could see his limits.
Tángshū Běn Zhuàn.
Zhōu Yǐ pointed to Gu Hé's heart and said: "What is in here?"
Gu Hé replied: "This is the most difficult place to fathom."
Jìnshū Gu Hé Zhuàn.
A single spiritual terrace,
Hard for even painting to depict.
Tángshū Péi Dù Zhuàn.
Various censors spoke incessantly on trivial matters,
And the Son of Heaven grew increasingly weary and annoyed.
Yáng Chéng was just drinking day and night with his two brothers and guests,
No one could discern his limits,
And all thought he had gained his reputation falsely.
Hán Yù wrote the "Zhēng Chén Lùn" to criticize him,
But Yáng Chéng paid no heed.
Tōngjiàn Táng Dézōng.
Biographies
Wáng Róng lived with Jī Kāng for twenty years,
Yet never saw any expression of joy or anger on his face.
Shì Shuō, Part I.
Grand Tutor Xiè showed neither anger nor joy.
Liú Yìqìng's Shì Shuō.
Sīmǎ Huī, when speaking with others,
Regardless of what was asked, good or bad, always said "good."
A fellow villager asked Huī: "Are you well?"
He replied: "Good."
Someone reported that his son had died,
He replied: "Very good."
His wife scolded him: "People tell you things because they consider you virtuous,
Why do you say 'good' upon hearing of someone's son's death?"
Huī said: "What you say is also very good."
Yīn Yún Xiǎoshuō.
Like holding a cup to drink from the river or sea,
One cannot know its depth.
Liú Xiàng's Shuō Yuàn.
Following the Tàiháng Mountains northward,
One also does not know the mountain's limits,
Just as with the Eastern Sea, one does not know its end.
Bówù Zhì.
Collections
Joy and anger, none can see their bounds.
Chǔ Yuān Bēi.
His understanding of the Way is empty and far-reaching,
Inner and outer fused and penetrating,
Profound as ten thousand qǐng,
Soaring straight up ten thousand rèn.
Servants and concubines never see his joy or anger,
Close attendants never see his relaxation.
Rèn Yǎnshēng.
Like a goose beyond the frontier, without peer,
Like the moon over the sea, hard to equal.
Mèng Dōngyě.
How can one fathom its shores and depths, or peer over its walls?
Táng Wén Cuì.
Who can distinguish between heart and trace,
Neither action nor concealment?
Bái Lètiān.
Look up to it, ever more lofty,
Majestic as a mountain;
Draw from it, ever more profound,
Deep as the sea.
Táng Wén Cuì.
Friends rarely hear words of gain or loss,
Family never see expressions of joy or anger.
Lǚ Héshū's writings.
Virtue's radiance, serene and full,
None can see its bounds.
Lǐ Yìshān.
If people wish to know the breadth of my mind,
See the autumn of Pénglí connecting with the ten-thousand-mile river.
Dù Mùzhī.
If one ascends Tàihuà and faces the vast sea,
Simply observe the accumulated heights and deep waters,
Not knowing the immense expanse that creates such vastness.
Ibid.
Our Dynasty
Moments suffice to fulfill the farmers' hopes,
Then收敛 the divine effort, silent as if nothing happened.
Hán Wèi Gōng's "Xǐ Yǔ Shī".
What you are capable of,
I cannot know.
Riding clouds, driving the wind,
Meeting with the vastness.
Dōngpō composed Wén Dìng Shéndào Bēi.
Your heart and mind,
Coiled like dragons and serpents.
Wind and clouds transform,
Rain and hail交织.
Suddenly wielding an axe,
Thunderbolts rumble like carts.
Those who encounter it,
Hearts startled, gall bladders fallen.
Collapsed like hemp,
In a moment it clears,
And looking around for a hundred miles,
Mountains, rivers, plants, and trees,
Sprout and bud.
Ōu Gōng's "Jì Sū Zǐměi".
Summoned, he does not come;
Waved away, he does not leave.
Cannot be made intimate,
Can he then be kept distant?
Pō's writings.
Talent like a cloud-reaching pine,
How can it be measured by inches?
Sū Zǐyóu.
Like Tàishān's lofty peaks,
One does not see their movement, yet the benefits reaching things

Dōngpō's "Jì Ōu Gōng Wén".
Zǐ
In the wilds, a crowd was pursuing a tiger.
The tiger backed into a mountain recess,
and no one dared to approach it.
Catching sight of Féng Fù,
they hurried to welcome him.
Féng Fù bared his arms and descended from the carriage,
and the crowd was pleased with him,
but those who considered themselves scholars laughed at him.
． _Mèngzǐ, Jìn Xīn Xià_.
Nánróng Chú arrived at Lǎozi's place.
Lǎozi said, "Just now, seeing between your eyebrows and eyelashes,
I have thereby understood you."
． _Zhuāngzǐ, Yǔ Sāng Chǔ_.
Duke Wèi of Qí was reading in his hall,
while Wheelwright Bián was chiseling a wheel below.
He asked, "What you, my lord, are reading
is merely the dregs of the ancients."
_Zhuāngzǐ_.
Yú Gōng planned to level the peril of Tàiháng Mountain,
and a widow from the capital city had a son who went to assist him.
The wise old man of Héqū laughed and tried to stop him, saying, "How extreme
is your lack of wisdom!
With your remaining years and strength,
you cannot even destroy a single hair of the mountain—
what can you do with the earth and stones?"
_Lièzǐ_.
Shǐ
Dòu Bóbǐ said: "The Mò'áo will surely be defeated.
He raises his feet high, his heart is not steadfast."
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 13 of Duke Wēi.
The Marquis of Qí held a covenant with the feudal lords at Kuíqiū.
Zǎi Kǒng returned first,
and encountering the Marquis of Jìn, said: "You may not attend the meeting.
The Marquis of Qí does not devote himself to virtue but is diligent in distant campaigns,
hence he attacked the Shānróng in the north,
campaigned against Chǔ in the south,
and now holds this meeting in the west.
His eastern campaigns are unknown,
but in the west, it is not so.
There will be disorder.
You should focus on quelling disorder,
and not labor in travels."
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 9 of Duke Xī.
Xì Ruì said: "Heavy gifts and sweet words—
they are luring us."
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 10 of Duke Xī.
Yáng Chǔfǔ of Jìn was on a mission to Wèi,
and on his return passed through Nìng.
Nìng Yíng followed him.
Upon reaching Wēn, he sent his wife back.
When asked,
Yíng said: "Because of his rigidity.
The Shāng Shū says: 'For the deep and submerged, use firmness to overcome;
for the lofty and bright, use gentleness to overcome.'
This gentleman embodies one aspect only,
will he not perish?
Heaven, with its firm virtue,
still does not interfere with the seasons,
how much more should men?
Moreover, he is showy without substance,
which gathers resentment.
To offend and accumulate resentment,
one cannot secure oneself.
I fear I will not gain benefits but encounter his calamities,
therefore I left him."
Jìn executed Yáng Chǔfǔ.
— From year 5 of Duke Wén.
Duke Mù of Qín, Rènhǎo,
died,
and had three sons of the Zǐchē family buried with him.
The gentleman thus knew that Qín would not campaign eastward again.
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 6 of Duke Wén.
Shì Huì returned to Jìn,
and Rào Cháo of Qín presented him with a策 (bamboo slip),
saying: "Do not say that Qín has no men—my plan was simply not used."
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 13 of Duke Wén.
Liú Kānggōng said: "Yuán Shū will surely face great calamity;
Heaven has taken away his spirit."
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 15 of Duke Xuān.
Shì Zhēnbó said: "The Earl of Zhèng looks about hastily and moves swiftly,
uneasy in his position,
likely he cannot last long."
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 6 of Duke Chéng.
Shì Yǎng said: "Luǎn Yǎn is excessively arrogant and cruel,
can he still avoid it? Will it be upon Yíng?"
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 14 of Duke Xiāng.
Shī Huì of Zhèng mocked Sòng, saying: "Surely there are no men here.
If there were still men,
how could they trade a minister of a thousand chariots
for a blind musician of lewd music?"
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 15 of Duke Xiāng.
Cross-reference "Neglecting the great for the small."
Shū Xiàng said: "Bó Yǒu is already extravagant,
what is called not lasting five harvests."
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 27 of Duke Xiāng.
Cross-reference "Estimation."
To be in mourning yet not sorrowful,
in grief yet with a cheerful countenance,
this is called lacking measure.
Those without measure
seldom avoid disaster.
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 31 of Duke Xiāng.
Hán Xuānzǐ went to Qí,
saw Zǐ Qí and said: "He is not one to preserve his family."
Yànzǐ said: "The gentleman, if he knows, has reason to know."
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 2 of Duke Zhāo.
Zhōu Yuán and Bó Lǔ disliked learning,
Mǐn Zǐmǎ said: "Learning
is like cultivation;
without learning, one will decline.
Will the Yuán family perish?"
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 18 of Duke Zhāo.
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ of Lǔ said: "Chǔ is not among the feudal lords anymore.
It merely preserves itself,
to maintain its lineage而已."
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 19 of Duke Zhāo.
Chǔ executed Wǔ Shē.
His son Yún went to Wú, speaking of the advantages of attacking Chǔ.
Prince Guāng said: "This man's clan was executed, and he seeks to avenge his enemy;
we cannot follow him."
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 20 of Duke Zhāo.
Cross-reference "Shifting blame."
Shūsūn Ruò was on a mission to Sòng, at Tóngmén.
The Yòu Shī met him,
spoke disparagingly of Sòng's great officers,
and belittled the Sīchéng clan.
Zhāozǐ told his followers: "Will the Yòu Shī perish?
A gentleman values himself,
and only then can he extend to others;
thus he has courtesy.
Now this gentleman belittles his great officers
and scorns his own clan,
which is scorning himself.
Can he have courtesy?
Without courtesy, he must perish."
— From Zuǒzhuàn, year 25 of Duke Zhāo.
Observe his demeanor and know his heart.
— From Guóyǔ.
Cross-reference "Estimation."
The Róng king sent Yóu Yú to Qín,
and Duke Mù of Qín showed him the palaces and stores.
Yóu Yú said: "This is what causes chaos in the Central States."
— From Shǐjì, Basic Annals of Qín.
Wèi Liáo advised the King of Qín.
The king treated Liáo as an equal,
sharing the same clothing, food, and drink.
Liáo said: "The King of Qín, in person,
has a prominent nose,
long eyes,
a chest like a bird of prey,
a voice like a jackal,
little kindness but a heart of tiger and wolf.
In hardship, he easily humbles himself before others;
when successful, he lightly devours men.
I am a commoner,
yet when he sees me, he often humbles himself before me.
If he truly achieves his ambition under heaven,
all under heaven will become his captives.
One cannot associate with him long."
So he left.
— From Shǐjì, Basic Annals of Qín Shǐ Huáng.
Wǔ Zǐxū saw the King of Wú,
advocating the advantages of attacking Chǔ.
Prince Guāng of Wú said: "That Wǔ Yún,
his father and elder brother died in Chǔ,
and Yún speaks of attacking Chǔ,
wanting to avenge his personal grudge,
not for Wú's sake."
So they stopped.
— From Shǐjì, Biography of the Assassin Zhuān Zhū.
Guǎn Zhòng is what the world calls a worthy minister,
yet Confucius thought little of him.
— From Shǐjì, Treatise on Guǎn and Yǎn.
Fàn Lǐ wrote to Minister Wén Zhǒng: "The King of Yuè, in person,
has a long neck,
a beak-like mouth;
one can share hardships with him,
but not enjoy success."
Zhǒng pleaded illness;
the king then gave Zhǒng a sword,
and he committed suicide.
— From Shǐjì, Hereditary House of Yuè.
Chǔ had Yǎng Yóujī,
skilled in archery.
He shot at willow leaves a hundred paces away,
hitting a hundred out of a hundred shots.
Thousands of onlookers
all praised his skill.
One man stood by his side,
saying: "You can be taught archery."
Yǎng Yóujī was angry,
but the man said: "Shooting at willow leaves a hundred paces away,
hitting a hundred out of a hundred shots,
if you don't rest at your peak,
soon when your energy wanes and strength tires,
with bow awry and arrow crooked,
one miss
nullifies all previous hits."
— From Shǐjì, Annals of Zhōu.
Cross-reference "One error invites a hundred faults."
The joy of a madman,
the wise mourn it.
— From Shǐjì, Hereditary House of Zhào.
When Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
Tiáohóu was appointed Grand Commandant.
Reaching Hénán,
he obtained Jù Mèng,
and joyfully said: "Wú and Chǔ undertake great deeds yet do not seek Mèng;
I know they can achieve nothing."
— From Shǐjì, Biographies of Wandering Knights.
Wú Jì Zhá went to Jìn,
and speaking with Zhào Wénzǐ, Hán Xuānzǐ, and Wèi Xiànzǐ, said:
"Will Jìn's power be concentrated in these three families?"
— From Shǐjì, Hereditary House of Wú.
King Xiāng of Zhōu sent Zǎi Kǒng to present sacrificial meat to the Marquis of Qí,
who encountered the Marquis of Jìn and said: "The Marquis of Qí is arrogant;
you'd better not go."
— From Shǐjì, Hereditary House of Qí.
Emperor Jǐng said: "Wèi Qí
is self-complacent,
often frivolous.
Hard to make him chancellor,
to bear heavy responsibilities."
— From Shǐjì, His Basic Biography.
I saw him looking at me intently and hastening away,
knowing I had learned the truth.
— From Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Annals of Zhōu.
King Xiàng, though fierce in his roars and shouts,
could render a thousand men helpless,
yet he was incapable of entrusting tasks to worthy generals,
which was merely the courage of an ordinary man.
When King Xiàng met people,
he was respectful, courteous, kind, and affectionate,
speaking in a gentle and amiable manner;
if someone was ill,
he would weep and share his food and drink with them;
but when it came to enfeoffing those
who had merits deserving of titles,
he would let the seal wear out
and could not bear to bestow it,
this is what is called the benevolence of a woman.
. "Tōng Jiàn: Western Hàn Gāo's Annals".
Cáo Cāo remarked: "Yuán Shào has grand ambitions but little wisdom,
fierce in appearance but timid at heart."
. "Tōng Jiàn: Eastern Hàn".
Zhòng Chángtǒng said to Gāo Gàn: "You have heroic aspirations but lack heroic talent."
Gān Níng said: "Liú Biǎo's foresight is short,
and his sons are incompetent,
they are not ones to inherit and sustain the legacy."
Same as above.
Zhū Bó, a man of small capacity who achieved quick success,
his wisdom ended right there.
. "Eastern Hàn Mǎ Yuán".
Cross-reference "Assessment".
Mǎ Yuán said: "While the world's fate between male and female is unsettled,
Gōngsūn does not spit out his food
to rush and welcome men of state to discuss success or failure,
but instead adorns his appearance like a puppet's form,
how can such a man long detain the talents of the world?"
. "Tōng Jiàn: Hàn Guāngwǔ's Annals".
Jīng Fáng studied the Yì with Jiāo Yánshòu of Liáng,
who often said: "The one who will lose his life by grasping my teachings
is Jīng Fáng."
. "Tōng Jiàn: Hàn Yuán's Annals".
Fán Zhòu incited the various barbarian tribes,
plotting to attach Wǔlíng to Liú Bèi in Hànzhōng.
Quán summoned and questioned Pān Jùn,
who replied: "With five thousand troops sent,
it is enough to capture Zhòu."
Quán asked: "Why do you underestimate him?"
Jùn said: "Zhòu is from an old family in Nányáng,
quite glib with words,
but in reality has no talent or strategy.
The reason I know this
is that Zhòu once prepared a feast for the province,
but by midday,
no food was to be had,
and he himself got up more than ten times,
this is like judging a dwarf by one joint—it proves the point."
. "Tōng Jiàn: Hàn Xiàn's Annals".
Huáng Yǔn and Jìn Wénjīng both relied on their intelligence and talent,
boasting fame far and wide,
yet declined appointments when offered.
They claimed to be seeking treatment in the capital,
not receiving guests,
while high officials sent their disciples morning and evening to inquire about their illness,
and minor officials crowded at their doors,
yet still could not see them.
Fú Róng said to Lǐ Yīng: "These two have no notable deeds or conduct,
yet set themselves up as heroes,
causing high officials to inquire after their health,
and royal attendants to sit at their gates.
I fear their petty ways undermine righteousness,
and empty praise contradicts reality,
so they should be particularly scrutinized."
Yīng agreed.
From then on, the two's reputation gradually declined,
their followers dwindled,
and within ten days,
they fled in shame and regret.
. "Tōng Jiàn: Hàn Huán's Annals".
Someone said to Yuán Shù: "If Jiān takes Luò,
he can no longer be controlled,
this is getting rid of a wolf only to gain a tiger."
. "Tōng Jiàn: Hàn Xiàn's Annals".
Dǒng Zhāo persuaded the governor of Hénèi, Zhāng Yáng, saying: "Though Yuán and Cáo are as one family,
their alliance won't last long.
Cáo, though weak now,
is truly a hero of the world."
As for Bù, he is crude, has few close relations,
rigid and without propriety,
merely a hero among common men.
Cáo Cāo said: "Lǚ Bù, upon gaining a province,
failed to secure Dōngpíng,
cut off the routes at Gāngfù and Tàishān,
and use the terrain to his advantage against me,
but instead stationed at Púyáng,
so I knew he could accomplish nothing."
Jiǎ Xǔ said: "Liú Biǎo is fit for the three highest offices in peaceful times,
but he fails to perceive changing circumstances,
is overly suspicious and indecisive,
and can achieve nothing."
Seeing Lǚ Bù, he turned to Liú Bèi and said: "Xuándé, you are a guest of honor here,
while I am a surrendered captive,
bound tightly with ropes;
can't you say a word for me?"
Cāo ordered the bonds loosened,
but Liú Bèi said: "No.
My lord, have you not seen how Lǚ Bù served Dīng Jiànyáng and Dǒng Tàishī?"
The above all from "Tōng Jiàn: Hàn Xiàn's Annals".
The regular palace attendant Zhào Zhōng said within the palace: "Yuán Běnchù sits and boosts his reputation,
fond of nurturing death-defying warriors;
what does this lad ultimately intend to do?"
"Hòu Hàn".
Lǐ Zàn said: "The times are about to fall into chaos.
No hero in the world surpasses Cáo Cāo."
"Yuán Shānsōng's Hòu Hàn Shū".
Yáo Yújùn said: "Zhāng Huìshù has much talent but little wisdom,
flashy without substance.
He gathers resentment,
and there is a calamity that will overturn his family.
I have seen the signs."
Not long after,
he met with failure.
. . "Tōng Jiàn: Three Kingdoms, Wèi Míng's Annals".
Someone said to the Emperor: "Liú Yè is not entirely loyal,
he is good at detecting the emperor's inclinations and aligning with them.
Your Majesty, try speaking with Yè,
asking him questions with reversed intentions;
if his answers are opposite to what you ask,
then he usually aligns with the imperial will.
If every answer matches the question,
then Yè's true nature cannot escape revelation."
The Emperor followed this advice to test him,
and indeed uncovered the truth.
. "Tōng Jiàn: Wèi Míng's Annals".
Sīmǎ Yì said to Jiǎng Jì: "The wisdom bag has gone."
Jì replied: "Huán Fàn is wise indeed,
but like a nag horse clinging to the stable beans,
Shuang will certainly not employ him."
. "Tōng Jiàn: Wèi Shàolíng Lì Gōng".
Guǎn Lù said: "Dèng's way of walking
shows tendons not restraining bones,
pulses not controlling flesh,
rising and leaning unsteadily,
as if without hands or feet;
this is called ghostly restlessness.
Hé's gaze shows his soul not abiding in its dwelling,
blood not coloring his skin,
essence floating like smoke,
countenance like withered wood;
this is called ghostly gloom.
Both are signs not of distant blessings."
. "Tōng Jiàn: Dèng Yáng and Hé Yàn".
Initially, Zhūgě Kè had a great reputation from youth,
and Emperor Wén deeply valued him,
but Kè's father, Jǐn, often worried,
saying: "He is not one to preserve the family."
His father's friend, General Fènwēi Zhāng Chéng, also believed Kè would bring ruin to the Zhūgě clan.
. "Tōng Jiàn: Wèi Gāoguì Qīng Gōng".
The Emperor once asked Chén Jiǎo: "Lord Sīmǎ is loyal and steadfast;
can he be called a minister of the state?"
Jiǎo replied: "He is the hope of the court,
but whether for the state, I do not know."
. "Tōng Jiàn: Wèi Míng's Annals".
The Lord of Wú, drunk,
asked Fèi Yī: "Yáng Yí and Wèi Yán are petty men, like shepherd boys;
though they often make some useful noise in current affairs,
once they are entrusted with tasks,
it's hard to dismiss them lightly.
If one day there is no Zhūgě Liàng,
they will surely cause calamity and chaos."
Same as above.
Lù Xùn once said to Kè: "Those above me, I must serve and rise with them;
those below me, I support and assist;
but now I see you overpowering those above,
and despising those below,
which is not the foundation of secure virtue."
. "Tōng Jiàn: Wèi Gāoguì Xiāng Gōng".
Zhōu Yú said: "Cáo, though posing as a Hàn minister,
is in fact a traitor to Hàn."
Huán Wēn invited Xiè Ān to be his military advisor,
and Gāo Sōng teased him: "You recline loftily on the Eastern Hill,
and people often say among themselves,
'If Ānshí refuses to come out,
what will become of the common people!'
Now, what will the common people become of you!"
Ān looked very ashamed.
. "Jìn Shū: Xiè Ān".
Cross-reference "Reproach".
Chén Dēng said to Lǚ Bù: "I told Lord Cáo: 'Treating the general is like raising a tiger;
you must feed it enough meat,
or it will bite people.'
The Lord said: 'Not so.
It should be like raising an eagle;
hungry, it serves you,
full, it flies away.' "
"Wèi Zhì".
Péi Wěi recommended Wéi Zhōng to Zhāng Huá,
who offered him a post,
but Zhōng declined due to illness and did not take office.
When asked the reason,
Zhōng said: "Zhāng Màoxiān is flashy without substance,
Péi Yìmín is greedy and insatiable,
abandoning canonical rites to attach to a thieving empress;
how can this be the conduct of a true man!
Yìmín often intends to entrust me with tasks,
I often fear that if he drowns in the deep abyss, the ripples will reach me;
how could I lift my robes and approach him!"
—from Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Hui of Jin.
Cross-reference "Not Casually Conforming."
Shān Tāo, upon seeing Wáng Yǎn, said: "What kind of old woman gave birth to such a tranquil child?
Yet the one who will mislead the common people under heaven is surely this man!"
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Book of Jin.
Wáng Měng said to Fú Jiān: "Mùróng Chuí and his son
are like dragons and tigers—
creatures that cannot be tamed.
If given wind and clouds,
they will become uncontrollable."
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Jin.
Wáng Chéng, Húwú Fǔzhī, and others
considered unrestrained freedom as sophistication,
sometimes even to the point of nudity.
Yuè Guǎng heard of it and laughed, saying: "Within the teachings of reputation, there is naturally a place of joy;
why must it be like this!"
—from Book of Jin: Biography of Yuè Guǎng.
Yáng Hù said to his guests: "Wáng Yífǔ now holds high office with great fame,
but the one who will corrupt customs and damage morals
is surely this man."
—from Book of Jin: Biography of Yáng Hù.
Dǒng Yǎng, upon seeing Wáng Mí, said to him: "You delight in chaos and calamity;
if turmoil befalls the world,
you will not remain among the gentry!"
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Shizu of Western Jin.
Táo Kǎn wrote in a letter to Xún Sōng: "Dù Zēng is vicious and cunning,
what is called 'a creature like an owl that eats its mother.'
If this man does not die,
the region will not know peace.
You should remember my words!"
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Min of Jin.
Fàn Tōng said to Wáng Jùn: "Your achievements are splendid,
but it is regrettable that the way you uphold them is not perfect.
When you return with your banners,
retire to your private residence in plain attire,
and do not speak of the conquest of Wú.
If someone asks,
simply say: 'It was the virtue of the sage ruler
and the strength of the commanders;
what power does an old man like me have!'
This is how Lìn Xiāngrú made Lián Pō yield;
could Wáng Hún feel no shame!"
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Shizu of Western Jin.
Liú Tán often marveled at Huán Wēn's talent,
but knew he had ambitions of disloyalty.
He said to Prince Wáng Yù of Kuaijī: "Wēn must not be placed in a strategic location;
his rank and title should always be restrained."
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Mu of Jin.
Liú Tán said: "I only fear that after conquering Shǔ,
Wēn will ultimately monopolize the court."
Ibid.
Wáng Xiànzhī once went with his elder brothers Wáng Huīzhī and Wáng Cāozhī to visit Xiè Ān.
The two elder brothers spoke mostly of mundane matters,
while Xiànzhī only exchanged brief greetings.
After they left,
a guest asked Ān about the comparative merits of the Wáng brothers.
Ān said: "The youngest is the best."
The guest asked why,
and Ān replied: "The words of a virtuous man are few;
because he spoke little,
I knew it."
—from Book of Jin: His Biography.
Hé Shàngzhī was promoted to Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
He took leave to visit his parents,
and the entire court saw him off.
When he arrived at the commandery,
his uncle Hé Shūdù asked him: "I heard that when you came here,
the entire court saw you off;
about how many guests were there?"
He replied: "Nearly several hundred."
Shūdù laughed and said: "They were sending off the Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
not concerning Hé Yàndé himself."
—from Book of Song.
In his later years, Xiè Hóngwēi once played chess with a friend.
His friend had a losing position in the southwest corner of the board,
and another guest remarked: "The southwest wind is strong;
perhaps a boat will capsize."
The friend understood and saved the position.
Hóngwēi was greatly angered,
throwing the board to the ground.
Those who understood knew it foretold his end-of-life affairs,
and indeed he passed away that year.
—from History of the Southern Dynasties.
Grand Tutor Liú Yìgōng wrote to Liú Yìxuān: "In the past, Yīn Zhòngkǎn borrowed troops,
and Huán Xuán soon brought disaster to his clan;
Wáng Gòng acted with sincerity,
yet Liú Láozhī quickly met defeat.
Zāng Zhì had few virtuous deeds from youth,
as you are fully aware.
Now he relies on the strength of Western Chǔ
to achieve his private aims;
if his sinister plot succeeds,
I fear he will not remain a mere pond creature."
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Shizu of Song.
Sū Zhàn said: "When planning great affairs,
one must seek extraordinary talents from under heaven to collaborate with;
now you are merely conspiring with gamblers of Cháng'ān—
does this have any chance of success?"
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Gaozu of Liang.
Gāo Huān said to Gāo Chéng: "Jǐng has controlled Hénán
for fourteen years now,
always harboring ambitions of arrogance and dominance.
It is only because I can control him
that he is not someone you can驾驭."
Ibid.
Lǐ Chóng, Guō Zuò, and Yóu Zhào said: "Bó Xù
(i.e., Sòng Wéi)
is vicious and reckless,
and will ultimately bring down the Sòng clan.
If he meets a violent death,
it would be fortunate!"
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Liang.
Wáng Xī said: "Since my youth,
I have seen many powerful figures.
Those who achieved success in their prime
rarely avoided downfall."
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Shizu of Chen.
Fù Jiǎ said: "Tàichū (Xiahou Xuan) has great ambitions but small capacity,
able to gather empty fame without real talent.
Hé Píngshù (He Yan) speaks loftily but is shallow in sentiment,
fond of debate but lacking sincerity—
truly what is called a person whose sharp tongue overturns states.
Dèng Xuánmào (Deng Yang) starts with action but lacks perseverance,
externally seeks profit and fame,
internally has no restraint,
values conformity and hates difference,
talks much and envies those ahead;
much talk brings many faults,
envying those ahead leaves one with no friends.
In my view, these three men
will all bring ruin to their families;
keeping away from them fears disaster may still reach,
how much more being intimate with them!"
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Wei.
"Lǐ Mì is cunning and fond of rebellion;
if we send him now,
it is like releasing a fish into the stream,
or setting a tiger free in the mountains—
he will certainly not return!"
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Gaozu of Tang.
Shèng Yànshī said: "Lǐ Mì claims to head toward Luò,
but actually intends to take people by surprise,
flee to Xiāngchéng,
and join Zhāng Shànxiàng."
After Mì crossed Shǎn,
he indeed went south over the mountains.
Ibid.
Zhāng Hào stated: "Xǔ Shūjì is cunning and full of deceit;
faced with difficulty, he will certainly turn traitor."
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Suzong of Tang.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng said to Zhāng Yuē: "Yǔwén Róng enjoys favor and wields power;
he is eloquent and full of schemes—
we must be prepared."
Yuē said: "What can such petty creatures do!"
Later, Róng and Lǐ Línfǔ impeached Yuē.
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Tang.
Cross-reference "Disasters Arise from Neglect."
Lù Yán assisted Cuī Xuàn in Huáinán,
serving as Commissioner of Finance.
Later, he entered the capital as Investigating Censor,
never leaving Cháng'ān city,
and in ten years rose to Chancellor.
When he moved from Investigating Censor to the Hanlin Academy,
Xuàn was still in Huáinán.
Upon hearing the news,
he said: "Lù Shí
(Yán)
has now entered the Hanlin Academy;
how can he grow old!"
It all turned out as Xuàn predicted.
—from Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Yizong of Tang.
Xú Kuàng,
courtesy name Wényuǎn,
was thoroughly versed in the Six Classics.
At that time, the elder scholar Shěn Zhòng lectured at the National University,
often teaching a thousand students.
Wényuǎn went to question him,
saying: "What you, sir, explain
are merely words on paper.
As for the profound realms,
you have not yet seen them;
what more is there to observe?"
—from New Book of Tang.
Zhāng Chānglíng and Wáng Gōngjǐn sat for the imperial examinations,
but both were rejected by Wáng Shīdàn.
Emperor Tàizōng asked the reason,
and he replied: "Chānglíng and others are flashy but lack substance;
their writing is frivolous and ornate—
they are not fine vessels."
—from New Book of Tang: Biography of Zhāng Chānglíng.
Yuán Jié lived by the Ráng River,
calling himself "the Wanderer."
When he obtained an official post,
people thought, "Can a wanderer also casually become an official?"
and called him "the Casual Gentleman."
Thus, "Casual" became prominent.
—from New Book of Tang: His Biography.
Péi Xíngjiǎn said: "Although Wáng Bó and others have literary talent,
Impetuous and shallow in exposure,
how could he be a vessel worthy of enjoying rank and emolument!"
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Tang Records_.
Zhāng Xiàozhōng said:
"One can start with Minister Zhū,
but it is hard to stay with him till the end."
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Tang Records_.
Lú Cángyòng lived in seclusion on Zhōngnán Mountain,
but later in life pursued power and profit.
When Sīmǎ Chéngzhèng summoned him to the court,
Lú Cángyòng pointed to Zhōngnán Mountain,
saying, "There are truly wonderful places within."

If one's face is dirty, one does not forget to wash it;

Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng had a younger brother named Shū Duàn,
whom Lady Jiāng favored.
Jì Zhòng advised to deal with him early,
but Duke Zhuāng said:
"He who repeatedly acts unjustly
will inevitably bring about his own downfall.
You should just wait for it."
Not long after,
Shū Duàn ordered the western and northern borders to pledge allegiance to him.
Gōngzǐ Lǚ requested to eliminate him,
but the Duke said:
"There is no need,
he will bring disaster upon himself."
Tàishū further took the dual allegiance territories as his own cities.
Zǐ Fēng said:
"If his power grows, he will win the masses."
The Duke said:
"Without righteousness, he lacks closeness;
with growing power, he will collapse."

He asked, "What did you find most enjoyable in your province?"

A man born in Yān,
raised in Chǔ,
returned to his native country in old age.
Passing through the state of Jìn,
his companions deceived him,
pointing to a city wall and saying: "This is the wall of Yān."
The man's expression changed to one of sorrow.
Pointing to an earth altar, they said: "This is the altar of your village."
He then sighed deeply.
Pointing to a house, they said: "This is your ancestor's cottage."
Tears welled up in his eyes as he wept.
Pointing to a mound, they said: "This is your ancestor's grave."
The man could not restrain his sobbing.
His companions burst into laughter,
saying: "We were deceiving you earlier;
this is actually the state of Jìn."

Zhào Gāo presented a deer,
calling it a horse.
Èrshì asked his attendants:
"Is this not a deer?"
The attendants all said:
"It is a horse."
Èrshì was astonished,
and from then on became confused.
He then summoned the Grand Diviner,
ordering him to perform a divination.
The Grand Diviner said:
"Your offerings to the ancestral temple spirits
and fasting rituals were not clear,
hence this has come to pass."
— Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Lǐ Sī.

In the second year of Yuánguāng, Lǐ Shàojūn appeared with a method to worship the stove deity and prevent aging.
Shàojūn excelled at making clever statements that remarkably hit the mark.
Once he attended a banquet with the Marquis of Wǔ'ān,
among the guests was an old man over ninety years old.
Shàojūn then mentioned a place where he had gone hunting with the old man's grandfather.
The old man had followed his grandfather there as a child,
recognized the place,
and the entire gathering was astounded.
Shàojūn said to the emperor:
"Worshipping the stove deity can summon things,
and with those things, cinnabar can be transformed into gold,
longevity can be increased,
the immortals of Pénglái can be seen,
and by performing the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices, one can achieve immortality,
as Huángdì did."
After a long time,
Lǐ Shàojūn died of illness,
but the Son of Heaven believed he had transformed and departed,
not truly dead.
Subsequently, more magicians from Yān and Qí along the coast spoke of matters concerning immortals and spirits.
— Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government, Annals of Hàn Wǔ.
In the fourth year of Yuánshòu,
a man from Qí named Shàowēng
appeared with methods for communicating with ghosts and spirits.
Shàowēng was appointed as General Wénchéng.
After over a year,
his methods became less effective,
and the spirits no longer appeared.
So he wrote on silk and fed it to a cow,
pretending not to know,
and said:
"This cow has something extraordinary inside its belly."
The cow was slaughtered,
and upon inspection,
a document was found,
containing very strange words.
The emperor recognized the handwriting,
questioned the man,
and it was indeed a forged document.
Thereupon, General Wénchéng was executed and the matter concealed.
In the second year of Yuándǐng,
Dīng Yì recommended the magician Luán Dà.
Dà dared to make grand claims,
and maintained them without doubt.
He boasted:
"I have traveled to and fro in the seas,
and seen Ānqī and Xiànmén and their like,
but they regarded me as lowly,
and did not believe me.
They also considered Kāngwáng merely a feudal lord,
unworthy of receiving their methods.
My master said:
'Gold can be produced, the breach of the Yellow River can be stopped,
the elixir of immortality can be obtained,
and immortals can be summoned.'"
In the fourth year of Yuándǐng,
a man from Qí named Gōngsūn Qīng said:
"Huángdì ascended to heaven as an immortal.
Huángdì mined copper from Shǒushān,
and cast a tripod at the foot of Jīngshān.
When the tripod was completed,
a dragon descended with drooping whiskers to welcome Huángdì.
He mounted the dragon,
and ascended to heaven with over seventy of his ministers and consorts."
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven said:
"Alas! If I could truly become like Huángdì,
I would regard abandoning my wife and children as merely shedding worn-out shoes!"
In the second year of Yuánfēng,
Gōngsūn Qīng reported:
"A divine being was seen at Dōngláishān,
as if wishing to see the Son of Heaven."
The Son of Heaven then went to Gōushì City,
and proceeded to Dōnglái,
staying there for several days,
but saw nothing,
except what was claimed to be the footprints of a giant.
Gōngsūn Qīng said that immortals prefer living in towers,
so the emperor ordered Cháng'ān to construct the Fēilián and Guàn towers,
and Gānquán to build the Yìshòu and Yánshòu towers,
setting up rituals with emblems to await the divine beings.
The Son of Heaven fell gravely ill at Dǐnghú.
Shamans and physicians tried every means,
but he did not recover.
Yóushuǐ Fàgēn said there was a shaman in Shàngjùn
who, when ill, was possessed by ghosts and spirits.
The emperor summoned and installed him,
making offerings at Gānquán.
When the emperor fell ill,
he sent someone to inquire of the spirit lord,
who said:
"The Son of Heaven need not worry about his illness.
When he is slightly better,
he should force himself to meet me at Gānquán."
The illness then greatly improved,
and a banquet was set up at the Shòu Palace.
The spirit lord could not be seen,
but his words were heard,
sounding like a human voice,
coming and going at times,
and when it came, it did so.
The emperor had the spirit lord's words recorded,
naming it "The Painting Method."
What it spoke of
was common knowledge in the secular world,
nothing extraordinary,
yet the Son of Heaven alone was pleased in his heart.
The matter was kept secret,
unknown to the world.
The emperor sacrificed at Huángdì's tomb on Qiáoshān,
and disbanded the army at Xūrú.
The emperor said:
"I heard that Huángdì did not die,
yet there is a tomb; why is that?"
Gōngsūn Qīng said:
"Huángdì had already ascended to heaven as an immortal,
and his ministers, missing him,
buried his clothes and cap."
When emotions do not match one's appearance and voice, it is called wěi (falseness);

Dòu Lú Gé and Wéi Shuō once asked Guō Chóngtāo:

Chén Yuántú Tú said to Zhèng Shēn Hóu:
"If the army passes between Chén and Zhèng,
our states will surely suffer greatly.
If instead it goes eastward,
displays military might to the Eastern Yí,
and returns along the coast,
that would be acceptable."
Shēn Hóu replied:
"Good."
Táotú reported this,
and the Marquis of Qí agreed.
Shēn Hóu had an audience,
saying:
"The army is weary;
if it goes eastward and encounters the enemy,
I fear it will be ineffective.
If it passes between Chén and Zhèng,
we can supply its provisions, grain, and footwear,
which would be acceptable."
The Marquis of Qí was pleased,
and arrested Yuán Táotú.
