"Analects".
The worthy avoid the age,
next they avoid the place.
. "Analects, Wēizǐ".
Zǐlù met an old man,
carrying a basket over his shoulder with a staff.
Zǐlù reported to the Master, saying: "A recluse."
Same as above.
Masters
Hidden in poor alleys and leaky houses,
even the Three Dukes cannot compete for fame with them.
"Xúnzǐ".
Abandoning glorious morning blossoms,
avoiding the dangerous path of overturned carts.
Chanting and laughing among the blue cliffs,
while all things turn to dust.
Contented face under lush branches,
while vermilion gates become rope-fastened doors.
Holding plows in vast fields,
command tallies suddenly like holding whips.
Sipping tea from rocky springs,
while grand feasts equal coarse greens.
Peaceful with abundant joy in the realm of non-action,
happily equalizing nobility and baseness in the land of non-contention.
Embracing purity and preserving simplicity,
free from desire and worry,
completing genuineness and emptying qi,
dwelling in peace and savoring blandness.
Vast and expansive,
equaling the primordial unity in its naturalness.
. "Bàopǔzǐ, Yáng Xuán".
Name mingling in court and market,
heart beyond the world.
"Wénzhōng" note.
History
Jiǎ Yì said: "I have heard that the ancient sages,
if they did not reside at the imperial court,
were surely found among diviners and physicians."
. _Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of Sīmǎ Jìwáng_.
Cross-reference: "Nowhere to go without finding contentment."
The Emperor in his youth studied with Yán Guāng,
and upon ascending the throne,
sought him out by description.
Only after repeated summons did he come.
He was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance,
but refused to accept.
He departed,
farming and fishing in the Fùchūn Mountains.
He died of old age at home.
. _Comprehensive Mirror: Reign of Emperor Guāngwǔ_.
The Four Haos,
concealed their brilliance and hid their radiance.
. _Book of Later Hàn: Biography of Guō Xuán_.
Their aspirations soared above the azure clouds,
while their persons remained obscure in the mud and filth.
. _Treatise on Hermits in the Book of Later Hàn_.
Fǎ Zhēn lived in seclusion and did not take office,
summoned four times in succession,
yet he never yielded.
His friend Guō Zhèng said: "Fǎ Zhēn's name can be heard,
but his person is hard to meet.
He flees from fame, yet fame follows him;
he avoids renown, yet renown pursues him."
. _Comprehensive Mirror: Reign of Emperor Shùn of Hàn_.
Cross-reference: "Wishing to remain obscure, yet becoming illustrious."
Pillowing on stones and rinsing with streams,
serene and detached in the vast realm of nature.
. _Records of the Three Kingdoms: Shǔ: Biography of Péng Yàng_.
Yīn Hàorepeatedly declined summons to office,
secluding himself at his ancestral gravesite,
for nearly ten years.
Contemporaries compared him to Guǎn Zhòng and Zhūgě Liàng.
. _Comprehensive Mirror: Reign of Emperor Mù of Jìn_.
He first dwelled beyond the dusty world,
loftily bidding farewell to human society,
laughing and chanting in the mountain forests,
roaming and sailing the rivers and seas.
At that time,
he had the untrammeled demeanor of one soaring amidst the clouds.
. _Book of Jìn: Biography of Xiè Ān_.
His name can be heard, but his person cannot be seen;
his virtue can be admired, but his form cannot be glimpsed.
. _Book of Jìn: Biography of Sòng Xiān_.
Nurturing purity in the mountain recesses,
vanishing from sight in the forest depths.
. _Eulogy for the Biographies of Hermits in the Book of Jìn_.
Zhōu Yóng resided in a mountain cottage.
Wáng Jiǎn asked him: "What do you eat in the mountains?"
He replied: "Red rice and white salt,
green mallows and purple knotweed."
When Prince Wénhuì asked Zhōu Yóng which vegetable dish tasted best,
Zhōu Yóng said: "Early leeks in early spring,
and late cabbage at autumn's end."
_History of the Southern Dynasties_.
The cliffs and valleys, secluded and distant;
the waters and rocks, clear and splendid.
. _Biographies of Hermits in the History of the Southern Dynasties_.
Cultivating simplicity in the hills and gardens.
. _Poem of Wěi Xiòng of Zhōu_.
Frolicking with fish and birds,
surrounded by lutes and books.
Gathering leftover grains and weaving with shed fur,
drinking from rocky springs and sheltering under pines and cypresses.
Releasing his spirit within the cosmos,
content within his own bosom.
His mind immersed beyond material things,
resolutely detached from worldly customs.
. _Biographies of Hermits in the History of the Northern Dynasties_.
Lù Guīméng was fond of tea,
and established a garden at the foot of Gùzhǔ Mountain.
He would ride a horse,
or ascend a carriage equipped with a canopy and mat,
carrying bundled books, a tea stove, a brush rest, and fishing gear on his travels.
He was called the "Leisurely Man of Rivers and Lakes,"
or also known as "Tiānsuízǐ" and "Master Fǔlǐ,"
comparing himself to Fú Wēng, the Fisherman, and the Old Man of the River.
Later, he was summoned as a man of lofty virtue,
but did not go.
. _New Book of Táng: His Biography_.
The highest among them
hide their persons, yet their virtue does not remain obscure;
thus, though they release themselves into the wilds,
fame goes and follows them,
and even the honor of the sovereign seeks them out by tracking their path and bestowing invitations;
The next level,
holding the tools to govern the age but unable to extend them,
or with such austere conduct that they cannot bend to custom,
even if they respond [to summons],
regarding rank and emolument,
they receive them with detachment,
and decline them with ease,
causing the ruler often to admire and aspire [to their virtue],
feeling wistful as if lacking something—
these are worthy of esteem;
The lowest category,
endowed with meager talents,
delighting in mountains and forests,
examining inwardly their own abilities,
conclude they ultimately cannot meet the choices of the age,
thus they flee to the hills and gardens and do not return,
causing people always to esteem their character and not dare to criticize them.
. _Preface to the Biographies of Hermits in the New Book of Táng_.
Tián Yóuyán dwelled on Mount Jī.
When Emperor Gāozōng visited Mount Sōng,
he personally went to his gate.
Yóuyán said:
"Your subject is what is called one whose bones are infused with springs and rocks,
and whose disease is an incurable addiction to mist and clouds."
. _New Book of Táng: His Biography_.
Pān Shīzhèng said: "Luxuriant pines and clear springs—
these are what your subject needs."
Same as above.
Collection
Dwelling in the secluded gates of the mysterious abode,
I nestle within rock crevices and hide in caves.
From "Chǔ Cì".
At dawn, I drink the falling dew from magnolias,
At dusk, I dine on the fallen petals of autumn chrysanthemums.
I drink from stone springs and rest beneath pines and cypresses.
Also from the same source.
My aspirations perch among the floating clouds.
From Zhāng Màoxiān's "Poem of Encouragement".
With lofty steps, I pursue Xǔ Yóu.
From Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Poems on History".
Striding high beyond the dusty world,
I salute and decline like Yí Qí.
Releasing my spirit beyond the azure skies,
I chew on petals and sip from flying springs.
From Guō Jǐngchún's "Poems on Roaming Immortals".
Letting my emotions roam beyond the blue clouds.
Minor hermits hide in forests and marshes,
Great hermits conceal themselves in courts and markets.
Both from Wáng Kāngjū's "Summoning the Recluse".
Resting on rocks, I draw from flying springs,
Climbing through woods, I pluck fallen blossoms.
From "Wénxuǎn, Xiè Língyùn".
Admirable seclusion like a coiled dragon,
Disdainfully transcending the world with lofty steps.
From "Wénxuǎn, Seven Admonitions".
Living hidden in a humble thatched hut,
Not interfering with power or influence.
From "Wénxuǎn".
Known among the cliffs and marshes.
From "Wénxuǎn, Epitaph for Guō Yǒudào".
Lying on grass, shaded by pines.
From Sūn Chuò's "Rhapsody on Tiāntāi".
Building a hut within human realms,
Yet no noise of carriages or horses disturbs.
Asked how this can be so,
The heart distant, the place naturally feels remote.
From Táo Yuānmíng's poem.
Like mud, coiled and unused.
From Shǔ Qín Mì's discourse.
The integrity that rises above vulgarity,
The carefree thought transcending the mundane,
Standing tall above material things, radiant beyond the clouds.
From Kǒng Déxíng's "Proclamation of the Northern Mountain".
Gradually delighting in fewer companions,
Dwelling in seclusion without seeking fame.
Though there may be visitors with carriages and horses,
No worldly clamor is heard.
Lying among clouds, my robes feel cold.
Also from Dù.
Encompassing the ways of governing the world in a sack,
Leaving the body amidst white clouds.
Throwing myself into misty peaks,
Vanishing into cloud-filled forests.
Drawing water from valleys, cultivating medicinal herbs.
Dwelling high in mountain valleys,
Farming the wilds through the years.
Living in mountains, feeding on trees,
Proud among forests and valleys.
Releasing myself to misty peaks,
Feasting on scenes in cloud-filled woods.
Unable to inquire of the lowly customs,
Unseen by the scholars of the time,
Gazing loftily through ancient times,
Laughing once at people of the past.
Keeping company with orchids and cassia,
Sharing fellowship with deer,
Carriages, robes, bells, and tripods—
All as if in a dream.
All from Chén Zǐ'áng.
Immortal fungi and numinous mushrooms in a dreamlike search.
From Lǐ Tàibái.
Casting a line with hidden bait,
Concealing traces by the Wèi River's bank.
Holding a jar to water the garden, cutting off
Cunning thoughts by the Hàn River's isle.
From Luò Bīnwáng.
The flower path never swept for guests,
The rustic gate now opened just for you.
My lazy nature has always lived by water and bamboos.
Wildflowers planted among ivy leaves,
Mountain wine sipped with wisteria blossoms.
From Luò Bīnwáng.
Deep within white clouds, there lies a rocky dwelling.
From Dù Mùzhī.
Growing old amidst mist and haze.
Few horses neigh at the wooden gate,
Rarely do visitors bow with ivy staffs.
Human voices answered by the empty mountains.
The pine trees I planted now aged and verdant,
Lying in the Peach Blossom Spring, the spring silent.
Only sesame seeds for chicken and millet,
White clouds coming and going, not despising my poverty.
My traces distant, befriending fish and birds.
Singing of magic mushrooms to escape the world,
Resigning office, drunk on chrysanthemums.
For a thousand years, the peach blossoms vainly bloom,
The people of Qín deeply unseen.
My fishing rod—my way is here,
Seagulls—the world is far away.
Building a thatched hut by the emerald slopes,
Clearing the overgrowth by cutting wood.
A lone peak leaning against the blue sky,
A single path leading endlessly away.
The Peach Blossom Cave full of dwellers,
On Cassia Tree Mountain, days pass leisurely.
Amidst myriad valleys and a thousand peaks, I shut my door alone.
Where I recline in seclusion among white clouds,
Is not told to the world.
All from Liú Chángqīng.
Brushing off my robes, I depart from here,
Taking lofty steps to tread on Huà and Sōng peaks.
Groping for vines and treading on moss.
Once heard of Páng Dé Gōng,
Who gathered herbs and never returned.
In golden streams, I consume magic mushrooms and atractylodes,
On stone beds, I lie amidst moss and lichen.
Pine and moonlight bring night's coolness,
Wind and springs fill my ears with clear sounds.
Building a hut against the rugged cliffs.
The bamboo house idle and serene,
Flowers and herbs connecting winter and spring.
Flat stones serving as desk for lute and inkstone,
Falling springs sprinkling my clothes and scarf.
Burning incense, I lodge on the flower-topped peak,
Drenched in dew, I gather numinous mushrooms.
Often treading on slippery moss,
Seeking the boundless realm.
All from Liú Yì's poems.
Closing my door, never to go out again,
Long estranged from worldly sentiments.
No carriage of vulgar scholars at my gate,
But the demeanor of an ancient emperor in my person.
Both from Mèng Hàorán.
Fearing only that the mountains are not deep enough,
The forests not dense enough,
Their influence obscure and faint,
Anxiously lest it be heard by others.
From Hán.
Beyond the material world, time is inherently unhurried.
From Hán's writings.
Retiring in plump seclusion, abiding in purity,
Nurturing innocence, cultivating integrity.
From Liǔ's writings.
Plowing in the wide, leisurely wilds,
Fishing by the lonely shores.
From Hán's writings.
Drinking herbal brews, boiling pines and cypresses.
From Mèng Dōngyě.
And wishing to leave my name behind,
How can I envy records on bamboo and silk?
Magic mushrooms and herbs sustain my provisions,
Mist and haze brush my turban.
In a fame-loving age, a forgetful guest of names,
In tumultuous times, a body free of affairs.
Laughing as I listen to the morning and evening drums' thud,
Which only urge on the market and court crowd.
Deep in clouds, no neighbors around.
Also from Liú Bīnkè.
The Four Hoary Ones of Nánshān,
Erudites of the Qín dynasty,
Facing a dark and obscure age,
Withdrew and sang: "Silent, lofty scholars,
In winding deep valleys.
Gleaming purple mushrooms,
Can cure our hunger.
Táng and Yú eras far gone,
Where shall we return?
High-canopied carriages and four horses,
Bring greater worries.
Wealth and honor that detain one,
Are不如 the freedom of poverty and lowliness."
Together they entered Shāng Mountain.
From Cuī Qí's "Ode to the Four Hoary Ones".
A small restraint in the mountains and forests.
Where people of the time do not reach,
No traces left on mossy rocks.
Only the sounds of chickens and dogs,
No noise of carriages or horses heard.
Ivy robes exchanged for official headwear,
A wooden staff replacing carriage and horse.
Chancing upon a tranquil realm,
Fulfilling a heart weary of worldly dust.
Then I realize true recluses
Need not be in mountains and woods.
Herb gardens and tea plantations as my estate,
Wild deer and forest cranes my companions.
Closing the door, leaning on a table,
Solitary and self-contained,
With a wooden form and ashen heart,
Even if an owl alights before or a withered willow sprouts behind, my heart remains unmoved.
In the human world, glory and connections are few,
Under the forest canopy, the aura of quiet leisure runs deep.
After nightfall, no sound of turtles breathing,
Come autumn, the crane's spirit grows.
Concealing traces, hiding light,
Erasing sound, veiling shadow.
Both from Vice-Minister Bái.
White clouds deep in a humble lane,
Withering grass all over the idle dwelling.
Leaning by streams and valleys, I turn my back on the times,
Entering misty vines, I find a place deep and secluded.
Year-round, I know nothing of city affairs,
The pines and bamboos I planted by hand have all grown shady.
Wearing orchids and resting under bamboos,
Cutting thatch and sitting on angelica.
Also by Wǔ Bócāng.
Sleeping at night on stones in secluded caves,
Breaking fast with white cloud vegetables.
Leisurely clouds always at the door.
Also by Yáo Shàojiān.
Under the bright moon, the pine-shaded rooms are quiet,
At sunrise, chickens and dogs clamor amidst the clouds.
Serene and pure in virtue,
Naturally simple in manner.
The lonely wooden gate sees no visitors,
In the empty woods, alone I return with the white clouds.
Also by Wáng Wéi.
Clouds and mountains encircling the house still seem too shallow,
I wish to row a fishing boat closer to the angling terrace.
The blue sky does not turn its carriage back,
White clouds long veil the gate.
Fragrance veils the scent of orchids,
Melodies lofty as the calls of phoenixes and cranes.
Returning to recline and nurture innate purity,
In deerskin coat and black horned headscarf.
Long idle and ill at Màolíng,
Drunken and ever poor at Péngzé.
Leisurely by nature, gulls recognize me,
With a distant heart, the crane knows first.
Also by Xǔ Yònghuì.
Teaching the blue crane to dance myself,
Gathering purple mushroom sprouts in parts.
Rolling up the blinds, no vulgar guests in sight,
Only clouds should come to visit.
Also by Zhāng Wénchāng.
Vines and creepers naturally form a canopy,
Why need the zither with wind and springs?
Monkeys and birds call out on their own,
Wind and springs stir each other's breath.
The qilin appears without response,
The wild goose flies into the void.
Also by Zhāng Jiǔlíng.
In remote lands, orchids and cassia grow long,
In sublime realms, mists and rosy clouds are extraordinary.
Leisurely at heart, fish and birds grow familiar,
Harmonious in body, mushrooms and atractylodes are fresh.
Also by Lǐ Yìshān.
Holding talent in secluded marshes,
Hiding brilliance in layered cliffs,
Renouncing the glory of court corridors,
Escaping the peril of the axe's blade.
Luò Bīnwáng.
Birds cry, flowers fall, human sounds cease,
Lonely mountain window veiled by white clouds.
From Lǐ Yìshān's writings.
Inviting white clouds as companions to ascend the hall,
Binding clear winds as guests to enter the room.
Dwelling where green hills are seen,
Proudly gazing at white clouds,
Gain and loss cannot shake their heart,
Glory and disgrace cannot move their will.
Shackled by official caps,
Mired in ranks and emoluments.
Lofty fame knows no hierarchy,
Untrammeled traces transcend all bounds.
Also by Pí Rìxiū.
In life, never having met the faces of nobles,
Till death, never leaving the herd of deer.
Dù Xúnhè.
Only the graceful Xiè Ānshí remains,
Brushing his sleeves, leading courtesans into Dōngshān.
Bái Lètiān.
Dreaming of mushrooms and atractylodes in spring.
Yáo Shàojiān.
Keeping company with pine and qiáo,
He is a man above Emperor Fúxī's time.
From "The Collected Works of Wáng Wéi".
When the world is full of troubles,
A man alone heads for rivers and lakes.
Where has his name changed?
When will gulls become intimate?
Jiǎ Làngxiān.
The wooden gate barred against vulgar guests.
From Lú Tóng's writings.
Dwelling in mountains, drinking from valleys.
From "The Collected Works of Wáng Wéi".
How would I know the changes in the marketplace?
I only feel the beauty of springs and rocks.
Mingling with herds of deer,
Wandering amidst lush grasses and tall woods.
Stone springs can wash away confusion,
Cloud-piercing pines can help forget the self and world.
No worldly dust flies here,
Human thoughts naturally drift far.
Also from "Wéncuì".
At dawn, drinking dew from flowers,
At night, sleeping under pines in the wind.
Wáng Chānglíng.
Broadly viewing ancient sages,
Roaming far beyond material things,
Tilling orchids, reclining in clouds,
Untouched by fame and gain.
From "Táng Wéncuì".
Holding a white feather fan,
Treading in green straw sandals.
Hearing of the crane missive's summons,
By the flowing stream, I still wash my ears.
Mèng Hàorán.
Though the wooden gate is often left unbarred,
A patch of cloud and a lone tree accompany my leisure.
Still disliking being known from long residence,
I plan to move my home further up the mountain.
Jiǎ Làngxiān.
Building a home among the blue cliffs,
Clouds and vines spread shade all around.
The empty room seems devoid of people,
Tall trees naturally form a forest.
Occasionally, a clear breeze arrives,
Faintly, the sound of woodcutting is heard.
From Chǔ Guāngxī's writings.
Smoke and fire never cease by day,
Weeds grow deeper in spring.
From Qián Qǐ's writings.
Fallen leaves cover the empty mountains,
Where to seek traces of passage?
From "The Collected Works of Wéi Yìngwù".
How high are the white clouds?
All belong to the old mushroom gatherer.
From "The Collected Works of Luó Yǐn".
Biographies
The graceful bright moon,
Shines distantly on mountain doors.
The solemn clear breeze,
Approaches from the side to valley windows.
From "Tōngdiǎn".
Xǔ Yóu lived in seclusion on Jīshān.
Having no cup or vessel,
He drank water by cupping his hands.
Someone gave him a gourd,
Which he used for drinking.
After drinking,
He hung it on a tree.
The wind blew it, creating a clattering sound,
Which he still found bothersome,
So he discarded it.
From "Yìshì Zhuàn".
Páng Gōng never entered Xiāngyáng city until old age.
From "Xiāngyáng Qíjiù Zhuàn".
Zhōu Xùzhī entered Lúshān to join Yuǎn Gōng's Pure Land society,
And together with Liú Yímín and Táo Yuānmíng, they were called the "Three Recluses of Xúnyáng".
See "Lúshān Jì: Eighteen Worthies' Biographies".
The recluse of Wǔlíng,
Concealed his traces in the Peach Blossom Spring.
In those Jìn dynasty years,
It was still considered the land of the tyrannical Qín.
From "Shǐ Tōng".
Our Dynasty
The bramble gate often stays closed,
Flowers bloom with few to know.
Purple mushrooms can satisfy hunger,
Fine grains and meat are not my craving.
From "Línchuān Jí".
Enduring cold and hardship,
Content with simplicity and detachment,
Keeping company with clear springs and white stones.
From Dōngpō's "Preface to Stone Calamus".
Pure, distant, carefree, and transcendent beyond worldly dust.
From Dōngpō's "Record of the Pavilion for Releasing Cranes".
Form endowed with the posture of pines and cypresses,
Breath imbued with the fragrance of mushrooms and atractylodes.
The recluse leans on his table in silence,
His heart amid the vanishing flight of wild geese.
Where the Daoist has the Way, the mountain is not lonely.
White clouds long had a pact to grow old together.
From Dōngpō's poems.
In the mountains, no calendar exists,
When cold ends, the year remains unknown.
From "Gǔjīn Shīhuà".
No need to bar the gate against vulgar guests,
How many who love leisure will come?
From Lǚ Wénjìng's poem.
Moving home, still fearing the green mountains are too shallow,
Leaning on the table, only aware the days grow long.
From Xiè Jǐngshān's poem.
See "Gǔjīn Shīhuà".
No worldly airs can find their way here,
Mist and fog serve as carriage guards.
From Huáng Lǔzhí's poem.
Rich with the joy of woods and springs,
Pure and free from the bustle of markets.
Shào Yáofū.
Avoiding the world in mountain forests,
Clad in grass, eating taro and chestnuts.
Favor and disgrace both lightly regarded, detached from worldly tastes,
Ice and frost do not reach, proudly defying nature's work.
From "The Collected Works of Sū Zǐyóu".
The topmost nine line of the Classic of Changes' Gu hexagram states:
"He does not serve kings and lords,
but elevates his own affairs."
． From the "Yi Gu Gua".
The topmost nine line of the Classic of Changes' Jian hexagram says:
"The wild goose gradually advances to the land,
its feathers can be used as adornments,
auspicious."
． The annotation on the "Yi Jian Gua" explains:
"Advancing to dwell in lofty purity without being burdened by position,
nothing can bend his heart or disturb his will,
towering and clear in distant aspirations,
his demeanor is worthy of honor."
A Confucian scholar neither serves the Son of Heaven above
nor attends to the feudal lords below.
． From the "Record of the Rites: Conduct of the Scholar".
Wealth and honor obtained through unrighteousness
are to me like floating clouds.
． From the "Analects: Shu Er".
Not lowering their aspirations,
nor disgracing their persons—
were these not Bó Yí and Shū Qí!
． From the "Analects: Wei Zi".
If the world were offered to him as emolument,
he would not look back;
if a thousand teams of horses were tethered before him,
he would not glance at them.
． From "Mencius: Wan Zhang Shang".
Erasing traces and relinquishing power,
he does not seek merit or fame.
． From "Zhuangzi: Shan Mu".
Considering glory and splendor as filth,
valuable treasures as dust and soil,
and reputation as morning dew.
． From "Baopuzi: Lun Xian".
Zǐsī said:
"Not taking from others is what I call wealth;
not yielding to others is what I call honor."
From "Kong Congzi".
In history,
Lǔ Zhònglián refused to hold office or take up duties,
preferring to uphold lofty principles.
． From "Records of the Grand Historian: His Biography".
Zhuāng Zhōu said:
"I would rather amuse myself in muddy ditches for my own pleasure
than be constrained by rulers of states,
never holding office my whole life,
to delight in my own will."
Same as above.
Spanning ages and transcending times,
he roamed far and alone.
From "Eulogy for Dōngfāng Shuò".
Taking nature as teacher and friend,
he is not enslaved by worldly customs.
Fishing in a single stream,
no worldly things can corrupt his will;
lingering on a single hill,
no worldly gains can alter his joy.
Not entangled in the sage's net,
nor sniffing the bait of arrogant rulers.
Unrestrained and following his will,
commentators cannot name or define him.
． From "Bān Gù's Epilogue to the History of the Western Han".
Aloof and detached from the mundane world.
． From "Biography of Wáng Bāo in the History of the Western Han".
Even among commoners,
within the confines of humble walls,
he remains content and self-satisfied,
not exchanging his state for the dignity of a sovereign—
how then can he be deemed lowly?
． From "Biography of Fán Yīng in the History of the Later Han".
Biographical records:
Gù Kuàng had distant and lofty aspirations;
when a high minister summoned him
to offer him a desirable official post,
Gù Kuàng replied with a poem:
"Now that the world is at peace,
why does the minister summon this madman?
This self is like a crane in a cage,
gazing eastward at the vast sea, crying out once."
Compiled by Lǐ Chuò of Zhào Commandery in "Shangshu Gushi".
The phoenix does not greedily crave food and eat recklessly.
From "Chǔ Cí".
I water my steed at Xiánchí,
And tie my reins to the Fúsāng tree.
Same as above.
Treading the distant traces of Hóngyá,
Continuing the severed path of Cháo Fǔ and Xǔ Yóu,
Soaring beyond the realm with outstretched wings,
Transcending the celestial path to stand aloft.
From Cài Yōng's "Epitaph".
Shedding the skin in the midst of filth,
Floating beyond the dust of the world,
Pure and unstained though emerged from mud,
Judging by this aspiration,
It can contend in brilliance with the sun and moon.
Bān Gù's preface to "Lí Sāo".
Not seeking fame or rank among the feudal lords.

From "History of the Northern Dynasties".

if he knew someone had a rare or exotic object,
he would inevitably seek to obtain it. He treated wealthy merchants and great traders kindly,
calling them his sons.
From "Book of Suí".
Lú Tǎn said: "Those who can amass wealth must have exploited the lower ranks to do so.
If their descendants are good at preserving it,
then Heaven is enriching unprincipled men;
it is better to let their unprincipled ways run their course,
so that it returns to the people."
． From "New Book of Táng, His Biography".
Wáng Pī made accepting bribes his business,
crafting a large chest to store gold and silk,
and he and his wife slept on top of it.
From "Comprehensive Mirror".
Cross-reference "obsessed with greed".
Vice Director of the Secretariat Dòulú Gé—
while the salaries of all officials were paid in discounted currency,
Gé and his son alone received payment in solid cash;
while all officials received theirs from May,
Gé and his son received theirs from January.
Same as above,
from "Táng Dynasty, Annals of Emperor Míngzōng".
Sāng Wéijìn's power and influence were at their peak,
and bribes from all directions
accumulated to tens of thousands each year.
From "History of the Five Dynasties".
The Western Capital Guardian and Vice Director of the Secretariat Wáng Shǒu'ēn
was by nature greedy and base,
devoted solely to amassing wealth.
Funeral carriages could not leave the city without paying a fee;
down to toilet cleaners and beggars,
none were exempt from his levies,
and sometimes he even let his subordinates rob people of their property.
When a wealthy family held a wedding,
Shǒu'ēn went with several entertainers as congratulatory guests,
and returned with several ingots of silver.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Later Hàn Dynasty, Annals of Emperor Yǐn".
Collected Texts
The valleys and gorges were emptied for it,
the rivers and streams were impoverished thereby.
From Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú".
Engaged in the exchange of goods and bribes.
． From the "Selection, Letter to Sūn Hào".
Greedy for trivial wealth,
they transgressed against the court's laws.
From "Biography of Chén Zǐ'áng".
Enriched themselves and adorned their homes.
Same as above.
Sheltered villains and coveted goods.
From the writings of Sīkōng Tǔshèng.
Classics
Yànzǐ wore one fox-fur robe for thirty years.
． From "Record of Rites, Tángōng Part Two".
The Master said: "Rare are those who err due to restraint!"
． From "Analects, Lǐrén".
In rites,
rather than extravagance,
prefer frugality.
From "Bāyì".
Histories
Yù Sūn said: "Frugality is the foundation of virtue."
． From Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Zhuāng 24th year.
Zhèng Shūduàn recited the poem "Cricket,"
Zhào Měng said: "He is the pillar of his family."
From Xiāng 27th year.
Jì Wénzǐ had no concubines clothed in silk,
no horses fed on grain,
no stored gold or jade,
and no duplicate vessels.
He served three rulers,
yet accumulated no personal wealth.
From Xiāng 5th year,
both in Zuǒzhuàn.
He wore no multicolored garments,
ate no varied dishes.
． From Western Hàn, Biography of Zhū Jiā.
Zhū Bó
did not indulge in wine, women, or feasts.
From poverty to wealth,
he ate no varied dishes.
Same as above.
"I guard the wealth for the empire,
how could I recklessly use it!"
． From Tōngjiàn, Annals of Emperor Shāng of Hàn.
Wèi's Gāo Yǔn and his brothers lived in just a few thatched huts,
wearing coarse robes,
with only salted vegetables in the kitchen.
Same as above,
from Sòng Shìzǔ.
Chángsūn Dàoshēng was frugal by nature,
using one bearskin saddle cloth
for decades without replacement.
Same as above,
from Sòng Tàizǔ.
Yǔ Gǎozhī
lived in poverty,
eating only leeks, shallots, and raw vegetables.
Rèn Fǎng teased him: "Who says Yǔ Láng is poor?
He always has twenty-seven dishes to eat."
Meaning three nines (韭).
From Qí Shū.
In the past, Yáng Zhèn, Zhào Zī and others all practiced simple burials,
knowing the soul leaves the body,
valuing swift decay.
Families with lavish burials follow vulgar customs,
considering extravagance as filial piety,
causing the dead to be exposed and desecrated—
is this not grievous!
If the dead are unaware,
they are no different from dirt—
why trouble with lavish burials?
If they are aware,
their spirit is not in the coffin—
why waste wealth on extravagance?
When I die,
dress me in ordinary clothes,
one set for each season."
． From New Táng Shū, Biography of Yáo Chóng.
Cuī Yǎn lived in humble conditions;
during rainy mud,
he would wear a rain hat and clogs to take his outer position.
Same as above.
Lú Huáijǐn
had no curtains on his door.
When wind and rain came,
he raised a mat as a shield.
At mealtime,
he served only two bowls of steamed beans and a few cups of vegetables.
Same as above.
Biographies
Táng's Zhèng Yúqìng was frugal and highly virtuous.
One day,
he suddenly invited several relatives, friends, and officials to dine,
telling his attendants: "Instruct the kitchen
to steam it thoroughly and remove the feathers,
but don't break the neck."
Everyone exchanged glances,
thinking it must be goose or duck.
Then came a bowl of millet rice
and one steamed gourd.
From Lúshì Zájì.
Collections
Living as if in poverty.
Liú Bīnkè.
Frugality means fewer pursuits.
Zhāng Wénchāng.
Our Dynasty
Kou Láigōng used one green bed curtain for over twenty years;
when it tore,
he ordered it mended.
When questioned,
he smiled and replied: "I cannot bear to discard it after long use."
From his biography.
See also "Cherishing the Old."
Wèi's Lǐ Chóng was wealthy yet frugal,
often eating no meat,
only leek dishes.
His guest Lǐ Yuányòu said: "Lǐ Yǔngōng eats eighteen dishes at one meal."
When asked why,
Yuányòu said: "Two leeks (二韭) make eighteen (十八)."
From Xù Shìshuō.
Classics
Indulgence destroys righteousness.
． From Shū, Bì Mìng.
Masters
What the heart desires to enjoy,
the ears desire to hear,
the eyes desire to see,
the mouth desires to taste—
even from distant lands,
not native to the ruler's domain—
all are obtained,
as if within a fence.
In the kitchens, fires never cease;
in the halls, music never ends.
． From Lièyáng Zhū Zhuàn.
Histories
Palaces and residences were lofty and extravagant.
． From "Zuozhuan, Eighth Year of Duke Zhao".
Extravagance is
the greatest of evils.
． From "Zuozhuan, Twenty-fourth Year of Duke Zhuang".
Qí's Qìng Fēng presented a carriage to Jì Wǔzǐ,
its glossy sheen could serve as a mirror
． From "Zuozhuan, Twenty-eighth Year of Duke Xiang".
Extravagance will lead to one's downfall by their own means.
． From "Zuozhuan, Twenty-ninth Year of Duke Xiang".
He built a residence surpassing all other mansions.
． From "Former Han, Biography of Tián Fén".
Luxury and excess cause inferiors to be disrespectful and the state to become poor.
． From "Western Han, Treatise on Rites and Music".
Cross-reference "Usurpation and Presumption".
Using wine to form a pool,
and hanging meat to create a forest.
． From "Records of the Grand Historian, Annals of the Yīn Dynasty".
Lord Chūnshēn had over three thousand retainers,
his honored guests all wore pearl-encrusted shoes.
． From "Historical Records, His Biography".
． The "Yì Zhuàn" says: "If the superior is not frugal,
the inferior will not be restrained,
and calamitous fire will burn their house."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Emperor Míng of Wèi".
Liú Mùzhī,
by nature extravagant,
his meals always covered a square zhàng,
each morning he would have food prepared for ten people,
never dining alone.
Ibid,
"Annals of Emperor Ān of Jìn".
Hé Zēng,
was by nature extravagant and ostentatious.
Whenever he feasted in private audience,
he would not eat what the imperial kitchen provided.
Spending ten thousand coins daily on food,
he still said there was no place to set his chopsticks.
． From "Jìn History, His Biography".
Hé Shào,
arrogant, extravagant, aloof, and noble,
also had his father's style.
His meals always included the rarest delicacies of all four seasons,
with a daily provision limited to twenty thousand coins.
． From "Jìn History, His Biography".
Shí Chǒng flaunted his wealth through extravagance and ostentation,
his toilet always had over ten maidservants in attendance,
all of them beautiful,
equipped with jiǎ jiān powder and chénxiāng juice,
and those who used the toilet
all changed into new clothes before leaving.
Ibid,
"Biography of Wáng Dūn".
Liú Shí once visited Shí Chǒng's home,
went to the toilet,
and saw crimson-patterned curtains,
with cushions and mattresses extremely luxurious,
and two maids holding incense pouches.
Shí immediately withdrew,
smiling and saying to Chǒng: "I mistakenly entered your inner chambers."
Chǒng said: "That is the toilet."
From "His Biography".
Shí Chǒng and the noble relatives Wáng Kǎi, Yáng Xiǔ and their ilk vied in extravagance and waste.
Kǎi used malt sugar to wash his cauldron,
Chǒng used wax instead of firewood.
Kǎi made a forty-lǐ purple silk screen,
Chǒng made a fifty-lǐ brocade screen to rival it.
Chǒng coated his walls with pepper, Kǎi used red stone ointment.
Ibid.
Shí Chǒng,
his wealth abundant and accumulated,
his houses grand and beautiful.
His rear chambers numbered in the hundreds,
all draped in embroidered silks, gold, and jade.
His musicians were the finest of the time,
his kitchen offered every delicacy of land and sea.
． Both from "Jìn History, His Biography".
Wèi's Gāoyáng King Yōng,
a single meal cost tens of thousands of coins.
Lǐ Chóng said: "Gāoyáng's one meal
equals a thousand days for me."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng".
Wéi Zhì,
prepared exquisite dishes to the utmost,
selected fertile land to grow grain seedlings,
used bird feathers to select rice,
every time he inspected the kitchen's waste,
its value still amounted to no less than ten thousand coins,
when feasting at the homes of dukes and marquises,
even with the finest delicacies of land and sea,
he never once set down his chopsticks.
． From "Tang History, His Biography".
Historical Records
On the Lantern Festival night, Yáng Guózhōng's sons and younger brothers
each had a thousand torchlights surrounding them.
"Tales of the Tiānbǎo Era".
Lǐ Déyù was extravagant.
Each time he ate a bowl of soup,
it cost about thirty thousand coins.
Mixed with pearls, jade, and treasures,
it was made by boiling cinnabar juice.
After three boilings, the dregs were discarded.
"Records of Unique Phenomena".
Yuán Zài built the Yúnhuī Hall.
Yún,
a fragrant grass,
white as jade.
Buried in soil, it does not decay,
ground into powder,
it was used to coat the walls.
He set up a purple silk gauze canopy,
in the depths of winter,
wind could not enter;
in midsummer, it remained cool and refreshing.
Táng's Sū È "Sūshì Yǎnyì".
Hán Yān enjoyed shooting pellets,
using gold for pellets,
losing over ten daily.
Cháng'ān had a saying about it: "Suffering hunger and cold,
chase the pellets."
The children of the capital,
whenever they heard Yān was out shooting pellets,
would follow him,
watching where the pellets fell,
and pick them up.
"Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital".
The Yáng family sons in summer carved mountains from large ice blocks to surround their banquet seats.
Wáng Rényù "Surviving Tales of the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo Eras".
Yáng Guózhōng,
in winter, selected plump maids and concubines,
lined them up in front,
to block the wind,
calling it a "flesh formation."
"Surviving Tales of the Kāiyuán Era".
Anthology
Wood clad in embroidered silk,
earth covered in vermilion and purple.
Zhāng Píngzǐ "Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital".
A set of spring clothes worth a thousand gold.
Vice Director Bái.
Exotic delicacies from mountains and seas discarded by the fences,
cooking calves and roasting lambs as if breaking sunflower stalks.
"Collection of Wéi Yìngwù".
Head ornaments bearing a thousand gold,
one meal consuming a thousand households.
"Táng Wéncuì".
Classics
Ministers of the king labor diligently,
not for their own sake.
． From "Yìjīng, Qiǎn Hexagram".
Masters
Loyal ministers do not flatter their ruler.
"Zhuāngzǐ".
History
Hán Xìn said: "One who rides another's carriage
shares their troubles;
one who wears another's clothes
carries their worries;
one who eats another's food
should die for their affairs."
． From "Records of the Grand Historian: Basic Biography".
The favored Lady Shèn of the emperor,
within the palace once shared a seat with the empress.
When returning to sit at the court officials' office,
Yuán Àng withdrew Lady Shèn's seat.
Saying: "What Your Majesty does for Lady Shèn,
will actually bring disaster upon her."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Han Records".
Loyal ministers do not avoid severe punishment but remonstrate directly.
． From "Western Han: Zhǔfù Yǎn's Biography".
Loyal ministers risk death to exhaust their wisdom.
From "Emperor Xuān's Annals".
Only by speaking forthrightly do they await death.
"Treatise on the Five Elements",
also from "Western Han".
Loyal ministers worry about the world,
offend the ruler's stern countenance,
criticize noble officials,
even to the point of being killed and having their families exterminated yet still do it,
why?
Because the duty between ruler and minister is weighty,
there are matters from which they cannot desist.
． From "Later Han: Hé Chǎng's Biography".
Emperor Chéng of Hàn wanted to ride a tower ship,
Xuē Guǎngdé remonstrated: "You should cross by bridge,
if Your Majesty doesn't listen to me,
I will cut my own throat,
staining the carriage wheels with blood."
From "Basic Biography".
Huáilǐ Magistrate Zhū Yún submitted a memorial saying: "I wish to be granted the Shangfang horse-beheading sword,
to cut off one sycophantic minister's head to warn the others!"
The emperor asked: "Who is it?"
He replied: "Ānchāng Hóu Zhāng Yǔ!"
The emperor was greatly angered,
saying: "A petty minister insults my teacher in court,
the crime deserves death without pardon!"
The imperial censor was about to take Yún away,
Yún grabbed the palace railing,
breaking it while shouting: "If I can follow Lóng Páng and Bǐ Gān underground,
that would be enough!
I wonder what will become of the sacred court!"
The imperial censor then took Yún away.
Left General Xīn Qìngjì removed his cap,
took off his official seal,
and kowtowed below the palace saying: "This minister has always been known for his wild honesty,
if his words are correct,
he should not be executed;
if his words are wrong,
he should naturally be tolerated.
I dare to dispute this with my life!"
Qìngjì kowtowed until he bled,
the emperor's anger subsided,
and only then was the matter settled.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Chéng of Hàn's Records".
Grand Minister over the Masses Hán Xīn,
fond of straightforward speech,
without concealment or taboos.
Before the emperor he testified that the year would bring famine and disaster,
pointing to heaven and drawing on earth,
his words were very firm and direct.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn's Records".
Wèi Jì submitted a memorial saying: "Unless one breaks their family for the state,
or kills themselves to complete their ruler,
who would dare to offend the countenance,
touch upon taboos,
establish one argument,
or open one discourse?"
From "Records of the Three Kingdoms: Wei".
Cuī Hóng,
pure, stern and unbending,
fond of pointing out others' faults to their face,
yet afterwards never spoke behind their backs.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Wǔ of Jìn's Records".
Gǔ Bì went to see the Wèi emperor,
who was playing Go with Attendant within the Gates Liú Shù,
his attention not on Bì.
Bì entered and attended for a long time,
unable to get a hearing.
Suddenly he stood up,
grabbed Shù by the head,
pulled him off the bed,
and beat his back,
saying: "The court's poor governance,
is actually your fault!"
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Sòng Tàizǔ".
The emperor appointed the dancing barbarian Ān Chìnu as a Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
Minister of Rites Lǐ Gāng remonstrated: "In ancient times, musicians were not ranked among scholars,
even the worthy like Zǐyě and Shī Xiāng,
all continued their profession for life through generations without change.
Only in late Qí was Cáo Miàodá enfeoffed as king,
and Ān Mǎjū made a Kaifu,
which rulers of states should take as a warning."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Gāozǔ".
Wèi Zhēng's appearance did not surpass average men,
but he had courage and strategy,
excelling at changing the ruler's mind,
often risking imperial displeasure with earnest remonstrance.
Sometimes when encountering the emperor's great anger,
Zhēng's expression would not change,
and the emperor would also calm his wrath because of it.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Tàizōng".
Chǔ Suìliáng: "If Your Majesty must change the empress,
I humbly request carefully selecting from the world's good families,
why must it be Wǔ Shì!
Wǔ Shì served the previous emperor,
as everyone knows,
the eyes and ears of the world,
how can they be blinded."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Gāozōng".
The Wèi emperor said to his ministers: "Like Gāo Yǔn,
this is a true loyal minister.
When I have faults,
he never fails to speak to my face,
even to the point of things I cannot bear to hear,
Yǔn avoids nothing.
I hear of my faults while the world remains unaware,
can this not be called loyalty!"
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Sòng Shìzǔ".
Forehead knocking on the dragon steps.
． From "New Book of Táng: Liú Qīchǔ".
Emperor Dézōng wanted to make Péi Yánlíng chancellor,
Yáng Chéng declared openly: "If Yánlíng becomes chancellor,
I will take the white hemp paper and destroy it,
weeping in the court."
The emperor did not make Yánlíng chancellor,
thanks to Chéng's efforts.
Same as above,
"Yáng Chéng's Biography".
Chǔ Suìliáng was upright and honest.
． From "New Book of Táng: Basic Biography".
Collection
devotes heart to remonstrance,
speaking forthrightly without concealment.
． From "Selected Policy Essays".
Honest speech without taboos endangers oneself.
． From "Selected Songs of Chǔ".
Spirit containing the reversed scales,
appearance showing self-sacrifice.
From "Essence of Táng Literature".
Maintaining integrity until death,
no loyalty is greater.
．． From "Preface to 'Ode to the Heroic Scholar'".
Accepting loyalty is the model for disputing ministers.
Liǔ Wén.
Lú Jǐngliàng presenting matters like water flowing to a valley.
Same as above.
Rectifying current ills,
admonishing the noble and close.
Without any顾虑,
knowing no action not taken.
Dù Mùzhī.
Bearing reputation for strong integrity,
still pursuing the name of unbending neck.
Zhāng Yuè.
Remonstrating tongue earnestly,
grinding the emperor's flaws above.
Sūn Qiáo.
Painstakingly exhausting heart and soul to speak of the world's affairs.
Yuán Zhěn.
Offending the heroic ruler's dragon scales,
treading the treacherous minister's tiger tail.
Táng Zhāng Yuè's "Inscription for Sòng Jǐng's Legacy of Love Stele".
Our dynasty
Lǔ Zōngdào as Assistant Administrator,
took loyalty and uprightness as his duty,
contemporaries called him: "Duke Fish-head, probably referring to him as bony and upright."
From "Gleanings of the Sacred Sòng".
Classic
Artful speech and ingratiating demeanor,
fawning and flattering.
． From "Book of Documents: Charge to Jiǒng".
Qúchú often watches people's expressions to form his words,
therefore cannot bow;
Qūshī,
lowers himself through expressions,
therefore cannot look up.
． From "Book of Songs: New Tower" annotation.
Artful speech and ingratiating demeanor,
seldom indicate benevolence.
． From "Analects: Learning".
Qúchú,
means mouth-softness.
Qūshī,
means face-softness.
Kuāpí,
means body-softness.

Collected
Hunching shoulders and flattering with a smile,
is more distressing than working in the summer vegetable plots.
Annotation from "Mèngzǐ":
"Xià qí refers to those who tend to vegetable plots in the summer months.
Engaging in such behavior
is more laborious than the work of those summer gardeners."
Those who covertly curry favor with the world
are the village honest men.
． From "Mèngzǐ Jīn Xīn Xià".
When the King of Qín fell ill and summoned physicians,
those who licked his hemorrhoids received five chariots.
． From "Zhuāngzǐ Liè Yù Kòu".
Anticipating intentions and guiding words
is called flattery.
From "Zhuāngzǐ".
Not considering where reason lies but toadying to gain favor,
there is no flattery worse than this.
． From the "Kǒng Cóng Zǐ Kàng Zhì" chapter.
Using improper conduct to lead others
is called sycophancy;
using improper conduct to harmonize with others
