History
Chǔ Qífù said to Zǐ Gé: "You, sir,
are the hope of the state of Chǔ!
Now when you speak with the king, it is like an echo.
What will become of the state?"
Criticizing him for complying with the king's heart like an echo responding to a sound.
. "Zuǒzhuàn, Twelfth Year of Duke Zhāo".
Chén Shèng rose up in Shāndōng,
and the Second Emperor summoned the scholars to inquire.
Shūsūn Tōng said: "These are merely a gang of thieves, stealing like dogs and rats.
They are not worth mentioning.
The commandery governors and captains are now capturing and judging them,
so there is nothing to worry about."
. "Shǐjì, Basic Biography".
Bowing humbly and approaching,
walking softly and speaking.
Same as above,
"Biographies of Diviners".
Not having any talent or ability,
but only valued and favored for being smooth and flattering.
"Biographies of Sycophants",
also from "Shǐjì".
When the Marquis of Wèi proposed plans that were incorrect,
the ministers all agreed as if with one voice.
Not examining the right or wrong of matters but delighting in others praising oneself—
nothing is more benighted than this;
not considering where principle lies but flattering to seek favor—
nothing is more servile than this.
. "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Chronicles of Zhōu".
Cross-reference "Flattery".
Huáng Bà served as chancellor,
and pheasants flew into the chancellor's office.
Bà considered them divine birds
and wanted to report it.
"Book of Hàn, Biography".
Turning one's face and defiling one's conduct
to serve flattering people.
"Biography of Zōu Yáng".
Complying with the ruler's wishes to do evil.
When Píng'ēn Hóu Xǔ Bó moved into his new residence,
the chancellor, imperial secretaries, generals, and officials of two thousand piculs all came to congratulate him.
Chángxìn Shǎofǔ Tán Chángqīng rose to dance,
performing as a monkey fighting with a dog.
Following and flattering, accommodating intentions,
to comply with the superior's wishes.
Fawning and evil ministers
seeking to gain fortune by luck.
"Biography of Zhái Fāngjìn".
Sīmǎ Chángqīng
lived at Màolíng.
Before he died,
he wrote a scroll,
saying: "If messengers come seeking this writing,
present it to them."
His posthumous manuscript discussed the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
"Biography of Sīmǎ Xiàngrú".
Lowering one's body and degrading one's form,
with pleasing expressions and subtle words,
smiling warmly and coaxing gently—
this is what men of purpose and humanity cannot bear to do.
"Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò",
also from "Book of Hàn".
Distorted words and flattery.
"Book of Later Hàn".
Pān Yuè and Shí Chòng flatteringly served Jiǎ Mì,
often waiting for him to go out,
and with Chòng, they would bow at the sight of his dust.
. "Book of Jìn, Biography of Pān Yuè".
Sīmǎ Zhāo was enfeoffed as Prince of Jìn.
Xún Yǐ said to Wáng Xiáng: "The Imperial Chancellor is highly respected;
today we should lead each other to bow to him."
Same as above,
"Biography of Wáng Xiáng".
Two peacocks flew from the Western Garden and gathered in front of the hall at Bǎochéng.
Personal guard captain Gāo Déru and over ten others saw them
and reported them as luán birds.
. "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Chronicles of Suí".
Like grease or softened leather,
bowing and creeping,
devouring filth to seek favor,
licking hemorrhoids to become intimate.
Fine words and flattering smiles
to enhance their joy,
feigned tears and hypocritical grief
to sympathize with their bereavements.
Same as above, Lú Sī's "Discussion of the Toilsome Life".
Zhāng Chāngzōng won favor with Empress Wǔ thanks to his charming appearance,
and Yáng Zàisī often said: "People say the Sixth Lad resembles a lotus blossom—
that's not so;
rather, it's the lotus blossom that resembles the Sixth Lad."
. "Book of Táng, Biography of Yáng Zàisī".
Emperor Míng of Táng was about to visit the Eastern Capital,
but the temple of the imperial ancestors collapsed.
Yáo Chóng said: "This is the old hall of Fú Jiān.
Mountains collapse due to decayed soil,
and wood breaks from being worm-eaten—
it's natural and not strange."
Same as above,
"Basic Biography".
Grand Astrologer Yuán Chōng submitted a memorial claiming: "Since the rise of Suí,
the days have gradually grown longer;
shadows are shorter and days longer—
rare since ancient times."
After this, all laborers and conscripts
had their workloads increased,
because the days were longer.
"Zīzhì Tōngjiàn".
Observing each other's expressions,
often not fully impartial.
"Táng Tàizōng".
Erudites Xiāo Chǔcái and others believed that preparing for unfortunate events
was not something subjects should discuss.
Jìngzōng and Yìfǔ strongly agreed,
so they burned the chapter "State Mourning",
and thus the rites for unfortunate events were omitted.
"Táng Gāozōng".
Tutor to the Heir Apparent Liú Nèyán once compiled a "Collection of Jests" and presented it to Heir Apparent Xián.
The emperor said to his attending ministers: "I have often sought advice with an open mind,
yet no one advises—
why is that?"
Lǐ Jì replied: "Your Majesty's actions are all perfect,
so the ministers have nothing to advise on."
Same as above.
Imperial physician Shěn Gāoqiú gained favor with the Empress Dowager,
and Huáiyì felt resentful.
That evening,
he secretly burned the Heavenly Hall,
and the fire spread to the Bright Hall.
Liú Chéngqìng requested suspending court and celebrations to respond to Heaven's reproach,
and the Empress Dowager was about to agree.
Yáo Shú said:
"In the past, the Xuān Pavilion of Chéngzhōu
foretold an even more prosperous reign;
when Hàn Wǔdì built the Jiànzhāng Palace,
his abundant virtue spread eternally."
"Táng Wǔzōng".
Yáng Zàisī served as censor,
solely relying on flattery to gain favor.
Zhāng Tóngxiū teased Zàisī: "Imperial Secretary Yáng looks like a Goryeo person."
Zàisī was pleased,
immediately cut paper to adorn his headcloth,
reversed his purple robe,
and performed a Goryeo dance,
making the whole assembly laugh heartily.
"Táng Zhōngzōng".
In the palace, it was said that a five-colored cloud rose from the empress's skirt in her clothes chest,
and the emperor ordered it depicted to show the officials.
Wéi Jùyuán requested it be proclaimed throughout the land.
Same as above.
Xuē Qiánguāng presented the "Inscription on the Yùzhōu Tripod" made by Empress Wǔ,
its end stating: "The supreme heaven descends to observe,
and establishes Lóngjī."
Considering it a sign of the emperor's mandate.
Yáo Chóng submitted congratulations,
requesting it be announced to the historians
and proclaimed to all, internal and external.
"Táng Xuánzōng".
Lǐ Shìzhī was careless and straightforward,
and Lǐ Línfǔ once said to Shìzhī: "Mount Huà has a gold mine;
mining it could enrich the state,
but the sovereign does not know of it."
Another day,
Shìzhī mentioned it while reporting matters.
The emperor asked Lǐ Línfǔ about it,
who replied: "I have long known,
but Mount Huà is Your Majesty's fate root,
the location of royal energy;
it is inappropriate to excavate it,
so I did not dare speak."
The emperor thought Lǐ Línfǔ loved him and considered Shìzhī
rash in considering matters,
saying to him: "From now on, when reporting matters,
you should first discuss with Línfǔ,
and not be so frivolous."
Shìzhī was thus restrained.
"Táng Xuánzōng".
The Tàiqīng Palace reported: "Academician Lǐ Qí saw Emperor Yuánxuán riding a purple cloud,
who informed him the state's fortune would prolong and flourish."
Same as above.
The emperor once said: "The Buddha speaks of retribution—
is it real or not?"
Yuán Zǎi and others reported: "The state's fortune is divinely long;
if not for previously planted blessings,
how could this be achieved!
Since blessings are already set,
though there may be minor disasters at times,
they ultimately cannot harm us.
Thus, when Ān and Shǐ's rebellions were at their peak, they suffered from their sons' misfortunes;
Púgù Huái'ēn raised troops to insult internally,
but fell ill and died upon departure;
the Huíhé and Tǔbō launched massive invasions deep inland,
yet retreated without battle: these are all beyond human power—
how can one say there is no retribution!"
"Táng Dàizōng".
Lǐ Jiān in Jiāngxī had monthly tributes,
Wéi Gāo in Xīchuān had daily tributes.
Prefects presenting tributes began with Jiān,
staff officers presenting tributes began with Suì.
"Táng Dézōng".
The emperor presided at Yányīng Hall,
asking the chancellor: "When will the world be at peace?"
Niú Sēngrú responded: "There is no fixed model of great peace.
Now the four barbarians do not invade each other,
the common people do not become displaced and scattered,
though not the ultimate governance,
it may be called minor prosperity.
If Your Majesty seeks another kind of great peace,
it is beyond what we ministers can achieve."
《Emperor Wénzōng of Táng》.
Locusts came from east to west,
blotting out the sun,
leaving barren land wherever they passed.
Jīngzhàoyǐn Yáng Zhīzhì reported: "Locusts entered the capital region,
but did not eat the crops,
instead they all clung to thorns and died."
All the chancellors offered congratulations.
《Emperor Yìzōng of Táng》.
The Grand Astrologer reported that the sun should have been eclipsed but was not.
Yáo Chóng submitted congratulations,
requesting it be recorded in the historical archives.
《Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng》,
both from《Comprehensive Mirror》.
Biographies
that discuss the sovereign's sageliness and wisdom
make the ruler equal to the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors;
narrating the chancellor's heroism and greatness,
make the ministers all like the Eight Talents.
《Shǐ Tōng》.
Collection
Fawning flatterers.
． 《Selected Admonition Poems》.
Breaking twigs and licking hemorrhoids.
． 《Selected Essay on Severing Ties》.
Speaking as if wounded,
bowing the body without bone.
Liáng Zhāng Zuǎn's《Memorial to the Minister over the Masses》.
Entering the door to flatter oneself.
Luò Bīnwáng.
Flattering and fawning upon each other,
a thousand faces with one expression.
Yuán Cìshān.
Being eloquent-mouthed and soft-faced for others.
Same as above.
Slavish countenance and kneeling like a true beggar.
Lù Guīméng.
Petty men hastening to serve inevitably change their expressions.
《Táng Wén Cuì》.
Our dynasty
Duke Kòu Láigōng served as chancellor,
Dīng Wèi rose from his mentorship,
becoming a participating chancellor.
While dining together at the capital hall,
soup stained the Duke's beard,
Wèi rose to wipe it off.
《Anecdotes》.
Bending and following others like a well-sweep.
Dōngpō's poem.
Emperor Zhōngzōng feasted with close ministers,
Zhù Qīnmíng volunteered to perform the "Eight Winds Dance",
shaking his head and rolling his eyes,
displaying all sorts of ugly postures.
《Continued World Anecdotes》.
When Empress Wǔ Zétiān was unwell,
she ordered Yán Cháoyǐn to go to Shàoshì Mountain to pray.
Cháoyǐn then twistedly expressed pleasing flattery,
using his own body as a sacrificial offering,
requesting to bear the emperor's suffering.
When Wèi Yuánzhōng lay ill,
all the censors went to visit him,
Guō Bà alone stayed behind,
requested to inspect the stool,
saying: "If the Grand Master's stool tastes sweet,
the illness may not heal.
Now it tastes bitter,
so it should soon be cured."
Creeping like an inchworm, crouching like a rat,
sycophantic words gushing like a spring.
Same as above.
Masters
As a subject,
seeing faults and not remonstrating,
thereby plunging the ruler into peril and ruin,
is among the gravest of crimes.
《The Kǒng Family Masters' Anthology》.
Shǐ
Fàn Xuānzǐ: "What the Son of Heaven favors,
one also favors;
what he opposes,
one also opposes."
． From Zuǒzhuàn, 11th year of Xiānggōng.
Zhāng Tāng
specialized in flattering the emperor's intentions.
What the emperor disliked,
he would accordingly disparage;
what the emperor desired,
he would accordingly praise.
． From Shǐjì, Biography of Jí Àn.
Chúnyú Kūn
made it his duty to follow intentions and observe expressions.
． From Shǐjì, His Biography.
Zhào Gāo presented a deer,
calling it a horse.
The Second Emperor asked his attendants, "This is a deer, isn't it?"
They all said, "It is a horse."
． From Shǐjì, Biography of Lǐ Sī.
The Grand General used gentleness and softness to ingratiate himself with the emperor.
． From Shǐjì, Biography of Wèi Qīng.
Flattering the ruler's preferences,
rising and falling with him.
． From Xī Hàn, Biographies of Harsh Officials.
Dù Zhōu largely imitated Zhāng Tāng,
excelling at observing and waiting.
He solely used the emperor's intentions to decide legal cases.
． From Xī Hàn, His Biography.
Wishing to accomplish something,
he subtly revealed his stance to his faction,
and following the emperor's will, prominently submitted memorials.
． From Xī Hàn, Wáng Mǎng.
Gěng Yù said, "Following and flattering according to direction,
to seek acceptance and favor."
． From Tōngjiàn, His Biography.
Tāng was a man full of deceit,
wielding cunning to control others.
At that time, the emperor was inclined towards literature,
so Tāng pretended to admire it,
serving Dǒng Zhòngshū and Gōngsūn Hóng, among others.
． From Tōngjiàn, Annals of Hàn Wǔdì.
If the emperor intended to punish someone,
he would associate them with supervisors and officials deeply implicated in crimes;
if the emperor intended to release someone,
he would associate them with supervisors and officials of light and fair judgment.
Same as above.
Gǔ Yǒng, knowing that Fèng was being trusted with power,
secretly sought to align himself.
Same as above.
Zhāng Yǔ said, "Young scholars of new learning,
confuse the way and mislead people,
should not be trusted,
but judged by classical teachings."
The emperor deeply trusted and loved him,
thus not doubting the Wáng family.
． From Tōngjiàn, Annals of Hàn Chéngdì.
The emperor intentionally had Dǒng Xián privately visit Kǒng Guāng.
Guāng, dressed formally, went out to wait,
seeing Xián arrive at the middle gate,
Guāng entered the inner chamber,
after Xián alighted from the carriage,
then came out,
bowing and greeting, sending and welcoming with great respect,
not daring to treat him as an equal guest.
The emperor heard of this,
and was pleased.
． From Tōngjiàn, Annals of Hàn Píngdì.
Hú Guǎng used humble words and respectful demeanor to curry favor with the times,
lacking the integrity of loyalty and straightforwardness,
thus the world looked down upon him.
Same as above,
Annals of Hàn Língdì.
Hóngnóng Prefect Liáng, following the orders of Fán Fēng and others,
sent officials to detain Yáng Zhèn's funeral procession in Shǎnxiàn,
leaving the coffin exposed by the roadside,
and forced Zhèn's sons to serve as couriers,
causing all on the road to shed tears.
Same as above,
Annals of Hàn Shāngdì.
Following the wind of intentions.
． From Dōng Hàn, Biography of Kǒng Róng.
Mǎ Róng, chastened by the Dèng family incident,
dared not oppose powerful families again,
thus drafted a memorial for Liáng Jì falsely accusing Lǐ Gù,
and also composed the "Western Mansion Eulogy" for the Grand General,
greatly shamed by the upright.
． From Dōng Hàn, His Biography.
Bān Gù served as Zhòng Hùjūn under Dòu Xiàn,
campaigning against the Xiōngnú,
participating in discussions.
When Xiàn fell from power,
Gù died in prison.
． From Dōng Hàn, His Biography.
Xiàhóu Xuán was brought to the Court of Judicial Review,
with Zhōng Yù handling the case.
Xuán sternly rebuked Yù, saying, "What crime am I guilty of!
You, as the investigating official, press me,
just write the confession for me!"
Yù, considering Xuán a renowned scholar,
of high integrity,
not to be forced,
and with the case needing conclusion,
wrote the confession at night,
making it fit the facts,
and tearfully showed it to Xuán.
． From Tōngjiàn, Gāoguì Xiāng Gōng.
Whenever Wáng Dǎo spoke,
no one present failed to praise him.
． From Jìn, Biography of Wáng Shù.
The emperor said to Liú Déyuàn, "If you weep for the Noble Consort,
those who grieve deeply will be richly rewarded."
Déyuàn immediately wailed in sorrow,
beating his chest and stamping his feet,
tears and mucus flowing together.
The emperor was very pleased,
thus appointed him as Governor of Yùzhōu as a reward.
The emperor also ordered the physician Yáng Zhì to weep for the Noble Consort,
and Zhì also sobbed with extreme grief.
Another day, someone asked Zhì, "How did you manage such ready tears?"
Zhì said, "That day, I was actually weeping for my deceased concubine."
． From Tōngjiàn, Sòng Shìzǔ.
Xú Yuàn was obsequious and skilled at serving others,
adept at welcoming and sending off,
leaving no trace from start to finish.
Same as above,
Annals of Sòng Tàizǔ.
Petty officials,
following orders and catching the wind,
manipulating texts and laws,
twisting facts to establish guilt.
Same as above,
Táng Tàizōng.
Lǐ Jì entered for an audience,
the emperor asked him, "I wish to make Wǔ Zhāoyí Empress,
but Chǔ Suìliáng stubbornly insists it cannot be done.
Since Suìliáng is a minister entrusted with the final decree,
should the matter be dropped?"
He replied, "This is Your Majesty's family matter,
why ask outsiders?"
Thus the emperor's mind was decided.
Xǔ Jìngzōng declared in court: "A rustic who harvests an extra ten hectoliters of wheat
still wants to change his wife;
how much more so for the Son of Heaven establishing an empress,
why should others interfere and recklessly raise objections!"
． From Tōngjiàn, Táng Gāozōng.
Attendant Censor Fù Yóuyì led over nine hundred commoners from Guānzhōng to the palace to submit a petition,
requesting to change the state's name to Zhōu,
and bestow the imperial surname Wǔ upon the emperor,
but the Empress Dowager refused;
Yóuyì was promoted to Jǐshìzhōng.
． From Tōngjiàn, Táng Wǔhòu.
Zhōu Lìyòng, Rǎn Zǔyōng, Lǐ Jùn, Sòng Zhīxùn, and Yáo Shàozhī all acted as eyes and ears for Wǔ Sānsī,
contemporaries called them the Five Dogs.
． From Tōngjiàn, Annals of Táng Zhōngzōng.
Shàngguān Jiéyú and others in the rear palace established many external residences,
coming and going without restraint,
court officials often socialized with them,
seeking advancement.
Princess Ānlè was especially arrogant and domineering,
with many officials below the rank of chancellor coming through her doors.
． From Tōngjiàn, Táng Ruìzōng.
Yáng Huì slandered Crown Prince Yīng, Prince È Yáo, and Prince Guāng Jū,
claiming they secretly plotted treason,
the emperor summoned his chancellors to discuss it.
Lǐ Línfǔ replied, "This is Your Majesty's family matter,
not something we should interfere with."
Thus the emperor's mind was decided.
． From Tōngjiàn, Táng Xuánzōng.
Gāo Lìshì built Bǎoshòu Temple in the Western Capital,
when the bell was completed,
Lìshì held a feast to celebrate,
the entire court gathered.
For each strike of the bell,
a donation of a hundred strings of cash was made,
those seeking to curry favor struck up to twenty times,
the least not fewer than ten strikes.
Same as above.
Tōngshì Shèrén of the Crown Prince, Lǐ Shè, knowing that the emperor's favor towards Tūtǔ Chéngcuǐ had not waned,
submitted a memorial through the petition box,
stating "Chéngcuǐ has merit,
long trusted as a close aide,
should not be hastily discarded."
． From Tōngjiàn, Táng Xiànzōng.
Lǐ Qíyùn used sweet words to flatter and comply.
From Tángshū.
Féng Dào served nine rulers previously without ever remonstrating.
From Wǔdài Shǐ.
Collection
Compliant and without a mind of one's own.
From Xuǎn Lùn.
Bending one's integrity as if the four limbs had no bones.
From Pān Ānrén's "Rhapsody on a Westward Journey".
This dynasty
Sū Shùnqīn supervised the Office of Memorials,
and during the October ceremonies to honor the gods,
he gathered colleagues at the office.
The censor Liú Yuányú impeached and imprisoned him,
charging him with embezzlement as the supervising official,
resulting in his removal from the register; all who attended the gathering
were also punished. Liú
said to the then chief minister Jiǎ Chāngcháo: "I have caught them all in one net."
From "Juànyóu Lù".
Classic:
Petty people are hard to serve but easy to please.
Even if pleased by improper means,
they are still pleased.
From "Yǔ Zǐlù".
Master:
To live among those who slander, flatter, and fawn face-to-face,
and yet desire to govern a state,
how can it be achieved?
From "Mèngzǐ Gàozǐ Shàng".
History:
Drowned in sycophantic words.
From "Zōu Yáng Zhuàn".
When the Marquis of Wèi proposed plans that were incorrect,
his ministers all echoed him as if with one voice.
Not examining the right or wrong of matters but delighting in others' praise of oneself
is the height of blindness;
not considering where reason lies but flattering to gain favor
is the depth of sycophancy.
From "Tōngjiàn Zhōu Jì".
Cross-reference "flattery and sycophancy".
Believing the slanderous whispers
(pronounced qiè)
of the treacherous.
From "Xīhàn Fǎn Sāo".
The sounds of praise and flattery
fill the ears daily.
False accolades intoxicate the heart,
while real disasters are obscured.
Same as above,
from "Lù Wēnshū Zhuàn".
Those trusted and beloved
are all flatterers and sycophants who curry favor.
From "Tōngjiàn Hàn Xiàndì Jì".
Wén Zhōngzǐ said: "To be pleased by praise
is the gateway to sycophancy."
From "Tōngjiàn Suí Jì".
With the slander and flattery of a hundred mouths and a hundred minds,
obscuring the clarity of two ears and two eyes,
unless one has an iron will and a heart of stone,
how can one not be deluded?
From "Táng Shǐ Chén Xuánzōng Zàn".
Collection:
Ears saturated with fawning talk.
From "Xuǎn Xù".
The nobles and dignitaries, once satisfied in their ambitions,
all delight in what is smooth and pleasing to the eyes and ears,
disliking to hear unvarnished truths,
and upon encountering them, immediately order their gates closed to shut them out.
From Hán Yù's "Wáng Jūn Mùzhì".
Mèngzǐ once said,
"The feudal lords of today
do not greatly surpass each other,
because they all 'prefer to have ministers whom they can instruct,
rather than those from whom they can receive instruction.'"
The present era, compared to Mèngzǐ's time,
is even further removed,
as all prefer those who obey commands and rush about,
and dislike those who uphold their principles and follow the Way.
Same as above,
from "Shàng Zhāng Jiànfēng Shū".
This dynasty:
Recently, scholar-officials have all developed insatiable and extravagant ambitions,
often wanting others to praise them as equal to Zhōu Gōng or Confucius,
and are dissatisfied
with anyone below Mèngzǐ.
From Sū Shì's "Dá Lǐ Zhì Shū".
Classic:
Will and spirit fill heaven and earth.
From "Jì Kǒngzǐ Xiánjū".
Not disheartened by poverty and low status,
nor overly elated by wealth and honor.
From "Jì Rú Xíng".
Cross-reference "integrity".
Wearing a shabby gown padded with old silk floss,
standing beside those clad in fox and badger furs,
yet feeling no shame—
is it not Yóu?
From "Lúnyǔ Zǐhǎn".
Master:
Dwelling in the broadest abode under heaven,
standing in the correct position under heaven,
walking the great path under heaven.
When achieving one's aims,
share them with the people;
when not achieving them,
practice the Way alone.
From "Mèngzǐ".
The worthy scholars of old
delighted in their Way and forgot the power of others,
so unless kings and dukes paid full respect and courtesy,
they could not frequently meet them.
From "Jìnxīn Xià".
Will
is the commander of the vital force.
From "Gōngsūn Chǒu Shàng".
I am good at cultivating my vast, flowing vital force.
This force,
supremely great and supremely strong,
if nourished with integrity and unharmed,
fills the space between heaven and earth.
Same as above.
When speaking to great men, regard them with contempt,
and do not be awed by their imposing manner.
From "Jìnxīn Xià".
Cross-reference "contempt".
They with their wealth,
I with my benevolence;
they with their rank,
I with my righteousness—
what do I lack?
From "Gōngsūn Chǒu Xià".
A person of purpose does not forget that he may end up in a ditch.
Also from "Mèngzǐ".
Regarding the peril of Tàiháng Mountain
as but a low hill.
From "Zǐhuázǐ".
With a cultivated will, one can look down on wealth and honor;
valuing the Way and righteousness, one can despise kings and dukes.
From "Xúnzǐ".
A hall several ren high,
with beams extending several feet—if I achieved my aims, I would not do such things.
Food laid out over a square zhang,
hundreds of concubines attending,
indulging in music and drink,
galloping in hunts,
with a thousand carriages following—
if I achieved my aims, I would not do such things.
From "Jìnxīn Xià".
Mèngzǐ said: "In terms of position,
you are the ruler,
and I
am your minister;
how dare I be friends with the ruler?
In terms of virtue,
then you should serve me;
how can you be my friend?
A ruler of a thousand chariots seeks to befriend him and cannot,
so how can he be summoned?"
Same as above,
from "Wànzhāng Xià".
Cross-reference "self-confidence".
Viewing three fu or three thousand zhōng
as no more than sparrows and mosquitoes passing before one's eyes.
From "Zhuāngzǐ".
Beside the sun and moon,
embracing the universe.
From "Qí Wù Lùn".
Roaming freely to the eight extremes.
From "Tián Zǐfāng".
Xiàng Yǔ did not learn a single art,
Hán Xìn did not plan for a single meal.
From "Liúzǐ".
Comparing lofty status to warts,
and all things to cicada wings.
From "Bàopǔzǐ Zhìlǐ Lùn".
Zǐgāo traveled to Zhào.
Among Lord Píngyuán's guests were Zōu Wén and Lǐ Jié,
with whom he was friendly.
When he was about to return to Lǔ,
after bidding farewell to all his old friends,
Wén and Jié saw him off for three days until the final parting.
Wén and Jié wept with tears streaming down their cheeks,
but Zǐgāo merely raised his hands in a formal salute.
His disciples asked him about it,
and Zǐgāo said: "I initially thought these two were true men,
but now I know they are like women.
How can men, unlike deer and pigs,
always gather in crowds?"
From "Kǒngcóngzǐ".
Crossing the Jiāng and Huái rivers
as if they were ordinary ditches.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
History:
You have ambitions to travel the four directions.
． From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, the 14th Year of Duke Xī".
He always had great magnanimity,
and did not engage in the livelihood and work of household management.
． From "Tōng Jiàn, Qín Records".
When the heroic officials heard that the magistrate of Pèi had a guest,
they all went to offer congratulations.
Xiāo Hé, as the master of ceremonies,
instructed the various officials, saying: "Those who contribute less than a thousand coins,
shall sit in the lower hall."
Gāozǔ, being a village chief,
had always looked down upon the various officials,
so he deceitfully wrote on his card "Congratulations with ten thousand coins",
though in reality he did not bring a single coin.
I too wish to go east;
how can I stay depressed here for long!
Same as above,
from "Hàn Gāo Records".
Guǒ Jiě
used his body to help friends seek revenge.
． From "Shǐ, Biographies of Rangers".
Xiàng Jí learned swordsmanship,
but did not master it,
so his uncle Xiàng Liáng was angry with him.
Jí said: "Swordsmanship can only defeat one person,
not worth learning;
I want to learn what can defeat ten thousand men."
． From "Western Hàn, His Biography".
He admired unconventional and great integrity.
． From "Western Hàn, Biography of Zhū Yún".
Zhào Wēn said: "A true man should soar like a male,
how can he crouch like a female!"
． From "Eastern Hàn, His Biography".
Simple and unrestrained.
． From "Western Hàn, Biography of Yáng Xióng".
See also "Simple".
Xǔ Sì said to Liú Bèi: "Chén Dēng is a man of lakes and seas,
his heroic spirit remains undiminished.
When I passed by Xiàpī,
I met Yuánlóng.
He showed no host's courtesy,
did not speak with me,
but took the large bed for himself to sleep on,
and had the guest sleep on the lower bed."
Bèi said: "Now the world is in great chaos,
you should worry about the country and forget your family,
having the intention to save the world.
Yet you only seek fields and inquire about houses,
your words offer nothing valuable,
this is what Yuánlóng despises;
why should he speak with you?
If it were me, I would sleep on a hundred-foot tower,
and have you sleep on the ground;
how could it be just the difference between upper and lower beds?"
． From "Eastern Hàn, Biography of Chén Qiú".
See also "Contempt".
In the Eastern Hàn, when the court arrested the partisans Lǐ Yīng, Dù Mì, and others, the attendant censor
Jǐng Yì's son had served Yīng but was not on the list,
so he was spared from the disaster.
Yì said: "I originally had my son serve Yīng,
which was the way to respect Lord Lǐ.
Now that he has encountered disaster,
how can I evade it?"
He then impeached himself.
Same as above,
from "His Biography".
Liáng Sǒng said: "A true man living in the world
should be enfeoffed as a marquis when alive,
and be offered sacrifices in the temple after death."
Same as above,
from "His Biography".
Yán Cén said: "A man should seek life in the face of death;
how can he sit still and be trapped in poverty!"
． From "Tōng Jiàn, Hàn Emperor Guāngwǔ Records".
A true man in the world
should sweep clean the empire;
why bother with one room?"
． From "Eastern Hàn, Biography of Chén Fān".
Mǎ Shí said:
"Fortunately born in a prosperous and enlightened age,
spared from being mere brick and tile,
endowed as a man,
I should establish a name for a thousand years,
and not be an empty being who dies in vain,
defiling the space between heaven and earth."
． From "Later Hàn, Xiè Chéng's Biography".
A man should die in the wild frontiers,
wrapped in horsehide for burial;
how can he lie in bed and die in the hands of women and children!"
Same as above,
from "Mǎ Yuán's Biography".
Bān Chāo, coming from a poor family,
worked as a government copyist.
Once he threw down his brush and said: "A man without great ambitions
should still emulate Fù Jièzǐ and Zhāng Qiān, achieving merits in foreign lands,
to earn a marquis title;
how can he long engage with brush and inkstone?"
Those around him laughed at him.
Chāo said: "How can petty minds understand the ambitions of a hero!"
． From "Eastern Hàn, His Biography".
Dèng Ài, poor in his youth, whenever he saw high mountains and great marshes,
would plan and point out locations for military camps.
From "Wèi Zhì".
Rènchéng King Zhāng said to his attendants: "A true man should become a Wèi or Huò,
leading a hundred thousand cavalry across the desert,
driving out the barbarians to achieve merit,
and establish a reputation;
how can one become a scholar?"
Same as above.
Shǔ's Liú Bā said: "A true man should befriend heroes from all corners."
From "Shǔ Zhì".
He was filled with emotion, aspiring to water his horse at the Hé and Luò rivers.
Same as above,
from "Biography of Zhūgě Liàng".
Qín's Wáng Měng,
unconventional and with great ambitions,
disdained trivial matters,
and was looked down upon by others.
Měng remained carefree and content;
hearing that Huán Wēn had entered the pass,
he went to see him in coarse clothes,
picking lice while discussing current affairs,
as if no one else was around.
． From "Tōng Jiàn, Jìn History".
See also "Contempt".
Zhōu Yǐ said: "This year I will kill the traitorous slave,
Wáng Dūn.
I'll take a gold seal as big as a dou measure and tie it to my elbow."
． From "Jìn History, His Biography".
His triumphant spirit enveloped the skies.
Same as above,
． From "Discourse on Hán Bó's Biography".
Huán Xuán said: "Liú Yì's family lacks even a dàn of grain in storage,
yet in gambling, he stakes a million at one throw."
． From "Tōng Jiàn, Jìn Records".
Taking the universe as his heart,
borrowing wind and clouds as his spirit.
．． From "Nán History, Preface to Recluses".
Zōng Què often said: "I wish to ride the long wind
and break through the ten-thousand-mile waves."
． From "Tōng Jiàn, Sòng Records".
Cáo Jǐngzōng said to his close ones: "In my youth in the countryside,
I rode swift horses like dragons,
with several dozen young riders,
drawing bowstrings with a thunderous sound,
arrows whistling like hungry owls,
chasing deer in the open marshes,
shooting them through the ribs,
drinking their blood when thirsty,
eating their flesh when hungry,
sweet as nectar.
Feeling the wind and dust behind my ears,
fire seeming to shoot from my nostrils,
such joy makes one forget death,
unaware that old age approaches.
Now in Yángzhōu as a noble,
I cannot move freely.
If I open the carriage curtain while traveling,
servants immediately say it's not allowed.
Shut inside the carriage,
like a bride of three days,
this depression drains all my spirit."
． From "Nán History, Qí History, His Biography".
When Péi Héngzhī became governor of Wúxīng,
he sighed: "If a true man attains wealth and honor,
he must make a hundred-panel quilt."
Same as above,
from "Liáng History".
Looking lightly upon the world,
considering all things insignificant.
．． From "Běi History, Preface to Recluses".
Gāo Áng devoted himself to galloping,
often saying: "A man should roam the world freely,
seeking wealth and honor on his own;
who can sit properly reading books,
to become an old scholar?"
Same as above,
from "His Biography".
Lǐ Bì said: "A man born into the world
must tread on blades to achieve merit and fame;
how can he mediocrarily climb the ranks for an official post?"
． From "Běi History, Later Zhōu, His Biography".
Lǐ Jìng often said: "A man's encounter with opportunity
should lead to achieving merit and fame for wealth and honor;
why stoop to being a textual scholar!"
． From "Táng History, His Biography".
When true men pledge mutual commitment,
do not mind minor grievances;
I will never believe slanders to harm the loyal and good."
． From "Tōng Jiàn, Táng Gāozǔ Records".
Mǎ Suì said: "A true man should make his achievements known throughout the world;
why grow old as a mere scholar!"
． From "Táng History, His Biography".
Shǐ Hóngzhào said:
"To pacify the court
and quell rebellions,
one only needs long spears and great swords;
what use are writing brushes!"
From "History of the Five Dynasties".
Biography
Lǐ Mì in his youth wrote a poem: "Heaven covers me,
earth carries me,
with purpose yet without.
Either I shall cease eating grains and ascend the celestial thoroughfare,
or I shall travel to the imperial capital with jade ornaments chiming.
How can I neither attain nobility nor depart,
merely becoming an imposing man in vain?"
From "The Family Biography of Marquis Lǐ Yè".
Hán Xīzǎi, having passed the imperial examination,
submitted a letter to Lǐ Biàn stating: "One who fishes for giant sea turtles
does not use bait meant for catching ordinary fish;
one who severs massive whales
would hardly employ a knife for slaughtering chickens."
He also said: "At my waist hangs a sword and in my sleeve rests a hammer,
in my mouth resides a tongue and in my hand lies a brush."
From "Surviving Accounts of the Southern Táng".

Páng Méng served as a local station master. When the county captain passed by, he greeted him with a bow to inquire about matters. After the captain left, he threw his tally stick to the ground and sighed, saying, "How can a true man always follow behind others?" Thereupon he left to pursue learning.
From "Records of the Eastern Hàn".

History
Emperor Gaozu of Hàn passed through Chénliú,
Lì Shēng sought an audience,
but the emperor said: "I am occupied with affairs of the realm,
and have no leisure to receive great Confucian scholars."
Lì Shēng declared of himself:
"I am a drunkard from Gāoyáng,
not a Confucian scholar." From Chǔ-Hàn Spring and Autumn Annals.
Gōngsūn Zàn said:
"With the uprising of armies across the land,
I believe it can be decided as easily as spitting on one's palm." From Jiǔzhōu Spring and Autumn Annals.
Xiàhóu Chēng at every feast,
overwhelmed the entire gathering with his aura. From Shì Shuō.
Fú Jiān deliberated on attacking Jìn,
saying: "If my troops cast their whips into the river,
it would be enough to block its flow.
I have resolved this within my heart!" From Cuī Hóng's Records of Former Qín.
Cross-reference "Self-confidence".
My nature can endure swords and spears,
but cannot bear whips and clubs.
Same as above.
When Lǐ Yuánzhōng first sought an audience with Qí's Gāo Huān,
and was not received immediately, he told the gatekeeper: "His Lordship is now summoning the talented and heroic,
yet I hear when a man of national stature arrives, he cannot interrupt his meal or stop washing to receive him.
His discourtesy is evident.
You may return my name card and not announce me." From The Chicken Feet Collection.
When Huángfǔ Shí composed the Fúxiān Temple stele for Péi Dù,
Péi promised a thousand strings of coins as reward.
Shí angrily said: "How meagerly you treat me!
My writing
is not that of ordinary men.
Apart from having once written a preface for Gù Kuàng,
I have never readily agreed to write for anyone.
The stele contains about three thousand characters,
each character worth three bolts of silk.
Now I won't accept a reduction of even half a coin."
Minister Péi paid him according to the count.
Shí accepted it
without any look of shame. From The Unrecorded History of Táng.
Lǐ Zhǐ, feeling his official rank did not match his clan's prestige though he had risen to provincial governor, in his letters only signed as "Lǐ Zhǐ of Guānxī".
From Lǐ Zhào's Supplement to National History.
To live in disgrace,
is worse than to die in glory.
From The Rites of Dài, "Zēngzǐ's Admonitions" chapter.
Zhāng Hù visited Lǐ Shēn,
introducing himself as "the guest who fishes for giant sea turtles".
Lǐ, greatly angered, asked: "What do you use as your fishing pole?"
He replied: "I use the rainbow as my pole."
"What do you use as your hook?"
Said: "I use the moon as my hook."
"What do you use as bait?"
Said: "I use Minister Lǐ (you) of short stature as bait."
Shēn fell silent,
then richly rewarded him. From Great Táng Anecdotes.

Our Dynasty
Táng presented scholar Zhāng Tuàn,
of lofty spirit,
never bowed or yielded to anyone.
He once said: "A true man has world-surpassing ambition,
yet confined to a lowly position,
is like standing in a low-roofed hut, unable to lift his head."
So he shook his robes and retreated to Sōng Mountain. From annotation to Dōngpō's poetry.
History
His mind was broad and open.
Always magnanimous,

Cìfēi said:

It's only a matter of abandoning the sword."

History
Lǔ Zhūjiā,
saved and harbored hundreds of courageous figures,
with countless ordinary people beyond measure.
Yet he never boasted of his abilities,
nor took pride in his virtues.
For all his frequent acts of charity,
he feared being acknowledged for them.
He relieved those in need,
starting with the poor and humble.
He devoted himself to others' emergencies,
prioritizing them over his own interests.
． _Records of the Grand Historian: Biographies of Wandering Knights_.
Moreover, crises are common to all.
When someone in distress knocks at the door,
they do not use family as an excuse,
nor absence as a pretext.
What the world looks up to
are solely figures like Jì Xīn and Jù Mèng.
． _Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of Yuǎn Āng_.
When Wèi Qí was in dire straits,
he sought refuge with Yú Qīng,
who abandoned his ministerial seal
and fled with Wèi Qí,
reaching Wèi.
． _Comprehensive Mirror: Chronicles of Zhōu_.
With the noble righteousness of the prince,

When King Zhào Áo's case was cleared,

and came to Hù.
Entrusting himself to Hù,
he ate with Lǚ Gōng's wife and an elderly woman.
Hù's wife and children grew weary of Lǚ Gōng.
Hearing this,
Hù shed tears and scolded his son, saying:
"Lǚ Gōng, in his impoverished old age, entrusted himself to me—
it is my duty to support him."
Thus, he cared for Lǚ Gōng until his death.
_Western Hàn_.
Cross-referenced under "entrustment," "old acquaintances," and "cherishing the past."
Zhāng Jiǎn incurred the wrath of the palace attendant Hóu Lǎn,
who issued a warrant for his arrest.
Having an old connection with Kǒng Róng's brother Bāo,
he fled to Bāo for refuge,
but did not find him.
Róng said, "Though my brother is away,
can I not act as the host?"
So he took Jiǎn in.
Later, the matter leaked,
and Bāo and Róng were arrested and jailed.
Neither knew who would be charged.
Róng said, "The one who sheltered and hid him
is I, Róng,
so I should bear the punishment."
Bāo said, "He came seeking me,
not my brother's fault;
I willingly accept the guilt."
The officials asked their mother,
who said, "Family matters fall on the eldest;
I should take the blame."
The whole family contended to die.
The edict ultimately sentenced Bāo.
． _Eastern Hàn: Biography of Kǒng Róng_.
Zhū Zhèn buried Chén Fān's body,
and hid his son Yì.
When discovered,
he was imprisoned,
with his whole family in shackles.
Though tortured,
Zhū Zhèn vowed to die without speaking,
and Yì thus escaped.
． _Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Líng of Hàn_.
Mǎ Yuán said, "Dù Jìliáng is righteous,
sharing others' sorrows
and joys."
． _Eastern Hàn: Biography of Mǎ Yuán_.
Dù Shàng and seven others were called the "Eight Providers,"
meaning they used wealth to save people.
Ibid.,
． _Preface to Biographies of the Partisan Prohibitions_.
Chén Zhòng, serving in the court,
had a colleague owing hundreds of thousands in debt,
with creditors coming daily,
pressuring relentlessly.
Zhòng secretly repaid the debt on his behalf.
_Xiè Chéng's History of Eastern Hàn_.
Tàishǐ Cí's mother told him, "You and Kǒng Běihǎi had never met,
yet after you left,
he provided for us diligently,
surpassing old friends."
At that time, Cí had fled to Liáodōng.
． _Records of the Three Kingdoms: Wú_.
Lǚ Sù distributed his wealth,
winning the hearts of his village.
When Zhōu Yú sought grain,
Sù had two granaries of rice,
each holding three thousand hú,
and he pointed to one, giving it to Yú.
Ibid.
Fàn Shūsūn aided the poor and relieved the urgent,
so his village honored his righteousness,
and none called him by name.
_Book of Sòng_.
Collection
Noble righteousness drives through past and present.
—Old Dù.
When others come in righteousness,
I pledge myself;
lifting my robes to rush to aid,
undaunted by cold or heat.
—Liǔ's text.
Elevating noble righteousness beyond common customs,

Ibid.
When Liú Mèngdé (Yǔxī) of Zhōngshān was exiled,
destined for Bōzhōu,
Zǐhòu wept, saying, "Bōzhōu is no place for humans,
and Mèngdé has his mother alive.
I cannot bear Mèngdé's plight,
with no words to explain to his elder,
and no reason for mother and son to go together."
He petitioned the court,
preparing to submit a memorial,
offering to exchange Liǔ for Bō,
even if doubly condemned, without regret.
When someone reported Mèngdé's case to the emperor,
Mèngdé was reassigned to Liánzhōu.
—Hán's text, _Epitaph for Liǔ Zǐhòu_.
Our dynasty
When Fàn Zhòngyān was demoted for his words,
and the purge of factions was intense,
Wáng Zhì alone, though ill, led his family to farewell at the east gate,
lingering for days.
A minister reproached him,
"Why trouble to entangle yourself in factions?"
He replied,
"Fàn is a worthy of the world;
how dare I aspire to that!
If I could be a faction member,
you'd bestow a great honor upon me."
—Ōu's writing, _Epitaph for Wáng Zhì_.
When Fàn Zhòngyān was demoted to Ráozhōu,
and censors remained silent,
Yǐn Shīlǔ wrote,
"Zhòngyān is my teacher and friend;
I wish to be demoted with him."
—Ōu's writing, _Epitaph for Yǐn Shīlǔ_.

Harmoniously ordering the nine clans.

By kin, the nine clans,

_Canon of Yáo_.
Revering ancestors thus honors the lineage;

． _Book of Rites: Minor Record of Mourning_.

Biographies
Kǒng Fěn was devoted to his flesh and blood.
_Eastern View: Hàn Records_.
Our dynasty
Bì Xián, upon achieving nobility,
used his salaries
to support needy clan members,
without discrimination.
_Kǒng's White Sixfold Compilation_.
Wéi Shéng raised orphaned young clan members without partiality.
Ibid.
Fàn Wénzhèng Gōng said, "To be wealthy yet not care for one's clan—
how will one face ancestors underground hereafter?"
_Anecdotes_.
Classics
Those who know how to protect, embrace, carry, and support their wives and children.
. From the "Shū·Zhàogào".
For families marrying off a daughter,
they keep candles burning for three nights without rest,
longing for the one who has parted.
. From the "Lǐjì·Zēngzǐ Wèn".
All beings born between heaven and earth,
those endowed with blood and vital energy,
must possess awareness;
among those with awareness,
none do not know to love their kind.
Now take these large birds and beasts:
if they lose their flock or companions,
even after months or seasons pass,
they will surely return and patrol,
passing through their former haunts,
hovering and circling there,
crying and calling out,
pacing to and fro,
lingering hesitantly,
and only then are they able to depart.
As for smaller creatures like swallows and sparrows,
they too have moments of chirping and twittering.
Only then can they bring themselves to leave.
Thus, among beings with blood and vital energy,
none are more aware than humans,
so humans, toward their parents,
cherish them unto death without end.
. From the "Lǐjì·Sānnián Wèn".
A child is born and for three years,
only then is it free from the bosom of its parents.
. From the "Lúnyǔ·Yánghuò".
Parents only worry about their children's illnesses.
From the "Lúnyǔ".
Regarding
the relationship between father and son is centered on affection.
. From the "Mèngzǐ·Gōngsūn Chǒu Shàng".
In ancient times, people exchanged sons to educate them,
so that between father and son, there would be no reproach over doing good.
From "Lílóu Shàng".
Historical Records
When the Jìn army attacked Qí,
Fàn Wénzǐ entered last.
Wǔzǐ said, "Did you not make me wait for you?"
From the "Zuǒzhuàn".
Left Minister Chù Lóng visited the Empress Dowager,
saying, "My humble son Shū Qí is the youngest,
and I deeply dote on him,
hoping he may fill a vacancy in the royal guards."
The Dowager said, "Do men also love their young sons?"
He replied, "Even more than women do."
He also said, "When parents love their children,
they plan deeply and far ahead for them."
. From the "Shǐjì·Zhào Shìjiā".
Bone and flesh are the closest kin,
akin to being one body.
. From the "Xīhàn·Lì Tàizǐ Zhuàn".
Zhāng Yǔ said, "I have four sons and one daughter,
and I love my daughter more than my sons."
From the "Xīhàn".
Yáng Biāo's son was killed by Cáo Cāo.
Cáo saw Yáng Biāo,
and asked, "Why have you grown so thin?"
Biāo replied, "I still harbor the love of an old cow
that licks its calf."
. From the "Dōnghàn·Běnzhuàn".
Affection is naturally bestowed by heaven.
. From the "Dōnghàn·Mǎ Hòu Jì".
The mother and son shared tender love,
remaining without the slightest rift from beginning to end.
. From the "Tōngjiàn·Hàn Míngdì".
Wèi Jiè was often ill and physically weak,
so his mother often forbade him from speaking.
. From the "Jìnshū·Běnzhuàn".
Cross-reference "Illness".
A father towards his sons,
should love them equally.
. From the "Tōngjiàn·Jìn Jì".
Wáng Shù's son Tǎnzhī,
even when grown,
was still held on his lap.
. From the "Jìnshū·Běnzhuàn".
Wáng Yǎn said, "Where deep emotions are concentrated,
is precisely among people like us."
Ibid,
"Běnzhuàn".
Xún Xiàn was seven years old,
and his father loved him so much
that he often sat Xiàn on his knee.
. From the "Jìnshū·Běnzhuàn".
Wáng Xīzhī led his sons,
carrying his young grandson,
and whenever there was a sweet morsel,
he would cut and share it,
to bring joy before their eyes.
From the "Jìnshū".
. Cross-reference the section "Human Relations: Grandchildren".
Zhèng Tánshǒu gathered with his brothers and their descendants,
letting the children play freely.
Sēngdá jumped to the ground pretending to be a tiger cub.
Sēngchǔ piled up ten gaming pieces,
neither letting them fall,
nor stacking them again.
Sēngchuò collected wax beads to make a phoenix,
which Sēngdá snatched and broke,
yet he showed no regret.
From the "Nánshǐ".
The Emperor said to Cén Wénběn, "Your younger brother has been overly social,
and I fear it may implicate you;
I intend to assign him an external post,
what do you think?"
Wénběn wept and said, "My brother was orphaned young,
and my elderly mother particularly dotes on him,
never having been apart from him for even two nights.
If he is sent away now,
my mother will surely languish;
without this brother,
there would be no old mother either."
. From the "Tōngjiàn·Táng Tàizōng Jì".
The Emperor said, "How can a son be left hanging upside down,
and his father not untie him?"
. From the "Tōngjiàn·Zhōu Shìzōng Jì".
On the day of the Dragon Boat Festival,
Emperor Sùzōng summoned the hermit Lǐ Táng for an audience.
The Emperor was holding his young daughter,
and said to Táng, "I am thinking of her,
do not find it strange."
. From the "Tángshū·Sùzōng Zhāng Hòu Zhuàn".
Lǐ Hè's mother searched his bag,
and seeing many written poems,
angrily said, "This boy will not stop until he vomits out his heart."
From the "Tángshū".
Biographies
Wángsūn Gǔ was fifteen years old,
and his mother said, "If you leave in the morning and return late,
I will lean against the door waiting for you;
if you go out at dusk and do not return,
I will lean against the village gate waiting for you."
From the "Zhànguócè".
Collections
Parents and their children,
even if their livers and intestines rot,
will cover up for them,
not wanting the village to hear of their faults.
From Wèi Wéndì's "Admonition to My Son".
The proud son never leaves my knees.
Dù Fǔ.
Returning alive to face the children,
as if forgetting hunger and thirst.
They compete to tug my beard asking questions,

Ibid.
The beloved daughter not yet weaned,
I cannot forget her in my thoughts.
Suddenly she seems before me,
as if I hear her crying.
Hán Tuìzhī.
Nowadays, people traveling a few hundred miles,

chattering endlessly.
. From Hán Wén's "Preface to Seeing Off Yīn Zhí on a Mission to the Uighurs".
Intimate words of children,
grudges and favors between you and me.
Hán Wén.
Streams of love form an ocean,
dust of passion becomes a mountain.
From the "Tóutuó Sì Bēi".
Though cutting off affection without a word,
it remains knotted in the heart.
Bái Jūyì.
Humans are not wood or stone; all have emotions.
Bái Jūyì.
Emotions give rise to numerous burdens.
From the "Wéi Yìngwù Collection".
The fierce tiger indulges in killing and violence,

Tigers and leopards do not eat their own young.

Hán Wèigōng in his youth was close to Yǐn Shīlǔ.

When he grew up,

He recommended him as a subordinate,
educating him like his own child.
"Records of Things Seen and Heard".
Ōu Gōng throughout his life was devoted to friends.
Such as Yǐn Shīlǔ, Méi Shèngyú, Sūn Míngfù after their deaths,
their families being poor,
the Duke strenuously managed their affairs,
enabling all to be self-sufficient.
He also recommended their sons to the court,
having all appointed to official posts.
"Epitaph".
Wú Kuí initially was good friends with fellow villager Wáng Péngnián.
Péngnián died away from home in the capital,

provided relief to his family,
and arranged marriages for his two daughters.
"Epitaph of Wú Kuí".

Same as above.

Masters
There was a man from Wei named Dōngmén Wú,
at forty had a son,
lost him but did not grieve.
His steward said: "Your love for your son,
was unmatched in the world.
Now that your son is dead, you do not grieve,
why?"
Dōngmén Wú said: "When I had no son, I did not grieve.
Now my son is dead,
it is the same as before when I had no son,
so why grieve?"

Being harsh to those one should treat well,

Being in mourning but not grieving,

Initially, Sīmǎ Yì of Jìn's founding emperor pleaded wind paralysis,

The Emperor was ill,

The affection between flesh and blood is thin.

Jìn King Liú's Lady was most favored.
Her father heard of her nobility,
went to the Wèi palace to visit the Lady.
The Lady was then competing for favor with other ladies,
each valuing family background,
ashamed of her own humble origins,
laughed loudly and said: "When I left home, I vaguely remember,
my father unfortunately died in the chaos of war,

What kind of country bumpkin dares to come here now!"
Ordered the old man Liú to be whipped at the palace gate.
"Comprehensive Mirror - Later Hàn Liáng Jūnwáng".
Wáng Róng was stingy and吝啬,

Róng's daughter married into the Péi family,
borrowed money.
When the daughter returned home,
Róng looked displeased,
only when the daughter returned the money did he become happy.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World".
Cross-reference "Stinginess".
Having already revealed the shame of seeking an axe,
how could one be ashamed of the ballad of the chi of cloth?
"Kǒng's White Six Scrolls".
Wèi Emperor Wén ordered Prince of Dōng'ā to compose a poem,
if not done within seven steps,
would face punishment,
he immediately responded with a poem: "Boil beans with beanstalks,
filter to extract the juice.
The stalks burn beneath the beans,
the beans weep in the pot.
Since we sprouted from the same root,
why press each other so urgently?"

Collection

Even among siblings,

From "Xuǎn Dá Kè Nán".
Once my fellow student friend,

A silk robe may not signify old ties,

Luò Bīnwáng.
To be unfeeling towards one's flesh and blood,

Liǔ Miǎn's "Lùn Wén Shū".
Even kin treat each other lightly,

A starving tiger does not eat its young,

Classic
Accumulation that can lead to subtlety.
From "Jì Qǔ Lǐ Shàng".
Distributing to others,

From "Rú Xíng".
Master
To share wealth with others,
Is called generosity.
From "Mèng Téng Wéngōng Shàng".
Taking joy in giving and being ashamed of hoarding.

History
Luán Huáizi delighted in giving,
And many scholars turned to him.
From "Zuǒ Xiāng Èrshíyī".
For all princes and descendants without stipends,
He privately distributed fiefs;
For the state's poor, constrained, orphaned, and widowed,

From "Zuǒ Zhāo Shí".
Loving to give,
Is the beginning of benevolence.
From "Shǐ Jì".
Wèi Chéng had a salary of a thousand zhōng,
Nine-tenths he gave away,
Only one-tenth he kept.
From "Shǐ Wèi Shìjiā".
Fàn Lǐ in Táo became Lord Zhū.
In nineteen years, he thrice amassed a thousand pieces of gold,

From "Shǐ Jì Huòzhí Zhuàn".
Lǐ Líng shared hardships and meager rations with his officers.

Initially, when the people suffered famine,

Mǎ Yuán in his youth lived farming and herding,

Generously dispersed goods and valuables,

Aided the poor and relieved the urgent,

If I skip a day of giving,

From "Hòu Qín Shū".
Fán Zhòng had lent millions to people,

The debtors felt ashamed,

His sons followed his decree,

From "Jìn Yáng Qiū".

Things are satisfied by righteousness.
From "Chén Zǐ'áng Jí".
Unfortunate and without self-support,

Liú Chángqīng.
Giving goods and effort,

Carrying a bottle to beg for water,
Holding reeds to seek fire,

From "Liú Zǐ".
