Not distinguishing between the orphaned and widowed,
showing no compassion for the impoverished and destitute.
"Zuo Wen Thirteen".
The family is wealthy with ten thousand gold,
yet not a single worthy person is seen at their gate.
"Records of Mèng Cháng Jūn's Biography".
Also see "Bǐ Lìn".
Worse than being stingy and miserly.
"Western Hàn Huò Zhí Biography".
Yán Shīgǔ said: "Xiān means petty,
sè means stingy."
The people of Lǔ were frugal and stingy,
and the Bǐng family was especially so;
the people of Zhōu were already petty,
and Shī Shǐ was particularly so.
"Western Hàn Huò Zhí Biography".
Closed their doors and did not interact even for fire or water.
"Western Hàn Sūn Bǎo Biography" note states: "Even with neighbors,
they did not associate."
Stingy with the flow of rivers,
not using it to wash the sides of boats;
sparing the light from the eastern wall,
not letting it shine into the eyes of poor women.
"Eastern Hàn Xiàhóu Zhàn Biography".
Would rather see thousands of coins rot away,
than reluctantly lend someone one coin;
well aware that stored grain spoils in the granary,
yet unwilling to lend others a single dou.
Family members resentful at home,
commoners cursing on the streets.
"Eastern Hàn Wáng Fú Biography".
Mǎ Yuán said: "When accumulating property,
the value lies in being able to give and aid,
otherwise, one is merely a money slave."
"Eastern Hàn Original Biography".
Cáo Hóng,
his family was wealthy but his nature was stingy.
"Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Three Kingdoms, Wèi Míngdì Annals".
Wáng Róng,
his family had good plums.
When selling them,
fearing others might obtain the seeds,
he often drilled through the pits.
"Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Jìn Annals".
Hé Qiáo,
his wealth rivaled that of a king, yet he was extremely stingy,
people called him "having a money obsession."
"Jìn Shū Original Biography".
Wáng Róng,
by nature greedy and stingy.
His gardens and fields spanned the land,
yet he often held the counting rods himself,
calculating day and night,
always as if it weren't enough.
"Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Jìn Huìdì Annals".
As parents, being stingy with their pickles and sauces,
though rich in all things, begrudging even one item.
"Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Liáng Gāozǔ Annals".
Wéi Zhuāng,
by nature miserly.
Counted grains of rice to cook,
weighed firewood to burn.
"Táng Shū".
The Vice Minister of Personnel, Zhāng Yǔn,
his family assets counted in the tens of thousands, yet he was stingy by nature.
Not even entrusting them to his wife,
he often tied all the keys under his clothes,
jingling like pendants as he walked.
"Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Zhōu Tàizǔ Annals".
Biographies
record Wáng Róng as frugal and stingy;
when his nephew got married,
he gave him a single garment,
but later demanded it back.
When Wáng Róng's daughter married into the Péi family,
she borrowed tens of thousands in cash.
Upon returning home for a visit,
Wáng Róng looked displeased;
only after she repaid the money did he become happy.
"Shì Shuō".
Also see "Heartless".
Collection
The wine jars sealed, moss grows green.
Bái Jūyì.
Fools cling to their wealth,
only to be mocked by later generations.
"Ancient Poems".
Classics
Excessive austerity cannot be steadfast.
"Yì Guà Jié" note: "If austerity is too harsh,
things cannot endure it."
Frugality not in accordance with propriety.
"Shī, Táng Guó Fēng, Xī Shuài".
Yàn Píngzhòng sacrificed to his ancestors,
with a pork shoulder not covering the sacrificial vessel.
Wearing washed clothes and a cleaned hat to court,
the gentlemen considered it narrow-minded.
"Jì Lǐ Yùn".
Classics
The gentleman uses thick virtue to carry all things.
"Yì Kūn Guà".
"A large cart used for carrying,"
means accumulation in the center does not lead to defeat.
"Dà Yǒu".
The breadth and thickness of the earth,
carrying Mount Huàyuè without being heavy,
holding rivers and seas without leaking.
"Jì Zhōng Yōng".
Masters
Heaven cannot kill it,
earth cannot bury it.
The eras of Jié and Zhí could not defile it;
none but a great Confucian can establish it.
"Xúnzǐ, Rú Xiào".
The world,
is of utmost weight,
without utmost strength,
none can bear it.
"Zhèng Lùn",
also from "Xúnzǐ".
History
Wáng Jiā served as Chancellor,
repeatedly advised against enfeoffing Dǒng Xián,
the emperor grew angry,
summoned the Chancellor to the court prison for interrogation.
His clerks wept,
together prepared poison for him to take,
but Wáng Jiā took the poison cup and threw it to the ground,
saying to his officials: "The Chancellor is fortunate to hold one of the Three Excellencies' positions;
having failed the state,
he should be executed in the market to show the multitude.
How could he be like a child or woman,
to die by taking poison!"
Wáng Jiā went out,
saw the envoy and received the edict.
"Western Hàn Original Biography".
Fú Jiān,
with a force号称 a million, camped at the Fèi River.
Xiè Xuán entered,
asking for strategy.
Xiè Ān showed no fear,
instead played Go and toured with Xuán,
not returning until night.
"Jìn Shū".
Firm and unmoving like a pillar,
positioned in a house like bones in the body.
"Suí Shū, Fáng Yànqiān Biography".
Lord Zhāng,
in discussing affairs, had the strength of four heavens.
"Táng Shū, Zhāng Yuánsù Biography".
Biographies
Once Dàntái Zǐyǔ, carrying a priceless jade disk, was crossing a river,
when the river god Yáng Hóu stirred waves,
and two flood dragons gripped the boat.
Zǐyǔ said: "I can be sought through righteousness,
but not coerced by force."
Drawing his sword, he slew the dragons.
The dragons dead,
the waves calmed,
he then threw the jade into the river,
but it leaped out three times after being thrown,
so he destroyed the jade and left,
showing no intention of regret.
"Shuǐ Jīng" annotation.
Collection
The axis of heaven and earth shakes the celestial pivot,
rousing primordial energy to thunder across the realm,
soaring over all rivers to rain upon the world.
From "Táng Wén Cuì".
His merits partake in creation,
his strategies align with cosmic design.
Within heaven and earth,
none surpass his command.
Towering and steadfast at the center,
he stands as heaven's pillar.
Thunder shatters valleys,
fierce beasts prostrate in awe.
Storms overturn oceans,
leviathans stumble and falter.
With long reins and sharp whips,
he governs the cosmos crosswise.
Holding the long river like a cup,
splitting Mount Tàihuá as if cracking a clod.
Severing the turtle's legs to mend the sky.
Vast, rivaling the earth's corners,
mighty, contending with heaven's strength.
Amidst raging currents,
one rebuke brings calm.
Heaven and earth churn for him,
rivers and mountains tremble in his wake.
Also from "Táng Wén Cuì".
Stemming all rivers to turn them eastward,
reversing furious waves already toppling.
From Hán Wén.
When the turtle rages, it kicks over the five peaks;
when the whale strikes, it shatters a hundred rivers.
Pí Rìxiū.
In our dynasty,
Hán Wèi Gōng, governing the northern capital, was presented with two jade cups.
He repaid the donor with a hundred gold pieces,
then hosted a banquet for esteemed guests.
He specially set a table to display the cups,
intending to pour wine and toast each guest.
Suddenly, a servant accidentally bumped it,
overturning the table,
shattering both jade cups.
All guests turned pale,
and the servant knelt awaiting punishment.
Hán, unshaken in expression, said: "Objects break at their destined time.
You erred,
but not intentionally.
What fault is there?"
From Liú Fǔ's "Hànfǔ Míngtán".
When Hán Wèi Gōng governed Xiàngzhōu,
during a Confucius ceremony fast,
he stayed overnight at the official residence.
A thief entered his room,
brandishing a blade, saying: "I cannot support myself,
so I seek aid from you."
Hán replied: "The vessels on the desk are worth a fortune;
take them all."
The thief said: "I wish to have your head
to present to the western foes."
Hán immediately offered his neck.
The thief kowtowed and said: "I heard of your immense magnanimity
and came to test you.
I've already received the items on the desk
as your gift;
I hope you won't reveal this."
Hán said: "Agreed."
He never told anyone.
Later, the thief was convicted for another crime
and sentenced to die in the market.
Before execution, he recounted the event, saying: "I fear that after my death,
your noble virtue will be lost to the world!"
From "Dùnzhāi Xiánlǎn".
When Kǒu Zhǔn was at Chányuān,
each evening he drank, gambled, sang, and bantered with Yáng Yì,
often until dawn.
If he slept,
his snore was like thunder.
The emperor sent someone to observe him,
and joyfully said: "With him like this,
what worries do I have?"
From "Wǔ Cháo Yán Xíng".
When Kǒu Láigōng was exiled to Léizhōu,
Dīng Wèi dispatched a palace envoy with an edict to deliver.
Kǒu was drinking with county officials;
all present were terrified,
but he remained composed.
He had someone tell the envoy: "If the court orders my death,
I wish to see the edict."
He then borrowed a green robe from the clerk,
received it kneeling in the courtyard,
ascended the steps, and resumed drinking,
continuing until evening ended.
From "Jì Lǘ".
Confronting great affairs,
deciding major policies,
gown straight, tablet held proper,
without changing expression,
he secures the world as stable as Mount Tài.
From Ōu Gōng's "Hán Wèi Gōng Zhàojǐn Táng Jì".
A lone boat overturns rivers,
bare hands capture rhinoceros and elephant.
From Sū Shī's poem.
Ten thousand oxen couldn't pull it forward,
yet he alone shouldered the burden.
From Huáng Lǔzhí's poem.
Draining the sea to seize the bright moon.
Same as above.
Zǐ
Lǔ burned the marsh's accumulation.
Heaven sent a north wind,
driving the fire southward,
threatening the state.
Duke Āi personally led the crowd to fight the fire.
But people chased beasts instead of fighting the fire.
Until Zhòngní ordered: "Those who chase beasts instead of fighting the fire
will be punished as if trespassing forbidden grounds."
Before the order fully spread,
the fire was extinguished.
From "Hán Fēi Zǐ".
History
Empress Dowager Lü established the various members of the Lü family as kings,
and Chén Píng pretended to comply.
When the Empress Dowager passed away,
Píng conspired with Grand Commandant Bó,
ultimately executing the entire Lü clan.
. _Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of Chén Píng_.
The reason the Crown Prince was not replaced
was due to the efforts of Liú Hóu in recruiting these four individuals.
Ibid,
_Biography of Liú Hóu_.
The Emperor intended to depose the Crown Prince,
and Empress Lü was fearful.
Zhāng Liáng said: "There are four men that even the Emperor cannot summon.
Have the Crown Prince write a letter
and persistently invite them."
The Crown Prince welcomed these four men.
The Emperor held a banquet,
with the Crown Prince in attendance.
The four men accompanied the Crown Prince.
The Emperor was surprised,
and inquired.
The four men stepped forward and replied: "We have heard that the Crown Prince is benevolent and filial,
respectful and fond of scholars.
All under heaven crane their necks, willing to die for the Crown Prince.
Therefore, we have come."
The Emperor said: "I trouble you, gentlemen, to take good care of the Crown Prince."
The Emperor summoned Consort Qī and said: "I wished to replace him,
but these four men assist him.
His wings are fully formed;
it is difficult to shake him now."
. _Biography of Zhāng Liáng of the Western Hàn_.
The Emperor resided in the Southern Palace,
and saw the generals whispering among themselves.
He asked Zhāng Liáng about it.
Liáng replied: "Your Majesty seized the empire with these men,
yet you have enfeoffed only old acquaintances,
and executed only personal enemies.
Now they fear being executed for any fault,
hence they gather to plot rebellion."
The Emperor said: "What should be done?"
Liáng said: "Select someone whom Your Majesty has long disliked,
the one most known to all ministers for this,
and enfeoff him first to show the ministers."
The Emperor enfeoffed Yōng Chǐ.
The ministers all rejoiced, saying:
"Even Yōng Chǐ has been made a marquis; we have nothing to fear!"
Initially,
Yōng Chǐ did not wish to serve Péi Gōng,
and Péi Gōng held a grudge against him.
Cross-reference "Shifting People's Hearts."
Tián Yánnián stepped forward,
left his mat, and pressing his sword said: "The late Emperor entrusted the young orphan to you, General,
and placed the empire in your care,
believing in your loyalty and virtue,
that you could secure the Liú family.
Now the ministers are in turmoil,
and the state is on the verge of collapse.
Moreover, the Hàn dynasty's posthumous title for emperors includes 'Filial'
to signify their lasting rule over the empire,
ensuring the ancestral temples receive sacrifices.
If the Hàn lineage is cut off,
even in death,
what face will you have to meet the late Emperor underground?
Today's decision
must be made without hesitation.
Any minister who responds late,
I ask to be beheaded with this sword!"
. _Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Xuān of Hàn_.
There was heavy rain in Guānnéi for over forty days.
The capital's populace panicked,
saying a great flood was coming,
and the people fled.
Grand General Fèng suggested:
"The Empress Dowager, the Emperor, and the rear palace can board boats, and order officials and people to ascend the walls of Cháng'ān to avoid the water."
Wáng Shāng alone said:
"Why would a great flood suddenly come? This must be a rumor!"
Shortly after,
Cháng'ān gradually stabilized;
upon inquiry,
it was indeed a rumor.
Fèng was greatly ashamed,
regretting his words.
Ibid,
_Annals of Emperor Chéng of Hàn_.
Cross-reference "Misspoken Words."
Laying an infant on the throne could bring peace to the court; leaving the imperial robe vacant could keep the empire from chaos.
_Biography of Jiǎ Yì of the Western Hàn_.
Changing what one wishes to do
is easier than turning over one's hand,
and as secure as Tài Shān.
_Biography of Méi Chéng_.
The Crown Prince indulged in drink,
enjoyed feasting and pleasure,
and the Emperor did not consider him capable.
He intended to make Shānyáng his heir.
When the Emperor was resting alone,
Shǐ Dān entered directly into the bedchamber,
kowtowed and prostrated on the green rush mat,
and tearfully said:
"There are rumors on the streets that the Crown Prince's position is being reconsidered.
I wish to be put to death first to show the ministers!"
Thus, the Crown Prince was confirmed as heir.
. _Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Yuán of Hàn_.
Zhuó commented:
"Zhāng wine is fine wine;
Lè Yàn means deep indulgence in feasting."
Shī Gǔ noted:
"The character 'lè' for music
is also pronounced with the fifth tone, xiào."
When Wáng Láng rose,
Emperor Guāngwǔ hurried to Xiàqūyáng.
News came that Wáng Láng's troops were behind,
and his followers were afraid.
Upon reaching the Hūtuó River,
scouts reported the river flowing with ice floes,
no boats,
making crossing impossible.
The officials were terrified.
Guāngwǔ ordered Wáng Bà to inspect.
Bà, fearing to alarm the crowd,
decided to press forward despite the water barrier,
and upon return deceitfully said:
"The ice is solid enough to cross."
The officials were all relieved.
Guāngwǔ laughed:
"The scouts indeed spoke falsely."
They advanced.
When they reached the river,
the ice had fused,
so he ordered Bà to oversee the crossing.
Just after a few cavalry crossed, the ice broke up.
Guāngwǔ said to Bà:
"That our people crossed safely was thanks to your effort."
. _Annals of the Eastern Hàn_.
After executing Wáng Láng,
they seized documents,
finding thousands of petitions from officials who had communicated with Láng and slandered [the court].
Guāngwǔ did not review them,
but gathered the generals and burned them,
to reassure the waverers.
Ibid.
Initially,
Lù Xùn was appointed Grand Commander,
but some generals were veterans from the campaign against rebels,
others were nobles or imperial relatives,
each arrogant and self-important,
refusing to obey orders.
Xùn drew his sword and said:
"We all bear the state's grace,
should cooperate harmoniously,
and together defeat the enemy,
repaying what we've received.
Yet you do not comply; why?
Though I am a scholar,
appointed by the sovereign,
the reason the state humbled you to follow me
is that I have some merit and can endure humiliation to bear heavy responsibilities.
Each of you must fulfill your duties;
how can you refuse?
Military discipline is constant;
it must not be violated!"
When they defeated Liú Bèi,
most strategies came from Xùn,
and the generals then submitted.
. _Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Wén of Wèi in the Three Kingdoms_.
Jiǎng Wǎn served as Secretary.
At the time, the commander had just died,
and Wǎn stood out among his peers,
placed above other officials.
He showed neither sorrow
nor joy,
his demeanor and conduct
as calm as usual,
gradually earning everyone's respect.
Ibid,
_Annals of Emperor Míng of Wèi_.
When Huán Wēn came for the imperial funeral,
he stopped at Xīntíng,
arrayed his troops grandly,
intending to shift the Jìn dynasty's rule,
and summoned Xiè Ān and Wáng Tǎnzhī,
planning to kill them at the meeting.
Ān calmly took his seat,
and after sitting,
said: "I have heard that when feudal lords uphold the Way,
their defense lies in the four borders.
Why does Your Excellency need to place men behind the wall?"
Wēn laughed:
"I simply had to do so."
They then chatted and laughed for a long while.
. _Book of Jìn: Biography of Xiè Ān_.
When Fú Jiān's million-strong army threatened the Wú River,
and Huán Wēn's imperial ambitions aimed to topple Jìn,
the officials changed their minds,
and near and far were shaken with fear.
Yet through composure, he thwarted treacherous plots;
through banquet strategies, he cleared the host of enemies.
Ibid.
Mùróng Gēn said to King Wěi of Yān:
"The Grand Tutor and Grand Preceptor are plotting treason; I request to lead the imperial guards to execute them." Kězúhúnshì was about to agree.
Wěi said: "These two lords are
close relatives and worthies of the state,
chosen by the late emperor,
entrusted with the care of the orphaned and widowed.
They certainly would not do such a thing.
How do we know it is not the Grand Tutor who intends to rebel!"
Thus, they stopped.
． From Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Jìn Hǎixī Gōng.
Yān had just suffered a great mourning,
and both inside and outside, there was fear and anxiety.
The Grand Tutor, Kè, behaved as usual,
and people did not see any sign of worry on his face.
Whenever he went out,
he was followed by only one person on foot.
Someone advised him that he should take strict precautions himself,
but Kè said: "People's hearts are just now fearful;
we should pacify them to calm them down.
Why should we alarm and disturb ourselves further?
What would the masses look up to then!"
From then on, people's hearts gradually settled.
Ibid.,
Jìn Jì.
The emperor passed away,
and the ministers did not dare to establish a successor.
Someone said: "We must wait for the Grand Marshal to decide."
Wáng Biāozhī said:
"When the Son of Heaven passes away,
the crown prince succeeds him.
How could the Grand Marshal have any objection!"
Ibid.
Wèi had over a thousand newly relocated Chìlè households,
who suffered under the generals and officials.
They planned to wait until the grass grew and the cattle and horses grew fat,
and then flee back to the northern desert.
Liú Jié and Ān Yuán petitioned to relocate them to Héxī.
The King of Wèi said: "These people's customs
have been free and scattered for a long time.
They are like deer in a pen:
if pressed, they will charge and break out;
if given ease, they will settle on their own.
I have my own way to handle them;
there is no need to relocate them."
． From Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Sòng Tàizǔ.
After Wén Dì of the Later Zhōu passed away,
Xiàomǐn Dì was still young.
Although the Duke of Zhōngshān, Hù, had received the dying mandate, his rank and status were originally low,
and the various lords each plotted to seize power.
Hù was deeply worried about this
and secretly consulted Yú Jǐn.
Jǐn said: "I have long received the special favor of the Prime Minister.
Today, I will certainly strive for this even at the cost of my life.
If we decide on a plan in front of everyone,
you, my lord, must not decline."
The next day,
the various lords held a meeting.
Jǐn said: "In the past, when the imperial house was in peril,
the Prime Minister was determined to save and restore it.
Now Heaven has sent down disaster,
and he has suddenly abandoned all his officials.
Although the heir is young,
the Duke of Zhōngshān is like a nephew in kinship,
and moreover, he received the dying entrustment.
Military and state affairs
should rightly be entrusted to him."
His words and expression were stern and forceful,
and everyone was moved and awed.
Hù said: "This is a family matter;
how dare I, Hù, decline!"
Since Jǐn was of equal status with Wén Dì and others,
Hù always showed him respect and courtesy.
At this point,
Jǐn then said: "If you, my lord, take charge of military and state affairs,
we, Jǐn and others, will have something to rely on."
He then bowed twice.
Pressed by Jǐn,
the various lords also bowed.
Thus, the consensus was settled.
． From Běishǐ, Yú Jǐn Běnzhuàn.
Someone advised the emperor, saying: "The reason the Turks repeatedly invade Guānzhōng is
because beautiful women, jade, and silk are all in Cháng'ān.
If we abandon Cháng'ān and do not make it the capital,
then the barbarian invasions will cease on their own."
The emperor thought this was right
and sent the Vice Director of the Secretariat, Yǔwén Shìjí, to cross the Southern Mountains to Fán and Dèng,
to survey habitable land,
intending to move the capital there.
The Crown Prince Jiànchéng, the Prince of Qí Yuánjí, and Péi Shū all supported this plan.
The Prince of Qín, Shìmín, remonstrated: "The troubles caused by the Róng and Dí
have existed since ancient times.
Your Majesty, with your divine martial prowess, rose like a dragon,
and brilliantly established yourself in the Central Plains.
You have a million elite troops,
invincible in all campaigns.
How can you, because of barbarian invasions disturbing the borders,
hastily move the capital to avoid them,
bringing shame upon the land within the Four Seas,
and becoming a laughingstock for a hundred generations!"
Thus, they stopped.
． From Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Táng Gāozǔ Jì.
Féng Àng was originally a person of Northern Yān
and was promoted to Commander due to military achievements.
Someone accused Àng of rebellion,
and Tàizōng issued an edict to dispatch troops to suppress him.
Wèi Zhèng remonstrated: "We should win him over with virtue."
The emperor then sent Wéi Shūxié to instruct Àng.
Àng sent his son Zhìdài to serve in the court.
The emperor said: "Zhèng's one word is worth more than a hundred thousand troops."
From Tángshū.
The emperor said to his attending ministers: "A diviner said that within five days, urgent troops will enter the palace.
You, my ministers, must prepare for me."
Zhāng Yuè said: "This must be a slanderer trying to sow discord with the Crown Prince.
I hope Your Majesty will have the Crown Prince oversee state affairs;
then the rumors will cease on their own."
． From Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Táng Xuánzōng.
Among the people, there was a rumor that the emperor was selecting women to fill the palace harem.
When the emperor heard this,
he ordered the relevant officials to prepare oxcarts at the Chóngmíng Gate,
and personally selected the useless women from the rear palace to be sent back to their homes.
He issued an edict: "Even within the private chambers of the palace,
I have ordered the dismissal and return of women;
among the common people,
this should be fully understood."
Ibid.
Guō Xī was in Bīnzhōu,
allowing his soldiers to commit violence,
and the Military Governor Bái Xiàodé was troubled by this.
Duàn Xiùshí volunteered to fill the post of Capital Military Police Chief.
After being appointed for a month,
seventeen soldiers from Xī's army entered the market to take wine,
stabbed the old wine seller with a knife,
and damaged the brewing vessels.
Xiùshí lined up soldiers, took the heads of the seventeen men, impaled them on spears,
and planted them at the market gate.
Xī's entire camp was in an uproar,
and all put on armor.
Xiàodé was frightened
and summoned Xiùshí, saying: "What shall we do?"
Xiùshí said:
"It's nothing serious.
Allow me to go and resolve it."
Xiàodé sent several dozen men to accompany him,
but Xiùshí declined them all,
asking only an old lame man to lead his horse to Xī's gate.
The armored soldiers came out,
and Xiùshí, smiling, entered,
saying: "To kill one old soldier,
why all this armor!
I have brought my own head here."
The armored soldiers were stunned.
He then admonished them: "Is the Regular Attendant letting you down,
or is the Vice Marshal letting you down?
Why do you want to ruin the Guō family with rebellion!"
Xī came out,
and Xiùshí reproached him, saying:
"The Vice Marshal's achievements fill heaven and earth;
he should think of maintaining them from beginning to end.
Now the Regular Attendant allows his soldiers to commit violence,
which will soon lead to rebellion.
If rebellion occurs, the Vice Marshal will be implicated;
if the rebellion stems from the Regular Attendant,
then how much of the Guō family's merit and fame
will remain!"
Before he finished speaking,
Xī bowed twice and said: "You have kindly taught me, Xī, with the right way;
your grace is immense,
how dare I not obey your command!"
He turned and scolded his attendants: "All of you, remove your armor
and disperse back to your squads.
Anyone who dares to make noise will die!"
． From Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Táng Dàizōng.
The Huíhé and Tǔbō combined forces to besiege Jīngyáng.
Guō Zǐyí said: "Now we are outnumbered and cannot match them;
it is difficult to win by force.
In the past, we had a very strong covenant with the Huíhé.
It would be better to go personally and persuade them;
we might subdue them without fighting."
He then went out through the gate with several cavalrymen,
and had someone shout: "The Lord of the Mandate has come!"
The Huíhé were greatly surprised.
Their great commander, Yàogéluó,
held his bow and fitted an arrow in front of the battle line.
Zǐyí removed his helmet, shed his armor, threw down his spear, and advanced.
The various chieftains of the Huíhé looked at each other and said: "It is him!"
They all dismounted and bowed in a circle.
Yàogéluó said: "Huái'ēn deceived us,
saying that the Heavenly Khagan had passed away,
and the Lord of the Mandate had also died,
and that China had no ruler.
That is why we dared to come with him.
Now we know that the Heavenly Khagan is in the upper capital,
and the Lord of the Mandate is again commanding troops here.
Huái'ēn has also been killed by Heaven.
How could we, my people, be willing to fight with you, my lord!"
Ibid.
Wáng Tóngzhī of Jīngzhōu plotted to rebel,
planning to act at dawn on the Xīnyǒu day when the alarm was sounded.
The night before,
someone reported this;
Duàn Xiùshí pretended to summon the timekeeper,
and scolded him,
Because they had lost their integrity,
he ordered that whenever the night watch came to report,
he would delay them for several moments,
thus causing the fourth watch to arrive at dawn,
and the mutiny did not materialize.
Same as above.
Wáng Hóng, the Military Commissioner of Róngguǎn, served as Junior Deputy of Hézhōng and administered the prefecture.
A subordinate general, Líng Zhèng, was violent and tyrannical,
and Hóng restrained him.
When his followers took advantage of the night to stage a rebellion,
Hóng learned of it,
so he intentionally shortened the water clock by several moments to alter the timing,
startling the rebels,
who fled in disarray.
Same as above.
Péi Dù, the Chief Minister of the Secretariat,
lost his seal.
Dù remained composed.
His attendants reported that the seal had been found in its original place,
but Dù did not respond.
When someone asked him the reason,
he said: "This must be a clerk who stole it to stamp documents;
if pressed urgently, he would throw it into water or fire,
but if handled leniently, it would return to its place."
People admired his wisdom and magnanimity.
*Comprehensive Mirror*.
False rumors spread of bandits approaching,
causing scholars and commoners to panic and flee in all directions,
raising dust everywhere.
Officials from various departments of the two bureaus heard of it,
and all ran away.
Zhèng Tán and Lǐ Shí were in the Secretariat,
watching as clerks and soldiers gradually escaped.
Tán said to Shí: "The situation seems unusual;
we should go out and avoid it."
Shí replied: "The position of chief minister is esteemed and weighty,
the focus of people's hearts,
and must not be taken lightly!
Now, the truth of the matter is unknown;
by sitting firmly and stabilizing it,
we may yet calm things.
If even the chief ministers flee,
then chaos will erupt both inside and outside.
Moreover, if disaster truly strikes,
avoiding it would not save us!"
Tán agreed with him.
Shí sat reviewing documents,
composed and unperturbed.
Chén Jūnshǎng, the Grand General of the Left Imperial Guard, led his troops to stand at the gate of Wàngxiān,
saying to the imperial envoy: "If bandits arrive,
it is not too late to close the gates;
let us observe the changes calmly,
and not show weakness!"
By late afternoon, order was restored.
That day,
had it not been for Shí and Jūnshǎng stabilizing the situation,
the capital would have nearly fallen into chaos again.
*Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Governance - Táng Wénzōng*.
Biographies
When Qián Liú was enfeoffed as the King of Wúyuè,
large-scale corvée labor was imposed,
causing soldiers to lament and resent.
Someone wrote on the government gate at night: "No end in sight,
no end in sight,
just finished building walls, now digging moats again."
Liú saw it upon exiting,
and ordered a clerk to write in response: "No end in sight,
no end in sight,
just finished spring clothes, now winter clothes."
The lamentations and resentment immediately ceased.
Táo Yuè's *Supplements to the History of the Five Dynasties*.
Collections
Eyebrows like pine trees and snow, matching the Four Haos,
with banter and laughter, they could secure the crown prince.
Lǐ Bái.
Using loyalty and righteousness to move those coerced into following,
with magnanimity to pacify those of wavering hearts.
Liú Bīngù.
When the steps of heaven are fraught with difficulty,
and the land within the seas is torn asunder,
the world is in turmoil,
a single word can bring peace.
Liú Chángqīng.
Sweeping away the filth and grime,
to secure peace for ten thousand generations.
Dù Mù.
Our Dynasty
There were false rumors that Nánzhào intended to invade Shǔ,
prompting the governor of Shǔ to mobilize troops and build city walls,
greatly alarming and disturbing the people.
The court heard of this,
and ordered Lord Zhāng Wéndìng to transfer to govern Western Shǔ.
The lord declared that this must be false.
Upon entering the region, he advocated calming it with composure,
issuing an order: "If bandits come,
I will face them myself.
Those who spread false rumors
will be executed."
He sent back all the mobilized troops,
halted the wall-building corvée,
and on the Lantern Festival,
kept the city gates open all night,
whereupon Shǔ became greatly pacified.
From Sū Dōngpō's epitaph for the lord.
Like Hàn's Jí Àn, Xiāo Wàngzhī, Lǐ Gù, Wú's Zhāng Zhāo, Táng's Lord Wèi Zhèng, and Dí Rénjié, all sacrificed themselves for righteousness,
not coming when summoned,
not leaving when dismissed,
standing solemnly in court,
so that wolves and foxes would devour each other,
thus able to dissolve calamity before it formed,
and rescue from peril before it culminated.
Same as above,
*In Praise of Wáng Yuánzhī's Portrait*.
When Zhāng Guāiyá governed Chéngdū,
in the aftermath of war,
people harbored rebellious intentions.
One day, during a grand military review as the troops assembled,
as soon as he appeared,
the crowd shouted "Wànsuì" three times,
and Guāiyá also dismounted,
faced northeast and shouted three times,
then took the reins and proceeded,
and the crowd did not dare to clamor.
From Wáng Qīngchén's *History of Dust*.
History
Jìn attacked Qí.
Zhōu Chuò attacked the eastern gate,
his left-side chariot horse was pressed,
so he turned back within the gate,
and counted the door leaves with a tally stick.
． The commentary in Zuǒ Zhuàn, 18th Year of Xiānggōng states: "To show he was not afraid."
Wú and Chǔ troops were short on provisions,
starving,
and wanted to retreat,
so they repeatedly challenged to battle,
but the enemy never came out.
At night,
panic broke out in the army,
with internal attacks and disturbances,
reaching even the commander's tent.
Zhōu Yàfū remained firmly lying down without rising.
After a short while,
calm was restored.
． From the "Biography of Zhōu Yàfū" in the History of the Western Hàn.
Jì Zūn served as a general,
and in selecting officers, he always employed Confucian methods.
When hosting banquets with music,
he would invariably perform elegant songs and play pitch-pot.
． From the "Biography of Jì Zūn" in the History of the Eastern Hàn.
The various generals, seeing the battle going unfavorably,
were mostly fearful.
Wú Hàn, however, remained composed as usual,
organizing and sharpening weapons,
and inspiring the officers and soldiers.
The Emperor said: "Wú Hàn somewhat meets expectations,
standing firm as an enemy state!"
Same source as above.
Zhāng Huàn served as a General of the Gentlemen of the Household.
The Wūhuán rebelled,
and set fire to the army gates.
Huàn sat within his tent,
discussing and lecturing with his disciples as if nothing was amiss,
and the crowd gradually calmed.
From the History of the Eastern Hàn.
The Wèi army encamped at Xīngshì,
Fèi Yī was granted the imperial tally,
and led troops to resist them.
The Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments, Lái Mǐn, came to bid Yī farewell,
requesting to play a game of wéiqí together.
At that time, urgent dispatches were flying back and forth.
Men and horses were armored,
and the solemn carriage was ready,
yet Yī and Mǐn focused intently on their game,
showing no sign of weariness.
Mǐn said: "I was just testing you!
You truly are a capable man,
one who will surely handle the enemy."
When Yī arrived,
the enemy retreated.
． From the "Biography of Fèi Yī" in the Records of Shǔ.
Cross-reference to "Victory Through Composure."
Fèi Yī succeeded Jiǎng Wǎn as Imperial Secretary,
handling affairs from morning till evening,
while also receiving guests in between,
and even engaging in board games without interruption.
From the Supplementary Biography of Fèi Yī.
Jìn's Yáng Hù governed Xiāngyáng.
In the army,
he often wore light fur and loose belts,
not donning armor himself,
and under his command tent,
he had no more than a dozen or so guards.
． From the Comprehensive Mirror in the Jìn Wǔdì Annals.
Liú Chóu took refuge in a fortress during the turmoil,
and hundreds of non-Hàn traders sought to harm him,
but Chóu showed no fear,
instead taking a reed pipe and playing it,
performing tunes of "Leaving the Frontier" and "Entering the Frontier,"
to stir their thoughts of wandering.
Thereupon, the group of non-Hàn people wept and left.
From the History of Jìn.
Cross-reference to "Shifting People's Hearts" and "Hearts Are Easily Moved."
Xiè Ài resisted Má Qiū, a general under Shǐ Jìlóng.
Ài rode in a light carriage,
wearing a white hat,
and advanced with drums beating.
Qiū was enraged,
and charged to attack him.
Ài's left and right were greatly disturbed.
They urged Ài to mount a horse, but Ài
refused,
instead dismounting and sitting on a folding chair,
directing and deploying troops.
The enemy did not dare advance.
From the History of Jìn.
Chái Shào campaigned against the Tǔyùhún,
and the enemy occupied high ground to shoot at Shào's army,
causing the soldiers to pale with fear.
Shào sat calmly,
sent someone to play the pipa,
and had two women dance,
which puzzled the enemy,
who stopped shooting to watch.
From the History of Táng.
Púgù Huái'ēn lured the Tǔbō and others southward,
urgently summoning Guō Zǐyí,
who stationed at Jīngyáng.
The Uighurs said: "We heard the Lord Guo had died.
If the Lord Guo is truly alive,
how can we see him?"
Zǐyí prepared to go out,
but the generals pleaded with him not to.
Zǐyí said: "The enemy outnumbers us many times over,
and our strength cannot match them now,
but utmost sincerity can move even gods,
let alone these enemies!"
The generals requested to select five hundred armored cavalry as escort,
but Zǐyí said: "That would only invite harm."
He then had it announced: "The Lord Guo is coming!"
The enemy was initially suspicious,
holding bows drawn and arrows ready.
Zǐyí slowly emerged with a few dozen cavalry,
removed his helmet, and addressed them: "Are you well?
We long shared loyalty and righteousness,
why has it come to this?"
The Uighurs all laid down their weapons, dismounted, and bowed in unison, saying: "It is truly our father."
Zǐyí summoned their chieftains,
served each wine,
gave them silks and brocades,
and they conversed joyfully as before.
He then sent the chieftains to the court.
． From the Old History of Táng, his biography.
Cross-reference to "Hearts Are Easily Moved."
Dáxī Bàohuī, the Military Commissioner of Shǎn-Guó, poisoned the Jiedushi Shǐ Zhāng Quàn,
and took over military affairs.
The Emperor said to Lǐ Mì: "I must trouble you to go."
He appointed Mì as the Defense and Transport Commissioner of Shǎn-Guó.
The Emperor wanted to send the Shence Army to escort Mì to his post,
and asked, "How many men do you need?"
Mì replied: "I request to enter alone on a single horse."
The Emperor said: "How can you enter alone on a single horse?"
Mì replied: "The people of Shǎn city
are not accustomed to defying orders;
this is solely Bàohuī's wrongdoing.
If we approach with a large army,
they will surely barricade themselves.
If I now go alone to the outskirts,
if they send a large force, I am no match,
but if they send a minor officer to kill me,
he might well be turned to my use."
The Emperor said: "I am about to employ you greatly;
I would rather lose Shǎn Prefecture
than lose you."
Mì replied: "No one else could surely enter."
Mì met with the reporting officials and officers from Shǎn Prefecture in Cháng'ān,
and told them: "The Sovereign, due to famine in Shǎn and Guó,
has not given me the tally but appointed me Transport Commissioner,
intending for me to supervise grain from Jiāng and Huái for relief.
The Shǎn Prefecture camp is at Xià County;
if Bàohuī is capable,
he should be made its commander.
If he achieves merit,
he will be granted the command tally."
Bàohuī's spies rushed to report this,
and Bàohuī felt somewhat reassured.
Mì then hastened forward.
Bàohuī did not send his officers to greet him,
only sending scouts in succession.
Mì lodged at Qūwò,
and the officers came to greet him without awaiting Bàohuī's order,
so Bàohuī also came out to meet him.
Mì praised his acting role in preserving the city's defenses,
entered the city to assume duty,
and thus those with rebellious inclinations were reassured.
Bàohuī then fled,
and his whereabouts were unknown.
． From the Comprehensive Mirror in the Táng Dézōng Annals.
Péi Dù served as Chancellor in the Secretariat,
and lost the seal.
Dù remained as composed as ever.
His attendants reported that the seal was found in its original place,
but Dù did not respond.
When asked the reason,
he said: "This must be a clerk stealing it to stamp documents;
if pressed, he would discard it in fire or water,
but if lenient, he would return it to its place."
People admired his discernment and magnanimity.
． From the Comprehensive Mirror in the Táng Annals.
Also cross-reference to "Composure in Human Affairs."
Zhāng Cóngbīn led troops into Luòyáng,
and officials in Dàliáng were all terrified,
but Sāng Wéijìn alone calmly directed military affairs,
his expression unperturbed,
receiving and responding to guests,
maintaining his usual demeanor,
which somewhat calmed the public mind.
．． From the Comprehensive Mirror in the Later Jìn Gāozǔ Annals.
Collection
Xiè Ānshí of the Eastern Mountains,
Amidst conversation and laughter, quelled the barbarian dust.
From "The Collected Works of Lǐ Tàibái".
Cross-reference: "Achieving victory through composure".
Official documents piled up like mountains,
Yet he handled them with ease.
From "The Collected Works of Liú Bīnkè".
In the state of
Zhào, King Wén delighted in swordsmanship.
Prince Kuī was troubled by this,
And sought among his attendants one who could sway the king's favor away from swords.
His attendants said, "Zhuāngzǐ would surely be capable."
Zhuāngzǐ, appearing before the king, said, "There is the sword of the Son of Heaven,
And there is the sword of the feudal lords.
With a single use of the Son of Heaven's sword,
The feudal lords are corrected,
And all under heaven submit.
The sword of the feudal lords,
Like the rumble of thunder,
Within the four borders,
Leaves none who do not pay homage.
The sword of the common man,
Is no different from cockfighting,
Once life is severed,
It is of no use to state affairs.
Now, Your Majesty holds the position of the Son of Heaven but favors the sword of the common man;
I secretly deem it unworthy for Your Majesty."
Thereupon, King Wén did not leave his palace for three months,
And the swordsmen all, in their places, submitted to their fate.
. From "Zhuāngzǐ Speaks of Swords".
Duke Āi of Lǔ wished to expand his residence westward,
The historian objected,
Considering westward expansion inauspicious.
Duke Āi changed countenance and grew angry.
His attendants repeatedly advised, but he would not listen.
So he asked his tutor, Zǎi Zhésuī,
Saying, "I wish to expand my residence westward,
Yet the historian deems it inauspicious.
What is your view?"
Zǎi Zhésuī replied, "Under heaven, there are three inauspicious things,
Westward expansion of a residence is not among them."
Duke Āi was greatly pleased and delighted.
After a moment,
He asked again, "What are the three inauspicious things?"
The response was: "Not practicing benevolence and righteousness,
Is the first inauspicious;
Insatiable desires and greed,
Are the second inauspicious;
Not heeding strong remonstrance,
Is the third inauspicious."
Duke Āi fell silent, deeply reflecting,
Sobered, he turned his thoughts inward,
And thus did not proceed with the westward expansion.
. From "Huáinánzǐ: Instructions on the Human World".
Cross-reference: "Skilled in speech".
Historian
The people of Chǔ attacked Xiāo.
The troops were suffering greatly from the cold.
The king inspected the three armies,
patting and encouraging them.
The soldiers of the three armies,
all felt as if clad in silk floss.
. "Zuǒzhuàn, Xuān'gōng 12th Year".
Cross-reference: "Being One with the Soldiers".
Duke Píng of Sòng was building a tower,
which hindered the agricultural harvest.
The builders sang work songs,
which Zǐhǎn heard.
He personally took a whip,
to urge on the builders,
saying: "We petty people,
all have houses to shelter from dryness, dampness, cold, and heat.
Now our lord is building a tower, and if it is not completed quickly,
what use is our labor?"
The singing then ceased.
. "Zuǒzhuàn, Xiāng'gōng 17th Year".
Duke Píng of Jìn shot at a quail but failed to kill it,
and had Shù Xiāng capture it, but he lost it.
The duke was angry, detained him, and was about to execute him.
Shū Xiàng said: "You must kill him quickly,
and not let the news spread far."
The ruler showed embarrassment on his face,
and then hastily released him.
"Guóyǔ".
Chǔ Yōu Mèng,
often used jokes and laughter to remonstrate.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ had a beloved horse,
which died.
He ordered his ministers to mourn it,
and wished to bury it with the coffin and outer coffin of a senior official.
Those around him argued against it,
but he would not listen.
Mèng entered the palace gate,
looked up to the sky and wailed loudly,
saying: "The great state of Chǔ,
what could it possibly lack?
Yet to bury it with the rites of a senior official,
is too meager.
I request to bury it with the rites of a ruler."
The king said: "How so?"
He replied: "I request a coffin carved from jade,
an outer coffin of patterned catalpa wood,
pián and maple trees and camphorwood for the outer enclosure,
dispatch armored soldiers to dig the tomb,
the old and weak to carry the earth,
with Qí and Zhào in attendance in front,
Hán and Wèi flanking behind,
sacrificial offerings of the Great Tài-láo sacrifice,
and a fief of ten thousand households to maintain it.
When the feudal lords hear of this,
they will all know that Your Majesty values horses above men."
The king said: "Has my fault reached such a point!"
Then he had the horse handed over to the Grand Provisioner,
ordering that the matter not be long known throughout the land.
. "Shǐjì, Guījī Lièzhuàn".
Cross-reference: "Reversing the Edge for Effect" and "Guījī".
The king of Zhào had newly ascended the throne,
and Qín urgently attacked Zhào.
Zhào sought help from Qí,
and Qí said: "You must send Prince Cháng'ān as a hostage,
then we will send troops."
The queen mother refused,
and the senior ministers strongly remonstrated.
The queen said:
"Whoever speaks of this again,
I will surely spit in their face."
Left Marshal Chù Lóng sought an audience,
and the queen awaited him with great anger.
The Left Marshal said:
"My humble son Shū Qí,
I dote on him in private,
and wish, before I fill the ditches, to entrust him to you."
The queen mother said: "Do men also love their young sons?"
He replied: "More than women!
I privately believe that if parents love their children, they plan deeply for them.
Now you, noble lady, honor Prince Cháng'ān's position but do not let him achieve merit for the state now,
once the mountains and hills crumble,
how will Prince Cháng'ān maintain himself in Zhào?
I consider your planning for Prince Cháng'ān to be short-sighted."
The queen mother said: "Very well.
Do as you see fit with him."
Thereupon he was sent as a hostage to Qí.
. "Shǐjì, Zhào Shìjiā".
Cross-reference: "Skillful in Speech".
Máo Jiāo said: "Your Majesty has committed reckless and perverse acts,
are you unaware of it?
You had your false father torn apart by chariots,
your two younger brothers beaten to death in sacks,
and exiled your mother to Yōng.
The actions of Jié and Zhòu did not go this far.
If the world hears of this,
it will completely disintegrate,
and none will turn towards Qín."
The king descended from the dais,
personally took his hand and said: "Sir, hasten to rise and dress,
I now wish to accept your advice!"
The king himself drove the carriage,
left the left seat empty,
went to fetch the queen mother,
brought her back to Xiányáng,
and restored their mother-son relationship as before.
. "Tōngjiàn, Qín Jì".
The emperor was in the Southern Palace,
and saw the generals talking in pairs.
He asked Zhāng Liáng about it.
Liáng said: "Your Majesty won the empire together with these men,
yet you have enfeoffed only old acquaintances,
and executed only personal enemies.
Now they fear being punished for any fault,
so they gather to plot rebellion."
The emperor said: "What to do?"
Liáng said: "Take someone you have long disliked,
whom all ministers know is the most extreme case,
and enfeoff him first to show the ministers."
The emperor enfeoffed Yōng Chǐ.
All the ministers were pleased,
saying: "Even Yōng Chǐ is made a marquis,
we have nothing to fear!"
Earlier,
Yōng Chǐ had not wished to serve the Lord of Pèi,
and the Lord of Pèi resented Chǐ.
Cross-reference: "Stabilizing Important Matters".
"Xī Hàn".
Liáng, through events, offered loyalty to change the emperor's mind,
ensuring the ruler above had no fault of favoritism,
the subjects below no schemes of suspicion and fear,
and the state was free from anxiety.
For later generations,
one like Liáng may be called skilled in remonstrance!
. "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Gāozǔ Jì".
Mòdú sent a letter full of obscenities and insults.
Fán Kuài said: "I wish to lead a hundred thousand troops to rampage through the Xiōngnú!"
Jì Bù said: "Kuài should be beheaded!
Previously, the Xiōngnú besieged Emperor Gāozǔ at Píngchéng,
the Hàn troops numbered three hundred twenty thousand,
with Kuài as supreme general,
yet he could not break the siege.
Now the songs and chants have not yet ceased,
the wounded are just recovering,
yet Kuài wants to shake the empire,
wildly claiming to rampage with a hundred thousand troops—
this is sheer deception.
Moreover, the barbarians are like beasts;
their good words are no cause for joy,
their bad words no cause for anger."
Empress Dowager Gāo said: "Well said!"
. "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Huìdì Jì".
Féng Táng said: "Even if Your Majesty obtained Lián Pō or Lǐ Mù,
you could not use them!"
The emperor was angry,
summoned him,
and reproached Táng: "Why do you insult me publicly,
could you not find a private moment!"
Táng said: "This rustic knows no taboos.
Wèi Shǎng was accused of a discrepancy of six heads in reported merits,
and Your Majesty stripped his rank and punished him."
The emperor was pleased.
He ordered Táng to bear the tally and pardon Wèi Shǎng,
reappointing him as governor of Yúnzhōng.
. "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Wéndì Jì".
The county authorities had no money,
and sought to borrow horses from the people.
Some people hid their horses,
so not enough horses were gathered.
The emperor was angry,
and wanted to execute the magistrate of Cháng'ān.
The Right Inner Secretary Jí Àn said: "The magistrate of Cháng'ān is not at fault.
Only if you execute your servant Àn,
will the people be willing to produce their horses."
The emperor fell silent.
. "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Wǔdì Jì".
The emperor casually said to the leader of the imperial guards Mǎ Yuán: "I deeply regret having executed so many governors and chancellors before."
He replied: "They died for their crimes;
how can that be many!
But since the dead are gone,
they cannot live again."
The emperor laughed heartily.
. "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Guāngwǔdì Jì".
In the past, Lǐngnán presented fresh longans and lychees,
with relay stations every ten lǐ,
and posts every five lǐ,
for day and night delivery.
Táng Qiáng submitted a memorial: "I have heard that the superior does not consider delicacies a virtue,
nor the inferior consider tribute meals an achievement.
I observe that the seven comman series of Jiāozhǐ present fresh longans and such;
the southern regions have scorching land,
vicious insects and fierce beasts,
ceaseless along the roads,
leading to the danger of encountering death.
The dead cannot live again,
but those to come can still be saved.
When these two items reach the palace,
they may not prolong life or increase longevity."
An edict was issued: "Order the Grand Provisioner to cease accepting such tributes."
. "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Hédì Jì".
Again, the practice of senior ministers observing the three-year mourning period was abolished.
. "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Gaozu of Sui."
After Empress Wende was buried,
the emperor built a multi-story tower in the garden,
to gaze toward Zhāolíng.
He invited Wèi Zhēng to ascend with him,
and after staring intently, Wèi Zhēng said: "Your servant's vision is dim and blurry,
I cannot see it."
The emperor pointed it out to him,
Wèi Zhēng said: "Your servant thought Your Majesty was looking toward Xiànlíng.
As for Zhāolíng,
your servant certainly sees it."
The emperor wept,
and had the tower demolished.
. "New Book of Tang: Biography of Wèi Zhēng."
The emperor went out hunting,
encountered rain,
and asked the Grand Master of Remonstrance, Gǔ Nàlǜ of Chānglè: "How can an oilcloth garment be made not to leak?"
He replied: "If it were made of tiles,
it certainly would not leak."
The emperor was pleased,
and because of this, he ceased the hunt.
. "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Gaozong of Tang."
Cross-reference "Quick in Response."
Quán Shàncái and Fàn Huáiyì mistakenly cut down a cypress tree at Zhāolíng.
Their crime warranted removal from office;
the emperor specifically ordered their execution.
Dí Rénjié memorialized: "The crime of these two does not deserve death."
The emperor said: "Shàncái and others cut down the cypress at the imperial tomb.
If I do not kill them, I would be unfilial."
Dí Rénjié persistently insisted without relenting.
The emperor's countenance changed,
and he ordered him to leave.
Dí Rénjié said: "To offend the ruler's countenance with straightforward remonstrance
has since ancient times been considered difficult.
Your servant believes encountering a Jié or Zhòu makes it difficult,
but encountering a Yáo or Shùn makes it easy.
Zhāng Shìzhī once said: 'Suppose there were a thief who stole a handful of soil from Chánglíng,
how would Your Majesty deal with him?'
Now, over a single cypress tree, you would kill two generals.
What will later generations say of Your Majesty?
The reason your servant dares not obey the decree
is the fear of plunging Your Majesty into unrighteousness,
and moreover, I would be ashamed to face Shìzhī underground."
The emperor's anger gradually subsided.
The two were removed from office
and exiled to Lǐngnán.
. "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Gaozong of Tang."
The emperor constructed a Mirror Hall.
When completed,
the emperor viewed it with Liú Rénguǐ.
Rénguǐ, startled, hurriedly descended from the hall.
The emperor asked the reason,
he replied: "Heaven has no two suns,
earth no two kings.
Just now I saw several emperors on the four walls—
what could be more inauspicious!"
Thereupon, the emperor immediately ordered them removed.
The emperor sent eunuchs along the river to transplant rare bamboos,
intending to plant them in the garden.
The eunuchs requisitioned boats to transport the bamboo,
and wherever they went, they acted violently and oppressively.
Passing through Jīngzhōu,
the Chief Administrator Sū Liángsì imprisoned them
and submitted a stern memorial of remonstrance.
The emperor issued a handwritten decree to comfort and instruct Liángsì,
ordering the bamboo to be discarded into the river.
Both from the same source above.
The Empress Dowager said to her attending officials: "Since Xìng,
Zhōu,
Jùnchén,
[and others] came,
upon their deaths,
there have been no more rebels."
Yáo Yuánchóng said: "Since the Chuígǒng era, those who have been executed for plotting rebellion
were mostly framed by Xìng and others,
who considered it their achievement.
When Your Majesty sent close ministers to interrogate them,
even the close ministers could not ensure their own safety—
how would they dare to change anything!
Those who were interrogated, if they recanted,
feared suffering cruel torture,
and preferred to die quickly.
Fortunately, Heaven enlightened the sage's heart,
and Xìng and others were executed.
Your servant guarantees with the lives of a hundred relatives
that from now on, no ministers inside or outside the court will rebel again.
If there were even slight concrete evidence,
I request to bear the crime of knowing but not reporting."
The Empress Dowager was pleased and said:
"In the past, the chief ministers all acquiesced to these matters,
making me appear as a ruler who indulged in cruel punishments.
Hearing your words,
they deeply accord with my heart."
. "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Empress Wǔ of Tang."
Lǐ Zhāodé spoke to the Empress Dowager, saying: "The Heavenly Emperor (Gāozōng)
was Your Majesty's husband;
the Crown Prince
is Your Majesty's son.
Your Majesty possesses the Son of Heaven's position,
which should be passed to your sons and grandsons as an enterprise for ten thousand generations.
How can you make a nephew your heir?
Since ancient times, I have never heard of a nephew becoming Son of Heaven and establishing a temple for his aunt."
The son of Yuè Sīhuì, not yet ten years old,
was confiscated into the Sīnóng administration,
reported an emergency,
and was granted an audience.
The Empress Dowager asked about the situation.
He replied: "My father is already dead,
my family is already ruined.
I only regret that Your Majesty's law is being manipulated by Jùnchén and others.
If Your Majesty does not believe my words,
I beg you to choose a court minister who is loyal, pure, and whom you normally trust,
to fabricate a confession of rebellion and give it to Jùnchén—
he will certainly accept it."
The Empress Dowager's mind was slightly awakened.
Both from the same source above.

There was heavy snow.
Sū Wèidào considered it an auspicious sign
and led the officials to offer congratulations.
The Palace Censor Wáng Qiúlǐ stopped him, saying: "Is snow in the third month considered auspicious snow,
and thunder in the twelfth month considered auspicious thunder?"
Wèidào did not listen.
After they entered,
Qiúlǐ alone did not congratulate,
but stepped forward and said: "Now, the warm yang energy is spreading,
plants and trees are sprouting and flourishing,
yet cold snow causes disaster—
how can one falsely claim it as auspicious!
Those offering congratulations are all flatterers."
The Empress Dowager dismissed the court because of this.
. "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Zhōngzōng of Tang."
Zhèng Pǔsī plotted rebellion.
When the affair was discovered,
the留守 of the Western Capital, Sū Huán, thoroughly investigated it.
Pǔsī's wife, the Fifth Lady, through sorcery, had gained favor with the Empress.
The emperor ordered Huán not to prosecute.

Empress Wǔ of Tang wanted to make Wǔ Sānsī the Crown Prince
and asked the chief ministers about it.
Dí Rénjié said: "Who is closer, aunt and nephew or mother and son?
If you establish the Prince of Lúlíng,
then after a thousand autumns and ten thousand years, he will eternally enjoy sacrifices in the ancestral temple.
If Sānsī is established, his temple would not include his aunt."
The Empress was moved and realized.

On the day of the Dragon Boat Festival,
Emperor Sùzōng summoned the hermit Lǐ Táng for an audience.
The emperor was holding his young daughter
and said to Táng: "I am thinking of her,
do not find it strange."
Táng said: "The Grand Emperor (Xuánzōng) today must also be thinking of Your Majesty."
The emperor shed tears.
. "New Book of Tang: Biography of Empress Zhāng of Sùzōng."
Since Prince Chéngtiān, Lǐ Tán, had been falsely accused by Zhāng Liángdì,
Sùzōng, in anger, imprisoned him until death,
and further sought to undermine the position of the future Emperor Dàizōng.
Lǐ Mì entered the court,
and during a casual conversation, the topic of Tán came up.
He said:
"I recall the 'Song of the Melons at the Yellow Terrace':
'Planting melons beneath the Yellow Terrace,
the melons ripen, the fruits abundant.
Picking one makes the melons better,
picking again leaves them sparse.
Picking three might still be tolerable,
picking four means returning with only the vines.'
Now one has already been picked—
I urge you not to pick again."
The emperor was startled,
and from then on, the plan to replace the heir was abandoned.
"Book of Tang."
Lǐ Guāngbì succeeded Guō Zǐyí in the Shuòfāng command.
The camps, soldiers, and banners remained unchanged,
yet as soon as Guāngbì issued his commands,
the army's spirit became even more sharp and vibrant.
. "Book of Tang: His Biography."
The Huíhé and Tǔbō joined forces and besieged Jīngyáng.
Guō Zǐyí said: "Now we are outnumbered and no match for the enemy,
it is difficult to prevail by force.
In the past, we had a very strong covenant with the Huíhé.
It would be better to go personally and persuade them—
we might succeed without fighting."
Thereupon, with a few cavalry, he rode out through the gate,
and had someone shout: "The Lord Prince has come!"
The Huíhé were greatly astonished.
Their great chieftain, Yàogēluó, held his bow with an arrow fitted, standing before the battle line.
Zǐyí removed his helmet and armor, threw aside his spear, and advanced.
The Huíhé chieftains looked at each other and said: "It is he!"
Géluó said: "Huái'ēn deceived me,
saying the Heavenly Khagan had already passed away,
and the Lord Minister had also departed this life,
that the Central Kingdom was without a ruler,
therefore I dared to come with him.
Now I know the Heavenly Khagan is in the upper capital,
the Lord Minister again commands troops here,
and Huái'ēn has been slain by Heaven,
how could we be willing to fight against you!"
． "Comprehensive Mirror of Emperor Dàizōng of Táng".

When Zhū Cǐ rebelled,
and the scholars were about to follow the rebellion,

Xīn Jīnggǎo killed a subordinate with private punishment,
the authorities reported that Xīn Jīnggǎo's crime deserved death,
and the Emperor was about to consent.
Lǐ Zhōngchén said: "Xīn Jīnggǎo should have died long ago!"
The Emperor asked the reason,
Zhōngchén said: "Xīn Jīnggǎo's uncles and brothers all died in battle,
only Xīn Jīnggǎo has survived until now,
I therefore think he should have died long ago."
The Emperor was moved with pity,
and demoted Xīn Jīnggǎo to Tutor of the Princes.
Zhōngchén seized opportunities to save people,
often in this manner.
． "Comprehensive Mirror of Emperor Dézōng of Táng".
When Hán Sīyàn was inspecting Jiànnán,
wealthy brothers in Yìzhōu were suing each other,
for years unresolved,

The two men realized,
and wept, saying: "Does the lord mean that brothers are born of the same milk!"
Then they requested to drop the lawsuit.
"History of Táng".
The Emperor asked Liǔ Gōngquán about brush techniques,
he replied: "If the heart is upright, the brush will be upright;
only when the brush is upright can it be emulated."
At that time, the Emperor was dissolute,
hence Gōngquán's reference.
The Emperor changed expression,
realizing he was using the brush to remonstrate.

Gāo Rénhòu besieged Zǐzhōu for long without capturing it,
so he wrote a letter and shot it into the city,
addressing its officers and soldiers: "Rénhòu cannot bear to see the city destroyed with jade and stone alike,
so I grant you a ten-day respite,
to let you accomplish your own merit.
If within ten days Yáng Shīlì is not sent out,
I will divide my visible troops into five rotations,
each taking turns day and night to attack,
which for us is quite easy,
but for you will surely be exhausting.
If not taken in five days,
we will advance from all sides,
and will certainly overcome it.
Consider this, gentlemen!"
After a few days,
Jūnxióng shouted to the crowd: "The Son of Heaven only punishes the chief villain,
others are not involved."
The crowd cheered "Long live!"
． "Comprehensive Mirror of Emperor Xīzōng of Táng".
The Emperor once hunted in Zhōngmóu,
trampling on the people's crops,
the magistrate of Zhōngmóu stood before his horse and admonished: "Your Majesty is the parent of the people,
how can you destroy what they eat,
causing them to die in ditches and gullies!"
The Emperor was angry,
shouted him away,
and was about to kill him.
Jìng Xīnmó chased and caught him before the horse,
reproaching him: "You, as county magistrate,
do you not know our Son of Heaven enjoys hunting?
Why let the people farm,
hindering our Son of Heaven's galloping!
Your crime deserves death!"
Then he requested execution,
the Emperor laughed and released him.
． "Comprehensive Mirror of Later Táng Zhuāngzōng".

Duke Jìng had a man care for his beloved horse,
the horse fell ill and died,
the duke was angry,
and ordered the horse keeper killed.
Yànzǐ requested to enumerate his crimes,
saying: "You have three crimes: having you care for the horse and you killed it,
first deserving death;
and killing the horse the duke always loved,
second deserving death;
causing the duke to kill a man over a horse,
the common people will surely resent and rebel,
the feudal lords will lightly attack our state,
third deserving death."
The duke sighed and said: "Pardon him."
"Spring and Autumn of Yànzǐ".
Wèi Wǔ on a campaign lost his way,

the plums sweet and sour can quench thirst."

When Zhènzhōu rebelled,
killing its commander Tián Hóngzhèng.
An edict ordered the lord to go and pacify.
Once on the way,
he sped forward and entered.
The lord announced:
"Men, let me clarify fortune and misfortune since the Tiānbǎo era for you.
Ān Lùshān, Shǐ Sīmíng, Lǐ Xīliè, Liáng Chóngyì, Zhū Cǐ, Wú Yuánjì, Lǐ Shīdào,
do any have sons or grandsons still alive?
Or any holding office?"
The crowd all said: "None."
He also said: "The Lord Minister returned Wèibó's six provinces to the court,
became military governor,
later reached Secretariat Director,
father and son both received command,
sons and grandsons even in childhood got good posts,
extreme nobility and favor,
glory shining throughout the land.
Liú Wù, Lǐ Yòu both governed major towns,
Wáng Chéngnián at just seventeen also held authority,
this all the army has heard."
The crowd then cheered: "The Vice Minister speaks rightly."
Huángfǔ Shí wrote "Conduct of Hán Yù".
Lǐ Huáiguāng rebelled.
The troops he led were all from Shuòfāng,
the lord knew his plan to join Zhū Cǐ,
was concerned,
went to Huáiguāng saying: "Your merit,
none in the land can match;
your faults,
have not reached the sovereign's ears.
If I go to the Emperor,
speak of your situation,
the Emperor is lenient and wise,
surely will pardon you,
how can you be a subject to Zhū Cǐ?
He, a subject, betrayed his lord,
if he succeeds,
what will you gain?
You are already Grand Commandant,
even if he favors you,
how can it surpass this?
He cannot serve his lord,
can he serve you?
If you can serve him,
can you not serve your lord?
He knows the land's anger,
faces execution soon,
so seeks accomplices in crime.
What benefit for you?
You have strength to oppose him,
better clearly break with him,
raise troops and attack him,
clear the palace and welcome the Son of Heaven,
then as a commoner submit and seek judgment from authorities.
Even with great faults,
they may be covered.
Who would dare criticize you then?"
After speaking,
Huáiguāng bowed: "Heaven sent you to save Huáiguāng's life."
Joyful and weeping,
the lord also wept.
Then he spoke to the officers and soldiers as to Huáiguāng,
they shouted: "Heaven sent you to save our army's lives."
Bowing and weeping,
the lord also wept,
thus Huáiguāng ultimately did not join Zhū Cǐ.
Hán's text "Conduct of Grand Tutor Dǒng".
People turned sorrow to joy,
the year changed from poor harvest to abundance.
Liú Bīnkè.
Cherishing owls yet expecting pleasant songs,

Severe winter turned to beautiful scenery,

Duke Wén Lǜ was governing Yìzhōu,
fond of excursions and banquets.
Once he feasted at the Qiánxiá's residence,
and the banquet did not conclude until late at night.
The attending soldiers began dismantling the horse stable for firewood,
and it could not be stopped.
When a military officer reported this to him,
the seated guests trembled with fear.
The Duke said: "The weather is indeed cold;
they may dismantle it for firewood."
His expression remained composed,
and he continued feasting as before.
The soldiers' morale deflated,
and they had no pretext for causing trouble.
From "Jì Wén".
When Wén Yànbó governed Yǒngxīng Army,
some claimed that Shǎnxī's iron coins were inconvenient
and requested they be entirely abolished.
Although the court did not comply,
many people learned of it,
and competed to use iron coins for purchases.
Sellers refused to accept them,
and many merchants in Cháng'ān closed their shops.
His subordinates requested to prohibit this,
but Yànbó said: "Doing so would only increase confusion and disturbance."
He then summoned silk fabric merchants,
brought out several hundred bolts of silk from his own household,
and had them sold,
saying: "Accept the payment entirely in iron coins;
do not use copper coins."
Thereupon, the public realized that iron coins would not be abolished,
and the markets stabilized.
Same as above.
During the Qìnglì era, a foreign merchant died in Guǎngzhōu,
and his pearls were confiscated by the state.
The Emperor ordered the pearls to be fetched
and used palace funds to purchase them for bestowal upon Consort Zhāng.
At that time, other consorts in the palace took this opportunity
to previously request imperial edicts for purchasing,
causing pearl prices in the capital to soar.
The Emperor became quite aware of this.
One day,
while admiring peonies in a side hall,
with consorts and concubines all gathered,
Consort Zhāng arrived last,
wearing the previously mentioned pearls as head ornaments
to boast among her peers.
As she approached the Emperor,
he saw them,
covered his face with his sleeve and said: "Covered all over with white clusters,
utterly without any taboo!"
The Consort felt ashamed,
blushed,
rose to change them,
and then he was greatly pleased.
From then on, no one in the palace wore pearls anymore,
and pearl prices greatly decreased.
From "Míng Dào Jí".
A single word directly breaks through a thousand words' confinement.
From Sū Dōngpō's poem.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of the Former Hàn,
someone killed a deer in the Shanglin Park.
The case was handed to the officials,
who sentenced him to death.
Dōngfāng Shuò said: "This man deserves death for three reasons: causing Your Majesty to kill a person over a deer,
is the first;
causing the world to hear that deer are valued more than people,
is the second;
if the Xiōngnú launch a sudden attack,
only deer can butt against them,
is the third."
The Emperor fell silent,
and then pardoned him.
