attacking and capturing commanderies and counties,
and the people fled in panic,
Hóng continued reciting classics unmoved.
From "Dōnghàn".
Anger without changing countenance,
joy without losing restraint,
these are most difficult to achieve.
From "Tōngjiàn: Hàn Xiàndì".
The integrity to drown oneself in the sea,
unmoved even by a thousand chariots.
From "Dōnghàn: Yímín Zhuàn Lùn".
Yíliáo faced the white blade with a steady expression.
From "Dōnghàn: Kǒng Róng Zhuàn".
When Kǒng Róng was executed,
his two sons were playing chess,
and remained unmoved when arrested.
Those around asked: "Your father is taken, yet you do not rise;
why?"
They replied: "How can the eggs remain unbroken when the nest is destroyed?"
Same as above.
Even when treading on a tiger,
his spirit remained tranquil.
From "Sānguó Míngchén Zàn".
When the First Sovereign entered Yìzhōu,
Liú Zhāng, Zhāng Fēi, and Zhūgě Liàng pacified the commanderies and counties.
Defeating Zhāng's general Yán Yán,
they captured him alive and said: "Our great army has arrived,
why not surrender?"
Yán said: "In our province, there are only beheaded generals,
no surrendering generals."
Fēi, enraged,
ordered his head be chopped off,
but Yán's expression did not change,
saying: "Chop it off if you must,
why the anger!"
Fēy, impressed, released him.
From "Shǔ Zhì".
Cross-reference "Unyielding".
Lù Xùn sent his confidant Hán Biǎn to present a memorial to the King of Wú,
but he was captured by patrols.
Zhūgě Jǐn, upon hearing, grew very fearful,
and wrote to Xùn: "The royal carriage has returned,
the enemy has captured Hán Biǎn,
and knows our situation fully;
moreover, the waters are receding,
we should leave quickly."
Xùn did not reply,
instead urging the planting of fēng and beans,
and playing chess and archery games with his generals as usual.
From "Tōngjiàn: Wèi Míng Jì".
The wise do not shift their gaze for small gains,
nor change their course for seeming intentions.
From "Tōngjiàn: Wèi Yuán Jì".
Jiǎ Chōng met Xiàhóu Xuàn.
He ordered courtesans to circle his boat three times,
but Tǒng acted as if he hadn't noticed.
Chōng said:
"This man from Wú is like a wooden figure with a stone heart."
"Jìn Shū".
Zhūgě Dàn was known for his inspiring spirit.
He often leaned against a pillar while reading,
and when thunder shook the pillar,
he continued reading undisturbed.
"Cáo Jiāzhī Jìn Jì".
When Kǒng Tǎn was dying,
Yǔ Bīng visited him
and wept.
Tǎn said indignantly: "A great man is about to die,
yet you don't ask about strategies to save the state and bring peace to the people,
but instead weep like women and children!"
Bīng deeply apologized.
"Tōng Jiàn Jìn Jì".
When Huán Wēn came to court,
some said he intended to kill Wáng and Xiè,
but Xiè Ān's expression remained unchanged.
Same as above.
When Yīn Hào was dismissed from office,
he continued discussing and chanting poetry without interruption.
Even his family members couldn't see
any sorrow of exile in him.
"Jìn Shū Běn Zhuàn".
Xiè Ān once went boating with Sūn Chuò,
when the wind rose and waves surged,
everyone else was frightened,
but Ān chanted and whistled calmly.
Same as above.
When Táo Kǎn was critically ill,
he submitted a memorial resigning his position.

He sent his Right Chief Clerk Yīn Xiàn to return the borrowed ceremonial banners, commander's insignia, canopy, the courtier's marten tail decoration, Grand Commandant's seal, and the official seals and credentials of the eight provincial governors;
all military supplies, weapons, livestock, and boats
had detailed inventories,
and the seals of warehouses
were personally kept by Kǎn.
He entrusted subsequent matters to Right Sima Wáng Qiānqī.
"Tōng Jiàn Jìn Chéng Jì".
Wèi Rǎn Mǐn sent Cháng Wěi as an envoy to Yān.
The ruler of Yān, Jùn, had Fēng Yù interrogate him with firewood piled nearby,
instructing Yù to privately persuade him,
saying: "Think carefully, sir,
don't pointlessly turn to ashes!"
Wěi sternly replied: "I've heard that the dead's flesh and bones return to earth,
while their spirit ascends to heaven.
If you grant me the favor
of quickly adding fuel and setting the fire,
enabling me to appeal to the Emperor above, that would suffice!
Since I came of age,
I haven't even deceived commoners,
let alone a ruler!
To distort my will for temporary agreement
is against my nature.
To speak honestly and fully,
even if it means sinking into the eastern sea,
I won't avoid it!"
"Tōng Jiàn Jìn Mù Jì".
Sun Shèng, the Secretary Supervisor from Tàiyuán, wrote "Jìn Chūnqiū",
recording events truthfully.
When Grand Marshal Wēn saw it,
he was angry
and said to Shèng's son: "The defeat at Fāngtóu was real,
but it wasn't as bad as your father described!
If this history is published,
it will concern the fate of your family!"
His son promptly bowed in apology,
requesting to revise it.
At that time, Shèng was elderly and living at home,
known for his upright and strict character
and adherence to rules.
His sons collectively wept and kowtowed,
begging him to consider the family's safety.
Shèng was furious
and refused.
So his sons secretly altered it.
However, Shèng had already made another copy
that was circulated abroad.
"Tōng Jiàn Jìn Hǎixī Gōng Jì".
Zhāng Róng was the magistrate of Fēngxī.
While traveling through dangerous mountains,
he was captured by Liáo bandits who intended to kill and eat him.
Róng remained calm,
and instead chanted in the Luòyáng style,
which so surprised the bandits that they spared him.
He sailed to Jiāozhōu,
encountering a storm at sea,
yet showed no fear,
chanting: "Dried fish can return to its homeland;
what is dried meat doing here?"
"Sòng Shū".
The Shānyīn Princess was licentious and willful,
and she fancied Chǔ Yànhuí,
so she told the Emperor.
The Emperor summoned Yànhuí to stay in the western upper chamber for ten days,
during which the princess visited him at night,
pressing him relentlessly.
Yànhuí stood upright,
from evening until dawn,
without wavering in his resolve.
The princess said to him: "You have a beard like a halberd,
why lack a man's desires?"
Yànhuí replied: "Though I am not clever,
how dare I initiate disorder?"
"Sòng Shū Běn Zhuàn".
When Zōng Ài held power in Wèi,
his authority shook the empire.
He once arrogantly received officials in the main hall,
and all the dukes and ministers below hurried to the courtyard to bow,
but only Gāo Yǔn ascended the steps and gave a deep bow without kneeling.
"Tōng Jiàn Sòng Wǔ Jì".
Liǔ Yuánjǐng knew disaster was imminent,
so he bid farewell to his mother,
donned his court robes, and rode in a carriage to answer the summons.
His younger brother, the Cavalry Sima Shūrén, in military attire,
led strong men to resist the order,
but Yuánjǐng firmly stopped him.
Once they left the alley,
soldiers arrived in force.
Yuánjǐng alighted and accepted execution.
"Tōng Jiàn Sòng Tàizǔ".
Wáng Jǐngwén was ordered to commit suicide.
When the edict arrived,
Jǐngwén was playing chess with a guest.
He opened the case and read it,
then placed it under the board,
his expression unchanged,
and continued to plan moves with his guest.
After the game ended,
he collected the pieces into the box,
and calmly said: "I have been ordered to die."
Only then did he show the edict to his guest.
"Tōng Jiàn Sòng Míng Jì".
Wáng Huì
was once by a winding stream
when a storm suddenly arose,
and all the seated guests scattered in panic.
Huì rose slowly,
no different from usual,
not altering his demeanor despite being drenched.
"Nán Shǐ".
The Emperor summoned Yǔn and asked: "Was the national history all written by Hào?"
Yǔn replied: "The 'Tàizǔ Jì'
was written by the former Editorial Director Dèng Yánhǎi;
the 'Xiāndì Jì' and the current record
I co-authored with Hào,
but I contributed more than he did."
The Emperor angrily said: "This is worse than Hào's case,
how can you survive?"
Jǐngmù interjected: "The Emperor's majesty is overwhelming,
causing Yǔn to be confused and misspeak.
When I asked earlier,
he said it was all Hào's work."
The Emperor asked: "Is that what the Crown Prince said?"
Yǔn responded:
"My crime deserves extermination of my clan,
so I dare not be untruthful.
His Highness, having had me as his tutor for long,
pities me and pleads for my life.
But he did not actually ask me,
and I cannot be confused."
The Emperor said to Jǐngmù: "How upright!
This is difficult for anyone to achieve,
yet he remains unwavering even facing death.
Moreover, he is honest with his ruler—
a loyal subject.
It's better to spare one guilty person
than to err."
"Běi Shǐ Gāo Yǔn Zhuàn".
Cross-reference to "Wú Yǐn".
Wèi Zhēng often remonstrated with the Emperor to his face,
and even when the Emperor was very angry,
his expression never changed.
Critics thought even ancient brave men like Bēn and Yù couldn't surpass him.
"Táng Shū Wèi Zhēng Zhuàn".
Lú Chéngqìng was in charge of evaluating officials,
and one official supervising transport
lost rice due to a storm.
His evaluation read: "Supervised transport and lost grain,
grade: middle-low."
The official remained composed,
and left without a word.
Chéngqìng, impressed by his poise,
changed it to: "Beyond his control,
grade: middle-middle."
The official showed neither joy
nor shame.
So it was changed again: "Undaunted by honor or disgrace,
grade: middle-high."
"Tōng Jiàn Táng Gāozōng Jì".
When Xú Gōng faced the thunderous wrath of authority,
he still upheld benevolence and forgiveness,
a match unseen in a thousand years.
"Táng Shū Xú Yǒugōng Zhuàn".
Yǒugōng
served as Chief Judge under Empress Wǔ,
who executed many people.
Liú Yīzhī secretly said to Jiǎ Dàyǐn: "Since the Empress has deposed the foolish and installed the wise,
It would be better to return governance. "
Dà Yǐn secretly memorialized this,
and the Empress Dowager ordered Wáng Běnlì to investigate it.
Běnlì proclaimed the imperial decree to him,
but Féi Zhī said: "Without passing through the Phoenix Pavilion and Luan Terrace,
how can it be called an imperial decree?"
The Empress Dowager was greatly angered,
and ordered his execution.
When Féi Zhī was first imprisoned,
Emperor Ruìzōng submitted a petition on his behalf pleading his case,
and all his relatives congratulated him,
but Féi Zhī said: "This will only hasten my death."
As he faced execution,
he bathed,
his expression calm as usual,
personally drafted a memorial of gratitude,
completing several pages immediately.
- From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Empress Wu of Tang"
Zhāng Chǔjīn and Wèi Yuánzhōng were both spared from death,
but exiled to Lingnan.
As they faced execution,
the Empress Dowager sent the Phoenix Pavilion Attendant Wáng Yǐnkè galloping on horseback to announce
their pardon.
The announcement reached the marketplace,
and those about to be executed all leaped for joy and cheered,
twisting and turning incessantly.
Only Yuánzhōng sat calmly as usual,
and when someone urged him to rise,
Yuánzhōng said: "We don't know if it's true or false."
When Yǐnkè arrived,
they urged him to rise again,
but Yuánzhōng said: "Wait until the decree is proclaimed."
Only after the decree was proclaimed
did he slowly rise,
performed the ceremonial dance,
and bowed twice, showing no expression of worry or joy throughout.
Same as above.
Lǐ Cháoyǐn successively dismissed over 1,400 irregularly appointed officials,
causing widespread resentment and criticism,
but Cháoyǐn paid no heed to any of it.
- From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Ruizong of Tang"
Yáng Guózhōng monopolized state affairs,
his power and influence were scorching hot,
and someone urged Zhāng Xún to meet him once,
promising prominent appointment,
but he replied: "He is precisely an ominous sign for the state,
and one cannot serve as an official in such court conditions."
- From "Book of Tang: Biography of Zhang Xun"
Líng Hú Chǔ served as the chief secretary in Tàiyuán.
When Zhèng Dān died suddenly at his post,
without having indicated arrangements for subsequent matters,
the army became tumultuous.
Suddenly several dozen cavalrymen with drawn swords forced Chǔ to the army gate at night,
with generals surrounding him,
ordering him to draft a final memorial.
Chǔ, amidst the naked blades,
grasped the brush and completed it immediately,
and when it was read aloud to the three armies,
all were moved to tears.
From then on, his reputation grew weighty.
From "Book of Tang"
Cross-referenced in the categories "Agility" and "Subordinates."
Lǐ Xīliè detained Yán Zhēnqīng and would not let him go.
Zhū Tāo, Wáng Wǔjùn, Tián Yuè, and Lǐ Nà each sent envoys to Xīliè,
presenting memorials declaring themselves subjects,
and summoned Yán Zhēnqīng to show him.
Zhēnqīng rebuked them, saying: "Do you know of Yán Gǎoqīng, who died cursing Ān Lùshān?
He was my elder brother.
I am eighty years old,
and know only to die upholding my integrity!"
Xīliè then had ten armored soldiers guard Zhēnqīng at his quarters,
dug a pit in the courtyard,
saying he intended to bury him alive.
Zhēnqīng remained composed,
and when he saw Xīliè, said:
"Life and death are already determined,
why so much ado!
Quickly give me a sword,
wouldn't that satisfy your mind!"
Xīliè then apologized to him.
- From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Annals of Emperor Dezong of Tang"
Sū Jiǎn repeatedly maneuvered to get Hán Wò appointed as chancellor,
and even sent a close subordinate to inform Wò,
but Wò said: "He actually wants to stain me with this!"
- From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Annals of Emperor Zhaozong of Tang"
Biographies
When Liú Yù reached Shānyáng,
he heard that Hé Wújì had suffered a major defeat,
so he packed his armor and advanced rapidly,
but when about to cross the river, the wind was fierce,
and everyone found it difficult,
but Yù said: "If it is Heaven's will,
the wind will cease of itself;
if Heaven does not aid us,
what is strange about boats capsizing and drowning?"
He immediately ordered embarkation,
and as the boats moved, the wind stopped.
From "Spring and Autumn Annals of the Thirty Kingdoms"
Though dwelling in grinding and dyeing,
he suffered no blackening or wearing away.
From a note in "A New Account of the Tales of the World."
As Jī Kāng faced death,
his complexion unchanged,
he asked his elder brother: "Has the zither come or not?"
His brother said: "It has arrived."
Kāng took it and tuned it,
playing "The Peaceful Prelude."
When the piece was finished,
he sighed and said: "'The Peaceful Prelude' ends today."
From "Biographies of Literary Men"
Xiàhóu Xuán
was once leaning against a pillar writing.
When lightning struck the pillar,
his expression remained unchanged,
and he continued writing as before.
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Collections
The strength of one who swallows states cannot overturn the resolve of one who would drown in the sea;
the might that bleaches bones cannot subdue the integrity of the Western Hills.
From Lù Jī's "Stringed Pearls"
Blazing fires that melt metal cannot burn shadows;
deep cold that congeals the sea cannot freeze the wind.
Swift winds and driving rain do not mistake the morning bird's discernment;
harsh shade and killing seasons do not wither the cold tree's heart.
Both from the same source.
One who acts without doubt though the whole world opposes him
is but one in a thousand or hundred years.
From Hán Yù's "Eulogy for Bó Yí"
Gold can be melted,
but cannot be made foul and rotten;
water can be muddied,
but cannot be made dust and dung.
From Yuán Jié
Cross-referenced in "True Integrity Is Hard to Destroy"
When power departs, one need not grieve;
when fortune comes, what is there to rejoice?
From Vice Director Bái
Cross-referenced in "Understanding Principle"
Waves and billows clamor with many mouths,
but wild greens quiet my thatched hut.
From Liú Chángqīng
Slanderous words stir like frost,
but bright sincerity stands firm as a mountain.
From Lǐ Yìshān's prose
Often undergoing grinding and dyeing,
yet unchanged in hardness and purity.
From Dù Mù
Should I be made the tip of an autumn hair,
I would still find myself sufficient, not seeing my smallness;
should I be made the slope of Mount Tài,
I would still have no surplus, not seeing my abundance.
From "Essence of Tang Prose"
Cross-referenced in "Cannot Be Diminished or Augmented"
Treading dangerous crises without changing heart,
caught in turmoil without forgetting the state,
pulling oneself up from the jaws of jackals and wolves,
the Way unstained and unerased.
Same as above.
A sword tempered becomes sharper;
jade burned does not burn.
From Sūn Kězhī's prose
The mythical beast offers its horn,
Bǐ Gān presented his heart.
Combining such fervor and integrity,
in you, sir, it is the tablet.
An angry tiger may be spat upon,
but the tablet cannot be thwarted.
Steep peaks may be uprooted,
but the tablet cannot be broken.
It props up Heaven without slanting,
points to the sun without eclipse.
Same as above.
Our Dynasty
Lǚ Duān was sent as an envoy to Gāolì,
encountering stormy waves,
the mast broke,
the sailors were terrified,
yet he calmly read his book,
as if in his study.
From "Yù Hú Qīng Huà".
The whole world wronged him,
yet his words never mentioned it himself;
he faced poverty until death,
but his wife and children never saw him express sorrow or joy.
From Ōu Yángxiū's "Memorial Ode for Yǐn Shīlǔ".
Since he could comprehend life and death through understanding destiny,
it was fitting that worries and hardships did not burden his heart.
Same as above.
Even if Mount Tài collapsed before him, his expression wouldn't change;
even if elk appeared to his left, his gaze wouldn't flicker.
From Lǎo Quán's writings.
Sīmǎ Wēngōng once said: "Among ten thousand horses galloping together,
who can halt their steps?
Is it Wáng Cún?"
From "Wáng Cún's Epitaph".
Successful yet flourishing without arrogance,
unsuccessful and worn thin without disgrace.
In company, not dependent;
alone, not fearful.
From Dōngpō's "Record of the Ink Gentleman Hall".
Praise and blame nearly reached countless extremes,
yet through calm and danger, he always maintained a single resolve.
From "Línchuān Collection".
Firm as metal and stone in heart,
unafraid of mosquitoes and gnats touching.
From "Sū Zǐyóu Collection".
Metal and stone do not follow the waves.
From Huáng Lǔzhí's poem.
Safely passing through a thousand layers of waves,
steadily descending from the hundred-foot pole's tip.
Chén Cóngyì wrote "Poem on Wáng Wénmù's Dismissal as Chancellor".
The recluse did not dream of Wū Gorge,
vainly the clouds and rain descended from Yáng Terrace.
From Chén Xīyí's poem,
seen in "Qīng Suì".
Mencius said:
Human nature is like rushing water,
channel it eastward and it flows east,
channel it westward and it flows west.
From "Mencius · Gàozi I".
History records:
Zǐxià, upon entering, heard the Master's Way and delighted in it,
but going out, he saw lavish splendor and was pleased.
From "Records of the Grand Historian · Biographies of Confucius' Disciples".
Wáng Mǎng executed Zhēn Fēng,
and those implicated in the accusations
were arrested without request.
At that time,
Yáng Xióng was collating texts in the Tiānlù Pavilion,
when the judicial envoy arrived,
intending to arrest Xióng.
Fearing he couldn't avoid it,
he jumped from the pavilion,
nearly dying.
From "Western Hàn Official Biography".
Cross-reference "Unable to Trust Oneself".
Some said the forthright advice was right,
others worried it was wrong,
uncertain how to decide.
From "Comprehensive Mirror · Hàn Zhāngdì Annals".
The Emperor asked Attendant-in-Ordinary Yuán Yán: "What kind of ruler am I?"
He replied: "Your Majesty is a middling ruler of Hàn."
The Emperor said: "How so?"
He said: "When Prefect of the Masters of Writing Chén Fān handles affairs, there is order;
when the Regular Palace Attendants and Huangmen intervene in governance, there is chaos.
Thus, I know Your Majesty can be led to do good,
and can be led to do wrong."
From "Comprehensive Mirror · Hàn Huándì Annals".
The bearded参军,
the short 主簿,
could make the Duke happy,
could make the Duke angry.
From "Book of Jìn · Biography of Xì Chāo".
The Emperor once asked Yuè Yùn: "What kind of person is the Crown Prince, in your words?"
He replied: "A middling man."
Asked: "What is a middling man like?"
He replied: "Duke Huán of Qí is an example.
With Guǎn Zhòng as minister, he became hegemon;
with Shù Diāo assisting, there was chaos.
He could be led to do good,
and could be led to do evil."
From "Comprehensive Mirror · Chén Xuāndì Annals".
One moment of doubt, one moment of confusion, in the blink of an eye;
self-approval, self-denial, changing within the bedchamber.
From "Comprehensive Mirror · Táng Tàizōng".
Biographies record:
There was a man with the same name and clan as Zēng Shēn who killed someone,
and someone told Zēngzǐ's mother: "Zēng Shēn killed a man."
Zēngzǐ's mother said: "My son does not kill people."
And continued weaving calmly.
After a while,
someone again said: "Zēng Shēn killed a man."
His mother still wove calmly.
Soon after,
another person told her: "Zēng Shēn killed a man."
His mother became afraid,
dropped the shuttle,
climbed over the wall and fled.
From "Strategies of the Warring States".
Cross-reference "Unable to Trust Oneself".
Collection:
Vaguely like a melody, just worth listening to,
then blown into a different tune by the wind.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán", recording a Táng poet's verse.
Classic:
Until death, I swear no other,
until death, I swear no change.
From "Shījīng · Cypress Boat".
My heart is not a stone,
it cannot be rolled away.
My heart is not a mat,
it cannot be rolled up.
Same as above.
A nobleman, though poor,
does not sell sacrificial vessels;
though cold,
does not wear sacrificial robes.
From "Lǐjì · Qū Lǐ".
The nobleman stands firm in poverty.
From "Analects · Wèi Línggōng".
Mencius said:
A good farmer does not stop plowing due to flood or drought,
a good merchant does not cease trading due to losses,
a scholar-nobleman does not neglect the Way due to poverty.
From "Xúnzǐ · Cultivating Oneself".
The Fool of the North Mountain,
aged ninety,
wanted to level the Tàiháng and Wángwū mountains.
Some laughed at him,
but the Fool said: "When I die, I have sons;
sons give birth to grandsons;
grandsons to sons: sons and grandsons,
endless and inexhaustible,
while the mountains do not grow larger.
Why worry about not leveling them?"
The mountain god holding snakes heard this,
fearing he wouldn't stop,
reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor ordered the two sons of Kuā'é Shì to carry the two mountains,
one placed east of Shuò,
one placed south of Yōng.
From "Lièzǐ".
Not letting things挫 one's will is called integrity.
From "Zhuāngzǐ".
History
Sīmǎ held his tally and died.
． From "Zuǒzhuàn, the Eighth Year of Duke Wén".
Duke Wén of Jìn said: "A cornered beast will still fight."
． From "Zuǒzhuàn, the Twelfth Year of Duke Xuān".
Chǔ attacked Sòng.
Huà Yuán entered the Chǔ army camp at night,
saying: "Our humble city exchanges children to eat,
splits bones for fuel.
Even so,
a treaty made under the city walls,
even if it means the state perishes,
we cannot comply."
． From "Zuǒzhuàn, the Fifteenth Year of Duke Xuān".
We ask to gather the remaining embers,
and fight one last battle with our backs to the city.
． From "Zuǒzhuàn, the Second Year of Duke Chéng".
Duke Wén of Jìn wandered in exile for nineteen years,
yet his resolve only grew firmer.
． From "Zuǒzhuàn, the Thirteenth Year of Duke Zhāo".
Wǔ Zǐxū was stranded by the river,
begging for food along the way,
but did his will ever forget Yǐng even for a moment?
Thus, he endured humiliation to achieve fame and merit;
if not a heroic man, who could have accomplished this?
． From "Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Wǔ Zǐxū".
Cross-referenced under "Heroic and Resolute".
Yǜ Ràng served Zhì Bó.
After Zhì Bó was destroyed,
Ràng hid a dagger to assassinate Xiāngzǐ,
but Xiāngzǐ spared him.
Soon after,
he lacquered his body to cause sores,
swallowed charcoal to become mute,
and begged on the streets,
saying: "The reason I do this
is to shame all ministers in the world and future generations who serve their lords with divided loyalties."
After a while,
when Xiāngzǐ went out,
Ràng hid under a bridge.
The horses were startled,
so Xiāngzǐ reproached Ràng,
to which Ràng said: "I am ready to die,
but I wish to strike your garment,
to express my intent of revenge,
then I will die without regret."
Xiāngzǐ gave his garment to Ràng,
who drew his sword, leaped three times, and struck it,
saying: "Now I can report to Zhì Bó below!"
． From "Records of the Grand Historian, His Biography".
Cross-referenced under "Heroic and Resolute".
Lìn Xiàngrú presented the jade of Zhào to Qín;
the King of Qín was pleased,
and passed it around for his attendants to see.
Xiàngrú saw that the King of Qín had no intention of ceding cities to Zhào,
so he said: "The jade has a flaw,
let me show it to Your Majesty."
The king handed him the jade,
and Xiàngrú, holding it, stepped back and leaned against a pillar,
his hair bristling with rage,
saying: "I observed that Your Majesty has no intention of compensating Zhào with cities,
so I took back the jade.
If Your Majesty presses me,
my head and the jade will shatter against this pillar together."
Xiàngrú held the jade, glancing at the pillar,
as if to smash it.
The King of Qín then apologized.
Xiàngrú kept the jade
and returned it to Zhào via a bypath.
Same as above.
Cross-referenced under "Heroic and Resolute".
Qū Yuán said: "Who can let his pure self be defiled by worldly filth?
I would rather throw myself into the Xiāng River and be buried in the bellies of fish.
How can I let my spotless whiteness be sullied by the dust of the world?"
Same as above.
Zhāng Yí said to his wife: "Look, is my tongue still there?"
His wife said: "Your tongue is still there."
Yí said:
"That is enough."
． From "Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Zhāng Yí".
Emperor Gāo defeated Xiàng Jí,
and led troops to surround Lǔ,
yet the scholars in Lǔ still lectured, recited, and practiced rituals and music,
the sound of strings and songs never ceasing.
． From "Records of the Grand Historian, Confucian Scholars".
The reason I endure humiliation and cling to life,
not refusing to be buried in dirt and filth,
is that I regret my unfulfilled aspirations,
and despise the thought of dying without my literary talents being known to posterity.
． From "Book of Hàn, Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān".
Mǎ Yuán said: "A man with ambition
should grow firmer in poverty,
and stronger in old age."
． From "Book of Later Hàn, His Biography".
Xiè Jǔ of Liáng, nephew of his elder brother.
He was once noble,
and one day had no food;
his son Qǐ wanted to pawn the "Book of Hàn" for money,
but he replied: "I would rather starve to death;
how can I use this to fill my stomach?"
From "History of the Southern Dynasties".
Zhāng Xún and Xǔ Yuǎn
can be called heroic men.
With tens of thousands of exhausted soldiers,
they defended a solitary wall,
resisting an unstoppable enemy,
blocking their throat and teeth,
preventing them from devouring,
tying up their front and rear,
and causing chaos in the regions of Liáng and Sòng.
They fought hundreds of battles, large and small,
and only died when their strength was exhausted.
． From "New Book of Táng, Their Eulogy".
Collected sayings
Also, for what my heart holds dear,
even if I die nine times, I will not regret it.
From "Chǔ Cí".
I would rather die suddenly and vanish
than bear such demeanor.
Same as above.
When they were under siege,
with no aid even as small as an ant,
all they wished to be loyal to
was the state and their lord.
From Hán Yù's writings.
As long as the tongue remains in the mouth,
it shall help the body fulfill its heart's desires.
From Jiǎ Lángxiān.
Not with the sorrowful cry of a wounded bird,
but with the heart of a cornered beast still fighting.
From Lǐ Wénráo.
Hands stretching empty fists,
strength exhausted but spirit bold.
From Liú Chángqīng.
Our dynasty
Gold, though dying a hundred deaths, does not change;
water, though winding ten thousand times, flows east.
From Chén Yíngzhōng.
Historical records
Wú attacked Lǔ.
Wēi Hǔ intended to attack the king's quarters,
privately leading seven hundred followers,
and they leaped three times in the tent courtyard.
The Prince of Wú heard of this,
and moved his camp three times in one night.
． From "Zuǒzhuàn, the Eighth Year of Duke Āi".
They submitted like grass bending to the wind.
． From "Book of Hàn, Biography of Hán Xìn".
Yǎng Yóu took aim, and the gibbon cried out.
． From "Book of Hàn, Bān Gù's Preface".
Fàn Pāng inspected his subordinates and officials,
who, knowing themselves corrupt,
surrendered their seals and fled at the mere sight of him.
． From "Book of Later Hàn, His Biography".
Fú Jiān was defeated at the Féi River,
his remaining troops fled in disarray,
hearing the wind and the cranes' cries,
they all thought the imperial army had arrived.
． From "Book of Jìn, Biography of Xiè Xuán".
Cross-referenced under "Fear" and "Mind Shifting with Events".
They fell as soon as the bowstring sounded.
． From "History of the Northern Dynasties, Biography of Lǐ Biāo".
They fled at the first sign of the enemy.
． From "New Book of Táng, Biography of Fáng Xuánlíng".
Of the twenty-four commanderies in Héběi,
was there not a single loyal minister?
． From "New Book of Táng, Biography of Yán Zhēnqīng".
Collected sayings
Appointed envoys to campaign west,
they advanced with the current,
wherever the wind reached,
none failed to submit.
From "Selections of Refined Literature".
Biographies and records
Villages fled at the sight of smoke,
cities crumbled at the sight of dust.
From "Diǎn Lùn".
Our dynasty
Wherever the horse's head turned,
all fled at the first sign.
From Sīmǎ Guāng's "Discussion on Wèi Yuán".
A fierce tiger dwelling in the deep mountains
makes all beasts tremble with fear
and dare not come out.
Not that I resist you,
but that you cannot withstand me.
From Sū Zhé's writings.
End
Zǐlù said: "I wish to have white feathers like the moon,
red feathers like the sun,
with the sound of bells and drums,
shaking the heavens above,
banners and pennants fluttering colorfully,
spreading across the earth below.
I would lead a troop to face the enemy,
surely seizing a thousand li of territory,
capturing flags and taking heads as trophies—
only I am capable of this."
． From "Family Sayings: Expressing Thoughts".
What Guǎn Zhòng and Zēng Xī would not do,
and you wish it for me?
． From "Mencius: Gongsun Chou I".
If Heaven does not yet wish to bring peace and order to the world,
but if it does wish to bring peace and order to the world,
in the present age,
who but me can accomplish it?
． From "Mencius: Gongsun Chou II".
In terms of rank,
you are the ruler,
and I,
a minister;
how dare I be friends with the ruler?
In terms of virtue,
you serve me,
so how can you be my friend?
A ruler of a thousand chariots seeks to be friends with him but cannot,
let alone summon him?
． From "Mencius: Wan Zhang II".
Cross-referenced under "spirit and bearing".
Yùzǐ at ninety years old
met King Wén.
King Wén said: "Alas,
you are old!"
Yùzǐ replied: "If you send me to catch tigers or chase deer,
then I am old;
but if you send me to strategize on state affairs,
then I am still young."
Thereupon, he was appointed as a teacher.
From "Yùzǐ".
Cross-referenced under "vigor and strength".
In the mountains and marshes, yet harboring the ambition of the court.
From "Wén Zhōng".
History
Luán Wǔzǐ said: "We cannot lose the allegiance of the feudal lords during our generation."
． (From Zuǒzhuàn, 16th year of Duke Chéng).
Máo Suì said: "Had I been placed in a sack earlier,
the tip would have already pierced through,
not merely showing its end."
． (From Shǐjì, Biography of Lord Píngyuán).
Cài Zé sought a physiognomy reading from Táng Jǔ,
and said: "Wealth and honor I already possess myself;
what I do not know is my lifespan."
(From Shǐjì).
King of Zhào longed to regain the services of Lián Pō,
and Lián Pō also longed to be employed again by Zhào.
The King of Zhào sent an envoy to summon Lián Pō.
Lián Pō met the envoy,
consumed a peck of rice and ten catties of meat in one meal,
donned his armor and mounted his horse,
to demonstrate his fitness for service.
． (From Tōngjiàn, Qín Annals).
Let us start with Guō Kuí.
． (From Tōngjiàn, Zhōu Annals).
Hán Xìn
was from a poor family.
When burying his mother,
he sought out high, dry ground,
so that space for ten thousand households could be placed beside it.
． (From Western Hàn, Basic Biography).
Hán Xìn said: "The more troops I command, the better I manage."
． (From Qián Hàn, Basic Biography).
At the village altar sacrifice, Chén Píng,
acting as butcher,
divided the meat very evenly.
He said: "Alas!
If I, Píng, could govern the world,
it would be just like this meat."
． (From Tōngjiàn, Annals of Hàn Gāozǔ).
Kuǎi Tōng titled his own collected arguments
"Juànyǒng".
． (From Western Hàn, Basic Biography).
Shī Gǔ said: "Juàn,
pronounced with the characters 'zì chōng fǎn',
means fat meat.
Yǒng
means long.
Because his arguments were very fine,
and their meaning profound and far-reaching."
Hán Ānguó said: "Can dead ashes alone not reignite?"
Zhōng Jūn volunteered to receive the long cord,
to bring the King of Nányuè captive before the palace gates.
Zhōng Jūn entered the pass on foot.
The pass officer gave Jūn a rú (silk pass tally).
Jūn asked: "What is this for?"
The officer said: "For your return pass,
to be matched upon coming back."
Jūn said: "A true man traveling west
will never return to have this pass checked."
He discarded the rú and left.
Both from the same source above.
Scholars suffer not from failing to understand the classics and arts;
if one understands the classics and arts,
attaining high office is as easy as bending down to pick up a mustard seed from the ground.
． (From Western Hàn, Biography of Xiàhóu Shèng).
Guō Dān said: "If I, Dān, do not ride in an envoy's carriage,
I will never leave this pass."
He left home for twelve years,
and indeed rode out of the pass in a high carriage.
． (From Eastern Hàn, Basic Biography).
Liáng Sǒng,
confident in his own talent,
said: "A true man living in this world
should be enfeoffed as a marquis while alive,
and receive temple sacrifices after death.
Positions in prefectures and counties
are merely toilsome for men."
Same as above.
Yú Xǔ laughed and said: "Without encountering gnarled roots and tangled knots,
one cannot distinguish a sharp tool.
This is precisely the season for me to achieve merit!"
． (From Tōngjiàn, Hàn Shāngdì Annals).
Mí Héng only esteemed Kǒng Róng,
and Yáng Xiū often declared: "My elder son is Kǒng Wénjǔ,
my younger son is Yáng Dézǔ.
The rest are mediocre and not worth counting."
． (From Eastern Hàn, Basic Biography).
Cáo Cāo casually said to Liú Bèi: "In the world today, the heroes
are only you, Sir, and myself!
People like Yuán Běnchū
are not worth counting."
． (From Tōngjiàn, Hàn Xiàndì Annals).
Hán Suì requested a meeting with Cáo Cāo.
At that time, Qín and Hú onlookers
crowded densely front and back.
Cáo Cāo laughed and said to them: "Do you wish to see Lord Cáo?
He is also just a man,
not with four eyes and two mouths,
only possessing much wisdom!"
Same as above.
Liú Bèi said: "Does Kǒng Běihǎi know there is a Liú Bèi in this world?"
(From Wú Zhì).
Liào Huà wished to go with Zōng Yù to visit Zhūgě Zhān.
Yù said: "We are both over seventy,
lacking only death.
Why should we seek out the younger generation and busily go to their door?"
Thus they did not go.
． (From Shǔ Zhì, Biography of Zōng Yù).
Wáng Jùn
was broad-minded and had great ambition.
Once, when building a residence,
he had the road in front of the gate opened to a width of several tens of paces,
saying: "I want it to accommodate long halberds and banners."
． (From Jìn Shū, Basic Biography).
Shān Tāo,
a commoner from a poor family,
said to his wife, Lady Hán: "Endure hunger and cold,
for I shall later become one of the Three Dukes."
Sūn Chuò showed his "Tiāntāi Fu" to his friend Fàn Róngqī,
saying: "Try throwing it on the ground—it should make a sound like metal or stone."
Xiè Kūn said: "In matters of hills and valleys,
I consider myself superior."
Superior to
Yǔ Liàng.
Zǔ Tì crossed the river,
struck the oar and swore: "If Zǔ Tì cannot clear the Central Plains and cross back again,
may I be like this great river!"
Both from the same source above.
Shí Lè said: "Had I met Emperor Guāngwǔ,
we would have vied for the Central Plains,
and who knows in whose hand the deer would die."
． (From Jìn Shū, Records of the States).
Zhōu Yǐ said: "This year I will kill all those villainous slaves,
and take a gold seal as big as a peck to tie at my elbow."
(From Basic Biography).
Xiè Ān's wife, seeing the family wealthy and noble while Ān alone remained quiet and retiring,
said to him: "A true man should not be like this."
Ān covered his nose and said: "I fear it cannot be avoided."
． (From Jìn Shū, Basic Biography).
Xiè Ān greatly respected Wáng Xiànzhī.
He thus asked him: "How is my calligraphy compared to my father's?"
Xiànzhī said: "They are certainly different."
Ān said: "External opinion does not say so."
Xiànzhī said: "How could others know!"
Same as above.
Liáng's Zhāng Yōng was arrogant, licentious, and tyrannical in the state,
and the people suffered from him.
Zhāng Tiānxī's close associate Liú Sù
said to Tiānxī: "We should quickly eliminate him."
Tiānxī said: "But who can do it?"
Sù said: "I, Sù, am that man."
Sù
was not yet twenty at the time.
Tiānxī said: "You are young;
should we seek further help?"
Sù said: "Zhào Báijū and I, Sù, are enough!"
． (From Tōngjiàn, Jìn Hǎixī Gōng Biography).
The Yān ruler Chuí deliberated on attacking Western Yān.
Chuí said: "As I approach old age,
I tap the wisdom in the bottom of my sack,
which is sufficient to take them.
I will ultimately not leave this villain to burden my descendants."
． (From Tōngjiàn, Jìn Wǔdì Annals).
Wáng Xīzhī said of himself: "My calligraphy compared to Zhōng Yáo's
should stand as an equal;
compared to Zhāng Zhī's cursive script,
it should still follow like geese in flight."
． (From Jìn Shū, Basic Biography).
Hú Fān said: "Liú Yì,
in every conversation and poetic recitation,
considers himself a hero."
． (From Tōngjiàn, Jìn Annals).
Cuī Hào
was delicate, handsome, and fair-skinned,
like a beautiful woman.
He often said of himself: "My talent equals Zhāng Liáng's,
and my knowledge of antiquity surpasses his."
． (From Tōngjiàn, Sòng Annals).
Wáng Jiǎn said: "Among the cultured and refined prime ministers south of the Yangtze,
only Xiè Ān—this is probably a self-comparison!"
． (From Sòng Shū, Biography of Wáng Jiǎn).
Péi Zǐyě said: "Other writers all achieve with their hands,
I alone achieve with my heart."
． (From Nán Shǐ, Basic Biography).
With a thousand scrolls of books stored in one's breast,
how can people not be awed and convinced?
． (From Běi Shǐ, Biography of Cuī Líng).
Wáng Kǎn did not socialize.
Relatives and friends urged him to take office.
Kǎn said: "If one has good farmland,
why worry about a late harvest?
I only regret lacking the talent and ability."
(From Běi Shǐ).
Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu said to Yáng Sù: "Strive hard on your own,
do not worry about not attaining wealth and honor."
Sù replied immediately: "I, your subject, only fear that wealth and honor will come forcing themselves upon me;
I have no mind to seek wealth and honor."
(From Suí Shū).
Suí's Wáng Pí said: "An old bear lies across the path;
how can a badger get past?"
Same as above.
To stir the turbid and raise the clear,
to hate evil and love good—
in these I surpass those several gentlemen by a day's length.
. "The Biography of Wáng Guī in the Book of Táng."
Lǐ Jìng once said: "A true man's encounter with opportunity
should lead to attaining wealth and status through achievements and fame;
why stoop to being a scholar of textual exegesis!"
. "The Main Biography in the Book of Táng."
Lǐ Shèng said to those close to him: "I grew up on the western frontier,
thoroughly familiar with the enemy's situation."
Same as above.
Péi Dù appointed Huángfǔ Shí as his adjutant.
When Péi Dù renovated the Fúxiān Temple,
intending to erect a stele,
he sought an inscription from Bái Jūyì.
Huángfǔ Shí was angered,
saying: "To bypass me nearby and seek from Bái Jūyì afar—
I request to resign from this moment."
. "The Biography of Hán Yù in the Book of Táng."
Hán Yù regarded himself as comparable to Yáng Xióng,
considering those below Gù as unworthy of discussion.
. "The Eulogy in the Book of Táng."
He compared himself to Mèng Kē,
viewing Xún Kuàng and Yáng Xióng as impure.
. "The Biography of Hán Yù in the Book of Táng."
Lǐ Huáiyuǎn,
when his clansmen wanted to use his high status for privilege,
Huáiyuǎn said: "Relying on another's power,
is something a noble scholar would be ashamed of.
To gain office through borrowed influence—
how could that be my aspiration?"
He passed the imperial examination in four categories.
. "The Main Biography in the Book of Táng."
Zhèng Rénbiǎo often said of himself:
"Heaven's auspice has the five-colored cloud,
humanity's auspice has Zhèng Rénbiǎo."
Same as above.
Biographies record
Lóu Jìng passing through Luòyáng,
saying: "My strategy can subdue without bloodshed,
effortlessly bridle the Xiongnu chieftain,
and present him before Your Majesty."
"Stories of the Three Capital Regions."
Lǐ Yuánlǐ,
held himself in high esteem,
aiming to take responsibility for the moral principles and judgments of the world.
"A New Account of the Tales of the World."
Zhāng Bīn said to his brothers: "I believe my wisdom, strategy, and insight are not inferior to Zhāng Liáng's,
only I haven't encountered an emperor like Gāozǔ."
Cuī Hóng's "Records of the Later Zhào."
Monk Zhī Dùn said: "Since one possesses the demeanor to soar to the skies,
how could one be willing to serve as an amusement for others' eyes and ears?"
"A New Account of the Tales of the World."
Yáng Dàyǎn of the Northern Wèi said: "If our banners and drums face each other,
with glaring eyes and fierce exertion,
it would be enough to make you lose your soul and courage."
"The Garden of Anecdotes."
A fierce tiger does not dwell in lowly positions,
a powerful eagle does not perch on drooping branches.
Jiǎng Zǐ's "Discourse on Myriad Opportunities."
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú was heading to the capital,
passing by the Shēngxiān Bridge in Shǔ Commandery,
inscribed on its pillar: "Unless I ride in a four-horse carriage,
I will not cross here again."
"Bái's Six Categories."
When Mr. Chǔqiū met Mèngcháng Jūn,
Mèngcháng Jūn said: "You are old, sir,
advanced in years,
and prone to forgetfulness!
What counsel can you offer me?"
The gentleman replied: "If you ask me to throw stones, leap far,
chase carriages and catch up with horses,
pursue deer and grapple with tigers and leopards,
then I am indeed old.
But if it's to devise strategies,
exert mental effort to resolve doubts,
speak upright words and stand above the feudal lords,
I am still in my prime;
how can I be considered old?"
Mèngcháng Jūn was taken aback,
sweating profusely to his heels,
and said: "I was mistaken!"
"The Biographies in Hán's Poetry."
Liú Chángqīng, whenever he inscribed a poem,
did not write his surname,
but only "Chángqīng."
"Discussions from Yúnxī."
Pí Rìxiū,
arrogant and unrestrained,
styled himself "Commoner of the Aura Between."
"Casual Words from the Northern Dream."
The monk Guànxiū,
beyond his literary talents,
was skilled in calligraphy.
Chéng Zhōnglìng asked about his brush techniques,
to which Guànxiū replied: "This matter requires an altar ceremony for transmission;
how can it be spoken of casually?"
Same as above.
After Zhōng Zǐqī died,
Bó Yá put away his qin and cut its strings,
never playing it again for life,
believing there was no one in the world worthy of his music.
Liú Xiàng's "Garden of Stories."
Collection
Those who understand me are few,
Thus I am all the more esteemed.
Yáng Xióng's "Resolving Difficulties".
The phoenix alights on the southern peak,
Ashamed to flock with swallows and sparrows.
From Liú Gōnggàn's poem.
Though roaming freely in grand mansions,
I yearn to strike fiercely across the central plains.
From Xuǎn Chuán Xuán's "Ode to the Eagle".
In life, one must glorify their name in the jade annals,
In death, inscribe great deeds in golden scrolls.
From Zhāng Jǐngyáng's "Seven Summons".
Cherishing the memory of the Yānshān stone inscription,
Longing to open the gates of Hángǔ Pass.
From Xú Jìngyè's "Writing at Lángyá City".
Pushing through vermilion gates alone and afar,
Rising to the blue clouds by one's own effort.
Not stealing light from a neighbor's wall,
Nor borrowing brilliance from a burning mirror.
Ultimately, dedicating oneself to achieve capability,
Never relying on others to accomplish deeds.
Luò Bīnwáng.
Though unable to release a transcendent melody from frosty marshes,
Crying out across the wilds with echoes reaching the ninth heaven;
Yet still gathering rare fragrance in dewy thickets,
Spreading a fragrance that perfumes ten paces around.
Same as above.
How can one compare with the quail,
Merely fluttering up to touch the elm tree?
Mèng Hàorán.
If in life one cannot be a model for the court,
Then one should grow old and die in the mountains and valleys.
Those who fuss over the dregs of wealth and goods,
And confine themselves to the gates of power and influence—
Even if they obtain bells and tripods,
How could they bear to accept them?
Yuán Cìshān.
In Dùlíng there was a commoner,
Growing older, his resolve turned more steadfast.
How foolish his self-expectations,
Comparing himself to Jì and Qì.
Unexpectedly, he became a failure,
Yet white-haired, he willingly endures hardship.
Only when the coffin lid closes will his endeavors cease,
This ambition ever hoping for fulfillment.
Year after year, grieving for the common people,
Sighing, his heart burns with anguish.
Not that he lacks the desire for rivers and lakes,
To wander freely through the days and months.
From Dù Fǔ's poetry.
The tiger's spirit must soar upward,
How could the dragon's form long remain hidden?
Same as above.
The heart harbors storms and clouds, unknown to the world.
From Lǐ Bái's poetry.
The thoroughbred is a heavenly steed,
Never meant to be a stable-bound pony.
Hán Xìn was ashamed to be compared with Jiàng and Guàn,
Mí Héng disdained to follow butchers and wine-sellers.
Rising to the blue clouds must be achieved by oneself,
Why seek the understanding of others?
Lǐ Tàibái in his "Letter to Prefect Péi" said: "Others' writings
Are like mountains without mist and glow,
Spring without grass and trees;
My writings,
Radiant and penetrating,
Stir the heart with every line."
All same as above.
Proud that none can match him.
From Hán Yù's "Song of the Fierce Tiger".
Nowadays, those blind in heart
Are all like Zhāng Jí,
Claiming only to be blind in eyes.
From Hán Yù's "Letter on Behalf of Zhāng Jí".
If the Way could be roughly transmitted through me,
Even if I died a million times, I'd have no regret.
From Hán Yù's "Reply to Mèng Jiǎn's Letter".
To carry on the ancestors' legacy rests on the grandson,
Only you are as a son to me.
From Hán Yù's writings.
Cross-referenced with "Expectation".
I consider that if the world had no Confucius,
I would not be among his disciples.
From Hán Yù's "Letter to Lǚ Yī, the Mountain Recluse".
Since I differ from oxen and horses,
Should I merely seek grass and water?
A flock of hens and a lone cock, intentions run wild.
Who will be the matchmaker to topple kingdoms,
I claim a value worth multiple cities.
Harboring rare talents and proud spirit,
Not following behind others.
The roc's wings spread wide, soaring to the sky,
The sword of service to the nation gleams cold.
If Heaven does not wish this man to have wisdom,
Then my fate cannot be hoped for;
But if this man is to have wisdom,
Who else but me?
His practice of the Way,
His writing of books,
His transforming the present,
His transmission to the future—
Surely there is a purpose.
All same as above.
Elaborating on the vast blessings of Heaven,
Extolling unparalleled great achievements,
They can be recorded in the books of "Poetry" and "History" without shame,
Placed between heaven and earth without flaw.
Even if the ancients were reborn,
I would not yield to them.
From Hán Yù's "Memorial of Thanks upon Arrival in Cháozhōu".
Matched with jade tablets, thus esteemed,
How could it be paired with mud and dregs?
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's "Rhapsody on Sifting Gold from Sand".
Gold, being a treasure,
Is ashamed to lie in the lower currents.
Same as above.
Hesitating, I lodge for now in a cage,
But soaring swiftly, I must fly beyond the heavens.
Bái Jūyì.
Cross-referenced with "Awaiting the Time".
With whips of Cuī and Dù descending together,
Reins of Yuáncháng driving side by side.
If not wearing a golden seal,
Then I shall cover myself with jade mushrooms.
All same as above.
Raising my arm, I can still risk one throw,
Who knows if this very moment won't bring the highest win?
Liú Yǔxī.
Seated, one should reach the clouds.
Liú Chángqīng.
The old tiger will eventually open its eyes,
The young insect will learn to kowtow.
As long as my tongue remains,
Why fear not being enfeoffed as a marquis?
From Zhāng Chéngjí's writings.
How could I contend with petty men over gains and losses in the eyes of one person?
From "Táng Wén Cuì".

Factions compare and praise each other.

History
Prince Bào of Sòng showed courtesy to the people of the state.
For those aged seventy and above,
he never failed to provide gifts,
occasionally adding rare delicacies.
The talented individuals of the state,
he never failed to employ;
from the Huán clan downward,
he never failed to show compassion.
*Zuǒ Zhuàn*.
Guàn Fū associated with
none but the bold and cunning.
His family wealth amounted to tens of millions,
with hundreds of retainers.
*Shǐ Jì* (Biography).
Guō Jiě entered Guānzhōng,
where the worthy and powerful, whether acquainted or not,
upon hearing his reputation,
vied to befriend him.
*Shǐ Jì* (Biographies of Wanderers).
He bribed the imperial relatives Xǔ and Shǐ,
exhausting his family fortune.
*Xī Hàn* (Chén Wànnián).
Bribes filled the courtyard,
envoys crowded the roads,
correspondence surpassed official documents,
private affairs outnumbered public duties.

The Wáng clan was at its peak,
guests filled their gates,
the five marquises each had their favorites,
yet none could win over all,
except for Lóu Hù of Cháng'ān,
who gained all their favor.
*Xī Hàn*.
Cross-reference "Rushing for Favor."
Close attendants all placed their confidants,

Cuī Liè became Minister over the Masses,
by having his nurse contribute five million cash.
*Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* (Hàn Língdì's Annals).
Dù Yù, while in his post,
frequently sent gifts to influential nobles in Luòyáng.
When asked the reason,
he replied, "I only fear causing harm,
not seeking benefit."

Xún Xī, as Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
engaged in extensive networking,
and whenever he obtained rare items,
he would send them to his relatives and nobles in the capital.
Yǎnzhōu was five hundred lǐ from Luòyáng,
and fearing the items would not stay fresh,
he acquired a thousand-lǐ steed,
so that each messenger
could depart at dawn and return by dusk.
Same as above.
Xiāo Zhìzhōng attached himself to Princess Tàipíng,
who recommended him as Minister of Justice.
*Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* (Táng Annals).
Cross-reference "Taking Shortcuts."
Lǐ Línfǔ was cunning and deceitful,
deeply ingratiating himself with eunuchs and the families of consorts,

so nothing escaped his knowledge.
Thus, whenever he reported,
it often pleased the emperor,
who favored him.
*Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* (Táng Xuánzōng).
Lǐ Línfǔ often bribed the emperor's attendants with gold and silk,
ensuring he knew every move.
Liǔ Zé submitted a memorial,

Liú Yōuqiú, Wèi Zhīgǔ, Cuī Shí, and Lù Xiàngxiān were appointed as chief ministers,
all at Princess Tàipíng's behest.
All same as above.
He sent gifts and thanks to every renowned scholar from all directions,

so they could not criticize him.

Lǐ Tīng had long won the favor of powerful officials through bribery,

Wáng Shūwén advised the crown prince, saying, "So-and-so can be chancellor,
so-and-so can be general,
I hope you will employ them in the future."
He secretly allied with Hànlín Academician Wéi Zhíyí and other court officials seeking rapid advancement, such as Lù Chún, Lǚ Wēn, Lǐ Jǐngjiǎn, Hán Yè, Hán Tài, Chén Jiàn, Liǔ Zōngyuán, and Liú Yǔxī,
forming a sworn brotherhood.

Wáng Shūwén relied on Wáng Pī,

for the privilege.
*Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* (Táng Annals).
Yáng Yúqīng, Zhāng Yuánfū, and Xiāo Huàn excelled at making connections,
attaching themselves to powerful figures,

Bó said: "I wish to see the chancellor but have no way,

Thereupon the retainer introduced Bó

Chasing current fashions to gain worldly resources.

following the times and attaching to power.

Luó Xīshì,

Carrying gold and transporting jade,

Hé Chāngyǔ was the minister of personnel,

Said: "Whose descendant are you?"

"History of the Southern Dynasties".

but was refused.
"Book of Táng".
Dòu Lú Gé and Wéi Shuō once asked Guō Chóngtāo,
who said: "Due to turmoil,
lost the genealogical records,
once heard ancestors say,
four generations above from Fényáng."
Gé said: "Then surely you are a cousin."

Wind and rain,

In Qí, there was a great famine.
Qián Áo set out food by the roadside,
waiting to feed the starving.
A starving man came, covering his face with his sleeve and dragging his shoes, stumbling along.
Qián Áo, holding food in his left hand
and drink in his right,
said, "Hey, come eat!"
The man raised his eyes and looked at him,
saying, "It is precisely because I will not eat 'hey, come eat' food
that I have come to this state."
Qián Áo then apologized to him,
but the man ultimately refused to eat and died.
． _Jì, Tángōng Xià_.
A scholar, when presented with wealth and goods,

does not compromise his righteousness for gain;
when threatened by the masses,

He does not lose heart in poverty and lowliness,

Same as above.

"Dōnghànshū".

Lí Zhū did not let clever dazzlement shift his gaze,
Shī Kuàng did not let new tunes change his hearing.
． "Dōnghànshū, Fàn Shēng Zhuàn".
The resolute do not drink from the Dào Quán spring,
the upright do not accept food given with contempt.
． "Dōnghànshū, Liènǚ Zhuàn".
The solitary bamboo starved long,
ashamed to eat the grain of Zhōu.
． "Dōnghànshū, Yìmín Zhuàn".
A thousand chariots cannot sway their resolve.
Ibid.
Chén Zhōng recommended Zhōu Xiè of Rǔnán and Féng Liáng of Nányáng for profound purity in learning and conduct,
they lived in seclusion, refusing office,
renowned in the world.
The emperor sent gifts of dark and red silks and lamb to invite them.
Xiè's clan urged him: "Cultivating virtue and establishing conduct
is to serve the state;
why alone do you guard the slopes of Dōnggāng?"
Xiè said: "Those who follow the Way gauge the time to act;
acting untimely,
how can one prosper!"
With Liáng, he traveled to a nearby county,
then claimed illness and returned.
． "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Hàn Shāngdì Jì".
Yáng Zhèn was Grand Commandant.
The emperor's uncle Gěng Bǎo recommended Lǐ Rùn's brother to Zhèn,
Zhèn refused.
Bǎo then visited Zhèn, saying: "Lǐ Chángshì is valued by the state;
he wishes you to appoint his brother,
I merely convey the emperor's intent."
Zhèn said: "If the court wishes the Three Excellencies to appoint him,
there should be a directive from the Imperial Secretariat."
He refused to consent.
"Dōnghànshū".
Yáng Zhèn was governor of Dōnglái.
En route to his command,
passing through Chāngyì,
his former protégé Wáng Mì, a talented scholar from Jīngzhōu, now magistrate of Chāngyì,
came by night with ten catties of gold for Zhèn.
Zhèn said: "Your old friend knows you,
but you do not know your old friend;
why?"
Mì said: "At night, no one knows."
Zhèn said: "Heaven knows,
earth knows,
I know,
you know;
how can you say no one knows!"
Mì left in shame.
． "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Hàn Shāngdì Jì".
Fàn Pāng's nephew Lǐ Sòng,
always ill-behaved,
was recommended by the eunuch Táng Héng to Zōng Zī,
who appointed him clerk;
Pāng delayed and did not summon him.
Zī vented his anger,
beating assistant clerk Zhū Líng,
who said: "Fàn Pāng's judgment is pure;
I would rather be beaten to death today
than defy Pāng."
Zī then stopped.
． "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Hàn Huándì Jì".
The emperor admired Yáng Qiáo's talent and looks,
wishing to marry him to a princess.
Qiáo firmly declined;
unheeded,
he sealed his mouth and fasted,
dying after seven days.
． "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Hàn Língdì Jì".
Eunuch Zhào Zhōng sent his brother Yán to show goodwill to Fù Xiè.
Yán told Xiè: "If Nánróng slightly obliges our eunuch,
a marquisate of ten thousand households is easily gained."
Xiè sternly refused: "To have merit unacknowledged is fate.
How could Fù Xiè seek private reward!"
"Běnzhuàn".
Earlier,
Liú Bèi had recommended Yuán Huàn.
Huàn was detained by Lǚ Bù,
who wanted him to write a letter insulting Bèi.
Huàn refused,
smilingly responding: "If Huàn one day served General Liú,
as he now serves you,
and upon leaving,
insulted you, would that be acceptable?"
． "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Hàn Xiàndì Jì".
Cáo Cāo, recalling Tián Chóu's merits,
regretted earlier accepting his refusal of reward,
and re-offered his former rank.
Chóu submitted a sincere memorial,
vowing to die rather than accept.
Cáo insisted,
attempting to confer it repeatedly,
but Chóu never accepted.
Chóu was close to Xiàhóu Dūn,
so Cáo sent Dūn to persuade him personally.
Dūn stayed overnight to urge him;
Chóu discerned his intent
and spoke no more.
As Dūn left,
he pressed Chóu again,
but Chóu said: "Chóu is but a man who betrayed duty and fled;
spared by grace,
I am already most fortunate,
how could I trade the fortress of Lúlóng for rewards and emoluments!
Even if the state favors me privately,
would I not feel ashamed in my heart!
General, you have long known me,
yet still act this way.
If there is no other choice,
I would rather die,
and cut my throat before you."
Same as above.
Not shifting one's gaze for petty gains,
not altering one's steps for casual companions.
. "Comprehensive Mirror: Records of the Three Kingdoms".
When the Regular Palace Attendant Huáng Hǎo held power,
Dǒng Jué and Zhūgě Zhān could not correct him,
and most officials attached themselves to him,
only Fán Jiàn did not associate with Hǎo.
The Palace Library Director Què Zhèng had long held an inner court position,
living next door to Hǎo,
moving in the same circles for over thirty years,
yet remained calm and self-possessed,
finding pleasure in books,
neither loved by Hǎo,
nor hated by him,
thus his official rank never exceeded six hundred piculs,
but he also avoided disaster.
. "Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Yuan of Wei".
Wú Yǐnzhī served as Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
and drawing water from the Greedy Spring, he composed a poem: "Even if Bóyí and Shūqí were to drink it,
they would never change their hearts."
. "Book of Jìn: Biography of Wú Yǐnzhī".
Cài Mó was appointed Minister over the Masses,
but for three years did not take up the post;
imperial edicts were repeatedly issued,
yet Mó ultimately did not accept.
The emperor appeared at the palace balcony,
dispatching the Palace Attendant Jì Jù and the Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Dīng Zuǎn to summon Mó;
Mó pleaded severe illness,
sending his Registrar Xiè Yōu to decline on his behalf.
From morning until late afternoon,
the messengers returned over ten times,
but Mó never came.
An edict dismissed Mó to commoner status.
. "Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Mù of Hàn".
Chǔ Yuān attended to Princess Shānyīn for ten days,
facing relentless pressure,
yet vowed to die rather than yield.
Shěn Yuē's "Book of Sòng".
Shěn Qìngzhī requested retirement due to age,
even kowtowing and weeping.
The emperor could not change his mind,
and allowed him to retire to his residence as Duke of Shǐxīng.
Later, the emperor wished to reappoint Qìngzhī,
sending Hé Shàngzhī to summon him.
Shàngzhī repeatedly conveyed the emperor's intent,
but Qìngzhī laughed and said, "I, Shěn, will not imitate you, Hé,
going and returning again."
Shàngzhī, ashamed, then desisted.
. "Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Wén of Sòng".
How could I be made to bend the truth in writing?
. "Book of Wèi: Biography of Yóu Zhào".
The recluse Wéi Xiòng of Zhōu,
aspired to a simple and unadorned life.
During the transition between Wèi and Zhōu,
he refused ten summons to office.
Emperor Shìzong treated him with great respect,
calling him "The Carefree Duke."
. "Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Gāozǔ of Chén".
Fù Zǎi
submitted a memorial criticizing the later emperor for excessive drinking and womanizing,
with blunt and accusatory language.
The later emperor was furious,
saying, "I wish to pardon you,
but can you reform your faults?"
He replied, "My heart is like my face;
if my face can be changed,
then my heart can be changed."
"History of the Southern Dynasties".
Liú Xíngběn
had a stern and unyielding nature.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu, he served as Grand Master in Charge of the Court,
responsible for the inkstone and brush according to protocol,
carrying them to the imperial seat,
where the Receiving Attendant would take them to present.
When Xíngběn was about to present them,
the Receiving Attendant tried to take them.
Xíngběn raised his voice and said to the Attendant, "You may not take the brush."
The emperor, surprised, asked why,
and he replied, "Since I do not carry the Receiving Attendant's knife,
how can the Receiving Attendant take my brush?"
"Book of Suí".
Cross-referenced under "Assuming Responsibility".
Wáng Shìchōng appointed Lù Démíng, a National University assistant instructor from Wú, as tutor to the Prince of Hàn,
ordering his son Wáng Xuánshù to perform the initiation ceremony at Lù's home.
Démíng was ashamed of this,
so he took a laxative made of croton seeds,
pretended to be ill in bed,
and when Xuánshù entered and knelt by the bed,
he had diarrhea in response,
and ultimately did not speak to him.
. "Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng".
Emperor Tàizōng said to Yùchí Jìngdé, "Your heart is firm as a mountain,
even if gold were piled up to the Dipper,
I know you would not waver."
The emperor also said to Yùchí Jìngdé, "I wish to give my daughter to you in marriage,
what do you say?"
Jìngdé kowtowed and declined, saying, "My wife may be humble and plain,
but we have shared poverty and hardship for a long time.
Though I am unlearned,
I have heard that the ancients did not abandon their wives upon gaining wealth."
Both from the same source.
Duàn Zhìyuán and Yǔwén Shìjí led troops guarding the Zhāngwǔ Gate,
when Emperor Tàizōng sent an envoy to the two generals at night,
Shìjí opened the door to admit the envoy,
but Zhìyuán refused, saying:
"The army gate does not open at night."
The envoy showed a handwritten edict,
but Zhìyuán said:
"I cannot verify it at night."
and did not admit him.
By dawn,
the emperor sighed and said:
"A true general indeed;
how could even Zhōu Yàfū surpass this!"
. "Book of Táng: His Biography".
When Princess Tàipíng disputed with a Buddhist temple over a watermill,
Lǐ Yuánhóng, the Registrar of Yōngzhōu, adjudicated in favor of the temple.
The Governor of Yōngzhōu, Dòu Cóngyī, was greatly alarmed,
and urgently ordered Yuánhóng to reverse the judgment.
Yuánhóng wrote boldly on the verdict:
"The Southern Mountain may be moved,
but this judgment cannot be shaken."
Cóngyī could not force him to change it.
. "Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Zhōngzōng of Táng".
Lǐ Shàngyǐn was promoted to Military Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
Upon his return,
some people collected money to gift him,
but Shàngyǐn said:
"My innate nature cannot be altered,
and it is not that I fear others knowing."
. "Book of Táng: His Biography".
Unyielding as a mountain.
. "Book of Táng: Biography of Lù Zhì".
Liǔ Hún and Zhāng Yánshǎng both served as chancellors,
Yánshǎng, abusing his power,
resented Hún's integrity,
and had a close associate
tell Hún:
"Your Excellency, with your virtuous reputation,
need only watch your words in court,
and you can keep your high position long."
Hún replied:
"Thank Chancellor Zhāng for me,
but Liǔ Hún's head may be severed,
his tongue will not be restrained."
"Book of Táng".
Holding fast to the heart and treading the path of righteousness,
with an iron will and stone resolve.
. "Book of Táng: Biography of Guō Zǐyí".
The Censor-in-Chief Gāo Yuányù wished to recommend Wéi Ào for promotion,
hinting that Ào should visit him.
Ào said:
"But I fear there is no such thing as a self-presenting censor."
. "Book of Táng: Biography of Wéi Ào".

Bó Chéng plowed in pairs, not coveting the glory of lords,
Yuàn Xiàn preferred his mulberry-wood door, not exchanging it for an official's mansion.

History
The State of Jìn sent Xiè Yáng to Sòng,
urging them not to surrender to Chǔ.
The people of Zhèng captured him and presented him to Chǔ,
where the King of Chǔ offered him substantial bribes
to reverse his message.
Yet he conveyed his lord's command.
He declared: "A minister can uphold orders to be faithful;
faithfulness allows no double commands.
Having received orders to go forth,
I would rather die than fail;
how could I be bribed?"
. *Zuǒzhuàn, Xuāngōng 15th Year*.
Zhèng's Zǐ Chǎn disputed the order of tribute,
the sequence of contributions.
Arguing from midday
until dusk,
he persuaded Jìn to agree.
. *Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāogōng 13th Year*.
Tián Héng's five hundred followers were at sea,
when the Emperor sent messengers to summon them.
Upon hearing of Tián Héng's death,
they all took their own lives.
. *Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Tián Dàn*.
As Grand General Wèi Qīng grew more esteemed,
with his sister as Empress,
Jí Àn maintained equal courtesy with him.
Someone advised Àn: "Since the Son of Heaven wishes his ministers to defer to the Grand General,
and the Grand General is noble and honored,
truly respected,
you must bow to him."
Àn replied: "If the Grand General has a guest who merely salutes him,
wouldn't that make him even more respected?"
. *Book of Hàn, Biography of Jí Àn*.
Xiāo Wàngzhī was dignified,
broken but unyielding.
. *Book of Hàn, His Biography*.
Gǒng Yǔ was Magistrate of Hénán,
reprimanded by his superior for official duties,
and removed his cap.
Yǔ said: "Once the cap is removed,
how can it be worn again?"
He then resigned.
Ibid.
Dǒng Xuān was Magistrate of Luòyáng,
and killed the servant of Princess Húyáng.
The Emperor summoned Xuān,
ordering him to kowtow and apologize to the princess.
Xuān refused;
forced to bow,
he pressed his hands on the ground,
but never lowered his head.
The Emperor commanded the stubborn-necked magistrate to leave.
. *Book of Later Hàn, His Biography*.
Dù Bóshān,
could not be made a subject by the Son of Heaven,
nor a friend by the feudal lords.
. *Book of Later Hàn, Biography of Mǎ Liáng*.
Yuèjī Commandant Zhèng Zhòng was sent to the Northern Xiōngnú,
and the Chányú ordered him to bow.
Zhòng would not submit.
The Chányú confined him,
cutting off water and fire;
Zhòng drew his sword and swore to die,
frightening the Chányú into stopping.
He then sent another envoy,
following Zhòng back to the capital.
. *Comprehensive Mirror, Hàn Míngdì*.
Cáo Cāo besieged Zāng Hóng in Guǎnglíng,
and Chén Róng, a fellow townsman of Yuán Shào, told Shào:
"I would rather die the same day as Zāng Hóng
than live the same day as you, General."
. *Book of Later Hàn, His Biography*.
Wáng Xiáng and Xún Yǐ went to visit Sīmǎ Yì,
Yǐ said: "We should bow."
Xiáng said: "How can the Three Excellencies of the Son of Heaven bow to others?"
He alone gave a long salute.
. *Book of Jìn, Biography of Wáng Xiáng*.
CH0F02D0 King of Qí - ; at a banquet ordered Attendant-in-ordinary Jī Shào to play the qin,
Shào replied: "You, sir, have restored the state,
and should set an example of proper conduct,
to be passed down to posterity.
Though I am unworthy,
I serve as a constant attendant,
girded and crowned,
with jade tinkling in the court and offices;
how can I handle silk and bamboo,
doing the work of an entertainer!"
. *Book of Jìn, Biography of Jī Shào*.
Prince Wǔlíng Xī heard that Dài Kuí was skilled at playing the qin,
and sent someone to summon him.
Kuí broke the qin before the messenger,
saying: "Dài Āndào will not be an entertainer at a prince's door!"
. *Book of Jìn, Biography of Dài Kuí*.
Táo Qián was Magistrate of Péngzé.
The commandery sent a Inspector to the county,
and clerks advised him to gird his belt to meet him.
Qián sighed: "I cannot bend my waist for five pecks of rice,
serving village petty men with earnestness!"
. *Book of Jìn, Biography of Táo Qián*.
Biàn Yán was Magistrate of Shàngyú,
and had a stern character.
When Měng Yǐ treated him as a subordinate,
he threw his cap to the ground,
and brushed off his clothes to leave.
*History of the Southern Dynasties*.
Wèi Commander Lǐ Zuǒ attacked Xīnyě,
captured Liú Sījì,
and asked him: "Will you surrender now?"
Sījì said: "I'd rather be a southern ghost,
than a northern subject!"
So they killed him.
. *Comprehensive Mirror, Southern Qí Míngdì Annals*.
Qí's Mùróng Yǎn said: "With my appearance like this,
people see me and bow;
how could I bow to others?"
*His Biography*.
The pine stands in the cold of winter,
frost and snow cannot wither its integrity.
*Suí Yángdì*.
Liú Rénguǐ lost ships transporting grain,
Lǐ Yìfǔ ordered Yuán Yìshì to interrogate him.
Yìshì said: "Whom have you offended in the court?
You should plan early."
Rénguǐ said: "If an official fails in his duties,
the state has fixed penalties;
I cannot escape my fate.
If I am to end myself to please my enemies,
I truly cannot bear it!"
He then reported the case fully.
He was dismissed.
. *Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Gāozōng*.
Xiāo Yǐngshì was like tempered steel,
unyielding.
. *New Book of Táng, Biography of Yuán Déxiù*.
Liǔ Gōngchuò was Governor of Jīngzhào.
When Gōngchuò first took office,
a junior officer of the Divine Strategy Army galloped across his procession.
Gōngchuò halted his horse,
and had him caned to death.
The next day,
he faced the Emperor at Yányīng Hall.
The Emperor was very angry,
questioning his unauthorized execution.
He replied: "It was my duty to cane him,
not to report it."
The Emperor said: "Then who should report it?"
He replied: "His own army should report it;
if he died in the main street,
the Jīnwú Street Commissioner should report it;
if within a ward,
the Left and Right Patrol Commissioners should report it."
The Emperor could not fault him.
Afterwards,
he told his attendants: "You must be careful with this man;
even I fear him."
. *Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Xiànzōng Annals*.
Chancellor Wéi Yīfàn's mother died,
but an edict recalled him to his post.
Hán Wò was to draft the appointment,
but he said to the Emperor: "It would be proper to summon him after the mourning period."
Academician-in-waiting Mǎ Cónghǎo pressed Wò for the draft,
Wò said: "My wrist may be broken,
but the hemp decree will not be drafted!"
. *New Book of Táng, Biography of Hán Wò*.
Biographies
Zhèng Zhòng said to the Xiōngnú: "I cannot bear to hold the great Hàn's emblem and bow alone to felt and fur!"
From "Dōngguān Hàn Jì".
Emperor Shùn of Hàn summoned Fán Yīng,
ordering the commandery and county to provide carriage and escort him on the road.
Fán Yīng had no choice,
arrived at the capital,
claimed illness,
and refused to attend.
He was then forcibly carried into the hall,
yet still would not yield with courtesy.
The emperor angrily said: "I can give you life,
or take it;
I can honor you,
or humble you;
I can enrich you,
or impoverish you.
Why do you slight me?"
Yīng replied: "I received my mandate from Heaven.
To fulfill it,
is Heaven's will;
to die fulfilling it,
is also Heaven's will.
How can Your Majesty kill me?
I regard a tyrant
as I would an enemy.
How could standing in court bring me honor?
Even as a commoner within humble walls,
content and self-satisfied, I would not exchange for the dignity of a sovereign—
how then could I be humbled?
How can Your Majesty humble me?
I do not accept ill-gotten riches;
not even ten thousand zhōng would I take.
To realize my aspirations,
even a basket of rice would suffice.
How can Your Majesty enrich me,
or impoverish me?" The emperor could not bend him.
From "Hàn Fán Yīng Lièzhuàn".
Emperor Shìzǔ of Wèi selected Dīng Hán for the post of court gentleman,
but Hán feigned illness and did not assume the post.
An edict inquired:
"Are you truly ill, or ashamed to be a court gentleman?"
He replied: "I am not actually ill,
but ashamed to be a petty official despite being a Xiàolián."

History
The ministers submitted a memorial: "It is appropriate to perform the Feng and Shan sacrifices on Mount Tài."
The edict responded: "Having been on the throne for thirty years,
the common people are filled with resentment.
'Whom would I deceive?
Would I deceive Heaven?'
'How could one say Mount Tài is less discerning than Lín Fàng?'
Why should I defile the records of the seventy-two generations!
If distant commanderies and counties send officials to offer congratulations,
extolling empty praises,
they shall surely be shaved bald,
and ordered to garrison the fields."
Subsequently, the emperor read the "Hétú Huìchāng Fú."
He proceeded to Mount Tài.
Performed the Shan sacrifice to the earth at Liángyīn.
． From "Tōng Jiàn Hàn Guāngwǔ."
In Wèi, for years, many generals and commanders were the favored and noble descendants,

There was a certain Minister Lǐ who, having left his post, lived in leisure,
his singing girls being the finest of the time.
Once he held a banquet,
but because Dù upheld the law,
did not dare to invite him.
Dù sent a messenger to convey his interest,
Lǐ promptly sent a letter to invite him,
and Dù came immediately upon receiving the summons.
At that time,
there were over a hundred female entertainers,
all of exceptional talent and beauty.
Dù sat alone in the southern row,
staring intently,
drained his cup,
and asked Lǐ: "I hear there is one called Zǐyún, which one is she?"
Lǐ pointed her out.
Dù gazed fixedly for a long time,
then said: "The fame is not undeserved;
you should give her to me."
Lǐ bowed his head and laughed,
and all the entertainers also turned around and broke into smiles.
Dù drank three more cups himself,
then rose chanting poetry. From "Original Story Poems".
Dù Mù served on the staff in Xuānchéng,
hearing that Húzhōu had many beauties,
went there for a visit.
Prefect Cuī organized a water festival for all the locals to watch,
and had Dù Mù observe.
Mù then saw a young girl and promised her: "If I do not come within ten years to govern this prefecture,
do not wait for me to marry." By the time Mù became prefect of Húzhōu, the girl
had been married for three years.
Mù then composed a poem: "It was my own delay in seeking spring,
no need to lament the passing of fragrant times."

Mǎ Róng calculated celestial motions but could not match them,

who solved it with one calculation.
When Xuán departed,
Róng envied him in his heart.
Xuán also suspected pursuers,
so he sat under a bridge,
resting his shoes on the water.
Róng indeed intended to pursue him,
but his attendants said: "Xuán is under earth, over water, resting on wood,
he must be dead."
Thus, they ceased pursuit.

In the early Tiānbǎo era,

earnestly and repeatedly showing kindness,
even promising him a high post,
then said: "The emperor values
Tǐngzhī of Jiàng Prefecture highly.
He should find a reason to excuse himself and return,
so he can meet the emperor
and be greatly employed."
Thus, he deceived Tǐngzhī into claiming illness,
wishing to seek medical treatment in the capital.
Once Lǐn Fǔ had the petition,

and ill,
and should be given a sinecure to recuperate.

Chancellor Lǐ, reading the Spring and Autumn Annals,
mistakenly pronounced Shūsūn Chuò as Chì Guǐ.

"I, following my teacher's teaching,

The chancellor said:
"Not so."

and indeed, it was pronounced Chì Lüè.
The chancellor was greatly ashamed,
and called the clerk his "one-character teacher."
