． From "Xīhàn Sūn Bǎo Zhuàn".
Jué means
to provoke or expose.
Exposing hidden and obscure faults.
． From "Xīhàn Zhào Hòu Zhuàn".
Collected sayings:
They love to conceal the beautiful and proclaim the ugly.
From "Chǔ Cí".
Cross-referenced under "covering virtues".
Classic:
Punishment does not extend to descendants.
． From "Shū Dàyǔ Mó".
Yán Huí did not transfer his anger.
． From "Yǔ Yōng Yě".
The Master said:
Do not punish a man's wife and children for his crime.
． From "Mèng Liánghuìwáng Xià".
History:
Enmity should not extend to descendants—
this is the way of loyalty.
． From "Zuǒ Wén Liù Nián".
Collected sayings:
Do not transfer anger to subordinates.
． From "Wénxuǎn Shū".
History:
During a great drought,
the duke wanted to burn the shamans and the deformed.
． From "Zuǒ Zhuāng Shíyī Nián".
If he couldn't handle it at the time,
what fault do later people have?
． From "Zuǒ Xuān Shíliù Nián".
Angry at home,
he shows it in the market.
． From "Zuǒ Zhāo Shíjiǔ Nián".
When Sītú Qī started a rebellion,
the duke,
Wèi Hóu Zhé,
fled to Chéngchú, saying: "Qī is behind this."
He ordered that anyone who had a grudge against the lady
should take revenge.
The lady was
Qī's sister.
Qī went on a mission to Yuè.
The duke attacked and seized his gifts.
Qī reported to the king,
who ordered their return.
The duke, enraged,
killed Qī's nephew, who was the crown prince.
Note: "Angry at Qī, he extended it to his sister, the lady,
and then to her son."
． From "Zuǒ Āi Èrshíliù Nián".
When Hán Xìn defeated the Qí army at Lìxià,
and advanced to Línzī,
the King of Qí, thinking Lì Shēng had betrayed him,
had him boiled alive.
． From "Tōngjiàn Hàn Gāo Jì".
King Zhào Lún, angry with Xiè Xì, said: "Even seeing a crab in water disgusts me,
let alone these brothers who disrespect me!
If this can be tolerated,
what cannot?"
He then had him killed.
From "Jìn Shū".
When Fú Jiān heard that Huán Wēn had deposed and installed rulers,
he told his ministers: "Wēn was defeated earlier at Bàshàng,
and later at Fāngtóu,
yet he doesn't reflect on his faults or humble himself;
instead, he deposes rulers to justify himself.
As the saying goes: 'Angry at his wife, he scowls at her father.'
This describes Wēn well."
． From "Tōngjiàn Jìn Jiǎnwén Jì".
Cross-referenced under "encroachment".
Lǐ Zhèn repeatedly took the imperial exams,
but never passed,
so he deeply resented the scholar-officials.
He said to Quán Zhōng: "These people always call themselves the pure stream;
we should throw them into the Yellow River,
to make them the turbid stream!"
． From "Tōngjiàn Táng Zhāozōng".
Biographies record
that Tàigōng said: "Those who do not love others
destroy even their walls."
Xūyú refers to
the walls of a village.
． From "Shàngshū Dàzhuàn Dàzhàn" chapter.
Cross-referenced under "hating someone and their belongings".
Where transferred anger reaches,
it destroys even ancestors.
From "Shǐ Tōng".
To hate someone
is to dislike all associated with them.
． From "Shuōyuàn Lì Zé" chapter.
Cross-referenced under "hating makes things ugly".
Jìn's Xīn'ān King Zūn said: "When I hear a surname with the wood radical,
I want to kill them,
how much more those with the Huán surname?"
From "Jìn Zhōngxīng Shū".
This dynasty:
Anger transferred to crabs in the water.
From Sū Shī.
Classic:
Rejoicing in heaven and knowing fate,
thus without worry.
． From "Yì Xì Cí".
Retiring from the world without discontent,
unrecognized without discontent.
Act when it brings joy,
avoid when it brings worry.
． From "Yì Qián Guà".
Whether attaining it or not,
remain self-content,
leaving it to heaven's will.
． From "Jì Biǎo Jì".
The nobleman dwells in ease awaiting fate.
Above, he does not blame heaven;
below, he does not blame others.
． Both from "Jì Zhōngyōng".
Employed, he acts;
set aside, he hides.
From "Lúnyǔ".
If the Way is to prevail,
it is due to fate;
if the Way is to fall,
it is due to fate.
． From "Yǔ Xiàn Wèn".
The Master said
Being neglected yet harboring no resentment,
being in dire straits yet feeling no distress.
． From "Mencius - Gongsun Chou II".
A noble person does not blame Heaven,
nor does they resent others.
Same as above.
Action and inaction are not within human control;
my failure to meet the Marquis of Lǔ,
is the will of Heaven.
． From "Mencius - King Hui of Liáng II".
Facing death without fear,
remaining calm in poverty,
is to understand destiny.
． From "Lièzǐ - Lì Mìng".
To accept the inevitable as destiny with equanimity,
only the virtuous are capable of this.
Zǐgòng said: "Those who attained the Way in ancient times,
were joyful in poverty,
and joyful in prosperity;
their joy did not stem from poverty or prosperity."
When it was time to come,
the Master complied with the timing;
when it was time to depart,
the Master followed the natural course.
Being at peace with the times and submitting to the natural order,
sorrow and joy cannot penetrate the heart. Confucius said: "I have long sought to avoid poverty,
yet could not escape destiny;
I have long sought prosperity, yet could not attain the right timing."
Both from "Zhuāngzǐ".
Rejoicing in Heaven and understanding destiny,
what have I to worry about?
Exhausting principles and fulfilling nature,
what have I to doubt?
From "Wénzhōngzǐ".
Historical Records:
Understanding destiny brings no sorrow.
Flowing with the current, one drifts away;
encountering obstacles, one comes to a halt.
． Both from "Hànshū - Biography of Jiǎ Yì".
A noble person, when the time is right, acts grandly;
when the time is not right, withdraws like a dragon or snake;
whether one meets opportunity or not is a matter of destiny.
． From "Xīhànshū - Biography of Yáng Xióng".
Huáng Xiàn remained composed and followed the natural order.
． From "Dōnghànshū - His Biography".
Guō Pǔ met Yán Hán,
wishing to divine for him,
but Yán Hán said: "I have my own destiny and life,
no need to trouble the yarrow stalks and tortoise shells."
． From "Tōngjiàn - Jìn Dynasty Annals".
Striving to avoid misfortune with intent,
is不如 surrendering to fate without intent.
． From "Tōngjiàn - Sòng Dynasty Annals".
Gù Kǎizhī often held that:
"People receive a fixed destiny and portion,
not alterable by intellect or effort;
one should only be reverent and uphold the Way;
yet the unenlightened fail to understand this,
recklessly seeking luck,
only damaging noble principles,
with no effect on gain or loss."
So he had his disciple Yuàn write "On Fixed Destiny" to explain it.
． From "Tōngjiàn - Emperor Shìzǔ of Sòng".
Lǐ Sìyuán said: "My heart bears no guilt toward Heaven and Earth,
when fortune or misfortune comes, there is no way to avoid it;
all is entrusted to destiny."
． From "Tōngjiàn - Táng Emperor Míngzōng".
Biographies:
Those who understand destiny,
remain unmoved by profit,
and face death without complaint.
Liú Xiàng's "Xīnxù".
Collections:
Entrusting to destiny and following principle,
one has no conflicts with things.
Zhāng Huá's "Ode to the Wren".
Equalizing all things, transcending to self-contentment;
entrusting life and fate, accepting departure or stay.
Jī Kāng's "Ode to the Lute".
Retiring in old age, leaving all to Heaven and Earth.
Dù Fǔ's poem.
Advancement indeed comes from destiny,
not from braving hardships.
From "Yuán Zhěn's Collection".
Poverty and low status are not without aversion,
but if the Way is present, why avoid them?
Wealth and honor are not without desire,
but when the time comes, they will come naturally.
Setting the heart to equate favor and disgrace,
submitting and following as actions dictate.
Is it the times or destiny?
I can do nothing about them;
Is it submission or compliance?
They can do nothing about me either.
When both are beyond control,
then one can truly achieve utmost compliance and unite with great harmony.
A guest asked Lètiān if he worried about illness,
he replied: "Knowing Heaven and destiny, I have no more worries."
Both from "Collection of Vice-Minister Bái".
In the vastness between Heaven and Earth,
submitting to fate brings endless joy.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng's essay.
Having coarse food daily,
rough clothing yearly,
sharing hunger and cold alike,
keeping family safe and sound,
this, beyond the contentment of submission,
brings added peace of mind.
From "Collection of Vice-Minister Bái".
Cross-reference "Contentment with Enough".
Where to go, what to follow?
Cease the judgments of turtle and stalk divination;
blooming and falling on their own,
leave glory and decay to Heaven and Earth.
From "Tángwéncuì".
Our Dynasty:
Teeth and hair entrusted to Heaven's care,
when worn and broken, beyond repair.
Sū Shì's poem.
Classics:
The noble person stores their tool within,
awaiting the time to act.
The inchworm's contraction,
is to seek extension;
the dragon and snake's hibernation,
is to preserve their lives.
． Both from "Yì Jīng - Xì Cí".
"Suppose there is a beautiful jade here,
should it be kept in a case and hidden?
Or should one seek a good price and sell it?"
The Master said: "Sell it!
． Sell it! I am waiting for the right price."
． From "Analects - Zǐ Hǎn".
Masters:
Though one may have tools,
it is better to await the right time.
． From "Mencius - Gongsun Chou I".
Historical Records:
Simply devote yourself to cultivating virtue,
and await the right time?
． From "Zuǒ Zhuàn - Eighth Year of Duke Zhuāng".
Like a farmer,
who weeds and mounds the soil,
though there may be famine,
there will surely be abundant years.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn".
Cross-reference "Being Prepared".
Folding fins and hiding wings,
awaiting the wind and clouds.
From "Jìnshū - Annals of Emperor Xuān".
Wáng Měng folded his wings, awaiting the time,
biding for the wind and clouds to act.
． From "Jìnshū - Biography of Wáng Měng".
Lù Fǎhé said: "When people pick fruit,
they should wait for it to ripen;
it will fall without being shaken."
． From "Tōngjiàn - Liáng Emperor Shìzǔ".
Yuán Wèi's Yú Jǐn said: "Positions in provinces and commanderies
were despised by people of the past;
high ministerial posts
must await the coming of the right time."
． From "Běishǐ - His Biography".
Collections
High or low, rich or poor, cannot be sought;
Upright in person, follow the Way and await the time.
Cáo Dà Gū's "Rhapsody on the Eastern Expedition".
Though lacking the demeanor of the black leopard,
I shall hide in the mist of the southern mountains.
Xiè Tiǎo's poem.
Confucius was a traveler,
King Wén endured obscurity.
If it is not their time,
even sages and worthies must lower their brows.
Lǐ Tàibái.
The heavenly horse neighs long, awaiting the harness.
Dù Fǔ's poem.
Not yet able to follow the eastern steed,
in vain I furl my wings aimed at the south.
Luò Bīnwáng.
Strive diligently to cultivate your fields,
and wait for the harvest at year's end.
Fill the windows, block the doors, be careful not to go out,
next year will bring warm breezes and sunny scenes.
Both from Hán Yù's writings.
Hovering low, I'll lodge within the cage for now,
but soaring swiftly, I must fly beyond the heavens in the end.
Bái Jūyì.
The hidden dragon must await a clap of thunder.
Dù Mù.
The six wings have not yet caught the wind.
Wǔ Bó Cāng.
A dragon coiled in mud lacks clouds,
unable to grow wings for ascending to heaven.
Zhāng Wénchāng.
The soaring scale in the vast sky,
once was a small spring's dormant creature.
Mèng Jiāo.
As for fine timber, pearls and gems,
precious swords and beauties like Máo Qiáng,
they never worry about being hidden in a case or bent—
"case" sometimes written as "cabinet",
"bent" sometimes written as "warped".
The worry lies in curtains,
and the obstruction by gnarled stones, leaden dullness, and the hunchbacked tumor,
only the timing of their emergence varies.
Quán Déyú.
The dormant dragon lies through the three winters,
the old crane has a heart for ten thousand miles.
"Táng Wén Cuì".
When winter goes, ice must melt;
when spring comes, grass grows on its own.
Féng Dào.
See also "Resignation and Compliance".
Our dynasty
Wandering and with wings drooping,
there will come a time with the autumn wind.
"Collection of Ōuyáng Xiū".
Dragons do not leap in winter,
fireflies can fly at night;
noble men and petty men,
each have their own time.
Shào Yōng.
Classic
Without knowing fate,
one cannot become a noble man.
"The Analects".
Masters
Those who resent premature death,
do not know fate.
"Lièzǐ - Strength and Fate".
Those who resent poverty,
do not know the times.
"Lièzǐ - Questions of Tāng".
History
Qu Yuán reached the riverside,
embraced a stone and threw himself into the Mìluó River to die.
"Records of the Grand Historian, His Biography".
Classic
Mèng Xiànzǐ said: "Those who keep carriages and horses do not bother with chickens and pigs;
families that use ice in sacrifices do not keep cattle and sheep;
families with a hundred chariots do not keep ministers who amass wealth."
"The Book of Rites - The Great Learning".
A noble man, when in office, does not farm;
when in the fields, does not fish.
"The Book of Rites - The Record of the Dykes".
In distribution, do not seek excess.
"The Book of Rites - The Ceremonial Usages, Part 1".
Masters
Knowing contentment brings constant satisfaction,
knowing contentment avoids disgrace.
"Lǎozǐ".
The wise do not act out of insufficiency.
"Zhuāngzǐ".
No blessing is greater than being free from misfortune.
"Xúnzǐ - Exhortation to Learning".
Scholars do not trade in goods and wealth,
rulers of states do not raise cattle and sheep,
ministers who have presented gifts do not raise chickens and pigs,
great officers do not manage gardens and fields.
"Xúnzǐ - Major Compendium".
Fame advances, the person retreats,
such is the Way of Heaven.
"Guǎnzǐ".
Also entered under "Natural Principles of Waxing and Waning".
Under heaven, there is the ultimate wealth that is not gold or jade;
being content with one's situation and knowing sufficiency is true wealth.
"Huáinánzǐ".
Brocades and dazzling finery,
what one wears only warms the body;
the three sacrificial animals and the great sacrifice,
what one eats only fills the belly.
Those who know how to take moderation for their person,
then know sufficiency;
if they know sufficiency,
then their will is not burdened.
"Kǒng Cóngzǐ - Residing in Wèi, Seventh Chapter".
Those who know sufficiency can then retreat fatly without being used,
nurturing their light in the mountains and forests.
They furl the wings of the phoenix and dragon,
nourish the vast and righteous energy.
In ragged clothes and rope belts,
they do not feel burdened by the dragon's emblem's brilliance.
Walking on foot with a staff,
they do not exchange it for the continuous line of four-horse carriages.
"Bàopǔzǐ - Chapter on Unfolding the Mysterious".
History
The state of Qí offered Yànzǐ the fief of Bèidiàn,
but he did not accept it.
He said: "The Qìng clan's cities were sufficient to satisfy their desires,
hence they perished.
My cities are not sufficient to satisfy desires.
By not accepting Bèidiàn,
it is not that I detest wealth,
but rather I fear losing wealth."
． *Zuǒzhuàn, Xiānggōng 28*.
Fàn Lǐ said: "In managing a household, one can accumulate a thousand pieces of gold;
in serving as an official, one can reach the position of minister or chancellor—
this is the utmost for a commoner.
To long enjoy a revered name
is inauspicious."
Thereupon, he returned his chancellor's seal,
dispersed all his wealth,
distributing it among close friends and fellow villagers,
and, carrying his valuable treasures,
left in secret,
settling in Táo.
． *Shǐjì, Yuè Shìjiā*.
Master Chǔ commented: "Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí, once encountering the rulers of ten-thousand-chariot states,
attained the positions of ministers and chancellors.
Now, you have accumulated decades of experience,
yet your office is no higher than that of a court gentleman,
and your position is merely that of a halberd-bearer.
Could it be that there is some flaw in your conduct?"
Master Dōngfāng replied: "That was one era,
this is another.
Had Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí been born with me in the present age,
they would not even have been able to obtain the post of a minor archivist,
how dare they aspire to be regular attendants or court gentlemen!"
*Dōngfāng Shuò Zhuàn*.
When offered a fief of thirty thousand households in Qí to enfeoff Zhāng Liáng,
Liáng said: "Your subject wishes to be enfeoffed in Liú, which is sufficient;
I dare not accept thirty thousand households."
． *Xīhàn Běnzhuàn*.
Gōngyízǐ served as chancellor of Lǔ.
Upon returning home and seeing silk being woven,
he became angry and dismissed his wife;
when eating at home and tasting the mallows,
he frowned and uprooted them,
saying: "I already receive an official's salary;
how can I also seize the profits of the gardeners and weavers!"
． *Xīhàn Dǒng Zhòngshū Zhuàn*.
Pìqiáng Hóu's son, Dé,
often adhered to the teachings of Lǎozǐ
on the principle of knowing contentment.
． *Xīhàn Chǔ Yuánwáng Zhuàn*.
Shū Guǎng said to Shòu: "I have heard that 'knowing contentment avoids disgrace,
knowing when to stop prevents danger,'
and 'withdrawing after achieving merit
is the way of Heaven.'
Now that we have reached the official rank of two thousand piculs,
if we do not know to withdraw,
I fear there will be regret later.
Would it not be better for father and son to leave the capital together,
return to our hometown in old age,
and live out our natural lives?
Is that not good?"
That very day, both father and son pleaded illness.
They submitted a memorial requesting retirement.
． *Xīhàn Běnzhuàn*.
Cross-reference to the "Contentment and Withdrawal" section.
Yīn Xīng said: "If the families of imperial consorts do not know humility and withdrawal,
marrying their daughters to marquises and kings,
and eyeing princesses for wives,
my foolish heart is truly uneasy.
Wealth and honor have their limits;
one should know contentment."
．． *Tōngjiàn, Hàn Guāngwǔ Jiànwǔ 7*.
Tián Yù served as Commandant of the Guards.
He requested to retire,
but Sīmǎ Xuānwáng would not permit it.
Yù said: "To hold office past the age of seventy
is like walking endlessly through the night after the bell has tolled and the water-clock has run dry—
that is to be a criminal."
Thereupon, he claimed illness.
*Wèi Zhì*.
Yú Wánzhī, in his old age, requested to retire.
His memorial stated: "One enters official service at forty,
and retires at seventy.
In youth, one drives forward;
in old age, one rests.
Knowing contentment avoids disgrace;
your subject knows contentment."
*Qí Shū*.
The Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments with the honors of Opening a Manor and having the same honors as the Three Excellencies,
Wáng Sēngqián firmly declined the appointment to the central government office,
saying to his nephew Wáng Jiǎn: "Your responsibilities at court are heavy,
and you are about to reach the rank of the Three Excellencies.
If I were to receive this appointment again,
it would mean one family has two officials of the highest rank,
which I truly fear."
*Wèi Zhì*.
Wěi Shìkāng was appointed Minister of Personnel.
Over more than ten years in that position,
he promoted and advanced many individuals.
He said to his children and younger relatives: "I have heard that withdrawing after achieving merit
is a constant principle of the ancients.
Now I am about to retire;
what do you all think?"
His son Fú Sì said: "Father, you have purified yourself and cultivated virtue,
achieving fame and official success.
To follow the example of the two Shūs,
we respectfully accept your esteemed decision."
*Suí Shū*.
Wěi Shìkāng served in the Ministry of Personnel for over ten years,
and was praised at the time for his integrity and fairness.
He often held the intention of knowing when to stop,
saying to his children and younger relatives: "Why must emolument be excessive?
Guard against fullness and then withdraw;
do not wait for the twilight years,
resign when illness comes."
． *Tōngjiàn, Suí Gāozǔ*.
Lǐ Yìyǎn's residence lacked a proper main hall,
so his younger brother bought timber and sent it to him.
Yìyǎn said: "To already hold a high official position
and also to expand one's residence
—without virtuous conduct,
one is bound to suffer calamity."
He did not allow it.
． *Jiù Tángshū Běnzhuàn*.
Zhāng Jiāzhēn did not accumulate family property.
When someone urged him to purchase fields and homes,
Jiāzhēn said: "I am honored to be a general and chancellor;
why should I worry about cold and hunger!
If I were to commit a crime,
even if I had fields and homes,
they would be of no use.
I have observed court officials extensively occupying good land,
but upon their death,
it only becomes funds for their unworthy sons to indulge in wine and women,
which I do not approve of."
Those who heard this agreed with him.
． *Tōngjiàn, Táng Xuánzōng Jì*.
Cross-reference to "Leaving a Legacy."
Lǐ Rìzhī was appointed Palace Attendant.
During the Xiāntiān era,
he requested retirement.
Rìzhī was about to make the request
without consulting his family.
Upon returning home, he began packing.
His wife, surprised, said: "Our property and assets are meager;
why retire so hastily?"
Rìzhī said: "To have reached this official rank
is already beyond my due.
How can one ever be satisfied?
If one is dissatisfied in heart,
no day will ever be enough."
． *Tángshū Běnzhuàn*.
Yuán Yánzǔ was appointed as an assistant magistrate of Chōnglíng,
but promptly resigned and left,
saying: "In life, clothing and food
should suffice to address hunger and fullness;
one should not seek more."
He often tended gardens and gathered firewood,
considering it "the duty of a living being;
beyond this, I do not think."
． *Tángshū Yuán Jié Zhuàn*.
Someone urged Cén Wénběn to establish family estates.
Wénběn said: "I was a commoner from the south,
who entered the capital on foot.
My hopes did not exceed becoming a secretary or a county magistrate.
Without the merit of battle,
I have reached the position of Secretariat Director through literary work,
which is the utmost.
How can I speak of estates further?"
． *Tángshū Běnzhuàn*.
Cross-reference to "Exceeding Expectations."
Biographies
state that ministers who accumulate
do not seek profits from the marketplace.
*Hánshī Wàizhuàn*.
Collection
Fearful of the extreme position's fullness and abundance.
Pān Ānrén's "Rhapsody on the Journey West".
Above, there is insufficiency,
yet below, there is surplus to compare with.
Zhāng Huà's "Rhapsody on the Wren".
The enlightened person knows when to stop and be content,
casting aside glory as if it were nothing.
Removing the hairpin and shedding court robes,
letting hair down and returning to the seaside.
Zhāng Jǐngyáng's "Poem on History".
My elder brother's virtue and conduct were lofty,
well-versed in prescriptions and medicines,
when eating, he always consulted the "Materia Medica",
yet his life ended at forty-two.
I am negligent and foolish,
eating without choosing taboos,
holding the position of a vice minister,
and have outlived my elder brother by fifteen years.
How can this be insufficient?
Where then to find sufficiency?
Moreover, to be able to die peacefully at home,
fortunate not to have lost great integrity,
and thus face my ancestors below,
can be considered glorious.
Hán Yù's "Account of Conduct".
Fortunate to live in a time of peace under heaven,
inheriting the legacy of my ancestors,
unaware of the toils of weapons, plows, attack and defense, or farming and harvesting.
Hán Wén's "Rhapsody on Two Birds".
Monthly spending of official salary,
yearly consumption of granary grains,
sons not knowing farming,
wife not knowing weaving,
riding horses with followers,
sitting idly and eating.
Hán Wén.
When I first came to the capital,
I brought only a bundle of books.
Through thirty years of hard work,
I have come to own this house.
Is this house not splendid?
For me, it is more than enough.
The main hall is high and new,
with ample meat and vegetables all seasons.
Same as above.
The Liǔ family is known as a great clan,
yet for five or six generations none have served as court officials,
how could it be
"how could it be" also written as "how could the ignorant"
that I alone surpass hundreds of others?
Considering this,
my official rank is already excessive,
my favor already deep.
Knowing sufficiency differs from knowing when to stop,
Zōng Yuán knows sufficiency.
If I were to stop now and not accept salary and position,
that is something I cannot do.
Liǔ's "Letter to Vice Minister Yáng Píng".
Hands cannot hold spears,
shoulders cannot carry hoes.
Fortunately, through skill with brush and inkstone,
I ascended the path of official advancement.
Bái Lètiān.
White-haired in human longevity,
gold-belted in worldly glory.
No descendants to concern about,
no property to manage.
One day of peace and leisure is worth ten thousand gold.
Cross-referenced under "Leisure and Comfort".
Carefree enjoyment of fortune and salary is even harder to dispel.
Cross-referenced under "Peace and Comfort".
Gaining years is not meager,
lasting fortune is singularly poor.
Suppose I were the creator,
abundance and ease would be just like this.
Compared to those with a single gourd and ladle,
I am now greatly wealthy and noble.
Do not dislike a poor livelihood,
for greater wealth means more toil of heart.
Having silk to ward off winter cold,
having grain to prevent year's famine.
Fuller than Dōngfāng Shuò,

From "Shàn Zāi Xíng".
Who, after all, distinguishes one's body and fame?
In the end, records and history will be worn away.
From Xiè Língyùn's "Yóu Shān".
Considering heaven and earth as a single morning,
And ten thousand ages as a fleeting moment.
Taking the sun and moon as windows and doors,
And the eight directions as courtyard and road.
Traveling leaves no wheel tracks,
Dwelling has no house or hut.
With the sky as curtain and earth as mat,
I follow wherever my will goes.
At rest, I hold a wine vessel;
In motion, I carry a wine pot.
From Liú Bólún's "Ode".
I, Táozi, am about to leave this inn of a temporary lodge,
And return forever to my original home.
Offering fine vegetables with reverence,
Presenting clear wine as tribute.
From Táo Qián's "Self-Eulogy".
Releasing the common attachments of the worldly realm,
Indulging in the transcendent lofty sentiments.
From Sūn Chuò's "Tiān Tāi Fù".
Roaming freely beyond the physical form.
From Wáng Xīzhī's "Lán Tíng Xù".
Once following the transformation into extinction,
What use is empty fame?
By Xiè Língyùn.
Seeking one day's fulfillment,
Equals a century's excess.
From Jìn Sūn Chuò's "Lán Tíng Shī Xù".
Profoundly leaving heaven and earth behind,
Riding transformation into infinity.
Sages value myriad affairs as precious,
While I find the world burdensome;
Sages honor the great treasure as supreme,
While I consider the world troublesome.
Both from "Collection of Chén Zǐ'áng".
Also see "Different Perspectives".
Heaven and earth are duckweed on water.
Glory and nobility are like dirt.
This body is like a floating cloud,
How can it be confined to north or south?
This body sober then drunk again,
Wherever I ride becomes home.
Lǐ Bái called himself an immortal in wine.
Life and world with twin disheveled hair,
In all heaven and earth, a single thatched hut.
Through all ages, one skeleton,
Neighbors welcome with songs and cries.
Releasing spirit beyond the eight extremes,
Looking up and down, all is desolate.
Through eternity, one life and death,
Why strive for name and status?
Both from Dù Fǔ's poems.
Raising my cup to invite the bright moon,
Facing my shadow makes three of us.
The moon, after all, doesn't understand drinking,
My shadow merely follows my body.
Just obtain the joy in drunkenness,
Don't convey it to the sober.
The enlightened discard heaven and earth.
Also by Lǐ Tàibái.
Rising to dance, first drunk, the tall pines crumble.
Floating with steps beyond the heavens,
How could I consent to be a prisoner within bounds?
Rather than being praised beforehand,
Better not to be slandered afterward;
Rather than pleasure for the body,
Better no worries in the heart.
No constraints of carriage or robes,
No application of knife or saw,
Unaware of order or chaos,
Unhearing of demotion or promotion.
Looking down on rule-bound scholars as slaves.
Also see "Contempt".
Noble men typically pity the crooked and unfortunate,
True men ultimately should bear no prejudice.
Chrysanthemums over the wall are good for buying wine,
Even if money and silk are gone, clothes can be pawned.
How can I grow long, great wings envious of clouds upon my body,
Riding the wind, shaking swiftly out of the six directions.
Cut off from floating dust,
Death, life, sorrow, and joy both abandoned,
Right, wrong, gain, and loss left to idle folk.
River fish cannot live in a pond,
Wild birds are hard to tame in a cage.
Both from Hán Yù's writings.
The most benevolent regard life and death as a relay station,
And high office as something that comes by chance.
Leaving a name for ten thousand generations has nothing to do with oneself.
Also from Liú Bīnkè.
Hearts and minds without any barrier,
Physical forms both unconstrained.
By Bái Shìláng.
The previous line also appears under "Contempt".
Within the vast heaven and earth,
In death we will surely meet.
Also appears under "Consolation".
Wherever one is content is home.
Despising the pettiness of small measures,
Mocking the stubbornness of clinging to trifles.
Piling gold behind you to prop up the North Star,
Is not as good as a single cup of wine while alive.
First, nothing equals meditation,
Second, nothing equals drunkenness.
Meditation can obliterate self and others,
Drunkenness can make one forget glory and decay.
Floating beyond the worldly dust,
How could even phoenixes catch up?
The physical form belongs to the sun and moon,
Growing old—why be startled?
Settling the mind in Buddhism,
Wandering traces in Lǎo-Zhuāng philosophy.
To be mired in the marketplace and court,
Or drowned in wife and children,
Is not enlightenment;
To be imprisoned in mountains and forests,
Or to reject blood relatives,
Is also not enlightenment;
If someone dwells among all creatures of an era,
They being they,
I being I,
Not purifying myself,
Not defiling myself,
Not being a Cháo Fǔ or Xǔ Yóu,
Not being a Yī Yǐn or Lǚ Shàng,
Making my heart like water,
My body like clouds,
Sinking, floating, disappearing, appearing,
Nowhere not content,
Is this not the enlightened person?
Also appears under "Content Everywhere".
I observe from the ninth rank to the first,
The essence and character are all similar.
Purple ribbons, red robes, blue cloth gowns—
Only the colors differ, that's all.
Entrust fate to its thickness or thinness,
Resign the heart to poverty or success.
In success, be a great roc,
Spreading wings to brush the blue sky.
In poverty, be a wren,
A single branch enough to shelter.
If one can know this way,
The body may be poor but the heart is not.
Merit and fame, when winnowed, are but dust.
Life is a floating cloud,
Death is the casting off of the shell.
From whence did it come?
To where does it go?
My nature does not move,
My form undergoes many changes.
Enough, enough,
Where can I go and not be content?
Why then be weary or attached in between?
Bólún always carried a spade with him,
Yuánliàng first wrote his own eulogy.
Leaving—what is there to look back on?
Staying—also no worry or disturbance.
Fame is a lock禁锢ing the body,
Wealth is a fire burning the self.
Both body and spirit are illusions,
Dreams and reality are equally unreal.
Asking myself what use are my remaining years,
I fear I'm just a superfluous tall figure in the human world.
Gazing at each other, parting for ten thousand miles,
We are all floating duckweed alike.
Both from Bái Lètiān.
The enlightened of old
Took life as a sojourn, a dream,
And death as a return, a homecoming.
By chance, vanishing into the great void,
The same as never having been born.
By Dù Mùzhī.
Principles touch on empty delights,
The mind immerses in
(immerses—alternatively, ascends)
quiet connections,
The room becomes
(becomes—alternatively, only)
bright with emptiness,
The person then contemplates mystery.
From Zhāng Yuèzhī's writings.
When power departs, no need to grieve;
When fortune comes, why rejoice enough?
Vice Minister Bái.
Cross-reference "Seeing with Settled Mind".
There is only the gate of non-duality,
Wherein there is no short or long life.
Same as above.
What is wealth and honor but dew on a blade of grass?
From Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Beginning and end
Are the great return of all things;
Life and death
Are the constant lot of a hundred years.
Luò Bīnwáng.
Existence and extinction, departure and stay,
Are like a single hair from nine oxen.
With dense woods and lush grass,
How could it differ from the gates of official offices?
Both from the Collected Works of Wáng Wéi.
Mansions are not my home,
They are but inns for temporary stay.
Children and grandchildren are not mine to keep,
They are but cast-off skins, nothing more.
Like a silkworm spinning a cocoon,
Or a flower bearing seed.
When the seed forms, the flower fades unseen,
When the cocoon is done, the silkworm dies of age.
Heaven and earth are my canopy and mat,
Wealth and honor are but mud and sand.
From the Collected Works of Bái Jūyì.
Why cling to the official seal at the waist,
Like a bird in a cage?
Wéi Yìngwù.
Cross-reference "Awakening".
Not grieving over the mayfly's brief evening,
Nor envying the tortoise and crane's long years.
Gain and loss both forgotten,
Cháo Fú and Xǔ Yóu return the same as nobles;
Favor and disgrace both retained,
Court and forest achieve alike.
Both by Luò Bīnwáng.
All outside the body is empty fame,
In wine lies complete virtue.
Lǐ Yìshān.
The cloudy mountains do not demand my correctness,
The woods and springs do not blame my faults.
Yuán Cǐshān.
If only I can stay drunk all day long,
No wine reaches the soil over Liú Líng's grave.
From Lǐ Hè's writings.
Renouncing the world, growing old in wine,
Planning for life, yet poor beyond books.
From Xǔ Yònghuì's writings.
Eyes clear, seeing through this fleeting life's dream.
Dù Xúnhè.
When you gain, sing loud; when you lose, just rest,
Too much sorrow and regret only bring weariness.
If I have wine in this life, I'll get drunk in this life,
Tomorrow's worries I'll face when they come.
From the Collected Works of Luó Yǐn.
Fame and merit are ten thousand miles away,
My heart's matters fit in a single cup.
Better to sing wildly in the marshes,
Than serve as an official in the dusty world.
Both by Gāo Shì.
Court robes left at the tavern.
I feel as if I've lost my home.
Both by Yáo Hé.
Delighting in the vast freedom beyond the world,
Sighing at the constraints of human life.
Ten thousand volumes of books in the belly,
A thousand cups of wine beyond the body.
Both by Wēn Tíngyún.
Heaven and earth
Are the inn of all things;
Time
Is the passing traveler of a hundred generations.
His mind far-reaching,
Soaring like a crane across ten thousand miles.
Drifting, unaware of the official hat on his head,
Vast, unknowing of the greatness of heaven and earth.
With hidden mechanism and careful path,
Though traces are bound, the heart is free,
Like a swan riding the clear wind,
Soaring on the ethereal air,
Finding contentment in the obscure realm.
Following the natural measures of great and small,
The long-lived and short-lived are equalized;
Forgetting longevity and brevity in the transformation of things,
Why distinguish between Péng Zǔ's long life and early death?
Without the movement of the four seasons,
Without traces of gain or loss, right or wrong, coming or going.
Gain is not my glory,
Loss is not my shame.
All from the Táng Wén Cuì.
One day, transformed along with all things,
The body merges with the soil and dirt.
After all, gold and silver
Are no different from mud and dust.
Noble and lowly, rich and poor,
Though high and low differ,
Joy and sorrow, benefit and harm,
Do not cross each other's bounds.
Thus the enlightened see
The great transformation as one path.
Both by Vice Minister Bái.
I do not regret a life of a hundred years being short,
But rather grieve that ten thousand aeons are too long.
No need to ask about current enemies,
Let external achievements and fame be as they may.
Wherever the clouds drift is home.
The ten-thousand-year turtle and the fleeting fungus are equal,

Both by Yuán Zhěn.
The nobleman is not bound by the world,
Quite equating glory and disgrace.
Wéi Yìngwù.
Our dynasty
Before a feast spread far, I eat till full and stop,
With a gourd of water to drink, joy knows no bounds.
From the Collected Works of Ōuyáng Xiū.
Metal and iron may corrode in time,
Mountains and peaks may crumble one day,
All forms are prone to decay.
Sū Xún.
Great troubles stem from having a body,

Viewed from the changing perspective,
Heaven and earth cannot last a single blink;
Viewed from the unchanging perspective,
Things and I are both endless.
Sū Shì.
Looking down, official ranks are like mud and silt.
What use in mourning lost achievements,

What use is undying fame, after all?
Wherever there is life, one can live in peace.
Fame and merit are a broken pot,
Discarded, why look back?
Already an earth-bound immortal in leisure,
In wine, I find heaven's completeness.
When others bestow upon the hall,
Like objects on a scale,
Every ounce of gain or loss

The hall receiving bestowals,
Like water reflecting shadows,
Though waves pass countless times,
None remain.
Waiting for dawn with boots full of frost,
Is不如 sleeping by the window till the sun is high and cool.
A pearl-shroud and jade-casket with thousands mourning at the northern tombs,
Is不如 sitting alone in tattered clothes, basking in the morning sun.
Wealth and honor in life,
Literary fame after death,
A hundred years fleeting, ten thousand ages bustling.
Bó Yí and the robber Zhí both lost their sheep—alike in futility,
不如 getting drunk now, forgetting both right and wrong, joy and sorrow.
What use is clinging to a petty official post?
In later years, it may only serve for an epitaph.
Ten thousand ages are but a cycle of dusk and dawn.
In life, I lodge with things but retain none,
At home, I learn the Zen of forgetting home.
Free and untrammeled, beyond trivial concerns.
Rise and fall—what do they matter?
They're equal, like the kingdoms of the snail's horns.
Soaring between heaven and earth,
Why cling to this capital?
In recent years, all matters are satisfied,
The only thing lacking is death.
Why choose where to settle?
The wide world is ample enough.
Like passing clouds before the eyes,
Or the calls of a hundred birds to the ears,
Do we not gladly receive them,
Then let them go without a second thought?
All by Sū Shì.
With the seats full of guests,
Who worries if a hundred flasks are emptied?
Posthumous fame is light,
Only the weight of one cup is felt.
Sū Shì's "Rhapsody on the Wondrous Principle of Unfiltered Wine".
Why calculate the gains and losses of chickens and worms?
The roc and the quail each know their own freedom.
Gathering the universe into a single pot,
Nothing in the world is worth a trifle.
Both by Wáng Ānshí.
Hometown is like any other road,
Where else can I call home?
Chén Shīdào.
Already equating the world to fine dust,
A floating flower in the sky, a body in a dream.
Having witnessed rise and fall, you should laugh,
Over the years, I've grown indifferent to honor and disgrace.
Lord Hé's lavish feast,
Yǔ Zhī's three vegetables,
Comparing abundance and frugality in dreams,
Ultimately both return to decay.
A hundred years, though long, must have an end,
A rich man's death may not be better than a poor man's life.
Both by Sū Shì.
Zǐ
Fāng qí mèng yě,
bù zhī qí mèng yě.
Mèng zhī zhōng yòu zhān qí mèng yān,
jué ér hòu zhī qí mèng yě.
Qiě yǒu dà jué ér hòu zhī cǐ qí dà mèng yě.
． "Zhuāng Qí Wù Lùn".
Xuān miǎn zài shēn,
fēi xìngmìng yě,
wù zhī tǎng lái jì yě.
． "Zhuāngzǐ Shàn Xìng" piān.
Rénshēng tiāndì jiān,
ruò báijū zhī guò xì,
hūrán ér yǐ.
． "Zhuāng Tián Zǐ Fāng".
Hù rù "kuàngdá".
Bù kěyǐ wú yá zhī zhì yì yǒu yá zhī shēn.
"Zhuāng".
Shǐ
Qū Yuán yuē:
"Zhòngrén jiē zuì,
ér wǒ dú xǐng."
． "Shǐ Qū Yuán Zhuàn".
Rénshēng rú qīng chén qī ruò cǎo ěr,
hé zhì zì kǔ nǎi ěr!
． "Tōng Jiàn Sānguó Zhì".
Zǎo zhī fùguì yǒu mìng,
hèn bù shí nián dúshū.
． "Nán Shǐ Shěn Yōuzhī Zhuàn".
Liáng Zhōngliè Shìzǐ yuē:
"Wú bùjí yú niǎo yuǎn yǐ.

rèn qí zhì xìng;
wú zhī jìntuì,
cháng zài zhǎngwò.

zé qù rénjiān rú tuō xǐ ěr."
． "Nán Shǐ Běn Zhuàn".
Zhuànjì
Fùguì zhī wèi rén,
bùrú pínjiàn zhī sì zhì.
Huángfǔ Shì'ān "Gāoshì Zhuàn".
Yì wǒ cái zhě sǔn wǒ shén,
shēng wǒ míng zhě shā wǒ shēn.
Tóng shàng.
Collection
Lamenting the unawakened ways of the mundane world,
Alone I transcend and am the first to realize.
Chéng Gōngzǐ Ān, "Rhapsody on Whistling".
If wealth and honor are hard to secure,
I halt my carriage to follow my desires.
Lù Shìhéng, "Poem Summoning the Recluse".
Knowing to turn back from a misguided path.
Qiū Xīfàn's letter.
Since I have let my heart be enslaved by my body,
Why grieve and sorrow alone?
Realizing the past is beyond remedy,
I know the future can still be pursued.
Indeed, I have not strayed far on this lost path,
Awakening to today's right and yesterday's wrong.
Táo Yuānmíng.
Reaching the edge and turning back,
Filling the measure and knowing to return.
．． "Preface to the Collected Works of Wáng Wénxiàn".
Knowing that fame and rank harm virtue,
Thus I neglect and do not seek them;
Knowing that rich flavors injure nature,
Thus I abandon and disregard them.
Jī Shūyè, "Essay on Nourishing Life".
Wine comforts the inner heart,
The spirit wanders to distant realms.
Smoke arises in the throat and tongue,
Bewildered as if gone mad.
Then peering into the well to watch the drawing of water,
Soon leaning over the river to gaze upon the stream.
Yet my stomach and intestines remain unsatisfied,
Relying on feasts and drinks but still wanting.
Thus I rush to the Jiǔjiāng River,
Race to the Five Lakes.
Searching until the great ocean,
Vast and merging with clarity.
How can your immensity
Not fill my capacity?
Before long in my deliberation,
Suddenly I see the shore.
Then I seek the ant hill,
Awaiting Gěng Gōng.
Ask Jiāngmǔ where she is,
Visit Shūrú wishing to follow.
Identify Kuāfù by the Wèi River,
Mourn Xiàngrú at Lín'áng.
All schemes exhausted,
The six viscera like ashes.
Sunlight slants through the window,
Mosquitoes fly around my temples.
Both startled and awakened,
It is both lamentable and laughable.
Not finishing the drink in the vessel,
My parched guts are already soothed.
Propping my chin, lost in thought,
The meaning grows ever deeper.
Through this day's dream of mine,
I see the hearts of those throughout history who were never content.
Hé Fěng, "Rhapsody on Dreaming of Thirst".
A commoner's life can last a lifetime,
How can favor and salary be relied upon?
Ruǎn Sìzōng, "Singing of My Feelings".
Cross-referenced in "Contentment with One's Lot".
Human life is not like metal or stone,
How can it last long and endure?
． "Selected Ancient Poems".
When delighted by what one encounters,
Temporarily attaining it for oneself,
Joyful and self-satisfied,
Unaware that old age is approaching.
And when one grows weary of what was pursued,
Feelings change with circumstances,
Regret and emotion follow.
What was once enjoyed,
In the blink of an eye,
Becomes a relic of the past.
Wáng Xīzhī, "Preface to the Orchid Pavilion Gathering".
Cross-referenced in "Lament".
Bells, tripods, jades, and silks,
Are not means for transcending the world;
Fame, rank, favor, and honors,
Are storehouses that burden the true self.
If one cannot stand independent of material things,
Transcend the world and endure long,
Shine equally with the sun and moon,
And match the lifespan of heaven and earth.
"Collected Works of Chén Zǐ'áng".
The great world is the mechanism that toils life,
Petty wisdom is no defense for preserving oneself.
Seeing the mantis clutching its shadow,
I fear the hidden crisis not yet pacified.
Seclusion and steadfastness are treasures of emptiness and purity,
Tranquility and silence are the gate to the great mystery.
Knowing that high rank comes by chance,
Understanding that glory and splendor are not attained by force.
Both by Luò Bīnwáng.
If waiting until achievement is made to brush off my clothes and leave,
The peach blossoms of Wǔlíng will laugh heartily.
Looking around, in the human world, it's easy to wither and decay.
Both by Lǐ Tàibái.
Human life in this world is like awakening from a dream,
What difference do gains and losses within it ultimately make?
While dreaming, there is joy and sorrow,
And after awakening, are they worth recalling?
Do not worry about worldly affairs and personal matters,
One must regard the human world as comparable to a dream.
Though the floating life has many paths,
The rush toward death is the same track for all.
Though one may find momentary pleasure,
It is like a swarm of flying mosquitoes.
Both by Hán Wén.
One dream enlightens a whole life.
The mind is the master, the body a guest.
Physical form and lifespan,
Fragile and perilous like floating smoke.
"Smoke" alternatively written as "cloud".
In the great world of human life,
Like a bird's feather in the wind.
Then I know that fame and possessions,
Both gain and loss are harmful.
Also know that the bonds of affection,
Are the sources of worry and distress.
Those with many companions often have more worries,
Not necessarily due to external fires burning.
Fearing to stain the clear, cool waves with dust,
I first shake off my cap tassels.
Without attaining the mind of non-birth,
Even white hair is premature death.
Only then do I know that the love of kin,
Is a gathering of sorrows and griefs.
Affection and love are originally illusions,
Temporarily relatives due to karmic union.
Vow to use the water of wisdom,
Eternally wash the dust of afflictions.
Not to let the child of affection,
Plant again the root of sorrow.
Moreover, this body of flesh and blood,
How can it long remain strong and healthy?
External burdens arise from the mind,
When the mind is calm, burdens cease of themselves.
Must realize all things are empty,
Do not let thoughts cling.
Beauty and color are empty flowers,
The floating life is like parched grain.
Obstructions must be burned by the lamp of wisdom,
Demons must be slain by the sword of insight.
Tempted by profit, nature is easily tainted,
Internal struggles, the mind is hard to conquer.
Sever folly, seek the sword of wisdom,
Cross suffering, attain the ferry of compassion.
In mountains and forests, first resting the shadow,
From morning to night, long toiling for life.
Worries and sufferings are all fires of the mind,
Prosperity and decay are dust in the eyes.
What people in the world value,
Are the minister's seal and the general's axe.
Tormenting the heart, the suffering of one body,
Scorching the hand, others feel the heat.
Not necessarily within the heart,
Can they be as carefree as I.
Guests enjoy, servants are well-fed,
Only then know that official positions serve others.
Official headgear temporarily assembled, empty fame remains,
Physical strength worn away, substantial deeds are void.
But if one can shake off worldly affairs,
Then one is a carefree immortal on earth.
Often see the wealthy in vermilion gates,
Before their gardens are complete, they lose their lives.
Flowing water, time urgent,
Floating clouds, wealth and honor slow.
Fine dishes and delicious wine,
Truly are the fat that rots the intestines.
Alluring sounds and beautiful colors,
Indeed are the blades that fell one's nature.
Speaking of dreams within a dream, doubly illusory.
Only fear that in the human world, it becomes a burden,
Better to be a remnant in the woods.
Gold and jade filling the hall are not one's own,
Descendants shed like cicada skin belong to others.
Only this single body should be cherished and protected,
Less let ice and charcoal torment the spirit.
An old hen under the rope has its tail cut off,
Fresh fish slices on the plate are from swallowing the hook.
Mistakenly entangled by the net of the world.
All by Bái Shìláng.
The sounds of strings and pipes are unreal,
The colors of floral ornaments are empty.
If this now were not a dream,
How much longer could it last than a dream?
Not asking whether the root of illness is deep or shallow,
This body should be born together with illness.
All by Bái Lètiān.
Only then do I know that between heaven and earth,
All things are impermanent.
Mèng Dōngyě.
Viewing the body as a relay station,
Observing the world passing like the eastern flow.
How can the physical body be my treasure?
When words reach the point of silence,
All people in the world are asleep.
Only those who understand the principles of life,
Should have no method to manage old age.
Only then realize the stupor of drunkenness,
Should surpass the bustle of constant striving.
After the day's music and songs scatter,
Amidst the wind and rain over the river, alone and sober.
Also by Yuán Zhěn.
Look at the lotus flower's purity,
Should know the unstained heart.
Mèng Hàorán.
Do not consult divination about life,
Good and ill fortune both come from oneself.
If Fúxī and King Wén had not died,
People today would not weep for the ancients.
Liú Yìwén.
Long bound by fleeting fame,
How could I not feel ashamed before the seagulls?
Liú Chángqīng.
As I age, I realize the burden of the body.
Same as above.
Clear in the deep night,
Perceptive in great drunkenness.
Huángfǔ Shí.
Official caps and robes are still like black dust.
All fame is a fearful path,
Only without affairs is the true essence.
Have you not seen the worldly wind, the lantern, and the hibiscus flower?
Also from Lǐ Yìshān's writings.
Fully aware of the peril on the path,
Who would willingly lighten the load in time?
Qián Qǐ's poem on the boat.
For generations, the body is in a dream,
A hundred years, clouds without roots.
Bào Róng's writings.
A road of ten thousand li, high and low outside the gate,
A body of a hundred years, honor and disgrace in a dream.
In the past, unaware of joy beyond fame,
In late years, first believing in the busyness of dreams.
Also by Xǔ Yònghuì.
How long can a human life be?
After all, it returns to formlessness.
From the "Collection of Wáng Wéi".
Always words that overstep bounds,
Long become traps for the self.
Dù Mù.
Only knowing events pass before the eyes,
Unaware that old age comes from the head.
From the "Collection of Luó Yǐn".
A floating life of seventy, now thirty,
Already half a lifetime in the human world.
Extinguish the fire in the heart, and it cools naturally.
After a hundred years, a mound of earth,

．． _Tōngjiàn, Sānguó Wèi Wén Dì_.
Cross-reference "self-preservation".
Lǐ Fēng, at seventeen or eighteen,
already had a pure reputation,
praised throughout the land.
His father, Tàipú Lǐ Huī, disapproved,
so he made him seclude himself and cut off visitors.
． _Tōngjiàn, Wèi Gāoguì Xiāng Gōng_.
Cáo Jiǒng said:
"If the tip is too large, it will break;
if the tail is too big, it cannot be wagged.
Even if the tail is part of the body,
it may not obey,
let alone a tail not of the body—
how can it be wagged!"
． _Tōngjiàn_.
Jìn Wǔdì wanted Yáng Hù to oversee the generals while bedridden,
but Hù said:
"Conquering Wú does not require my presence,
but after pacification,
Your Majesty will have to labor over it."
． _Tōngjiàn, Jìn Jì_.
Initially,
Hé Zēng attended a feast with Wǔdì,
and upon leaving,
told his sons:
"The emperor founded a great enterprise,
yet in feasts, I never hear grand strategies for the state,
only concerns for his lifetime—
his successors are in peril!
You might be spared."
Pointing to his grandsons, he said:
"They will surely face disaster."
When Suí died,
his elder brother Sōng wept:
"Was my grandfather almost a sage!"
． _Tōngjiàn, Jìn Huái Dì Jì_.
Wáng Měng was gravely ill,
and Fú Jiān personally visited his residence,
consulting on future matters.
Měng said:
"Although Jìn resides remotely in Jiāngnán,
it upholds the legitimate succession,
with peace above and below.
After my death,
do not plan against Jìn.
The Xiānbēi and Xīqiāng are our enemies,
and will eventually cause trouble—
gradually eliminate them."
． _Tōngjiàn, Jìn Wén Dì Jì_.
Xiè Zhān saw his brother Huì's residence crowded and narrow,
and said:
"Influence overwhelming the court—
is it a blessing for the family?"
． _Tōngjiàn, Jìn Ān Dì Jì Xià_.
Wáng Yàn's cousin Ruǎn Xiàoxù also knew Yàn would fall;
Yàn often visited his door,
but he hid and refused to see him.
Once, he tasted delicious sauce,
and upon learning it came from Yàn's house,
spat it out and poured it away.
． _Tōngjiàn, Qí Gāozōng Jì_.
Cross-reference "avoiding disaster externally".
The Wèi emperor, critically ill,
told Minister Xíe:
"The state relies on you.
Huò Zǐmèng and Zhūgě Kǒngmíng, as non-relatives, received临终托付,
let alone you, a close and worthy—
can you not strive?"
Xíe wept:
"Even the great sage Zhōu Gōng and the wise King Chéng faced suspicion,
how much more me!
Thus, for Your Majesty to love me,
it would lack a perfect end."
． _Tōngjiàn, Qí Dōng Hūn Hóu_.
Gāo Huān said:
"Only Mùróng Shàozōng can match Hóu Jǐng.
I deliberately did not honor him,
leaving him for you."
． _Tōngjiàn, Liáng Gāozǔ_.
Ultimately, fear the tail outgrowing the body,
the heel thicker than the thigh,
stubborn and unyielding,
fierce and hard to tame.
_Tōngjiàn_,
same as before.
The Liáng crown prince lectured on Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzǐ in Xuán Pǔ,
and Hé Jìngróng told scholar Wú Zī:
"Formerly, Western Jìn esteemed emptiness and mystery,
leading to the Central Plains' fall to the Hú and Jié;
now the crown prince does the same—
will Jiāngnán also become barbarian land?"
． _Tōngjiàn, Liáng Gāozǔ_.
The Huáinán giant whale,
though said to be beheaded;
the Xiāngyáng short fox,
not fully reformed.
． _Tōngjiàn, Liáng Gāozǔ_.
Qí Xiǎnzǔ's alcoholism led to illness,
unable to eat,
knowing his time was short,
told Empress Lǐ:
"Death is inevitable for all—
why regret it!
Only pity Zhèngdào is young,
Should they run wild,
there would be no ground to retreat and seek withdrawal.
It's not that I do not desire high-ranking positions,
but I have thought it through thoroughly."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Wen of Chen".
Húlǜ Jīn, the Left Director of the Qi dynasty, had his eldest son Guāng as a Great General,
and his second son Xiàn along with many grandsons were enfeoffed as marquises, achieving great prominence.
Their family produced one empress,
two crown princesses,
and three princesses,
serving the Qi through three reigns,
unmatched in honor and favor.
Yet Jīn took no joy in this,
once telling Guāng: "Although I am uneducated,
I have heard that few maternal relatives in history have preserved their clans.
If a daughter is favored,
she incurs jealousy among the nobles;
if not favored,
she earns the emperor's disdain.
Our family should attain wealth and status through merit,
why rely on a daughter's favor!"
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Records of Chen".
Sū Wēi had a good reputation from youth,
and Zhōu's Duke of Jìn, Yǔwén Hù, forcibly married his daughter to him.
Seeing Hù's monopolization of power,
Sū Wēi feared disaster would befall him,
so he secluded himself in a mountain temple,
finding solace in reading and reciting.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Records of Chen".
Suí's Prince of Cài, Zhì Jī, had five sons
and taught them only the "Analects" and "Classic of Filial Piety",
fearing that if they had talent, it might lead to disaster.
Same as above.
If a ruler, upon seeing desirable things, thinks of contentment;
when about to undertake construction, thinks of knowing when to stop;
in high and perilous positions, thinks of humility and descent;
facing fullness and surplus, thinks of reduction;
encountering leisure and pleasure, thinks of moderation;
in peace and comfort, thinks of future troubles;
to prevent obstruction, thinks of openness and acceptance;
hating slander and evil, thinks of self-correction;
when bestowing honors and rewards, thinks of excess due to joy;
when imposing punishments, thinks of abuse due to anger.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Tàizōng of Táng".
The emperor had decreed that imperial clan members and officials inherit titles as provincial governors,
but Left Tutor Yú Zhìníng believed ancient and modern circumstances differed,
fearing it was not a way to lasting peace,
and submitted a memorial in opposition.
Attendant Censor Mǎ Zhōu also memorialized,
arguing: "If children inherit offices,
should they become arrogant or foolish,
the people would suffer and the state face ruin.
If you wish to end it,
the good governance of Zǐ Wén remains;
if you wish to retain it,
the evils of Luán Yǎn are already evident.
What was meant as love
may恰恰 harm them."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Tàizōng of Táng".
The emperor told the crown prince: "Lǐ Shìjì has ample talent and wisdom,
but you share no bond of gratitude with him,
fearing he may not submit willingly.
I will now demote him;
if he departs promptly,
after my death,
you can appoint him as Chief Minister,
trusting and employing him;
if he hesitates and looks back,
then he should be executed."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Tàizōng of Táng".
Prince Pei, Lǐ Xián, hearing that Wáng Bó was skilled in writing,
summoned him as a compiler.
When princes were competing with gamecocks,
Bó playfully wrote a "Proclamation Against Prince Zhōu's Chicken".
The emperor saw it,
and angrily said: "This is the start of sowing discord."
He expelled Bó from the Prince of Pei's residence.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Gāozōng of Táng".
The emperor ascended the Xiángluán Pavilion,
to watch a grand feast.
Music was divided into eastern and western teams,
with Prince Yōng, Xián, leading the east,
and Prince Zhōu, Xiǎn, leading the west,
competing for amusement.
Hǎo Chǔjùn admonished: "The two princes are still young,
their inclinations not yet set;
they should practice sharing and yielding,
united as one.
Now divided into teams,
competing and boasting in turn,
with entertainers and petty men
using unrestrained language,
I fear they will contend for victory,
mocking and losing propriety,
not promoting ritual and righteousness,
nor encouraging harmony."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Gāozōng of Táng".
Yáo Chóng divided his assets,
assigning fixed shares to each son.
His testament said: "I've seen many descendants of high officials fall into poverty and greed,
competing over trifles,
regardless of right or wrong,
all ridiculed
and slandered.
When fields, houses, and mills are shared,
they lean on each other until all is neglected and ruined.
Lù Jiǎ and Shí Bāo,
wise men of old,
also set fixed shares first to prevent future disputes."
． From "New Book of Táng: His Biography".
Lǐ Jì, on his sickbed,
told his younger brother, Vice Minister of the Imperial Guard, Bì: "I've seen Fáng Xuánlíng and Dù Rǔhuǐ toil all their lives,
barely establishing their households,
only to have unworthy sons
utterly destroy them.
I have these descendants,
now all entrusted to you.
Should any show improper ambition
or keep bad company,
beat them to death first."
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance".
Jí Xū said: "Mixing earth and water into clay,
is there contention?"
The Empress replied: "None."
He continued: "Dividing it half for a Buddha,
half for a celestial deity,
is there contention?"
She said:
"There is contention."
Xū kowtowed and said: "If imperial clansmen and maternal relatives keep to their proper places,
the empire is at peace.
Now, with no crown prince appointed and maternal relatives still princes,
Your Majesty is driving them to inevitable future conflict,
where neither side finds peace."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Empress Wǔ of Táng".
After the Zhāng brothers were executed,
Luòzhōu Chief Official Xuē Jìchǎng told Zhāng Jiǎnzhī and Jìng Huī: "Though the two villains are gone,
their kin, like Chǎn and Lù, remain;
if the roots aren't removed,
they will regrow."
The two said: "The major deed is done,
they are but meat on the cutting board,
what can they do!"
Jìchǎng sighed: "I know not where I shall die!"
Liú Yōuqiú also told Huàn Yànfàn and Jìng Huī: "While Wǔ Sānsī lives,
you will have no burial place;
if not planned early,
regret will be too late."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Zhōngzōng of Táng".
Cross-referenced under "Foresight".
Wise men of old never wished to accept favors from barbarians,
for they foresaw their insatiable demands would become future troubles.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Ruìzōng of Táng".
Qí Huàn stated: "Gě Fúshùn commands the imperial guards,
he should not marry into Máo Zhòng's family.
Máo Zhòng is a petty man;
excessive favor breeds treachery.
If not addressed early,
I fear it will become a future calamity."
He added: "If a lord is not discreet, he loses his ministers;
I hope Your Majesty will keep this secret."
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance".
Zhāng Jiāzhēn did not accumulate family property;
when urged to buy land and houses,
he said: "As a respected chancellor,
why worry about cold or hunger!
If I am convicted of a crime,
even with land and houses,
they would be of no use.
I've seen court officials amass vast fertile lands,
only for their unscrupulous descendants
to use them as funds for wine and women after their death;
I will not follow that."
Same as above.
The emperor recalled Guō Zǐyí to the capital.
The Shuòfāng troops appreciated Zǐyí's leniency
and feared Lǐ Guāngbì's strictness.
Zhāng Yòngjì and other officers plotted to lead elite troops into the eastern capital,
expel Guāngbì,
and request Zǐyí's return.
Kāng Yuánbǎo said: "If you use troops to request Lord Guō,
the court will suspect he instigated it,
thus ruining his family.
How has Lord Guō, with his hundred relatives, wronged you!"
Yòngjì then desisted.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Sùzōng of Táng".
Guō Zǐyí, when receiving guests,
always had his concubines nearby.
But when Lú Qǐ came to inquire about his health,
Zǐyí dismissed all attendants,
leaning alone on a table to await him.
Asked why,
he said: "Qǐ is ugly but sinister;
if women saw him, they would laugh,
and if he ever gains power,
our clan would be exterminated!"
． From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Dézōng of Táng".
Even a commoner who loves his child
knows to seek a wise teacher for instruction,
how much more should the heir of an emperor, on whom the fate of the realm depends!
Gěng Chún led his clan to submit to Emperor Guāngwǔ,
fearing some might not be in agreement,
burned down their houses,
cutting off any thought of turning back.
From "Dōngguān Hànjì".
In the world, what is inexhaustible
is wisdom and talent.
Chén Píng devised six remarkable strategies,
but feared disaster would befall him.
Lù Jiǎ advised him,
to befriend the Grand Commandant,
and also outlined several matters regarding the Lǚ clan.
Chén Píng followed his advice,
and eventually eliminated the various Lǚs.
Thus, Jiǎ's wisdom and strategy
surpassed even that of Píng.
From "Kǒngshì Záshuō".
Mutually entered under "Strength Meets Strength".
Collection
Holding counting rods to calculate,
not a single error in ten thousand.
From Méi Chéng's "Seven Stimuli".
The blade of wisdom thus renews daily.
From "Selection Temple Stele".
Classic
If a person lacks long-term considerations,
they are bound to have immediate worries.
From "Analects, Duke Líng of Wèi".
Without thought, how can one gain?
From "Book of Documents, Tàijiǎ Part Two".
If I myself am not spared,
how can I have leisure to care for my descendants?
From "Book of Songs, Gǔ Fēng".
Turning away from this without reflection,
what more can be said?
From "Book of Songs, Méng".
Plans that are not far-sighted.
From "Book of Songs, Bǎn".
Masters
If plans are not settled in advance,
one cannot respond to sudden events.
From "Dèng Xīzǐ".
History
Zǐfú Huìbó said: "The nobleman has long-term considerations,
while the petty man follows the immediate.
If one does not care for hunger and cold,
who has leisure to think of the future?"
From "Zuǒzhuàn, 28th Year of Duke Xiāng".
Mù Shū said to Mèng Xiàobó: "Zhào Mèng is about to die.
His words are heedless."
Xiàobó said: "How long is a human life?
Who can avoid being heedless?
If morning does not reach evening,
what use is planning for the future?"
Mù Shū went out and told others: "Mèng Sūn is about to die.
I spoke to him about Zhào Mèng's heedlessness,
and his is even worse."
From "Zuǒzhuàn, 31st Year of Duke Xiāng".
Zhào Mèng said: "I fear only crimes and faults,
how can I care for the distant future?
We merely eat heedlessly,
with no plan from morning to evening,
how can we think long-term?"
From "Zuǒzhuàn, 1st Year of Duke Zhāo".
Zhào Mèng looked at the shadows and said: "Morning and evening do not connect,
who can wait for five?"
Five years passed.
From "Zuǒzhuàn, 1st Year of Duke Zhāo".
Generally, human wisdom
can see what has already happened,
but cannot see what is about to happen.
From "Comprehensive Mirror".
Indulging in petty pleasures without planning for great disasters.
From "Western Hàn, Biography of Jiǎ Yì".
In planning affairs and proposing advice,
not aiming for the stability of ten thousand generations,
but relying on temporary matters for a short while,
cannot endure long.
From "Western Hàn, Appraisal of the Xiōngnú".
Qí Hé Shìkāi said: "One day of pleasure
can rival a thousand years!"
From "Comprehensive Mirror, Chén Dynasty".
Kǒng Fàn said: "The various generals
are only a match for ordinary men.
Deep insight and far-reaching plans,
how could they possibly know!"
From "Comprehensive Mirror, Later Lord of Chén".
Classic
Fāng Shū, the venerable elder,
could greatly expand his strategies.
From "Book of Songs, Cǎi Qǐ".
At forty, one begins official service,
then plans and deliberates on affairs.
From "Book of Rites, Nèi Zé".
Loving to plan and thereby succeed.
From "Analects, Shù'ér".
Masters
Combining talent and valuing strategy,
calculating on the right and left.
From "Yáng Chónglí".
Pooling strategies and uniting strengths.
Same as above.
史
Bì Chén, when deliberating in the wilds, achieved success;
when deliberating in the city, he did not.
"Zuǒzhuàn".
Calm and profound, thus possessing strategy.
． "Shǐjì Dì Xū Jì".
Sū Qín feared that Qín would undermine the vertical alliance,
and thought of no one who could be employed in Qín,
so he sent someone to subtly influence Zhāng Yí,
secretly providing him with carriages, horses, gold, and coins,
for whatever he desired to use,
supplying him as needed,
without informing him.
Zhāng Yí thus managed to see King Huì of Qín.
King Huì appointed him as a guest minister,
and consulted with him on attacking the various states.
Sū Qín's retainer took his leave.
Zhāng Yí said: "Thanks to you, I have gained prominence,
and I am just about to repay your kindness,
why are you leaving?"
The retainer said: "I did not recognize your worth,
it was Sū Jūn who recognized you.
He worried that Qín would attack Zhào and break the vertical alliance,
believing that no one but you could gain power in Qín,
so he deliberately provoked you,
sent me to secretly provide you with funds,
all part of Sū Jūn's scheme.
Now that you are employed,
I ask to return and report."
Zhāng Yí said: "I was in Sū Jūn's plan without realizing it,
I am clearly not as astute as Sū Jūn!
Moreover, I have just been employed,
how could I plot against Zhào?
Please convey my thanks to Sū Jūn,
while Sū Jūn is alive,
how would I dare speak against him."
． "Shǐ Běn Zhuàn".
Fàn Jū said: "Your Majesty should befriend distant states and attack nearby ones,
gaining an inch makes it Your Majesty's inch,
gaining a foot makes it Your Majesty's foot."
． "Shǐ Běn Zhuàn".
Gān Luó was young,
devised an ingenious plan,
and his reputation endured in later generations.
He too was a strategist of the Warring States period.
． "Shǐ Běn Zhuàn".
Yú Qīng assessed events and gauged situations,
devised strategies for Zhào,
how masterful he was!
． "Shǐ Běn Zhuàn".
Cài Zé said to Fàn Jū: "As chancellor of Qín,
your plans are made without leaving your mat,
your strategies are formed within the court,
you control the feudal lords from your seat,
your achievements have reached the peak!"
． "Shǐ Cài Zé Zhuàn".
Hóu Yíng said: "I hear that Jìn Bǐ's military tally is in the king's bedchamber,
and Rú Jī, being the most favored,
has the means to steal it.
I have heard that you, young master, avenged her father's death for Rú Jī,
she is willing to die for you,
without hesitation.
If you truly ask her,
you can obtain the tiger tally to seize Jìn Bǐ's troops,
rescue Zhào in the north and repel Qín in the west,
this would be an achievement rivaling the Five Hegemons."
The young master followed his advice,
and repelled Qín.
． "Tōngjiàn Zhōu Jì".
Six ingenious plans were employed,
and the feudal lords submitted to Hàn;
in the matter of the Lǚ family,
Chén Píng was the mastermind.
Zǐfáng's strategies,
tackled difficulties through simplicity,
achieved greatness through subtlety.
Both from "Tàishǐgōng Zìxù".
Someone submitted a letter accusing Hán Xìn of rebellion.
The Emperor asked Chén Píng,
who said: "To raise troops and attack him
would hasten him to battle.
Your Majesty should instead pretend to tour Yúnmèng,
where he will surely come to the outskirts to greet you.
When he greets you,
capture him;
this is merely a task for one strong warrior."
The Emperor agreed,
toured Yúnmèng,
and Hán Xìn indeed came to the outskirts to greet him.
Warriors bound him,
and placed him in a following carriage.
． "Shǐ Chén Píng Shìjiā".
Zhāng Liáng returned to Hàn,
often ill,
never specifically commanded troops,
but always devised strategies.
． "Tōngjiàn Hàn Gāo Jì".
Zhāng Liáng said:
"The King of Jiǔjiāng, Yīng Bù,
a fierce general of Chǔ,
has a rift with King Xiàng;
Péng Yuè, with Qí, rebels in Liáng territory;
these two can be urgently employed.
And among the King of Hàn's generals,
only Hán Xìn can be entrusted with great affairs,
holding his own front.
If you are willing to assign these three men,
then Chǔ can be defeated."
Same as above.
Yuán Shēng advised the King of Hàn: "I hope Your Majesty will march out of Wǔguān,
King Xiàng will surely lead his troops southward,
you fortify your defenses deeply,
allowing the area between Xíngyáng and Chénggāo to rest.
Send Hán Xìn and others to pacify the northern Zhào lands,
then you can return to Xíngyáng,
not too late.
This way,
Chǔ will have many fronts to defend,
its forces divided,
Hàn can rest,
and then engage them in battle,
surely defeating Chǔ."
King Xiàng heard the King of Hàn was in Wǎn,
and indeed led his troops south.
Hàn fortified its walls and did not engage in battle.
． "Shǐjì Hàn Gāo Jì".
Chén Píng, from his initial service until the empire was settled,
followed in campaigns against Zāng Tú, Chén Xī, and Qíng Bù.
In all, he devised six ingenious plans,
the world never learned of them.
Hán Xìn, having defeated Qí,
sent a message: "If not made acting king,
I fear I cannot pacify Qí."
The King of Hàn wanted to attack him.
Liú Hóu said: "Better to enfeoff him accordingly,
letting him guard it himself."
So he sent Zhāng Liáng with the seal to establish Hán Xìn as King of Qí.
． "Shǐjì Hàn Gāozǔ".
Xiàng Yǔ urgently besieged the King of Hàn,
who plotted with Lì Yìjī to undermine Chǔ's power.
Lì Shēng said: "If Your Majesty restores the descendants of the six states,
they will all vie to uphold your virtue and righteousness,
willing to be your subjects."
The King of Hàn said: "Good.
Hasten to carve the seals."
Before Lì Shēng could depart,
Zhāng Liáng came from outside to see the King of Hàn,
who fully informed him of Lì Shēng's plan.
Liáng said: "Who devised this plan for Your Majesty?
Allow me to borrow your chopsticks to strategize.
Moreover, the wandering scholars of the empire,
leaving their families,
abandoning their ancestral graves,
parting from old friends,
follow Your Majesty,
hoping day and night for a small piece of land.
Now if you restore the six states' descendants,
the wandering scholars will return to serve their own lords,
rejoin their families,
and return to old friends,
with whom will Your Majesty conquer the empire?
If this plan is adopted,
Your Majesty's cause is lost."
The King of Hàn stopped eating, spat out his food,
and cursed:
"This pedant,
nearly ruined your lord's affairs!"
Ordered to hasten the destruction of the seals.
． "Xīhàn Zhāng Liáng Zhuàn".
The King of Hàn scheduled a joint attack on Chǔ with the King of Qí, Xìn, and the Chancellor of Wèi, Yuè;
Xìn and Yuè did not arrive.
Zhāng Liáng said: "Chǔ's army is about to be defeated,
these two have no allocated lands,
their not coming is natural.
Now if you can grant the area from Suīyáng north to Gǔchéng to Péng Yuè as king,
and from Chén east to the sea to the King of Qí, Xìn.
Xìn's family is in Chǔ,
he desires to regain his hometown.
If you can cede these lands to promise the two,
letting them fight for themselves,
then Chǔ can be easily defeated."
The King of Hàn agreed.
Thereupon, Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè both led their troops to come.
． "Tōngjiàn Hàn Gāo Jì".
The Grand Commandant again ordered Lì Jì and the Diplomat Liú Jiē to first persuade Lǚ Lù: "The Emperor has ordered the Grand Commandant to guard the Northern Army,
wishing you to return to your fief.
Quickly return the general's seal and depart.
Otherwise,
disaster will arise."
Lǚ Lù believed Lì Kuàng was not deceiving him,
so he handed over the seal to the Diplomat,
and the troops to the Grand Commandant.
． "Tōngjiàn Hàn Gāo Jì".
The various Lǚs monopolized power,
and Chén Píng was troubled by it.
Lù Jiǎ said: "The empire's safety or peril,
depends on the generals and ministers.
If the generals and ministers are harmonious,
then the scholars will gladly submit."
Why don't you form an alliance with the Grand Commandant?
Chén Píng employed his strategy,
presenting five hundred gold pieces as a birthday gift to Jiàng Hóu,
and the Grand Commandant reciprocated in kind.
The two men formed a deep bond,
and the plots of the various Lǚ clan increasingly fell apart.
. "Biography of Lù Jiǎ from the Former Hàn".
Chén Tāng was a person of deep courage and great foresight,
abounding in strategies and schemes.
. "Main Biography from the Western Hàn".
His mastery of classical arts and refinement were sufficient to counsel on royal affairs,
and to decide state policies.
. "Biography of Xuē Xuān from the Western Hàn".
Cross-referenced under "Refinement".
Wisdom, strategy, and planning,
were the deep pools of the court.
. "Biography of Fú Zhàn from the Eastern Hàn".
Cross-referenced under "Wisdom and Foolishness".
Mǎ Yuán's strategies flowed like a gushing spring.
. "Biography of Mǎ Yuán from the Eastern Hàn".
He was brave, fierce, and possessed wisdom and strategy.

Lǐ Zhèngjǐ of Zīqīng, during the reign of Emperor Dézōng, feared the emperor's decisive authority,
and offered a tribute of three hundred thousand strings of coins,
to test the court's response.
The emperor suspected deceit,
and was unsure how to respond.
Cuī Yòufǔ, serving as chancellor,
said: "If Lǐ Zhèngjǐ is indeed deceitful,
it would be better to send an envoy to reward his army,
using the tribute to bestow upon his officers and soldiers.
If he obeys the edict,
it shows Your Majesty's grace reaches his troops;
if not,
he will incur their resentment,
and the army may revolt.
This prevents the border tribes from viewing the court as easily bribed."
The emperor said: "Excellent."
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ felt ashamed and submitted.
Contemporary critics praised his strategic planning.

Lǐ Déyù served as Minister of War.
Initially,
Lǐ Zōngmǐn had a rift with Lǐ Déyù,
and when Lǐ Déyù returned from Xīchuān,
the emperor held him in high regard,
and he was soon to become chancellor,
but Lǐ Zōngmǐn tried every means to obstruct him without success.
The Capital Governor Dù Cóng,
an ally of Lǐ Zōngmǐn,
once visited Lǐ Zōngmǐn,
saw his worried expression,
and asked: "Is it because of the great general?"
Lǐ Zōngmǐn said: "Yes.
How can you save me?"
Dù Cóng said: "I have a plan
that can settle the old grudge,
but I fear you may not use it."
Lǐ Zōngmǐn said: "What is it?"
Dù Cóng said: "Lǐ Déyù is learned but did not pass the imperial exams,
and often resents this;
if you let him oversee the examinations,
he would surely be pleased."
Lǐ Zōngmǐn remained silent for a while,
then said: "Think of another way."
Dù Cóng said: "Otherwise, appoint him as Grand Imperial Secretary."
Lǐ Zōngmǐn said: "That would work."
Dù Cóng then went to see Lǐ Déyù.
Greeting him, he said: "Why have you come to this quiet place?"
Dù Cóng said: "Chancellor Jìng'ān sent me to convey his intentions."
He then informed him of the appointment as Grand Imperial Secretary.
Lǐ Déyù was pleasantly surprised and shed tears,
saying: "This is a high-ranking position;
how can someone like me deserve it!"
He repeatedly expressed his gratitude.

Confucius served as prime minister of Lǔ.

From "Family Sayings".
When the roasted sacrificial meat did not arrive,

From "Mèngzǐ".

From "Liúzǐ".
In history,

saying: "When the flying birds are gone,
the good bow is stored away;
when the cunning hares are dead,
the hunting dog is cooked."
From "Historical Records: House of Yuè".
Fàn Lǐ served King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè,
and after more than twenty years finally destroyed Wú,
avenging the shame of Kuàijī.
Upon returning to the state,
he sent a letter resigning to Gōu Jiàn,
who said: "I will share the state with you and possess it together.
If not,
I will impose punishment upon you."
Fàn Lǐ said: "The ruler issues commands,
the minister follows his will."
Thereupon, he packed his light treasures, pearls, and jades,
and with his private followers sailed away by sea,
never to return.
He settled in Táo,
calling himself Lord Táo Zhū.
Same as above.
When Confucius could not gain employment in Wèi,
he planned to go west to see Zhào Jiǎnzǐ.
Upon reaching the river, he heard of the deaths of Dòu Míngdú and Shùn Huá,
and sighing by the river, said: "How beautiful is the water,
so vast and boundless!
That I cannot cross
must be fate!"
Zǐgòng hurried forward and asked:
"May I ask what you mean?"
Confucius said: "Dòu Míngdú and Shùn Huá
were worthy senior officials of the state.
When Zhào Jiǎnzǐ had not yet achieved his ambitions,
he needed these two men to then administer governance;
once he had achieved his ambitions,
he killed them to then govern.
I have heard that
if one cuts open wombs and kills the young, the qílín will not approach the suburbs;
if one drains ponds and dries up fisheries, the jiāolóng will not harmonize yīn and yáng;
if one overturns nests and destroys eggs, the fènghuáng will not soar.
Why is this?
Because the nobleman avoids harming his kind.
Even birds and beasts know to avoid what is unjust,
how much more should I!"
He then returned and rested in Zōu xiāng,
composing the "Zōu Cǎo" to mourn them.
From "Historical Records: House of Confucius".
Those who know early

From "Historical Records: Biography of Yuè Yì".
Beneath success,
one cannot dwell for long.

Yuán

Before the hónghú has hatched from the egg,
a single finger can crush it,
leaving it formless and dissolved;
but once its sinews and bones have formed,
and its wings and feathers are complete,
it flaps its wings and shakes its pinions,
ascending past floating clouds,
bearing the blue sky on its back,
brushing the crimson sky with its breast,

Our Dynasty
When Xiàng Jí was crossing the river,
Pèi Gōng began to marshal his troops toward the pass.
If Jí had quickly led his army to Qín at that time,
using their sharp momentum,
he could have occupied Xiányáng and controlled the empire.
Not realizing this approach,
he instead contended with Qín generals for momentary survival,
and after securing Jùlù, still lingered between Hénán and Xīn'ān,
reaching Hángǔ
only after Pèi Gōng had entered Xiányáng months earlier.
Ultimately, he established his capital at Péngchéng,
allowing Pèi Gōng to pacify the Three Qín.

what good did it do?

The Master's words
were actually criticizing him.

thinking the Master was praising Jì Lù,
thus acting on momentary impressions
