pass the nine thorn bushes,
consult the multitude of ministers,

yet ultimately avoided punishment and execution,
because their words were upright.
From "Shǐjì, basic annals and eulogies".
Qín Shǐhuáng sent Wáng Jiǎn to conquer Shǔ,
who requested many fine fields, houses, gardens, and ponds.
Someone said: "General, your begging is
excessive."
Jiǎn said: "The King of Qín is suspicious
(pronounced cū)
and distrustful of others.
Now he empties Qín's armored forces and entrusts them solely to me;
if I do not request many fields and houses as assets for my descendants to secure myself,
he would surely sit and doubt me!"
From "Shǐjì, basic biography".
Sū Qín advised the King of Yān: "If I stay in Yān, I cannot make Yān weighty,
but if I go to Qí, then Yān becomes weighty."
From "Tōngjiàn, Zhōu records".
Hearing that the king intended to reprimand him,
he slipped away alone and left.
From "Shǐjì, Xiàng Yǔ's annals".
Zhāng Ĕr preserved himself through wisdom.
From "Shǐjì, basic eulogies".
Zhāng Liáng entered to apologize: "Pèi Gōng cannot handle alcohol,
and is unable to bid farewell."
From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Gāozǔ's annals".
Jīzǐ feigned madness,
Jiēyú avoided the world.
From "Shǐjì, Zōu Yáng's biography".
I wish to abandon worldly affairs and follow Chìsōngzǐ in wandering.
From "Shǐjì, Zhāng Liáng's biography".
Lǚ Xū repeatedly slandered Chén Píng to Empress Lǚ: "The Chancellor does not attend to duties,
drinking strong wine daily and amusing himself with women."
"People" in one version is "women".
Píng heard this,
and intensified it daily.
From "Hànshū".
Lǐ Yì praised Bān Chāo: "Embracing his beloved wife,
holding his beloved son,
content in a foreign land,
with no mind for home."
Chāo heard this and sighed: "I am not Zēng Shēn, yet face triple slander;
I fear being doubted in these times!"
Thus he sent away his wife.
From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Zhāngdì's annals".
Méi Fú knew Wáng Mǎng would usurp the Hàn throne,
so one morning he abandoned his wife and children and left,
none knew where he went.
Later,
someone saw Fú in Kuàijī,
having changed his name to become a gate guard in Wú market.
From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Píngdì's annals".
Páng Méng of Běihǎi told a friend: "The three bonds are severed;
if I do not leave,
disaster will reach me!"
He immediately took off his official hat and hung it on the eastern capital's city gate,
returned home,
took his family across the sea,
and settled in Liáo.
Same as above.
Dōngpíng King Cāng, being a close relative in government,
saw his prestige grow daily,
felt uneasy,
and repeatedly submitted memorials stating:
"Since Hàn's founding,
no imperial clansman has held high ministerial office;
I beg to return the seal of General of Agile Cavalry,
and retire to my fiefdom."
His pleas were earnest,
so the emperor allowed Cāng to return,
but not to surrender his general's seal.
From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Míngdì's annals".
Jìng King Mù of Běihǎi loved learning from youth,
beloved by both Emperor Guāngwǔ and the current emperor;
once he sent a grand master to the capital for court greetings,
and summoned him: "If the court inquires about me,
how will you respond?"
The envoy said: "Your Majesty is loyal, filial, kind, and benevolent,
respecting the worthy and delighting in scholars;
how dare I not answer truthfully!"
Mù said: "Alas, you endanger me!
That was my youthful, ambitious conduct.
You should say that since I inherited the title,
my will has declined,
I amuse myself with music and women,
and indulge in dogs and horses;
that would show true affection."
Such was his cautious wisdom.
From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Míngdì's annals".
Xià Fù heard of Zhāng Jiǎn's flight,
and sighed:
"Misdeeds are self-made,
yet they unjustly implicate the good;
one man flees death,
and disaster reaches ten thousand households—
why live on!"
He then cut off his beard and altered his appearance,
entering the Línlǜ mountains.
Fàn Pāng told Yīn Táo et al.:
"Now you follow me,
which multiplies my disaster."
From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Língdì's annals".
Sīmǎ Yì,
was intelligent and perceptive from youth,
with great strategic vision.
Cáo Cāo heard of him and summoned him,
but Yì declined citing paralysis.
Cáo Cāo,
angered, intended to arrest him,
so Yì, fearing,
took the post.
From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Xiàndì's annals".
Shēntú Pán said:
"In the Warring States era,
recluses debated freely,
and kings of various states
even swept paths for them,
yet ended with the burning of books and burying of scholars—
this is like today."
So he vanished between Liáng and Dàng,
building a hut among trees,
living like a laborer.
After two years,
Pāng and others indeed suffered the partisan prohibition,
with hundreds punished,
only Pán transcended, free from suspicion.
From "Hòuhànshū, Shēntú Pán's biography".
Some urged Guō Tài to pursue office,
to which he replied: "I observe celestial signs at night,
and human affairs by day;
what Heaven discards
cannot be supported."
From "Hòuhànshū, Guō Tài's biography".
A white crane in the clouds
cannot be caught by quail nets.
From "Wèizhì, Bǐng Yuán's biography".
King Gǔn of Běihǎi was cautious and studious.
His literary officials and advisors submitted a report praising Gǔn.
Gǔn heard this,
was greatly alarmed,
and reproached them: "Cultivating oneself and maintaining integrity
is ordinary conduct;
yet you report it to the emperor,
which only adds to my burden."
From "Tōngjiàn, Three Kingdoms Wèi".
Also cross-referenced under "Long-term planning".
Junior tutor Kuǎi Qīn,
cousin of Yáng Jùn,
often offended Jùn with blunt words,
others feared for him,
but Qīn said: "Yáng Wéncháng, though dull,
knows not to kill the innocent;
he will only distance me,
and by being distanced,
I can avoid disaster;
otherwise,
we would perish together."
From "Tōngjiàn, Jìn Huìdì's annals".
Fàn Téng,
amidst the empire's turmoil,
resigned and returned home.
He sighed: "Born in chaotic times,
if noble yet able to be poor,
one can avoid disaster."
He distributed half a million in family wealth
among his clan.
From "Jìnshū".
Ruǎn Jí originally had ambitions to save the world,
but during the Wèi-Jìn transition,
with much turmoil in the empire,
few noted scholars survived intact,
so he withdrew from worldly affairs,
and took to heavy drinking as normal.
From "Jìnshū, basic biography".
Cross-referenced under "Foresight".
In Later Zhou, Yǔ Jǐn, feeling he had long held significant power,
and having already established his merit and fame,
wished to preserve a life of ease and leisure.
He thus presented the fine horses he had previously ridden and the armor he had worn, among other items.
. "History of the Northern Dynasties, Basic Annals".
Cross-referenced under "Knowing the Subtleties".
Xiè Fěi, the Palace Attendant, requested to be sent out to serve as the Governor of Wúxīng.
Upon arriving at the commandery,
he sent several hu of wine to his younger brother, Yuè, the Minister of Personnel,
with a letter saying: "Drink this to your heart's content,
but do not meddle in human affairs!"
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Emperor Gaozong of Qi".
Wáng Yàn's maternal cousin from Wèishì, Ruǎn Xiàoxù, also knew that Yàn was bound to fall.
Though Yàn repeatedly visited his gate,
Xiàoxù fled and hid, refusing to see him.
Once, he tasted some delicious sauce,
but upon learning it came from Yàn's household,
he spat it out and poured the rest away.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Emperor Gaozong of Qi".
Cross-referenced under "Long-term Considerations".
Yáng Shèngjīn was appointed to oversee the duties of the Censor-in-chief.
At that time, Lǐ Línfǔ held exclusive power,
and any high official's advancement
that did not come through his influence
was inevitably removed on some charge.
Shèngjīn therefore firmly declined the post,
not daring to accept it.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Emperor Xuanzong of Tang".
The Emperor went to drink with Lǐ Bì,
and they slept sharing the same couch.
Bì said, "Now that I have repaid Your Majesty's kindness sufficiently,
to become a man of leisure again—
what joy could compare to that!"
The Emperor said, "Why are you so eager to leave?"
Bì replied, "There are five reasons why I cannot stay.
I beg Your Majesty to allow me to depart,
and spare me from death."
The Emperor asked, "What do you mean?"
He answered, "I met Your Majesty too early,
you have entrusted me with too much responsibility,
favored me too deeply,
my achievements are too great,
and my path too extraordinary—
these are the reasons I cannot remain."
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Emperor Suzong of Tang".
Guō Zǐyí, as a senior general,
commanded strong armies,
yet despite the endless slanders from Chéng Yuánzhèn and Yú Cháo'ēn,
a single edict summoning him
would see him set out the very same day,
thus rendering the slanders ineffective.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Emperor Dezong of Tang".
Guō Zǐyí, having been slandered and maligned,
was stripped of his military command.
Yet upon hearing the order in the morning,
he set out on the road by evening,
without the slightest hint of resentment or suspicion.
Preserving his integrity and lofty principles,
he shone brilliantly alone.
. "New Book of Tang, Eulogy on Guō Zǐyí".
Cross-referenced under "Without Shame".
Péi Dù, in his later years, drifted somewhat aimlessly, seeking only to secure his own safety.
. "New Book of Tang, Basic Eulogy".
In Shǔ, all the princes held command of armies,
but Prince Péng Zōngdǐng said to his brothers, "For imperial princes to command troops
is the root of disaster and turmoil.
Now the ruler is young and the ministers powerful,
slander and discord will surely arise.
To train soldiers and repair armor
is not fitting for us."
He thus firmly declined the military command,
and the King of Shǔ permitted it,
so he merely built a study and planted pines and bamboos for his own enjoyment.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Emperor Modi of Later Liang".
Cross-referenced under "Long-term Considerations".
Wèi Gōngzǐ Wújì, knowing he had been ruined again by slander,
pleaded illness and ceased attending court.
He spent his days drinking through the night with guests,
consuming strong wine,
and often keeping company with women.
Day and night, he indulged in merry drinking.
. "Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Annals".
Biographies
Sīmǎ Huī resided in Jīngzhōu,
believing that Liú Biǎo would surely face upheaval, and thinking to withdraw and protect himself,
he ensured his own safety. Whenever he spoke with others,
he only said, "Excellent." His wife
reproached him for making no distinctions.
Huī replied, "What you say
is also quite excellent,
and in the end, we avoided calamity."
"Records of Xiāngyáng".
The phoenix treasures its feathers,
the tiger and leopard treasure their claws,
for these are what preserve their bodies.
"Garden of Persuasions".
Wáng Yǔnzhī, still in his youth,
was favored by his paternal uncle, Dūn.
Once, at a night banquet,
Yǔnzhī claimed drunkenness
and lay down to sleep
on a separate couch.
Dūn was plotting rebellion with Qián Fèng,
and Yǔnzhī overheard all their words,
whereupon he vomited profusely where he lay.
Dūn, thinking him heavily intoxicated,
suspected nothing further.
"Records of the Jin Restoration".
Cross-referenced under "Keen Insight".
Collections
The phoenix soars among the azure clouds,
thus no arrow can reach it.
The dragon dives in the whirling depths,
its body untouched by nets or snares.
Knowing that greed for bait brings death near,
better to swim downstream in clear waves.
Preserving life, avoiding harm,
free from the world's troubles.
Both from "Songs of Chu".
The phoenix cries from the high ridge,
keeping far from traps and nets.
. "Selected Works: Chén Lín's Proclamation".
Not hoarding treasures to invite harm,
not adorning appearances to attract trouble.
Zhāng Huá's "Rhapsody on the Wren".
In roaming, one must choose the place,
hover before settling.
Not falling into traps,
not entangled in nets.
Xīliáng Emperor Wǔ's "Ode to the Qílín".
Desolate, with wings tucked under the weeds,
even hawks and kites—what can they do to you?
"Collected Works of Lǐ Bái".
Roosting birds choose the deepest branches.
Hidden fish do not bite the hook,
fleeing deer do not look back.
With short wings, I only wish to nest in deep thickets.
Both from Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Ants and moles plan for deep burrows.
How can a bird, freed from its cage, not choose its forest?
Both from "Collected Works of Bái Jūyì".
It is not my wish for the dark swan to descend.
Dù Mùzhī.
Often I fear my frank nature,
may bring ruin for a cup of wine.
Lately, I decline the company of heavy drinkers,
humbling myself behind ten thousand men.
Dù Gōngbù.
The path to the blue clouds is not long ahead,
yet I must proceed slowly, steadily holding the reins.
Vice-Minister Bái.
Our Dynasty
The cunning silkworm spins no cocoon,
stiffening before its time.
Forever spared the agony of boiling water,
it drifts transcendent, beyond all bounds.
Dōngpō's poetry.
Classics
Disaster comes from one's own actions.
. From the Yì, the Hexagram of Sòng (Conflict).
This is how one brings calamity upon oneself.
. From the Yì, the Hexagram of Lǚ (Travel).
A ram butts against the hedge,
and finds its horns entangled.
. From the Yì, the Hexagram of Dà Zhuàng (Great Strength).
Negligence in storing things teaches others to steal;
seductive attire teaches lewdness.
With meager virtue yet a high position,
little wisdom yet great ambitions,
and small strength yet heavy burdens,
few escape disaster.
"Carrying burdens while riding in a carriage,
invites robbers to come,"
is to beckon thieves.
. All from the Yì, the Xì Cí (Appended Judgments).
Jìn means
to advance,
and advancement inevitably incurs harm.
. From the Yì, the Xù Guà (Sequence of the Hexagrams).
Receiving a rank without yielding,
leads to one's own ruin.
. From the Shī, the poem "Jiǎo Gōng" (Horned Bow).
The Master said:
"Making promises without fulfilling them brings resentment and disaster upon oneself."
. From the Lǐ Jì, "Biǎo Jì".
To be foolish yet love to rely on oneself,
lowly yet love to act arbitrarily,
ensures disaster strikes one's person.
. From the Lǐ Jì, "Zhōng Yōng".
To love what others hate,
and hate what others love,
is to go against human nature,
and disaster will surely befall one.
. From the Lǐ Jì, "Dà Xué".
The Master said: "To act solely for profit invites much resentment."
. From the Lúnyǔ, "Lǐ Rén".
Yì was skilled in archery,
Ào excelled in naval warfare,
yet neither died a natural death.
. From the Lúnyǔ, "Xiàn Wèn".
It is like
riding in a cart without linchpins,
approaching a thousand-ren chasm,
and hoping it won't overturn—
that is difficult indeed.
From the Jiāyǔ.
Those who hoard pearls and jade
will surely face calamity.
. From the Mèngzǐ, "Jìn Xīn Xià".
With evil and filth within,
resentment gathers against one.
. From the Xúnzǐ, "Quàn Xué".
Words can summon disaster.
Same as above.
High position brings peril,
heavy responsibilities lead to downfall,
monopolizing favor invites disgrace,
all can happen in an instant or as quickly as a meal is cooked.
. From the Xúnzǐ, "Zhòng Ní".
To throw an egg against a stone,
or stir boiling water with a finger,
is like plunging into water or fire—
one will be scorched and submerged.
. From the Xúnzǐ, "Yì Bīng".
Mountain trees are felled for their own wood.
From the Zhuāngzǐ.
The Yú family,
ascended a high tower,
overlooking the main road,
set out music and laid out wine,
and played dice upstairs.
Knights-errant passed by below.
A flying kite happened to drop a rotten rat, hitting one of them.
The knights-errant said among themselves: "We did not provoke them,
yet they insult us thus;
we must destroy their household."
On the appointed night,
they gathered a crowd and armed forces to attack and annihilate the Yú family.
. From the Lièzǐ, "Shuō Fú".
Cross-reference "Events Occur Beyond Expectation."
Riding a galloping horse without reins,
treading on thin ice while bearing a heavy load.
From the Dèng Xīzǐ.
Carrying priceless treasure,
sleeping alone in the wilderness,
is more perilous than piling up eggs.
From the Fùzǐ.
Treading on thin ice while waiting for summer,
climbing a rotten branch while awaiting a strong wind.
From the Bàopǔzǐ.
When tigers and wolves approach,
to play the qín and recite poetry instead of brandishing weapons,
I have never seen one's safety assured.
Same as above.
Where disaster arises,
it must stem from accumulated resentment.
From the Liúzǐ.
History
War is like fire;
if not contained, it will consume itself.
． _Zuozhuan, Fourth Year of Duke Yin_.
A common man is guilty of no crime,
but possessing a precious jade becomes his crime.
． _Zuozhuan, Tenth Year of Duke Xuan_.
Receiving emoluments without virtue
brings calamity.
． _Zuozhuan, Second Year of Duke Min_.
Cross-reference "Exceeding One's Station".
Wearing inappropriate clothing
brings disaster upon oneself.
It is fitting.
． _Zuozhuan, Twenty-fourth Year of Duke Xi_.
Cross-reference "Unsuited".
Showy without substance,
it gathers resentment;
offending others and accumulating resentment
makes it impossible to secure one's person.
． _Zuozhuan, Sixth Year of Duke Wen_.
Now, the master's arrogance
is the way to invite misfortune.
． _Zuozhuan, Fourteenth Year of Duke Xuan_.
When Zǐsì of Zhèng redistributed the fields,
the Sī, Dǔ, Hóu, and Zǐshī clans all lost their lands,
so the five clans gathered discontented people to start a rebellion,
killing Zǐsì.
． _Zuozhuan, Tenth Year of Duke Xiang_.
A petty man carrying jade cannot cross the countryside safely.
． _Zuozhuan, Fifteenth Year of Duke Xiang_.
Confucius said: "Though possessing the wisdom of Zāng Wǔzhòng, he was not tolerated in the state of Lǔ.
There must be a reason for this:
he acted against propriety and practiced without forgiveness."
． _Zuozhuan, Twenty-third Year of Duke Xiang_.
Duke Zhuāng of Qí whipped his attendant Jiǎ Jǔ yet kept him close,
thus enabling Cuīzǐ
Cuī Zhù
to spy on the duke.
． _Zuozhuan, Twenty-fifth Year of Duke Xiang_.
Cross-reference "Failing to Guard Against".
Qìng Fēng of Qí presented a chariot to Jì Wǔzǐ,
its glossy surface could reflect one's shoes;
Zhuāng Shū, upon seeing it, said: "The chariot is too glossy,
its owner will surely suffer,
it is fitting that he should perish."
． _Zuozhuan, Twenty-eighth Year of Duke Xiang_.
Gāo Zhǐ of Qí liked to take credit for affairs,
hence difficulties befell him.
． _Zuozhuan, Twenty-fifth Year of Duke Xiang_.
Shū Xiàng said: "Extravagance and arrogance to excess
bring disaster upon oneself."
． _Zuozhuan, Fifth Year of Duke Zhao_.
Seeking great emoluments without great merit
invites resentment.
Accumulating more wealth
gathers more hatred.
The eight Xì families, with five high officials and three ministers,
were greatly favored.
Yet they were wiped out in a single morning,
solely for lacking virtue.
Both from _Guoyu_.
He whose courage and strategy alarm his sovereign endangers himself;
he whose achievements overshadow the world receives no reward.
． _Western Han, Biography of Kuǎi Tōng_.
This is what is called probing the tiger's mouth.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Lì Shēng_.
Fond of fame and boasting of worth,
he ultimately met ruin because of it.
．． _Records of the Grand Historian, Discussion on Biography of Cháo Cuò_.
He who occupies the position of a gentleman but acts like a commoner
will inevitably meet with calamity.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Reign of Emperor Wu of Han_.
Knowing the jealousy of the many concubines,
why must one flaunt one's moth-like eyebrows?
Eyebrows,
pronounced méi.
Criticizing Qū Yuán for displaying his fine eyebrows,
thus incurring collective envy.
． _Western Han, Biography of Yáng Xióng_.
Zhāng Tāng frequently acted as chancellor,
and knowing the three senior officials were traditionally esteemed,
he deliberately humiliated them,
treating them harshly through his subordinates,
so the three senior officials all resented him.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Reign of Emperor Wu of Han_.
Zhāng Tāng issued an unfavorable decree,
Yán Yì did not respond,
but slightly curled his lips.
Zhāng Tāng accused Yán Yì of internal dissent,
and Yán Yì was executed.
． _Book of Han, Treatise on Food and Money_.
A rat that cannot fit in its hole
is carrying a basket.
． _Western Han, Biography of Yáng Yùn_.
Yán Shǐgǔ said: "A jù sǒu
is a carrying basket."
In the past, Guó Wǔzǐ liked to expose others' faults,
thus incurring resentment and hatred.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Reign of Emperor Zhi of Han_.
Formerly, Duke Yì punished Bǐng Chù's father,
seized Yán Zhí's wife,
yet made these two men his carriage attendants,
eventually leading to the disaster in the bamboo grove.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Reign of Emperor Huan of Han_.
Chén Fán intended to eliminate the eunuchs,
so he submitted a memorial stating: "I wish my memorial to be publicly shown to those around,
so that all treacherous ministers know how I detest them."
The above cross-referenced with "Negligence".
Those who heard were all terrified,
but before the plot could be carried out,
Cáo Jié, Wáng Fǔ, and others forged an edict and killed him.
． _Eastern Han, His Biography_.
Judging people's worth,
condemning the corrupt and praising the virtuous,
is like stroking a viper's head,
stepping on a tiger's tail,
leading to severe punishment for oneself,
disaster befalling friends,
the scholar class annihilated and the state perishing with them.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Reign of Emperor Ling of Han_.
Kǒng Róng was executed in the market.
Kǒng Róng, relying on his talent and reputation,
often insulted and mocked Cáo Cāo.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Reign of Emperor Xian of Han_.
Guān Yǔ was rigid and arrogant,
Zhāng Fēi was violent and unkind,
and they met defeat due to their shortcomings.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Three Kingdoms, Wei Wendi_.
Zhāng Fēi respected gentlemen,
but showed no compassion to common soldiers.
The Former Lord often warned him: "You are excessive in punishments and killings,
and daily whip strong soldiers,
yet keep them by your side;
this is the way to invite disaster."
Zhāng Fēi did not reform.
His own officers killed him.
_Records of Shu_.
Hé Zēng looked down upon others,
and his village hated him like an enemy.
By the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
the Hé clan was completely exterminated.
_Book of Jin_.
Cross-reference "Arrogance".
A common man standing alone,
incurs hatred from powerful clans.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Reign of Emperor Shizu of Western Jin_.
Xiè Língyùn, relying on his talent, acted recklessly,
often belittling others,
thus meeting with disaster.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Emperor Taizu of Song_.
Cuī Hào recorded the early history of Wèi,
with all details accurate,
and displayed it on public roads,
so passersby could see and talk about it.
The northern people were universally enraged,
and the emperor angrily had him killed.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Emperor Taizu of Song_.
Lǐ Yánshòu commented: "For a wicked man to advance himself,
he must rely on times of chaos.
Cáo Shuǎng applied the ways of a chaotic era in ordinary times,
so his defeat was fitting!"
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Emperor Taizu of Song_.
Cuī Hào of Wèi said: "Creating empty fame invites real disaster."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Emperor Taizu of Song_.
Liú Xiàochuò, relying on his spirit and talent,
often belittled others,
and at court gatherings,
he would say nothing among the ministers,
instead calling guards to ask about roadside affairs,
thus offending many.
He was dismissed five times in total.
．． _History of the Southern Dynasties, Biography of Liú Xiàochuò_.
Hèruò Bì was again imprisoned for an offense,
and the emperor enumerated his faults: "You have three excesses: an overly fierce jealousy,
an overly fierce tendency to judge others,
and an overly fierce disrespect for superiors."
_Comprehensive Mirror_.
Wáng Yìfāng, due to his hatred of evil, was not tolerated in his time.
． _Book of Tang, His Biography_.
Like fire meeting water,
how could he not fail?
． _Book of Tang, Commentary on Empress Wu Zetian_.
Wáng Yīn, whenever he went out,
had several hundred attendants.
Wáng Yīn requested to be provided with armor and weapons
for patrol purposes.
The emperor found it troublesome.
When the emperor fell ill,
Wáng Yīn entered to pay respects,
and was seized and killed.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Later Zhou, Emperor Taizu_.
Sheltering rotten wood,
riding a glue boat.
． _Book of Tang, Biography of Wéi Chéngqìng_.
Cross-reference "Foolish Obscurity".
Zhāng Chānglíng presented a eulogy,
and Emperor Tàizōng told him: "In the past, Mí Héng and Pān Yuè both relied on their talent and looked down on others,
leading to untimely deaths."
_Book of Tang_.
Biographies
often remain hidden and unused,
which is called a repository of grievances.
． From "Shuō Yuàn Cóng Tán".
Zhōu Bó Rén as a person,
had great ambitions but limited talent,
held a prestigious reputation but lacked insight,
and took pleasure in others' misfortunes,
which is not a way to preserve oneself.
Sōng's nature was arrogant and unyielding,
thus he was also not tolerated by the world.
From "Shì Shuō".
Collection
piling eggs like stacking chess pieces.
From Zuǒ Tài Chōng's "Wèi Fù".
Wealth and powerful favor,
draw sidelong glances from all under heaven.
From Yǔ Yuán Guī's memorial.
Upholding solitary integrity leads to envy,
confronting wickedness results in conflict.
Liú Cháng Qīng.
How different is it from sailing a glue boat on vast waters,
or holding rotten reins to control galloping horses?
Like moths flying towards a bright candle,
or a clod of earth falling into an empty valley.
Unaware that they are heading towards destruction,
unable to extricate themselves.
All from "Táng Wén Cuì".
I foolishly triggered a deadly mechanism,
and plummeted into deep waters.
Liú Bīn Kè.
Magpies chatter noisily in their nests,
crows caw raucously.
Struggling within the courtyard,
trying to protect oneself from attacks.
Hán Wén.
Cross-referenced in "Yīn Yán".
Speaking too frankly and exposing others' faults
was why Guó Wǔ Zǐ was killed in Qí.
Hán Wén.
Same as above.
Not choosing words and speaking recklessly,
is indeed where troubles gather.
Driving a long shaft without yielding,
navigating the towering nine bends.
Turning the startled oar across the river,
against the soaring waves reaching the sky.
From Liǔ's "Chéng Jiù Fù".
Amassing wealth to adorn one's house,
invites disaster and endangers oneself.
Bái Lè Tiān.
Stepping into the gate of misfortune.
Pí Rì Xiū.
Gaining momentary honor,
wipes out a clan for a hundred generations.
Dù Mù Zhī.
Our dynasty
majestic as a dragon,
relinquishing its storm-riding power for the comfort of domestication,
remaining unawakened till the end,
until its belly is torn and limbs split,
landing on a commoner's cutting board.
From Dōng Pō's "Letter to Grand Marshal Hán".
Classics
His heart felt shame and disgrace,
as if whipped in the marketplace.
． From "Shū·Shuō Mìng Shàng".
When the bottle is empty,
it is the jar's shame.
． From "Shī·Liǎo É".
A gentleman has five shames: holding a position without appropriate words,
or without corresponding actions,
a gentleman is ashamed of these.
． From "Jì·Zá Jì Xià".
A gentleman is ashamed to wear the robes without the demeanor,
ashamed to have the demeanor without the speech,
ashamed to have the speech without the virtue,
ashamed to have the virtue without the actions.
To make people feel encouraged and ashamed,
so they can practice their words.
． Both from "Jì·Biǎo Jì".
Knowing shame is close to courage.
． From "Jì·Zhōng Yōng".
Artful words,
ingratiating expressions,
excessive courtesy,
Zuǒ Qiū Míng was ashamed of these,
and I, Qiū, am also ashamed of them.
Hiding resentment and befriending someone,
Zuǒ Qiū Míng was ashamed of this,
and I, Qiū, am also ashamed of it.
． From "Yǔ·Gōng Yě Cháng".
When the state is well-governed,
being poor and lowly is a shame;
when the state is ill-governed,
being wealthy and noble is a shame.
． From "Yǔ·Zǐ Lù".
When the state is well-governed,
taking salary is acceptable;
when the state is ill-governed,
taking salary is shameful.
． From "Yǔ·Xiàn Wèn".
Masters
The heart of feeling shame and disgust
is the beginning of righteousness.
． From "Mèng·Gōng Sūn Chǒu Shàng".
If given with a shout,
even a passerby would not accept it;
if given with a kick,
even a beggar would disdain it.
． From "Mèng·Gào Zǐ Xià".
A gentleman is ashamed of not cultivating virtue,
not of being slandered;
ashamed of being untrustworthy,
not of not being trusted;
ashamed of incompetence,
not of not being employed.
． From "Xún Zǐ·Fēi Shí Èr Zǐ".
Ashamed not to avoid wrongdoing.
From "Guǎn Zǐ".
History
Suí Huì could be humble yet have a sense of shame.
． From "Zuǒ·Wén Shí Èr".
Whenever I think of this shame,
sweat always pours down my back and soaks my clothes.
． From "Xī Hàn·Sī Mǎ Qiān Zhuàn".
Blushing and sweating,
the shame of Kuài Jī.
From "Hàn Shū".
A gentleman, even in poverty,
does not accept salary from a chaotic ruler.
From "Shuō Yuàn".
Collection
The shame of death is a momentary pain,
the shame of life is a lifelong disgrace.
Mèng Dōng Yě.
Cross-referenced in the "Valuing Spirit" section.
Classics
Petty people are not ashamed of being unvirtuous.
． From "Yì·Xì Cí".
With a brazen face.
． From "Shī·Hé Rén Sī".
If the "Bái Huá" is neglected, integrity and shame are lacking.
． From "Shī·Liù Yuè".
The flaw of the Yīn people
was winning without a sense of shame.
． From "Jì·Biǎo Jì".
Masters
Without a sense of shame and disgust,
one is not human.
． From "Mèng·Gōng Sūn Chǒu Shàng".
Throughout the state, no one would stop to talk with him.
Eventually, he went to the eastern outskirts among the graves,
begging for leftovers from sacrificers,
and when not enough,
he looked around and went to others—
this was his way to satisfaction.
． From "Mèng·Lí Lóu Xià".
The shame of having no shame
is true shamelessness.
． From "Mèng·Jìn Xīn Shàng".
Shame is of great importance to a person.
Those who engage in cunning schemes
have no use for shame.
Not ashamed of being inferior to others,
how can one surpass them?
Same as above.
Their lack of guilt and unawareness of shame
is extreme.
． From "Zhuāng Zǐ·Zài Yòu".
Thick-skinned and enduring humiliation.
． From "Xún Zǐ·Jiě Bì".
No disgrace is greater than being without shame.
． From the "Guǎn Lǎng" chapter of "Wén Zhōng Zǐ".
The Queen Dowager of Qín engaged in an illicit affair with Lào'ǎi,
and all matters were decided by Lào'ǎi.
Numerous guests sought official positions,
becoming retainers of Lào'ǎi, numbering over a thousand.
- From "Records of Lǚ Bùwéi" in Shǐjì.
Abandoning ritual and righteousness, discarding integrity and shame grew increasingly severe.
- From "Biography of Jiǎ Yì" in the Western Hàn.
Stubborn and shameless,
lacking integrity and restraint,
failing to establish a sense of shame,
and not even self-respecting,
they would do anything if it seemed feasible.
Same as above.
With little integrity and scant shame,
customs would not foster lasting honesty.
- From "Biography of Sīmǎ Xiàngrú" in the Western Hàn.
When hunger and cold befall one,
they disregard integrity and shame.
- From "Treatise on Food and Money" in the History of the Former Hàn.
Turning one's face and defiling one's conduct
to serve flatterers,
seeking closeness to those in power.
- From "Biography of Zōu Yáng" in Shǐjì.
Sīmǎ Chángqīng stole wealth from the Zhuō family,
while Dōngfāng Shuò gave up his share to his wife.
- From "Biography of Yáng Xióng" in the Western Hàn.
Liáng Sūnlián was cunning and skilled in officialdom,
leading contemporaries to mock him with a riddle about shoes: "Prick the nose and it doesn't sneeze,
step on the face and it doesn't get angry,
gnaw the ground to count steps,
with this, one wins over others."
Satirizing his disregard for shame and humiliation
in pursuit of fame and position.
- From "Biography" in the History of the Southern Dynasties.
Zǔ Tǐng, a scholar of Qí, was literate
and skilled in many arts,
but careless and lacking in virtue.
Once, while serving under Emperor Gāozǔ, a golden cup was lost during a banquet,
and it was found in Zǔ Tǐng's hair knot.
- From "Tōngjiàn: Chén Shìzǔ."
Cross-reference "Inconsistent in Deed and Word."
When the Liáng ruler visited Yè,
the Zhōu ruler played the pipa himself,
and the Liáng ruler danced, saying, "Since Your Majesty personally strums the five strings,
how dare I not join like the hundred beasts?"
- From "Tōngjiàn: Chén Jì."
Cuī Rìyòng feasted in the inner court,
and when drunk,
he rose
to perform a swirling dance,
seeking an academic post.
From "Tángshū."
Yáng Zàisī, as a high official,
solely relied on flattery to gain favor.
Zhāng Tóngxiū teased Yáng, saying, "Minister Yáng looks like a Goryeo person."
Yáng gladly
cut paper to adorn his headscarf,
draped a purple robe backward,
and performed a Goryeo dance.
The entire assembly laughed heartily.
- From "Tōngjiàn: Táng Zhōngzōng."
Cross-reference "Flattery."
In the first year of the Yǒngzhēn era of Emperor Shùnzōng of Táng,
Wáng Shūwén, Wáng Pī, and others held power,
and the gates of over ten households
were as bustling as a market.
Guests waiting to see Shūwén and Pī
even stayed overnight in bakeries
or under tavern eaves in their neighborhoods,
paying a thousand coins per person
for the privilege.
From "Tōngjiàn."
Cross-reference "Rushing for Favor."
Féng Dào held positions as general, chancellor, and among the three excellencies across multiple reigns,
floating with the tides to maintain favor,
and once wrote "A Narrative of the Longevity of an Elder,"
detailing his glorious experiences through successive dynasties.
- From "Tōngjiàn: Five Dynasties, Later Zhōu Tàizǔ."
Biographies
record that Wáng Wǔzǐ loved the braying of donkeys.
After his burial,
Emperor Wén attended the funeral
and said to his companions, "Prince Wǔ loved donkey brays;
let each of us make the sound to send him off."
All the mour present brayed like donkeys in unison.
From "Shìshuō."
Cross-reference "Unrestrained Behavior."
During Empress Wǔ's reign,
Hóu Zhīyī was old
and ordered to retire,
but he went to the court hall,
jumping and running about
to demonstrate his agility.
From "Records of Court and Country."
Cross-reference "Greed and Obsession."
Jìnshì Wáng Yuánsuǒ relentlessly sought favors from the powerful,
sometimes suffering beatings and insults,
yet showing no remorse.
Contemporaries said of Wáng
that "his shame was as thick as ten layers of iron armor."
From Wáng Rényù's "Surviving Tales of the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo Eras."
Classics
state: Women hold their proper place inside,
men hold their proper place outside.
When men and women are correct,
it embodies the great principle of heaven and earth.
Maintaining order in the household prevents regret.
- All from "Yìjīng: Family."
Setting up multiple gates and sounding the night watch
to guard against violent intruders.
- From "Yìjīng: Xì Cí."
Defending oneself with ritual.
- From "Shījīng: Qí Ào."
Using jade tallies to mobilize armies
and manage military defense.
- From "Zhōulǐ: Diǎn Ruì."
For paternal aunts, sisters, and daughters
who have married and returned home,
brothers should not sit on the same mat with them
nor eat from the same vessel.
- From "Lǐjì: Qū Lǐ Shàng."
Cross-reference "Returning to Visit Parents" and "Sisters" sections.
Outside matters should not enter the women's quarters,
and inside matters should not leave the women's quarters.
- From "Lǐjì: Qū Lǐ Shàng."
Cross-reference "Limits and Rules."
Men and women should not sit together indiscriminately,
not share clothes racks,
not share towels or combs,
not hand things directly to each other,
and sisters-in-law and brothers-in-law should not exchange inquiries.
- From "Lǐjì: Qū Lǐ Shàng."
Cross-reference "Avoiding Suspicion."
When driving a carriage for a woman,
advance the left hand
and follow with the right.
- From "Lǐjì: Qū Lǐ Shàng."
Punished individuals should not be near the ruler.
Same as above.
Note: "To prevent harboring resentment and ensure careful consideration."
Men and women should not exchange clothing.
When a man enters the inner quarters,
he should not whistle or point,
and if walking at night, he must use a candle;
without one, he should not go.
When a woman goes out,
she must cover her face,
and if walking at night, she must use a candle;
without one, she should not go.
- From "Lǐjì: Nèi Zé."
If a husband dies
and there are no brothers in his clan,
the husband's relatives should oversee the funeral.
The wife's relatives,
even if close, should not take charge.
If the husband has no clan,
then neighbors from front, back, east, and west
should do so;
if none exist,
the village chief should preside.
- From "Lǐjì: Zá Jì Xià."
Great precautions are taken:
ritual to guard against moral failings,
punishment to prevent licentiousness,
and commands to curb desires.
- From "Lǐjì: Fāng Jì."
The ruler does not share a carriage with those of the same surname,
and when sharing with those of a different surname, they do not wear the same attire.
Same as above.
The ancient kings established the ritual of one round of drinks with toasts,
where host and guest bow a hundred times,
allowing drinking all day without becoming drunk,
thus preventing the troubles of alcohol.
- From "Lǐjì: Yuè Jì."
Ritual prevents the arising of disorder,
just as a dam stops the source of flooding water.
- From "Lǐjì: Jīng Jiě."
The Master said...
The outer screen is meant to prevent outsiders from seeing inside,
while the inner screen is meant to prevent those inside from seeing out.
． From "Xúnzǐ: Dà Lüè".
Cross-reference to "Limitations".
Wearing a crown is to dignify the head,
wearing shoes is to honor the feet.
Robes flowing gracefully,
swords and pendants clinking sonorously,
all serve to guard against impulsiveness.
From "Wénzhōngzǐ".
Historical Records
Women do not go beyond the gate to see guests off or welcome them,
and do not cross the threshold when meeting their brothers.
． From "Zuǒzhuàn: Xī 22".
A woman has her home,
a man has his household,
they should not defile each other.
． From "Zuǒzhuàn: Wēi 18".
When feudal lords meet,
military guards are not withdrawn,
as a precaution.
． From "Zuǒzhuàn: Xuān 12".
Zhào Mèng said:
"Words from the bedchamber should not cross the threshold,
how much less in the open fields?"
． From "Zuǒzhuàn: Xiāng 27".
Confucius said:
"Sacrificial vessels do not leave the gate,
auspicious music is not performed in the wild."
． From "Zuǒzhuàn: Dìng 10".
In the early Hàn dynasty,
copper tiger tallies and bamboo envoy tallies were made with commandery governors.
Yìng Shào explained:
"The copper tiger tallies are numbered from one to five.
When the state needs to dispatch troops, an envoy is sent to the commandery to match the tallies.
Only when they match
are the orders accepted.
The bamboo envoy tallies are made of five bamboo arrows,
each five inches long,
engraved with seal script,
numbered from one to five."
Zhāng Yàn said:
"Tallies replaced the ancient guī and zhāng jades,
for the sake of simplicity."
Shī Gǔ noted:
"Making tallies with commandery governors means
splitting them into halves,
keeping the right half in the capital,
and giving the left half to them."
． From "Xīhàn: Xiàowén Jì".
Liú Hé said:
"The vicious minions have many eyes and ears;
I fear before the plan is set,
we will suffer disaster first."
． From "Tōngjiàn: Hàn Líng Jì".
It is like keeping a hawk:
when hungry, it clings to people,
but whenever it hears the wind rise,
it often aspires to soar to the skies.
We should precisely secure its jesses and cage;
how can we release it
to follow its desires?
． From "Tōngjiàn: Jìn Wǔ Jì".
Someone said to Prince Yǎn of Chángshān:
"When a fierce bird leaves its nest,
there is surely the risk of its eggs being taken.
Why should Your Highness go out today?"
． From "Tōngjiàn: Chén Jì".
Cuī Shénqìng said:
"Officials of the fifth rank and above wear turtle tokens
to guard against fraudulent summonses,
producing the inner turtle to verify commands."
． From "Xīn Tángshū: Běn Zhuàn".
Lǐ Línfǔ, aware of having many enemies,
often feared assassins.
When going out, he had over a hundred foot and horse guards
forming wings to his left and right.
The Imperial Guards cleared the streets,
with vanguards hundreds of steps ahead.
In one night, he moved his bed multiple times,
so even his family did not know his location.
． From "Tōngjiàn: Táng Xuánzōng".
Cross-reference to "Self-Restraint".
Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng replaced the Suì bamboo envoy tallies
with silver rabbit tallies,
later changed to copper fish tallies,
used for mobilizing troops and changing governors.
． From "Xīn Tángshū: Chēfú Zhì".
Those carrying heavy treasures
do not travel at night.
From "Zhànguócè".
Collection
Tiger and leopard guard the nine passes.
Heaven's gate has nine layers,
with divine tigers and leopards guarding its passes.
From "Chǔcí".
Those who dwell in the mountains,
knowing the harm of fierce beasts,
will surely heighten their fences and set traps outside to await them;
those who dwell in the capital,
knowing the theft by burglars,
will surely raise their walls and secure locks inside to guard against them.
From Hán Yù's "Shǒujiè".
Biographies
A wall of a thousand ren,
misfortune does not enter the gate.
From Jiāo Gòng's "Yì Lín".
Historical Records
Duke Zhuāng of Qí whipped his attendant Jiǎ Jǔ yet kept him close,
which led to the Cuī clan
(Cuī Zhù)
spying on the duke.
． From "Zuǒzhuàn: Xiāng 25".
Cross-reference to "Inviting Disaster".
When Cén Péng encamped
(while attacking Gōngsūn Shù)
at a place named Péngwáng (Péng's Demise),
he heard the name and disliked it,
intending to move.
At dusk,
a Shǔ assassin pretended to be a runaway slave surrendering
and stabbed Péng to death at night.
． From "Dōnghàn: Běn Zhuàn".
Lái Xī attacked Gōngsūn Shù;
the people of Shǔ were greatly afraid
and sent an assassin to stab Xī.
Though not fatally wounded,
he wrote a memorial himself:
"After the night watch began,
I was wounded by an unknown person,
striking my vital spot."
From "Běn Zhuàn".
Previously, Duke Yì punished Bǐng Chù's father,
took Yán Zhí's wife,
yet had these two ride with him,
leading to the disaster in the bamboo grove.
． From "Tōngjiàn: Hàn Huán Jì".
Cross-reference to "Inviting Disaster".
Zhāng Fēi respected gentlemen
but showed no care for commoners.
The First Sovereign often warned him:
"You not only overdo punishments and killings,
but also daily whip strong soldiers
yet keep them by your side—
this is the way to invite disaster."
Fēi did not reform.
His tent general killed Fēi.
From "Shǔ Zhì".
Cross-reference to "Inviting Disaster".
The Shǔ general Fèi Yī held a grand gathering with other generals at Hànshòu;
Guō Xún was present.
Yī drank joyfully and sank into drunkenness;
Xún rose and stabbed Yī,
killing him.
Yī was by nature broadly affectionate,
trusting others without suspicion.
Zhāng Yì once wrote to caution him:
"In the past, Cén Péng leading troops and Lái Xī as envoy
both fell to assassins.
Now you, General, hold high rank and great power,
yet trust new followers too much.
You should learn from past events
and be somewhat vigilant."
Yī did not heed this.
． From "Tōngjiàn: Wèi Jì".
Yì Kāng believed to himself:
"We are the closest of brothers,
no need to maintain the formalities of ruler and subject,
acting from the heart,
without any suspicion or guard."
． From "Tōngjiàn: Sòng Tàizǔ".
Prince Yǎn of Qí was frivolous and unguarded;
How could one not go out early and late?
But fear the path is drenched with dew.
. From "Shī·Xíng Lù".
Do not let the long-haired dog bark.
. From "Shī·Yě Yǒu Sǐ Jūn".
Men and women do not sit together indiscriminately,
do not share clothes racks,
do not share towels or combs,
do not hand things directly to each other,
and sisters-in-law and brothers-in-law do not exchange inquiries.
. From "Lǐjì·Qū Lǐ Shàng".
Cross-reference to "prevention and boundaries".
The son of a widow,
unless he shows exceptional qualities,
should not be made a friend.
Same as above.
The sons of rulers and high officials dare not refer to themselves as "this unworthy youth",
the sons of high officials and scholars dare not call themselves "the heir",
and one dares not share the same name as the crown prince.
. From "Lǐjì·Qū Lǐ Xià".
When a woman is ill,
one may inquire after her,
but not about the specifics of her illness.
To avoid suspicion of flirting.
. From "Lǐjì·Fáng Jì".
A widow should not cry at night.
To avoid suspicion of longing for intimacy.
. From "Lǐjì·Fáng Jì".
A subject should not engage in external relations,
daring not to show divided loyalty to his ruler.
. From "Lǐjì·Jiāo Tè Shēng".
In the state of Lǔ, there was a man living alone,
and a widow next door also lived alone.
One night, a sudden storm arose,
destroying her house.
She rushed to his door for shelter,
but the man of Lǔ shut his door and refused her.
From "Kǒngzǐ Jiāyǔ".
In history,
Wèi Qīng, as Grand General,
respected and honored, dared not act arbitrarily,
even when authorized to execute commands beyond the borders.
. From "Western Hàn, his biography".
Between father and son,
matters are hard to speak of.
. From "Qián Hàn, Chē Qiānqiū's biography".
Cross-reference to "suspicion".
Sūn Huìzōng wrote to Yǎng Yùn, saying:
"A dismissed high official
should shut his doors in fear,
showing a pitiable demeanor;
he should not manage property,
entertain guests,
or seek praise."
. From "Western Hàn, Yǎng Yùn's biography".
Shutting his doors and resting at ease,
he is considered foremost among the wise.
. From "Western Hàn, Gǔ Yǒng's biography".
Upon returning to his private residence,
he shut his doors to cultivate dignity and gravitas.
. From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Guāngwǔ's reign".
Wú Yòu's father, Wú Huī,
served as Governor of Nánhǎi,
and Yòu accompanied him to his post.
Huī intended to prepare bamboo slips to copy classics,
but Yòu advised: "The local custom values rare treasures;
if these books are completed,
they will require double the carts to transport.
In the past, Mǎ Yuán was slandered over coix seeds, and Wáng Yáng sought fame with simple belongings—
in matters of suspicion, the wise ancients were truly cautious." Huī then desisted.
. From "Eastern Hàn, his biography".
When Wèi Wén was Crown Prince,
Bǐng Yuán did not pay respects to Wèi Wǔ.
When asked why,
Yuán said: "I have heard that when the state is in peril, one does not serve the prime minister;
when the ruler is aged, one does not attend the heir."
. From "Sānguó Zhì, Wèi".
Dù Xī was appointed to the Ministry of Personnel
and dared not employ a single fellow townsman.
From "Jìn Shū".
Lǐ Jìng shut his doors, claiming illness,
fearing the proximity of power and its pressures.
His achievements were great, yet the ruler did not suspect him.
. From "Táng Shū, his biography's eulogy".
Guō Zǐyí was slandered by Chéng Yuánzhèn and Yú Cháo'ēn
while commanding troops abroad;
yet, upon the emperor's summons, he set out immediately,
without the slightest hesitation,
so that rumors and discord could not take hold.
. From "Táng Shū, his biography".
Lù Zhì, exiled to a remote place,
often kept his doors shut,
so that no one saw his face.
To avoid slander,
he wrote no books.
. From "Táng Shū, his biography".
Péi Dù no longer harbored ambitions for statecraft;
he built a residence in the eastern capital,
wore rustic clothes in leisurely repose,
composed writings with Bái Jūyì and Liú Yǔxī,
drinking day and night in joy,
unconcerned with worldly affairs.
. From "Táng Shū, his biography".
In historical records,
Yán Shūzǐ lived alone in his house,
and the widow next door also lived alone.
One night, a storm destroyed her house,
and the woman rushed to his door.
Shūzǐ let her in and had her hold a candle,
which burned out by dawn;
he then dismantled part of his roof to continue the light.
From "Máo's Commentary on the Shījīng".
When Wáng Xīzhī was young,
General Wáng Dūn adored him,
often letting him sleep in his tent.
Once, before he rose,
Qián Fèng entered,
dismissed others to plot rebellion.
Xīzhī awoke,
heard their discussion,
and knew he would not be spared.
So he induced vomiting,
soiling his face and bedding,
feigning deep sleep.
When Dūn opened the curtain,
he saw saliva and mess everywhere,
thus Xīzhī survived.
From "Shì Shuō", with Liú Xiàobiāo's note: "Various texts attribute this to Wáng Yǔn;
here it says Xīzhī,
likely an error."
In collections,
he received guests at his gate,
recommended scholars,
with attendants present daily.
Yet in private, he treated them
with such detachment as if indifferent.
From Hán Yù's writings.
The duty of a deputy
is to assist the magistrate.
The deputy's position is delicate,
typically avoiding decisions to prevent suspicion.
When documents were processed,
a clerk would bring the completed file to the deputy,
rolling up the front part,
holding it with his left hand,
and pointing to the end with his right,
walking in like a goose,
standing level and glancing sidelong: "Sign here."
The deputy would carefully dip his brush and sign in his place,
looking at the clerk,
asking if it was acceptable;
the clerk would say, "Approved,"
and then leave,
not daring to review the content,
utterly unaware of the matter.
From Hán Yù's "Record of Lántián".
Many in the capital say your household hoards wealth,
so those who value a reputation for integrity
fear to speak well of you,
keeping it to themselves,
holding it in heart,
biting back words,
for public justice is hard to discern,
and the world is full of suspicion.
Once spoken,
scoffers would think they received heavy bribes.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's "Letter to Wáng Cānyuán on the Fire".
In history,
after Marquis Jiàng, Zhōu Bó, returned to his fief,

Bó, fearing execution,
would don armor
and have his family bear weapons to meet them.
Later, someone accused Bó of plotting rebellion,
and he was handed to the court justice.
. From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Wéndì's reign".
Tián Fén, as Chancellor,
recommended men who rose to high ranks,
shifting power from the emperor.

I too wish to make some appointments."
. From "Hàn Shū, Dòu Yīng's biography".
Wèi Qīng said: "Since the days of Wèi Qí and Wǔ'ān hosting many guests,
the Son of Heaven has often gnashed his teeth in anger."
. From "Western Hàn, his eulogy".
Yǎng Yùn was dismissed to commoner status,
managed his estate at home,
built houses,
amusing himself with wealth.
His friend Sūn Huìzōng warned him,
saying: "A dismissed high official
should shut his doors in fear,
showing a pitiable demeanor."
. From "Western Hàn, his biography".
Classics
When water is above fire (the image of Jì Jì),

thinks of potential calamities and takes preventive measures against them.

Setting double gates and sounding the clapper to guard against violent intruders
is derived from the idea of preparation.
． _Yì Jìng, Xì Cí_.
The superior man, in security, does not forget danger;
in preservation, does not forget ruin;
in order, does not forget chaos.

Cross-reference to "Foresight".
Only by preparing for every affair can one be equipped;

Before the heavens darken with rain,

With three years of farming,

In all affairs, preparation leads to success;

Anticipating and considering calamities

In the grand scheme of heaven and earth,

Even with epidemics or drought disasters,
the people will not suffer poverty or become refugees.
． _Huái Nán Zǐ, Zhǔ Shù Xùn_.
History
Wèi Jiàng said: "Yet I wish you to enjoy your pleasures while thinking of their end."

Preparing for the unforeseen

"All gentlemen,
none escape periods of shortage."
This means preparation must never cease.

The wise prepare for calamities before they take shape.

Accumulating reserves

If grain is abundant and wealth plentiful,

In attack, one can conquer;
in defense, one can hold firm;
in battle, one can win;

Yáo had nine years of floods,

Cut off what is continuous,
block what is trickling.

Cross-reference to "Caution in Small Matters".
If the dikes are intact,
even prolonged heavy rains cannot cause damage.

Cross-reference to "Foresight".
Those skilled in healing
prevent conditions from becoming critical;
those skilled in disaster relief
prevent the need for extensive aid.

while saving many depletes state funds,
and depleted funds lead to heavier taxation.
． _Táng Shū, Liú Yàn Zhuàn_.
Biographies
When Duke Táo governed Jīngzhōu,
he ordered ship officials to save all sawdust,
without limit,
and store it all,
which puzzled everyone at the time.
Later, at the New Year's assembly,
during snowfall,
on the day it cleared,
the snow was cleared in front of the hall,
but the ground was very wet,
so they used the sawdust to cover it,
and it caused no inconvenience at all.
_Shì Shuō Xīn Yǔ_.
Collections
Those wearing light linen in summer do not suffer the stifling heat;
those clad in furs in winter do not fear the bitter cold.
Why?
Because having the means makes preparation easy.
Wáng Bāo, "In Praise of a Sage Lord Gaining Worthy Ministers".
In a year of drought,
people prepare boats;
in three months of heat,
people prepare furs.
Liú Bīnkè.
Those who store grain do not fear famine years;
those who hoard pearls and jade do not worry about starvation.
Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
Our Dynasty
Like storing medicines for illness,
like planting catalpa and lacquer trees for future use.
Sū Dōngpō, "Hán Wéi's Father Hán Yì Edict".
Classics
Negligent and unprepared.
． _Yì Jìng, Dà Yǒu Guà_.
Masters
Affairs without preparation will fail.
． _Guǎn Zǐ, Bà Yán Piān_.
Thus, a state without nine years' reserves
is called insufficient;
without six years' accumulation,

without three years' stores,

． _Huái Nán Zǐ, Zhǔ Shù Xùn_.
To seek fur coats only when great cold arrives—

History
Without preparation and foresight,

Jǔ relied on its remote location,

In the battle of Chéngpú,

． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Zhāo Year 5_.

． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Āi Year 2_.
If shaming an ordinary man requires preparedness,
how much more so shaming a state?
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Zhāo Year 5_.
If things are not prepared in advance,
one cannot respond to emergencies.
． _Shǐjì, Qín Shìjiā_.
If the state lacks a year's储备,

． _Xīhàn, Gǔ Yǒng's Biography_.
Lǐ Zuòjū said: "Transporting grain a thousand miles,

《Hán Xìn's Biography》.
Collection
I have often thought that people in peacetime do not read a single prescription,
but when ill, entrust their lives to quacks.
Liú Bīnkè.
Our dynasty's
military campaigns
are just like a private family building a house.
For a house of certain size,
the cost of materials and stones, grain and coins are all calculated,
budgeted and fixed,
with no room for excess or shortage;
yet when workers enter,
the sound of axes and adzes clanging,
and countless expenses arise,
beyond any prior calculation—
this is the fault of not planning ahead.
Starting construction then gathering grain,
cutting timber then seeking materials,
the cost will surely double,
and the work will not be sturdy.
Sū Dōngpō's _Reply to Lǐ Cóng's Letter_.
Classic
When facing times of worry and regret,

though minor, must not be treated lightly,

Are grievances only in the open?
Plan for the unseen.
． _Shū, Wǔzǐ Zhī Gē_.
Grievances need not be great.
． _Shū, Kànggào_.
Consider the subtlest thoughts,

《Shū》annotation.

． _Shī, Yì_.
Able to be cautious in small matters and humble to subordinates.
． _Shī, Jírì_.
Hear the soundless,

． _Lǐjì, Qū Lǐ Part 1_.
The transformation by rites is subtle,

The nobleman is watchful over what is not seen,

Masters

This Dynasty
Bái Qǐ, with a single doubt in mind,
buried brave warriors like lice;
Shí Chóng, with a moment of pleasure,
cut down beauties like straw dolls;
Lǐ Sī, with one act of ruthlessness,
left corpses across the land;

ignited disasters for a century.
Their beginnings were very slight,
but their consequences vast.
From *Collection on Enlightening the Way*.

To distinguish the virtuous from the wicked,
