but left without staying overnight;
then proceeded
to visit Xiàn,
and stayed for days before returning.
Fàn Yè commented:
Huáng Xiàn's words and demeanor,
are not passed down;
yet gentlemen who met him,
all deeply admired him from afar,
shedding pettiness,
as if his way was complete and nature whole,
though his virtue cannot be named!
My great-grandfather Mùhóu believed:
"Xiàn,
composed in his compliance,
profound as if embodying the Way,
none can reach his depth,
nor discuss the measure of his purity."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Eastern Hàn Emperor Shāng's Annals".
When Guō Tài first visited Luòyáng,
none knew him,
but Chénliú's Fú Róng upon meeting him,
marveled at his uniqueness,
and introduced him to Governor of Hénán Lǐ Yīng.
． From "Hàn Emperor Huán's Annals".
Select the refined and upright,
expel the cunning and evil.
From "Comprehensive Mirror".
Someone asked Mí Héng:
"Why not follow Chén Zhāngwén and Sīmǎ Bódá?"
He said:
"How could I follow sons of butchers and wine-sellers?
I only value Kǒng Róng and Yáng Xiū,
often saying:
'My elder son Kǒng Wénjǔ,
younger son Yáng Dézǔ,
the rest are mediocre,
not worth counting.'"
． From "Eastern Hàn Original Biography".
Cáo Cāo said:
"To have a son, one should have Sūn Zhòngmóu;
as for Liú Jǐngshēng's sons,
they are but pigs and dogs."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Eastern Hàn".
Guǎn Lù said:
"When I speak with the Liú brothers of Yǐngchuān,
it refreshes my spirit,
keeping me awake though drowsy.
Besides them,
I'd likely sleep in broad daylight."
From "Book of Jìn".
When Wú established a Chancellor,
the consensus favored Zhāng Zhāo,
but the King of Wú said:
"It's not that I grudge Zǐbù the position;
but the Chancellor's duties are heavy,
and this gentleman is by nature stern.
If his advice is not followed,
resentment will arise,
which would not benefit him."
．． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Three Kingdoms Wèi Emperor Míng's Annals".
Jī Kāng once visited recluse Jíjùn's Sūn Dēng,
who said:
"You have much talent but little wisdom,
and will find it hard to escape in this age."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Wèi Emperor Yuán's Annals".
Lǚ Méng at fifteen,
followed Dèng Dāng to attack bandits,
and Sūn Cè saw and found him extraordinary,
placing him by his side.
Zhāng Zhāo recommended Méng,
who was appointed Separate Department Major.
From "Records of Wú".
Jìn Emperor Wǔ heard of Wáng Yǎn's fame,
and asked Wáng Róng:
"Who today can compare with Yífǔ?"
Róng said:
"I've seen none his equal.
One must seek among the ancients."
． From "Book of Jìn Original Biography".
Mǐn Hóng saw Lù Yún,
found him extraordinary,
and said:
"If this child is not a dragon colt,
he must be a phoenix chick."
Shān Tāo, as Head of Personnel, selected and promoted individuals,
categorizing each with labels.
Ruǎn Jí could show blue or white eyes,
turning white eyes to ritualistic conventionalists.
Jī Xǐ came to offer condolences,
and Jí made white eyes at him.
When his younger brother Jī Kàng visited,
Jí was greatly pleased,
and showed him the black of his eyes.
． From "The Official Biography in the Book of Jìn".
When the Hé jade was still in the Jīng Mountains,
and the Suí pearl lay hidden in deep rivers,
had they not met the right person,
would they have gained the value of multiple cities and the fame of illuminating carriages?
． From "The Biography of Zhāng Zài in the Book of Jìn".
Wáng Shù had a calm disposition.
Often when guests engaged in heated debates,
he remained serene amidst them.
At thirty years old,
he was still unknown,
and people called him foolish.
Wáng Dǎo recruited him due to his family background.
After meeting him,
he only asked about the price of rice in the east,
and Shù stared without answering.
Dǎo said:
"Assistant Wáng is not foolish;
why do people say he is?"
． From "The Records of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn in the Comprehensive Mirror".
Shí Lè gathered scholars and officials separately into a Camp of Gentlemen.
From "The Jìn Annals".
When Sūn Quán conquered Jīng Province,
all the officials submitted and joined him.
Pān Jùn did not go to see Quán,
who sent someone to bring him,
appointing him as Manager of the Army in Jīng Province and consulting him on all matters.
From the "Jiāngbiǎo Biography" annotated in "The Records of Wú".
Mǎ Xiù said:
"When Yáng Xióng wrote 'The Great Mystery',
only Huán Tán believed it would be passed down to later generations."
． From "The Biography of Wáng Chángwén in the Book of Jìn".
The Wèi emperor often had Cuī Hào accompany him into his private quarters.
Once, pointing to Hào, he told a newly surrendered leader of the Gāochē tribe:
"You see this man as frail and weak,
unable to bend a bow or wield a spear,
yet what he harbors in his mind
surpasses armor and weapons."
． From "The Records of Emperor Tàizǔ of Sòng in the Comprehensive Mirror".
Uncut fine jade
is no different from tiles and stones;
an untested steed
mixes with ordinary horses.
But once cut and polished,
and galloped to test it,
then jade and stone, steed and nag, are distinguished.
． From "The Biography of Sū Chǔ in the History of the Northern Dynasties".
When Xīn Yànzhī was appointed as Governor of Suí Province,
at that time, many provincial governors presented rare treasures,
but only Yànzhī offered items for sacrificial use, which Emperor Gāozǔ praised.
Turning to his court officials, he said:
"How can one not learn? Yànzhī's tribute is the result of studying the ancients."
From "The Book of Suí".
The Vice Minister of Personnel, Gāo Xiàojī, was renowned for judging character.
Upon seeing Fáng Xuánlíng, he said:
"I have seen many people,
but never one like this young man."
Seeing Dù Rǔhuì, he told him:
"You have the talent to adapt to change,
and will surely bear the weight of a pillar."
He entrusted both with the care of his descendants.
． From "The Records of Emperor Gāo of Suí in the Comprehensive Mirror".
Zhāng Chānglíng and Wáng Gōngjǐn were both skilled in writing,
and their fame shook the capital.
The Examination Officer, Wáng Shīdàn, in charge of the imperial examinations,
rejected them,
leaving the entire court puzzled.
When the results were reported,
the emperor noticed the absence of their names
and questioned him.
Shīdàn replied: "Although these two have literary talent,
their style is frivolous,
and they will not become outstanding figures.
If placed high on the list,
I fear later scholars would emulate them."
． From "The Records of Emperor Tàizōng of Táng in the Comprehensive Mirror".
Cross-reference "Deep Insight and Great Judgment".
Wáng Jù and Sū Wèidào were both unknown,
but Péi Xíngjiǎn, upon meeting them once,
said: "You two will successively oversee official appointments in the future.
I have a young daughter,
and I wish to entrust her to you."
． From "The Records of Empress Wǔ of Táng in the Comprehensive Mirror".
Sū Guàn's son, Sū Tǐng, was exceptionally bright in his youth,
and it was recorded:
"The ancients spoke of advancing a thousand li in a day;
such is Sū."
From "The Book of Táng".
Dúgū Xìn, upon seeing Sūn Sīmiǎo, said:
"A vessel too great is hard to employ."
． From "His Biography in the Book of Táng".
Dí Rénjié said: "You are like an essential in my medicine chest,
indispensable for even a day."
． From "The Biography of Yuán Dàn in the Book of Táng".
Eagles and hawks,
how can they be peers of common birds?
． From "The Biography of Wéi Sīqiān in the Book of Táng".
Sòng Jǐng reported that Lǐ Yōng, Assistant Officer of Kuò Province, and Zhèng Miǎn, Military Administrator of Yí Province, both had talent, strategy, and literary skill,
but their natures were unorthodox,
fond of controversy and change.
If fully promoted,
they would surely bring regret;
if long neglected,
their talents would be wasted.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror Volume 213".
Jí Wēn was the Magistrate of Xīnfēng.
Xuē Yí recommended Wēn's talent,
and the emperor summoned him for an audience.
Turning to Yí, he said:
"This is a man of ill character,
I will not employ him."
． From "The Records of Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng in the Comprehensive Mirror".
Lǐ Huá was skilled in writing
and friendly with Xiāo Yǐngshì.
He wrote "Essay on an Ancient Battlefield",
stained it to look old,
and placed it
among Buddhist texts.
He and Yǐngshì found it while reading Buddhist books.
Huá asked him:
"What do you think of this essay?"
Yǐngshì said:
"It's acceptable."
Huá said:
"Among contemporary writers,
who can match this?"
Yǐngshì replied:
"If you refine your thoughts a bit more,
you can reach this level."
Huá was taken aback.
． From "His Biography in the Book of Táng".
Biographies record
that Wáng Róngchōng and Péi Shūzé visited Zhōng Shìjì in their childhood.
A guest asked:
"Who are these two boys?"
Zhōng said:
"Péi Kǎi is clear and profound,
Wáng Róng is concise and essential.
In thirty years,
these two worthies will become Ministers of Personnel."
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World".
The wife of Wáng Xīzhī, Lady Xì, said to her two younger brothers
Xì Yīn and Xì Tán:
"When the Wáng family sees the two Xiè,
Ānshí,
they
some versions have "empty the trunks"
overturn the shelves;
when they see you coming,
they are merely indifferent."
From the latter part of "A New Account of the Tales of the World".
Cross-reference "Women's Insight".
If an owl does not hoot,
it is not an auspicious bird;
though a fierce tiger may crouch,
can it equal a benevolent beast?
． From "Continued Tales of the World, Chapter 10".
A mirror reflecting the sun and moon.
From "The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons".
The yes-men of the crowd
are not as good as Zhōu Shě's outspokenness.
From "Han's Outer Commentary on the Classic of Poetry".
Those promoted by Liǔ Cóng
were all praised by the world.
The locals said of him: "Gaining a box of gold
is not as good as being recognized by Liǔ Bóqiān!"
From "The Biographies of Elders of Yì Province".
Collection
Cài Yōng took refuge south of the Yangtze River,
lodging at Kē Tíng.
The inn had bamboo rafters;
looking up at them, he said,
"Fine bamboo indeed."
He took some to make a flute,
and its extraordinary sound was uniquely sublime.
- From Cài Yōng's "Preface to the Ode on the Long Flute."
When a fine steed neighs,
Bó Lè recognizes its ability;
when a black hound howls mournfully,
the Hán state official knows its talent.
- From "Wén Xuǎn: Cáo Zhí's 'Memorial on Self-Recommendation'."
A kind father cannot love a worthless son,
nor a benevolent ruler retain useless ministers.
Same as above.
He promoted Lǚ Méng from the ranks of soldiers,
and recognized Pān Jùn among captives.
From Lù Jī's "Discourse on the Fall of Wú."
He recognized Lǚ Méng amidst the troops.
From Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Chǔ selected the finest timber,
Hàn's gardens welcomed the finest steeds.
Do not spread that a deer is a horse,
nor believe an owl is a phoenix.
Such qualities must be sought in the ancients.
All from the same source.
The dragon sword, long unpolished,
lay obscured in mud and sand.
Had it not been for Zhāng Mào Xiān,
who would have discerned its stellar glow?
From Quán Dézhi's writings.
With an open heart and broad love,
yet clear as the separate rivers Jīng and Wèi.
From "Táng Wén Cuì."
The three commentaries on the Spring and Autumn Annals shelved high,
he alone embraced the classic to explore its entirety.
From Hán Yù's writings.
In Bó Lè's stable, many fine horses;
in Biàn Hé's chest, many precious jades.
From Hán Yù's "Preface to Seeing Off Scholar Quán."
The song of the ox horn,
crude in words and clumsy in meaning;
the words spoken in the hall,
unrecorded in annals.
Yet Duke Huán of Qí promoted him to minister,
and Shū Xiàng took his hand to rise.
Thus, it is not that speaking is hard,
but finding one who listens and understands is rare!
From Hán Yù's "Letter to Vice Minister Lǐ Yì of the Ministry of War."
Cross-reference to "Knowing People."
When Bó Lè passed through the fields of Jìběi, the herds of horses were emptied.
Since Jìběi has more horses than anywhere under heaven,
even if Bó Lè excels at recognizing them,
how could he empty the herds?
The explainer said: "By 'emptied,'
I mean not without horses,
but without fine horses.
Bó Lè knows horses;
encountering a fine one,
he takes it,
leaving no fine steeds in the herd.
If no fine ones remain,
even if said to have no horses,
it would not be an empty statement."
From Hán Yù's "Preface to Sending Wēn Zào, the Recluse, to Héyáng Army."
The benevolent qílín and wise dragon,
are auspicious but for a time.
Not like the noble person,
a blessing to human relations.
From "The Collected Works of Liú Bīnkè."
Like a faint string's lonely note,
briefly catching the ear,
it is not the sound of grand music.
Same as above.
Do not disdain the straight, broken sword,
for it surpasses the curved, intact hook.
From "The Collected Works of Bái Jūyì."
While others disdain, I alone appreciate.
Loyal, diligent, and earnest,
fit to stand by one's side as a close aide.
Do not send him where all eyes can see,
valuing domestic fowl over the wild crane.
All from the same source.
With white eyebrows, his spirit soars above the crowd.
From "The Collected Works of Yuán Zhěn."
To know where the finest flowers bloom,
look deep within the thicket.
Same as above.
Pine and cypress may symbolize integrity,
but not literary talent.
From Huángfǔ Shí.
The usurping purple hue,
cannot be called legitimate.
From Sūn Kèzhī's writings.
When Jiǎ Sù headed the Ministry of Rites,
court officials sought his favor for the imperial exams in vain,
and some strongly slandered and mocked him.
Jiǎ Sù said:
"I only need Dù Mù
to rival hundreds of others."
From "The Collected Works of Dù Mù."
Cross-reference to "Quality Over Quantity."
In our dynasty,
Huán Xuán recognized Gāo Róu in his youth,
and singled out Wáng Jī as a child.
From "Lèi Yào."
Like ivory, rhinoceros horn, pearls, and jade,
though they do not alleviate hunger or cold,
they must not be left in the mud.
From Sū Shì's writings.
Only the eye of heaven recognizes the celestial being.
From Sū Shì's poetry.
Rare treasures and steeds drawing carts cross the path,
but who recognizes them? Only Ōuyáng Xiū.
From Chén Shīdào's "To Sū Shì."
At a glance, he empties the herds of Jìběi.
From Chén Shīdào.
Classics
The Master said: "Yóu,
in a state of a thousand chariots,
can be entrusted with its military levies.
Qiú,
in a town of a thousand households or a family of a hundred chariots,
can be made its steward.
Chì,
girded and standing in court,
can converse with guests."
- From "The Analects: Gōngyě Cháng."
The Master said: "In virtue: Yán Yuān, Mǐn Zǐqiān, Rǎn Bóniú, Zhòng Gōng.
In speech: Zǎi Wǒ, Zǐgòng.
In governance: Rǎn Yǒu, Jìlù.
In culture: Zǐyóu, Zǐxià."
- From "The Analects: Xiān Jìn."
Masters
Duke Huì of Fèi said: "Towards Zǐsī, I treat him as my teacher;
towards Yán Bān, as my friend.
Wáng Shùn and Cháng Xī
are those who serve me."
From "Mencius."
Yuèzhèngzǐ
stands between the second and fourth ranks.
- From "Mencius: Jìn Xīn Part Two."
Yànzǐ,
a minister of practical service,
is not equal to Zǐchǎn;
Zǐchǎn,
a benevolent man,
is not equal to Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng's character
emphasized achievement over righteousness,
wisdom over benevolence,
making him a rustic man,
unfit to be a high minister of the Son of Heaven.
- From "Xúnzǐ: General Summary."
In Shǔ, there was one Zhòng Yuán,
who did not bend his will,
nor burden his person,
neither aloof nor accommodating,
balancing between approval and denial.
From "Yángzǐ."
History
Fēng Shū asked Jiǎ Jì: "Between Zhào Cuī and Zhào Dùn, who is more worthy?"
He replied: "Zhào Cuī is
like the winter sun;
Zhào Dùn is
like the summer sun."
. "Zuǒzhuàn, Wén 7th Year".
The Zuǒshì is ornate and rich,
its flaw being exaggeration;
the Gǔliáng is clear and subtle,
its flaw being brevity;
the Gōngyáng is argumentative and decisive,
its flaw being vulgarity.
. Fàn Nìng's "Preface to the Gǔliáng Commentary".
In hunting,
the hounds chase and kill the beasts,
but the one who tracks and points out where the beasts are is the human.
Now, you all can only run and catch beasts,
thus your merit is that of hounds;
as for Xiāo Hé,
he tracks and gives directions,
so his merit is that of a human.
. "History of the Western Hàn, Biography of Xiāo Hé".
Even if we were to lose a hundred like Cáo Cān now,
what would Hàn lack?
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Hàn Gāozǔ Annals".
Among the court officials of Hàn,
only Jí Àn was fond of straightforward admonishment,
maintaining integrity and dying for righteousness,
hard to mislead with falsehoods;
as for persuading Chancellor Gōngsūn Hóng and others,
it was like brushing off dust or shaking down leaves!
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Hàn Wǔdì Annals".
The strategies and awareness of Jīngzhào Yǐn Zhāng Chǎng were not as good as Zhào Guǎng Hàn's.
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Hàn Xuāndì Annals".
Zhuó Mào's conduct lay between purity and turbidity.
"History of the Eastern Hàn".
Guō Línzōng said: "Fènggāo
Yuán Hóng's
capacity is like an overflow,
clear but easy to scoop.
Shūdù is vast like a thousand-qǐng pond,
unclear when settled,
unturbid when stirred,
impossible to measure."
. "History of the Eastern Hàn, Biography of Huáng Xiàn".
Zhèng Tài paid respects to Dǒng Zhuó, saying: "You, illustrious lord, hail from Xīzhōu,
have been a commander since youth,
well-versed in military affairs.
Yuán Běnchù is a scion of nobles,
raised in the capital;
Zhāng Mèngzhuó is an elder of Dōngpíng,
who does not peer beyond his hall;
Kǒng Gōngxù engages in lofty talk,
exhaling the withered and blowing life into things.
None have talent for military campaigns;
facing blades and deciding battles,
they are no match for you."
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Hàn Xiàndì Annals".
Páng Dé Gōng often said: "Kǒngmíng is the sleeping dragon,
Shìyuán is the young phoenix,
Décāo is the ice
(or 'water')
mirror."
Same as above.
Jìng and his cousin Shào were both renowned in youth,
known for judging character's good and bad.
. "History of Shǔ, Biography of Xǔ Jìng".
Xǔ Shào and his elder brother Jìng were both highly famed,
fond of critically discussing local figures,
changing their evaluations monthly,
hence the Rǔnán custom of 'first-day assessments'.
. "History of the Eastern Hàn, Biography of Xǔ Shào".
When Cáo Cāo was obscure,
he often used humble words and rich gifts,
seeking an evaluation.
Xǔ Shào said: "You are a villain in times of peace,
a hero in times of chaos."
Same as above.
Sūn Quán, discussing Zhōu Yú, Lǔ Sù, and Lǚ Méng with Lù Xùn, said: "Gōngjǐn was heroic and fierce,
with surpassing courage and strategy,
thus he defeated Mèngdé,
expanding into Jīngzhōu,
rarely matched.
Zǐmíng in youth,
I thought him merely unafraid of hardship,
bold and daring;
but as he grew,
his learning broadened,
his strategies became remarkably astute,
placing him next to Gōngjǐn,
though his eloquent discourse fell short.
In plotting to capture Guān Yǔ,
he surpassed Zǐjìng."
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Hàn Xiàndì Annals".
When Sūn Lǐ and Lú Yù first joined the military office,
Cuī Yǎn said: "Sūn is candid and fervent,
resolute and decisive;
Lú is alert and clear-minded,
tempered yet unyielding,
both are talents for high office."
They later rose to top positions.
. "History of the Three Kingdoms, Wèi".
The Wèi crown prince had Hú Zǒng compile 'Guest Evaluations': "For outstanding talent surpassing peers,
there is Zhūgě Kè;
for keen insight into timing,
penetrating the subtle,
there is Gù Tán;
for profound debate and broad understanding,
resolving knots with words,
there is Xiè Jǐng;
for exhaustive learning and discerning subtlety,
matching Zǐyóu and Zǐxià,
there is Fàn Shèn."
Yáng Dào privately rebutted: "Yuánxùn is talented but careless,
Zǐmò is sharp but harsh,
Shūfā is eloquent but shallow,
Xiàojìng is deep but narrow."
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Wèi Míngdì Annals".
Yuánzǐ discussed: Some say,
"Shàofǔ Yáng Fù, seeing his lord err,
directly rebuked his faults and publicized his wrongs—
this can be called straightforward,
but not loyal.
Thus, the late Minister Chén Qún was different;
he debated all day,
yet never spoke of his lord's errors;
submitted dozens of memorials,
unknown to outsiders.
Gentlemen say Qún was thus an elder statesman."
Same as above.
For sincere and utmost conduct,
there is Tàizhōng Dàfū Hán Jì;
for upright and pure character,
there is Sīlì Xiàowèi Cuī Lín;
for steadfast and unadulterated virtue,
there is Tàicháng Cháng Lín.
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Wèi Shàolíng Lì Gōng Annals".
Yǔ Ái saw Hé Qiào and sighed: "Qiào stands towering like a thousand-zhàng pine,
though knotted and gnarled,
when used in a great hall,
it serves as a beam."
. "History of the Jìn, Biography of Hé Qiào".
Wáng Yǎn and his brother Chéng
enjoyed evaluating people,
and the world took their standards as models.
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Jìn Huìdì Annals".
Wáng Chéng, Wáng Xuán, and Wáng Jì all had great fame,
yet all ranked below Wèi Jiè.
The world said:
"Three sons of the Wáng family
are not equal to one child of the Wèi family."
"History of the Jìn".
Someone told Wáng Róng: "Yesterday in a crowd, I first saw Jī Shào,
towering like a wild crane among chickens."
Róng said: "You haven't seen his father yet."
Same as above.
Péi Kǎi had the insight to judge people;
he once said: "Xiàhóu Xuán is solemn as entering an ancestral temple,
where only ritual vessels are seen.
Zhōng Huì is like viewing an armory—
only spears and halberds ahead.
Shān Tāo is like climbing mountains overlooking waters,
profound and far-reaching."
. "History of the Jìn, Biography of Jī Kāng".
Wáng Yǎn spoke with facile judgments,
and court and public followed him unanimously.
. "History of the Jìn, His Biography".
Wáng Róng had discernment in judging character;
he often regarded Shān Tāo as unpolished jade or unrefined gold—
people admire its value,
but none know its true measure;
Wáng Yǎn had a transcendent demeanor,
like jade trees in a fairy forest,
naturally standing above the worldly dust.
Same as above.
Zhōu Yǐ and others held high positions together.
Once at a winter solstice feast,
their mother offered a toast to her three sons;
Sōng said: "Bórén has great ambition but little talent,
heavy reputation but dim insight,
fond of exploiting others' weaknesses—
not a way to preserve himself.
I, Sōng, am stubborn and blunt,
and also unwelcome in the world.
Only Ānú is mediocre,
and should remain under our mother's care."
Ānú was
the childhood name of Sōng's younger brother Mó.
"History of the Jìn".
Huán Yí said: "Jìyě has the Spring and Autumn Annals in his heart."
Meaning he showed no outward judgment,
but held inner praise or blame.
. "History of the Jìn, Biography of Chǔ Póu".
The Wèi sovereign Sì asked: "How does Liú Yù's talent compare to Mùróng Chuí?"
The reply: "He surpasses him.
Chuí relied on his father and brother's legacy,
restoring the former enterprise,
with people flocking to him like night insects to fire;
with little support,
he easily achieved merit."
Liú Yù rose from humble origins,
without inheriting an inch of land,
yet he suppressed Huán Xuán,
revived the Jìn dynasty,
captured Mùróng Chāo in the north,
and beheaded Lú Xún in the south.
Wherever he marched, none could stand before him.
Had his talent not surpassed others,
how could he have achieved this?"
From the Comprehensive Mirror.
Cuī Hào of Wèi remarked:
"Gāo Yǔn possesses abundant talent and broad learning,
a fine scholar of his generation,
but what he lacks
is an unyielding moral integrity."
From the Comprehensive Mirror: Records of Sòng.
Kǒng Huàn said:
"Jiǎng Zǒng has the literary brilliance of Pān Yuè and Lù Jī,
but lacks the noble spirit of Dōng Yuángōng and Qǐ Lǐ Jì."
From the Book of Chén.
The Crown Prince asked Hè Ruòbì:
"Yáng Sù, Hán Qínhǔ, and Shǐ Wànsuì are all praised as fine generals—
how do they compare in merit?"
Bì replied:
"Yáng Sù is a fierce general,
not a strategic one;
Hán Qínhǔ is a warrior general,
not a garrison commander;
Shǐ Wànsuì is a cavalry general,
not a grand general."
From the Comprehensive Mirror: Records of Suí Gāozǔ.
The Emperor said:
"Zhǎngsūn Wújì excels at avoiding suspicion,
responds to affairs with swift adaptability,
and decides matters with clarity unsurpassed by the ancients;
however, commanding troops in battle
is not his strength.
Gāo Shìlián is well-versed in past and present,
clear-minded and perceptive in thought,
unchanging in integrity when facing adversity,
and free from factionalism in office;
what he lacks is the boldness to admonish directly.
Táng Jiǎn is eloquent and quick-witted,
skilled at reconciling others;
serving me for thirty years,
he has never offered advice on governance.
Yáng Shīdào is pure and gentle in nature,
naturally without fault;
yet he is truly timid,
unreliable in times of urgency.
Cén Wénběn is honest and sincere by nature,
with elegant and rich writings;
moreover, his arguments always adhere to enduring principles,
ensuring he never fails in his duties.
Liú Jì has the firmest integrity,
and is beneficial in affairs;
however, he values promises highly,
showing favoritism to friends.
Mǎ Zhōu perceives matters swiftly,
his character very upright and just;
in evaluating people,
he speaks with straightforward honesty,
and in my appointments,
he often meets my expectations.
Chǔ Suíliáng has considerable learning,
and his nature is also firm and upright;
he constantly expresses loyalty,
and attaches himself closely to me,
like a bird relying on a person,
evoking natural affection."
From the Comprehensive Mirror: Tàizōng.
Biographies
Yán Zhòngbì is like a crane calling over the marshlands,
a white steed in an empty valley.
Yán Yànxiān resembles the qín and sè among the eight tones,
the dragon's pattern among the five colors.
Zhāng Wēibó is like the lush pine in winter,
the escaping light in the dark night.
Lù Shìhéng and Lù Shìlóng are like swans hovering,
a suspended drum awaiting the mallet.
From A New Account of the Tales of the World.
Yǔ Dàojì said:
"Lián Pō and Lìn Xiàngrú, though millennia have passed,
still emanate a vital, awe-inspiring spirit;
Cáo Chú and Lǐ Zhì, though alive today,
are as lifeless as those in the nine springs below.
Grand General Wáng praised Wáng Yífǔ,
standing among the crowd,
like pearls and jade amidst tiles and stones."
From A New Account of the Tales of the World.
Collections
Fù Yì compared to Bān Gù
are only a hair's breadth apart.
From Wèi Wéndì's "Diǎn Lùn".
Criticizing and evaluating merits and faults.
From the "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" in the Selections of Refined Literature.
Judgments flow from their lips,
distinctions between right and wrong stem from their assessments.
From "On Severing Relations" in the Selections of Refined Literature.
The world regards you, noble sir, as the arbiter of literature,
the scale for evaluating people;
once appraised by you,
one becomes a fine scholar.
From Lǐ Bái's "Letter to Prefect Hán of Jīngzhōu".
Subtle critiques on the tongue,
unspoken judgments in the heart.
From Duàn Chéngshì's writings.
At that time,
seeing the prince at the northern pavilion,
he was like a dragon or tiger in high mountains and deep forests,
unpredictable in transformation,
a man of outstanding eminence.
Upon retiring to see the junior tutor,
he was like emerald bamboos and verdant parasol trees,
with phoenixes perched serenely,
one who can preserve his heritage.
The youngest son, graceful, quiet, and elegant,
adorned with jade rings and ear ornaments,
like an orchid sprouting its buds,
worthy of his family's name.
From Hán Yù's "Epitaph for the Late Junior Supervisor of the Palace Mǎ Jūn".
Our Dynasty
The recluse Dīng Zhòng was skilled in judging character.
Observing Yú Cóng, he said to Lù Ruò:
"Vice Director Yú possesses elegant demeanor and tidy appearance,
with humble and respectful manners.
Like a vessel capable of holding a hundred hú,
it is still half empty—
how can his emolument and rank not increase?"
From the Continued Tales of the World.
Qí's Hé Diǎn often praised:
"Lù Huìxiǎo is like a mirror,
reflecting everything it encounters with clarity;
Wáng Sīyuǎn is always as if holding ice,
exuding a frosty chill even in the summer heat."
Some versions say "aura".
Classics
To understand others is wisdom.
From the "Counsels of Gāo Yáo" in the Book of Documents.
The people of Jìn said of Wénzǐ that he understood people.
From the "Tángōng" chapter in the Record of Rites.
Fán Chí asked about wisdom,
the Master said:
"To understand others."
From the Analects, "Yān Yuān" chapter.
Masters
Nothing is more difficult than understanding others.
From the "Conduct of Disciples" in the Family Sayings of Confucius.
To recognize the worthy is called discernment.
From the "Dispelling Obscurity" chapter in the Writings of Xúnzǐ.
A gentleman cannot be deceived about people.
I was profoundly struck by his uniqueness.
From the Zhuāngzǐ.
To perceive what is yet unheard,
to discern what is yet unformed,
and to assess their spirit and wisdom,
recognizing their talents and abilities—
this can be called understanding others.
If one only recognizes them after achievements are made and deeds accomplished,
Zǐsāng was loyal,
he understood people,
and was capable of promoting the virtuous.
． _Zuozhuan, 3rd Year of Duke Wen_.
Confucius heard of the turmoil in Wèi,
and said:
"Chái will come,
but Yóu will die."
． _Zuozhuan, 15th Year of Duke Ai_.
Bào Shū recommended Guǎn Zhòng,
placing himself beneath him.
The world praised Guǎn Zhòng's worthiness and Bào Shū's ability to recognize talent.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Biography_.
The emperor asked Bǐng Jí: "Who can replace you?"
He replied: "Dù Yánnián, Yú Dìngguó, and Chén Wànnián."
Later, when they assumed their posts, all were deemed competent,
and the emperor praised Bǐng Jí for understanding people.
． _Book of Han, Basic Biography_.
Cross-referenced under "Self-replacement."
Dìwǔ Lún recommended many who reached the rank of two thousand piculs,
and his era considered him a judge of character.
_Book of the Later Han_.
Wú Jìyīng
(Yòu)
had the insight to understand people.
． _Book of the Later Han, Basic Biography_.
Sīmǎ Huī was pure and refined,
possessing the discernment to understand people.
Páng Dé Gōng once said of Dé Cāo
(Sīmǎ Huī)
that he was like ice
(or "water")
as a mirror.
_Comprehensive Mirror_.
Tài was intelligent and understood people,
encouraging and instructing scholars,
and the world acclaimed the discernment of Xǔ and Guō.
． _Book of the Later Han, Basic Biography_.
Xún Shù encountered Huáng Xiàn at an inn,
when the latter was fourteen years old,
and Xún was struck with awe and found him extraordinary,
bowed to him and spoke with him,
lingering for a long time unable to leave.
He said: "He is my model and teacher."
_Book of the Later Han_.
Sīmǎ Huī said: "Páng Shìyuán is not talent for a hundred-li district;
if given the responsibilities of a治中 or別駕,
he will unfold his steed's stride."
． _Records of the Three Kingdoms, Biography of Páng Tǒng_.
Zhūgě Liàng said: "Jiǎng Wǎn,
is a vessel for the state,
not talent for a hundred-li district."
． _Records of the Three Kingdoms, Basic Biography_.
Zhōu Bì saw Péi Wěi and sighed: "Like an armory,
with weapons纵横,
a hero of the age."
_Book of Jin_.
Wáng Róng had the discernment to judge character.
． _Book of Jin, Basic Biography_.
Wáng Dǎo, from a young age, had keen judgment,
with clear and far-reaching insight.
At fourteen,
the eminent scholar Zhāng Gōng saw him and found him remarkable,
saying to his cousin Dūn: "This child's appearance and ambition
mark him as prime ministerial material."
Same as above.
Cross-referenced under "Expectations."
Xiè Ān, at the age of twenty,
visited Wáng Méng,
engaged in pure conversation,
and after he left,
Méng said: "This young man is impressively compelling."
Same as above.
At that time, Grand Commandant Xì Jiàn sent a disciple to seek a son-in-law from Wáng Dǎo,
who had him go to the east wing to observe all the young men.
The disciple returned,
and told Jiàn: "All the Wáng youths are excellent,
but upon hearing the messenger had arrived,
they all became reserved.
Only one person was lying bare-bellied eating in the east bed,
as if he hadn't heard."
Jiàn said: "That's the perfect son-in-law!"
Upon inquiry,
it was Xīzhī.
． _Book of Jin, Biography of Wáng Xīzhī_.
Cross-referenced under "Choosing a Son-in-Law."
Wáng Xīzhī at twelve,
Zhōu Yǐ found him extraordinary.
At the time, ox heart roast was highly valued,
and before the seated guests had tasted it,
Yǐ first cut a piece and gave it to Xīzhī to eat,
and thus Xīzhī became known.
_Book of Jin_.
Those recommended by Rénjié,
such as Zhāng Jiànzhī, Huán Yànfàn, Jìng Huī, Yáo Chóng, etc.,
all became famous ministers of the restoration.
． _Book of Tang, Basic Biography_.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān asked Dí Rénjié,
wishing to find a rare talent to employ,
and Rénjié said: "The Chief Clerk of Jīngzhōu, Zhāng Jiànzhī,
though old,
truly has the talent of a prime minister!"
_Continued World Sayings_.
Lǐ Yōng was renowned throughout the land for his literary talent.
Lú Cángyòng said:
"Yōng is like the swords Gānjiàng and Mòyé,
hard to contend with,
but I fear he may break."
． _Book of Tang, Basic Biography_.
Cross-referenced under "The Unyielding Must Break."
Dúgū Xìn saw Sūn Sīmiǎo and said: "A great vessel is hard to employ."
Xí Yù promoted many from humble and distant backgrounds to high office,
and was praised in his time for understanding people.
Wáng Qǐ presided over the imperial examinations,
and those he recommended all became well-known,
earning admiration for his discernment.
Cross-referenced under the "Examiner" section.
Jiǎ Sù presided over the imperial examinations three times,
and many of his candidates became famous ministers and prime ministers.
Same as above.
Collection
Clearly understands Shān Tāo's discernment.
Dù's poem.
The song of the ox horn,
though crude in words and clumsy in meaning;
the words from the hall,
are not recorded in the annals.
Duke Huán of Qí raised him to be prime minister,
Shū Xiàng took his hand and ascended,
yet it is not that words are hard to utter,

Hán's writing.

Our dynasty
Wáng Yí Gōng composed the "Ode on the Undifferentiated Completion,"
and those with insight knew he would certainly become prime minister.
_Records of Hearsay and Sight_.
Yàn Yuánxiàn, as prime minister, sought a son-in-law from Fàn Wénzhèng,
who said: "For your daughter, you must seek a national talent,
none better than Fù Bì."
Same as above.
Ōu Gōng was prefect of Yǐngzhōu,
with Lǚ Gōngzhù as his deputy,
a man of virtuous conduct who kept deeply to himself,
not widely known at the time.
Later, when Ōu returned to court,
he strongly recommended him.
_Anecdotes_.
Classics
Examining sounds to understand music,
examining music to understand harmony.
． _Record of Music, Book of Rites_.
Masters
Confucius was in Wèi,
rising early at dawn,
with Yán Huí attending by his side,
they heard a mourner's cry, very sorrowful.
The Master said:
"Huí,
do you know what this mourning is about?"
"This mourning cry is not only for the dead,
but also for the living parted."
The Master said: "How do you know?"
He replied: "Huí has heard of the birds of Héng Shān,
which bear four chicks,
and when their wings are fully grown,
they will part to the four seas,
their mother sadly cries as she sends them off,
her mournful sound resembles this,
for they go and do not return,
and Huí privately recognized it by the similarity in sound."
Confucius had someone ask the mourner,
who indeed said: "My husband died, the family is poor,
I sold my child to bury him,
and now part with him forever."
The Master said: "Huí is skilled in discerning sounds."
_Family Sayings of Confucius_.
Bó Yá excelled at playing the qin,
and Zhōng Zǐqī excelled at listening.
When Bó Yá played the qin,
his thoughts were on high mountains.
Zǐqī said: "Excellent!
Towering like Tài Shān!"
When his thoughts were on flowing water,
Zǐqī said: "Excellent!
Vast like the rivers!"
Whatever Bó Yá thought of,
Zǐqī always grasped it.
_Liezi_.
The Master wandered by the Fén pavilion,
playing the qin,
when a fisherman passed by,
and said: "How beautiful,
the meaning of the qin!
It holds the ambition of the court while in the mountains and marshes."
_Wenzhongzi_.
Cross-referenced under the "Meeting of Wits" section.
History
When the people of Jìn heard that the Chǔ army was coming,
Shī Kuàng said: "No harm.
I repeatedly sang the northern airs,
and also sang the southern airs.
The southern airs were not strong,
full of dying sounds.
Chǔ will surely achieve nothing."
． _Zuǒzhuàn, 18th Year of Xiānggōng_.
When Bó Shí was first born,
his aunt went to see him,
but upon hearing his cry, she turned back,
saying: "This is the cry of a jackal or wolf.
The wild ambition of a wolf's cub —
if not this one,
none will bring ruin to the Yángshé clan."
． _Zuǒzhuàn, 28th Year of Zhāogōng_.
Confucius learned to play the qín from Master Xiāngzǐ,
but after ten days had not progressed.
Master Xiāngzǐ said: "You may advance now."
Confucius said: "I have mastered the melody,
but not yet the technique."
After some time,
he said: "You have mastered the technique,
you may advance now."
Confucius said: "I have not yet grasped its spirit."
After some time,
he said: "You have grasped its spirit,
you may advance now."
Confucius said: "There is a solemn depth in contemplation,
and a joyful gaze reaching far with lofty aspirations."
He said:
"I have perceived the man —
dark and somber,
tall and slender,
with eyes gazing into the distance like a shepherd,
as if ruling over the four states.
If not King Wén, who could have composed this!"
Master Xiāngzǐ rose from his mat and bowed twice,
saying: "My master said it is indeed the 'Wén Wáng Cāo'."
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Hereditary House of Confucius_.
When someone invited Cài Yōng with food and drink,
a guest played the qín behind a screen.
Yōng, arriving at the gate, listened secretly and said:
"I was summoned with music, yet there is a murderous intent —
why?"
He then turned back.
The host pursued and asked the reason,
and Yōng told him everything.
The qín player said: "Earlier I saw a mantis stalking a cicada,
about to leave but not yet flying away,
and the mantis advanced and retreated accordingly.
My heart was tense,
fearing only that the mantis would miss the cicada.
Could this have manifested as a murderous intent in the sound?"
Yōng sighed and said: "That indeed explains it."
_History of the Eastern Hàn_.
When Cài Yōng broke a string while playing the qín at night,
Yǎn said: "The second string."
Yōng said: "You guessed it by chance."
So he broke another string and asked her,
and Yǎn said: "The fourth string."
． _Later Biography_.
Zhōu Yú was skilled in music from a young age.
After three cups of wine,
if there was any error in the music,
Yú would surely notice it,
and upon noticing, he would turn to look.
Thus, people of the time sang:
"When a melody has an error,
Zhōu Láng turns his head."
_History of Wú_.
In the 14th year of the Kāihuáng era,
a decree was issued to perform the new music.
Wàn Bǎocháng, upon hearing the performance by the Tàicháng office,
shed tears and said: "The music is licentious, harsh, and sorrowful —
the world will soon come to an end!"
At that time, the empire was at its peak,
and all thought it untrue;
but by the end of the Dàyè era,
his words proved true.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Suí Wén Records_.
Hán Huǎng understood music theory.
Once, while watching a qín performance,
when it reached "Zhǐxī",
he sighed and said: "Marvelous!
When Jī Kāng composed this piece,
it must have been during the transition from Wèi to Jìn!
Its tone is centered on shāng,
and shāng represents autumn.
Autumn is when
heaven causes withering and stern killing —
is it not the year's decline?
Moreover, Jìn succeeded through metal's phase,
and shāng corresponds to metal's sound.
This is how I know it was the end of Wèi and the rise of Jìn.
Slowing the shāng string
to match the gōng tone
signifies a minister usurping the ruler.
This is how I know the Sīmǎ clan would seize the throne."
． _Old Book of Táng, Biography of Hán Huǎng_.
Lǐ Yǔ, while going to morning court through Yǒngxīng Lane,
heard the sound of a flute
and asked his attendants: "Is that a musician from the Tàicháng office?"
They replied: "Yes."
Another day, he recognized the musician and asked:
"Why were you playing while lying down?"
The flutist was startled and apologized.
Also, upon hearing Kāng Kūnlún play the pipa,
he said: "There is too much 'pí'
and too little 'pá' —
this cannot be played on the 54-string large silk instrument."
Musicians say striking upward from below is called "pí",
and striking downward from above is called "pá".
． _Combined Examination of Táng History_.
Xún Xù once encountered a cowbell from a Zhào merchant on the road
and recognized its sound.
Later, when in charge of music,
the tones were not harmonious,
so he said:
"If we get a Zhào cowbell, it will harmonize."
He then ordered all commanderies
to send cowbells,
and indeed found a harmonious one.
_Book of Jìn_.
Biographies
When Confucius played the sè,
Zēngzǐ, upon hearing it, said:
"My master's sè sound has the ambition of greed and cruelty,
and the conduct of depravity —
how unmerciful
and excessively profit-seeking!"
Zǐgòng went in and reported this.
The Master said: "Shēn
is a worthy man of the world,
well-versed in music.
Just now, as I played the sè,
a mouse came out to roam,
a wildcat saw it on the roof,
crept along the beam,
and tried to catch it but failed.
I expressed this with the sound of my sè.
For Shēn to think me greedy and depraved
is quite fitting, is it not?"
_Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn_.
A man from Wú was burning paulownia for fuel,
and Cài Yōng, hearing the crackling sound,
said: "This is fine paulownia."
He then asked for it to carve into a qín.
_Sōushén Jì_.
Yú Dí had a guest play the qín,
and his sister-in-law, who understood music,
said: "In three parts,
one part is zhēng sound,
two parts are pipa,
with no qín charm at all."
_Supplement to the National History_.
Collection
Recognize the tune and hear its truth.
． _Selected Ancient Poems_.
Though I cherish the ancient melodies,
most people today do not play them.
I offer you this piece,
for the rarity of a true understanding is precious.
Liú Chángqīng.
See also "Àn Tóu".
Classics
The Master said: "With the wisdom of Zāng Wǔzhòng,
the lack of desire of Gōng Chuò,
the courage of Biàn Zhuāngzǐ,
and the arts of Rǎn Qiú,
adorned with ritual and music,
one may indeed be considered a complete person."
． _Analects, Xiàn Wèn_.
Masters
The utility of Huáinánzǐ's writings
is not equal to that of Grand Historian Simǎ Qiān's.
The Grand Historian —
the sage would have something to select from him.
Now emerging, now withdrawing —
that is Huáinánzǐ;
elegant but of little use —
that is Sīmǎ Xiàngrú;
loving much and sparing none —
that is Simǎ Zǐcháng.
Zhòngní loved much,
loving righteousness;
Zǐcháng loved much,
loving the extraordinary."
． _Yáng Yuān Qiān_.
Bó Zhí,
still smells of mother's milk,
cannot match Hán Xìn.
Féng Jìng,
though virtuous,
cannot match Guàn Yīng.
Xiàng Tuō,
cannot match Cáo Cān.
． 《Tōng Jiàn Hàn Gāo Jì》.
Xún Yuè said: "The Zhào troops left their state to engage in battle,
advancing when they saw an opportunity,
retreating when they knew it was difficult,
harboring thoughts of looking back home,
without a plan to fight to the death;
Hán Xìn's army was isolated by the river,
his soldiers were determined to die,
without any second thoughts,
this is why Hán Xìn defeated them.
The King of Hàn deeply entered enemy territory,
held banquets and grand gatherings,
his soldiers were at ease and comfortable,
their will to fight was not firm;
Chǔ, with its mighty power, had lost its capital,
its soldiers were filled with indignation and fervor,
rushing to save their defeat and impending doom,
staking their lives in a single day,
while Hán responded with lazy and negligent troops,
this is the same situation but with different circumstances."
《Tōng Jiàn》.
Zǐfáng, Xiāo Hé, Hán Xìn,
these three were all outstanding men,
I was able to employ them,
this is how I gained the world.
Xiàng Yǔ had one Fàn Zēng,
yet could not use him,
this is why he was captured by me.
Same as above.
Cháo Cuò was keen on planning for the state's long-term but failed to see the harm to himself,
his father foresaw it,
dying in a ditch without helping to save,
his failure was not like Mother Zhào pointing out Kuò's flaws,
to preserve his clan.
． 《Qián Hàn Běn Zàn》.
The talents of Wáng and Gòng,
were superior to Gōng and Bào.
Holding fast to the good way unto death,
Shèng truly practiced it.
． 《Tōng Jiàn Hàn Píng Jì》.
Grand Administrator of Tàiqiū Chén Shí.
Shí's son, Court Minister of State Guests Jì,
Jì's son, Minister of Works Qún,
Qún's son Tài,
for four generations in the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
all had great reputations, but their virtue gradually diminished.
Contemporaries said of them: "The Duke shames the Minister,
the Minister shames the Administrator."
《Sān Guó Wèi Chén Qún Zhuàn》note.
Wáng Sù was upright, knowledgeable, and capable of analyzing responsibilities.
Liú Shí believed that Sù was subservient to superiors but liked inferiors flattering him,
this is the first contradiction.
Only craving honor and wealth but not seeking improper alliances,
this is the second contradiction.
Stingy with wealth but maintaining personal integrity,
this is the third contradiction.
《Sān Guó Wèi Wáng Sù Zhuàn Píng》.
Wáng Chǎng was Minister of Works of Wèi,
open-minded and insightful,
profound and simple in nature,
with a magnanimous demeanor,
had the expectation of becoming a high minister.
Pure and detached with few desires,
not embellishing his words.
Famous ministers after Jìn crossed the river, like Wáng Dǎo, Wèi Jiè, Zhōu Yǐ, Yǔ Liàng, and others,
all ranked below him.
From Chǎng to Chéng, generations had high reputations, but critics,
believed the grandfather was not as good as the grandson,
the grandson not as good as the father.
《Jìn Shū》.
Fàn Lóng said: "I have always been ashamed that Suí Hé Lù lacked military prowess,
and Jiàng Guàn lacked literary talent.
Suí Hé Lù met Emperor Gāo but could not establish the feat of enfeoffment,
Jiàng Guàn met Emperor Wén but could not promote education in schools."
． 《Tōng Jiàn Jìn Shì Zǔ》.
Zhāng Fǔ once wrote an essay arguing that Guǎn Zhòng was not as good as Bào Shū,
Bān Gù不及Sīmǎ Qiān,
Wèi Wǔ不及Liú Bèi,
Yuè Yì was inferior to Zhūgě Liàng.
《Jìn Shū》.
Cuī Hào said: "Wáng Měng's governance of the state,
was Fú Jiān's Guǎn Zhòng;
Mùróng Kè's assistance to the young ruler,
was Mùróng Wěi's Huò Guāng;
Liú Yù's suppression of turmoil,
was Sīmǎ Dézōng's Cáo Cāo."
． 《Tōng Jiàn Jìn Jì》.
The Wèi sovereign Sì said: "How does Yù's talent compare to Mùróng Chuí?"
The reply was: "He surpasses him.
Chuí relied on the resources of his father and brother,
restored the former enterprise,
the people of the state rallied to him,
like night insects drawn to fire,
with little additional support,
it was easy to achieve merit.
Liú Yù rose from humble origins,
without a foot of land to start with,
campaigned to eliminate Huán Xuán,
revived the Jìn court,
captured Mùróng Chāo in the north,
beheaded Lú Xún in the south,
advancing unopposed wherever he went,
if not for his exceptional talent,
how could he have achieved this!"
． 《Tōng Jiàn Jìn Gōng Jì》.

At the start of the two Hàn dynasties,
butchers, vendors, convicts, and slaves emerged
to become dukes, marquises, ministers, and chancellors—no other reason,
they inherently possessed the capacity for such roles.
Meeting untimely eras led to their suppression;
their initial misfortune
was not due to encountering Gāozǔ or Guāngwǔ and counting it as luck.
By the end of Hàn and Jìn,
dukes, marquises, ministers, and chancellors were robbed, killed, starved, and died huddled against walls—
no other cause,
they were fated for such ends.
Meeting untimely times brought this forth;
only their initial fortune
was not due to encountering Dǒng Zhuó or Liú Yào before disaster struck.
Liǔ's "On Universal Appropriateness".
Zhōu Rén, as a high official, governed as a two-thousand-bushel official; Xǔ Jìng,
through others' praise, rose to one of the three highest offices—
recent times particularly favor such types,
considering them virtuous elders.
From gatekeepers and night watchmen
upward, they receive the most recommendations and favor.
Those deemed simple and harmless
may serve as commoners in rural villages.
Even if called virtuous elders,
it is acceptable;
but from gatekeepers and watchmen upward,
they must respect their duties.
The higher they rise, the greater their impact—
why employ useless simplicity!
Nowadays, it is said:
"So-and-so is a virtuous elder,
fit for high office"—mostly unlike the ancients' so-called elders.
Then they are mere clay and wood.
To place clay and wood in the high halls,
draped in royal robes, flanked by attendants scurrying about—
what good does it do for the people's toils and hardships!

Hán Yù once wrote a rhapsody,

Commanderies and counties select those skillful in writing and adept at account books who can deceive their superiors,
placing them in high positions;
when villainy becomes uncontrollable,
they then take the fierce and bold who can achieve merit at the people's expense,
and those who use harshness and cruelty to intimidate subordinates,
placing them in great offices.
Thus, the unrighteous who possess wealth become prominent in the world,
the deceitful who are skilled writers are honored at court,
the rebellious and fierce are esteemed in office.
Hence, the common saying: "Why practice filial piety and fraternal duty?
Wealth brings glory.
Why observe ritual and righteousness?
Skill in writing brings official position.
Why be cautious and prudent?
Fierceness qualifies one for office."
Thus, even those branded, mutilated, and shaven still thrust their sleeves forward to govern the world,
their conduct no better than dogs and pigs,
yet their families rich and power sufficient,
directing with glances and commanding with breath,
this is considered worthy.

History
The wise eliminate slander to secure themselves.

Shàngguān Jié resented Huò Guāng and had someone forge a letter from the King of Yān to the emperor,
claiming that Guāng, when leaving the capital with the Yǔlín troops,
had his path cleared and proclaimed a rapid advance.
He also arbitrarily increased the number of officers in his headquarters.
Upon hearing this,
Guāng did not enter the court.
The emperor asked, "Where is the Grand General?"
Jié replied, "Because the King of Yān accused him of crimes,
he dares not enter."
An edict was issued: "Summon Guāng."
Guāng removed his official hat.
The emperor said, "General, put on your hat!
I know this letter is forged,
you are not guilty.
General, you appointed the officers
less than ten days ago;
how could the King of Yān have known about it?"
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Han Emperor Zhao's Annals".
Cross-reference to "Thorough Investigation".

each time it is polished,

Biographies
Zhūgě Liàng arrived in Nánzhōng,
and wherever he went, he achieved victory in battle.
Hearing that Mèng Huò
was respected by both the Yi people and the Hàn,
he sought to capture him alive.
Once captured,
he had him observe the camp formations,
and asked, "How do you find this army?"
Huò replied, "Previously, I did not know the actual situation,
hence I was defeated."
Liàng laughed,
released him to fight again,
capturing and releasing him seven times,
yet Liàng still sent Huò away.
Huò stopped and did not leave,
saying, "You, sir,
possess the might of heaven.
The southern people will not rebel again."
From "Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū".

Initially,
the Emperor heard that in the Western Regions there was a deity,
named Buddha,
so he sent envoys to Tiānzhú to seek his teachings,
obtaining his scriptures and bringing back monks.
These scriptures generally took emptiness as their foundation,
valuing compassion and non-killing;
believing that when people die,
their spirit does not perish,
but immediately takes another form;
the good and evil deeds performed during life
all receive retribution,
therefore what is valued is cultivating the spirit,
until one becomes a Buddha;
skillfully using grand and magnificent words to persuade and entice the ignorant masses.
Those proficient in this path
were called Shāmén.
Thus China began to transmit these techniques,
depicting his images,
and among the nobility and high officials,
only King Yīng of Chǔ was the first to favor it."
