in matters great and small,
consulting diviners and invocators,
thus Wáng Yú and Lí Gàn advanced through heterodox methods.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Dàizōng".
The Emperor, gravely ill,
ordered monks to shave his head,
leaving instructions to be buried in a stūpa.
Same as above.
Biographies
When Sūn Ēn attacked Kuàijī,
Wáng Níngzhī told officials and people: "No need for precautions,
I have already petitioned the Great Dào,
which has promised to dispatch ghost troops to assist,
the rebels will defeat themselves."
Since no preparations were made,
he was consequently killed by Ēn.
Wáng shì pǔ seen in "Shì Shuō" commentary.
Serving ghosts to seek blessings,
is what the Mohist school believed.
From "Shǐ Tōng".
Collections
How extreme!
People's fondness for the strange.
Not seeking its origins,
not inquiring into its ends,
only desiring to hear of the strange.
Hán Wén's "Yuán Dào".
The Yuè people believe in omens and readily sacrifice.
When ill and distressed,
they gather shamans,
using chicken divination.
First they sacrifice small animals,
if ineffective,
then medium animals,
if still ineffective,
then large animals,
and if again ineffective,
they bid farewell to relatives,
prepare funeral affairs,
saying: "The spirits will not spare me."
Thereupon they stop eating,
cover their faces and die.
From "Liǔ Sì Jì".
Virtue is the true token of receiving the mandate,
to establish eternal sacrifice; later those licentious,
deluded, dim-witted, and fond of the strange,
then began to present great lightning,
great rainbows,
mysterious birds,
giant footprints, white fish,
flowing fire, and crow tokens,
considering these as auspicious signs.
All are deceitful, exaggerated, and absurd,
truly shameful.
Liǔ Zhēnfú.
From Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, Liú Xiàng, Yáng Xióng, Bān Biāo, to his son Bān Gù, all followed this foolish tradition,
inferring ancient auspicious objects to match the receipt of mandate,
their words resemble those of licentious shamans and blind historians,
deceiving and confusing later generations,
incapable of understanding the sage's foundation for establishing standards,
revealing ultimate virtue,
promoting great achievements,
greatly missing their true purpose.
Same as above.
Our Dynasty
Fearing ghosts and spirits, listening to shamans and wizards,
is the folly of common women.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Sùzōng".
History
Zhūgě Zhān,
son of Liàng.
After Liàng's death,
the people of Shǔ, remembering Liàng's virtue,
all loved Zhān's talent and quickness,
whenever there were good governance or fine deeds,
even if not established by Zhān,
all would tell each other: "This was done by Lord Zhūgě."
Thus his fine reputation exceeded reality.
From "Shǔ Zhì".
Cross-referenced under "Enduring Love".
Zhāng Huá loved learning,
excelling in literary composition.
Court officials, because Huá lacked hereditary status,
competed to reject and slander him.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Chén Hòuzhǔ".
Collections
The crow on the elder's roof—
if the man is good, the crow is deemed good too.
From Dù's poetry.
By chance titled as the Wood Dwelling Scholar,
endless fortune-seekers then gather.
From Hán's writings.
If indeed all that the earth produces were usable,
then the bamboo arrows of the southeast,
even if crooked and twisted,
could all pierce rhinoceros hide;
the trees of the northern mountains,
even if grotesque, sap-filled,
hollow and standing dry,
could all beam hundred-foot towers;
sail across thousand-fathom depths;
the soil of Jì's north,
where horses are born,
all those with large ears and short necks,
contorted and stumbling,
thin-hoofed and dragging,
could all bear heavy loads,
gallop a thousand miles;
the clods of Yōng,
could all serve as whetstones;
the manure-soil of Xú,
could all mound the great altars;
the thatch of Jīng,
could all filter wine;
the great tortoises of Jiǔjiāng,
could all be used for divination;
the stones of the Sì riverbanks,
could all be struck for sound,
yet if so, few would escape great error.
Applying this to people,
then Lǔ's morning sheep-waterers,
cart-wheel turners,
could all become teachers and scholars;
those of Lú who buy fame,
could all become great physicians;
in Xīshī's village,
the ugly frowners,
could all serve as lords and kings;
Shānxī's reckless and greedy,
ruthless and enduring,
could all breach fatal gates,
command beyond the threshold;
Shāndōng's blunt and simple,
devoted to farming,
date and chestnut eaters,
could all strategize in the court halls.
Such would utterly defy order and reason,
how different is this from those objects?
From Liǔ's writings.
Cross-reference "Lacking Discernment".
Our dynasty
Hán Wèigōng said: "In earlier times, when Dīng and Kòu served at court,
the world attributed every good deed to Láigōng,
though not all necessarily came from him;
every misdeed was attributed to Jìngōng,
though not all necessarily came from him.
Thus, the world's good and evil vied to be ascribed to them."
From "Yí Shì".
The Classics
Choose the good and follow it,
the bad and correct it.
• From "Analects, Shù'ér".
Cross-reference "Decision Making".
Those who tackle tigers barehanded or cross rivers on foot,
and die without regret,
I do not accompany.
It must be those who approach tasks with caution,
and succeed through good planning."
Same as above.
Accept those who are acceptable,
reject those who are not.
• From "Analects, Zǐzhāng".
Mencius
If it contradicts the Way,
not even a basket of rice should be accepted from others;
if it aligns with the Way,
then Shun accepting the world from Yáo,
is not considered excessive.
From "Mencius".
If people in the same house fight,
to rescue them,
even with hair disheveled and cap strings tangled, is acceptable.
If neighbors fight,
to rush disheveled to rescue them,
would be deluded;
even shutting the door is permissible.
Same as above.
Cross-reference "Same Matter, Different Context".
Fish
is what I desire,
bear's paw is also what I desire;
if I cannot have both,
I forsake fish for bear's paw.
Life is what I desire,
righteousness is also what I desire;
if I cannot have both,
I forsake life for righteousness.
• From "Mencius, Gàozǐ Shàng".
Speaking of being satiated with benevolence and righteousness,
thus not craving others' rich flavors.
Widespread renown bestowed upon oneself,
thus not craving others' embroidered robes.
Same as above.
Seek and you will gain it,
abandon and you will lose it,
this seeking benefits the gain,
for it depends on oneself.
Seek it by the Way,
gain it by fate,
this seeking does not benefit the gain,
for it lies outside oneself.
• From "Mencius, Jìn Xīn Shàng".
If taking is permissible or not,
taking may harm integrity;
if giving is permissible or not,
giving may harm generosity.
• From "Mencius, Lílóu Xià".
Rather than stooping oneself for wealth and honor,
it's better to uphold principles in poverty and lowliness.
Stooping puts one under others' control,
upholding principles leaves no shame against the Way.
From "Kǒng Cóngzǐ".
Cross-reference "Having Integrity".
The position of the three banners,
I know is nobler than a butcher's stall;
the emolument of ten thousand zhōng,
I know is richer than a butcher's profit.
But how can I crave titles and stipends,
and let my lord bear the name of reckless bestowal?
• From "Zhuangzi, Ràng Wáng".
Zhuangzi was fishing in the Pú River,
when the King of Chǔ sent two ministers to approach him first,
saying, "We wish to burden you with the affairs of our state!"
Zhuangzi said, "I hear Chǔ has a sacred turtle,
dead for three thousand years,
kept wrapped in cloth and boxed in the ancestral temple.
This turtle—
would it rather die to leave its bones honored,
or live dragging its tail in the mud?"
The two ministers said, "It would rather live dragging its tail in the mud."
Zhuangzi said, "Go then!
I will drag my tail in the mud."
• From "Zhuangzi, Qiū Shuǐ".
Human nature
seeks the lesser harm in the midst of harm,
and the greater benefit in the midst of benefit.
• From "Huáinánzǐ, Miù Chēng Xùn".
History
For those who strategize on behalf of a ruler,
nothing is more important than first clarifying what to adopt and what to discard.
Once the standards for adoption and discard are firmly established internally, the signs of safety and danger will manifest externally.
The King of Qín's desire to honor the ancestral temple and secure his descendants
was the same as that of Tāng and Wǔ.
However, Tāng and Wǔ expanded their virtuous conduct,
maintaining it for six to seven hundred years without loss,
while the King of Qín governed the empire for over a decade before suffering a great defeat.
This was due to no other reason: Tāng and Wǔ determined what to adopt and discard with clarity, whereas the King of Qín did so without clarity.
． "Tōng Jiàn Hàn Wén Jì".
Zhào Chōngguó said: "A cornered enemy
should not be pursued.
If given leeway, they will flee without looking back;
if pressed hard, they will turn and fight to the death."
． "Tōng Jiàn Hàn Xuān Jì".
If there is suspicion in the heart,
even fine delicacies like guǐ sūn zhuàn bù are deemed unworthy of eating,
as exemplified by Jīng Mǎo.
If the mind is free of doubt,
even a hundred pieces of premium gold can be declined without reluctance,
as exemplified by Mèng Kē.
． "Dōng Hàn Zhāng Héng Zhuàn".
If righteousness outweighs life,
one may sacrifice life;
if life outweighs righteousness,
one may preserve life.
． "Dōng Hàn Lǐ Gù Zhuàn Lùn".
As for chicken ribs,
eating them yields little gain;
discarding them,
seems a pity.
． "Hòu Hàn Yáng Xiū Zhuàn".
To plant fragrant orchids,
one must clear away thorns.
"Sān Guó Míng Chén Zàn".
Rather drink the water of Jiànyè,
than eat the fish of Wǔchāng;
rather return to Jiànyè to die,
than stay in Wǔchāng to live.
． "Tōng Jiàn Jìn Wǔ Dì".
If the way of benevolence is near,
one gives up life to follow righteousness;
if it is weightier than life,
one sacrifices oneself to fulfill it.
"Běi Shǐ".
Biographies
A good merchant does not haggle over prices with others,
but carefully observes the timing.
When prices are low, they buy—
even if expensive, it is cheap for them;
when prices are high, they sell—
even if cheap, it is expensive for them.
"Zhàn Guó Cè".
Collections
Rather be the mud in clear waters,
than the flying dust on a muddy road.
Cáo Zhí.
There are those who bear the name of a Ruist but follow Mòist practices;
inquire into their name and it seems correct,
but examine their actions and they are wrong—
can one associate with them?
Or those with a Mòist name but Ruist conduct;
inquire into their name and it seems wrong,
but examine their actions and they are correct—
can one associate with them?
Yáng Zǐyún stated: "If at the gate, drive them away;
if among the barbarians, advance them."
I take this as my rule.
Hán Wén.
Compared to the eastern capital,
I barely saw his countenance;
though I had not yet spoken with him,
my heart already found him remarkable,
but I dared not judge solely by appearance.
Knowing others is difficult even for Yáo and Shùn,
and having heeded the warning of Zǎi Yǔ,
I did not dare to embrace him decisively,
nor could I casually forget him.
Though the good may not align with me,
I will strive to adhere to it;
though the bad may not repel me,
I will strive to reject it.
Rather than praise beforehand,
is it not better to avoid slander later?
Rather than pleasure in the body,
is it not better to have no worries in the heart?
Also Hán Wén.
Cross-referenced under "Broad-mindedness".
Is it better to be known and impoverished,
or unknown and prosperous?
Is it better to be upright and stumble,
or mixed and successful?
Liǔ Wén.
Those who raise falcons—
do they truly desire them to prey on crows and kites,
or to prey on phoenixes?
"Táng Wén Cuì".
Our dynasty
Fàn Wénzhèng Gōng said: "When recruiting staff for the administration,
one must only recruit those who can serve as teachers,
not even friends should be recruited."
"Yí Shì".
Rather than be noble and constrained,
better to be free and humble.
Línchuān.
Not necessarily discarding the giant tree,
but using even the small sapling.
Dōngpō shī.
Classics
Do not engage in useless pursuits that harm the useful,
and achievements will be made;
do not value exotic things over practical ones,
and the people will be content.
． "Shū Lǚ Áo".
While parents are alive,
do not promise friends to die for them.
． "Jì Qū Lǐ Shàng".
Cross-referenced under "Filial Duty".
When building a palace,
do not cut down trees on the graves.
． "Jì Qū Lǐ Xià".
Chén Qiánxī fell ill,
and instructed his son Zūnjǐ: "When I die,
make sure to build a large coffin for me,
and have my two maids lie beside me."
When Chén Qiánxī died,
his son said: "Burying the living with the dead
is against the rites."
So he did not carry it out.
． "Jì Tán Gōng Xià".
Do not let small plans ruin great undertakings,
do not let favored concubines resent the legitimate queen,
do not let favored courtiers resent the upright officials, ministers, and nobles.
． "Jì Zī Yī".
The Ruist does not treasure gold and jade,
but holds loyalty and trust as treasures;
does not pray for land,
but establishes righteousness as his land;
does not pray for great accumulation,
but considers broad learning as wealth.
． "Jì Rú Xíng".
Returning the guī and zhāng jades after the betrothal
demonstrates the principle of valuing ritual over wealth.
． "Jì Pìn Yì".
Before the sacrificial vessels of a senior official are completed,
he does not make vessels for personal use.
． "Jì Wáng Zhì".
The stables burned.
The Master returned from court and asked,
"Was anyone hurt?"
He did not ask about the horses.
． "Yǔ Xiāng Dǎng".
The noble person seeks the Way, not food.
The noble person worries about the Way, not poverty.
． "Yǔ Wèi Líng Gōng".
The Master
When Confucius left Qí,
he departed while rinsing rice.
When leaving Lǔ, he said: "Slowly, slowly I make my journey—
this is the way to leave the land of one's parents."
． _Mencius, Wàn Zhāng II_.
"If a villager is older than one's elder brother,
when pouring wine, whom should one serve first?"
The reply was: "Serve the villager first."
． _Mencius, Gào Zǐ I_.
Do not let the small harm the great,
nor let the base harm the noble.
"Which is more important: ritual or food?"
The answer: "Ritual is more important."
"Which is more important: desire or ritual?"
The answer: "Ritual is more important."
Both from the same text above.
Fú Zǐjiàn was the magistrate of Shànfù.
When the Qí army attacked Lǔ,
their route passed through Shànfù.
The elders requested: "The wheat is ripe,
and now the Qí invaders are coming.
Please allow the people to go out
and harvest the wheat near the city walls—
it can increase our food supply,
and won't benefit the enemy."
After three requests, Fú Zǐjiàn refused,
saying: "If we have no wheat this year,
we can plant more next year.
But if we let those who didn't farm reap the harvest,
it would make the people welcome invaders.
Moreover, one year's wheat from Shànfù
won't strengthen Lǔ if kept,
nor weaken it if lost.
But if we let people develop the habit of taking things for themselves,
the harm would last for generations."
_Family Sayings of Confucius_.
Cross-referenced under "Profound Insight and Great Principles".
Human nature is such that,
even for Jié or Zhí,
who would willingly harm what they love for what they hate?
． _Xúnzǐ, Discussion on Military Affairs_.
If a halberd is raised to one's head,
one wouldn't hesitate to lose ten fingers.
Not that one doesn't value them,
but there's an order of priority in emergencies.
． _Xúnzǐ, On Strengthening the State_.
The sage does not prize a foot-long jade disk, but values every inch of time.
_Huáinánzǐ_.
Lín Huí abandoned a priceless jade disk,
and carried an infant while fleeing.
_Zhuāngzǐ_.
With a rhinoceros or tiger behind,
and the Marquis of Suí's pearl in front,
one wouldn't stop to pick it up—
avoiding harm comes before seeking gain.
． _Huáinánzǐ, Sayings and Admonitions_.
Cutting a boil is not painless,
drinking bitter medicine is not pleasant,
yet we do it for the body's benefit;
drinking when thirsty is refreshing,
eating heavily when hungry is satisfying,
yet we refrain when it harms our nature.
． _Huáinánzǐ, Exposition of Sayings_.
Jīng Kē and Zhū Hài didn't show minor courage among the timid,
Mèng Bēn and Féng Fù didn't wield weapons against packs of jackals.
_Bàopǔzǐ_.
History:
Jìn's Wèi Wǔzǐ had a favored concubine
who bore no sons.
He ordered Wèi Kē: "You must marry her off."
When gravely ill,
he said: "You must bury her with me."
After his death,
Kē married her off,
saying: "In illness, one's mind is confused;
I follow his rational order."
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xuān 15th Year_.
When Confucius read the historical records about Chǔ restoring Chén,
he said: "How worthy was King Zhuāng of Chǔ!
He valued a single promise over a state of a thousand chariots."
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Chén Hereditary House_.
When Pei Gong entered Xiányáng from the west,
his generals all rushed to the treasuries to seize gold, silk, and goods.
Only Xiāo Hé first collected the maps and records from the Qín chancellor's office and stored them,
enabling Pei Gong to know all about the empire's strategic passes, population numbers, and strengths and weaknesses.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Hàn Gāozǔ Annals_.
An enlightened ruler values the five grains and disdains gold and jade.
． _Qián Hànshū, Treatise on Food and Money_.
Leaving your children a full basket of gold is not as good as one classic.
_Hànshū_.
Lìn Xiàngrú feared not the King of Qín but yielded to Lián Pō—
for the state's sake.
． _Later Hànshū, Biography of Kòu Xún_.
Even if all sand and gravel turned to southern gold,
and tiles and stones became Hé's jade,
if the people had nothing to drink when thirsty,
nothing to eat when hungry,
even with the pure virtue of Fúxī and Shénnóng,
the civilization of Táng and Yú,
they could not preserve peace within their own walls.
For the people can go a hundred years without goods,
but not a single day without food.
． _Later Hànshū, Biography of Liú Táo_.
Zhāng Gāng was inspecting provinces and commanderies
when he buried his carriage wheels at the Luòyáng capital post station,
saying: "With wolves blocking the road,
why bother with foxes!"
． _Later Hànshū, His Biography_.
Cross-referenced under "Hatred of Evil".
Cài Yōng said: "Troubles on the borders are like scabies on the limbs;
crises in the central states are like ulcers on the chest and back."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Later Hàn_.
The Emperor sent men to Wú to trade horses for pearls, jadeite, and tortoiseshell.
The Lord of Wú said: "These are things I have no use for,
and I can get horses for them—
why should I begrudge them?"
He gave them all.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Wèi Míngdì Annals_.
Shí Lè said: "I am not pleased to get Yōuzhōu,
but pleased to get two men."
Wáng Xiàn and Sūn Chuò.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Jìn Mǐndì Annals II_.
Yān's heir apparent Bǎo said to Chuí: "I hope you won't let personal feelings and small favors
make you forget the importance of the state."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Jìn Wǔdì Annals_.
Lǐ Mì said: "A man with ten thousand volumes of books—
what need has he for a hundred cities and a throne?"
_History of the Northern Dynasties_.
The Emperor told Xuē Rénguì: "All my generals are old;
I want to find a new, brave leader for them—
none compares to you.
I am not pleased to have Liáodōng,
but pleased to have you."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Tángshū His Biography_.
Dí Rénjié said: "In yellow scrolls, I face the sages and worthies—
when would I have time to chat with vulgar officials?"
Same as above.
Emperor Míng of Táng wanted to capture Shíbǎo Fortress.
Wáng Zhōngsì opposed it.
Lǐ Guāngbì urged him,
but Zhōngsì said: "We cannot take Shíbǎo Fortress without killing tens of thousands.
If I disobey the decree now,
at most I'll offend the Son of Heaven—
as a general,
I'll return to guard duty!
Otherwise,
I might become a minor official in Qiánzhōng?"
He also said: "How could I bear to trade tens of thousands of lives for one official post?"
_Tángshū_.
_The Record_ says: "Better keep a thieving minister."
A thieving minister is indeed detestable,
but he harms only one person.
If a extortionate minister is employed,
the regular laws are ruined,
and the people suffer endless harm.
． _Tángshū, Treatise on Food and Money_.
Lǐ Jiàng said: "Money spent can be regained,
but a lost opportunity cannot be recovered."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Annals_.
Cross-referenced under "Seizing Opportunities".
Biographies and Records
During the reign of Lord Sì of Wèi,
a convict
who was a capable minister committed a crime.
He fled to Wèi,
and Wèi offered a hundred pieces of gold to ransom him,
but it was not accepted.
They then offered the territory of Zuǒshì.
A city of Wèi.
The ministers said:
"Using land worth a hundred pieces of gold
to ransom a mere convict—
is that not inappropriate?"
The lord replied:
"In governance, nothing is trivial;
in chaos, nothing is minor.
If the people are guided by education,
a city of three hundred households
is sufficient for orderly rule;
if the people lack shame,
even with ten Zuǒshì,
how could they be of use?"
From *Strategies of the Warring States*.
Niè Zhèng said:
"While my aged mother lives,
I dare not pledge my life to others."
Same source as above.
Cross-referenced under "Way of the Son."
Mòzǐ asked Qín Gǔlí:
"In a famine year,
if I gave you a Suí pearl,
and also a bell of grain,
which would you choose?"
Lí replied:
"The grain would suffice."
From Liú Xiàng's *Garden of Persuasions*.
Cross-referenced under "Practical Benefits."
Duke Wén followed Jiù Fàn's advice
and defeated Chǔ at Chéngpú.
Upon returning to bestow rewards,
Yōng Jì was placed above him.
His attendants remonstrated:
"The victory at Chéngpú
was due to Jiù Fàn's strategy.
Should you use his advice but then rank him lower?"
The Duke said:
"Yōng Jì's words
benefit a hundred generations;
Jiù Fàn's words
address a momentary need.
How can momentary needs precede benefits for a hundred generations?"
From *Mr. Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Collection:
If a trap clamps the foot, even a fierce tiger
will sever its paw;
if a viper bites the hand,
a strong man will cut off the joint.
Why? Because what is preserved is weighty,
and what is discarded is light.
From Chén Lín's proclamation.
Duke Huán of Qí did not hold a grudge over the arrow hook incident,
thus achieving the feat of nine assemblies;
Duke Mù of Qín did not let one fault obscure virtue,
thus avenging the shame of nine defeats.
From Lord Lù Xuān's writings.
Value reputation over office.
Lǐ Tàibái.
Each person has but one death,
which may be weightier than Tài Shān
or lighter than a goose feather.
If death outweighs righteousness,
it is regarded as Tài Shān;
if righteousness outweighs death,
it is seen as a goose feather.
Thus, without righteousness,
a noble person does not lightly give life;
in its proper place,
a noble person does not cling to life.
From the *Báichuán Collection*.
Ōuyáng Zhān,
a man of Mǐnyuè,
with aged parents,
left their daily care
to come to the capital,
his heart set on gaining something
to return and honor his parents.
Even his parents felt the same:
with Zhān by their side,
though free from separation's sorrow,
their hearts were not joyful;
with Zhān in the capital,
though separated and sorrowful,
their hearts were content.
Thus, Zhān exemplified
nourishing their will with his own.
From Hán's writings.
Is plumpness in appearance
better than richness in virtue?
Seeking from others,
better than seeking from oneself?
From Sūn Kězhī's writings.
Our dynasty:
When Lord Fù served as envoy to the barbarians,
his achievements were great,
yet he never boasted of them.
While governing Qīngzhōu,
he saved over four hundred thousand from famine,
and often said of this:
"It surpasses serving as Secretariat Director for twenty-four evaluations."
From *Records of Things Seen and Heard*.
If a tiger is hunting a deer,
and a bear seizes its den,
grappling its cubs,
how can the tiger not abandon the deer and return?
From the *Lǎoquán Collection*.
Recently troubled by accumulated ailments,
the doctor said:
"Given the illness,
it should be purged,
and cured in a day.
If not purged,
it will heal in half a month.
But after middle age,
each purge weakens one,
and accumulated weakness
is a lifelong worry."
I considered privately:
not to trade a day's relief
for a lifetime of anxiety.
From the *Dōngpō Collection*.
A child of a wealthy family does not die at the hands of thieves—
why?
Because his life is precious,
and thieves are not worth dying for.
From Dōngpō's "Essay on Liú Hóu."
Ōu Gōng said:
"Writings only adorn the self,
but governance can benefit all."
From the *Zhāng Yúnsǒu Collection*.
Mencius:
Now, kindness sufficient to reach animals,
yet benefits not extending to the people—
why is that alone so?
From *Mencius*, King Huì of Liáng, Part I.
Why honor carpenters and wheelwrights
but slight those who practice benevolence and righteousness?
From *Mencius*, Duke Wén of Téng, Part II.
If a person's chickens or dogs stray,
they know to seek them;
if their heart strays, they do not know to seek it.
From *Mencius*, Gàozi, Part I.
A small tung or catalpa tree,
if one wishes it to live,
all know how to nurture it.
Yet for their own person,
they know not how to nurture it—
is loving oneself less than loving trees?
If a gardener
abandons his fine trees
to nurture thorns,
he is deemed a poor gardener.
Nurturing one finger
while losing the shoulder and back,
unaware of it,
makes one a reckless person.
Both from the same source above.
Unable to observe the three-year mourning,
yet scrutinizing the minor mourning rites;
gobbling food and gulping soup,
yet questioning the lack of teeth-breaking etiquette.
From *Mencius*, Exhausting the Heart, Part I.
Using a Suí pearl
to shoot a sparrow a thousand ren high—
the world will laugh,
for what is used is heavy,
and what is sought is light.
From *Zhuangzi*, Yielding the Throne.
Killing a warhorse to catch a fox,
grasping two turtles but losing a divine tortoise,
severing a right arm to vie for a hair,
breaking a Mòyé sword to fight over an awl.
Using wisdom thus—
is it worthy of praise?
To gain one man and lose a whole state,
to ally with the wicked and abandon the good,
is not good strategy.
． _Zuozhuan, Duke Zhuang 12th Year_.
To exchange a minister of a thousand chariots
for a blind musician of lewd music.
． _Zuozhuan, Duke Xiang 15th Year_.
Earlier,
Chǔ's Zǐ Yù made for himself a jade cap and jade-decked tassels,
but had not yet worn them.
Before the battle,
he dreamed the River God said to him: "Give them to me,
and I will grant you the marshlands of Mèng Zhū."
He did not offer them.
Dà Xīn and Zǐ Xī sent Róng Huáng to remonstrate,
but he would not listen.
Róng Jì said: "If dying could benefit the state,
one might still do it,
how much more so with jade ornaments?
They are but dirt and dust,
yet they can aid the army,
why should you begrudge them?"
He did not listen.
After leaving,
Róng Huáng told the two men: "It is not the god who defeated the Prime Minister;
the Prime Minister failed to diligently serve the people,
and thus brought defeat upon himself."
． _Zuozhuan, Duke Xi 28th Year_.
Neglecting the respect due to elders and kin while honoring the rites for guests,
weakening the affection for flesh and blood while deepening the love for friends,
forgetting the way of self-cultivation while seeking the praise of the masses,
cutting into the livelihood of food and clothing to supply the pleasures of feasts.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Emperor Wu of Hàn_.
Blocking streams and springs to create stagnant ponds.
． _History of Hàn, Treatise on Food and Money_.
Zhào Yī said: "Though one's belly is filled with literary works,
it is not worth a bag of coins."
． _Later Hàn History, His Biography_.
The emperor sent someone to trade horses for pearls, jade, kingfisher feathers, and tortoiseshell with Wú;
the ruler of Wú said: "These are things I have no use for,
yet I can obtain horses with them,
why should I begrudge them?"
He gave them all.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Emperor Ming of Wèi_.
Mutually enters "knowing what is light and what is heavy."
Chuán Zài said: "Not attending to the great spirits of the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
but exclusively currying favor with licentious and deluded ghosts."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Later Chén_.
Dèng Jìngshān had a subordinate general who committed a crime deserving death;
the generals pleaded for him,
but he refused;
his younger brother requested to die in his brother's place,
and he also refused;
they requested to contribute a horse to redeem the crime,
and only then did he agree.
The generals angrily said: "Are we worth less than a horse!"
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Emperor Dàizōng of Táng_.
In our dynasty,
holding a priceless jade disc to seek a clay pot,
how close is it to being discarded into the ditch?
Lǎo Quán.
Classic
The gentleman bows three times before advancing,
and declines once before withdrawing.
． _Record of Rites, Biǎojì_.
If in agreement, advance;
if not in agreement, withdraw.
． _Record of Rites, Rúxíng_.
At a sign of trouble, he rises and flies away,

． _Analects, Xiāngdǎng_.
Serving men with the upright Way,

Serving men with a crooked way,
why must one leave the land of one's parents?
． _Analects, Wēizǐ_.

As for a commoner,
if summoned for labor, he goes to labor;
if the ruler wishes to see him,
he is summoned but does not go to see him.
． _Mencius, Wànzhāng II_.
Three circumstances for taking office,
three for leaving it.
． _Mencius, Gàozǐ II_.
History
When a small state serves a large state,
if it is virtuous,
then it is like a man;
if not virtuous,
then it is like a deer.
． _Zuozhuan, Duke Wén 17th Year_.
The bird chooses the tree,
how can the tree choose the bird?
． _Zuozhuan, Duke Āi 11th Year_.
Fèi Wújí said: "Shē's sons are talented;
if they are in Wú,
they will surely trouble Chǔ;
why not summon them by pardoning their father?
If they are benevolent,
they will surely come.
If not,
they will become a threat."
The king sent to summon them,
saying: "Come,
and I will pardon your father."
Táng Jūn Shàng said to his brother Yuán: "You go to Wú,
I will return to die.
My wisdom falls short,
I can die,
you can seek vengeance.
Hearing the order to pardon our father,
we cannot fail to go;
with kin being killed,
we cannot fail to seek vengeance.
To go to death and save our father is filial;
to weigh merits and act is benevolent;
to choose one's task and go is wise;
to face certain death without avoidance is courageous.
Our father cannot be abandoned,
our name cannot be ruined.
Do your best,
to follow each other is better."
． _Zuozhuan, Duke Zhāo 20th Year_.
Collection
Should I be sincere and earnest,
simple and loyal?
Or should I socialize and entertain,
following the crowd endlessly?
Should I clear weeds and thorns,
and labor in farming?
Or should I court the great,
to make a name?
Should I speak truth without concealment,
and risk my life?
Or should I follow the crowd to wealth and honor,
and live carelessly?
Should I rise aloof and transcendent,
to preserve my true self?
Or should I flatter and fawn,
ingratiating myself,
stammering and stuttering,
to serve women?
Should I be honest and upright,
to keep myself pure?
Or should I be slick and slippery,
following customs,
like grease or leather,
soft and pliable?
Should I be proud and lofty like a thousand-mile steed?
Or should I drift like a duck in water,
rising and falling with the waves,
just to save my skin?
Should I pull the yoke with noble steeds?
Or follow in the tracks of nags?
Should I soar wing to wing with the yellow crane?
Or fight for food with chickens and ducks?
_Chǔcí_.
Circling the tree three times,
which branch can I rely on?
Cáo Cāo "Short Song Style".
A bright pearl is hard to throw in the dark.
Guō Pú "Roaming Immortal Poems".
One must know the world's paths are hard to tread lightly,
it's not that the lord's gate is not wide open.
Dù Mù.

If it is not the right place to go, he does not go;
if it is not the right place to dwell, he does not dwell.
． _Yángzǐ, Learning and Conduct_.
Those who follow Yáo, Shùn, King Wén, and King Wǔ
follow the right way;
those who do not follow Yáo, Shùn, King Wén, and King Wǔ
follow other ways.
． _Yángzǐ, Inquiring about the Way_.
History
If you emulate Bó Gāo and fall short,
you can still be a cautious and diligent man,
as they say, if carving a swan fails, it still resembles a duck.
If you emulate Jì Liáng and fall short,
you risk becoming a frivolous man of the world,
as they say, if drawing a tiger fails, it nearly resembles a dog.
． _Later Hàn History, Biography of Mǎ Yuán_.
Sòng's Yuán Shù wrote a poem: "Plant orchids, avoid the gate;
cherish jade, do not go to Chǔ.
Chǔ has few who discern jade;
the gate is no place to plant orchids."
_Continued Tales of the World_.
Also seen in _History of the Sòng_.
Classical Texts
Like a boat adrift,
knowing not where it shall moor.
． "Xiǎobiàn" from the Book of Songs.
It is like a blind man without a guide,
wandering aimlessly—where can he go?
Just as searching all night in a dark room,
without a torch, what can one see?
． "Zhòngní Yànjū" from the Book of Rites.
Masters
You leave a spacious dwelling unused,
abandon the right path untrodden.
． "Lílóu I" from Mencius.
The man Hé of Chǔ obtained a piece of jade,
and presented it to King Lì;
the king had a jade artisan appraise it,
who said, "It is but a stone."
The king deemed Hé deceitful,
and amputated his left foot.
When it came to King Wǔ,
he presented it again;
the king had a jade artisan appraise it,
who again said, "It is but a stone."
The king again thought it deceitful,
and amputated his right foot.
Hé then embraced the uncut jade and wept at the foot of Mount Chǔ.
Han Feizi.
Cross-reference "Blindly Casting."
Tapping the ground to find the way,
is but walking in darkness.
． "Cultivation of the Self" by Yáng.
To forsake boats and cross a river,
is futile;
to abandon the Five Classics and seek the Way,
is futile.
If one discards common delicacies and craves exotic dishes,
how can they be said to know taste?
If one rejects the great sages and favors the various philosophers,
how can they be said to know the Way?
． "My Child" by Yáng.
Collections
In the past, the King of Qí loved the yú flute;
one seeking office in Qí went there carrying a sè,
and stood at the king's gate for three years without gaining entry.
Hán Yù's "Letter in Reply to Chén Shāng."
Sailing a boat yet not knowing the four directions,
crossing the vast, boundless waters.
Hán Yù's "Rhapsody on Lamenting Oneself."
Cross-reference "Losing One's Support."
Weeping profusely, presenting the jade thrice.
Liú Chángqīng.

Public affairs are not discussed privately.

In the court, women are not spoken of.
Ibid.

Ibid.
A gentleman is ashamed to prepare funeral paraphernalia in advance;

Masters
Mìzǐjiàn served as magistrate of Shànfù.
When the Qí army attacked Lǔ,
their path led through Shànfù.
The elders requested: "Allow the people to go out
and harvest the wheat around the city walls,
to increase our grain supply,
and prevent it from aiding the enemy."
After three requests, Mìzǐjiàn refused,
saying: "If we lose the wheat this year,
we can plant it again next year.
But if we let those who did not farm reap the harvest,
it would make the people delight in having enemies.
The wheat of Shànfù for one year
does not strengthen Lǔ if kept,
nor weaken it if lost.
If we instill in the people a mindset of taking for themselves,
the harm will last for generations."
Family Sayings of Confucius.
Cross-reference "Knowing What Is Important."
As for Master Lǔ,
he can be said to have nurtured his resolve.
． "Lílóu II" from Mencius.
Jìsūn was chancellor of Lǔ.
In the sixth month, a long ditch was dug, and Zǐlù privately provided a meal for the workers.
Confucius overturned the meal and said: "How can the people of Lǔ accept
(alternatively "receive")
this? Why?"
Han Feizi.
Histories
Chǔ Chéng Déchén attacked Chén,
and upon returning after fortifying Dùn,
Zǐwén considered it his achievement,
and appointed him as Lìngyǐn.
Shūbó said: "What will become of the state because of you?"
He replied: "I use this to stabilize the state.
For one who has great achievements but no high office,
how many of such men can remain peaceful?"
. _Zuǒzhuàn, Xī 23rd Year_.
Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng passed away,
and preparations were being made to clear the way for the burial.
There was a house belonging to the tomb official that stood in the path;
if it were demolished,
the burial could be held in the morning;
if not demolished,
it would have to wait until noon.
Zǐtàishū requested to demolish it,
saying: "What about the guests from other states?"
Zǐchǎn said: "If the guests from other states
can come to attend our funeral,
why would they fear waiting until noon?
With no harm to the guests
and no detriment to the people,
why not proceed?"
Thus, it was not demolished,
and the burial was held at noon.
The gentleman commented: "Zǐchǎn understood ritual.
Ritual
does not involve destroying others to achieve one's own ends."
. _Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāo 12th Year_.
Hán Xuānzǐ of Jìn possessed a jade ring,
with its counterpart held by a merchant of Zhèng.
Xuānzǐ appealed to the Duke of Zhèng for it,
but Zǐchǎn refused to give it,
saying: "It is not an artifact guarded by the government,
and our humble ruler is unaware of it."
. _Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāo 16th Year_.
Hán Zhāohóu had a pair of worn trousers,
which he ordered to be stored away.
An attendant said: "Your Majesty is ungenerous.
Instead of bestowing them on your attendants, you store them away!"
Zhāohóu replied: "I have heard that a wise ruler values every frown and smile,
as each expression serves a purpose for me.
Now, are these trousers merely like a frown or a smile?
I must reserve them for someone who has achieved merit."
. _Tōngjiàn, Zhōu Jì_.
The Lord of Pèi arrived in Xiányáng,
and his generals rushed to the treasuries for gold, silk, and valuables,
while Xiāo Hé alone collected the maps and books of Qín.
. _Xīhàn, Xiāo Hé Biography_.
The Emperor ordered Zhōu Chāng to select strong men from Zhào who could be made generals,
and he presented four men.
Each was enfeoffed with a thousand households,
and appointed as generals.
The attendants remonstrated,
but the Emperor said: "This is beyond your understanding.
Chén Xī has rebelled,
and the lands of Zhào and Dài are all under his control.
I have summoned troops from across the land with urgent dispatches,
but none have arrived.
Now, the only troops we can count on are those in Hándān.
Why should I begrudge four thousand households,
if it can comfort the sons of Zhào!"
_Tōngjiàn_.
Cáo Shēn left Qí,
and instructed his successor: "Entrust the markets and prisons to care,
and be careful not to disturb them."
. _Xīhàn, His Biography_.
Emperor Wén asked: "How many legal cases are decided in the empire in a year?
How much money and grain are received and spent annually?"
Chén Píng replied: "There are officials responsible for each."
The Emperor asked: "Who are the responsible officials?"
He said: "If Your Majesty asks about legal cases,
hold the Tíngwèi accountable;
if about money and grain,
hold the Zhìsù Nèishǐ accountable."
. _Xīhàn, Chén Píng Biography_.
Someone presented a thousand-lǐ horse.
The Emperor said: "With ceremonial banners ahead,
and auxiliary carriages behind,
on auspicious journeys we travel fifty lǐ a day,
on military marches thirty lǐ.
If I ride a thousand-lǐ horse,
where would I go alone ahead?"
Thereupon, he returned the horse.
. _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Wén Jì_.
Tián Shū returned from investigating the affair in Liáng,
and upon reaching Bàchāng Stable,
he took a torch and burned all the legal documents concerning Liáng,
then came back empty-handed to see
the Emperor,
who asked: "Is there truth to the Liáng affair?"
He replied: "I deserve death.
There is."
The Emperor asked: "Where is the evidence?"
Tián Shū said: "Your Majesty should not inquire further into the Liáng affair."
The Emperor asked: "Why?"
He said: "If the King of Liáng is not executed,
it means Hàn law is not enforced;
if he is executed, the Empress Dowager will find no flavor in her food,
and no rest in her bed,
and this worry will fall upon Your Majesty."
. _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Jǐng Jì_.
Cross-reference "Handling Matters Appropriately."
His governance focused on non-action,
adhering to the greater principles,
unconstrained by legal formalities.
. _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Wǔ Jì_.
The wise may fail to see some things,
the discerning may fail to hear some things.
. _Xīhàn, Dōngfāng Shuò Biography_.
Féng Fèngshì, as a guard envoy bearing the tally, was sent to escort missions from Dàyuān and other states.
He then used his authority to inform the kings of these states,
mobilized their troops,
advanced south to attack Suōjū,
and captured its city.
All the states were pacified.
The Emperor was very pleased,
and proposed enfeoffing Fèngshì.
Xiāo Wàngzhī believed: "Fèngshì, on his mission,
presumptuously forged orders and disobeyed commands,
raising troops from various states.
Though he achieved success,
this should not set a precedent.
If we enfeoff Fèngshì,
it will open the way for future envoys to cite his example for their gain,
competing to raise troops,
seeking merit from a hundred lǐ away,
and causing troubles for the state among the barbarians.
Such a trend must not be encouraged.
Fèngshì should not be enfeoffed."
. _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Xuān Jì_.
Bǐng Jí served as Chancellor.
The Emperor was magnanimous,
valued courtesy and deference,
and did not involve himself in minor matters.
Contemporaries considered him to understand the greater principles.
Same as above.
Adopting the proposal of Chén Héng,
the Tàizhì altar at Gānquán was abolished.
Liú Xiàng said: "Even common families do not wish to cut off their lineage,
let alone abandon the state's divine treasures and ancient altars!
Moreover, the Gānquán, Fényīn, and the five altars at Yōng were established
only after divine responses were received,
and then they were constructed—
not arbitrarily.
During the reigns of Wǔ and Xuān, these three deities were honored,
with rituals reverently and fully prepared,
and divine radiance was especially evident.
The ancient positions of the deities established by our ancestors
truly should not be lightly altered.
First, we adopted Gòng Yǔ's proposal,
and later generations followed suit,
making many changes.
The _Yì Dàzhuàn_ says: 'Those who deceive the gods bring calamity for three generations.'
I fear the blame will not rest solely on Yǔ and others!"
The Emperor regretted his decision,
and also due to the long absence of an heir,
in winter,
the tenth month,
on the Gēngchén day,
the Emperor reported to the Empress Dowager,
ordering the officials to restore the Gānquán Tàizhì and Fényīn Hòutǔ as before,
along with the five altars at Yōng, the Chénbǎo shrine, and the prominent temples in Cháng'ān and the commanderies.
All were reinstated.
. _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Chéng Jì_.
The intent of a sovereign
is not to pry into the private matters of bedchambers,
nor to listen to gossip from within.
Same as above.
Hé Wǔ served as Regional Inspector,
and if a two-thousand-dàn official committed a crime,
he would report it promptly.
For others, whether worthy or not,
he treated them with equal respect.
Mǎ Yuán was Governor of Lǒngxī,
delegating duties to his subordinates,
while he oversaw the broader picture.
When various officers reported external affairs,

why trouble me with it?
If powerful families oppress the common people,
or cunning clerks disobey orders,
then it is the governor's affair."

Establishing laws and prohibitions
cannot completely block all wickedness in the world,
nor satisfy everyone's desires.
Generally, if they bring more convenience and benefit to the state,
that is sufficient.
. _Dōnghàn, Huán Tán_.
Sòng Jūn said: "Civil officials are accustomed to deceit,

which does not help the people fleeing in exile,
nor the harm caused by bandits."
. _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Míng Jì_.
Zhōu Yǔ of Xiàpī became Magistrate of Luòyáng.
Upon taking office,
he first asked for the names of the great families;

how could they know this vegetable-selling commoner!"
Thereupon, the officials under his command, sensing his intent,

causing the noble relatives to tread cautiously,

From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Hàn Zhāngdì's Annals".
Cross-referenced under "Showing people one's intent" and "Not fearing the powerful".
He focused on the main principles,
simplifying and omitting harsh details.
From "Book of Later Hàn: Xuān Bǐng's Biography".

could be said to be utmost affection,
yet he still allowed Shēntú Jiā to carry out his will.
When one is entrusted like this,
what worry is there about petty officials on the left and right?
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Hàn Shāngdì's Annals".
Zhūgě Liàng once personally checked the account books,
when his secretary Yáng Yóng entered directly
and admonished: "Governing has its proper form,

those who act and implement it

Thus Bǐng Jí did not ask about the dead lying across the road but worried about an ox panting,

personally checks the account books,

From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Wèi Míngdì's Annals".

and replied:

not to be disclosed."
Yáng Fù became angry,
caned the official one hundred strokes,
and rebuked him: "Does the state not share secrets with the nine ministers,

Same as above.
Initially,
during Chancellor Liàng's time,
some said that the Duke was sparing with pardons,
to which Liàng replied: "A well-governed world relies on great virtue,
not on small favors,
hence Kuāng Héng and Wú Hàn were unwilling to issue pardons.

but they never spoke of pardons.

From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government".

which others could not decide,
Shū would slowly plan for them,
often surpassing the collective opinions.
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Wèi Dynasty Annals".

governing with excessive scrutiny?"
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Eastern Jìn Yuándì's Annals".

imperial sacrifices have often been accompanied by pardons,

expecting a pardon with every sacrifice,
will become opportunistic in their hopes!"
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Jìn Mùdì's Annals".
Xiè Ān in governance
emphasized the main principles,
and did not bother with minor details,
so his contemporaries compared him to Wáng Dǎo.
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Jìn Wǔdì's Annals".
Huán Xuán once intended to use Xiè Ān's residence for military quarters,
but Xiè Kūn said: "Even the benevolence of Shào Bó
benefitted the gǎntáng tree;
shall the virtue of Wénjìng
not protect his five-acre estate?"
Huán Xuán, ashamed upon hearing this, desisted.
From "Book of Jìn: Xiè Kūn's Biography".
Xiè Hóngwēi said: "For relatives to quarrel over wealth
is most despicable.
Now that even the women can remain silent,
how can we lead them to dispute?"
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Qí Tàizǔ's Annals".
Wèi Yuánhuái had a tolerant and straightforward nature,
disliking pettiness,
often saying: "Those in high positions should focus on the main principles,
why must they attend to every detail!
It is like building a house:
if it looks tall and impressive from outside,
with beams and pillars straight,
and foundations and walls solid,
that is enough;
if the axe marks are uneven,
or the carving not fine,
it is not a flaw of the house."
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Liáng Gāozǔ's Annals".
Xú Miǎn served as Minister of Personnel.
Once at a night gathering with literary officials,
a guest Yú Gǎo requested a position in the household of the heir apparent,
but Miǎn sternly said: "Tonight we can only discuss the breeze and the moon,
not public affairs."
His contemporaries admired his impartiality.
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Liáng Wǔdì's Annals".
In Wèi, a great drought occurred,
and the Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Xíng Luán memorialized: "The wise kings of old valued grain and cloth,
and despised gold and jade.
Why?
Because grain and cloth nourish the people and secure the state,
while gold and jade are useless and corrupt virtue.
The late Emperor deeply understood extravagance,
and promoted frugality,
to the extent of using paper and silk for curtains and screens,
and copper and iron for bridles and reins;
the gold in the treasury
was only for necessary use,
not hoarded to waste state resources.
By the beginning of the Jǐngmíng era,
inheriting a time of peace,
the four borders were tranquil,
and people from near and far came to submit.
Then tributes arrived in succession,
merchants brought goods in,
and all the offerings
far exceeded the usual,
so gold and jade were often in surplus,
while state funds were often insufficient.
If we do not set limits,
I fear the annual accounts will not balance;
from now on, let us not accept anything that is not essential."
The Emperor of Wèi accepted his advice.
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Liáng Wǔdì's Annals".
Qūtū Tōng went to Lǒngxī to inspect the horse pastures,
and discovered over twenty thousand hidden horses.
The Emperor was furious,
and intended to execute the Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud Mùróng Xìdá and fifteen hundred supervising officials.
Tōng remonstrated: "Human life is most precious,
how can Your Majesty kill over a thousand people for the sake of livestock!
I dare to plead with my life!"
Then he kowtowed and said: "I alone am ready to die,
begging Your Majesty to spare the lives of over a thousand people."
The Emperor was moved and realized,
and Xìdá and others had their sentences commuted from death.
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Suí Gāozǔ's Annals".
Cross-referenced under "Transforming people's minds".
Niú Hóng asked Liú Xuàn: "In the 'Zhōu Lǐ', there are many scholars but few clerks,
yet now the number of clerks is a hundred times more than before,
and reducing them would cause inefficiency;
what is the reason?"
Xuàn replied: "The ancients delegated and held accountable,
assessing performance at year's end,
without rechecking files repeatedly,
and documents were not overly detailed;
the duty of clerks
was to handle key points only.
Nowadays, we constantly worry about re-examining documents,
and if the forging is not严密,
we pursue evidence from thousands of miles away for cases a century old.
Hence the proverb: 'Old clerks die clutching their files.'
Affairs are complex and governance flawed,
and this is the cause.
Reducing officials is not as good as reducing tasks;
if official tasks are not reduced, how can we expect ease?"
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Suí Yángdì's Annals".
Qín Wáng Shìmín, whenever he defeated armies and captured cities,
while his officers competed for treasures,
Xuánlíng alone gathered talented individuals,
and brought them into his headquarters.
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Táng Gāozǔ's Annals".
The Grand Governor of Yìzhōu, Dòu Guǐ, reported that the Lǎo people were rebelling,
and requested troops to suppress them.
The Emperor said:
"The Lǎo rely on the mountains and forests,
occasionally coming out to steal like rats,
which is their custom;
if the local officials can安抚 them with kindness and trust,
they will naturally submit.
How can we lightly mobilize troops,
preying on their people like hunters,
treating them as beasts—is that the intention of being parents to the people?"
In the end, he did not permit it.
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Táng Tàizōng's Annals".
Dù Yān memorialized: "I fear there may be delays or losses in the documents of various offices,
please order the censors to inspect them at the offices."
The Emperor asked Féng Déyí about it,
who replied: "Officials are appointed and duties divided,
Each has their own responsibilities.
If there are indeed faults or transgressions,
the censors should naturally impeach and report them;
if they were to go through all the departments,
searching for flaws and defects,
it would be extremely troublesome and trivial. "
When Princess Chánglè was about to be married,
an edict ordered the officials to provide a dowry twice that of Princess Yongjiā.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying: "In the past, Emperor Ming of Hàn wanted to enfeoff his sons,
and said: 'How can my sons compare with the sons of the late emperor!'
He ordered them all to receive half of what was given to the princes of Chǔ and Huáiyáng.
Now, providing a dowry for the princess
that is double that of the elder princess,
is this not contrary to Emperor Ming's intention?"
Dèng Shìlóng requested to compile the emperor's writings.
The emperor said: "My decrees and speeches,
if they benefit the people,
are all recorded by historians,
which is enough to make them immortal.
If they are of no benefit,
what use is compiling them!
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, his son, Emperor Hòuzhǔ of Chén, and Emperor Yáng of Suí all had literary collections circulated in the world,
yet what did it do to save them from ruin!
A ruler should worry about lacking virtuous governance;
what is the use of literary compositions!"
The emperor said to Fáng Xuánlíng and Dù Rúhuì: "You, as chief ministers,
should broadly seek out worthy men,
appoint them according to their talents,
this is the duty of a chancellor.
Recently, I've heard that you spend your time hearing lawsuits,
with no leisure throughout the day;
how can you assist me in seeking the worthy!"
Thereupon, he decreed: "Minor affairs of the Department of State Affairs shall be handled by the vice directors,
only major matters that should be reported
are to be referred to the chief ministers."
The vice director Wéi Cōng found that the official price of timber from the Court of the Imperial Granaries was higher than the market price,
and reported their embezzlement.
The emperor summoned the chief minister of the Court of Judicial Review, Sūn Fújiā, to record the crimes of the Court of the Imperial Granaries.
In response, he said: "It is precisely because the official timber is expensive
that private timber is cheap.
If the official timber were cheap,
private timber would have no reason to be cheap.
I only see that the Court of the Imperial Granaries understands the greater principle;
I do not see their fault."
Zhāng Chānglíng and Wáng Gōngjǐn were both skilled in writing,
and their fame spread throughout the capital.
The examination official Wáng Shīdàn, who presided over the examinations,
rejected them,
and no one in the court understood the reason.
When the results were reported,
the emperor was surprised not to see their names,
and questioned him.
Shīdàn replied: "Although these two have literary talent,
their style is frivolous,
and they will ultimately not become accomplished individuals.
If they were placed in high ranks,
I fear later scholars would imitate them."
All from the same source above.
Liú Xiǎo submitted a memorial discussing: "The Ministry of Rites selects scholars
solely based on literary compositions for ranking,
thus scholars throughout the land
all abandon virtue and conduct to pursue literary skill.
There are those who pass the top examination in the morning and face punishment by evening;
even if they recite ten thousand words a day,
what does it have to do with the principles of governance!
Composing a poem within seven paces,
is not enough to transform people.
Moreover, devoting one's mind to flowers and trees,
and wielding the brush amidst mists and clouds—
for this to become a custom,
is it not a great error!"
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Táng Gāozǔ_ .
Dài Zhìdé served as right chief minister,
and Liú Rénguǐ as left chief minister.
They took turns daily receiving petitions and lawsuits.
Rénguǐ often granted them with kind words,
while Zhìdé would inevitably question them based on reason,
never making arbitrary decisions.
For those who were truly wronged,
he secretly submitted memorials to argue on their behalf.
Because of this, contemporary praise all went to Rénguǐ.
When someone asked the reason,
Zhìdé said: "The power to reward and punish is the prerogative of the ruler;
how can subjects presume to take it!"
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Táng Gāozōng_ .
Selecting generals should be based on wisdom and strategy as the foundation,
and courage and strength as secondary.
Now, the court's use of people
often chooses sons of military families and those from households of the deceased in service;
they are all mediocre men,
how can they be fit for external commands!
Lǐ Zuǒjū, Chén Tāng, Lǚ Méng, Mèng Guān—
all came from poverty and low status yet achieved extraordinary merits;
we have not heard that their families were generations of generals.
The director of the imperial workshops, Péi Fěishū,
was skilled at profiteering,
and proposed selling horse dung from the imperial gardens,
estimating an annual income of two hundred thousand strings of cash.
The emperor asked Liú Rénguǐ about it,
who replied: "The profit is indeed substantial,
but I fear later generations will say the Táng family sold horse dung,
which is not a good name."
Both from the same source above.
The inspector of the imperial gardens, Péi Fěigōng,
planned to sell vegetables and fruits from the gardens to make a profit.
Sū Liángsì said: "In the past, Gōngyí Xiū served as minister of Lǔ,
he could uproot his melons and dismiss his weavers,
but I have not heard of the lord of ten thousand chariots selling vegetables and fruits."
Thus, it was stopped.
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Táng Wǔhòu_ .
Dí Rénjié served as participating chancellor,
and the Empress Dowager said to Rénjié: "When you were in Rǔnán,
you had very good governance;
do you wish to know the names of those who praised you?"
Rénjié declined, saying:
"If Your Majesty considers me at fault,
I beg to correct it;
if you know I am without fault,
that is my fortune,
and I do not wish to know the names of the praisers."
A ban on slaughter was imposed throughout the land.
The remonstrance official Zhāng Dé,
three days after his son was born,
secretly slaughtered a sheep to feast his colleagues.
The supplementary official Dù Sù took a piece of meat,
and submitted a memorial accusing him.
The next day,
the Empress Dowager, in court audience,
said to Dé: "I heard you have a son,
I am very pleased."
Dé bowed in thanks.
The Empress Dowager said: "Where did you get the meat?"
Dé kowtowed and admitted his crime.
The Empress Dowager said: "I banned slaughter,
but auspicious and inauspicious occasions are exceptions.
However, from now on when you invite guests,
you must also choose your company."
She then showed Sù's memorial to him.
Sù was greatly ashamed,
and the entire court wished to spit in his face.
Liú Zhījī submitted a memorial stating four matters.
The first: "That amnesty decrees are incessant,
recently even twice a year,
and in the past not a year has been missed.
At the new year's court,
they anticipate the emperor's grace,
on the Double Ninth Festival,
they await the imperial pardon.
As they speculate,
all are indeed released.
Some are about to be convicted,
their crimes nearly decided,
but they secretly engage in bribery,
seeking ways to circumvent,
thus causing delays,
until they all receive leniency.
Those who do good do not share in the grace,
while those who do evil alone gain undeserved fortune.
An ancient saying goes: 'The good fortune of petty men
is the misfortune of gentlemen.'
This is what it means."
The Empress Dowager asked the vice minister and participating chancellor Lù Yuánfāng about external affairs,
who replied: "I hold the position of chancellor;
if it is a major matter, I dare not fail to inform you;
trivial matters among the people,
are not worth troubling Your Majesty's attention."
Because of this, he offended her.
Both from the same source above.
Zhū Jìngzé served as chancellor,
prioritizing the use of talent,
and paid no attention to other minor affairs.
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Táng Zhōngzōng_ .
Zōng Chǔkè ordered Yuán Shǒuyī to memorialize, saying: "When Wǔ Zétiān was formerly at Sānyáng Palace and fell ill,
Dí Rénjié requested that Your Majesty oversee the state,
while Yuán Zhōng secretly memorialized that it should not be done."
The emperor said to Yáng Zàisī and others: "In my consideration,
subjects serving their ruler
must be of one mind;
how could it be that upon the ruler's minor illness,
they immediately request the crown prince to take charge!
This was Rénjié seeking to build personal favor,
and I see no fault in Yuán Zhōng.
Shǒuyī wants to use past events to frame Yuán Zhōng;
how can this be allowed?"
Same as above.
Yáng Fú,
impeached and corrected without avoiding the powerful,
and the powerful avoided him.
The emperor said: "When a hawk catches a cunning rabbit,
it must act swiftly to save it,
or else it will be bitten in return.
The censors restraining the wicked are the same.
If the ruler does not protect them,
they too will be bitten by the wicked."
. _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Táng Xuánzōng_ .
The emperor ordered Sòng Jǐng and Sū Tǐng to devise names for the imperial princes and their fief titles,
and also commanded them to create an additional fine name and title to present.
Jǐng and others submitted a memorial saying: "The equal nurturing of seven sons
is recorded in the 'Airs of the States.'
Now, the names we have devised number over thirty,
indiscriminately submitted together,
to manifest Your Majesty's impartial virtue that shelters all without bias."
The Emperor greatly approved of this.
When a major locust plague struck Shāndōng,
Lú Huáishèn believed that killing too many locusts
might disrupt the harmony of nature.
Yáo Chóng said:
"In the past, King Zhuāng of Chǔ swallowed a leech and recovered from illness;
Sūnshū Áo killed a snake and obtained blessings.
How can we bear to spare locusts
yet tolerate people starving to death?
If there is calamity for killing locusts,
I request to bear it."
The Empress's brother-in-law, Imperial Wardrobe Attendant Zhǎngsūn Xīn, held a minor grudge against Censor-in-chief Lǐ Jié.
Xīn and his brother-in-law Yáng Xiānyù waylaid Jié in an alley and beat him.
Jié submitted a memorial,
and the Emperor was enraged,
ordering Xīn to be caned to death at the court assembly hall,
to apologize to the officials,
and sending a letter to comfort Jié.
Mutually entered "dedication to public duty over personal interests."
The Emperor wished to appoint Niú Xiānkè as a Minister,
but Zhāng Jiǔlíng said: "It cannot be."
Lǐ Línfǔ told the Emperor:
"Xiānkè has the talent of a chancellor;
what issue is there with him being a Minister?
Jiǔlíng is a bookish scholar
who does not grasp the greater picture."
The Emperor was pleased.
The next day,
the Emperor said: "Do you disdain Xiānkè for his humble origins?
What noble lineage do you yourself have?"
Jiǔlíng replied: "I am but a lowly orphan from Lǐnghǎi,
not like Xiānkè born in the Central Plains.
However, I have served in the central institutions,
managing imperial edicts for years.
Xiānkè is a minor official from the border regions,
illiterate,
and if given great responsibility,
I fear he may not meet public expectations."
When the former Governor of Guǎngzhōu, Péi Zhòuxiān, was imprisoned,
the Emperor discussed his punishment with the chancellors.
Zhāng Jiāzhēn requested caning,
but Zhāng Yuè said: "I have heard that punishments do not extend to high officials,
because they are close to the ruler
and to cultivate their sense of honor.
Thus, a scholar may be killed but not humiliated.
When I previously inspected the northern border,
I heard of Jiāng Jiǎo being caned in the court assembly hall.
Jiǎo had reached the third rank,
and had minor achievements;
if his crime deserved death, he should die,
if exile, then be exiled.
How can we lightly add the shame of caning,
treating him like a menial?
What's done cannot be undone,
but Zhòuxiān's case warrants exile according to the facts;
how can we repeat past mistakes!"
The Emperor deeply agreed.
The Emperor once casually spoke with Lǐ Mì about Lǐ Línfǔ,
wishing to order generals to capture Cháng'ān,
exhume his tomb,
and scatter his ashes.
Mì said: "Your Majesty has just stabilized the empire;
why仇仇 the dead?
What does those dry bones know?
It only shows a lack of magnanimity in your sage virtue."
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Táng Sùzōng".
The Emperor also said to Lǐ Mì: "Liangdi's grandmother
was the sister of Empress Zhāochéng,
remembered by the Retired Emperor.
I wish to install her as Empress
to comfort the Retired Emperor's heart."
Mì replied: "We should await the Retired Emperor's command,
it will only be a matter of months."
The Emperor complied.
Wáng Qùróng killed his county magistrate out of personal enmity
and deserved death.
The Emperor, because of his skill with catapults,
spared him.
The Secretariat Drafter Jiǎ Zhì did not immediately issue the decree,
instead submitting a memorial,
arguing: "Qùróng acted without principle,
killing his county's ruler.
If one skill with catapults can exempt from capital punishment,
now in the armies, those with peerless skills
are numerous.
They will surely rely on their abilities
to defy authority everywhere;
how then can we stop them?
If we spare one Qùróng for his talent,
we will inevitably have to kill ten others like him;
would that not cause more harm?"
Also from the same source.
Péi Xū came to report affairs,
and the Emperor asked: "The profit from the liquor monopoly,
how much is the annual income?"
Xū did not answer for a long time.
The Emperor asked again,
and he replied: "I came from Hédōng,
and along the way saw beans and grains not yet planted,
farmers full of sorrow and complaint.
I thought Your Majesty summoned me
to first inquire about people's hardships,
yet you press me on profits;
hence I dared not respond."
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Táng Dàizōng".
The Capital Governor Lí Gàn reported that autumn rains damaged crops,
but Hán Huàng reported that Gàn's account was untrue.
The Wèinán County Magistrate Liú Zǎo, currying favor with the Finance Commission,
claimed no damage in his county.
The Emperor said: "The rain was widespread;
how could Wèinán alone be spared?"
He ordered a censor to inspect,
and over three thousand qǐng were found damaged.
Dàizōng sighed long,
saying: "A county magistrate,
an official who nurtures the people,
should report damage even if there is none;
how can he be so unkind!"
If not foolish and deaf,
one cannot be the family elder;
the private words of children in their chambers,
are not worth listening to.
Zhū Cǐ presented a cat and mouse nursing together without harm as an auspicious sign,
and Cháng Gǔn led officials in congratulations.
Only the Secretariat Drafter Cuī Yòufǔ did not congratulate,
saying: "When things defy nature, it is an omen.
A cat catching mice
is its duty;
now they nurse together,
it is an omen.
Why congratulate?"
Also from the same source.
When Dàizōng's funeral procession was to depart,
the Emperor saw
the hearse was not on the main path,
slightly off to the side,
and asked why.
The officials replied:
"Your Majesty's birth branch is at wǔ;
we dare not oppose it."
The Emperor wept: "How can we divert the spirit carriage for personal benefit!"
He ordered it straightened to head directly through wǔ.
From "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government: Táng Dézōng".
Heaven does not cease growth because the earth has bad trees,
nor should the Son of Heaven cease listening because there are petty men.
For one person's hearing and sight to exhaust all changes in the universe,
for one person's vigilance to overcome the treachery of millions,
the more refined the use of wisdom,
the farther one strays from the Way.
Xiàng Jí accepted the surrender of two hundred thousand Qín troops,
but fearing their deceit and rebellion,
had them all buried alive in one move.
In terms of precaution,
it was excessive.
Hàn Gāozǔ, open-minded and magnanimous,
welcomed all scholars under heaven,
employing them without suspicion.
His preparedness might be called lax,
yet Xiàng's house perished,
while Liú's thrived.
Hoarding suspicion versus extending trust—
their outcomes surely differ.
Qín Shǐhuáng was stern, majestic, and deeply suspicious,
yet Jīng Kē pursued his secret plot;
Guāngwǔ was tolerant and broad-minded,
and Mǎ Yuán offered his sincere loyalty.
Is it not because treating others with an open heart
makes them wish to attach;
employing schemes to control things,
things ultimately do not draw close?
When feelings wish to attach, they are moved and pleased,
even enemies can transform into trusted aides;
when intentions are not close, they fear and resist,
even kin can become foes.
Intelligence surpassing all things
breeds contempt for ministers;
thoughts encompassing myriad duties
fosters the idea of ruling the realm alone;
schemes to swallow all strategies
lead to excessive caution in defense;
clarity illuminating all sentiments
brings foresight before events;
strict control over all officials
establishes a pattern of relying on punishment;
awe commanding the four quarters
embodies the will to conquer cruelty by force.
Liú Cóngyī visited Xiāo Fù, saying:
"Qīnxù conveyed the decree,
ordering me to discuss with you the matter mentioned this morning,
then memorialize for implementation,
without letting Lǐ and Lú know."
Fù said: "If Lǐ and Lú are unfit as chancellors,
then dismiss them.
But since they are in office,
how can we not consult them?"
Lǐ Mì said: "The duty of chancellor
cannot be divided.
It is not like the case of reviewing officials where there are oversights in personnel or military matters, or where dra
The Son of Heaven does not inquire whether the feudal lords possess wealth or not,
does not speak of how many chariot households there are,
and does not keep ministers who amass wealth through extortion.
From the writings of Lù Xuān Gōng.
The reason why people of old covered the broken cap tassel and drank with the horse thief
was not necessarily because they forgot their personal feelings,
but because they understood the proper way of being a ruler!
Same as above.
A good physician
does not look at whether a person is thin or fat,
but examines whether their pulse is healthy or not;
a good strategist for the world
does not look at whether the world is safe or in danger,
but examines its legal and social order.
Therefore, even if the four limbs are unharmed,
they cannot be relied upon;
it is the pulse that matters;
even if all under heaven is peaceful,
it is not something to be proud of;
it is the legal and social order that matters.
From the writings of Hán Wén.
With will as nourishment,
what need is there for cattle and sheep?
Duke of Zhōu composed poems without avoiding taboos,
Confucius did not avoid using both characters of a two-character name,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals did not criticize avoiding homophones.
The grandson of King Kāng Zhāo was indeed King Zhāo.
Zēng Shēn's father was named Xī,
yet Zēng Zǐ did not avoid the word "xī" (past).
During the Zhōu dynasty, there was Qí Qī,
and during the Hàn dynasty, there was Dù Dù;
how should their sons avoid these names?
If they avoid homophones,
would they then avoid their surnames as well?
Or would they not avoid homophones?
The Hàn dynasty avoided Emperor Wǔ's name "Chè" by using "Tōng" instead.
But we have not heard that they avoided the character "zhé" in "chē zhé" (wheel rut) by replacing it with another character.
They avoided Empress Lǚ's name "Zhì" by using "yě jī" (wild chicken),
but we have not heard that they avoided the character "zhì" in "zhì tiānxià" (governing the world) by replacing it with another character.
Nowadays, in memorials and edicts, we do not hear of avoiding "hǔ," "shì," "bǐng," or "jī,"
only eunuchs and palace maids dare not mention "yù" and "jī,"
considering it an offense.
When scholars and gentlemen establish their words and conduct,
what should they adhere to?
In serving parents, if one can be like Zēng Shēn,
they can be considered filial;
in conduct, if one can be like the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius,
they can be considered to have reached the pinnacle.
Scholars of today
do not strive to emulate the conduct of Zēng Shēn, the Duke of Zhōu, and Confucius,
but in avoiding their parents' names,
they strive to surpass Zēng Shēn, the Duke of Zhōu, and Confucius.
This shows their confusion!
Since the Duke of Zhōu, Confucius, and Zēng Shēn cannot be surpassed,
to surpass them in this regard
is to compare oneself to eunuchs.
Does this mean that the filial piety of eunuchs and palace maids towards their parents
is superior to that of the Duke of Zhōu, Confucius, and Zēng Shēn?
Same as above.
In our dynasty,
when Rénzōng first appointed Yīngzōng as crown prince,
he ordered the Secretariat to summon an academician to draft the edict.
Academician Wáng Guī was on duty,
and when summoned to the Secretariat and instructed,
Wáng said, "This is a major matter;
I must receive the imperial decree in person."
Thereupon, he requested an audience.
The next day, he reported in person,
received the decree,
and then drafted the edict.
All the officials considered Wáng to truly understand the role of an academician.
From the Collected Works of Ōu Gōng.
Yǐn Shī Lǔ,
in all matters, if there was something small yet worthy of compassion,
he would always show a pained expression, unable to bear it;
but when facing major principles,
and deciding important matters,
he would be as firm as metal or stone,
even if cauldrons and boiling oil were before him,
he would not waver.
From Ōu Gōng's "Epitaph."
Cross-referenced with "Brave in Big Matters, Timid in Small Ones."
Court discussion: officials who reach seventy years of age but do not retire
should be dealt with by the relevant authorities according to the records.
Hú Sù believed that to nurture integrity and shame,
and to enrich customs,
there should be a gradual process,
and to handle everything according to bureaucratic discussion
is hardly the way to honor the elderly and encourage merit.
The matter should be slightly delayed,
allowing people to speak for themselves and preserve their good reputation.
From Ōu Gōng's "Epitaph for Hú Sù."
When Chén Zhízhōng was chancellor,
Fàn Shǔ Gōng once criticized him for lacking learning and being unfit for the role of chancellor.
Later, when Chén Zhízhōng's
favorite concubine
beat a maid to death,
the censor impeached him, seeking his removal.
Fàn said, "Now yin and yang are not in harmony,
wealth is scarce, the people are distressed,
bandits run rampant,
and prisons are full;
Chén Zhízhōng should bear the blame for these.
Private matters within the household
are not what a chancellor should be held accountable for."
Those with understanding agreed with him.
From the Epitaph of Fàn Zhèn.
Ōuyáng Xiū, Yú Jìng, Cài Xiāng, and Wáng Sù wanted to recommend Shí Jiè,
but Fàn Wénzhèng Gōng said, "If Shí Jiè becomes a remonstrance official,
he will surely hold the ruler accountable for impossible tasks,
and if his will is slightly opposed, he will pull at robes, break thresholds,
kowtow until bleeding,
and stop at nothing.
Our sovereign is without fault,
and governance is well-maintained;
what need is there for such a remonstrance official?"
The others were convinced by his words.
From the "Dōngxuān Notes."
When Hán Wèi Gōng was chancellor,
Zēng Gōng was vice-chancellor,
and Zhào Kāngjìng and Ōuyáng Gōng were participating in governance.
For matters related to government decrees, they would say, "Ask the Jíxián Institute;"
for matters of precedent, "Ask the East Hall;"
for literary matters, "Ask the West Hall;"
but for major affairs, they would decide themselves.
People considered this the proper way of a chancellor.
From the "History of Dust."
Someone wanted to buy the Lǜyě Hall for Fàn Xīwén,
but Fàn Xīwén refused,
saying, "In the Táng dynasty, someone like Jìn Gōng
is worthy of respect.
To take his possessions for myself
— how could I be at peace?
I would rather let it be farmed to ruin or let someone else capable acquire it;
I cannot take it myself."
From the "Records of Words and Deeds."
The sun and moon traverse the sky,
broadly able to cover the four seas,
yet narrowly may not enter under a single roof;
they certainly have no use for such trivial, small brightness.
From Lǎo Quán.
In the past, when Xiè Ān defeated Fú Jiān,
the report arrived,
but Xiè Ān continued playing go with his guest without stopping,
