Zhào Bāo's mother, wife, and children were taken hostage,
used to attack the commandery.
Zhào Bāo led twenty thousand cavalry to face the bandits in battle formation;
the bandits presented his mother to him;
Zhào Bāo wept in grief,
saying to his mother: "As a son, I have failed in my duties;
I wished to support you with my humble salary day and night,
never expecting to bring disaster upon you.
Once a son to you,
now I am a subject of the king;
duty forbids me to prioritize personal affection,
to ruin loyalty and integrity.
I can only face death ten thousand times,
with no way to atone for my crime."
His mother and wife were both killed.
After burying them,
Zhào Bāo told his fellow villagers: "To evade hardship while receiving official salary
is not loyalty;
to cause my mother's death to uphold righteousness
is not filial piety.
How can I face the world after this!"
He then vomited blood and died.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Annals of Hàn Língdì."
Qiáo Xuán had a grudge against Chén Lín;
yet when in high office,
he recommended Chén Lín as Commandant of Justice.
"Later Han Dynasty."
A nobleman in office does not act for himself; in duty, his thoughts know no worry.
. "Biography of Zhāng Shēng from the Eastern Han Literary Circle."
Sū Zhāng was promoted to Governor of Jìzhōu.
An old friend of his was Governor of Qīnghé,
and Sū Zhāng, while on inspection, investigated his corruption.
He then invited the Governor,
set out wine and food,
and reminisced about their lifelong friendship joyfully.
The Governor happily said: "Everyone has one heaven,
but I alone have two."
Sū Zhāng said: "Tonight, Sū Rúwén drinks with an old friend—
that is personal affection;
tomorrow, the Governor of Jìzhōu investigates matters—
that is public law."
He then exposed and rectified his crime.
. "Biography from the Eastern Han Dynasty."
Cross-referenced in "Balancing Public and Private."
Whenever Zhūgě Jǐn was sent as an envoy to Shǔ,
he and his brother Liàng only met at official gatherings,
with no private meetings afterward.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Annals of Hàn Xiàndì."
Dǒng Xún said: "I have heard that upright men of old
spoke their minds fully for the state,
undeterred by death;
thus, Zhōu Chāng compared Gāozǔ to Jié and Zhòu,
and Liú Fǔ likened Empress Zhào to a servant girl.
Heaven endows loyalty and integrity;
even facing blades and boiling water,
they press on without looking back,
truly out of concern for their ruler and the realm.
I am but a single hair on an ox;
alive, I bring no benefit,
dead, what loss is there!"
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Annals of Wèi Míngdì."
Lǐ Xǐ, while serving at court,
shared clothing and meals
with relatives and old friends,
yet never privately secured official posts for them.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Annals of Jìn Shìzǔ."
The Dí tribesman Qí Wànnián rebelled;
court officials resented Zhōu Chǔ for his strong integrity,
assigning him under Xiàhóu Jùn for the western campaign.
Sūn Xiù advised him: "You have an elderly mother;
you can use this as an excuse to decline."
Zhōu Chǔ said: "The paths of loyalty and filial piety—
how can both be fulfilled!
Having left my parents to serve the ruler,
how can I still act as a son to them?"
. "Book of Jìn, Biography of Zhōu Chǔ."
Hé Chōng selected and appointed officials based on merit,
showing no favoritism to relatives or friends.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Annals of Jìn Mùdì."
When Wáng Tǎnzhī was dying,
he wrote to Xiè Ān and Bó Chōng in his final moments,
concerned only with state affairs,
with no mention of personal matters.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Annals of Jìn Wéndì."
After Qiè Chāo's death,
his father Qiè Yīn grieved until he fell ill;
a disciple presented
secret correspondences with Bó Wēn.
Qiè Yīn then angrily said: "That brat deserved to die sooner!"
and ceased mourning.
. "Book of Jìn, Main Biography."
Wáng Wéndù spoke without involving personal matters.
"Book of Jìn."
Yuánní Xū, a general of Huáishuò Garrison in Wèi, was an old friend of Yuán Huái;
he was corrupt and disgraced,
and hosted a banquet for Yuán Huái,
saying: "My life's length
rests on your words;
surely you can show some leniency!"
Yuán Huái replied: "Today, Yuán Huái drinks with an old friend—
this is not a court of law.
Tomorrow, the public hall will be where the envoy examines the general's crimes."
Yuánní Xū wept, with no retort,
and was tried and punished for his offenses.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Annals of Liáng Wǔdì."
Cross-referenced in "Balancing Public and Private."
Cuī Kǎi of Wèi served as Governor of Yīnzhōu.
Some advised him to leave his family behind
and go to his post alone;
Cuī Kǎi said: "I have heard that those who eat another's food share their worries;
if I go alone,
which officer or soldier would stay resolute?"
So he moved his entire family to his post.
When Gě Róng besieged the city,
Cuī Kǎi encouraged the troops to resist;
all fought zealously,
saying: "Lord Cuī does not spare his hundred-strong family;
why should we cherish our single lives!"
They battled incessantly,
with corpses piling up,
yet none betrayed their resolve.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Annals of Liáng Gāozǔ."
Qūtū Tóng followed the campaign against Wáng Shìchōng.
At that time, his two sons were in Luòyáng;
the Emperor said: "Now I entrust the eastern campaign to you,
what of your two sons?"
Qūtū Tóng replied: "I am old,
and unworthy of such a heavy responsibility.
But in the past, Your Majesty released this captive,
bestowing grace and courtesy,
granting me a new life;
then I vowed with heart and mouth
to repay the state with my death.
On this campaign,
I should lead the vanguard;
if my sons die, it is their fate,
I will never let personal matters harm righteousness."
. "New Book of Táng, Biography of Qūtū Tóng."
In office, he was strict and upright; those who broke the law,
even if relatives, received no leniency.
Same as above.
The Emperor entrusted all military supplies, equipment, and records to Cén Wénběn;
he worked diligently day and night,
personally allocating resources, never putting down his pen,
until his spirit was exhausted,
and his speech and actions
differed greatly from usual.
The Emperor saw this and worried,
telling his attendants: "Wénběn came with me,
but I fear he may not return with me."
That day,
he succumbed to a sudden illness and passed away.
. "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Táng Tàizōng."
Wáng Yìfāng impeached Lǐ Yìfǔ.
Lǐ Yìfǔ said to him: "Academician Wáng became a Censor
through my recommendation.
In this matter today,
do you feel no shame?"
He replied: "The righteous path serves the public interest,
not private interests."
Book of Tang.
While Zhāng Yìzhī and Zhāng Chāngzōng held power in the court,
Bǎi Yànfàn plotted to eliminate them.
Yànfàn informed his mother of the matter,
to which she said: "Loyalty and filial piety cannot be fully achieved together,
it is acceptable to prioritize the state over the family."
Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Emperor Zhongzong of Tang.
When Empress Dowager was moved to Shàngyáng Palace,
Yáo Yuánzhī alone wept with sobs,
saying: "My previous actions in following you to eliminate treacherous rebels,
were the duty of a subject;
today's parting with the former sovereign,
is also the duty of a subject.
Even if I incur punishment,
I am truly content."
Ibid.
A true man should dare to speak out,
must open his eyes wide and summon courage to repay the Son of Heaven,
how can he muddle along merely to protect his wife and children?
Book of Tang, Biography of Wéi Sīqiān.
Sincerely straightforward and outspoken,
not favoring personal connections.
Book of Tang, Biography of Sòng Jǐng.
The empress's brother-in-law, Fèngyù Chángsūn Xīn, had a minor dispute with Censor-in-chief Lǐ Jié.
Xīn and his own brother-in-law Yáng Xiānyù waited for Jié in an alley and beat him.
Jié submitted a memorial,
the emperor was greatly angered,
ordered him to be caned to death at the court assembly,
to apologize to all officials.
Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Emperor Xuanzong of Tang.
Cross-referenced in "Profound Understanding of the Greater Good".
Lǐ Guózhēn governed the army strictly,
the officers and soldiers of Shuòfāng were discontent,
all missing Guō Zǐyí,
so Wáng Yuánzhèn started a rebellion for them.
When Zǐyí arrived at the army,
Yuánzhèn considered himself meritorious,
but Zǐyí said: "You were facing enemy territory,
yet you killed your commanding officer;
if the enemy had exploited this rift,
Jiàngzhōu would have been lost.
As the chancellor,
how could I accept the private interests of a single soldier!"
He arrested Yuánzhèn and forty accomplices,
and executed them all.
Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Emperor Daizong of Tang.
Guō Zǐyí prohibited riding horses without reason in the army.
The son of the wet nurse of his wife, the Lady of Nányáng, violated the ban,
and the capital rectifier caned him to death.
Zǐyí's sons tearfully complained to him,
speaking of the capital rectifier's tyranny,
but Zǐyí scolded and sent them away.
The next day,
he told his subordinates about the matter and sighed: "All my sons
are nothing but servant material.
They don't commend their father's capital rectifier but mourn their mother's wet nurse's son—
if not servant material, what are they!"
Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Tang Annals.
Lǐ Shèng said: "I am fortunate to hold the positions of general and chancellor;
if I remain silent to preserve myself,
how can I claim to confront wrongdoing without concealment?"
Book of Tang, His Biography.
Cuī Yòufǔ had not been chancellor for a year,
yet he appointed nearly eight hundred officials,
mostly considered appropriate.
The emperor said: "Some criticize that the officials you appoint
often involve relatives and old friends,
why is that?"
Yòufǔ replied: "Proposing appointments requires knowing their talents and conduct.
If I am acquainted with them,
I can roughly assess;
if I have never heard of them,
how can I know their words and deeds?
The reason for the criticism
lies precisely in this."
Old Book of Tang, His Biography.
Cross-referenced in "Unconstrained by Formalities".
Duke Jìn of Péi left no last words concerning family matters.
Book of Tang.
Lǐ Yíjiǎn impeached Yáng Píng,
who was demoted to Línhè Commandant.
No relatives or friends dared to see him off,
but Xú Huì alone went to Lántián to bid farewell.
Quán Déyù asked him: "Won't this implicate you?"
He replied: "Since my humble days,
I have been recognized and encouraged by Lord Yáng;
now that he is exiled far away,
how can I not bid him farewell?"
A few days later,
Yíjiǎn recommended him as Investigating Censor.
Huì thanked him: "I have never had the honor of meeting you,
how did you come to select me!"
Yíjiǎn said:
"You did not betray Yáng Línhè,
how would you betray the state!"
Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Emperor Xianzong of Tang.
Cross-referenced in "Judging People by Their Actions".
Péi Jì was dignified and stern,
no one dared to approach him for private favors.
Once an old friend visited from afar,
Jì provided generous support,
and conversed cordially.
The person seized the opportunity to request the position of a judge in the capital,
but Jì said: "Your talent does not suit this post,
I dare not harm the court's utmost impartiality for a friend's private sake.
If someday a blind chancellor pities you,
you might obtain it,
but from me, it is impossible."
Ibid.
Lǐ Gùyán recommended Cuī Qiú as Court Diarist,
but Zhèng Tán repeatedly objected,
saying: "Do not oppose me in official matters!"
Tán said: "If all chancellors always agree,
then surely some are deceiving Your Majesty!"
Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Emperor Wenzong of Tang.
Lǐ Déyù appointed Liǔ Zhòngyǐng as Governor of the Capital.
Zhòngyǐng had long been friendly with Niú Sēngrú,
and thanked Déyù: "I never expected the Grand Commandant's favor and encouragement to reach this extent;
to repay your kindness,
I dare not differ from the disciples of Duke Qízhāng."
Déyù did not take offense.
Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Emperor Wuzong of Tang.
Gāo Jìchāng sent Chief Commander Ní Kěfú with ten thousand soldiers to repair the outer walls of Jiānglíng,
Jìchāng inspected the work,
rebuked the slow progress,
and caned him.
Jìchāng's daughter was married to Kěfú's son, Zhījìn,
Jìchāng told his daughter: "Go tell your father-in-law: I only intended to assert authority to get things done."
He gave him several hundred taels of white silver.
Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Emperor Jun of Later Liang.
Cross-referenced in "Serving Both Public and Private Interests".
Liú Rénshàn's youngest son, Chóngjiàn, tried to cross the Huái River north by boat at night,
but was captured by a junior officer,
Rénshàn ordered him cut in half at the waist.
Zhōu Tínggòu pleaded with the lady for mercy,
the lady said: "It's not that I don't love Chóngjiàn,
but military law cannot be bent for private feelings,
and integrity must not be compromised.
If we pardon him,
the Liú family would become disloyal,
how could I and you face the officers and soldiers!"
She ordered the execution,
and then held the funeral.
Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou.
Biographies
Duke Wén of Jìn asked Jiù Fàn,
who could be Governor of Xīhé,
he replied: "Zǐgāo."
The Duke said: "Is he not your enemy?"
Fàn said: "You asked who should govern,
not who my enemy is."
When Zǐgāo met him to thank him,
Jiù Fàn said: "Recommending you was a public matter;
I will not let private affairs harm public duty."
Garden of Stories.
Xǔ Yǔn was Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and often appointed his fellow villagers.
Emperor Míng of Wèi sent imperial guards to arrest him,
Yǔn said: "These villagers of mine,
I know them well."
New Account of the Tales of the World.
Cross-referenced in "Local Ties".
Yàn Liáng Chēn was sent as envoy to Qín,
his cousin Yì,
was previously a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat in Qín,
when the mission ended,
the King of Qín wanted Chēn to stay at Yì's residence,
Chēn told the officials: "Previously, the Zhūgě brothers served in three different states,
and when they met on missions,
they saw each other at court,
but never privately afterward.
Yì repeatedly came to the guesthouse,
to inquire about conditions in the eastern state,
Chēn said:
"Now the three powers stand like a tripod,
we brothers both enjoy favor,
our loyalties lie in different places,
if I were to speak of eastern state affairs to you,
I fear it is not what the western state wishes to hear,
why do you ask?"
Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms.
Marquess Wén of Wèi asked Xiè Hú: "I wish to appoint a Governor for Xīhé,
who should I use?"
He replied: "Jīng Bóliǔ is a worthy man."
The Marquess said:
"Is he not your enemy?"
He replied: "You asked about the governorship,
not about my enemy."
When Bóliǔ met Xiè Hú to thank him,
Hú said: "Recommending you was public;
resenting you is private."
Han Ying's Commentary on the Book of Songs.
Collection
Throwing oneself into the fray of blades and spears,
How can one cling to concerns for life?
Parents are set aside without regard,
Let alone speaking of children and wife.
Enrolled in the roster of valiant warriors,
One must not dwell on private affairs.
Sacrificing life to answer the nation's crisis,
Death is regarded as a homeward stride.
． From "Selecting a White Horse".
A man vows to dedicate himself to the state,
What room remains for resentment or regret?
From Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Knowing to serve the ruler with principle,
One does not fear martyrdom;
Admiring to act in office with integrity,
One does not seek personal gain.
From Hán Yù's writings.
Confucius' mat had no time to warm,
Mòzǐ's chimney never turned black.
Wishing to rid the sage court of malpractices,
How could I, in old age, cling to my remaining years?
Both from Hán Yù's writings.
An ant's life is very light,
The state's plans are profoundly weighty.
From "The Collected Works of Bái Jūyì".
Not enriching oneself but enriching the ruler,
Not prospering the family but prospering the state.
From "Táng Wén Cuì".
State affairs demand utmost loyalty,
Family wealth is not hoarded for descendants.
From "The Collected Works of Luó Yǐn".
In our dynasty,
Duke Wèi of Hán delighted in employing renowned scholars,
Sometimes without having met them;
Once appointed,
The individuals did not know who had recommended them.
From a biographical account.
When Fù Bì was sent as envoy to the Qìdān, upon receiving the order he learned of a daughter's death,
Upon a second assignment, he heard of a son's birth,
Yet he proceeded without turning back;
Receiving a letter from home,
He burned it unopened.
From "The Spirit Path Stele".
When Kǒng Dàofǔ died,
A guest said to the duke, "He was your adversary."
The duke replied gravely, "Lord Kǒng spoke out of duty,
How could he be my foe?
It's a pity the court has lost an upright minister."
Thereafter, the speaker felt lifelong shame.
From Ōu Yángxiū's "Inscription for Wáng Déyòng".
While Fàn Zhōngxuān served as chancellor,
Whenever recommending talents,
He always followed public consensus;
Those recommended never knew it came from him,
And he never showed favor to anyone.
From "Records of Words and Deeds over Three Reigns".
Cross-referenced under "Avoiding Fame".
Zhāng Zhībái told his colleagues, "We, as scholars,
Have reached these positions;
Only by upholding public duty over self-interest
Can we repay the state."
From "Gleanings from the Sagely Sòng".
Classic
Seeking profit without regard for one's ruler
Shows benevolence unworthy of praise.
． From "Record of Tángōng Part Two".
Master
A hundred schemes for their families, not one for the state;
Ten visits to private doors,
But not one to the court.
． From "Guǎnzǐ's Chapter on Clear Laws".
Frequent visits to influential men's doors,
But not once to the sovereign's court;
A hundred considerations for private convenience,
Not one plan for the ruler's state.
． From "Hán Fēi's On Standards".
History
Zhào Chōngguó said: "All of you manipulate documents for self-preservation,
rather than loyally planning for the state."
From "Biography of Zhào Chōngguó in the History of Western Hàn."
Though Zhāng Yǔ resided at home,
as a Special Advance minister he served as the emperor's teacher.
Whenever the state had major policies,
he was always consulted to decide them.
At the time, many officials and commoners submitted memorials discussing the responses to calamities and anomalies,
criticizing that they were caused by the Wáng clan's monopolization of power.
The emperor agreed with this view,
but had no clear evidence.
So he went to Zhāng Yǔ's residence,
dismissed his attendants,
and personally asked Zhāng Yǔ about the celestial changes,
then showed him what the officials and commoners had said about the Wáng clan.
Zhāng Yǔ, seeing himself old,
his sons and grandsons weak,
and having conflicts with the Marquis of Qūyáng,
feared incurring resentment.
Thus he told the emperor: "Young students of new learning
confuse the way and mislead people;
they should not be trusted.
Decide matters based on classical teachings."
The emperor deeply trusted and favored Zhāng Yǔ,
and from then on did not suspect the Wáng clan.
From "Comprehensive Mirror in the Reign of Emperor Chéng of Hàn."
Cross-referenced under "Ingratiation."
Gǔ Yǒng submitted over forty memorials in total,
solely attacking the emperor's person and the inner palace,
while allying himself with the Wáng clan.
The emperor knew this,
but did not closely trust him.
From "Biography of Gǔ Yǒng in the History of Western Hàn."
Xún Yuè said: "Private affairs outnumber official duties."
From "Comprehensive Mirror of Western Hàn."
Though Wáng Yǎn held the important position of chancellor,
he did not concern himself with state affairs but thought of plans for self-preservation.
He appointed his younger brother Chéng as Inspector of Jīngzhōu
and another younger brother Dūn as Inspector of Qīngzhōu.
Then he told Chéng and Dūn: "With you two outside,
and me remaining here,
we have enough to form three burrows."
From "Biography of Wáng Yǎn in the History of Jìn."
Lǐ Línfǔ wanted to block military governors from becoming chancellors.
Since the Hu people were illiterate,
he memorialized: "Civil officials as generals
fear arrows and stones;
it's better to use Hu people from humble clans.
Hu people are brave, decisive, and skilled in war;
those from humble clans are isolated and have no factions.
If Your Majesty truly wins their hearts with kindness,
they will surely give their lives for the court."
The emperor was pleased with his words
and began employing Ān Lùshān.
This led to replacing all regional military governors with Hu people,
stationing elite troops in the northern border,
causing an imbalance in the empire's power distribution,
which eventually allowed Lùshān to overthrow the empire,
all stemming from Lǐ Línfǔ's schemes to monopolize favor and secure his position.
From "Comprehensive Mirror in the Táng Annals."
Lǐ Kuí, Minister of Rites, was appointed as envoy to the Tǔbō for a covenant meeting.
Kuí had talent and reputation,
which Lú Qǐ resented,
so he sent him to the Tǔbō.
The emperor said: "Isn't Kuí too old?"
He replied: "Sending to distant barbarians requires someone familiar with court precedents.
Moreover, if Kuí goes,
then those younger than him
will not dare decline distant missions."
From "Comprehensive Mirror in the Reign of Táng Emperor Dézōng."
Lǐ Xīliè attacked and captured Rǔzhōu.
The emperor asked Lú Qǐ for advice,
who replied: "Xīliè is a young, brave general,
arrogant due to his achievements,
and no aides dare admonish him.
If a cultured senior minister
could proclaim the imperial grace,
explaining the consequences of rebellion and loyalty,
Xīliè would surely repent and reform,
and we could subdue him without military action.
Yán Zhēnqīng,
a veteran minister of three reigns,
known for loyalty, integrity, and decisiveness, respected throughout the land,
trusted by all,
is the right person."
He ordered Zhēnqīng to go to Xǔzhōu to pacify Xīliè.
When the edict was issued,
the entire court was aghast.
Lǐ Shèng once commanded the Divine Strategy Army garrisoning Chéngdū,
and upon returning,
took the camp courtesan Gāo Hóng with him.
Zhāng Yánshǎng, Military Governor of Western Chuān, angrily pursued and returned her,
causing a rift between them.
When the emperor summoned Yánshǎng to become chancellor,
Shèng submitted a memorial detailing his faults.
The emperor, reluctant to oppose his wish,
appointed Yánshǎng as Left Vice Director.
Zhāng Yánshǎng and Qí Yìng served as chancellors together.
Yìng was known among the chancellors for his outspokenness,
so Yánshǎng claimed Yìng was unfit to be chancellor,
and Yìng was transferred as Prefect of Kuízhōu.
Lú Qǐ, over personal grievances, had Yáng Yán killed,
pushed Yán Zhēnqīng to his death,
and provoked Lǐ Huáiguāng to rebel.
The Deputy Commissioner of Wéizhōu under Tǔbō, Xīdámóu, surrendered
and led all his followers to Chéngdū.
Lǐ Déyù sent Yú Cángjiǎn, Acting Prefect of Wéizhōu, to lead troops and occupy the city.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
alternatively recorded as "Shēn,"
he reported the situation in detail,
stating: "This is what Wéi Gāo regretted all his life not achieving!"
The matter was referred to the Department of State Affairs,
where all officials gathered to discuss,
and all supported Déyù's strategy.
Niú Sēngrú said: "The Tǔbō territory spans ten thousand li in all directions;
losing one Wéizhōu
does not harm their power.
What use is gaining a hundred Wéizhōus?"
The emperor ordered Déyù to return the city to Tǔbō,
arrested Xīdámóu,
and all who came with him,
returning them to Tǔbō,
where they were all executed at the border,
in an extremely cruel manner.
Also from the same source.
Huáng Cháo headed north toward Xiāngyáng,
where Jù Róng resisted and heavily defeated the rebel forces.
Some urged Jù Róng to pursue and annihilate the rebels completely.
Jù Róng said: "The state often betrays people;
in crises, it cares for generals and troops, sparing no official rewards.
Once peace comes, it discards them,
or they even face charges. Better to keep the rebels as a means to wealth and honor."
The troops then stopped.
From "Comprehensive Mirror in the Reign of Táng Emperor Xīzōng."
Classic:
"The rain waters our public fields,
and then our private lands."
From "The Book of Songs: Greater Field."
Zhào Wénzǐ said: "Suí Wǔzǐ benefits his lord without forgetting himself,
plans for himself without neglecting his friends."
From "The Record of Rites: Tángōng."
"Serving the ruler, one dares not forget his lord,
nor dare neglect his ancestors."
Same as above.
"Serving parents, one exerts his strength;
serving the ruler, one devotes his person."
From "The Analects: Learning."
"Filial piety begins with serving one's parents,
continues with serving the ruler,
and ends with establishing oneself."
From "The Classic of Filial Piety."
"Without personal affection, one is not a filial son;
without public righteousness, one is not a loyal minister.
The gentleman does not let personal matters harm public duty,
nor use family affairs to avoid royal service."
From the commentary on "The Book of Songs."
The Master said:
"Only after public duties are finished
dare I attend to private matters."
From "Mencius: Duke Wén of Téng Part Two."
"Today's affair
is the ruler's business;
I dare not neglect it."
He drew an arrow,
tapped the wheel,
removed its metal head,
shot four arrows, and then returned.
From "Mencius."
Guǎnzǐ said: "As for Xí Péng's character,
at home, he does not forget the public gate;
at the public gate, he does not forget his home.
He serves his ruler without divided loyalty,
yet does not forget himself."
From "Guǎnzǐ."
History
Shí Shē,
was the chancellor of King Zhāo of Chǔ.
There was a murderer,
who turned out to be his own father.
After letting his father escape, he bound himself and
sent someone to inform the king: "The murderer
is my father;
I deserve death for my crime."
The king said, "You need not face punishment."
Shē replied,
"Not favoring one's father
makes one an unfilial son;
disobeying the king's command
makes one a disloyal minister.
If the king pardons my crime,
it is his great kindness;
but accepting execution
is my duty."
He thus refused the order
and cut his own throat to die.
． From "Records of Upright Officials" in Shǐ Jì.
Cross-referenced under "Integrity and Good Governance."
Sū Zhāng was promoted to Governor of Jìzhōu.
An old friend served as Governor of Qīnghé.
While inspecting the region,
Sū Zhāng uncovered his friend's corruption and bribery.
He then invited the governor to a banquet,
where they reminisced fondly about their past friendship.
The governor joyfully said, "Everyone has one heaven,
but I alone have two."
Sū Zhāng responded, "Tonight, Sū Rúwén drinks with an old friend—
that is personal affection.
Tomorrow, the Governor of Jìzhōu investigates matters—
that is public law."
He then duly reported the crimes.
． From "Biography of Sū Zhāng" in the Book of the Later Hàn.
Cross-referenced under "Favoring Personal Ties Over Public Duty."
Xún Xī served as Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
His maternal cousin sought a military position.
Xún appointed him as a commander,
but when he later broke the law,
Xún executed him under full authority.
His aunt kowtowed, pleading for mercy.
He did not listen,
but afterward, he donned mourning clothes and wept for him,
shedding tears as he said, "The one who killed you
was the Governor of Yǎnzhōu;
the one mourning his brother
is Xún Dàojiàng."
Such was his adherence to the law.
From the Book of Jìn.
Yuán Huái was dispatched as an envoy to inspect the northern frontier.
Yuánníxū, a commander at Huáishuò Fort and an old acquaintance of Huái's,
was deeply corrupt.
He hosted a banquet for Huái, saying, "My fate lies
in your words;
surely you can show some leniency."
Huái replied, "Today's gathering
is where Yuán Huái drinks with an old friend;
it is not a court for trying cases.
Tomorrow in the public hall
is where the inspector examines the commander's offenses."
Níxū could only weep in response.
Huái then submitted an impeachment.
From the History of the Northern Dynasties.
Cross-referenced under "Upholding Public Duty Over Personal Ties."
Zhāng Zhènzhōu was appointed Governor of Shūzhōu.
Shūzhōu was his hometown.
Zhāng prepared ample wine and food,
returned to his old residence in Wàngjiāng,
and gathered all his old friends and relatives for a joyous feast.
For ten days, they relaxed and reminisced about old times.
He gave them money and silk,
then tearfully told his guests, "Until now, Zhāng Zhènzhōu has been enjoying time with old friends.
From today onward, it is the Governor of Shūzhōu who governs the people.
The relationship between ruler and people forbids casual interaction,
so we must part forever."
From then on, he showed no leniency to any relative who broke the law,
and the region became orderly.
． From "Biography of Zhāng Zhènzhōu" in the Book of Táng.
Lù Zhì said, "I have not failed the emperor above,
nor have I failed what I have learned below."
． From "Biography of Lù Zhì" in the Book of Táng.
During a period near imperial tombs, slaughter was prohibited.
A subordinate of Guō Zǐyí secretly slaughtered a sheep
and brought it into the city.
General Péi Xǔ of the Right Imperial Guard reported it.
Someone said to Péi, "Lord Guō has rendered great service to the state;
why not give him some leeway?"
Péi replied, "This is precisely how I give him leeway.
Lord Guō has high merit and prestige;
the new emperor fears many officials side with him.
So I expose a minor fault
to show that Lord Guō's power is not to be feared.
This way, I honor the emperor above
and reassure the ministers below."
． From "Records of Táng Emperor Dézōng" in Zīzhì Tōngjiàn.
Initially,
when Lǐ Huáiguāng lifted the siege of Fèngtiān,
the emperor appointed his son Lǐ Cuǐ as a censor.
As Huáiguāng stationed at Xiányáng without advancing,
Cuǐ secretly told the emperor, "My father will surely betray Your Majesty;
I urge you to prepare early.
I believe ruler and father are one in principle,
but in the current situation, Your Majesty cannot punish my father,
while my father can endanger you.
I cannot bear to remain silent."
The emperor, startled, said, "I know you are a minister's beloved son;
please try to mediate and report back."
Cuǐ replied, "My father does not love me less,
nor do I love my father and clan less.
But I have exhausted my efforts and cannot change his course!"
The emperor asked, "Then how will you save yourself?"
Cuǐ answered, "My advice
is not to seek personal survival.
If my father falls, I will die with him;
what strategy could there be?
If I betrayed my father to live,
how could Your Majesty use me?"
The emperor said, "Go to Xiányáng and persuade your father,
so that both ruler and minister, father and son, may be preserved.
Would that not be good?"
Lǐ Mì said, "Lǐ Cuǐ is truly virtuous;
he will surely die with his father.
If he does not,
he would not be worthy of esteem."
When Huáiguāng died,
Cuǐ first killed his two younger brothers
and then himself.
Same as above.
Gāo Jìchāng sent commander
Ní Kěfú with ten thousand soldiers to repair the outer walls of Jiānglíng.
During an inspection,
Gāo criticized the slow progress
and had him caned.
Gāo's daughter was married to Kěfú's son, Zhījìn.
Gāo told his daughter, "Tell your father-in-law: I only meant to enforce discipline to get things done."
He then gave him several hundred taels of silver.
． From "Records of Liáng Emperor Jūn" in Zīzhì Tōngjiàn.
Cross-referenced under "Upholding Public Duty Over Personal Ties."
Sāng Wéihàn, Chancellor of Jìn, was a protégé of Péi Hào.
Once, he visited Péi,
who neither welcomed nor saw him off.
When asked why,
he replied, "When I see Wéihàn at the secretariat,
he is a junior official.
When Wéihàn sees me at my private residence,
he is my protégé.
What need is there for welcomes or farewells?"
From the History of the Five Dynasties.
Collection
At home, I often rise early,
worrying for the state, wishing for a bountiful year.
From Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Cross-referenced under "Concern for the World."
Use filial piety to enrich the family;
use loyalty to strengthen the state.
From Táng Wén Cuì.
Our Dynasty
Duke Wèi of Hán said: "During the Qìnglì era,
I served with Fàn Xīwén and Fù Yànguó in the Western Bureau.
We debated fiercely before the emperor,
yet parted ways after court
without losing harmony,
as if we had never argued."
From Bié Lù.
In the Yuánfēng era, Duke Wén of Lù, as Grand Commandant, oversaw the Western Capital.
Before assuming his seal,
he first went to his residence
and received officials as a peer.
The next day,
after taking office,
he greeted them according to official protocol.
When asked why,
he said, "Before handling official duties,
I met them as a senior minister to juniors;
after receiving the seal as Governor of Hénán,
it was the prefect meeting his supervisors."
From Wén Jiàn Lù.
Recently,
an edict ordered officials to revise the rules for hereditary appointments,
requiring candidates to pass examinations
before receiving office.
This not only cultivates talents for the state
but also helps ministers establish their families.
From the Collected Works of Ōuyáng Xiū.
Classics
When it is time to stop, stop;
when it is time to act, act.
In motion and stillness, do not miss the right timing;
thus, the path is bright.
． From the Gèn hexagram in the Yì Jīng.
When employed, one acts;
when set aside, one remains hidden.
． From the Analects, "Shù Ér."
End
When in obscurity, one cultivates personal integrity;
when eminent, one benefits the whole world.
． _Mencius: Jin Xin I_.
In obscurity, one does not abandon righteousness,
thus the scholar maintains self-possession;
when eminent, one does not depart from the Way,
thus the people are not disappointed.
Same as above.
In obscurity, one is sure to have renown;
when eminent, one is sure to have influence.
_Xúnzǐ_.
The ancients who attained the Way
were joyful in obscurity,
and joyful in success.
． _Zhuāngzǐ: Ràng Wáng_.
History
Zhāng Héng said: "The primordial dragon greets summer by soaring through the clouds with vigor,
while the scaled creature faces winter by churning mud and lying hidden."
_Hòu Hàn_.
Collection
Unfurled, it aids myriad people;
rolled up, it perfects the self.
Bái Shìláng.
Applying it, one achieves the deeds of Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng;
storing it, one embodies the virtue of Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozi.
Responsive yet not stagnant,
cultivating oneself with principles.
When the time comes,
be the cloud-borne dragon,
be the wind-borne roc,
bursting forth suddenly,
exerting strength to emerge.
When the time departs,
be the mist-hidden leopard,
be the sky-hidden swan,
vast and silent,
withdraw while preserving oneself.
Cross-reference "Different Encounters".
The enlightened person, in stillness, subtly merges with the yin;
in action, expansively flows with the yang.
Also same as above.
Concealing and obscuring it,
like unpolished gold and uncut jade,
is the way of the noble person;
revealing and illuminating it,
like the dragon soaring and the tiger transforming,
is the pattern of the great person.
_Táng Wén Cuì_.
Advancing, benefiting the world;
retiring, having fame for a hundred generations.
Prominent, becoming a teacher to the feudal lords;
silent, establishing laws for ten thousand ages.
Same as above.
In stillness, the dragon hibernates, preserving spirit in a single stream without distress;
in motion, the phoenix soars, displaying virtue from a thousand ren to present itself.
Lǐ Yìshān's writing.
Masters
The fish that swallows boats
does not swim in branch streams;
the swan flies high,
not gathering in muddy ponds.
． _Lièzǐ: Yáng Zhū_.
Riding the clouds,
driving flying dragons,
and roaming within the four seas.
． _Zhuāngzǐ: Xiāo Yáo Yóu_.
History
He cleansed himself from the mire and filth,
shed his skin like a cicada from the foulness,
to float beyond the dust of the world,
untainted by the world's grime,
pure though in mud, unstained.
Extending this aspiration,
even vying in brilliance with the sun and moon
is possible.
． _Shǐ Jì: Qū Yuán Zhuàn_.
The wild goose flies high,
soaring a thousand miles at once.
． _Shǐ Jì: Zhāng Liáng Zhuàn_.
Aloof, transcending the vulgar and leaving the world.
． _Xī Hàn: Wáng Bāo Zhuàn_.
Biographies
The divine dragon does not dwell in waters with nets;
the phoenix does not fly in lands with snares.
_Rénwù Kǎo_.
Collection
The phoenix soars in the azure clouds,
thus arrows and strings cannot reach it.
The dragon hides in the swirling depths,
its body untouched by nets.
_Chǔ Cì_.
The dark crane flies high,
ascending into the blue heavens.
The phoenix soars aloft,
then gathers in the wilderness of the great emperor.
Circling the four extremes and returning,
it descends only upon seeing great virtue.
The sage's divine virtue
keeps him far from the turbid world, hiding himself.
If the qílín could be tethered and tied,
how would it differ from dogs and sheep?
The swan's first flight
traverses the winding curves of mountains and rivers.
Its second flight
beholds the square and round of heaven and earth.
How can one with clear insight
endure the world's obscurity?
And how can one of pristine purity
be sullied by the dust of the世俗?
Cross-reference "Not Following Others".
Is there no fine steed in this age?
Seeing the one holding the reins is unfit,
it leaps and goes far away.
Also same as above.
The phoenix soars at a thousand ren,
descending only upon seeing virtuous radiance.
Jiǎ Yì's rhapsody.
Lamenting the narrowness of the世俗,
he lightly rose and traveled far.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody of the Great Man".
Looking down, all things appear chaotic,
like duckweeds on the Yangtze and Han rivers.

Shake my clothes on a thousand-ren peak,

Narrow and perilous are the paths of the world,
I look up to the heavenly road and stride high.

Soaring high, brushing the great purity,
forever free from the fear of arrows.
Chǔ Guāngyì's writing.
Cleaving great abysses, rubbing the great purity,
viewing the three mountains as cups, the five lakes as mere sights.
Lǐ Bái's "Rhapsody on the Roc".
Stirring three thousand miles to rise abruptly,
beating ninety thousand to swiftly journey.
Same as above.
Dense are the nets,
distant the high swans,

profound the hidden dragons.
How remote is their calamity and ruin,
cut off like Hú and Yuè!
_Chén Zǐ'áng Collection_.
Is there no phoenix facing the morning sun?
It shames to contend with petty things.
_Yuán Zhěn Collection_.
Cross-reference "Knowing What to Cherish".
Long dwelling on the path of blue clouds,
no reason for arrows to target.
_Liú Bīnkè Collection_.
To see all hills as small,
one must ascend Tài Shān's peak;
to see all streams as tiny,
one must sail the deep blue sea

deep.
Hán Wén.
Who can drive a flying chariot,
to accompany me and view the sea's breadth?
Same as above.
Seeing through ten thousand ages.
． Lǐ Hàn's "Preface to Hán Wén's Collection".
The divine phoenix does not peck at rank food.
_Bái Lètiān Collection_.
The yellow swan once gone,
the blue heavens have no limit.
Liǔ Wén.
Looking down, the three realms seem narrow,
only the stench of the five turbidities is heard.
_Táng Wén Cuì_.
Leisurely, the swan by the isle,
nourishes itself at will.
Not pecking at the granary's grain,
not drinking from the square pond's water.
Shaking feathers, lifting through floating clouds,

Our dynasty
Lofty peaks cannot be saluted,
Distant as swan geese among the clouds.
Ōu Gōng.
Coolly observing the people of this world.
Dōngpō's poetry.
Transcendent and free from worldly dust,
Standing alone beyond all things;
Riding the wind and driving the ether,
To wander with the Creator.
Dōngpō's "Letter in Reply to Huáng Lǔzhí".
Living aloof and enjoying a lifetime.
Passing through the old capitals of Qín and Hàn,
Freely gazing upon the heights of Zhōngnán and Sōng Huà,
Looking north at the rushing flow of the Huáng Hé,
With deep emotion imagining the heroes of antiquity.
Arriving at the capital,
Looking up at the grandeur of the Son of Heaven's palaces,
And the wealth and vastness of granaries, treasuries, city walls, and parks.
Only then realizing the magnificent splendor of the world.
"Luánchéng Collection".
Soaring up to the Milky Way,
Looking down upon thousands of miles.
Same as above.
One day weary of snail's horns,
Riding on the back of a roc for ten thousand miles.
"Wáng Zhífāng's Poetic Remarks".
Lofty feelings like flying swans,
Not easily lured by handfuls of grain.
"A Hundred Hu of Bright Pearls".
Classic
Studying alone without friends,
Then one becomes isolated and poorly informed.
． "Record of Learning".
Master
You are truly a man of Qí,
Knowing only Guǎn Zhòng and Yànzǐ.
． "Mencius, Gōngsūn Chǒu I".
Chén Zhòngzǐ lived in Yúlíng.
His ears heard nothing,
His eyes saw nothing.
． "Mencius, Téng Wéngōng II".
Hearing little is called shallow,
Seeing little is called narrow.
． "Xúnzǐ, Cultivating Oneself".
A frog in a sunken well said to a turtle from the Eastern Sea: "I leap and play upon the railing of the well,
Rest in the crevices of the broken brickwork;
When I enter the water, it reaches my armpits
(another version says "supports my chin"),
Holding my chin,
Stirring the mud covers my feet and submerges my insteps;
Looking back at the larvae, crabs, and tadpoles,
None can compare to me.
Moreover, to command the waters of this one gully,
And enjoy the pleasure of straddling this sunken well,
This is the ultimate joy.
Why don't you come in and see for yourself sometime?"
． "Zhuāngzǐ, Autumn Floods".
Cross-reference to "judging others by oneself".
Shallow and poorly informed.
Kuǎn means
empty.
Like empty hearing,
What one sees is small.
． "Zhuāngzǐ, Full Understanding of Life".
Long ago in the state of Sòng there was a farmer,
Who often wore worn-out hemp clothes to pass the winter.
When spring ploughing came,
He basked in the sun.
Not knowing that under heaven there were spacious houses and warm rooms,
Silk wadding and fox furs.
He turned to his wife and said: "The warmth of the sun on my back,
No one else knows about this,
If I present it to our lord,
I will surely receive a great reward."
A wealthy man from his village told him: "Once there was a man who found beans delicious,
And enjoyed hemp stems, wild celery, and duckweed seeds,
Praising them to a local magnate.
The magnate took them and tasted them.
They stung his mouth,
And pained his stomach,
The crowd laughed at and scolded
(another version says "resented")
him,
And the man was greatly ashamed.
You, sir,
are like him."
． "Lièzǐ, Yáng Zhū".
You cannot speak of the sea with a frog in a well—

He is bound by his teachings.
． "Zhuāngzǐ, Autumn Floods".
When the Hú people see hemp, they do not know it can be made into cloth;

"Huáinánzǐ".
A tiny fish swimming in a puddle

"Bàopǔzǐ".
Cross-reference to "judging others by oneself".
Seeing a tiger,

Shūsūn Tōng's disciples arranging ritual mats,

Holding a flickering candle in a dark corner,

The Hú people see cloth and suspect it is felt,

do not vainly hope for luck."

Dǒng Yǔn succeeded Fèi Yī as Imperial Secretary.
Within ten days,
many affairs were delayed.
Yǔn sighed: "The disparity in talent and ability is so great,
it is beyond my reach."
． _Records of the Three Kingdoms, Shu, His Biography_.
Cross-referenced under "heartfelt admiration".
Xú Miǎo was appointed Minister of Works.
He sighed: "The Three Excellencies are positions for discussing the Way.
If no suitable person is found, the post should remain vacant.
How can it be defiled by an old and sick man?"
He firmly declined the appointment.
． _Records of the Three Kingdoms, Wèi, His Biography_.
Cross-referenced under "content with retirement".
When Jìn was screening court officials, Wèi Shū said: "I am one of those."
He packed his belongings and left,
leaving his colleagues all ashamed.
． _Book of Jìn, His Biography_.
Shí Lè said: "How can one not know oneself?
If I had met Hàn Gāozǔ,
I would have served him facing north,
standing shoulder to shoulder with Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè."
． _Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Book of Jìn_.
When Wáng Dǎo was first appointed Minister over the Masses,
he told others: "If Liú Zǐqiáo had crossed the river,
I would not have been made a Duke."
． _Book of Jìn, Biography of Liú Kuǐ_.
Kuǐ's son, Chóu,
styled Zǐqiáo.
Zhōu Sōng said: "I am by nature upright and unyielding,
and cannot be tolerated by the world."
_Book of Jìn_.
Wáng Jì was handsome, sharp-witted, and graceful,
but whenever he saw Wèi Jiè,
he would sigh: "With such a jewel by my side,
I feel the shabbiness of my own appearance."
． _Book of Jìn, Biography of Wèi Jiè_.
Yuán Fǔ from Huáinán once visited Hé Xù,
claiming he could govern a large county.
Xù asked: "Why only wish to be a county magistrate,
and not hold a central government position?"
Fǔ replied: "Each person has what they can and cannot do."
． _Book of Jìn, His Biography_.
Cài Mó was promoted to Minister over the Masses.
He submitted a memorial firmly declining,
telling his close ones: "If I become Minister over the Masses,
I will be laughed at by later generations;
in righteousness, I dare not accept."
Lù Wán was promoted to Minister of Works.
He told his guests: "Making me one of the Three Excellencies
means there is no one else in the world."
Both from the same source.
Wèi Yuánshùn said: "I have but the petty talent of a clerk,
fit only for desk work;
how should I defile the imperial court?"
． _Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Liáng Annals_.
Cén Wénběn was appointed Zhongshu Ling
and looked worried.
His mother asked why,
and he replied: "I have no great merit nor long service,
yet the responsibility is heavy and the position high—
that is why I worry."
When people came to congratulate him,
he would say:
"Today I accept condolences,
not congratulations."
． _Book of Táng, His Biography_.
Cross-referenced under "caution and prudence".
Diligently serving the state,
knowing what should be done and doing it—
in this, I am inferior to Fáng Xuánlíng.
Versatile in both civil and military arts,
able to lead armies and govern as minister—
in this, I am inferior to Lǐ Jìng.
Presenting memorials clearly and in detail,
handling communications with fairness—
in this, I am inferior to Wáng Yánbó.
Managing complex and arduous tasks,
ensuring all duties are accomplished—
in this, I am inferior to Dài Zhòu.
Dedicated to remonstrance,
ashamed if the ruler falls short of Yáo and Shùn—
in this, I am inferior to Wèi Zhèng.
． _Book of Táng, Biography of Wáng Guī_.
Cross-referenced under "deference and humility".
Lú Huáijǐn served as Tong Pingzhangshi,
but believing his talent inferior to Yáo Chóng's,
he deferred in all matters without making independent decisions.
． _Book of Táng, His Biography_.
Xǔ Yuǎn, considering himself less capable than Zhāng Xún,
requested to receive military orders from him and serve under him.
． _Book of Táng, Biography of Zhāng Xún_.
Chéng Yì also knew he was unpopular,
and after over a month as chancellor,
dared not take up the seal or hold the brush.
． _Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Táng Xiànzōng_.
Lǐ Déyù said: "I have no reputation,
my actions are inappropriate,
and I am not a Jìnshì."
． _Táng History, Treatise on Selection_.
Zhèng Qì was appointed Tong Pingzhangshi
and laughed: "With Xiēhòu Zhèng Five as chancellor,
you can imagine how things will go!"
． _Book of Táng, His Biography_.
Liú Fén ranked first in the imperial examination,
but the examiners dared not select him.
Among those selected,
Lǐ Hé said:
"Fén is rejected while I remain—
how thick-skinned am I!"
He then submitted a memorial: "My answers were far inferior to Fén's;
I feel deep shame within,
yet call myself virtuous and capable.
What will people say!
I beg to return the appointment
to honor Fén's integrity."
． _New Book of Táng, His Biography_.
Liǔ Càn, at his execution, cried out: "Traitor Liǔ Càn,
deserves to die!"
． _Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Táng Zhāozōng_.
Biographies and records.
Lord Xú of the northern city
was the most handsome man in the state of Qí.
Zōu Jì asked his wife, concubine, and guests, "Who is more handsome, I or Lord Xú?"
They all thought Lord Xú could not compare.
The next day, Lord Xú came.
After gazing at him intently,
Zōu Jì considered himself inferior.
Peeking in the mirror and looking at himself,
he felt far from matching him.
From "Strategies of the Warring States".
Wáng Yífǔ sighed to himself, "When I talk with Yuè Lìng,
I don't realize my words are becoming verbose."
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World".
In our dynasty,
Prince Xiàolíng of Liáng commandery wrote in his petition to decline the post of Governor of Dānyáng: "Having examined myself and understood my limits,
I am unfit for public discussion,
and find myself especially inadequate."
From "Taiping Imperial Encyclopedia".
The
divine turtle could appear in a dream to Lord Yuán,
but could not escape the net of Yú Qiē;
its wisdom allowed it to be divined seventy-two times without error,
yet it could not avoid the calamity of being gutted.
From "Zhuangzi: External Things".
Cháng Hóng
was an expert in calculations during King Xuān of Zhōu's reign.
The qi of heaven and earth,
the movements of the sun and moon,
the changes of wind and rain,
the numbers of pitch-pipes and calendars,
there was nothing he did not comprehend.
Yet he did not foresee his own death by dismemberment.
From "Huainanzi".
Minister Wén Zhǒng knew how to strengthen Yuè,
but did not know how to preserve himself;
Cháng Hóng knew how Zhōu could survive,
but did not know why he himself would perish.
From "Huainanzi: Discourse on Mountains".
In history,
Duke Huán knew that Xiàng could be destroyed,
but did not realize that he himself could not be eliminated.
From "Guliang Commentary".
It is like the eye seeing a fine hair,
but not seeing its own eyelashes.
From "Records of the Grand Historian: Hereditary House of Yuè".
Sūnzi's strategies
were clear to Páng Juān.
Yet he could not save himself early,
suffering the misfortune of punishment.
Wú Qǐ advised Marquis Wǔ,
that terrain is not as important as virtue.
But when implementing it in Chǔ,
due to his harshness and lack of kindness,
he lost his life.
From "Records of the Grand Historian: Biographies of Sūnzi and Wú Qǐ".
With Sīmǎ Qiān's vast knowledge and wide learning,
he could not preserve himself.
From "Book of Han: Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān".
Bān Gù lamented that although Sīmǎ Qiān was erudite and well-informed,
he still suffered a severe punishment.
This is why the ancients discussed the metaphor of the eyelashes.
From "Book of Later Han: Treatise on Bān Gù's Biography".
Warning others of disaster shows wisdom,
yet he could not avoid slander and discord himself.
From "Book of Later Han: Treatise on Mǎ Yuán's Biography".
Wáng Yàn's cousin Sīyuǎn told Yàn, "Most people are unskilled at planning for themselves."
From "Comprehensive Mirror: Chronicle of Emperor Gāozǔ of Qí".
Skillful in assessing others,
clumsy in planning for oneself.
From "New Book of Tang: Eulogy for Lǐ Guāngbì".
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng said, "The trouble with people is that they lack self-awareness."
From "Comprehensive Mirror: Basic Annals".
Liú Fén warned the emperor against careless speech,
yet he himself recited words in the court.
From "New Book of Tang: Basic Eulogy".
In biographies,
a family may have a worn-out broom,
but value it as worth a thousand pieces of gold,
which is the flaw of not seeing oneself clearly.
From Emperor Wén of Wèi's "Discourses on Literature".
Cross-reference "Unselfconscious".
Ordinary people are blind to their own faults,
considering themselves worthy.
Ibid.
In collections,
Lǐ Chì was skilled at composing poetry,
similar to Lǐ Bái,
and was famous in the world.
Initially, as a scholar,
he was no different from others.
Once deluded by a monster,
his actions became thus,
even considering the world as filthy,
and the filth as the emperor's pure capital,
his intentions were clear.
Now everyone laughs at Lǐ Chì's delusion,
but when it comes to making decisions on right and wrong, acceptance and rejection, alignment and opposition, without becoming like Chì,
how many are there?
If one cultivates oneself,
free from desires for profit,
and does not let preferences and aversions disturb one's spirit irreversibly,
that would be fortunate.
How then is there leisure to laugh at Chì!
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's "Biography of Lǐ Chì".
Cross-reference "This One Should Not Laugh at That One".
Wén Zhǒng knew that Wú could be conquered,
and that Yuè could be strengthened,
but did not know his own course of action regarding advancement, retreat, survival, or demise.
From "Collection of Lǐ Yuánbīn".
The people of Qín had no time to lament themselves,
so later people lamented them.
If later people lament them but do not learn from them,
they will also be lamented by later people in turn.
By Dù Mù.
Bronze mirrors do not see themselves,
only meant to reflect others until old.
From "Collection of Luó Yǐn".
Laughing at the lack of skill in predecessors,
forgetting one's own deeds are already clumsy.
From "Generalities on History".
In our dynasty,
Emperor Gāozōng criticized Yì Yǎn for, as chancellor,
oppressing his maternal family.
Yet he himself had slandered and killed his uncle
Wú Jì.
Unaware of his own vice,
how could he blame his ministers for being unkind to their maternal relatives?
From Fàn Zǔyǔ's "Mirror of Táng".
In classics,
When an elder gives to a younger,
the inferior dare not decline.
From "Book of Rites: Summary of Ceremonies Part 1".
When feudal lords are bestowed with bows and arrows,
then they may campaign; when bestowed with axes,
then they may execute; when bestowed with jade libation cups,
then they may make fragrant wine.
From "Book of Rites: Royal Regulations".
A junior officer does not receive congratulations from a senior officer.
If a junior officer has a celebratory event and does not hear of it,
and a senior officer comes personally to congratulate him,
he dare not change his demeanor out of respect for the superior.
From "Book of Rites: Jade Adornments".
The lowly do not eulogize the noble,
the young do not eulogize the elder.
From "Book of Rites: Questions of Zēngzǐ".
Clan members should not claim kinship
in the presence of the ruler, out of respect for the ruler's position.
From "Book of Rites: Great Treatise".
One who does not hold the position,
does not plan its policies.
From "Analects: Tàibó".
A nobleman's thoughts
do not go beyond his position.
From "Analects: Xiàn Wèn".
In texts,
Duke Jǐng of Qí summoned the gamekeeper for a hunt,
using a banner, but he did not come.
From "Mencius: Wàn Zhāng Part 2".
Even if the cook is not attending to the cooking,
the priest does not cross over the sacrificial vessels to replace him.
From "Zhuangzi".
History
The Marquis of Qí wished to make Jìng Zhòng a minister,
but he declined, saying: "I am a wandering minister, fortunate to receive pardon.
What I have gained is already plenty.
How dare I disgrace a high position,
thereby hastening official censure?"
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Zhuāng 22nd Year_.
A minister does not cross the border without the sovereign's command.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Zhuāng 27th Year_.
The King offered Guǎn Zhòng the rites for a high minister,
but he declined, saying: "I am a lowly official,
and there are the two guardians of the Son of Heaven, Guó and Gāo, present.
If they come in spring and autumn to receive the King's command,
how could I be treated with such rites?
I, a retainer minister, dare to decline."
He accepted the rites for a lower minister and returned.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xī 12th Year_.
Nìng Wǔzǐ of Wèi said: "I, a retainer minister, come to renew old friendships,
how dare I violate the great rites,
thereby bringing fault upon myself?"
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Wén 4th Year_.
Zōng Lì said: "I am a household servant,
and dare not involve myself in state affairs."
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Zhāo 25th Year_.
A hat, though worn, must be placed on the head;
shoes, though new, must be worn on the feet—
such is the distinction between high and low.
． _Shǐjì, Biographies of Confucian Scholars_.
Cross-reference to "Míngfèn".
The sovereign's dignity is like a hall,
his ministers like the steps,
and the common people like the ground.
Thus, with nine steps and the upper edge far from the ground, the hall is high;
with no steps and the edge near the ground, the hall is low.
． _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Wén Dì's Annals_.
When ranks are clearly distinguished and the Son of Heaven is elevated above them,
his dignity becomes unattainable.
Ibid.
Wèi Qīng said: "Although I had the authority to behead a general,
given my honored and favored position, I dared not arbitrarily execute within the borders,
but reported all to the Son of Heaven,
for him to decide himself,
thereby showing that as a subject, one dares not monopolize power—
is that not appropriate?"
． _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Wǔ Dì's Annals_.
Honoring the honorable and debasing the debased,
strengthens the trunk and weakens the branches.
． _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Hé Dì's Annals_.
Lǐ Sù entered Càizhōu.
The next day,
Péi Dù arrived,
and Sù, bearing his bow case, awaited Dù at his horse's head.
_Tángshū_.
Classics
The woman's proper place is within,
the man's proper place is without.
． _Yìjīng, Family_.
Mourning garments and ominous objects do not enter the palace,
concealed weapons and tools of harm do not enter the palace,
strange attire and eccentric people do not enter the palace.
． _Zhōulǐ, Gatekeeper_.
Father and son do not share the same mat.
． _Lǐjì, Qū Lǐ Part One_.
A father does not offer sacrifices to his son,
nor a husband to his wife.
Rites do not extend to the common people,
punishments do not reach the great officers.
Dogs and horses are not presented in the hall.
Note: "They are not gifts or tributes."
Outside matters are not discussed within the threshold,
inside matters are not discussed beyond the threshold.
Both ibid.
Cross-reference to "Fángxián".
A collateral son does not offer sacrifices;
if he sacrifices, he must inform the ancestral son.
． _Lǐjì, Qū Lǐ Part Two_.
Also, _Xiǎo Jì on Mourning Attire_ states: "A son by a concubine does not sacrifice to his father,
to clarify the lineage."
Those without land or stipend
do not set up sacrificial vessels.
Wearing fine or coarse hemp,
one does not enter the ducal gate.
Straw sandals,
tucked lapels,
a pressed mourning cap,
do not enter the ducal gate.
Both ibid.
A nobleman, without great cause,
does not lodge outside.
． _Lǐjì, Tán Gōng Part One_.
Side dishes do not surpass the sacrificial animal,
informal robes do not surpass sacrificial attire,
and sleeping garments do not surpass temple wear.
． _Lǐjì, Royal Regulations_.
With land, one offers sacrifices;
without land, one presents offerings.
On the road,
men keep to the right,
women to the left.
Both ibid.
From commissioned scholars upward,
fathers and sons have separate residences.
． _Lǐjì, Domestic Rules_.
Men do not discuss internal affairs,
women do not discuss external affairs.
Great officers at informal meals
have minced meat but not dried meat,
or dried meat but not minced meat.
Scholars do not have two kinds of soup or meat,
and common elders do not eat without dishes.
Such are the distinctions of rank.
Both ibid.
A family does not treasure tortoise shells,
hoard jade tablets,
nor build tower gates.
． _Lǐjì, Ritual Vessels_.
Singers are placed above,
gourd and bamboo instruments below.
． _Lǐjì, Jīao Tè Shēng_.
Following kindness from the father, ascending through ancestors,
step by step upward,
until the founding ancestor,
is called lightness.
Following righteousness from the ancestor,
descending in order,
until the father,
is called weight.
One light, one heavy—
such is the principle.
In terms of affection,
parents are weighty and ancestors light.
In terms of righteousness,
ancestors are weighty and parents light.
For those heavy in affection, three years of mourning;
for those heavy in righteousness, one year of mourning attire.
． _Lǐjì, Great Tradition_.
Severed lineages have no transferred mourning.
Ibid.
A father does not take precedence over his son,
nor an elder brother over his younger.
． _Lǐjì, Great Record of Mourning_.
A state should not exceed a thousand chariots,
a capital city's walls not over three hundred zhang,
a family's wealth not over a hundred chariots.
． _Lǐjì, Fáng Jì_.
Father and son do not hold the same rank.
Ibid.
When ritual and righteousness are established,
then nobility and baseness are distinguished.
． _Lǐjì, Record of Music_.
Masters
Those who eat with their hands
cannot establish ancestral temples.
． _Xúnzǐ, Discourse on Rites_.
An outer screen is to avoid seeing outside,
an inner screen to avoid being seen inside.
． _Xúnzǐ, Great Summary_.
Cross-reference to "Fángxián".
History
The system of the former kings:
a large city not more than one-third of the capital,
a medium one-fifth,
a small one-ninth.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Yǐn 1st Year_.
In rites, a family's influence does not extend to the state,
and great officers do not appropriate public benefits.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Zhāo 26th Year_.
Merchants may not wear embroidery or ride in carriages,
and descendants of market folk may not hold office or serve as officials.
． _Shǐjì, Treatise on the Balanced Standard_.
Emperor Míng of Hàn wished to enfeoff his son,
saying: "How can my son be equal to the sons of the late emperor?
Let him have half of Chǔ or Huáiyáng."
_Hòu Hàn Jì_.
Classics
To abandon office and leave one's post.
． _Shūjīng, Yìn's Expedition_.
Masters
To speak of high matters from a low position
is a crime.
_Mèngzǐ_.
History
Luán Zhēn said: "To encroach on another's office is presumption,
to neglect one's duty is disrespect,
to leave one's post is treachery."
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Chéng 16th Year_.
Sì Qín of Zhèng was a favorite minor officer,
yet often displayed a minister's carriage and robes in his courtyard.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Āi 3rd Year_.
Masters
Cut off the long to supply the short.
． From "Mèngzǐ: Téng Wéngōng Shàng".
Orderly and well-arranged,
systematic and methodical.
From "Xúnzǐ".
In each prefecture and county, garrison commanders were appointed to take charge of affairs,
taking away the authority of the prefects and county magistrates,
and acting arbitrarily with power and favor.
If the prefects had been allowed to perform their duties,
then even if there had been treacherous and ambitious men like Ān Lùshān and Shǐ Sīmíng,
they certainly could not have rebelled with just one prefecture.
The three prefectures of Dé, Dì, and Jǐng under my jurisdiction,
I have already issued documents returning their administrative duties to the prefects,
and all troops within the prefectures should be commanded by the prefects."
In summer,
the fourth month,
an edict was issued that all troops and horses in the subordinate commanderies under the various military commissioners, regional defense commissioners, and frontier commanders
should be commanded by the prefects.
Since the Zhìdé era,
the power of military commissioners had grown heavy,
with garrison troops established in each of the prefectures under their control,
commanded by senior generals,
whose tyranny and violence caused trouble, hence Chóng Yìn discussed this.
Afterwards, among the various garrisons in Héběi,
only the Héng Hǎi garrison was the most obedient to the court's orders,
because Chóng Yìn handled it appropriately.
. *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government, Táng Xiànzōng*.
Lú Tǎn served as the observation commissioner of Xuānzhōu and Shèzhōu.
Upon his arrival,
there was drought and famine,
and grain prices increased daily.
Some requested to suppress the prices.
Tǎn said: "The land of Xuānzhōu and Shèzhōu is narrow and grain is scarce,
relying on supplies from all directions.
If the price is cheap,
then merchant ships will not come again,
and the hardship will worsen."
Soon, rice reached two hundred cash per dou,
merchants and travelers gathered like spokes to a hub,
and the people relied on this to survive.
The emperor wanted to appoint Wáng Chéngzōng as the acting military commissioner of Chéng Dé,
separating its Dé and Dì prefectures to form another garrison to weaken its power,
and also make Chéngzōng pay two taxes,
and request officials,
exactly like Lǐ Shīdào."
Lǐ Jiàng and others replied:
"We hope that when the envoy for condolences and sacrifices arrives there,
he can instruct Chéngzōng in his own words,
ordering him to submit a memorial requesting the same treatment as Shīdào,
without letting him know it comes from Your Majesty's intention.
In this way,
if he fortunately obeys the order,
it is naturally reasonable and smooth;
if he does not obey,
there is also no loss of dignity."
The emperor then sent the junior governor of the capital, Péi Wǔ, to Zhēndìng to offer comfort.
Chéngzōng received the edict very respectfully and said:
"The three armies forced me, leaving no time to await the court's decree.
I request to offer the two prefectures of Dé and Dì to demonstrate my sincerity."
Same as above.
Previously,
the court sent a palace envoy to bestow seasonal clothing to Zhū Kèróng.
Kèróng considered it coarse and inferior,
and detained the imperial envoy.
He also memorialized:
"The troops in my jurisdiction have insufficient spring clothing this year,
I request the Ministry of Revenue to supply three hundred thousand bolts of cloth."
He also memorialized:
"I wish to lead five thousand troops and laborers to assist in repairing the palace."
The emperor was troubled by this,
and asked the chief ministers,
wanting to send a high-ranking official to proclaim comfort,
and also to demand the return of the imperial envoy.
Péi Dù replied: "Kèróng's lack of propriety is extreme,
he is probably about to perish!
It is like a fierce beast roaring in the mountains and forests,
after leaping and struggling for a long time, it will naturally become exhausted,
and certainly will not dare to rashly leave its lair.
I hope Your Majesty does not send anyone to proclaim comfort,
nor demand the return of the imperial envoy.
After ten days,
slowly bestow an edict saying:
'I have heard that the palace envoy there,
somewhat lost proper conduct.
Upon his return,
I will personally deal with it.
Regarding the seasonal clothing,
the responsible officials were not careful in its manufacture,
I very much wish to punish them,
and have already ordered it to be handled.
As for the spring clothing for the troops,
it has never been supplied by the court,
but always prepared by the local command itself.
I do not begrudge several hundred thousand bolts of goods,
but there has never been such a precedent,
and I cannot give it solely to Fànyáng.'
His claim of assisting in repairing the palace,
is all empty words.
If you wish to directly thwart his treachery,
you should say 'the laborers should come quickly'—he will certainly panic and lose his plan.
If you wish to show tolerance for now,
then say:
'The matter of repairing the palace is handled by the responsible officials,
there is no need for laborers to come from afar.'
That is all,
it is not worth troubling Your Majesty's concern."
. *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government, Táng Jìngzōng Annals*.
In Wú, the co-administrator of affairs Xú Zhīxùn,
was arrogant, licentious, and violent.
The military commissioner of Wēiwǔ,
and administrator of Fǔzhōu, Lǐ Déchéng, had several tens of household entertainers.
Zhīxùn requested them.
Déchéng sent an envoy to decline, saying: "All those in my household are of advanced age,
some have children,
and are not fit to serve a noble person.
I should seek younger and more beautiful ones for you."
. *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government, Later Liáng Jūnwáng*.
Cáo Bīn was sent as an envoy to Wúyuè.
After completing his mission, he hurriedly returned,
not accepting any gifts.
The people of Wúyuè pursued him with light boats to give them,
up to three or four times.
Bīn said: "If I ultimately do not accept,
it is to steal fame.
I will fully record the amount,
and upon returning, present it."
The emperor said: "Previous envoys,
begged and were insatiable,
causing all regions to look down on the court's commands.
That you could act like this,
is very good.
However, since they gave it to you,
you may take it for yourself."
Bīn then bowed and accepted,
but distributed it all among relatives and acquaintances,
keeping none at home.
. *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government, Zhōu Shìzōng*.
Collection
Do not exceed the ancients,
do not neglect what future generations will see.
*Táng Wén Cuì*.
For those who respect themselves,
revere them as a minister serves a ruler;
for those beneath oneself,
be kind to them as a mother nurtures a child;
for those equal to oneself,
befriend them as brothers.
Then none will fail to achieve their aspirations.
Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
Our dynasty
The Western Xià's Zhào Démíng reported that the people were starving,
and requested a million hu of grain.
Emperor Zhēnzōng asked Wáng Dàn.
Dàn requested to order the responsible officials to prepare a million hu of grain in the capital,

Yuánhào sent an envoy seeking communication,
while the Khitan had a conflict with Yuánhào,
and sent an envoy to make an agreement with us.
When it was requested to reject them,
the authorities wanted to reject the Khitan,
and accept Yuánhào.
Lord Zhāng Wéndìng and Lord Sòng Qí submitted a memorial saying: "If we do this,
we gain a newly submitting minor Qiāng tribe,
but lose a long-peaceful strong enemy.
We should bestow an edict to Yuánhào saying: 'The court accepts you,
and the sincerity was originally due to the Khitan's request.
Now I hear you have lost the joy of the uncle-nephew relationship,
and the Khitan has sent an envoy to speak about it.
You should carefully handle this matter.'
Once the discord is resolved in the morning,
then the investiture will be granted."
They proceeded like this in the evening.
Regarding the northwest, it achieved two gains,
and people of the time admired their profound insight.
Sū Dōngpō composed *Epitaph for Zhāng Āndào*.
Cài Què, while administrator of Ānzhōu, wrote poems,

Lord Sū secretly submitted a memorial to the court saying: "If we treat Què's crime lightly,
then it is insufficient for the emperor's filial governance.
If we deeply punish Què,
then it becomes a minor burden for the Grand Empress Dowager.
I suggest the emperor issue an edict,
establish a tribunal to arrest and try him,
and then the Grand Empress Dowager issue a handwritten edict pardoning him.
Then both benevolence and filial piety are achieved."
Sū Zǐyóu composed *Epitaph for Dōngpō*.
