Cunningly hastening for profit.
． From "Shījīng · Gé Jù".
If one acts based on profit,
it will lead to much resentment.
． From "Lúnyǔ · Lǐ Rén".
Petty men understand profit.
Same as above.
Masters
Putting profit before righteousness,
they are never satisfied without seizing more.
． From "Mèngzǐ · Liáng Huìwáng I".
The king asks: "How to profit my state?"
The ministers ask: "How to profit our families?"
Scholars and commoners ask: "How to profit ourselves?"
When high and low contend for profit,
the state is endangered.
Same as above.
To bend a foot and straighten eight feet
is spoken in terms of profit.
If it is for profit,
then bending eight feet to straighten a foot for gain,
could that also be done?
． From "Mèngzǐ · Téng Wéngōng I".
There is a base man
who must seek a垄断 (monopoly) to climb upon,
looking left and right
to net all the market's profit.
From "Mèngzǐ".
As ministers,
they serve their lord with profit in mind;
as sons,
they serve their father with profit in mind;
as younger brothers,
they serve their elder brothers with profit in mind.
Same as above.
Preserving profit and abandoning righteousness
is called the utmost baseness.
From "Xúnzǐ".
Wherever profit lies,
there is nothing they will not overturn.
． From "Xúnzǐ · Bù Gǒu".
It is human nature
that upon seeing profit, none can avoid pursuing it.
Thus, where profit is found,
even a mountain of a thousand rèn,
they will climb it;
beneath deep sources,
they will enter it.
． From "Guǎnzǐ · Jìn Cáng".
The king of Qín was ill,
and summoned a doctor to lick his hemorrhoids,
rewarding him with five chariots.
From "Zhuāngzǐ".
History
They only look to profit.
． "Zuozhuan, 12th Year of Duke Cheng".
Shū Xiàng said: "Even the tip of an awl or knife,
they will strive to seize it all."
． "Zuozhuan, 6th Year of Duke Zhāo".
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said: "Profit is truly the beginning of chaos."
．． "Shǐjì, Preface to Mencius' Biography".
Profit makes one's mind confused.
"Biography of Plain Yuán".
Fond of profit and untrustworthy,
they know not ritual, righteousness, virtue, or conduct.
If there is profit to be had,
they care not for kin or brothers,
acting like beasts.
． "Shǐjì, Hereditary House of Wèi".
Lǚ Bùwéi bought cheap and sold dear,
amassing a fortune of a thousand gold at home.
． "Shǐjì, His Biography".
Zǐgòng traded goods between Cáo and Lǔ.
． "Shǐjì, Biographies of Money-makers".
Being a traveling merchant
is a lowly occupation for a man,
yet Yōng Yuèchéng prospered from it.
Selling grease
is a disgraceful trade,
yet Yōng Bó made a thousand gold.
Selling juice,
a petty business,
yet the Zhāng family made tens of millions.
Sharpening knives,
a meager skill,
yet the Zhì family dined from tripods.
From this we see,
in wealth, no trade is insignificant;
thus goods have no constant owner.
The capable gather like spokes,
the unworthy disintegrate.
All under heaven hustle hither for profit;
all under heaven bustle thither for profit.
The king of a thousand chariots,
the marquis of ten thousand households,
the lord of a hundred chambers,
still fear poverty—
how much more so the common folk of registered households?
All from the same source above.
When a commoner monopolizes profit,
it is called robbery.
． "Shǐjì, Annals of Zhōu".
Wherever profit lies,
they know not ritual or righteousness.
． "Shǐjì, Biography of the Xiōngnú".
Yuè Yì entered Línzī,
took treasures and ritual vessels,
and transported them to Yān.
． "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Zhōu Annals".
Stubborn and greedy for profit.
． "History of the Western Hàn, Biography of Chén Píng".
They chase profit without a second thought,
disregarding conduct.
． "History of the Western Hàn, Biography of Jiǎ Yì", note says: "In their pursuit of profit,
they only consider whether it is profitable or not."
Sāng Hóngyáng
was the son of a merchant from Luòyáng.
Skilled in calculation,
he became a palace attendant at age thirteen.
He analyzed profit matters down to the finest detail.
． "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Annals of Hàn Wǔdì".
Rushing to profit like water flowing downhill,
they go in all directions without discrimination.
． "History of the Former Hàn, Treatise on Food and Money".
Merchants take advantage of the ruler's urgency,
doubling their selling prices.
Accustomed to commercial calculations,
they deal in minute fractions.
Seeking profit
means taking it.
Wealthy merchants and great traders
have no means to seize profit.
Both from the same source above.
Embroidering patterns
is not as good as leaning by the market gate.
．． "History of the Western Hàn, Preface to Biographies of Money-makers".
When the path of righteousness closes,
then the gate of profit opens.
． "History of the Eastern Hàn, Biography of Lǐ Gù".
Minister over the Masses Yuán Wěi
wished to find a marriage for his niece.
Seeing Huáng Yǔn, he sighed: "To have a son-in-law like this
is sufficient."
Yǔn heard this and divorced his wife to send her away.
． "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Annals of Hàn Huán".
Cross-referenced under "son-in-law gate" and "heartlessness".
Wáng Róng had a nature fond of pursuing profit.
He often held his own ivory tally sticks,
calculating day and night,
always as if it were not enough.
． "History of the Jìn, His Biography".
Wèi's Chéngyáng King Yuī fled to the south of the mountains,
reaching the home of former Luòyáng Magistrate Kòu Zǔrén.
Zǔrén's family had three provincial governors,
all promoted by Yuī.
Due to past kindness,
he sought refuge there.
Yuī carried a hundred catties of gold,
and fifty horses.
Zǔrén coveted his wealth;
outwardly he accommodated him,
but privately told his sons: "I hear Ěrzhū Zhào is offering a reward for Chéngyáng King;
the one who captures him will be enfeoffed as a thousand-household marquis.
Today, wealth and honor have arrived!"
He then frightened Yuī, saying official capture was imminent,
made him flee elsewhere,
and had men ambush and kill him on the road,
sending his head to Zhào.
． "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Liáng Gāozǔ".
All circuit inspection offices recruited fast runners,
setting up relay stations within sight of each other.
Goods and prices from all regions,
their fluctuations and other matters,
however distant the profits and losses,
within a few days,
were known as he rode to court each morning,
calculating with his whip.
． "History of the Táng, Biography of Liú Yàn".
Initially, Jí Wēn advanced through Lǐ Línfǔ's influence,
but as Yáng Zhāo's favor deepened,
Wēn left Línfǔ to attach to him,
planning for Zhāo
a strategy to replace Línfǔ in power.
． "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Táng Xuánzōng".
Biographies record:
The king's dogs,
whether lying or rising,
walking or stopping,
do not fight each other.
Throw them a bone,
and they lightly rise,
baring teeth at each other.
"Strategies of the Warring States".
Tián Yīng said: "Those who die for righteousness
do not fear the threat of axes and halberds;
those impoverished for righteousness
do not accept the gift of high carriages and official caps.
To live without righteousness
is worse than to die with righteousness."
"Garden of Persuasions".
Seeking profit through lowly associations,
without any shame.
Profits of minute fractions,
they know and must contend for.
Same as above.
Collection:
Eyes fixed on sums, expressions shifting,
brows moving, noses blocked.
They discuss wisdom in tiny spaces,
peeping for gains in minute margins.
Jìn Chéng Bóyáng's "Rhapsody on the Pínglè Market".
They compete for feathers' lightness,
rush for awl-tip profits.
Liú Xiàobiāo's "Expanded Discourse on Cutting Off Friendships".
Profit weighs more than Tài Mountain,
the Way lighter than a goose feather.
Zhōu Zhī's "Admonition on Steadfast Friends".
Marketers gather at midday,
competing for awl-tip profits.
Dù Fǔ's poem.
A skilled doctor sucks others' sores,
contains their blood—
not out of flesh-and-bone kinship,
but for the profit involved.
Hán Yù's prose.
The brokers of contracts,
the cliques of monopolists,
join together
and inflate prices.
With clever words praising good and bad,
they manipulate measures and weights with risky hands, creating hair's-breadth differences.
Wagging tongues, crude and clamorous,
boasting of deceit and outdoing each other,
strange postures横行而出.
Drums of noise and uproar,
clouds of dust and smoke.
"Collected Works of Liú Bīngkè".
Principal and interest frequently multiply,
goods and trade daily merge and acquire.
Seeking pearls, they sail the vast sea;
gathering jade, they ascend Jīng and Héng mountains.
Buying horses from Dǎngxiàng in the north,
capturing parrots from Tǔbō in the west.
From Yánzhōu, cloth washed by fire;
from Shǔ lands, brocade woven complete.
"Collected Works of Yuán Zhěn".
Ships compete to navigate profitably,
coming and going with wind and tide.
Liú Chā's writing.
Our dynasty
Those sycophantic individuals,
do not know where righteousness lies,
but only follow profit,
hence this behavior.
If profit lies with the ruler or father,
they follow the ruler or father;
if profit lies with powerful ministers,
they attach themselves to powerful ministers;
if profit lies with enemy states,
they befriend enemy states;
if profit lies with barbarians,
they become intimate with barbarians.
Wherever profit is found,
they follow it;
wherever profit departs,
they abandon it.
Fàn Zǔyǔ's "Reflections on the Táng Dynasty".
Classics
Do not ascend heights,
do not approach depths.
． "Book of Rites·Qū Lǐ I".
Feudal lords do not pursue beauty like fishing.
． "Book of Rites·Fáng Jì".
The noble person, with every step,
dares not forget filial piety.
With every lift of the foot,
dares not forget parents.
Therefore,
they take the main road rather than shortcuts,
use boats rather than swim.
． "Book of Rites·Jì Yì".
Cross-reference to "Way of the Child".
On the road, do not contend for advantages of danger or ease,
in winter and summer, do not contend for harmony of yin and yang.
Cherish one's life to await opportunities,
nurture one's body to accomplish deeds.
． "Book of Rites·Rú Xíng".
The noble person does not for a single day let themselves become contemptible,
as if unable to last the day.
． "Book of Rites·Biǎo Jì" note: "A look of being lightly regarded."
Dare not endanger the body inherited from parents.
Malicious words do not leave the mouth,
angry words do not return to the body.
Do not disgrace oneself,
do not shame one's parents.
． "Book of Rites·Jì Yì".
Cross-reference to "Way of the Child".
The body
is the branch of one's parents.
How dare one not respect it?
． "Book of Rites·Āi Gōng Asks".
Cross-reference to "Way of the Child".
If the noble person is not dignified,
then they command no authority.
． "Analects·Xué Ér".
How can one be like ordinary men and women keeping petty fidelity,
hanging themselves in ditches,
with none knowing of it?
． "Analects·Xiàn Asks".
Mencius
There is not an inch of skin
one does not love.
Then there is not an inch of skin
one does not nurture.
． "Mencius·Gào Zǐ I".
Those who understand destiny
do not stand beneath dangerous walls.
． "Mencius·Jìn Xīn I".
Duke of Zhōu said: "The noble person may have strength like an ox,
but does not contend in strength with the ox;
may run like a horse,
but does not contend in running with the horse."
"Xúnzǐ".
One who possesses a sword from Gān or Yuè,
stores it in a case,
dares not use it,
this is the ultimate treasuring.
． "Zhuāngzǐ·Kè Yì".
On a speeding chariot, there is no Confucius;
under an overturned boat, there is no Bóyí.
"Hán Fēizǐ".
History
The child of a wealthy family
does not die in the marketplace.
"Records of the Grand Historian".
Everyone loved themselves,
and hesitated to break the law.
． "Records of the Grand Historian·Treatise on the Balanced Standard".
The child of a hundred gold
does not ride on the balustrade.
． "Book of Hàn·Yuán Áng Biography".
Wáng Yáng was the Chief Clerk of Yìzhōu.
Arriving at Jiǔzhé Slope,
Yáng said: "Carrying the body inherited from ancestors,
how can I repeatedly traverse such danger?"
． "Western Hàn Original Biography".
A thousand-jūn crossbow
is not triggered for a mouse.
A ten-thousand-shí bell
is not struck with a reed to produce sound.
． "Comprehensive Mirror·Hàn Xiàn Dì Annals".
Biographies
The southern mountains have a patterned leopard,
that during seven days of fog and rain does not descend to eat,
why?
It wishes to moisten its fur,
and complete its patterns.
"Biographies of Exemplary Women".
Collections
A family accumulating a thousand gold,
sits not under the eaves.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Memorial Advising Against Hunting".
Strive to cherish yourself.
． "Selections of Refined Literature·Lǐ Líng's Reply to Sū Wǔ's Letter".
Using a bright moon pearl to shoot at a bird a thousand ren high,
I cannot do it.
Chén Zǐ'áng.
How could one be willing to compete with petty people,
deciding gain and loss through one man's eyes,
and feel joy or sorrow over it?
Hán Yù's Prose.
Never recklessly joining the flock of swallows and sparrows.
"Wáng Wéi Collection".
Is there no phoenix facing the morning sun?
It is ashamed to compete with insignificant creatures.
"Táng Literary Essence".
Cross-reference to "Soaring High and Seeing Far".
This Dynasty
Hán Wèi Gōng said that when beginning learning and conducting oneself,
one should be like gold and jade, not accepting the stain of fine dust.
"Anecdotes".
Fàn Zhōngxuān Gōng said: "For a grand carriage to race with a firewood cart,
a phoenix to compete for food with an owl,
a priceless jade to contend with tiles and stones,
a noble person to struggle in strength with a petty person—
not only can one not win,
but it is also improper to win.
Not only is it improper to win,
even winning would be wrong."
Fàn Zhōngxuān Gōng's Conduct Record.
Trembling with care,
as if a maiden in her chamber;
cautiously,
as if carrying a priceless jade disk while walking.
Sū Shì's "Explanation of Yáng Jiàn's Style Name".
Common saying: Péng Zǔ observing a well,
first tied himself to a large tree above it.
Covered the well with a cart wheel,
then dared to look.
"Sū Shì Collection".
To shoot a rat,
why trouble to draw a six-jūn bow?
Same as above.
The child of a wealthy family does not die at the hands of thieves,
why?
Because their own body is precious,
and thieves are not worth dying for.
Sū Shì's "Essay on Liú Hóu".
Cross-reference to "Knowing What to Value".
The bright pearl naturally has a thousand-gold value,
do not make it into a pellet for travelers.
"A Hundred Hú of Bright Pearls".
Classics
If feudal lords, except for inquiring after illness or mourning,
enter the homes of their ministers,
this is called ruler and minister jesting.
． "Book of Rites·Lǐ Yùn".
Descending the hall to meet feudal lords
is the Son of Heaven's breach of etiquette.
． "Book of Rites·Jiāo Tè Shēng".
Fighting tigers barehanded, crossing rivers on foot, and dying
without regret.
． "Analects·Shù Ér".
Mencius
Using the pearl of the Marquis of Suí
to shoot at a bird a thousand ren high.
"Zhuāngzǐ".
History
Yú Fān was by nature careless and straightforward,
often made mistakes due to drink,
and also enjoyed contradicting others,
so many people slandered and defamed him.
． "Comprehensive Mirror·Wèi Míng Dì Annals".
Collections
Zǐhòu in his youth was bold in acting for others,
not valuing himself highly.
He believed that achievements could be instantly accomplished.
Hán Yù's "Epitaph".
Classics
To be gentle yet not hindered in decision-making,
is to have mastered the art of control.
"Yi Lüe Li Shang".
The
poem from Bèi states: "Holding the reins like weaving silk,
the side steeds dance in unison."
Confucius remarked: "The composer of this poem
understands governance, does he not?
For the weaver,
gathers threads at one end,
creating patterns at the other—meaning
actions taken nearby
extend their influence afar.
Applying this method to governing people,
would it not transform them?"
． "Jiā Yǔ Sān Shù".
Liáng Yǎng, a herdsman under King Xuān of Zhōu,
could nurture birds and beasts.
Even tigers and wolves
became tame under his care.
Yǎng said: "The way to raise tigers
is to please them and they rejoice,
oppose them and they rage—
such is the nature of creatures with blood and breath.
One dares not feed them live prey,
lest killing stir their fury.
Nor give them whole carcasses,
lest tearing them apart provoke anger.
Regulate their hunger and fullness,
understand their wrathful hearts.
Thus tigers and humans,
though different species, become endeared to their keeper."
"Liè Zǐ".
The rule of a sage monarch
resembles Zào Fǔ's skill in driving:
harmonizing rein and bit movements,
moderating pace through gentle commands,
maintaining balance in the heart,
directing rhythm through the hands.
Inner alignment with one's core
matches outward accord with the horse's spirit.
Hence,
advancing or retreating with ease,
following straight paths or curves,
fitting perfectly to rules,
journeying far without exhaustion,
with strength to spare—
truly mastering the method."
"Huái Nán".
When control follows the right way,
even the cunning of the world become servants.
"Yáng".
Historian
records: "Cart tracks leave dust,
horses mark with hooves,
the driver
never loses control of the gallop."
"Gǔ Liáng".
Yīng Bù and Suí Hé joined Hàn.
Upon arrival,
the king was lounging while having his feet washed,
yet summoned Bù for audience.
Bù grew furious,
regretted coming,
and contemplated suicide.
But when escorted to quarters,
he found lavish food and drink,
attendants rivaling the king's own—
Bù's joy surpassed all expectation."
． "Xī Hàn Yīng Bù Zhuàn".
Whenever Hán Xìn captured Wèi or defeated Dài for Hàn,
he would have their elite troops recruited
to defend Xíngyáng against Chǔ."
． "Tōng Jiàn Hàn Gāo Jì".
In combat with others,
without gripping their throat
(pronounced gāng,
meaning throat)
and pressing their back,
one cannot achieve total victory."
． "Xī Hàn Lóu Jìng Zhuàn".
Hán Xìn said: "Your Majesty cannot command troops,
but excels at commanding commanders."
． "Xī Hàn Hán Xìn Zhuàn".
For governing the realm peacefully,
nothing surpasses multiplying authorities.
Establish many lords but limit their power—
weakened, they become manageable.
Small states bound by righteousness
lose rebellious intent.
Now the empire's structure
resembles the body moving arms,
arms moving fingers—
all obey without resistance."
． "Tōng Jiàn Hàn Wén Jì".
Even runaway horses
and unruly talents
depend solely on how they are managed."
． "Xī Hàn Wǔ Jì".
Tigers, leopards, horses, oxen—
creatures deemed uncontrollable—
when trained to utmost familiarity,
can be led, harnessed, and ridden,
obeying human command alone."
． "Xī Hàn Gōngsūn Hóng Zhuàn".
Maintain loose reins without severing ties."
． "Xī Hàn Sīmǎ Xiàngrú Zhuàn".
Despite Kòu Dèng's high merits
and Gěng Jiǎ's grand achievements,
their fiefs spanned but a few large counties,
with only titular honors added."
． "Dōng Hàn Èrshíbā Jiàng Lùn".
Cáo Cāo declared: "I employ the world's wisdom and strength,
guiding them with principle—
nothing is impossible."
． "Tōng Jiàn Hàn Xiàn Jì".
When Lǚ Bù surrendered to Lord Cáo,
he was bound tightly.
Lǚ Bù complained: "The ropes chafe too hard."
Lord Cáo replied: "Binding a tiger
demands severity."
"Wèi Shū".
Liú Yè of Wèi advised: "Like anglers who hook big fish—
first give line and follow,
then reel in when controllable—
thus nothing escapes capture."
． "Tōng Jiàn Wèi Jì".
Cuī Hào said: "To strike a snake,
first hit its head.
Once the head is crushed,
the tail cannot thrash."
． "Tōng Jiàn Sòng Tàizǔ".
Lǐ Chóng was appointed governor of Yǎnzhōu.
Yǎnzhōu suffered rampant banditry,
so Chóng ordered each village to erect a tower
with drums hung atop.
Where robbery occurred,
drums were beaten wildly.
Neighboring villages hearing it
responded with one beat as initial signal,
then two, then three—
within moments,
the alarm spread a hundred lǐ,
prompting guards to secure strategic points.
Thus no bandits escaped capture."
． "Tōng Jiàn Qí Tàizǔ".
Ěrzhū Róng kept a vicious horse in his stable.
He ordered Gāo Huān to groom it.
Huān trimmed it without restraints
and rose unharmed by bite or kick, declaring: "Managing wicked people
resembles handling this horse."
"Běi Qí Shū".
Nurturing tigers and wolves without crossing their nature
prevents rage from arising."
"Tōng Jiàn".
The bold crave to assert their will,
the greedy rush for profit,
the foolish ignore mortal peril."
． "Tōng Jiàn Táng Tàizǔ".
Dozens of veteran generals,
all nobles and dignitaries,
obeyed Guō Zǐyí's slightest gesture—
advancing or retreating like privates."
． "Táng Shū Guō Zǐyí Zhuàn".
Beyond remote territories,
rebellions warrant no costly campaigns,
surrenders warrant no laxity.
Maintain strict defense
so raiding becomes impossible
and defection untenable."
．． "Táng Tūjué Zhuàn Xù".
Historical records state:
Utilize the wise,
employ the brave,
exploit the greedy,
deploy the foolish."
Huáng Shí Gōng "Sān Lüè".
A massive ox, ten arm-spans round,
is driven by a mere shepherd boy."
"Lùn Héng".
A hundred horses with shared reins
are driven by Zào Fǔ alone."
Wèi Míngdì "Shàn Zāi Xíng".
Collection
To shoot a man, first shoot his horse;
to catch bandits, first catch their chief.
From Dù Shī.
The Mǐn people are fierce and unruly,
the Yí customs are brittle and hasty.
Govern them with kindness and trust,
and they will rest peacefully like hibernating insects.
From Liú Bīnkè.
In employing heroes and outstanding men,
rulers must control them with authority
and bind them with kindness.
If not restrained by heroic spirit,
but indulged with leniency,
they will become arrogant and unreliable.
If not bound by affection,
but only by strict etiquette,
they will hold resentment and not serve willingly.
From "Collected Works of Lǐ Wénráo".
Governing heroes and fierce generals differs from
associating with righteous and upright scholars.
One should not rely on elaborate rituals and superficial appearances,
nor on empty rhetoric
(zú, departing tone)
to suffice.
Instead, one should open one's heart,
reveal sincerity to intimidate their courage,
and win their hearts with kindness.
Even if summoned while washing one's feet,
it would not be considered disrespectful.
Same as above.
Though a hundred hits depend on oneself,
the final call rests with the ruler.
From Gāo Dáfū.
In our dynasty,
a thousand-jūn ox
is controlled by a three-foot child.
It lowers its ears and submits,
unlike a monkey leaping freely in the mountains.
Why is this?
Because authority lies with humans.
From Sū Wén.
Those who rear animals
do not give them complete freedom.
Shepherds
remove the troublemakers from the flock
and whip the laggards.
Falconers keep their hawks hungry.
From Huángshān Wén.
Classic:
When those above lose the Way,
the people have long been dispersed.
From "Analects, Zǐzhāng".
It is like driving a horse without bit or bridle,
relying solely on whip and spur—
its uncontrollability is certain.
From "Family Sayings of Confucius".
Tight reins and frequent whipping
are not the way to drive a thousand-mile journey.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
If governance loses its way,
all under heaven will become cunning enemies.
From Yáng.
History:
Jìn's Xì Quē said: "If rebellion is not punished,
how can authority be shown?
If submission is not softened,
how can kindness be demonstrated?
Without authority or kindness,
how can virtue be displayed?"
From "Zuǒzhuàn, 7th Year of Wén".
Favorite concubines inside
plunder freely in the markets;
favored ministers outside
issue unauthorized orders in the borders.
From "Zuǒzhuàn, 20th Year of Zhāo".
Handling affairs perversely and erroneously,
losing proper governance.
From "Qián Hàn".
Holding the sword by the blade,
handing the hilt to Chǔ.
From "Western Hàn, Méi Fú's Biography".
Governing and controlling in wrong ways.
From "Tōngjiàn, Táng Dé's Annals".
Collection:
Driving a lame donkey without a whip—
what path can it reach?
From "Chǔ Cí".
If the reins are not controlled,
the yoke will break and the shafts shatter.
Same as above.
Classic:
If one served one's parents,
one avoids the names of grandparents.
If one did not serve one's parents,
one does not avoid grandparents' names.
From "Book of Rites, Qū Lǐ I".
Meaning orphans who never knew their parents
feel no obligation to avoid grandparents' names.
Father's father is called wángfù,
father's mother is called wángmǔ.
From "Ěryǎ".
History:
Zhèng Dāngshí's friends
were all of his grandfather's generation.
From "Western Hàn, His Biography".

History
Xún Yōu,
styled Wéndá,
his grandfather was Xún Tán.
Yōu was orphaned young,
and when Tán passed away,
a former subordinate Zhāng Tuī requested to guard Tán's tomb.
Yōu, then thirteen years old,
grew suspicious of him.
He said to his uncle Xún Qú:
"This official
has an unusual expression,
perhaps he intends to commit treachery."
Qú, realizing this, interrogated him.
It turned out he was a fugitive murderer,
and because of this, Yōu was regarded as extraordinary.
"Wèi Zhì."
Cáo Cāo was unrestrained in his youth.
His uncle repeatedly reported this to Sōng,
and Cāo resented it.
Later, he met his uncle on the road,
and feigned a distorted face and mouth.
The uncle reported this.
Sōng called Cāo and said:
"Your uncle said you had a stroke;
are you better now?"
Cāo replied:
"I never had a stroke,
but I've lost my uncle's favor,
so he deceived you."
． "Jìn Shū, Cáo Mán Zhuàn."
Wáng Zhàn,
styled Chǔchōng,
was the younger brother of Minister Wáng Hún.
His nephew Wáng Jì
looked down on him.
Once, Jì visited Zhàn
and saw the "Zhōu Yì".
He asked, "Uncle, what use is this to you?"
Zhàn replied, "When I'm unwell,
I occasionally read it."
"Occasionally" is sometimes written as "inwardly".
This is likely incorrect.
Jì asked him to explain,
and Zhàn analyzed its profound subtleties,
revealing remarkable insights.
Though Jì's talent surpassed Zhàn's,
he had shown no respect as a nephew,
but upon hearing his words,
he became reverent in heart and demeanor.
Wáng Zhàn possessed hidden virtues,
and his clan all thought him foolish.
Emperor Wǔ asked Jì, "Has your foolish uncle died yet?"
Jì replied, "My uncle is not foolish,"
and praised his excellence.
Same as above.

Same as above.

who by then had died.
Liú Xuàn argued that since she had no nurturing kindness,
he should not be relieved from his post for mourning.
Liú Zǐyì refuted him,
saying: "The 'Commentary' states: 'A stepmother
is like a birth mother.
She should, by virtue of her position alongside the father,
occupy the role of mother,
and the mourning rituals and staff
should be the same as for a birth mother.'
If the stepmother is in the father's household,
then the mourning is the same as for a birth mother.
If one claims she had no nurturing kindness
and treats her as a stranger,
what mourning should there be?
If mourning is observed, then heart-mourning applies;
how can it be different now?
To decree that he should not be relieved
is highly erroneous,
since birth and stepmothers are equal in closeness.
Thus, heart-mourning cannot differ;
if one argues the stepmother came
after the child had left,
and the mourning should be lighter,
checking the classics and commentaries,
no such text is found.
In the past, Wáng Bì from Chángshā,
in the late Hàn, went to the capital as a reporter.
Later, Wú and Wèi were cut off,
and Bì, in the inner state,
remarried and had a son, Chāng.
After Bì died,
Chāng became Chancellor of Dōngpíng
and only then learned that his mother in Wú had died.
He immediately requested to observe heavy mourning
and withdrew from his duties.
At that time, the debaters
did not consider this wrong.
Thus, between step and birth mothers,
there is no difference in sentiment.
If one insists on nurturing from birth for mourning rites, what of Wáng Chāng?
What more need be said?
Also, Jìn General Zhèngnán Yáng Hù had no son.

When Hù died,
Yī did not observe heavy mourning.
Hù's wife reported this to the court,
and Yī explained:
'Uncle raised me during his lifetime,
and I did not dare disobey.
But without my father's command,
I return to my birth family.'
Minister Péng Quán argued:

must have the father's command.
Without command, it is rebellion.'
Thereupon, an edict followed his view.
Thus, the system of heart-mourning

Moreover, the father's subsequent wife
gains the title of mother through the father.
If as you propose,
could one also have no heart-mourning for the birth father?

The matter was reported, and Zǐyì's argument was followed.

If a wife has matters to attend to,

if itchy, she dare not scratch;

was listed among the famous scholars south of the Miǎn River.

with yellow hair and dark skin,
but her talent is a match for yours."
Kǒngmíng agreed,
and Huáng sent her to him.
People of the time found it amusing,
and a local proverb arose: "Don't imitate Kǒngmíng choosing a wife,
who ended up with old Chéng's ugly daughter."

In biographies,
a wife may be dismissed for seven reasons: disobedience to parents,
childlessness,
licentiousness,
jealousy,
affliction with a foul disease,
garrulousness,
theft.
Disobedience to parents is due to opposing virtue;
childlessness means cutting off the lineage;
licentiousness disrupts the clan;
jealousy disrupts the household;
foul disease means she cannot participate in sacrifices;
garrulousness alienates kin;
theft violates righteousness.

The rites for being a good child are:
to warm in winter and cool in summer,
to settle in the evening and inquire in the morning,
and not to contend among peers.
. From "Jì Qūlǐ".
For those who are children,
even with three bestowals, carriages and horses are not to be received.
For those who are children,
their travels must have regularity,
their studies must have a profession,
and in constant speech, they do not refer to themselves as old.
For those who are children,
they do not occupy the main corner of the room,
sit in the center of the mat,
walk in the middle of the path,
or stand in the center of the doorway.
They do not climb heights,
approach depths,
criticize lightly,
or laugh frivolously.
They do not serve in darkness,
nor climb dangerous places,
fearing to bring disgrace upon their parents.
While parents are alive,
they do not pledge their lives to friends,
nor possess private wealth.
While parents are alive, their caps
and garments are not purely white.
When parents are ill,
those wearing caps do not comb their hair,
walk without swinging their arms,
speak without laziness,
do not play the qín or sè,
eat meat without changing its taste,
drink wine without altering their countenance,
laugh without showing their gums,
or get angry without cursing.
Same as above.
In serving one's parents,
if after three remonstrations they do not listen,
then one should weep and follow them.
. From "Jì Qūlǐ Xià".
When a parent is ill and
takes medicine,
the child should taste it first.
Same as above.
In serving parents, there is concealment
but no offense; attending to them closely,
without fixed methods, serving diligently,
and upon their death, observing mourning for three years.
From "Tángōng Shàng".
Those who have not taken office
dare not give gifts to others.
If giving gifts,
it must be by the command of father or elder brother.
They do not manage family wealth alone,
as giving means bestowing upon others.
Same as above.
Parents' clothing, quilts, mats, pillows, and small tables are not passed on,
but moved aside.
Their staffs and shoes
dare not be approached.
From "Nèizé".
In the presence of parents,
if there is a command,
respond with "yes" and answer respectfully.
Dare not belch, sneeze, cough, yawn, stretch, limp, lean, or glance askance;
dare not spit or sniffle;
if cold, dare not add layers;
if itchy, dare not scratch;
dare not bare the shoulders.
If parents have faults,
with subdued breath and pleasant expression,
advise them in a soft voice.
If the advice is not accepted,
maintain respect and filial piety.
If they are pleased, advise again;
if displeased, rather than offending the local community,
is it better to advise persistently?
Even after parents have passed away,
when intending to do good, think
of leaving parents a good name,
and then act decisively.
When intending to do wrong, think
of bringing shame upon parents,
and then refrain.
If a son is very fond of his wife,
but parents are displeased, he should divorce her.
If a son dislikes his wife,
but parents say she serves them well,
he should perform the duties of husband and wife,
without decline for life.
What parents love, he also loves;
what parents respect, he also respects,
even down to dogs and horses.
Same as above.
When parents are alive, in performing rites for others, refer to one's father.
If someone gives a gift,
refer to the father and bow in thanks.
Matters are unified under the尊 (zūn, elder).
. From "Jì Yùzǎo".
When called by father's command,
respond with "yes" and not "acknowledged".
If holding work,
drop it.
If food is in the mouth,
spit it out.
Run without delay.
When parents are old,
do not change directions when going out,
and return without exceeding the time.
If parents are ailing, one's expression should not be cheerful.
Same as above.
The body
is what parents have left behind.
In actions,
it is parents' legacy.
How dare one not be respectful?
From "Jìyì".
If parents love them, rejoice and never forget;
if parents dislike them, fear but hold no resentment;
if parents have faults, advise but do not oppose.
Not a single step is taken without remembering parents.
Hence, take the main road and not shortcuts,
use boats and do not swim.
Dare not endanger the body left by parents;
not a single word is spoken without remembering parents.
Hence, harsh words do not leave the mouth,
and angry words do not return to oneself.
Do not disgrace oneself,
nor shame one's parents.
A filial child with deep love
must have a harmonious spirit.
One with a harmonious spirit
must have a cheerful countenance.
One with a cheerful countenance
must have a gentle demeanor.
After parents have passed away,
conduct oneself carefully,
leaving no bad name for parents,
which can be called fulfilling to the end.
Parents give birth to one whole,
and one returns whole,
which can be called filial piety!
Same as above.
There are three ways for a child to serve parents:
in life, provide for them;
after death, mourn them;
after mourning, sacrifice to them.
From "Jìtǒng".
While parents are alive,
one dare not claim ownership of one's body,
nor keep private wealth.
From "Fāngjì".
Credit good deeds to parents,
and blame faults on oneself.
A gentleman overlooks his parents' faults
and respects their virtues.
Obey without resentment,
advise subtly without weariness,
labor without complaint.
While parents are alive,
do not call oneself old.
Speak of filial piety, not parental kindness;
within the household, jest
but do not sigh.
While parents are alive,
gifts do not include carriages and horses.
Same as above.
A benevolent person serves parents
as serving heaven.
From "Āigōng Wèn".
The body
is a branch of one's parents.
How dare one not be respectful?
If one cannot respect one's own body,
it harms one's parents.
Harming one's parents
is harming the root.
Same as above.
Dare not take on important matters alone,
thereby humbling oneself and honoring ancestors.
From "Guànyì".
Serve parents with gentle remonstrance;
if they do not heed your intent,
still respect and do not disobey,
laboring without complaint.
. From "Yǔ Lǐrén".
Thus, in the face of injustice,
a child must not fail to dispute with the father.
From "Xiàojīng".
The Master said: "In serving parents,
is it not about compliance?"
From "Zhōngyōng".
Child
A filial son does not flatter his parents.
"Zhuāngzǐ".
A filial son is not born in a household with a compassionate father.
"Shènzǐ".
As a child,
one should show reverence, love, and utmost refinement.
"Xúnzǐ".
Follow righteousness,
not necessarily one's father.
Ibid.
There are three instances where a filial son does not obey commands.
If he obeys, his parent will be in danger;
if he disobeys, his parent will be safe—
this is the loyalty of a filial son in not obeying.
If he obeys, his parent will be disgraced;
if he disobeys, his parent will be honored—
this is the righteousness of a filial son in not obeying.
If he obeys, he becomes like a beast;
if he disobeys, he cultivates refinement—
this is the respect of a filial son in not obeying.
"The Way of a Son".
In history,
Shǐ Zǐ was filial yet admonishing.
"Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāogōng Year 26".
Niè Zhèng said: "While my mother is alive,
I dare not pledge my life to anyone."
"Records of the Grand Historian, His Biography".
When a parent has a stern guest,
one rolls up
the sleeves and
wears a archer's armguard,
pronounced bèi.
Bowing
means bending.
It is read as jì,
same as "kneel",
meaning to kneel slightly.
Serving wine in front.
"Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Chún Yú Kūn".
Classic
Dreaming of bears and brown bears
is an omen of a son.
When a son is born,
he is laid to sleep on a bed.
He is dressed in robes,
and given a jade tablet to play with.
"Book of Songs".
History
Xú Líng's mother, Zāng Shì,
once dreamed of a five-colored cloud transforming into a phoenix,
which perched on her left shoulder.
Soon after, she gave birth to Líng.
At that time, there was a monk named Bǎo Zhì,
whom the world praised as enlightened.
When Líng was a few years old,
his family took him to see Bǎo Zhì,
who patted his head and said: "A stone from heaven,
a qílín indeed."
"History of the Southern Dynasties".
Biography
Wáng Zhèn'è was born on the fifth day of the fifth month,
and his family wanted to abandon him.
His grandfather, Wáng Měng, said: "In the past, Mèng Chángjūn was born on this day
and eventually became chancellor of Qí.
This child will revive our clan,
so name him Zhèn'è (Subdue Evil)."
"Summary of the Song Dynasty".
Collection
A boy should uphold the family,
from birth his eyes shine with spirit.
Fǔ Xuán's "Song of Yùzhāng".
The family declines and fortune is thin,
late in life I have a son.
"Selected Works, Memorial of Chenqing".
The jade tree grows new branches.
Wéi Yìngwù's poem.
Who would have thought the temples
(or "beard")
would turn to snow,
just as I see the palm holding a pearl.
"Collection of Bái Jūyì".
When can he feed me in return,
to nurture the white-headed crow together?
Moreover, there is hope to continue the family line,
why complain about having a son late?
Ibid.
A palm-pearl of a son at three years old,
a father of sixty with snow-white hair.
Ibid.
Uncertain who will lead the household,
but for now, spare the books from being given to others.
Liú Chángqīng.
Newborns sent by Lǎozi and Buddha,
all are heavenly qílín children.
Dù Fǔ's poem.
Colt of a steed,
chick of a phoenix.
Breed of Wòwā sweat-blood horses,
heavenly qílín child.
Among the crowd, seeing his fur and bones,
he is still a qílín child.
A single feather from a phoenix's nest.
Greedily gaining a new pearl in the palm.
Mǎ Fàn congratulating someone on having a son said: "Joyfully obtained a pearl in the palm."
See annotation in Dù Fǔ's poem.
Last year, a son was born named Tiāndīng,
intending for him to serve the nation in farming.
Hán Yù's "Poem for Lú Tóng".
Nursing below, outstanding and lofty,
peppercorns abundant, crying loudly.
The nurse holds the young child standing aside,
eyebrows and eyes like a painting, hair jet black,
skin like jade and snow, utterly adorable.
Ibid.

History
Initially, Shū Xiàng wished to marry a daughter of Shēn Gōng, but his mother wanted him to marry her own kin.
Shū Xiàng said, "My mother has many concubines but few children; I take warning from my maternal uncles."
《Zuǒ Zhuàn, 28th Year of Zhāo Gōng》.
Meaning the mother had many concubines, and the scarcity of half-siblings suggests the mother's nature was not broad-minded, etc.
Wéi Tāo memorialized: "In the 'Mourning Apparel' section, for maternal uncles, three months of light mourning; for maternal aunts and maternal grandparents, five months of minor mourning.
Maternal grandparents, being of high honor, share the same mourning as maternal aunts; while aunts and uncles are of the same rank, their mourning differs in weight.
For cousins of the maternal line, though kinship is not distant, if the bond is broken, no mourning is worn.
For aunts-in-law, though connected to the maternal clan, they do not receive the same mourning as those who shared the hearth.
I believe the ancient intent is not fully expressed; I propose elevating maternal grandparents to nine months of major mourning.
Maternal aunts and uncles should both have five months of minor mourning.
Maternal cousins and aunts-in-law should be elevated to the level of baring the arm and headband mourning.
《Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Dynasty》.
Wéi Shù argued: "The maternal kin compared to the paternal clan cannot be treated equally, that is clear."

Edict: "Since maternal aunts and uncles already wear minor mourning, aunts-in-law should not be fully downgraded; they should wear light mourning, and maternal cousins should wear bared arm and headband mourning."
《Táng Dynasty Records》.

According to Qín law,

． From "Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of Fàn Jū".
Hé Wǔ recommended upright and virtuous scholars,

From "His Biography".
Sòng Hóng recommended Huán Tán,
and the emperor ordered Tán to play the zither,
growing fond of its elaborate melodies.
Hóng heard of this
and was displeased.
Waiting until Tán exited the palace,
he sat in his office in full court attire.
The emperor sent an official to summon him,
but when Tán arrived, Hóng did not offer him a seat
and reproached him,
saying, "Can you reform yourself?
Or shall I have the chancellor enforce the law upon you?"
Tán kowtowed,
apologizing for a long time,
before Hóng dismissed him.
Later, when the emperor had Tán play the zither again,
Tán, upon seeing Hóng,
lost his usual composure.
The emperor found it strange and asked why,
whereupon Hóng rose from his mat,
removed his cap,
and apologized, saying, "The reason I recommended Huán Tán
was in the hope that he would guide Your Majesty with loyalty and integrity,
yet he has caused the court to indulge in the music of Zhèng.
This is my fault."
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Eastern Hàn, Reign of Emperor Guāngwǔ".
Lǐ Chōng initially recommended Lǐ Biāo,
but once Biāo felt he had gained the ruler's favor,
he no longer relied on Chōng.
Chōng gradually distanced himself from him,
only bowing respectfully in public settings
without any further reverence as a patron.
Chōng grew increasingly resentful,
and eventually compiled all of Biāo's past and present faults,
confining Biāo in the Department of State Affairs.
He submitted a memorial impeaching Biāo for arrogance and lack of restraint,
elevating himself and disregarding others; his words
might sound like those of ancient loyal and benevolent sages,
but examining
(some texts read "comparing")
his actions,
he is truly a villain of flattery and violence in the world.
From "Qí, Reign of Emperor Míng".

In the Tang Dynasty, Lǐ Jiàng served as chancellor under Emperor Dézōng.
People accused him of favoring his fellow examination graduate,
Xǔ Jìtóng.
Emperor Dézōng asked him:
"Do people naturally have affection for those who passed the imperial examination in the same year?"
Lǐ Jiàng replied:
"Fellow graduates are people from all corners of the realm
who coincidentally passed the examination in the same year.
Some only became acquainted after succeeding in the examinations—
what affection could there be?
If someone is truly talented,
even if they were among my own brothers or nephews,
I would still recommend employing them,
let alone a fellow graduate?"
. "Comprehensive Mirror of the Tang Dynasty".

. From "Zuo Zhuan, Seventh Year of Duke Zhao".
No action is more disgraceful than bringing shame upon one's ancestors.
. From "Western Han, Sīmǎ Qiān".
Lǐ Líng surrendered alive and brought ruin to his family's reputation.
From "Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān".
Pronunciation: tuí.
At that time, Emperor Chéng of Hàn had no heir,
and governance was controlled by the Wáng clan.
Liú Xiàng then submitted a sealed memorial,
vehemently admonishing
that the Wáng and Liú clans could not coexist,
for if below there is the stability of Mount Tài,
then above there is the peril of piled eggs.
After Liú Xiàng's death,
his son Xīn was recommended by Wáng Mǎng as a court gentleman,
and when Wáng Mǎng held power,
he retained Xīn as Right Assistant.
In the first year of the Jiànpíng era,
he changed his name to Xiù,
and when Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
Xīn became the State Preceptor.
. From "Biography in Western Han History".
To be someone's descendant,
and to guard their achievements,
acting like this—is it not a betrayal?
. From "Comprehensive Mirror, Chapter 33, Annals of Emperor Chéng of Hàn".
Zǔ Yuē
was the younger brother of Zǔ Tì.
After Zǔ Tì's death,
he succeeded Tì as General of Western Pacification
and Inspector of Yùzhōu. When Wáng Dūn raised troops,
Yuē returned
to defend the capital.
He considered his reputation and seniority no less than Xì and Biàn's,
and hoped to establish a private secretariat,
but many of his memorials and requests were not approved,
so he harbored resentment.
When Sū Jùn raised troops,
he推崇 Yuē,
and Yuē, hearing this, was greatly pleased.
After Jùn captured the capital, he appointed Yuē as Palace Attendant,
but later Yuē fled to Shí Lè and died.
. From "Biography in Jin History".
Fáng and Dù toiled diligently all their lives,
barely able to establish their family's standing.
But encountering unworthy sons,
it was completely overturned and lost.
. From "Comprehensive Mirror, Tang Records, Chapter 300".
Lǐ Jì, ill, said to his younger brother Bì: "I have seen Fáng Xuánlíng, Dù Rúhuì, and Gāo Jìfǔ all laboriously built their family's standing,
hoping to leave it to their descendants,
yet all were ruined by their unworthy sons."
. From "New Book of Tang, Biography".
Dí Rénjié served as Governor of Wèi Province,
implementing benevolent governance,
for which the common people established a lifetime shrine for him.
Later, his son Jǐnghuī became Registrar of Wèi Province,
but was greedy and cruel,
causing people to suffer,
so they destroyed his statue.
. From "Comprehensive Mirror, Chapter 207, Emperor Zhōngzōng of Táng".
Fáng Xuánlíng's son, Yí'ài,
married the daughter of Emperor Tàizōng of Táng.
Yí'ài was arrogant and unrestrained,
plotting to depose his elder brother Yízhí
and seize his title and fief.
During the Yǒnghuī era,
he falsely accused Yízhí of disrespecting him.
Emperor Gāozōng ordered Chángsūn Wújì to investigate the matter,
thus uncovering the conspiracy between the princess and Yí'ài to rebel.
Yí'ài was executed.
. From "Old Book of Tang, Biography".
Dù Rúhuì's son Gòu inherited the title and became Governor of Cí Province.
Implicated in his younger brother Hé's plot to rebel,
he was exiled to the southern regions.
Same as above.
Biographies
Hán Chǎng,
son of Hán Yù.
His nature was dull and inferior;
he served as Collator in the Jíxián Hall.
Historical records mentioned a "gold-root carriage,"
but Chǎng, misunderstanding it entirely,
changed "root" to "silver."
. From "Shàngshū Gùshí".
Cross-reference "Ignorance".
Unworthy descendants undergo three transformations: the first into locusts,
meaning they sell estates to eat;
the second into bookworms,
meaning they sell books to eat;
the third into tigers,
meaning they sell slaves and maids to eat.
Such consumers—
in which era are they absent?
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Collection
The family line is not prosperous.
Rěn Yànshēng, "Letter".
Alas, your lineage emerges
from a household so lofty.
Yet you do not cultivate your conduct,
rare are those as base and shallow as you.
Why not feel shame before your ancestors,
brazenly unaware of return?
Hán Yù's writings.
Classics
Meeting with misfortune in the family.
. From "The Book of Songs, Mǐn Yú Xiǎo Zǐ".
History
Luán, Xì, Xū, Yuán, Hú, Xù, Qìng, and Bó descended to the status of servants.
. From "Zuo Zhuan, Third Year of Duke Zhao".
Shū Xiàng said: "Of the eleven clans of Xì's lineage,
only the Yángshé clan remains."
Same as above.
Wèi Zhēng's great-great-grandson, Wèi Chóu, was extremely poor,
and mortgaged the old residence to someone for money.
. From "Comprehensive Mirror, Tang Records, Chapter 53".
The emperor
halted Shū Yù's marriage,
and toppled the erected stele,
seeing his family in decline.
. From "Táng History, Biography of Wèi Zhēng".
Collection
The family declines and blessings are thin.
. From "Selections, Lǐ Lìngbó's 'Memorial Expressing Feelings'".
To inherit the legacy of our ancestors—
among the grandsons, only you remain,
among the sons, only I.
The Hán family for two generations,
only this remains.
Hán Yù's writings, "Eulogy for My Nephew, the Thirteenth, Lǎo Chéng".
Classics
His father stole a sheep,
and the son testified against him.
From "The Analects".
History
Yuè Yíng said: "A retainer's minister can exert effort for the royal house,
but his son Yǎn cannot preserve the labors of his father."
. From "Zuo Zhuan, Twenty-First Year of Duke Xiāng".
Sòng Huá Ŏu said: "Your servant's former minister, Dū,
offended against Duke Shāng of Sòng,
and his name is recorded in the annals of the feudal lords."
. From "Zuo Zhuan, Fifteenth Year of Duke Wén".
Classics
He plans for his descendants,
to protect and assist his sons.
From "The Book of Songs".
Leaving abundance for later generations.
. From "The Book of Documents, Announcement of Zhònghuǐ".
Able to prosper his descendants.
From "The Book of Songs".
Initiating achievements by oneself,
diligent and untiring,
to set an example for one's descendants.
. From "The Book of Documents, Charge to Cài Zhòng".
May his body be healthy and strong,
and his descendants meet with good fortune.
. From "The Book of Documents, Great Plan".
Masters
Not leaving wealth for sons and grandsons.
. From "Lièzǐ, Yáng Zhū".
History
Thus they inherited Heaven's blessings,
and their descendants relied on them.
. From Zuo Zhuan, 28th Year of Duke Zhao.
When Yànzǐ was near death,
he carved a pillar and stored writings inside,
telling his wife: "The pillar records the days,
show it to our son when he comes of age."
From Yànzǐ Chūnqiū.
Shūxiàng said: "Formerly, Luán Wǔzǐ had not even the land of one battalion,
his office did not possess the full ancestral vessels,
yet he displayed his virtuous conduct,
followed the established laws,
and thereby avoided calamity.
When Huánzǐ became arrogant and extravagant,
his greed knew no bounds,
he should have met with disaster,
but he relied on Wǔ's virtue,
and thus ended his days."
. From Guóyǔ, Jìnyǔ.
Píng Dàng became chancellor,
and the emperor wished to enfeoff him.
Dàng was gravely ill and did not respond to the summons,
someone asked if Dàng had no concern for his descendants?
Dàng said: "I hold high office yet have failed in my duties,
rising from plain meals,
to receive a marquis' seal,
then returning to lie down and die,
my death would leave residual guilt.
My not rising now,
is precisely for my descendants' sake."
From Qián Hànshū.
Cross-reference "Retiring Modestly".
Shū Guǎng requested retirement,
the emperor bestowed twenty catties of gold.
Someone urged Guǎng to use the gold to establish estates for his descendants,
Guǎng said: "Am I so senile
as to not think of my descendants?
But we already have old fields and huts,
if my descendants work diligently there,
it will suffice for food and clothing like ordinary people.
Now to add more for surplus,
would only teach my descendants idleness!
If worthy, more wealth damages their ambition;
if foolish, more wealth increases their faults.
Moreover, the wealthy
attract others' resentment.
Since I cannot educate my descendants,
I wish not to increase their faults and generate resentment."
. From Xī Hànshū, Shū Guǎng biography.
Wěi Xuánchéng succeeded his father Xián as chancellor,
the folks of Zōu and Lǔ sang: "Leaving your son a box full of gold,
is not as good as teaching him one classic."
. From Xī Hànshū, his biography.
Emperor Wén cautioned the crown prince: "Should emergency arise,
Zhōu Yàfū is truly fit to command troops."
When the revolt of seven states was reported,
the emperor appointed Commandant of the Center Zhōu Yàfū as Grand Commandant General,
to attack Wú and Chǔ.
. From Tōngjiàn vol.16, Hàn Jǐngdì chronicle.
Xuē Guǎngdé returned to his county,
his comfortable carriage,
he passed down to his descendants as an honor.
. From Tōngjiàn vol.28, Hàn Yuándì chronicle.
Páng Gōng left plowing at the ridge,
his wife and children weeded before him.
Liú Biǎo asked why the gentleman labored in fields but refused official salary,
what would he leave to his descendants?
Páng Gōng said: "The world leaves danger to theirs,
I alone leave safety to mine,
though what is left differs,
it cannot be said nothing is left."
From Hòu Hànshū.
Yáng Zhèn was incorruptible by nature,
his descendants often ate plain food and walked.
Some wanted him to start estates,
Zhèn said: "To have posterity call them pure officials,
this legacy I leave my descendants,
is it not abundant!"
. From Dōng Hànshū, his biography.
When Sòng Gāozǔ was obscure,
he farmed personally at Dāntú,
upon receiving the mandate,
some farming tools remained,
he ordered them preserved,
to leave to later generations.
. From Nánshǐ, his biography.
Zhāng Xù said to Qí's Liǔ Shìlóng: "You should leave a pure name to your descendants!"
He replied: "Beyond one's person, what more is needed?
If descendants lack talent,
it will become a source of strife.
If they have talent,
better than classics is nothing."
From Nánshǐ.
Gāo Huān said: "Only Mùróng Shàozōng
can match Hóu Jǐng.
I deliberately did not honor him,
to leave him for you."
. From Tōngjiàn vol.159, Liáng Gāozǔ.
Cross-reference "Foresight".
Fáng Yànqiān told his son Xuánlíng: "All become rich from salaries,
I alone remain poor as an official.
What I leave my descendants
is purity alone."
From Suíshū, his biography.
The emperor told the crown prince: "Lǐ Shìjì has ample talent and wisdom,
but you share no bond with him,
I fear he won't submit wholeheartedly.
I now demote him;
if he departs promptly,
after my death,
you may appoint him as Púyè,
and trust him closely.
If he hesitates and looks back,
you should kill him."
. From Tōngjiàn vol.199, Táng Tàizōng chronicle.
Zhāng Jiāzhēn did not accumulate family wealth,
some urged him to buy fields and homes,
Jiāzhēn said:
"As chancellor, highly honored,
why fear cold or hunger?
If I offend the law,
even with fields and homes, they'd be useless.
I've seen court officials amass fertile lands,
upon their death,
just becoming funds for worthless descendants' feasts,
I won't follow this,"
hearers approved.
. From Tōngjiàn, Táng Xuánzōng chronicle.
Cross-reference "Contentment".
For renowned families and great clans,
none but stem from ancestors
loyal, filial, respectful, and frugal,
thus establishing them.
. From Tángshū, Liǔ Pín biography.
Yìng Shào said: "The record
of Luán
—worthy yet covering darkness."
Commentary on Yōutōng Fù,
see Wénxuǎn.
Our family has been poor and frugal for generations,
following ancestral instruction
always fearing property would make descendants idle.
Thus our home lacks even land for gathering firewood.
Yuán Zhěn.
Later, if I possess gold and jade,
I surely won't hoard them for you.
Cuī Zhāoshēng, Cuī Yún, Lǐ Jiānshēng, Kū Láng.
Piling coins by the hundred,
the house collapses, how wild the dispersal.
Now though not immediately dying,
starving and freezing, nearly stiffened.
Dù Mù.
Cross-reference "Failure to Inherit".
Classic
If not taken now,
later will surely worry descendants.
From Lúnyǔ.
History
Wǔzǐ's beneficence faded,
while Yǎn's resentment truly manifested.
From Zuǒzhuàn.
Qín Shǐhuáng's palaces so magnificent,
yet his descendants couldn't find a hut to dwell in;
his roads so splendid,
yet his descendants couldn't find a path to tread on;
his burials so lavish,
yet his descendants couldn't find a weed-covered mound to bury in.
. From Hànshū, Jiǎ Shān's "Zhìyán".
Collection
Yìng Shào said: "Yǎn, wicked, harmed the full."
. See Wénxuǎn Yōutōng Fù commentary.
Swallow wings unlike,
ending as starving souls.
From Liú Bīnkè Collection.
Behind closed doors, not understanding,
planting peach and plum trees everywhere,
only to hear thorny caltrops growing.
From Báijūyì Collection.
Cross-reference "Retribution".
Classic
Below the mountain is thunder,
symbolizing Nourishment;
the noble person thereby guards his speech
and moderates his eating and drinking.
. _Yì Jīng_, Hexagram Yí.
The noble person fasts and purifies himself,
dwelling he must cover his body,
do not be agitated.
Cease music and beauty,
do not let them approach,
make flavors mild,
do not seek harmony,
moderate desires and cravings,
settle the mind and vital energy.
.. _Lǐ Jì_, Yuè Lìng, Mid-Summer.
Ears and eyes clear and sharp,
blood and vital energy harmonious and balanced.
. _Lǐ Jì_, Yuè Jì.
Depraved sounds and chaotic sights do not linger in ears and eyes,
perverse music and improper rites do not connect with the mind's workings,
lazy, arrogant, evil, and corrupt energies are not set upon the body.
Same as above.
The firm energy does not become anger,
the soft energy does not become fear,
the four (energies) flow freely and interact within,
and manifest outwardly in actions.
Same as above.
If one does not allow the mind to go astray,
how can harmful energy connect with it!
Same as above.
Mencius said:
Maintain your will,
do not abuse your vital energy.
_Mèngzǐ_.
For nourishing the heart, nothing is better than having few desires.
_Mèngzǐ_.
Preserve your mind,
nourish your nature.
_Mèngzǐ_.
Do not, through likes and dislikes,
injure your body internally.
. _Zhuāngzǐ_, chapter Dé Chōng Fú.
Combine the essence of the six energies.
Even and easy, calm and mild,
then worry and hatred cannot enter,
and evil energy cannot assail.
Thus one's virtue remains whole and spirit undiminished.
Also said: "Pure and unadulterated, without mixture,
tranquil and unified, without change,
detached and non-active,
acting in accordance with the movements of Heaven,
this is the way to nourish the spirit."
Also said: "The spirit and essence extend in all four directions,
reaching everywhere without limit."
. _Zhuāngzǐ_, chapter Kè Yì.
Evil and foul energies,
how
(one version reads "cannot")
can they connect?
_Xúnzǐ_.
One with a clear spirit,
desires and cravings cannot disturb.
. _Huáinánzǐ_, chapter Chù Zhēn Xùn.
Calmness and harmony nourishing the spirit brings inner peace;
clarity and emptiness housing the mind prevents external seduction;
with spirit calm and mind clear, the body remains unburdened.
_Liúzǐ_.
History:
Zǐ Chǎn said: "Regulate and disperse his vital energy,
do not let it become blocked, stagnant, or congealed,
so as to expose his body (to illness)."
. _Zuǒ Zhuàn_, Zhāo 1.
Nourish the essence and let the spirit roam.
. _Western Hàn Shū_, biography of Dōngfāng Shuò.
One who cultivates the body,
considers refining the spirit as precious.
. _Eastern Hàn Shū_, Lǐ Gù.
Mèng Shuō said: "One who cultivates his nature,
should not let good words leave his mouth."
_Xīn Táng Shū_.
Sūn Sīmiǎo said: "One who cultivates his nature,
must first know self-discipline."
_Xīn Táng Shū_.
Liǔ Gōngdù said: "I do not use my qì sea to warm cold things,
nor cook raw things,
nor use my primordial qì to fuel joy or anger,
(thus I) reached eighty-nine years of age."
Same as above.
Sūn Sīmiǎo said: "One should not take medicine without cause,
as medicine has biased assistance,
which can imbalance the visceral energies."
. _Táng Shū_, biography of Péi Yíng.
Biographies record:
To nourish the spirit,
one must first nourish the vital energy.
_Xiūzhēn Mìjué_.
Collection:
The noble person knows the body relies on the spirit to stand,
and the spirit requires the body to exist,
understanding that the principle of life is easily lost,
and knowing that a single fault can harm life.
Therefore, cultivate nature to preserve the spirit,
pacify the mind to protect the whole body,
let love and hate not dwell in emotion,
let worry and joy not linger in thought,
serenely unaffected, the body's energy becomes harmonious and balanced.
Jī Shūyè's _Yǎngshēng Lùn_.
Nourish nature and prolong life.
Jī Shūyè's _Yōufèn Shī_.
May you, Prince, cherish your jade-like body,
that we both may enjoy the age of yellowed hair (old age).
Cáo Zǐjiàn's _Zèng Báimǎ Wáng Biāo_.
I study the methods of nourishing life,
rejecting glory and splendor,
abandoning rich flavors.
. _Wén Xuǎn_, Jué Jiāo Lùn.
Not loving his body,
but sparing his spirit.
. _Wén Xuǎn_, Yùn Mìng Lùn.
Reduce reading to preserve eyesight,
simplify affairs to nourish the mind-king.
Liú Bīnkè.
Nourish nature and preserve life,
partake of jade and drink dew.
_Táng Wén Cuì_.
Newly bathed, limbs feel free,
sleeping alone, spirit and soul are at peace.
Bái Lètiān.
Rinse and sip sweet fluids,
immerse and swim in harmonious energy.
_Táng Wén Cuì_.
Preserve harmony and spare the spirit.
Same as above.
Concentrate harmony and preserve the spirit.
Same as above.
Our dynasty:
Sweep clean body and mind,
bathe and cleanse spirit and energy.
_Dōngpō Jí_.
Using neither shānxiōng nor wheat yeast,
walking mud and sleeping dew, ultimately without illness.
_Lúan Chéng_.
Nourishing vital energy is like nourishing a child.
_Dōngpō Jí_.
The Master
Confucius said: "There are three kinds of death that are not due to fate,
but are taken by oneself.
Sleeping and rising at improper times,
eating and drinking without moderation,
overexertion or idleness beyond measure,
disease will kill such a person."
. _Jiā Yǔ_, Wǔ Yí Jiě.
The body labored without rest will deteriorate,
the essence used without cease will toil,
toil leads to exhaustion.
. _Zhuāngzǐ_, chapter Tiān Yùn.
One should not use limitless knowledge
to drive a body with limits.
_Zhuāngzǐ_.
Cross-reference "Admonition and Warning".
If ears and eyes indulge in the pleasures of music and beauty,
then the five viscera will be agitated and unsettled.
The five viscera agitated and unsettled,
then the blood and vital energy will surge and swirl without rest.
Blood and vital energy surging without rest,
then the spirit will gallop outside and not remain guarded.
Galloping outside and not guarded,
then when fortune or misfortune arrive,
even if as large as a mountain,
one will have no way to recognize them.
. _Huáinánzǐ_, chapter Jīngshén Xùn.
An agitated spirit causes the heart to waver,
a wavering heart injures the body.
_Liúzǐ_.
Eyes loving colorful sights are called the axe that hacks one's nature,
ears delighting in depraved sounds are called the drum that assaults the heart,
the mouth craving flavors are called the medicine that rots the intestines,
the nose pleased by fragrances are called the smoke that chokes the throat,
the body comfortable in carriages and teams is called the mechanism that summons collapse.
_Liúzǐ_.
Cross-reference "Admonition and Warning".
History
When the spirit is overused, it becomes exhausted;
when the body is overworked, it becomes worn out.
With both body and spirit in turmoil,
to desire longevity matching heaven and earth
is something I have never heard of.
"The Autobiography of Grand Historian".
Rich foods and delicacies ruin one's palate,
music and women ruin one's hearing,
lofty halls and deep chambers,
granaries, treasuries, and servants ruin one's inner self,
pleasures and feasting ruin one's heart.
"Jiǎ Yì's Five Lures from the Book of Former Hàn".
To expose one's delicate jade-like body
to the vexations of toil and trouble
is not the way to preserve
the foundation of longevity.
"Comprehensive Mirror, Chapter 34, Annals of Hàn Emperor Xuān".
Excessive memorization harms the heart,
excessive speech depletes vital energy.
When heart and energy are internally impaired,
and body and spirit externally depleted,
though initially unnoticed,
over time it becomes detrimental.
"Book of Táng, Biography of Liú Jì".
People often say one bout of anger cannot harm one's nature,
one episode of grief cannot injure one's body,
thus indulging lightly and recklessly.
This is like ignoring the benefit of a single irrigation
while expecting fine grain from drought-stricken sprouts.
Jī Kāng's "Essay on Nourishing Life".
When the spirit is agitated within, the form deteriorates without.
Same as above.
The five emotions have already been wounded,
how can one naturally grow old?
Mèng Jiāo.
People fail to perceive
beyond the five grains,
indulging in music and beauty,
eyes bewildered by colors,
ears pursuing lewd tunes,
flavors scorching their organs,
alcohol boiling their intestines and stomach,
fragrances rotting their marrow,
anger and joy perverting their vital energy,
worry and thought consuming their spirit,
sorrow and happiness damaging their inner harmony.
With such a small body assaulted
not from one direction but easily depleted,
facing enemies both internal and external,
the body is not wood or stone—
how can it last long?
Same as above.
Medicine is for curing illness,
not for daily consumption.
Moreover, metals and minerals are intensely potent and toxic,
further intensified by fiery energy,
likely more than human organs can endure.
"Comprehensive Mirror, Chapter 241, Táng Emperor Mùzōng".
Sūn Sīmiǎo once said:
"Medicinal properties have biased effects,
causing imbalance in the organ energies."
"Comprehensive Mirror, Chapter 243, Táng Emperor Mùzōng".
Accumulation of slight harms leads to damage,
accumulation of damage leads to decline.
"Essay on Nourishing Life".
Historical Records
Rich meats and strong wines, sought for self-strengthening,
are called:
"food that rots the intestines."
"Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals".
The skin's energy dissipates inwardly,
like the waves at the tail drain;
the spirit and will are injured outwardly,
akin to the trees on Niú Mountain.
"The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons".
Anthology
Riding in carriages and litters is called the mechanism of paralysis and atrophy,
deep chambers and cool palaces are called the媒介 of fevers and chills,
bright teeth and fine brows are called the axe that hacks at nature,
sweet, crisp, rich, and strong foods are called the medicine that corrodes the intestines.
"Seven Stimuli from the Anthology".
Combining ice and fire to wage war,
only torments one's own body.
Bái Jūyì.
Our Dynasty
Frying and boiling the heart, spleen, stomach, and kidneys,
has turned my hair to autumn frost in surprise.
"Collection of Lúanchéng".
Classics
Shēn Bó, a loyal minister,
did not wish to leave the royal house.
Annotation to "Shīsōng, Song of Shōng Gāo".
Though your body is abroad,
your heart is never absent from the royal house.
"Book of Documents, Announcement of King Kāng".
Former minister Bǎo Héng said:
"If I do not make my sovereign a Yáo or Shùn,
my heart feels ashamed,
as if whipped in the marketplace."
"Book of Documents, Charge to Yuè, Part 2".
King Wǔ fell ill,
unwell, the Duke of Zhōu
built three altars on the same field.
Praying with a scroll, he said:
"Let Dàn take his place."
"Book of Documents, Golden Coffer".
The Master said:
"Serving a ruler, one should desire to remonstrate, not to expose."
The Book of Songs says:
"In my heart, I love him,
why not speak of it?
I hold it in my heart,
never forgetting it day after day."
"Book of Rites, Biǎo Jì".
Praise should be attributed to the ruler,
faults to oneself.
"Book of Rites, Fáng Jì".
Shēn Shēng, heir of Jìn, sent a message to Hú Tū:
"My lord is old,
my brother young,
the state faces many troubles.
If you, Bó, do not come out to aid my lord,
but if you do, Shēn Shēng would be blessed."
Shēn Shēng accepted the charge and died.
"Book of Rites, Tán Gōng, Part 1".
Masters
Unless it is the way of Yáo and Shùn,
I dare not present it before the king.
"Mencius, Gōngsūn Chǒu, Part 2".
I tarried three nights before leaving Zhòu,
and in my heart, it still felt too hasty.
I hoped the king might change,
and if he did, he would surely recall me.
But after leaving Zhòu,
the king did not pursue me,
and then I felt a vast resolve to return home.
Even so,
how could I abandon the king?
"Mencius".
Failing to gain the ruler's favor heats the heart.
"Mencius".
In the state of Sòng, there was a farmer
who often wore hemp padding,
barely enough to pass the winter.
Come spring, working in the east,
he basked in the sun,
unaware of the world's great mansions and warm rooms,
or silken waddings and furs of fox and raccoon.
Turning to his wife, he said:
"The warmth of the sun on my back—
no one knows of it;

During the Kāiyuán era,
a Dàoshi named Lǚ Wēng passed through Hándān,
and stayed at an inn.
A young man from the city, Lú Shēng,
was also staying at the same inn.
The innkeeper was steaming huángliáng millet to share,
and when it was cooked,
Lú, unaware,
heaved a long sigh.
Lǚ asked him about it,
and he explained: "I have suffered hardships in this life."
Lǚ took a pillow from his bag,
and handed it to Lú, saying: "Pillow this,
and you will achieve glory and fulfillment as you wish."
Lú bowed his head and only remembered entering the hole of the pillow,
then arriving at his home.
Soon, he passed the imperial exams with high honors,
served in high offices,
and for fifty years, moved between positions as a general and a minister.
His sons and grandsons all held prominent official posts,
unmatched in glory and prosperity.
He submitted a memorial saying: "I am over eighty years old,
have held the three highest offices,
but have failed to repay the deep favor,
and now bid farewell to this sage era forever."
That evening, he died.
Lú Shēng stretched and woke up,
with Lǚ Wēng beside him,
and the huángliáng millet was not yet cooked.
Lú thanked him, saying: "This, sir, is how you curb my desires;
I dare not refuse your teaching."
He bowed twice and left.
Chén Hàn's "Collection of Strange Tales".
Chún Yú Fén lived in Guǎnglíng,
with an ancient locust tree south of his house.
He often drank heavily under it,
and once fell ill from drunkenness.
Two friends helped him back to lie down in the eastern wing, where he dreamed.
Two envoys in purple clothes said: "The king of Huái'ān Kingdom invites you."
Chún Yú followed the two envoys into a carriage.
They pointed to the ancient locust tree and entered a hole.
A large city with vermilion gates was inscribed: "Great Huái'ān Kingdom."
A rider called out: "The imperial son-in-law has arrived from afar."
They led Chún Yú into a grand hall,
where he saw a man in plain white attire,
wearing a crimson flowered crown,
and was told to bow to the king.
The king said: "Previously, following your honored father's command,
I promised my daughter Yáo Fāng to serve you as your wife."
Several dozen fairy maidens,
playing music,
held candles to guide them,
with golden and emerald curtains,
exquisitely continuous.
They reached a gate named "Xiūyí Palace",
where a woman called "Princess Golden Branch" looked like a celestial being.
They celebrated the wedding,
and their affection grew daily.
The king said: "The affairs of my Nánkē Commandery are in disarray;
I must trouble you to govern it."
He ordered officials to provide gold, jade, brocades,
servants, concubines, carriages, and horses,
displayed along the broad road,
to bid farewell to the princess.
The queen cautioned her daughter: "Chún Yú Láng is of a stern nature
and fond of drink;
the way of a wife values gentleness and obedience.
Serve him well."
After several days,
they reached the commandery.
Officials, monks, Daoists, and musicians came to welcome them.
He dismounted,
observed local customs,
and investigated hardships,
bringing great order to the commandery,
for twenty years in all.
The people built a shrine in his honor,
the king granted him a noble title and lands,
and he rose to the highest ministerial rank,
fathering five sons and two daughters,
with unmatched glory and prosperity.
The princess fell ill and passed away.
Chún Yú requested to escort the funeral to the capital; the king and queen, in plain clothes, wept bitterly in the suburbs,
with full ceremonial guards, feather canopies, and music,
burying the princess at Pánlóng Ridge.
Chún Yú, as a noble relative, grew increasingly powerful.
Someone submitted a memorial,
saying celestial signs indicated a great terror for the kingdom,
the capital would move,
and the ancestral temple would collapse,
with the trouble lying within the court walls.
Contemporary opinion attributed this to Chún Yú's extravagance.
The king thus ordered Chún Yú: "You may return to your hometown for a while,
to see your relatives.
Your grandchildren will stay here;
do not worry."
He again sent two envoys to escort him out of a hole,
whereupon he woke to see his servant sweeping the courtyard,
and his two friends washing their feet by the couch.
The setting sun had not yet disappeared,
the remaining wine in the west wall,
was still clear by the east window.
He then went with his two friends to search under the ancient locust tree,
where a hole was clear and bright,
large enough to hold a couch.
Above was soil,
formed like city walls, towers, and palaces.
There were several hú of ants,
with two large ants having white wings
and red heads—
these were the king of Huái'ān Kingdom.
Exploring another hole,
straight along a southern branch,
a group of ants also resided there—
this was Nánkē Commandery.
Yet another hole,
twisted like a dragon or snake,
with a small mound over a foot high—
this was Pánlóng Ridge.
Chún Yú reflected with emotion,
and quickly had the holes covered.
That night, a storm arose,
and by morning, looking at the holes,
he found the ants had disappeared.
No one knew where they had gone.
The kingdom's great terror,
and the capital's migration,
this was its proof.
Ibid.
