white hair and wrinkled face await专门.
From the Táng Wén Cuì.
High reputation is hard to maintain.
Liú Chángqīng.
Heavy power is hard to hold long,
high position's influence easily穷尽.
Fullness is the peak of things,
aging the end of fate's count.
These four are like bandits,
attacking day and night.
The favored guard against regret and blame,
the powerful harbor worry and fear.
To those in high-canopied carriages,
fear it's not true富贵.
Close to the sun, favor though heavy,
cloud-high, influence劫孤.
Turn over and fall from the heavens,
misstep and tumble into the mud.
Obscurity is the medicine for preserving self,
brightness the weapon that hacks nature.
Don't mistake complexity for wisdom,
nor rashness for noble simplicity.
Fortunate to tread smooth paths,
do not follow crooked ways.
Don't raise a lean colt,
don't keep a young singing girl.
The outcome is right before your eyes,
if you don't believe, just look.
When the horse fattens, it gallops away,
when the girl grows, she sings and dances.
In three to five years,
you'll hear she has a new master.
Ask between old and new masters,
who enjoys and who suffers.
Cross-referenced in "Preparing Ground for Others."
Ask the owners of ponds and terraces,
mostly they are generals and ministers.
Never setting foot there in their lives,
only unrolling paintings to view.
Moths should stay far from lamps and candles,
rabbits avoid nets and snares.
Fighting over snail's antennae,
gaining but an ox hair.
Don't dislike a narrow place with small forest pavilion,
don't resent a poor home with meager livelihood.
Many grand gates lock wide estates,
whose owners never return till old.
I observe the powerful,
suffering, sacrificing self for things.
Hands scorching, blazing outwardly,
treading ice, trembling inwardly.
Must remove the obstacle of self-love,
don't become a prisoner of home attachment.
Fame is a public vessel, take not much,
profit is personal disaster, seek little.
Regret then, what use biting the navel?
Powerful gates and key roads are personal disasters,
retired grounds and idle living harbor fewer misfortunes.
Don't dwell on past events under bright moonlight,
it harms your complexion and shortens your years.
All from the Collected Works of Bái Shìláng.
If dwelling doesn't keep its measure,
then lofty buildings and high towers assault it.
If sight and hearing don't keep their measure,
then seductive sounds and beautiful colors assault them.
If joy and anger don't keep their measure,
then excessive rewards and cruel punishments assault them.
If hobbies and pleasures don't keep their measure,
then goods that hinder conduct,
and instruments that unsettle the mind assault them.
If advice and contributions don't keep their measure,
then slanderous words and schemes of extortion assault them.
If methods and arts don't keep their measure,
then recipes for immortality and ways to avoid life assault them.
Thus being so,
how can one not fortify the inner guard more than city walls,
and defend against external assaults more than against bandits and invaders?
From the Collected Works of Bái Lètiān.
All know the enemy's enmity,
but not how great the benefit can be.
All know the enemy's harm,
but not how immense the advantage.
Qín had the six states,
vigilant, it grew strong.
Once the six states were removed,
complacent, it perished.
From Liǔ's writings.
Wealth, rank, and nobility,
are what people greatly desire.
Yet maintaining it is even more difficult.
Gained through achievements,
it may be lost through lack of virtue.
Gained in one's own person,
it may be lost by one's descendants.
Hán Wén.
Time does not come again,
glory is hard to long rely upon.
"Táng Wén Cuì".
You dislike my house for being too low to dwell in,
yet even carved beams and painted pavilions know the meaning of spaciousness.
You must carefully choose a safe place to nest,
lest when the nest is built, it brings no peace.
"Dù Xúnhè Jí".
Look all over the plain at the numerous grave mounds,
once occupied by restless souls from the city.
All say gold can adorn a house,
but who considers that the desolate bones soon turn to dust?
Same as above.
Cross-referenced under "Greed and Delusion".
Yáo and Shùn ruled the world,
valuing farmers over soldiers.
Qín and Hàn plundered the mountains,
casting weapons instead of plows.
May Heaven and Earth not produce gold,
for when gold appears, people start conflicts.
Mèng Dōng.
A screen inscription says: Guard your tongue like a sealed vase,
defend your mind like a fortified city.
"Cháo Shì Kè Yǔ".
Deep-seated hatred and malice instead harm harmony.
"Chén Hòushān Jí".
Cross-referenced under "Excessiveness".
Classic
One should not use water as a mirror,
but use the people as a mirror.
. "Shū·Jiǔ Gào".
The mirror of Yǐn is not far away,
it lies in the age of Xià Hòu.
. "Shī·Dà Yǎ".
Masters
Borrowing clarity as a mirror.
"Huáinán Zǐ".
History
Not forgetting past events serves as a guide for the future.
. "Shǐ Jì·Zhèng Shì Jiā".
Those who mirror themselves in water
know their facial features.
Those who mirror themselves in others
know good and bad fortune.
. "Shǐ·Cài Zé Zhuàn".
When the front carriage overturns,
the rear carriage takes warning.
The reason why the Qín dynasty perished so quickly
is that its tracks are visible.
Yet if one does not avoid them,
then the rear carriage will also overturn.
"Tōng Jiàn".
Past events are what inform the present.
. "Hòu Hàn Shū·Féng Yì Zhuàn".
The clear mirror is not far,
the overturned carriage seems like yesterday.
. "Hòu Hàn Shū·Chén Fān Zhuàn".
A local saying goes: "A clear mirror is for reflecting one's form,
ancient events are for understanding the present."
. "Tōng Jiàn·Wèi Shàolíng Lì Gōng".
Lǐ Xíyán said: "Changing laws is not as good as nurturing people,
altering systems is not as sound as preserving the old ways!
Hán Jiàn amassed countless treasures,
yet initiated affairs with Zhū Wēn;
Wáng Kē changed laws like hemp fibers,
and one day surrendered to the enemy;
the city of Zhōngshān was not without steep walls,
the troops of Shàngcài were not few;
past events are very clear,
and can serve as a warning."
. "Tōng Jiàn·Táng Zhāozōng".
Biographies
Those who use a mirror to reflect themselves
see their appearance.
Those who use others to reflect themselves
see good and bad fortune.
"Tài Gōng Yīn Móu".
Collections
The previous mirror is not far,
overturned carriages follow the same tracks.
. "Xuǎn·Yùn Mìng Lùn".
The goat's path retains the tracks of overturns.
"Liú Chángqīng Jí".
Initially, the extravagant families of Jìn,
such as the Luán, Qí, and Yángshé clans, numbering in the tens,
could not protect themselves,
due to coveting the state's benefits.
The five ministers
tore them apart and consumed them.
The Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
greedy for others' lands,
encroaching on others' power,
were again torn apart and consumed by the three ministers.
Liǔ Zōngyuán's "Yú Zhě Duì".
Cross-referenced under "Greed and Delusion".
Not forgetting past events
serves as the great guide for future affairs.
"Bái Lètiān Jí".
A clear mirror for a moment,
an overturned carriage for a thousand years.
Wáng Wúgōng.
Classic
Violating the taboos of the times,
the crime is not in its magnitude.
Losing one's proper place,
the fault is not in its depth.
"Yì Lüè Lì Shàng".
For their crimes, it is not that they are great,
nor that they are many.
. "Shū·Kāng Gào".
Punish intentional crimes, no matter how small.
Not heeding and intentionally offending,
even if minor, must be punished.
. "Shū·Dà Yǔ Mó".
Destroying norms and disrupting customs,
even for three minor offenses, there is no pardon.
. "Shū·Jūn Chén".
History
To punish evil and encourage good,
seeking fame leads to loss.
Trying to cover up only makes it more evident,
thus Qí Bào is recorded as a robber,
and the names of the three rebels are listed.
. "Zuǒ Zhuàn Xù".
Zhào Chuān attacked Lord Líng in the Peach Garden.
Xuānzǐ had not yet left the mountains when he returned.
The Grand Historian wrote: "Zhào Dùn assassinated his ruler."
and displayed it at court.
Xuānzǐ said: "That is not so."
The reply was: "You are the chief minister,
yet when you fled, you did not cross the border,
and when you returned, you did not punish the culprit,
if not you, then who?"
. "Zuǒ·Xuān Èr".
Duke Dǎo of Xǔ had malaria and drank medicine,
the Crown Prince Zhǐ offered it,
and he died from the drug.
It is recorded: "Assassinated his ruler."
. "Zuǒ·Zhāo Shíjiǔ".
Sòng Dū killed Kǒng Fù and took his wife.
The Duke was angry,
Dū feared,
so he assassinated the Duke.
The gentleman considers Dū as having no regard for his ruler,
and then acted wickedly.
. "Zuǒ·Huán Èr".
Towards the ruler and parents, there should be no intent to harm,
and if there is, it must be punished.
"Gōngyáng Zhuàn".
A minister should have no intent to harm,
and if he does, it is rebellion,
a crime punishable by death without pardon.
. "Shǐ·Shū Sūn Tōng Zhuàn".
Gōngsūn Hóng said: "Guō Xiě, as a commoner, acted as a knight-errant wielding power,
killing people over trifles.
Guō Xiě did not know,
but this is worse than if Guō Xiě had knowingly killed them."
. "Xī Hàn·Guō Xiě Zhuàn".
Collections
The Spring and Autumn Annals record the king's law,
without punishing the person himself.
Hán Wén's "Dú Huángfǔ Shí Shī".
Táng's Cuī Hàng served as the chief penalty officer.
His same-year graduate Lú Càn,
just before the border feast, requested leave to go to Luòyáng.
Upon his return,
the same-year graduates had already feasted at the Qǔjiāng Pavilion. Càn,
with a carved carriage carrying courtesans,
in plain clothes watched from afar,
was exposed by the banquet officials.
Hàng judged thus:
"Deeply hidden under a hat,
secretly screened by a felt carriage,
on the purple path seeking spring,
you missed the faces of your same-year peers;
but when you find your way to high office,
we shall see the heart you show in days to come."
Táng Cuī Hàng's judgment on same-year graduate Lú Càn.
Teaching a thief to break through a wall,
the cabinet yielded much gold and jade, yet he did not share with his accomplices;
does that not make him a thief?
"Dù Mùzhī Jí".
Current dynasty
In Shǔ, followers of Lǐ Shùn who were guilty and fled,
while Zhāng Yǒng governed Yìzhōu, were granted the chance to surrender themselves.
He detained one's mother for ten days, but the fugitive did not appear.
Releasing her,
he then detained the man's wife,
who came within one night.
The official judged:
"Detaining the mother for ten nights,
yet keeping the wife for just one evening—
how indifferent to the longing gaze at the door, and how deep the affection for the marital bond?"
Thereupon, he had him executed.
From "Yǔlù".
Regarding Yán Líng's favor and Vù Zhì's dismissal,
Zhào Jǐng truly aided in it,
making Jǐng's offense grave.
If judged by the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Jǐng would be the first to deserve punishment.
From Fàn Zǔyǔ's "Táng Jiàn".
In the Táng dynasty, Yuán Zhěn, in drafting an appointment for Lǐ Cóngyì as Zōngchéng, wrote:
"In the past, the descendants of the Liú clan numbered over a hundred thousand in the registry."
Upon examining the era when Wáng Mǎng acted as regent,
he issued a grand proclamation stating:
"The outstanding members of the imperial clan number four hundred."
Mèng Kāng annotated:
"Referring to those of the Liú clan still alive.
Why such a difference in numbers?
Could it be that after Mǎng's ruthless purges,
the so-called four hundred were all those who flattered Mǎng to steal the Hàn's legacy, living indulgently?
Otherwise, how could they survive to that point,
even being called 'outstanding' by Mǎng?"
From "Hóu Qīng Lù".
The warning against rebellion is deeply inscribed in the Lǔ classics;
the punishment for speaking against the way is hard to escape under Hàn law.
From "The Edict Demoting Dīng Wèi".
The master said:
"It is like chasing a runaway pig:
once it has entered the pen,
you then go on to beckon it."
From "Mèngzǐ: Jìn Xīn Xià".
Fearing the horse might stumble
("stumble" sometimes written as "avoid"),
one dares not ride it.
Apprehensive that the carriage might overturn,
one dares not board it.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
If someone chokes to death while eating,
and on that account, eating is banned throughout the land;
if someone suffers a mishap with a carriage or horse,
and on that account, riding is forbidden everywhere—
is that not absurd?
One who has never been burned may still dare not grasp fire,
having seen it burn something.
One who has never been injured may still dare not grasp a blade,
having seen it harm someone.
Also from the same text.
If someone dies from taking medicine,
and on that account, one wishes to ban all medicine in the world—
that is wrong!
If someone dies in a boating accident,
and on that account, one wishes to ban all boats in the world—
that is wrong!
From the "Bīng Dào" chapter of "Kāng Cāng Zǐ".
History records:
When human feelings are frustrated and humiliated,
the ethos of righteousness and integrity suffers.
From the "Hòu Dù Lín Zhuàn".
Yáng Hù said:
"To hesitate when a decision should be made,
to not take what Heaven offers—
is it not that those with experience regret acting too late?"
From "Jìn Shū: Běn Zhuàn".
To skip a meal because of a hiccup.
From "Liáng Shū: Hè Chēn Zhuàn".
Hán Xiǎnzōng said:
"How can we abolish the position of chancellor just because there is no one like Zhōu Gōng or Shào Gōng in our time?"
From "Hòu Wèi".
To shut one's door and bite one's tongue.
From "Xī Hàn: Huái Fū Zhuàn".
In the past, there was one who fell ill from a single choke
and decided to stop eating altogether.
From "Táng Shū: Chén Zǐ'áng Zhuàn".
One scalded by hot soup blows on cold minced pickles;
a bird injured by a bow startles at a curved branch.
From "Táng Shū: Fù Yì Zhuàn".
Wèi Yuánzhōng returned from Duānzhōu
to serve as chancellor,
but no longer offered strong remonstrance,
instead conforming with the times,
disappointing both court and country.
From "Tōng Jiàn: Táng Zhōngzōng".
Déyù stated:
"In the past, Xuánzōng, as the Prince of Línzī, quelled internal strife,
and thereafter grew suspicious and wary of the imperial clan,
not allowing them to leave their residences.
This is why they were all preyed upon by Ān Lùshān and Zhū Cǐ,
because they were confined to one palace."
From "Tōng Jiàn: Táng Wénzōng".
Biographies record:
Gēng Léi was with the King of Wèi under the eaves,
when a pair of wild geese flew from the east.
(Another version says:
"coming from the east.")
Gēng Léi shot a blank, and the goose fell.
The King of Wèi asked:
"Can archery achieve this?"
Gēng Léi replied:
"It flew slowly and its cry was mournful.
Flying slowly indicates its wound pains it;
crying mournfully means it long lost its flock.
Thus, its pain not yet eased,
its fear not yet gone,
it fell upon hearing the bowstring."
From "Zhànguó Cè".
Because of one choke,
one stops eating grains entirely.
Because of one stumble,
one refrains from walking.
From the "Tán Cóng" chapter of "Shuō Yuàn".
Collections:
Scalded by hot soup, one blows on cold minced pickles.
From "Chǔ Cí".
Having been scalded by soup, one blows on minced pickles—
why not change this mindset?
From "Chǔ Cí: Shàng".
A wounded bird startles at the bowstring;
a weary traveler dreads parting.
Poem by Sòng Bàozhāo.
A wounded bird detests the startling bowstring.
From "Wénxuǎn: Dōngmén Xíng".
A precarious leaf fears the wind;
a startled bird is easily felled.
From "Wénxuǎn: Cè Wén".
To treat an illness without the true medicine,
compounding and taking it,
the illness gradually worsens,
unaware of being deceived.
Instead, one claims the prescription is unreliable,
and the medicine is useless for curing,
thus abandoning it.
Thereafter, one dares not take any more medicine,
and turns to shamans and witches.
Even if death results,
it is acceptable!
From Wáng Fú's "Qián Fū Lùn".
Punished by cruelty, wounded by severity.
To stop eating because of one choke;
to avoid proper women due to a mistaken marriage.
Both from "Chén Zǐ'áng Jí".
A blank string fells a startled bird.
From "Lǐ Tàibái Jí".
A stranded fish startles at the reflected wheel tracks;
a fallen feather fears the empty bend of the bow.
By Luò Bīnwáng.
Like one who, after the pain subsides, recalls the time of suffering,
not knowing how they endured it.
From Hán Wén.
Completely avoiding mention of current affairs,
striving for loftiness and depth,
to block the mouths of the envious.
From Hán Wén's "Letter to Lǐ Shàngshū".
The wild goose fears the mere bow's threat.
From "Yuán Wēizhī Jí".
Hearing the string, still startled,
the fearful heart unsettled,
ears drooping long,
its long cry deeply mournful.
Thus, it makes later ascendants to the altar
each time they ponder, afraid to achieve merit.
Both by Liú Bīnkè.
An empty bow-bend startles the goose;
a void draw makes the ape weep.
From "Bái Shìláng Jí".
Never has it been heard that a caged bird,
once flown out, would willingly return.
From "Bái Lètiān Jí".
The newly startled bird, not yet over its bow-wound.
By Bái Lètiān.
The wound fears another bow injury.
By Liú Chángqīng.
In the past, some stopped eating due to a choke,
others drowned themselves for fear of drowning—
in their efforts to overcorrect and prevent disaster,
were they not excessive?
From Lù Xuàngōng's writings.
Having concern for the state,
yet keeping silent and not speaking out.
From "Táng Wén Cuì".
Our dynasty
I, having fallen victim to slanderous mouths and landed in this plight,
find every glib tongue I hear utterly detestable.
From "The Collected Works of Ōu Yáng Xiū".
In recent years, I've practiced mute silence.
Under a tranquil sky, the wounded wild goose still folds its wings;
In the bright moonlight, the startled magpie finds no branch to rest on.
Both from Sū Shì's poetry.
To erase all traces and vanish from human sight,
Like a hare escaping into the bushes.
From "The Collected Works of Dōngpō".
Just as there are those who kill others with their plows while farming,
Some might argue that farming should therefore be abandoned.
Long submerged in muddy depths,
One trembles at the sound of thunder;
Deeply confined in a cage,
One doubts oneself upon feeling a fresh breeze.
Both from "The Collected Works of Lúan Chéng".
Classic
He so devoted himself that he forgot to eat,
Found such joy that he forgot his sorrows,
Unaware that old age was approaching.
From "The Analects".
Master
As for the outstanding individuals,
Even without King Wén, they would still rise.
From "Mencius: Jin Xin Part I".
History
Initially, though with drooping wings,
He ultimately soared with vigorous flight.
From "The Biography of Féng Yì, Book of the Later Hàn".
Where there's a will, there's a way.
From "The Biography of Gěng Yǎn, Book of the Later Hàn".
While Táo Kǎn governed, with little to occupy him,
He would move a hundred bricks outside his study in the morning,
And move them back inside in the evening.
When asked the reason,
He replied, "I am dedicated to reclaiming the Central Plains.
If I indulge in leisure and comfort,
I fear I'll become unfit for the task."
His discipline and diligence
Were consistently of this nature.
From "The Book of Jìn".
Liú Cí was promoted to Tuánliàn Shǐ for his merits,
Yet he often slept in armor with his spear as a pillow, saying,
"I attained wealth and honor through this;
How could I forget it for even a day?
Moreover, human nature tends to grow accustomed to ease;
If I once let my strength and vigor decline,
How could I serve the country when needed?"
From "The History of the Five Dynasties".
Collections
If words alone cannot move listeners,
One must resort to provocation to stand out.
If actions alone cannot reach far,
One must hone oneself to seek fame.
By Liú Bīnkè.
When pines and cypresses unfortunately sprout within rocky crevices,
The weak and brittle ones will grind their buds and perish beneath.
What chance do they have to strive upward?
But these pines and cypresses,
Though just sprouting with youthful vigor,
Maintain their noble nature unblemished.
As they mature,
Their strength contends with the rock.
Riding the force of the sun,
Lamenting their own oppression,
They strive to rise,
Yet ultimately cannot overcome the pressure,
Their courage stifled and pent-up,
Their resentment bursting forth in protest,
Until their deformity becomes manifest,
And the world points at them as freakish trees.
Alas!
Is it any different for humans?
Those endowed with great talent,
If not employed early in life,
Remain suppressed and unfulfilled.
As their pent-up energies ferment and intensify daily,
Their paths blocked and opportunities seized by force,
They ultimately succumb to adversity,
Crying out and clamoring,
Pouring forth their grievances,
Until their extraordinary brilliance erupts in literary expression,
And the world labels them as eccentric.
From Lù Guīméng's "Portrait of a Strange Pine".
Without struggle and effort,
One cannot rise from the mire.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
Our Dynasty
Dare I not sharpen and cleanse my wearied spirit,
And diligently revive my long-neglected studies?
From "Línchuān".
Classic
Following virtue and reforming conduct.
From "The Book of Documents: The Charge to Cài Zhòng".
So devoted that he forgot to eat.
From "The Analects: Shuō Ér".
If students are not eager, I do not enlighten them;
If they are not struggling, I do not inspire them.
From "The Analects: Shuō Ér".
Master
When Heaven is about to confer a great responsibility on someone,
It first tests their resolve with suffering,
Exhausts their body with toil,
Subjects them to hunger and hardship,
Frustrates their endeavors,
And confounds their actions.
This is to stir their spirit, toughen their nature,
And enhance their capabilities.
From "Mencius: Gào Zǐ Part II".
Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn conceived his ambition for hegemony while in Cáo,
King Gōujiàn of Yuè nurtured his in Kuàijī,
And Duke Wēi of Qí, Xiǎo Bái, fostered his in Jǔ.
From "Xúnzǐ: Yòu Zuò".
Had Sū Qín possessed fertile land near the city walls,
He would not have worn the seals of six states;
Had Zhǔfù not been scorned by relatives and friends,
He would not have aspired to the feast of five tripods;
Had Zhāng Yí not suffered the humiliation at the hall's base,
He would not have resolved to enter Qín;
Had Fàn Jū not endured the disgrace in the latrine,
He would not have harbored thoughts of vengeance against Wèi;
Nìng Yuè, spurred by hardship, cultivated learning,
And eventually became the teacher to King Wēi of Zhōu;
Bān Chāo, driven by indignation, trained in martial arts,
And ultimately achieved merit in the Western Regions.
All these men kindled their ambitions through adversity,
And gained fame by overcoming hardship.
From "The Masters of Liú".
History
Treating Qín as barbarians,
they ostracized and rejected it,
preventing it from participating in the alliances and covenants of the Central States,
whereupon Duke Xiào resolved to strengthen Qín.
. _Tōng Jiàn Zhōu Jì_.
The King of Yuè brooded over Wú's retaliation.
In summer, he grasped fire;
in winter, he embraced ice.
_Wú Yuè Chūnqiū_.
With bitter heart and aching head.
. _Zuǒ Zhuàn, Chéng 13_.
When King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè returned to his state,
he tormented his body and anguished his thoughts,
placing a gall bladder in his seat.
Sitting or lying, he would look up at the gall bladder,
and when drinking, he would also taste the gall.
Saying: "Have you forgotten the shame of Kuàijī?"
He personally engaged in farming,
ate without extra meat,
wore no double layers of colorful silk,
humbled himself to treat worthies with respect,
generously received guests,
relieved the poor and mourned the dead."
Sharing the toils with the common people.
. _Shǐ Jì Yuè Shì Jiā_.
Sū Qín returned in poverty and distress,
his elder brothers, sisters, and wife all laughed at him,
not even pausing their weaving.
Sū Qín then secluded himself to study the _Zhōu Shū_ and _Yīn Fú_,
later uniting the six states in a vertical alliance,
appointed as prime minister of the six states,
his chariots, cavalry, and supplies
rivaled those of a king.
_Shǐ Jì_.
Xúnzǐ detested the corrupt governance of a turbulent age,
thus promoting the practices of Confucianism, Mohism, and Daoist virtues,
composing works totaling tens of thousands of words.
. _Shǐ Jì Běn Zhuàn_.
Yú Qīng, finding no satisfaction,
wrote a book passed down through the ages titled: "The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Yú Clan."
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said: "Had Yú Qīng not been impoverished and sorrowful,
he could not have written books to make himself known to later generations."
_Shǐ Jì_.
If not distressed, how can one be stirred?
. _Shǐ Jì Cài Zé Zhuàn Lùn_.
Sū Qín formed the vertical alliance,
and the leading feudal lords each sent envoys to escort him, rivaling a king's treatment,
whereupon he sighed: "Had I possessed two qǐng of land near Luòyáng's outer walls,
how could I have worn the prime minister seals of six states?"
. _Shǐ Jì Běn Zhuàn_.
King Wén of the Western Zhōu was imprisoned and elaborated the _Zhōu Yì_,
Confucius composed the _Spring and Autumn Annals_,
Qū Yuán was exiled and then wrote the _Lí Sāo_,
Zuǒ Qiū lost his sight and thus produced the _Guó Yǔ_,
Sūnzǐ had his feet amputated and cultivated the _Art of War_,
Lǚ Bùwéi was banished to Shǔ, leaving behind the _Lǚ's Annals_,
Hán Fēi was imprisoned in Qín and wrote "Shuì Nán" and "Gū Fèn".
The three hundred poems of the _Shī Jīng_,
were largely works composed by sages and worthies in their resolve and frustration.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng without sight,

Withdrawing, they discussed and wrote books and strategies,
to vent their frustrations,
hoping to leave behind empty words to make themselves known.

Dí Fāngjìn served in the governor's office as a minor official.
Repeatedly insulted and humiliated by the clerks,
Fāngjìn grieved over his plight,
then went west to the capital,
to study the _Spring and Autumn Annals_.
After more than ten years of accumulation,
he became well-versed in the classics,
and his followers grew daily.
Praised by the Confucian scholars,
he passed the top grade in the examination and became a court gentleman.

Resolved and sincere.

Zhōu Chù in his youth did not attend to minor virtues,
and the local community was troubled by him.
Chù, aware that he was disliked,
felt deeply and resolved to reform himself,
asking the elders: "Now that the times are peaceful and the harvest abundant,
why is there no joy?"
The elders replied: "The three scourges are not yet eliminated,
what joy can there be?"
Chù asked: "What are they?"
They answered: "The white-fronted beast of the southern mountains,
the flood dragon under the long bridge,
and you make the third."
Chù then entered the mountains and shot the tiger,
plunged into the water and killed the flood dragon,
encouraged his will and pursued learning,
aspiring to righteousness and fervor,
after a year of self-discipline,
both the provincial and central governments vied to recruit him.
. _Jìn Shū Běn Zhuàn_.

You have long been in distress and hardship,

Generally, when things are unsettled, they sound out;
plants and trees are silent,
but when wind disturbs them, they sound;
water is silent,
but when wind agitates it, it sounds.
When it leaps,
it is stirred by something;
when it flows swiftly,
it is obstructed by something;
when it boils,
it is heated by something.
Metal and stone are silent,
but when struck, they sound.
So it is with human speech;
they speak only when compelled,
their singing has thought,
their weeping has feeling.
All that comes from the mouth as sound,
must it all stem from some disquiet?
Hán Yù's "Preface to Seeing Off Mèng Jiāoyè".

Táo Yuānmíng, by nature unversed in music, kept a plain qin with
strings and tuning pegs incomplete.
Whenever friends gathered for wine,
he would stroke it in accompaniment,
saying:
"If one comprehends the delight within the qin,
why trouble with the sound from its strings?"
． _Jìnshū Běnzhuàn_
Wáng Huīzhī once dwelt in Shànyīn.
One night after clearing skies,
the moonlight shone bright and pure,
casting a gleaming white in all directions.
He drank wine and recited Zuǒ Sī's "Summoning the Recluse."
Suddenly recalling Dài Kuí at that moment,
with Kuí then in Shàn,
he took a small boat by night,
journeying to visit him through the night.
Upon reaching the gate, he did not enter but turned back.
When asked the reason, he replied:
"I set out following my whim,
and now that the whim has passed, I return.
Why must I see Āndào?"
_Jìnshū_

Confucius, passing through a valley, saw an orchid thriving alone,
sighed, and said:
"The orchid should be the king's fragrance,
yet now it flourishes alone,
mingling with common weeds."
He halted his carriage,
took up the qin and played it,
lamenting his own misfortune in timing,
expressing it through the fragrant orchid.

Collections
In the past, Zhāng Xǔ delighted in cursive script,
devoting no effort to other skills.
Joy or anger, distress or poverty,
sorrow, pleasure, or idleness,
resentment, longing,
drunkenness, or boredom—
any unrest in his heart
would find release in cursive script.
Observing the world,
he saw mountains, waters, cliffs, and valleys,
birds, beasts, insects, and fish,
flowers of plants and trees,
sun, moon, and stars,
wind, rain, fire, and water,
thunder, lightning,
singing, dancing, battle, and strife—
all changes in heaven, earth, and things,
whether delightful or startling,
were embodied in his writing.
Thus, Zhāng Xǔ's calligraphy
changed like ghosts and gods, unfathomable,
and with this, he spent his life, leaving a name for posterity.

Zhāng Liáng was traveling.
In Xiàpī, there was an old man
who came to Liáng's place wearing coarse clothes.
He deliberately dropped his shoe under the bridge,
turned and said to Liáng: "Young man, go down and fetch my shoe."
Liáng was startled,
and wanted to hit him,
but because the man was old,
he restrained himself and went down to get the shoe.
He then knelt and offered it to the old man,
who extended his foot to receive it,
laughed, and left, saying: "You are worth teaching!
In five days, at dawn,
meet me here."
Liáng said: "Yes."
After five days,
Liáng went,
but the old man was already there,
and angrily said: "Meeting an elder and arriving late,
why?
Come again in five days,
earlier."
After another five days,
Liáng went in the middle of the night.
After a while,
the old man also arrived,
and said happily: "This is how it should be."
He took out a book,
saying: "Read this, and you will be a teacher to kings."
． From the Biography of Zhāng Liáng in History of the Western Hàn.

King Wēi of Qí summoned the magistrate of Jímò,

the officials without troubles,
and the eastern region thus peaceful.
This is because you do not serve my attendants to seek help."
He enfeoffed him with ten thousand households.
He summoned the magistrate of Ē,
and said to him: "Since you guarded Ē,
praises have come daily.
I sent people to inspect Ē,
and found the fields uncultivated,
the people poor and hungry.
This is because you bribe my attendants heavily to seek praise."
That day,

Sūn Liàng went to the Western Garden,
was eating raw plums,
sent a eunuch to the central storehouse to fetch honey to pickle the plums.
The honey contained rat droppings,
he summoned and questioned the storehouse official,
who kowtowed.
Liàng asked the official:
"Did the eunuch ask you for honey?"
The official said:
"He asked before,
I truly dared not give it."
The eunuch pleaded innocence,
attendants Diāo Xuán and Zhāng Bīn reported the conflicting statements of the eunuch and the official,
requested to send them to prison for investigation.
Liàng said:
"This is easy to determine."
Ordered the rat droppings broken open,
the inside was dry.
Liàng laughed heartily,
said to Xuán and Bīn:
"If they had been in the honey long,
inside and out would be wet.
Now the inside is dry,
surely the eunuch did it."
The eunuch confessed,
all around were shocked and fearful.

History: In the Hàn dynasty, Páng Cān served as governor of Hànyáng.
A county man named Rèn Táng had extraordinary integrity
and lived in seclusion.
Cān paid him a visit;
Táng did not speak to him,
but only placed a large bulb of scallions
and a bowl of water
in front of the door screen.
Then, holding his grandson, he knelt by the door.
The registrar thought it was arrogance,
but Cān pondered and said: "The water
means he wants me to be clear.
Pulling up the large scallion
means he wants me to strike the powerful clans.
Holding the child at the door
means he wants me to open the door and care for the orphans."
From "History of the Later Hàn".

Cross-reference to "Evidence and Proof".
Yuán Àng had always disliked Cháo Cuò.
Wherever Cuò was seated,
Ǎng would leave;
where Ǎng sat,
Cuò would also depart.
The two never spoke together in the same hall.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Annals_.
Cross-reference to "Grudges and Rifts".
Xiāngzǐ of Zhào held a grudge against Zhì Bó.
He lacquered his skull to make a drinking vessel.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Yù Ràng_.
Day and night clenching their wrists,
glaring with gnashing teeth.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Zhāng Yí_.
Gōu Jiàn said: "Day and night with parched lips and dry tongue,
I desire to follow in King Wú's footsteps to death."
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Duānmù Cì_.
Guàn Fū tyrannized Yǐngchuān,
the folks of Yǐngchuān sang: "When the Yǐng River runs clear,
the Guàn clan is safe;
when the Yǐng River runs muddy,
the Guàn clan is doomed."
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Annals_.
From the highest ministers down to the common people,
all pointed at Tāng.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Zhāng Tāng_.
Wáng Wēnshū executed many people in Huáiyáng.
Upon his death,
his enemies sought to burn his corpse.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Annals_.
Cross-reference to "Grudges and Rifts".
Zhū Màichén visited Zhāng Tāng.
Tāng sat on his couch,
and his officials treated Màichén without courtesy.
Màichén, a man of Chǔ,
harbored deep resentment,
and often wished to cause his death.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Zhāng Tāng_.
The fathers and brothers of Qín resented these three men,
their hatred penetrating to the marrow.
_Records of the Grand Historian_.
All looked askance at Wàng Zhī and his associates.
． _Book of Hàn, Biography of Liú Xiàng_.
Gōngsūn Hóng also eyed Jǐ with sidelong glances.
． _Book of Hàn, Biography of Yuán Gù_.
Often pointed at and stared at.
． _Book of Hàn, Biography of Chén Shèng_.
Cháo Cuò's father said to Cuò: "Many speak ill of you with resentment."
． _Book of Hàn, Basic Biography_
Bit his tongue and committed suicide.
． _Book of Hàn, Biography of Guàn Fū_.
Lǐ Wén had a rift with Zhāng Tāng.
Later, as Imperial Censor,
when matters arose that could harm Tāng,
he showed no leniency.
． _Book of Hàn, Biography of Zhāng Tāng_.
His words were always filled with gnashing teeth.
． _Book of Hàn, Biography of Wáng Mǎng_.
I encountered this disaster due to slander,
greatly ridiculed by my fellow villagers.
Defiling my ancestors,
what face have I to approach my parents' graves again?
Even after a hundred generations, the shame would only deepen!
Thus, my guts churn nine times a day,
at home I am absent-minded as if having lost something,
going out I know not where to go.
Whenever I recall this shame,
it never fails to bring forth tears,
soaking my garments.
． _Book of Hàn, Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān_.
Carrying hatred into the netherworld.
． _Book of Later Hàn, Biography of Féng Yǎn_.
Sūn Xiù was a minor official,
serving Yuè, cunning and self-satisfied.
Yuè detested his character,
often whipping and humiliating him,
and Xiù always harbored resentment.
When King Zhào Lún assumed regency,
Xiù became Secretariat Director,
Yuè asked Xiù in the ministry: "Director Sūn, do you recall our past interactions?"
He replied: "I keep it in my heart,
never forgetting it for a day!"
Yuè then knew he could not escape.
Soon, Xiù falsely accused Yuè, Shí Chóng, and Ōuyáng Jiàn of conspiring with Huáinán Wáng Yǔn and Qí Wáng Jiǒng to rebel,
had them executed,
and exterminated their three clans.
． _Book of Jìn, Biography of Pān Yuè_.
Cross-reference to "Retribution of Evil".
When Zhāng Huá and Péi Wěi were executed,
King Zhào Lún and Sūn Xiù, bearing old grudges, arrested Xiè Xì and his brothers.
King Liáng Róng tried to save Xì,
but Lún angrily said: "Even seeing a crab in water disgusts me,
let alone these brothers who slight me?
If this can be tolerated,
what cannot?"
Thus, he had them killed.
_Book of Jìn_.
Crush them,
pulverize them,
slaughter them,
dismember them,
still it would not suffice to atone.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Sòng Tàizǔ_.
Hóu Jǐng said to his attendants: "I always knew that old man Wú had a shallow heart."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Liáng Gāozǔ_.
Lú Qǐ, pardoned, was appointed Prefect of Ráo Prefecture.
The Imperial Secretary Yuán Gāo, tasked to draft the appointment,
held it and told Lú Hàn and Liú Cóngyī: "All officials despise him as an enemy,
the armies long to eat his flesh."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Dézōng_.
Shǐ Hóngzhào particularly despised scholars,
often saying: "These people are contemptuous and unbearable,
always calling us soldiers."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Five Dynasties, Hàn Yǐndì_.
Zhūgě Liàng returned to his hometown,
and for life never sat facing the imperial court.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Western Jìn, Chūzǔ Records_.
Wú Xiè Lì said: "Grand Guardian Pān often gnashes his teeth at you,
only lacking a reason to act."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Wèi, Jùalíng Lìgōng Records_.
Jìn's Empress Dowager Lǐ lay ill in Jiànzhōu,
with no medicine or treatment,
only weeping with the Jìn ruler, looking up to heaven,
pointing and cursing Dù Chóngwēi and Lǐ Shǒuzhēn: "I will not rest in death until you are dealt with!"
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Later Hàn Records_.
Liú Shū was dismissed from Qīngzhōu and returned,
long attending court audiences,
yet not assigned an official post,
often pointing angrily at the ministers.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Later Hàn Records_.
Biographies and Records
Eternal words of resentment and shame,
neither life nor death can express.
Looking up to heaven and down to earth,
how can one live on?
With teeth in mouth and hair on head,
how can one face others?
_Generals of History_.
The King of Wú granted Zǐxū the sword Zhǔlòu.
Zǐxū fell on the sword and died,
the King of Wú took Zǐxū's corpse,
placed it in a leather sack,
and cast it into the river.
Zǐxū then rode the waves with the current,
coming and going with the tides,
washing and eroding the banks.
． _Later Hàn, Zhào Yè, Annals of Wú and Yuè_.
The King of Yuè granted Wén Zhǒng the sword Zhǔlú, and he died,
the King of Yuè buried Zhǒng in the Western Hills of the state,
for a year.
Wǔ Zǐxū came from the sea, pierced the mountain's flank, and took Zhǒng away,
floating together with him on the sea.
Thus, the vanguard of the tidal bore
is Wǔ Zǐxū;
the following heavy waters
are Grand Master Zhǒng.
Ibid.
Collections
Glaring eyes and gnashing teeth.
． _Selections, Ode to the Virtue of Wine_.
How is the Way of Heaven?
Many swallow their regrets.
． _Selections, Rhapsody by Bào Zhāo_.
Swallowing hatred and stifling sobs.
Rhapsody by Jiāng Wéntōng.
Classics
For a father's enemy, avoid them beyond the seas,
for a brother's enemy, avoid them a thousand miles away,
for a cousin's enemy, do not reside in the same state.
An enemy of one's lord is regarded like that of a father,
an enemy of a teacher or elder,
is regarded like that of a brother,
an enemy of a patron or superior is regarded,
as that of a cousin.
From "Zhōu Lǐ".
With a father's enemy, one cannot share the same sky;
with a brother's enemy, one does not retreat without a weapon;
with an enemy from social circles, one does not share the same state.
From "Jì Qǔ Lǐ".
Historical Records:
Zhōu and Zhèng became mutually hostile.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn".
Zhèng and Xī had disagreements.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Yǐn 11".
The duke and his minister first developed animosity.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Āi 26".
Hán Jiǎnzǐ and Zhào Wénzǐ were mutually hostile,
Wèi Xiāngzǐ also bore enmity with Fàn Zhāozǐ.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Dìng 13".
The three families were not harmonious.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Dìng 13".
Sharing borders with us,
yet for generations they have been sworn enemies.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Āi 1".
Jiǎn Xuān once had a rift with Tāng,
and pursued the matter to its extreme.
From "Shǐ Jì, Zhāng Tāng Zhuàn".
Wáng Wēnshū died,
and his enemies sought to burn his corpse.
From "Shǐ Jì, Běn Zhuàn".
Cross-reference "Resentment and Hatred".
Between ruler and ministers, there were many estrangements.
Meaning a rift.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Āi 27".
The general and I have a grudge.
From "Xī Hàn, Gāo Jì".
There were minor grievances within.
From "Xī Hàn, Sūn Bǎo Zhuàn".
Cháo Cuò had long been on bad terms with Wú's chancellor Yuán Àng.
Wherever Cuò sat,
Àng would avoid;
wherever Àng sat,
Cuò would also avoid.
The two never spoke in the same hall.
From "Tōng Jiàn".
Cross-reference "Resentment and Hatred".
Cáo Shēn served as chancellor,
and had a rift with Xiāo Hé.
From "Xī Hàn, Běn Zhuàn".
Zhào Wēn and Guō Fàn contended over trivial grievances,
leading to a feud of immense weight.
From "Dōng Hàn, Zhào Wēn Zhuàn".
Hatred over minor slights,
turned into suspicion and discord.
From "Wèi Zhì".
Wáng Xún married a daughter of the Wàn family,
and Wáng Mín's younger brother married a daughter of the Ān family.
Both marriages ended poorly,
thus creating a rift with the Xiè family.
From "Jìn Shū, Xiè Yǎn Zhuàn".
Lǐ Bàozhēn and Mǎ Suì harbored deep resentment and discord,
and ceased to see each other.
From "Tōng Jiàn, Táng Dézōng".
Collected Sayings:
Sharing meals from the same plate,
they often glanced at each other,
without exchanging a word.
By Dù Mù.
Classics:
To go without returning is against ritual;
to come without going is also against ritual.
From "Jì Qǔ Lǐ".
Historical Records:
The one repaying is weary,
while the one giving is not satisfied.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Xī 24".
When Jìn's prince Chóng'ěr reached Chǔ,
the lord of Chǔ feasted him and said: "If you return to Jìn,
how will you repay me?"
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Xī 23".
Chǔ's minister Zǐ Qí had done favors for the king,
but did not know moderation.
Allying with the Yǎng family,
he sought endlessly without satisfaction.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Zhāo 14".
Collected Sayings:
Who can give without expecting return?
From "Chǔ Cí".
Classics:
If not for your sake,
why would I be in the dew?
From "Shī Jīng, Shì Wēi".
Do not keep your words like gold and jade,
while harboring distant thoughts.
From "Shī Jīng, Bái Jū".
You claim not to know,
yet you already hold a child.
From "Shī Jīng, Yì".
If you lovingly think of me,
lift your garments and cross the Zhēn.
If you do not think of me,
are there no others?
From "Shī Jīng, Qiān Cháng".
Are there no others?
But none compare to my own kin.
From "Shī Jīng".
Why pass by my weir,
yet not enter my door?
Why pass by my weir,
yet not come to console me?
At first, it was not so,
now you say I am not acceptable.
I hear your voice.
If you turn and enter,
my heart will be at ease.
If you turn away and do not enter,
it is hard to know why.
If only you would come once,
it would set my mind at rest.
From "Xiǎo Yǎ, Hé Rén Sī".
That cunning lad,
who does not speak with me,
all because of you,
I cannot eat.
From "Zhèng Fēng".
Forgetting my great virtues,
dwelling on my minor faults.
From "Biàn Xiǎo Yǎ, Gǔ Fēng".
Whom, then, do you hate?
From "Shī Jīng, Zhēng Yuè".
Even if I do not go,
why do you not send word?
From "Shī Jīng, Zǐ Jīn".
Cross-reference "Forgiving Oneself and Blaming Others".
Look at the trapped hare, someone might free it;
where there is a dead body, someone might bury it;
but a gentleman's heart—how can it be so cruel?
From "Yōu Yǎ, Xiǎo Biàn".
In life and death, separated or together,
we made our pact.
Holding your hand,
I vowed to grow old with you.
Alas, the distance,
that keeps me from living with you.
Alas, the long separation,
that keeps me from keeping my vow.
From "Shī Jīng, Jī Gǔ".
Far from my brothers in the end,
I call another 'father'.
Calling another 'father',
yet he does not regard me.
From "Shī Jīng, Wáng Fēng, Gé Lěi".
Philosophers:
If one cultivates conduct but their name
is not renowned, it is the fault of their friends.
From "Jiā Yǔ".
Cross-reference "Fault Lies Somewhere".
After settling in your lodging,
should you then seek to see the elders?
From "Mèngzǐ, Lí Lóu Shàng".
As parents to the people,
if you make them toil wearily,
laboring all year long,
unable to support their own parents,
and then borrow to make ends meet,
causing the old and young to perish in ditches and gullies,
how can you be called parents to the people?
From "Mèngzǐ, Téng Wén Gōng Shàng".
Historical Records:
Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
Zhèng sent a messenger to inform Jìng Zhī,
Wǔzǐ had the messenger reply: "You received orders from Chǔ,
yet did not send a single envoy to inform our humble ruler,
but instead found comfort with Chǔ."
． From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Xiāng Gōng 8th Year".
A solitary envoy,
Jí hè fǎn.
The duke went to Jìn to request a welcoming from Jìn,
the people of Jìn said: "Heaven brought disaster to the ruler of Lǔ,
who lingers in distress abroad.
You also did not send a single envoy to disgrace our humble ruler,
but instead found comfort with your maternal uncles."
． From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Xiāng Gōng 28th Year".
A lone envoy,
Gǔ hè fǎn.
Moreover, when I was abroad,
my uncle did not convey any message.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn".
Yuè Shífù, a worthy man, was in prison,
Yànzǐ untied his left-side horse to ransom him,
carried him back and entered the inner chamber; after a long time,
Yuè Shífù requested to sever ties.
From "Yànzǐ".
Startled, he said: "Although Yǐng is not benevolent, I rescued you from distress,
why do you seek to sever ties so quickly?"
Shífù said: "I have heard that a gentleman may be misunderstood by those who do not know him,
but is trusted by those who do.
When I was in prison,
they did not know me.
Since you, sir, were moved to ransom me,
that means you know me.
To know me yet show no courtesy,
is certainly worse than being in prison."
． From "Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Yàn Píngzhòng".
King Huì of Yān sent someone to reprimand Yuè Yì and apologize to him, saying: "General, you have misunderstood,
and because of a rift with me,
you abandoned Yān and returned to Zhào.
If you are acting for your own plans, that is acceptable,
but how then will you repay the late king's intention in treating you as he did?"
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Zhōu Chronicles".
Empress Lǚ sent Lǚ Zé to say to Zhāng Liáng: "How can you, sir, now rest easy on your high pillow?"
From "Biography of Zhāng Liáng".
The world's reproaches,
come from all directions.
． From "Western Hàn, Biography of Gǔ Yǒng".
To be grieved yet not shown distinction,
who can bear it without resentment?
． From "Western Hàn, Biography of Dù Yè".
Zhāng Ràng reproached Hé Jìn, saying: "I only wished to entrust myself to your household.
Now you want to exterminate our kind,
is that not too extreme?"
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Chronicles of Hàn Xiàndì".
Zhāng Liáng said: "I hear the general intends to reprimand him."
From "Western Hàn".
Attendant Gentleman Mǎ Róng,
was responsible for drafting memorials for Liáng Jì.
Wú Yòu said to Róng: "Lǐ Gōng's crime was sealed by your hand;
if Lǐ Gōng is executed,
what face will you have to look upon the world?"
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Chronicles of Hàn Zhìdì".
Lǐ Gōng,
refers to Lǐ Gù.
Lǐ Gù died in prison.
Before his death, he wrote a letter to Hú Guǎng and Zhào Jiè, saying: "Gù received the state's generous favor,
thus I exhausted my strength,
disregarding life and death,
intent on supporting the royal house,
to rival the prosperity of Kings Wén and Xuān.
How could I foresee that one day the Liáng clan would be deluded and erroneous,
and you gentlemen would yield to them,
turning good fortune into disaster,
and success into failure!
The Hàn dynasty's decline,
begins from this.
You gentlemen receive generous salaries from the sovereign,
yet when the state totters, you do not support it,
overturning great affairs;
will future good historians show any partiality!
My life is over,
in righteousness I have gained it,
what more is there to say!
Guǎng and Jiè, upon receiving the letter, were grieved and ashamed,
and could only sigh deeply and shed tears.
From "Comprehensive Mirror".
The emperor summoned Tián,
Yóu Yán to be Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
but in the Eastern Palace, he offered no admonitions or benefits.
Vice Commander of the Right Guard Jiǎng Yǎn wrote to reproach him: "If you had previously refused to eat Zhōu's grain, sir,
how would you dare accept salary for yourself?
With what will you repay this?"
Yóu Yán ultimately could not reply.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Gāozōng".
Lú Qǐ detested Tàizǐ Shǎoshī Yán Zhēnqīng,
and wanted to send him out to the provinces,
Zhēnqīng said to Qǐ:
"When the head of your late father, the Vice Censor, was sent to Píngyuán,
I, Zhēnqīng, licked the blood from his face with my tongue.
Now can you, sir, bear to not tolerate me?"
Qǐ started up and bowed in alarm,
but hated him even more.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Dézōng".
Xiè Ān repeatedly declined summons and did not take office; Jiǎn,
Emperor Wén, while serving as chancellor, said: "Since Ānshí shares joy with others,
he must inevitably share worries with them.
If summoned, he will certainly come."
． From "Jìn Shū, Basic Annals".
In the Wǔdé era,
the Turkic Khans Jiélì and the second Khan reached Yuánzhōu,
Tàizōng said to them:
"Do you not remember the words spoken over the incense fire in the past,
that you come now to invade?"
From "Táng Shū".
Biographies and Records
For the general, one battle brings achievement,
how can he bear to see the hundred-war veterans on the sandy field?
From "Nán Táng Jìnshì".
Collections
Long a wanderer, I often receive letters from friends,
plain letters, a bundle every month.
My vain reputation only brings inquiries about my well-being,
superficial affection does not save me from the disgrace of poverty.
From Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Cross-reference "Letters and Inquiries".
Old friends do not show compassion,
new acquaintances, how could they be sympathetic?
From Lǐ Bái's poetry.
Although I may receive a gift of a thousand gold daily,
and be promoted nine times in one year,
I may feel gratitude.
But to proclaim to the world:
"You know me,"
that is not so. From Hán Yù's writings.
The fēihuáng steed soars away,
unable to look back at the toad.
From Hán Yù's writings.
Now you, sir, are satisfied with fine food,
how could you still remember my times of poverty and lowliness?
From Mèng Jiāo.
Why is it that the noble in high carriages and caps,
do not speak with the commoner in cloth clothes?
From "Collection of Wáng Wéi".
Relatives and friends are like the clouds in the sky,
visible but beyond reach.
From "Collection of Gāo Shì".
If you uphold Píngzhòng's
long-standing promise,
do not spare the poet's
precious inquiries.
From Zhāng Jiǔlíng's writings.
You do not blame the quilt for being slept in,
but believe the quilt is worn through.
From Lú Tóng's writings.
Cross-reference "Lack of Trust".
Our Dynasty
What wrong have I done to you,
that you bring calamity upon me?
From "Collection of Ōuyáng Xiū".
Just as I was listening intently,
hoping for a continuation of the admonitions from the garden of remonstrance.
If you have something to say, awaiting the moment,
perhaps you can compose a discourse on the disputatious minister.
From "Collection of Sū Shì".
Pitiful Dí Rénjié,
still betrayed Lóu Gōng.
From "Collection of Sū Zhé".
Do not say there are no qílín or phoenixes in the central plains,
it is only that the royal net is woven too loosely.
From "General Turtle of Poetic Remarks".
Who knows how hard it is to part in old age,
news should come continuously.
From "Collection of Chén Shīdào".
Classics
How can it be said:
"I have no clothes? I have seven,
but none are as comfortable and auspicious as yours." From the "Poetry Classic, No Clothes".
Masters
Yú Shìjī said: "I move under the threat of arrows,
like you, master."
Wáng Tōng.
One may call it obscure.
Both from "Wénzhōngzǐ".
History
Gōngsūn Qīng said: "The Yellow Emperor ascended to heaven as an immortal,
the Yellow Emperor mined at Shǒushān.
Cast a bronze tripod at the foot of Jīngshān,
once the tripod was completed,
a dragon descended with its beard hanging down,
welcoming the Yellow Emperor upward.
Riding the dragon with his ministers,
and over seventy members of the harem, all ascended to heaven together.
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven said: 'Alas!
If I could truly be like the Yellow Emperor,
I would regard leaving my wife and children,
as merely taking off a sandal.'"
"Tōng Jiàn".
Shū Guǎng and his son requested to retire and leave,
onlookers along the road all said: "How virtuous!
These two great officers."
Some sighed in admiration,
shedding tears for them.
"Xīhàn Běnzhuàn".
Cáo Qiūshēng said to Jì Bù: "How did you, sir, gain such a reputation between Liáng and Chǔ?"
"Qiánhàn Běnzhuàn".
Scholars who received his reception,
were said to have ascended the dragon's gate.
"Dōnghàn Lǐ Yīng Zhuàn".
Guō Línzōng and Lǐ Yīng crossed the river in the same boat,
guests watching from afar thought they were immortals.
"Dōnghàn Guō Tài Zhuàn".
Yuán Shù saw Sūn Cè,
and sighed, saying: "If I had a son like the young lord Sūn,
what regret would I have in death!"
"Dōnghàn Běnzhuàn".
Cross-reference "resentment" "having a son".
King Fú Jiān of Qín sighed: "Zhōu Mèngwēi stood firm in the front,
Dīng Yànyuǎn maintained purity in the rear,
Jí Zǔchōng died with sealed lips,
how many loyal ministers does the Jìn house have!"
"Tōng Jiàn Jìn Chéng Jì".
Cross-reference "resentment" "maintaining integrity".
Táng Tàizōng established the College of Literature,
gathering talented individuals,
appointing Dù Rúhuì and others as academicians.
At that time,
those selected,
were admired throughout the land,
hailed as ascending Yíngzhōu.
"Tángshū Chǔ Liàng Zhuàn".
Consort Yáng was favored.
A folk song said: "Do not rejoice at a son's birth,
nor grieve at a daughter's.
Now see how a daughter upholds the family's honor."
"Tōng Jiàn Táng Xuánzōng".
Bān Jǐngqiàn entered the capital as Vice Minister of Justice,
passing through Dàliáng,
Ní Ruòshuǐ bid him farewell,
stood watching the dust of his departure,
only returning after a long while,
saying to his subordinates: "Bān's journey this time,
is no different from ascending to immortality!"
"Tōng Jiàn Táng Xuánzōng Jì".
Emperor Liáng said:
"To have a son, one should wish for Lǐ Yàzǐ,
thus Kèyòng's line does not perish.
As for my son,
he is but a pig or dog!"
"Tōng Jiàn Wǔdài Liáng Jì".
Cross-reference "having a son".
Biographies
Cuī Rìzhī regretted not reaching the eighth rank,
serving as Minister of Ceremonies.
He built a tower facing the Department of State Affairs,
people called it Cuī Gōng's Gaze-at-the-Ministry Tower.
"Guóshǐ Zuǎnyào".
During Táng Wénzōng's reign,
the imperial examination candidates were particularly prominent.
Examinees said:
"A presented scholar,
is not worth exchanging for a prefect of a superior prefecture."
"Lúshì Záshuō".
Táng Xuānzōng paid close attention to the imperial examinations,
inscribing on a palace pillar: "Local tribute scholar Lǐ Mǒu."
"Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Collections
Minister Lù delighted in the western capital,
Guō assessed human relations in the eastern state,

Lù Jiǎ had five sons;

sold them for a thousand gold,
divided among his sons,
each getting two hundred gold,
for their livelihood.
Jiǎ often rode in a comfortable carriage with four horses,
followed by ten attendants singing and playing se,
with a precious sword worth a hundred gold,
and said to his sons: "I make an agreement with you:
when I visit you,
you provide men, horses, wine, and food to the utmost,
and I move on after ten days.
Wherever I die,
that household gets the sword, carriage, horses, and attendants.
In a year, I will visit other guests in between,
generally not more than twice per visit,
often enjoying fresh kills,
so I won't trouble you for long."
