History
Zǐ Hǎn said: "We common folk
all have our humble homes
to avoid dryness, dampness, cold, and heat."
From "Zuǒzhuàn, 17th year of Xiāng Gōng".
Zhèng Xuán admonished his son Yì Ēn, saying: "Our family is now somewhat better off than before."
From "Hòu Hàn Shū • His Biography".
Cross-referenced under "Easily Satisfied".
Resources are moderately sufficient.
From "Táng Jiǎn".
Classics
The king bestows triple honors.
From "Yìjīng • Shī Guà".
Receiving heaven's favor.
Also from the same source.
Horses are bestowed in abundance,
received three times in a single day.
From "Jìn Guà".
Having met the noble man,
one becomes honored and glorified.
From "Xiǎo Yǎ • Liǎo Xiāo".
Hǔ bowed low, touching his head to the ground,
responding to and extolling the king's grace.
From "Dà Yǎ • Jiàng Hàn".
Father and son both served as Minister of Education for Zhōu.
From "Lǐjì • Zī Yī".
To be near the light of the Son of Heaven.
From "Shūjīng • Hóng Fàn".
Masters
If a ruler employs them,
they will enjoy peace, wealth, honor, and glory.
From "Mèngzǐ • Jìn Xīn Shàng".
Fù Yuè was elevated from among the builders,
Jiāo Gé from among the fish and salt traders,
Guǎn Yíwú from among the prisoners,
Sūn Shū'áo from the seashore,
Bǎilǐ Xī from the marketplace.
From "Mèngzǐ • Gào Zǐ Xià".
Cross-referenced under "Life's Unpredictability" and also see "Humble Abode".
History
Shénwǔ Gōng Gédòulíng Yì replied: "I have heard that qílín and fènghuáng,
though obtained, are of no use.
How could they compare to Délín,
who is both an auspicious sign and useful!"
"Chronicles of Chén".
The Emperor said: "To admonish and correct my faults,
I cannot be without you for even a day."
"Annals of Táng Tàizōng".
When Wèi Zhēng passed away,
the Emperor personally composed his epitaph,
and also wrote it himself.
The Emperor could not cease missing Zhēng,
and said to his attendants: "With Wèi Zhēng gone,
I have lost a mirror."
Lǐ Jī once suffered a sudden illness,
and it was said that burnt beard ashes could cure it,
so the Emperor cut off his own beard to mix the medicine.
Also from "Táng Tàizōng".
Wéi Sìlì was then the magistrate of Láiwú,
when Empress Wǔ summoned him,
saying: "Your father once said that his two sons
were fit to serve Your Majesty.
You and your brother in office
truly match your father's words,
so I now appoint you in your brother's place,
with no need for another."
That same day, he was appointed Shèrén of the Fènggé Pavilion.
"Annals of Táng Wǔhòu".
Cross-referenced under "Brothers".
Empress Wǔ trusted and valued the Neìshǐ Liáng Wénhuì
and Lord Dí Rénjié.
No other officials compared,
and she often called them 'State Elders' without using their names,
saying: "Every time I see you bow,
I feel pain in my own body."
"Annals of Táng Zhōngzōng".
Cross-referenced under "Respect and Courtesy".
Empress Wǔ said: "Táng Xiūjǐng is well-versed in border affairs,
you others are not even one-tenth his equal."
Same as above.
Lǐ Mì said: "I reside in the palace,
from my undergarments to my shoes, all are bestowed by Your Majesty, leaving me
with nothing but my own person."
The Emperor said: "I wish for you to eat meat and drink wine,
have a family,
receive a salary and position,
and be an ordinary man."
Mì wept and said: "I have abstained from grains for over twenty years;
why must Your Majesty make me abandon my resolve?"
He arranged for Mì to marry a daughter of the Lú family,
with all expenses covered by the state.
He bestowed a residence in Guāngfú Ward,
ordering Mì to stay there for several days,
and at the Pénglái Court for several days.
"Annals of Táng Dàizōng".
Dù Cóng was appointed Tóngpíngzhāngshì.
The Emperor commended him, saying: "I know you have the heart to guide your sovereign,
now having you as chancellor is like gaining another Wèi Zhēng."
"Annals of Táng Wǔzōng".
Lù Zhì, as a Hànlín academician, was trusted and favored by the Emperor.
During times of hardship,
even in matters great and small concerning the chancellor,
the Emperor would consult Zhì.
Thus, he was called the 'Inner Chancellor' at the time,
and the Emperor would always have him by his side.
"Annals of Táng Dézōng".
Lǐ Mì requested to retire due to old age.
The Emperor said: "My father and I relied on you for safety,
and now I entrust my descendants to you,
wishing you and your lineage everlasting wealth and honor in return for your virtue."
Same as above.
Both from "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn".
The Emperor once considered hunting near the Huāzhōng to the west of Pénglái Pond,
but told his attendants: "Lǐ Jiàng will surely remonstrate,
so we might as well stop."
"Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Annals of Táng Xiànzōng".
The Emperor praised Cuī Qún for his forthrightness and appointed him as an academician.
From then on,
all memorials required Cuī Qún's co-signature
before being presented.
Same as above.
Lǐ Déyù was promoted to Tàiwèi,
but he firmly declined.
The Emperor said: "I regret there is no higher office to reward you with."
"Annals of Táng Wǔzōng".
Lǐ Déyù requested to retire to a less demanding post.
The Emperor said: "Every time you resign,
it leaves me unsettled for ten days."
Same as above.
The Emperor ordered the relevant office to appoint Lǐ Sùlì as Jiānchá Yùshǐ,
a seventh-rank pure and important post.
The office proposed Yōngzhōu Sīhù instead.
The Emperor said: "That post
is important but not pure."
They then proposed Mìshū Láng,
and the Emperor said: "This post
is pure but not important."
So he was promoted to Shì Yùshǐ.
"Annals of Táng Gāozǔ".
Hán Xiū was stern and upright,
unconcerned with glory or profit.
When he became chancellor,
he lived up to the expectations of the time.
If the Emperor feasted in the palace
or hunted in the rear gardens,
even for minor faults,
he would ask his attendants: "Does Hán Xiū know?"
No sooner had he spoken,
than the memorial of remonstrance would arrive.
The Emperor sighed: "When Xiāo Sōng reports, he often
follows my wishes and leaves,
yet I cannot sleep peacefully."
"Táng Xuánzōng",
also from "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn".
My having Kǒngmíng
is like a fish having water.
"Biography of Shǔ's Zhūgě Liàng".
Thrice he visited my thatched cottage,
consulting me on the affairs of the time.
Same as above.
"Chūshī Biǎo".
Fú Jiān said to Wáng Měng: "I found you extraordinary at first sight,
and you also saw me as unique with one word;
our spirits aligned, a meeting
of a thousand years."
"Jìn Zǎijì".
Shān Táo was determined to retire,
but an edict stated: "Shān Púyè recently left temporarily,
and due to minor illness has not returned;
this is not my intent in awaiting you by the empty seat.
Send a clerk with this decree to convey my will:
if your health is not yet fully recovered,
have him bring you back to your office by carriage."
Unable to refuse,
Shān Táo resumed his duties.
"His Biography in Jìnshū".
Since Suí unified the realm, Lǐ Délín
often advised on plans to conquer Chén.
Gāozǔ, visiting Tóngzhōu,
pointed south with his horsewhip, saying: "Once Chén is pacified,
I will adorn you with the seven treasures."
"Suíshū".
Sòng's Wáng Yù,
courtesy name Jǐngwén.
Emperor Wén held him in high esteem,
so he married Jǐngwén's sister to Emperor Míng and used Jǐngwén's name
to name Emperor Míng.
Emperor Wǔ's fifth daughter, Princess Xīn'ān, was first married to Tàiyuán's
Wáng Jǐngshēn, but after divorcing,
she was to marry Jǐngwén.
Jǐngwén firmly declined,
and the marriage did not take place.
"His Biography in Sòngshū".
Yáng Xuánbǎo was transferred to be Prefect of Wú Commandery.
Tàizǔ once said: "Whenever I have a good official vacancy,
I always think of Yáng Xuánbǎo first."
Same as above.
Jì Zhì served as Zhōngshū Lìng,
while his father Liàng was Shàngshū Lìng.
At court assemblies,
the Emperor used a mica screen to separate their seats.
"Wú Lù".
Zhāng Shuài was promoted to Mìshū Chéng.
Gāozǔ said: "Mìshū Chéng is a pure post in the empire;
among the descendants of the southeast,
none have held it.
Now I place you here
to establish your reputation."
"Qí Shū".
Kǒng Língchǎn, as Guānglù Dàfū, refused to take office.
Tàizǔ gifted him a white feather fan and a plain stool, saying: "You have the style of the ancients,
so I bestow upon you the attire of the ancients."
Same as above.
Zhōu Tàizǔ consulted Sū Chuò,
straightening his clothes and sitting upright,
unconsciously leaning forward on his knees,
until dawn without weariness.
"Běishǐ".
Wáng Sù was appointed Dàzhōngzhèng of Yángzhōu.
Later, Wèi Xiàowén summoned him to court,
writing in an edict: "I have adorned a lodge in Huálín,
and prepared a mat to await you."
"His Biography".
The Emperor held Cuī Hào's hand, showing him to Měngxùn's envoy, saying: "The one called Lord Cuī
is this man.
The excellence of his talent and strategy
is unmatched in the present day."
"Wèi's Biography of Cuī Hào",
also from "Běishǐ".
When Xuánzōng appointed a chancellor,
he would first write the name and place it on his desk.
Once, the Crown Prince entered,
and the attendant lifted a golden bowl covering the name, saying: "This is the chancellor's name."
Sùzōng said: "Is it not Cuī Lín or Lú Cóngyuàn?"
"Tángshū".
The Prince of Qín appointed Rúhuì and Yuánlíng as Hóngwénguǎn academicians,
with their portraits displayed and titles honored,
known as the Eighteen Academicians.
Those who entered the academy
were said by contemporaries to have "ascended to Yíngzhōu."
In the fifth year of Yuánhé,
Lǐ Jiàng was promoted to Zhōngshū Shèrén.
He retained his previous position as Hànlín Academician,
and the emperor bestowed upon him golden purple robes,
personally selecting a fine hu tablet for Jiàng.
Emperor Tàizōng personally untied his own girdle dagger,
to bestow upon Fáng Xuánlíng and Wèi Zhēng.
When Lù Zhì entered the Hànlín Academy, the Son of Heaven
often addressed him by his generational rank instead of his personal name.
"Basic Biography."
Lù Zhì accompanied the emperor to Shānnán,
the road was arduous and dangerous,
the escort could not keep up,
and he became separated from the emperor,
not arriving for one night.
The emperor decreed:
"Whoever finds Zhì will be rewarded a thousand in gold."
The next day,
Zhì had an audience,
and the emperor's joy showed on his face.
On the day of Wèi Zhēng's death,
Emperor Tàizōng ascended a tower overlooking the road to weep and offer sacrifices,
composed a stele inscription for him,
and wrote it in his own hand.
When Péi Dù lay ill,
Emperor Wénzōng sent a palace envoy to bestow a poem upon Dù, which said:
"Focused thoughts await you, Yuán,
I regret not knowing you earlier in my life.
You are the pillar and cornerstone of the state,
in worry, I learn from Qiū's prayers."
Líng Hú Táo served as a Hànlín Academician.
Emperor Xuānzōng summoned him at night,
to discuss the hardships of the people,
and sent him back with a golden lotus torch from the imperial carriage.
The courtyard officials saw it from afar,
thinking the Son of Heaven had come,
but when Táo arrived,
they were all astonished.
Emperor Táng Tàizōng said:
"People say Wèi Zhēng's demeanor is careless and rude,
but I find him even more charming."
Both from "Táng Shū."
Liǔ Gōngquán
was summoned by Emperor Xuānzōng to ascend the front of the imperial hall and write on three sheets of paper.
The Military Commissioner Xīmén Jìxuán held the inkstone,
and the Privy Councilor Cuī Jùyuán passed the brush.
"Old Táng Shū Basic Biography."
Liǔ Gōngquán,
during Emperor Wénzōng's reign, served as Zhōngshū Shèrén,
and Hànlín Academician.
Whenever summoned, even when the candle wick was nearly burnt out and his words unfinished,
he dared not take the candle,
so palace maids would knead paper with wax tears,
to continue.
Same as above.
Empress Zétiān, because Wáng Fāngqìng's family had many books,
once sought the surviving works of Yòujūn.
Fāngqìng presented twenty-eight individuals,
with a total of ten volumes of calligraphy.
Zétiān presided at Wǔchéng Hall,
showing them to the assembled officials.
She then ordered Zhōngshū Shèrén Cuī Róng to compile the "Precious Chapters Collection,"
to narrate the event.
She also bestowed it upon Fāngqìng,
which was considered a great honor at the time.
Same as above.
"Wáng Fāngqìng Biography."
Dí Rénjié later personally embroidered twelve golden characters on his robe,
to express his loyalty,
and was reappointed as Píngzhāng Shì.
"New Táng Shū Basic Biography."
Liú Yàn, at eight years old, presented a eulogy,
the emperor marveled at his youth,
and ordered Chancellor Zhāng Yuè to test him, saying: "A national treasure."
He was immediately appointed to Zhèngzì,
with invitations from high officials coming incessantly,
hailed as a child prodigy,
his fame shaking the era.
Same as above.
"Basic Biography."
Cross-referenced under "Intelligence."
Wēn Dàyǎ successively rose to Huángmén.
Emperor Tàizōng said:
"I started the uprising in Jìnyáng,
all for your family alone."
Cross-referenced under "Brothers."
Biography
Liáng Liǔ Chuò,
was appointed as Mìshū Chéng.
Emperor Wǔdì said:
"The first official position
should be given to the number one person."
"Tōngdiǎn."
Emperor Dézōng called Lù Zhì as Lù Jiǔ,
and once took off his own imperial robe
to bestow upon him.
"Táng Xiǎoshǐ."
When Lǐ Bái faced Emperor Mínghuáng drafting edicts,
the weather was cold and the brush froze,
so the emperor ordered palace maids
to hold the ivory brush and warm it with their breath.
"Kāiyuán Tiānbǎo Yíshì."
Lǐ Mì abstained from grains for many years.
During Emperor Sùzōng of Táng's reign,
he would personally roast two pears each time
to bestow upon him.
Lǐ Yèhóu "Family Affairs."
Xú Jiān, for his extensive knowledge of classical precedents,
entered the library seven times.
"Great Táng Yíshì."
Cross-referenced under "Erudition."
Liú Yàn, at eight, presented a text for the eastern sacrifice.
Emperor Mínghuáng ordered the chancellor to set a topic,
conducted the test at the Zhōngshū Department,
and led Yàn into the inner palace,
seating Yàn on the Consort's lap.
He personally drew eyebrows and tied his hair in twin tufts,
while palace maids threw flowers and fruits.
"Kāiyuán Chuánxìn Jì."
When Duke Wèi Lǐ was ill,
Emperor Tàizōng personally issued edicts,
four times.
One said:
"There is a saying: day and night I watch over your illness,
let an old woman send one person here,
I wish to be thoroughly familiar with the state of your daily life."
Upon seeing this edict, Duke Wén
often wept and said:
"The relationship between ruler and minister
is indeed like this."
Wéi Duān "Record of Duke Wèi's Belongings."
Emperor Táng Xuānzōng favored Confucian elegance,
and paid close attention to imperial examinations.
A discourse on a once-in-a-thousand-years encounter,
undoubtedly soaring with ease.
Like a swan feather meeting a favorable wind, flourishing freely;
like a giant fish released into a vast abyss.
Wáng Bāo's "Eulogy".
The Orchid Terrace and Golden Gate,
alternating lodgings and successive residences.
"Rhapsody on the Western Capital".
Having gained access through the Golden Gate register,
then sipping jade banquet wine.
"Selections of Refined Literature".
Noble and lofty, Zǐjìng,
rose from obscurity among the weeds.
"Selections of Refined Literature".
Asked what merit I have,
thrice I entered the Chéngmíng Lodge.
Yīng Jù's poem.
Encountering a glorious gathering of a thousand years.
Pān Ānrén's "Rhapsody on a Journey West".
His words were like stones cast into water,
none could oppose them.
Lǐ Xiāoyuǎn's "Discourse on Fate and Fortune",
also in "Selections of Refined Literature".
The sovereign bestows his favor,
reputation soaring above the mist and rainbow.
Lǐ Tàibái.
Winds and clouds stirred, rising from butcher and fisherman.
Cross-reference "The Unfathomability of Human Life".
Like fish and water, united through three visits,
winds and clouds arose across the four seas.
Both from the same source as above.
Climbing with dragons and following phoenixes, their momentum unstoppable.
Dù Fǔ's poetry.
The Son of Heaven said: "The writings of Wáng Mǒu,
are most fit for imperial edicts,
possessing ancient style—how could he remain long?"
Employing him with official duties,
he was appointed as a Secretary in the Secretariat.
Hán Yù's "Stele for Wáng Zhòngshū".
Cross-reference "Critique of Literature".
Wáng Zhòngshū and Yáng Chéng jointly thwarted Péi Yánlíng,
preventing him from becoming chancellor.
Emperor Dézōng long praised him,
and later, when entering the court for consultation, said to the chancellor: "The one in such position must be Wáng Mǒu."
Indeed it was,
and within over a month, he was promoted to Vice Director.
Same as above.
Emperor Xuánzōng summoned Lǐ Bái to the Golden Bells Hall,
descended from his carriage to welcome him as if meeting Yuán and Qǐ,
bestowed a feast before him on a jewel-adorned square mat,
personally seasoned the soup with his imperial hand,
uttered virtuous words of praise,
such grace to one in coarse cloth,
unprecedented before.
Thus he was directly appointed to the Hanlin Academy, solely in charge of confidential decrees.
Another day, while boating on the White Lotus Pond,
with the Duke absent from the banquet,
the imperial joy being harmonious,
he was summoned to compose a preface.
At that time, the Duke was already intoxicated in the Hanlin courtyard,
yet the tall General-in-Chief was ordered to support him onto the boat.
Fàn Chuánzhèng's "Stele for Lǐ Bái".
Riding a red-wheeled carriage to the commandery residence,
trailing long robes at the prince's gate.
Fame and office reaching this point,
it cannot be said he was unfulfilled.
"Collected Works of Bái Jūyì".
May he wear sable ornaments and stand by my side,
attending with ease, ready for consultation.
Same as above.
Imperial notes piled on the desk,
heavenly fragrance fills the robes.
Lǐ Wénráo.
Awakening to a single word and attaining the chancellorship,
with three inches of tongue becoming the emperor's teacher.
Same as above.
Winter clothes and medicine all from the sage's compassion,
every horse and person selected by the emperor.
Lǚ Héshū's writings.
In our dynasty,
Dí Qīng battled the western rebels,
accumulating merits,
until he became Deputy Military Commissioner.
Yet the emperor had not seen his face,
so ordered a portrait to be submitted,
whereby all under heaven knew his name.
"Records from the Eastern Studio".
Repeated and detailed favors.
"Línchuān Collection".
Classic
I was born at an inopportune time.
The worthy of Wèi,
served as a court musician.
"Cypress Boat" speaks of benevolence,
yet he did not find fulfillment.
During the time of Duke Qǐng of Wèi.
The benevolent man unfulfilled,
petty men at the side.
Both from "Máo's Version of the Classic of Poetry".
Master
When a nag and a steed are yoked together,
Bó Lè sighs over it;
when jade and stone are mixed,
Hé Shì laments it.
"Kǒng Cóngzǐ: The Confucian Garb" chapter.
A floating chime stone silent,
indistinguishable from common rocks.
"Bàopǔzǐ".
Duke Yuè first saw the Master,
and encountered the Palace Secretary, Duke Xuē, who said: "Have you met Wáng Tōng?"
Duke Xuē said: "He is my townsman,
his family tradition spans seven generations.
All possessed the way of statecraft,
yet none encountered opportunity."
Duke Yuè said: "How can there be seven generations without opportunity under heaven?"
Duke Xuē said: "When the way of the gentleman wanes, ten generations without opportunity
can occur."
"Wénzhōngzǐ: Rituals and Music" chapter.
History
Six egrets flew backward.
． _Zuozhuan, Year 16 of Duke Xi_.
Since Qū Yuán drowned himself in the Mìluó River,
over a hundred years had passed.
In the Hàn dynasty, there was Jiǎ Shēng who served as the Grand Tutor to the King of Chángshā,
and when crossing the Xiāng River, he cast a letter into the water
to mourn Qū Yuán.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Qū Yuán_.
Sū Qín traveled abroad,
and after several years,
returned in great distress.
_His Original Biography_.
Zhòngní (Confucius) approached over seventy lords,
yet found no ruler to employ him.
_Biographies of Confucian Scholars_.
Confucius left Lǔ,
was rejected in Qí,
expelled from Sòng,
and trapped between Chén and Cài in Wèi.
_Confucius' Hereditary House_,
also from _Records of the Grand Historian_.
Zhū Mǎichén walked alone,
singing on the road,
carrying firewood among the tombs.
His former wife and her husband's family went to sweep the graves,
saw Mǎichén hungry and cold,
and called him over to give him food and drink.
_Book of Hàn_.
Zhāng Shìzhī went ten years without promotion,
Féng Táng reached old age still a lowly court attendant.
Xún Yuè's _Annals of Hàn_.
Emperor Wén said: "It's a pity Lǐ Guǎng was born at the wrong time;
had he lived in Emperor Gāozǔ's era, a marquis with ten thousand households
would have been nothing remarkable!"
． _Western Hàn, Biography of Lǐ Guǎng_.
Why is an official's career so bleak?
_Biography of Yáng Xióng_.
Féng Táng served as a court attendant;
the Emperor asked him, "Why are you, an elder, still a lowly attendant?"
Yán Shǐgǔ commented: "He was already old."
_His Original Biography_.
Zhāng Shìzhī purchased the position of a cavalry attendant,
served under Emperor Wén,
yet for ten years received no promotion,
remaining unknown.
_His Original Biography_.
Yáng Xióng served three reigns without a single promotion.
_His Original Biography_.
Lǐ Guǎng's fate was often thwarted.
Mèng Kāng explained: "He never found his match or opportunity."
_Biography of Lǐ Guǎng_.
Left behind and unmatched.
_Biography of Huò Qùbìng_.
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú long served as an official but never succeeded.
_Biography of Sīmǎ Xiāngrú_,
also from _Book of Hàn_.
Mǎ Róng served as a collator for ten years
without a transfer or promotion.
． _Later Hàn, His Original Biography_.
Holding precious jade only to be covered in dust,
embracing pillars and beams,
yet trapped in ditches and valleys.
_Book of Jìn_.
In Zhào, there was the recluse Máo Gōng who hid among gamblers,
and Xuē Gōng who concealed himself among drink sellers.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Fifth Scroll of Zhōu_.
In Wèi, Gāo Yǔn served as a court attendant for twenty-seven years
without promotion.
Same as above.
_Annals of Emperor Wǔ of Sòng_.
Liú Cángqì at seventy
became a Secretary in the Department of State Affairs.
_Annals of Emperor Gāozōng of Táng_.
Wáng Yìfāng, a hero of his time,
died in obscurity among the grasses.
Same as above.
Jí Àn, with his upright spirit,
starved to death in Huáiyáng.
Dǒng Zhòngshū, with his great talent,
was relegated to the position of a feudal lord's chancellor.
_Memorial on Sealing Matters_.
Among Confucius' three thousand disciples who achieved understanding,
none held the rank of a viscount or baron.
Also from _Táng_.
Biographies and Records
Wáng Bō was orphaned and poor in his youth,
once staying at Mùlán Temple in Yángzhōu,
joining the monks for meals,
but the monks grew tired of him,
so by the time Bō arrived, they had already eaten.
_Records of Selected Sayings_.
Yán Sì said to Emperor Wǔ: "Emperor Wén favored literary men, but I was martial;
Emperor Jǐng preferred the aged, but I was still young;
Your Majesty favors the young, but I am already old—
thus through three reigns, I found no opportunity."
_Stories of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn_.
Chancellor Duàn Wénchāng was poor in his youth,
and whenever he heard the meal bell at Zēngkǒu Temple,
he would go to eat,
until the temple monks grew annoyed,
and rang the bell only after the meal.
Later, when he became chancellor
and was stationed south of the capital,
he inscribed at Zēngkǒu Temple: "Once I encountered the meal bell after the monks had eaten."
_Trifling Tales from North of Meng_.
Collections
More than half the year has already passed,
Yet I remain stranded in hardship and stagnation.
From "Chǔ Cì".
Is there truly no fine steed in this age?
Indeed, there is no Wáng Liáng skilled in handling the reins.
Holding gems and grasping jades,
Yet in poverty, I know not to whom to present them.
Bó Yá broke his strings,
For without Zhōngzǐ Qī, who would listen?
Hé, embracing his uncut jade, wept tears of blood,
How could he find a skilled artisan to discern its worth?
Also from "Chǔ Cì".
My reputation is in disarray, my talents unwieldy,
A life full of troubles, bitterly winding.

were penalized with drinking.

Huán asked, "What is 'jūyú'?"
He replied,
"In the tribal language, fish is called 'jūyú.'"
Huán said, "Why use tribal language in a poem?"
Lóng replied, "I traveled a thousand lǐ to serve you,
only to become a tribal commander's adviser—
how could I not use tribal language?"

There was a traveler who fell from a thousand rèn while traversing the perilous Sāntú path,
looking up from the road, crying out for help from passersby.
Hundreds passed by daily without a glance,
and even those who pitied him and looked,
merely grasped a tree, bowed their heads,
sighed deeply for a while, and then left.
In the end, there was no solution.
Yet the man still hoped without ceasing.
Suddenly, a strong man like Wū Huò appeared,
holding a long rope a thousand xún long,
passing slowly by.
His strength was sufficient,
his tools adequate.
But when called, he did not look back;
looking back, he said: "If I cannot help, the man knows he must die in the great ravine.
Why?
This is a moment not meant to be met, yet by chance it is.
Why not seize it when encountered?
Only then did he realize his fate was exhausted and his situation dire.
Finally, he cried out in despair and perished,
no longer hoping for rescue from above."
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
Cross-reference "Pleading for Mercy".
Fallen leaves do not rest again,
broken tumbleweeds do not return.
From Hán's "Poem on Fallen Leaves".
Rain that falls cannot return to the sky,

Xì Xiànzǐ rushed to save him.

Xìzǐ then ordered the immediate public display of the body and told his attendant: "I did this to share the blame."

A singer of Sòng's walls chanted: "The pale one from Zémén,

Zǐ Hǎn heard this,

striking the lazy builders until they ceased their idleness.

Do not let one alone bear the ill repute.

Chén Shí, serving as a merit officer,
was asked by the regular attendant Hóu Lǎn to have the prefect Gāo Lún appoint an official.
Lún instructed to assign him as a literary official.
Shí, knowing the man unfit,
carried the document and requested an audience, saying: "This man should not be appointed."
But Hóu the regular attendant's wish could not be opposed.
Shí begged to appoint him externally, and Lún agreed.
Local opinion criticized the improper appointment, but Lún later explained: "I previously appointed an official for Hóu the regular attendant.
Chén Jūn secretly returned the instruction and arranged it externally.
When it became known, critics faulted me for this.
The fault lies with me, fearing the powerful.
Chén Jūn can be said to claim the fault as his own."
Shí insisted on taking the blame himself,
and those who heard sighed in admiration.
. From "Eastern Hàn, his biography".
Cross-reference "Judgment Settled Over Time".
Biographies
A loyal minister lets criticism fall on himself,
and praise go to his superior.
The ruler of Sòng seized the people's time
to build a terrace, and the people criticized him.
It was because there was no loyal minister to cover for him.
Zǐ Hǎn, as minister of works, took up the whip,
so the people blamed Zǐ Hǎn
and praised their ruler.
In Duke Huán of Qí's palace,
there were seven markets and women's quarters;
the seven hundred families of the state criticized him.
Guǎn Zhòng built a triple-terraced mansion
to cover Duke Huán's faults,
taking the blame upon himself from the people.
The Spring and Autumn Annals record ministers killing rulers—
all were ministers who had gained praise.
When a minister gains praise,
it is not a blessing for the state.
From "Zhànguócè".
Our dynasty
Yú Ní was possessed by a ghost and foretold events,
some of which came true, attracting crowds of scholars and commoners. After these incidents,
he was imprisoned for spreading heretical teachings.
An imperial decree appointed officials to investigate, and they obtained letters from various gentlemen.
From Hán Zēng downwards,
all had them,
but Duke Lù alone had none.
The emperor asked the reason.
The duke said: "I simply did not know about it;
had I known, I would have written too."
Contemporaries praised him for sharing the blame.
"Wēn Gōng's Daily Records."
Duke Yàn Yuánxiàn said: "I am not one who dislikes feasts and outings;
if I had money,
I would go too.
But having no money,
I cannot go out."
"Brush Talks."
Classic
The Jì family was about to attack Zhuānyú.
Rǎn Yǒu and Jì Lù visited Confucius and said: "The Jì family is going to attack Zhuānyú."
Confucius said: "Qiú,
is this not your fault?
Zhuānyú,
the former kings appointed as lord of Dōngméng,
and it lies within our state's borders,
being a minister of the altars of land and grain.
Why attack it?"
Rǎn Yǒu said: "Our master wishes it;
we two ministers
both do not desire it."
"Analects, Jì Shì chapter."

When people die, they say:
'It was not I; it was the year.'
How is this different from stabbing someone to death
and saying:
'It was not I; it was the weapon.'"
"Mencius, Liáng Huì Wáng I."
Mencius went to Pínglù and said to its high official: "If your spearman
loses his place three times in one day, do you dismiss him?"
He said: "I would not wait for three times."
"Then you have lost your place many times as well.
In years of famine and hunger,
your people,
the old and weak are left in ditches,
the strong scatter to the four directions,
nearly a thousand of them."
He said: "This is not something Jùxīn could prevent."
"Mencius, Gōngsūn Chǒu II."

Now if people in the same house

The emperor ordered the arrest and delivery to the Palace Domestic Service for interrogation.
Lǐ Shèng heard of this,
and immediately fell to the ground, saying:
"My clan will be exterminated." Lǐ Mì asked him the reason,
and Shèng said:
"I have recently suffered slander and vilification.
There are over a thousand family members at home and abroad.
If even one of them is involved in the faction,
then even you, elder brother, would not be able to save me." Lǐ Mì then secretly memorialized:
"Once a major case is initiated,
the number of people implicated will surely be many,
causing alarm and fear among the populace.
I request that it be handed over to the Censorate for investigation." The emperor complied,
and no court officials were implicated.
Also from "Annals of Emperor Dézōng of Táng".
Dù Jiān falsely accused Lǐ Fān of unsettling military morale
upon the death of Zhāng Jiànfēng.
The emperor was furious
and secretly ordered Dù Yòu to execute him.
Yòu, who had always respected Fān, held the edict for ten days without bearing to carry it out.
He then led Fān out and showed him the edict.
Fān's expression did not change.
Yòu said:
"Be careful not to speak of this. I have already secretly argued and staked my family's hundred lives to guarantee you." The emperor summoned Fān to Cháng'ān,
and upon seeing Fān's dignified and composed demeanor,
exclaimed:
"How could this man be an evildoer?" He immediately appointed him as a Gentleman of the Imperial Library.
"Annals of Emperor Dézōng of Táng".
Cross-referenced under "Turning Calamity into Blessing".
Quán Shàncái and Fàn Huáiyì mistakenly cut down a cypress tree at the Zhāolíng mausoleum,
an offense warranting dismissal from office;
but the emperor specifically ordered their execution.
Dí Rénjié memorialized:
"The two men's crime does not deserve death." The emperor said:
"If I do not kill Shàncái and others for cutting the mausoleum cypress, I would be unfilial." Despite Rénjié's persistent remonstrance,
the emperor became angry
and ordered him to leave.
Rénjié said:
"Offending the ruler with blunt advice
has always been considered difficult since ancient times.
I believe it is difficult when encountering Jié or Zhòu,
but easy when encountering Yáo or Shùn. Zhāng Shìzhī once said:
'If someone were to steal a handful of soil from the Chánglíng mausoleum,
how would Your Majesty deal with it?'
Now, for one cypress tree, you would kill two generals.
What will later generations say of Your Majesty?
The reason I dare not obey the decree
is that I fear it would plunge Your Majesty into unrighteousness,
and I would be ashamed to face Shìzhī in the afterlife." The emperor's anger subsided slightly,
and the two were dismissed from office,
exiled to Lǐngnán.
"Annals of Emperor Gāozōng of Táng".
Cross-referenced under "Shifting Public Sentiment".
Wéi Sìlì
was the half-brother of Chéngqìng.
Their mother, née Wáng,
treated Chéngqìng very harshly.
Whenever she caned Chéngqìng,
Sìlì would invariably remove his clothes and beg to take the punishment in his stead.
If their mother refused,
he would often cane himself in private,
and eventually, the mother became more lenient.
"Annals of Empress Wǔ of Táng".
Cross-referenced under "Brothers".
The recluse Wéi Yuèjiāng submitted a letter accusing Wǔ Sānsī of secretly communicating with the palace.
The emperor was enraged
and ordered his execution.
Sòng Jǐng petitioned for an investigation, saying:
"If you insist on executing Yuèjiāng, please execute me first.
Otherwise, I dare not obey the decree." "Annals of Emperor Zhōngzōng of Táng".
An edict stated:
"Wáng Yǎn's entire entourage shall be executed."
After it had been stamped and approved,
the Privy Councilor Zhāng Jūhàn
wiped the character for "entourage" off the palace pillar
and changed it to "family".
"Annals of Emperor Míngzōng of Later Táng".

Dòu Jiàndé captured Jǐngchéng

"The Registrar is incomparably pure and conscientious.
If you kill him, Great King,
how will you encourage goodness?" "Annals of Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng".
Zhāng Jiǔlíng contested every matter, great or small.
Consort Wèi tearfully complained to the emperor:
"The Crown Prince has secretly formed a faction
to harm me and my son, and he has also spoken disrespectfully of Your Majesty." The emperor was furious
and told his ministers,
intending to depose them all.
Jiǔlíng said:
"The Crown Prince is the foundation of the empire
and must not be shaken.
In the past, Duke Xiàn of Jìn, believing the slander of Lí Jī, killed Shēnshēng,
leading to three generations of chaos.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn trusted Jiāng Chōng's false accusations against the Crown Prince Jù,
causing bloodshed in the capital.
Emperor Huì of Jìn, heeding Jiǎ Hòu's calumny, deposed Crown Prince Mǐnhuái,
plunging the central plains into misery.
Emperor Wén of Suí, accepting the words of Empress Dúgū, dismissed Crown Prince Yǒng
and established Yáng,
leading to the loss of the empire.
From this, it is evident
that caution is necessary.
If Your Majesty insists on this course,
I dare not obey the decree." Thus, until Jiǔlíng was dismissed from his post,
the Crown Prince remained secure.
"Annals of Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng",
also from "Comprehensive Mirror".
Lǐ Déyù served as Minister of War.
Initially, Lǐ Zōngmǐn had a grudge against Déyù.
When Déyù returned from Xīchuān,
the emperor held him in high regard
and was about to make him chancellor soon.
Zōngmǐn tried every means to obstruct him but failed.
Dù Cóng once visited Zōngmǐn and said:
"I have a plan
to settle the old grievance,
but I fear you may not use it." Zōngmǐn asked:
"What is it?" Cóng said:
"Déyù is learned but did not pass the imperial examinations,
which often bothers him.
If you let him oversee the examinations,
he would surely be pleased." Zōngmǐn remained silent for a while and then said:
"Think of another option." Cóng said:
"Otherwise, appoint him as Grand Master of Remonstrance." Zōngmǐn said:
"That would work." Cóng then went to see Déyù.
Déyù greeted him and asked:
"Why have you come to this quiet place?" Cóng said:
"Minister Jìng'ān sent me to convey his intentions."
and informed him of the appointment as Grand Master.
Déyù was pleasantly surprised and shed tears,
saying:
"This is a high-ranking position; how can someone like me deserve it!" "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Emperor Wénzōng of Táng".

Differed in their ancestral foundations.

During the Kāiyuán era, over seventy mints cast coins nationwide,
Yielding a million in annual revenue,
Now only over ten mints remain,
Bringing in one hundred and fifty thousand yearly,
With coins hoarded by merchants or flowing out to border tribes.
Moreover,
Before the Dàlì era, Zīqīng, Tàiyuán, and Wèibó traded using lead and iron coins,
While Lǐngnán used gold, silver, cinnabar, and ivory,
Now only standard coins are used.
Under these circumstances,
How can money not be devalued!
Now, taxes should be paid in grain and silk,
With increased minting and bans on hoarding or export,
Then currency will gradually multiply.

Fēng Píng was enfeoffed as Hóu of Hùyǒu.
Píng declined, saying: "If not for Wèi Wúzhī,
how could I have been advanced?"
The Emperor said: "Like you,
one can be said not to forget one's origins."
． *Qián Hàn Shū, Chén Píng's Biography*.
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Sòng was in humble circumstances,
he personally farmed at Dāntú.
After receiving the Mandate, the farming tools
that remained
were all ordered to be stored,
to be left for posterity.
． *Nán Shǐ, Basic Annals*.
Zhōu Pánlóng went from General Who Pacifies the North to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Emperor Wǔ jested with him: "How do you feel
wearing the marten tail and cicada wing emblem?"
He replied: "This emblem comes from within the helmet."
． *Qí Shū*.
Sūn Zhěng's disciples Fèi Cí and Zǎi Yì
went to the prison
to clarify Zhěng's innocence.
Zhěng said: "I chose not to betray the two Lùs unto death;
it is my duty. Why are you doing this?"
They said: "Since you did not betray the two Lùs,
how could we betray you?"
． *Tōngjiàn, Jìn Huìdì's Annals*.
Zhāng Chāo said: "Zǐyuán is a righteous man of the world,
who will never forget his origins."
． *Tōngjiàn, Hàn Xiàndì's Annals*.
The Emperor arrived at Xiǎnrén Palace and said: "When I passed here before,
I bought food to eat
and rented a room to stay.
Now with such lavish provisions,
how can one still complain it's not enough?"
． *Tōngjiàn, Táng Tàizōng*.
Wáng Shīfàn said: "I respect my homeland
to teach my descendants not to forget their roots."
． *Tōngjiàn, Táng Xīzōng*.
Initially, the Prince of Qín repelled them with a large arrow.
Later, one large bow
and five large arrows remained.
They were treasured through generations and at suburban altars,
always displayed at the forefront of ritual objects
to commemorate military achievements.
． *Táng Shū*.
Cross-referenced under "Achievements."
Biographies
state: Those who eat from a vessel
do not destroy it;
those who rest under a tree
do not break its branches.
． *Hán Shī Wàizhuàn*.
Wearing a single color reminds one of women's labor;
consuming a grain makes one sympathize with farmers' toil.
． *Shì Yào Lùn*.
Collections
dare to betray kindness and forget beginnings.
Mí Zhèngpíng's rhapsody.
The weak are meat for the strong to eat.
Now that Wénchàng and I live securely and eat leisurely,
wandering carefree through life and death,
differing from beasts,
how can we not know whence this comes?
Hán Wén.
Who enriches the river
without admiring its source?
Same as above.
All day fine food and drink,
all year fine clothes to wear.
Fine clothes and good food have their origins;
one should feel ashamed before Sāng Hóngyáng.
The Salt Merchant's Wife.
． *Bái Shìláng Jí*.
Frost descends, water returns to the valleys;
wind falls, wood goes back to the mountains.
Without the virtue of ancestors,
who would inspire later generations?
Both same as above.
If one embodies heaven and earth's essence,
all are bodies of heaven and earth.
Mèng Dōngyě.
Who says the heart of an inch-long grass
can repay the warmth of three spring months?
Same as above.
Our Dynasty
Someone advised Dí Qīng to remove the character between his temples. He said: "The reason I've reached this position
is because of this."
． *Wénjiàn Lù*.
Fàn Zhōngxuān Gōng was banished to Yǒngzhōu.
His sons wanted to explain that Zhōngxuān and Sīmǎ Gōng differed
on corvée laws,
seeking to clear his name.
He said: "I became chancellor through Jūnshí's recommendation;
disagreeing in court discussions is one thing,
but your current words are unacceptable.
Better to die without shame
than live with it."
Same as above.
Always a stick of incense,
reverently offered to Zēng Nánfēng.
． *Hòushān Jí*.
Masters
Féng Méng learned archery from Yì
and mastered all of Yì's skills.
Thinking only Yì in the world surpassed himself,
he then killed Yì.
． *Mèngzǐ, Lílóu II*.
Jǐ Chāng learned archery from Fēi Wèi,
and after exhausting Wèi's techniques,
plotted to kill Wèi.
． *Lièzǐ*.
Valuing the bright pearl but despising the deep pool,
cherishing the Hé jade but hating Jīng Mountain,
not knowing the deep pool
is where the bright pearl comes from,
and Jīng Mountain
is where the Hé jade is produced.
． *Bàopǔzǐ, Wēizhǐ Piān*.
Eating grain but scorning the fields,
wearing silk but laughing at silkworms—
this is delusion.
． *Chénzǐ Yàoyán*.
Ice is born from water yet ice blocks water;
smoke arises from fire yet smoke stifles fire.
． *Liúzǐ*.
History
As the saying goes: "To seek shelter under a tree and then wield an axe against it."
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Wén Year 7_.
To rely on another's strength,
and then to harm them is unrighteous.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xī Year 30_.
Yáng Qiú arrested Wáng Fǔ, Duàn Jǐong and others and sent them to Luòyáng prison,
including Fǔ's son, the Shǎolè Shàofǔ Méng.
Qiú personally interrogated Fǔ and the others,
whereupon Méng said to Qiú: "Spare my old father."
Qiú said: "Your crimes are heinous,
death cannot absolve your guilt,
and yet you seek leniency!"
Méng then cursed: "You served my father and me like a slave,
how dare a slave rebel against his master!
Today you push us into the pit,
but your turn will come!"
． _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Língdì Annals_.
Huángfǔ Lì said: "Recently,
Dǒng Gōng's power was known to you, General.
Lǚ Bù received his favor,
yet plotted against him."
． _Tōngjiàn, Hàn Xiàndì Annals_.
Zuǒ Xióng recommended Zhōu Jǔ for Shàngshū,
but when Xióng recommended Féng Zhí who was implicated in bribery,
Jǔ impeached Xióng for this.
Xióng said: "Promoting you, sir,
has become my own undoing."
． _Tōngjiàn, Shùndì Annals, Yǒnghé Year 2_.
When Liú Zhàn entered court,
Yīn Jǐngrén actually recommended him.
Once Zhàn arrived,
seeing that Jǐngrén's position and favor did not surpass his own,
yet he was suddenly ahead,
he felt deeply resentful,
and had Yì Kāng slander Jǐngrén to the Emperor.
Jǐngrén sighed to his kin and old friends:
"I brought him in,
and once in, he bites people."
． _Tōngjiàn, Jìn Tàizǔ_.
In the ruined Yīnshì where Gāozǔ once lived, the bedhead had an earthen partition wall,
on which hung a gé lantern,
and a hemp duster.
Shìzhōng Yuán Yì thus praised Gāozǔ's virtue of frugality,
but the Emperor did not reply.
He only said: "A country fellow getting this was already excessive!"
． _Tōngjiàn, Sòng Shìzǔ Annals_.
Lǐ Chōng initially recommended Lǐ Biāo,
but once Biāo felt he had gained the sovereign's favor,
he no longer relied on Chōng,
gradually distancing himself,
only straightening his sleeves in public,
with no further respect as his patron.
． _Tōngjiàn, Qí Míngdì Annals_.
Initially, Lǐ Déyù was in power,
and brought Bái Mǐnzhōng in as Hànlín Xuéshì.
When Wǔzōng passed away,
Déyù lost influence.
Mǐnzhōng seized the court's anger,
exerting himself to oust him,
having his associate Lǐ Xián
accuse Déyù of crimes.
． _Tōngjiàn, Táng Wǔzōng_.
Cuī Hóng recommended Qiè Shēn,
but Shēn later impeached Hóng.
Hóng said: "I recommended Assistant Qiè, and he impeaches me in return,
this is drawing the bow to shoot myself."
． _Jìnshū, Cuī Hóng Biography_.
See also "Zuòzhǔ".
Like borrowing another's spear,
and turning it to stab them.
_Táng Shǐchén Sùzōng Zàn_.
Collected
Just as hatchlings, newly feathered,
run wild and recklessly turn to bark at their master.
_Cáo Gōng's Proclamation Against Wú_.
Beasts forget kindness once fed,
wasps and scorpions nurtured turn venomous.
_Yàn Gōng Collection_.
Any who call themselves disciples yet do not know the source of their favor,
are not human.
Liǔ Wén.
Many guests eat, but who repays the kindness?
Liú Chángqīng.
One by one, fed by mouth,
until their feathers grow.
Once grown, they chirp and fly away,
each to the four directions.
At dusk, the empty nest remains,
a lone hen returns.
_Wáng Wéi Collection_.
This Dynasty
Wáng Yí Gōng (Wáng Zēng) repeatedly recommended Lǚ Yíjiǎn,
but once Yíjiǎn attained high office,
he became at odds with Yí Gōng.
_Dōngxuān Bǐlù_.
Lǚ Bù served Dīng Yuán,
then killed Dīng Yuán;
he served Dǒng Zhuó,
then killed Dǒng Zhuó.
Liú Láo zhī served Wáng Gōng,
then rebelled against Wáng Gōng;
he served Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn,
then rebelled against Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn.
_Luánchéng Collection_.
Classics
Without Guǎn Zhòng,
we would be wearing our hair loose,
and fastening our garments on the left.
． _Lúnyǔ, Xiàn Wèn_.
Masters
They would make him a corpse and pray to him,
establish him as an altar and sacrifice to him.
_Zhuāngzǐ_.
Amidst storms and harsh rains,
then one knows the great house as a shelter.
_Yángzǐ_.
Histories
Zhào Dùn said: "Without you, Jī Shì,
I would be a man of the Dí."
_Zuǒzhuàn_.
Without Chǔ's grace, I would not have reached this.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xī Year 28_.
Without that man's strength,
I would not have reached this.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xī Year 30_.
Without Wǔzǐ's strength, I would not have reached this;
even if my bones return to Jìn,
you, like a son, give them flesh.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Zhāo Year 13_.
Wèi's Nìngzǐ monopolized power, Gōngsūn Miǎnyú
requested to kill him.
The Duke said: "Without Nìngzǐ,
I would not have reached this."
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xiāng Year 27_.
I see Shēn Shū,
truly one who gives life to the dead and puts flesh on bones.
_Zuǒzhuàn_.
He clothed me with his own garments,
fed me with his own food.
． _Western Hàn, Hán Xìn Biography_.
Whenever Hé Wǔ reported affairs in the capital,
Dài Shèng never failed to visit his door to give thanks.
． _Western Hàn, Hé Wǔ Biography_.
Hastily, at Wúlóu Pavilion, bean porridge,
at Hūtuó River, wheat meal,
your deep kindness long unrepaid.
． _Eastern Hàn, Féng Yì Biography_.
Yáng Tán was dearly regarded by Xiè Ān.
When Ān passed away,
Tán ceased music for a full year,
and never took the road to Xīzhōu again.
． _Jìnshū, Xiè Ān Biography_.
Féng Yì said: "Your humble servant
dares not forget the kindness of the head-scarfed carriage."
． _Tōngjiàn, Guāngwǔ Annals_.
Táng's Lǐ Yíjiǎn impeached Yáng Píng.
Píng was demoted to Línhè,
only the wèi Xú Huì went to Lántián to bid farewell.
Quán Déyù said: "Won't this implicate you?"
He said: "Huì, from my commoner days, received Lord Yáng's recognition and encouragement;
today he is exiled far,
how could I not bid him farewell!
If, for instance, you, sir,
were one day driven out by slanderers,
would Huì dare treat you as a stranger?"
_Tōngjiàn_.
Biographies
When Bào Shū died,
Guǎn Zhòng lifted his lapel and wept for him,
tears falling like rain.
His follower said: "He was not your ruler or father."
Guǎn Zhòng said: "My father gave me life,
but Bào Zǐ knew my heart.
A scholar dies for one who knows him,
how much more should I mourn him?"
_Shuōyuàn_.
Yǔ Tàiwèi in youth was recognized by Wáng Wǔzǐ.
When Yǔ crossed the river,
he praised Wáng: "Under his eaves' shelter,
one forgets cold and heat."
_Shìshuō_, middle scroll.
Collected
Engraved in my heart forever.
From Dù Fǔ's poetry.
In the past, during the journey to Sháozhōu,
I received orders from my elder brother, saying:
"You were raised by your sister-in-law from a young age;
you must observe mourning for her for a full term.
How dare I forget Heaven now?
It truly oversees this."
From Hán Yù's writings.
Cross-referenced under "sister-in-law's gate."
Even as autumn's energy shifts and fades,
I remain grateful for the kindness in my case.
From Zhāng Jiǔlíng's essay.
Receiving the grace of special favor,
I feel as if I've grown wings.
To repay an unexpected promotion,
I should tear out my liver and intestines.
From Dù Mù.
In our dynasty,
the master's protective grace,
is more than just a silk robe.
From Línchuān.
Even if I fall headfirst and carve out my heart,
I know it's not enough to repay.
Same as above.
In this life, if kindness is unreturned,
my eyes will not close in death.
From Hòushān.
The Classic says:
"No virtue goes unrewarded."
From the Odes, "Yì" chapter.
History records:
Initially, the Zhōu people gave land to the Fàn clan,
and Gōngsūn Páng taxed it.
The Zhào clan captured and presented him,
and the officials requested his execution.
Zhào Mèng said: "He acted for his master—
what crime is that?"
He spared him and gave him land.
During the battle of Tiě,
he led five hundred men in a night attack on the Zhèng army,
capturing the bee banner from under Zǐ Yáo's tent, saying:
"I request to repay my master's virtue."
From Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Āi, 2nd year.
Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn said:
"If by your grace I return to Jìn,
and our armies meet in the central plains,
I will retreat three encampments for you."
From Duke Xī, 22nd year.
Zǐ Fàn said:
"Without Chǔ's favor, we would not be here;
retreating three encampments is how we repay it."
From Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xī, 28th year.
Wèi Kē saw an old man twisting grass to trip Dù Huí.
Dù Huí stumbled and fell.
That night, he dreamed the old man said:
"I am the father of the woman you remarried.
You followed your father's wise order,
so I repay you thus."
From Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xuān, 15th year.
Duke Líng of Jìn planned to kill Zhào Dùn,
setting an ambush during a feast.
Earlier, Xuānzǐ hunted at Shǒushān,
rested under a mulberry tree,
and saw Líng Zhé starving.
Asked his condition, he said:
"I haven't eaten for three days."
He fed him,
and later, as a guard for the duke,
Líng Zhé turned his spear to defend him.
He helped him escape;
asked why,
he said: "I am the starving man from the mulberry tree."
From Zuǒzhuàn.
Initially, Sū Qín went to Yān, borrowing a hundred coins for funds.
When he gained wealth and honor,
he repaid with a hundred gold pieces.
He widely repaid all who had shown him kindness.
From Shǐjì, his biography.
Fàn Jū would repay even the kindness of a single meal.
From Shǐjì, his biography.
When Qín lost a good horse,
over three hundred villagers under Qíxià ate it,
and officials caught them.
Duke Mù said:
"A gentleman does not harm people over livestock."
He pardoned them.
When they heard Qín was attacking Jìn,
all three hundred pushed forward to fight to the death,
repaying the kindness of the horse meal.
From Shǐjì, Qín annals.
Zhū Hài,
a retainer of Lord Wújì of Wèi,
said:
"The reason I didn't thank you then
was that small courtesies are useless.
Now is the time for me to devote my life."
From Shǐjì.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ destroyed Zhì Bó.
His minister Yù Ràng fled to the mountains,
saying: "Alas!
A scholar dies for one who knows him,
a woman adorns herself for one who pleases her.
Now Zhì Bó knew me;
I must die avenging him
to repay Zhì Bó,
so my spirit will feel no shame!"
Same as above.
Hàn Gāozǔ enfeoffed Xiàng Bó and three others as marquises,
granting them the surname Liú.
They had earlier rendered service to Hàn.
From Western Hàn annals.
Yùzǐ swallowed charcoal to disguise himself,
and Fèng Jiàn showed difference to the Qí guest,
falling headfirst at the public gate
to repay kindness shown.
From Western Hàn, Gǔ Yǒng's biography.
I sigh secretly at the ancients'
repayment of a single meal.
From Eastern Hàn, Lǐ Gù's biography.
Emotions are moved by grace,
life is lightened by righteousness.
From Eastern Hàn, commentary on Zhū Huī's biography.
Tàishǐ Cí avoided trouble in Liáodōng;
Kǒng Róng, Chancellor of Běihǎi, sent someone to inquire after his mother
and sent provisions.
When Róng was besieged by Guǎn Hài,
Cí went alone to see Róng,
then sought help from Liú Bèi,
obtaining troops to lift the siege.
From Wúzhì.
Qiè Jiàn once provided for Zhōu Yì.
After Jiàn's death,
Yì, recalling the nurturing grace,
resigned his post, spread a mat,
and observed three years of heart-mourning.
From Jìnshū.
Yīn Kēng was at a feast,
saw the cup-bearer,
and turned to give him wine and roast meat.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Kēng was captured by bandits,
and someone saved him.
When Kēng asked why,
it was the former cup-bearer.
From Chénshū.
Biographies record:
Wǔ Zǐxū fled to Wú, reaching Lìyáng,
where a woman was washing by the stream.
Zǐxū begged for food;
she gave him a basket of rice and pot of soup.
After Zǐxū left,
he looked back after five steps—
the woman had thrown herself into the water.
Later, when Zǐxū attacked Chǔ,
he passed Lìyáng again,
repaid with a hundred gold pieces,
threw them into the stream, and left.
From Wúyuè Chūnqiū.
The Marquis of Suí once spared a large snake,
releasing it instead of killing it.
Later, the snake brought a bright pearl
to repay the Marquis of Suí.
From Shèng Hóngzhī's Jīngzhōu Jì.
Yáng Bǎo, at nine years old,
saw a yellow sparrow attacked by an owl,
fallen under a tree, beset by ants.
He took it home,
placed it in a box,
and fed it yellow flowers.
After over a hundred days,
its feathers grew, and it flew away.
Vowing to remain steadfast unto death to repay kindness.
By Mí Zhèngpíng's rhapsody.
Even common men and humble women,
can still dedicate their lives for a single meal.
From "Letter to Péng Chǒng".
Ghosts resisted and brought Qín to ruin.
From "Wénxuǎn".
Willing to turn to ashes and grind bones to fulfill a heartfelt wish.
By Chén Zǐ'áng.
Tying the cap-strings and falling on the sword,
to slightly repay one ten-thousandth of the debt.
Cutting open the heart and grinding the heels,
to repay the one to whom I owe my all.
From Jiāng Wéntōng's letter.
Moved by your deep grace, I pledge my life to you,
Casting Mount Tài aside as lighter than a goose feather.
By Lǐ Tàibái.
How could the heart of a minnow
repay the kindness of the Eastern Sea?
By Bái Lètiān.
With the private affection of crows, I find joy in nurturing;
Like a dog or horse with feeble strength, I vow to devote my life in gratitude.
Same as above.
The mountain of heavy grace remains unrequited.
By Dù Mùzhī.
Repaying kindness is as bright as the sun.
By Wǔ Bócāng.
Qín Xī's head shattered for a confidant;
Yù Ràng's body, moved by being treated as a national scholar, could be lacquered.
From Zhāng Jiǔlíng's writings.
The vast kindness of Sōng and Dài mountains,
was eventually repaid by an ant hill.
By Luò Bīnwáng.
In vain, I think of repaying virtue with a tiny stream.
Note: "功" is sometimes written as "空".
From "Táng Wén Cuì".
Surely it is the day to repay grace,
Today I feel my life is light.
From "The Collection of Wáng Wéi".
In our dynasty,
Hán Yù was orphaned young,
and was raised by his elder brother and sister-in-law.
When his sister-in-law passed away,
he observed the mourning period for her,
to repay her kindness.
From "Zǔ Wúzé's Extensive Records of Wén Gōng".
History
Going out, he relied on their resources;
entering, he used their favor.
He ate their grain when hungry,
yet after three acts of kindness, he gave no repayment,
hence this came about.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn".
Turning one's back on kindness shows no closeness,
and is what the people reject.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Year 14 of Xī".
When Jìn suffered famine,
Qín supplied them with grain;
when Qín had famine,
Jìn closed its grain markets to them.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Year 15 of Xī".
Betraying favor and breaking promises.
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, Year 28 of Xī".
Wáng Mǎng sent Anyang Hóu Shùn to see the Empress Dowager.
The Dowager said: "Your clan, fathers, sons, and kinsmen have benefited from the Hàn dynasty's power,
enjoying wealth and honor for generations.
Having given no repayment,
you accepted the orphan's trust,
and taking advantage of the opportunity,
seized their state,
no longer caring for grace or righteousness.
People like this,
even dogs and pigs would not eat.
How could there be
any brothers like you under heaven?"
From "Tōng Jiàn, Annals of Hàn Míngdì".
Collection
In a mere foot's space, the heat and cold change with the seasons,
My anxiety for you, how could you know?
From "The Collection of Wéi Yìngwù".
In our dynasty,
Before the ink recommending Mí had dried,
The bow to shoot down Yì was already bent.
From "The Collection of Ōu Gōng".
Scholars under Ōu Gōng
betrayed him in an instant.
From Dōngpō's "Preface to the Poem for Qín Shàngrén".
Classics
Repaying resentment with resentment,
then the people will have something to fear.
From "The Record of Biǎojì".
Repay resentment with uprightness.
From "The Analects".
Masters
When Zhào Xiāngzǐ killed Zhì Bó,
Yù Ràng sought to avenge the grievance,
fearing others would recognize him,
he knocked out his teeth to alter his appearance.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
History
Chǔ Wǔ Shàng said to his younger brother Yuán: "I can die,
and you can take revenge."
． From *Zuǒzhuàn*, Zhāogōng 20th Year.
Zhèng attacked Sòng,
to avenge the battle of the Eastern Gate.
． From *Zuǒzhuàn*, Yǐngōng 5th Year.
Fū Chāi had someone stand in the courtyard,
and whenever he came in or out,
they would say to him: "Fū Chāi, have you forgotten that the King of Yuè killed your father?"
He would then reply: "I dare not forget."
After three years, he took revenge on Yuè.
From Dìnggōng 14th Year.
Yuè attacked Wú,
Wángsūn Míyōng saw the flag of Gūmiè and said: "That is my father's flag;
I cannot see the enemy and not kill them."
From *Zuǒzhuàn*.
Duke Āi of Qí was boiled alive by Zhōu,
after Jì Hóu slandered him.
Duke Xiāng sought to avenge this,
though Jì was nine generations removed from their ancestor.
Can revenge be taken after nine generations?
Even after a hundred generations, it is permissible.
Is it permissible for a family?
It is said: "No,
but why is it permissible for a state?
Because the ruler and the state are one.
The shame of a former ruler
is like the shame of the current ruler."
From *Gōngyáng Zhuàn*.
Zhāng Yí served as chancellor of Qín,
and issued a proclamation to the chancellor of Chǔ, saying: "When I drank with you before,
I did not steal your jade disk,
yet you had me flogged.
You'd better guard your state well,
for I intend to steal your cities!"
． From *Shǐjì*, his biography.
Resentment and hatred in people
run deep indeed!
Even a king cannot impose it on his ministers,
let alone among peers?
When Wǔ Zǐxū was stranded by the river,
begging for food along the way,
did he ever forget Yǐng for a moment?
Thus, he endured humiliation to achieve fame and merit;
if not for a man of fierce determination,
who could have accomplished this?
From the commentary in his biography.
Gōu Jiàn said: "I was once trapped at Kuàijī,
the pain piercing to the marrow.
Day and night I fretted,
lips parched and tongue dry,
only wishing to die following the King of Wú—
that was my desire."
From the biography of Duānmù Cì.
Cross-reference "Resentment and Hatred."
Borrowing strength to avenge his father's shame.
From the biography of Wǔ Zǐxū.
Lǐ Guǎng was ransomed to become a commoner.
He arrived at night at Bàlíng, where the captain
shouted to stop him.
Not long after,

The actual number of bandits is large,
but they reduce and report it as small."
. From Tōngjiàn, Suí Yángdì.
The emperor wanted to broadly seek talents from across the land,
ordering those proficient in at least one art to come to the capital.
Lǐ Línfǔ, fearing that scholars from the countryside might criticize his treachery and evils in their responses,
proposed: "Most examinees are lowly and foolish,
and I fear their vulgar words might tarnish the imperial virtue,
so order the local officials to rigorously test and train them,
and only those truly outstanding
should have their names sent to the ministry for re-examination by the Department of State Affairs."
. From Tōngjiàn, Táng Xuánzōng.
The emperor worried that rain would damage the crops,
Yáng Guózhōng took the best ears of grain,
and presented them,
saying: "Though the rain is heavy,
it does not harm the crops."
The emperor believed it to be so.
. From Tōngjiàn, Táng Xuánzōng.
The emperor passed Biàn Bridge,
an old man, Guō Cóngjǐn, offered advice: "Beyond the palace gates,
Your Majesty knows nothing,
the nine gates are strict and deep,
my humble heart
has no way to reach upward,
had matters not come to this,
how could I have the chance to see Your Majesty's face and speak of it?"
Same as above.
Yuán Zài, wielding exclusive power,
feared that those reporting affairs would expose his private wrongdoings,
so requested: "All officials discussing matters
must first inform their superiors,
the superiors inform the chancellor,
and only then present it to the emperor."
Yán Zhēnqīng submitted a memorial: "Believing that those discussing matters
must first inform the chancellor
is to blind and deafen oneself.
Tàizōng established the 'Simén Regulation,' stating: 'Those without gate access
who have urgent reports
should all be escorted by the gate officers and guards to present them,
without obstruction.'
This was to prevent blockage.
After the Tiānbǎo era,
Lǐ Línfǔ served as chancellor,
deeply hating those who spoke out,
people on the streets communicated with their eyes.
The emperor's will did not reach below,
the people's sentiments did not rise above,
deceived and silenced,
eventually leading to the disaster of fleeing to Shǔ.
The decline to this day
has been gradual."
. From Tōngjiàn, Táng Dàizōng.
Even within the court, one cannot speak freely,
how can one communicate across the vast universe?
. From Tōngjiàn, Táng Mùzōng.
Xiānyú Zhòngtōng's campaign against Nánzhāo ended in a great defeat,

Zhòngtōng barely escaped with his life.
Yáng Guózhōng concealed the defeat,
and instead reported it as a military success.
Lǐ Mì attacked Nánzhāo,
was captured,
and the entire army was lost,
Guózhōng hid the defeat,
and instead reported a victory.
From Jiù Tángshū.
If Lí Lóu's eyes are blinded,

With the slander and flattery of a hundred mouths and a hundred minds,
obscuring the clarity of two ears and two eyes.
From Táng Xuánzōng's Eulogy.

The emperor believed it to be so,
yet Cǐ personally led troops to press toward Fèngtiān.
From Jiù Tángshū.
Wèi Zhēng said: "Qín Èrshì hid himself away,
trusting Zhào Gāo,
and was unaware of the rebellions across the land.
Liáng Wǔdì trusted Zhū Yì,
and was unaware when Hóu Jǐng approached the palace.
Suí Yángdì trusted Yú Shìjī,
and was unaware when bandits spread across the land.
Thus it is said: 'If the ruler can listen broadly,
then treacherous men cannot block, and the sentiments below will be communicated.'"
. From Xīn Tángshū, his biography.
Péi Dù said: "The emperor's face is not even a foot away,

how can it enlighten the imperial hearing?"
. From Tángshū, his biography.

Went to Eastern Zhōu,
Divulging all intelligence of Western Zhōu.
Western Zhōu was enraged,
Féng Dàn said:
"I can kill him."
The ruler gave him thirty catties of gold.
Féng Dàn sent a man carrying gold and a letter,
To covertly deliver to Chāng Tuó.
It said: "If the matter can be accomplished,
Strive to complete it;
If it cannot be accomplished,
Flee immediately.
If prolonged, it will be exposed,

Eastern Zhōu immediately executed Chāng Tuó.
From "Zhànguócè".
King Xiàng and Fàn Zēng urgently besieged Xíngyáng.
King Hàn was troubled by this,
So he used Chén Píng's stratagem to sow discord with King Xiàng.
When King Xiàng's envoy arrived,
A grand feast was prepared,
Intending to present it.
Upon seeing the envoy,
He feigned surprise and said: "I thought you were envoy of Father Yà,
But you are King Xiàng's envoy."
Then took it away,
And fed King Xiàng's envoy with poor food.
The envoy returned and reported to King Xiàng,
King Xiàng then suspected Fàn Zēng of having secret dealings with Hàn,
Gradually stripping him of his authority.
From "Shǐjì: Xiàng Yǔ Běn Jì".
Interlinked with "Using the Opponent's Own Tactics Against Them".
King Hàn gave Chén Píng forty thousand catties of gold,
To sow discord among the Chǔ sovereign and ministers.
From "Shǐjì: Hàn Gāozǔ Běn Jì".
Duke Mù of Qín asked his Internal Historiàn Liào about Yóu Yú: "Yóu Yú is worthy,
But he is a Róng tribesman.
He is a threat to me,
What should I do?"
Liào said: "The Róng king lives in seclusion,
And has not heard the music of the Central States.
You should try sending him female musicians,
Request Yóu Yú's presence,
To create distance between them;
Detain him and do not send him back,
Making him miss his deadline.
The Róng king will find it strange,
And will surely suspect Yóu Yú.
When there is discord between sovereign and minister,
Then you can capture him."
Duke Mù sent sixteen female musicians to the Róng king,
The Róng king accepted them and was delighted,
And did not return for a whole year.
Thereupon, Qín sent Yóu Yú back.
Yóu Yú repeatedly remonstrated but was not heeded,
Duke Mù also repeatedly sent agents to invite Yóu Yú,
Who then left and surrendered to Qín.
From "Shǐjì: Qín Běn Jì".
Qín attacked Zhào,
Lián Pō of Zhào fortified his defenses and awaited Qín,
Despite repeated challenges,
The Zhào troops did not engage.
The King of Zhào repeatedly reprimanded him.
The Qín chancellor sent agents to spend a thousand catties of gold in Zhào for counter-espionage,
Saying: "What Qín fears,
Is only that Lord Mǎfú's son, Zhào Kuò, will command;
Lián Pō is easy to deal with,
And will soon surrender."
The King of Zhào was angry that Lián Pō did not fight,
And upon hearing the counter-espionage words,
Thus sent Zhào Kuò to replace Lián Pō.
Kuò was defeated,
Died,
And four hundred thousand men surrendered to Lord Wǔ'ān.
From "Shǐjì: Bái Qǐ Lièzhuàn".
Lord Wújì of Wèi's prestige shook the world,
The King of Qín was troubled by this,
Spent gold to slander the lord before the King of Wèi, saying:
"The commanders only hear of Lord Wèi,
Not of the King of Wèi.
The lord also wishes to take this opportunity to establish himself as king."
He repeatedly sent counter-espionage agents,
Falsely congratulating the lord on his imminent enthronement before the King of Wèi.
The King of Wèi heard these slanders daily,
Could not help but believe them,
And eventually sent someone to replace the lord as commander.
From "Shǐjì: His Biography".
King Huì of Yān, since his time as crown prince,
Had often been displeased with Yuè Yì.
Tián Dān of Qí heard of this,
Then spread counter-espionage in Yān, saying:
"The cities of Qí that remain uncaptured are but two.
The reason they are not taken sooner is that,
It is heard that Yuè Yì and the new king of Yān have discord,
And he wishes to prolong the war and remain in Qí to become king of Qí.
What Qí fears,
Is only that another general will come."
King Huì already suspected Yuè Yì,
And upon receiving Qí's counter-espionage,
Sent Jì Jié to replace him as commander.
From "Shǐjì: Yuè Yì Lièzhuàn".
Lǐ Mù of Zhào greatly defeated the Qín army,
Qín gave much gold to Guō Kāi, the favored minister of the King of Zhào, for counter-espionage,
Saying: "Lǐ Mù wishes to rebel against Zhào."
Thus sent Yán Jù to replace Mù,
Arrested and executed him.
From "Shǐjì: His Biography".
Qín spent a thousand catties of gold to undermine Lián Pō,
Hàn scattered ten thousand catties to alienate Father Yà.
From "Xīhàn: Fù Xǐ Zhuàn".
Biographies
In ancient times, espionage was used in various ways:
Some targeted sovereigns,
Some targeted relatives,
Some targeted the worthy,
Some targeted the capable,
Some targeted allies,
Some targeted friendly neighbors,
Some targeted those in close service,
Some targeted horizontal and vertical strategists.
Zǐgòng, Shǐ Liào, Chén Zhěn, Sū Qín, Zhāng Yí, Fàn Suī, etc.,
All achieved success by relying on these methods.
From "Lǐ Wèigōng Bīngfǎ".

Observing the Nourishment hexagram is to observe what it nurtures;

Planning for oneself,

Being kind and harmonious to enrich the family,

In times of chaos,
The nobleman flaunts his merits to oppress the petty man,

From "Shǐjì: Guàn Fū Zhuàn".
The Chǔ army had little food,

King Hàn said:
"My father is your father;
If you insist on cooking your father,
Chǔ was at fault,

Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody on the Shanglin Park".

Although Líng showed ingratitude,

"Selected Ancient Poems".

"Tōngjiàn".

Collected sayings
In criticizing others, they are meticulous;

Being lenient with oneself makes it hard to do good;
being lenient, one demands little of oneself.
Having no virtue, one says: "I am good at this,

Having no ability, one says: "I can do this,
and this is enough."
Outwardly deceiving others,
inwardly deceiving one's own heart—
stopping before achieving even a little.
Is this not treating oneself with excessive leniency?
As for others, they say:

it is not worth praising.

it is not commendable."
Picking on one fault,
ignoring ten merits;

Not knowing to clarify one's own concerns,

Biographies
Qí Xípí.
