Master:
Yángzǐ would not pluck a single hair from his body to benefit the world.
． From "Mèngzǐ, Jìn Xīn Shàng".
Yángzǐ said: "The world's affairs cannot be helped by one hair."
From "Lièzǐ".
History:
Caring only for oneself,
with no concern for the people.
From "Zuǒzhuàn".
Dù Mì said: "Liú Shèng holds the position of senior official,
yet knowing good men, he does not recommend them;
hearing of evils, he remains silent;
concealing the truth and sparing himself,
he is like a cicada in winter."
From "Hòuhànshū".
Privately enriching himself.
． From "Tōngjiàn, Jìn Jì".
Collection:
Entering the gate, each has their own flatteries,
who would willingly speak for others?
From "Chángchéng Kū".
Classic:
Do not exalt yourself by belittling others.
． From "Shūjīng, Xián Yǒu Yī Dé".
The great officers trek through hardships,
and my heart is troubled.
． From "Shījīng, Zǎichí".
When a neighbor has a funeral,
do not sing while pounding grain;
when there is a burial in the lane,
do not sing in the streets.
． From "Lǐjì, Qūlǐ Shàng".
What you dislike in subordinates,
do not use to serve superiors;
what you dislike in superiors,
do not impose on subordinates.
． From "Lǐjì, Dàxué".
What you do not wish done to yourself,
do not do to others.
． From "Lǐjì, Zhōngyōng".
Wishing to establish oneself, one establishes others;
wishing to succeed oneself, one helps others succeed.
． From "Lúnyǔ, Yōngyě".
When eating beside mourners,
he never ate his fill.
From "Lúnyǔ".
Zǐgòng asked: "Is there one word
that can guide one throughout life?"
The Master said: "It is 'shù' (reciprocity)!
Do not impose on others
what you yourself do not desire."
． From "Lúnyǔ, Wèi Línggōng".
I do not wish others to impose on me,
nor do I wish to impose on others.
From "Gōngyě Cháng".
History:
When Jìn's Xún Wú besieged Gǔ,
some in Gǔ offered to betray the city.
Mùzǐ said: "If someone betrayed our city,
we would deeply detest it.
How could I favor others betraying theirs to us?"
． From "Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāogōng 15th Year".
The King of Chǔ said: "Do others love their sons
as much as I do!"
． From "Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāogōng 13th Year".
Jìn's Zǔ Tì had a officer Tóng Jiàn
who killed the prefect Zhōu Mì
and surrendered to Later Zhào's Shí Lè.
Lè sent the head to Zǔ Tì, saying:
"Traitorous ministers and fleeing officials
are my deep enemies;
what you detest, I detest as well."
． From "Tōngjiàn, Jìn Yuán Dì".
Cross-referenced under "Detesting Evil".
Jù Bóyù felt ashamed to be the only gentleman.
From "Dōnghànshū".
Gù Róng, feasting with colleagues, noticed the roast bearer
looking desirous of the meat,
so he cut a piece and gave it to him.
When asked why, he said:
"How can one handle it all day
without knowing its taste?"
． From "Jìnshū, His Biography".
Yǔ Liàng's horse had a white forehead,
and Yīn Hào thought it ill-omened for its master,
urging Liàng to sell it.
Liàng said: "How can I transfer my own discomfort to another?"
． From "Jìnshū, His Biography".
Qín king Fú Jiān summoned Dài's senior official Yàn Fèng,
asking about Dài's turmoil.
Fèng explained in detail.
Fú Jiān said: "Evil is one under heaven,"
and had Shí Jūn seized.
When Jīn reached Cháng'ān,
he was torn apart by chariots.
． From "Tōngjiàn, Jìn Wǔ Dì".
Yīn Kēng once feasted with guests
and, seeing the wine server,
turned to offer him wine and meat,
saying: "We drink all day,
while the cup bearer knows not the taste—
this is against human feeling."
From "Nánshǐ".
The southern mountains are warm.
The emperor, seeing the troops had no spring clothes,
also wore unlined garments himself.
． From "Tōngjiàn, Dèzōng".
Biography:
Yànzǐ said: "The wise of old,
being full, knew others' hunger;
being warm, knew others' cold."
From "Yànzǐ Chūnqiū".
Collection:
All birds delight in having nests,
and I too love my hut.
From Táo Yuānmíng.
Seeing others' suffering
is like having ulcers on one's own body.
From "Liú Bīnkè Jí".
If all were as comfortable and warm as I,
there would be no cold people under heaven.
From Bái Jūyì.
If one, being at ease, thinks of how to ease others;
being comfortable, thinks of how to comfort things;
not ignoring the woes of the widowed due to one's own joy,
nor forgetting the toil of farming due to one's own leisure—
"toil" sometimes written as "diligence".
From Lǚ Héshū's writings.
Master:
The frog in the sunken well
said to the turtle of the Eastern Sea: "I leap and play upon the coping of the well,
rest within the broken-bricked bank.
When I enter the water, it holds me up to my armpits and supports my chin;
when I tread in the mud, it covers my feet and submerges my insteps.
Looking back at the water fleas, crabs, and tadpoles,
none can match me.
Moreover, to command the water of one gully and straddle the joy of a sunken well—
this is the ultimate!
Why don't you come in from time to time to see for yourself?"
． From "Zhuangzi·Qiū Shuǐ".
Cross-reference "Shallow and Narrow Knowledge".
A swarm of ants observed a sea turtle hidden like a mountain;
an ant said: "His carrying mountains on his head—
how is it different from my carrying a grain leisurely,
or burrowing atop a mound of soil?
It's just a dwelling."
From "Fúzǐ".
Collection
Lílóu with his faint gaze,
the blind man thought he had no sight.
From "Chǔcí".
One who relishes foul carrion
tries to feed a yuānchú with a dead rat.
From Jī Shūyè's letter.
Our Dynasty
This is a Warring States strategist
measuring Yǐyīn by his own standards.
From Dōngpō.
Classics
When others have intentions,
I ponder and measure them.
． From "Shījīng·Qiǎo Yán".
Conjecturing often hits the mark.
From "Lúnyǔ".
Bringing warfare upon myself,
whom else can I blame?
． From "Yìjīng·Xiè Guà".
When petty people resent and curse you,
you should earnestly cultivate your own virtue.
． From "Shūjīng·Wú Yì".
Blaming others is not difficult;
only accepting blame like flowing water
is truly hard!
． From "Shūjīng·Qín Shì".
The Master said: "When walking in a group of three,
I am sure to find a teacher among them.
I select their good qualities to follow,
and their bad qualities to correct in myself."
． From "Lúnyǔ·Shù Ér".
Rectify oneself without demanding of others, and there will be no resentment.
． From "Lǐjì·Zhōng Yōng".
The gentleman seeks it in himself.
From "Wèi Línggōng".
The Master said:
"When you see a worthy, think of equaling them;
when you see an unworthy, turn inward and examine yourself."
The gentleman worries about his lack of ability,
not about others not recognizing him.
． Both from "Lúnyǔ·Lǐ Rén".
Do not worry that others do not recognize you;
worry that you lack ability.
． From "Lúnyǔ·Xiàn Wèn".
When introspection finds no guilt,
what is there to worry or fear?
． From "Lúnyǔ·Yán Yuān".
Cross-reference "Without Shame".
Masters
What I call hearing
is not about hearing others,
but about hearing oneself.
What I call seeing
is not about seeing others,
but about seeing oneself.
． From "Zhuangzi·Pián Mǔ" chapter.
If you love others and they are not affectionate, reflect on your benevolence;
if you govern others and they are unruly, reflect on your wisdom;
if you are courteous to others and they do not respond, reflect on your respect.
Whenever you do not achieve your aim,
turn inward and seek within yourself.
． From "Mèngzǐ·Lí Lóu Shàng".
Upon self-reflection, if I find myself in the wrong,
even against a commoner,
I shall not intimidate him.
Upon self-reflection, if I find myself in the right,
even against thousands and tens of thousands,
I shall go forward.
． From "Mèngzǐ·Gōngsūn Chǒu Shàng".
An archer corrects himself before shooting;
if he shoots and misses,
he does not resent those who surpass him,
but turns inward to seek the cause in himself.
Same as above.
If someone here
treats me with rudeness,
the gentleman will certainly reflect on himself.
From "Mèngzǐ".
Zēngzǐ said: "If I associate with others and am not loved,
I must be lacking in benevolence.
If I interact with others and am not respected,
I must be lacking in diligence.
If I face wealth and am not trusted,
I must be untrustworthy.
With these three faults in myself, how can I blame others?"
． From "Xúnzǐ·Fǎ Xíng".
Seeing goodness,
one should thoughtfully seek to preserve it in oneself;
seeing badness,
one should seriously examine oneself for it.
． From "Xúnzǐ·Xiū Shēn".
Rather than praising Yáo and condemning Jié,
it is better to shut off cleverness and return to cultivating the Way.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
Lǐ Mì asked about heroes;
the Master said,
"Knowing oneself is called yīng (intelligence),
conquering oneself is called xióng (valor)."
From "Wénzhōngzǐ".
History
Chǔ's Jiāo Jǔ said: "Only one without flaws
can punish others."
． From "Zuǒzhuàn·Zhāo 4".
Fù Chén said: "If even we brothers are not harmonious,
how can we blame the feudal lords for their discord?"
． From "Zuǒzhuàn·Xī 23".
If the heart is without flaw,
why worry about having no home?
． From "Zuǒzhuàn·Mǐn 1".
The people of Zhèng gathered at the village school
to discuss the government.
Rán Míng wanted to destroy it.
Zǐchǎn said: "I have heard that loyalty and goodness reduce resentment,
not that authority prevents resentment."
． From "Zuǒzhuàn·Xiāng 31".
Even if they do not speak of my faults,
am I not ashamed in my own heart?
． From "Shǐjì·Xiàng Yǔ Běn Jì".
Gazing at the river and coveting fish,
it is better to go home and weave a net.
． From "Xī Hàn·Yáng Xióng Zhuàn".
Cross-reference "First Attack Oneself".
The wisdom of observing things
lies in the introspection of oneself.
． From "Dōng Hàn·Mǎ Yuán Zhuàn".
When others slander you, you should withdraw and examine yourself.
If you have conduct that can be slandered,
then their words are appropriate.
If you have no conduct that can be slandered,
then their words are false.
If appropriate, do not resent them; if false,
it does not harm you.
Why retaliate?
A proverb says: "To ward off cold, nothing beats a heavy fur;
to stop slander, nothing beats self-cultivation."
This saying is true.
． From "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn·Wèi Míng Dì Jì".
Yán Hán said: "I have heard that when attacking a state,
one does not consult a benevolent man.
Earlier Féng Zǔsī asked me about cunning;
do I possess wicked virtue?"
． From "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn·Jìn Jì".
Ruǎn Yù was in Shàn;
he once had a fine carriage
that he lent to anyone who asked.
Someone was burying his mother
and wished to borrow it but dared not ask.
Later, Ruǎn Yù heard of this
and sighed: "I have a carriage that makes people afraid to borrow it—
what use is the carriage?"
He ordered it burned.
From "Jìn Shū".
Yáng Zhāojiǎn said: "Carving stone to record merits
is not as good as issuing an edict of mourning;
writing praises with brush
is not as good as proclaiming a self-accusing text."
． From "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn·Jìn Gāozǔ".
A tomb robber excavated Guō Zǐyí's father's grave;
they hunted for him
but did not catch him.
People, knowing Yú Cháo'ēn had long disliked Zǐyí,
suspected he was behind it.
When Zǐyí came to court from Fèngtiān,
the court worried he would revolt.
Zǐyí saw the emperor.
The emperor mentioned the incident;
Zǐyí wept and said: "I have long commanded troops
and could not prevent violence;
my soldiers often excavated graves.
That it has come to this today
is Heaven's punishment,
not a human affair."
The court was then reassured.
． From "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn·Dà Lì Yuán Nián".
Collection
Brother Qíshēng was a renowned minister of his time,
and the great officials at court were all his old friends.
When Qíshēng took the imperial examination,
the examiners thereby repeatedly wronged him.
Qíshēng did not complain but instead said:
"It is because I have not yet reached the required standard;
how could the examiners have wronged me?
I shall sharpen my tools and await the right time."
Carrying his scholarly works,
he returned east to his home.
I observe that among people,
many who fail to achieve their ambitions blame their superiors,
without considering their own shortcomings.
As for Qíshēng,
though he did not achieve his ambition,
he said, "I have not yet reached the standard,"
and did not resent the examiners.
Is this not rare indeed!
Hán Wén's "Preface to Seeing Qíshēng Off After Failing the Examination."
In our dynasty,
when gentlemen associate with petty men
and are bullied by them,
they cultivate self-reflection, act with caution and avoidance,
stir their hearts and endure their nature,
increasing their virtues and taking preventive measures.
Lǎoquán.
Cross-reference "Reaching the Essence Through the Coarse."
Classic:
Those who are not good at learning
cause the teacher to labor with only half the result,
and then go on to resent him.
• "Record of Learning" from the Book of Rites.
Petty men demand from others.
• Analects, "Wèi Línggōng."
Collection:
A mirror is bright but does not reflect itself.
Lú Tóng's writings.
To blame Bó Yì after drowning in a well,
to blame Suìrén after a fire.
Classic:
A man from Lǔ mourned in the morning and sang in the evening;
Zǐlù laughed at him.
The Master said: "Yóu, you criticize others
endlessly."
• Book of Rites, "Tángōng I."
The Master said: "Petty men in employing others
seek perfection."
• Analects, "Zǐlù."
Masters:
Those who are harsh and troublesome
find it difficult to be respectful.
Qiáo Zǐ's "Admonitions on Law."
Blaming the sun, moon, and stars for not shining into an overturned pot.
• Bàopǔzǐ, "Biàn Wèn" chapter.
History:
Sūn Jìshū drank with Shí Chóng, behaving excessively arrogant and disrespectful.
Chóng wanted to petition for his dismissal,
but Péi Kǎi said to Chóng: "You make people drink,
then blame them for the madness of the liquor;
is that not contrary to proper ritual?"
• "Biography of Péi Kǎi" in the Book of Jìn.
Kùdí Fúlián, troubled by flies in his residence,
struck the gatekeeper and said: "Why did you let them in?"
History of the Northern Dynasties.
Collection:
He himself threw the five-colored ball,
which flew into another's house.
Then he seized the servant,
and beat him three hundred times with a jade whip.
"Discourse on Poetry."
Classic:
The nobleman receives others with emptiness.
• I Ching, Xián hexagram.
To give up oneself and follow others.
"Counsels of the Great Yǔ."
Masters:
The ancient kings,
though their knowledge encompassed heaven and earth, did not rely on their own thoughts;
though their eloquence could adorn all things,
they did not speak of themselves;
though their abilities could cover the world,
they did not act for themselves.
• Zhuāngzǐ, "Tiāndào" chapter.
History:
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu read a hundred books in the morning
and received seventy scholars in the evening,
yet still feared it was not enough.
Comprehensive Mirror.
Only by not relying on oneself
can one employ others.
• Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Dézōng.
If Lǐ Jiàng did not remonstrate for a long time,
the emperor would ask him: "Is it that I cannot accept advice,
or that there is nothing to remonstrate about?"
• Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Xiànzōng.
Biographies:
Using the eyes of the world to see,
then nothing remains unseen.
Using the ears of the world to listen,
then nothing remains unheard.
Using the minds of the world to ponder,
then nothing remains unknown.
"Six Secret Teachings" of Tàigōng.
Collection:
An empty boat responds to things.
Luò Bīnwáng.
The secluded valley has no selfishness—
when something arrives, it echoes.
The great bell, empty and receptive,
responds to all that comes.
"Head Monastery Stele."
Our dynasty:
All things turn their heads like a fallen pot;
alone in this floating world, as if in an empty boat.
"Remarks on Poetry."
Classic:
Powerful ministers arrogate authority.
• Book of Songs, "Cunning Boy."
The foolish are fond of acting on their own;
the lowly are fond of being autocratic.
• Doctrine of the Mean from the Book of Rites.
Masters:
Fools like to monopolize affairs
and envy the worthy and capable.
• Xúnzǐ, "Confucian Effects."
The rooster that monopolizes the perch,
the pheasant that dominates the marsh.
Bàopǔzǐ.
History:
When Zhèng Zǐkǒng was in power,
the people of the state killed him for his autocracy.
• Zuǒzhuàn, 19th year of Xiānggōng.
Jì Zhòng was autocratic,
and the Earl of Zhèng was troubled by it.
• Zuǒzhuàn, 15th year of Wēigōng.
Zǐchǎn said: "The anger of the multitude is hard to oppose;
a selfish desire is hard to achieve."
• Zuǒzhuàn, 10th year of Xiānggōng.
Lú Pú Piè conducted government affairs from his home.
Zuǒzhuàn.
Qí Gāo Zhǐ liked to take credit for affairs and
was autocratic.
Hence, disaster reached him.
• Zuǒzhuàn, 29th year of Xiānggōng.
Zāng Wénzhòng said: "To make others follow one's desires rarely succeeds."
• Zuǒzhuàn, 20th year.
Exclusive listening breeds treachery;
sole authority creates chaos.
• Comprehensive Mirror, Liáng Wǔdì's Annals.
Monopolizing benefits and harms.
• Comprehensive Mirror, Qín's Annals.
Lú Qǐ held power as Vice Minister of Personnel,
Guān Bō as Vice Director of the Secretariat,
both participating in policy-making.
The emperor once discussed matters with his ministers;
Bō thought something was wrong
and stood up to speak,
but Qǐ signaled him with his eyes and he stopped.
Later, at the Secretariat, Qǐ said to Bō: "Because you are upright and reserved,
I recommended you for this position. Why then
did you start to speak?"
• Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Dézōng.
Wielding authority in the court.
• History of the Former Hàn, "Table of Feudal Kings."
Autonomy leads others to undermine one.
• History of the Former Hàn, "Treatise on the Five Elements."
Arbitrary and self-indulgent authority.
• Records of the Grand Historian, "Biography of Zhào Gāo."
The principles of the Spring and Autumn period were lost;
the Hàn laws included rectifying decrees.
• History of the Former Hàn, "Biography of Féng Fèngshì."
With the insignificance of a commoner,
usurping the power over life and death.
• History of the Western Hàn, "Biographies of Wandering Knights."
Tián Fén was Chancellor;
when he recommended someone, they could rise to high rank,
shifting power from the emperor.
The emperor said: "Have you finished appointing officials?
I too wish to appoint some."
Once he requested land from the workshop to expand his residence;
the emperor angrily said:
"Why not just take the armory!"
• History of the Western Hàn, "Biography of Tián Fén."
Collection:
Dominating the arena, boasting of beak and spur.
Hán Wén.
Classic.
You abandon your divine turtle,
and gaze at my bulging cheeks - ominous.
. From the "Yì, Yí Guà".
Mencius said:
People often neglect their own fields,
yet weed others' fields.
They demand much from others,
but take little responsibility themselves.
. From "Mèngzǐ, Jìnxīn Xià".
By hunting improperly, one might catch ten in a single morning.
. From "Mèngzǐ, Téng Wéngōng Shàng".
Huáng Xiē plotted with the crown prince: "
Initially, Xiē and the crown prince were hostages in Qín.
It would be better to flee Qín together with the envoy.
I request to face death in your stead."
The crown prince then disguised himself as a Chǔ envoy,
and drove through the pass,
while Huáng Xiē guarded the residence,
often claiming illness on behalf of the crown prince.
Estimating the crown prince was far away,
he confessed to the king: "The Chǔ crown prince has returned,
and is now far away.
Xiē wishes to receive death."
. From "Tōngjiàn, Zhōu Jì".
Lǐ Yún submitted a memorial,
angering the emperor.
He ordered officials to arrest Yún,
then Hóngnóng's official Duàn Zhòng sympathized with Yún,
who was punished for loyal remonstration,
and submitted a memorial wishing to die the same day as Yún.
. From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Huán Jì".
Zhū Zhèn collected and buried Chén Fān's corpse,
hiding his son Yì,
but the affair was discovered,
and he was imprisoned,
with his whole family in shackles.
Zhèn endured torture,
vowing to die without speaking,
thus Yì escaped harm.
. From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Líng Jì".
Attendant Censor Jǐng Yì's son Gù was a disciple of Lǐ Yīng,
but not registered,
thus avoiding punishment.
Yì exclaimed: "I believed Yīng was virtuous,
so I sent my son to learn from him.
How can I seek safety
just because his name was omitted!"
He then resigned voluntarily.
. From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Líng Jì".
Collection
Scholars with plans to govern the world,
often lack strategies to save themselves.
Yáo Quán.
Mencius said:
The otter drives fish into the deep,
the sparrowhawk drives birds into the thickets.
. From "Mèngzǐ, Lílóu Shàng".
Cross-reference "Giving Advantage to Others".
Mòzǐ advocated universal love,
wearing himself out from head to heel
to benefit the world.
From "Mèngzǐ".
History
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng said: "I govern from the third watch,
finishing before noon if matters are few,
or eating only at sunset if busy.
Once my waist exceeded ten spans,
now it's barely over two feet.
Whose fault is this?
It's for saving others."
. From "Tōngjiàn, Běnjì".
Collection
How can one weave fine silk,
yet wear ragged clothes oneself?
Mèng Jiāoyě.
Guests enjoy and servants are full,
then I know my official post serves others.
From "Báilètiān Collection".
Cross-reference "Awakening" and "Giving Advantage to Others".
Yearly they say my silkworms toil hard,
so why am I clad in coarse hemp?
From "Dù Xúnhè Collection".
Silkworms mature, cocoons form, yet don't shelter them,
bees starve, honey ripens, but belongs to others.
Báilètiān.
Classic
The sun goes, the moon comes;
the moon goes, the sun comes.
Sun and moon push each other, thus light is born.
Cold goes, heat comes;
heat goes, cold comes.
Cold and heat push each other, thus the year completes.
. From "Yì, Xìcí".
The sun at zenith must decline,
the full moon must wane.
Heaven and earth wax and wane with time,
how much more so humans?
Same as above.
Dùn means
retreat.
Things cannot retreat forever,
hence Dàzhuàng follows.
Yang flourishes, Yin declines,
the noble path grows.
From "Xùguà".
Jìn means
advance, but advance may bring harm,
hence Míngyí follows.
The sun at zenith must decline,
the full moon must wane.
Things cannot be difficult forever,
hence Jiě follows.
Rising endlessly must lead to exhaustion,
hence Kùn follows.
Both from "Xùguà".
Contraction and expansion push each other.
One contracts, one expands,
alternately giving way.
From "Yì Lüèlì".
Wealth hoarded, the people scatter;
wealth shared, the people gather.
. From "Lǐjì, Dàxué".
Mencius said:
The sun at zenith must shift,
the moon full must wane.
From "Lǎozǐ".
What thing, full to the extreme,
does not overturn?
From "Jiāyǔ".
Rivers dry, valleys empty;
hills flatten, abysses fill.
From "Zhuāngzǐ".
Retire after fame is achieved,
such is heaven's way.
From "Guǎnzǐ".
Cross-reference "Knowing Satisfaction".
A tree bearing fruit twice,
its roots will surely suffer.
From "Wénzǐ".
History
Extreme beauty
must have extreme ugliness.
. From "Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāo 20".
Prosperity has decline,
as morning must have evening.
. From "Xīhàn, Hán Ānguó Zhuàn".
Reaching heights brings danger,
fullness leads to overflow,
the full moon wanes,
the zenith sun shifts.
. From "Hòuhàn, Lǐ Gù Zhuàn".
Fortune favors humility, shuns excess.
Same as above.
Biography
When Jupiter is in Chou,
ask for broth, get wine;
when in Si,
sell wife and children.
Fortune and misfortune alternate,
expansion and contraction cycle.
Liú Zhījī's "Shǐ Tōng".
Hard times must turn smooth,
dark fate must turn bright.
Yán Yánnián's "Shìdiàn Shī".
Human affairs never stay prosperous long.
From "Qí Ōu Xíng".
First flourishing, then withered, ever shifting.
From "Lǐtàibái Collection".
Fullness and emptiness depend on each other,
comings and goings are never constant.
From Liú's letter.
Heaven and earth long stagnant, suddenly prosper and calm;
sun and moon long dim, suddenly clear and bright;
thunder long silent, suddenly roars and shocks;
clouds long dense, suddenly scatter and clear.
The way of Zhòngní,
stagnant in Zhōu and Qín,
dim in Hàn and Wèi,
silent in Jìn and Sòng,
dense in Chén and Suí,
but met in our Táng:
the grievance of ten thousand generations,
released by one Hán.
Huángfǔ Shí's "Memorial to Enshrine Hán Gōng".
Fate thwarted in one's time,
blessings flow to descendants.
From "Bái Collection".
First to green, first to wither.
Báilètiān's poem.
Our dynasty
A year's toil leads to a winter's leisure.
From "The Collected Works of Dōngpō".
How apt are
Sīmǎ Guāng's words: "All things born between heaven and earth
have but this fixed measure;
if not in the hands of the people, then in the coffers of the state.
It is like the rain:
if summer brings floods, autumn will bring drought."
Dōngpō.
A decade's accumulation spent in a single startling moment,
waves shatter mountains, winds shake the earth.
From Hòushān's "Song of Alas".
The Classic
says: "Treading on frost, solid ice will follow." The commentary explains: "Treading on frost, solid ice—
this signifies the yin energy begins to congeal;
if it proceeds along its path,
it will reach solid ice."
From "The I Ching, Kūn Hexagram".
Like that falling snow,
first gather the sleet.
From "The Book of Songs, Guì Biàn".
What are the auspicious dreams?
Dreams of bears and brown bears
are signs of a son's coming;
dreams of vipers and snakes
are signs of a daughter's coming.
From "The Book of Songs, Sī Gàn".
The household thrives and multiplies.
From "The Book of Songs, Wú Yáng".
When desires are about to arise,
there must first be an opening.
From "The Record, Confucius at Leisure".
Heaven sends timely rain,
mountains and rivers emit clouds.
Same as above.
When fortune or misfortune approaches,
the good will surely know it beforehand,
and the wicked will surely know it beforehand.
From "The Record, Doctrine of the Mean".
When a state is about to flourish,
there must be auspicious omens;
when a state is about to perish,
there must be sinister portents.
Same as above.
The Master said: "Last night,
I dreamed I was seated between two pillars, receiving offerings;
I am likely to die soon."
He then lay ill for seven days and passed away.
From "The Book of Rites".
A person
whose eyes are about to go blind
will first see the finest autumn hairs;
one whose ears are about to go deaf
will first hear the buzz of gnats.
From "Lièzǐ".
When a person is about to fall ill,
they must first lose their taste for fine grains and meats;
when a state is about to perish,
it must first detest loyal and honest words.
From "Yànzǐ".
One leaf falls, and the autumn of the world is known.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
History
records someone shouting in the Sòng grand temple: "Hiss, hiss, out, out,
birds cry at Bó."
Shè Rú said: "Alas!
Alas!
In the year Jiǎwǔ, Sòng suffered a great disaster."
From "Zuǒzhuàn, 30th Year of Xiānggōng".
Duke Wén of Jìn passed through Wèi
and begged for food from a rustic.
The rustic gave him a clod of earth,
enraging the duke,
who wished to whip him.
Zǐ Fàn said: "It is a gift from heaven."
They bowed their heads to the ground,
accepted it, and carried it away.
From "Zuǒzhuàn".
The Marquis of Jìn fell ill
and sought a physician from Qín.
Before the doctor arrived,
the duke dreamed his illness took the form of two boys saying: "He is a skilled physician;
I fear he will harm us;
where can we escape?"
One said: "Let us dwell above the huāng
and below the gāo;
what can he do to us then?"
When the doctor arrived, he said: "The illness is incurable.
It lies above the huāng,
below the gāo,
where needles cannot reach,
moxa cannot penetrate,
and medicine cannot arrive;
it cannot be treated."
From "Zuǒzhuàn, 10th Year of Chénggōng".
In the second year of King Yōu of Zhōu,
the three rivers of Western Zhōu all shook.
Bó Yángfǔ said: "Zhōu is about to perish.
In the past, the Yī and Luò rivers dried up, and Xià fell;
the Yellow River dried up, and Shāng fell."
From "Records of the Grand Historian, Annals of Zhōu".
Yīn's Yuè dreamed and arose at Fùyán,
Zhōu's Wàng saw an omen by the Wèi riverbank.
From "Western Hàn, Bān Gù's Preface".
Fortune has its foundation,
misfortune has its embryo.
From "Western Hàn, Méi Chéng's Biography".
When Mount Mín collapsed,
blocking the river for three days,
the river water dried up.
Liú Xiàng deeply dreaded it: "In the past, Mount Qí collapsed,
the three rivers dried up,
and King Yōu perished.
Mount Qí
was where Zhōu rose.
Hàn's origin lies in Shǔ and Hàn;
now, in the land of its rise, mountains collapse and rivers dry up;
it is likely to perish."
From "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Hàn Emperor Chéng".
At Liǔgǔkou in Zhāngyè, water surged forth,
bearing a stone with a chart,
shaped like a divine turtle,
standing west of the river,
with seven stone horses,
and images of phoenixes, qílins, white tigers, sacrificial oxen, huáng jués, the eight trigrams, constellations, and comets.
Yú Chuò asked Jùlù's Zhāng Jiàn,
who secretly told him: "Now Hàn has long fallen,
and Wèi has taken its place;
why seek signs of revival!
This stone
is an omen of present change and a portent of the future."
From "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Wèi Emperor Míng".
Sūn Jùn plotted with the Wú ruler to invite Zhūgě Kè to a banquet.
On the night before Kè's arrival,
his spirit was agitated,
restless throughout the night.
Moreover, his home had seen many strange occurrences,
making Kè suspicious.
From "Annals of Wèi's Gāoguìjié Gōng".
A proverb says: "If a cock crows at night,
it bodes ill for military campaigns;
if a large pack howls, the palace will be emptied;
if weapons stir and horses startle,
the army will be defeated and not return."
From "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Jìn Emperor Wǔ".
Dù Yān said: "When Qí was about to fall,
they composed 'Jade Tree Backyard Blossoms',
its melody full of sorrow and longing;
passersby who heard it all wept."
From "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Táng Emperor Tàizōng".
Yáng Zhèn declined appointments from the provincial government for decades,
then a stork flew to his lecture hall carrying three shad fish in its beak,
and the assistant lecturer took the fish and presented them, saying:
"The shad
symbolizes the attire of high ministers.
The number three
represents the three highest offices.
From this, you shall rise, sir!"
He later rose to the position of Grand Commandant.
From "Eastern Hàn, His Biography".
During Sūn Hào's reign, the Qiántáng Lake burst open,
and some said it meant peace under heaven,
when the green canopy entered Luòyáng.
Hào asked Chén Xùn about it, who said: "The green canopy entering Luò
foretells a surrender with a coffin and jade in mouth."
Soon after, Wú fell.
From "Book of Jìn".
Sūn Xiù falsely accused Pān Yuè and Shí Chǒng of rebellion, executing their three clans.
Shí Chǒng was already at the execution ground,
Pān Yuè arrived later,
and Chǒng said: "Ānrén,
you too end like this?"
Yuè replied: "We can say, 'Together we return in white-haired old age.'"
Yuè's "Jīngǔ Poem" had said: "I entrust my fate to my stone-hearted friend,
together we return in white-haired old age."
Thus, it became a prophecy fulfilled.
From "Book of Jìn, Biography of Pān Yuè".
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi once dreamed of three horses
eating from one trough.
Later, Emperor Xuān, Jǐng, and Wén successively served as chancellors,
and they overthrew the Cáo family.
From "Sòng, Records of Auspicious Signs".
When Zhū Yì was first appointed Central Secretariat Gentleman,
it was autumn,
and as he received the appointment,
a flying cicada alighted on his cap.
All took it as an omen of the cicada emblem,
and eight years later, he became Palace Attendant.
From "History of the Southern Dynasties, His Biography".
Wáng Rényù loved poetry from youth.
He once dreamed someone cut open his intestines and stomach,
washing them with the West River's water, and looking back,
he saw the river's sand and stones
all inscribed with seal script.
From then on, his literary talent greatly advanced.
From "History of the Five Dynasties".
Biography
There was a star, red and with sharp rays,
flowing from northeast to southwest,
and plunging into Zhūgě Liàng's camp;
it plunged three times and returned twice,
going large and returning small.
Soon after, Liàng died.
"Jìnyáng Qiū".
Auspicious signs are the forerunners of fortune,
ominous signs are the forerunners of disaster.
"Lǚshì Chūnqiū".
Emperor Suí Yáng in the palace,
once held a small gathering for character analysis,
and turning to Consort Xiāo said:
"Can you analyze the character 'zhèn' (朕)?"
The consort said:
"Moving the left stroke to the right,
isn't it the character 'yuān' (渊)?"
At that time, popular expectation largely favored Duke Táng,
the Emperor heard this,
and was displeased.
He then said:
"If I cannot know this matter,
am I not a sage?"
Thereafter, treachery arose within,
and bandits attacked from without.
"Suí Dàyè Jì".
When the magpie chirps, travelers arrive;
when spiders gather, all affairs bring joy.
"Xījīng Zájì".
In Shǔ county there was a fire well; during the heyday of the Hàn dynasty,
its flames blazed fiercely, a display of majestic power.
When the fire's force gradually waned,
Zhūgě Liàng glanced at it, and it grew strong again.
Mulberry and grain trees grew together in the court,
and in one day became as thick as arms under Wǔ Dīng.
Feudal lords who cultivated virtue came to court,
from six states.
During Wǔ Dīng's sacrifice, a flying pheasant perched on the tripod's handle,
and crowed; within three years, those who came to court through interpreters,
were from six states.
"Shàngshū Dàzhuàn".
Our dynasty
A halo around the moon foretells wind,
dampness on the plinth foretells rain.
Lǎo Sū.
Son
No disaster is greater than not knowing contentment.
"Lǎo Zǐ".
For those who do good,
Heaven repays with fortune;
for those who do evil,
Heaven repays with disaster.
"Jiāyǔ, Zài È" chapter.
Fortune and disaster none do not come from seeking them oneself.
"Mèngzǐ, Gōngsūn Chǒu I".
Fortune is lighter than a feather,
yet none know how to bear it; disaster is heavier than
earth, yet none know how to avoid it.
"Zhuāng Zǐ".
No fortune is greater than being without disaster.
"Xúnzǐ, Quànxué" chapter.
Cross-reference "Knowing Contentment".
When disaster comes,
it is brought by man himself; when fortune comes,
it is accomplished by man himself.
Disaster and fortune come from the same gate,
benefit and harm are neighbors.
"Huáinán Zǐ".
History
Què Zhì said:
"When disaster is great,
what fortune can there be?"
"Zuǒzhuàn, Chéng 12th Year".
The capable
nurture it to attain fortune;
the incapable
ruin it and incur disaster.
"Chéng 13th Year".
Fortune and disaster have no gate,
they are summoned only by men.
"Zuǒzhuàn, Xiāng 23rd Year".
When fortune arrives,
it is brought forth by man himself.
When disaster arrives,
it is created by man himself.
"Shǐjì, Guīcè Lièzhuàn".
Zhū Yīng said to Chūnshēn Jūn:
"In the world, there is unforeseen fortune,
and also unforeseen disaster."
"Shǐjì, Chūnshēn Jūn Lièzhuàn".
Disaster arises from resentment,
fortune springs from virtue.
"Xī Hàn, Wén Dì Jì".
Fortune has its foundation,
disaster has its embryo.
"Xī Hàn, Méi Chéng Lièzhuàn".
Cross-reference "Portents".
As for auspicious and inauspicious events for humans,
they are like shadow and echo;
yet those who do good often obtain auspicious outcomes,
while those who unfortunately encounter inauspicious ones,
do exist; those who do evil never fail to meet with misfortune,
yet those who luckily avoid it also occur occasionally.
But petty men, in their considerations,
thus believe the way of Heaven is hard to know,
that doing good may not bring fortune,
and doing evil may not bring disaster.
Ōuyáng Gōng's "Táng Shǐ, Zhōng Zōng Zàn".
Collection
Fortune's focus often has omens,
disaster's arrival surely has causes.
"Jūnzǐ Xíng" poem.
Generally, the coming of disaster, fortune, auspiciousness, or inauspiciousness seems not up to me,
but for gentlemen, encountering disaster is unfortunate,
while for petty men, encountering disaster is normal.
Gentlemen obtaining fortune is normal,
while petty men obtaining fortune is unfortunate.
Because their actions seem to have ways of inviting these outcomes,
one must not say:
"Gentlemen are always auspicious,
and petty men are always inauspicious."
Hán Wén.
Classic
In my dealings with people,
whom do I defame, whom do I praise?
"Lúnyǔ".
Son
There is unexpected praise,
and criticism seeking perfection.
"Mèngzǐ".
The goodness of the Three Dynasties
is the accumulated praise of a thousand years.
The slander against Jié and Zhòu
is the accumulated criticism of a thousand years.
"Huáinán Zǐ".
Praise of the ruler is followed by slander.
Same as above.
I have not seen one who rejoices at hearing slander,
or fears upon hearing praise.
"Wénzhōng Zǐ, Tiāndì" chapter.
History
Jì Bù said:
"Because of one person's praise, I am summoned;
because of one person's slander, I am dismissed."
"Qián Hàn, Jì Bù Lièzhuàn".
Cross-reference "Lack of Scrutiny".
The origins of slander and praise, love and hate,
are the mechanisms of fortune and disaster.
"Wèi Zhì, Wáng Chǎng Lièzhuàn".
Slander and praise are coerced by power and profit.
"Jìn Jì Zǒng Lùn".
He who gets angry upon hearing slander
is a trap for calumny.
He who rejoices upon seeing praise
is a medium for flattery.
Eliminate the trap and remove the medium,
and calumny and flattery will stay far away.
"Tōngjiàn, Suí Gāozǔ Jì".
Trap,
pronounced yú, zhōu initial.
Also read as wǔ gē final.
Collection
Generally, when people receive slander or praise from others,
there are also respective reasons.
A gentleman in a lower position often receives slander,
When the bed is stripped to the skin, it brings misfortune.
． From the Book of Changes, Hexagram Bō.
As trees grow from the earth and rise,
the noble person cultivates virtue accordingly,
accumulating the small to achieve greatness.
． From the Book of Changes, Hexagram Shēng.
Petty people deem small acts of goodness useless,
and thus do not perform them;
they consider minor wrongs harmless,
and thus do not abandon them.
Hence, evil accumulates until it can no longer be concealed, and crimes
become too great to be resolved.
． From the Appended Phrases of the Book of Changes.
It is not a matter of a single morning or evening;
its origin develops gradually.
． From the Book of Changes, Hexagram Kūn.
Like the falling snow,
it begins with scattered sleet.
． From the Book of Songs, Ode "Kuǐ Biàn".
Now, a mountain begins with a handful of stones,
yet when it becomes vast and great,
grass and trees grow on it,
birds and beasts dwell on it,
and treasures flourish there.
Water starts with a single spoonful,
yet when it becomes immeasurable,
turtles, alligators, dragons, fish, and tortoises thrive in it,
and goods and wealth multiply there.
． From the Record of the Doctrine of the Mean.
The way of the noble person begins
with ordinary men and women, yet at its utmost,
it illuminates heaven and earth.
Ibid.
A
tree large enough to embrace
grows from a tiny sprout.
A nine-story tower
rises from heaps of earth.
A journey of a thousand miles
begins beneath one's feet.
From the Laozi.
A piece of wood an inch square
can be made taller than a lofty tower.
． From Mencius, "Gào Zǐ II".
The River begins from Mínshān,
its source so shallow it can barely float a wine cup.
But when it reaches the river crossings,
without a boat
and facing the wind,
one cannot cross it.
． From the Family Sayings of Confucius and also from the Xunzi, chapter "The Way of Heaven".
The waters of rivers
do not flow from a single source.
From the Mòzǐ.
Hills and mountains accumulate from lowliness to become high;
rivers and seas combine waters to become great.
． From the Zhuangzi, chapter "Xú Wúguǐ".
Counting by the day seems insufficient,
but by the year, it proves ample.
From the Zhuangzi.
When water drips continuously,
it bores through soft stone;
when insects gnaw persistently,
they decay weak wood.
The dripping is not a drill for the stone,
nor are the insects borers for the wood.
Yet with their subtle and fragile forms,
they penetrate hard and solid substances.
Is this not the result of gradual accumulation?
From the Kǒng Cóngzǐ.
Cross-reference "Softness Can Overcome Hardness".
What is lacking in a month may be abundant in a year.
From the Guǎnzǐ.
With unceasing half-steps,
a lame turtle can journey a thousand miles.
With uninterrupted piling of earth,
a hill or mountain will be grandly formed.
From the Xúnzǐ.
Accumulate earth to form a mountain,
and wind and rain will arise there;
accumulate water to form an abyss,
and dragons will thrive there.
Accumulated earth is called a mountain,
accumulated water is called a sea,
accumulated dawns and dusks are called a year,
and accumulated goodness fully realized is called a sage.
A sage
is what a person becomes through accumulation.
Both from the Xúnzǐ.
Without accumulating half-steps, one cannot reach a thousand miles;
without accumulating small streams, one cannot form rivers and seas.
． From the Xúnzǐ, chapter "Encouraging Learning".
Earthworms boring through a dike
can flood an entire town;
a wisp of smoke leaking from a chimney
can soot a thousand homes.
From the Liúzǐ.
Where water accumulates, fish large enough to swallow boats are born;
where earth accumulates, trees like pián, nán, and yùzhāng grow.
From the Yǐnzǐ.
The goodness of the Three Dynasties
was the accumulated praise of a thousand years.
The slander against Jié and Zhòu
was the accumulated condemnation of a thousand years.
From the Huáinánzǐ.
Cross-reference "Praise and Blame".
Accumulate goodness, and achievements will follow;
accumulate evil, and calamity will peak.
． From the Huáinánzǐ, "Advice for Rulers".
When the River's waters first emerge from Mínshān,
one can lift his robes and wade across.
But by the time it flows downstream,
passing Dòngtíng, startling Shíchéng, and flowing through Dān,
it stirs up waves,
and boats cannot cross it in a single day.
Like fire meeting dryness
or water meeting dampness,
it soaks and grows ever larger.
The growth of a living tree
is imperceptible day by day,
yet over time it becomes tall.
Whetstones and grindstones
show no visible loss,
yet over time they wear thin.
Thus, accumulated affection becomes blessing,
and accumulated resentment becomes disaster.
Both from the Huáinánzǐ.
History
The disaster of minor steps.
． From the Zuǒzhuàn, Third Year of Duke Yǐn.
Accumulated goodness in a person
is like the lengthening of days—unnoticed by others;
accumulated evil in a person
is like fire consuming oil—unseen by others.
． From the Book of Hàn, Biography of Dǒng Zhòngshū.
Many littles make a much,
accumulating small to achieve greatness.
Ibid.
Gathered mosquitoes create a thunderous noise;
collected breaths can move a mountain.
． From the Book of Hàn, Biography of Zhōngshān Jìng King Shèng.
Whetstones and grindstones show no visible loss,
yet over time they wear away.
Planting and rearing show no visible gain,
yet over time they flourish.
Accumulating virtue and conduct, one is unaware of their goodness,
yet in time they prove useful.
Abandoning righteousness and reason, one is unaware of their evil,
yet in time they lead to ruin.
． From the Book of Hàn, Biography of Méi Chéng.
The dripping from Tàishān bores through stone;
a single rope's persistence cuts through a well beam.
It is not a drill for the stone or a saw for the wood,
but gradual erosion
that causes this.
Ibid.
Safety does not come in a single day,
nor does danger arise in a single day.
Both result from gradual accumulation,
which must not go unexamined.
． From the Former Hàn, Biography of Jiǎ Yì.
The water that breaches cliffs and shatters rocks
originates from a trickling spring;
the tree that reaches the clouds and blocks the sun
starts from a green sprout.
． From the Book of Later Hàn, Biography of Dīng Hóng.
A dike collapses from an ant hole; air leaks from a needle's eye.
From the Biography of Chén Zhōng.
Gathered mosquitoes create a thunderous noise.
From the Biography of the Fifth Lún.
Accumulated days form a month.
Both from the Book of Later Hàn.
Accumulated discord breeds hatred;
accumulated harmony fosters affection.
． From the Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Emperor Xuánzōng Annals.
Biographies
A Róng person born in Róng speaks the Róng language;
a Chǔ person born in Chǔ speaks the Chǔ language,
without knowing how they acquired it.
Now, if a Róng person were raised in Chǔ,
and a Chǔ person in Róng,
then the Chǔ person would speak Róng,
and the Róng person would speak Chǔ.
From the Annals of Lü Buwei.
Cross-reference "Habit".
Collection
Water gradually forms rivers and seas.
From Huán Kuān's "Discourses on Salt and Iron".
A tiny patch of cloud can bring nourishing rain.
From Cáo Zǐjiàn's poetry.
Ant holes can breach a river,
Dripping water can topple mountains.
From Fùzǐ's "Inscription on the Mouth".
The lofty is built upon the low, the vast originates from the minute,

From Zhāng Màoxiān's "Poem Encouraging Ambition".
Ant tunnels leak through mountains and rivers,

From "The Selected: A Thoughtful Gentleman".
Solid ice begins with frost underfoot,

From "Wénxuǎn".
It is said that a patch of shade

From "Collection of Liú Bīnkè".
Mosquitoes gather like thunder invading a room.
Same as above.
Mountains grow gradually higher,
Marshes accumulate and lengthen.
Same as above.
Straight from the sprout it rises,

From "Collection of Vice-Minister Bái".

Embroidery begins with one thread,

Both same as above.
Unchecked trickles
Will eventually turn into mulberry fields.
Unquenched sparks
Can blaze across the plains.
From Lord Lù Xuān's writings.
Dripping water finely wears through stone,
A thin rope can sever a trunk.
From "Táng Wéncuì".
Though advancing by a spoonful,

A fist-sized accumulation
Can secure a region.
Same as above.
Accumulated errors become decay.
Same as above.
A single breath of waves

From "Collection of Pí Rìxiū".
Originally from the light of struck stones,
It led to sky-scorching heat.
From Liǔ Yǔxī's poetry.
Our dynasty
That overflowing from a wine cup,
With frogs leaping and minnows swimming,
Swelled to embrace the mountains,
Was what Shén Yǔ worried about.
From "Collection of Dōngpō".
A single torch holds the danger of prairie fire,
And an overflowing cup has the calamity of flooding the sky.
Same as above.
The towering hundred-foot pine
Starts from a one-inch root.
From "Collection of Luánchéng".
The eunuchs' calamity
Began with Emperor Míng,

Classic
Ministers and officials
Acted without measure.
From the "Wēizǐ" chapter of the "Book of Documents".
Cross-reference "Shared Evils".
Corrupt customs of extravagance and beauty,
Flow the same through all ages.

Shāng customs were addicted to profit and glib talk,

Same as above.
The young of the moth
Carried by the wasp, taught and nurtured,
Your sons shall follow goodness like this.

Masters
Living with good people is like entering a room of orchids,
After long, one no longer smells their fragrance,

Living with bad people,

After long, one no longer notices the stench,

Same as above.
Orchids and angelicas
Steeped in honeyed wine.

Línglíng produced many good scholars,
Largely due to Xún Qīng.

From "Yángzǐ".

A man of Línjiāng caught a young deer,
And kept it.
Daily, he carried it to the dogs,
Accustomed them to it,
And let them play together.

They grew more familiar,
The deer forgot it was a deer.
Going outside, it saw other dogs,
And went to play with them.
The outside dogs killed it together,
The deer died without realizing why.

Biographies
Confucius passed through a valley,
Saw an orchid growing alone and lush,
Sighed: "The orchid should be the king's fragrance,
Yet now it blooms alone,
Mingling with the common grass."
Then he stopped his carriage,
Took up his lute and played,
Grieving that he was born at the wrong time,
Expressing his feelings through the fragrant orchid.
"Qín Cāo".
