A cold official with no duties, his dwelling deep and still.
Same as above.
Faded temples treading remnants over snowy peaks,
A stout heart subdued, banners drooping in the wind.
From "Ōu Gōng's Collection".
A few white hairs tell my worries,
A stretch of green hills, my entire life.
From "A Hundred Peaks of Bright Pearls".
In life, one shouldn't wish for talent,
For talented men are plagued by constant奔走.
From "Luánchéng Collection".
A stout heart entrusted to the east-flowing stream.
Talent short as a silkworm, only entangling itself.
An official's comings and goings like autumn swallows,
A meager salary wrapped up like spring silkworms.
This body long like a horse harnessed to the shaft,
When will it become a fish swimming free in the abyss?
Once wrapped in official robes,
Forever caught in the web of duties.
A red heart turned to ashes.
The old grow weaker, lazier each year,
While worldly affairs bloom anew like flowers.
Also same as above.
Body like a sick crane with short wings,
Heart like tangled threads, endless worries.
From Huáng Shān Gǔ's poetry.
In vain, I've read thirty thousand volumes in my life,
Yet a silken cap must come from a warrior's helmet.
From "Chén Hòushān's Collection".
Those who shared my fame in youth achieved early success.
Same as above.
Zǐ
Now, in the great furnace where metal is cast,
The metal leaps up and says, "I must become a Mò Yé sword."
From "Zhuāng Zǐ".
Shǐ
Máo Suì said: "Had I been placed in a pouch earlier,
the tip would have pierced through and emerged.
It's not merely that the tip wasn't visible."
． From "Records of Píngyuán Jūn" in Shǐjì.
Dōngfāng Shuò submitted a memorial stating: "Your subject Shuò lost his parents at a young age,
and was raised by his elder brother and sister-in-law.
At age thirteen, I began studying writing,
and in three winters, had mastered literature and history sufficiently.
At fifteen, I learned swordsmanship,
at sixteen, studied the Shī and Shū,
reciting 220,000 words,
at nineteen, studied the military strategies and battle formations of Sūn and Wú,
the teachings of drums and gongs,
also reciting 220,000 words.
Your subject Shuò is twenty-two years old,
stands nine feet three inches tall,
with eyes like hanging pearls,
teeth like arranged shells.
As brave as Mèng Bēn,
as agile as Qìng Jì,
as incorruptible as Bào Shū,
as trustworthy as Wěi Shēng.
With such qualities,
I am fit to be a great minister to the Son of Heaven!"
． From "Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò" in Qián Hànshū.
Like clay on the potter's wheel,
it is shaped only by the potter's hands;
like metal in the crucible,
it is cast only by the smelter's design.
． From "Biography of Dǒng Zhòngshū" in Qián Hànshū.
When the Xiānlíng rebelled in Zhào,
Chōng Guó was over seventy years old.
The emperor asked who could lead the army?
Chōng Guó said: "None surpass this old minister."
From his "Original Biography".
Even a blunt lead knife can cut through rotten wood,
capable of making a single cut.
From Bān Gù's "Preface to the Biography".
Although I am worn-out and inept,
I have occasionally heard of the enduring legacy of the elders.
From "Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān",
also in "Western Hàn".
If a green-boned falcon is confined in a cage by heavy frost,
how can it demonstrate its skill in capturing the eastern hare from the falconer's glove?
If a white ape or female leopard is hidden behind bars,
how can one know their ability to leap for branches at a thousand ren?
． From "Biography of Zhāng Zǎi" in Jìnshū.
The Hé jade in Jīngshān,
the Suí pearl hidden in deep rivers—
if not encountered by the right person,
how would they gain the value of multiple cities,
or the fame of illuminating a carriage?
Same as above.
Jìn's Prince Qiáo Yǒng said: "You have not yet been recognized,
but can a lead knife not make at least one cut?"
． From "Jìn Records" in Zīzhì Tōngjiàn.
If it receives the leftover moisture of heavenly dew,
even a decayed stump or rotten wood,
though unable to grow anew,
can still produce mushrooms,
regarded as auspicious objects.
． From "Biography of Liǔ Zōngyuán" in Tángshū.
My clothes do not cover my body,
and I often depend on others for food.
I deeply fear dying in a ditch,
and beg for the emperor's compassionate decree,
following the precedent of former ministers,
to lift me from long disgrace in the mud,
so that my writings,
though not worthy of promoting the Six Classics,
in depth of emotion and rhythmic intensity,
and timely responsiveness,
may approach those of Yáng Xióng and Méi Gāo.
With a minister like me,
how can Your Majesty bear to abandon him!
From "Biography of Dù Fǔ" in Tángshū.
Yuán Dàn said to Dí Rénjié: "A subordinate serving a superior is like a wealthy household,
storing resources for self-sufficiency.
Dried meat provides flavor,
ginseng and herbs prevent illness—
your household is filled with a hundred delicacies!
I wish to serve as one medicinal stone among them,
would that be acceptable?"
． From "His Biography" in Tángshū.
Collection
Ashamed of the cook's solitude,
I draw in the priest to assist myself.
From "On Severing Ties".
Birds not yet caught in light snares,
fish not yet hooked by bait,
fear that angling and shooting techniques
may not be fully mastered.
In the past, Jiǎ Yì in his youth sought to test his skills in a vassal state,
asking to bind the neck of the Chányú and control his fate.
Zhòng Jūn, in his prime years, was sent to Yuè,
wishing to obtain a long tassel
to tether their king.
Though utterly inadequate myself,
my ambition lies in devoting my life,
hoping to achieve even the slightest merit
to repay the grace I have received.
To offer the utility of an awl or knife,
enabling me to serve under the Great General in the west, leading a troop,
or under the Grand Marshal in the east, commanding a contingent,
I would surely tread peril and risk danger,
gallop boats and spur steeds,
confront blades and meet spears,
leading the soldiers from the front.
Though unable to capture Quán or behead Liàng,
I hope to capture their leaders,
annihilate their vile kind,
and achieve a momentary victory
to erase lifelong shame.
Even if my body is torn in Shǔ's borders,
my head hung at Wú's gates,
it would be as if I were still alive.
If my meager talent goes untested,
unknown till death,
merely adorning my form
and fattening my body,
alive, I bring no benefit to affairs,
dead, I cause no loss to fate.
Vainly holding high position and disgracing heavy salary,
like birds and beasts idling until white-haired,
this is but raising creatures in pens,
not what I aspire to.
From Cáo Zhí's "Petition for Self-Recommendation".
Hoping that dust and dew's insignificance
may supplement mountains and seas.
The faint light of fireflies and candles
adds brilliance to the sun and moon.
Ibid.
Recovering Mèng Míng after three defeats,
demanding success from Cáo Mò in one move.
Enabling those with broken arms or severed feet
to groom themselves anew,
hoping to serve under the whip's command.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
Fluttering short wings among elms,
aspiring to brush against lofty branches;
rinsing fresh scales in trickles,
yearning for a drop from the vast waves.
Hoping for a glance in winding streams,
grooming to enhance value,
then a lead knife may serve for one cut,
a lame turtle may journey a thousand miles.
From Luò Bīnwáng.
Cf. "Seeking Aid".
If able to share a dipper of water,
to aid a parched fish with moistening foam,
bestow leftover light,
to shine on a shivering widow in her humble abode.
Enabling a worn-out nag at the trough
to hope for a steed's pace and trot;
a fluttering insect in hiding
to preen feathers among phoenixes.
Ibid.
An auspicious unicorn in Lǔ's marshes
hopes to present itself to Confucius;
a stray steed at Wú's slope
truly longs to neigh for Sūn Yáng.
What is valued lies in being recognized,
what bends and stretches depends on a confidant.
Ibid.
Under your roof not for a day,
born in Jiàng Shí's garden,
raised in Bó Lè's stable.
If unknown here,
even if seen by others,
what worth in thousands?
From Hán Yù's "Letter Seeking Recommendation for Another".
Jí excels at poetry;
if his mind is not troubled by food and clothing,
when you, sir, have leisure,
summon him to your side,
have him kneel and present his works.
You, leaning on the table, listen—
it may not be less pleasing than bamboo flutes, silk strings, or metal and stone percussion.
From Hán Yù's "Letter on Behalf of Zhāng Jí to Vice Censor-in-Chief Lǐ".
Wood from a large ditch,
same as that for sacrificial vessels.
If uncarved and unpolished,
it becomes mere firewood.
Paint it vermilion or indigo,
it can still be made into a vessel.
If warped and twisted,
unworthy of axe and adze,
it wishes to be a courtyard torch,
to illuminate honored guests.
From Liú Yǔxī.
Fortunately fit for seasoning the cauldron,
I hope you will pluck and pick.
From Wáng Wéi's Collection.
Though iron armor is stiff and dull,
the precious blade can still be tested.
If granted the grace of polishing,
it should turn sharp and keen.
From Liú Chángqīng.
A treasure worth cities awaits
a King Wén of Chǔ to be presented;
a melody to collapse mountains waits
for a Zhōng Zǐqī to be played.
From Selections of Táng Literature.
In our dynasty,
a worn-out cart, though useless,
can still serve as firewood;
a discarded mat, not forgotten,
may again grace a splendid hall.
From Línchuān Collection.
Rotting wood can still sprout mushrooms and lingzhi.
From Sū Shì's poem.
Anecdote:
Xuē Tán learned singing from Qín Qīng.
Before mastering Qīng's skills,
he claimed to know all,
and bid farewell to return.
Qín Qīng did not stop him,
but feasted him at the suburban road,
beating time in a mournful song that shook the trees,
its echo halting the clouds.
Tán then apologized and begged to return,
never daring to speak of leaving again.
From Lièzǐ, "Questions of Tāng".
Cf. "Small Vessels Easily Filled".
History:
King Xiàng said, "Even if my elders east of the river pity and make me king,
what face have I to see them?
Even if they say nothing,
should I not feel shame in my heart?"
From Records of the Grand Historian, Basic Annals.
Cf. "Self-Reproach".
Lǐ Guǎng said, "As governor of Lǒngxī,
the Qiāng rebelled and were enticed to surrender;
over eight hundred surrendered,
but I deceitfully killed them all the same day.
To this day, I regret only this."
From History of the Western Hàn, his biography.
There is nothing to say to bear such guilt.
From History of the Later Hàn, Biography of Zhāng Bù.
Chǔ Póu attacked the Later Zhào,
defeated, returned to Jīngkǒu,
hearing many cries,
asked his attendants.
They replied, "All are families of those who died at Dàibēi."
Póu, ashamed and enraged, fell ill
and died.
From Jìn Mùdì's Annals.
Wáng Dǎo said, "Though I did not kill Bó Rén,
Bó Rén died because of me.
In the netherworld,
I bear this guilt toward a good friend."
From History of the Jìn, Biography of Zhōu Yǐ.
Cf. "Knowing Remorse".
Dí Rénjié said, "Lord Lóu's virtue is great;
I am tolerated by him.
Now I know I fall far short!"
From New Book of Táng, Biography of Lóu Shīdé.
Wáng Shūwén's downfall left Wéi Zhíyì
also losing his footing.
Knowing disaster approached,
though still chancellor,
he often felt uneasy,
listless and dispirited.
Hearing footsteps,
he would startle and pale with fear.
From Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Shùnzōng's Annals.
Collections:
Ashamed, sweat like broth.
From Luò Bīnwáng.
Cf. "Stating Feelings".
Introspecting with shame and fear,
as if falling into an icy valley.
From Liú Yǔxī.
Sweating crimson with shame.
From Dù Mù.
History
Zhāng Yí once drank with the prime minister of Chǔ,
later the prime minister lost a jade disc,
his attendants suspected Zhāng Yí, saying:
"Yí is poor and lacks integrity,
he must have stolen the prime minister's jade disc."
They together seized Zhāng Yí,
flogged him hundreds of strokes,
but he did not confess,
so they released him.
His wife said:
"Had you not studied books and traveled persuading,
how could you have suffered this humiliation?"
Zhāng Yí said to his wife:
"Look, is my tongue still there?"
His wife laughed and replied:
"It is."
Yí said:
"That is enough."
From "Records of the Grand Historian: Basic Biography."
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
"If Zhāng Yí and Sū Qín were born with me in the present age,
they could not even hold the position of a minor official,
how would they dare aspire to be regular court attendants?"
At that time, Shuò was already a palace attendant.
From "Records of the Grand Historian: Basic Biography."
If one has fertile land,
why worry about a late harvest?
From "History of the Northern Dynasties: Biography of Yáng Kǎn."
See also the "Preparation" section.
Hán Yù, with his great talent,
was repeatedly dismissed from office,
so he wrote "An Explication on Progress in Learning" to express himself.
From "New Book of Tang: Basic Biography."
When Jìzǐ returned,
the people of Lǔ were pleased that he alleviated their crisis.
From "Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor An of Hàn."
The emperor said:
"Emperor Suí Yáng conscripted laborers to build the Great Wall,
to defend against the Tūjué.
Ultimately, it was of no benefit.
I merely placed Lǐ Shìjì in Jìnyáng,
and the border remained undisturbed.
As a 'Great Wall,'
is that not even more magnificent?"
From "Comprehensive Mirror: Annals of Emperor Tàizōng of Táng."
Sū Yuánmíng said:
"I am unfortunate to live in a decadent age, yet not ashamed,
for I know Yuán Zǐzhī."
From "New Book of Táng."
Guō Zǐyí once recommended someone for a local official post,
but it was not approved.
His aides said to each other:
"With your merit and virtue, yet a recommendation for a subordinate is not accepted,
how can the prime minister be so unreasonable?"
Zǐyí, hearing this,
told his staff:
"Since the military campaigns began,
many regional commanders have been arrogant.
Whenever they made requests to the court,
it often yielded to them out of consideration.
This is for no other reason
than suspicion towards them.
Now that my recommendation
was deemed unfeasible by the sovereign and set aside,
it shows I am not treated as a typical military officer but with intimacy and trust.
You should congratulate me,
why wonder at it?"
Those who heard were all convinced.
From "Comprehensive Mirror: Emperor Dàizōng of Táng."
Péi Hào wrote a quatrain:
"The official path values literary judgment most,
Heaven grants this fool a great name.
Thrice presiding over the examinations,
now eighty disciples,
I see my disciples' disciples."
From "History of the Five Dynasties."
Collection
Position demoted, but virtue upheld,
body in hardship, spirit at ease.
From "Selections of Refined Literature."
Teeth lost, yet not a heartless man,
tongue remains, only to lament at a dead end.
Dù Fǔ's poem.
Newly returned, comfort your heart,
why speak of livelihood?
Alive, facing the children,
as if forgetting hunger and thirst.
Vast within heaven and earth,
my path stretches far and long.
Since ancient times, there have been wanderers,
why should I grieve bitterly?
Before my eyes, no vulgar matters,
often ill, yet feeling light.
A letter from home is worth ten thousand gold.
In this life, spared from bearing arms.
Don't ponder endless worldly affairs,
just enjoy the limited cups in life.
Friends and family fill the world.
Freed from the duties of a minor official,
I begin to part with the cane's punishment.
Recalling when I presented three rhapsodies at the Pénglái Palace,
marveling how my fame soared in a single day.
All from Dù Fǔ's poems.
In a fruitful year, the poor heart finds peace.
Liú Yǔxī.
Travelers, don't laugh at the white-haired drunk,
few are the old who get drunk among flowers.
Same as above.
Once I thought I'd be abandoned in the mud,
growing old and dying in the wilds.
Now the spirit within me surges anew,
there's a path to official advancement again.
Hán Yù's prose.
Pity the lofty ambitions turned to white bones,
yet in remaining life, I await the bloom of youth.
Same as above.
Clearly seeing my homeland in my eyes,
knowing there's a day of return, my brows will ease.
Same as above.
Suddenly casting off official robe and tablet, I feel light.
Yáo Hé.
This morning, starting to realize before the flowers,
half the sorrow when sober has passed.
Yuán Zhěn.
I love my upright and cautious nature,
standing as a stubborn and clumsy self.
Though seldom in harmony in life,
now free from stain and wear.
Bái Jūyì's poem.
Yesterday, due to illness, I was resigned to eternal rest,
today, meeting the warm sun, I feel somewhat recovered.
Like having packed for a long journey,
lingering a while longer does no harm.
I am one who has settled all worldly matters.
My ears, though old, are not too deaf.
In the deep village, shepherd's purse flowers and elm seeds
also say the spring breeze comes for me.
With the burden of marriage light, why fear old age?
Accustomed to hunger and cold, I do not worry about poverty.
Wine stirs the joy before me,
poetry leaves a name behind.
From now on, time is my own,
the past days belonged to the court.
See also the "Leisure and Contentment" section.
Family reunion can also be glorious.
Already a renowned figure in the land,
also among the long-lived in the world.
Letters from court worthies have ceased,
but understanding friends among country folk are many.
Not destined for worldly wealth and honor,
but my writings will surely have fame after death.
Passing the exams is not the real honor,
congratulating one's parents brings true glory.
All from Bái Jūyì's poems.
A leisurely person like me is unmatched in the world.
Dù Mù.
Flowers and novelties seem to hold intention.
From "Línchuān Collection".
Why must one cleanse in water,
When originally no dust sullies the cap's tassel?
From "Ōu Gōng Collection".
In this world, rises and falls hold no regrets,
Before the wine cup, robust health is a priceless asset.
From "Luánchéng Collection".
Still there is the pure task of reading,
Not allowing spring slumber to rival a thousand cups.
From "Dōngpō Collection".
Gaining leisure through illness is not so bad,
Peace of mind is the best medicine, with no other prescription needed.
Same as above.
But exchange poverty and sorrow for lasting health.
Retreating to the fields,
Calling myself an old servant.
Recounting the fortunes encountered from start to finish,
To astonish the elders of the village.
Like awakening from drunkenness,
Like a mute finding voice,
Like a paralytic rising,
First returning to the hometown,
First seeing father and elder brothers.
Without office, one's body feels light,
With a son, all matters are fulfilled.
All from the same source as above.
In life, never doing things that cause frowning,
Under heaven, there should be no one grinding their teeth in anger.
From Shào Yáofū's poem.
Sūn Shì retired to Yùn,
Held a banquet,
And told his guests: "Bái Jūyì said:
'How many vermilion gates lock empty mansions,
Their masters never return when the time comes.'
Now this old man has returned,"
His joy evident in his expression.
From "Chéngshuǐ Yàntán".
A courtyard full of blooming flowers does not seem like poverty.
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì".
An annual stipend of two thousand, parents aged eighty,
Who in the world enjoys such honor at this time?
From Chén Hòushān's poem.
Withdrawing the body like thinning ice melting away,
Placing the pillow as secure as Mount Tài.
From Huáng Shān Gǔ's poem.
Wishing to reform and start anew.
From "Xī Hàn Xíngfǎ Zhì".
Cleansing the heart to renew oneself.
From "Dōng Hàn Píng Dì Jì".
Purifying the heart to turn toward goodness.
From "Hòu Guō Tài Zhuàn".
A rooster that missed the dawn,
Again thinks to crow once.
From "Sānguózhì Zhūgě Jǐn's Words".
Zhu Jǐngxiù said: "If allowed to start anew,
I would swallow knives to cut my intestines,
Drink ashes to cleanse my stomach."
From "Nánshǐ Qí Shū Xún Bóyù Zhuàn".
You should focus on forgiving faults,
I too ask to amend my actions.
From Hán Yù's writings.
A mother wise and kind,
I have no one to command.
With seven sons,
The mother toils in hardship.
With seven sons,
None comfort the mother's heart.
From "Máo Shī Kǎifēng".
Quietly speaking and thinking of it,
I mourn for myself.
From the poem "Méng" in the Shījīng.
Xuān Zǐ said: "I have been shallow as a man."
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, 19th Year of Xiāng Gōng".
Zhào Měng said: "I truly lack virtue,
And using a servant's wall to house the lords,
This is my fault,
I apologize for my incompetence."
From "31st Year of Xiāng Gōng".
When Jìn Dào's wife fed the laborers building the wall of Qǐ,
A man from Jiàng County was of advanced age.
Joining in the meal, Zhào Měng asked the county official,
Who turned out to be his subordinate.
Summoning him, he apologized for his fault,
Saying: "I, Wǔ, lacking talent,
Bear the great affairs of the ruler,
Yet with Jìn's many troubles, I could not follow your lead.
Causing you to suffer long in the mud,
Is Wǔ's crime,
I dare apologize for my inadequacy."
From "30th Year of Xiāng Gōng".
Even pulling out all of Jiǎ's hair to count his crimes
Would still not be enough.
From "Shǐjì Fàn Suī Zhuàn".
Even if they do not speak of my disgrace,
Would I not feel shame in my heart?
From "Qián Hàn Xiàng Jí Zhuàn".
Cross-reference to the "Self-Shame" section.
When his wife and children had faults,
He would often remove his cap and blame himself.
From "Dōng Hàn Qiú Lǎn Zhuàn".
Sins piled high as mountains and rivers,
Deep and inerasable.
From "Liú Yuèshí Zhuàn".
Better that others wrong me,
Than I wrong others.
From "Tōngjiàn Táng Dézōng Jì".
Cross-reference to the "Generosity" section.
As the ash tube frequently shifts,
Dust and dew offer no remedy.
From Liú Bīnkè.
Vague as in a drunken dream,
Unaware of the words that escape.
From Dōngpō's "Memorial on Exile to Huángzhōu".
Reflecting on the causes of my misfortunes,
All stem from reputation exceeding reality.
Which the Creator cannot tolerate,
Equating with receiving a thousand measures without merit,
The sin is the same.
Closing the gate and sweeping away visitors,
Gathering my scattered spirit.
Just when speaking out leads to exhaustion,
Pulling out hair couldn't count the crimes.
All from "Dōngpō Collection".
Long arrows cannot be fully drawn,
Missing the target, no blame on the bow.
From "Luánchéng Collection".
The weak cannot save themselves,
They must rely on the strong.
From "Yì Lüè Lì".
Appealing to the great states.
From the Shījīng poem "Zǎichí".
Searching all night in a dark room,
Without a candle, what can be seen?
From "Lǐjì Zhòngní Yānjū".
Knocking on people's doors at dusk.
From "Mèngzǐ".
In the rut of a cart,
A crucian carp said: "I am a subject of the Eastern Sea's waves.
How could a mere dipper of water
Save my life?"
From "Zhuāngzǐ Wàiwù" chapter.
Mèng Xiàn Zǐ said: "I wish to borrow your assistance."
From "Zuǒ Zhuàn, 4th Year of Xiāng Gōng".
Gān Mào said to Sū Qín: "A poor man's daughter and a rich man's daughter were spinning together.
The poor man's daughter said: 'I have nothing to buy a candle with,
But your candlelight fortunately has surplus.
You could share your extra light with me,
Without diminishing your brightness and gaining a convenience.'"
From "Shǐjì".
Though occasional rain falls from heaven,
It still awaits clouds rising from the four peaks.
From "Běishǐ Wèi Kǎi Zhuàn".
Xiāo Jiǒng was the Governor of Hénán,
Once involved in a case at the Western Office.
Jí Wēn was sent to investigate him,
And Wēn pressed Jiǒng severely.
Later, when Wēn became the Deputy of Wànnián briefly,
Jiǒng became the Governor of Jīngzhào,
Wēn had long been connected with Gāo Lìshì.
When Lìshì returned from the palace,
Jiǒng was sure to visit to thank for his post,
So Wēn went first to see Lìshì and chatted with him.
Joking and shaking hands warmly,
When Jiǒng arrived later,
Wēn pretended to avoid him in surprise,
But Lìshì called out: "Jí Qī, no need to avoid,
This is also my old acquaintance."
Summoning him back to sit with Jiǒng,
Jiǒng received him very respectfully,
Not daring to hold a grudge over the past incident.
Another day,
Wēn visited Jiǒng and said: "In the past,
I dared not compromise the state's laws.
From now on, I ask to cleanse my heart and serve you."
Lord Jiǒng then enjoyed his company fully.
From "Tōngjiàn Táng Xuánzōng Jì".
A scholar is not jade or璧,
His worth is spoken by those who discuss him.
From "Wùlǐ Lùn".
Cross-reference to the "Valued Through Others" section.
Hoping to borrow the faint light of a night candle,
seeking the modest favor from a wealthy household.
Liú Xiàobiāo's "Guǎng Jué Jiāo Lùn".
The cold valley awaits the sounding pitch-pipe.
"Wénxuǎn".
Just like hibernating insects sealed in their burrows dying,
there is no difference from those withering to death.
With one clap of spring thunder,
they are bound to lift their heads eagerly and come to life.
Moreover, if there is someone to blow the pitch-pipe,
summoning the east wind to warm them,
their transformation will be even faster.
"Liú Bīnkè Jí".
Sòng Guǎngpíng, while serving in a lowly position,
met Sū Gōng Wèidào, who was an envoy.
Sòng Guǎngpíng presented him with the "Plum Blossom Fu",
which Sū praised highly,
and from then on, he was recognized among the renowned.
This shows that even outstanding talents cannot rely solely on their literary works;
they still need a few words of recommendation from predecessors,
riding on their influence to then raise their heads high.
How much more so for the mediocre,
who can distinguish themselves?
Ibid.
Cross-reference "Valued through Association".
Applying a single yang at the extremity of decline,
rescuing the drowning from the depths of the abyss.
Those who have fallen,
desiring to rise, will surely cry out for help;
the sick,
wishing to recover, will moan and seek a doctor.
Both from the same source.
A lone beast runs, searching for its herd.
Cáo Zǐjiàn's "Poem to Báimǎ Wáng Biāo".
Without the brightness of the multitude of stars,
they borrow the light of the sun and moon.
Wèi Wéndì's "Letter to Wú Zhì".
I wish to borrow the glow from the eastern wall,
that its remaining light may shine on a poor girl.
"Lǐ Bái Jí".
Hoping the receding waves will save the parched.
Dù Fǔ's poetry.
The vast sea can be fished without a hook,
and floating clouds also have a ladder.
Under your command, thanks to you, I am included;
how could I alone have no intention of joining the fishermen and woodcutters?
Yáng Xióng also had the "Hédōng Fù",
only waiting to be blown and sent up to the heavens.
Both from Dù Fǔ's poetry.
If the jade of Jīng does not meet with suspicion,
and the night-luminous pearl is not met with a hand on the sword,
then even if my bones sink in nine deaths,
I still hope to hold the pearl in gratitude;
bowing my head in the three springs,
I merely wish to tie grass in return.
Luò Bīnwáng.
A stranded fish relying on drops often despairs of the whale's waves;
a bird with broken wings, tossed about, much desires to move to the phoenix tree.
Ibid.
If your remaining light can shine upon me,
perhaps cold ashes may reignite.
If your grace extends to me, benefiting from the leftover moisture of Dōnglǐ,
I shall humbly follow your guidance, lightly entrusting my dreams to the southern branches.
Beating short wings among the elms,
hoping for a touch from your high standard;
washing fresh scales in a trickle,
longing for a sprinkle from the vast waves;
what I hope is that your glance may flow towards me,
that your grooming may enhance my value;
then a leaden knife may serve for one cut,
and a lame turtle may journey a thousand miles.
Cross-reference "Self-Dream".
If you can share a dipper of water,
to save a parched fish relying on drops,
bestow your leftover light,
to shine upon a shivering woman living in widowhood;
then may a worn-out nag at the trough,
trot like a thoroughbred;
a creature hiding in flight,
preen its feathers among phoenixes.
Cross-reference the "Self-Recommendation" section,
both from "Luò Bīnwáng Jí".
Those treading water and fire seek rescue from others,
not only from those who love them like fathers, brothers, or sons,
that they may go and save them.
If there is someone nearby,
even if they are hated or resented,
as long as they do not
wish for their death,
they will cry out loudly,
hoping that person will save them.
Hán Yù's writings.
A great tree in the mountains,
a horse in the market,
if passed by without a glance,
even by thousands daily, it does not mean they are worthless
or inferior.
But until the master carpenter passes without a look,
or Bólè passes without a glance,
then it is known they are not timber for pillars,
nor feet for surpassing speed.
Hán Yù's "Letter Seeking Recommendation for Someone".
Cross-reference "Abandonment".
At the shore of heaven and earth,
by the banks of the great river,
there is a strange creature,
surely not of the common scale or shell kind, its match!
If it gets water,
it can change into wind and rain, moving between heaven and earth without difficulty.
If it lacks water,
it is confined to a space of ordinary size.
There are no high mountains, great ridges, wide roads, or extreme dangers blocking it,
yet in its parched state,
it cannot reach the water on its own,
and has been laughed at by otters
for almost eight or nine years.
If a powerful one
pities its plight and moves it,
it would be but the effort of lifting a hand or moving a foot.
Yet this creature,
proud of its uniqueness among the masses,
says: "I would rather
rot to death in the sand and mud;
to lower my head, droop my ears,
wag my tail and beg for pity—
that is not my will."
When a powerful one encounters it and looks closely,
it is as if unseen.
Whether it lives or dies,
is indeed unknown.
Now there is another powerful one before it,
so it tentatively lifts its head and cries out once.
How can it know if the powerful one will not pity its plight,
and not spare the effort of a hand or foot,
to transfer it to clear waves?
If he pities it, it is fate.
If he does not,
it is fate.
Knowing it is fate yet still crying out—
that too is fate.
Hán Yù's writings.
Moreover, under the bustling sky, I alone moan.
Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
The wave of kindness naturally knows to save the parched fish.
Liú Chángqīng.
Even if there is a time to repay kindness by holding flowers,
who would allow a perch when choosing a tree?
Ibid.
Borrowing wings.
"Wáng Wéi Jí".
A broken tally can honor the withered,
a lost hairpin should not be discarded.
If the beauty of springtime could be lent,
the cold valley would turn to mist and breeze.
Wēn Fēiqīng.
Ashamed I lack the grace of a phoenix,
with short wings, I fly back in vain.
Who will lend me feathers,
to chase along the clouded path?
"Wéi Yìwù Jí".
Thread enters through the needle,
the arrow is shot by the string.
Although there is thread
and an arrow, without the needle
and string, to achieve it on one's own
is impossible.
"Bái Jūyì Jí".
On the road, I plead with a confidant,
presenting my card not seeking ignorance.
Mèng Hàorán.
Without a single relative in court,
nor an old acquaintance to glance back on the road,
is like a lone root planted in barren land.
Unreached by everyone's weeding,
untouched by any household's irrigation,
if its branches wash and grow,
and it bears flowers and fruit,
is it not due to heaven's utmost benevolence in rich rain,
and the earth's boundless spring sunshine?
You, sir, are the timely rain from heaven,
assisting the earth's boundless spring,
the one who makes things grow;
how will you place me?
Ōuyáng Xíngyán's writings.
Grasping the wind, capturing shadows,
casting wood, carving water.
I dare not seek your favor or knowledge,
but only hope for your refinement.
Dù Mùzhī.
Those fallen into a well seek a way out,
those holding something hot wish to wash.
Ibid.
I feel ashamed as a gate-sweeping scholar;
who will be the one to beg for fire?
Ibid.
Lost hairpins and dropped shoes should be remembered;
now, the disciples are only lowly officials.
Luó Yǐn's poetry.
If asked late at night in the Xuānshì Hall,
could you entirely forget the unburned ashes?
Same as above.
This dynasty
lacks the engraving of supervision and praise,
borrowing warmth from the cold valley.
From Ōu Yángxiū's poetry.
Must be like the sword Mòyé,
all melted and cast into one.
From "Yàn Gōng's Classified Essentials".
If you would pity the sincerity of one humble person,
I wish to borrow the aid of even half a word.
From Línchuān.
Soon to see wealth and honor pressing close,
borrowing residual warmth from the scorching hand.
From "The Collected Works of Dōngpō".
Specially borrowing your teeth and words,
to subtly complete my wings.
Same as above.
History
The King of Chǔ besieged Zhèng.
After three months,
he captured it.
The Earl of Zhèng, baring his shoulder and leading a sheep,
went to meet him, saying: "I, the orphan, am not favored by heaven and unable to serve you, my lord,
causing your anger to reach my humble city,
is my crime.
How dare I not obey your command?
If you take captives to the south of the river,
to populate the coastal regions,
I will also obey.
If you divide and bestow us upon the feudal lords, making us your servants and concubines, I will also obey.
But if you kindly remember our former friendship,
and seek blessings from Lì, Xuān, Huán, and Wǔ,
not extinguishing our altars of land and grain,
allowing us to change and serve you, ranking among the nine districts, that would be your grace,
and my wish,
though I dare not hope for it.
I venture to bare my true feelings,
and it is for you, my lord, to consider them."
From "Zuǒzhuàn, Xuāngōng 12th Year".
King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
and captured it.
The Earl of Zhèng, baring his shoulder and leading a sheep,
went to meet him, saying: "I, the orphan, am not favored by heaven,
unable to serve you, my lord.
You have become angered,
which is my crime.
How dare I not obey your command?
If you banish me to the southern sea,
or bestow me as a servant or concubine to the feudal lords,
I will also obey.
If you do not cut off our altars of land and grain,
and allow me to change and serve you,
that is my wish.
Though I dare not hope for it,
I venture to bare my true feelings."
From "History of Chǔ Leaving Home".
Yuán Ní, the garrison commander of Huáishuò.
Being an old friend of Yuán Huái,
yet corrupt and disgraced,
set a banquet to invite Huái.
He said to Huái: "The length of my life
depends on your words;
how can you not show some leniency?"
From "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Chronicle of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng".
Wèi Qí flogged Fàn Suī,
breaking his ribs and knocking out his teeth.
Suī feigned death and curled up,
was placed on a mat and put in the toilet.
He had drunk guests
take turns urinating on him.
Fàn Suī said to the guard:
"If you can get me out,
I will surely reward you handsomely."
The guard then requested to dispose of the dead person in the mat.
Wèi Qí, drunk, said: "Alright."
From "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Zhōu Chronicle".
The King of Jìn beheaded Liú Shǒuguāng.
Shǒuguāng said: "I, Shǒuguāng, am skilled in riding and archery;
if you, my king, wish to achieve hegemony,
why not spare me to let me prove myself?"
His two wives, Lǐ shì and Zhù shì,
rebuked him, saying: "Emperor, matters have come to this;
what good is living anymore?
We beg to die first."
They immediately stretched their necks to be executed,
while Shǒuguāng wept and begged pitifully until his death.
From "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Later Liáng, King Jūn".
Dīng Gōng was a general under Xiàng Yǔ.
He pursued and cornered Gāozǔ west of Péngchéng,
and close combat ensued.
The King of Hàn urgently turned to Dīng Gōng and said: "Should two worthy men oppress each other?"
Dīng Gōng then led his troops and withdrew.
From "Western Hàn, Biography of Jì Bù".
Bào Shèngzhī intended to execute Wáng Xīn.
Xīn said: "Killing Xīn will not enhance your authority;
it would be better to show leniency at times,
to demonstrate your grace and mercy."
Shèngzhī admired his words and pardoned him.
From "Former Hàn".
A fierce tiger in the deep mountains shakes all the valleys,
but when trapped in a pit,
it wags its tail begging for food.
From "Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān".
Collection
Minister Yuán in Zhèdōng's guest residence had a secretary named Xuē,
who, after drinking, offended the minister's nephew and was expelled from the staff.
After leaving,
he composed ten poems on separation,
and presented them.
Separation of the dog from its master,
the brush from the hand,
the horse from the stable,
the parrot from its cage,
the swallow from its nest,
the pearl from the palm,
the fish from the pond,
the eagle from the flock,
the bamboo from the pavilion,
the mirror from its stand.
The dog poem says: "Tamed at the red gate for four or five years,
with fragrant fur and clean feet, the master pities.
For no reason, it bit a beloved guest,
and can no longer sleep on the red silk carpet."
The brush poem says: "Yuè tubes and Xuān hairs first suited the mood,
on red paper, scattering floral jades.
All because long use has worn the tip away,
it can no longer startle in Xī Zhī's hand."
The parrot poem says: "Alone in Lǒngxī, a solitary figure,
flying back and forth onto the brocade mat.
All because its speech lacked discretion,
it can no longer call out from the cage."
The swallow poem says: "Entering and leaving the red gate, unwilling to leave,
the master often loved its chirping sounds.
But carrying mud defiled the coral mat,
it can no longer build a nest between the beams."
From "Records of Gathering", the rest not recorded.
Classics
To perceive the situation,
one who acts directly will meet resistance.
Commentary on "Brief Examples of the Yì" says: "Perceiving the other's situation,
acting will surely succeed.
Acting without assessment,
the other will surely resist."
Having seen the gentleman,
how can I not be joyful?
From "Shījīng, Odes of the States, Wind and Rain".
Having seen the gentleman,
he is the dragon, he is the light.
From "Shījīng".
It is heard that when first meeting a gentleman,
one should say: 'I sincerely wish to have my name heard by the messenger.'
To an equal, one says: 'I sincerely wish to meet.'
For rare meetings, one says:
'I have heard of your name.'
For frequent meetings, one says: 'Morning and evening.'
Commentary on "Lǐjì, Minor Rites of the Junior" says: "Frequent means many times.
To a gentleman, one says: 'I wish morning and evening to have my name heard by the messenger.'
To an equal, one says: 'I wish morning and evening to be seen by the messenger.'"
Masters
Do I not know if I can continue this and meet again?
From "Mèngzǐ".
I hope to tread under your curtain.
From "Zhuāngzǐ, Chapter on Robber Zhí".
Waiting below the wind,
fortunate to hear the sound of your cough and spit.
From "Zhuāngzǐ, Chapter on the Old Fisherman".
History
Zǐchǎn said: "My humble city dares not rest peacefully,
coming to meet at the appointed time,
but encountering your busy schedule and not being able to see you,
and not receiving your command,
I do not know when the meeting will be."
From "Zuǒzhuàn, Xiānggōng 31st Year".
Zōu Yáng said: "At which king's gate
cannot one drag long robes?"
From "Western Hàn, His Biography".
I wish to have an audience.
Same as above.
Ěr and Yú paid a visit.
From "Western Hàn, Biography of Zhāng Ěr".
He called upon the various dignitaries.
From "Western Hàn, Biography of Zhāng Tāng".
Vast as clouds parting to see the sun.
What joy can compare?
From "Eastern Hàn, Biography of Yuán Shào".
Bowing at the guest's steps.
Presenting the card of rank and hometown.
From "Records of the Wèi".
Lǚ Sēngzhēn had a son.
Sòng Jìyǎ went to congratulate him, inscribing the envelope: "One thousand coins."
The gatekeeper thought it too little,
and did not announce him until forced to do so.
From "Book of Liáng".
Cross-reference "Celebrations and Congratulations".
Collection
Receiving grace beneath your countenance.
Lù Shìyún's "Banquet Gathering Poem".
Alone ashamed to engage in solicitation.
Dù Gōngbù's "Poem for Zhào Fèngxiān".
When you go out, I come in,
As if avoiding each other.
Hán Wén.
Zhèng Guāngyè had a large leather case,
Whenever someone presented a laughable tribute,
He would toss it inside,
Calling it the "Sea of Bitterness".
"Zhìyán".
In ancient times, before paper, they shaved bamboo and wood
To inscribe names,
Hence called "calling cards".
Later using paper for writing,
Thus termed "name cards".
When Táng's Lǐ Déyù became powerful chancellor,
People sought to show extra respect,
Changing to prepared documents inquiring after his well-being,
Called "gate petitions".
"Jíyùn".
Classic
The sun and moon cling to heaven,
All grains, grasses, and trees cling to earth.
． "Yì·Lí Guà" note: "Each finds its place to adhere,
Yīchuān says between heaven and earth,
There is nothing that does not cling."
What finds its proper place
Must become great.
Therefore it is followed by Fēng (Abundance).
"Xù Guà".
Weak yet not fearing enemies
Comes from having secure footing.
Worried yet not fearing chaos
Comes from having proper position.
"Yì Lüèlì Shàng".
The sun and moon, attaining heaven, can shine perpetually.
． "Yì·Héng Guà".
Fish cling to water,
Beasts cling to mountains.
． "Yì Xìcí" note.
Lush are the artemisias,
Growing in those broad valleys.
． "Shī·Jīngjīng Zhě É".
The wild geese fly,
Gathering in the central marsh.
"Juǎn Ē" poem.
Cross-reference "Being in the Right Place".
Fish are among the algae,
Resting by the rushes.
． "Shī·Yú Zǎo".
Masters
Frost-geese rely on autumn winds
To achieve effortless flight.
"Lièzǐ".
Release fish into deep pools,
Place monkeys in trees.
"Wénzhōngzǐ".
When a great mansion is completed, swallows and sparrows congratulate each other.
． "Huáinánzǐ·Shuōlín Xùn".
Cross-reference "Residences" category.
History
The Marquis of Qí invited Jìng Zhòng to be minister, but he declined saying:
"I am a traveling minister,
Fortunate to obtain pardon under lenient governance,
Forgiven for lacking proper instruction and spared punishment -
This is the ruler's kindness.
What I've gained is already plenty."
． "Zuǒzhuàn·Zhuāng 22nd Year".
Shrine mice aren't flooded out,
House mice aren't smoked out.
Why? Because their refuge makes it so.
． "Qián Hàn·Zhōngshān King Biography".
Giant fish swim in vast abysses.
． "Qián·Wáng Bāo Biography".
Stars clinging to heaven
Resemble all states adhering to the king.
． "Hòu Hàn·Xiāng Kǎi Biography".
Like morning breezes gathering
In northern woods, or dragon-fish seeking
Marshy wetlands.
． "Jìn Shū·Xiàomǐn Emperor Annals".
Fish obtain water to swim,
Birds ride wind to soar.
． "Táng Shū·Yuán Zhěn Biography".
Birds live in deep forests,
Beasts dwell in lush grasslands.
"Bái Jūyì Biography".
Biographies
Shrine wasps aren't attacked,
Shrine mice aren't smoked.
Their refuge makes it so.
"Hán Shī Wàizhuàn".
Phoenixes nest in palace eaves.
"Tōnglì".
Collection
Returning birds reach tall woods,
Fluttering and strengthening wings.
Cáo Zǐjiàn's "To White Horse Prince Biāo".
Having land for shelter.
"Rèn Yǎnshēng Collection".
Hedgehog-tangles and ant-gatherings,
Find reliance in water and grass.
"Wénxuǎn".
Dew-drenched autumn cypress, crane cries clear.
Dù Xúnhè.
Before asking about well-being, first
Congratulate them on obtaining a worthy host.
Hán Tuìzhī for Zhāng Jí.
Round, round within compass stars,
Not necessarily bright as moon.
Tracking near Polaris,
Circling heaven never sinking.
Yuán Zhěn.
Powerful frontier carriage-horse land,
Serving as commandant brings glory.
"Wéi Yìngwù Collection".
Carrying mud into magnificent houses.
Same as above.
Not seeing the thousand-year crane,
Often perched on hundred-fathom pines.
"Bái Shìláng Collection".
Beasts delight in mountains and valleys,
Fish delight in ponds and pools.
Insects delight in deep grass,
Birds delight in high branches.
Same as above.
Cross-reference "Different Orientations".
Deep waters bring fish extreme joy.
Dù's poetry.
Classic
Dragons fight in the wild,
Their way exhausted.
． "Yì·Kūn Guà".
Like crossing great waters,
With no shore in sight.
． "Shū·Wēizǐ" chapter.
On whom shall I rely?
． "Shū·Wǔzǐ Zhī Gē".
My feathers bedraggled,
My tail disheveled.
My nest precarious,
Tossed by wind and rain.
． "Shī·Chīxiāo".
Wild geese fly over land.
． "Shī·Jiǔ Yù".
Not connected to fur,
Not attached to lining.
． "Xiǎoyǎ·Xiǎopiàn".
Nowhere to settle.
． "Shī·Xiǎoyǎ".
Masters
Descend from tall trees into dark valleys.
． "Mèngzǐ·Téng Wéngōng Shàng".
The reed warbler builds its nest with feathers woven with hair,
Tied to reed spikes.
When wind comes,
The reeds break,
Eggs shatter and chicks die -
Not that the nest was incomplete,
But its attachment caused this.
． "Xúnzǐ·Quànxué" chapter.
History
Qì Shè declared: "If the skin doesn't exist,
How can the fur adhere?"
． "Zuǒzhuàn·Xī 14th Year".
Adrift with nothing to rely on.
． "Shǐjì·Huáiyīn Biography".
Losing one's place constitutes fault.
． "Shǐjì·Confucius Hereditary House".
Cannot even find a side path
To set foot on.
． "Qián Hàn·Jiǎ Shān Biography".
Though the universe is vast,
Nowhere to accommodate oneself.
． "Tōngjiàn·Jìn Mù Annals".
There is a bird
That builds its nest atop reed tips,
When heavenly winds come, the reeds break and nest destroys -
Because its perch is fragile.
"Hán Shī Wàizhuàn".
Collection
Vast and boundless with nowhere to anchor.
From "Chǔ Cì".
Flowers wither when separated from their stems,
Branches dry up when severed from their trunks.
From Cài Yōng's "Shì Huì".
Escaped from the cage with clipped wings,
Stranded in ruts like a dying fish.
By Luò Bīnwáng.
Sailing a boat yet knowing not the four directions,
Crossing the endless expanse of great waters.
From Hán Wén's "Mǐn Jǐ Fù".
Interchangeable with "obscure in direction".
If water does not enter the sea,
How can it ride the celestial waves?
If wood does not grow in mountains,
How can it stretch its boughs to the sun?
By Mèng Dōngyě.
Thorns and brambles vainly host the phoenix.
By Liú Chángqīng.
Swallows that once graced the halls of Wáng and Xiè,
Now fly into commoners' humble homes.
By Liú Bīnkè.
If a hundred rivers do not flow to the sea,
Though they rush and surge wildly,
They will ultimately become parched land.
From Tián Yūn's letter to Yáng Xíngmì in the Táng dynasty.
Dejected like a stray dog with no home.
From "Records of the Grand Historian: Confucius' Hereditary House".
The Mohist Yí Zhī sought to meet Mencius through Xú Pì.
From "Mèngzǐ".
In history,
Wèi Yāng, through Jǐng Jiān,
Sought an audience with Duke Xiào.
From "Comprehensive Mirror: Reign of King Xiǎn of Zhōu".
Someone had previously recommended.
From "Biography of Zōu Yáng in Western Hàn".
Yán Shígǔ commented: "‘Xiān yóu’
means to introduce and recommend."
Gnarled roots of coiled trees,
Twisted and peculiar,
Yet become vessels for the emperor—
Because those around him first prepared their form.
From the aforementioned "Biography of Zōu Yáng".
If someone speaks first,
Even withered wood and rotten stumps can achieve merit and be remembered.
Same as above.
Classic:
Pursuing a deer without a forester,
One merely enters the forest.
From the commentary on "Yì Jīng: Hexagram Zhūn": "Though one sees the game, without the forester, entering the forest alone—
how can it be captured?"
In history,
Scholars in humble circumstances,
Trapped in poverty and weakness,
Even if endowed with the wisdom of Yáo and Shùn,
The eloquence of Yī Yǐn and Guǎn Zhòng,
The integrity of Lóng Péng and Bǐ Gān,
Yet lacking any prior introduction,
Though exhausting their spirit,
Wishing to offer loyalty to the rulers of their time,
Would surely meet sovereigns who grasp their swords and glare suspiciously.
From "Biography of Zōu Yáng in Western Hàn".
The bright moon's pearl,
The night-shining jade,
If thrown at someone darkly on the road,
All would grasp their swords and glare—
Why? Because they appear without cause.
Same as above.
None would put me first.
From "Biography of Lì Yìjī".
Without the backing of powerful relatives,
To rely on in advance.
Commentary on "Biography of Jiǎ Yì": "To have support and connections."
Throughout history, employing people
Must involve intermediaries;
As for those who achieve success,
None lacked prior introduction.
From "Biography of Zhāng Xíngchéng in Táng".
Collection:
Without the means of introduction,
How can one approach the nobles and ministers?
From "Discussion of Four Scholars on Virtue".
Lacking any connections.
From "Biography of Chén Zǐ'áng".
No steps to advance,
Yet sitting to reach the clouds.
Same as above.
In the past, Emperor Gāo of Yīn
Found a worthy assistant in his dreams.
Who among his attendants introduced him?
It was heaven's accord and divine match.
From Hán Wén's "Ode to Two Birds".
Resonating without being struck,
Uniting without introduction.
By Liǔ Qǐ.
Inspired and self-achieved,
With no intermediary in between.
By Lǚ Héshū's writings.
Classic:
Going straight would be contrary.
Commentary on "Yì Jīng: General Principles": "The example of ‘pursuing a deer without a forester’
fits this."
Walking alone, solitary and unsupported.
From "Shī Jīng: Dì Dù".
In history,
Without a day's acquaintance,
Or introduction from attendants.
From "Biography of Gǔ Yǒng in Western Hàn".
Isolated with little support.
From the same source.
Zhèng Chāng petitioned in defense
Of Gài Kuānráo, saying: "Above, he lacked connections like Xǔ and Shǐ;
Below, he had no backing like Jīn and Zhāng."
From "Comprehensive Mirror: Reign of Emperor Xuān of Hàn".
Without a single recommendation from high ministers,
Or supportive words from those around.
From "Biography of Mǎ Yuán in Later Hàn".
Standing alone among the powerful,
With not a single word of support beside him.
From "Eastern Hàn".
Biographies:
Clad in rough cloth, holding jade within,
Yet no way to present oneself.
From "Shī Tōng".
Humble families in modest gates,
Unheard for generations.
Same as above.
Collection:
All clans have their place,
Only the lone cloud has no support.
From "Selected Poems: The Poor Scholar".
Lacking connections for recommendation.
From Hán Shī.
The court is filled with officials,

fearing execution;
wishing to surrender to Qí,
but having killed many from Qí.
Fearing humiliation after surrender,
said: "Rather than be killed by others,
I'd kill myself."
Then committed suicide.

. *Book of Jìn, Wāng Dǎo's Biography*.
Hé Chōng once visited Wáng Dǎo,
who pointed with his yak-tail chowry to the couch, calling Chóng to sit together,
saying: "This is your seat."
When Dǎo passed away,
Chōng participated in the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
. *Book of Jìn, Hé Chōng's Biography*.
Wáng Xún and Xiè Xuán served as clerks under Huán Wēn,
who once said of them,
saying:
"Clerk Xiè at forty will surely command troops with authority,
and Clerk Wáng will become a dark-haired Excellency."
*Book of Jìn*.
Liú Yù said to Yìlóng:
"Wáng Tánshǒu is profound, resolute, and dignified,
a talent for chancellor."
. *Comprehensive Mirror, Jìn Gōngdì's Annals*.
Wáng Jiǎn from childhood was devoted to learning,
and Wáng Sēng, upon seeing him, said:
"Like a cypress or camphor tree,
though small, it already has the bearing of a pillar and beam.
He will surely undertake the affairs of family and state."
*History of the Southern Dynasties*.
Xú Miǎn loved learning.
His clansman Xú Xiàosì, upon seeing him, said:
"This is what is called a qilin among men,
and he will surely achieve a thousand miles."
. *History of the Southern Dynasties, Liáng Basic Biography*.
Xú Líng, when just a few years old,
was taken by his family to visit the monk Bǎozhì, who
touched his head, saying:
"A stone qilin from heaven."
. *History of the Southern Dynasties, Basic Biography*.
Gāo Xiàojī, upon seeing Fáng Xuánlíng, said: "I have observed many people,
but never one like this.
This young man will be a vessel of the state,
only regretting that I may not see him soar above the ravines and reach the skies."
. *Book of Táng, Basic Biography, Comprehensive*.
*Mirror* changed the character "observe" to "review".
for the character "inspect".
Cuī Hóng, upon seeing Gāo Yǔn, said:
"Gāo Zǐ is inwardly refined like the yellow center,
outwardly shining with culture and brightness,
and will surely become a great vessel of his generation."
. *Northern History, Basic Biography*.
Yáng Sù appointed Fēng Lún as Supervisor of Construction,
often discussing matters of chancellorship with him,
remaining tireless throughout the day,
then patting his couch, saying:
"Young Fēng will surely occupy this seat of mine."
He recommended him to Emperor Wén.
*Book of Suí*.

Our dynasty
Chén Zhēn asked: "Previously in Qí,
the king offered a hundred yi of double-refined gold, yet you did not accept it;
in Sòng,
when seventy yi were offered, you accepted;
in Xuē,
fifty yi were offered and you accepted.
If the previous refusal was right,
then today's acceptance
is wrong.
If today's acceptance is right,
then the previous refusal
is wrong.
You, Master, must be guilty of one of these!"
From the "Mèngzǐ."
Chén Jiǎ said: "Zhōu Gōng sent Guǎn Shū to oversee Yīn,
and Guǎn Shū used Yīn to rebel. If he knew and still sent him,
that was unkind.
If he did not know and sent him,
that was unwise.
Kindness and wisdom,
Zhōu Gōng did not fully possess."
Wūlúzǐ said: "When the Master went to Rèn, he visited Jìzǐ;
when he went to Qí, he did not visit Chǔzǐ.
Was it because Chǔzǐ was a prime minister?"
When Lǔ Pínggōng was about to visit Mèngzǐ,
Zāng Cāng said: "My lord, you are lowering yourself to prioritize a commoner,
thinking him worthy?
Ritual and righteousness come from the worthy,
yet Mèngzǐ observed later mourning more lavishly than earlier mourning.
My lord, do not see him!"
From "Liáng Huìwáng Xià."
Some say, "Yī Yǐn used cooking to win over Tāng."
From "Wàn Zhāng Shàng."
Some claimed that when Confucius was in Wèi, he stayed with Yōng Jū;
in Qí, he stayed with the eunuch Jí Huán.
Same as above.
Wàn Zhāng asked: "Some say, 'Bǎilǐ Xī sold himself to a livestock keeper in Qín
for five sheepskins,
fed cattle,
to win over Qín Mùgōng.'
Is it true?"
Mèngzǐ said: "No,
it was made up by busybodies."
Same as above.
All from the "Mèngzǐ."
The roc migrates ninety thousand li,
and the cicada and little dove laugh at it, saying: "We burst up and fly,
reaching for the elm and sandalwood trees.
If we don't make it, we just land on the ground.
Why go ninety thousand li to the south?"
The quail laughs and says: "Where is it going?
I leap up,
no more than a few yards high, then come down,
soaring among the brushwood and weeds—
that's the ultimate in flying too.
So where is it going?"
From the "Zhuāngzǐ: Free and Easy Wandering" chapter.
Petty arguments ruin the great Way.
From the "Kǒng Cóngzǐ: Gōngsūn Lóng" chapter.
Each person affirms what they affirm
and denies what they deny;
then whom shall we have to judge them?
From "Yángzǐ."
False praise is a thief of benevolence;
false slander is a thief of righteousness.
Same as above.
From the "Yuān Qiān" chapter.
Commoners have never seen dragons, unicorns, phoenixes, or luan birds,
so they say there are no such things in the world,
thinking the ancients invented auspicious omens.
From the "Bàopǔzǐ: Chàng Xuán" volume.
Historical Records:
Zǐchǎn of Zhèng instituted the qiū tax,
and the people slandered him, saying: "He has become a scorpion's tail."
From "Zuǒzhuàn, Fourth Year of Zhāo."
Jì Kāngzǐ summoned Zhòngní; Gōng Zhīyú said: "In the past, our former lord employed him but not to the end,
and he was laughed at by the feudal lords.
Now if we use him again and cannot see it through,
it will mean being laughed at by the feudal lords once more.
We must summon Rǎn Qiú."
From "Shǐjì: Confucius' Hereditary House."
When Confucius went to Zhèng,
someone from Zhèng said: "He looks weary, like a homeless dog."
Zǐgòng told Confucius, who said: "The appearance may not be right,
but resembling a homeless dog—
indeed, that's so!"
From "Shǐjì: Hereditary House."
Zhuāngzǐ wrote "The Old Fisherman,"
"Robber Zhí," and "Rifling Trunks"
to slander Confucius and his followers.
From "Shǐjì: Basic Biography."
Liú Bāng appointed Chén Píng as commandant.
He made him his chariot companion and director of the army guard.
The generals all complained, saying: "The king, in one day, gets a deserter from Chǔ,
not knowing his worth, and immediately shares his carriage with him,
even having him oversee us elders."
From "Tōngjiàn: Western Hàn, Gāozǔ's Annals."
Lóng Qiě said: "I've long known Hán Xìn's character—
easy to deal with.
He relied on a washerwoman for food,
had no means to support himself,
suffered the humiliation of crawling between legs,
lacked the courage to face others—
not worth fearing."
Same as above.
Generally, slandering the sages
is considered bizarre and impractical.
From "Yáng Xióng's Biography."
They are content with what they're used to
and slander what they haven't seen.
From "Treatise on Literature."
They mocked the Three Dynasties.
From "Table of Feudal Lords and Kings."
Jiàng and Guàn said: "Though Píng is a handsome man,
like jade on a cap,
he may have little substance inside."
From "Chén Píng's Biography,"
all from Western Hàn.
Confucius, a great sage,
was not spared slander from Wǔ Shū.
Zǐlù, a man of utmost worth,
still faced accusations from Bó Liáo.
From "Eastern Hàn: Biographies of Exemplary Women, Yuán Wěi's Wife."
How can floods and droughts
be blamed on Yáo and Tāng?
From "Cài Yōng's Biography."
Today's youth
enjoy slandering their elders.
From "Kǒng Róng's Biography."
They like to discuss others' faults,
arbitrarily judge laws and policies.
From "Mǎ Yuán's Biography,"
all from Eastern Hàn.
Common opinion says that recluses merely steal empty fame.
From "Tōngjiàn."
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi decreed: "In the past, Zhí Bùyí had no elder brother, yet people said he seduced his sister-in-law.
Dìwǔ Bóyú married orphaned girls three times, yet people said he beat his father-in-law.
Wáng Fěng monopolized power,
yet Gǔ Yǒng compared him to Shēn Bó.
Wáng Shāng was loyal and righteous,
yet Zhāng Kuāng called him heretical.
These are all cases of turning white into black,
deceiving heaven and the ruler."
From "Wèi Zhì."
Cross-reference to "deception."
Huán Chōng said: "Xiè Ānshí has the capacity for court affairs,
but is unskilled in military strategy.
Now with a great enemy approaching, he's busy with idle talk,
sending inexperienced youths to resist them.
The troops are few and weak; the fate of the empire
is clear. We shall be barbarians!"
From "Tōngjiàn: Jìn, Xiàowǔ's Annals."
Shǐ Sīmíng said: "Lǐ Guāngbì is good at defending cities,
but now he's out in the open—
he's sure to be captured!"
From "Tōngjiàn: Táng Annals."
Collections:
Street gossip and alley talk.
From Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital."
They claim Yáo was imprisoned,
petty scholars' absurd fabrication that Yǔ was tortured—
narrow-minded men's forced interpretations.
From Zhāng Wèi's "Stele for Emperor Yú."
This is like blaming the carpenter for not using a peg as a pillar or slandering the doctor
for prescribing chāngyáng to prolong life
while wanting to promote his pig's tuckahoe.
From Hán Yù's "An Exegesis on Learning."
Lǎozǐ belittled benevolence and righteousness—
not to slander them,
but because his perspective was narrow.
Sitting in a well and saying the sky is small—
it's not the sky's fault.
He took petty kindness for benevolence,
trivial acts for righteousness,
so his belittling of them was natural.
Thus, his so-called Way is his own way,
not what I call the Way.
His so-called virtue is his own virtue,
not what I call virtue.
From Hán Yù's "On the Origin of the Way."
In life, before transforming into a kun,
others' opinions are as light as a goose feather.
From Liú Chángqīng.
Like a vinegar fly discussing the roc,
or a summer insect discussing layered ice.
From "Táng Wén Cuì."
Our dynasty:
No different from beating a well's mud and discussing the Eastern Sea,
or sitting on a mosquito's back and laughing at the ninety-thousand-li journey south.
From Jiāng Mínbiǎo's "Essay on the Mind."
Cross-reference to "not knowing one's limits."
Classical texts.
He served as a guest in the royal house.
． "The Decree to Wēizǐ" from the Book of Documents.
To honor the noble,
is because they are close to the sovereign.
． "The Meaning of Sacrifices" from the Book of Rites.
When respecting elders who are of a higher rank than oneself,
one should not dare to ask their age.
"Shǎo Yí" from the Book of Rites.
When a senior official reaches seventy, he retires from his post;
if he is not allowed to decline,
he must be granted a small table and a staff,
and ride in a comfortable carriage.
"Qū Lǐ Shàng" from the Book of Rites.
A ruler of a state does not address senior ministers and official wives by their names,
a senior official does not address veteran ministers and their female relatives by their names,
a scholar does not address the family steward and senior concubines by their names.
"Qū Lǐ Xià" from the Book of Rites.
When five people live together,
the eldest must have a separate mat.
When consulting with elders,
one must carry a small table and a staff to follow them.
Both from the Book of Rites.
Mèngzǐ
In the past, did Lord Mù of Lǔ not have anyone
by Zǐsī's side,
so he could not put Zǐsī at ease?
． "Mèngzǐ: Gōngsūn Chǒu Xià".
When Guǎn Yíwú of Qí held the state's administration,
he was addressed as:
"Zhòng Fù." "Lièzǐ".
He bent the dignity of a thousand chariots to visit a humble alley.
"Yángzǐ".
History
The Song state was descended from earlier dynasties,
and was treated as a guest by the Zhou.
When the Son of Heaven had sacrificial ceremonies, he would send them sacrificial meat;
when there was mourning, he would bow to them.
From "Zuǒzhuàn".
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ had Guǎn Zhòng bound and handed over to the Qí envoy,
who accepted him and departed.
Upon arrival,
he was anointed three times
with fragrant substances.
He was bathed three times.
Duke Huán personally welcomed him in the suburbs.
From "Guóyǔ".
King Wén of Zhōu encountered Lǚ Wàng at Pánxī,
and King Wǔ honored him as mentor,
calling him Tàigōng,
with the appellation Shàngfù.
From "Shǐjì".
Xiàng Yǚ respected Fàn Zēng as Yàfù (Second Father).
Same as above.
Prince Wújì of Wèi was benevolent and treated scholars with humility;
in Wèi there was a recluse named
"Hóu Yíng, the prince with his carriage and retinue, vacated the left seat to personally welcome Master Hóu."
Master Hóu, adjusting his worn clothes and hat,
went straight up and took the honored seat,
without declining.
The prince held the reins even more respectfully.
From "Tōngjiàn Zhōu Jì".
When General-in-Chief Qīng served in the palace, the emperor would look at him while squatting over the toilet.
When Chancellor Hóng was received at banquets,
the emperor sometimes wore no crown.
But when Jiǎn came to audience,
if not properly crowned, he would not receive him.
Once the emperor was seated in the military tent,
and Jiǎn approached to present matters,
the emperor, uncrowned,
saw Jiǎn coming,
hid within the tent,
and had someone else approve his memorial.
Such was the respect he received.
From "Xīhàn Jí Àn Zhuàn".
Cáo Shēn served as chancellor of Qí,
and heard that in Jiāodōng there was a Master Gài skilled in governance
through Huáng-Lǎo teachings, so he sent generous gifts to invite him.
Shēn then vacated the main hall
and lodged Master Gài there.
From his "Běnzhuàn".
Holding a broom to lead the way.
From "Yáng Xióng Zhuàn".
Bào Shèngzhī saw Juàn Bùyí's dignified appearance
and rose to welcome him, slipping into his shoes.
Both from "Xīhàn".
General-in-Chief Yuán Shào commanded troops in Jìzhōu,
and sent an envoy to invite Zhèng Xuán to a grand gathering of guests.
Xuán arrived last,
yet was ushered to the seat of honor.
From "Dōnghàn Zhuàn".
Kǒng Róng deeply respected Zhèng Xuán,
hurrying to his door with shoes on backwards.
He petitioned Gāomì County to establish a special district for Xuán,
saying:
"In the past, Qí established a 'Village of Good Men',
and Yuè had an 'Army of Gentlemen',
all intended to honor the worthy.
Now Master Zhèng's district should be called 'Lord Zhèng's Village'."
From "Hòuhàn Zhèng Xuán Zhuàn".
Rising from the mat and changing countenance.
From "Hòuhàn".
Zhāng Zhāo of Wú
was called Zhòngfù (Uncle) in Wú.
From "Wú Zhì Zhuàn".
Xú Shù said:
"This man can be visited, but cannot be summoned to come."
Liú Bèi therefore went to see Liàng,
and only after three visits did he meet him.
From "Tōngjiàn Hàn Xiàn Jì".
Wàn Zhāng served as Governor of Jīngzhào.
His attendant followed him to the palace hall,
where nobles and dignitaries vied to greet Zhāng,
but none spoke with the Governor.
From "Xīhàn".
See also "Comparative Matters".
Sūn Cè attacked Yùzhāng,
first sending Yú Fān to see Huà Xīn.
Xīn greeted Cè wearing a commoner's scarf,
and Cè said to Xīn:
"Your honor's virtue and reputation
are admired far and wide.
I, Cè, am young and immature,
and should perform the rites of a junior."
Thereupon he bowed to Xīn.
From Hú Chōng's "Wú Shū".
Sūn Cè said:
"In the past, when Guǎnzǐ served as Qí's minister,
first called Zhòngfù, then again Zhòngfù,
and Duke Huán became the model for hegemons."
From "Wú Zhāng Zhāo Zhuàn".
Xǔ Jìng was over seventy years old,
fond of people and welcoming guidance,
tirelessly engaging in pure conversation with younger scholars.
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng
would bow to him.
From "Shǔ Zhì".
Jìn's Wáng Dǎo served as Chancellor.
Emperor Yuán entrusted him with increasing favor,
the court and public admired him,
and he was called Zhòngfù.
From "Jìnshū Běnzhuàn".
Guō Yì served as Magistrate of Yěwáng.
Yáng Hù once passed through,
and Yì sighed:
"Yáng Shūzǐ surpasses ordinary men far!"
He then escorted Hù beyond his jurisdiction,
and was dismissed from office for traveling hundreds of li.
From "Jìnshū Guō Yì Zhuàn".
Yú Fān was in Wú,
and Emperor Wén of Wèi once set an empty seat for Fān.
From "Sānguó Wú Zhì Běnzhuàn".
Guō Zǐyí of Táng
was granted the title "Shàngfù" by Emperor Dézōng.
From "Tángshū Běnzhuàn".
Guō Zǐyí
was addressed by Emperor Dàizōng as "Great Minister" rather than by name.
From "Jiù Tángshū Běnzhuàn".
Wèi Zhēng said:
"People say Your Majesty wishes to visit Nánshān,
and all outside have prepared strictly,
yet you ultimately do not go.
Why?"
The emperor laughed:
"I initially had this intention,
but feared your reproach,
so stopped midway."
The emperor once obtained a fine hawk,
and was holding it on his arm,
when he saw Zhēng approaching,
hid it in his robe.
As Zhēng reported matters,
it took so long
that the hawk died in his embrace.
From "Tōngjiàn Táng Tàizōng Jì".
The Empress Dowager trusted and valued Grand Master of the Palace Secretariat Di Rénjié, Lord Wénhuì of Liáng,
beyond any other minister.
She often called him "State Elder" without using his name,
saying:
"Every time I see you bow,
I also feel physical pain."
From "Tōngjiàn Táng Wǔhòu Jì".
Emperor Xuánzōng honored and treated Yáo Chóng with respect,
each time meeting in the side hall,
he would rise for him,
and often saw him off from the balcony—
no other minister received such treatment.
From "Tángshū Běnzhuàn".
Páng Dégōng had long enjoyed great fame,
and whenever Zhūgě Liàng visited his home,
he would bow alone below the couch.
From "Sānguózhì".
Wáng Wéi's fame peaked during the Kāiyuán era,
and nobles would vacate the left seat to welcome him.
From "Tángshū".
The emperor went to Qūfù to visit Confucius's temple,
saying:
"Confucius is the teacher of emperors and kings for a hundred generations.
How dare I not respect him?"
He then bowed to it,
and also bowed at Confucius's tomb.
He prohibited woodcutting in the Cemetery of Confucius.
He sought out descendants of Confucius and Yán Yuān,
appointing them as Magistrate and Registrar of Qūfù.
From "Tōngjiàn Wǔdài Zhōu Tàizǔ Jì".
Fán Zōngshī met Liú Yì and bowed alone.
From "Tángshū Běnzhuàn".
Records and Accounts
After Fàn Suí departed,
Táo Kǎn pursued and sent him off incessantly
for nearly a hundred li.
From "Shìshuō".
Anthology
When Zǐxià dwelled by the Western River,
Marquis Wén wielded the broom.
When Zōuzǐ resided in the shade of Shǔ Valley,
King Zhāo accompanied him in the carriage.
From "Wénxuǎn".
The King of Yān honored Yuè Yì,
wishing to share the state and rejoice together.
From "Chén Zǐ'áng Collection".
I have humbled Hán Yù to serve as Governor,
and should order that he not be subject to the Censorate,
not bound by old conventions.
From Hán Yù's "Shéndào Bēi".
At that time, he was Governor with the rank of Censor-in-Chief.
Wherever Lǐ Bái went, the local governor would greet him in the suburbs.
From Lǐ Yángbīng's "Preface to Lǐ Bái's Collection".
In our dynasty,
Lord Ōuyáng was fond of scholars,
and was considered the foremost in the realm.
"Lěng Zhāi Yè Huà".
Cross-referenced under "Delighting in Goodness".
Sū Míngyǔn arrived in the capital during the Zhìhé era,
and once recognized by Lord Ōuyáng,
his fame surged.
Hán Zhōngxiàn and other dignitaries treated him as a distinguished guest.
Once on the Double Ninth Festival, Zhōngxiàn hosted a banquet at his private residence,
attended only by Wénzhōng and a couple of high officials.
Yet Míngyǔn, as a commoner, joined their company,
which the capital's residents regarded as an exceptional honor.
"Shí Lín Yàn Yǔ".
The Master said:
When speaking to the great, despise them,
do not regard their imposing stature.
"Mèngzǐ".
Cross-referenced under "Spirit".
They rely on their wealth, I
on my benevolence;
they rely on their rank, I
on my righteousness.
What have I to feel lacking?
"Mèngzǐ: Gōngsūn Chǒu II".
Mèngzǐ served as a minister in Qí,
and was sent to offer condolences in Téng,
with Wáng Huān appointed as his deputy.
Though Wáng Huān saw him morning and evening
throughout the journey to and from Qí and Téng,
Mèngzǐ never discussed official matters with him.
Ibid.
History:
Máo Suì said:
"You all are mediocre,
precisely what is called those who achieve things through others."
"Shǐ Jì: Biography of Lord Píngyuán".
Why worth mentioning between teeth?
"Xī Hàn: Biography of Shūsūn Tōng".
Persuading Chancellor Hóng to submit
was like removing a blindfold.
"Xī Hàn: Biography of Huáinán King Ān".
"Tōng Jiàn" records Wǔ Bèi saying:
"Persuading Chancellor Hóng and others
is like shaking off dust from a blindfold!"
Gēngshī, upon seeing Zhào Xǐ, said:
"A calf the size of a silkworm cocoon or chestnut,
how could it travel far?"
"Dōng Hàn".
Xǔ Sì, speaking with Liú Bèi, said:
"Chén Yuánlóng is a scholar from Huáihǎi,
his haughty spirit remains unchecked."
Sì, while passing Xiàpī,
saw Yuánlóng showed no host-guest courtesy,
and did not converse with him.
Yuánlóng took the upper bed to sleep,
leaving the guest to sleep on the lower bed.
Bèi said:
"Now the realm is in great turmoil,
you should worry about the state, forgetting home,
and harbor intentions to save the world.
Yet you seek fields and inquire about houses,
your words offer nothing adoptable,
which is what Yuánlóng despises.
Why should he speak with you?
If it were me, I'd sleep atop a hundred-zhang tower,
leaving you to sleep underground—
how much more than just upper and lower beds?"
"Dōng Hàn: Biography of Chén Qiú" annotation.
Cuī Lín said:
"A great man acts for the chance encounters;
as for you people,
are you truly worthy of esteem?"
"Tōng Jiàn: Dōng Hàn".
Huáng Zhōng was appointed Rear General,
and Guān Yǔ, hearing Huáng Zhōng's rank equaled his,
angrily said:
"A great man does not stand alongside an old soldier."
He refused the appointment.
At that time, Yǔ was being appointed Front General.
"Tōng Jiàn: Hàn Xiàndì Annals".
Cross-referenced under "Valuing Pride".
Someone asked Mí Héng:
"Why not follow Chén Chángwén and Sīmǎ Bódá?"
He said:
"How could I follow butchers and wine-sellers?"
Asked again about Xún Wénruò and Zhào Zhìcháng,
he said:
"Wénruò could lend his face for mourning,
Zhìcháng could supervise the kitchen."
"Dōng Hàn: Original Biography" annotation.

The term "sharing the same hatred in bamboo-slips" refers to mutual compassion.

Sharing concern for disasters and dangers,

Natural disasters spread,

Rescuing from troubles and sharing in disasters.

Saving people from distress,

Jì Bù was renowned in Chǔ,
and repeatedly cornered the King of Hàn.
After Xiàng Yǔ perished,
Emperor Gāozǔ offered a thousand in gold for Bù's capture,
so Bù hid with the Zhōu family.
The Zhōus shaved and shackled Jì Bù,
dressed him in coarse garments,
placed him in a willow cart,
and along with several dozen of their servants,
sent him to Lǔ to be sold by Zhū Jiā.
Zhū Jiā knew in his heart it was Jì Bù,
so he bought him and settled him on his land,
instructing his son: "Follow this slave's lead in farm work,
and be sure to eat with him."
_Biography of Jì Bù_.
Qín imprisoned Lord Mèngcháng,
plotting to kill him.
Lord Mèngcháng sent someone to appeal to King Zhāo's favored consort for help.
The consort said, "I wish to have your lord's white fox fur."
At that time, Lord Mèngcháng had one white fox fur,
worth a thousand in gold,
unmatched under heaven,
which he had presented to King Zhāo upon entering Qín,
leaving him no other such fur.
Lord Mèngcháng worried over this,
asking all his guests,
but none could respond.
The lowest-seated guest, skilled in dog-like theft,
said, "I can obtain the white fox fur."
So that night, he acted like a dog,
entering the Qín palace treasury,
retrieved the presented white fox fur,
and offered it to the king's favored consort.
She spoke on his behalf,
and Lord Mèngcháng was released,
immediately galloping away.
King Zhāo of Qín later regretted releasing him,
and finding he had already left,
sent men on fast carriages to pursue him.
When Lord Mèngcháng reached the pass,
the pass rule was to let guests out at cockcrow;
fearing pursuit would catch up,
a lower-seated guest skilled in imitating roosters
made all the roosters crow,
and thus they departed through the pass.
_Main Biography_.
Lǐ Tóng advised Lord Píngyuán: "When scholars are in peril and hardship,
they are easily won over by kindness."
_Main Biography_.
Wǔ Zǐxū fled to Wú, reaching Zhāoguān,
where the pass guards tried to arrest him.
Wǔ Zǐxū barely escaped his pursuers,
later arriving at the river,
where a fisherman in a boat,
knowing Wǔ Zǐxū's desperation,
ferried him across.
_Main Biography_,
also in _Records of the Grand Historian_.
Bào Xuān was imprisoned in the court,
Wáng Xián raised a banner at the Imperial Academy, saying:
"Those who wish to save Commissioner Bào, gather here."
Over a thousand scholars assembled,
blocking Chancellor Kǒng Guāng's carriage,
preventing it from moving,
and Bào's sentence was reduced by one degree from death.
． _Western Hàn Main Biography_,
cross-referenced in "Admiration".
A diviner reading auras

Guō Rǎng went to the commandery prison at night,
but Bǐng Jí barred the door against the envoy,
refusing entry,
saying:
"Even if the imperial great-grandson were an innocent commoner,

let alone the direct great-grandson?"
They held their ground until dawn,
and he could not enter.
． _Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Emperor Xuān of Hàn Annals_.
Protecting each other in times of urgency.
． _Book of Hàn, Empress Xǔ of Emperor Xuān_.
Hé Yǒng and Yuán Shào were close friends in flight,

seeking rescue and strategies for renowned scholars implicated in factional disputes,
enabling them to escape and hide,
thus saving many.
． _Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Emperor Líng of Hàn Annals_.
Initially, Cài Yōng had a grudge against Yáng Qiú, the Minister of Works.
Qiú was the son-in-law of the eunuch Chéng Huáng,
and had someone swiftly submit a memorial accusing Yōng,
leading to his imprisonment in Luòyáng,
charged with "harboring resentment against public duty,
plotting harm to high officials,
disloyalty and disrespect,
punishable by public execution."
When the case was reported,
the eunuch Lǚ Qiáng of Hénán, pitying Yōng's innocence,
strongly pleaded for him.
Yáng Qiú sent assassins to waylay and kill Yōng,
but the assassins, moved by his righteousness,
all refused to act.
Qiú also bribed Yōng's jailer to poison him,
but the bribed man instead warned Yōng of the plot,
thus he was spared.
Ibid.
Zhào Qí fled from trouble,
selling cakes in Běihǎi.
Sūn Sōng saw Qí and took him in his carriage home,
hiding him in a double-walled room,
for several years.
． _Eastern Hàn Main Biography_.
Qiú Lǎn and others petitioned accusing Zhāng Jiǎn and twenty-four others from the same commandery of forming a faction,
so an arrest warrant was issued for Jiǎn.
Jiǎn, trapped and desperate, fled,
seeking refuge door to door,
and all who revered his reputation and conduct
risked their families to shelter him.
Those who harbored him faced severe punishment,
with dozens of clans exterminated,
and commanderies and counties devastated as a result.
． _Eastern Hàn Main Biography_.
Zhāng Jiǎn was resented by the eunuch Hóu Lǎn,
who issued a warrant for his arrest.
Jiǎn was acquainted with Kǒng Róng's elder brother Bāo,
and fled to him but did not find him,
so Róng said, "Though my brother is away,
can I not host you, my lord?"
Thus he took him in,
but later the matter was exposed, and Bāo was executed.
． _Eastern Hàn, Biography of Kǒng Róng_.
Wáng Xiáng gradually gained renown,
which his mother deeply resented,
secretly attempting to poison him.
His younger brother Lǎn found out,
directly rose to take the wine,
Xiáng struggled to stop him, but he wouldn't yield,
and their mother quickly snatched it back.
After that,
whenever their mother gave Xiáng food,
Lǎn would always taste it first.
． _Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Emperor Yuán of Wèi Annals_.
Cross-referenced in "Brothers".
Lǐ Jǐngzhuāng grew old in the examination halls,
often failing,
and his mother would beat Jǐngràng
(Jǐngzhuāng's elder brother).
The prime minister told the examiner: "This year, Lǐ Jǐngzhuāng must be accepted;
pity the old man who gets beaten every year!"

An edict stated: "Wáng Yǎn's entire group shall be executed."
The Privy Councilor Zhāng Jūhàn wiped the character "group" from the palace pillar and changed it to "family."
． _Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Emperor Míngzōng of Táng Annals_.

Huáng Bà was governor of Yǐngchuān.

Public statement.
In ancient times, when ministers were dismissed for lack of integrity,
it was not called lack of integrity,
but "unadorned sacrificial vessels";
when dismissed for lewd and promiscuous behavior without distinction between men and women,
it was not called lewdness,
but "untidy curtains and screens";
when dismissed for weakness and incompetence,
it was not called weakness,
but "subordinates not fulfilling their duties".
Thus, even when high ministers were confirmed guilty,
they were not directly and openly denounced,
but rather, circumlocution was used to cover for them.
Therefore, those in the realm of major condemnation and inquiry,
upon hearing the condemnation, would don a white hat with yak-tail tassels,
carry a tray of water with a sword on it,
and go to the petition room to request punishment.
The emperor would not have them bound and dragged away.
Those with moderate offenses,
upon hearing the order, would discipline themselves,
and the emperor would not have someone...
and impose it.
When someone has committed a grave offense,
upon hearing the command, they face north and bow twice,
then kneel and take their own life,
so the ruler does not have to drag and punish them.
It is said: "You, the great officer, have your own faults,
but I have treated you with courtesy."
From "The Biography of Jiǎ Yì,"
also in "History of the Western Hàn."
