cultivating demeanor in the garden of rites,
soaring in the orchard of documents.
Xīhàn Sīmǎ Xiàngrú Zhuàn.
Learning's influence on people
surpasses that of vermilion and azure.
I have seen vermilion and azure fade over time,
but never seen prolonged learning fade.
Jìn Yú Pǔ Zhuàn.
It molds the spirit and disposition,
enlightens the ears and eyes.
Běishǐ Wèi Cháng Shuàng Zhuàn.
Zhòngní accumulated learning to become a sage.
Tángshū Dòu Wēi Zhuàn.
Biographies
Learning is like planting trees:
in spring, enjoy their blossoms;
in autumn, reap their fruits.
Explaining texts and writings
is the blossom of spring.
Cultivating oneself and benefiting conduct
is the fruit of autumn.
Yánshì Jiāxùn.
Collections
Feasting in the groves and marshes of benevolence and righteousness.
Bān Gù "Diǎnyǐn".
Ingesting the ancient and containing the modern,
without beginning or end.
Huángfǔ Shí composed "Hán Yù Mùzhì".
Endowed with natural innate wisdom,
his learning stood above Yóu and Xià.
Dù Shī.
Immersing deeply in the meaning of teachings,
repeating sentence structures,
polishing one's endeavors,
and exerting vigor in literary works.
Hán Wén.
The reason humans can be human
is because their minds hold the Shī and Shū.
Hán Wén.
Learning stored within oneself,
remains abundant as long as one lives.
Same as above.
Classics
The noble person strives tirelessly for self-improvement.
Yì Qián Guà.
Cross-reference "Effort".
The noble person advances virtue and cultivates work,
desiring to seize the timely moment.
Same as above.
Only by learning with a humble mind,
diligently and promptly attentive,
will cultivation come.
Thinking constantly of learning from start to finish,
one's virtue improves unconsciously.
Shū Yuè Mìng Xià.
Daily diligence,
daring not to indulge in ease.
Jūn Chén.
Strengthening learning day and night to await questions.
Jì Rú Xíng.
If there is something not learned,
learn it without stopping until mastered;
if there is something not asked,
ask without stopping until understood;
if there is something not debated,
debate without stopping until clear;
if there is something not practiced,
practice without stopping until steadfast.
Zhōngyōng.
If others succeed with one effort,
I use a hundred;
if others succeed with ten efforts, I use a thousand.
If one truly follows this path,
even the dull will become wise,
even the weak will become strong.
Same as above.
That refined noble person,
like cutting and filing,
like carving and polishing.
Shī Qí Ào.
Daily progress and monthly advancement.
Jìng Zhī.
To learn and timely practice it,
is that not a pleasure?
Yǔ Xué Ér.
The Master said: "I have tried not eating all day,
not sleeping all night,
to think,
but it was of no benefit.
It is not as good as learning.
Learning is like chasing what you cannot catch,
yet fearing to lose it."
Tàibó.
I see him advance,
but never see him stop.
Zǐ Hǎn.
Daily knowing what he lacks,
monthly not forgetting what he can.
Zǐ Zhāng.
Broad learning and steadfast will,
earnest questioning and close reflection.
Same as above.
Masters
Flowing water does not stagnate,
because it moves;
a door pivot does not get worm-eaten,
because it turns.
Zǐ Huá Zǐ.
A spring's water gushes forth,
never ceasing day or night,
filling the hollows before advancing,
until it reaches the four seas.
Mèng Lílóu Xià.
When concentration is undivided,
it becomes focused like spirit.
Lièzǐ Huángdì.
Many loved writing,
but only Cāngjié is remembered, due to singularity;
many loved farming,
but only Hòujì is remembered, due to singularity;
many loved music,
but only Kuí is remembered, due to singularity.
Chuí made the bow,
Fú Yóu made arrows,
and Yì excelled in archery;
Xī Zhòng made carts,
Chéng Dù invented horse riding,
and Zàofǔ excelled in driving.
The world has never seen duality achieve excellence.
Xún Jiě Bì.
The noble person strengthens learning and practices diligently.
Yángzǐ Xiūshēn.
Oh time,
time!
Why do you come so slowly,
yet depart so swiftly?
The noble person races against it.
Yáng Wèn Míng.
The supremely sage Zhōu Gōng read a hundred chapters daily;
the heaven-endowed Zhòngní wore out the leather bindings thrice;
the great worthy Mò Dí filled carts with writings;
the era-defining Zhòng Shū never glanced at gardens.
Ní Kuān carried classics while weeding;
Lù Shēng cut cattails to write on;
Huáng Bà studied while in fetters;
Nìng Zǐ doubled efforts day and night.
Bàopǔzǐ.
Hearing what one has not heard,
seeing what one has not seen.
Yángzǐ.
Even at his end, Xuānní never let go of scrolls;
nearing death, Zhòng Shū never ceased reciting;
Yǒuzǐ, hating to doze, seared his own palm;
Sū Shēng, troubled by sleep, personally pricked his thigh.
With the nature of sages and worthies,
they still loved learning untiringly.
Liú Zǐ.
The heart as if intoxicated by the Six Classics.
Wénzhōng Zǐ.
Histories
. In his later years, Confucius delighted in the "Yì Jīng," composing the "Tuàn," "Xì," "Xiàng," "Shuō Guà," and "Wén Yán."
He read the "Yì Jīng"
so intensively that the leather thongs binding the bamboo strips broke three times,
and said, "If I were granted a few more years,
like this,
I would be thoroughly versed in the 'Yì Jīng'."
. From "Shǐ Kǒngzǐ Shìjiā."
Dǒng Zhòngshū immersed himself in study, lowering his curtain to read,
not glancing at the garden for ten years,
such was his dedication.
. From "Qián Hàn Běnzhuàn."
Ní Kuān carried the classics while hoeing.
Same as above.
Diligently, ceaselessly, day and night.
. From "Qián Hàn Zhāng Chǎng Zhuàn."
Delving into texts and records,
to illuminate his own person.
. From "Xī Hàn Bān Gù Xùzhuàn."
Pillowing on the classics and resting on books.
. From "Xī Hàn Bīn Xì."
Liú Xiàng devoted his thoughts to the classics, reciting by day and reading commentaries,
observing the stars by night,
sometimes staying awake until dawn.
. From "Xī Hàn Běnzhuàn."
Róng studied in Cháng'ān,
with unflagging energy,
not returning home for fifteen years.
. From "Hòu Hàn Gèn Róng Zhuàn."
On New Year's Day, after Emperor Guāngwǔ's court congratulations ended,
he ordered officials who could discuss the classics to debate their meanings,
and if anyone failed to respond,
their mat was taken away.
Dài Píng thus accumulated fifty layers of mats.
Hence, the capital said of him, "The inexhaustible interpreter of classics, Attendant Dài."
From "Hòu Hàn."
Closing his door to lecture and recite,
cutting off worldly affairs.
. From "Dōng Hàn Gěng Gōng Zhuàn."
At dawn, combing his hair,
he sat in the guest hall.
In the morning, he recited the Yì of Fú Xī and King Wén, the books of Yú and Xià,
went through the rituals of Duke Zhōu,
perused the Spring and Autumn Annals of Confucius;
in the evening, he wandered the inner steps,
chanting the "Shī Jīng" by the southern window,
with the hundred schools and various scholars,
seizing moments to produce works, abundantly filling his ears,
brilliantly overflowing his eyes,
joyfully and busily, how he delighted alone!
At such times,
he did not know the sky as a canopy,
nor the earth as a carriage;
he did not know there were others in the world,
nor that he himself had a body.
. From "Dōng Hàn Yán Dǔ Zhuàn."
Lǐ Gù,
son of Lǐ Hé,
loved learning from youth,
often changing his name,
wielding a staff to drive a donkey,
carrying books on his back to follow teachers,
not minding the thousand miles.
Thus, he thoroughly studied ancient texts,
becoming a great Confucian of his time.
Whenever he went to the Imperial Academy,
he secretly entered the official residence to check on his parents,
not letting his fellow students know he was Hé's son.
. From "Tōngjiàn Hàn Ān Jì."
Huángfǔ Mì indulged in the classics,
forgetting sleep and food,
so people of his time called him a book addict.
. From "Jìn Shū Běnzhuàn."
Chē Yìn's household often lacked oil,
so in summer, he filled a sack with dozens of fireflies to read by,
continuing day into night.
From "Jìn Shū."
Zuǒ Sī focused solely on composing the "Sān Dū Fù,"
cutting off all social interactions.
Dù Yù was engrossed in the classics,
compiling a commentary on the "Spring and Autumn Annals and Zuǒ's Commentary,"
claiming to have an obsession with the Zuǒ Commentary.
Same as above.
Jiāng Mì read by the moonlight,
climbing onto the roof with his scroll when it slanted.
From "Nán Shǐ."
Lǐ Xuàn, due to scarce literary collections in his hometown,
traveled to the capital,
to read books he had never seen.
. From "Běi Shǐ Běnzhuàn."
Lǐ Yōng said he hadn't read all books,
wishing to see the secret collections.
Lǐ Qiáo remarked,
"The secret archives hold ten thousand volumes;
how can one master them in a short time?"
Yōng insisted,
and was temporarily assigned to the secretariat.
From "Táng Shū."
Dù Yòu was addicted to learning,
and though noble,
still read late into the night.
Liǔ Zhòngyǐng loved learning,
once taking bear gallbladder pills at night to stay diligent.
Same as above.
Lù Guīméng studied diligently,
never letting the scroll leave his hand.
. From "Xīn Táng Shū Běnzhuàn."
Biographies
Chǔ Táo was calm and quiet,
amusing himself with ancient texts.
He told his close ones,
"The sages and worthies are all in these yellow scrolls;
what else should one seek beyond this?"
From an annotation in "Shì Shuō."
A good learner is like the King of Qí eating chicken,
he must eat the feet,
consuming thousands before being satisfied.
From "Lǚ Shì Chūnqiū."
Sūn Kāng's family was poor and had no oil,
so he read by the light of snow.
From "Sūn Shì Shìlù."
Lǐ Pín said,
"With just five-character verses,
I'll exhaust a lifetime's heart."
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Cross-referenced in the "Poetry" section.
While Liú Xiàng was collating texts in the Tiānlù Pavilion,
an old man in yellow clothes appeared at night,
holding a green staff,
and taught Xiàng the "Hóng Fàn" from the Five Elements,
saying, "I am the essence of Tàiyǐ;
the Heavenly Emperor heard that among the descendants of Jīnmǎo,
there is a profound scholar,
so I descended to observe."
From Jìn Wáng Jiā's "Shí Yí Zhuàn."
Kāng Héng studied diligently without a candle;
his neighbor had one,
so he bored a hole to borrow its light for reading.
From "Xī Jīng Zá Jì."
Guǎn Níng lived in seclusion, fond of learning,
with his rush bed half worn through.
From "Gāo Shì Zhuàn."
Zhāng Yí and Sū Qín worked as scribes;
when encountering sage writings,
if they had no means to record,
they wrote with ink on their palms and thighs,
and at night,
split bamboo to transcribe them.
From "Wáng Zǐ Shí Yí."
Yīn Liàng,
during the Jiànwǔ era, served as a court scholar,
and in debates among Confucians, the winner was given a mat;
Liàng accumulated eight or nine layers.
The Emperor said, "Shouldn't learning be like this?"
From "Yīn Shì Shì Zhuàn."
Collection
Reciting the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents,
and the words of the hundred schools of thought.
Lips worn and teeth falling out,
yet holding them close to the heart without letting go.
． From "Dōngfāng Shuò's Reply to a Guest's Challenge" in the Selections.
Gathering fireflies and reflecting on snow,
weaving reeds and binding willows.
． From the "Recommendation Memorial" in the Selections.
Plowing with the brush to make a living.
From the "Selections" memorial.
Writing brushes worn out from a thousand hares,
poems composed as thick as two oxen's waists.
From the Collected Works of Lǐ Tàibái.
Dying with white hair over verses and lines.
Same as above.
Galloping through the forest of books in the morning,
soaring in the garden of arts in the evening.
From Hán Yù's "Rhapsody on Restoring Ambition".
Cross-reference to "never forgetting goodness for a moment".
Never ceasing to chant the texts of the six arts;
never stopping to peruse the compiled works of the hundred schools.
For records of events, one must extract their essentials;
for compiled sayings, one must probe their profundities.
Greedy for more and striving to gain,
neglecting nothing big or small.
Burning oil to extend the daylight,
often toiling tirelessly throughout the year.
From Hán Yù's writings.
Mending gaps and plugging leaks,
illuminating the obscure and subtle.
Searching for the vast, lost threads,
alone, delving widely and connecting to the distant past.
Ancient histories scattered left and right,
the Book of Songs and Documents placed before and after.
How different from a bookworm,
living and dying among words.
All from the same source as above.
Even in daily life, never parting with books, whether eating or sleeping,
using them as a pillow when tired,
savoring them like food to delight the palate.
From the epitaph for Hán Wéngōng.
Aiming ambitions in the forest of books,
savoring the Airs of the States and the Sao in the Seven Summaries;
cultivating the garden of emotions and righteousness,
resting among the texts of the nine schools of thought.
From Luò Bīnwáng.
Repeatedly adding orchid-scented oil to the lamp,
still grinding ink with a rabbit-hair brush.
From the Collected Works of Yuán Zhěn.
Indulging in literary works,
focusing on diligent study.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
Studying deeply and researching thoroughly,
almost to the point of not peering beyond the garden well.
From the Collected Works of Yuán Wēizhī.
Opening a book and gaining insight,
then joyfully forgetting to eat.
From the Collected Works of Táo Yuānmíng.
Taking the Way as drink,
and literature as food.
From the Collected Works of Pí Rìxiū.
Intelligent and fond of learning,
unwilling to be an ordinary person.
From Liú Yǔxī.
Penetrating to the bone of scholarship.
From the Essence of Tang Literature.
Even after retiring from public duties, still plowing with the brush.
From Liú Yǔxī.
Reading until the eyes grow dim,
holding the brush until calluses form on the hands.
From Bái Jūyì.
Yáo and Shùn emaciated,
Dà Yǔ with calloused hands and feet,
they were sages.
I am but a commoner,
if not diligent,
how can I be the support for my wife and children?
From Lù Guīméng.
Like waves flowing into rivers,
and rivers pouring into the sea,
day and night, never knowing when to rest.
From the Essence of Tang Literature.
In our dynasty,
in farming and horse wisdom, I yield to none.
From Hòushān's "Poem Sent to Dù Shìzhī".
The poet's thoughts are bitter, his frame gaunt.
From the Collected Works of Sū Zhé.
Heaven moves daily,
hence it is vigorous;
the sun and moon travel daily,
hence they are bright;
water flows daily,
hence it never exhausts;
human limbs move daily,
hence they remain free of illness;
tools are used daily,
hence they do not decay.
From the Collected Works of Sū Shì.
Still engaged in the pure task of reading,
never letting spring sleep rival a thousand cups.
From Sū Shì's poetry.
Xú Xuàn demoted to Bīnzhōu,
at seventy years old,
never let go of his books.
Often personally wrote in clerical script,
copying one volume of Xǔ Shèn's "Shuōwén Jiězì".
From "Anecdotes from the Sacred Song Dynasty".
Classic:
Not learning is like facing a wall.
． From the "Zhōu Guān" chapter of the Book of Documents.
Even if there is the ultimate Way,
without learning it,
one cannot know its goodness.
． From the "Record of Learning" in the Book of Rites.
Jade uncut
does not become a vessel;
a person without learning
does not understand the Way.
From the "Record of Learning".
Cross-reference to "correction and refinement".
If a person does not study the "Zhōu Nán" and "Shào Nán",
is it not like standing facing a wall?
． From the Analects, "Yáng Huò" chapter.
The Master said: "When an ignorant person asked me,
I was completely empty."
From "Zǐ Hǎn" chapter.
Struggling yet not learning,
such people are the lowest.
From "Jì Shì" chapter.
The Master said: "Loving benevolence
without loving learning
leads to the flaw of foolishness;
loving wisdom
without loving learning
leads to the flaw of aimlessness;
loving trustworthiness
without loving learning
leads to the flaw of harm;
loving straightforwardness
without loving learning
leads to the flaw of harshness;
loving courage
without loving learning
leads to the flaw of disorder;
loving firmness
without loving learning
leads to the flaw of arrogance."
The Master's disciple
Bǔ Shāng returned to Wèi,
and saw someone reading a historical record,
who said: "The Jìn army attacked Qín,
three pigs crossed the river."
Zǐxià said:
"That's not right!
It was the jǐhài day."
The reader asked the Jìn historian,
who indeed said: "Jǐhài."
Thus, Wèi regarded Zǐxià as a sage.
． From the "Seventy-Two Disciples" chapter of the Family Sayings of Confucius.
If a person does not learn,
even without worries,
how are they different from birds and beasts?
． From Yáng Xióng's "Conduct of Learning".
All shallow individuals,
hollow and empty,
resemble the parable of the Shǔ people's gourd pot.
With not a single sheet of knowledge in their chest,
only concerned with wine and roast meat.
What is called coveting goods and bribes, greedy for food and drink, the worthless sons recorded in the Zuǒzhuàn.
From the Master Who Embraces Simplicity.
Cross-reference to "worthlessness".
History
Zhōu Yuán Bólǔ took no pleasure in learning,
Mǐn Zǐmǎ said:
"Learning is like cultivation;
without it, one will decline.
Is the Yuán family heading toward ruin!"
From "Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāogōng 18th Year."
Cross-reference "What the discerning perceive."
Fàn Xiànzǐ was on a diplomatic mission to Lǔ,
and asked about Jù Mountain and Áo Mountain.
The people of Lǔ answered with their local names.
Xiànzǐ said,
"Aren't they called Jù and Áo?"
They replied,
"Those are the taboo names of former lords Xiàn and Wǔ."
Xiànzǐ returned and said,
"I mentioned two taboos by name—
I've become a laughingstock,
all for lacking learning."
From "Guóyǔ."
Cross-reference "Clear about self-awareness."
The Qín official reported that the planet Tàibái (Venus) was punishing the star Jǐng in the Eastern Well constellation,
indicating that the Qín region would surely see violent soldiers rise in the capital.
The Qín ruler Fú Shēng said,
"Tàibái entering the Well—
it's just thirsty,
what's strange about that?"
From "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Jìn Annals."
Jiāngzhōu Governor Chén Bózhī,
illiterate,
upon receiving documents and lawsuits,
could only make grand gestures of assent.
From "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Vol. 145, Liáng Gāozǔ."
Northern Qí's Yuán Shī,
acting head of the Ministry of Sacrifices,
once reported to Gāo Ēnàgōng:
"The dragon has appeared; it's time for the rain sacrifice."
Ēnàgōng exclaimed in surprise,
"Where has a dragon appeared?
What color is it?"
Shī said,
"The dragon star has first appeared;
by ritual, we should hold the rain sacrifice,
it's not a real dragon."
Ēnàgōng angrily said,
"You Hàn people are meddlesome,
forcing knowledge of the stars."
Thus, no sacrifice was held.
From "Chén Annals."
Also seen in "Sānguó Diǎnlüè."
Sixty-four candidates were selected for official ranks,
and the emperor summoned them for a face-to-face examination.
Zhāng Shì held the paper
but failed to write a single character all day,
leading contemporaries to call it "dragging blank."
From "Táng Xuánzōng Annals."
Guāng was unlearned and lacking in skill.
From "Xīhàn Huò Guāng Biography."
To live in the world without learning
is like dwelling in a cave—
what can one possibly see?
From "Běishǐ Léi Shào Biography."
Ministry of Revenue Vice-Minister Xiāo Jiǒng misread "zhēng cháng fú là" as "fú liè,"
and Yán Tǐngzhī reported to Zhāng Jiǔlíng, saying,
"Can the ministry have a 'hunting' vice-minister?"
From "Táng Yán Jùn Biography."
"Zīzhì Tōngjiàn" records.
Lǐ Línfǔ had no scholarly learning;
once, a candidate Yán Jiǒng used the characters "dì" and "dù" in his judgment,
which Línfǔ did not recognize.
He asked the Vice-Minister of Personnel Wéi Zhì,
"What does this 'zhuàng' and 'dù' mean?"
Zhì bowed his head, not daring to speak.
From "Tángshū."
Zāng Xīràng had no scholarly learning;
among the nobility, he forcibly cited ancient sayings to appear virtuous,
but what he knew was mostly picked up from hearsay,
and when he spoke, it was full of errors,
laughed at by scholars.
Same as above.
Rèn Huán said,
"Everyone knows Cuī Xié cannot read characters,
yet he holds an empty reputation
as a 'wordless stele.'"
From "Wǔdài Shǐ Rèn Huán Biography."
Biographies
Hán Chǎng,
son of Hán Tuìzhī,
was dull and incompetent.
As a collator in the Jíxián Academy, he encountered "gold-root carriage" in historical texts,
and mistakenly
changed all "root" characters to "silver."
From "Shàngshū Gùshí."
Cross-reference "Unable to inherit."
Huò Guāng had no learning,
not knowing a single classic.
From "Shǐ Tōng."
During Emperor Huán's time, someone appointed to a government office
hired another to write his memorials.
From Hándān's "Xiàolín."
Cross-reference "Ghostwriting."
Zhāng Yóugǔ had no scholarly training;
he lamented in public that Bān Gù's writings were not included in the "Wénxuǎn,"
to which the crowd pointed out "Liǎngdū Fù" and "Yānrán Míng."
Yóugǔ said,
"That's by Bān Mèngjiān,
not Gù."
From Táng Wēn Tíngyún's "Gànmìan Zǐ."
Lǐ Jiànxún, as chancellor of Jiāngnán,
was stationed in Yùzhāng.
One day, while touring the Western Hills,
he saw an old man in a thatched hut teaching village children.
The lord drank at his cottage
and ate several pears in a row.
A guest remarked,
"Pears are called the 'five viscera's axe'—
they shouldn't be eaten in excess."
The old man laughed and said,
"The 'Hèguànzǐ' says 'five viscera,'
using the character for 'parting,' not 'pear.'
It means parting from one's chest feelings
feels like an axe."
He then took a small book from the shelf,
dusted it off, and presented it to the chancellor—
it was the "Hèguànzǐ."
From Wú monk Wén Yǐng's "Xiāngshān Yělù."
In Jiāngnán, there was a powerful noble
who read a corrupted version of the "Shūdū Fù,"
where the annotation "dūn chī means taro" was mistaken for "sheep."
When someone sent him mutton,
he replied in a letter,
"Thank you for the gift of dūn chī."
From Northern Qí's Vice-Minister of the Imperial Secretariat Yán Zhītuī's "Yánshì Jiāxùn."
This dynasty:
Court Minister of Ceremonies Jiāng Dù had a son,
and Lǐ Línfǔ wrote a congratulatory note,
saying, "I hear you have the joy of 'playing with the deer.'"
Guests saw it and covered their mouths in laughter.
From "Xù Shì Shuō."
Classics:
The noble person strives tirelessly to strengthen themselves.
From "Yìjīng, Qián Guà."
High achievement comes only from ambition,
and broad accomplishment only from diligence.
From "Shūjīng, Zhōuguān."
If there is something lacking,
one dares not fail to exert effort.
From "Lǐjì, Zhōngyōng."
If learning it doesn't lead to ability,
or asking doesn't bring understanding,
or thinking doesn't yield results,
or discerning doesn't bring clarity,
or practicing it isn't steadfast,
one does not stop.
If others manage with one effort,
I'll use a hundred;
if others need ten,
I'll use a thousand.
If one can truly follow this path,
even the foolish will become wise,
and the weak will become strong.
Same as above.
Philosophers:
If one borrows something long without returning it,
how can we know it wasn't originally theirs?
From "Mèngzǐ."
Practice earnestness strenuously,
and nothing is closer to benevolence.
From "Jìnxīn Shàng."
Though the path may be near,
without walking, it won't be reached;
though the task may be small,
without doing, it won't be accomplished.
From "Xúnzǐ, Xiūshēn."
Carve without ceasing,
and even metal and stone can be engraved.
From "Xúnzǐ, Quànxué."
History:
Zǐshùn said,
"Everyone acts;
if one acts without stopping,
they become a noble person.
If acting without change,
habit and nature form as one,
then it becomes natural."
From "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn."
Strive diligently in learning,
and one's knowledge will broaden,
wisdom grow clearer;
strive diligently in practicing the Way,
and virtue will daily rise,
achieving great merit.
From "Xīhàn Dǒng Zhòngshū Biography."
Biographies:
Whip the jade and grind the blunt.
Chén Zǐ'áng.
Grind lead and re-sharpen,
Whip the lame and race again.
Bái Shìláng.
It is not like the foot of Mount Tài Shān,
Where one stops and cannot ascend,
But rather like a river that never ceases to flow!
Liǔ Wén.
Classic
The lazy farmer seeks ease,
Not toiling diligently,
Not tending the fields,
Thus failing his duties,
And reaping no millet or grain.
． "Shū Pán Gēng".
The nature of the average person is to love comfort and pleasure.
Annotation to "Wú Yì".
If one does not act,
How can one achieve?
"Tài Jiǎ Xià".
Indulging in ease,
One degenerates daily.
． "Jì Biǎo Jì".
Comfort and pleasure know no bounds.
． "Shī Bái Jū".
The Master said: "Not cultivating virtue,
Not discussing learning,
Hearing what is right but not following it,
Failing to correct one's faults."
． "Yǔ Shù Ér".
Rǎn Qiú said: "It is not that I do not delight in your Way,
But my strength is insufficient."
"Yōng Yě".
To eat one's fill all day,
Without applying one's mind to anything—
How difficult it is!
"Yáng Huò".
To gather all day,
Speaking without touching upon righteousness.
"Wèi Líng Gōng".
A scholar who clings to comfort
Is not worthy of being called a scholar.
"Xiàn Wèn".
Master
Zǐgòng said: "I am weary of learning,
Perplexed by the Way,
May I rest for a while?"
"Jiā Yǔ".
One who lives in constant ease
Will not have broad aspirations.
Ibid.
Advancing and retreating alternately,
Even six fine steeds cannot reach the destination.
． "Xúnzǐ Xiū Shēn".
As for a person,
One with many idle days
Will not go far in or out.
Lazy, cowardly, and shirking duties,
Without shame yet craving food and drink,
Such a one may be called a vile youth.
Both from the same text.
Rotted flesh breeds worms,
Dried fish gives rise to moths.
Negligence and laziness make one forget oneself,
Then disasters arise.
"Qín Xué".
History
Comfort and ease
Truly ruin one's reputation.
． "Zuǒ Xī Èrshísān".
Guǎn Jìngzhòng said: "Ease and pleasure are like poisoned wine,
Not to be cherished."
． "Zuǒ Mǐn Yuán".
We, common folk, live carelessly,
Not planning beyond the morning for the evening.
． "Zuǒ Zhāo Yuán".
Governing the people,
Wasting years and idling away days.
"Zhāo Yuán".
Idle,
Pronounced kǔ gài qiē.
Sparrows and rats cling greedily to life,
Merely begging to survive.
． "Tōng Jiàn Bāshíyī Dōng Hàn Shì Zǔ Jì".
Gathering together to live on heedlessly,
Like fish swimming in a cauldron,
Knowing it cannot last long,
And only gasping for a moment's breath.

The lazy cannot cultivate themselves.
Hán Wén "Yuán Huǐ".
Our Dynasty
Sitting and wasting time.
Línchuān.
Brush and inkstone gather dust, idling away the days.
"Luán Chéng Jí".
Classic
The noble person is harmonious but not conformist,
That is strength;
Firmly neutral and unbiased,
That is strength;
When the state has the Way,
Remaining unchanged in adversity,
That is strength;
When the state is without the Way,
Remaining unchanged until death,
That is true strength!
． "Jì Zhōng Yōng".
Jade uncut
Does not become a vessel;
A person who does not learn
Does not understand the Way.
"Xué Jì".
Cross-reference to "Not Learning".
Master
Zǐlù said: "The bamboo on the southern mountain,
uncarved yet naturally straight,
when cut and used,
pierces through rhinoceros hide.
From this perspective,
what need is there for learning?"
Confucius replied:
"If feathered with arrows,
and sharpened on a whetstone,
would its penetration not be deeper?"
． From "The Family Sayings: Zǐlù Chapter".
If uncut jade remains intact,
who would make sacrificial vessels?
If white jade is unpolished,
who would create guī and zhāng tablets?
． From "Zhuangzi: Horses' Hooves".
Jì Shěngzǐ was raising fighting cocks for King Xuān of Qí,
After ten days,
he was asked: "Are the cocks ready?"
He said: "Not yet.
They're still vainly arrogant and rely on spirit."
After ten more days,
he was asked again,
and said:
"Not yet,
they still respond to echoes and shadows."
After another ten days he was asked,
and said:
"Not yet,
they still glare fiercely and are full of vigor."
After ten more days,
he was asked again,
and said:
"Almost there.
Though other cocks may crow,
they remain unchanged,
looking like wooden cocks,
their virtue complete."
． From "Zhuangzi: Mastering Life".
Xīmén Bào had an impatient nature,
so he wore soft leather to remind himself to be calm;
Dǒng Ānyú had a sluggish nature,
so he wore a taut string to urge himself to haste.
From Hánfēizǐ.
Wood straight as a plumb line,
bent into a wheel,
its curve matches compasses;
even when dried,
it won't straighten again,
bending made it so.
． From "Xúnzǐ: Exhortation to Learning".
Warped wood must be straightened with tools,
then it becomes straight;
metal must be ground and sharpened,
then it becomes sharp.
． From "Xúnzǐ: Human Nature is Evil".
Jade uncarved,
yúfán gems don't become vessels.
From Yángzǐ.
Sea oysters unopened,
then bright pearls don't appear;
Kūnlún bamboo uncut,
then phoenix notes don't sound.
From Wénzǐ.
Wú bows naturally strong,
but without arrow feathers, not used for hunting;
Yuè swords naturally sharp,
but unsharpened, not keen.
Ibid.
Wait for arrows that straighten themselves,
then for generations not one arrow;
await wood that rounds itself,
then for millennia not one wheel.
From Hánfēizǐ.
Borrowing scholar's robes and books,
wearing them and reading,
for three months not returning them,
who says he's not a scholar?
From Yángzǐ.
History
Tigers, leopards, horses, oxen,
beasts that cannot be tamed,
yet when trained and accustomed,
can be led, ridden, and harnessed,
obeying only humans.
． From "Western Hàn: Gōngsūn Hóng's Biography".
The way to cultivate nature:
examine what you have in excess,
and strengthen what you lack: the intelligent and perceptive
guard against being too sharp;
the poorly informed and inexperienced
guard against being blocked;
the brave and strong
guard against being too violent;
the kind and gentle
guard against indecision;
the calm and relaxed
guard against delay;
the broad-minded and ambitious
guard against forgetfulness.
From "Kǒnguāng's Biography".
Gold in the mine,
what value has it?
Well smelted and forged into vessels,
people then treasure it.
． From "Táng History: Wèi Zhēng's Biography".
See also "Selection and Promotion".
Collection
Shaving square to make round.
From "Chǔcí".
Like metal whetted on stone,
like clay on the potter's wheel.
From Zhāng Màoxiān's "Poem Encouraging Ambition".
Wood straightens by the line,
metal hardens by quenching,
must be ground and whetted,
to achieve sharp edges.
From Cài Yōng's "Exhortation to Learning".
Without vermilion and blue,
how change plain silk's nature?
From Jìn Wáng Jiǎn's memorial.
Wood's nature is straight, yet craftsmen
bend it into wheels;
metal's nature is hard,
yet workers shape it into vessels.
Is this human effort?
Only the supremely wise and foolish
inherit unique qualities;
those of average talent
depend entirely on training.
From Yú Shìnán's "Essay on Noble Sons".
Strictly discipline conduct,
as if obeying Shāng Yāng's laws,
fearing Qín's punishments.
From Huángfǔ Shí.
Our Dynasty
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng, naturally fierce,
brave to the point of disregarding kin,
yet could revere righteousness, love worthies,
humble himself to accept advice,
rigorously reform himself,
striving to do good.
This is how he achieved the Zhènguān era's governance.
From Fàn's "Táng Mirror".
Classics
The gentleman extensively learns from past words and deeds.
． From "Yìjīng: Great Accumulation".
Loving antiquity,
erudite and refined gentlemen.
． From "Shūjīng Preface".
The gentleman's learning is broad.
A scholar is broadly learned without limit.
． From "Lǐjì: Conduct of Scholars".
Broad learning without fixed method.
． From "Records: Domestic Rules".
How great!
Confucius's broad learning,
yet without specializing in fame.
From "Analects".
Masters
Extensive hearing is called erudition,
extensive seeing is called familiarity.
． From "Xúnzǐ: Cultivating Character".
Broad learning and detailed explanation.
From "Mèngzǐ".
History
Zǐchǎn of the state of Zhèng paid a diplomatic visit to Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn was ill,
and Hán Xuānzǐ said: "Our sovereign has been bedridden with illness,
for three months now.
Recently he dreamed of a yellow bear entering the chamber door.
What vengeful spirit could this be?"
Zǐchǎn replied: "Long ago, Yáo executed Gǔn at Yǔshān,
and his spirit transformed into a yellow bear,
which entered the Yuān of Yǔ.
He is in fact honored in the Xià dynasty's suburban sacrifices,
and was worshipped throughout the three dynasties.
Since Jìn is the leader of the alliance,
perhaps you have not sacrificed to him."
Hán Xuānzǐ then performed the Xià suburban sacrifice,
and the Marquis of Jìn recovered.
(From the Zuǒ Zhuàn)
The wife of Duke Dào of Jìn provided food to the laborers building the wall for Qǐ.
An elderly man from Jiàng County,
who had no sons and had gone
to partake of the food.
Someone doubted his age,
so they asked him his age.
He said: "I am but a humble man,
and do not know how to count years.
In the year I was born,
the first month began on a jiǎzǐ day.
Since then, 445 jiǎzǐ cycles have passed,
with the last cycle now one-third complete."
The officials hurried to ask at court,
and Shī Kuàng said: "That was the year when Lǔ's Shūzhòng Huìbó met Xì Chéngzǐ at Chéngkuāng,
seventy-three years ago."
Shǐ Zhào said: "The character 'hài' has two heads and six bodies,
with the lower two like the body,
this indicates the number of days."
Shì Wénbó said: "Then it is twenty-six thousand six hundred and sixty days."
Dù's commentary states: "The character 'hài' has two strokes above,
combined with three sixes as the body,
like the six on a counting rod."
Same as above.
Wú attacked Yuè,
destroyed Kuàijī,
and obtained a bone joint that filled a cart.
Wú sent an envoy to ask Zhòngní: "Which bone is the largest?"
Zhòngní said: "When Yǔ assembled his ministers at Mount Kuàijī,
Fángfēng shì arrived late,
so Yǔ executed and exposed his body.
His bone joint filled a cart,
this is the largest."
(From the Shǐjì)
A falcon fell on the courtyard of Chén and died,
pierced by an arrow of thorn wood,
with a stone arrowhead measuring one chǐ and eight cùn.
Duke Mǐn of Chén sent to ask Zhòngní,
who said: "This falcon has come from afar,
this is an arrow of Sùshèn.
Long ago, when King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
he opened routes to the various barbarian tribes,
ordering each to bring their local products as tribute.
Then Sùshèn offered arrows of thorn wood with stone arrowheads,
measuring one chǐ and eight cùn.
The former king gave them to his eldest daughter Dàjī,
who married Yú Húgōng and was enfeoffed in Chén."
They searched the old treasury,
and indeed found them.
Same as above.
Zhuāngzǐ in his studies,
left nothing unexamined.
(From the Shǐjì basic biography)
Master Chǔ loved reading unofficial histories and anecdotal works.
(From the Shǐjì Jījí biography)
Dōngfāng Shuò was extensively learned,
and studied unofficial works.
Suǒyǐn states: "Unofficial works are not limited to classics and histories,
but include biographies and miscellaneous texts."
(From the Shǐjì Jījí biography)
Tián Fén studied works like Pányú.
(From the basic biography)
Liú Xiàng and Yáng Xióng,
were profoundly learned across all texts.
(From the Western Hàn Simǎ Qiān praise)
Simǎ Qiān served as Grand Historian,
(pronounced chōu)
and compiled historical records from the stone chamber and metal chests.
(From the Tàishǐgōng zìxù)
His broad learning spanned widely,
connecting classics and commentaries,
ranging across ancient and modern times.
(Western Hàn)
Bān Gù's praise of Simǎ Qiān.
Men of extensive knowledge throughout the land.
(From the Western Hàn Rúcái biography)
Yán Shīgǔ said: "Men of broad learning."
Jǐng Dàchūn of the discordant Five Classics.
(From the Hòu Hàn)
Zhōu Jǔ was comprehensively learned,
revered by Confucian scholars,
and the capital praised him: "Zhōu Xuānguāng of the far-reaching Five Classics."
Immersed in ancient texts,
he became a Confucian literary forest.
(From the Hòu Hàn Cuī Shí biography)
Zhòngní considered it shameful not to know any single thing.
(From the Jìn Zhāng Héng biography)
The more one reads, the broader one's knowledge;
the more one studies, the greater one's learning.
Daily hearing what one has not heard before,
daily seeing what one has not seen before.
(From the Jìn Yú Pǔ biography)
When giant bones emerged in Wú,
a falcon gathered in Chén's courtyard,
a yellow bear entered a bedchamber,
and hài had two heads,
none but the comprehensively learned
could recognize their origins.
(From the Dōng Hàn Xiè Gāi biography)
Dù Yù of Jìn
was called "Armory" by court and commoners alike,
meaning he possessed knowledge of everything.
(From the Jìnshū basic biography)
Wáng Càn knew many things and had a strong memory,
when asked,
there was nothing he could not answer.
(From the Wèi Zhì)
Péi Wěi was learned and investigated antiquity,
and Zhōu Bì saw him and sighed: "Like the five weapons in an armory,
he is an outstanding talent of the time."
(From the Jìnshū Péi Wěi biography)
Xún Xù encountered a cowbell from Zhào merchants on the road,
recognized its sound,
and when in charge of music found the tones unregulated,
said: "If we obtain Zhào cowbells,
they will harmonize."
So he ordered all commanderies to send cowbells,
and indeed obtained harmonious ones.
Once, while seated with the emperor,
during a meal,
he told those present: "This was cooked with fatigued wood."
The emperor sent to ask the cook,
who confirmed they used old cartwheels,
and everyone admired his keen discernment.
(From the Jìnshū)
All the rare secrets under heaven,
and things scarce in the world,
were all in Zhāng Huá's possession,
thus he was comprehensively learned and well-informed,
unmatched in his time.
During Emperor Huì's reign,
someone obtained a three-zhàng-long bird feather,
and showed it to Huá.
Huá saw it and grew distressed,
saying: "This is called a sea duck's feather,
when it appears,
the world will fall into chaos."
Lù Jī once gave Huá some preserved fish,
with many guests present,
Huá opened the container,
and immediately said: "This is dragon meat."
The crowd did not believe him.
Huá said: "Try washing it with vinegar,
and something unusual will happen."
Soon, five-colored light arose.
Jī went back to ask the fish provider,
who indeed said they found a white fish under the garden's thatch pile,
of extraordinary substance and appearance,
made into exceptionally delicious preserved fish,
hence offered as a gift.
The armory was tightly sealed,
yet suddenly a pheasant crowed inside,
Huá said: "This must be a snake transformed into a pheasant."
Upon opening and inspection,
beside the pheasant lay a snakeskin.
When the Línpíng riverbank in Wú commandery collapsed,
a stone drum emerged,
but striking it produced no sound.
The emperor asked Huá about it,
who said: "Take tóng wood from Shǔ,
carve it into fish shape,
and striking it will produce sound."
Following his advice,
the sound indeed carried for several lǐ.
Earlier,
before Wú was destroyed,
purple energy often appeared between Dǒu and Niú constellations,
and Daoist practitioners all thought Wú was still strong,
not yet conquerable,
only Huá thought otherwise.
After Wú was pacified,
the purple energy grew brighter.
Huá heard that Léi Huàn of Yùzhāng excelled in astrological signs,
so invited Huàn to stay overnight,
dismissed others and said: "Let us study astronomy together,
to know future fortunes."
They then ascended a tower and gazed upward.
Huàn said: "I have observed this for long,
only between Dǒu and Niú
there is rather unusual energy."
Huá said: "What omen is this?"
Huàn said: "The essence of precious swords,
piercing up to the heavens."
Huà said:
"Your words are correct.
When I was young, a fortune-teller
said that after I turned sixty, I would hold one of the three highest offices,
and would obtain a precious sword to wear.
Could this prophecy be coming true?"
Then he asked: "In which commandery is it?"
Huàn said: "In Fēngchéng, Yùzhāng."
Huà said: "I wish to trouble you to serve as magistrate,
and secretly search for it together.
Is that acceptable?"
Huàn agreed.
Huà was overjoyed,
and immediately appointed Huàn as magistrate of Fēngchéng.
When Huàn arrived at the county,
he dug up the foundation of the prison building,
going four zhàng into the ground,
where he found a stone case,
radiating extraordinary light and energy.
Inside were a pair of swords with inscriptions,
one called 'Lóngquán',
the other 'Tài'ē'.
That night, between the constellations Dǒu and Niú,
the aura was no longer seen.
Huàn used soil from the northern cliff of Xīshān in Nánchāng to wipe the swords,
making them gleam brilliantly.
He placed the swords on a large basin filled with water,
setting them atop it.
Those who looked at them
were dazzled by the radiant glow.
He sent one sword along with the soil to Huà,
keeping the other for himself.
Someone said to Huàn: "You obtained two but sent only one;
how could you deceive Lord Zhāng?"
Huàn replied:
"This dynasty is about to fall into chaos,
and Lord Zhāng will suffer its calamities.
This sword is destined to be hung on the tomb tree of Lord Xú.
Such spiritual marvels
will eventually vanish,
not remaining long in human possession."
Huà obtained the precious sword,
cherished it,
and often kept it by his seat.
Huà thought the soil from Nánchāng inferior to the red soil of Huàyīn,
so he wrote back to Huàn: "Upon close examination of the sword's patterns,
it is indeed Gānjiàng;
could Mòyé also be found?
Although not, divine objects born of heaven
are destined to reunite."
Thus, he sent one jīn of Huàyīn soil to Huàn.
Huàn used it to wipe the sword again,
making it even more brilliant.
When Huà was executed,
the sword was lost.
After Huàn's death,
his son Huà served as a state official.
While passing through Yánpíng Ford with the sword,
it suddenly leaped from his waist
and fell into the water.
He had someone dive to retrieve it,
but the sword was not seen;
instead, two dragons, each several zhàng long,
coiled with patterned scales, appeared.
The diver, frightened, returned.
Moments later, brilliant light illuminated the water,
waves surged tumultuously,
and the sword was lost.
Huà sighed: "My father's words about its vanishing,
and Lord Zhāng's theory of reunion—
is this their fulfillment!"
Huà's vast knowledge often resembled this,
too numerous to record in detail.
Zhāng Huà's erudition and wide learning
were unmatched in his time.
Fú Yuándá was skilled in discerning flavors,
able to distinguish the origins of all salts, vinegars, and meats.
Someone once killed a chicken to serve him,
and Yuándá said: "This chicken often roosted half-exposed."
Investigation proved it true.
He also ate goose meat,
knowing whether it was from a black or white goose.
People doubted him,
but recording and testing it
showed no error.
Contemporaries considered him a connoisseur of taste.
Also from the same source.
Lǐ Shǒusù mastered the study of surnames,
earning the nickname 'Living Genealogy'.
Yú Shìnán said: "In the past, Rén Yànshēng was versed in classics,
hailed as 'Five Classics Repository';
now, we call the Personnel Officer 'Records of Personalities',
is that fitting?"
From "The Book of Táng".
Wáng Yuángǎn
was known as the 'Guide to the Five Classics'.
Same as above.
Yīn Jiànyóu was profoundly learned,
Hè Zhīzhāng called him 'Five-Gathering Turtle',
meaning: a turtle gathers once every two hundred years, so after a thousand years, it knows all,
and there is nothing it does not know when asked.
From "The New Book of Táng".
Liú Yǎo comprehensively studied numerous books,
and from Shěn Yuē, Rén Fǎng onward,
whenever they had forgotten something,
they would consult him.
From "The History of the Southern Dynasties".
Wáng Biāozhī was widely informed and knowledgeable;
regarding old matters of Jiāngdōng,
he kept them in a green box,
leading the world to call it the 'Wáng Family Green Box Learning'.
Same as above.
Chéng was extensively read,
omniscient.
Wáng Jiǎn prided himself on being more knowledgeable than Chéng,
but after Jiǎn finished speaking,
Chéng discussed hundreds of omitted points,
all unseen by Jiǎn.
Jiǎn then sighed in admiration:
"Lord Lù is a walking bookcase!"
From "The History of the Southern Dynasties: Biography of Lù Chéng".
Liú Xiàozhì's son Liàng
knew all the historical events of the Jìn Dynasty,
earning the nickname 'Jìn History Under the Skin'.
From "The History of the Southern Dynasties: His Biography".
Zhū Yì studied all five classics thoroughly,
dabbled in literature and history,
and excelled in board games, calligraphy, and arithmetic.
All were his strengths.
Shěn Yuē said:
"You are young;
how can you be so greedy?"
Yì did not understand,
so Yuē said:
"Under heaven, only literary meaning, chess, and writing remain,
and you take them all at once;
you could be called greedy."
From "The Book of Liáng".
Fáng Huīyuǎn
inherited Confucian scholarship through generations,
and Niú Hóng called him the 'Repository of the Five Classics'.
From "The Book of Suí: His Biography".
For ancient matters, ask Zhòngshū.
Gāo.
For current matters, ask Lín—why doubt?
From "The Book of Táng: Biography of Cuī Lín".
Cháng Shuǎng was known as the Confucian Scholar.
From "The History of the Northern Dynasties".
Gǔlǜ Nà was deeply versed in numerous books,
and Chǔ Suìliáng called him the 'Repository of the Nine Classics'.
From "The Book of Táng: His Biography".
Biographies and Records
Yáng Xióng carried lead tablets
and wooden slips, following scribes,
visiting officials everywhere,
to compile the "Fāngyán".
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital".
During Emperor Hàn Wǔ's reign,
a bell in front of the Wèiyāng Palace rang without cause,
and the emperor consulted Dōngfāng Shuò,
who said:
"Copper is the child of earth;
speaking by analogy, the child
responds when the mother is affected.
I fear a mountain may collapse or shift,
hence the bell rang first."
Three days later,
the southern commandery reported a mountain collapse.
From "The Outer Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò".
Xú Jiān knew many historical典故,
and entered the imperial library seven times.
From "Great Táng Anecdotes".
Cross-reference "Opportunities".
Encompassing all diversity,
containing the nine treasuries.
From "Generalities on History".
Regardless of time's distance,
or matter's magnitude,
one must rely on broad hearing
to achieve extensive knowledge.
Same as above.
Collection
Embracing the entire forest of books.
． From Yáng Xióng's "Rhapsody on Tall Poplars".
Fifty schools of military strategy,
Your belly serves as a box for scrolls.
From Dù Shī.
Gathering the lost writings of a hundred generations,
Collecting the lingering rhymes of a thousand years;
Viewing past and present in an instant,
Embracing the four seas in a blink.
From Lù Jī's "Rhapsody on Literature".
Literature abundant as overflowing granaries.
From Hán Wén.
My parched guts hold only five thousand volumes of writing.
From Lú Tóng's "Song of Tea".
All that has existed since the times of Yáo and Shùn,
Preserved in compiled bamboo slips,
Vast as rivers and seas,
Lofty as mountains and peaks,
Bright as sun and moon,
Mysterious as spirits and ghosts,
Delicate as pearls, blossoms, and fruits,
Changing as thunder, lightning, wind, and rain,
With extraordinary expressions and profound meanings,
All are thoroughly comprehended.
From Hán Wén.
No book left unread,
Yet properly utilized to nourish poetry.
From Hán Yù's "Epitaph for Lú Yīn of Fànyáng".
Hooking and linking, threading through,
Encompassing the great while including the small,
Like the stores of the great granary,
Or the burdens of a lofty mountain,
Vast and boundless beyond comprehension.
From Liǔ Wén.
Mastering the six scripts of calligraphy,
His learning covers the seven catalogs.
From Liǔ Jìwén.
An arsenal,
Where spears and halberds stand dense;
A study,
Where rituals and music are fully preserved.
From Yáo Chóng's Inscription.
In our dynasty,
Duke Yàn's "Classified Essentials",
In upper, middle, and lower volumes,
Totals seventy-four chapters.
The six classics, Sima Qian, the sayings of various schools, the writings of poets and literati,
Down to geographical records, clan genealogies, the numerous theories of Buddhism, Daoism, and technical arts,
Extending even beyond the nine provinces,
． Recording the remote and elusive barbarian tribes, their strange transformations and wonders,
All were examined and unraveled.
And regarding the three realms and all things, their changes and true nature,
The principles of right and wrong, rise and fall,
The intricacies of the manifest and hidden, the fine and great,
None were not exhaustively explored.
From Lǎo Quán.
Marvelous books can be studied,
Knowing Yáng Xióng's earnest effort;
Lost books restored,
Relying on Zhāng Ānshì's memorization.
From "The Collected Works of Dōngpō".
Cross-reference "Powerful Memory".
Five thousand volumes of writing propping up my intestines and filling my belly.
From Dōngpō's poem.
Learning is like a rich merchant amassing broadly,

From Dōngpō's poem.
History
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn visited Hédōng,
Three cases of books were lost,
When inquired by edict,
None could recall,
Only Zhāng Ānshì remembered them,
And detailed their contents.
Later, when the books were sought and obtained,
Upon comparison,
Nothing was missing.
From "History of the Western Hàn".
Huò Guāng asked Zhāng Qiānqiū about battle strategies,
And the terrain of mountains and rivers,
Qiānqiū answered about military affairs orally,
Drawing maps on the ground,
With nothing omitted.
． From "Biography of Zhāng Ānshì in History of the Western Hàn".
Huáng Zǔ's eldest son, Shè,
Once traveled with Mí Héng,
And together read Cài Yōng's stele inscription.
Shè regretted not copying it,
Héng said: "I can remember it at a glance,
Only two characters are missing in the stone."
Thereupon he wrote it out,
Producing it,
Shè sent someone swiftly to copy the stele,
Compared,
It matched exactly what Héng had written.
． From "Biography of Mí Héng in History of the Eastern Hàn".
Mí Héng,
Whatever his eyes saw once,
He could immediately recite;
Whatever his ears heard briefly,
He never forgot in his heart.
Same as above.
Wáng Qǐ,
Read every book under heaven,
Once seen,
Never forgotten.
From "New History of the Táng".
Fèi Yī served as Imperial Secretary,
His understanding surpassed others,
Whenever reviewing documents,
With a brief glance,
He grasped their meaning entirely,
His speed several times that of others,
And never forgot them.
． From "Records of Shàolíng Lì Gōng of Wèi in Comprehensive Mirror".
Táng Yǒng was well-versed in military documents,

Rotations and movements,
Quality of equipment,
Status of supplies,
All were familiar to him.
． From "Emperor Shìzǔ of Liáng in Comprehensive Mirror".
Liú Yú secretly reviewed the military registers and warehouses of the realm,

． From "Emperor Huái of Jìn in Comprehensive Mirror".
Yáng Yīn had a powerful memory,
Meeting someone once,
He never forgot their name.
A candidate,
Lǔ Mànhàn claimed to be lowly and insignificant,

Yīn said: "You previously at Yuánzǐsī Lane,
Riding a short-tailed donkey,
Saw me but did not dismount,
Covering your face with a square fan,
Why wouldn't I recognize you?"
Mànhàn was astonished and convinced.
． From "Emperor Jìng of Liáng in Comprehensive Mirror".
Wáng Càn watched people play weiqi,
The board was disturbed,
Càn reset it,
Not a single stone misplaced,
Such was his powerful memory.

Wáng Càn was walking with others,

Someone asked:

He said:
"Yes."
Thereupon they had him recite it from memory,
Without missing a single character.
Same as above.
Zhū Huán had strong recall,
Meeting someone once,
He remembered for decades,
Recognizing all his subordinates, their wives and children.
． From "Biography in Records of Wú".

Zhāng Xún read books,

Sǔ Tǐng could read a thousand words at a glance,

From "History of the Táng".

Zhāng Yàngōng summoned and questioned him,

He replied:
"Yes."
When tested with ten thousand characters,
he mastered them perfectly after just seven readings.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì".
When Tàizōng campaigned against Liáo,

From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Collection:
He possessed a powerful memory for reading,

How magnificent the writings of the sages,

Whatever passed before his eyes,

From "Táng Wén Cuì".
Xún said:

Sōng was astonished,

Sōng then took various books from the shelves to question Xún,

Having been with Xún for long,

Our dynasty:
In former times, a worthy wrote the "Cáo É Bēi",

Every book he read once,

Learning based merely on memorization and inquiry

The flying squirrel has five skills but ends up helpless.

Toiling until the end of one's days in a decadent age,

Someone wrote a Qīxī poem saying:

Someone wrote a poem about trees saying:

Also, I've seen people call boastfulness "flattery",

Collection:
Superficial learning from skin-deep reception.
From Zhāng Héng's "Dōng Jīng Fù".
Classic:
Following and expounding upon traces,

the person copied it,

On the day of examination,

In Hàn times, someone drafting a memorial for his office

Not originating from one's own mind,

Collection:
Following and expounding upon each other.

Following and imitating harms through plagiarism.

Cross-reference "Critiquing Literature".
Treading in the words and phrases of predecessors.
From Hán Yù's "Epitaph for Fán Shàoshù".
Peeking at old chapters to steal.

Literary scholars

Our dynasty:

Masters

drawing from it deeply,
he finds its source wherever he turns.
． _Mèngzǐ, Lílóu II_.
The noble person broadly learns and daily examines himself,
then knowledge becomes clear and actions are without fault.
． _Xúnzǐ, Encouraging Learning_.
Seeing goodness,
one must seriously reflect on preserving it in oneself;
seeing badness,
one must anxiously reflect on examining oneself.
When goodness is in oneself,
one must steadfastly cherish it;
when badness is in oneself,
one must regard it as calamitous and hate it.
_Cultivating the Self_.
To be able to correct one's seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting
was what our former teacher revered.
． _Yáng Quǎnqiān_.
Collection
Adorning the highest virtue,
polishing the fine model.
．． _Preface to Selected Poems_.
Classic
If the branches and leaves are unharmed,
but the root is first damaged.
．． _The Book of Songs, Greater Odes, Dàng_.
Injuring its root and branches,
leads to its perishing.
． _The Rites, Duke Āi_.
Zǐ
Mèngzǐ said: "The trees of Niú Mountain were once beautiful,
but because it bordered a great state,
axes and hatchets hewed them down.
Could they remain beautiful?
Yet through the days and nights they grew,
moistened by rain and dew,
and not without new sprouts springing forth,
but then cattle and sheep came to graze upon them,
thus leaving them so bare.
People see their bareness
and think there were never any trees there.
Is this the mountain's true nature?
So in humans,
is there no heart of benevolence and righteousness?
The reason they lose their good heart
is also like axes hewing trees:
hewn day after day,
can it remain beautiful?
What grows in them day and night,
the dawn's fresh energy,
their likes and dislikes barely differ from others',
but their daytime actions
fetter and destroy it.
Fettered repeatedly,
their night breath cannot sustain it;
the night breath cannot sustain it,
then they are not far from beasts.
People see their beastly state
and think they never had any capacity.
Is this human nature?
Thus, if properly nourished,
nothing fails to grow;
if nourishment is lost,
nothing fails to perish.
． _Mèngzǐ, Gàozǐ I_.
Even with the most easily growing thing under heaven,
if exposed to sun for one day
and chilled for ten days,
it cannot survive.
Mutilating the willow tree
to make cups and bowls.
Now thorns block your mind.
_Jìnxīn II_.
If a person
has many desires,
even if some goodness remains,
it is little.
Same as above.
Is loving one's body not like loving the tong and zǐ trees?
They simply do not think enough.
_Mèngzǐ_.
Though wood may be worm-eaten,
without a strong wind it won't break;
though a wall may crumble,
without heavy rain it won't collapse.
_Guǎnzǐ_.
History
If this heart is not clear,
it brings chaos to all measures.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāo 1_.
Classic
The Way is something
from which one cannot stray for even a moment.
—The Doctrine of the Mean.
Rites and music must not leave one's person even briefly.
—The Book of Rites, Records of Music.
The more I look up at it, the higher it appears;
the more I drill into it, the harder it becomes;
I see it before me,
yet suddenly it is behind.
—The Analects, Zǐ Hǎn.
Standing, I see it arrayed before me;
in the carriage, I see it leaning against the crossbar.
—Wèi Líng Gōng.
The Master said: "A noble person does not abandon benevolence even for the space of a meal;
in moments of haste, they adhere to it;
in times of distress, they adhere to it."
—Lǐ Rén.
Collection
The mouth never ceases reciting the texts of the Six Arts;
the hands never stop unrolling the scrolls of the Hundred Schools.
—Hán Wén.
By morning, one gallops through the forest of books;
by evening, one soars in the garden of arts.
—Mutually entered under "Love of Learning".
Walk upon
the path of benevolence and righteousness;
wander through
the source of the Odes and Documents.
Both from the same source above.
Classic
To build a mound nine fathoms high,
the work falls short by one basket.
—The Book of Documents, Lǚ Áo.
A noble person follows the Way and acts,
but gives up halfway.
—The Doctrine of the Mean.
To practice rites without basing them on righteousness
is like plowing without sowing;
to practice righteousness without studying it through learning
is like sowing without weeding;
to study it through learning without uniting it with benevolence
is like weeding without harvesting;
to unite it with benevolence without securing it with music
is like harvesting without eating.
It is like building a mound;
if one basket short of completion,
I stop because I choose to stop.
—The Analects, Zǐ Hǎn.
Master
If one digs a well nine fathoms deep but does not reach the spring,
it is still an abandoned well.
—Mèngzǐ, Jìn Xīn Shàng.
Hills learn from mountains but do not reach their height,
hence I detest those who limit themselves.
—Yáng Xué Jìng.
Collection: Just as one is cutting an axe handle,
can one discard the axe?
—Wén Cuì.
Classic
The Master said: "As for Huí's character,
he chose the Mean.
Upon obtaining one good,
he would clasp it firmly to his breast
and never lose it."
—The Doctrine of the Mean.
When Zǐlù heard something
and was unable to put it into practice,
he would fear to hear more.
—The Analects, Gōng Yě Cháng.
A good person does good,
as if each day were insufficient.
—The Book of Documents, Tài Shì.
When it comes to benevolence, do not yield even to your teacher.
—The Analects, Wèi Líng Gōng.
See goodness as if you cannot reach it.
Practicing benevolence depends on oneself;
can it depend on others?
—Yán Yuān.
Master
Hearing one good word,
seeing one good deed,
is like the bursting of a river,
overflowing and unstoppable.
—Mèngzǐ.
Rising at cockcrow,
diligently doing good.
Looking up and pondering it,
night and day,
fortunate to grasp it,
sitting up to await the dawn.
—Lí Lóu Xià.
History
Following goodness as a flowing stream.
—Zuǒ Zhuàn.
The emperor asked Dōngpíng King about managing his household,
and the king said that doing good brings the greatest joy.
—Eastern Hàn, Basic Biography.
Classic
Loving to ask makes one ample.
—The Book of Documents, Zhòng Huǐ Zhī Gào.
Shùn loved to ask
and was fond of examining commonplace sayings.
—The Doctrine of the Mean.
Not ashamed to ask those below.
—The Analects.
When the Master entered the Grand Temple,
he asked about everything.
Asking the incapable despite his ability,
asking the few despite his abundance.
—Tài Bó.
Master
When Confucius went to Zhōu,
he asked Lǎo Dān about the rites,
and consulted Cháng Hóng about music.
—Family Sayings.
Received texts from Lǐ Yù,
studied the Odes from Xià Diàn,
inquired about rites from Guān Zǐ,
clarified proper music from Huò Jí,
examined the Changes with Zhòng Huá.
—Wén Zhōng Shì Jiā.
History
When Tán Zǐ came to court,
Zhāo Zǐ asked about Shǎohào's naming of officials after birds,
and Tán Zǐ said: "He is my ancestor,
I know of this."
Zhòngní heard of it,
saw Tán Zǐ and learned from him.
—Zuǒ Zhuàn, Zhāo 17th Year.
At that time, Zhòngní was eighteen years old.
Confucius learned to play the zither from Master Xiāng Zǐ.
—Records of the Grand Historian, Confucius' Hereditary House.
He asked about affairs incessantly, Jiā the Long-Head.
—Book of the Later Hàn, Biography of Jiǎ Kuí.
Biographies
With the sagehood of Zhòngní,
he visited Tán Zǐ
and first heard of Shǎohào's officials;
with the worth of Shū Xiàng,
he consulted Guó Qiáo
and thereby discerned the specter of the yellow bear.
—Shǐ Tōng.
Collection
No affair is left unconsulted.
—Elegy for Yáng Jīngzhōu.
Classic
He chooses the Mean,
but cannot hold it for even a month.
—The Doctrine of the Mean.
As for the rest, they only reach it now and then.
—The Analects.
As a virtue, the Mean
is supreme indeed,
but among the people, it has long been rare.
—Yōng Yě.
Master
If the five grains do not ripen,
they are inferior to weeds.
—Mèngzǐ, Gào Zǐ.
Classic
When Yán Zǐ had a fault,
he never failed to recognize it.
Recognizing it,
he never repeated it.
—The Book of Changes, Xì Cí.
Returning not far, without great regret.
—Fù Guà.
A noble person, having faults, corrects them.
—Yì Guà.
Being without blame lies in skillfully remedying faults.
—Xì Cí Shàng.
Correcting faults without stinginess.
—The Book of Documents, Zhòng Huǐ Zhī Gào.
Not repeating faults.
—The Analects.
Having faults,
do not fear to correct them.
—Xué Ér.
Master
Zǐlù was playing the sè,
which Confucius heard,
and said:
"Practicing the music of a fallen state,
can one preserve a six-foot body?"
Rǎn Yǒu informed Zǐlù of this,
who became fearful and regretted on his own,
quietly reflecting without eating,
until he was reduced to skin and bones.
From "Family Sayings".
Also see "Courage in Correcting Faults".
There was a man from Jìn named Féng Fù,
skilled at fighting tigers,
who eventually became a virtuous man.
From "Mèngzǐ, Wànzhāng I".
Zǐlù,
when told of his faults,
would be pleased.
From "Gōngsūn Chǒu I".
To hear of one's faults and show joy,
Chéng Yuán was capable of this.
From the chapter "Lǐ Yuè" in "Wénzhōngzǐ".
History:
Wú Jìzhá went to Jìn,
and was about to lodge at Qī,
the fief of Sūn Línfǔ.
Hearing the sound of bells there,
he said:
"The master has offended the ruler,
and here, fear is still not enough,
yet what joy is there?"
Wénzǐ
(i.e., Sūn Línfǔ)
heard this,
and never listened to the qín or sè again for life.
From "Zuǒzhuàn, 28th Year of Xiānggōng".
Who among men is without faults?
To have faults and be able to correct them,
there is no greater good.
From "2nd Year of Xuāngōng".
A nobleman who can know his faults,
will surely have good plans,
aided by Heaven.
From "Zuǒzhuàn".
Correct the past and reverse faults.
From "Xīhàn, Gǔ Yǒng's Biography".
There was a cow thief,
caught by the owner,
who pleaded: "I accept punishment or death,
but beg that Wáng Yànfāng not know of it."
Liè heard of it,
and sent someone to console him,
giving him a bolt of cloth.
When asked the reason,
Liè said: "The thief feared I would hear of his fault,
showing he has a sense of shame.
Since he feels shame,
he will surely correct his fault,
hence I encouraged him thus."
Later, an old man dropped his sword on the road,
and a passerby
saw it and guarded it,
until evening,
when the old man returned to search,
found the sword,
and curiously asked his name,
then reported the matter to Liè.
Liè had it investigated,
and it turned out to be the former cow thief.
From "Dōnghàn, Wáng Liè's Biography".
Zhōu Chù in youth did not attend to minor conduct,
troubling his locality.
Knowing he was disliked by others,
he resolutely resolved to reform,
saying:
"Now with peace and good harvests,
why is there no joy?"
The elders said: "The three scourges remain,
what joy is there?"
Chù asked:
"What do you mean?"
They replied: "The white-browed beast of South Mountain,
the flood dragon under Long Bridge,
and you make the three."
Chù then entered the mountain and killed the tiger,
dove into the water and slew the dragon,
devoted himself to learning,
aspired to righteousness and fervor,
restrained himself for a year,
and was recruited by both provincial and central governments.
From "Jìnshū, His Biography".
Also entered under "Determined Effort".
The wise correct faults and turn to good,
thus their virtue renews daily.
From "Tōngjiàn, Táng Dézōng's Annals".
Lù Zhì said: "I hear Zhònghuǐ praised Chéng Tāng,
not for having no faults but for correcting them;
Jīfǔ eulogized Zhōu Xuān,
not praising his flawlessness,
but his mending of flaws.
Thus the sage's intent is clear and evident,
valuing the ability to correct faults,
not prizing the absence of faults."
From "Tōngjiàn, Táng Dézōng's Annals".
Collection:
Restrain oneself and self-chastise.
Hán Wén.
Matters often change former preferences.
Yánzǐ not repeating faults means
he could stop them
at their inception,
cut them off before they took form—
this is the conduct of not repeating faults.
Both from the same source.
Féng Fù loved fighting tigers,
yet became a virtuous man.
Zhōu Chù was wild and unruly,
but once reformed his character,
both able to master themselves.
Liǔ Wén.
This dynasty:
Now I must earnestly reform myself,
thrice cleansing and thrice purifying.
Huáng Tíngjiān.
Classic:
Words that are model speech,
can one not follow them?
But to reform is precious.
To follow without reforming,
I can do nothing with such a person!
From "Analects".
Masters:
A man who daily stole his neighbor's chicken
was told: "This is not the way of a nobleman,
please reduce it.
Steal one chicken a month,
wait until next year,
then stop."
If he knows it is wrong,
he should stop quickly;
why wait until next year?
From "Mèngzǐ, Téng Wéngōng II".
History:
I see that former emperors who rejected advice
often said: "I've already done it."
Or: "I've already promised it."
And never changed,
thus how could they avoid peril and ruin?
From "Tōngjiàn, Táng Tàizōng's Annals".
Also see "Persisting in Error".
Collection:
The worry is not knowing one's faults;
once known,
if one still cannot correct them,
that is cowardice.
Hán Wén.
Classic:
Petty men think small faults harmless,
and do not rid themselves of them.
Thus faults accumulate and cannot be concealed,
crimes grow great and cannot be pardoned.
From "Yì Jīng, Xì Cí".
Also see "Clinging to Errors".
Do not be shameless and persist in wrongs.
From "Shū Jīng, Yuè Mìng".
To have faults and not correct them—
that is truly a fault.
From "Analects, Wèi Línggōng".
I have not seen one who can see his faults
and inwardly reproach himself.
From "Gōngyě Cháng".
He avoids saying he desires it,
yet always finds excuses for it.
From "Jì Shì".
Not being able to correct what is not good—
that is my worry.
The faults of a petty man
are always glossed over.
Both from "Analects".
Masters
The gentlemen of today,
when they err, they go along with it.
Not only do they go along with it,
but they also follow up with excuses for it.
． _Mencius, Gōngsūn Chǒu II_ .
Ugliness must rely on goodness,
to explain itself;
evil must cover itself with righteousness,
to make excuses for itself.
They travel without discussing the state,
serve in office without choosing the position,
and act without avoiding corruption.
They say:
"This is the way of Yī Yǐn: dividing and contending for wealth, relatives and brothers harboring grudges, and kin harming each other."
They say:
"This is the righteousness of Zhōu Gōng: acting without shame,
enduring disgrace without dying."
They say:
"This is the pursuit of Guǎn Zhòng: practicing bribery, courting the powerful, establishing private interests at the expense of public good, and forming cliques to gain favor."
They say:
"This is the method of Confucius."
． _Huáinánzǐ, Tài Zú Xùn_ .
In history,
to err and not correct it,
and to persist in it over time,
until regret forms,
what benefit is there in that?
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Xuān 17th Year_ .
Words,
are enough to cover up wrongs.
． _Records of the Grand Historian, Shāng Dynasty Annals_ .
Have you not seen the widows in common households?
At first, when they restrained themselves,
their hearts admired Sòng Bó Jī and Chén Xiào Fù,
but unfortunately, once defiled by bandits,
they then indulged in debauchery.
They knew it was improper,
but could not revert to their former selves,
and I am just like this.
． _Western Hàn, Biography of Yuán Shè_ .
Cross-reference "Embracing Error as Right."
Dòu Yīng said: "The marquisate was obtained by me,
and lost by me,
I have no regrets."
． _Western Hàn, Biography of Tián Fén_ .
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn said: "I imprisoned the chancellor,
to let the people hear of my faults."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Hàn Gāozǔ Annals_ .
Foolish people are ashamed of their errors and thus persist in them,
persisting in errors only accumulates their wickedness further.
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Dézōng Annals_ .
Gōngsūn Hóng apologized, saying: "Those who know me,
consider me loyal,
those who do not know me,
consider me disloyal."
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Hàn Wǔdì Annals_ .
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, facing the rebellion at Táichéng,
sighed and said: "I obtained it myself,
and I lost it myself,
what regret is there?"
． _Comprehensive Mirror, Basic Annals_ .
Zhái Zhuāng said: "Greedy for the bait, I swallowed the hook—
was it really me?"
． _Jìn Shū, His Biography_ .
Xiè Kūn,
courtesy name Yòu Yú,
flirted with the neighbor's daughter Gāo Shì,
who threw a shuttle and broke two of his teeth.
People at the time said of him: "Indulging in wantonness unceasingly,
Yòu Yú lost his teeth."
Xiè Kūn heard this,
and proudly chanted aloud: "It still doesn't stop me from singing."
_Jìn Shū_ .
Sūn Zǐjīng said to Wáng Wǔzǐ: "I should pillow on the stream and rinse my mouth with stones."
Wáng Wǔzǐ said: "Stones cannot be used to rinse,
nor can a stream be used as a pillow."
Sūn said: "The reason for pillowing on the stream
is to wash my ears;
the reason for rinsing with stones
is to sharpen my teeth."
_Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū_ .
Cross-reference "Embracing Error as Right."
Lǐ Línfǔ's son, Lǐ Xiù,
seeing the overwhelming power and influence,
said: "Father, you have held this position for long,
with thorns piled before you.
Once disaster strikes,
how could you compare to those ordinary people?"
At that time, Xiù wept upon seeing heavily laden carts.
Lǐ Línfǔ was displeased,
saying: "The situation is already thus,
what can be done?"
_Táng Shū_ .
Cross-reference "Fear."
Biographies
Xǔ Jìngzōng was frivolous by nature,
often forgetting people he met,
some said he was not sharp,
to which he replied: "You are hard to remember yourself.
If I met Cáo, Liú, Shěn, or Xiè,
even groping in the dark,
I could recognize them."
_National History Compilation of Anecdotes_ .
Cross-reference "Contempt."
Jiǎ Chōng asked Sūn Hào: "Why do you peel people's faces?"
Hào replied: "I hate their thick-skinned faces."
_Yǔlín_ .
Our Dynasty
During Emperor Rénzōng's reign,
Wáng Ānshí served as a drafter.
One day,
at a flower-viewing and fishing banquet for the eunuchs,
each had a golden plate with fishing bait pellets placed on the table,
and Wáng Ānshí ate them all.
The next day,
the Emperor said to his ministers: "Wáng Ānshí is a hypocrite.
If he had mistakenly eaten one pellet of fishing bait,
that would be it,
but eating them all
is insincere."
_Records of Hearsay and Sight_ .
Cross-reference "Seen Through by the Discerning."
Classics
Self-reliance leads to pettiness.
． _Shū, Announcement of Zhòng Huǐ_ .
Not following the ancients' ways,
not planning great strategies.
_Shī_ .
All say, 'We are sages.'
． _Shī, First Month_ .
Thinking only themselves good,
having their own hearts and minds.
． _Shī, Sāng Róu_ .
Ah, this Huáng Fù,
how can it be said he is not timely?
． _Shī, Tenth Month Intersection_ .
Foolish yet fond of self-assertion,
lowly yet fond of self-determination.
Born in today's world,
yet reverting to ancient ways.
_The Doctrine of the Mean_ .
Masters
Considering themselves right,
they cannot enter the way of Yáo and Shùn.
_Mencius_ .
A fool of Sòng
found a Yān stone and hid it,
thinking it a great treasure.
A visitor from Zhōu heard of it and came to see,
the host, in formal black attire, opened it.
The treasure chest had ten layers,
wrapped in ten orange cloths.
When the visitor saw it,
he chuckled and laughed,
saying: "This is a Yān stone,
no different from a tile."
The host was furious,
and hid it even more securely.
_Quēzǐ_ .
Not following teachers' methods,
but fond of self-reliance,
is like the blind distinguishing colors,
or the deaf distinguishing sounds.
． _Xúnzǐ, Cultivating Oneself_ .
Today's recluses
claim ability where they have none,
and knowledge where they are ignorant.
． _Xúnzǐ, Against Twelve Masters_ .
History
Wú Qǐ as a person,
was rigid and self-satisfied.
． "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Zhou Annals".
He exerted his private wisdom,
without learning from ancient origins.
． "Records of the Grand Historian, Annals of Xiàng Yǔ".
Affairs not modeled on antiquity that can long endure,
I have never heard of.
． "Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Lǐ Sī".
Gentlemen in the imperial carriage,
considering themselves in an age of Yáo and Shùn,
how dare they speak recklessly?
"Book of Jìn".
Zǐsī said: "When the ruler speaks,
he considers himself correct,
and the ministers dare not correct his errors.
When the ministers speak,
they also consider themselves correct,
and the scholars and commoners dare not correct their errors."
"Comprehensive Mirror".
The emperor said: "I have already appointed him,
it cannot be revoked."
． "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Táng Gāozǔ".
Zōng Què governed Yùzhōu,
with Wú Xǐ as diǎnqiān.
Whenever Zōng Què implemented punishments or administration,
Wú Xǐ often obstinately opposed,
enraging Zōng Què,
who said: "Zōng Què is nearly sixty,
having risked his life,
only to obtain a province as small as a dipper,
and cannot govern it together with a diǎnqiān!"
Self-willed,
unable to heed magnanimous advice.
． "Comprehensive Mirror, Qín Annals".
Classic
No one recognizes the faults of their own children.
． "Book of Rites, Great Learning".
History
A man who loved his dog,
which often urinated in the well,
was seen by his neighbor,
who wanted to tell him,
but the dog guarded the door and bit him.
． "Comprehensive Mirror, Zhou Annals".
Líng Hú Táo held power for many years,
his son Líng Hú Hào extensively sought power and accepted bribes,
critics attacked his faults,
yet Líng Hú Táo pleaded his son Líng Hú Hào's innocence.
． "Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Xuānzōng".
Collection
Bóhóu, afflicted with a fatal illness,
raged at Biǎn Què's foresight.
Jī Shūyè's "Essay on Nourishing Life".
This dynasty
When people today have faults,
they dislike others admonishing them,
like concealing illness and avoiding doctors,
preferring to perish
without awakening.
Zhōu Dūnyí's "Penetrating the Book of Changes".
Classic
Petty men consider small evils harmless,
and do not eliminate them.
Thus evils accumulate until they cannot be concealed,
and crimes grow too great to be resolved.
． "Appended Judgments of the Book of Changes".
Cross-reference "persisting in error".
Obstinately persisting in crime merits punishment.
． "Book of Documents, Canon of Shùn".
Day and night, incessantly.
Note: "Perpetrating evil without cease."
． See "Book of Documents, Yì and Jì".
Villains doing evil,
also find the day insufficient.
． "Book of Documents, Great Declaration".
Foul virtue becomes widely known.
Same as above.
Accustomed to treachery.
． "Book of Documents, Jūn Chén".
Arrogant and boastful,
they will end in evil.
． "Book of Documents, Charge to Bì".
While your evil is rampant,
I behold your spears.
． "Book of Songs, Joint Mount South".
Hoping you would act virtuously,
instead you emerge to do evil.
． "Book of Songs, Rain Without Right".
Much will blaze fiercely,
beyond remedy.
． "Book of Songs, Board".
History
Persisting in evil without reform,
leads to self-destruction.
． "Zuǒzhuàn, Yǐn 6".
Not considering slander.
Read as such.
Undaunted by gods or spirits,
spirits angered, people pained,
yet no remorse in heart.
． "Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāo 20".
Sòng Zǐyú said: "The calamity is not yet over,
insufficient to chastise the ruler."
． "Zuǒzhuàn, Xī 21".
In the Yì, one fault is a mistake,
twice is treading,
thrice without correction,
brings annihilation, a dire omen.
"Records of the Three Kingdoms, Wèi".
Biographies
Wasps and scorpions,
if not abandoning venom towards people,
will not be tranquil.
． "Garden of Persuasions, Chapter on Power and Strategy".
Collection
Even facing nine deaths, I would still not regret.
"Songs of Chǔ".
Wasps and scorpions always harbor poison.
Dù Fǔ's poetry.
The owl's cry unceasing,
the kite's spread ever fiercer.
"Collection of Bái Jūyì".
History
Wú Jìzhá intending to lodge at Qī,
fief of Sūn Línfù.
Hearing bell music there,
said: "Our host has offended his ruler and is here,
fear is still not enough,
what joy can there be?"
"Zuǒzhuàn".
Wèi Hóu Kàn returned to Wèi,

those who met him at the gate, he only nodded to.

Cross-reference "arrogance" section.
The King of Qí fled into exile,

whose ruler vacated palaces to host him,
addressed him as sovereign,

The King of Qí was disrespectful,

The King of Qí left for Zōu and Lǔ,

so he fled to Jǔ.
． "Comprehensive Mirror, Zhou Annals".
Xiàng Yǔ crossed the Huái River,
with only twenty-eight cavalry,
pursued by thousands of Hàn troops.
Xiàng Yǔ said: "I rose in arms over seventy years ago,
every battle I fought, I conquered,
never defeated,
now suddenly trapped here,
Heaven destroys me,
not due to faults in battle.
Today I wish to fight decisively,
behead generals and capture flags,
to show you all it is Heaven destroying me,
not faults in battle."
． "Records of the Grand Historian, Annals of Xiàng Yǔ".

Without moisture,

To express the desires of the heart,

The historian's
words,

words lead to disorder.
Mí Zhèng Píng's rhapsody.
Words that wear down sharp edges.
Yuán Wēi Zhī.
In our dynasty,

Have you not seen bells and drums?
When struck,
they then resound,
with clanging and booming,

If they sound without being struck,

To be able to speak and not speak,

"Yū Shū".
To speak with intent,

"Dōng Pō".
The Classic

"Yì Jīng".

. "Yì Xì Cí".

. "Shī Yì".

. "Shī Dàng".

. "Jì Zī Yī" note:
Once a mistaken word is out,

A gentleman is sparing in speech.
. "Jì Fāng Jì".
A gentleman speaks little but acts,

. "Jì Zī Yī".

. "Jì Jì Yì".
A gentleman, in his speech,

In the ancestral temple and court,

. "Yǔ Xiāng Dǎng".

. "Yǔ Yán Yuān".
Be cautious in the rest of your speech,

The "Yǔ" says.

Better to preserve stillness.

In Hòu Jì's temple,
there stood a bronze figure,

Do not talk much,

"Jiā Yǔ".
The mouth may be used for eating,

"Guǐ Gǔ Zǐ".
If words do not align with benevolence,

"Xún Zǐ: Fēi Xiāng".
Words in the mouth

"Liú Zǐ".
Once spoken, words cannot be taken back;

When the bow is drawn but not released,

Words are like the wind,

Liú Bīnkè.
