History
Gù Yōng served as chancellor and managed the affairs of the imperial secretariat.
Gù Yōng was a man of few words,
and the ruler of Wú also said:
"When Lord Gù is present,
it makes people uncomfortable."
Such was the awe he inspired.
Xú Xiànzhī carried himself with dignified composure,
speaking only at the appropriate time.
"Tōng Jiàn: Jìn Gōng Jì".
Wáng Xiànzhī once went with his elder brothers Wáng Huīzhī and Wáng Cāozhī to visit Xiè Ān.
The two elder brothers talked much about mundane matters,
while Xiànzhī only exchanged brief pleasantries.
After they left,
a guest asked Xiè Ān about the comparative merits of the Wáng brothers.
Ān said:
"The youngest is the best."
When asked why,
he replied:
"The words of the virtuous are few;
because he spoke little,
I knew."
"Jìn Shū: Běn Zhuàn".
Ruǎn Qiānlǐ met Wáng Róng,
who asked him:
"The sages value the teachings of names,
while Lǎo Zǐ and Zhuāng Zǐ elucidate naturalness.
Are their tenets the same or different?"
Ruǎn replied:
"Perhaps they are not different."
Wáng Róng then recruited him,
and contemporaries called him "The Official of Three Words."
"Jìn Shū".
Xiè Ān once praised Wáng Méng,
saying:
"Chancellor Wáng speaks very little,
yet one can say he possesses admirable speech."
"Jìn Shū: Wáng Méng Zhuàn".
Wèi Jiè was often ill and physically weak,
so his mother usually forbade him from speaking.
On fine days,
relatives and friends would occasionally ask him to say a word,
and all would sigh in admiration,
considering his words profoundly insightful.
Lángyá's Wáng Chéng, who had a high reputation,
whenever he heard Wèi Jiè speak,
would sigh repeatedly and be utterly amazed.
"Jìn Shū: Wèi Jiè Zhuàn".
Cross-reference: "Appreciating excellence."
And "Words are not spoken idly."

Lǚ Āigōng wanted to expand his residence westward,
the historian opposed it,
believing that westward expansion was inauspicious.
Āigōng changed countenance and grew angry,
his attendants repeatedly admonished him,
but he wouldn't listen.
He then asked his tutor Zǎi Zhésuī: "I wish to expand my residence westward,
but the historian considers it inauspicious,
what do you think?"
Zǎi Zhésuī replied: "There are three inauspicious things in the world,
and westward expansion is not among them."
Āigōng was greatly pleased,
and after a moment asked again: "What are the three inauspicious things?"
He replied: "Not practicing ritual righteousness
is the first inauspicious thing;
having insatiable desires
is the second inauspicious thing;
not listening to strong admonitions
is the third inauspicious thing."
Āigōng fell silent in deep thought,
soberly reflected on himself,
and consequently abandoned the plan to expand westward.
. From "Huáinánzǐ, Rénjiānxùn".

Histories
Chǔ Zǐyù requested battle,
Jìn Luán Zhī replied: "The grace of the king of Chǔ,
I have not dared to forget,
therefore I am here,
and for the sake of you, the great officer, I retreat.

Jìn Shū Xiàng went to Zhèng,

Same as above.
The king of Zhào was newly enthroned,
Qín urgently attacked Zhào,
Zhào sought aid from Qí,
Qí said: "You must send Cháng'ān Jūn as a hostage,
then troops will be dispatched."
The queen dowager refused,
the great ministers strongly remonstrated,
the dowager said: "Whoever speaks of this again,
this old woman will certainly spit in his face."
Left Tutor Chù Lóng saw the dowager,
she was full of anger and awaited him,
Left Tutor said: "Your servant's lowly son Shū Qí,
I privately love him,
and wish, before I fill the ditches, to entrust him."
The dowager said: "Do men also love their young sons?"
He said: "More than women do.
Your servant privately believes that your love for Yānhòu is more worthy than that for Cháng'ān Jūn."
The dowager said: "Not as much as for Cháng'ān Jūn."
Left Tutor said: "When parents love their children,
they plan deeply and far for them.
Now you honor Cháng'ān Jūn's position,
but do not take the present opportunity to let him achieve merit for the state.
Once the mountains and hills crumble,
how will Cháng'ān Jūn entrust himself to Zhào?
Your servant considers your planning for Cháng'ān Jūn to be short-sighted."
The dowager said: "Very well.
Do as you think best in employing him."
Thereupon he was sent as hostage to Qí.
． From Shǐjì, Zhào Shìjiā.
Cross-reference to "Transforming People's Hearts."
Wáng Chéng said: "Húmǔ Yànguó uttered fine words,
like sawdust from wood,
fluttering unceasingly,
he is a leader of the later generation."

Yuè Guǎng excelled at discussion,
often using concise words to analyze principles,

The king of Zhào went out incognito,
was captured by Yān troops,
Yān thereupon sought to demand ceded territory,
envoys went to request,
Yān repeatedly killed them.
A groom-soldier went to the Yān camp,
saw the Yān general and said: "Do you know what Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú desire?"
He said:
"They desire to recover their king."
The Zhào groom-soldier laughed and said: "You do not know what these two men desire.
Now Wǔ Chén, Zhāng Ěr, and Chén Yú,
wielding horsewhips, conquered dozens of Zhào cities,
each also desires to face south and be king,
how could they wish to be ministers and chancellors forever?
Now you have imprisoned the king of Zhào; these two men,
in name seek the king of Zhào,
but in truth desire Yān to kill him, so these two men
can divide Zhào and establish themselves.
Now with one Zhào they could still easily overcome Yān,
how much more with two worthy kings supporting each other,
and condemning the crime of killing a king?
Destroying Yān would be easy!"
The Yān general then returned the king of Zhào,
the groom-soldier drove the carriage and returned.
． From Tōngjiàn, Qín Jì.
Jiāo Hé engaged in lofty discourse reaching the clouds.
． From Tōngjiàn, Eastern Hàn.
Kǒng Gōngxù engaged in pure talk and lofty discourse,
reviving the withered and blowing life into things.
Same as above.
Cáo Cāo captured Chén Gōng,
said to Gōng: "What about your aged mother?"
He said: "Gōng has heard that those who govern the world with filial piety
do not harm people's parents.
Whether my aged mother lives or dies lies with you, my lord,
not with Gōng."
Cáo said: "What about your wife and children?"
Gōng said: "Your servant has heard that those who implement benevolent government in the world
do not cut off people's sacrifices.
Whether my wife and children live or die lies with you, my lord,
not with Gōng."
． From Tōngjiàn, Hàn Xiàn Dì Jì.
Kǒng Róng engaged in lofty discourse,

cold and heat mix;
when human ether is not harmonious,

when terrestrial ether is not harmonious,

Now Your Majesty, being a woman, occupies the yang position,

Your Majesty calls it an auspicious mountain,

． From Tōngjiàn, Táng Wǔ Hòu.
Lǐ Zhāodé said to the empress dowager: "Tiānhuáng is Your Majesty's husband,
the crown prince is Your Majesty's son.
Your Majesty personally possesses the empire,
should transmit it to your sons and grandsons,
as an enterprise for ten thousand generations.
How can you make a nephew your heir?
Since ancient times, there has never been a case where a nephew became Son of Heaven
and his aunt was established in the ancestral temple."
． From Tōngjiàn, Táng Wǔ Hòu.
The emperor said to Lǐ Bì: "Now employing you,
I wish to make an agreement with you:
you must not take revenge,
as for those who have shown you kindness,
I will repay them for you."
He replied: "Your servant has always followed the Way and does not bear grudges against others.
Lǐ Fǔguó and Yuán Zài both harmed your servant,
but now they have perished by themselves.
Those I have long been friendly with or who showed me kindness
are mostly already prominent and successful,
or have declined and fallen,
your servant has none to repay."
Bì said: "Lǐ Shèng and Mǎ Suì have rendered great service to the state.
I have heard there are those who slander them,
though Your Majesty certainly will not listen.
However, your servant today speaks of these two men,
wishing them not to harbor doubts themselves.
Shèng and Suì already have sufficient wealth and honor.
If Your Majesty treats them with openness,
enabling them to protect themselves without worry,
when the state has affairs,
they go out to join campaigns,
when there are no affairs, they attend court audiences—
what joy could compare to this!
Therefore, your servant hopes Your Majesty will not, because of these two ministers' great achievements, become suspicious of them,
and these two ministers will not, because of their high positions, doubt themselves.
Then the empire will forever be without troubles."
Shèng and Suì both rose and wept in gratitude.
． From Tōngjiàn, Táng Dézōng.
The emperor suffered from the muggy heat,
ordered the palace garden commissioner Wáng Yǔnpíng to build another tower for relief from the heat.
A eunuch said: "Guō Chóngtǎo often frowns in displeasure,
because Kǒng Qiān discusses insufficiency of funds.
Even if Your Majesty wishes to construct buildings,
it ultimately cannot be done."
Then he sent a palace envoy to tell him: "This year the intense heat is exceptionally abnormal.
In the past, I was at the river confronting the Liáng people,
the camp was low and damp,
wearing armor and riding horses,
personally facing arrows and stones,
yet there was not such heat as this.
Now in the deep palace,
the heat is unbearable—
what is to be done?"
He replied: "When Your Majesty was at the river in the past,
a powerful enemy was not yet destroyed,
you deeply brooded over hatred and shame,
although there was intense heat,
it did not enter your sacred thoughts.
Now external troubles are already eliminated,
within the seas all submit,
therefore even with precious towers and secluded lodges,
you still feel stifling heat.
If Your Majesty does not forget the times of hardship,
then the heat will naturally dissipate."
The emperor fell silent.
． From Tōngjiàn, Later Táng Zhuāngzōng.
With a three-inch tongue,

When Duke Wén of Jìn received Yuán from the king,
he found it difficult to decide its governor.
He asked the eunuch Bó Dī,
who recommended Zhào Xiāng.
I say that governing Yuán
is a major affair of state,
and should not be discussed with base intimates,
thus disgracing the king's command.
Yet the ruler of Jìn, in selecting a great responsibility,
did not seek public counsel at court,
but private discussion in the palace;
did not broadly consult ministers and chancellors,
but solely consulted a eunuch.
Although perhaps Xiāng's virtue was sufficient to govern,
and the state's affairs were not ruined,
the origin of harming virtue and failing governance
sprang from this.
Alas!
Gaining a virtuous minister to govern a great city
is not a misappointment,
yet it still shamed that time
and misled later generations.
How much more so when both the question and the appointment are flawed?

When Tián Dān of Qí attacked Liáochéng but could not capture it,
Lǔ Lián then tied a letter to an arrow,
and shot it into the city,
sending a letter to the Yān general saying: "I have heard that
the wise do not miss opportunities and abandon advantages,
the brave do not fear death and tarnish their reputation,
loyal ministers do not put themselves before their lord.
Now you act on momentary anger,
disregarding that the King of Yān is left without a minister,
which is not loyalty;
to die and lose Liáochéng,
yet your authority not trusted by Qí,
is not courage;
achievements ruined and reputation destroyed,
with no praise from later generations,
is not wisdom.
These three make a ruler not regard you as a minister,
and persuaders not record your deeds.
Hence, the wise do not hesitate in planning,
the brave do not fear death.
Now life and death, honor and disgrace,
nobility and baseness, respect and humility,
this moment will not come again,
I hope you consider carefully and not follow the common way."
The Yān general saw Lǔ Lián's letter,
wept for three days,
then committed suicide.
Liáochéng fell into chaos,

The King of Chǔ asked about the tripod's size and weight,
Zhōu's Wángsūn Mǎn replied:
"It lies in virtue,
not in the tripod.
In the past, when Xià possessed virtue,
distant regions depicted images,
contributed nine pieces of metal,
and cast the tripod with these images.
Jié had depraved virtue,
the tripod moved to Shāng,
for six hundred years of sacrifices.
Shāng Zhòu was tyrannical,
the tripod moved to Zhōu.
When virtue is splendid and bright,
even if small,
it is heavy;
when it is wicked, chaotic, and depraved,
even if large,
it is light.
King Chéng fixed the tripod at Jiárǔ,
divined thirty generations,
divined seven hundred years,
it is the mandate of Heaven.
Although Zhōu's virtue has declined,
Heaven's mandate has not changed,
the tripod's weight,
cannot be inquired about."

They sacrificed to Confucius at Quèlǐ and his seventy-two disciples,
the Emperor said to Kǒng Xī:
"Today's gathering,
does it bring glory to your clan?"
He replied:
"You have personally condescended with ten thousand chariots,
humbly visited our humble village,
this is to honor the former teacher with rites,
and enhance the splendor of your sage virtue.
As for glory,
it is not what I dare claim."
The Emperor said:
"If not a sage's descendant,
how could there be such words?"
*Zīzhì Tōngjiàn*, Hàn Hé Dì Annals.
The King of Wú sent Zhào Zī to offer apologies,
the Emperor asked:
"How many in Wú are like you, Great Officer?"
He replied:
"The exceptionally intelligent and outstanding,
number eighty or ninety.
Those like your subject,
are as numerous as cartloads and bushels,
uncountable."
*Zīzhì Tōngjiàn*, Sān Guó, Wèi Wén Dì Annals.
Dèng Ài saw Zōng Yù,
said: "By rites,
at sixty one does not bear arms,
yet you accept troops,
why?"
Yù said:
"You at seventy have not returned the troops,
I at sixty,
why should I not accept them?"
*Sān Guó Zhì*, Shǔ Zhì.
Cross-reference "Forgiving oneself and blaming others."
Ruǎn Fú said to Biàn Kǔn:
"You are often without leisure and ease,
as if holding tiles and stones in your mouth,
is it not too laborious?"
Kǔn said:
"All you gentlemen promote magnanimity and elegance in morals and manners,
who but Kǔn would uphold meanness and stinginess?"
*Zīzhì Tōngjiàn*, Jìn Chéng Dì Annals.
Féng Yánsī once teased Sūn Chéng:
"What abilities do you have?"
The Mid-Department Lang Sūn Chéng said:
"Chéng is a rustic scholar from Shāndōng,
my writing is not as good as yours,
my wit and humor are not as good as yours,
my flattery and deceit are not as good as yours.
However, the sovereign sent you to accompany the Prince of Qí in recreation,
intending for you to guide him with benevolence and righteousness,
not merely to be a friend for music, women, dogs, and horses.
Chéng truly has no ability,
but abilities like yours,
are precisely enough to be the state's calamity."
*Zīzhì Tōngjiàn*, Five Dynasties, Jìn Gāo Zǔ Annals.
The Emperor once discussed Jīn Mìdī with Dù Tǎn,
saying:
"I regret there are no more such people today."
He said:
"If Mìdī were born in this age,
he would be too busy tending horses,
how could he manage to be recognized?"
The Emperor changed countenance and said:
"Why do you judge the court so lightly?"
Tǎn said: "From your subject's perspective,
I originally belonged to a high clan of Zhōnghuá,
but with the Jìn's collapse and chaos,
we moved to Liáng territory,
yet our family profession was passed down,
not losing its former status.
Simply because we did not cross south early enough,
we are treated as rustic northerners and kept at a distance."
Jīn Mídī was a Hu tribesman,
working as a herdsman,
yet he rose to serve in the inner court,
and was ranked among the virtuous worthies.
Although the sage court does promote talent,
I fear this might not be possible."
The Emperor fell silent.
. *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Taizu of Song*.
Emperor Wei held the ministers of Qi in high regard,
and said to his courtiers:
"Jiāngnán has many good ministers."
Lǐ Yuánkǎi responded:
"Jiāngnán has many good ministers,
yet their rulers change every year;
Jiāngběi has no good ministers,
but their rulers change only once in a century."
. *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Taizu of Qi*.
Emperor Liáng issued an edict,
planning to return to Jiànkāng,
but Hú Sēngyòu, Zōng Lǐn, and Liú Gǔ advised against it:
"The royal aura of Jiànyè has already faded,
and Jīngzhōu is destined to produce an emperor."
Zhōu Hóngzhèng and Wáng Bāo said:
"Now the people have not seen Your Majesty's carriage enter Jiànkāng,
they may think you are merely a feudal lord;
we hope Your Majesty will heed the expectations of the realm."
At the time, many courtiers were from Jīngzhōu,
and they all said:
"Hóngzhèng and others are easterners,
so they wish to go east;
this may not be a sound plan."
Hóngzhèng refuted them directly,
saying:
"Easterners advise going east,
and you say it's not sound;
but you westerners want to go west—
how can that be a good strategy?"
. *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Shizu of Liang*.
The hermit Lǐ Táng had an audience,
and the Emperor was holding his young daughter,
so he said to Táng:
"I am thinking of her,
do not find it strange, sir."
Táng replied:
"The Grand Emperor longs to see Your Majesty,
likely just as Your Majesty loves the princess."
. *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Daizong of Tang*.
Emperor Xīzōng of Táng once said to the actor Shí Yězhū:
"If I were to take the polo scholar examination,
I would surely be the top candidate."
Yězhū replied:
"If Yáo and Shùn were the Ministers of Rites,
I fear you might be rejected."
. *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: First Year of Huángmíng in Tang Records*.
The Empress Dowager summoned Xú Yǒugōng,
and greeted him saying:
"You have been handling cases lately,
why so many wrongful acquittals?"
He replied:
"Wrongful acquittal is a minor fault of a minister,
but valuing life is the great virtue of a sage."
The Empress Dowager fell silent.
. *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Empress Wu of Tang*.
Lǐ Xīliè plotted to declare himself emperor,
and sent someone to ask Yán Zhēnqīng about the ceremonies,
who replied:
"This old man once served as a ritual officer,
but I only recall the rites for feudal lords paying homage to the Son of Heaven."
. *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance: Emperor Dezong of Tang*.
Xiāo Fù was appointed to pacify and comfort Shānnán and other regions,
but Liú Cóngyī and other courtiers frequently petitioned to keep him,
so the Emperor said to Lù Zhì:
"I consulted with the chancellor and courtiers,
and all agreed it was proper.
Now they reverse themselves like this,
leaving me distressed for days.
Could it be that Fù regrets going,
and prompted them to argue?"
Zhì memorialized:
"If Xiāo Fù had requested this,
how could Cóngyī and others conceal it!
If Cóngyī and others are somewhat evasive,
then Xiāo Fù should not be doubted.
Why does Your Majesty hesitate to clarify,
and instead simply feel distressed!"
Ibid.
The First Sovereign sent Yī Jí as an envoy to Wú,
and Sūn Quán, hearing of his eloquence,
wanted to overwhelm him with words.
As Jí entered and bowed,
Quán said:
"Is it tiresome to serve a ruler without virtue?"
Jí replied:
"A single bow and rise—
hardly tiresome."
*Records of the Three Kingdoms: Shu*.
Zhōng Huì visited Jī Kāng,
but Kāng did not show him courtesy;
after a long while, as Huì left,
Kāng asked:
"What did you hear that brought you here?
What did you see that makes you leave?"
Huì replied:
"I heard what I heard and came,
saw what I saw and left."
. *Book of Jin: Biography of Jī Kāng*.
At the time, Méi Táo and Zhōng Yǎ often discussed affairs,
and Zǔ Nà would corner them,
saying:
"You gentlemen from Rǔyǎn,
are sharp as awls;
we from Yōujì,
are blunt as mallets.
With our blunt mallets striking your sharp awls,
all would break."
Táo and Yǎ
both claimed to have divine awls,
that no mallet could break.
Nà said:
"If there are divine awls,
there must be divine mallets."
. *Book of Jin: Biography of Zǔ Nà*.
Mutually entered under "neither yielding to the other."
Yuán Hóng had outstanding talent,
and Xiè Ān often admired his quick and clever responses.
Later, when Hóng was appointed as governor of Dōngyáng,
Ān wanted to test him with a sudden challenge;
at parting, he took his hand,
and told attendants to fetch a fan to give him,
whereupon Hóng immediately said:
"I shall uphold benevolent winds,
to comfort the common people."
*Book of Jin*.
Gù Yuèzhī was the same age as Emperor Jiǎnwén,
but his hair turned white early.
The Emperor asked the reason,
and he replied:
"The nature of pines and cypresses
is to flourish even after frost;
but the substance of willow trees
withers at the approach of autumn."
. *Book of Jin: His Biography*.
Sūn Chuò composed "Rhapsody on Tiāntāi,"
and showed it to Fàn Róngqī,
saying:
"Try tossing it to the ground—
it should ring like metal or stone."
Róngqī said:
"I fear this metal and stone may not be in tune."
Ibid.
Hé Chéngtiān was appointed as Editorial Director,
already old while his assistants were all young men from famous families;
Xún Bózǐ mocked him,
often calling him "wet nurse."
Chéngtiān said:
"You should say 'the phoenix leads nine chicks'—
why mention 'wet nurse'?"
*Book of Song*.
Emperor Wén once went with his courtiers to Tiānquán Pond,
and after fishing for a long time without a catch,
Wáng Jǐngwén stepped forward and said:
"I believe the one angling is so pure
that he does not catch the greedy bait-takers."
*Book of Song*.
Hé Yǎn said to Liú Yǔ:
"Why is your horse so slow?"
Yǔ replied:
"A fine steed restrained by reins
naturally falls behind."
Yǎn said:
"Why not whip it
to gallop a thousand miles?"
Yǔ answered:
"With one leap, it reaches the blue clouds—
why compete on the road with nags?"
*Book of Song*.
Zhōu Pánlóng served as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and Emperor Wǔ of Qí teased him:
"How do you like wearing the marten tail and cicada wing hat?"
Pánlóng, in his helmet, replied:
"This marten and cicada hat
grew out of a helmet."
. *Book of Qi: His Biography*.
When the Later Liáng ruler Xiāo Kuí surrendered,
Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu played the pipa himself
and ordered Kuí to dance,
saying:
"Can the King of Liáng dance for me?"
Kuí replied:
"Since Your Majesty plays the five-stringed instrument,
how dare I not join the hundred beasts?"
*Book of Later Liang*.
In Eastern Wèi, Yáng Yīn oversaw official selections,
and when a clerk called out names,
he mistakenly called Lú Shìshēn as Shìchēn;
Shēn stated his correct name,
and Yīn said:
"Gentleman Lú is so brilliant and refined,
we added the jade radical."
*Annals of the Three Kingdoms*.
He said to him:
"How will you govern such a challenging district?"
Yán Shīgǔ commented:
"One doesn't use an ox-cleaver to kill a chicken."
From Suí Shū.
His responses were eloquent and quick-witted.
From Táng Shū Lǐ Shàn Zhuàn.
Yǔwén Róng was divinely alert and sharp,
answering questions as swiftly as an echo,
so much so that even the Son of Heaven could not bend his will.
From Táng Shū Běn Zhuàn.
Xǔ Jìngzōng's grandson Bó Yàn,
son of Áng,
in his later years, Jìngzōng no longer wrote himself;
all major imperial documents
were composed by Bó Yàn.
He once jokingly said to Áng:
"My son is not as good as your son."
The reply was:
"His father is not as good as Áng's father."
From Xīn Táng Shū Jiān Chén Běn Zhuàn.
Lú Tǎn served as captain of Hénán,
Dù Huángshang was the prefect,
who summoned Tǎn to stand below the hall,
saying:
"A certain family's son associates with villains,
squandering his inheritance;
why not investigate him?"
Tǎn replied:
"Generally, officials who are honest,
even if they hold high positions, do not amass great wealth;
those who can accumulate much
must have exploited their subordinates to do so.
If their descendants manage to preserve it,
it means Heaven enriches unjust families;
better to let their injustice benefit others.
I, Tǎn, deem it fitting,
hence I do not investigate."
Huángshang looked at him in astonishment.
From Xīn Táng Shū Lú Tǎn Zhuàn.
Later, Lǐ Áo wrote Tǎn's biography,
stating that as an official,
Hénán's knowledge of capturing thieves, Dù Huángshang, as the prefect of Hénán,
said to Tǎn:
"A certain family's son associates with villains,
depleting the old family wealth;
you, in charge of capturing thieves,
why not investigate him?"
Tǎn looked up and said:
"Officials who remain honest and pure throughout,
relying only on their salaries,
even if they reach high office,
do not accumulate much wealth;
whereas those who amass much
must have exploited their subordinates to achieve it.
If their descendants preserve it well..."
The rest is the same.
See Lǐ Áo Wénjí.
Emperor Gāozōng went hunting and encountered rain,
so he asked the Remonstrance Official Gǔ Nàlǜ:
"How can an oiled cloth garment not leak?"
The reply was:
"If made of tiles,
it certainly wouldn't leak."
From Xīn Táng Shū Běn Zhuàn.
Lù Jī visited Wǔzǐ,
who had several dou of goat cheese placed in front,
pointing and saying to Lù:
"What in Jiāngdōng can rival this?"
Lù said:
"We have water shield soup from a thousand lǐ away,
only it hasn't been seasoned with salted fermented beans yet."
Contemporaries considered this a famous retort.
From Shì Shuō.
Sūn Chuò planted a pine tree in front of his studio,
Gāo Shìyuǎn, then a neighbor,
said to Sūn:
"This young pine tree,
is not without its delicate charm,
but it will never be of use as a beam or pillar."
Sūn replied:
"Even if maple and willow trees grow thick enough to embrace,
what use are they?"
From Shì Shuō, part one.
A guest asked Chén Jìfāng:
"What virtues and achievements does your esteemed father have,
to bear such a great reputation under heaven?"
Jìfāng said:
"My father is like a cassia tree,
growing on the slopes of Mount Tài.
Above, it has the immense height of ten thousand rèn,
below, the unfathomable depths of the abyss;
above, it is moistened by sweet dew,
below, nourished by spring waters.
At such a time,
how can one know the height of Mount Tài,
the depth of the spring waters,
or whether there are merits and virtues or not?"
From Shān Shuō.
Cross-referenced under "Father" category.
Wèi Jiè met Ruǎn Zhān,
teasing him:
"With one word, one can be summoned to office;
why need three?"
Ruǎn said:
"If one is renowned throughout the land,
they can be summoned without a word;
why rely on even one?"
From Wèi Jiè Bié Zhuàn.
Collection
Responding as smoothly as turning a circle.
From Dù Shī.
This dynasty
Wáng Jīnggōng, when first participating in governance,
looked down upon the court as if no one was there;
one day,
during a dispute over new policies,
he glared at the officials and said:
"You all sit here without having read books."
Zhào Qīngxiàn alone refuted him:
"You are mistaken;
in the times of Gāo Yáo and Qì,
what books were there to read?"
Jīnggōng fell silent.
From Shào Shì.
In Jìn, Xiè Tiǎo oversaw official selections in the Ministry of Personnel,
when a person named Tán requested an official post,
Tiǎo said:
"Duke Huán of Qí extinguished the state of Tán;
how can there be you?"
The reply was:
"The son of Tán fled to Jǔ,
hence there is your servant."
From Dīng Yònghuì's Zhī Tián Lù.
Classics
Using clever speech to deal with others,
often incurs dislike.
From Lúnyǔ Gōngyě Cháng.
Masters
Exhausted by the knowledge of the hundred schools,
and the debates of numerous mouths.
From Zhuāngzǐ Qiūshuǐ.
Strength sufficient to resist enemies,
eloquence enough to gloss over faults.
From Zhuāngzǐ Dào Zhí.
Zhào's Gōngsūn Lóng
engaged in debates on hardness and whiteness, similarity and difference.
From Xúnzǐ Hòu Xù.
Histories
When rhetoric surpasses reason,
one will ultimately be defeated.
From Tōngjiàn Zhōu Jì.
Words sufficient to conceal wrongs.
From Shǐjì Yīn Jì.
Reversing words and altering phrases,
yet forming elegant compositions.
From Liú Xiàng's Shuō Yuàn.
Dù Zhōu served as a history official in the Court of Judicial Review,
a guest said: "You administer justice for the empire,
yet do not follow the three-foot law,
but solely base judgments on the emperor's intentions."
He replied: "Where does the three-foot law come from?
What previous rulers affirmed was recorded as statutes,
what later rulers affirmed was elaborated as edicts;
what is appropriate at the time is followed,
why adhere to antiquity?"
From Xī Hàn Běn Zhuàn.
Using sophistry to harm others.
From Xī Hàn Zhào Wáng Péngzǔ Zhuàn.
Sūn Chǔ wished to live in seclusion,
said to Wáng Jì: "I want to pillow on stone and rinse my mouth with stream water."
But mistakenly said: "Rinse stone and pillow on stream."
Jì said: "One cannot pillow on a stream,
nor rinse with stone."
Chǔ said: "The reason for pillowing on the stream
is to wash my ears;
the reason for rinsing with stone
is to sharpen my teeth."
From Jìn Shū Běn Zhuàn.
Liáng's Xiāo Chēn, drunk at an imperial banquet, lay down;
Emperor Wǔ threw a date at Chēn,
who then took a chestnut
and threw it back,
hitting the emperor squarely in the face.
The emperor said: "Do you have an explanation for this?"
He immediately replied: "Your Majesty bestowed upon me a red heart (date),
how dare I not repay with trembling (chestnut)?"
From Nán Shǐ.
Cross-referenced under "Líng Jì".

Yīn Hào said to Sūn Ānguó: "Don't be a stubborn-mouthed horse."
From Shì Shuō.

Skilled at clever but deceptive speech.

so everyone feared his tongue,

One heart with a hundred tongues, how chaotic!

who never had an elder brother,
was slandered as having stolen his sister-in-law;
Dìwǔ Bóyú married three orphaned women,
yet the world accused him of "beating his father-in-law";
this is like listening for an echo where there is no sound,

an extreme form of false accusation.

_Book of Jìn_ .
Xíng Shào was skilled in writing,
and when nobles in Luòyáng received appointments,
many relied on Shào to draft their gratitude memorials.
Once, a newly appointed noble,
with Yuán Fān and Shào both present,
Fān assumed the host had entrusted him to write the declination memorial,
but Shào was ordered to compose it instead.
Fān was displeased,
and often told others:
"That Xíng youngster,
hired to write memorials,
even buys yellow paper himself to write and deliver them."
_Book of Later Wèi_ .
Previously, in the examination for virtuous and capable candidates,
Lǐ Zōngmǐn, Niú Sēngrú, and Huángfǔ Shí gave very forthright responses,
and upon grading their papers,
all ranked third.
Powerful officials resented their criticism and,
along with those who failed the exam,
annotated their responses,
collectively spreading slander.
_Book of Táng_ .
Historical records
mention that Wèi Wénhóu ordered Yuè Yáng to lead troops,
attack Zhōngshān,
and capture it after three years.
Upon Yuè Yáng's return,
when discussing merits,
Wénhóu showed him a chest full of slanderous letters.
_Later Narratives of the Spring and Autumn Period_ .
Cross-reference "Showing Intent to Others."
Collected sayings
Jade turns to stone,
pearls become gravel,
all due to slander.
_Discourses Weighed in the Balance_ .
Accumulated slander melts bones.
From Jiāng Yǎn's letter.
Barking at Yáo, slandering Shùn.
_Collection of Yán Gōng_ .
Even great sages like the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius,
faced slander from Guǎn and Cài earlier,
and Shū Xiàng later.
Pí Rìxiū.
Masters
Adjusting one's cap and gown,
maintaining a solemn expression,
and remaining silent all day with a humble demeanor—
such is the lowly scholar of Zǐxià.
． _Xúnzǐ, Critiquing Twelve Masters_ .
A person who speaks little
is like a woman without adornment.
． _Huáinánzǐ, Explanations of Mountains_ .
History
Tied the bag and said nothing.
． _Western Hàn, Biography of Gōngsūn Hè_ .
If speaking of ruler and minister,
one should remonstrate;
if of friends,
there should be mutual critique.
How can one, knowing it will not succeed,
merely wilt, bite one's tongue,
and fold hands to follow the crowd?
． _Eastern Hàn, Biography of Mǎ Yuán_ .
Concealing the truth, sparing oneself,
like a silent cicada in cold.
． _Eastern Hàn, Biography of Dù Mì_ .
The emperor frequently made demands,
and ordered the regional commands
not to let the chancellor know.
Lǐ Bì heard of this,
felt distressed but dared not speak.
． _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Táng Dynasty, Dézōng's Reign_ .
Mǎ Yǐnsūn served as Vice Minister of the Secretariat,
and people of the time called him "Three Not Opens"—
meaning his mouth, seal, and door.
． _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Five Dynasties, Gāozǔ's Annals_ .
Cross-reference "Holding Position Without Merit."
During the thorough investigation of King Yīng of Chǔ's case,
Investigating Censor Hán Lǎng said: "Returning home,
though I do not speak,
I look up at the ceiling and sigh in secret."
． _Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Later Hàn_ .
Collected sayings
Gagged mouth and rolled-up tongue.
From Jiāng Yǎn's letter.
If honest words are not spoken,
all states remain sealed.
Yuán Cìshān.
Not outspoken like Zhōu Shě,
but accommodating like Hú Guǎng.
From Xú Líng's _Letter to Yáng Zūnyǎn_ .
Sparing oneself by not speaking,
looking up at the ceiling and sighing in secret.
From Lǐ Shēnzhī's writings.
Classics
Bantering, frolicking, laughing, and mocking.
． _Book of Songs, Zhòng Fēng_ .
Skilled at jesting,
yet not crossing into cruelty.
． _Book of Songs, Qí Ào_ .
Masters
Àizǐ saw an old woman in mourning clothes weeping bitterly,
and asked: "Whose wife are you?"
She replied: "Péng Zǔ's."
Àizǐ said: "Péng Zǔ lived eight hundred years before dying,
surely not a short life,
so you need not regret."
The woman said: "But there is one who lived nine hundred years and hasn't died yet—
wouldn't that be regrettable?"
_Àizǐ_ .
Àizǐ saw a creature at sea,
round and flat,
with many legs,
and called it a mantis shrimp.
Another, slightly smaller,
he called a crab.
Then another,
similar to the previous ones,
but much smaller,
he called a crayfish.
Àizǐ remarked: "Truly, one crab is worse than the last."
Same as above.
Living in seclusion, amusing oneself with the world,
adapting to the times without encountering trouble—
is this not the essence of wit?
_Yángzǐ_ .
History
Words subtly hitting the mark
can also resolve disputes.
． From Simǎ Qiān's "Preface to the Biographies of Jesters".
Chǔ's Yōu Mèng once used jokes to satirize and advise.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ had a beloved horse that died,
He ordered his ministers to mourn it,
wishing to bury it with the rites of a senior official, including inner and outer coffins.
Those around him argued against it,
but he wouldn't listen.
Mèng entered the palace gate,
looked up to the sky and wailed loudly: "With Chǔ's grandeur,
what could it possibly lack?
To bury it with the rites of a senior official
is too meager—I request it be buried with the rites of a sovereign."
The King asked, "How so?"
He replied, "I propose a jade-carved inner coffin,
a patterned catalpa outer coffin,
with nán and camphor woods for the burial mound.
Mobilize soldiers to dig the tomb,
the elderly and weak to carry the earth,
have Qí and Zhào envoys accompany in front,
Hán and Wèi guard the rear.
Sacrifice a grand offering at the temple,
and bestow a fief of ten thousand households."
． From "Records of the Grand Historian: Biographies of Jesters".
Qín Èr Shì wanted to lacquer the city walls,
Yōu Zhān,
a dwarf entertainer of Qín,
said: "Excellent! Lacquered smooth and vast,
enemies couldn't climb it."
But then added, "It's easy to lacquer,
just hard to build a drying room for it."
Èr Shì laughed at this.
Same as above.
Qín's Chūlǐzǐ,
witty and clever,
was called the "Wisdom Sack" by the people of Qín.
From "Records of the Grand Historian".
Dōngfāng Shuò
was a master of wit.
． From "Eulogy in the Western Hàn Annals".
Shuò deceived the dwarfs, saying,
"The Emperor finds you useless to the state,
unable to farm as well as others,
incapable of governing in office,
unsuited for military service against enemies,
of no benefit to the nation,
just consuming food and clothing,
so he plans to kill you all."
The dwarfs were terrified.
． From "Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò in Western Hàn".
For wit,
there were Dōngfāng Shuò and Méi Gāo.
． From "Eulogy for Gōngsūn Hóng et al. in Western Hàn".
Dōngfāng Shuò said,
"The dwarfs are over three chǐ tall,
receiving one bag of grain,
and 240 coins.
I, Shuò, am nine chǐ tall,
also getting one bag of grain,
and 240 coins.
The dwarfs are stuffed to death,
while I'm starving to death."
The Emperor laughed heartily.
． From "Main Biography in Western Hàn".
Initially,
when Cáo Cāo attacked and slaughtered Yè City,
the Yuán family suffered many abuses,
and Cáo Cāo's son Cáo Pī privately took Yuán Xī's wife, Zhēnshì, for himself.
Kǒng Róng then wrote to Cáo Cāo, stating,
"King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
and gave Dájǐ to the Duke of Zhōu."
Cáo Cāo, puzzled, later asked which classic this came from?
He replied,
"Judging by today's events,
I assumed it must have been so."
Later, when Cáo Cāo campaigned against Wūhuán,
Róng mocked him again:
"The great general campaigns far away,
desolate beyond the seas.
Once Sùshèn didn't offer tribute arrows,
and Dīnglíng stole Sū Wǔ's cattle and sheep—
both cases can be settled together."
． From "Biography of Kǒng Róng in Eastern Hàn".
Once, Xí Zàochǐ and Sūn Chuò were walking together.
Chuò, straightforward and fond of teasing,
was ahead when he turned and said to Zàochǐ,
"After washing and sifting,
the pebbles come last."
Zàochǐ retorted,
"After winnowing and tossing,
the chaff is in front."
From "Book of Jìn".
Also under "Mutual Undercutting".
Xiè Ān initially cherished a desire to retire to the Eastern Hills.
Huán Wēn noticed the herb yuǎnzhì among medicines
and asked Xiè, "This herb is also called xiǎocǎo.
Why does one thing have two names?"
Before Xiè could answer,
Cānjūn Hǎo replied,
"When rooted, it's yuǎnzhì (high ambition);
when sprouted, it's xiǎocǎo (little grass)."
Xiè looked quite ashamed.
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World".
Dèng Ài stuttered,
often repeating "Ài, Ài."
Emperor Wén of Jìn teased,
"How many Àis is 'Ài Ài'?"
Dèng replied,
"Fèng xī, fèng xī—
still one phoenix."
Huán Xuān and Yīn Zhòngkǎn were exchanging perilous phrases.
Huán said,
"Washing rice on a spearhead, cooking over a sword tip."
Yīn said,
"A centenarian climbing a dead branch."
Gù Kǎizhī added,
"Placing a baby on a well's windlass."
A cānjūn present said,
"A blind man on a blind horse,
midnight at a deep pool's edge."
Yīn exclaimed, "Intimidating!"
Because Zhòngkǎn had a blind eye.
Both from the same source.
Shěn Zhāolüè was wildly eccentric.
Seeing Wáng Yuē, son of Wáng Jǐngwén, he said,
"You're Wáng Yuē,
so why so fat and foolish?"
Yuē retorted,
"You're Shěn Zhāolüè,
so why so thin and mad?"
Zhāolüè laughed loudly,
"Thin beats fat,
mad beats foolish."
From "Book of Sòng".
Hé Chéngtiān was appointed Editor,
already old at the time,
while his assistants were all young from famous families.
Xún Bózǐ mocked him,
often calling him "wet nurse."
From "Book of Sòng".
Military Commissioner Lǐ Zhōngchén, during an audience,
was told by Emperor Dézōng,
"Your ears are large,
a sign of nobility."
Zhōngchén replied,
"I've heard donkey ears are large,
dragon ears small.
My ears may be big,
but they're donkey ears."
The Emperor was amused.
From "Book of Táng".
Lǐ Tāo loved humor
and was unconcerned with appearances.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Zhōu Shìzōng".
Féng Dào was witty and clever.
． From "Comprehensive Mirror: Zhōu Tàizǔ Annals".
Biographical records:
Xú Huì loved drink,
Shěn Chuánshī loved food.
Yáng Sìfù remarked,
"Xú's lungs,
Shěn's spleen—
truly at ease!"
From "Forest of Sayings".
Lǐ Bái teased Dù Fǔ with a poem:
"On Fànkē Mountain, I met Dù Fǔ,
wearing a bamboo hat in the midday sun.
Asked why he'd grown so thin since we parted,
he said it's all from laboring over poetry."
From "Solutions to Music Bureau Poems".
The Master said,
"The multitude are bustling and merry,
as if partaking of the Great Sacrifice,
as if ascending a terrace in spring."
． From "Laozi: Abandon Learning and Have No Sorrows Chapter".
Mèngzǐ said:
"A gentleman in governing may keep people at a distance,
how could he assist every single person?"
． From "Mencius: Lilou II".
Harmonizing with things to create spring.
． From "Zhuangzi: The Great and Venerable Teacher".
Duke Āi inquired about governance,
the Master replied:
"The most urgent matter in governance
is nothing greater than
making the people prosperous and long-lived.
Reduce labor services and lighten taxes,
then the people will prosper;
promote ritual teachings and keep them from crime,
then the people will enjoy longevity."
The Duke said:
"I wish to implement your words,
but fear my state would become poor."
The Master said:
"A benevolent gentleman
is like the parent of the people.
Never has there been a case where children are wealthy while parents remain poor."
From "The School Sayings of Confucius".
Zǐlù governed Pú for three years.
When Confucius entered the territory,
he praised its excellence three times,
saying:
"Upon entering his territory,
I see fields completely transformed,
wastelands well cultivated,
and irrigation channels well maintained.
This shows his reverence and trustworthiness,
thus his people exert their full effort.
Entering his city,
walls and tiles are solid and complete,
trees are luxuriant.
This shows his loyalty and leniency,
thus his people are not deceitful.
In his court,
all is tranquil and orderly,
subordinates follow commands.
This shows his clear judgment in speech,
thus his governance causes no disturbance."
Same as above.
Someone said:
"In governance,
punish first, then instruct."
The reply was:
"Does heaven bring autumn before spring?"
Shì Huì commanded the central army,
and the bandits of the Jìn state
fled to Qín.
. From "Zuǒzhuàn, Xuāngōng 16th Year".
Zǐ Tàishū was in charge of governance,
unable to bear harshness and thus lenient,
leading to many bandits in the Zhèng state.
. From "Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāogōng 20th Year".
Zǐ Chǎn said: "Governance is like farming,
thought of day and night.
Think of its beginning and achieve its end,
act upon it morning and evening.
Actions should not exceed thoughts,
just as farming has its boundaries.
Then mistakes will be few."
. From "Zuǒzhuàn, Xiānggōng 25th Year".
Zhào Xuānzǐ of Jìn was in charge of state affairs,
established regulations,
corrected laws and penalties,
opened up judicial proceedings,
supervised fugitives,
reformed old corruptions,
restored ritual ranks,
continued regular duties,
and promoted the滞留 talents.
After completion,
he presented them to Grand Tutor Yángzǐ and Grand Preceptor Jiǎ Tuó,
to be implemented throughout the Jìn state,
as the permanent law.
. From "Zuǒzhuàn, Wéngōng 6th Year".
Bó Qín was enfeoffed in Lǔ,
and reported on governance after three years.
Tàigōng was enfeoffed in Qí,
and reported on governance in five months.
. From "Shǐjì, Lǔ Shìjiā".
Zǐ Chǎn governed Zhèng,
the people could not deceive him;
Zǐ Jiàn governed Shànfù,
the people could not bear to deceive him;
Xīmén Bào governed Yè,
the people dared not deceive him.
Among these three, whose talent and ability
was the most worthy?
The "Suǒyǐn" says: "Zǐ Chǎn governed Zhèng,
benevolent and discerning,
so people did not deceive him;
Zǐ Jiàn in governance,
serene, only playing the qin,
transformed the area without leaving his hall in three years,
so people could not bear to deceive him;
Xīmén Bào used authority to transform customs,
so people dared not deceive him."
. From "Shǐjì, Guójì, Xīmén Bào Biography".
Duke Zhōu said: "Governance,
if not simple and easy,
the people will not be close.
Plain and easy to approach the people,
the people will surely turn to it."
. From "Shǐjì, Lǔ Shìjiā".
None did not crane their necks to observe his governance.
. From "Shǐjì, Qín Jì".
Zǐ Chǎn served as prime minister for one year,
youths stopped frivolous play,
the elderly no longer carried burdens.
Children did not plow near boundaries.
In the second year,
markets had no inflated prices.
In the third year,
lost items were not picked up on the road.
In the fourth year,
farming tools were not returned (as they were not lost).
In the fifth year,
scholars had no records of misconduct,
mourning periods were observed without orders.
. From "Shǐjì, Xúnlì Zhuàn".
Governor Wú Gōng of Hénán,
his governance was the best in the land.
. From "Shǐjì, Jiǎ Shēng Biography".
Zhào Guǎnghàn was the Capital Governor,
summoned a local chief to the western border,
who jokingly said: "When you reach the office,
give my many thanks to Lord Zhào."
When the chief arrived,
after Guǎnghàn finished questioning him,
he said: "The border chief sent words to thank me,
why didn't you convey the greeting?"
The chief kowtowed and admitted it was true.
His ability to uncover hidden crimes was godlike,
all similar to this.
From "Qián Hànshū".
Huáng Bà was the Governor of Yǐngchuān,
once sent an honest official to observe people's affairs,
warning him to be thorough and not leak.
The official left,
dared not stay at post stations,
ate by the roadside,
where a bird snatched his meat.
Later, when the official returned,
Bà saw him,
welcomed and consoled him,
saying: "Very hard on you.
Eating by the roadside,
and having your meat stolen by a bird."
The official was greatly shocked,
thinking Bà knew all his movements,
dared not hide the slightest in his reports.
From "Qián Hànshū".
Hán Yánshòu governed Zuǒ Féngyì,
where brothers disputed over land.
Yánshòu closed his door to reflect on his faults,
leading the disputing family to blame each other,
the two brothers deeply regretted,
shaved their heads, bared their shoulders to apologize,
yielding the land to each other,
never disputing again till death.
Thereafter, no one dared bring lawsuits lightly.
From "Qián Hànshū".
Cross-reference to "Silent Influence" section.
Féng Yěwáng and his brother Féng Lì had similar governance, praised in a folk song: "Great Féng Jūn, little Féng Jūn,
brothers succeeding one another in continuity.
Wise and knowledgeable, benefiting officials and people,
governance like Lǔ and Wèi, virtue equally spread,
even Duke Zhōu and Kāng Shū resemble these two lords."
From "Qián Hànshū".
Cross-reference to "Brothers" section.
Zhāng Chǎng was the Capital Governor,
faced with many thieves in the market.
Chǎng summoned several thief chiefs,
questioned and reproached them,
then pardoned their crimes,
ordering them to capture other thieves to redeem themselves.
A chief said: "If summoned to the office now,
other thieves might panic,
we wish to be temporarily appointed as officials."
Chǎng made them all officials,
sent them back to rest,
set up a feast,
where all the thieves came to congratulate,
each getting drunk,
and the chiefs marked their robes with red dye.
Red dye,
is red clay.
Officials sat in the neighborhoods,
inspecting passersby for red stains,
arresting them immediately,
capturing hundreds in one day,
all punished according to law,
hence the market had no more thieves.
From "Qián Hànshū".
Cross-reference to "Fighting Poison with Poison" section.
Huáng Bà was the Governor of Yǐngchuān,
vigorously promoted education,
and only then imposed punishments.
Lenient outwardly but discerning inwardly,
won the hearts of officials and people,
his governance was the best in the land.
. From "Qián Hànshū, his biography".
Officials and people praised him incessantly.
. From "Xī Hànshū, Zhào Guǎnghàn Biography".
Good governance brings harmony immediately,
like drumbeats matching the drumstick.
. From "Xī Hànshū, Lǐ Xún Biography".
Xuē Xuān brought order wherever he served,
becoming a model for officials of the time.
. From "Xī Hànshū, his biography".
Wáng Zūn was the Capital Governor,
comforting the poor and weak,
suppressing the powerful.
. From "Xī Hànshū, his biography".
Gōng Suì governed Bóhǎi,
where people carried swords and knives,
he made them sell swords to buy oxen,
sell knives to buy calves,
saying: "Why carry oxen and calves on your belt!"
. From "Xī Hànshū, his biography".
Jiǎ Cóng was the Governor of Jiāozhǐ,
praised in a street song: "Father Jiǎ came late,
making us rebel first.
Now seeing peace and clarity,
officials dare not take bribes!"
. From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Língdì纪".
Dù Jī was in Hédōng for sixteen years,
often ranked top in the land.
. From "Tōngjiàn, Hàn Xiàndì纪".
Zhāng Jiànfēng governed with leniency and discipline,
not sparing anyone from the law,
so his subordinates both feared and admired him.
. From "Tōngjiàn, Táng Dézōng纪".
Hóu Bà was the Grand Governor of Huáipíng,
renowned for capable governance.
Gēngshǐ sent an envoy to summon him,
the people, old and young, wept together,
blocking the envoy's cart or lying on the road,
all saying: "We beg Lord Hóu to stay one more year."
From "Hòu Hànshū".
Jiǎ Cóng was the Governor of Jìzhōu,
where tradition had escort carriages with triple horses,
hanging red curtains,
welcoming at the border.
When Cóng took office and mounted the carriage,
He said: "A regional inspector should observe broadly and listen widely,
investigating both merits and faults.
How can one lower the carriage curtains to isolate oneself?"
He then ordered his driver to raise them.
All cities trembled at his reputation,
and those with hidden misdeeds
fled upon hearing of him, resigning their official seals.
(Book of the Later Hàn)
Fàn Shào served as magistrate of Jùnyí.
Two men were disputing over silk
in the market.
He adjudicated by having them split it equally.
After they left,
he sent someone to secretly observe them,
noticing one appeared pleased while the other angered.
Thus he apprehended them,
and they confessed their crime.
(Book of the Later Wèi)
The alarm drum remained silent.
(Dǒng Xuān of the Eastern Hàn)
Zhuō Mào served as magistrate of Mì County.
Neighboring counties and prefectural officials considered him incompetent.
The Hénán governor appointed an acting magistrate,
yet Zhuō continued governing calmly.
After several years,
his moral influence spread widely,
with no one picking up lost items on the road.
(Yuán Hóng's Records of the Hàn)
Yán Dǔ served as capital governor,
governing with leniency and benevolence.
Previously,
Biān Fèng held the position
and was also renowned for ability.
Local people said:
"First came Zhào Guǎnghàn, Zhāng Chǎng,
respected Wáng Zhāng and Wáng Jùn."
Wáng Yǎn served as Yuánchéng magistrate,
engaged in philosophical discourse all day,
yet county affairs remained orderly.
(Book of Jìn biography)
Cáo Shū served as Línzī magistrate.
Prison held death-row inmates.
At year's end,
he pitied them:
"You unfortunate souls facing death,
while others celebrate the New Year -
wouldn't you wish to briefly see your families?"
The prisoners wept:
"If we could return temporarily,
we'd die without regret."
He released them all from prison.
Officials strongly objected,
but Cáo said:
"Though these are common folk,
they won't betray my trust.
I take full responsibility."
On the appointed day,
all returned together,
astonishing the entire county.
(Book of Jìn)
Xiàhóu Kuí served as Yùzhōu governor.
His elder brother Dǎn previously held the post,
both showing kindness.
People sang:
"Elder brother first, younger brother after,
governing with excellence."
(History of the Southern Dynasties)
Cross-reference "Brothers" section.
Fù Yǎn's father Sēngyòu served as Shānyīn magistrate,
renowned for capability.
Fù Yǎn served as Wùkāng magistrate,
both earning fame.
Both counties called them "Fù Sages",
people saying the Fù family had "county governance manuals".
(History of the Southern Dynasties)
Kǒng Yǐ served as senior clerk,
prone to drunkenness.
When drunk,
he'd remain unconscious for days.
Yet he understood governance clearly,
making impeccable judgments when sober.
All said:
"Lord Kǒng drunk twenty-nine days monthly
surpasses ordinary people sober twenty-nine days."
Fù Yǎn served the Qí dynasty
as Shānyīn magistrate.
Two villagers disputed a chicken.
He asked each what they fed it.
One said millet,
the other beans.
He had the chicken cut open,
found millet inside,
and convicted the bean-claimant.
(History of the Southern Dynasties)
Sòng Shìliáng served as Qīnghé governor,
skilled in administration.
Peach trees grew in prison yards,
weeds filled the compounds.
Daily the court stood empty,
with no litigants,
called the "Divine Gate".
When his successor arrived,
an elderly man approached weeping:
"I'm ninety years old,
have seen thirty-five administrations,
but you, governor, not only governed well,
were utterly incorruptible.
Now we lose a worthy,
how shall we manage?"
All clung to his carriage weeping.
(History of the Northern Dynasties)
Liú Kuàng served as Píngxiāng magistrate,
seven years in office,
achieving great moral transformation.
Prisons grew weeds,
courtyards could host bird nets.
(History of the Northern Dynasties)
Gāo Qiānzhī served as Héyīn magistrate.
Someone filled a bag with rubble,
claiming it was money,
cheated a horse trader,
and escaped.
An arrest order was issued.
Gāo had a prisoner shackled
in the horse market,
announcing him as the cheat.
Secretly he sent agents to observe whisperers.
Two men met,
rejoicing:
"No more worries!"
Arrested and interrogated,
the whole gang was captured.
(History of the Northern Dynasties)
Long-standing villains and crafty schemers restrained themselves.
(Táng History: Liú Qīchǔ biography)
Cuī Xián transferred to Shǎnzhōu,
serving as inspector.
Daily he drank heavily with guests and staff,
seldom sober.
At midnight he handled affairs,
decisions precise and brilliant,
without the slightest error.
Clerks called him divine.
(Táng History)
Zhāng Yǔnjì served as Wǔyáng magistrate.
A Yuánwǔ man left his cow with in-laws,
it bore over ten calves.
When retrieving it,
the in-laws refused.
Zhāng had the man bound and hooded,
taken to the in-laws,
claiming they caught a cow thief.
He ordered all cows produced
to identify their origin.
The unsuspecting in-laws quickly said:
"This is our son-in-law's cow,
we're not involved."
He immediately removed the hood,
saying:
"Very well,
return this cow to its owner."
(Táng History)
Liǔ Zhòngyǐng served as capital governor,
governing with strict clarity.
Later as Hénán governor,
he governed with leniency.
When questioned about inconsistency,
he replied:
"The capital requires control,
local governance needs nurturing."
(Táng History)
Cross-reference "Adapting to Circumstances".
Cuī Yǎn served as Tángzhōu governor,
governing leniently,
not flogging anyone for months.
In Èzhōu,
he enforced strict laws,
showing no mercy.
Same source.
Cross-reference same.

Jì knelt in apology,

He immediately impeached Jì,

The Governor of Hénán, Bù Yí,

Wú Shù was appointed magistrate of Wǎn,

Shù said: "Petty villains and corrupt elements,

The illustrious general holds a high command,
should honor the virtuous and good,
to remedy court deficiencies.
Since I sat in attendance,
I haven't heard you praise a single worthy person,
but mostly entrust matters to the wrong people,
which I truly dare not heed."
Jì fell silent, displeased.
Shù arrived at the county,

Thereupon, his subordinates, sensing his intent,

Liǔ Gōngchuò served as the governor of the capital.
When Gōngchuò first went to his office,
a junior officer of the Divine Strategy Army galloped on horseback and charged through his procession.
Gōngchuò halted his horse,
and had the officer beaten to death with a staff.
The next day,
when he went to the court at Yányīng Hall to answer,
the emperor looked very angry,
questioning him about the unauthorized execution.
He replied: "It was within your subject's duty to have him beaten;
it was not necessary to memorialize."
The emperor said: "Then who should have memorialized?"
He replied: "His own army should have memorialized.
If he died in the main street,
the Jīnyǔ street patrol should have memorialized.
If within a ward,
the left or right patrol should have memorialized."
The emperor had no way to blame him.
After he left,
the emperor said to his attendants: "You all must be careful;
I too am in awe of this man."
. Tōngjiàn Táng Xiànzōng Jì.

Zhāng Yìzhī and his brother both held high ministerial ranks,
yet they always feared Jǐng.
They vacated a seat and bowed to Jǐng, saying:
"You are the foremost person,
why are you in a lower seat?"
"Continued Shì Shuō".
Wáng Dūn long harbored rebellious intentions,
but feared Zǔ Tì,
and dared not act.
"Book of Jìn, Liú Kūn's Biography".
Xiè Ān wanted Wáng Xiànzhī to inscribe the plaque for the Tàijí Hall,
but found it difficult to say directly.
He tested him by saying:
"During the Wèi period, the plaque for the Língyún Hall was not yet inscribed,
and the craftsmen mistakenly nailed it up.
It couldn't be taken down,
so they had Wéi Zhòngjiāng write on it while suspended on a ladder."
Xiànzhī discerned his intent,
and said sternly:
"Zhòngjiāng was a high minister of Wèi;
how could such a thing happen?
If it were so,
it would show that Wèi's virtue was not long-lasting."
Thus, he did not press him further.
"Book of Jìn, Xiànzhī's Biography".
Cross-reference "Having Integrity".
Wáng Dūn always feared Zhōu Yǐ,
and whenever he saw Yǐ,
his face would flush hot.
Even in winter,
he couldn't stop fanning his face and hands.
"Book of Jìn, Zhōu Yǐ's Biography".
Liáng's Gù Xié was pure and upright from youth,
with strong will and integrity.
When he first served as Commandant of Justice,
in midwinter,
he wore thin clothing.
The Chief Minister of the Court, Cài Fǎdù, wanted to give him his padded coat,
but feared his stern integrity,
and dared not speak of it.
He told others:
"I wish to give my coat to Gù Láng,
but Gù Láng is hard to provide for in terms of clothing and food,"
and ultimately dared not offer it to him.
"His Biography".
Fàn Shūsūn helped the poor and aided the needy;
the village honored his righteous deeds,
and no one called him by his name.
"Book of Sòng".
Sīkōng Tú resided in Wángguān Valley;
when bandits passed through,
though they committed atrocities elsewhere, they alone did not enter his area,
and scholars relied on him for refuge.
"Táng Dynasty Biography".
Emperor Míng once hunted in the imperial park;
if music was played too extravagantly,
he would immediately look at his attendants and ask:
"Does Hán Xiū know?"
"Book of Táng".
Lái Tián recaptured Héluò in the north,
repeatedly crushing enemy formations.
When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
the bandits called him "Lái the Iron-Chewer."
"Minor Táng History".
Lǐ Língyào occupied Biànzhōu,
blocking all public and private wealth and taxes,
yet only Guō Zǐyí's sealed funds,
when passing through his territory,
he dared not detain,
but instead provided armed escort.
Such was the awe he commanded even among jackals and wolves.
"Old Book of Táng, Guō Zǐyí's Biography".
Duàn Xiùshí served as Prefect of Jīngzhōu;
for three or four years,
the Tǔbō dared not invade the frontier.
"Book of Táng".
When Huáng Cháo rebelled,
Zhèng Qǐ was Prefect of Lúzhōu;
he issued a proclamation not to violate his prefecture.
Cháo restrained his troops,
and the prefecture alone remained intact that year.
When Cháo left,
a surplus of a thousand strings of coins
was stored in the treasury.
Later, other bandits never touched Prefect Zhèng's money.
"His Biography".
Powerful relatives and influential officials were subdued.
"Wèi Zhēng's Biography".
Biographies
All four seats changed their expressions because of this.
"Shì Shuō" Part I.
Liú Zhěng lived extravagantly at home,
and told people:
"Gauze and crepe are my everyday wear."
But when Cài Zǐ was present,
he felt uneasy all day.
"Cài Kè's Separate Biography".
Collection
Spies dared not peek eastward,
camels and horses dared not graze southward.
"Inscription for King Zhāo's Stele".
A thousand chariots stopped at his thatched hut.
Zuǒ Tàizhōng's "Ode to Wèi".
I shall cleanse my ears
to listen to your jade-like words.
"Seven Exhortations".
All four seats recoiled in awe.
Dù's Poem.
Distant tribes knew of the true Hàn minister,
vying to kneel and behold his dignified form.
Liú Bīnkè.
Cáo Cāo dared not advance rashly with his strong army,

all due to the influence of that minister.
Shàng Chí, "Stele for Marquis Wǔ of Zhūgě".
Cunning officials startle at the falcon,

Liú Chángqīng.
The entire gathering felt a chill of awe.
Liú Chā's Prose.
The traces of Cuī and Xǔ are not forgotten,
a thousand years bowing to their legacy.
Same as above.
Relatives and guests viewed him anew,
servants felt fresh respect.
"Táng Wén Cuì".
When the gray eagle stands alone,
evil birds dare not fly.
Same as above.
The Three Dukes dared not treat him as a subordinate.
"Táng Wén Cuì".
The sun and moon shine within an inch of heart—
without seeking or deceiving others,
Fàn Zhòngyān was stationed in Yán'ān,

for this young Fàn
Yōng
has tens of thousands of armored soldiers in his breast - he is not like the elder Fàn who could be deceived."
From "Records of Words and Deeds of Five Dynasties".
When Sīmǎ Wēngōng served as chancellor,
the Liáo people instructed their border officials,
saying:
"The Central Plain has Sīmǎ as chancellor now,
be careful not to cause trouble
or create border conflicts." From "The Spirit Way Stele of Wēngōng".
When Wén Lǜgōng was at court,
the Khitan envoys Yēlǜ Yǒngchāng and Liú Xiāo came on a diplomatic mission.
As the envoys entered for audience,
they saw the duke in the hall,
halted outside the gate,
and changed their expressions, saying:
"Is this Wén Lǜgōng?
This is what they call one who conquers others with virtue."
From Sū Dōngpō's "Record of the Hall of Virtue and Power".
Fù Qīnzhī wanted to meet Chén Shīdào,
knowing he was extremely poor,
so he carried gold to give him.
But when he saw his appearance
and heard his discourse,
he ultimately dared not bring it up.
From "The Dàoqīng Collection".
The treacherous and the flattering,
their courage broken and bones startled.
From "Ōuyáng's Collection".
When the young men in the village heard the sound
of his coughing,
they would often flee and hide.
If they couldn't hide in time,
they would bow their heads in fear and shame.
Línchuān.
Bristling his beard and striking the table,
he routed the petty villains;
hearing his name and seeing his image,
already made the wicked tremble with fear.
Dōngpō.
The unkind dare not approach his wall,
the unjust dare not pass his gate.
Same as above.
Stark as autumn frost and summer sun,
not to be treated lightly.
From "The Dōngpō Collection".
All along, a stick of incense
reverently offered to Zēng Nánfēng.
From Chén Hòushān's poem.
His great virtue now stands as our elder.
From Chén Hòushān's poem.
Zǐ
Mèngzǐ said:
"As for what I wish,
it is to learn from Confucius."
From "Mencius - Gōngsūn Chǒu".
When the Master walked, I walked;
when the Master hurried, I hurried;
when the Master ran, I ran.
From "Zhuāngzi - Tián Zǐfāng" chapter.
Yán Chánghé once looked up to the Master,
Zhèng Kǎofǔ often admired Yǐn Jífǔ,
and Prince Xīsī frequently emulated Zhèng Kǎofǔ.
From "Yángzǐ - Learning and Conduct".
The rituals and righteousness of dress and conduct,

I wish to follow Zǐ Zāng's example,
so as not to fail in integrity."
． From "Zuǒzhuàn, Xiānggōng 14th Year".
Between Yān and Qí,
they all established shrines for Luán Bù,
called "Lord Luán's Shrine".
． From "Records of the Grand Historian, His Biography".
Cross-referenced under "Enduring Love".
Shí Qìng served as Chancellor of Qí,
the entire state of Qí admired his conduct,
and built a shrine for Chancellor Shí.
From "His Biography".
Bào Xuān was sent to the Court of the Commandant,
when doctoral student Wáng Xián
raised a banner below the Imperial Academy,
shouting: "Those who wish to save Commandant Bào, gather here!"
Over a thousand scholars assembled.
． From "Western Hàn, His Biography".
Cross-referenced under "Rescue".
Chén Zūn lived in Cháng'ān,
where court officials and noble relatives all esteemed him highly.
When governors were appointed to office,
and when local magnates from commanderies and states came to the capital,
none failed to visit Zūn's door.
Wherever he went, the gentry cherished him,
fearing they might be left behind.
． From "Western Hàn, His Biography".
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú admired Lìn Xiàngrú's character,
and changed his name to Xiàngrú.
． From "Western Hàn, His Biography".
Yáng Xióng's family was poor but he loved wine,
and there were enthusiasts who brought wine and food

From "History of the Former Hàn".
From east of the Hángu Pass onward,
none did not crane their necks hoping to befriend him.
． From "Western Hàn, Biography of Zhū Jiā".
Guō Línzōng was caught in the rain,
and one corner of his headscarf got soaked and drooped;
people then intentionally folded one corner of their scarves,
calling it the "Línzōng scarf".
Such was the admiration he received.
． From "Eastern Hàn, His Biography".
Zhāng Bà was widely read in the Five Classics,
and students like Sūn Lín, Liú Gù, Duàn Zhù admired him,
all buying houses near his,
to study with him.
From "History of the Later Hàn".
Lǐ Yīng was aloof by nature,
and rarely socialized.
Fán Líng from Nányáng sought to be his disciple.
Xún Shuǎng once visited Yīng,
and took the role of his carriage driver;
upon returning,
he joyfully said:
"Today I finally got to drive for Lord Lǐ!"
Such was the admiration he received.
Ibid.
Cài Yōng believed that the classics had long been distant from the sages,
with many textual errors,
so he personally wrote on steles,
had craftsmen carve them outside the Imperial Academy,
and later scholars all took them for correction.
When the steles were first erected,
those who came to view and copy them
filled the streets with over a thousand carriages daily,
blocking the roads.
． From "Eastern Hàn, His Biography".
Scholars who received his reception
were said to have "ascended the dragon's gate".
． From "History of the Later Hàn, Biography of Lǐ Yīng".
Cross-referenced under "Admiration".
Zhuó Mào was benevolent and tolerant by nature,
and though fellow villagers and old acquaintances might differ in conduct or ability,
they all loved and admired him joyfully.
． From "Eastern Hàn, His Biography".
Ruǎn Xiū, styled Xuānzǐ,

Wáng Dūn and others pooled money for his marriage;

Those who admired him at the time
sought to contribute but couldn't.
From "History of the Jìn".
Cross-referenced under "Marriage".
Xiè Ān was naturally skilled at the Luòyáng scholars' recitation style.
Having a nasal ailment,
his voice was husky.
Eminent figures loved his recitation but couldn't match it,
so some pinched their noses to imitate him.
． From "History of the Jìn, His Biography".
Xí Zàochǐ served as Héng Wēn's Registrar in Jīngzhōu,

From "History of the Jìn".
Xiè Kūn was Chief Clerk to Wáng Dūn.

such was the admiration he inspired.
From "History of the Jìn".
On the day Xì Chāo died,

From "Jìn Revival Records".
Táo Qián of the Jìn dynasty, as Governor of Jiāngzhōu,

Upon meeting,
they drank together cheerfully.
From "History of the Southern Dynasties".
Dúgū Xìn was Governor of Qínzhōu;

From "History of the Northern Dynasties".

Yáng Chéng was admired far and wide for his conduct,
and the tracks of those coming to study with him lined the roads.
From "Táng History".

Hè Zhīzhāng of the Táng dynasty was known for his witty conversation.
Lù Xiàngxiān,
a cousin of Zhīzhāng on his maternal side,

． From "Old Táng History, His Biography".
Lǐ Huá wrote the epitaph for Yuán Déxiù's tombstone,

From "Táng History".

For the tombstones of high officials and ministers' families,

Lú Zhīyóu was skilled in calligraphy,

From "Táng History".
Liú Yì heard that Hán Yù welcomed scholars from everywhere,

． From "Táng History, His Biography".
During the Dàlì era,

Eminent and upright scholars nationwide

From "Táng History".
Biographies

Jiāng Wěi was skilled in calligraphy,
and those who obtained his handwritten notes

From "Separate Biography of Jiāng Wěi".
After Bái Jūyì was buried at Lóngmén Mountain,

Emulating their virtue and achievements

Soaring above all officials,

Words shine like paintings,

Straight trunk a hundred xún tall,

Words akin to a brocade market,

Graceful demeanor as bright as autumn moon,

Embracing the virtues of celestial bodies,

Aura imbued with wind and clouds,
bearing the weight of sun and moon. Shěn Yuē.
Like climbing a pearl tree,
vainly admiring the glow of a carriage's radiance;
As if treading on jade fields,
unaware of the value illuminating the corridors. Suí Jiāng Zǒng.
Harmony with the Way through spiritual connection,
Huáng Shí imparting strategies of an imperial mentor;
Virtue endowed by heaven,
white clouds bestowing the essence of a jade assistant. The above all by Luò Bīnwáng.
Winning battles a thousand miles away,
achieving Lǔ Lián's merit in casual talk;
Exemplary for an era,
Guō Tài's pinnacle in human relations.
Three thousand leagues compared,
striking Shùn's sea like a swimming fish;
Ninety thousand soaring south,
gazing at Yáo's clouds with uplifted wings.
A model for a hundred generations,
overshadowing Liáng and Dòu like gathering clouds;
Prominent for a time,
towering over Yuán and Yáng like a mountain.
Words like a spring gushing afar,
startling waterfalls with flying waves;
Literary river clear and deep,
holding woven brocade and turning waves.
Flying blossoms from a phoenix nest,
adorned with five colors like dazzling flowers;
Cleansed tips in a dragon spring,
immersed in nine layers to nurture moisture.
Heart's waves deep as the Milky Way,
swimming essence in Huáng Pí;
Emotions' peaks reaching the sky,
holding wind and clouds on jī yǎn.
Sparse trunk stirring streams,
Lóngmén opening waves of bamboo arrows;
Securing earth with a horizontal base,
goose wings standing at Lotus Peak.
Rising waves bathing in light,
deep spiritual streams holding pearls;
Rising trunk touching clouds,
assisting high cliffs with towering cassia.
Jade-moist and golden-voiced,
orchid-fragrant and cassia-rich.
Hanging autumn fruits in the literary forest,
adorning spring flowers in the garden of letters.
Pure standards deep and brilliant,
shining in monthly critiques with eloquent discourse.
Simple theories condensed in mystery,
opening night-lustre in exquisite debate.
Conversations exuding fragrance,
veiling lingering aura in nine orchids;
Pen sea flowing with waves,
startling great waves in the eight rivers. The above all by Luò Bīnwáng.
Learning as rich as Yī Dùn's wealth,
writing like the music of a clear temple. Huángfǔ Shí.
Spirit towering ahead of the proud,
how could grace lag behind others? Lǐ Tàibái.
Vast and deep strategies gush like rivers and seas,
unrestrained energy rushes like wind and thunder.
Uttering words precious as pearls and jade,
writing brushes turn back wind and frost.
Spreading culture to revive declining waves,
upholding virtue to lead all human relations. All from the same author.
Young, he displayed the beauty of marsh orchids;
grown, he became a vessel of the clear temple.
In public appraisal,
all regarded him as first-rate.
Benevolent unicorn and wise dragon are auspicious for a time,
yet none match the gentleman's auspice in family bonds.
Elegant lineage from Guānxī,
refined attire from Zhàoběi capital.
Truly sounding like a Hàn chancellor,
flawless, surpassing Suí pearls.
High tone like metal and stone,
virtuous appearance like jade tablets.
Night talks and road conversations,
lute, books, and witty banter,
all flow from literary art. The above all by Liú Bīnkè.
Condensed into harmony, gathering five blessings;
released as spring, dispelling six calamities.
Nourishing oneself with filial piety and friendship,
perfuming conduct with benevolence and trust.
Words and deeds cautious and upright,
character and demeanor proper and dignified.
Solemn in ritual bearing,
a vessel of the clear temple.
Descended from heavenly harmony,
standing as a human hero.
Calmly deciding major events,
vigorously proposing extraordinary plans.
Endowed with natural nobility,
writing as the nation's splendor.
Actions rooted in source,
words without superfluity.
Standing firm without leaning,
sounding clear when struck like metal.
Dignified with a minister's bearing,
gentle and refined with a gentleman's writing.
Integrity like gold and jade,
appearance like a phoenix.
Mind vast and grand,
appearance very majestic,

Pure and lofty as golden stem dew,

Collection
Though green garments are plentiful,

Though paths may be expedient,
none surpass the straight one.
From Jìn Péi Wěi's "Admonitions for Women Historians."
Living, they are laughed at by the world;
dead, they become foolish ghosts.
From "Selected Writings."
Though the fierce tiger is said to be vicious,
it too has its companions.
Traveling in packs through deep valleys,
all beasts lower at the mere rumor of its approach.
It feeds on the yellow bear's father,
and its young devour the red leopard's fawn.
Choosing prey among bears and giant pandas,
would it deign to glance at hares and foxes?
Sleeping in the valley at broad daylight,
its eyes hold a terror that spans a hundred paces.
Proud of having no match,
its temper runs wild and unchecked.
In morning rage, it kills its own offspring;
by evening, it dines on its mate.
Companions scatter in all directions,
leaving the fierce tiger to dwell alone.
Lonely, it cries by the four sides of the door,
as crows and magpies gather to clamor around it.
Driven out, it chases monkeys into their dens,
the tiger knows not where to return.
Who says the fierce tiger is evil?
On the midway path, it weeps in sorrow.
Leopards come to seize its tail,
bears come to snatch its jaw.
The fierce tiger does not fear death,
but is ashamed of its past deeds.
If even tigers and rhinos die unaided,
how much more so someone as insignificant as you?
Therefore, trust should bind relationships,
and intimacy should be tied with personal bonds.
If even kin and old friends are not secure,
who will trust what you do?
From Hán Yù's writings.
The Qín loved extravagance and luxury,
yet each person also cared for their family.
Why then take everything to the last bit,
and spend it as recklessly as mud and sand?
Making the pillars that bear the beams
more numerous than farmers in the southern fields,
the rafters that frame the roof
outnumber the women working at looms,
the gleaming nail heads
exceed the grains in granaries,
the uneven tile seams
are more than the threads in one's clothing,
the straight railings and horizontal balustrades
surpass the city walls across the nine regions,
and the music of pipes and strings
drowns out the chatter of market-goers.
From Dù Mù's "Rhapsody on the Ēpáng Palace."
Though leaping high,

What is called reputation preceding reality,
is not only used in warfare,
but also applies to scholars.
Like those today seeking the jìnshì degree from local prefectures to the authorities,
numbering hundreds each year,
mostly composing ornate writings,
discoursing on past and present,
vying in extravagance,
striving for richness.
The authorities receive nearly ten thousand words at once,
reading less than one-tenth,
then reclining exhausted,
dizzy-eyed, unwilling to look,
mind weary, unwilling to manage.
Claiming under such circumstances not to miss talents,

Only those with prior reputation,
when their writings are read,
receive focused mind and eye,
thus rarely fail.

Masters
Confucius trapped between Chén and Cài,
went seven days without food.
Zǐgòng bought grain from villagers,
obtaining one dàn of rice.
Yán Huí and Zhòng Yóu cooked it,
when soot fell into the rice.
Yán Huí picked it out and ate it.
Zǐgòng saw this and was displeased,
thinking he had stolen food.
He entered and asked Confucius,
who said: "I have long believed in Huí's benevolence.
Even if you witnessed something,
do not doubt him.
Perhaps there is a reason?"
Summoning Yán Huí to inquire,
he replied:
"Just now soot fell into the rice.
To leave it
would be unclean;
to discard it
would be wasteful.
So I ate it."
Yán Huí left,
Confucius turned to his disciples: "My trust in Huí is long-standing,
not just today."
. "Family Sayings, In Distress" chapter.
His speech to others,
is always trusted,
like Zēng Shēn.
"Family Sayings".
Calmly as if by nature possessing it,

History
Shū Xiàng of Jìn said: "Minister Qí, in recommending externally, does not discard his enemies,
and in recommending internally, does not overlook his kin.
Would he alone leave me out?"
． From the 21st year of Xiānggōng.
Cross-referenced under "Self-confidence."
Yáng Hù and Lù Kàng faced each other across borders.
Kàng once fell ill,
and Hù sent him medicine.
Kàng took it without suspicion.
Many advised against it,
but Kàng said, "Is Yáng Hù the kind to poison someone?"
． From the "Biography of Yáng Hù" in the Book of Jìn.
The Comprehensive Mirror records: "How could he poison anyone?
That Yáng Shūzǐ!"
Gentlemen say that Qí Xī was able to recommend the worthy.
Praising his enemy
was not flattery;
establishing his son
was not favoritism;
recommending his subordinate
was not factionalism.
． From the third year of Xiānggōng in the Zuǒzhuàn.
Shè from Xiǎo Zhū came to defect with Jùyì,
saying, "If Jì Lù gives me his word,
I need no covenant, Master Jì."
Kāngzǐ said, "A state of a thousand chariots distrusts its covenants
but trusts your words—
how are you dishonored!"
． From the 14th year of Duke Āi in the Zuǒzhuàn.
The praise of a single word
surpasses the gift of embroidered robes;
the censure of a brief remark
exceeds public flogging.
． From the Preface to the Gǔliángzhuàn.
Sū Qín served as chancellor of Yān,
and the people of Yān spoke ill of him to the king.
The king grew angry, gripping his sword,
yet fed him swift steeds.
Bái Guī rose to prominence in Zhōngshān,
and the people of Zhōngshān spoke ill of him to Marquis Wén of Wèi,
yet the marquis bestowed upon him a luminous jade.
Why so?
Because the two rulers and their ministers
trusted each other with open hearts,
unswayed by empty words!
From the Records of the Grand Historian.
Gaining a hundred catties of gold
is not as good as a single promise from Jì Bù.
． From the "Biography of Jì Bù" in the Book of Hàn.
The arguments of the two Xún scholars
grew more trusted over time.
． From their biographies in the Records of Wèi.
Receiving a single letter from Lord Liú
is worth more than ten assistants.
． From the "Biography of Liú Hóng" in the Book of Jìn.
When a follower of Shàngguān Jié slandered Huò Guāng,
the emperor grew angry,
saying, "The Grand General is a loyal minister,
appointed by the late emperor to assist me.
Dare to slander him, and you will be punished."
From then on, Jié and others dared not speak again.
． From the Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Emperor Zhāo of Hàn.
When Huáng Qióng passed away,
and was about to be buried,
six to seven thousand renowned scholars from near and far gathered.
Xú Zhì went to mourn him,
offered a libation,
wept sorrowfully, and left,
unknown to anyone.
The scholars inquired at the funeral,
and the steward said, "Earlier, a scholar came,
dressed in coarse clothes, weeping bitterly—
I don't recall his name."
The crowd said, "It must be Xú Rúzǐ."
． From the Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Emperor Huán of Hàn.
The ruler of Wú granted Grand Ceremonialist Pān Jùn authority
to suppress the Wǔxī tribes.
Jùn's cousin-by-marriage Jiǎng Wǎn served as Zhūgě Liàng's chief clerk,
and Wèi Jiū reported that Jùn had secretly contacted Wǎn,
plotting to align himself.
The king of Wú said, "Chéngmíng would not do such a thing."
． From the Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Emperor Míng of Wèi.
When Páng Huǎng and others spoke ill of Gāo Jiǒng to the emperor,
the emperor grew angry,
dismissed them all,
and said to Jiǒng, "Duke Dúgū is like a mirror—

． From the Comprehensive Mirror, Suí Dynasty, Emperor Gāozǔ.
Shìmín said to Yùchí Jìngdé, "Your heart is steadfast as a mountain;

． From the Comprehensive Mirror, Táng Dynasty, Emperor Gāozǔ.
When Lǐ Wěi was appointed Minister of Revenue,

and the reply was, "Upon hearing of Lǐ Wěi's appointment,

making Wěi prefect of Luòzhōu instead.

Zhōu Tàizǔ entrusted Sū Chuò wholeheartedly,

Upon returning,

From the Comprehensive Mirror.
The "Wèi Wǔ's Strict Laws" stated: "If trouble arises in the capital,

A single word of his was valued at a thousand pieces of gold.
