Biographies
record: Duke Líng of Wèi sat with his wife one night
when they heard carriage wheels,
which stopped at the gate,
then resumed passing.
The lady said, "This must be Qú Bóyù."
The duke asked, "How do you know?"
She replied, "I have heard that according to ritual,
one should dismount at a noble's gate and salute the horses.
Now, Qú Bóyù is a worthy man—
surely he would not neglect courtesy in the dark."
The duke sent someone to check,
and it was indeed as she said.
From the Biographies of Exemplary Women.

Histories
When Lord Yè of Chǔ arrived,
someone encountered him and said:
"Why does my lord not wear his helmet?
The people of the state look to you,
as they look to loving parents.
If the arrows of bandits
should wound you,
it would cut off the people's hopes.
Why not wear your helmet?"
So he put on his helmet.
Then he met another person,
who said: "Why does my lord wear his helmet?
The people of the state look to you,
as they look forward to the harvest.
Day and night they count the days,
hoping to see your face,
for that would bring them comfort.
If the people know you are alive,
yet you cover your face,
thus cutting off their hopes,
is that not excessive?"
So he removed his helmet and advanced.
. *Zuǒzhuàn*, Duke Āi 16th year.
Bì Chén said:
"Heaven has long brought disaster upon Zhèng;
it must surely make Zǐchǎn end it,
only then can there be stability,
and peace.
Otherwise,
it will perish."
. *Zuǒzhuàn*, Duke Xiāng 29th year.
Yáng Huí went to see Zhào Jiǎn,
and said:
"I was driven out three times while living in my village,
and dismissed five times while serving a lord.
Hearing that you value scholars,
I have come to see you."

When Xiàngrú arrived,
the entire assembly was captivated.

They submitted sincerely, returning to benevolence.

When Chén Zūn made requests,

When Zhào Guǎnghàn served as Governor of the Capital,

When he was released from prison,
the markets and neighborhoods of the capital all shouted "Long live!"
Same as above.

Same as above.
Liú, Governor of Yùzhōu,

Same as before.
When the imperial carriage campaigned south,

Cross-reference "Banquets."

*Tángshū*.

one feels warm without wearing clothes."
*Sòngshū*.

*Tōngjiàn*.

all congratulated one another.

Liú Zhān served as Minister of Justice.
When Zhān was demoted,
people, whether worthy or foolish,
all felt deep regret.
When he returned,
the people of Cháng'ān's two markets

Hearing of this,
Zhān changed his route and entered by another road.
*Tōngjiàn*.
Biography

"The teeth of dogs and horses are worn out,
with neither physical strength,
nor evaluation merits.

is the profound courtesy and esteem from Your Excellency,
which I cannot bring myself to sever."

Unable to contain the feelings of a loyal dog or horse.

All rivers flow to the vast sea.

Entire villages emptying out,

Once ascending the dragon's gate,

In deep waters, fish are extremely joyful;
in dense forests, birds know to return.
By Dù Gōngbù.
Although Heaven and Earth do not seek benevolence from straw dogs,
even field ditches think of contributing their moisture to the vast ocean.

Though I am but a petty man who cherishes kindness,

Humbly staying at your gate in silence,

From Hán Yù's "Fù on Restoring Ambition".
Anxiously,
fearing only that I might not emerge from the gate of a great worthy.

Settling firmly in place,
scholars and friends gather around.

Scaly and shelled creatures revere the turtle and dragon.

Our Dynasty
Visitors from all directions
feel as if returning home,
so happy they forget to leave.
After the carriage is hitched,
even the horse looks back at its stable and neighs.
From "Collection of Dōngpō".

Sīmǎ Guāng went to the palace to mourn.

saying:

Classics
In the ceremony of audience,
the Son of Heaven does not descend from the hall to receive the feudal lords.
Descending from the hall to receive them
is a breach of etiquette by the Son of Heaven,
starting from King Yí onward.
From "Record of the Single Victim at the Border Sacrifices".
Masters
A person must first invite insult themselves,
then others will insult them;
a family must first destroy itself,
then others will destroy it;
a state must first attack itself,
then others will attack it.
From "Mencius, Lí Lóu I".
Actions can bring about disgrace.
From "Xúnzǐ, Exhortation to Learning".
History
Xiāo Chēn once attended an imperial banquet,
got drunk and slumped over.
The Emperor threw a date at Chēn,
whereupon Chēn took a chestnut
and threw it, hitting the Emperor in the face.
From "Book of Liáng".
Cross-reference "Insult and Offense".
Zhāng Xuánzǔ, at eight years old, had a missing tooth.
A senior who knew he was extraordinary
teased him, saying:
"Why has your mouth opened a dog hole?"
He replied:
"Just so that people like you can come out from it."
From Liú Zhāo's "Biographies of Young Children".
Cross-reference "Wit and Insight".
Liú Dàozhēn, caught in turmoil by the river,
was pulling a boat himself.
He saw an old woman shucking rushes,
and said to her:
"Woman, why don't you adjust your loom and shuttle deftly instead of shucking rushes?"
The woman replied:
"Man, why don't you mount a horse and wield a whip instead of pulling a boat?"
From Péi Qǐqī's "Forest of Conversations".
Cross-reference "Women's Words".
Our Dynasty
When Sūn Hào was defeated by the Jìn,
Emperor Wǔ asked Hào:
"I hear southerners like to compose 'you-and-thou' poems."
Hào said:
"Once I was your neighbor,
now I am your subject.
I offer you a cup of wine,
may you live ten thousand springs."
From "Talks on Poetry Past and Present".
Classics
Weeding out confusion and disorder,
cutting away flowery language,
lifting the great guiding principles,
extracting the essential points,
sufficient to establish teachings for posterity.
From "Preface to the Classic of Documents".
Studying deeply and pondering thoroughly,
extensively examining the classics and texts,
gathering various sayings
to establish commentaries and traditions.
Condensing the text and elaborating the meaning,
expounding and clarifying its intent,
hoping it may be of some benefit to the future.
Same as above.
Confucius returned to Lǔ from Wèi,
whereupon the music was corrected and the Yǎ and Sòng each found their proper place,
then he edited the "Shī" and finalized the "Shū",
appended commentaries to the "Zhōu Yì",
and composed the "Chūnqiū".
Mencius withdrew from Qí and Liáng,

all galloping like thoroughbreds for a thousand miles,
raising their hooves in unison and racing side by side.
From Wèi Wéndì's "Discourse on Literature".
Literary compositions are a grand undertaking for governing the state,
an eternal and magnificent endeavor.
Lifespans have their inevitable end,
glory and pleasure cease with one's body,
both bound to a fixed term,
unlike literature, which is boundless.
Thus, ancient writers
immersed themselves in ink and brush,
expressing their thoughts in books and records,
relying not on the words of skilled historians,
nor on the influence of rapid advancement,
yet their fame naturally passed down to posterity.
Ibid.
The essence of literature is one, but its branches differ: memorials and proposals should be elegant,
letters and discourses should be reasoned,
inscriptions and eulogies value sincerity,
poetry and rhapsodies aspire to beauty;
these four categories differ,
and those skilled in them are often specialized;
only the comprehensively talented can master all forms.
Literature is primarily governed by qì (vital force),
which has its substance in clarity and turbidity,
and cannot be forced into being.
Analogous to music,
though the melodies may be uniform,
and the rhythms follow the same measure,
the breath control varies,
with inherent skill or clumsiness,
so even among fathers and brothers,
it cannot be transferred to sons or younger brothers.
From Wèi Wéndì's "Diǎn Lùn".
Poetry follows emotion and is ornate,
rhapsodies embody objects and are lucid.
Stele inscriptions blend elegance with substance,
eulogies are poignant and sorrowful.
Inscriptions are concise and gentle,
admonitions are rhythmic and vigorous.
Odes are leisurely and richly adorned,
discourses are subtle and clear.
Memorials are calm and refined,
persuasions are brilliant and deceptive.
From Lù Jī's "Wén Fù".
In grasping ideas, it values cleverness,
in employing words, it prizes beauty.
To place a brief phrase in a crucial position,
is the alerting whip of the entire piece.
Though all words may be orderly,
they must rely on this to achieve effect.
Ibid.
Xiàngrú excelled in descriptive language,
Zhòngxuǎn took qìzhì as his style.
From "Xuǎn Fù Xù".
Resplendent as embroidered brocade,
poignant as dense strings.
From Lù Jī's "Wén Fù".
Earthenware and gourd instruments differ,
yet both provide aural delight;
embroidered patterns vary,
but all serve as visual pleasures.
From Liáng's "Zhāomíng Wénxuǎn".
Chén Sī's literary works,
are like having Zhōu Gōng and Confucius in human relations,
the qílín and phoenix among scales and feathers,
shēng and yú pipes in music,
or intricate embroidery in women's work.
If Confucius's gate were to judge by poetry,
then Gōnggàn would ascend the hall,
Sī Wáng would enter the chamber,
while Pān and Lù could only sit in the corridors.
Liú Zhēn's literary style originated from "Ancient Poetry".
Relying on qì and loving the unusual,
his works often shock and awe.
His steadfast bones defy frost,
his lofty style transcends the vulgar.
But his qì surpasses his refinement,
regrettably lacking in polished elegance.
Yet, from Chén Sī downward,
Zhēn is deemed peerless.
From Zhōng Róng's "Shī Píng".
From Qū Yuán and Sòng Yù onward, writers
based their works on sorrow and beauty,
striving for exaggeration and fantasy,
losing the essence of bǐxìng (comparison and evocative imagery).
From "Liǔ Miǎn Jí".
With the rise of the Sāo poets, excessive beauty flourished,
and literature split from teaching into two.
From Liǔ Miǎn's "Lùn Wén".
Sitting as if forgotten, walking
as if lost, solemn
as if in deep thought, vast
as if bewildered? When drawing from the heart
and pouring it out by hand,
one must strive to eliminate clichés,
how gratingly difficult it is!
From Hán Wéngōng's writings.
It must originate from oneself,
not plagiarizing a single word or phrase from predecessors,
and how difficult that is!
It must encompass benevolence and righteousness,
its richness like nurturing all things,
possessing the capacity of the sea and the burden of the earth,
unrestrained and free-ranging,
without rigid structure,
yet naturally conforming without the need for carving or shaping.
From Hán Wén's "Fán Zōngshī".
In antiquity, words were necessarily one's own,
but later generations, unable to do so,
resorted to plagiarism.
Later ones pointed to earlier ones, openly imitating,
from the Hàn dynasty to the present, all following the same pattern.
From Hán Wén's "Epitaph for Fán Zōngshī".
Cross-reference "plagiarism".
A dragon-patterned cauldron weighing a hundred hú,
its weight borne by the strength of the brush alone.
From Hán Wén's poetry.
The Son of Heaven said: "The writings of Wáng Mǒu,
are most suited for proclamations,
possessing an ancient style."
From Hán Wén's "Stele for Wáng Chōngshū".
Cross-reference "opportunity".
In composing essays,
they overflow and accumulate,
profound and boundless without shore.
From Hán Wén's "Epitaph for Liǔ Zǐhòu".
In the Hàn dynasty, everyone could write,
but only Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, the Grand Historian, Liú Xiàng, and Yáng Xióng were the best.
Thus, those who delve deeply
gain fame that endures.
If one merely floats with the times,
without establishing oneself,
even if not scorned in their era,
they will surely not be remembered by posterity.
From Hán Wén's "Letter to Liú Zhèngfū".
Peaceful and harmonious tones are bland,
while sounds of sorrow and thought are exquisite.
Joyful and pleasant words are hard to perfect,
but expressions of hardship and suffering easily excel.
Therefore, literary compositions
often emerge from sojourners and the rustic wilds,
whereas nobles and dignitaries,
content and fulfilled,
unless naturally inclined and fond of it,
have no leisure to engage in it.
From Hán Wén's "Preface to the Poetry Exchange of Jīngtán's Péi Jūn and Yáng Píng".
To be recorded in the annals of literature,
influencing later generations.
Gazing loftily among all things,
standing majestically through the ages.
From Liǔ's "Letter on Literature".
Hailed as a "master of literature".
From Liǔ's "Letter to Yáng Píng".
The fēnggǔ (wind and bone) of Hàn and Wèi,
was not transmitted to Jìn and Sòng.
Qí and Liáng poetry competed in ornate brilliance,
but xìngjì (evocative imagery and allegory) was entirely lost.
From "Chén Zǐ'áng Jí".
Scholars who maneuvered adeptly in the literary arena
could none match or compare to him.
From Liǔ Wén's "Preface to Poetry Exchange".
Literature has two paths:
one of rhetoric and judgment,
rooted in authorship;
the other of guidance and admonition,
rooted in bǐxìng.
The stream of authorship
originates from the "Councils" and "Instructions" in the "Shū",
the "Images" and "Appendices" in the "Yì",
the "Recording" and "Editing" in the "Chūnqiū";
its essence lies in grandeur and substance,
with upright words and complete reasoning,
deemed fit for preservation in archives.
The stream of bǐxìng
stems from the songs of Yú and Xià,
the "Fēng" and "Yǎ" of Shāng and Zhōu;
its essence lies in beautiful norms and clear resonance,
with fluent speech and elegant meaning,
deemed fit for circulation in ballads and chants.
These two,
examining their intents,
diverge and do not align.
Liǔ Zǐhòu wrote the "Preface to Collection of Evaluator Yáng".
Before the Shāng and Zhōu dynasties,
writing was simple and rustic;
from the Wèi and Jìn onward,
it became unrestrained and decadent.
Achieving the mean in this,
was the Hàn dynasty.
By the Eastern Hàn, it had declined.
Liǔ Zǐhòu wrote the "Preface to Classified Writings of the Western Hàn".
Those revered by Hán Tuìzhī,
were Sīmǎ Qiān and Yáng Xióng.
Between Qiān and Tuìzhī,
they were indeed comparable.
As for someone like Xióng,
works such as "Tài Xuán", "Fǎ Yán",
and "Four Sorrows Fu",
Tuìzhī simply hadn't composed them;
had he certainly written them,
they would have been even more magnificent and extraordinary.
As for his other writings,
they far surpassed Xióng's.
Xióng's writing in diction and conception,
is rather constrained and stagnant,
not like Tuìzhī's wild and uninhibited flow.
Liǔ's "Letter in Reply to Hán Gě".
Consult the Gǔliáng Commentary,
to sharpen its vigor;
consult Mèngzǐ and Xúnzǐ,
to smooth its branches;
consult Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozǐ,
to unleash its origins;
consult the "Guóyǔ",
to broaden its interests;
consult the "Lí Sāo",
to attain its profundity;
consult Grand Historian's records,
to highlight its purity.
Liǔ's writings.
The writings of the Sāo poets,
are works of venting indignation,
often self-praising,
quite arrogant in demeanor;
the writings of Xiàngrú and Zǐyún,
are works of indirect admonition,
forming their own school,
yet lacking upright spirit;
the writings of Jiǎ Yì,
are works of transformative culture,
elaborating on the ways of emperors and kings,
vividly clear before the eyes;
the writings of Sīmǎ Qiān,
are works of structured accomplishment,
galloping through thousands of years,
as if with energy to spare;
the writings of Dǒng Zhòngshū and Liú Xiàng,
are works of comprehensive scholars,
elucidating classical arts,
exhaustively exploring heaven and humanity.
Péi Dù's "Letter to Lǐ Áo".
The difference in writing,
lies in the height of its spirit and style,
the depth of its thought and conception,
not in fragmenting phrases and sentences,
or abandoning rhythm and rhyme.
Same as above.
Writing is like a thousand troops and ten thousand horses,
yet with wind calm and rain cleared,
silent without human sound,
this is probably what is meant.
Lǐ Déyù's "On Writing".
Writing as an entity,
is of natural ethereal energy,
arriving indistinctly,
coming without deliberate thought.
Lǐ Déyù's "On Writing".
The eight tones communicate with governance,
and writing rises and falls with the times.
The writing of the Three Dynasties,
declined by the Warring States period,
revived through the Qín and Hàn;
Hàn writing,
declined by the era of divided states,
revived with the rise of Táng.
When governance becomes chaotic and land splits,
the energy of the three lights and five peaks divides,
the great sound is incomplete,
thus it must mix before unifying.
Liú Bīnkè's "Preface to Liǔ's Writings".
The Táng stabilized the realm,
swiftly demonstrating with culture.
The sounds of Sháo and Yīng music intermingled with war drums.
Thus, those who rose to high ministers through writing,
Wèi Wénzhēn became prominent through remonstrance,
Mǎ Gāotáng rose through wisdom and strategy,
Cén Jiānglíng became known for literary refinement,
without the toil of founding chaos or battlefield merit,
yet met with appointments above the meritorious officials.
How Táng valued writing!
Same as above.
Gaining the words of student Dǒng,
ethereal like grasping a jade screen,
floating on layered waves,
what meets the eye and ear,
are not things of the mundane world,
also like bright gold and gathered feathers,
obtained from distant,
borders—how could one not treasure them?
His words very concise yet profoundly flavorful,
with long vigor as the trunk and writing as the branches.
Rhapsodies, edicts, memorials, petitions, songs, dedicatory notes, inscriptions, and proclamations of merit,
like a great bell startling the ear,
a jade zither cleansing the bone,
moving the lungs and liver,
making every hair stand on end.
Painting scenes to transform,
shining brilliantly over the regions,
like ethereal mist and auspicious wind,
adorning all things.
Observe how he issues virtuous words to bless the people,
abundantly like timely rain,
praises elder statesmen and instructs the meritorious,
solemnly like the seasonal winds,
the edict appointing a chancellor harmonious and dignified,
the proclamation appointing a general clear and resolute.
All above seen in "Collection of Liú Bīnkè".
Lǐ Bái could not even reach his outer fences,
let alone the inner hall!
Yuán Zhěn wrote "Epitaph for Dù Zǐměi".
Since the Jiànwǔ era,
writing declined and substance was lost.
Vying with flowers and contending leaves,
upside-down styles became the vogue.
Until my brother did it with thought,
moving ghosts and gods.
Stripping away the embellishments,
he grasped the root.
Uniting the strange and startling,
driving waves and surging clouds.
The style of the "Six Classics",
cut off yet renewed.
Scholars have a guide to return to,
greatly transforming writing.
Lǐ Áo's "Eulogy for Hán Yù".
Two hundred years after Confucius passed away,
the Sāo poets emerged,
whereupon the method of graceful beauty and empty extravagance prevailed.
Two hundred years after the rise of Hàn,
Jiǎ Yì and Sīmǎ Qiān stood as giants,
modeling rites and music,
possessing the demeanor of mature elders;
peers like Chángqīng and Zǐyún,
with myriad marvelous and bizarre changes,
were also extraordinary scholars.
Pity that their words for lords and nobles,
drowned in frivolous rhetoric and lacked prominence.
Thereafter, Bān, Zhāng, Cuī, Cài, Cáo, Liú, Pān, Lù,
followed the wave and wrote,
though falling short of great elegance,
yet their legacy and remaining influence,
still held classical form.
From Sòng and Qí onward,
it became haggard,
meandering and declining,
flowing into decadence,
until Xú and Yǔ,
heaven seemed about to destroy this culture.
Later scholars like Shàngguān Yí emerged in succession,
whereupon the way of the "Fēng" and "Yǎ",
was swept clean from the ground.
Táng Lú Cángyòng's "On Writing".
Biographies and records
Yáng Xióng said:
"During military campaigns,
urgent dispatches and proclamations employ Méi Gāo;
within court halls,
elevated writings and grand documents employ Xiàngrú."
Records of the Western Capital.
Yǔ Xìn, upon moving from the Southern Dynasties to the North,
admired only the "Stele of Hánshān Temple" composed by Wēn Zǐshēng.
Someone asked Yǔ Xìn, "How is the North?"
He replied, "Only the stone tablet of Hánshān
is worth conversing with;
the rest are like the braying of donkeys and barking of dogs."
Yùquánzǐ.
Zhèng Yì often taught his son using the Literary Selections,
his elder brother said, "Why not teach him to read the Classic of Filial Piety and the Analects,
to prevent him from imitating Shěn Yuē and Xiè Tiǎo,
mocking the wind and chanting the moon,
tainting one's conduct?"
Outer History: Táowù.
See also "Teaching Children."
Táng's Zhāng Jiǔlíng once perused Sū Tíngshuò's literary collection,
and told his colleagues:
"Sū's brilliance and richness are unmatched,
truly a commanding general in the literary battlefield."
The emperor ordered Yú Shìnán and forty others to select literary works,
from the Songs of Chu to the Daye era,
compiling a collection of five thousand volumes,
titled the Comprehensive Collection of Literary Works,
and selected two thousand skilled calligraphers as imperial scribes,
to copy the texts.
Records of the Southern Court's Splendors.
Now, literary writings
originate from the Five Classics.
Edicts, commands, strategies, and proclamations stem from the Book of Documents;
prefaces, narratives, discussions, and debates stem from the Book of Changes;
songs, chants, rhapsodies, and recitations stem from the Book of Songs;
sacrificial rites, elegies, and eulogies stem from the Rites;
memorials, petitions, admonitions, and inscriptions stem from the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Court regulations and military oaths
spread benevolence and righteousness,
illuminate merits and virtues,
govern the people and establish states—
they cannot be absent even briefly
(some versions say "serve many purposes").
As for cultivating one's nature,
reciting leisurely,
savoring the flavors,
it is also a joyful pursuit.
If one has energy to spare,
then one may practice it.
Yet since ancient times, many literary men have fallen into frivolity: Qū Yuán displayed his talent and promoted himself,
exposing his ruler's faults;
Sòng Yù, with his handsome appearance,
was treated like an entertainer;
Dōngfāng Shuò was humorous but lacked elegance;
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú stole wealth and had no integrity;
Wáng Bāo erred in writing the Servant Contract;
Yáng Xióng's virtue faltered with In Praise of the New;
Lǐ Líng surrendered and was disgraced among barbarians;
Liú Xīn wavered during Wáng Mǎng's reign;
Fù Yí aligned himself with the powerful;
Bān Gù plagiarized his father's history;
Zhào Yuánshū's memorials were excessively confrontational;
Féng Jìngtōng was ostracized for his flashiness;
Mǎ Jìliáng was ridiculed for his flattery;
Cài Yōng was executed for association with evil;
Wú Zhì defamed his hometown;
Cáo Zhī was rebellious and broke the law;
Dù Dǔ was insatiable in borrowing;
Lù Cuì was extremely narrow-minded;
Chén Lín was indeed crude and careless;
Fán Cān lacked restraint by nature;
Liú Zhēn was stubborn and sent to hard labor;
Wáng Càn was rash and disliked;
Kǒng Róng and Mí Héng died due to their arrogance and eccentricity;
Yáng Xiū and Dīng Yì met their ends for stirring trouble;
Ruǎn Jí breached etiquette and corrupted morals;
Jī Kāng met a violent end for belittling others;
Fù Xuán was dismissed for contentiousness;
Sūn Chǔ was boastful and overbearing;
Lù Jī courted danger by defying authority;
Pān Yuè risked peril for greed;
Yán Yánnián was dismissed for his haughtiness;
Xiè Língyùn was empty-headed and disrupted order;
Wáng Róng brought disaster upon himself as a troublemaker;
Xiè Tiǎo incurred wrath for his insolence.
All these individuals,
being the most outstanding,
cannot all be recorded,
but the general picture is as such.
Family Instructions of the Yán Family.
In writing literary works,
it is like riding a fine steed:
though it may have unbridled spirit,
one must control it with the reins,
lest it strays from the path
and dashes recklessly into pits and banks.
Literature should take reasoning and intent as its heart and kidneys,
tone and style as its bones and sinews,
content and allusion as its skin,
and elegance as its crown.
Nowadays, traditions passed down
chase the trivial and abandon the essential,
mostly being flashy and ornate.
When form competes with substance,
form prevails and substance is buried;
when content vies with talent,
content overwhelms and talent diminishes.
The unrestrained drift aimlessly and forget to return;
the forced patch up endlessly and never suffice.
With customs as they are,
how can one alone resist?
Just strive to avoid excess.
Ibid.
Shěn Yuē said: "Literature should follow three easinesses: easy to understand the references,
first;
easy to recognize the characters,
second;
easy to read and recite,
third."
Ibid.
Pheasants are colorful but soar only a hundred paces,
for their flesh is heavy and strength sinks;
eagles and hawks lack brilliance but fly high to the sky,
for their bones are strong and spirit fierce.
Literary talent and strength are similar.
If there is vigor but lacks ornament,
it is like hawks gathering in the literary grove;
if there is ornament but lacks vigor,
it is like pheasants scurrying in the garden of letters;
only when both brilliance and soaring height combine
can it be the crying phoenix of literature.
The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons.
Memorials, petitions, reports, and discussions
should aim at classical elegance;
eulogies, praises, songs, and poems
should model clarity and beauty;
tallies, proclamations, letters, and dispatches
should exemplify clarity and decisiveness;
historical commentaries, prefaces, and annotations
should follow thoroughness and conciseness;
admonitions, inscriptions, steles, and eulogies
should embody breadth and depth;
linked pearls and seven-style rhapsodies
should engage in skill and beauty.
This is adapting the form to establish momentum,
succeeding through adaptation to change.
Although they may interconnect and overlap,
and the rhythm and ornament vary,
they are like brocade of five colors,
each based on its inherent hue.
Ibid.
Literature follows learning,
but ability lies in natural talent.
Thus talent emerges from within,
while learning is acquired externally.
Some have ample learning but meager talent,
others abundant talent but poor learning.
Those poor in learning struggle with content and allusion,
those meager in talent labor over expression and emotion—
this is the difference between inner and outer.
The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons.
Since the Warring States period, writers composing texts
falsely set up hosts and guests,
feigning exchanges and replies.
Generalities on History.
What is called literature
is not merely holding scrolls at Confucian doors,
wielding brushes for the splendor of ink,
but values the profundity of creation and the richness of ritual and music.
Lù Jǐng's Classics and Edicts.
Since the decline of the Liáng dynasty,
the way of belles-lettres was lost,
level tones and rising tones
were particularly avoided at the time.
Parallel phrases and paired diction
became盛行 in common practice.
Generalities on History.
Poetry includes Wèi Mèng's "Satirical Admonition" rhapsody,
Zhào Yī's "Resentment of Evil" piece,
then Jiǎ Yì's "Discourse on Faulting Qín,"
then Bān Biāo's "On the Mandate of Kings,"
Zhāng Huá's admonition for the female historian,
Zhāng Zǎi's inscription on the Sword Gate,
Zhūgě Liàng's memorial on launching a campaign,
Wáng Chǎng's family letter admonishing his son,
Liú Xiàng and Gǔ Yǒng's memorials,
Cháo Cuò and Lǐ Gù's policy responses,
Xún Bózi's impeachment writings,
Shān Táo's official petitions—
all these words became models of conduct,
serving as mirrors for the world.
Generalities on History.
Zhào Mù emulated Lǐ Hè in composing short songs,
said to be like embroidering with gold thread,
leaving no trace of seams.
Collected Sayings.
Shěn Guāng wrote the "Rhapsody on the Music of Dòngtíng Lake,"
Wéi Xiù said:
"This rhapsody is a symphony of palace melodies."
From "Records of Hearsay from North of Meng"
Collection
When writing is flawed, then it becomes extraordinary;
without extraordinariness, it cannot startle the vulgar.
Lù Guīméng.
His writings,
trample Yáng and Mò on barren ground,
and crush Shì and Lǎo in uninhabited realms.
Pí Rìxiū's "Petition for Hán Yù to Be Honored in the Temple."
Mysteriously, like a soaring dragon,
luxuriantly, like a leaping tiger or phoenix,
resoundingly, like the music of Sháo and Jūn,
bright as sunlight, pure as jade.
． Lǐ Hàn wrote the "Preface to Hán Yù's Collected Works."
His writings
never imitate the words of predecessors,
yet naturally stand alongside them.
From the end of the Zhèngyuán era,
scholars of later generations
with aspirations for ancient-style prose
all regarded him as their model.
Hán Yù's biography.
He savors the ancient and encompasses the modern,
without boundaries or limits,
vast and boundless,
impossible to fully discern.
And when he is in full creative flow,
with swift brushstrokes and bold characters,
strangeness bursts forth across the page,
like whales crashing or spring's splendor,
astounding the world.
Yet, intricate and subtle,
with well-arranged chapters and fitting sentences,
so refined and capable,
it reaches the point of entering the divine and emerging from the heavens.
"Epitaph for Hán Wéngōng."
Between the Liáng and Chén dynasties,
writings mostly did no more than mock wind and snow,
or chant of flowers and grass.
"Collected Works of Bái Jūyì."
Writing is like warfare:
with the first drum, spirit is roused;
with the second, it wanes;
with the third, it is exhausted.
Ibid.
Clear sorrow and pure beauty,
quiet joy, ancient elegance,
all attain the fragrance of orchids,
the plumage of phoenixes.
Pí Rìxiū.
Intertwining clouds and mist
cannot match its grace;
the far-reaching flow of water
cannot match its sentiment;
the vibrancy of spring
cannot match its style;
sailing ships in wind and horses in battle array
cannot match its courage;
clay coffins and inscribed tripods
cannot match its antiquity;
seasonal flowers and beautiful women
cannot match its color;
deserted capitals and crumbling palaces,
overgrown mounds and hilltop graves,
cannot match its sorrow and regret;
whales sucking and tossing,
ox-headed ghosts and snake-bodied spirits,
cannot match its emptiness and fantastical absurdity.
Dù Mù.
Yān Gōng's writing
is like the branches and trunk of a fine wood,
constructing a great hall,
with beams above and eaves below,
nurturing an aura,
able to alter yīn and yáng,
and endure cold and heat,
seating the Son of Heaven and receiving feudal lords;
like ritual bells and drums,
sheng pipes and chime stones,
with adorned stands and feathered banners,
arranged in palace suspension,
fit to serve deities,
and honor ancestral temples.
Lǐ Běihǎi's writing
is like red-feathered arrows and black armor,
stretching across the plains,
like wind, like clouds,
with fierce beasts and tigers,
thundering drums,
truly fearsome.
Jiǎ Chángshì's writing
is like a tall hat and ornate hairpin,
dragging robes and jingling jades,
standing in the court,
speaking only according to law,
fit to be regarded as wings,
and modeled for its righteousness.
Lǐ Yuánwài's writing
is like a golden carriage and jade chariot,
carved dragons and colorful phoenixes,
externally painted,
graspable, yet internally,
its substance remains unweakened.
Dúgū Shàngshū's writing
is like perilous peaks and sheer cliffs,
piercing the sky,
with tall pines and strange rocks,
tumbling into streams and gorges,
yet somewhat lacking harmony,
so those of refined virtue avoid it.
Yáng Yázhōu's writing
is like a newly built long bridge,
iron cavalry crossing at night,
majestic and fierce,
startling to the heart and ears,
yet when drums sound,
often cautious to gentlemen.
Quán Wéngōng's writing
is like a grand red-door mansion,
imposing and spacious,
with corridors and storerooms,
windows and doors all complete,
yet it cannot offer new vistas or superior views,
to make people gaze in awe.
Hán Lìbù's writing
is like the autumn Yangtze, pouring down,
a single course for a thousand miles,
with raging winds and turbulent waves,
muddy flow never stagnating,
yet when used for irrigation,
it may sometimes fall short.
Lǐ Xiāngyáng's writing
is like night geese in Yān market,
or dawn cranes in Huátíng,
their cries startling to hear,
yet talent and strength are both scant,

The Classic

From "Shī Xù".
To rectify gains and losses,
move heaven and earth,
affect ghosts and spirits,
nothing comes closer than poetry.
The ancient kings used it to regulate husband and wife,
fulfill filial piety and respect,
enrich human relationships,
beautify education,
and transform customs.
Thus, poetry has six principles: Fēng, Fù, Bǐ, Xìng, Yǎ, Sòng.
The superior uses Fēng to transform the below;
the below uses Fēng to admonish the superior;
through elegant language and indirect remonstrance,
the speaker is without fault,
the listener is sufficiently warned,
hence it is called Fēng.
When the kingly way declines,
ritual and righteousness are abandoned,
government and education fail,
states have different policies,
families have different customs,
then transformed Fēng and transformed Yǎ arise.
The state historians, understanding the traces of success and failure,
grieving over the abandonment of human relationships,
lamenting the harshness of punishments and governance,
chant and express their nature and emotions,
to admonish their superiors,
comprehending changing events while cherishing old customs.
Thus, transformed Fēng arises from emotion,
but stops within ritual and righteousness.
Arising from emotion
is human nature;
stopping within ritual and righteousness
is the legacy of the ancient kings.
Therefore, affairs of one state,
tied to one person's origin,
are called Fēng;
speaking of the world's affairs,
shaping the customs of all regions,
are called Yǎ.
Yǎ means
correct,
speaking of the rise and fall of kingly governance.
Governance has minor and major,
hence there are Minor Yǎ,
and Major Yǎ.
Sòng means
praising the forms of great virtue,
announcing their successes to the spirits.

Our dynasty
Shěn Yuē of the Liáng dynasty said: "There are eight poetic defects: First is píngtóu (level head),
where the first and second characters must not share the same tone with the sixth and seventh characters.
For example, in 'Jīnrì liáng yànhuì,
huān lè nán jù chén.'
'Jīn'
and 'huān'
are both level tones.
Second is shàngwěi (rising tail),
where the fifth character must not share the same tone with the tenth character.
For example, in 'Qīngqīng hé pàn cǎo,
yùyù yuán zhōng liǔ.'
Both are rising tones.
Third is fēngyāo (wasp waist),
where the second character must not share the same tone with the fifth character.
For example, in 'Wén jūn ài wǒ gān,
qiè yù zì xiūshì.'
'Jūn' and 'gān' are both level tones,
'yù' and 'shì' are both entering tones.
Fourth is hèxī (crane knee),
where the fifth character must not share the same tone with the fifteenth character.
For example, in 'Kè cóng yuǎnfāng lái,
yí wǒ yī shū zhá.
Shàng yán cháng xiāngsī,
xià yán jiǔ líbié.'
'Lái' and 'sī' are both level tones.
Fifth is dàyùn (major rhyme),
such as with the sound
'míng' as the rhyme, the preceding nine characters
must not use 'jīng', 'qīng', 'píng', 'róng'.
Sixth is xiǎoyùn (minor rhyme),
aside from the intended rhyme character,
no two characters within the verse should share the same rhyme.
For example, 'yáo' and 'tiáo' should not appear in the same line.
Seventh is pángniǔ (lateral homophones),
eighth is zhèngniǔ (direct homophones),
two characters within ten characters sharing initial consonants is zhèngniǔ,
if not from the same phonetic group but sharing initial consonants,
it is pángniǔ,
such as 'liú' and 'jiǔ' being zhèngniǔ,
'liú' and 'liǔ' being pángniǔ.
Among the eight, shàngwěi and hèxī are most to be avoided,
the other defects are also generally applicable.
From Lǐ Shū's 'Shī Yuàn' of our dynasty.

Monk Jiǎorán said: 'Poetry has four avoidances, four depths, two essentials, two abandonments, four separations, six delusions, seven perfections, and seven virtues.
Four avoidances: spirit high but not angry,
force strong but not offensive,
emotion abundant but not obscure,
talent ample but not negligent.
Four depths: atmosphere profound,
deep in structure and momentum;
conception grand,
deep in artistic execution;
use of rules fluid,
deep in tonal parallelism;
use of allusions indirect,
deep in meaningful categories.
Two essentials: essential strength complete without harshness,
essential spirit full without aggression.
Two abandonments: though wishing to abandon artifice for directness,
imaginative thought cannot be direct;
though wishing to abandon words for meaning,
classical elegance cannot be omitted.
Four separations: wishing to express emotion but separated from obscurity,
wishing to use classics and history but separated from pedantry,
wishing for lofty detachment but separated from remoteness,
wishing for dynamic movement but separated from frivolity.
Six delusions: considering emptiness and grandiosity as sublime antiquity,
considering slowness as serene elegance,
considering bizarre disparity as novelty,
considering mistaken intent as unique excellence,
considering overfamiliarity as subtlety,
considering weak spirit as ease.
Seven perfections: most perilous yet not obscure,
most extraordinary yet not erroneous,
most arduous yet traceless,
most immediate yet meaning distant,
most unrestrained yet not circuitous,
most difficult yet appearing easy,
most beautiful yet natural.
Seven virtues: understanding principle, sublime antiquity, classical elegance, romantic flair, vital spirit, substantial quality, and proper form.'
Poetry has three types of borrowing.
Borrowing language,

such as Fù Xuán's 'Rìyuè guāng tài qīng',

Borrowing meaning,

Táng's Shàngguān Yí said: 'Poetry has six parallelisms: First is zhèngmíng duì (direct name parallelism),
'Heaven-Earth', 'Sun-Moon' are examples;
Second is tónglèi duì (same category parallelism),
'Flower-Leaf', 'Grass-Bud' are examples;
Third is liánzhū duì (linked pearl parallelism),
'Xiāoxiāo', 'Hèhè' are examples;
Fourth is shuāngshēng duì (alliterative parallelism),
'Huáng huái', 'Lǜ liǔ' are examples;
Fifth is diéyùn duì (rhyming compound parallelism),
'Pánghuáng', 'Fàngkuàng' are examples;
Sixth is shuāngnǐ duì (double simile parallelism),
'Spring tree', 'Autumn pool' are examples.'
Also said:
'Poetry has eight parallelisms: First is démíng duì (exact name parallelism),
'Sending wine southeastward,
Welcoming lute northwestward.'
is an example;
Second is yìlèi duì (different category parallelism),
'Wind weaves pondside trees,
Insects bore leaf patterns.'
is an example;
Third is shuāngshēng duì (alliterative parallelism),
'Autumn dew fragrants fine chrysanthemums,
Spring breeze scents beautiful orchids.'
is an example;
Fourth is diéyùn duì (rhyming compound parallelism),
'Unrestrained in myriad thoughts,
Hesitant with a single heart.'
is an example;
Fifth is liánmián duì (continuous parallelism),
'Fading river like a ribbon,
New moon as an eyebrow.'
is an example;
Sixth is shuāngnǐ duì (double simile parallelism),
'Discussing the moon, eyebrows rival the moon,
Speaking of flowers, cheeks surpass flowers.'
is an example;
Seventh is huíwén duì (palindromic parallelism),
'Fresh feeling arises from intent,
Intent follows fresh feeling.'
is an example;
Eighth is géjù duì (alternate line parallelism),
'Yearning then remembering,
Nightly tears soak the clothes,
Vain sighs then vain weeping,
Daily you do not return.'
is an example.'

Jiǎ Dǎo one day, while riding a donkey, composed the lines: "Birds nestle in the poolside tree,
a monk knocks at the gate under the moon."
Initially, he intended to use the word "push,"
then considered using "knock,"
refining it undecidedly,
so on the donkey, he mimed pushing and knocking gestures,
unconsciously traveling half a block,
astonishing onlookers.
At that time, Hán Gōngquán was the capital governor,
known for his stern and upright demeanor,
his authority shaking the imperial roads.
As the third patrol shouted warnings,
Jiǎ Dǎo still hadn't stopped his gestures.
Suddenly, he was pushed off the donkey by officials,
and escorted before the horse,
only then did Jiǎ Dǎo realize what happened.
The governor questioned him, intending to reprimand him,
to which Jiǎ Dǎo replied fully: "I happened upon a couplet,
unsettled on perfecting one word,
my spirit wandered in the realm of poetry,
thus offending Your Excellency."
The governor remained on horseback for a long while,
pondering it,
and said to Jiǎ Dǎo:
"Using 'knock' is better."
Then he entered the government office with Jiǎ Dǎo.
Later, Jiǎ Dǎo became a monk,
changing his name to Wúběn.

History
The "Spring and Autumn Annals" is the name
of the historical records of Lǔ.
In recording events,
they link events to days,
days to months,
months to seasons,
and seasons to years.
This is how they mark distances and proximities,
and distinguish similarities and differences.
Therefore, what the historians record
must indicate the year to commence the events.
As a year has four seasons,
they alternately select these to form the name of the record.
The Zhōu rites had historiographers
in charge of affairs from the state and four quarters,
conveying the records from all regions.
The feudal lords also each had their own state histories.
Major events were written on bamboo slips bound together,
while minor events were recorded on simple bamboo or wooden tablets.
Mèngzǐ said: "In Chǔ, it is called 'Táowù',
in Jìn, it is called 'Shèng',
and in Lǔ, it is called 'Spring and Autumn Annals',
but their essence is the same."
When the virtue of Zhōu declined,
officials lost their duties,

Directly recording the events,

History
Marquis Wén of Wèi was drinking with his ministers,
enjoying himself when it began to rain.
He ordered his carriage to go to the outskirts.
His attendants said: "Today you are enjoying the wine,
and it is also raining.
Where does my lord intend to go?"
The Marquis replied: "I have an appointment with the gamekeeper to hunt;
although I am enjoying myself,
how can I fail to keep a single meeting?"
From "Comprehensive Mirror: King Wèiliè's Annals".
Fàn Shì and Zhāng Yuánbó were friends;
the two parted in the capital in spring,
setting an appointment for late autumn.
Yuánbó killed a chicken on the fifteenth of September to await him.
His mother said:
"A thousand lǐ separate you;
how can you trust him so?"
Before she finished speaking, he arrived.
From "History of the Later Hàn".
Cross-reference "Not Making Promises Lightly".

Zǐgāo traveled to Zhào,
Where he befriended Zōu Wén and Lǐ Jié.
They became close companions.
When he was about to return to Lǔ,
Wén and Jié saw him off, staying together for three nights.
At parting,
They wept until tears streamed down their cheeks,
While Zǐgāo merely raised his hand in farewell.
He said to his disciples: "At first, I thought these two were men of fortitude,
But now I see they are like women.
Are humans deer and pigs,

History
Shǎn Jiǎn governed Xiāngyáng,
where the various Xí clan gentry families of Jīngzhōu had exquisite gardens and ponds.
Jiǎn often went out for leisurely excursions,
frequently visiting these ponds.
He would set out wine and get drunk,
and at that time children sang:
"Where does Lord Shān go?
He heads to the Gāoyáng Pond.
At dusk he returns lying down in his carriage,
wearing his white hat backwards."
- From "Jìnshū Běnzhuàn".
When Shāng Hào and others ascended the South Tower,
they didn't notice Liàng's arrival,
and everyone was about to rise and avoid him.
Liàng said:
"Gentlemen, stay a while. This old man's spirits here are quite high."
Then he sat leaning against a folding chair,
chatting and reciting poetry with Hào and others.
- From "Jìnshū Běnzhuàn".
Also see "Unrestrained Behavior".

living together in Wūyī Lane,

As mentioned in Kūn's poem:
"Once we gathered in Wūyī, all were close kin."

Emperor Jiǎnwén toured the Huálín Garden,
turned to his attendants and said:
"A place that captures the heart need not be remote.
Amidst these shaded woods,
one naturally thinks of the Háo and Pú rivers,
feeling that birds, beasts, and fish
come close to people of their own accord." - From "Shì Shuō".
He ordered all officials to take ten-day breaks in spring,

From the prime minister to vice ministers,

taking turns to have them dance,
until all had enjoyed themselves before leaving.

not removing the mourning girdle.
.. From the Record: Questions and Traditions. Annotation by Mèng Kāng of the Western Hàn: "The mourning hut,
leans against the wall to the ground,
and is made without lintels or pillars."
For the mourning of parents, weeping has no set time.
. From the Record: Tán Gōng Part One.
Observing mourning for three years.
Same as above.
Gāozǐ Gāo, in mourning for his parents,
wept tears of blood for three years,
and never showed his teeth.
. From the Record: Qu Li Part One.
Yán Dīng was skilled in observing mourning.
At the beginning of death,
he was anxious,
as if seeking something but not finding it;
at the encoffining,
he looked expectantly,
as if following but not catching up;
after burial,
he sighed,
as if not returning and resting.
. From the Record: Tán Gōng Part Two.
During mourning, read the mourning rites;
after burial, read the sacrificial rites.
The Book of Rites.
Zēng Shēn asked Zēngzǐ: "When weeping for parents,
is there a constant sound?"
He said: "Like an infant on the road who has lost its mother,
how can there be a constant sound?"
. From the Record: Miscellaneous Records.
For the mourning of parents,
one does not avoid weeping when meeting others.
Same as above.
Annotation: "Utmost grief has no adornment."
Women should not bare their arms, expose their chests, beat their hearts, or leap like sparrows.
Feet should not leave the ground.
With heavy and continuous sounds,
like a collapsing wall.
. From the Record: Questions on Mourning.
For the mourning of parents by officials and scholars,
they return after the练祭 (liàn jì).
Annotation: "Return to their residence."
On the first day of the month and the anniversary of death,
they return to weep in the ancestral temple.
Annotation: The home of the clan elder.
. From the Book of Rites: Great Records of Mourning.
For the three-year mourning,
one bows in mourning.
Kowtow and then bow.
. From the Record: Miscellaneous Records.
Mourning has no rites for receiving guests.
Those in mourning do not send gifts,
but others send them.
Even wine and meat are accepted.
Confucius said: "If the body has a sore, then bathe;
if the head has a sore, then wash the hair;
if ill, then drink alcohol.
Emaciation leading to illness,
a gentleman does not do."
Also from the same source.
A gentleman, in mourning for his parents,
does not let water or gruel enter his mouth for three days,
and can only rise with a staff.
. From the Record: Tán Gōng Part Two.
During the three-year mourning,
one speaks but does not converse.
Speaking,
refers to one's own affairs.
Speaking for others is conversing.
One responds but does not inquire in the hut,
in the plain chamber,
one does not sit with others.
Unless it is the time to see the mother,
one does not enter the gate.
. From the Record: Miscellaneous Records Part Two.
Mourning does not consider residence.
Means spending on the house to serve the mourning.
Because there is no temple,
do not harm oneself to the point of danger.
Means becoming haggard to the point of losing life.
Because there would be no heirs.
. From the Record: Tán Gōng Part Two.
Mourning allows no secondary matters.
. From the Record: Royal Regulations.
Not allowing involvement in governance.
If ill during mourning,
one may eat meat and drink alcohol,
but must have the flavor of plants and trees,
meaning ginger and cinnamon.
. From the Record: Great Records of Mourning.
For the mourning of parents,
dwell in the mourning hut without plastering.
Sleep on straw and use a clod as a pillow,
and speak only of mourning matters.
Same as above.
The three-year mourning is like a cut.
. From the Record: Miscellaneous Records Part Two.
The coarse hemp mourning garment is not mended.
. From the Record: Four Regulations of Mourning Attire.
Dwelling in the mourning hut,
grieves that the parent is outside;
sleeping on straw and using a clod as a pillow,
grieves that the parent is in the earth.
. From the Record: Questions on Mourning.
A man from Biàn had his mother die,
and wept like a child.
Confucius said: "Grief is grief,
but it is hard to sustain.
Rites,
are meant to be passed on,
are meant to be sustained,
hence weeping and leaping have their measures."
. From the Record: Tán Gōng Part One.
See also "Matters should be sustainable."
Lǔzǐ asked: "During the three-year mourning, should one offer condolences?"
Confucius said: "During the three-year mourning, even after the练祭 (liàn jì),
one does not stand in groups,
nor travel together."
This is to avoid casual talk and forgetting grief.
A gentleman uses rites to express emotions;
during the three-year mourning, to offer condolences and weep,
is that not false?
. From the Record: Questions of Lǔzǐ. Annotation: "Grieving for others means not focusing on one's own;
grieving for one's parent,
then offering condolences is insincere."
Miscellaneous Records says: "During the three-year mourning,
even with lighter mourning garments, one does not offer condolences."
Those in mourning do not attend to matters unrelated to the corpse or coffin.
. Annotation from the Record: Minor Ceremonies.
If there is the mourning for a father,
as if the mourning period is not over,
and the mother dies,
when removing the mourning for the father,
wear the removal garments,
and after the event, return to the mourning attire.
. From the Record: Miscellaneous Records Part Two.
Zǐgòng asked about mourning. The Master said: "Reverence is foremost,
grief is next,
emaciation is last.
Complexion should match the emotion,
and sorrowful countenance should match the attire."
Same as above.
The bald do not bind their hair,
the hunchbacked do not bare their arms,
the lame do not leap,
the old and ill do not abstain from wine and meat,
all these are regulated by flexibility.
. From the Record: Four Regulations of Mourning Attire.
Do not harm oneself to the point of losing life,
do not use death to injure life.
For the mourning of parents,
wear the coarse hemp mourning cap, rope-tasseled hat, and straw sandals.
Same as above.
Damages the kidneys, dries the liver, scorches the lungs, and abstains from lighting fires.
From "Jì Wènsāng".
At the end of the Dàgōng mourning period,
one may cap one's son,
and marry off one's daughter.
At the end of the Xiǎogōng mourning period for one's father,
one may cap one's son,
marry off one's daughter,
and take a wife.
Even if one is in Xiǎogōng mourning oneself,
one may cap and take a wife.
When Dàgōng mourning is approaching,
avoid playing the qín and sè.
When Xiǎogōng mourning arrives,
do not cease music.
From "Jì Zájì Xià".
At the end of the Jī mourning period,
after the final wailing, resume governance.
For the nine-month mourning period,
resume governance after burial.
For Xiǎogōng and Sī mourning periods,
resume governance after the encoffining.
Same as above.
For one's wife,
if parents are alive,
do not use a staff,
and do not kowtow with the head touching the ground.
If the mother is alive,
do not kowtouch with the head touching the ground.
From "Zájì Shàng".
For the mother or wife while the father is alive.
In the nine-month mourning period,
one may eat meat and drink alcohol. In the Jī mourning period,
one may eat meat and drink alcohol,
but not enjoy it with others.
From "Jì Sàngdàjì".
What is the staff for?
It is said: "Both bamboo and tong wood are the same."
Why is it used?
It is said: "Because the filial son is physically ill and weak,
he uses the staff to support his illness.
If the father is alive,
he dares not use the staff,
because the respected one is present."
From "Jì Wènsāng".
The wailing for Zhǎncuī mourning
is like going without returning;
for Zīcuī mourning,
it is like going and returning;
for Dàgōng mourning,
it is three modulations with a drawn-out sound.
For Xiǎogōng and Sīmá mourning,
a sorrowful expression is sufficient.
From "Jì Wènzhuàn".
In Zhǎncuī mourning, one responds but does not answer;
in Zīcuī mourning, one answers but does not speak;
in Dàgōng mourning, one speaks but does not discuss;
in Xiǎogōng and Sīmá mourning,
one discusses but does not touch upon music.
In Dàgōng mourning,
one sleeps on a mat.
In Xiǎogōng mourning,
a bed is permissible.
Same as above.
When Bó Yú's mother died,
he still wailed after the mourning period had ended.
The Master heard it
and said, "Who is that wailing?"
The disciples said, "It is Lǐ."
The Master said, "Alas,
that is excessive."
Bó Yú heard this
and then ceased.
From "Jì Tángōng".
Great wounds take long to heal,
severe pain delays recovery.
The three-year mourning period
is established according to human emotion,
to express the utmost grief.
From "Jì".
Mourning garments, a rush staff, living in a hut, eating congee, sleeping on firewood, and using a clod as a pillow
are to adorn the utmost grief.
The three-year mourning period
ends in twenty-five months,
though sorrow is not fully exhausted
and longing not forgotten.
Yet the rites set this limit—
is it not because sending off the dead must have an end,
and returning to life must have moderation?
From "Jì Sānnián Wèn".
Zēngzǐ asked, "If an acquaintance is in mourning,
may he participate in sacrifices?"
Confucius said, "Even in Sī mourning, one does not sacrifice;
how much less should one assist others?"
From "Jì Lǔzǐ Wèn".
A gentleman in mourning
finds no sweetness in fine food,
no joy in music,
and no comfort in his dwelling.
From "Yǔ Yánghuò".
In mourning,
let grief be sufficient.
From "Yǔ Zǐzhāng".
When a filial son mourns his parent,
his wailing is without modulation,
his demeanor lacks grace,
his speech is unadorned,
he feels uneasy in fine clothes,
finds no joy in music,
and no sweetness in fine food—
this is the expression of grief.
After three days, he eats,
teaching people not to harm the living for the dead,
nor to destroy one's nature through excessive grief—
this is the rule of the sages.
Mourning does not exceed three years,
to show the people it has an end.
Provide a coffin, grave clothes, and shroud to enshroud the body,
set out the fǔ and guǐ vessels to express sorrow,
beat the breast, leap, and weep
to send off the deceased with grief.
Choose the burial site and inter the body peacefully.
Establish an ancestral temple
to make offerings as to a spirit;
offer spring and autumn sacrifices
to remember them in season.
From "Xiàojīng".
Zǐ
suffered calamity from Heaven,
encountered hardship and distress,
with a troubled heart and a weary body.
From "Mèngzǐ Xù".
The three-year mourning period,
the hemmed sackcloth garments,
the congee diet—
from the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
were shared by the three dynasties.
From "Mèng Téng Wéngōng Shàng".
Shǐ
grieved in heart and lost counsel.
From "Zuǒzhuàn".
Deep in mourning garments and headband.
When Qí's Yàn Huánzǐ died,
Yàn Yīng wore a rush headband, girdle, staff, and straw sandals.
Same as above,
from "Xiāng Shíqī".
To be in mourning without grief,
and to have a cheerful countenance in sorrow,
is called impropriety.
Same as above,
from "Xiāng Sānshíyī".
Severe frost falls in summer.
From Fàn Nìng's "Gǔliángzhuàn Xù".
Looked up to heaven, beat his breast, and wept tears of blood.
From "Xīhàn Lǐ Líng Shū".
Again stole a breath to live on.
From "Sānguó Wúzhì Yú Fān Zhuàn".
Wept with eyes like a bursting river.
From "Shìshuō".
Lived in a hut by the tomb, wailing and longing.
From "Tángshū Yáng Yán Zhuàn".
In one leap, three tears fell.
From "Guō Zǐyí Jiāzhuàn".
Ordered that those in Jī or Dàgōng mourning who had not completed the period
should not attend banquets.
From "Jiù Tángshū Wáng Fāngqìng Zhuàn".
Collection
Due to perilous circumstances,
I encountered misfortunes early on.
Lǐ Lìngbó's "Memorial Expressing My Feelings".
My five emotions were shaken with grief, bowing to heaven,
treading the earth as if with no place to hide.
． "Xiè Píngyuán's Memorial".
Walking in shadows, my heart mourns,
with sour nose and aching bones.
Jiāng Wéntōng's letter.
Looking up to the vast sky, unrewarded,
I lament the futile grasp of the gentle wind.
Xiè Xīyì's "Elegy for the Noble Consort of Sòng".
Weeping blood while awaiting dawn.
Rěn Fǎng's petition.
With meager salary and humble means,
I initially hoped to provide for my parents with a joyful countenance.
Personal wishes unfulfilled,
I never anticipated such calamitous punishment.
My aged father passed away,
how could my clinging and wailing reach him?
"Collection of Chén Zǐ'áng".
Your humble servant says:
"This solitary minister faced sudden disaster,
humbly received heaven's posthumous gift,
kowtowed to accept the command,
wailed until fainting, lost and confused."
Surviving breathlessly, how dare I show my face.
With a tormented heart and emaciated body.
Grieving in the mourning hut,
bearing sorrow throughout the mourning period.
Grief shatters me like brambles,
thoughts congeal in the cold springs.
All above from "Collection of Chén Zǐ'áng".
Deep pain wrenches my innards.
Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Crying for three years,
as if the bereavement just began.
Hán Yù's prose.
A hundred sorrows assail my heart,
tears and mucus streaming down.
Soul and dreams trembling,
grief piercing to the bone,
instead mourning my solitary survival.
Liú Yǔxī.
Forced by ritual not to die,
thus contracting a chronic illness.
Appealing to heaven, touching the earth,
blood staining the mourning clothes.
Also from the same source.
Guilty of heinous crimes,
unaccepted by the world.
Yet still mindful of continuing the lineage,
I dare not die immediately.
Barely sustaining my breath,
greatly fearing the lack of an heir for sacrifices,
thus disgracing your great virtue.
Liǔ Zōngyuán's prose.
The wound is vast, the pain persistent,
wailing to the high heavens.
Holding my head, drenched in tears,
kowtowing until a mound forms.
Chest sunken, eyes decaying,
spending all seasons in the hut.
Plants wither and die,
birds and beasts falter.
Different tribes and species,
also share in the sorrow.
Liǔ Zōngyuán's "Inscription for the Gate of Filial Piety".
Heart turned to ashes, body defiled,
weeping tears of blood continuously.
Under the pines and catalpas,
my life remains but a remnant.
Rather than living on in loneliness and suffering,
it would be better to die and be reunited.
Wishing to end myself and be destroyed,
yet fearing to fail in the filial duty of preserving the body whole.
Vice Minister Bái.
Whenever the thought comes,
my guts burn and bones ache.
Also from the same.
Swallowing tears and bearing grief.
Bái Jūyì.
Emaciated as firewood, bones protruding.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng's prose.
Liver and chest torn asunder.
Lǐ Shūzhī.
Crying and wailing mournfully,
moving others to emotion.
Dù Mù.
Holding sorrow and enduring grief.
Wáng Wúgōng.
Tears fewer than blood,
bones more than body.
"Collection of Wáng Wéi".
As if bereaved in all emotions,
not redeemable even with a hundred lives.
Also from the same.
Wailing until emaciated.
"Táng Wén Cuì".
Dwelling by the grave,
weeping without restraint.
Dust and grime accumulating on the head,
grass growing among the hair.
Bearing grief until gaunt.
Also from the same.
Our dynasty
Spirit scattered, liver and innards severed,
tears of blood covering the face, never drying.
"Collection of Línchuān".
Grief surpassing others,
emaciation worse than average.
"Lèi Yào".
Actions betraying the spirits,
personally inviting blame and misfortune.
Emaciated nearly to the loss of life.
Enduring sorrow while containing grief.
Heart aching, weeping snowy tears.
Mourning garments stained with blood.
Also from the same.
If there is a sound, it should pierce the heavens,
if there are tears, they should reach the springs.
Hòushān.
Classic
Mournful, my parents,
who bore me with toil.
． "Interpretation of the Poem 'Lù'".
Without a father, on whom to rely?
Without a mother, on whom to depend?
Going out, I bear sorrow;
returning home, I find no haven.
Also from the same.
The "Shī" says: "Awake through the dawn,
thinking of two people."
Referring to parents.
． "Record of Sacrificial Meanings".
A gentleman, once orphaned, does not change his name.
． "Record of Ritual Propriety, Part 2".
The filial piety of ancient kings:
their parents' images never forgotten before their eyes,
their voices never ceased in their ears,
their hearts' desires and wishes never forgotten in their minds.
Utmost love makes them ever-present,
utmost sincerity makes them vivid,
vivid presence never forgotten in the heart.
This is remembrance.
． "Record of Sacrificial Meanings".
When frost and dew have descended,
and the gentleman treads upon them,
he must feel a heart of sorrow,
not because of the cold.
When spring rain and dew have moistened,
and the gentleman treads upon them,
he must feel a heart of trepidation,
as if about to see them.
Also from the same.
When going to escort the deceased,
he looks anxiously,
urgently,
as if chasing something he cannot reach.
When returning to weep,
he is restless,
as if seeking something he cannot find.
Thus, when going to escort,
he is like one longing; when returning,
he is like one doubting, seeking but finding nothing.
Entering the gate, he does not see them;
ascending the hall, again he does not see them;
entering the room, again he does not see them.
Gone,
lost,
never to be seen again.
Therefore, he weeps, beats his chest, and stamps his feet,
until his grief is fully expressed.
． "Record on Inquiring about Mourning".
The three-year mourning period,
ends after twenty-five months,
yet the grief is not exhausted,
the longing and remembrance not forgotten.
． "Record on the Three-Year Mourning Inquiry".
Think of their dwelling places,
think of their laughter and words,
think of their will and thoughts,
think of what they enjoyed,
think of what they delighted in.
． "Record of Sacrificial Meanings".
When a filial son's parent dies,
sorrow and distress overwhelm his heart,
so he crawls and weeps for them,
as if they could return to life,
but how could that be possible?
Thus, they are taken and encoffined.
Therefore it is said: "The encoffining after three days
is to wait for their revival."
． "Record on Inquiring about Mourning".
Son
Gazing up at the rafters above,
Looking down at the mats and tables below.
The vessels all remain,
But their owner is nowhere to be seen.
Reflecting thus on sorrow,
Then the grief becomes palpable.
． From *Family Sayings: Five Norms*.
Cross-referenced under "Grief and Mourning".
The tree desires stillness, but the wind never ceases;
The son wishes to care for his parents, but they await him not.
What goes and does not return
Is the years.
What cannot be seen again
Are one's parents.
． From *Family Sayings: Expressing Thoughts*.
History:
After the mourning period ended, the longing remained,
Lifelong as if in bereavement.
． From *History of the Southern Dynasties: Biography of Guō Shìtōng*.
Jīnmìdī's mother
Raised her sons with discipline,
And the emperor praised her.
After her death,
An edict commissioned her portrait in the Gānquán Palace.
Whenever Jīnmìdī saw the painting,
He would often bow,
Facing it with tears before departing.
． From *Official Biography in the Western Han History*.
Anthology:
Facing the grave, I cry out to the blue heavens,
Tears falling like strands of rope.
． From *Selections: Ode to History*.
Far into eternity, they do not return.
From *Wénxuǎn*.
Reflecting on the swiftness of life as a glimpse through a crack,
Lamenting the river that flows without pause.
Treading on frost and dew in sorrow,
Holding the fire-drill and tinder, tears fall.
From Emperor Liáng's "Rhapsody on Filial Longing".
The joy of being at one's parents' knees
Has already passed like a glimpse through a crack.
The longing for the mats and tables—
On what can it rely?
From Rén Yǎnshēng's petition.
Dew gives way to frost,
Sun and moon pass by.
From Zuǒ Tàichōng's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Wú".
Eternal remembrance of the grace of nurturing,
Long-lasting pain of longing and admiration.
From Luò Bīnwáng.
Soaked by dew, treading on frost—
Who does not have eternal remembrance?
From Liú Bīnkè.
Frost descends, dew soaks,
Filial longing knows no bounds.
From *Collection of Bái Jūyì*.
The meaning and words in letters
Are all vivid as ever.
Only the soul and spirit—
I know not where they have gone.
Each time I unroll a scroll,
It feels like a knife twisting my lungs and guts.
Each time I read a passage,
Blood drips upon the words.
Same as above.
If voice and countenance were still here,
On what day would my resolve be fulfilled?
From Lǐ Xízhī.
Trembling at the frost and dew.
From *Táng Wéncuì*.
Jīnmìdī wept upon seeing the portrait.
From *Collection of Yuán Zhěn*.
Classics:
Unwavering in spring and autumn,
Offering sacrifices without error.
From the *Book of Songs*.
Purified and prepared as offerings,
This is how filial piety is shown.
Presenting the seasonal sacrifices,
To the former dukes and kings.
． From the *Book of Songs: Tiān Bǎo*.
Offering with clear wine,
Followed by a red bull,
To the ancestral temple.
． From *Xiǎo Yǎ: Xìn Nán Shān*.
Fragrant and abundant,
The sacrificial affairs are most illustrious.
From the *Book of Songs*.
Presenting the annual offerings to the imperial ancestors.
From the *Book of Rites*.
In spring and autumn, offer the seasonal foods.
From the *Doctrine of the Mean*.
On the day of sacrifice,
Entering the chamber, one feels a solemn presence,
Surely seeing them in their place;
Moving around the position,
Exiting the door, one is reverent,
Surely hearing
Their vocal expressions; stepping out,
And listening, one sighs deeply,
Surely hearing
The sound of sighs.
A filial son, about to sacrifice,
Must prepare for the affairs without neglect.
Gathering the items in time,
Must be done without omission,
With a focused mind to manage it.
This is like anticipating the moment.
Focused mind
Means not thinking of other matters.
With this trance-like state,
To commune with the spirits,
Perhaps they will partake.
Confucius once, while presenting offerings to his parents,
Was sincere in his actions,
Hastening with reverence.
Sacrifice is the means to continue nurturing and uphold filial piety.
． All from *Records: Meaning of Sacrifices*.
Offering the new harvest like the first-of-the-month sacrifice.
． From *Records: Tángōng Part I*.
In spring and autumn, perform sacrifices,
To remember them in season.
From the *Classic of Filial Piety*.
Note: "The change of cold and heat
Increases the feeling of loss;
Seasonal sacrifices
Express one's filial longing."
Masters:
In sacrificial affairs, serve their spirits.
． From *Xúnzǐ: Discourse on Rites*.
To preserve the form of the departed,
And connect with the distant and severed,
Only fasting can achieve this.
Note: "Sacrifice as if present;
Filial piety is utmost."
History:
Sacrifices are the means
To manifest filial piety, serve ancestors, and communicate with the divine.
． From *Western Han History: Treatise on Sacrifices*.
Classics
When going to a grave mound, one does not ascend it.
． From "Records: Qu Li Part I".
When going to a grave mound, one does not sing.
Confucius said: "In ancient times, they did not repair tombs."
Also from the same source above.
After Confucius had buried his parents together at Fáng,
he said: "I have heard that,
in ancient times, tombs were made without mounds.
But now I, Qiū,
am a man who travels east, west, south, and north.
I cannot leave it unmarked."
Thereupon, he raised a mound over it four feet high.
． From "Records: Qu Li Part II".
Burying in a tomb
is a means to send off the departed.
． From "Records: Tán Gōng Part I".
When Jìzǐ of Yánlíng's son died,
he was buried between Yíng and Bó.
The pit was dug not deep enough to reach the water table.
After the burial, it was mounded over,
covering the pit broadly and roundly,
with a height one could lean on.
After mounding,
he bared his left arm and wailed three times,
saying: "Flesh and bones return to the earth;
it is fate."
． From "Records: Tán Gōng Part II".
Confucius said: "The people of Wèi, in joint burials,
separate them."
Fù
means joint burial.
"Separate them"
means to leave a space between the coffins in the outer coffin.
The people of Lǔ, in joint burials,
join them together—this is good.
Among the ruins and tombs,
even without imposing grief upon the people,
the people grieve.
Flesh and bones return to the earth.
． Also from "Records: Tán Gōng Part II".
Grave mounds are not to be heaped up.
． From "Records: The Four Regulations of Mourning Attire".
Chéngzǐ Gāo said: "In life, I benefited others;
in death, I should not harm the people.
How can I, in death, harm others?
When I die,
choose unproductive land to bury me."
． From "Records: Tán Gōng Part I".
The Master said: "I have seen mounds shaped like a hall,
built up into a ridge.
I have seen some like a dam,
with sides sloping down to a flat top.
I have seen some like an overturned Xià house,
thatched with tiles.
Xià house
refers to today's door eaves."
I have seen some like an axe,
with sides sloping to a long, sharp top.
I follow the axe-shaped one."
Confucius found the sharp top difficult to ascend and narrow,
yet easy to construct.
This is called the horse-mane mound.
． Commonly known from "Records: Tán Gōng Part I".
Altering a tomb is not ancient practice.
Clearing away vegetation.
Same as above.
Divining the burial site and placing the coffin there peacefully.
From "The Classic of Filial Piety".
The master
vanishes into the formless,
content in the abode of eternal night.
From "Huáinánzǐ".
In history,
"White poplars, much sorrowful wind,
rustling, sorrow enough to kill a man."
From "Records of the Grand Historian".

Generally, a person's deeds,
unless of great virtue or great evil,
are unknown to the public,
so by old custom, information was sought from others,
and the xíngzhuàng was taken as basis.
Nowadays, those who write xíngzhuàng,
if not disciples,
then former subordinates,
all falsely add benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom,
falsely claim loyalty, respect, kindness, and harmony,
or speak of great virtue and grand achievements,
shining brighter with distance,
or of upright ways and honest words,
immortal after death,
so they cannot straightforwardly narrate the facts,
making good and evil mixed and unclear.
As for Xǔ Jìngzōng, Lǐ Yìfǔ, Lǐ Línfǔ,
treacherous ministers of our dynasty,
having their disciples or former subordinates write xíngzhuàng,
not pointing to the actual facts,
falsely praising loyalty and trustworthiness added to them,
then such could be transferred to Yuánlíng, Wèi Zhèng, Péi Yán, Xú Yǒugōng.
This is not only due to their insincerity,
but merely wanting to falsely glorify those from whom they received favor.
Thus, matters lose their essence,
writing harms principle,
and xíngzhuàng becomes unreliable.
If one points to facts and writes truthfully,
without embellishing false words,
then surely some would know the truth or falsehood.
Otherwise,
even if disciples or former subordinates write it,
they should not wrongly fabricate virtuous deeds to add.
Now, I request that those writing xíngzhuàng,
not vainly speak of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom,
loyalty, respect, kindness, harmony,
great virtue and grand achievements,
upright words and honest ways,
cluttering the records,
untrustworthy,
but point to facts and speak truthfully,
directly recording the words,
so that good and evil, merits and deeds,
all based on facts, become self-evident.
For example, transmitting Wèi Zhèng,
just record his remonstrating words,
enough to show his uprightness.
Transmitting Duàn Xiùshí,
just record his using the Sìnóng Temple seal backward to recall rebel troops,
and striking Zhū Cǐ with an ivory tablet,
enough to show his loyalty and fierceness.
Nowadays, those writing xíngzhuàng,
do not point to the facts,
generally using empty praise,
so without Wèi Zhèng's remonstrance,

The Qín people poisoned the upper reaches of the Jīng River,

When Jìn fought against Chǔ,

set up two banners and then retreated,
while Luán Zhī had chariots drag brushwood to feign retreat.
． (From Zuǒzhuàn, 28th year of Xīgōng).
When Jìn attacked Qí,
the Marquis of Qí ascended Mount Wū to observe the Jìn army.
The Jìn commander ordered scouts to reconnoiter the dangerous mountains and marshes,
and even where they did not go,
they were sure to display banners and spread out formations.
They had chariot riders place real soldiers on the left and decoys on the right,
with banners leading the way,
and chariots dragging brushwood following behind.
When the Marquis of Qí saw this,
he feared their numbers,
and fled back without his armor.
． (From Zuǒzhuàn, 18th year of Xiānggōng).
Yān sent Qì Jié to replace Yuè Yì.
Qí's Tián Dān gathered over a thousand oxen in the city.
He dressed them in crimson silk robes,
painted with multicolored dragon patterns,
tied sharp blades to their horns,
and tied oil-soaked reeds to their tails,
setting the ends on fire.
He then dug dozens of holes in the city walls,
released the oxen at night,
with five thousand warriors following behind.
The oxen, enraged by their burning tails, charged into the Yān army.
Those they gored were all killed or wounded.
Taking advantage, they attacked,
and achieved a great victory.
They recovered over seventy cities of Qí.
． (From Shǐjì, Tián Dān's biography).
When Wèi and Zhào attacked Hán,
Hán sought urgent help from Qí,
which sent Tián Jì to march directly toward Dàliáng.
Wèi general Páng Juān heard of this,
left Hán and returned to Qí,
while Sūn Bìn had the Qí army enter Wèi territory,
and prepared a hundred thousand cooking stoves.
The next day, they prepared fifty thousand stoves.
The day after, they prepared twenty thousand stoves.
After three days of marching, Páng Juān
exclaimed joyfully, "I always knew the Qí army was cowardly.
Three days into our territory,
and more than half their soldiers have deserted."
He then led his light, elite forces, marching double time to pursue them.

When Zhào Kuò attacked Qín,

When Hán Xìn attacked Zhào,

The Zhào troops saw this and laughed heartily,

Hán Xìn abandoned his drums and banners,

Zhào was crushed,

． (From Tōngjiàn, Hàn Gāozǔ's chronicles).
When Chǔ's Lóng Qiě and Hán Xìn faced off across the Wéi River,

attacked Lóng Qiě,

As Lóng Qiě pursued Hán Xìn,
Hán Xìn had men break the sandbag dam,

trapping most of Lóng Qiě's troops on the far side.
He then attacked and killed Lóng Qiě.
． (From Xīhànshū, Hán Xìn's biography).
When Hán Xìn attacked Wèi king Bào,
he created decoy troops,

． (From Tōngjiàn, Hàn Gāozǔ's chronicles).
When Lǐ Guǎng attacked the Xiōngnú,
he ordered, "Dismount and remove your saddles."
His cavalry asked, "The enemy is numerous and close,
what if they attack urgently?"
Lǐ Guǎng said, "They think we will flee,
but now we remove our saddles to show we won't,
to strengthen their suspicion."
Thus, the Hú cavalry dared not attack.
． (From Shǐjì, Lǐ Guǎng's biography).
Zāng Gōng served as General Fǔwēi,
stationed with troops in Yuè.
At that time,
Gōngsūn Shù's general Rén Mǎn,
was confronting Cén Péng in Jīngzhōu.
Zāng Gōng had few troops,
and lacked strength to control the situation.
Just then, subordinate counties delivered several hundred supply carts,
so Zāng Gōng had men secretly cut the city gate sills at night,
and ordered the carts to rumble in and out until dawn.
The Yuè scouts,
hearing the endless cart noises,
and seeing the broken gate sills,
thought the city was breached,
and Gōngsūn Shù was defeated.
(From Hòuhànshū).
When the Northern Xiōngnú invaded in force,
Lián Fàn, governor of Yúnzhōng, resisted them.
His officers, due to their small numbers,
wanted to send messages to neighboring commanaderies for help,
but Lián Fàn refused.
As dusk fell,
he ordered the troops to eat in their beds,
and at dawn, they advanced to attack,
beheading several hundred enemies.
． (From Tōngjiàn, Hàn Míngdì's chronicles).
Yǔ Xǔ was governor of Wǔdū.
With less than three thousand troops,
he was besieged by over ten thousand Qiāng tribesmen.
Yǔ Xǔ deployed his troops to exit the city's east gate,
and enter through the north gate,
changing clothes,
and circling multiple times,
frightening the enemy into retreat.
He then set an ambush and attacked them,
achieving a great victory.
(From Hòuhànshū).
Yǔ Xǔ possessed the stratagems of a general,
and was appointed governor of Wǔdū.
Several thousand Qiāng tribesmen
intercepted him at Chéncāng Xiáogǔ.
Yǔ Xǔ halted his army and did not advance,
instead proclaiming he would send a report,
requesting troops and would advance only when they arrived.
The Qiāng heard this,
and went to plunder nearby counties' granaries.
Yǔ Xǔ took advantage of their dispersed forces to advance day and night,
covering over a hundred lǐ in double time,
and ordered each soldier to prepare two cooking stoves,
doubling the number daily.
The Qiāng dared not press close,
and someone asked,
"Sūn Bìn reduced stoves, yet you increase them.
The Art of War says: 'March no more than thirty lǐ a day,
to guard against the unexpected.'
But now you cover nearly two hundred lǐ daily,
why?"
Yǔ Xǔ replied, "The enemy is numerous, our troops few.
Moving slowly would make us easy to catch,
speeding ahead makes us unpredictable.
The enemy sees our stoves increase daily,
they will think commandery troops have come to reinforce,
many in number and fast in movement,
and will fear to pursue us.
Sūn Bìn showed weakness,
I now show strength,
the situations differ,
that is why."
． (From Tōngjiàn, Hàn Shāngdì's chronicles).
When Hú Zūn and Zhūgě Dàn attacked Dōngxīng,
Wú general Dīng Fèng, seeing their vanguard had few troops,
ordered his men to remove armor and spears,
keeping only helmets and swords with shields,
and climb the embankment bare-chested.
The Wèi troops saw this and laughed,
not preparing defenses immediately.
The Wú troops ascended,
then beat drums and shouted,
breaking through the Wèi vanguard,
and the Wèi army panicked and scattered in flight.
． (From Tōngjiàn, Wèi Shàolíng Lì Gōng's chronicles).
Mǎ Lóng attacked Shù Jī,
capable of surprising the enemy,
he piled magnetite along the road,
and the rebels, wearing iron armor,

Mǎ Lóng's troops all wore rhinoceros hide armor,

and all thought it miraculous.
(From Jìnshū).
