A woman holds no rank of her own,
but follows her husband's rank,
and is seated according to his seniority.
A woman is one who follows others:
in youth, she follows her father and brothers;
married, she follows her husband;
widowed, she follows her sons.
． From "Jiāo Tè Shēng" of the Lǐ Jì.
If her husband belongs to the father's generation,
the wife is considered of the mother's generation;
if her husband belongs to the son's generation,
the wife is considered of the daughter-in-law's generation.
． From "Yù Zǎo" of the Lǐ Jì.
A woman does not reside in the mourning hut,
nor sleep on straw,
and when her parents die,
she returns home after the first anniversary of mourning.
． From "The Great Record of Mourning" of the Lǐ Jì.
A woman
follows the teachings of men,
with no right to autonomous decisions,
but adheres to the three obediences.
Her instructions do not go beyond the women's quarters,
her duties are merely to provide food and drink,
with no involvement in matters outside the inner chambers.
From the Family Sayings of Confucius.
In history,
a woman does not go beyond the door to see guests off or welcome them,
and does not cross the threshold to meet her brothers.
． From the 22nd Year of Duke Xī in the Zuǒ Zhuàn.
Fù Chén said: "A woman's virtue knows no extremes,
a woman's resentment knows no end."
． From the 24th Year of Duke Xī in the Zuǒ Zhuàn. Close, they do not know when they have enough favor; distant, they harbor endless resentment.
A maiden serves others,
a married woman attends to affairs righteously.
． From the 20th Year of Duke Xiāng in the Zuǒ Zhuàn.
A woman does not act independently,
her actions must always follow another.
From the Gǔliáng Zhuàn.
Confucius said: "The words of that woman
can drive one to flee.
The requests of that woman
can lead to death and ruin."
From the Records of the Grand Historian.
Even with the virtue of Wén Mǔ,
she must be connected to her son.
From the Biography of Dù Yè.
Women may not participate in affairs.
． From the Biography of Gǔ Yǒng in the Western Hàn.
Women's nature is easily pleased.
A woman considers her husband's family as inner and her parental family as outer.
． Both from the Comprehensive Mirror in the Reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
No matter how noble a woman is,
she remains the subordinate part of her state.
． From the Biography of Dù Yè in the Western Hàn.
Collection
Adjusting the lapel and tying the bridal sash,
she reverently manages the household provisions.
From the Admonitions for Women.
Our dynasty
In ancient times, a woman's
rank derived from her husband,
her honor from her son.
Even if she had exceptional talent
or extraordinary conduct,
it was not manifested in the world.
From the Dōngpō Collection.
Though a woman may possess virtue, talent, and wisdom,
she cannot apply them in affairs;
though she may have eloquence and literary skill,
they remain unknown to others.
How much more so for those who are benevolent but short-lived,
or virtuous but unrecognized?
This is why poets compose about the red tube,
and historians compile biographies of exemplary women.
Choosing a husband, she obtained Wén Qiáo,
bearing a son, she surpassed Wáng Jì.
Both from the Dōngpō Collection.
Classics
The second sister, Rén by name,
her heart is sincere and profound.
Gentle and kind to the end,
virtuous and careful in her person.
． From the poem "Swallows" in the Book of Songs.
The annotation says: "Rén means to be trusted through kindness and closeness."
Graceful and dignified,
like a mountain, like a river.
． From the poem "The Nobleman Grows Old Together" in the Book of Songs.
Annotation: "The mountain accepts all,
the river moistens all."
Zhuāng Jiāng was virtuous but not favored.
． From the poem "The Tall Lady" in the Book of Songs.
The quiet maiden is lovely,
she gives me a red tube,
the red tube gleams brightly.
． From the poem "The Quiet Maiden" in the Book of Songs.
Women value a single virtue,
not multiple accomplishments.
． From the commentary on the "Autumn Offices" in the Rites of Zhōu.
History
A woman's virtue does not necessarily require exceptional talent.
Serene, chaste, and calm,
preserving integrity and orderliness,
acting with a sense of shame,
and behaving according to rules in action and repose,
this is called womanly virtue.
． From the Biographies of Exemplary Women of the Eastern Hàn.
The way of earth is soft and tranquil,
the constant principle of the feminine.
． From the Biography of Lǐ Xún in the Eastern Hàn.
Gentle, serene, and courteous.
． From the Annals of Empress Míngdé in the Eastern Hàn.
Biographies and Records
In the Eastern Hàn dynasty, virtuous women,
such as Xú Shì, wife of Qín Jiā,
acted in accordance with rites,
and spoke according to rules.
From the Shǐ Tōng.
Collection
Following the clear teachings of Fāng Zhīmíng from Zūnyì,
and adhering to the classical admonitions of women's histories.
From Pān Ānrén's "Rhapsody on the Widow".
Guǐ
(pronounced wǔ lèi qiē)
Huà, serene and secluded.
From Sòng Yù's "Rhapsody on the Goddess".
Possessing virtuous and cautious character,
and the worthiness of gentleness,
Pearls, jade, and jadeite are her proper ornaments,
yet washing and cleaning water plants does not alter her integrity.
Thus my noble man,
befriends her with qin and se.
From "Collection of Chén Zǐ'áng".
The matron's discussions on wine and food,
the complexity of women's weaving work,
all were governed by her pure heart,
greatly exemplifying virtuous principles,
abiding by the elegant teachings of duckweed and water plants,
harmonizing with the fragrant ways of ponds and islets.
Ancient texts praise Jìng Jiāng, the poem says: "The virtuous woman's appearance matches her virtue,
perhaps none can surpass."
Endowed with a gentle nature,
containing pure essence and hidden elegance.
The beauty of gentleness,
the grace of loveliness.
Chaste integrity sterner than winter pines,
beautiful demeanor fairer than warm jade.
Gentle, kind, benevolent, and harmonious,
sincere, respectful, cultivated, and amiable,
her actions follow rules,
her movements adhere to ritual classics.
Strict and respectful in management,
family members skilled in music.
Harmonizing with the noble man,
embracing magnanimity and brilliance.
As for ancestral temples,
she shows reverence, respect, benevolence, and filial piety;
harmonious with sisters-in-law,
she is humble and compliant;
preparing pure food and wine,
is her feminine duty;
embroidering black and yellow patterns,
is her womanly work.
Expanding these four virtues,
and attending to the six relations,
she can serve as a model of maternal conduct,
illuminating the principles of womanhood.
Externally supporting her husband's virtue,
internally glorifying household management.
Her enduring style and simple model,
spread like blooming orchids and irises.
Her kind heart shines sincerely,
perfuming ponds and islets.
The hall strict with womanly teachings,
fragrant with maternal examples.
Gentle and excellent in household management,
sisters-in-law follow her example.
Also from "Collection of Chén Zǐ'áng".
Those who gaze upon her,
feel like the lingering sun rippling on water;
those who observe her speech,
see like light winds turning fragrant herbs.
From Zhāng Yuè's writings.
Generations like Bān Gù's history,
fragrant as Mèng Mǔ's neighbor.
From Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Constantly self-disciplined,
never wasting days with flute songs;
always following ritual laws,
never using smiles for mere appearance.
From "Epitaph by Zhāng Yàngōng".
Truly possessing complete virtue,
serving as clan mentor for nine generations.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
In her small home,
no laughter heard by neighbors.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's "Epitaph for Madame Cuī".
Humble, gentle, dignified, respecting parents,
harmonious with sisters-in-law without trace.
From Hán Yù's poetry.
Graceful, restrained, diligent, and humble,
gaining harmony from all relatives.
From "Quán Zàizhī's Collected Epitaphs".
Her way as wife: chaste and obedient,
should always be embodied;
suspicions and doubts,
never sprout in her heart;
anger and resentment,
never show on her face.
Conforming while matching ritual,
graceful while maintaining correctness.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
The equality of magpie's nest,
the caution of family members,
the respectful demeanor in rituals,
the harmonious ceremony of qin and se,
the lady possessed all.
From Quán Děyù.
Achieving harmony with inner and outer relatives,
like gentle wind and sweet rain,
nourishing all living things.
Promoting friendship and harmony,
sisters-in-law showing mutual respect,
thus comforting parents-in-law.
Same as above.
Formerly Qī Shì and Tí Yíng,
were exemplary women,
but as wives,
left no fame;
wives of Bó Zōng and Liáng Hóng,
were wise women,
but as mothers,
left no fame;
Wén Bó's mother Mèng,
was a virtuous mother,
but as girl or wife, also left no fame.
Now this lady as daughter was filial and friendly,
as Yuán's wife richly maintained family sacrifices,
as mother personally taught reading,
instructing two sons,
both achieving office through classical learning.
Such excellence as daughter,
such virtue as wife,
such example as mother,
perfect in all three,
can be called supreme through past and present.
From "Bái Jūyì's Collected Epitaph for Madame Yuán".
Gentle and wise in nature,
warm and kind in self-preservation,
quietly cultivating speech and appearance,
moving with measured regularity.
Receiving instruction from matrons,
becoming bride to a good man.
Flourishing in four virtues like fragrant orchids,
pure in hundred conducts like spotless jade.
Developing into virtuous reputation,
becoming fragrant example.
Glory to relatives,
model for women's quarters.
Quiet without breaching ritual,
thus weaving has constant instruction;
moving with proper measure,
thus girdle jades have constant sound.
Also same as above.
Ritual demeanor needs no artificial ornaments,
skillful work also lies in weaving.
From "Collection of Wáng Wéi".
Though pearls and jade fill the hall,
never forgetting washing duties;
though musical instruments stand in rows,
still valuing historical records.
From Shěn Quánqī's writings.
Like katydids without jealousy,
like phoenixes singing in harmony.
From Lǐ Bái's writings.
Her words become the books of great families,
her deeds the model for all women.
From "Collection of Wáng Wéi".
Diligence in respectful washing and food preparation,
unrelenting through heat and cold;
tasks of mixing ash and mending seams,
completed with mere glances.
From "Collection of Lǚ Wénjǐn".
For grand sacrifices and important guests,
personally handling water plant affairs;
rising early and retiring late,
able to wear washed clothes.
Same as above.
Our dynasty
The quiet maiden does not vie for favor,
Her secluded grace seems self-content.
From Ōu Yángxiū's poetry.
Serving her in-laws with filial devotion,
She is a virtuous daughter-in-law;
Attending her husband with gentleness and obedience,
She is a worthy wife;
Educating her children with reverence, frugality, and impartiality,
She is an exemplary mother.
From Ōu Yángxiū's writings.
In youth, as a maiden,
She was diligent without maternal instruction.
From the "Dōngpō Collection".
With the restraint of珩璜,
Her actions always followed ritual;
In offering water plants as tribute,
She was reverent and dignified.
Ibid.
Gentle, kind, serene, and devoted,
She came as a bride to a great household.
From the "Línchuān Collection".
Through obedience, she was a good wife;
Through strictness, she was a wise mother.
Ibid.
In the splendor of ceremonial robes,
Her virtue matched the mountains and rivers;
With the solemnity of the red-tube brush,
Her purity rivaled jade tablets.
From Lúan Chéng.
Quiet and upholding propriety,
She preserved the customs of Jiāng and Hàn;
In action, always dignified,
She embodied the majesty of mountains and rivers.
Ibid.
From the tying of the sash to the laying of the funeral silk,
The nine clans had no criticism.
From "Classified Essentials".
Anecdote:
Xǔ Yǔn's wife was exceptionally ugly.
After the wedding ceremony,
He refused to enter the bridal chamber.
Xǔ said, "A wife should have four virtues;
How many do you possess?"
She replied, "What I lack
Is only beauty.
But a scholar should have a hundred conducts;
How many do you have?"
He said, "I have them all."
The wife said, "You favor looks over virtue.
How can you claim to have them all?"
Xǔ felt ashamed,
And thereafter they respected each other.
From "The Tales of Guō".
History:
Bān Jiéyú said, "'Life and death are fated,
Wealth and honor lie with Heaven.'
Cultivating rectitude has not yet brought blessings;
What hope is there in doing evil?
If the spirits are aware,
They will not heed a disloyal plea;
If they are not,
Pleading is futile.
Hence, I do not do it."
From "The Original Biography of the Western Hàn".
Cross-reference: "Upholding Integrity".
A wife's speech
Need not be eloquent or sharp.
Choosing words carefully when speaking,
Avoiding harsh language,
Speaking at the right time,
Not wearying others—
This is called a wife's speech.
From "Biographies of Exemplary Women of the Later Hàn".
Emperor Wǔ once played dice with Consort Hú,
And she injured his finger.
The emperor angrily said, "You really are of military stock!"
Consort Hú replied, "You campaigned north against Gōngsūn,
And west against Zhūgě—
If not of military stock, what are you?"
From "The Biography of Consort Hú of Jìn".
Xiè Dàoyùn was the wife of Wáng Néngzhī.
Once, his younger brother Xiànzhī was debating with guests
And was on the verge of losing the argument.
Dàoyùn sent a maid to tell Xiànzhī,
"I wish to help my brother-in-law break the siege."
She set up a blue silk screen
And elaborated on Xiànzhī's earlier points,
Leaving the guests unable to refute her.
From "Biographies of Exemplary Women of the Jìn History".
Cross-reference: "Sister-in-law Section".
Biographical Account:
Liú Dàozhēn, caught in turmoil,
Was pulling a boat by the river
When he saw an old woman rowing.
He said, "Why does a woman not work the loom but rows instead?"
She replied, "Why does a man not ride a horse with a whip but pulls a boat?"
From Péi Qǐqī's "Forest of Tales".
Cross-reference: "Inviting Insults".
A woman of Qí named Xú Wú
Joined her neighbors in spinning by candlelight at night.
Being poor, she could not contribute candles.
The neighbors asked her not to join at night.
Xú Wú said, "Because I am poor,
I always arrive first and
Leave last,
Sweeping and preparing mats
For those who come.
I always sit in the lower seat
Due to my poverty.
Now, in one room,
Adding one person
Does not make the candle brighter;
Removing one
Does not make it darker.
Why begrudge the leftover light from the east wall?"
None could reply,
So she continued spinning with them at night.
From "Biographies of Exemplary Women".
Cross-reference: "Insight".
Collection:
Fàn Chuánzhèng, while inspecting Xuān and Chí,
Sought out Lǐ Bái's descendants.
He found two granddaughters,
One married to Chén Yún,
The other to Liú Quàn,
Both commoners.
Summoned to the commandery office,
They met and conversed.
Though dressed rustically
And appearing simple and unrefined,
Their demeanor was graceful,
Their responses detailed and precise.
Their ancestral virtue seemed present,
The Confucian air still vivid.
Asked about their circumstances,
They said, "Our father Bó Qín died in the eighth year of Zhēnyuán,
Leaving one elder brother
Who traveled away twelve years ago
And is now missing.
Our father held no office in life,
And left no fame in death.
With a brother we cannot rely on,
We are among the world's destitute.
Without mulberries, we cannot silkworm,
Though we know weaving;
Without land, we cannot farm,
Though we know cropping.
As women, we are unfit for labor,
Clad in cloth skirts, eating coarse food—
On what can we depend?
Married to farmers,
We barely escape death.
Long we dared not inform the authorities,
Fearing to disgrace our ancestors.
Pressed by the village,
We bear shame to tell our tale."
Tears fell as they finished.
From "The Collection of Lǐ Bái".
Classic:
Her artful smile, so radiant,
Her girdle gems, how they tinkle.
A maiden rides with me,
Her face like a hibiscus flower.
We are about to soar, about to soar,
With girdle gems of precious stone.
That beautiful Mèng Jiāng,
Truly lovely and elegant.
The quiet maiden is lovely,
The quiet maiden is fair.
From "The Quiet Maiden",
Both in the "Book of Songs".
History:
A wife's appearance
Need not be of striking beauty.
Washing away dust and grime,
Wearing clean and fresh clothes,
Bathing to await duties,
Keeping the body unsoiled and unashamed—
This is called a wife's appearance.
From "Biographies of Exemplary Women of the Later Hàn".
Lady Wáng had a spirit clear and free,
Hence possessing the air of a woodland recluse;
The wife of the Gù family, pure-hearted and jade-like,
Was naturally the flower of the women's quarters.
From "Biographies of Exemplary Women of the Jìn History".
Cross-reference: "Elegance" section.
Collection
She wears no rouge applied,
Nor any balm beside.
． From "The Goddess of the River Luò Rhapsody".
With powder touched, her face would be too pale;
With rouged lips, too rosy to prevail.
． From "The Goddess of the River Luò Rhapsody".
Her beauty would put flowers to shame;
Her face outshines the lotus fair.
She washes silk in ripples blue,
And plays with water clean there.
By Lǐ Tàibái.
Gentle and graceful her bearing,
Elegant and dignified her appearance.
Though her family was poor,
And she could not change clothes yearly,
Yet her natural beauty remained pure and solemn,
Always as if adorned with pearls,
Dressed in fine silk,
Untouched by dust and impurity.
Both from Liǔ Wén.
Classics
They cut it and they boil it,
Making fine cloth and coarse.
From "Gě Tán".
Women have no public affairs;
They should rest from silkworm rearing and weaving.
． From "Dà Yǎ: Zhān Yǎng".
Handling hemp and flax,
Managing silk and cocoons,
Weaving and braiding,
Learning women's work to provide clothing.
Observing sacrificial rites,
Presenting wine, offerings, pickles, and sauces.
． From "Lǐ Jì: Nèi Zé".
History
Women's work
Need not surpass others in skill.
Focus on spinning and weaving,
Not fond of idle laughter,
Preparing clean and orderly food and drink,
To serve guests,
This is called women's work.
． From "Hòu Hàn Liè Nǚ Zhuàn".
Biographies
Lady Zhào, wife of the King of Wú, could weave brocade between her fingers,
Known as "the ultimate loom";
On a square inch of silk, she embroidered the five mountains, rivers, and seas,
Known as "the ultimate needle";
Using divine glue to join hair into a hat,
And splitting a single strand into threads,
Known as "the ultimate silk".
From Wáng Jiā's "Shí Yí Jì" of the Jìn dynasty.
During the reign of Emperor Shùnzōng,
A remarkable woman named Lú Méiniáng was presented as tribute from Nánhǎi,
Who could embroider the Fǎhuá Sūtra on a foot of silk,
With characters as small as millet grains.
She also made a flying immortal canopy,
Using a single strand of silk for the canopy,
Within its five layers were the ten continents and three islands.
From Sū È's "Sū Shì Yǎn Yì" of the Táng dynasty.
Anthology
The beauty carefully irons it smooth,
Sewing with no trace of needle and thread.
From Dù Shī.
Sewn into garments for a peerless beauty.
From Lǐ Bái.
Classics
At the funeral of Wén Bó,
Jìng Jiāng leaned against his bed but did not weep,
Saying: "Formerly, I had this son,
I thought he would become a virtuous man,
I never had him attend the court.
Now that he has died,
None of his friends or ministers have shed tears,
Yet all the women of the household wail uncontrollably.
This son of mine
Must have often neglected the rites."
． From "Lǐ Jì: Tán Gōng Xià".
Masters
When Gōngfǔ Wén Bó died,
His wives and concubines all wailed uncontrollably.
Jìng Jiāng admonished them, saying: "I have heard that those who favor external affairs
Are mourned by scholars;
Those who favor internal affairs
Are mourned by women.
Now my son died young,
And I detest that he be known for favoring internal affairs.
You women who wish to serve the ancestral sacrifices,
Please show no emaciated appearance,
No waving away of tears,
No beating of the breast,
No sorrowful countenance,
No extra mourning garments,
But follow the rites quietly,
Thus illuminating my son."
Confucius heard of this,
And said: "The wife of the Gōngwén family
Is wise indeed.
She dissects emotions and analyzes rites,
To show that her son possessed virtuous conduct."
． From "Kǒngzǐ Jiāyǔ: Zǐgòng Wèn".
History
The mother of Ruì Bó Wàn, Ruì Jiāng,
disliked his having many favorites.
Therefore, she drove him out,
and he went to reside in Wèi.
． _Zuǒzhuàn, Duke Xī 3rd Year_
Gōngfǔ Wénbó retired from court,
and paid respects to his mother,
who was spinning.
Wénbó said: "In a household like Chù's, for the mistress to still spin
fears to provoke Jì Sūn's anger,
thinking that Chù is incapable of serving his lord!"
His mother sighed and said: "Have you forgotten?
Were you made an official while still a youth and have not heard this?
Sit,
and I will tell you.
The feudal lords attend court to cultivate their sovereign's affairs,
at midday examine their state duties,
in the evening review their laws and punishments,
at night warn the officials,
to prevent indulgence and excess,
and only then rest.
Ministers and high officials attend court to examine their duties,
at midday recite about various administrative matters,
in the evening,
arrange their tasks,
at night manage their households,
and only then rest.
Scholars receive their lessons in the morning,
study and connect them at midday,
review and practice in the evening,
reflect on their faults at night without regret,
and only then rest.
From the commoners down,
they work from dawn,
rest at dusk,
without a day of idleness."
． _Guóyǔ, Lǔyǔ_
Zhào Kuò, from a young age, studied military tactics,
discussed warfare,
believing no one in the world could match him.
He once discussed warfare with his father, Shē,
who could not refute him,
yet did not praise him.
Kuò's mother asked Shē the reason,
Shē said:
"Warfare,
is a matter of life and death,
yet Kuò speaks of it lightly.
If Zhào does not make Kuò a general, all is well;
if he must command,
the one who will destroy Zhào's army,
will surely be Kuò."
When Kuò was about to depart,
his mother submitted a letter to the king, saying: "Kuò should not be made general."
The king said: "Why?"
She replied: "When I first served his father,
as a general,
those he personally served meals to
numbered in the tens,
those he befriended,
in the hundreds,
and what was bestowed by nobles and the royal clan,
he entirely gave to his officers and officials.
From the day he received command,
he did not inquire about household affairs.
Now Kuò, upon becoming general,
faces east to receive homage,
with officers not daring to look up at him.
The gold and silk bestowed upon him,
he takes home to store,
and daily looks for advantageous fields and properties to buy,
and buys them.
What does Your Majesty think compared to his father?
Father and son have different hearts;
I wish Your Majesty would not send him."
． _Shǐjì, Biography of Zhào Shē_
Chén Yīng's mother said to Yīng: "Since I became a wife in your family,
I have never heard of any noble ancestors.
Now suddenly gaining great fame
is inauspicious.
It is better to align with someone;
if successful, you may still be enfeoffed as a marquis,
if failed, it's easier to flee,
not being notably targeted by the world."
． _Shǐjì, Annals of Xiàng Jí_
Zhāng Tāng committed suicide,
his brothers and sons wanted to bury him lavishly.
Tāng's mother said: "A great minister of the Son of Heaven died under accusations;
what use is a lavish burial?"
They carried him in an ox cart,
with a coffin but no outer coffin.
The emperor heard of this,
and said: "If not for such a mother,
such a son would not be born."
． _Xīhàn, Biography of Zhāng Tāng_
Juàn Bùyí,
each time he toured the county reviewing prisoners,
upon returning,
his mother would ask Bùyí: "Have you exonerated any,
saved how many people?"
If Bùyí had exonerated many,
his mother would happily laugh,
and prepare food and drink.
If there were none to release,
his mother would be angry,
and refuse to eat because of it.
． _Xīhàn, Main Biography_
Zhào's mother pointed out Kuò's faults,
thus preserving her clan.
． _Qiánhàn, Commentary on Cháo Cuò's Biography_
Zhái Fāngjìn bid farewell to his stepmother,
to go to the capital and study classics.
His mother pitied his youth,
followed him to Cháng'ān,
and wove sandals to support Fāngjìn.
_Xīhàn_
Xiàng Yǔ captured Wáng Líng's mother,
and placed her in the army.
When Líng's envoy arrived,
Líng's mother was seated facing east,
to signal Líng.
The mother privately saw off the envoy,
weeping and saying:
"Tell Líng for me:
Serve the King of Hàn well,
do not be of two minds because of your old mother.
I send off the envoy with my death."
Then she fell on her sword and died.
． _Xīhàn, Biography of Wáng Líng_
Yán Yánnián was the governor of Hénán,
Hénán called him the "Butcher Chief."
His mother came from Dōnghǎi,
arrived in Luòyáng,
saw prisoners being executed,
was greatly shocked,
stopped at a post station,
and did not enter the prefecture.
When Yánnián came to pay respects,
his mother closed the gate and refused to see him,
Yánnián removed his cap and kowtowed below for a long time,
then she saw him.
Thereupon, she reprimanded Yánnián:
"You are fortunate to serve as a commandery governor,
yet I hear not of benevolent love and education,
to protect and pacify the ignorant people,
but instead of much punishment and killing,
wishing to establish authority.
I did not expect in my old age
to see my grown son face punishment and execution.
Go now,
I leave you and return east,
to prepare the burial ground."
Then she left,
over a year later,
Yánnián was executed in the market,
Dōnghǎi praised his mother.
_Qiánhàn_
Jīnmìdī's mother,
educated her two sons with great discipline.
The emperor heard and commended her,
when she fell ill and died,
he ordered her portrait placed in Gānquán Palace.
_Xīhàn_
In the second year of Jiànníng,
there was a great persecution of the partisans,
Pāng heard of it,
and went to the prison himself.
He bid farewell to his mother,
his mother said:
"You now share fame with Lǐ and Dù,
what regret is there in death?"
． _Dōnghàn, Biography of Fàn Pāng_
Guō Dān's stepmother,
sold clothes and belongings,
sold property,
to accompany him to study in Cháng'ān.
_Hòuhàn_
The Duke of Gāoguìxiāng was deposed.
Wáng Jīng was arrested.
Jīng apologized to his mother,
his mother's expression did not change,
she smiled and responded:
"Who does not die?
I only fear not dying properly,
to die together for this,
what regret is there?"
． _Tōngjiàn, Wèi Wéndì Annals_
Sū Jùn raised an army,
Biǎn Kǔn died in battle,
his two sons, Zhěn and Xū,
seeing their father fall,
followed him to fight the rebels,
and were killed simultaneously.
Their mother, Péi, caressed her sons' bodies,
and cried: "The father a loyal minister,
the sons filial children,
what regret is there?"
． _Jìnshū, Main Biography_
Wěi Chěng was young,
his mother, Sòng, gathered firewood by day,
At night she taught Chěng,
who thus achieved fame.
Táo Kǎn served as a minor official in Xúnyáng County.
Once while supervising a fish weir,
he sent some pickled fish to his mother.
Zhàn returned the fish along with a letter,
reproaching Kǎn: "You, as an official,
sending me government property,
not only fails to benefit me,
but actually increases my worries."
Fàn Kuí remarked:
"Without such a mother,
such a son would not have been born."
When Yú Tán was dispatched to subdue Sū Jùn,
his mother, née Sūn, admonished him:
"I have heard that loyal ministers come from filial sons' households.
You should sacrifice your life for righteousness,
and not let my old age be a burden to you."
Both stories from Biographies of Exemplary Women.
Táo Kǎn was orphaned early and lived in poverty.
When Fàn Kuí once visited Kǎn,
they had nothing to entertain the guest in their haste.
His mother cut off her hair,
obtaining a hairpiece to exchange for wine and dishes.
From History of the Jin Dynasty.
Hé Wújì was drafting a proclamation behind a screen at night,
when his mother,
sister of Liú Láozhī,
climbed onto a stool to secretly observe him.
Weeping, she said:
"If you can do this,
what regrets could I have?"
When asked who his co-conspirators were,
he replied:
"Liú Yù."
His mother was especially pleased,
and explained the principle that "Xuán must fail,
and your undertaking must succeed" to encourage him.
From Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Annals of Emperor An of Jin.
When Gāo Jiǒng first became vice director of the department of state affairs,
his mother warned him:
"You have reached the peak of wealth and honor,
but there remains only the risk of losing your head.
You must be cautious."
From Book of Sui.
While Zhāng Yìzhī and Zhāng Chāngzōng held power at court,
Jìng Yànfàn plotted to eliminate them.
Yànfàn informed his mother of the matter,
who said:
"Loyalty and filial piety cannot be fully achieved simultaneously.
Putting the state before family is acceptable."
From Annals of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang.
Lǐ Jǐngràng's mother, née Zhèng,
came from a poor family.
When her sons were all young,
she educated them herself.
When the house wall collapsed due to rain,
a boatload of coins was discovered.
The servants joyfully ran to tell the mother,
who went and burned incense, praying:
"I have heard that unearned gains
bring personal disaster.
If Heaven is bestowing this due to my late husband's accumulated virtue,
pitying our poverty,
then I wish my orphaned sons would achieve scholarly success in the future,
which would fulfill my aspiration.
I dare not accept this."
She immediately ordered the coins covered and the wall rebuilt.
All three sons passed the imperial examinations.
Even when Jǐngràng had achieved high office,
with hair already graying,
if he committed minor errors,
he still received caning.
From Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Annals of Emperor Wuzong of Tang.
Liú Xuánzuǒ, military commissioner of Xuānwǔ, possessed authority and strategy.
Though his mother enjoyed noble status,
she wove a bolt of silk daily,
telling Xuánzuǒ:
"You originally came from humble circumstances.
The emperor has enriched and honored you to this extent,
you must repay him with your life."
Thus Xuánzuǒ never failed in his duties as subject.
From Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Annals of Emperor Dezong of Tang.
Púgù Huái'ēn,
no longer employed by the court,
conspired with Lǐ Jiéchéng, a general of Hé dōng, against Tàiyuán.
The officer Bái Yù killed his son Yáng.
Huái'ēn went in to inform his mother,
who said:
"I told you not to rebel.
The state has treated you well.
Now that popular sentiment has turned,
disaster will surely reach me.
What should be done?"
Huái'ēn did not reply,
but bowed twice and left.
His mother chased him with a knife,
saying:
"I will kill this traitor for the state,
take his heart,
and apologize to the three armies."
Huái'ēn fled quickly and escaped.
He then crossed the Yellow River north with three hundred followers.
From Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Governance, Annals of Emperor Daizong of Tang.
Cuī Xuánwěi repeatedly served as vice minister.
His mother, née Lú, once admonished him: "I heard from my cousin, Xīn Xuányù, director of the state farms bureau:
'When someone says of an official son that he is impoverished and struggling to survive,
this is good news.
If I hear he has ample wealth,
with fine clothes and horses,
this is bad news.'
I have always valued these words,
considering them true.
Recently I've seen many relatives and acquaintances in office
presenting money and goods to their parents,
who only feel joy
without inquiring where these things came from.
If they are surplus from salary,
that is indeed good.
But if obtained improperly,
how is this different from theft?
Even without major punishment,
wouldn't one feel inner shame?
Mèng's mother refusing the gift of pickled fish
was for this reason.
Now you receive official salary,
enjoying much honor already.
If you cannot be loyal and honest,
how can you face heaven and earth?
Confucius said:
'Even if three sacrificial animals are provided daily, it still may be unfilial.'
And:
'Parents only worry about their children's faults.'
You should particularly cultivate yourself and maintain purity,
not disappointing my intention."
From Old Book of Tang, his biography.
When Wáng Guī and his friends Fáng and Dù visited his home,
Guī's mother observed them and
joyfully said: "These two guests have the talent of ministers.
Your future nobility is certain."
Same source as above.
Cross-reference "Insight."
Xiāo Fǔ's mother, née Wéi,
was virtuous and wise,
managing the household strictly.
Even when Fǔ became chancellor,
she treated him as if he were still in commoner's clothes.
From New Book of Tang.
Biographies
Mèngzǐ, having completed his studies, returned home,
and his mother Mèng Mǔ inquired about his academic progress.
Mèngzǐ appeared self-satisfied.
Mèng Mǔ took a knife and cut through the cloth she was weaving,
saying: "Your abandonment of learning
is like my cutting this woven fabric."
From Biographies of Exemplary Women.
When Chǔ Zǐfǎn returned after defeating the Qín army,
his mother closed the gate and refused him entry,
sending someone to reprimand him: "When King Gōujiàn of Yuè attacked Wú,
a guest presented a vessel of fine wine,
the king had it poured upstream,
allowing the soldiers to drink downstream,
yet the flavor did not diminish.
Another day,
someone offered a bag of provisions,
and the king again had it distributed among the troops,
who shared and ate it,
its sweetness not surpassing their throats.
Now your soldiers share beans and grains to eat,
while you alone feast on fine meats morning and night,
why is this?"
Same as above.
When Mèngzǐ's wife was alone in her room,
sitting with legs stretched out,
Mèngzǐ entered and saw her,
then told his mother: "My wife is without propriety,
I request to dismiss her."
His mother said: "It is not your wife who lacks propriety,
but you who are without propriety.
Does not the Book of Rites say: 'When about to ascend the hall,
one must raise one's voice;
when about to enter a room,
one must lower one's gaze.
This is to avoid catching others unprepared.'
Now you entered the private quarters
without making a sound,
causing her to be seen sitting with legs stretched out;
this is your lack of propriety,
not your wife's."
Thereupon Mèngzǐ blamed himself,
and dared not dismiss his wife.
From Hán Shī Wài Zhuàn.
Tián Zǐ served as chancellor,
and after three years returned home on leave,
presenting his mother with a hundred yì of gold.
His mother said: "Ill-gotten gains
should not enter this house.
To be disloyal as a minister
is to be unfilial as a son.
You should leave."
Tián Zǐ walked out in shame,
returned to the king to give back the gold,
and requested to resign and face imprisonment.
Same as above.
Mèng Mǔ lived near a cemetery,
where Mèngzǐ played
at funeral matters.
Mèng Mǔ said: "This is no place to raise my child."
So they left.
They settled next to a market,
where her son played
at merchant hawking.
Mèng Mǔ again said: "This is no place to raise my child."
Then they settled beside a school,
where her son played
at arranging sacrificial vessels,
practicing bows and courtesies.
Mèng Mǔ said: "This is truly where we can raise our child."
So they settled there,
and when Mèngzǐ grew up,
he studied the six arts,
eventually becoming a great scholar.
From Biographies of Exemplary Women.
Cross-referenced under "Neighborhood."
Mèng Rén studied under Lǐ Sù in his youth,
and his mother made him a thick mattress and large quilt,
saying: "My child lacks virtue,
and many visiting scholars are poor,
so I make this wide quilt
hoping you may connect with kindred spirits."
When appointed as Fish Pond Supervisor,
he caught fish and made pickled fish,
sending some to his mother.
His mother scolded him: "You serve as fish official,
yet send me pickled fish—
this avoids no suspicion."
From Wú Lù.
Collection
At the end of the Qín dynasty,
local leaders jointly supported Chén Yīng to become king,
but Yīng's mother stopped him,
saying: "Since I became your family's bride,
we have been poor and humble through generations;
sudden wealth and honor
bring ill fortune."
Yīng followed her advice,
and the Chén family remained safe.
From Bān Shūpí's On the Mandate of Kings.
Only by following the Mèng family's example
can one strongly become a motherly teacher.
From Liǔ Zōngyuán's writings.
Our Dynasty
I, Xiū, was unfortunate,
orphaned at four years old.
My widowed mother vowed to preserve her chastity;
though living in poverty, she supported us through her own efforts,
providing clothing and food,
nurturing and educating me,
until I reached adulthood.
My mother told me: "Your father as an official
was incorruptible and generous,
fond of hosting guests.
Though his salary was meager,
he never allowed surplus.
Saying:
'Do not let this become my burden.'
Thus when he died,
there was not a single tile for shelter
nor a field for cultivation,
nothing to depend on for livelihood.
What could I rely on to maintain my resolve?
I knew your father
well enough
to place hopes in you.
Since I joined your family,
I never met your grandmother,
but I knew your father provided well.
You were orphaned and young,
I couldn't know if you would achieve anything,
but I knew your father would surely have descendants."
From Oūyáng Xiū's Tombstone Inscription at Lǒnggāng.
Recording a son's virtue and achievements
reveals his mother's integrity.
From Oūyáng Xiū's Epitaph for Lady Lǐ.
Cultivating virtue within oneself
to establish a family;
bringing blessings to descendants
to bequeath to children and grandchildren.
From Línchuān Collection.
When Sū Shì was ten,
his mother personally taught him reading.
Once while reading Eastern Hàn history,
upon reaching the Biography of Fàn Pāng,
he sighed deeply.
Sū Shì asked his mother: "If I were to become like Fàn Pāng,
would you allow it?"
His mother replied: "If you can be Fàn Pāng,
can I not be Fàn Pāng's mother?"
From Sū Zhé's epitaph for his elder brother.
Not only should families have long-lived mothers,
but they should also produce extraordinary people for the court.
From Sū Shì's poetry.
Classics
If a son is dissatisfied with his wife,
but his parents say: "She serves us well,"
From The Book of Rites: Internal Rules.
Wives should have no private possessions,
no private goods,
no private savings,
no private use of utensils,
and no private lending or giving.
All household matters must be approved by elders.
In the presence of parents-in-law,
one must not belch, sneeze, cough, yawn, stretch, lean limply, or glance sideways,
nor spit or snivel.
Any wife,
unless ordered to her private room,
may not withdraw.
Same as above.
A wife who has not adorned herself
may not appear before her parents-in-law.
From The Book of Rites: Tángōng.
Cross-referenced under "Parents-in-law."
A wife serving her parents-in-law
should serve them as her own parents:
with subdued voice and pleasant tone,
inquiring if they are warm or cold,
if they suffer pain or itch,
respectfully massaging and scratching for them;
when they go out or come in,
either preceding or following them,
respectfully supporting them.
From The Book of Rites: Internal Rules.
Cross-referenced under "Parents-in-law."
When a wife needs to do something,
whether major or minor, she must ask her parents-in-law.
From The Book of Rites: Internal Rules.
History
The wife listens and is gentle.
． From "Zuo Zhuan, Sixth Year of Duke Zhao".
Bào Xuān's wife, Bǎi Shì,
pulled the deer-cart together with Xuān,
returned to their hometown,
after paying respects to her mother-in-law,
carried a jar to fetch water.
She cultivated wifely virtues,
and was praised throughout the region.
Her son Yǒng became governor of Lǔ Commandery,
Yǒng's son Yù asked Shaojūn: "Does the lady still remember pulling the deer-cart?"
She replied: "My late mother-in-law said,
'In preservation, do not forget loss,
in safety, do not forget danger,'
how dare I forget?"
． From "Biographies of Exemplary Women of Eastern Han".
Bān Zhāo wrote in "Admonitions for Women": "Relying on the classical teachings of mothers and teachers,
at age fourteen,
I took up broom and dustpan in the Cáo family,
and now over forty years have passed.
Trembling with fear,
constantly fearing disgrace,
lest I bring shame upon my parents,
or increase burdens upon the family,
I toiled day and night,
diligent without complaint."
Bān Zhāo died in her seventies,
submitting sixteen memorials as final instructions,
compiled by her daughter-in-law Dīng Shì,
who also wrote "Eulogy for the Great Lady."
Both from the same source.
Jiāng Shī
served his mother with utmost filial piety,
his wife obediently served with deep devotion.
The mother enjoyed drinking water from the Jiāng River,
the wife often fetched it upstream,
once encountering wind,
she couldn't return in time,
the mother grew thirsty,
Shī reproached and dismissed her.
The wife then lodged with neighbors,
spinning day and night,
buying delicacies,
having the neighbor's mother give them to her mother-in-law.
This continued for a long time,
the mother-in-law grew suspicious and asked the neighbor,
who explained everything.
Moved and ashamed, the mother called her back.
． From "Biography of Jiāng Shī's Wife of Eastern Han".
Cross-reference "Human Hearts Are Easily Moved".
The virtue of women
lies in reverently serving parents-in-law,
diligently working day and night—
this is wifely integrity.
From "Book of Tang".
Biographies
record: Wèi Guàn's son Xuān married Princess Fánchāng,
eunuchs slandered them,
so he separated from the princess,
writing to his mother as "your former daughter-in-law".
． From "Accounts of Jin Nobles".
In ancient times, daughters-in-law served parents-in-law,
staying by their side morning and night,
no different from their own children.
． From "Family Instructions of the Yán Clan of Northern History".
Cross-reference "Parents-in-Law".
Classics
Present offerings for sacrifices.
． From "Book of Documents, Announcement about Drunkenness".
Gathering white southernwood,
shows the lady not neglecting her duties.
If the lady can perform sacrifices,
she does not neglect her duties.
From "Book of Songs".
Gathering duckweed,
shows the official's wife can follow rules.
Being able to follow rules,
she can honor ancestors,
and participate in sacrifices.
From "Book of Songs".
Where to place the offerings?
In the ancestral hall under the window.
Who presides over it?
A reverent young maiden.
． From "Book of Songs, Gathering Duckweed".
Collections
Washing makes all pure and excellent,
rituals brilliantly clear.
From Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital".
Presenting seasonal sacrifices to show devotion,
sweeping and cleaning to fulfill duties.
From Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on the Widow".
In spring and autumn ancestral rites, presiding over ritual vessels,
making pure offerings to please bright spirits.
From Hán Yù's writings.
Classics
A wife can pity her husband,
yet encourage him with righteousness.
． From "Book of Songs, Banks of the Rǔ".
A family can sympathize with his labors,
urging him with duty.
． From "Book of Songs, The Distant Thunder".
At Mù Bó's funeral,
Jìng Jiāng wept by day.
At Wén Bó's funeral,
she wept day and night.
Confucius said: "She understands ritual."
． From "Book of Rites, Tángōng".
Histories
Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn passed through Qí,
Duke Huán married a woman to him,
and the prince felt content there.
His followers plotted under a mulberry tree,
a silkworm maid reported this to Jiāng Shì,
who killed her.
She then told the prince: "You have ambitions to travel the four directions,
and the one who overheard this,
I have killed."
She then conspired with Zǐ Fàn,
made the prince drunk, and sent him away.
. "Zuǒzhuàn, Xī 22nd Year".
The Marquis of Qí encountered Qǐ Liáng's wife,
offering condolences to her in the suburbs,
but she declined, saying: "My late husband's humble cottage is still below,
I cannot receive condolences in the suburbs."
The Marquis then offered condolences at her home.
"Zuǒzhuàn, Xiāng 23rd Year".
Cross-reference "Condolences and Comfort".
Bó Zōng of Jìn, every time he went to court,
his wife would warn him: "Thieves hate the master,
the people detest their superiors,
you are fond of speaking bluntly,
and will surely meet with disaster."
. "Zuǒzhuàn, Chéng 15th Year".
Prince Yǔ of Jìn was a hostage in Qín,
planning to escape back home,
said to Yíng Shì: "Shall we return together?"
She replied: "You are the crown prince of Jìn,
humiliated in Qín,
your desire to return,
is it not appropriate?
My lord ordered me to serve you with towel and comb,
to secure your position.
To follow you back
would abandon my lord's command,
I dare not follow,
nor dare I speak of it."
"Zuǒzhuàn".
Zhào Jī of Jìn, considering Dùn talented,
insistently requested the duke,
to make him the heir,
and placed her three sons beneath him,
appointing Shū Wěi as the principal wife,
while she herself took a lower position.
. "Zuǒzhuàn, Xī 24th Year".
Xī Fùjī's wife said: "I observe that the followers of Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn
are all capable of assisting a state,
if with such support,
he will surely return to his country,
and achieve his ambitions among the feudal lords."
. "Zuǒzhuàn, Xī 23rd Year".
A widow does not worry about her loom's threads,
but grieves for the fall of the ancestral Zhou.
. "Zuǒzhuàn, Zhāo 24th Year".
Qí and Jìn battled at Ān,
the Qí army was defeated,
and the Marquis of Qí entered from Xúguān.
A woman asked: "Has the lord escaped?"
He said: "He has."
"Has the Sharp司徒 escaped?"
He said: "He has."
She said: "If the lord and my father have escaped,
what more could I ask?"
Later, it was learned
she was the wife of the Pi司徒,
and he granted her Shíliù.
"Zuǒzhuàn".
Cross-reference "Enfeoffment and Titles".
Yànzǐ was the chancellor of Qí,
once going out,
his charioteer's wife watched her husband from the door,
her husband driving for the chancellor,
proud and elated,
very self-satisfied.
After returning home,
his wife requested to leave,
saying: "Yànzǐ is not even six chǐ tall,
yet he serves as chancellor of Qí,
renowned among the feudal lords.
You are eight chǐ tall,
but serve as a servant driver,
and in your heart,
you feel content,
that is why I wish to leave."
. "Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Yànzǐ".
King Xiāng made the daughter of the Grand Historian his queen,
after King Xiāng died,
his son Jiàn succeeded,
the queen served Qín diligently,
and kept faith with the feudal lords,
thus for over forty years,
they suffered no military attacks.
Emperor Qín Shǐ Huáng once sent an envoy with a linked ring to the queen,
saying: "Is Qí wise enough to solve this ring?"
The queen showed it to her ministers,
who could not solve it,
so the queen took a hammer,
shattered the ring,
and replied to the Qín envoy: "Respectfully, it is solved."
"Strategies of the Warring States".
Gōngfǔ Wénbó held office in Lǔ,
fell ill and died,
and sixteen women
committed suicide in their rooms for him.
His mother heard of it,
but refused to weep.
The steward said: "How can a mother not weep for her dead son?"
The mother said: "Confucius,
a wise man,
was exiled from Lǔ,
and this man did not follow.
Now that he's dead, sixteen women died for him,
if so,
he treated the wise lightly and women heavily."
Thus, from a mother's perspective,
she is a worthy mother;
from a wife's perspective,
she would inevitably be seen as jealous.
So the words are the same,
but spoken by different people, the perception changes.
Ibid.
Lady Lǐ was critically ill,
Emperor Wǔ personally visited her,
but she covered herself with a quilt,
apologizing: "I have been ill long,
my appearance ruined,
I cannot see the emperor."
Her sisters reproached her: "Can you not see the emperor once,
to entrust your brothers?"
Lady Lǐ said: "Not seeing the emperor
is precisely to deeply entrust my brothers.
Those who serve through beauty,
when beauty fades, love wanes.
The emperor's fond memory of me
is based on my former appearance.
If he sees me now, ruined,
my looks not as before,
he will surely fear and dislike me,
how then would he still care for my brothers?"
. "Western Hàn, Biography of Lady Lǐ".
Lǚ Lù visited his aunt Lǚ Xū,
who angrily said: "You are a general yet abandon the army,
the Lǚ clan now has no place!"
She then scattered all her jewels and treasures in the hall,
saying: "Why guard them for others?"
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Hàn Empress Gao".
The emperor began traveling incognito,
once night fell at Bǎigǔ,
he sought lodging at an inn,
asking for drink.
The innkeeper said: "No drink,
only piss here."
Suspecting the emperor of being a thief,
he gathered youths to attack him.
The innkeeper's wife, seeing the emperor's unusual demeanor,
stopped her husband: "This guest is no ordinary man,
and he is prepared,
do not plot against him."
The husband不听,
so she made him drink wine,
got him drunk and tied him up,
the youths dispersed,
and she killed a chicken to feast the guest as apology.
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn".
The King of Qín favored lewd music,
so Queen Yèyáng refused to listen to Zhèng and Wèi melodies;
King Chǔ Zhuāng loved hunting,
so Fán Jī refrained from eating bird and beast meat.
. "Western Hàn, Biography of Zhāng Chǎng".
King Chǔ Zhuāng loved hunting,
his wife Fán Jī repeatedly advised against it to no avail,
so she ate no bird or beast meat for two years,
moved by this, the king
devoted himself to governance.
"Biographies of Exemplary Women".
Duke Bǎi of Qí indulged in pleasure,
so Consort Wèi refused to listen to Zhèng and Wèi music.
Ibid.
Once, Chén Yīng's mother,
considering their family's generations of poverty,
believed sudden wealth and honor
were inauspicious,
ordered Yīng not to claim kingship.
Wáng Líng's mother,
knowing the Hàn king would gain the empire,
fell on her sword to die,
firmly urging Líng onward.
Yīng's mother knew decline,
Líng's mother knew rise.
. "Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of Emperor Guāngwǔ".
King Xuān rose late,
so Queen Jiāng removed her hairpin;
Duke Bǎi of Qí loved music,
so Consort Wèi made no sound.
. "Eastern Hàn, Biography of Wáng Yì".
Yuè Yángzǐ from Hénán sought a teacher,
studied for a year,
and returned home.
His wife knelt and asked the reason.
Yáng Zǐ said: “Long travels breed longing thoughts,
with no other unusual feelings.”
His wife then took up a knife and approached the loom,
saying: “This weaving begins from silkworm cocoons,
is completed on the loom and shuttle;
one thread accumulates,
until it becomes an inch;
accumulating inches without cease,
eventually forms yards and bolts.
Now if this weaving is cut off,
then the previous effort is wasted,
and time and months are delayed and lost.
You, sir, accumulate learning;
if you return midway,
how is it different from cutting off this weaving?”
. From Biographies of Exemplary Women of the Eastern Hàn.
King Zhāo of Chǔ was feasting and traveling,
and the Yuè concubine accompanied him.
He said to her: “I wish to live and die with you like this.”
The concubine said: “Your Majesty enjoys traveling,
yet demands that I die;
I dare not obey such a command.”
Later, the king fell ill,
and the Grand Historian requested to transfer the illness to the generals and ministers.
The king said: “The generals and ministers are to me like limbs.”
He did not listen.
The concubine said: “Great indeed
is Your Majesty’s virtue!
I beg to follow the king in death.
In the past, during the travels and pleasures,
that is why I dared not obey the command;
now the king has returned to propriety,
and the people of the state would die for Your Majesty—
how much more should I?”
Then she killed herself.
From the Eastern Hàn.
Bào Xuān’s wife, of the Bǎi family, was sent off with very lavish dowry and trousseau.
Xuān said to his wife: “Shǎojūn, you were born into wealth,
accustomed to pride and fine adornments.
But I am poor and lowly,
and dare not accept such ceremony.”
So she returned all the attendants, carriages, clothing, and ornaments,
and changed into short cloth garments.
From the Dōngguān Hànjì.
Yīng Chāo took Zhào Áng’s son Yuè as a hostage.
Áng said to his wife Yì: “My plan is thus;
the matter is sure to be perfectly safe,
but what shall we do about Yuè?”
Yì sternly replied: “To wash away the great shame of your lord and father,
losing one’s head is not too heavy a price—
how much more a single son?”
. From the Tōngjiàn Hàn Xiànjì.
Liáng Hóng’s wife entered the household adorned in finery.
For seven days, Hóng did not respond to her.
Then she knelt by the bed to ask for his reproach.
Hóng said: “I wanted a person in coarse garments,
one who could go with me to hide in the deep mountains.
Now you wear silks and gauzes,
apply powder and makeup—
how could this be my wish?”
His wife said: “I have my own garments for living in seclusion.”
Then she changed to a mallet-shaped bun,
wore plain cloth clothes,
and came forward to work.
. From the Eastern Hàn Original Biography.
If you wish to emulate the lofty examples of Bào Xuān and Liáng Hóng,
then I too beg to follow the deeds of Shǎojūn and Mèng Guāng.
. From Biographies of Exemplary Women of the Eastern Hàn.
Earlier,
the Dānyáng governor Lǐ Héng
repeatedly encroached upon the Prince of Lángyá in various matters.
His wife, of the Xí family, admonished him,
but Héng did not listen.
When the Prince of Lángyá ascended the throne,
Lǐ Héng became worried and fearful.
He said to his wife: “I did not heed your words,
and so have come to this.
I wish to flee to Wèi—
what do you think?”
His wife said: “You must not.
The Prince of Lángyá has always been fond of goodness and admired reputation;
he now wishes to display himself to the world.
He will certainly not kill you over a private grievance.
This is clear.
You should instead imprison yourself and go to the court,
submit a statement listing your past faults,
openly seeking to receive punishment.
In this way,
you will likely be met with generous treatment,
not merely be spared alive.”
Héng followed her advice.
The Wú ruler issued an edict: “The Dānyáng governor Lǐ Héng,
because of past grievances,
has confined himself to the Office of Justice.
Let Héng be sent back to his commandery.”
. From the Tōngjiàn Wèi Yuándì.
Gěng Fàn’s wife said: “Earlier, you wished to behead the Xúzhōu governor Zōu Qí;
everyone said you were hard to serve under.
Now you are ashamed to submit to Lǚ,
Lǚ Zhāo Fàn.
It is also hard to serve above you.”
. From the Wèi Zhì, Biography of Cáo Shuǎng.
Earlier,
the Jìn High Ancestor,
Sīmǎ Yì,
declined office on grounds of wind-paralysis,
unable to rise or move about.
While airing books, he encountered rain;
the High Ancestor got up to collect the books.
Only one maidservant in the household saw this.
Empress Zhāng, fearing the words might leak out,
then killed her with her own hands,
and personally did the cooking.
From the Jìn Shū.
Bó Xuán’s later wife, of the Liú family, had wisdom and discernment.
She said to Xuán: “Liú Yù moves like a dragon, strides like a tiger;
his gaze and bearing are extraordinary.
I fear he will not remain under others forever;
it would be better to eliminate him early.”
. From the Tōngjiàn Jìn Āndì Jì.
Shān Gōng and Jī, Ruǎn were as close as metal and orchid.
Shān Gōng’s wife, of the Hán family, sensed these two men were different from ordinary people,
and spied on them.
Another day, when the two came,
the wife secretly watched them.
Shān Gōng asked: “What are these two like?”
His wife said: “You are far inferior;
it is only in knowledge
and judgment that you compare.”
From the Shì Shuō.
Wáng Yòujūn’s wife, Lady Xiè, said to her two younger brothers
Xīnyīn and Tán:
“When the Wáng family sees the two Xiè—
Ān and Wàn—
they empty their baskets and rush out in their slippers.
When they see you all come,
it is just ordinary.”
From the Shì Shuō, part two.
Cross-referenced in “Discernment and Distinction.”
Fú Chéngzǔ was just then in power,
and relatives by marriage vied to flatter and attach themselves for gain.
His maternal aunt, Lady Yáng, wife of the Yáo family,
alone did not.
She once said to Chéngzǔ’s mother: “Sister, though you have momentary glory,
it is not like me, who have carefree joy.”
Her elder sister gave her clothes,
but she mostly would not accept them.
. From the Tōngjiàn Qí Tàizǔ.
Prince Xǔ’s mother, Consort Hú,
was first selected into the rear palace.
Her peers, following precedent, wished her well,
saying: “May you bear princes and princesses,
but not a crown prince.”
Consort Hú said: “My aspiration differs from others’;
why should I fear death for myself,
and let the state have no heir?”
When she became pregnant,
her peers urged her to get rid of it.
Consort Hú would not,
and secretly vowed: “If I am fortunate to bear a son,
and he should be the eldest in succession,
even if I die giving birth to a boy,
I will have no regrets!”
. From the Tōngjiàn Liáng Gāozǔ.
Dòu Yì’s daughter heard that Suí had received the abdication,
threw herself down in the hall,
beat her chest and sighed deeply: “How I regret not being a man,
to save my maternal uncles’ calamity!”
Yì and Princess Xiāngyáng covered her mouth,
saying: “Do not speak recklessly—
you will exterminate our clan.”
Yì thus considered her extraordinary.
When she grew up,
she was married to the Duke of Táng, Lǐ Yuān.
. From the Tōngjiàn Chén Jì.
Empress Zhǎngsūn had always been fond of reading,
and often calmly discussed ancient matters with the Emperor,
thereby offering criticism and suggestions,
which provided great benefit.
Sometimes the Emperor would reprimand or grow angry at palace women without just cause;
the Empress would also feign anger,
request to personally interrogate them,
then order them imprisoned,
waiting until the Emperor’s anger subsided,
before slowly pleading their case.
Because of this,
within the palace,
punishments were not unjust or excessive.
The Emperor fell ill,
and for years did not recover.
The Empress attended him,
day and night never leaving his side.
She often carried poison tied to her sash,
saying: “If the unmentionable happens,
in duty I will not live alone.”
The Empress had long suffered from illness;
the Crown Prince said to her: “Medicine and treatment have been exhausted,
yet the illness does not heal.
I request to petition for amnesty for prisoners,
When it came to converting people to Taoism,
hoping to obtain posthumous blessings."
The Empress said: "Life and death are fated,
not something that intelligence or effort can change.
If doing good brings blessings,
then I have done no evil;
if it is not so,
what benefit is there in vainly seeking?"
When her illness became critical,
she bid farewell to the Emperor, saying: "On days when Your Majesty is unwell,
I vowed to follow the imperial carriage in death,
unable to bear the situation like Empress Lǚ Zhì did."
On the Yǐmǎo day,
she passed away in the Lìzhèng Hall.
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Tàizōng".
Zhǎngsūn the Empress once compiled stories of women's successes and failures since ancient times,
creating "The Women's Principles" in thirty volumes.
Same as above.
When Wèi Zhēng passed away,
the Emperor ordered all officials of the ninth rank and above to attend the funeral,
providing feather canopies,
and musical accompaniment for burial at Zhāolíng.
His wife, Madame Péi, said: "Zhēng lived a frugal and simple life;
now burying him with first-rank ceremonial honors
goes against the deceased's wishes."
She declined all offerings,
burying him with a coffin carried on a plain cart.
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Tàizōng".
Xiāo Yǔ's son Ruì inherited the title and married the Emperor's daughter, Princess Xiāngchéng.
The Emperor wanted to build a separate residence for them,
but the princess firmly declined, saying: "As a wife serving parents-in-law,
I should attend them morning and night;
if living in a separate residence,
much would be lacking."
When the Emperor built the Yùhuá Palace,
he insisted on frugality and simplicity,
only having the main hall roofed with tiles,
while the rest used thatch,
fully accommodating the Great Wall.
Xú Huì, seeing that the Emperor campaigned against Gāolì in the east,
fought against Qiūcí in the west,
and successively built Cuìwēi and Yùhuá palaces,
with continuous construction,
along with rather extravagant clothing and playthings,
submitted a memorial advising, roughly saying: "Using finite agricultural resources
to fill endless vast waves,
seeking what is not yet obtained,
others lose what they have,
our army achieves it.
In the past, the Qín king annexed the six states,
but instead hastened the foundation of peril and fall;
the Jìn Wǔdì briefly held three regions,
yet turned it into a cause for collapse and defeat.
Was it not due to boasting of achievements, relying on size,
abandoning virtue, and轻视ing the state,
seeking profit and endangering scholars,
indulging emotions and desires?
Thus, it is known that vast territory
is not the means to lasting peace;
people's toil
is the source of容易混乱.
Even if showing restraint with thatch,
it still wearies wood and stone greatly;
hiring labor from the people,
it unavoidably has the flaw of causing disturbance.
Precious playthings and craft
are the axes that destroy the state;
pearls, jade, brocade, and embroidery
are indeed the poison that bewilders the heart.
If laws are made with frugality,
there is still fear of luxury;
if laws are made with luxury,
how can later generations be controlled?"
Also from the same source.
Hóu Mǐn, the Superintendent of the Imperial Parks, often flattered Lái Jùnchén.
His wife, Madame Dǒng, warned him: "Jùnchén is a traitor to the state;
he will fall from power soon;
you should distance yourself from him."
Mǐn followed her advice,
angering Jùnchén,
who had him demoted to Magistrate of Wǔlóng.
Mǐn hesitated to go,
but his wife said: "Go quickly,
do not stay."
When Jùnchén fell,
his followers were all exiled to Lǐngnán,
but Mǐn alone was spared.
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Wǔhòu".
When the Emperor fell ill,
the eunuchs wanted to invite Empress Dowager Guō to reign as regent,
but the Empress Dowager said: "In the past, Empress Wǔ reigned,
nearly overthrowing the state;
our family has always upheld loyalty and righteousness,
not comparable to Empress Wǔ.
Since ancient times, has there ever been a woman ruling the world
who could achieve the governance of Yáo and Shùn?"
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Jìngzōng".
Tàizōng once discussed rewards and punishments with the Empress,
and she said: "When a hen crows at dawn,
it signifies the family's decline; I,
a woman, dare not interfere in state affairs."
Tàizōng insisted on speaking with her,
but she ultimately did not reply.
． "Continued Tales of the World: Empress Zhǎngsūn".
See also "Rites and Laws".
Zhū Wēn was orphaned young,
and with his brother Xùcún, followed their mother, Madame Wáng, to rely on Liú Chóng's family in Xiāo County.
Chóng often whipped and humiliated them,
but their mother alone pitied them,
warning the family: "Zhū Sān is no ordinary person;
treat him well."
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Táng Xīzōng".
Zhōu Xíngféng's wife, Madame Dèng, Lady of Xūn State,
said: "Taxes
are government property.
You, as a military governor,
not paying taxes first,
how can you lead your subordinates?
And do you not remember being a village head,
paying taxes for others,
to avoid whipping and punishment then?"
． "Comprehensive Mirror: Zhōu Shìzōng".
Shǔ's Empress Dowager Lǐ, due to inappropriate military appointments,
told the Shǔ ruler: "Now Wáng Zhāoyuǎn comes from menial origins,
Yī Shěnwēi, Hán Bǎozhēn, Zhào Chóngtāo,
are all pampered, milk-smelling youths,
untrained in warfare,
merely placed above others due to old favors.
If border conflicts arise one day,
how can they resist great enemies?
From what I see,
only Gāo Yànchóu,
a veteran from Tàiyuán,
will never betray you;
the rest are not worthy of appointment."
Same as above.
Wáng Guī was close to Fáng and Dù,
and when they visited his home,
Wáng Guī's mother observed them,
and joyfully said: "These two guests have the talent of ministers;
your nobility is assured."
． "Táng Book: Wáng Guī Biography".
See also "Motherly Way".
Biographies.
There was a woman from Qí named Xú Wú,
who joined her neighbor women in spinning at night by shared candlelight.
Being poor,
she could not contribute her share of candles.
The neighbor women requested that she not join them at night,
but Xú Wú said:
"Because of my poverty,
I always rise first
and leave last,
sweeping and arranging the mats
to await the arrivals.
I always sit in the lowest place
due to my poverty.
Now in this single room,
adding one person
doesn't make the candle burn brighter,
nor does removing one person
make it burn dimmer.
Why begrudge the spare light from the eastern wall?"
None could respond to this,
so she continued spinning with them at night. From Biographies of Exemplary Women.
Cross-referenced under "Women's Words."
Lǎo Láizi lived in seclusion on Méng Mountain.
The King of Chǔ personally came to his gate,
and when his wife asked who it was,
he replied: "The King of Chǔ."
His wife said:
"Those who can be fed with wine and meat
can also be beaten with whips;
those who can accept official salaries
can also be followed by executioners' axes.
If you accept an official salary from others,
you will be controlled by them.
I cannot be one who is controlled by others."
His wife then left. From Biographies of High-Minded Scholars.
There was a woman from the town of Qīshì in Lǔ
who had passed marriageable age without marrying.
During the time of Duke Mù,
when the ruler was old and the crown prince young,
the woman leaned against a pillar and sighed deeply.
A neighbor woman asked:
"Why do you sigh so sorrowfully?
Do you wish to marry?"
The woman replied:
"How could I be sorrowful about not marrying?
I worry that the ruler of Lǔ is old while the crown prince is young." From Biographies of Exemplary Women.
Fán Yí recommended her sister,
Hé Dé, who was beautiful in appearance.
The Emperor summoned her to the palace.
When Hé Dé had just bathed,
she applied perfumed ointment nine times,
used sinking incense,
styled her hair in curled locks,
called the "New Rise Chignon,"
painted her eyebrows thinly,
called "Distant Mountain Eyebrows,"
applied light rouge,
called "Languid Makeup,"
and those around her clicked their tongues in admiration.
During Emperor Xuān's time, the erudite of Pīxiāng, Nào Fāngchéng,
white-haired and teaching in the palace,
called "Lady Nào,"
spat behind the Emperor and said:
"This is a flood of disaster
that will surely extinguish the fire." From The Unofficial Biography of Empress Zhào.
Chén Zìdìng,
courtesy name Zǐzhòng,
was offered one hundred yì of gold by the King of Chǔ's envoy
to appoint him as chancellor.
Zhòngzǐ said:
"I have a wife who handles the broom and dustpan.
Please allow me to consult with her."
He then told his wife:
"If I become chancellor today,
tomorrow we'll have carriages and riders in procession,
with fine food spread before us."
His wife said:
"The joy of being chancellor today
lies within oneself.
With countless carriages and riders,
the comfort needed is only knee-room;
with fine food spread before you,
the sweetness enjoyed is but one portion of meat.
Now for the comfort of knee-room
and the taste of one portion of meat,
to bear the worries of the state of Chǔ
in a chaotic world full of dangers
—I fear you won't preserve your life, sir."
Zhòngzǐ and his wife fled
to work watering gardens for others. From Huángfǔ Mì's Biographies of High-Minded Scholars.
The Grand Administrator of Táo governed for three years
without gaining a good reputation,
but his family wealth tripled.
His wife angrily said:
"To hold high office with little ability
is to invite harm;
to prosper without merit
is to accumulate calamity.
In the past, the Prime Minister of Chǔ governed the state
with his family poor but the state rich.
The ruler respected him, the people supported him,
thus blessings reached his descendants,
and his name passed to later generations.
Now you greedily seek wealth and greatness,
disregarding future harm.
I ask to leave." From Biographies of Exemplary Women.
Zhōu Qǐ, courtesy name Mèngyù,
had a disciple who committed murder and was convicted.
Qǐ went to the prefecture
and died in prison with his disciple.
His brother's wife did not weep for her son,
but wept for Mèngyù,
thus was considered noble. From Comprehensive Meaning of Customs.
The queen of King Mǐn of Qí
had a large tumor on her neck,
thus called "Sùliú" (Congenital Tumor).
Initially,
when King Mǐn went on an excursion,
all the common people watched,
but Sùliú continued gathering mulberry leaves as before.
The King found it strange
and asked her.
She replied:
"I received my parents' teaching to gather mulberry leaves,
not teaching to watch the Great King."
The King ordered her to be carried in his rear carriage.
The girl said:
"With my parents at home,
if I follow the King without their teaching,
I would be an eloping woman.
How could the King use me?"
The King was greatly ashamed,
sent an envoy with gifts and one hundred yì of gold
to formally propose marriage.
Her parents were startled
and wanted her to bathe and change clothes,
but the girl said:
"If I meet the King like this,
changing my appearance and clothing,
I won't be recognized."
Thus she went as before
with the envoy
and King Mǐn made her his queen. From Biographies of Exemplary Women.
Cross-referenced under "Steadfast Chastity."
Fán Jī moved the King of Zhuāng
by not eating fresh game;
the woman of Wèi emulated Bó Yí,
her ears averse to harmonious music.
Their will was stern, their righteousness high,
and two rulers changed their hearts.
The black bear climbed the railing,
Féng Yuān advanced quickly—
was she without fear?
She knew death was not to be avoided.
Bān Jiéyú had words,
cut off joy and shared the carriage—
was she without feeling?
She guarded against the subtle and considered the distant. Zhāng Huá's Admonitions for Women Historians.
Collection
Fàn Chuánzhèng conducted inspections in Xuānzhōu and Chízhōu
and searched for Lǐ Bái's descendants.
He found two granddaughters,
one married to Chén Yún,
the other to Liú Quàn,
both commoners registered as peasants.
He summoned them to the commandery
and told the two women
he would remarry them to scholar-official families.
They both said:
"The way of husband and wife
is fate,
also one's lot.
In our loneliness and poverty,
though we've lowered ourselves,
to rely on powerful influence
and seek support from other families
—even if we steal comfort in life,
what face would we have to see our grandfather underground after death?
To ruin our kind
is what we cannot bear to hear." From The Collected Works of Lǐ Bái.
Even with the understanding of an ordinary woman,
one can still deduce principles of affairs
and probe the mechanisms of fortune and misfortune.
Yīng's mother knew about decline,
Líng's mother knew about rise. From Discourse on the Mandate of Kings.
History
Niè Zhèng's sister Róng declared: "How could I fear the punishment of death,
and thus extinguish the name of my worthy brother!"
She then greatly alarmed the people in the Hán market.
Crying out to heaven three times,
she died by Zhèng's side.
When Jìn, Chǔ, Qí, and Wèi heard of this,
they all said:
"She is a woman of exemplary conduct."
. _Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of Niè Zhèng_.
"Róng" is also written as "Yīng".
Wǔ Zǐxū fled to Wú,
reaching Lìyáng,
where a woman was beating laundry in the water.
Zǐxū passed by and begged for food,
the woman fed him with a pot of broth,
and after Zǐxū left,
the woman threw herself into the Lài River.
_Annals of Wú and Yuè_.
Emperor Yuán visited the tiger enclosure,
with the rear palace ladies all seated.
A bear escaped the enclosure and climbed the railing,
those nearby all fled in panic,
but Féng Jiéyú stepped forward directly,
standing before the bear.
The emperor asked: "Why did you step forward to face the bear?"
She replied: "I have heard that fierce beasts stop when they catch a person.
I feared the bear would reach Your Majesty's seat,
so I used my body to block it."
_Book of Hàn_.
Guī Lǎn, the Grand Governor of Dānyáng, killed the Grand Administrator Sūn Yì,
and sought to force himself upon Yì's wife, Xú Shì.
Xú deceived him, saying: "I beg for time until the last day of the month,
to set up a sacrifice and remove mourning garments,
after which I will comply."
Lǎn agreed.
Xú Shì secretly sent her confidants
to inform Yì's close former generals Sūn Gāo and Fù Yīng,
to join in plotting against Lǎn.
On the last day of the month,
she set up the sacrifice,
Xú Shì wept and mourned,
after fully expressing her grief,
she removed her mourning clothes, perfumed herself, bathed, and spoke and laughed joyfully.
The household felt sorrowful,
finding her behavior strange.
Lǎn secretly observed,
and had no further suspicions.
Xú Shì called Gāo and Yīng to hide inside the door,
then had someone summon Lǎn to enter.
Xú Shì came out the door,
bowed to Lǎn,
just as she finished one bow,
Xú loudly called: "You two gentlemen may rise!"
Gāo and Yīng both came out,
and together killed Lǎn.
. _Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance: Reign of Hàn Xiàndì_.
Sūn Quán married his sister to Liú Bèi,
this sister was talented, quick, firm, and fierce,
having the demeanor of her brothers,
with over a hundred maidservants
all personally holding knives and standing in attendance.
Whenever Liú Bèi entered,
his heart was always filled with trepidation.
_Records of Shǔ_.
Zhào É's father was killed by Lǐ Shòu,
so É concealed a sword in her sleeve in a curtained carriage,
and in broad daylight assassinated Shòu at the capital pavilion,
then went to the county office,
her complexion unchanged.
She said:
"My father's enemy is slain,
I request to receive execution."
The county magistrate tried to release her,
but É refused,
so he forcibly carried her back home,
and she was pardoned by a general amnesty.
_Records of Wèi_.
Liú Shì had courage and strategy,
Shí Lè involved her in military decisions,
and she assisted Lè in achieving merit,
possessing the style of Empress Lǚ,
but without jealousy,
even surpassing her.
. _Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance: Reign of Jìn Chéngdì_.
Sūn Ēn captured Kuàijī,
Wáng Níngzhī fled,
Ēn captured and killed him,
along with his several sons.
Níngzhī's wife, Xiè Dàoyùn,
daughter of Xiè Yì,
upon hearing the bandits arrived,
remained composed in her actions,
ordered her maids to carry her sedan and drew a knife,
went out the gate and personally killed several people,
before being captured.
. _Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance: Reign of Jìn Chéngdì_.
Zhū Xù defended Xiāngyáng,
Fú Jiān sent a general to besiege Xù.
His mother, Hán Shì, personally walked on the city walls,
and said the northwest corner would be the first to fail,
so she led over a hundred maids and the city's women
to build a slanting wall over twenty zhàng long at that corner.
When the enemy attacked the northwest corner,
it indeed collapsed,
but the crowd then defended the newly built wall,
and the enemy withdrew.
People called this wall the "Lady's Wall."
_Book of Jìn_.
Same as above.
Zhōu Jùn once went hunting,
encountered rain,
and stopped at the Lǐ family's home.
It happened that the brothers were not home,
Lǐ Shì, hearing Jùn had arrived,
with one maid inside, slaughtered pigs and sheep to prepare enough
food for ten people,
very exquisitely arranged,
without any sound of people.
Jùn thus sought to take her as a concubine,
and she gave birth to Zhōu Yǐ.
. _Book of Jìn: Biographies of Exemplary Women_.
When the Former Liáng's Zhāng Tiānxī fell ill,
his beauties Yán Jī and Xuē Jī both committed suicide.
Tiānxī had often said to them: "After I die,
you will become someone else's wives."
They both said: "If Your Honor passes away,
we beg to die before you,
to clean and sweep for you in the underworld,
with no other intentions."
_Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms_.
The wife of Féng Bǎo, the Grand Administrator of Gāoliáng of Chén, Xiǎn Shì,
pacified and gathered the tribes,
bringing peace to several provinces.
By the Suí dynasty,
when Wáng Zhòngxuān rebelled,
the Lady Xiǎn of Gāoliáng in Lǐngnán rescued Guǎngzhōu.
It was preserved intact,
and Xiǎn Shì was enfeoffed as "Lady of Qiáo."
She established a headquarters in Lǐngnán,
set up officials,
and acted according to circumstances.
. _Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance: Liáng Dynasty_.
Cross-reference to "Enfeoffments and Titles."
Cuī Níng battled Yáng Zǐlín,
and suffered several defeats.
Cuī Níng's concubine Rén Shì used her family wealth of several hundred thousand to recruit soldiers,
gathering several thousand men,
led them to attack Zǐlín,
defeated him,
and Zǐlín fled.
. _Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance: Táng Dàizōng_.
When Mòchuò attacked Fēihú County,
the wife of Gǔ Yuányìng was able to firmly defend it,
and by decree was enfeoffed as "Lady of Xúnzhōng County."
. _New Book of Táng: Biographies of Exemplary Women_.
Cross-reference to "Enfeoffments and Titles."
During the rebellion of Shǐ Sīmíng,
