After Yuán Zǎi's downfall,
his wife, née Wáng, said:
"I am the daughter of a certain circuit military governor,
and for eighteen years, the wife of a chancellor.
Today, my husband has committed a crime,
and I would die content.
To make me a springtime maid-servant—
I would rather die."
The authorities reported this to the emperor,
and soon she was also ordered to commit suicide.
From Liú Yǔxī's "Jiāhuà".
History
Bān Biāo's daughter,
named Zhāo,
also named Jī,
was erudite and highly talented.
Her elder brother Bān Gù was writing the "Book of Hàn",
but its "Eight Tables" and "Treatise on Astronomy" were not completed at his death.
Emperor Hé ordered Zhāo
to go to the library at the Eastern Lodge
and continue the work to completion.
She also wrote seven chapters of "Admonitions for Women",
which aided in female education.
Her writings included fu, eulogies, inscriptions, dirges, questions, commentaries, lamentations, letters, discourses, memorials, and final instructions,
totaling sixteen pieces.
She also wrote "Eulogy for the Great Lady".
Cài Yōng's daughter,
named Yǎn,
courtesy name Wénjī,
was erudite, talented, and eloquent,
and also excelled in music.
Cáo Cāo asked her:
"I have heard that your family possessed many classical texts;
can you still recall them?"
Wénjī replied:
"In the past, my late father bestowed over four thousand scrolls of books,
but amidst the turmoil and suffering,
none remain.
What I can now recite from memory
is only over four hundred pieces.
I beg for paper and brush,
and will write them in regular or cursive script as commanded."
Thereupon, she transcribed the texts and presented them,
with no omissions or errors.
Later, moved by the sorrows of displacement and turmoil,
she reminisced with grief and indignation,
and composed a poem.
Both from the "Biographies of Exemplary Women" in the "Book of the Later Hàn".
The wife of Qínzhōu Governor Dòu Tāo,
daughter of Péngchéng Magistrate Sū Dào,
was talented and learned.
She wove a brocade with a reversible-pattern poem
to redeem her husband from punishment.
When read cyclically,
the verses were very clear and graceful.
From the "Book of Jìn".
Wéi Chěng, the Minister of Ceremonies, had a mother née Sòng,
who inherited her father's learning
and mastered the pronunciation and meaning of the "Zhou Rites".
Fú Jiān then established a lecture hall at the Sòng family home,
with 120 students,
who studied behind a crimson silk curtain,
and honored Lady Sòng as Lady Xuānwén.
From the "Biographies of Exemplary Women" in the "Book of Jìn".
Xiè Dàoyùn was intelligent, knowledgeable, and eloquent.
Once, her uncle Xiè Ān held a family gathering,
when suddenly snow began to fall.
Ān said:
"What does it resemble?"
Ān's nephew Lǎng said:
"It roughly compares to salt scattering in the air."
Dàoyùn said:
"Better said, willow catkins riding on the wind."
Same as above.
Empress Zhēn, at age nine,
loved books,
using her elder brothers' writing brushes and inkstones.
Her brothers said to her:
"Do you intend to become a female scholar?"
She replied:
"The virtuous women of ancient times
all studied the successes and failures of former ages
to serve as their own warning.
Without knowing books,
how could one learn from them?"
From the "Records of Wèi".
Xú Fēi's wife,

She was Liú Xiàochāo's younger sister.
From the "Biography of Liú Xiàochāo" in the "History of the Southern Dynasties".
Biographies
Cài Yǎn's husband died, leaving no son,
and she returned to her parental home.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, she was captured by Hú cavalry,
and lived among the Left Virtuous Prince's tribe.
In a spring month, ascending a Hú hall,
moved by the sound of a reed pipe,
she composed a poem, saying:
"The Hú reed pipe stirs, the frontier horses neigh."
From "The Separate Biography of Cài Yǎn".
Liǔxià Huì's wife wrote a eulogy for her husband,

From the "Biographies of Exemplary Women".
When Xiàngrú was about to take a maiden from Màolíng as a concubine,

Chángqīng (Xiàngrú) died of diabetes,
and Wénjūn wrote a eulogy that was passed down through the ages.
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital".
Bān Jiéyú was literate,
favored by Emperor Chéng of Hàn.
When the emperor later favored Zhào Fēiyàn,

From the "Music Bureau Poems".
Yáng Yíngchuān's niece, named Rónghuá,

"The roosting birds, startled from sleep, have ceased;
the room and windows open at dawn.
The phoenix hairpin, gold threaded;
the phoenix mirror, jade as its stand.
The makeup seems to emerge by the pond;
the person is suspected to have come down with the moon.
Pitying myself, in the end unseen,
wishing to leave, yet I linger."
From "Records from Court and Country".
Dù Gāo's wife, née Liú, was skilled at poetry.
Dù Gāo repeatedly failed the imperial examinations.
As he was about to return home,
his wife first sent him a poem, saying:
"My husband truly has remarkable talent;
Why is it that year after year you are sent back?
Now my face is ashamed before yours;
If you come, come under cover of night."
Gāo saw the poem,
and immediately turned back.
Soon he passed the examinations,
and his wife again sent a poem, saying:
"From Cháng'ān, it's not far from here;
Luxuriant and vibrant, auspicious air floats.
My husband, triumphant in his youth—
In which tower will you lie drunk tonight?"
From "New Book of the South".
Hàn Wáng Zhāojūn went to the Chányú,

and composed a song of resentment and longing, saying:
"What am I alone?
Changing the past, altering the constant.
The high mountains are lofty;
The river waters are vast.
Father, mother, wife, and children—
The road is long and far."
From "Accounts of the Lute".

History:
In Zhèng, Xú Wúfàn's younger sister was beautiful;
Gōngsūn Chǔ had already betrothed her,
but Gōngsūn Hēi also forced a betrothal gift upon her.
Zǐchǎn suggested letting the maiden choose for herself.
Zǐxī entered in splendid attire,
laid out the gifts, and left.
Zǐnán entered in military dress,
shot arrows to left and right,
leaped into his chariot and departed.
The maiden watched from her room and said,
"Zǐxī is indeed handsome,
but Zǐnán is a true man."
She married into the Zǐnán clan.
From "Zuǒzhuàn."
Long ago, a man of Jiǎ was ugly,

Driving to the marsh,

The Mèng family had a daughter,
plump and plain in appearance,
who refused to marry until she found a match,

Her parents asked her the reason,
and she said, "I wish to find someone as worthy as Liáng Bóluán."
Liáng Hóng heard of this and sought her hand.
The maiden said, "I have privately heard of your high principles,
having rejected several women;

History:
The wife of Xǔ Shēng of Wú was a daughter of the Lǚ family.
Shēng in his youth was a gambler,
neglecting his conduct.
His wife often urged him to pursue studies,
and whenever he erred,
she would weep and offer admonition.
Shēng, moved and inspired,
sought teachers and studied afar,
eventually achieving fame.
From "Biographies of Exemplary Women of the Eastern Hàn."
At the end of the Jiànzhōng era,

His wife, Yáng shì, said: "If the county is not defended,
it becomes bandit territory;
the granaries and treasuries become their stores,
and the people become their soldiers.
I request to recruit warriors willing to die."
The bandits then withdrew,
the county was preserved,

Biography:
The Duke Píng of Jìn ordered an artisan to make a bow,
which took three years to complete.
When shot,
it could not pierce a single layer of armor.
The duke was angry and intended to kill the artisan.
His wife appeared before the duke and said: "My husband made this bow
with great toil,
yet it cannot pierce a single layer—this is because you, my lord, do not know how to shoot.
I have heard the way of shooting: the left hand is like a square,
the right hand like clinging to a branch;
when the right hand releases,
the left hand remains unaware."
The duke used her words as guidance
and pierced seven layers of armor.
The artisan was rewarded with three yi of gold.
From "Biographies of Exemplary Women."
Our dynasty:
That I am not burdened in heart by poverty or
wealth and honor
is due to the help of my wife.
I have often spoken with scholars and officials,
and Xiè shì would listen from behind the door or screen;
she could thoroughly discuss their talents, worthiness or lack thereof,
and the merits and faults of current affairs,
all with clear reasoning.
When I served in Wúxīng,
upon returning from outside,
she would always ask:
"With whom did you drink and enjoy today?"
If she heard they were worthy,
she was pleased;
if not,
she would sigh and say: "The people you associate with
are all the finest of the time.
How can you drink and rejoice with such a person?"
From Ōu Yángxiū's epitaph for Méi Shèngyú's wife, Xiè shì.

Beside the one who has not yet died.

calls herself 'the one who has not yet died'."
Yú Gōng planned to level the peril of Tàiháng Mountain,
and a widow in the capital had a son
who went to assist him.
. _Lièzǐ, "Tāng Wèn"_.
When Qǐ Liáng died,

According to rites,

she calls herself 'the one who has not yet died'.
. _Hòu Wèi Shū_.

alas, how sorrowful!
Your soul and spirit have departed;
your posthumous title should be Huì!"

During a fire in Sòng,
Bó Jī of Sòng perished,
because she waited for her governess.
Female preceptor.

that if her matron is not present,
she does not descend from the hall,"
and thus she was caught in the fire and died.

When Dù Tāo reached Chángshā,
he captured the two daughters of the former Shàoxīng governor Yǐn Yú,

Intending to marry them,
they said: "Our father was a two-thousand-bushel official,

From Dèng Càn's Records of Jìn.
Wáng Níng served as household registrar of Guózhōu,
and died in office.
His family was poor,
with one son still young,
so his wife Lǐ Shì took the child to return home.
Passing through Kāifēng prefecture,
the innkeeper saw her, a woman,
traveling alone with one child,
and grew suspicious,
refusing her lodging.
Lǐ Shì saw that night had fallen,
but unwilling to leave,
the innkeeper pulled her by the arm and ejected her.
Lǐ Shì looked up to heaven and wailed bitterly,
saying: "I am a woman;
if I cannot preserve my chastity,
and this hand has been grasped by a man,
I cannot let one hand defile my whole body."
Immediately she took an axe and cut off her own arm.
Passersby who witnessed this
gathered around and sighed,
some clicking their tongues in sympathy,
others shedding tears.
The prefect of Kāifēng heard of it,
reported the matter to the court officials,
had medicine bestowed to dress her wound,
provided generous support to Lǐ Shì,
and flogged the innkeeper.
Alas!
Scholars who do not cherish their own integrity
and endure shame to cling to life—
upon hearing of Lǐ Shì's example,
should feel some shame!
． From Miscellaneous Biographies of the History of the Five Dynasties.
Biographies

The wife of a man from Cài

Her husband had a foul disease,

how can I leave him?
The way of marriage

how much more so between husband and wife?"
Same as above.
Virtuous women contend with sages and martyrs for undying fame,

The wife of King Zhāo of Chǔ
was a woman of Qí.
When King Zhāo went on an excursion,
he left his wife at the Jiàntái tower.
The river rose greatly,
and he sent a messenger to fetch her,
but he forgot the tally.
The lady said: "The king made a pact with the palace women
that summons must be with the tally;
now the messenger has no tally,
so I dare not go."
Thereupon the messenger returned,
but before he could fetch the tally and come back,
the tower collapsed,
and she drowned.
The queen of King Mǐn of Qí
had a large tumor on her neck,
called the "persistent tumor."
Initially,
when King Mǐn went on an excursion,
all the commoners came to watch.
The tumor-bearing woman went on picking mulberry leaves as before,
and the king, surprised, asked why;
she replied: "I received from my parents the duty to pick mulberry leaves,
not the duty to watch the great king."
He ordered her to be taken in his rear carriage,
but the woman said: "If I, with my parents at home,
follow the king without their instruction,
I would be an eloping woman.
How could the king employ me?"
The king was greatly ashamed,
and sent a messenger with gifts plus a hundred yì of gold
to betroth and marry her.
Her parents were startled,
and wanted her to bathe and change clothes,
but the woman said: "If I meet the king like this,
altering my appearance and changing clothes,
he will not recognize me."
So she went as before,
followed the messenger to court,
and King Mǐn made her his queen.
The wife of Chén Zhòng,
sister of Zhāng Shūmíng,
named Zhī.
When she and her two sisters-in-law fell among bandits,
fearing violation,
they said to each other: "A woman holds it highest not to defile her body,
and most beautiful not to compromise her virtue;
how can we surrender ourselves to await disgrace?"
Thereupon they stabbed themselves.
All from Liè Nǚ Zhuàn.

had relations with him,

She became pregnant,

History
The prime minister of Chǔ, Zǐwén, wanted to seduce Lady Wén,
built a lodge near her palace,
and performed the Wàn dance there.
Lady Wén wept and said: "The late lord used this dance,
to practice military readiness,
now the prime minister does not seek it among enemies,
but beside this widow,
is it not strange?"
Seduction with lewd affairs.
． "Zuǒzhuàn, 28th Year of Duke Zhuāng".
The widow Qīng,

and monopolized its profits.
Qīng,
able to maintain their enterprise,
used her wealth to defend herself.
Qín Shǐhuáng considered her a chaste woman and treated her as a guest,
building for her the Nǚhuáiqīng Tower.
"Shǐjì".
Cáo Shuǎng's cousin Wénshū's wife,
Xiàhóu Lìngnǚ,
widowed early with no children,
her father Wénníng wanted to remarry her,
so Lìngnǚ cut off both her ears,
to vow her resolve.
She usually lived with Shuǎng,
and when Shuǎng was executed and his family punished,
her family petitioned to annul the marriage,
forcibly brought her back,
and again intended to remarry her.
Lìngnǚ secretly entered the bedroom,
took a knife and cut off her own nose,
her family was shocked and lamented,
saying to her: "Life is like light dust on weak grass,
why must you torment yourself so?
Moreover, the husband's family is completely annihilated,
whom are you guarding this for?"
Lìngnǚ replied: "I have heard that the benevolent do not change their integrity due to prosperity or decline,
the righteous do not alter their hearts because of survival or demise.
When the Cáo family was at its peak,
I still wished to remain faithful till the end,
how much more now in their decline and fall,
how could I bear to abandon them?
Such is the behavior of beasts,
how could I do it?"
Sīmǎ Yì heard of this and admired her virtue,
allowing her to adopt a son to raise,
to continue the Cáo lineage.
． "Tōngjiàn, Three Kingdoms".
Liáng Yángshì said: "My parents sold me to the Dī people,
to seek wealth and honor,

how could it happen again?"
． "Tōngjiàn, Jìn Records".

Biographies
A man from Lǔ named Qiū Hú married his wife and after three days left to pursue an official career,
returning on leave after three years.
His wife was gathering mulberry leaves in the suburbs,
and Hú, not recognizing her,
was attracted to her,
so he offered her a yi of gold.
His wife said:
"My husband has been away as an official and has not returned,
for three years now,
and I have never been insulted as I am today."
She paid him no heed,
and Hú, ashamed, withdrew.
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital".
The wife of Qín Jiā of the Eastern Hàn,
disfigured herself and did not remarry,
grieving to the point of endangering her life.
From "Generalities on History".
Táo Yīng of Lǔ was widowed,
and a man from Lǔ sought to marry her.
Upon hearing this,
Yīng feared she could not avoid it,
so she composed a song to express her unwavering fidelity.
The poem said:
"I mourn the early widowhood of the yellow swan,
for ten years without a mate;
bowing its head and folding its wings,
it does not mingle with the flock;
at times it flies and calls,
walking alone in solitude;
heaven's decree has made it so,
ashamed, I bear eternal sorrow;
moved by the bird's plight as my own,
tears fall in streams;
alas, how sorrowful,
the dead are not forgotten;
if even a bird is thus,
how much more a chaste and virtuous woman?
Though there may be worthy suitors,
I will never tread that path again."
The man from Lǔ heard this and said,
"This woman cannot be won."
He dared not seek her again.
From Liú Xiàng's "New Biographies of Exemplary Women".
The chaste widow Gāo Xíng of Liáng,
widowed early and refusing to remarry,
was sought after by nobles of Liáng.
The King of Liáng heard of this
and sent to betroth her.
Gāo Xíng said:
"My husband unfortunately departed before me like a dog or horse filling a ditch,
and I ought to dedicate myself to his coffin and tomb,
caring for our orphaned child,
unable to focus elsewhere.
I have heard that a woman's duty
is unchanging once committed,
to preserve her chastity and faithfulness.
To forget death and rush toward life now
would be faithless."
Then she took a sword and knife,
cut off her nose, and said,
"I have mutilated myself;
the reason I do not die
is that I cannot bear to leave our young heir doubly orphaned."
Ibid.

Treading the path of Gòng Jiāng with a clear vow,

Her lofty integrity pierces the autumn frost.

Like dodder and duckweed,

Zhuō Wángsūn had a daughter, Wén Jūn,

Xiàng Rú tempted her with his zither,

From "Western Hàn Biography of Xiàng Rú".
Cài Yōng's daughter Yǎn,

Amid the turmoil of the realm,

spent twelve years among the Hú,

Cáo Cāo ransomed her with gold and jade,

From "Later Hàn Biographies of Exemplary Women".
In the Hàn, Liú Yào made Lady Yáng his empress.
Yào asked her,
"How do I compare to the son of the Sīmǎ family?"
Lady Yáng said:
"He had one wife, one son, and himself—three in all—
yet could not protect me.
At that time, I truly did not wish to live,
thinking all men in the world were like that.
But since serving you with towel and comb,
I have learned that there are real husbands in the world."
From "Comprehensive Mirror: Jìn Annals".
Biographies
Cài Shì, wife of Dǒng Sì,
bore children among the Hú,
suffered humiliation in the barbarian court,
abundant in literary talent,
but lacking in integrity.
From Liú Zhījī's "Generalities on History".
Classics
It speaks of the katydid,
if not jealous,
then having numerous descendants.
From "The Book of Songs: Katydid".
If the wife is without jealous behavior,

From "The Book of Songs: Little Star".

History
In Jìn, Lady Zhào made Shū Wěi her principal wife

From "Zuǒzhuan: 24th Year of Duke Xī".
The daughter of Liáng Shāng became a noble lady,

but calmly declined to the emperor, saying:
"For the yang, broad generosity is virtue;
for the yin, non-monopoly is righteousness.
The katydid
is the source of all blessings.
I hope Your Majesty considers the equal distribution of cloud and rain,
recognizes the order of strung fish,

From "Eastern Hàn Biography of Empress Liáng".
Biographies
The wife of Bào Sū of Sòng was not jealous,

From "Biographies of Exemplary Women".
Collected
She treated other consorts' sons as her own,

Without envious or jealous behavior,

From Liǔ's "Epitaph for Cuī".
Our Dynasty
Hearing you have a virtuous wife,

Why not empty your purse,

From Dōngpō.
Classics
Having a principal wife but not using her attendants to complete the number.
Shū Xiàng said: "My mother had many [co-wives], yet few half-siblings."
Annotation: "Meaning the father had many concubines,
but few children by them.
This avoids suspicion that the mother's nature was not tolerant."
A beautiful woman enters the household,
an ugly woman becomes her enemy.
"Records of the Grand Historian".
What a woman uses to serve her husband

yet jealousy is her inherent emotion.
"Strategies of the Warring States".
The King of Chǔ favored a new consort,

cover it when you see him."
She then told the king: "She hates your odor."
The king ordered her nose cut off.
Same as above.
Féng Yǎn's wife, Rén Shì, was fierce and jealous,
not allowing him to keep concubines,
so their children often had to do household chores themselves.
"Book of the Later Hàn".
The daughter of Sīlì Féng Fāng fled turmoil to Yángzhōu,
Yuán Shù saw and fancied her,
thus took her in,
and doted on her greatly.
The other women resented her favor,
telling her: "The general, a noble man, values resolve and integrity;
you should often weep and show sorrow,
and you will surely earn long-lasting respect."
Féng Shì followed their advice.
Later, the women jointly strangled her,
hanging her in the restroom, making Yuán Shù
believe she died of despair.
Páng Chǒng's wife threw her stepchild into a well.
"Book of the Later Hàn".
Cross-reference "Cruelty".
Jiǎ Chōng's wife Guō Wěi suspected him of eyeing the wet nurse,
flogged her to death,
and her son missed the nurse,
refusing other milk,
thus died;
when another son was born, it happened again,
so Jiǎ Chōng had no heirs.
"Book of Jìn".
Xún Xù said: "The noble consort is young;
jealousy is common among women,
it may lessen as she grows older."
． "Comprehensive Mirror in Aid of Governance, Jìn Huì Chapter".
Wáng Dǎo was chancellor,
his wife Cáo Shì was jealous by nature,
and Wáng Dǎo feared her greatly,
so he secretly built another residence
to house his concubines.
When Cáo Shì found out and was about to go there,
Wáng Dǎo, fearing the concubines would be shamed,
hurriedly called for his carriage.
"Book of Jìn".
Gān Bǎo's father had a favored maid,
and his mother was very jealous;
when his father died,
the mother buried the maid alive in the tomb.
Gān Bǎo and his brothers were young,
and unaware of this.
Same as above.
Biographies
Fáng Rúfù's wife Cuī Shì was jealous by nature,
forbidding her maids to wear heavy makeup or high buns.
"Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng".
The First Ruler of Shǔ placed a jade figure beside Gān Hòu to admire,

"Records of Omissions".
Xiè Tàifù's wife, Liú Fūrén, forbade him to have other consorts;
as the duke deeply enjoyed music and women,
he wished to keep singing girls and concubines.
His nephews and nephews-in-law subtly understood his intent,
and together advised Liú Fūrén,
citing that "Guān Jū" and "Zhōng Sī" praise the virtue of non-jealousy,
but the lady knew they were mocking her,
so she asked: "Who wrote these poems?"
They replied: "The Duke of Zhōu."
She said: "The Duke of Zhōu was a man,
so he spoke for himself;
if the Dame of Zhōu had written the poems,
they wouldn't have such lines."
"Records of Jealousy".
Zhāng Bá wanted to take a concubine,
his wife said: "Try reciting 'Song of White Hair',
and I'll listen."
Bá felt ashamed and stopped.
"Combined Examination".
Collection
Many women envy the moth-eyebrows.
"Songs of Chǔ".
Entering the gate, they meet with envy;
the moth-eyebrows refuse to yield to others;
hiding sleeves, they attack with slander,
seductive charms偏偏能迷惑 the ruler.
"Collection of Luò Bīnwáng".
Having the beauty of Xī Shī,
slander and jealousy enter to boast.
"Songs of Chǔ".
Though the king loves the moth-eyebrows' beauty,

Lǐ Bái.
Who knew Simǎ's wife was so jealous,

Vice Minister Bái.
On the screen, Zhōu Fǎng painted slender waists,

Leaning by the jade window, the phoenix-haired maiden

Dù Mùzhī.
Destroying the magpie's nest,
failing the dove's benevolence.
Lú Tóng's writing.
Our Dynasty
In Yánpíng, the Wú sisters, six in all,
were all jealous and fierce,
dubbed the "Six Tigers".
The fifth tiger was the worst,
having personally killed over ten maids in her lifetime,
married three times,
each ending before midnight.
Often, noises were heard in the halls,
frightening all in the house,
but the fifth tiger angrily said: "Mad ghosts dare this? Open the door!"
She moved her bed to the central courtyard,
slept alone with a knife,
and all was quiet till dawn;
people said the fifth tiger's fierceness
even scared ghosts.
Written by Chén Zhèngmǐn in "Leisurely Readings from the Dùnzhāi Studio".
Classics
A woman has no exclusive control over household affairs.
． Annotation to "The Odes - Sī Yú".
When a woman has matters to attend to,
whether great or small, she must ask her parents-in-law.
． "Book of Rites - Jīao Tè Xìng".
When a woman's compliance is complete,
then the household is harmonious and orderly;
when the household is harmonious and orderly,
then the family can endure long.
． "Book of Rites - Hūn Yì".
A woman's compliance means
being obedient to her parents-in-law,
harmonious with the household members,
and then fitting to her husband.
． "Book of Rites - Hūn Yì".
Household members
refer to those in women's work,
sisters-in-law, and other women.
The man leads the woman,
the woman follows the man.
A woman is one who follows others:
in youth, she follows her father and brothers;
married, she follows her husband;
widowed, she follows her sons.
． "Book of Rites - Jīao Tè Xìng".
The matron's teaching
is to be gentle and obedient.
． "Book of Rites - Nèi Zé".
Masters
Women follow the teachings of men,
having no authority to act independently,
but adhering to the three obediences.
"Family Sayings of Confucius".
Do not disobey your husband;
to be compliant is the proper way,
the way of a wife or concubine.
． "Mencius - Duke Wén of Téng Part Two".
If the husband is courteous,
then she is gentle, obedient, and attentive.
． "Xúnzǐ - On the Way of a Ruler".
History
A woman is one who follows others,
not acting independently,
but must have someone to follow.
"Gǔliáng Commentary".
Biographies
A woman's duty is to be compliant and obedient,
thus a wife serves her husband in five ways: at dawn, with hair pinned, she pays respects, embodying the solemnity of ruler and subject;
washing hands and serving food, she shows the reverence of father and child;
reporting and returning from errands, she follows the way of brothers;
being punctual and sincere, she demonstrates the trust of friends;
and through the intimacy of the bed,
then she fulfills the righteousness of husband and wife.
"Biographies of Exemplary Women".
Collection
A wife follows her husband's direction.
Hán Wén.
Classic
A hen should not herald the dawn;
If a hen heralds the dawn,
it brings ruin to the household.
． _Shū: Mù Shì_.
That hornless goat grows horns.
． _Shī: Yì_. Note: "Tóng refers to
a goat without horns,
yet it acts as if it has them.
The hornless goat
symbolizes the queen.
Growing horns
metaphorically harms governance.
Alas, that clever woman
becomes an owl or a screech-owl.
． _Shī: Zhān Yǎng_.
Cross-reference "bewitchment."
A woman with a long tongue
is the step to calamity.
． _Shī: Zhān Yǎng_.
Philosophers
The Master said: "When women meddle in affairs,
the Hàn dynasty's way is endangered!"
． _Wén Zhōng Zǐ: Shù Shǐ_ chapter.
Note: "Lady Lǚ,
Empress Liáng."
History
Since it is said of a clever woman,
she too brings ruin to the household.
． _Hòu Hàn Shū: Ān Dì Zàn_.
A rainbow descending and a hen transforming
are both caused by women interfering in governance.
． _Dōng Hàn Shū: Cài Yōng Zhuàn_.
A hen heralding the dawn
means the family's decline.
_Táng Shū_.
Biographies
When the wife controls the husband,
the yang yields to the yīn.
_Fēng Sú Tōng_.
Collections
Yīn is obscure, Kūn follows—
these are the constant virtues.
To emerge argumentative and strong
is not a woman's capability.
Hán Wén.
Classic
Only discuss food and drink.
． _Shī: Sī Gān_.
Note: "A woman's duties
are solely to discuss food and drink."
A woman has no public affairs;
she rests from her silkworms and weaving.
． _Shī: Zhān Yǎng_.
History
The way a wise woman brings prosperity to the family.
． _Dōng Hàn Liè Nǚ Zhuàn_.
Wáng Níngzhī's wife Xiè Dàoyùn
managed her household with ease and order.
_Jìn Shū_.
Biographies
Cuī Shū's wife
governed the household with strict order,
her demeanor dignified and beautiful,
and forbade the maids from wearing trendy makeup.
_Yīn Huà Lù_.
Our dynasty
The women's quarters were so quiet no human sound was heard.
_Xù Shì Shuō_.
Classic
Her hands like soft reeds,
her skin like congealed fat.
Her neck like the grub of a cicada,
her teeth like melon seeds.
Her forehead like a cicada's, her brows like silkworms,
her artful smile so charming,
her beautiful eyes so clear.
． _Shī: Shuò Rén_.
That beautiful maiden.
． _Shī: Dōng Fāng Zhī Rì_.
How fair is the brow's whiteness.
． _Shī: Jūn Zǐ Xié Lǎo_.
Yáng:
above the eyebrows.
Xī:
fair-skinned.
Her face like a hibiscus flower.
． _Shī: Yǒu Nǚ Tóng Chē_.
There is a beautiful one,

． _Shī: Yě Yǒu Màn Cǎo_.
Qīngyáng: between the eyebrows and eyes.
Her thick hair like clouds,
disdaining a wig.
． _Shī: Jūn Zǐ Xié Lǎo_.
A beauty of the state.
Same as above.
Philosophers
A tender heart and soft bones.
． _Liè Zǐ: Tāng Wèn_.
Skin like ice and snow,
graceful as a maiden.
． _Zhuāng Zǐ: Xiāo Yáo Yóu_.
The young daughter of Cài,
the tender beauty of Wèi.
． _Huái Nán Zǐ: Xiū Wù Xùn_.
History
Sòng Huáfǔ Dū saw Kǒngfǔ's wife on the road
and said, "Beautiful and dazzling."
． _Zuǒ Zhuàn: Huán Yuán Nián_.
Lí Jī
was a beauty of the state.
_Gōngyáng Zhuàn_ 5, Hé Xiū's note: "Her beauty was the choice of the whole state."
Charming and delicate,
graceful and serene.
Her walk composed and calm.
Bright teeth gleaming,
lovely smiles radiant,
long brows arched delicately,
with a subtle, distant gaze.
． _Xī Hàn Shū: Sīmǎ Xiàngrú Zhuàn_.
Zhào Fēiyàn was so light
she could dance on a palm.
Utterly unique and aloof from the vulgar,
enchanting and elegant,
exquisitely adorned.
Also from the same text.
A glance worth a million,
a smile worth a thousand gold.
． _Dōng Hàn Shū: Cuī Yīn Zhuàn_.
Biographies
Wénjūn's eyebrows needed no ink;
they resembled distant mountains,
her cheeks always like lotus blossoms,
her skin like cream.
_Xī Jīng Zá Jì_.
Guóguó Fūrén used no makeup,
naturally beautiful and dazzling,
often appearing barefaced before the emperor.
_Yáng Fēi Wài Zhuàn_.
Collections
With vermilion lips and pearly teeth,
Plump flesh and delicate bones,
Lovely eyes that suit a smile,
Fine brows so graceful and long,
Her demeanor elegant and refined,
And a youthful, rosy complexion.
From "Chǔ Cì".
A generous heart and graceful posture,
A slender waist and elegant neck.
Powdered white and darkened with mascara,
She applies fragrant oils.
With dimpled cheeks and rare teeth,
Her smile is perfectly suited.
Her body is lithe and graceful.
With a gaze both tender,
And a smile so fitting.
A beautiful face and graceful form.
Ibid.
Her glance leaves behind a radiant light,
Her long laughter carries the scent of orchids.
From Cáo Zhí's "Ode to a Beautiful Woman".
Máo Qiáng hiding her sleeves,
Cannot match her standard;
Xī Shī covering her face,
Pales in comparison, losing all color.
From "Rhapsody on the Goddess".
Empress Wèi was famed for her thick hair,
Zhào Fēiyàn was favored for her lightness of body.
From Zhāng Héng's "Rhapsody on the Western Capital".
With a subtle sidelong glance,
Her arched brows curve gracefully.
Long sleeves swirling around,
Her silk stockings tread softly.
Ibid.
Wèi's hair shone like a mirror,
Zhào's figure was slender and lovely.
From Pān Yuè's "Rhapsody on a Western Journey".
The exquisite maiden of the eastern capital,
The beauty of the southern land.
With an orchid heart and delicate quality,
A jade-like face and crimson lips.
From Bào Zhào's rhapsody.
Graceful and leisurely in elegance.
From Lù Jī's "Discourse on Literature".
Plump but not short,
Slender but not tall.
From Sòng Yù's "Rhapsody on the Goddess".
Her appearance full and dignified in beauty,
Enveloped in a warm, smooth jade-like face.
Her brows, delicate and arched like moth antennae,
Her vermilion lips bright as cinnabar.
Moving in a misty gown with slow steps,
Brushing the steps with a rustling sound.
Gazing at my curtain with an extended look,
Like flowing waves about to ripple.
Offering fine words in response,
Exhaling a fragrance like orchids.
Ibid.
Her form and appearance are graceful and beautiful.
From Sòng Yù's "Rhapsody on the Fondness of Beauty".
Lovely in form and enchanting in beauty,
She needs no adornment.
Holding joy in a gentle smile,
Stealing glances with flowing charm.
Ibid.
The maiden from the eastern neighbor:
Add one inch, and she'd be too tall;
Subtract one inch, and she'd be too short.
Apply powder, and she'd be too pale;
Apply rouge, and she'd too red.
Her brows like kingfisher feathers,
Her skin like white snow,
Her waist like a bound silk ribbon,
Her teeth like contained shells.
With a captivating smile,
She bewilders Yángchéng,
And enchants Xiàcài.
From Sòng Yù's "Rhapsody on the Fondness of Beauty".
Vague as light clouds veiling the moon,
Floating as the swirling wind tosses snow.
Gazing from afar,
Bright as the sun rising over morning clouds;
Observing up close,
Radiant as a lotus emerging from green waves.
Plumpness and slenderness in perfect balance,
Height and build in ideal proportion.
Shoulders as if carved,
Waist like a tied silk ribbon.
An elongated neck and elegant nape,
Revealing a fair complexion.
No added perfumed oils,
No application of lead powder.
Her cloud-like chignon towering,
Her long brows delicately arched.
Red lips bright externally,
White teeth gleaming within,
Bright eyes skilled in sidelong glances,
Dimples complementing her cheekbones.
Her graceful form dazzling and elegant,
Her demeanor calm and composed.
Gentle emotions and a graceful posture,
Charming even in speech.
In rare attire surpassing the world,
Her bone structure matches painted ideals.
Poised lightly like a crane standing,
As if about to fly yet not soaring.
Treading lightly over waves with subtle steps,
Her silk stockings seem to stir dust.
Turning her gaze with flowing brilliance,
Her jade-like face glowing and smooth.
Words held back, not yet spoken,
Her breath like secluded orchids.
Her magnificent form so graceful,
It makes me forget to eat.
From Cáo Zhí's "Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luò River".
Her radiant beauty rivals the morning sun.
From Yán Yánnián's "Qiū Hú Poem".
Who would not gaze upon one who topples cities?
Ibid.
Her flowing glances emit charming grace,
Her words and laughter exude fragrance.
From Ruǎn Jí's "Poems of My Heart".
Elegant steps highlighting her slender waist,
A clever smile revealing pearly teeth.
From Lù Jī's "To My Wife".
Pushing up sleeves to reveal fair hands,
White wrists adorned with golden bracelets.
Her beauty shines like the morning sun,
Who does not admire her lovely face?
From "Ode to a Beautiful Woman".
Lovely in red and powder makeup,
Delicate, fair hands emerging.
From "Selected Ancient Poems".
Displaying grace within the bedchamber,
Composed in her glances,
Abundantly graceful and at ease.
From Zhào Zhì's letter.
Brilliant as such flowers,
Truly a beauty of the state.
From "Eulogy for the Sòng Noble Consort".
Her appearance and color are dignified and beautiful.
From Fàn Yè's "Discourse on Empresses".
Mystically standing in ethereal mist,
Jade terrace descending with fragrance,
Táng hall cleansed by rain,
Wū Mountain lush with clouds.
Emanating orchid-like grace,
Gazing at the moon, rivaling the moon goddess,

Ibid.
In the southern land, there is a lovely lady,

From Cáo Zhí's "Miscellaneous Poems".
Observing her in detail,
She captivates one's eyes.
From "Rhapsody on the Goddess".
In a fleeting moment,
Beauty arises unrestrained;
Brilliant as flowers,
Warm as polished jade.
Her eyes flow with sidelong glances like rippling waves.
Ibid.
Icy blossoms and jade-like demeanor,
Fairy elegance and divine beauty.
From Jiāng Yān's rhapsody.
Elegant, refined, and charming.
From Cài Yōng's rhapsody in his biography.
Delicate and lovely with beautiful eyes and brows.
From Bào Zhào's poem.
Swirling skirts and turning pendants create endless charms.
From "Later Songs of the Jade Terrace".
Chǔ songs, Wú maidens, too delicate to fully perform,

Xiè Ān sought the courtesans of Dōngshān,
Strolling hand in hand through forests and springs everywhere.
From Lǐ Bái.
With blue-black painted brows and red brocade boots,
She sings coquettishly, mispronouncing words.
From Lǐ Bái's "Facing Wine".

Her brows and eyes outshine the stars and moon.

The beauty about to drunk, her rosy face flushed.

Her brows and eyes outshine the dark moth eyebrows.

With a beaming smile that ripples like a wave,

Same as above.

Both from the same source.

From Chén Zǐ'áng's writings.
Her stunning beauty startles the lotus flowers.
The Qín family maiden of Xīmén,
Her fair looks resemble jade flowers.
From Lǐ Bái.
Her face like polished jade,
She wears no common household attire.
From "The Collected Works of Bái Jūyì."

The palace ladies of King Wén of Zhōu,

Hence called "step-shakers."
In Qín Shǐhuáng's palace, the "gazing-at-immortals chignon" was worn,

Wèi Wǔdì's palace ladies painted connected eyebrows.
Jìn Huìdì's palace ladies wore "lotus chignons,"

In Suí Wéndì's palace, the "nine-perfected chignon" was worn.
During Táng Wǔdé era,
"Pacifying-barbarians chignons" and "eternal-joy chignons" were worn,

Biographies and Records
In the Hàn palace, there was a lady named Lì Juān,
renowned for her singing,
with a delicate physique,
so frail she could barely bear the weight of her clothes.
She often performed the "Song of the Whirling Wind,"
causing courtyard leaves to flutter down as if in autumn.
From "Records of Penetrating Truth."
Her voice shook the trees in the forest,
its resonance halting drifting clouds,
the lingering sound spreading through the woods,
not fading for days.
From "Records of Jīngzhōu."
As for the modern "Three Terraces" drinking催促 song,
some say:
"In Yè, there were three terraces,
where Shí Chóng held feasts and outings,
and musicians used it to hasten drinking."
Another account states:
"Cài Yōng visited three terraces within three days,
and because he understood music theory,
the Music Bureau composed this tune,
hoping for generous rewards from him."
From Lǐ Zhèngwén's "Collection of Leisurely Reflections."
Songs like "Waves Returning," "Oriole's Spring Song," and "Crows Cawing at Night"
are termed soft dances.
While "Zhèzhī," "Great Wèizhōu," and "Bodhidharma's Branch"
are called vigorous dances.
From "Records of the Music Bureau."
Minister Bái's singing girl,
Fán Sù, excelled in singing,
while Xiǎo Mán was skilled in dancing.
From "Solutions to Music Bureau Problems."
During the Kāiyuán era,
a palace lady named Xǔ Zǐhé,
from a musical family in Yǒngxīn County, Jízhōu,
entered the palace and was thus named Yǒngxīn.
She could innovate new melodies;
on a clear autumn night under a bright moon,
with just one note,
her voice traveled across all streets.
One day,
during a grand feast at the Qínzhèng Tower,
amid the clamor of the crowd,
no one could hear the sounds of the various performances,
so Yǒngxīn brushed back her hair and raised her sleeves,
singing in a melodious voice directly,
and the entire square fell silent,
as if not a soul was present.
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Music Bureau."
Dancing is the expression of music,
with gestures like the great drooping hand
and the small drooping hand.
Some movements resemble startled swans,
others like soaring swallows.
"Pósuō" describes the dance posture,
while "mànyán" refers to the dance formation.
There are vigorous dances, soft dances, character dances, flower dances, and horse dances.
Dance tunes include "Lǜ Yāo," "Sūhéxiāng," "Qū Zhè," "Hú," "Wèizhōu," "Tuányuán Xuán," "Gānzhōu," among others.
In character dances, dancers bend close to the ground
to form characters.
In flower dances, they wear green garments,
leaning to compose the character for "flower."
In horse dances, grooms in colorful attire
whip and dance on platforms,
their steps matching the rhythm closely.
Ibid.
